title: Netanyahu strikes back at ex-Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar over Oct. 7 contact claims in lawsuit
body: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected former Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) director Ronen Bar's allegation that he couldn't contact him on the morning of October 7, 2023, because "unlike previous prime ministers, he never provided the plaintiff with his personal telephone number."The prime minister struck back at Bar on Wednesday, saying, "Ronen Bar, who saw the warning signs on the night of October 7 and didn't call me, says today that he didn't have my phone number. Ronen, are you serious? After all, you had my red phone number and could have called me immediately, as all heads of the security establishment do.""The Shin Bet security detail, your subordinates who are with me 24/7, could have reached me within minutes. How many lives could we have saved if only you had called on time?" Netanyahu added in the X/Twitter post.רונן בר, שראה את הסימנים המעידים בליל ה-7 באוקטובר ולא התקשר אליי, אומר היום שלא היה לו את מספר הטלפון שלי. רונן, אתה רציני? הרי היה לך את מספר הטלפון האדום שלי, ויכולת מייד יכול להתקשר אליי כפי שעושים כל ראשי מערכת הביטחון. מאבטחי השב״כ, פקודיך, שנמצאים איתי 24/7, היו יכולים להשיג אותי תוך דקות. כמה חיים היינו יכולים להציל אם רק היית מתקשר בזמן.— Benjamin Netanyahu - בנימין נתניהו (@netanyahu) October 14, 2026Bar's lawsuit stated that "It is worth noting that the prime minister did not get back to the head of the Shin Bet and did not intervene even after the massacre began."The lawsuit also presents evidence from the night of October 7 that refutes the claim that the Shin Bet concealed information. It details how, contrary to the prime minister's claims, the Shin Bet began distributing warnings to all security agencies as early as 3:03 a.m."As the head of the service, I bear responsibility for the Shin Bet's failure to provide the intelligence required regarding the October 7 attack and its timing," Bar said in a statement issued on his behalf.Eisenkot calls for Oct. 7 state commissionYashar party chair Gadi Eisenkot responded to the revelatory allegations by pushing for a State Commission of Inquiry into the October 7 massacre by saying, "Netanyahu was warned and did not act. A State Commission of Inquiry that we will establish will investigate the disaster. The heads of the systems took responsibility and resigned long ago. We will not allow the master of evaders to escape the truth." נתניהו הוזהר ולא פעל. ועדת חקירה ממלכתית שנקים תחקור את האסון. ראשי המערכות לקחו אחריות והתפטרו מזמן. לא ניתן לאדון המשתמטים לחמוק מהאמת. https://t.co/znqEmekExL— Gadi Eisenkot - גדי איזנקוט (@gadi_eisenkot) October 14, 2026Opposition leader and former prime minister, Yair Lapid, also pressed the attack, accusing Netanyahu of prioritizing Qatari information over Israel's establishments.On X, he wrote, "Netanyahu can no longer claim that he didn't know. All the materials were on his desk. The only question is why he preferred to listen to Qatar's agents in his office instead of the IDF and Shin Bet?"נתניהו לא יכול להגיד יותר שהוא לא ידע. כל החומרים היו על שולחנו. השאלה היחידה היא למה הוא העדיף להקשיב לסוכנים של קטאר בלשכה שלו במקום לצה״ל ולשב״כ?— יאיר לפיד - Yair Lapid (@yairlapid) October 14, 2026"We can no longer say 'we didn't know,'" former prime minister Naftali Bennett wrote on X."The IDF chief of staff raises 10 red flags about the collapse of the army, and cabinet member [Shas leader Arye] Deri tells him: We intend to continue on the same path and institutionalize the evasion. Voting for Netanyahu, [Finance Minister Bezalel] Smotrich, or Deri is a vote for draft evasion, for 150 reserve duty days a year, and for billions every year from the pockets of those who serve to the dodgers," he wrote, while promising to transfer NIS 30b. "from the dodgers to the serving."עכשיו כבר לא נוכל להגיד ״לא ידענו״. נתניהו ימשיך לממן את המשתמטים, ובתמורה דרעי יעניק לו את השלטון - הכל על חשבון המשרתים. הרמטכ״ל מרים 10 דגלים אדומים על קריסת הצבא, וחבר הקבינט דרעי אומר לו: אנחנו מתכוונים להמשיך באותה הדרך ולמסד את ההשתמטות. הצבעה לנתניהו, סמוטריץ׳ או דרעי היא הצבעה להשתמטות, ל-150 ימי מילואים בשנה ולמיליארדים בכל שנה מהכיס של המשרתים למשתמטים. אנחנו לא ניתן לזה לקרות. נחולל את מהפכת המשרתים וניצור במדינת ישראל סדר חברתי חדש. נעביר 30 מיליארד שקלים מהמשתמטים למשרתים.— Naftali Bennett נפתלי בנט (@naftalibennett) October 14, 2026Amir Bohbot contributed to this report.

title: Turkey appoints trustee to run pro-opposition Halk TV amid opposition crackdown
body: Turkish authorities appointed a government trustee to run pro-opposition broadcaster Halk TV, prosecutors said on Wednesday as police raided its Istanbul office, extending a crackdown on the opposition and prompting fresh concerns over media freedom.The Istanbul Chief Prosecutor's Office said its financial crimes unit had conducted an investigation into Halk TV Chairman Cafer Mahiroglu over "bribery, tender-rigging, and laundering of assets derived from crime."Prosecutors ordered the detention of 17 people, including Mahiroglu, and 11 have been detained, the statement said, with firms linked to Mahiroglu seized and the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF) appointed as trustee.Mahiroglu is currently outside Turkey and being sought by the authorities.The channel's live broadcast was cut at 6:30 a.m. (0330 GMT), after which pre-recorded material began airing. "Hundreds of police" were inside, and entry into the premises was not being permitted, it said on its website. A Halk TV programmer said negotiations with the trustee delegation to continue broadcasts had yielded no results.The move comes days after Kemal Kilicdaroglu, the court-appointed chairman of Turkey's former main opposition Republican People's Party (CHP), publicly criticized Halk TV and Mahiroglu over its coverage. He said the CHP had complained to Turkey's RTUK television watchdog but no action was taken.Kilicdaroglu lost the CHP leadership to Ozgur Ozel in 2023, but was reinstated by a court ruling in May amid an unprecedented legal crackdown on the opposition. He has refused to call new party elections, while his rhetoric has become more aligned with the government.The CHP later criticized Wednesday's raid on Halk TV as a "shameful" example of "systematic pressure" on opposition media.The European Parliament's Turkey rapporteur Nacho Sanchez Amor criticized the move on X/Twitter, saying that the government was "not happy with controlling 90% of media" and was "aiming for the 100%.""Amidst detentions of journalists & broad online censorship, freedom of media & expression will soon be just a memory."Crackdown on press freedomWednesday's move makes Halk TV the fifth major Turkish news outlet to have a trustee appointed, following similar legal decisions for Flash TV, Eko Turk, Haberturk and Tele1.Authorities have appointed trustees in recent years to take over many municipalities, previously seizing those run by pro-Kurdish opposition mayors in southeastern Turkey and more recently major municipalities - including Istanbul and its districts - won by the opposition, prompting some mayors to join President Tayyip Erdogan's ruling AK Party.Rights groups and Western countries have criticized the government over its use of the judiciary, its record on rights, and its crackdown on press freedom in recent years as it establishes tighter control over mainstream media. Several opposition or independent outlets have experienced access bans, fines, and other restrictions.The government says Turkey's judiciary is independent. It has not commented publicly on the latest moves against Halk TV.Opposition head decries Turkish authorities as 'impotent, cowards'Ozel, who now leads the main opposition New Party, condemned Wednesday's move, as did the pro-Kurdish opposition DEM Party."Dawn raid on a television channel, appointing a trustee — only dictators would do such a thing," Ozel said on X. "Those who appoint trustees to municipalities and trample the people's will have now appointed a trustee to Halk TV, watched by millions. Because THEY ARE IMPOTENT AND COWARDS!"The raid on Halk TV came as Erdogan's biggest political rival, jailed Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu, was expected to start his defense on Wednesday in a sweeping corruption trial of more than 400 defendants linked to the Istanbul municipality."On such a day, a trustee was appointed to Halk TV, one of the most-watched news channels in Turkey," Turkish Journalists' Union Chairman Gokhan Durmus told Reuters, adding Turkey was facing another "dark chapter" in terms of freedom of press and expression."It remains unclear what the fate of our 200 colleagues working inside (Halk TV) and its editorial line will be from now on."

title: UK Green Party gambling on anti-Israel politics, former deputy leader warns 'Post' - exclusive
body: The UK Green Party has undergone an ideological transformation that has accelerated under leader Zack Polanski, with antisemitism, Islamist influence, and electoral opportunism increasingly shaping its political direction, its former deputy leader Shahrar Ali told The Jerusalem Post in an interview on Tuesday.Ali warned that the changes are no longer simply an internal Green Party matter, but pose a danger to wider British society.“When a political party, any political party that has de facto power, gets into positions of influence, and that gets subverted and corrupted beyond recognition, it's a danger to society.”Ali has been a member of the Green Party for “the best part” of 20 years. He served as deputy leader of the Green Party of England and Wales from 2014 to 2016, and as the party's policing and domestic safety spokesperson in 2021.Ali has a history of disciplinary disputes with the party. In 2022, he launched legal action against the Greens over alleged discrimination concerning his gender-critical beliefs, later securing a ruling that his dismissal had been procedurally unfair and that he had been subjected to “unlawful discrimination.”He was excluded from the party for two years in September 2024 over comments on the same issue, and was suspended again on October 7, 2026, following his condemnation of the “Zionism is racism” motion and his calls for voters not to support the Greens.For Ali, these “weaponized disciplinary processes” indicate increasing extremism within the party. “I was criticizing the motion long before the time it was passed, way back in spring, when it first reared its ugly head at the Spring conference,” he told the Post.A party transformed under PolanskiAli told the Post that the current radical approach taken by the Greens has “accelerated to devastating effect, particularly since Polanski became leader of the party.”While he said it was “in gestation, even prior to that,” the culture of the party has predominantly shifted since autumn 2025, when the Jewish leader took over.“The authoritarian drift and the rot, it's set in more deeply from Polanski's tenure as leader. Now we're seeing the old guard like Caroline Lucas and Adrian Ramsay, and also some of the MPs, notably Ellie Chowns, getting far more agitated around the direction of the party. But it's too little too late, unfortunately.”Ali attributed much of this transformation to the rapid expansion of the party's membership and what he described as a failure to scrutinize the political beliefs of those joining.“During the last 12 months, the party's seen a huge increase in membership but a corresponding lack of control regarding who is entering the party and why. There are a lot more pro-Palestine campaigners, Corbynista types who were kicked out of the Labour Party because of antisemitism.”Ali said he thinks the shift to more overt antisemitism in the Green Party is two-pronged: one is the actual ideologues of the party who are strongly anti-Israel and often antisemitic; the other is a political ploy to take voters from the Labour Party and to secure support from Muslim voters, including those he believes hold Islamist views in the UK.He cited the example of Hannah Spencer, who won the Greens' first-ever parliamentary by-election in Gorton and Denton earlier this year, with major Muslim support. Her winning campaign was heavy on Gaza messaging.However, Ali thinks the issue is more endemic than that.“Unfortunately, the membership and the activist base has also changed,” he told the Post.“I do think we're dealing now with ideological zealotry of a very ugly sort, where members, some of whom may self-identify as Muslim, have extreme views around Israel and the right of Jews to a homeland.”While he said it is difficult to put a figure on it, he thinks a large number of members and councilors have been resigning or threatening to resign as a result.The controversy has also raised questions about Polanski's own position on Israel.Asked by the BBC on Friday whether he believed Israel has a right to exist, Polanski refused to say.Other members have been more overt, calling for the end of the Jewish state. “They're not going to get disciplined, I'm sure. Whereas I've been disciplined for criticizing the motion,” Ali said.He said this is no longer a purely party-related issue but a much bigger issue involving wider politics and society.“The Green Party has had an absolute blind spot; I think I've been quite vocal about it, including Polanski, around the exponential rise of antisemitic hatred in this country, in the UK, which is horrific. They hardly say anything about it, or next to nothing about it. I think they're in complete denial about the impact of their campaign upon the rise of antisemitic hatred.”Islamism and the Green Party's changing identityAli also spoke about the issue of Islamism in the party, which is now in the strange place of “both attracting Muslims and targeting Muslims.”He argued that the problem extends beyond the party's stance on Israel, describing what he sees as an erosion of its traditional eco-focused secular identity.He cited Mothin Ali, the Green Party's deputy leader.“I've never once heard him criticize Islam. And that's a problem. I think that is the beginnings of Islamism. The reason it's Islamism is because it means the religion is beyond reproach, irrespective of the fact that it keeps popping up in the news cycle in ways which are directly relevant.”“So what we're ending up with is a party which is no longer occupying a secular space – where all religions and the non-religious are equal. It now seems to be promoting a Muslim agenda.”Ali said that this is evident with respect to the Middle East.“The Greens are going out of their way to target Muslim voters on Palestine issues, who have a kind of visceral reaction to the suffering of the Palestinian people, but this is to the exclusion of the suffering that's happened to Israelis and Jews on and since October 7”“The complete absence of sympathy, empathy, or compassion for innocent Jews is just staggering.”Can Gaza-focused campaigning continue to deliver votes?The key question here is, will the Greens' strategy of Gaza-centric politics pay off? The party didn't win the by-election seat in Holborn and St. Pancras on October 8 (just days after the controversial motion passed), but nevertheless made gains compared with previous years.Ali told the Post that “it could go either way.”“Many traditionally-Green voters will recoil at voting for the Greens. So they will lose a lot of support. And I can think of a couple of MPs who probably at the moment would lose their seats.”“But what the party's gambling on is that there are enough young cosmopolitan activists who are sufficiently misguided in various cities and towns, and students who will still vote for this antisemitic party. And so that's just profoundly dangerous. So the extremists in the party are probably calculating that they actually want to carry on with this strategy.”The Post pointed out that only around 1% of the party's membership voted in the conference last week, and suggested that it is possible that the other 99% would have voted down the “Zionism is racism” motion.Despite this, Ali does not believe the result necessarily misrepresents the wider party.He argued that the party's membership had increased dramatically under Polanski and that the motion could still pass if put to a wider membership vote.“I do think the activists often represent the critical mass of the membership. For every activist, there'll be other voters who are influenced by those activists.”Why did senior Greens wait to speak out?Ali also expressed skepticism over why, only after the failure to secure the by-election seat, did several senior Greens come out to voice their concerns about the “Zionism is racism” motion, as well as extremism in their party.He suggested that the timing of their criticism reflected political calculations rather than principled opposition to the motion.“If Polanski had won the by-election, it's unlikely that there would have been furore around the motion. I interpret it more as they're only objecting strongly now because they can see it can cause the party electoral damage. That is very concerning.”When reached for comment, a spokesperson for the Green Party told the Post that “Mr. Ali is entitled to his views but is no longer a member of the party. We are proud to be a party that bravely stands up for some of the most vulnerable people in the world.”

title: UVision moves beyond loitering munitions with sensor-to-strike network
body: WASHINGTON – UVision unveiled new launch and ISR integrations at the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Annual Meeting & Exposition in Washington, DC, expanding its portfolio beyond loitering munitions with a networked sensor-to-effect architecture built around its CORTEX mission-management system. The company displayed an eight-canister launcher for the Hero120 alongside new airborne  intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) links designed to tie sensing and strike nodes into a single operational loop.The Multi-Canister Launcher, shown in an eight-round configuration, is designed for remote operation and can be deployed on mobile, fixed, or containerized platforms across land and maritime environments. Itzik Huber, general manager of UVision, told Defense & Tech by The Jerusalem Post at AUSA that the containerized solution can hold up to 20 Hero-120 or Hero-400 loitering munitions.Integrated with CORTEX, the launcher operates as part of a distributed network connecting surveillance assets, decision tools, and precision-strike capabilities.At the exhibition, UVision promoted persistent border defense as one application with launch nodes positioned along extended border areas and tied into CORTEX with ISR platforms, enabling continuous monitoring and rapid response across multiple sectors.“We have changed the concept to a multi-layer, multi-solution instead of a single solution for a single soldier,” Huber said, explaining that one soldier can now strike several targets rather than just one.At the exhibition, the company also demonstrated an expanded sensing layer through the integration of Wayland Autonomy's IRIS airborne ISR payload with Tactical CORTEX. IRIS is a compact, platform-agnostic airborne ISR payload that provides wide-area surveillance and onboard target generation, including in GPS-denied environments, allowing UVision to fuse airborne sensing with its growing portfolio of launchers and effectors across the Hero, Viper, and Peregrine families.“It's not just about having more effects in the field. It's about having them where you need them, when you need them, and giving forces the flexibility to use the right capability for the mission,” said Dr. Ran Gozali, CEO of UVision. “That's what we're focused on: bringing sensing, mission management, and a broader range of effects together in a way that gives forces more options and greater operational flexibility.”Expanding global footprintHeadquartered in Emek Hefer, UVision has a strong foothold in Israel, India, and the United States, where it is continuing to expand its footprint. The company's Hero-120 is supporting the army's Lethal Unmanned Systems program, and Hero-90 is participating in the Low Altitude Stalking and Strike Ordnance effort. The company is also building out domestic manufacturing, integration, and training capacity as it moves toward a more comprehensive mission-solutions role.The war in Ukraine has forced European governments, that for years have neglected their defenses, to recognize that major conflict on the continent remains a reality. That has led European nations to accelerate their investment in autonomous weapons and unmanned systems.And the wars that have been raging in Europe and the Middle East have fundamentally altered battlefield requirements. Huber argued that autonomy and artificial intelligence will be among the most consequential technologies shaping future conflicts."AI and autonomy will be more influential on future battlefields," he said.And with that, UVision sees a future battlefield built around layered, networked capabilities rather than single platforms. According to Huber, "It's a different way of thinking. It's a more complex, holistic solution."

title: Iran's central bank governor dismisses claims of economic collapse amid US blockade
body: US claims that Iran's economy is collapsing are an illusion, the governor of Iran's central bank said on Wednesday at an International Monetary Fund meeting in Bangkok, as Tehran faces a US naval blockade aimed at driving its oil exports to zero and draining state coffers.Washington reinstated its blockade of Iranian ports in July and launched "Operation Economic Outcast" on August 24, a campaign aimed at severing Iran's remaining financial and commercial links with the global economy.According to energy intelligence platform Vortexa, Iran's seaborne crude exports fell to zero in the second week of September from a 14-day average of 230,000 barrels per day at the start of the month, and remained there as of October 5.US pressure has coincided with a sharp fall in the Iranian rialIn September, Washington expanded the campaign to target Iranian airlines, further isolating the country and making links to the outside world more limited and costly.US pressure has coincided with a sharp fall in the Iranian rial. According to exchange-rate data from Iranian currency tracker Bonbast, the rial has lost nearly 35% of its value against the US dollar since July.Hemmati said the central bank was prioritizing curbing inflation, stabilizing inflation expectations, preserving financial stability and maintaining banking and payment services, while securing foreign currency for medicine and essential goods. Annual inflation reached 73.6% in September, according to the Statistical Center of Iran.Iran's central bank launched a program in late September to sell up to $2 billion through state banks to support the rial.

title: Three seriously injured in suspected gas cylinder explosion at Intel chip plant in southern Israel
body: Three people were seriously injured in a blast at an Intel factory in Kiryat Gat on Wednesday, caused by what Israel Police suspect to be a gas cylinder explosion.Israel's Fire and Rescue Authority initially warned that hazardous chemicals may have leaked following the explosion. Firefighters worked to identify the source of the chemicals and extinguish the ensuing fire, which has since been put out.The Fire and Rescue Authority said the incident involved nitrogen trifluoride (NF3), a non-flammable gas with oxidizing properties.Following the explosion, Mayor Kfir Suissa said, "After an on-site assessment of the situation in cooperation with all relevant parties, the fire at the factory was completely extinguished. As of this time, there are no special instructions for residents, and there is no danger to the public. We ask that you not come to the area of ​​the incident, in order to allow the security and rescue forces to complete their work at the scene without interruption."Intel's Kiryat Gat factory, also known as FAB 28, manufactures semiconductor chips used in the company's processors. The facility is one of Intel's key manufacturing sites in Israel and plays a role in the company's global semiconductor production operations.Three in serious condition after Intel blast in Kiryat GatUnited Hatzalah medical teams treated three people who suffered burns across their bodies following the incident in Kiryat Gat, the emergency medical service said.Yanaki Weinberg, deputy head of United Hatzalah's Kiryat Gat branch, and paramedic Moshe Winfeld said they treated a man around 45 who was critically injured and suffered burns across his body. He was transported by a United Hatzalah ambulance to meet an intensive care ambulance while resuscitation efforts were underway. The team delivered two electric shocks using a defibrillator during the journey, and the man's heart miraculously began beating again. He was then transferred to Soroka Medical Center by intensive care ambulance.Hila Rinkoff and Zvi Levin, paramedics with a second United Hatzalah ambulance team at the scene, said they evacuated another man, around 30, who was also critically injured, to meet an intensive care ambulance while resuscitation efforts were underway.A third man, around 25, was treated at the scene and evacuated in moderate-to-serious condition, they added.Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spoke with MDA director-general Eli Bin to inquire about the condition of those injured in the explosion, the Prime Minister's Office said later on Wednesday.The prime minister wished the injured a speedy recovery and thanked the emergency responders for acting quickly and decisively, the statement added.

title: Iran's stock market climbs despite US blockade, energy shortages, collapsing currency
body: Iran's stock market has recently rallied despite its plummeting economy.Iran International reported on Tuesday that the Iranian stock market has seen an influx of Investments, despite increasing power outages, a shortage of foreign currency, and the rate of the rial tanking.The report noted that this could mean one of two things: either investors believe Tehran and Washington will reach a peace deal soon, or they have no other way to stop their savings from losing value.Iran International points to a few competing analyses of the situation to better explain investors' choices.One analysis from Farau indicates that a lack of foreign exchange currency in the country, energy shortages, and uncertainty over the war are the primary stressors for Tehran's economy.Why is Iran's stock market rallying?Iranian oil exports have effectively stopped under the US blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, leaving Iran with a dwindling supply of foreign currency. The report noted that Khabar Online cited a 35,000-toman rise ($.003495) in the free-dollar market in the last month alone.Additionally, energy shortages in Iran are exacerbating the problems. Iran's energy sector was already underfunded before the war began, and strikes on Iranian energy infrastructure have further strained production.On top of that, Iranian investors are unsure what comes next. The economic effects of a third round of war would be disastrous, but diplomatic efforts continue.Businesses that rely on imported goods are feeling these effects, as they face higher operating costs with less access to foreign currency, Iran International added. These factors significantly complicate long-term investment and leave Iranians seeking assets that will preserve their value.Some analyses indicated that investors are optimistic about a deal. Rouydad24 argued that investors expect a deal and believe more access to international markets is on the horizon.However, Iran International noted that other analyses show a different picture.Just because the market is rising does not mean that investors in Iran are optimistic about the country's economic prospects. Instead, it might indicate that Iranian's lack alternatives for preserving their wealth.The rial's value has tanked, property is losing value, and bank deposits are losing purchasing power, making domestic equities more attractive to investors, the report noted. This could offer a more stable assessment than the first: investors may be buying domestic stocks out of fear that cash will lose value in the country.This comes as the International Monetary Fund forecasted that Iran's economy would contract by 7.6% in 2026, as compared to the rate of 5.4% projected in July.Notably, Iran International noted that the Middle East and Central Asia were expected to contract by 0.3%.

title: First ever Israeli fashion museum anticipated to open in Tel Aviv in early 2027
body: Israel's first museum dedicated entirely to fashion as a cultural field is expected to open in Tel Aviv in early 2027, marking a new chapter for fashion exhibitions in the country.The Tel Aviv Fashion Museum, a joint initiative by Azrieli Group and fashion historian and curator Dr. Ya'ara Keydar, will be housed at Azrieli Sarona.In Paris, London, and New York, fashion museums have long been part of the cultural landscape, while fashion exhibitions at the Metropolitan Museum of Art attract blockbuster crowds. In Israel, by contrast, fashion has entered exhibition spaces only through a handful of shows. The opening of the new museum is expected to change that.The museum is a joint venture between Azrieli Group, led by CEO Danna Azrieli, and Keydar, and the project has been underway for about three years. Located at Azrieli Sarona, it will cover approximately 1,150 square meters across three floors and include exhibition spaces for rotating shows, an auditorium for lectures and events, and a museum shop.Alongside the exhibitions, the museum plans to offer educational activities, guided tours, and themed evenings. Its founders aim to attract more than 250,000 visitors annually.Azrieli malls intertwined with fashion industryThe choice of location is no coincidence. Azrieli operates some of Israel's largest shopping malls, and the museum continues the group's ties to the fashion industry."The group's malls are spaces where the public encounters brands, designers, and trends from Israel and around the world, and the museum expands on that encounter," Danna Azrieli said.She also described a personal connection to the world of fashion: Her grandfather, Rafael Hirsch Azrilovich, was a tailor and workshop owner in Poland.Keydar is perhaps the figure most closely associated with bringing fashion into Israeli museums. Over the past decade, she has curated 12 exhibitions in Israel and abroad, including four presented at the Design Museum Holon: an exhibition dedicated to Ronit Elkabetz, The Ball, an exhibition on Alber Elbaz, and Heroines. Together, the four exhibitions attracted more than half a million visitors.A graduate of the fashion design department at Shenkar College of Engineering, Design and Art, Keydar holds a master's degree from New York University and a doctorate from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. She also trained at the Metropolitan Museum of Art's Costume Institute.Museum will promote Israeli designers, build relationships with institutions abroadAccording to Keydar, the museum will present original exhibitions, promote Israeli designers, and develop relationships with institutions abroad."Especially in a complex reality, we need spaces of beauty," she said.Ilan Jarbi, the group's director of strategic content initiatives and a partner in establishing the museum, added that the opportunity to build a museum from scratch makes it possible to rethink both exhibitions and the visitor experience.The theme of the museum's inaugural exhibition will be revealed at a later date.

title: Maccabi Tel Aviv 1-4 in Euroleague after tight loss to Barcelona
body: Maccabi Tel Aviv came up short at Barcelona 90-87 as Justin Robinson's 3-pointer with time winding down proved to be the winning shot to send the yellow-and-blue to the devastating Euroleague defeat.Both teams brought their “A” game to the table as Kevin Punter and Yam Madar put on a show for their respective sides, but it was the Blaugrana who came out on top to take the dramatic victory thanks to Robinson's heroics. Next up for Maccabi, now 1-4 in Euroleague play, is a date at Valencia on Thursday night and sits at 4-1 on the season,Madar scored a career high 22 points, Iffe Lundberg put in 13 points and Bonzie Colson put in 12 points in the win as Punter scored 19 points, Umoja Gibson added 13 points while Joel Parra and Robinson each scored 11 points for Barca in the win.'There were a lot of situations that could have been different'Maccabi coach Oded Katash spoke about the loss and some decisions that were made on the floor.“There were some strange things going on here, but we were there in the game. The first half we could have used our fouls a bit better and our offense wasn't at its best while we gave up a bit too many points in the first eight seconds of the clock. There were a lot of situations that could have been different.”Barcelona coach Aleksander Sekulic reflected on his side's win.“Very tough match and loud atmosphere which was a big help for us as Maccabi has a team with a lot of tools. But we also have quality and talent. We only had one day to prepare but the guys excited and left their hearts on the court.”Madar also summed up the game.“This is the Euroleague. There are a lot of games, some tougher than others; we'll watch the video and learn from it. We have a tough team to face on Thursday, but this was a very frustrating game. We managed to fight our way back and tie it up and obviously, the basket at the end is very frustrating. But we have to deal with it and look at what we didn't do well.”See more Israeli sports coverage at www.sportsrabbi.com/en

title: Known criminal serving as police agent aids in mass arrest of 28 drug traffickers across Israel
body: Police arrested 28 suspected drug traffickers in raids across Israel early Wednesday following a 10-month undercover operation in which a known criminal recruited as an agent helped gather evidence against dozens of suspects involved in supplying drugs to Jerusalem.The agent, a known criminal who had spent years building connections in the underworld, was recruited by the Jerusalem District Police's Central Unit (YAMAR) and helped establish an evidentiary basis against dozens of suspects involved in drug trafficking.The operation was designed to reach dealers behind the drug supply chains operating in Jerusalem. According to police, the reputation the agent had built in the criminal underworld allowed him to gain the trust of dealers and carry out dozens of controlled drug transactions under the direction of YAMAR's undercover agents division.During the operation, the agent purchased commercial quantities of cocaine, ecstasy, and other drugs, with a total value of hundreds of thousands of shekels. The transactions were conducted under the supervision of the Jerusalem District Attorney's Office, and the evidence gathered was used to build cases against the suspects.When the investigation entered its overt phase, officers from the Jerusalem District and other police districts, along with Border Police officers, National Guard personnel, and the canine unit, launched the arrest operation.During searches, police seized more than NIS 100,000 in cash, drugs, and 12 vehicles suspected of having been used to transport drugs and carry out transactions. Police intend to seek the forfeiture of the vehicles as part of the subsequent legal proceedings.Operation aimed to undermine trust among criminals, police sayAt a ceremony on Wednesday marking the agent's public unveiling, Jerusalem District Police Commander Maj.-Gen. Avshalom Peled said the operation was intended not only to target drug suppliers but also to undermine trust among criminals."We can certainly say this morning that we achieved the two main objectives we set for this operation. The first was to strike at the criminals operating the supply chains and bringing drugs into the capital, targeting those in their closest circles. The second was to undermine the trust between criminals and their ability to rely on one another, thereby making it harder for them to operate," Peled said.He added, "No criminal involved in this field knows this morning whether the next deal will be the one that ends his criminal career and puts him behind bars."The suspects are expected to be brought before a court later Wednesday for hearings on extending their detention. The investigation remains ongoing.

title: Rogue AI models could self-replicate in your smart ovens or TVs: Anthropic
body:
A new warning about artificial intelligence from Anthropic caused a stir in cybersecurity circles on Tuesday, a day after the company warned that AI models could be months away from self-replicating across the internet.
In a post late Monday, Anthropic raised the possibility that rogue AI could spin up a botnet, spread quickly, fight takedown attempts and even break into data centers to turbocharge its growth. Some experts said Tuesday that they shared the company’s concern, although at least one said the company appeared to be engaging in “vendor exaggeration.”
Monday’s post fleshed out a warning last month from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who floated the idea that within the next year or even sooner, AI might be able to hijack “the entire internet” with “a persistent botnet.”
Cybersecurity experts who pushed back on the doomsday scenario argued that models would be too big to move around efficiently and could not draw on enough computer power to operate independently.
The post made an early attempt to articulate how those challenges could be overcome. The company said its experiments showed medium-sized AI models with 30 billion parameters or less could already perform many of the individual tasks required for self-replication, even if they struggled to complete the entire process reliably.
Anthropic said the models could then stitch together the required compute by hijacking inexpensive internet-connected devices. It added that the models were able to replicate across a simplified test network.
“A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off,” the company said.
The report adds to broader concerns about the security risks tied to increasingly capable AI systems, including their potential to automate cyberattacks, operate with limited human oversight and circumvent safeguards.
The advances in models have prompted a series of often dire warnings from industry heads and AI company employees about the possibility of severe, even existential, risks of runaway AI development.
Some cybersecurity experts were skeptical.
“‘We managed to run a small model on cheap TVs,’ does not a security crisis make,” said Ciaran Martin, a former head of Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre. He said the post came across as an “interesting technical paper with a more than hint of vendor exaggeration.”
Zhengxiong Li, an assistant professor of computer science and engineering at the University of Colorado Denver, said that while the testing had been done in controlled conditions, he still found it worrying that an AI could effectively become a “worm,” a self-replicating program that could improvise ways to hijack devices on the fly.
“If it runs across many devices without depending on a central service, there may be no single place to shut it down,” he said.
Anthropic said that if smaller models continue improving at their historical rate, they could reach the capability required for autonomous replication by the end of 2026. It also floated the idea that the models might find ways to target more powerful computing resources, including data-center processors, that could potentially enable them to draw on much bigger pools of computer power.
One researcher said it made sense to think of the Anthropic post as more of a hypothetical than a prediction.
It made sense to consider the possibility of AI models proliferating autonomously given the past three months of revelations over rogue AI activity, said Jessica Ji, a senior research analyst at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology. But she said, “we don’t know yet what the likelihood of that actually happening is — it’s not zero, but nor is it guaranteed.”

title: Arleigh Burke-class destroyer USS John Basilone joins U.S. naval forces in Europe
body: The ship will serve alongside units assigned to Commander, Task Force 65 and Destroyer Squadron 60. Commissioned in late 2024, the Arleigh Burke-class destroyer can conduct air defense, anti-submarine warfare and surface warfare missions. “Operating in the European theater provides our crews valuable opportunities to project combat power, maintain operational readiness, and defend the maritime approaches to the Homeland,” said Vice Adm. J.T. Anderson, commander of U.S. 6th Fleet. “We welcome USS John Basilone and look forward to the ship joining our forward-deployed units.” “We are proud to welcome USS John Basilone and her crew to Team Rota,” said Capt. Charles Chmielak, commander of U.S. Naval Activities Spain and Naval Station Rota. “Naval Station Rota remains committed to providing the operational support our Sailors and ships need to remain ready, responsive, and prepared to meet the challenges of an increasingly complex security environment.” “Our crew is honored to bring Gunnery Sgt. Basilone’s legacy to Europe,” said Cmdr. T. Max Murphy, John Basilone’s commanding officer. “We are eager to integrate into the Rota community, work alongside our Spanish hosts, and support America’s ability to deter and win future conflicts.” The destroyer, designated DDG 122, is named after Marine Corps Gunnery Sgt. John Basilone. He received the Medal of Honor for his actions at Guadalcanal in 1942 and was posthumously awarded the Navy Cross for bravery at Iwo Jima in 1945. Basilone was the only enlisted Marine in World War II to receive both decorations. His namesake ship now operates in the region served by U.S. 6th Fleet, headquartered in Naples, Italy. The fleet conducts joint and naval operations across Europe and Africa. Those operations frequently involve allied and partner forces supporting maritime security and stability.

title: Diesel exports to boost oil refining, budget revenues — Novak
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Russian diesel fuel exports will make it possible to boost domestic oil refining and increase budget revenues, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters on the sidelines of the Russian Energy Week forum.
"This is a positive signal on the whole for our economy, associated with the increase of refining volumes at oil refineries, increase of production volumes, additional taxes to the budget, and the opportunity of budgeting social expenditures," Novak said.
"These are the opportunities for investments in particular," he added.

title: Guard at the Center of Prison Sexual Abuse Allegations Left Georgia’s Penitentiary System
body: Giorgi Varabiovi, a prison staffer identified in media reports as being among the guards featured in the alleged sexual assault of inmate Giorgi Davitadze, has left the Georgian Penitentiary Service, the agency confirmed to Civil.ge. Varabiovi, reportedly 22, left the service several months ago at his own request, the agency said, without providing further details about his departure. The agency later specified to RFE/RL’s Georgian service that Varabiovi left in March 2026. Media reports identified Varabiovi as the guard wearing the rubber gloves in the footage showing the incident in the de-escalation room of Rustavi’s No. 6 prison, during which, according to Davitadze, he was sexually assaulted. Davitadze, 36, the son of Avtandil Davitadze, a former Georgian Dream member of the Tbilisi City Council, alleged that prison guards sexually assaulted him with a finger during an inspection in a de-escalation cell. Following Davitadze’s allegations in court, the Special Penitentiary Service released footage from December 21, 2025, when the alleged assault occurred, rejecting his accusations as “a complete lie.” The footage, which contains no audio, shows the guards bending the inmate over the bed to inspect him. It includes, however, episodes where guards position themselves in ways that obscure parts of Davitadze’s body, making it impossible to determine the exact nature of the procedures carried out on him. At least one guard – reportedly Varabiovi – involved in restraining and inspecting him appears to be wearing rubber gloves. The allegations sparked further controversy and tensions at the prison. On October 4, the Penitentiary Service said Davitadze had swallowed an unidentified object and refused hospitalization, while the Public Defender’s Office later reported that he was refusing medical treatment until three inmates allegedly placed in de-escalation cells for protesting in his support were returned to their cells. Separate allegations emerged that several inmates were physically assaulted for similarly protesting in solidarity with Davitadze. The Penitentiary Service denied that the three inmates had been punished for protesting, saying they had been transferred after physically attacking prison employees, releasing muted footage showing what appears to be inmates assaulting guards. The Prosecutor’s Office of Georgia subsequently charged three inmates with assaulting prison staff in two separate incidents on October 2 and 4 at Penitentiary Institution No 6. The charges carry penalties of up to 12 years in prison. The allegations, as well as the footage released by authorities, sparked calls for a more thorough investigation of the incident, including a release of the full footage and audio recordings. However, on 10, the Prosecutor’s Office announced closing the probe into the incident, saying that “he evidence obtained shows that no violence or criminal act was committed against Giorgi Davitadze during his examination in the de-escalation room of the prison.” Also Read: 05/10/2026 – Family Disputes Suicide Account After Inmate Is Found Dead in Rustavi Prison 02/10/2026 – Inmate Alleges Sexual Abuse in Prison, Penitentiary Service Denies 20/05/2026 – Georgia Has Fourth-Highest Prison Population Rate in Council of Europe’s 2025 Report 18/02/2026 – CoE Committee for Prevention of Torture Publishes Report on Georgia

title: OPEC+ countries boost oil output by 2.31 mln bpd in September but miss targets — IEA
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. OPEC+ countries participating in the oil production restraint agreement increased output by 2.31 million barrels per day (bpd) in September 2026, yet still fell significantly short of their targets, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).
According to IEA data, the target level for OPEC+ countries voluntarily limiting oil production was 34.45 million bpd in September, while actual output stood at 29.03 million bpd. Thus, the underproduction relative to the target amounted to approximately 5.42 million bpd.
In September, according to the IEA, among seven key OPEC+ nations, Kuwait cut production by 550,000 bpd, Iraq increased it by 520,000 bpd, Saudi Arabia raised output by 2.33 million bpd, Oman increased it by 20,000 bpd, and Russia increased it by 70,000 bpd.
Meanwhile, Kazakhstan and Algeria kept production levels unchanged from the previous month.
Total production across all OPEC+ nations rose by 2 million bpd in September, reaching 34.8 million bpd.

title: Russia expects adjustment of global petroleum product prices — Novak
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Russia expects a price adjustment for petroleum products globally after the start of its diesel fuel supplies to the market, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters on the sidelines of the Russian Energy Week forum.
"Europe is one of participants of the world energy market, including oil and petroleum products. Therefore, the petroleum product price will be adjusted when rebalancing demand and supply worldwide," Novak said.
TASS is the information partner of the Russian Energy Week.

title: Man Utd to sanction Martinez after outburst – Reports
body: Manchester United are considering disciplinary action against defender Lisandro Martinez following his public criticism of the club’s hierarchy after their 2-0 defeat to Atletico Madrid in the UEFA Champions League. According to reports, the club is assessing a possible fine for the Argentine international after he questioned the team’s summer recruitment and called for greater investment to strengthen the squad. Speaking after Tuesday’s defeat, Martinez expressed frustration with the club’s management, particularly technical director Jason Wilcox, over its failure to bring in more players. “We did a fantastic season last season and now we expect more from the top, more players to compete because many teams bring many players as well,” he said. “I expect more [investment]. 100 per cent. I expect more from our technical director. “Tonight it is easy to blame the coach, easy to say the players, but also we have to see other areas.” The defender also questioned United’s approach to changing managers without addressing other areas of the club. “You can’t keep changing, changing, changing the manager. What about other areas?” he asked. According to The Athletic’s Manchester United correspondent, Laurie Whitwell, the club considers a fine for Martinez “inevitable”, although other players in the dressing room reportedly share his concerns about the club’s recruitment and overall direction. Football transfer journalist Fabrizio Romano also reported on Wednesday that United were considering a possible sanction against the defender. “Lisandro Martínez not the only player at Manchester United with that view of the situation at club level. Man United assessing possible sanction/fine for Licha, as reports,” Romano wrote on X. He added that Martinez’s contract situation remained a factor, with his current deal due to expire in June 2027, although the club has an option to extend it until 2028. Martinez reportedly reinforced his position in a subsequent interview, insisting that he would not “close my mouth” over his concerns and calling for greater ambition from the club. The defender’s remarks have generated debate over whether his criticism was justified, with some arguing that United’s recruitment strategy needs scrutiny, while others believe public criticism could undermine team unity. United have struggled for consistency this season, with Tuesday’s defeat to Atletico extending their winless run to five matches. The club is expected to face Leeds United in the Premier League on Sunday as manager Michael Carrick seeks to improve the team’s results amid growing scrutiny of the club’s leadership and recruitment decisions. The post Man Utd to sanction Martinez after outburst – Reports appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Iron Dome architect behind new counter swarm system
body: A defence technology company founded in Washington and Israel has unveiled what it describes as the world’s first native counter swarm defence system, designed from the outset to engage large numbers of drones at once instead of picking off one target at a time, according to the company. Skapion said the system has been designed by its founding architect, General (retired) Pini Yungman, who was the architect of Iron Dome and formerly general manager of Rafael’s air and missile defence division. It is built around what the company calls a native many-to-many architecture, allowing multiple interceptors to engage multiple targets at the same time. The company said the mobile, fully kinetic system is designed to engage more than one hundred targets simultaneously with an interception rate above 97 per cent, at a significantly lower cost per interception than conventional air defence. A vertical launch arrangement gives 360 degree coverage, and the company said it is designed for deployment from ground, airborne and maritime platforms. Ido Bar-On, co-founder and chief executive, said: “The next generation of threats cannot be defeated by simply stacking yesterday’s air-defense solutions. A swarm is not just a larger number of discrete drones. It changes the dynamics of the engagement, the number of simultaneous decisions, the speed at which they must be made and the economies of every interception. Native Counter-Swarm means designing the entire system from day one for simultaneous mass engagement.” Most air defence systems were developed to engage single targets or small numbers of them, which creates capacity and cost constraints against simultaneous mass attack. Skapion cited the wars in Ukraine and Iran, where it said legacy air defence is being saturated by swarms built to exhaust the defender’s magazines and budgets. A Shahed type one-way attack drone costs tens of thousands of dollars. The interceptors fired at it can cost hundreds of thousands or more, and the magazine on any launcher is finite, so an attacker who can generate enough cheap airframes wins on arithmetic even when every shot is defeated. Bringing the cost per interception down, and the number of simultaneous engagements up, is what several companies on both sides of the Atlantic are now chasing. At the centre of the Skapion system is an AI command and control architecture that fuses data from the company’s own sensors or from third party systems, evaluates and prioritises threats, allocates interceptors and manages engagements in real time. The company said it can run with full end-to-end autonomy or with a single human operator in the loop, depending on customer policy, and that the open, sensor-agnostic design allows integration with existing command and control and other counter-drone systems. The post Iron Dome architect behind new counter swarm system first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: How this year’s Economics Nobel helps us understand the Gulf economies
body: This year’s Nobel Prize in Economics was awarded to an American duo – Prof Robert Hall of Stanford University and Prof Michael Woodford of Columbia University – for their work on the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”. Their research emphasised that keeping the economy on a steady path requires understanding how ordinary businesses and consumers make decisions at an individual level rather than treating them as a homogenous whole. The insights provided by their work could help us understand the potential trajectory of the Gulf economies as they continue to diversify away from oil. In fact, the energy policies pursued by Arab oil-exporting countries during the 1970s contributed to the genesis of Prof Hall and Prof Woodford’s work, but the story begins much earlier. Before the interwar period of the early 20 th century, the kind of macroeconomic policy that is pursued by governments around the world today to stabilise their economies was essentially absent. Policymakers perceived the role of economic authorities very narrowly: balance the state budget and ensure liquidity in the financial system by managing the money supply and overseeing banks. A key reason for this limited, self-imposed mandate was the lack of macroeconomic data, such as gross domestic product, consumer price inflation and unemployment figures. In other words, even if governments had a theory of how to intervene in the economy to soften the boom-and-bust cycle, they lacked the information needed to put it into practice. Things changed between the First and Second World Wars for two reasons. On the one hand, the deepest economic crisis in modern history struck in 1929, making it essential for scholars and policymakers to develop methods of stabilising the economy. On the other hand, governments began collecting macroeconomic data systematically, equipping themselves with the tools needed for active macroeconomic management. This process accelerated during the 1960s and 1970s, as the substantial expansion in data availability was complemented by advances in computing technology that enabled sophisticated statistical analysis. As a result, on the eve of the first oil shock in 1973 , economic authorities around the world were well-versed in collecting macroeconomic data, as well as using fiscal and monetary instruments to smooth the economy’s peaks and troughs. Crucially, policymakers relied on historical statistical relationships to guide their interventions. One influential example was the Phillips Curve , which linked higher inflation to lower unemployment. Suppose historical data showed unemployment averaging 6 per cent when inflation was 2 per cent, but only 4 per cent when inflation was 4 per cent. Accordingly, when unemployment was actually 6 per cent and this was considered undesirably high, policymakers might loosen monetary policy through interest rate cuts to push inflation towards 4 per cent, expecting unemployment to fall towards 4 per cent as well. This approach assumed that the historical relationship would remain reliable when policymakers deliberately tried to exploit it. However, the oil crisis of the 1970s exposed the inadequacies of this approach and set the stage for Prof Hall and Prof Woodford to contribute to a paradigm shift in economics. The tipping point was the phenomenon of “stagflation”: inflation and unemployment rising simultaneously, in direct contradiction to the conventional interpretation of the Phillips Curve. This left economic authorities in oil-importing countries bereft of ideas. Prof Hall and Prof Woodford were part of a new cohort of economists who went back to basics. Rather than taking historical relationships between macroeconomic variables at face value, they recognised that each macroeconomic variable represents an aggregation of millions of microeconomic decisions. For example, aggregate consumption across an economy is the sum of individual households’ consumption decisions. Accordingly, to understand how a macroeconomic variable behaves and how it relates to other macroeconomic variables, we must first understand the relationships between the underlying microeconomic variables from which these aggregate measures are derived. Unemployment provides a good illustration. Economists must not treat economy-wide joblessness as the starting point for their statistical analysis. Instead, they must understand how individual members of the labour force and businesses make employment decisions and then build their analysis from the ground up. The result of this novel way of thinking was a new generation of economic models with two features that their predecessors lacked. First, they helped explain the phenomenon of stagflation and provided clear reasons for its occurrence, including the role of the energy shocks of the 1970s. Second, they offered governments a new set of tools for stabilising the economy. As the global financial crisis of 2008 demonstrated, the problem was by no means solved. Nevertheless, Prof Hall, Prof Woodford, their contemporaries and their successors have continued to advance our understanding of these issues. In the context of the Gulf economies, the legacy of Prof Hall and Prof Woodford can be seen clearly in several aspects of macroeconomic policy. The region’s success will ultimately depend on translating ambitious national strategies into millions of individual decisions that collectively sustain prosperity beyond oil One of the most salient is the challenge of maintaining a sustainably high rate of economic growth. There is growing recognition that aggregate economic expansion depends on innovation at the level of small and medium-sized enterprises . Gulf governments understand that they must work from the bottom up rather than rely on fleeting relationships between observed economic growth rates and other macroeconomic variables. In this regard, the subsequent work of other Nobel laureates – such as Paul Romer, Peter Howitt and Philippe Aghion – has been instrumental in shaping the region’s growth-enhancing policies, including subsidies for research and development and support for venture capital. Another illustration of the influence of Prof Hall and Prof Woodford’s work is the Gulf currencies’ pegs to the US dollar (with the exception of the Kuwaiti dinar). These arrangements reflect the belief that investors and consumers are forward-looking decision-makers who value the certainty afforded by fixed exchange rates. They might be far more reluctant to spend and invest if Gulf currencies were to adopt a free-floating regime that exposed them to exchange-rate risk. For the regional economies , the enduring lesson of Prof Hall and Prof Woodford’s work is that effective macroeconomic policy begins with understanding how households and businesses make decisions. As diversification progresses, policymakers will do well to ensure that their reforms encourage people to invest, innovate and create jobs while providing a credible framework for economic stability. The region’s success will ultimately depend on translating ambitious national strategies into millions of individual decisions that collectively sustain prosperity beyond oil.

title: Elections delayed: A generation of Palestinians is being denied its right to choose - opinion
body: What pains me most about the postponement of the Palestinian elections is that I know the faces of those who were waiting for them. I spoke with them, heard their dreams, and saw how the prospect of voting restored some of their confidence in themselves and their country. They were not expecting a miracle. They wanted a simple right: to choose their representatives and have a say in their future. Then the door was closed.Based on my close observation of the political process leading up to the decision, I hold Vice President Hussein al-Sheikh and Jamil Mezher primarily politically responsible for pushing for this postponement. This does not absolve others of responsibility. But it prevents those who drove the decision from hiding behind vague phrases about “national consensus” and “creating the right conditions.” Palestinians have the right to know who closed the door, and why. Those responsible have a duty to answer.In my assessment, Sheikh worked persistently to prevent the election decree from being issued last July. Once it was issued, he continued his efforts to cancel the date it had set. He succeeded in securing the postponement. The painful irony is that his success in closing the path to elections followed a series of failures in areas that should have opened a way out of the crisis.Postponement of the electionsInternal dialogue within Fatah and national dialogue were used to justify the postponement. Yet these are two processes the vice president helped lead over many years. Numerous capitals hosted lengthy meetings without achieving reconciliation or ending the division.How does the failure of dialogue become a reason to deny people elections? Why should citizens pay the price for their leadership's failures and then be denied the democratic means to hold it accountable?As for Palestinian-American relations, where is the breakthrough ordinary citizens can see? And as for civilian coordination with Israel, ask the worker cut off from his job, the student arriving late to university, or the employee who leaves home before dawn without knowing when he will arrive.The occupation bears direct responsibility for the checkpoints, restrictions, and humiliation. But the Palestinian official entrusted with coordination must also be held accountable for the results he has achieved in protecting people's interests. It is not enough for the office to remain in place while citizens' lives become harder every day.Holding leadership accountableI have known Sheikh since his release from prison in the early 1990s, after many years of detention. At the time, I headed Fatah's youth movement in Jerusalem and served in its leadership across the West Bank and Gaza Strip. He was a member of Fatah's Higher Movement Committee: well liked, cheerful, and close to ordinary people and the youth movement's activists. We had a strong relationship, as he did with many leaders of our generation.I do not know what these long years have done to the leader we once knew. But I know that the young man who once defended his generation's right to participate has now become, in my assessment, one of the leading figures denying that same right to a new generation.These young people are present within Fatah, too. In recent weeks, I saw its members and activists eager to stand as candidates and participate. According to the information I followed, more than 430 people in Hebron alone applied for a place on the movement's electoral list, including many young grassroots leaders. This was a clear expression of a desire to take part in political life, and of talent waiting for an opportunity, even within the organization to which the vice president belongs.As for Mezher, deputy secretary-general of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, who holds a leading role while Secretary-General Ahmad Sa'adat remains imprisoned, his responsibility raises a question no less painful: How can an organization with such a substantial political history and popular following accept a role in closing the path to political renewal?For me, that question has a face and a name: Nidal al-Rabadi.He was my friend and schoolmate, and a supporter of the Popular Front. During a demonstration in Jerusalem in 1988, a bullet struck him and he fell beside me. We were 15. Lying on the ground, he looked at me and spoke his last words: “Don't leave me.”I have never left him behind in my memory. To this day, I keep his photograph in my home beside those of my children, and I cannot hold back my tears whenever his name is mentioned.When I think about Mezher's position on the elections, I remember Rabadi and ask: How do we honor that generation by denying its children the right to choose? What future do we preserve for their sacrifices if young people remain outside our institutions, waiting for permission to participate from those who have held their positions for decades? I invoke Rabadi because politics, to me, means responsibility toward people's lives and toward those who died believing their sacrifices would open a better path for future generations.The Popular Front was once the second-largest force in the Palestine Liberation Organization, with a clear grassroots presence during the First Intifada. In my assessment, that presence has diminished considerably over the years. Recently, I have witnessed young people and activists moving from its ranks to other political groups and electoral lists, including Masar Jadid.This phenomenon extends beyond any single organization. Many of my colleagues in Masar Jadid and I came from other political movements. We brought our history and convictions with us, but we sought a space where we could work, make a difference, and participate. When organizations fail to make room for their members' abilities, people look for other doors. Postponing elections will not resolve this alienation. It will deepen it.The cost of delayThe cost of waiting is visible in almost every Palestinian household. Employees receive delayed portions of their salaries, workers have lost their incomes since October 2023, and families borrow money to pay rent and buy food. I have met people overwhelmed by loans, checks, and obligations they can no longer meet. Fear of creditors and the courts has become part of their daily lives.In education, the financial crisis affects both regular schooling and teachers' lives. When a teacher must seek additional work or sell goods on the street to support a family and afford the journey to school, the future of all our children is at risk.In Gaza, families – many displaced into tents – are approaching a third winter since the war began. Mothers and fathers spend their days searching for the bare minimum of food, water, and medicine for their children.Amid these conditions, I spoke for hours every day with young men and women from Gaza by phone, Zoom, and social media. Their education, knowledge, and capacity to think and act impressed me. I was moved by the hope in their voices simply because a political organization existed that allowed them to express their views and participate.For them, elections offered a chance to become decision-makers in a society accustomed to treating them as recipients of aid. How painful it is to see these abilities buried once again beneath a closed bureaucracy and leaders who refuse to make room for them.There are Palestinians approaching 40 who have never once voted in a national election. There are leaders who have held their positions for most of these young people's lives. This imbalance cannot be corrected through more waiting or through dialogue that continues for years without restoring people's rights – especially when the cost of postponement extends beyond our internal affairs.French President Emmanuel Macron invested significant political effort in supporting recognition of Palestinian statehood and advancing an international path toward a two-state solution. Those efforts were linked to Palestinian commitments to reform, renew democratic legitimacy, and hold elections.When we postpone this vote again, we confront our partners with a difficult question: How can they defend support for Palestinian institutions that deny their own people the opportunity to choose their representatives?I cannot say with certainty that donor countries will freeze their assistance. But I fear this decision will weaken their willingness to honor their commitments and make it harder to defend support for us before their parliaments and taxpayers. When our institutions and public services depend on that support, international trust becomes a direct Palestinian interest. Squandering it places an additional burden on citizens who are already suffering. Even so, I still see an opportunity to correct course, and I place cautious hope in it.President Mahmoud Abbas has the authority on the Palestinian side to bring the date forward. Macron can use his diplomatic influence to support that correction and link the reform process to a clear electoral timetable in the near future.We may have missed the opportunity to hold elections on November 28, 2026, but that does not justify waiting until September 11, 2027. I call for presidential and legislative elections to be brought forward to no later than March 2027, with preparations beginning immediately and conditions created that allow all Palestinian lists and political forces wishing to stand to carry out their preparatory work and activities on the ground.Elections alone will not solve all our crises. But they give people a peaceful means of demanding accountability, open institutions to new talent, and rebuild trust between citizens and their leadership. Every day we postpone this opportunity makes it harder to recover.At Masar Jadid, we will continue reaching out to everyone who can help. We will use the political, administrative, and legal means available to advocate for an earlier date. We will participate in every serious national dialogue that leads to a clear outcome: returning the decision to the people.I hold Sheikh and Mezher politically responsible for pushing for the postponement. I call on Abbas to correct the decision he signed, and I urge Macron to help protect the opportunity that remains.Thirty-eight years ago, Rabadi told me: “Don't leave me.”Today, in those words, I hear the voice of an entire Palestinian generation waiting for someone to open the door.We have a duty not to leave them behind.Samer Sinijlawi is a Palestinian political figure from Jerusalem and the founder and president of Masar Jadid (New Path), a Palestinian political movement advocating democracy, nonviolence, reform, and regional peace.

title: Russia condemns strikes on civilian targets in Saudi Arabia — deputy foreign minister
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Russia is monitoring the situation in the Middle East with concern and condemns strikes on civilian targets, Deputy Foreign Minister Georgy Borisenko said in an interview with RTVI, commenting on the strikes on the international airport in Riyadh.
"We, of course, are watching with great concern what is happening in Yemen and around it. In 2022, hostilities there effectively ceased thanks to the agreements reached between the Yemeni parties with the participation of Saudi Arabia," he said.
"And, of course, Russia condemns attacks on any civilian facilities, on any civilian infrastructure. We also said this in relation to the attacks that occurred on Riyadh International Airport."

title: Fighting erupts between rival SPLM-IO factions in Leer
body: Fighting between forces loyal to rival acting chairpersons of the opposition SPLM-IO erupted in Rupkong and Bow payams in Leer County, Unity State, the birthplace of SPLM-IO leader Riek Machar, with clashes continuing on Wednesday, local military officials said. The clashes involved forces aligned with Regina Joseph and Oyet Nathaniel, both of whom identify themselves as the movement’s acting chairpersons. James Yoach Bading, the military commissioner of Leer County aligned with Oyet, accused forces aligned with Joseph of attacking his faction’s position in Rupkong, saying his fighters had been defending themselves since Tuesday. “The group of Regina Joseph attacked our position in Rupkong, but we have been defending ourselves since yesterday,” Bading told Radio Tamazuj. Bading said the fighting had killed 14 people from the two sides, including four from his faction and 10 from the opposing group. He added that eight people had been injured and transferred to Leer County Hospital for treatment. Dhoal Koryom Lingling, the SPLM-IO military governor aligned with Joseph, confirmed that clashes had broken out between the rival factions, describing the fighting as an internal conflict involving supporters of Nathaniel and Joseph. Koryom said his side had recorded three injuries and no deaths, adding that further details of the clashes were still being collected as fighting continued on Wednesday morning. The casualty figures provided by the two officials could not be independently verified. The fighting comes amid a deepening leadership crisis within the SPLM-IO following the detention of its leader, Riek Machar, in March 2025. The dispute intensified in August 2026, when acting chairman Oyet Nathaniel Pierino suspended interim Secretary-General Regina Joseph and other senior officials. Joseph rejected the move and issued a counter-order suspending Oyet, with both sides claiming authority under the movement’s internal rules. The post Fighting erupts between rival SPLM-IO factions in Leer appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Ukrainian drones reportedly hit Sberbank data center in Russia
body:
A Ukrainian overnight attack reportedly targeted a data center under construction belonging to Russian state lender Sberbank in Balakovo in Saratov Oblast, deputy chief executive Alexander Vedyakhin said on Oct. 14.
Saratov regional governor Roman Busargin said that Ukrainian drones had attacked the region on the morning of Oct. 14, according to Russian state news agency TASS.
Vedyakhin confirmed the attack to TASS, saying that all systems and services of the bank continued operating, and that no employees were injured in the attack. Busargin also said that "all infrastructure facilities" operated normally.
Nonetheless, Russian users reported disruptions to the online services of Sberbank, including its AI service GigaChat, the independent Moscow Times said.
Russian authorities announced construction of the facility in 2020, expecting it to cover about 60,000 square meters (about 645,800 square feet), while Russian state-aligned media Vedomosti said it will house a new supercomputer worth 500 billion rubles.
Ukrainian defense company Fire Point commented in a social media post on Wednesday morning, saying "You didn’t think it would stop with just Yandex, did you?" after it trolled Russian tech giant Yandex on Oct. 12, following reported damage to another of its data centers, disrupting access to its financial services.
Yandex's data center in Vladimir Oblast completely shut down following a reported drone attack on Oct. 11, Russian state news agency TASS said on Oct. 11, citing the company.
The strike marked the third attack on a Yandex data center in four days, following confirmed strikes in Ryazan and Kaluga oblasts on Oct. 8 and 9.
On Oct. 11, Yandex Cloud reported power disruptions in an availability zone identified as being located at the company's data center in Vladimir.
Sberbank remains heavily isolated under Western sanctions , having been entirely cut off from the SWIFT international payment messaging network.
Ukrainian authorities did not comment on the strike.

title: EU provides EUR 228 bln to Ukraine since 2022 - commissioner
body:
The European Union’s support for Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022 has reached EUR 228 billion, European Commissioner for Economy and Productivity Valdis Dombrovskis said at the 10th ministerial roundtable on support for Ukraine on Wednesday, on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank in Bangkok.
“The EU is doing its part: EUR 228 billion in support of Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion, and that is not all, more to come,” he said on X after the roundtable, which was closed to the press.
Dombrovskis stressed that international partners must join these efforts.
He did not give Interfax-Ukraine other details, but a meeting of the Ukraine Financial Coordination Group with the commissioner is scheduled for Friday, October 16, on the sidelines of the annual meetings.
Several roundtable participants told Interfax-Ukraine that it did not address specific commitments that Kyiv’s partners are ready to make in the future, but that in general they confirmed their readiness to keep supporting Ukraine.
The Ukrainian side outlined its external financing needs for 2027 and said its sources must be confirmed before the IMF mission in November for the combined second and third reviews of the Extended Fund Facility (EFF) program.
IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva traditionally took part in the roundtable and left after a while, and the fund was then represented by First Deputy Managing Director Daniel Katz, an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent said. Before joining the IMF last year, Katz was U.S. deputy treasury secretary and worked on creating the American-Ukrainian investment fund.
World Bank Vice President Antonella Bassani, European Bank for Reconstruction and Development President Odile Renaud-Basso, International Finance Corporation (IFC) Managing Director Makhtar Diop and IFC Vice President Alfonso Garcia Mora, and European Investment Bank President Nadia Calvino were also present.
Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky spoke for Ukraine online, as did Finance Minister Serhiy Marchenko, who stayed in Kyiv because of his report to the Verkhovna Rada on Monday and the adoption of laws important for external financing later in the week. National Bank of Ukraine Governor Andrei Pyshnyy, Economy and Environment Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko and Deputy Finance Minister Olha Zykova also attended.
During the IMF annual meetings, which run on October 12-18, the Ukrainian delegation will discuss with the fund the implementation of the new four-year EFF program of $8.1 billion, approved in late February this year. It is part of total external financing of $136.5 billion in 2026-2029 under the base scenario.
