In July, the fund completed the first review of the program and released a second tranche of about $690 million, bringing total financing under the new program to $2.2 billion. Delays in meeting some of the program’s structural benchmarks were recorded. The program, updated after the first review, gained eight structural benchmarks, seven of them fiscal.
The plan now is to combine the second and third reviews and bring them to the executive board by December, together with approval of the combined third and fourth tranches totaling about $1.65 billion.
“Bringing this to the board depends on receiving sufficient and reliable financing assurances to cover the projected funding gap on terms consistent with ensuring Ukraine’s debt sustainability,” IMF spokeswoman Julie Kozack said in early October.
Marchenko said that before the IMF mission’s expected visit in November it would be desirable to get confirmation of all sources of the $52.6 billion of external financing of the state budget in 2027, while about $32.6 billion of that still needs additional confirmation.
He said Kyiv counts on the EU to keep its commitment to cover two-thirds of Ukraine’s external financing needs next year as well, which would add about $17.5 billion to confirmed financing. As for the remaining roughly $15 billion, there are a number of sources for covering it, he said, including bilateral financing and guarantees and programs with international financial institutions.
The first such roundtable took place at the IMF and World Bank spring meetings on April 21, 2022, and the second at the autumn meetings on October 12 that year. They have been held twice a year at these events since.
At the first meeting, the IMF head pointed to Ukraine’s monthly need in 2022 of $5 billion to finance the state budget deficit amid the war Russia unleashed. At the second, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy proposed that the global financial community take three urgent steps in support of Ukraine: create a ‘financial Ramstein,’ ensure economic recovery and help for Ukrainians, and create a mechanism to support investment and insure it against war risks.
At the third, Zelenskyy asked the IMF and World Bank to approve a Support Program to cover priority Rapid Recovery projects worth $14.1 billion, and urged them to work out specific mechanisms for using frozen Russian assets to compensate for the damage Russia caused.

title: Two Veterans With Prosthetic Legs Conquer 6,476-Meter Himalayan Peak in Tribute to Ukraine’s Defenders
body:
Two veterans who each lost a lower leg while defending Ukraine have summited Mera Peak in Nepal, reaching an altitude of 6,476 meters (21,247 feet) and dedicating their ascent to Ukrainian service members fighting Russia’s full-scale invasion and those who have died in the war .
Christopher John Park-Greenwood, a former British soldier who served in Ukraine’s military, and Roman Havryliak, a Ukrainian veteran, completed the climb using prosthetic legs as part of an expedition organized with Second Wind, a Ukrainian community supporting service members and veterans with limb loss through adaptive mountain sports.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The expedition began on Oct. 1, Ukraine’s Defenders Day. The climbers dedicated their ascent to those continuing to defend the country and to the memory of those who have given their lives.
According to Second Wind, the team faced demanding high-altitude conditions, including temperatures below freezing, up to three meters of fresh snow and avalanches in close proximity. The multi-day expedition required gradual altitude gain and acclimatization before the final push to the summit.
For Greenwood and Havryliak, Mera Peak marked another milestone in a mountaineering journey that began after their combat injuries. The climb followed their ascent of Mount Ararat in Turkey, which stands at 5,137 meters (16,854 feet), in the summer of 2026.
Both climbers spent more than a year preparing for the expedition through regular training, climbing-gym sessions and increasingly challenging routes in Ukraine’s Carpathian Mountains.
Greenwood, originally from Yorkshire, England, is a career soldier who previously served in the British Army and the French Foreign Legion.
Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, he joined the Armed Forces of Ukraine ’s (AFU) 73rd Naval Special Operations Centre. He sustained a severe combat injury in 2023 that resulted in the loss of his lower leg.
Two veterans summited Mera Peak in Nepal with the support of the Second Wind Foundation team. (Photo courtesy of the Second Wind Foundation)
Two veterans summited Mera Peak in Nepal with the support of the Second Wind Foundation team. (Photo courtesy of the Second Wind Foundation)
Havryliak, known by the call sign “Hava,” is from the Lviv region. He volunteered to join the AFU following the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion and served as a drone operator with the 80th Separate Air Assault Brigade. He also sustained a severe combat injury that led to the loss of his leg.
After more than a year of treatment and multiple surgeries, Havryliak set himself a new goal: returning to the mountains.
Both veterans subsequently became active members of Second Wind, a charitable foundation and community that brings together Ukrainian service members and veterans who use prostheses, taking part in its training sessions and mountain programs.
The expedition was accompanied by Gennady Gazin, Anna Vozna and Oleksii Aleksieienko, the founders of the organization.
Second Wind grew out of the documentary project Second Wind, which followed five Ukrainian service members who climbed Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa’s highest mountain. The foundation currently runs regular adaptive mountain sports programs in Ukraine and organizes mountain expeditions for its community members.
Ukrainian veterans are increasingly taking on mountain-climbing challenges at home and abroad as part of their rehabilitation after severe combat injuries.
Many of these expeditions involve service members who have undergone amputations and climb using prosthetic limbs, demonstrating how adaptive mountaineering can help veterans return to physically demanding activities.
In early 2025, five Ukrainian veterans completed a group ascent of Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa’s highest peak, at 5,895 meters (19,341 feet). The expedition was described as a world first for a group of veterans with combat-related injuries.
The participants included Roman Kolesnyk, known by the call sign “Dobriak,” a veteran of the 3rd Assault Brigade who underwent an amputation after a severe injury; border guard Vladyslav Shatilo, known as “Shatia,” who lost a limb; and Mykhailo Matviiv, or “Grizzly,” a member of the Omega Special Forces Detachment of the National Guard of Ukraine who was injured by a landmine near Vuhledar.
The group also included Oleksandr Mikhov, known as “Ragnar,” an Omega special forces fighter who uses a prosthesis, and a servicewoman known by the call sign “Vysota” (“Height”), who sustained severe injuries twice while serving at the front.
In May 2025, Ukrainian military intelligence veterans Ivan Taran and Oleksandr Dashko, both of whom had undergone major amputations, reached the Everest Base Camp in Nepal at an altitude of approximately 5,400 meters (17,717 feet), using prosthetic limbs. The expedition was organized by Ukrainian mountaineerc Tetiana Yalovchak.
Veterans have also taken on mountain challenges within Ukraine. Volodymyr Voropai, a veteran of the 73rd Naval Special Operations Centre who lost a leg during the war, helped pioneer climbs of Mount Hoverla (2,061 meters, or 6,762 feet) for veterans with amputations.
In October 2026, service member Maksym Bashynskyi, who was wounded near Huliaipole, climbed Mount Vysokyi Verkh in the Carpathians, which stands at 1,176 meters (3,858 feet), as part of the Travel Therapy project. Volunteers assisted him using a specialized all-terrain mobility cart known as “Julietta.”
Group ascents of Mount Hoverla have also brought together dozens of veterans. Among the initiatives reported in late 2025 and 2026 were a climb involving 50 veterans from the Kyiv region and an ascent by Special Operations Forces (SSO) personnel who carried a fellow veteran with an amputation to the summit of Ukraine’s highest mountain.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: FACTBOX: SpaceX restricts access to Starlink for Ukrainian military
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. SpaceX limited the speed of Starlink satellite internet terminals used by the Ukrainian army overnight, Sergey Beskrestnov, Vladimir Zelensky’s external adviser and expert in communications and unmanned systems, said.
Below are the main facts on the subject.
- SpaceX imposed restrictions on the operation of Starlink terminals for the Ukrainian army overnight, disrupting its operations, Sergey Sternenko, a former adviser to Ukraine’s defense minister, wrote on Telegram.
- Sternenko speculated that SpaceX had acted at the request of US President Donald Trump’s administration.
- Zelensky’s external adviser Beskrestnov later confirmed the reports on Telegram.
- According to him, the restrictions currently apply to the ‘military package’ of Starshield services, with the speed limit set at 100 miles per hour (about 160 kilometers per hour - TASS).
- This "disrupted a number of missions," Beskrestnov said.
- In his view, "this action cannot be a coincidence and has to do with the current political situation."
- Ukraine once again received no intelligence warning from its Western partners last night, Vladimir Zelensky said.
- The US warned Ukraine that it could suspend intelligence sharing, Zelensky said in an interview with NPR. According to him, Ukrainian generals reported that they had been notified of this possibility at the military level.
- Ukraine received no intelligence warnings regarding the first wave of Russian ballistic missile launches overnight into October 14, but warnings about subsequent attacks did come in, RBC Ukraine quoted Ukrainian Air Force Spokesman Yury Ignat as saying.
- A slowdown in Starlink service is making it virtually impossible to launch medium-range drones, and some missions involving them have already been cancelled since the start of the day, the 7th Corps of the Ukrainian airborne assault troops reported on Telegram.
- The Ukrainian armed forces rely entirely on Starlink satellite internet, so the Kiev authorities must travel to the US to negotiate the lifting of access restrictions, Verkhovna Rada lawmaker Alexey Goncharenko (listed in Russia as a terrorist and extremist) said.
- The Ukrainian army will no longer be able to counter Russian jet-powered drones due to the reduced speed of the US Starlink satellite Internet service, Zelensky’s external adviser on communications and unmanned systems, Beskrestnov, said.
- As the adviser pointed out, Kiev uses Starlink to counter jet-powered drones, but restrictions on its operation will now prevent the Ukrainian military from doing so.
- Beskrestnov said that through their actions Ukraine’s partners "actually deprive" Kiev of one of the few chances to intercept such drones.
- The slowdown of Starlink terminals caught the Ukrainian military by surprise, occurring entirely without warning, the British newspaper Financial Times (FT) wrote citing sources.
- The report says that Ukrainian drones relying on Starlink terminals are experiencing signal disruptions at speeds above 160 kmph.
- The reduction in intelligence-sharing from the United States, combined with Starlink's operational restrictions, is seriously hampering the Ukrainian military, unmanned aviation expert and CEO of the Center for Integrated Unmanned Solutions Dmitry Kuzyakin told TASS.
- According to him, the Kiev regime’s unchecked actions are irritating both the US president himself and a segment of the American establishment that has heavily invested in Ukraine.
- A number of cyber operations by the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) against Russia may be disrupted or delayed due to SpaceX restricting the speed of Starlink satellite Internet terminals used by Ukrainian security agencies, Sergey Trukhachev, a technical and digital security expert, told TASS.
- He also noted that the SpaceX restrictions would directly impact the Ukrainian armed forces as well.
- This would primarily affect Ukrainian operators of high-speed unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), the expert added.
- Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski warned US entrepreneur and SpaceX owner Elon Musk on social media platform X, amid reports that connection speeds for Starlink satellite internet terminals used by the Ukrainian military have been throttled.

title: IN BRIEF: First hearing of Nord Stream blast case takes place in Germany
body:
HAMBURG, October 14. /TASS/. The first hearing in the case of the Nord Stream gas pipeline explosions took place at the Higher Regional Court in Hamburg, Germany, amid tightened security measures.
The trial began four years after the attack. Ukrainian national Sergey Kuznetsov is the defendant in the case. The Office of the German Federal Prosecutor believes that what he did can be classified as a war crime.
TASS has compiled the key details about the hearing.
- Ukrainian national Sergey Kuznetsov is the defendant in the case.
- He was detained in Italy in August 2025 and transferred to Germany.
- During the first hearing, Kuznetsov confirmed his identity and said that he had been born in Omsk on January 2, 1976.
- Another Ukrainian citizen was detained in Croatia recently.
- The Office of Germany’s Federal Prosecutor believes that Kuznetsov’s actions should be considered a war crime, a TASS correspondent reported from the courtroom.
- The suspect and his accomplices, also service members, acted on orders from Ukrainian government agencies, a prosecutor from the German Federal Prosecutor's Office said during the Hamburg hearing.
- Investigators believe that the saboteurs used forged documents to rent a sailing yacht from a German company and transported explosives to the Nord Stream pipelines.
- Earlier, the court admitted the indictment against the Ukrainian national for trial on the merits and opened the main proceedings.
- Judges came to the conclusion that there was enough evidence to suspect Kuznetsov of committing a war crime using banned methods of warfare by attacking civilian facilities, carrying out a blast, damaging property, and disrupting public services.
- Kuznetsov declined to speak to the court, exercising his right to remain silent.
- Kuznetsov’s defense team said that, as a service member, he was unable to discuss the circumstances of the incidents, the people who gave him orders and the details of those orders.
- According to his lawyer, this makes a fair trial is impossible.
- The defense also argued that the Nord Stream pipelines could not be considered as purely civilian facilities in the context of the Ukraine conflict.
- The defense team plans to seek a dismissal of the charges.
- The first hearing of the case took place at the Hamburg Higher Regional Court.
- The hearing lasted a little over two hours.
- The next hearing is set for October 27.
- The court has scheduled 24 hearings through the end of the year.
- Further hearings are planned for February, but they have yet to be finalized.
- Over 100 journalists have been accredited to cover the trial.
- A rally calling for an investigation into the sabotage of the Nord Stream gas pipelines took place in Hamburg ahead of the first hearing.
- The rally was organized by the BSW party.
- On September 26, 2022, unprecedented damage was recorded on three strings of the Nord Stream pipelines and the never-commissioned Nord Stream 2 pipeline.
- The Russian Prosecutor General’s Office opened a criminal case over an act of international terrorism.
- Russian Ambassador to Germany Sergey Nechayev said earlier that all of Moscow’s initiatives regarding the investigation into the sabotage of the Nord Stream and Nord Stream-2 gas pipelines were being ignored.

title: Former SIC Savings and Loans MD Amma Frimpomaa Dwumah honours EOCO invitation
body: Former Managing Director of SIC Life Savings and Loans, Amma Frimpomaa Dwumah, has honoured an invitation from the Economic and Organised Crime Office (EOCO). The Office says she is cooperating with investigators probing an alleged criminal conspiracy linked to a revised financial loss of about GH¢27 million. In a statement dated October 13, 2026, EOCO said investigations into the alleged conspiracy, which has resulted in financial losses to SIC Savings and Loans Company Limited, were progressing steadily. The Office also confirmed that the Member of Parliament for Suame, John Darko, had reported to its offices at exactly 12 noon on Tuesday to assist investigators with information relevant to the case. According to EOCO, Mr Darko was cooperative and responsive throughout the investigative process and was subsequently granted enquiry bail. The Office said its decision to grant him bail took into consideration the circumstances of the case, the applicable law and his level of cooperation with investigators. EOCO stressed that the investigation remains active and that no conclusion has been reached regarding the culpability or otherwise of any person connected to the matter. It said the ongoing investigation was proceeding according to its case theory but did not provide further details about the alleged conspiracy.

title: Escaped Russian POW Reportedly Shoots 5 Ukrainian Troops Dead Near Kharkiv
body:
Five soldiers serving in Ukraine’s 72nd Mechanized Brigade were shot dead in a residential house near Kharkiv on Tuesday, Oct. 13, and investigators are checking whether the attacker was a Russian soldier who escaped from captivity.
Ukrainska Pravda , citing the investigation, said a man opened fire on the soldiers while they were inside the house. All five died of their wounds.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
On Wednesday, the Kharkiv District Prosecutor’s Office opened a pre-trial murder investigation, with law enforcement working to establish the attacker’s identity, his whereabouts and all circumstances of the crime.
Investigators are examining several theories, including whether the suspect was linked to a Russian sabotage and reconnaissance group.
BBC Ukraine , citing its source “among the military command in the Kharkiv region,” said the murder was committed by a Russian soldier who escaped from captivity in the Kharkiv region.
The 72nd Brigade, named after the Black Zaporozhians, confirmed that the victims were its personnel and called the incident a “tragic event.”
It expressed condolences to the families, urged the media and public not to spread unverified information, and said it was withholding further details for security reasons. The brigade also raised the possibility of Russian involvement.
Other Ukrainian outlets reported additional details. Public broadcaster Suspilne , citing its sources in law enforcement, said the attacker was a man in civilian clothes carrying an automatic weapon. He allegedly killed one soldier outside the house, then continued shooting inside.
The shooting reportedly lasted about two hours, after which the suspect fled. But Suspline also mentioned a version where the shooter was a Russian man who escaped Ukrainian captivity.
The shooting follows a series of documented killings of Ukrainian service members by Russian forces. Those cases involve soldiers captured at the front, and investigators have not linked them to the Kharkiv district incident.
On April 12, Russian troops executed four captured Ukrainian soldiers near the village of Veterynarne in the Kharkiv region during the Orthodox Easter ceasefire. The incident came about a day after Ukraine and Russia each released 175 prisoners of war.
In July, Russian troops reportedly executed a Ukrainian prisoner of war in the Donetsk region right after interrogation. A month later, a captured Ukrainian soldier was shot near Myrne in the Donetsk region’s Volnovakha district.
In September, two captured Ukrainian soldiers were killed in the Donetsk region near Dobropillia.
Russia executed at least 337 captured Ukrainian soldiers as of late 2025, according to Dmytro Lubinets , Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman.
The investigation into the Kharkiv district shooting is ongoing.
Anastasiia Bzova is journalist covering politics, culture and current affairs. She focuses on delivering accurate, accessible reporting that helps readers understand the issues shaping their opinions.

title: Russia attacked Ukrainian retailer Epicentr’s warehouse 10 times in one day, destroying about 85% of goods, company says
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Russian forces attacked Epicentr’s hub in Khmelnytskyi, a city in western Ukraine, 10 times on 13 October, starting five large fires that destroyed about 85% of the goods stored inside, the company said . Epicentr is a Ukrainian chain of home-improvement and household-goods stores. The attack adds pressure to Ukraine’s logistics network, already damaged by Russian strikes. On 10 September, Ukrainian entrepreneur Ruslan Shostak, co-owner of the popular retail chains Eva and Varus, said that 2.1 million square meters of Ukraine’s modern warehouse space had been destroyed since Russia’s full-scale invasion began. He put the country’s total modern warehouse space at approximately 5 million square meters. The strike on the hub came the same day Russia opened a barrage of 39 ballistic missiles on Ukraine’s power grid. About 30 drones in the sky kept the fire from being put out, and the hub burned down completely overnight, Epicentr said. None of its people were hurt, the company said. “The most important thing is that all our people are alive,” Epicentr wrote. Russia had earlier completely destroyed Epicentr’s two largest logistics complexes, in Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast, the company said. The Khmelnytskyi hub had remained effectively its only surviving large warehouse complex. Goods were sent from there to the company’s shopping centers, and people worked there every day “so that millions of Ukrainians could buy what they need,” it wrote. Epicentr described every such attack as a blow to Ukrainian businesses’ ability to operate, pay wages, preserve jobs, and support the country’s economy. Epicentr’s earlier losses Epicentr said in August that 10 of its shopping centers had been completely destroyed since February 2022. Another 13 retail sites had been damaged, and one in Melitopol remained under Russian occupation, it said. At the time, the company operated 70 shopping centers, down from 80 at the end of 2021. Earlier, during a Russian missile attack overnight on 5 August, Epicentr’s logistics center in Kyiv burned down completely, Epicentr’s Yulia Chudnovets said . The company’s ceramic tile plant in Kalynivka, one of the largest in Ukraine, was effectively lost, she said. One employee was killed and three were injured, she added. Explore further A fourth Ukrainian pharmaceutical warehouse has burned in a Russian strike since the start of the month On 25 May 2024, Russian airstrikes on an Epicentr hypermarket in Kharkiv killed 19 people, Interior Minister Ihor Klymenko said . Attacks across Khmelnytskyi Oblast Fires broke out at enterprises in Khmelnytskyi and Shepetivka districts on 13 October, Serhii Tiurin, head of the Khmelnytskyi Oblast Military Administration, reported. He did not name the enterprises. On 14 October, Tiurin said one of the fires had been put out, and crews were still fighting the other. Khmelnytskyi Mayor Oleksandr Symchyshyn said six people were injured in Khmelnytskyi district that day, where Russian strikes damaged private enterprises, a gas station, and a medical facility.
