title: NATO reconnaissance plane spends nearly 4.5 hours near Kaliningrad Region
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. A US-registered NATO reconnaissance aircraft spent almost four and a half hours near Russia’s Kaliningrad Region, a source in air traffic control services told TASS.
"The Bombardier Artemis II reconnaissance aircraft flew in the area of the Kaliningrad Region from its home base in Constanta, Romania. It then spent nearly four and a half hours circling the Russian region, using the airspace of Poland and Lithuania as well as areas over the neutral waters of the Baltic Sea," the source said.
According to the source, the aircraft was detected near the Kaliningrad Region for the first time this week. Previously, its flight had been monitored over the neutral waters of the Black Sea, where it spent seven hours flying east and west in the southern part of the sea. On Monday, the Bombardier Artemis II also flew over central Latvia, Lithuania, and Estonia, turning near the Estonian coast of the Gulf of Finland.
"The aircraft did not approach Russia's borders at that time, and during the flight over the Black Sea, it did not enter the airspace of any coastal country other than Romania, from where it took off and where it subsequently landed," the source noted. During these flights, the aircraft operates outside civil aviation routes, usually at an altitude of around 10.5 kilometers.

title: Igbo group urges Tinubu to tackle erosion in South-East
body: By Ugochukwu Alaribe UMUAHIA — The Igbo Community Association, Abuja, has appealed to President Bola Tinubu to urgently intervene in the gully erosion crisis ravaging communities across the South-East. The association said immediate Federal Government intervention was necessary to prevent further destruction of communities, protect lives and property, and restore hope to thousands of affected residents. The President-General of the Igbo Community Association, Federal Capital Territory, Engr. Ikenna Ellis-Ezenekwe, made the appeal at a stakeholders’ meeting on the erosion menace. Ezenekwe expressed concern over the destruction of homes, livelihoods and communities across the region, particularly in Nanka, Anambra South Senatorial District, where advancing gullies have reportedly displaced families and threatened ancestral homes. He said vulnerable residents, including children and the elderly, faced the risk of losing their homes if urgent measures were not taken. “Many families, including vulnerable children and the elderly, are currently facing imminent displacement as their ancestral homes are threatened daily. “They need their hopes renewed, and they need the Federal Government of Nigeria to come to their rescue immediately. We are appealing to President Tinubu to intervene urgently and save the people,” he said. The association’s president-general argued that the scale of the erosion crisis exceeded the financial and technical capacity of individual state governments in the region. “We acknowledge that the scale of gully erosion remediation is beyond the financial and technical capabilities of the five South-East state governors. “The state governors can only proffer prophylactic solutions given their resource limitations. This is a capital-intensive environmental ecological disaster that falls within the powers and constitutional responsibilities of the Federal Government,” he said. Seeks stronger SEDC intervention To address the crisis, the association urged Tinubu to adequately fund and empower the newly established South-East Development Commission (SEDC) to coordinate erosion control and remediation projects across affected states. It also proposed the establishment of a high-powered presidential committee to assess the extent of the damage and develop and implement a comprehensive, long-term remediation plan. The group further called for international collaboration, urging the President to use Nigeria’s diplomatic relationships to secure technical expertise, development funding and other forms of assistance to address the environmental crisis. It said coordinated action involving the Federal Government, the SEDC, state governments and international partners was needed to achieve lasting solutions to gully erosion in the South-East. The post Igbo group urges Tinubu to tackle erosion in South-East appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: “It finances an economy geared toward total war”—Ukraine’s third president on the Russian diesel Washington just cleared
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Viktor Yushchenko, Ukraine’s president from 2005 to 2010, has written an open letter to US President Donald Trump and posted it on Facebook on 14 October. Without naming it, the letter takes aim at the green light Washington gave Russian diesel trade five days earlier, after a call between Trump and Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin. Russia banned its diesel exports in July amid a fuel crisis at home, after Ukrainian strikes on refineries had already cut those exports, and last week’s US waiver and the supply deal Trump announced with Moscow would put that fuel back on world markets while Russian strikes still kill Ukrainian civilians. What Yushchenko says Russian fuel buys Yushchenko wrote that Russian ballistic missiles, Iranian Shahed drones, and aerial bombs strike homes every day and night in Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa, Dnipro, and Kharkiv. Whenever there is talk of “concessions” or deals with Putin, he wrote, the Kremlin answers with more missiles, more drones, and more bloodshed. Explore further Trump’s Russian diesel deal, which drew fury in Ukraine, is unlikely to lower prices, experts say Yushchenko rejected calls for Ukraine to “restrain its strikes against the infrastructure that finances and sustains Russia’s war.” “Money paid for Russian fuel is not an abstraction called ‘commerce.’ It finances an economy geared toward total war,” he wrote. Nuclear arms, Pearl Harbor, and Iwo Jima Yushchenko wrote that Ukraine inherited “one of the largest nuclear arsenals in the world” and agreed to give it up, trusting the words and signatures of great powers. In his view, by signing the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, America took on a moral responsibility toward Ukraine. He compared trade in Russian energy to America’s trade with Imperial Japan, which included strategically important materials, before the US entered World War II. Washington hoped for years to avoid a wider war in the Pacific, he wrote, but economic pressure and diplomacy could not prevent catastrophe. Explore further Ukraine warns of “a new type of humanitarian crisis” as Russia aims at its biggest cities Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941. America knows how dangerous it is to believe that trade can tame an aggressor, Yushchenko wrote, adding: “History taught us that lesson at a terrible price.” He also named two men he called Ukrainian. One was Sergeant Michael Strank, whose family, Yushchenko wrote, came from Lemkivshchyna. The son of immigrants from Czechoslovakia, Strank took part in the famous raising of the US flag on Iwo Jima, according to the Marine Corps. The other was Oleksandr Silvashko, “a Ukrainian boy from the Cherkasy region,” who, Yushchenko wrote, was the first to embrace US Lieutenant William Robertson when American and Soviet forces met at the Elbe in April 1945. “One does not negotiate with tyrants—one stops them,” Yushchenko concluded. title: Russia to supply diesel fuel to the US after making contract — Novak
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. A certain amount of time will be needed to make a contract and load a tanker for the delivery of the first Russian diesel fuel batch to the United States, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters on the sidelines of the Russian Energy Week forum.
"A contract should be made and loading of supplies should be provided. It will require some time," he said.
The work on contracts is currently underway with the US counterparts at the level of executive authorities and companies, Novak added.

title: AFCON 2027Q: ‘We should assemble the best squad’ – George Afriyie speaks on Black Stars’ team
body: Former Ghana Football Association (GFA) Vice President, George Afriyie, has urged the Black Stars to organize the country’s strongest players for their remaining 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) qualification matches. Afriyie’s comments follow a difficult start to Ghana’s qualifying campaign, where the four-time African champions lost their opening two matches. Ghana first suffered a 2-0 defeat against Côte d’Ivoire in Bouaké, followed by a humiliating 4-2 loss at home. The national team was severely weakened after several key players missed the matches due to injuries. Following the back-to-back defeats, former head coach Carlos Queiroz mutually parted ways with the GFA. “Black Stars’ chances of qualifying for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) are not over,” Afriyie said. “We should assemble the best squad for the rest of the games. It’s a league format, so if we can win the rest of the games, hopefully we will qualify,” he told sporty FM . The Black Stars will face Somalia in November with a crucial double-header against Somalia at the Accra Sports Stadium with the aim of gaining maximum points. Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda will co-host the 2027 AFCON in East Africa.

title: Inflation sizzled in September -- and Social Security benefits will get a boost
body:
Rising gasoline and diesel prices pushed inflation higher in September. The cost of living index was up 3.7%, according to a report Wednesday from the Labor Department. Isabelle Souriment/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
Nights are getting colder, but inflation is heating up.
A report from the Labor Department on Wednesday showed consumer prices in September were up 3.7% from a year ago. That's a larger annual increase than the previous month.
A spike in energy prices tied to the U.S. war with Iran drove the cost of living higher. Prices jumped 0.6% between August and September.
"It's not looking good," said economist Brian Bethune of Boston College. "The main problem, of course, that everybody knows is gasoline prices. But also heating oil."
Heating oil is a close cousin of diesel fuel. The cost of the fuel oil has jumped 74% in the last year, which is hard on families in New England who rely on heating oil to stay warm.
Stripping out volatile energy and food prices, what's known as "core inflation" was 2.6% in September. That's also a bigger annual increase than was tallied in August.
The artificial intelligence boom has raised the cost of memory chips, affecting all sorts of consumer electronics. Apple, for example, raised the price of older-model iPhones last month by $100 apiece.
Shortly after the inflation report was released, the Social Security Administration announced that benefits will increase by 3.6% next year . The annual cost-of-living adjustment is based on prices in July, August and September.
The jump in benefits amounts to an extra $75 a month for the average Social Security recipient.
Advocates for seniors welcomed the increase.
"It helps millions of Americans keep up with rising costs for groceries, routine bills, healthcare and other everyday expenses," said AARP CEO Myechia Minter-Jordan.
But critics complain that the cost-of-living adjustment doesn't reflect seniors' actual expenses, which often include higher costs for healthcare.
"It won't be enough for most seniors to even tread water financially," said Max Richtman, president of the National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare.
Treading water would be an improvement for most workers, whose paychecks are not keeping pace with today's rising prices.
Average wages in September rose just 3%, so the typical worker's buying power has eroded over the last year.
"People are kind of saying, 'Something isn't right with that,'" Bethune said. "I'm working harder. I'm more productive. And this is not a square deal."
Inflation is not nearly as high as it was in 2022, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. But every time prices start to level off, the economy is rattled by a new supply shock, such as President Trump's double-digit tariffs or the war with Iran.
Beth Hammack, who heads the Cleveland Federal Reserve Bank, worries the cumulative effect of these shocks could make inflation more entrenched. Hammack told a group of economists this week about a Cleveland-area retailer she'd heard from who is raising prices not just to cover today's costs but the higher costs that may come in the future.
"This could be a sign that an inflationary mindset is taking hold," Hammack said. "When people expect higher prices, they make decisions with this in mind. It can become a self-fulfilling prophecy that makes it harder for monetary policy to bring inflation back down."
Policymakers at the Federal Reserve will weigh the new inflation data when they meet in two weeks to discuss interest rates. Investors now see about a 50-50 chance the Fed will raise its benchmark rate in October in an effort to combat inflation.
An earlier version of this story said that inflation was higher in 2002, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The invasion and the resulting spike in prices were in 2022.
