title: Russia to continue economic cooperation with US — Dmitriev
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Russia will continue to engage with the US on economic projects and explain that American sanctions harm the US itself, Kirill Dmitriev, the Russian President’s Special Representative for Investment and Economic Cooperation with Foreign Countries and head of the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF), told reporters on the sidelines of Russian Energy Week (REW).
"We will continue economic cooperation, as instructed by Russian President Vladimir Putin. It is not just about the diesel deal. There are many other opportunities for economic and investment cooperation with the US - opportunities that benefit Russia, the United States, and global markets alike. We also see that such examples demonstrate that US sanctions primarily harm the US itself; <…> therefore, we will continue to engage with the States on economic and investment projects and continue to explain, using concrete examples, that American sanctions primarily harm the American people and American farmers," he said.
The Russian Energy Week international forum is taking place in Moscow from October 14 to 16, supported by the Russian government, the Ministry of Energy, and the Moscow government. The forum is organized by the Roscongress Foundation. TASS is an information partner of the event.

title: African security chiefs strategise to tackle exploitation of social media, digital technologies by terrorists
body:
African security chiefs are worried about the increasing use of digital technologies and social media platforms by terrorist groups that hold sway over ungoverned territories across the Sahel and West Africa region.
The security leaders, according to Punch, expressed their concerns on Tuesday at a three-day regional conference on detecting and disrupting terrorists’ exploitation of information and communication platforms as well as emerging technologies.
Participants were drawn from across the volatile region, including representatives from the African Union (AU), the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) and the Multinational Joint Task Force (MNJTF), among other regional and international bodies.
Idriss Lalalli, the acting director of the AU Counter-Terrorism Centre, acknowledged the expanding digital footprints of Islamic State and al-Qaeda affiliates in the region.
PREMIUM TIMES reports that Islamic State Sahel Province (ISSP), Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), Boko Haram and other terror groups are consolidating their presence in the Sahel and Lake Chad basin states, deploying new technologies in an unconventional war already overstretching state and regional forces.
JNIM, for instance, has conducted several drone attacks in the Sahel since its first AI-enabled aerial assault on military positions in Bandiagara, Mali, in 2023. The ISSP also deployed a drone for the first time in its attack on Niamey airport earlier this year.
Also, these groups continue to exploit many digital platforms for propaganda and recruitment, gaining territory control and winning hearts and minds beyond their physical strongholds, a trend Mr Lalalli said poses threats faster than security agencies could respond.
“Across West Africa and the Sahel today, ISWAP, Boko Haram and JNIM are extending their reach through technology,” Mr Lalalli said. “They recruit on social media platforms, move and conceal funds via mobile money, gift cards and cryptocurrencies.”
The regional defence chief alleged that these terror groups purchase weapons on “darknet marketplaces,” fly drones, communicate over satellite links, and use AI “to tailor propaganda and evade detection.”
“What makes this difficult is speed and cost,” he continued. “A [terror] cell with a modest budget can now reach audiences far beyond its physical presence and move faster than our procedures can respond.”
Mr Lalalli called for specialised training, regional coordination and stronger collaboration with private sector operators.
In his remarks, Nigeria’s National Security Adviser (NSA), Nuhu Ribadu, noted that emerging technologies further complicate Africa’s security landscape.
Represented by Adamu Laka, the coordinator of the National Counter Terrorism Centre (NCTC), Mr Ribadu said AI-created content, drones and autonomous systems “can expand operational capabilities,” noting that these assets can pave the way for new terror financing channels.
“We must, therefore, strengthen our ability to anticipate, detect, analyse and disrupt threats before they materialise,” the NSA advised.
Beyond acquiring sophisticated equipment, Mr Ribadu said the continent needs technical knowledge, institutional coordination and cooperation among security agencies.
He also urged West African and Sahelian countries to strengthen cross-border intelligence cooperation and share actionable cyber threat information promptly.
“Nigeria recognises that no institution, country or sector can defeat terrorism alone,” he said.
The NSA added that Nigeria was working with the African Union Counter-Terrorism Centre to secure accreditation for the NCTC as a regional centre of excellence for counterterrorism in West Africa and the Sahel.
He said the initiative followed President Bola Tinubu’s declaration at the High-Level Africa Counterterrorism Summit in April 2024.
Mr Lalalli said the conference would train participants in cyber threat intelligence, open-source intelligence, digital forensics and blockchain analysis to help them track online recruitment networks, preserve digital evidence and trace cryptocurrency transactions.
He said the skills needed to be integrated to strengthen investigations and prosecutions.
The AU official also urged stronger collaboration with social media companies, telecommunications operators and financial service providers, noting that terrorist groups often exploit privately owned infrastructure.
“You leave as this continent’s first cohort of trainers in this domain. You will leave here not just carrying home a certificate, but a responsibility. The Centre will stand behind you. But the multiplier is you,” he said.

title: Behind the scenes: Kyiv Independent's September digest
body:
Welcome to the Kyiv Independent's monthly digest, where we share company updates, milestones, and the stories behind our work.
In September, we gave our travel series a home of its own, launched a new way to reach readers, saw our community's support translate into practical help for journalists on the front line, and met our community at events in Brazil and the Netherlands.
On Sep. 11, the Kyiv Independent War Crimes Investigation Unit presented its latest investigative documentary, Last Seen in Crimea , which investigates a system of secret prisons in Russian-occupied Crimea where Ukrainian civilians have been held without contact with the outside world, often without formal charges, and subjected to torture and other forms of abuse.
Olesia Bida , the film author, shared that the main goal of the investigation was to identify those, who are directly responsible for these unlawful detentions. “Systems like this do not operate on their own — they depend on those who run them and those who carry out their orders,” she says.
The documentary is available to watch on the Kyiv Independent Youtube channel .
Our travel series, Dare to Ukraine , now has its own YouTube channel . The series explores Ukraine beyond the headlines, from its culture and history to its landscapes and, above all, its people. All 11 episodes from both seasons are now available in one place. As our deputy chief editor, Toma Istomina , put it, the series "captures the heart and soul of Ukraine." We hope the new channel will help even more people discover it.
We've also launched a WhatsApp channel , giving readers another way to follow our work. It brings our field reports, investigations , analysis , and long-form stories straight to your phone, alongside a weekly recap of the most important developments in Ukraine.
We also have an update on a project made possible by our community . In May, ahead of World Press Freedom Day, we launched our No News is Bad News collection to help protect journalists reporting near the front line. Through sales of the collection, plus additional donations, our community raised more than $24,000 .
The funds enabled the Institute of Mass Information to purchase 26 Vydun 7.5 FPV drone detectors for independent regional journalists working near the front line, exceeding our original goal of funding 20 detectors. The Institute had been seeking funding for the equipment for months, as many potential donors were unable to support purchases of equipment suitable for military use. The detectors provide early warnings of approaching drones, giving journalists crucial time to seek cover.
Our editor-in-chief, Olga Rudenko , spent part of September meeting audiences and fellow journalists abroad.
First, she traveled to São Paulo for the Festival piauí de Jornalismo , held under the theme "In the eye of the hurricane: editors-in-chief in times of turmoil." Joining newsroom leaders from eight countries, Olga spoke about what it takes to lead an independent newsroom in a country under attack.
Later in the month, she traveled to Deventer to speak at the Nederlands Journalistiek Festival . In a session titled "The Kyiv Independent: building independent journalism in wartime," she joined Wendelmoet Boersema, the editor-in-chief of Dutch newspaper Trouw and a former correspondent in the post-Soviet countries.
Their conversation explored the challenges of journalism under fire, the importance of holding those in power to account, and why independent reporting is particularly vital when a country is fighting for its future.
In the meantime, Francis Farrell and Olena Zashko travelled to Bucharest, Romania for a screening of Can You Hear Me? The Invisible Battles of Ukrainian Military Medics , the Kyiv Independent documentary co-authored by them. The film follows a group of Ukrainian military medics as they travel from the front-line in Ukraine to the quiet forests of Sweden, for a short mental health retreat.
September also brought opportunities to share our journalists' experiences and perspectives with international audiences.
Our deputy chief editor, Toma Istomina , spoke to Canadian Affairs about daily life in Kyiv under the threat of Russian aerial attacks. The city is now under round-the-clock air-raid alerts, forcing residents to weigh the risks of carrying on with their lives against the need to seek shelter. Toma also shared her mother's experience of receiving a cancer diagnosis and undergoing treatment during the war, explaining how interrupted sleep and the constant stress of attacks make recovery even harder.
Olga's visit to Brazil also drew interest from local media. In an interview with Marie Claire Brasil , she discussed leading an independent newsroom in wartime. She also spoke to Poder360 about the debate over holding elections in Ukraine during wartime.
For a deeper look at the issue, you can also watch Olga Rudenko and our deputy chief editor, Oleksiy Sorokin, discuss wartime elections on the Kyiv Independent's YouTube channel .
Meanwhile, Helsingin Sanomat , Finland's largest daily newspaper, featured Kyiv in a story exploring how younger Ukrainians view President Volodymyr Zelensky. Its reporters traveled to the Ukrainian capital to hear their perspectives firsthand.
September also brought us two awards that recognized not only our journalism, but also the work that makes it possible to keep that journalism free to read.
Our chief operating officer, Zakhar Protsiuk , was named among INMA's 2026 30 Under 30 honorees . The International News Media Association's awards recognize young professionals making an impact on the news industry. INMA highlighted Zakhar's role in growing the Kyiv Independent's membership from 6,000 to more than 35,000 members, with reader revenue now covering more than 70% of our budget.
We also received the 2026 Online Journalism Award for Innovation in Revenue Strategy from the Online News Association, in the Medium Newsroom category. This marks our second consecutive win in the category. The judges praised our "authentic and transparent membership model" and its central principle: keeping independent journalism freely accessible during wartime.
Neither milestone would have been possible without the people who choose to support us. Consider joining our community of members today .

title: AI won’t decide outcome of 2027 general election – INEC Chairman
body:
The Chairman of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), Joash Amupitan, has said Artificial Intelligence (AI) must not be allowed to determine the outcome of Nigeria’s 2027 general election.
Mr Amupitan said this on Wednesday in Abuja while delivering a keynote address at the AI and Democracy Forum 2026, organised by Yiaga Africa in partnership with INEC, Microsoft, TikTok, the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID), Dataphyte, the MacArthur Foundation, the International Foundation for Electoral Systems (IFES), the German Agency for International Cooperation (GIZ) and other partners.
The two-day forum, themed “Safeguarding the 2027 General Elections in the Age of Artificial Intelligence,” brought together representatives of electoral commissions from Senegal, Kenya, Gambia, Liberia, Sierra Leone and Togo, as well as security agencies, civil society organisations, the media, technology companies and students.
Mr Amupitan said the forum was aimed at moving discussions around artificial intelligence beyond identifying risks to developing practical responses ahead of the 2027 elections.
“Will algorithms decide the 2027 votes?” he asked.
“I consider our gathering here today not merely as an academic exercise or a routine policy consultation. This is a strategic imperative.”
He answered the question himself, saying the choice of who leads Nigeria must remain with the electorate.
“No, algorithms will not and must never decide the 2027 vote.
“2027 votes must be decided by the sovereign people of Nigeria,” he said.
According to him, AI would nevertheless have a significant influence on the information environment in which voters make decisions and on the administration and security of elections.
“AI will undeniably shape the information environment in which citizens form their choices, influence the speed and security of electoral logistics, and alter the tactics of both democratic actors and anti-democratic actors,” he said.
He urged INEC and its partners to ensure that AI was deployed to strengthen the electoral process rather than undermine it.
“Our task, therefore, at this forum and within the commission, is to ensure that AI remains a servant of democracy, not its master,” he said.
Mr Amupitan said the scale of Nigeria’s electoral process made the use of technology increasingly necessary.
He said INEC was preparing to manage more than 100 million registered voters across 176,846 polling units in 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory.
The presidential and National Assembly elections are scheduled for 16 January 2027, while the governorship and state Houses of Assembly elections are scheduled for 6 February.
The chairman said INEC would have to deploy personnel and sensitive materials to difficult terrains across 774 local government areas, including remote and riverine communities and areas affected by insecurity.
He cited Kabi Ward in Kuje Area Council of the FCT as an example of the logistical difficulties faced by the commission.
According to him, reaching the area could take about three hours and there was limited network coverage.
Mr Amupitan said AI could help the commission overcome some of these challenges through predictive modelling, geospatial analysis and dynamic routing.
“Machine learning algorithms can analyse historical traffic patterns, weather forecasts, road conditions and security incidents to generate optimal deployment routes for logistic vehicles across the terrains,” he said.
He added that AI-powered systems could also help INEC predict demand for non-sensitive materials, monitor warehouse stock and identify supply-chain bottlenecks before they affect election-day operations.
Mr Amupitan said INEC had tested some of these systems during elections conducted since he assumed office, adding that there had been improvements in the early deployment of election materials and commencement of voting.
The INEC chairman also listed several areas where the commission had incorporated technology into the electoral process.
He said the commission had digitised its candidate nomination process through the INEC Candidate Nomination Portal, which he said had processed more than 15,000 nominations from 22 political parties ahead of the 2027 elections.
He also said INEC had introduced online voter registration, allowing Nigerians to begin the registration process remotely using digital devices.
Mr Amupitan said the commission had also experimented with downloadable voter cards, including during the Osun governorship election, for voters whose cards had been lost or damaged and who were unable to receive replacements before the election.
He said AI could also assist with detecting anomalies in election results.
According to INEC boss, algorithms could identify mathematical inconsistencies, unusual patterns and image-quality problems in uploaded polling-unit results before they were accepted into INEC’s results management system.
He said this would complement, rather than replace, human oversight and the statutory processes for declaring election results.
Mr Amupitan also said AI was being used to improve the voters’ register by helping the commission identify duplicate biometric records.
“With over 13 million records in our national register of voters, AI-enhanced automated biometric identification systems drastically accelerate deduplication processes, detecting facial and fingerprint duplicates with unprecedented speed and accuracy,” he said.
The chairman disclosed that INEC had established an AI unit within its Information and Communication Technology department.
He said the commission was also finalising a governance framework for the use of artificial AI in elections, with support from IFES and other partners.
He said the framework would be guided by principles including integrity, transparency, human intervention and public auditing.
Mr Amupitan warned that the same technology that could strengthen elections could also be exploited to attack electoral systems and manipulate public information.
He said INEC’s digital infrastructure, including its results management and candidate nomination platforms, could become targets for malicious cyber actors.
“Every day we check, working with experts in this area, to detect faults and threats to our systems,” he said.
He added that AI-powered cyber-security systems could help detect denial-of-service attacks, brute-force attacks and other threats to electoral infrastructure.
The Executive Director of Yiaga Africa, Samson Itodo, said rebuilding public confidence would be one of the major challenges ahead of the 2027 elections.
Mr Itodo said Nigerians’ distrust of the electoral process remained high, partly because of the role technology played in the 2023 election.
“Just last week, Yiaga Africa issued a national voting intention survey report, where it is obvious that Nigerians doubt the credibility of the process, and that their votes will not count in 2027,” he said.
The survey was designed to assess voter interest and participation and identify factors that could encourage or discourage Nigerians from taking part in the elections.
He said the deployment of technology alone would not guarantee credible elections, stressing that the integrity of those managing the systems was equally important.
“It is one thing to deploy technology; it is another thing for the personal integrity of those managing those technologies to deliver,” he said.
Mr Itodo also raised concerns about the growing number of AI-powered platforms being developed to aggregate election results ahead of the 2027 elections.
He said only INEC had the legal authority to declare election results and winners, although other organisations could independently aggregate results for monitoring and oversight.
“We encourage stakeholders to continue to use different tools and platforms to keep an eye on the results process,” he said.
He urged organisations deploying AI for results aggregation to ensure that their systems were accurate, transparent and auditable.
“For us, as an organisation, we’re very open and transparent about the methodologies that we use,” he said.
Mr Itodo said organisations using AI in elections should be guided by the principles of integrity, transparency and auditability to prevent the technology from becoming a source of political instability.
The forum is expected to develop practical recommendations for governing the use of AI in Nigeria’s electoral process ahead of the 2027 general elections.

title: Toronto police to give update on 2 Canadian soldiers facing 49 charges
body:
Three Canadian Armed Forces members are among seven people facing 82 charges after a kidnapping call snowballed into a larger probe, Toronto police say.
Police Chief Myron Demkiw and Supt. Joe Matthews said Wednesday military ammunition was recovered during the investigation, which began on July 25 when officers were called to a reported abduction near Finch and Bayview avenues.
The victim in that case was targeted as he approached his vehicle and was abducted at gunpoint, Demkiw alleged. The victim was handcuffed and assaulted while the suspects allegedly tried to access his cryptocurrency assets, he added.
Matthews said the victim was released and was threatened not to call police. Within 24 hours, two suspects were arrested.
The investigation that unfolded led to further arrests in August and September, and the discovery that three of the seven people arrested are members of the military.
“Their training that they had received through the military is quite concerning, not only to the victims of this type of violence but also to our officers who may encounter them,” Matthews said.
“These are highly trained individuals with access to firearms and that creates a lot of concern for not only our community but our officers.”
The Department of National Defence (DND) announced last week that Bombardiers Sachintha Fernando and James Moreau were arrested . Matthews identified Jack Miley, 24, as being a member of the military Wednesday. He did not share details about his role in the army.
Fernando, 22, and Moreau, 29, were arrested on Aug. 11 and face a total of 49 charges, including kidnapping for ransom, forcible confinement and use of a firearm during the commission of an indictable offence.
Miley has been charged with multiple offences, including kidnapping for ransom with a firearm, unauthorized possession of a firearm in a motor vehicle and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence.
All three men are members of the 7th Toronto Regiment, according to the DND.
Moreau enrolled in the Canadian Army as a reservist in March 2018 and Fernando enrolled in the Canadian Army as a reservist in January 2020, the spokesperson said.
Fernando has not been deployed on a CAF operation, whereas Moreau served on Operation LASER in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Miley, a master bombardier, enrolled in the Canadian Army as a reservist and deployed on Operation REASSURANCE in 2025, a DND spokesperson told Global News on Wednesday.
All three soldiers were removed from military duties after their arrests, and their access to military equipment, facilities and bases was restricted, the DND spokesperson said.
They remain members of the military pending the outcome of an administrative review, a formal process used to assess matters that may affect a member’s continued service while providing procedural fairness.
The DND said military police are cooperating with the Toronto police investigation as well as undertaking its own administrative review.
“We are actively working to strengthen verification and oversight of ammunition holdings, including inventory validation and stock-count requirements, to improve the accuracy and reliability of our records. Beginning this fall, we are also taking steps to modernize ammunition management, to improve accuracy, traceability, and accountability across the CAF,” the spokesperson said.
Shortly after police made their first arrests, investigators identified additional suspects and began executing search warrants across the Greater Toronto Area, Matthews said.
By Sept. 24, seven people were arrested and 82 charges were laid.
A shotgun, two 9 mm firearms with 3D printed receivers, a third 9 mm firearm that was not safely stored, two silencers, cell phones, portable radios, a money counter, firearm storage boxes, methamphetamine and cocaine were some of the items seized, Matthews said.
Police also recovered roughly 2,500 rounds of assorted ammunition that Matthews said belonged to the military.
“What began as an abduction investigation became a firearms investigation, a drug investigation and ultimately a much broader criminal investigation,” he said.
“Our responsibility is to adapt alongside those threats. Whether offenders use intimidation, firearms violence or technology to commit these crimes, our investigators will continue to pursue them and hold them accountable.”
Toronto residents Raheem Bishop-Jackson, 24, Saiefeddine Adem, 22, Christian Darbandi, 39, and Suhaib Alekozai, 39, are also facing charges.
Police aren’t seeking additional suspects, but the investigation remains ongoing, Matthews said.
Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

title: 2027: Build your own results machinery or don’t contest – Agbakoba tells parties
body: Senior Advocate of Nigeria, Dr. Olisa Agbakoba, has told political parties that those unable to collect and preserve their own election results have no business on the ballot, warning that they cannot lean on the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to prove their case in court. Speaking on ARISE NEWS on Wednesday, Agbakoba said parties that want to challenge INEC’s declarations in 2027 must be ready to present authenticated results of their own, gathered through agents deployed across polling units. “If you’re not ready to monitor the elections right across Nigeria, don’t go on the ballot. Or don’t complain,” he said. He criticised the common practice of parties heading to court to ask judges to compel INEC to release results from its Result Viewing Portal (IReV), describing it as “lazy.” In his view, party agents already sign the polling unit result sheets (Form EC8A) and should hold those records themselves. Agbakoba explained that INEC is presumed to have acted regularly in official matters, a presumption parties can only overcome with credible evidence. A party that shows up in court with its own verified records, he said, puts the court in a position to see “something else that is coming from the same source,” which can rebut that presumption. A party without such records, he added, has “no reason to question” it. The senior lawyer noted that this approach has never been tested in earlier presidential election petitions, but said he hopes it will change in 2027. He predicted that parties would use AI tools to pull results from IReV and produce faster tallies, and that such parallel compilations could pressure INEC to be more accurate because it would know it was being watched. On the right to publish results, Agbakoba cited the 1984 case of NUJ v. FEDECO (INEC’s predecessor), saying it affirmed that anyone may publish results already in the public domain. INEC’s exclusive power, he said, is only to declare a winner. He added that the Electoral Act itself penalises publishing fake results, which implies that publishing genuine ones is allowed. For media houses using AI to collate and project outcomes, he set one condition: results must come from IReV and be clearly attributed to it. The post 2027: Build your own results machinery or don’t contest – Agbakoba tells parties appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: IAI says Lockheed Martin supplier awards recognize its F-35 and F-16 production performance
body: The F-35 wings program received the Ahead of Ready Award. IAI’s F-16 wings, vertical fins and conformal fuel tank programs received the Mission Focused Award. Lockheed Martin Aeronautics selects a limited number of award recipients each year from more than 1,400 active suppliers worldwide. Senior company representatives presented the awards to IAI leadership at a ceremony held at IAI. IAI has participated in the F-35 program since 2014 and delivered its 350th wing to Lockheed Martin in February 2026. It has supplied major F-16 structures for more than 30 years, including the conformal fuel tank jointly developed by the two companies. “The partnership between IAI and Lockheed Martin spans nearly four decades and is built on mutual trust, technological cooperation and a shared commitment to supporting critical aerospace and defense programs,” said Guy Bar Lev, IAI’s president and chief executive. “Over the years, our companies have worked together to meet evolving operational needs and deliver advanced capabilities to customers worldwide.” “We look forward to continuing to strengthen this partnership in the years ahead,” Bar Lev said. The relationship dates to the late 1980s and covers aerostructures development and production. “Trust is the foundation of our partnership with Lockheed Martin,” said Yaacov Berkovitz, executive vice president and general manager of IAI’s Aviation Group. “For years, our teams have worked side by side, delivering quality, value, and on-time performance with consistency and reliability.” “This shared commitment to excellence enables us to support critical programs, meet demanding requirements, and help ensure success for Lockheed Martin and its customers around the world,” Berkovitz said. Kyle Franklin, vice president of Global Supply Chain at Lockheed Martin Aeronautics, described receiving both awards as “an outstanding achievement by IAI.” The supplier awards assess quality, delivery, operational performance and customer support. IAI’s wider aerostructures business manufactures and assembles complex composite and metallic structures for military and commercial aircraft programs.

title: Petition to cut mobilization age to 55 gets 25,000 votes
body:
A petition on the Cabinet of Ministers website calling for the upper age limit for mobilization to be lowered to 55 has gathered the number of votes needed for consideration, according to the government's petition platform.
The petition was submitted on July 27 and had collected the required 25,000 votes by October 14.
"Practical experience of carrying out combat and special tasks shows the need to review the rule and lower the age limit to 55," the petition says.
Its author believes that men aged 55-60 in most cases have persistent age-related health changes and chronic diseases, which significantly reduce their physical endurance in extremely difficult field and combat conditions.
She also believes that staffing units with personnel according to their physical capabilities would improve the overall combat readiness and mobility of military units.
In addition, she said, citizens in this age group are highly qualified specialists whose work in the civilian sector and at critical infrastructure enterprises provides significant support to the economy.
The author proposes drafting and submitting to the Verkhovna Rada a bill amending the laws 'On Military Duty and Military Service' and 'On Mobilization Preparation and Mobilization' to lower the upper age limit for military service under martial law from 60 to 55 for privates, sergeants, petty officers and officers. It would also establish the right of servicemen who reach 55 under martial law to leave military service at their own request.
General mobilization is in effect in Ukraine, covering men liable for military service aged 25-60.
Earlier petitions on the Cabinet website calling to allow demobilization of servicemen over 55 who have served more than three years, to lower the upper draft age from 60 to 58 and to demobilize men over 55 who have earned the right to a civilian pension for work in hazardous conditions did not gather the votes needed for consideration.

title: Russian drone debris damages artwork of famous contemporary artist at museum in northwestern Ukraine
body:
Debris from a Russian drone damaged artwork by one of Ukraine's most prolific contemporary artists at the Korsak Art Museum in Lutsk, a northwestern Ukrainian city, the museum staff reported on Oct. 14.
Petro Antyp's polyptych "Cosmogony," a Ukrainian interpretation of the world's origin, spans thousands of square meters. The museum's founder, Viktor Korsak, described the damage inflicted upon the panel "The Future" as a "symbolic and at the same time terrifying coincidence."
The museum was damaged in a fire caused by a Russian drone attack against Lutsk on Oct. 13, the staff said. "Now the war itself has intervened in a work about the future. And I wonder: perhaps we should not fully restore the damaged section? Perhaps these traces of war should remain as a historical artifact and a warning to future generations? But the most important thing is that we continue to create!" Korsak wrote. Established in 2018, the Korsak Museum is the country's largest museum of contemporary Ukrainian art. The museum has received international recognition for its curatorial work, including a Special Commendation at the 2025 European Museum of the Year Awards. Although the Oct. 13 attack damaged part of the collection, Roman Korsak, Viktor's son and the museum's owner, told the Kyiv Independent that the museum continues to operate. "We know the collection remains at risk. But we believe the greater loss would be to hide art away from people and close our doors at such a difficult time," Korsak said. Ukraine's cultural heritage has long been a target of Russian aggression. The Culture Ministry reported that, as of September 2026, Russia has damaged or destroyed at least 2,161 cultural heritage sites and 2,665 cultural institutions since the start of the full-scale war.
Tens of thousands of artworks are also estimated to have been looted by Russia from Ukraine's museums in the occupied territories and active combat zones.
Russia attacked Ukraine's northwest again on Oct. 14, exacting a deadly toll : at least six people were killed and 20 injured in Volyn Oblast, including Lutsk, and in neighboring Rivne Oblast.

title: Netanyahu on October 7: Nobody told Bush to 'go home' after September 11 attacks
body: Intelligence failures surrounding the October 7 massacre should not automatically lead to a premier's dismissal, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a radio interview with Army Radio on Wednesday, arguing that "nobody told [former US president George W.] Bush to go home after" the September 11 attacks.Netanyahu compared Israel's intelligence failures to those preceding the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor and the September 11 attacks on the World Trade Center in New York, arguing that those disasters had not automatically led to the removal of the countries' political leaders."There was blindness here," he admitted, "And I can tell you: There was also blindness at Pearl Harbor, when the Japanese bombed the United States. Yes, there was blindness. There was also blindness on September 11, at the Twin Towers. Nobody said: Okay, you have to go home. They didn't say that to Roosevelt; they didn't say that to President Bush."Netanyahu defended his proposal to establish a "national" inquiry committee with equal representation for coalition and opposition members.He argued that a government-appointed commission would lack public trust among opposition voters, while a state commission appointed through the existing judicial framework would be rejected by many of his own supporters. He also suggested modeling the investigation on the bipartisan US commission established after September 11.Additionally, the prime minister doubled down on the position that had he been awakened and informed of the reported unusual Hamas activity on the night before October 7,  he would have ordered military preparations and canceled the Nova music festival.The prime minister insisted that Israel's security establishment had repeatedly assessed that Hamas was deterred and had not expected an imminent major attack from Gaza."The answer is no," he said when asked whether he had recognized the warning signs before the attack.Netanyahu warns Iran against attacking Israel ahead of electionHe also warned Iran that any attempt to attack Israel would trigger an unprecedented response."If Iran makes that mistake, [unclear word], and tries to attack us, it will encounter a response it cannot even imagine," Netanyahu said, responding to questions about possible Iranian military action ahead of Israel's October 27 election and the US midterm elections."We are prepared for all those scenarios. I hope we won't have to resort to them, but I can say one thing: Israel will not allow - I will not allow - Iran to have nuclear weapons. As long as I am prime minister, Iran will not have nuclear weapons."He said Israel had completed approximately 60% of its security objectives against the Iranian axis and suggested further operations could be necessary."Just a year ago, I'm saying this as emphatically as I possibly can, Iran was poised to destroy us. We removed a threat to the State of Israel. That is the most important thing," he said.Asked whether Israel was coordinating with Saudi Arabia over recent Houthi attacks, Netanyahu declined to discuss specific countries or security cooperation.He nevertheless claimed Israel's military successes had created opportunities for new regional alliances, saying countries both inside and outside the Middle East were increasingly interested in cooperation.Netanyahu also pointed to what he described as an International Monetary Fund projection of 4.5% economic growth for Israel, arguing that the economy's performance demonstrated the success of his security and economic policies.Netanyahu says election is 'extremely close,' pushes against smaller partiesThe prime minister said he hoped the election would proceed as scheduled but warned that Israel's enemies could attempt attacks or rocket fire to create an impression of Israeli vulnerability.Netanyahu also described the contest as extremely close."I'm worried because this election, right now, is tied," he said, adding that he had begun traveling across the country to encourage Likud supporters to vote.Discussing the government he hopes to establish after the election, Netanyahu said his first preference was a right-wing coalition consisting of his existing political partners.However, he did not completely rule out cooperation with opposition parties, including those associated with former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot.Netanyahu said any potential coalition partner would have to accept his opposition to Palestinian statehood and support his government's security policies."If you accept our policies, of course we will talk with them," he said, while emphasizing that he intended to form a right-wing government first.He criticized Eisenkot's positions during the war in Gaza, accusing him of supporting a premature end to military operations and withdrawal before Israel had achieved its objectives."I'm telling you that after October 7, I had to struggle, struggle against Gadi, who wanted to stop the war and withdraw. He said: We'll come back after two years and see."Netanyahu: Defense Ministry will remain in Likud's handsNetanyahu also said Likud would keep the Defense Minister portfolio in a future government, while cautioning against distributing ministerial positions before the election results were known.His statement came as National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir continued his campaign to secure the portfolio for himself in a future Netanyahu-led government. Ben-Gvir has repeatedly affirmed he would demand the position of defense minister as a condition for joining Netanyahu's coalition.The prime minister repeatedly warned right-wing voters against supporting smaller parties that might fail to enter the Knesset, arguing that such votes could undermine the chances of forming another government under his leadership.He said he planned campaign stops in Kiryat Malachi, Kiryat Gat, Beersheba and Beit Shemesh on Wednesday to encourage turnout.Netanyahu also defended his government's settlement policies, claiming it had established or legalized 104 communities and more than 100 farms. He pledged to continue pursuing security measures and settlement construction while criticizing the High Court of Justice's intervention in government decisions.

title: Machar links trial to failed Tumaini talks, alleges political plot
body: South Sudan’s former First Vice President Riek Machar on Wednesday linked his ongoing trial in Juba to a political dispute between the ruling SPLM and the opposition SPLM-IO, alleging that the court proceedings are politically motivated. Machar, the fifth accused in the case, resumed his defence testimony during the court’s 121st session, questioning why he had been designated accused number five rather than accused number one. “I do agree that this trial is political trial between SPLM-IG and SPLM-IO,” Machar said, referring to the faction aligned with President Salva Kiir and the opposition faction he leads. He said he intends to present video footage that he believes would support his claim that the proceedings are politically motivated. Accused designation Machar argued that his designation as accused number five contradicts official state documents, including a statement by the former minister of justice and constitutional affairs and a warrant establishing the special court issued by the chief justice. “My defence team has made a number of attempts throughout the proceedings of this court to uncover the reason why I am not designated as accused number one. However, no satisfactory explanation has been given as to why I am designated as accused number five in lieu of number 1,” Machar told the panel of judges. He said he had expected the list of the eight accused persons to follow the order in which their names appeared in the justice ministry’s statement and the warrant establishing the court. “Both the minister and the chief justice appropriately listed my name as the first accused,” he said, adding that the court had been established under Article 127(1)(b) of the Constitution of South Sudan, as amended. Machar maintained that the constitutional provisions governing the establishment of the special court should take precedence over police records in determining the order of the accused. “In spite of this, the Honorable Court has designated me as accused number five. I view this as a political plan to deny me my right to be tried in accordance with the appropriate constitutional provisions as the First Vice President of the Republic, and instead force me to be tried in the shadow of my junior colleagues in the SPLM-IO,” he said. 2018 Peace agreement Machar linked the case to the collapse of peace initiatives and subsequent military confrontations between the SSPDF and the SPLM-IO. He said the failure of the December 2024 Nairobi peace talks over the proposed Tumaini Peace Initiative was followed by attacks on SPLM-IO positions in Western Equatoria and Western Bahr el Ghazal states in January and February 2025, before the Nasir incident on March 3 and 4 that year. “I will first expose how this political plan was developed following the failed attempt by the SPLM-IG to replace the R-ARCSS with the Tumaini Consensus during the December 2024 Nairobi peace talks,” Machar said. He alleged that the failure of the Nairobi talks led the transitional government and the ruling SPLM to effectively abandon implementation of the Revitalised Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in South Sudan (R-ARCSS) and launch attacks against SPLM-IO forces. Machar said he would discuss the alleged military campaigns against the SPLM-IO in greater detail later in his testimony. Constitutional changes Machar also said that provisions of the R-ARCSS, the transitional constitution and the electoral law had been amended unilaterally during his arrest, detention and ongoing trial. He further said that the Revitalised Transitional Government of National Unity (RTGoNU) had been dissolved on Sept. 22, 2026, and replaced by a caretaker government tasked with preparing for elections scheduled for Dec. 22, 2026. According to Machar, the elections had been declared on June 22, 2026, without adequate preparation or consultation with key political parties that are signatories to the 2018 peace agreement. He described the changes and election plans as unconstitutional and said they had plunged the country into political and security crises. “These unilateral and unconstitutional amendments and declarations of general elections have plunged the country into uncalled-for and unwanted constitutional and security crises,” he said. Machar said he would address the constitutional provisions and legal procedures he believes should have been followed in his trial later in his testimony. Video evidence Machar also asked the court to allow him to display video footage containing public statements by senior government officials made before and after his arrest during the state burial and funeral rites of the late General David Majur Dak. He said the recordings would support his argument that government officials had publicly prejudged the case against him and other SPLM-IO leaders before the special court was established. In his statement, Machar described the proceedings as a politically motivated trial and said the footage would help demonstrate how the political plan had developed. The prosecution objected to the defence request to display the video exhibits. The defence characterised the prosecution’s objections as unfounded, while the prosecution disputed the defence’s position. Court proceedings The proceedings also featured a disagreement between the defence and prosecution over the conduct of Machar’s examination. Lead defence lawyer Geri Raymond Legge argued that Machar should be allowed to present his statement without interruption, citing provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure Act of 2008. The prosecution, represented by Deny Achuil Adija, disputed aspects of the defence’s interpretation of the proceedings. Machar said he would use his testimony to address the constitutional and legal issues surrounding the trial, as well as the political and military developments he believes led to his arrest and prosecution. The court adjourned the proceedings until Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. The panel of judges is expected to rule on Machar’s request to display the video exhibits, while Machar is expected to continue presenting his oral defence testimony. The post Machar links trial to failed Tumaini talks, alleges political plot appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Public money belongs to the people, not government officials – Ato Forson
body: Finance Minister Dr. Cassiel Ato Forson has called on public officials to account for every cedi entrusted to them and build systems that make the recovery of public money an exception rather than an annual ritual. He was speaking at an engagement on the Auditor-General’s Report attended by regional ministers and metropolitan, municipal and district chief executives. Dr. Forson stressed that government officials are custodians of the nation’s resources, not their owners, and must manage those resources with a clear sense of responsibility to citizens. “Public money does not belong to government officials, we are only the custodians of those resources,” he said. “Those resources belong to the people of Ghana: Our constituents, our citizens!” He urged officials to reclaim every recoverable cedi, underscoring their obligation to account for the public funds placed in their care. “So let us recover every cedi, that is recoverable! Let us account for every cedi that is entrusted to us as public officials,” he stated. The Finance Minister, however, made clear that accountability must go beyond recovering money. He called for stronger systems to protect public resources, rather than allowing recovery to become a recurring feature of public financial management. “But above all, let us build systems where recovery becomes the exception, not an annual ritual,” he said.

title: UK Prosecutor Tells Jury Russell Brand A ‘Sexual Predator’
body: Comedian Russell Brand was a “sexual predator” who was “ruthless, calculated and manipulative” when targeting women for sex, a British prosecutor told a UK jury Wednesday at the start of his rape and sexual assault trial. The one-time left-wing personality, 51, who shot to fame as a television and radio presenter, faces seven sexual offence charges involving six women. He denies all the alleged offences. Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones said the alleged offences took place between 1999 and 2009, when Brand’s career was beginning to flourish. Addressing the jury, she gave graphic details of accusations by women, saying the youngest was 21 at the time of the alleged offences. They came forward to police after seeing media coverage about Brand in 2023 and after he was initially charged in 2025, the court heard. Brand was “not deterred” when some of the women said no, she said, adding his desire for sexual contact was “indiscriminate and voracious”. He used charm and comic talents when he wanted something but would then be “demanding and entitled… childlike in his expectation that his every desire should be met,” Karmy-Jones told the jury of eight men and four women. Bragging “He was ruthless, calculated and manipulative, and the prosecution say — a sexual predator,” she added. The identities of the women will not be revealed during the trial. Brand, dressed in a dark suit, black-and-white striped shirt and long white tie, arrived for the start of the case at London’s Southwark Crown Court in a black Mercedes-Benz van accompanied by his wife Laura. In each woman’s case, Brand responded to police with a prepared statement saying he did not remember the women and any sexual activity was consensual. Karmy-Jones said Brand’s acquaintances recalled him bragging that he wanted to “bed 5,000 women in his lifetime”, adding, “you have to tell them what they need to hear”. It was a clear indication of “how manipulative the defendant could be,” she said. Brand has in recent years reinvented himself as a conservative and faith-based guru for millions of social media followers. He has pleaded not guilty to all seven of the charges — three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one charge of indecent assault. The first woman met Brand when he was performing at a Labour Party conference in Bournemouth in southern England in 1999. She invited him to her hotel room where he pushed her onto the bed before raping her without using a condom, the prosecutor said. One woman said Brand in 2001 tried to drag her into a toilet cubicle at MTV’s office, but she resisted. Another woman met Brand at a London bar in 2004 and said he grabbed her breasts and pulled her into a toilet cubicle, orally raping her, after telling her not to be a “spoilsport”. Yet another woman said Brand visited the radio station where she worked in 2004 or 2005, and kissed her “very aggressively” then grabbed her breasts and bottom. One woman, who was 21 at the time, said she had consensual oral and then vaginal sex with Brand in 2009 at his house but he then forced her into anal sex without her consent “with full force” without a condom, the prosecutor said. Massage In the final charge, a woman employed by Channel 4 television said she was working with Brand in a record studio in 2009. Members of his production team told her she must give him a massage and he then pressed his face into her groin. The trial at London’s Southwark Crown Court should last around six weeks but could stretch into December. The trial is attracting intense media scrutiny, with numerous British outlets launching dedicated podcasts and US channels reporting from outside the court. Born to working-class parents in Essex in eastern England, Brand launched a successful stand-up comedy career as a teenager. He became a household name as a television presenter on MTV, Channel 4 and the BBC, also penning newspaper columns and two autobiographies. He then made a foray into Hollywood, starring in several hit films, and was in a brief but high-profile marriage to US pop star Katy Perry. Now remarried and living in Florida with his young family, he has gained a new following as an influencer, with six million subscribers on YouTube, 10.1 million on X and 4.9 million on Instagram. The post UK Prosecutor Tells Jury Russell Brand A ‘Sexual Predator’ appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Digital Development Ministry helps Yandex find additional sites after data center attacks
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. The Digital Development Ministry helped Yandex secure additional sites to relocate key systems following attacks on its data centers, Digital Development Minister Maksut Shadayev told RBC.
"The Digital Development Ministry assisted Yandex in securing additional sites for the relocation of key systems. Despite the unprecedented attack on the data centers, the company managed to promptly transfer the operations of key systems to pre-prepared backup facilities," the minister said.
He noted that distributing infrastructure geographically helps reduce reliance on individual large facilities and preserve service availability even in the event of severe damage. The company is continuing restoration work and transferring its remaining systems to third-party sites.
Yandex's press service told RBC that the company has spent years building a distributed infrastructure and backup capacities at independent sites, without revealing details regarding their locations.
On October 11, Yandex completely halted operations at its Vladimir data center following a UAV attack. On October 9, part of the company's data center infrastructure in Kaluga was also damaged in a drone attack, leaving several modules completely out of service. A fire broke out at Yandex's data center in Sasovo, Ryazan Region, following a UAV attack, damaging part of the infrastructure.

title: Power, politics and the battle for electoral credibility: Is Ghana’s electoral commission truly independent?
body: Nothing tests the strength of a democracy quite like an election. Elections ignite hopes, heighten anxieties, expose political rivalries and sometimes deepen national divisions. Beyond determining who governs, they provide a peaceful mechanism for resolving political competition and confer legitimacy on those entrusted with public power. But what happens when the very institution responsible for safeguarding the people’s mandate becomes the subject of political suspicion? That is the uncomfortable question confronting Ghana as the controversy surrounding the appointment of two Deputy Electoral Commissioners by President John Dramani Mahama reignites debate about the independence, credibility and impartiality of the Electoral Commission (EC). Why is the New Patriotic Party (NPP) so concerned about the appointments? Is its opposition rooted in legitimate institutional concerns, partisan calculations, or a mixture of both? And, more fundamentally, what do these political battles reveal about the independence of Ghana’s electoral management body? These are questions that deserve more than partisan talking points. They demand a closer examination of the constitutional framework, the history of appointments to the Commission and the political circumstances that have shaped public perceptions of its neutrality. THE INDEPENDENCE QUESTION: WHAT DOES THE CONSTITUTION REALLY GUARANTEE? Ghana’s 1992 Constitution establishes the Electoral Commission as an independent constitutional body entrusted with responsibilities central to the country’s democratic survival. Article 45 outlines the Commission’s functions, including the compilation of the voters’ register, the conduct and supervision of public elections and referenda, and voter education in collaboration with the National Commission for Civic Education (NCCE). Article 43 provides for the composition of the Commission, while Article 46 expressly guarantees its independence by stipulating that, in the performance of its functions, the Commission shall not be subject to the direction or control of any person or authority. On paper, the constitutional safeguards are clear. The EC is expected to operate independently, free from political interference and undue influence. Yet constitutional guarantees and institutional realities are not always the same. Article 70 gives the President a central role in appointing the Chairperson, Deputy Chairpersons and other members of the Commission, acting in consultation with the Council of State. Article 195 also establishes the President’s role in public-service appointments, subject to the constitutional provisions governing the relevant offices. This arrangement raises an important institutional question: Can an electoral management body be perceived as completely independent when the President, who is also the leader of a political administration, plays a decisive role in appointing its top officials? The question is not whether presidential appointment automatically makes an Electoral Commissioner partisan. It does not. Rather, the issue is whether the appointment process provides sufficient safeguards to inspire confidence across the political spectrum. The absence of a parliamentary confirmation process for these appointments, for instance, limits the extent to which nominees are subjected to public scrutiny through a formal legislative vetting process. Questions also arise about the Commission’s financial autonomy, administrative arrangements and the procedures governing appointments within the institution. CHARLOTTE OSEI’S EXIT: THE CONTROVERSY THAT REFUSES TO DISAPPEAR To understand the current debate, Ghana must revisit one of the most contentious episodes in the recent history of its Electoral Commission: the removal of Charlotte Osei and her two deputies in 2018. Appointed in June 2015 under President John Dramani Mahama, Osei became the first woman to serve as Chairperson of Ghana’s Electoral Commission. Her tenure, however, was marked by tensions and controversy that culminated in her removal in June 2018 under President Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo. The removals followed an investigation initiated through a committee constituted under the authority of the then Chief Justice, Sophia Akuffo, after allegations of misconduct were raised against the Commission’s leadership. The officials were removed following the constitutionally prescribed process. Nevertheless, the episode left a lasting political and institutional legacy. For critics of the process, the circumstances surrounding the removal intensified concerns about the vulnerability of the Commission’s leadership to political developments at the highest levels of government. For others, the constitutional procedure demonstrated that even senior electoral officials were not beyond accountability. The controversy became even more politically charged because the NPP, then in government, had previously been a vocal critic of Osei’s leadership while in opposition and profess her removal if they won the 2016 election. That history inevitably raises a difficult question: Did the change in the Commission’s leadership strengthen public confidence in its independence, or did it deepen suspicions that the institution’s leadership could become entangled in partisan power struggles? The answer cannot be established by political rhetoric alone. It requires evidence, institutional analysis and a careful assessment of the Commission’s conduct before, during and after elections. FROM ONE LEADERSHIP TO ANOTHER: HAS THE TRUST DEFICIT BEEN RESOLVED? Following the 2018 removals, President Akufo-Addo nominated Jean Adukwei Mensa as Electoral Commission Chairperson, alongside Samuel Tettey and Eric Bossman as Deputy Commissioners, and Adwoa Asuama Abrefa as another member. The new leadership was sworn into office on 1 August 2018. The appointments marked a new chapter in the Commission’s history, but they did not end the broader debate about presidential influence over electoral administration. The real test of an Electoral Commission is not simply the political identity of the appointing authority or the public reputation of its appointees. It is whether the institution consistently demonstrates impartiality, transparency, procedural fairness and accountability. An electoral management body may act lawfully and still struggle to convince a section of the public that it is impartial. Equally, political accusations against the body do not, by themselves, establish that it has acted improperly. This distinction is crucial. In a highly competitive multiparty system such as Ghana’s, electoral decisions are routinely scrutinised through partisan lenses. An appointment that one party regards as administratively sound may be interpreted by another as politically consequential. That is precisely why the appointment process must be sufficiently transparent to withstand suspicion, scrutiny and political disagreement. THE TWO DEPUTY COMMISSIONERS: WHY THE POLITICAL TEMPERATURE? The controversy surrounding the appointment of two Deputy Electoral Commissioners by President Mahama on Monday, October 12, 2026 raises a broader question about how Ghana manages the relationship between constitutional authority and public confidence. W Why is the NPP raising concerns about the appointments of Emelia Affi Agbenyo and Joseph Kwaku Asamoah, PhD? What specific constitutional, procedural or substantive objections has the party advanced? Does it challenge the qualifications of the nominees, the appointment process, the potential implications for electoral administration, or the broader institutional arrangement? These questions must be answered against the documented statements and the actual circumstances of the appointments. The NPP’s position should not automatically be dismissed as partisan obstruction. Equally, its objections should not be accepted uncritically merely because they are presented as a defense of electoral independence. A credible analysis must apply the same standard to every political party, whether in government or opposition. If the party believes the appointments threaten the Commission’s neutrality, it must explain precisely how. If its concerns relate to the absence of adequate consultation, transparency or institutional safeguards, those arguments deserve serious public examination. But if the objections are inconsistent with the party’s previous positions on presidential appointment powers, that inconsistency also deserves scrutiny. The central issue is not simply who gets appointed. It is whether the process protects the Electoral Commission from partisan capture and gives Ghanaians compelling reasons to trust its decisions. That is a national democratic concern, not the exclusive property of any political party. BEYOND PARTISAN POLITICS: FOUR TESTS OF ELECTORAL INDEPENDENCE The independence of the EC should be assessed against clear institutional criteria rather than the changing political interests of the parties. First: Appointment and tenure. Are the procedures for appointing and removing commissioners sufficiently transparent and protected against arbitrary political influence? Do they inspire confidence among competing political parties and the wider public? Second: Financial and administrative autonomy. Does the Commission have adequate control over the resources and administrative arrangements necessary to carry out its constitutional mandate without undue external pressure? Third: Operational impartiality. Does the EC apply electoral laws, regulations and procedures consistently, irrespective of which party stands to benefit? Are its decisions explained clearly and communicated in a timely manner? Fourth: Transparency and accountability. Does the Commission provide sufficient information to enable citizens, political parties, civil society organisations and independent observers to scrutinise its decisions? Are complaints handled fairly and through credible procedures? These four tests provide a more meaningful framework for examining electoral independence than the political affiliations or perceived loyalties of individual commissioners. They also provide a basis for assessing the Commission’s performance across elections, including the conduct of the 2020 polls. Any claim that the EC favoured or disadvantaged a particular party must be supported by verifiable evidence, documented decisions and a defensible analysis of its actions. Suspicion alone cannot substitute for proof. WHY PUBLIC CONFIDENCE MATTERS The implications of this debate extend far beyond the appointment of Emelia Affi Agbenyo and Joseph Kwaku Asamoah, PhD. The Electoral Commission of Ghana as it is in other civilised democracies derive much of their authority from public confidence in their impartiality. Their decisions must be respected not because they are immune from criticism, but because the institutions making those decisions are seen to operate according to fair and predictable rules. When confidence deteriorates, even routine administrative decisions can become flashpoints for political confrontation. Voter registration, ballot administration, results collation and the declaration of winners may all attract heightened suspicion. The danger is that persistent distrust can weaken the perceived legitimacy of electoral outcomes, regardless of whether particular decisions are legally defensible. THE BIGGER QUESTION: WHO PROTECTS THE ELECTORAL COMMISSION FROM POLITICS? Ultimately, the controversy over the appointment of the two Deputy Electoral Commissioners exposes a constitutional and democratic dilemma that Ghana has yet to resolve fully. The Constitution guarantees the EC’s independence, but the process through which its leadership is appointed leaves room for continuing debate about the relationship between executive authority and electoral autonomy. The answer is not necessarily to declare every presidential appointment illegitimate. Nor is it to dismiss every objection as political mischief. Rather, Ghana must confront the institutional weaknesses and perceptions that allow electoral appointments to become recurring sources of partisan conflict. Reforms could include greater transparency in the nomination process, clearly articulated and publicly accessible qualification criteria, stronger safeguards for tenure, and a more open framework for scrutinising nominees. Any proposed reform must be carefully designed to preserve the Commission’s independence rather than transfer political influence from one institution to another. The ultimate objective should be to ensure that commissioners command confidence because of their competence, integrity and demonstrable impartiality—not merely because a particular government appointed them. CONCLUSION: A TEST FOR GHANA’S DEMOCRACY The NPP’s opposition to the two Deputy Commissioner appointments presents an opportunity to confront a question that transcends party politics: is Ghana doing enough to insulate its Electoral Commission from political influence and protect public confidence in its work? The party must substantiate its objections. The government must demonstrate that the appointment process is constitutionally sound and institutionally defensible. The Electoral Commission must continue to uphold transparency, impartiality and accountability. Above all, Ghanaians must insist that electoral institutions serve the Republic rather than the interests of the political parties that compete to govern it. Because, in the final analysis, the credibility of an election is determined not only by the ballots cast or the results declared, but also by whether citizens have compelling reasons to believe that the institution overseeing the process has acted fairly. The real battle, therefore, is bigger than two appointments. It is a battle for public trust, institutional independence and the future credibility of Ghana’s democracy.

title: Lavrov arrives in Azerbaijan to participate in CICA summit
body:
BAKU, October 14. /TASS/. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov arrived in Azerbaijan to take part in the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA).
His plane landed in the country’s capital Baku, a TASS correspondent reported.
The Russian Foreign Ministry said the event will focus on further development of the organization. Besides, the participants will exchange opinions on pressing international and regional issues.
CICA is an inter-governmental forum for resolving key regional problems and developing cooperation between member states.
CICA has 28 member countries: Azerbaijan, Afghanistan, Bahrain, Bangladesh, Cambodia, China, Egypt, India, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Kuwait, South Korea, Sri Lanka Mongolia, Pakistan, Palestine, Qatar, Russia, Tajikistan, Thailand, Turkey, United Arab Emirates, Uzbekistan and Vietnam.
Belarus, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Saudi Arabia, Turkmenistan, Ukraine, the United States, the Philippines, and Japan, as well as the UN, the Arab League, OSCE (Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe) and the Parliamentary Assembly of Turkic-Speaking Countries have observer status.

title: Lagos begins 35-day Lekki-Epe road repairs Thursday
body: Releases traffic advisory for motorists By Olasunkanmi Akoni LAGOS — The Lagos State Government will on Thursday commence a 35-day rehabilitation of damaged sections of the Eti-Osa-Lekki-Epe Expressway, covering Bonny Camp to Admiralty Way Junction and areas around Victoria Garden City (VGC). The government said traffic diversion arrangements would be introduced to minimise congestion and ensure the safety of road users during the rehabilitation. The Special Adviser to the Governor on Infrastructure, Olufemi Daramola, disclosed this on Wednesday during a stakeholders’ engagement organised by the Ministry of Works and Infrastructure to discuss the scope of work and traffic management plans. Daramola said the meeting was part of the government’s policy of consulting residents, businesses and road users before embarking on major infrastructure projects, adding that feedback from stakeholders would inform the implementation process. He appealed to residents and motorists to cooperate with the government during the exercise, particularly as Lagos prepares for increased traffic during the festive season. According to him, the rehabilitation is expected to improve road safety and ease movement along the strategic corridor, which connects residential communities, commercial centres and major industrial investments across the Lekki-Epe axis. The expressway provides access to the Lekki Free Zone, Dangote Refinery, Dangote Fertiliser Factory, Lekki Deep Sea Port and Eleganza Industrial Estate. It also serves major housing developments and educational institutions, including Pan-Atlantic University and Lagos Business School. However, rapid urbanisation, growing commercial activities and increasing traffic have accelerated the deterioration of some sections of the road. Daramola said the government was also addressing drainage concerns along the corridor, adding that the proposed Green Line rail project formed part of broader plans to improve transportation infrastructure in the area. He said the state had so far reconstructed and rehabilitated 69.44 kilometres of the expressway, comprising 49.7 kilometres of reinforced concrete pavement and 19.76 kilometres of flexible pavement. Residents raise concerns At the meeting, the Chairman of the Victoria Island and Ikoyi Residents Association, Prince Akin Fadoju, called for improved drainage infrastructure to address flooding in the area. Fadoju acknowledged that drainage problems predated the current administration but stressed the need for urgent intervention. Other stakeholders urged the government to ensure that traffic management officials were deployed throughout the construction period to direct motorists and prevent gridlock. They also called for the maintenance of alternative routes and adequate security for road users during the rehabilitation. The intervention is part of broader efforts to rehabilitate the Eti-Osa-Lekki-Epe Expressway. The government had earlier awarded the first phase, covering 18.75 kilometres from Eleko to Epe T-Junction in Ibeju-Lekki, in November 2020. The project was completed and commissioned in February 2023. Phases IIA and IIB, covering the stretch from Eleko Junction to Abraham Adesanya, were subsequently awarded, while rehabilitation works between Admiralty Intersection and Ajah Jubilee Flyover have also been completed. In April 2025, the government awarded early infrastructure development works for the proposed Green Line mass transit project. The proposed rail corridor will run from Marina through the Eti-Osa-Lekki-Epe axis towards the planned Lekki International Airport, connecting Lagos Island with the state’s rapidly developing eastern corridor.
