title: From Protest to Procedure
body:
Oleksandr Larin, Founder of ‘Idealist Media’ platform, General Secretary of the Basketball Federation of Ukraine (2011-2015), Deputy Minister of Sport of Ukraine (2010)
Recently Ms. Stella Zakharova, Olympic champion and Vice President of the Ukrainian Gymnastics Federation submitted a report to the Gymnastics Ethics Foundation, the body responsible for ethical and disciplinary matters within the World Gymnastics system. The report is based on documented actions by Russian gymnastics structures in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine. It was prepared not as a political declaration, but as a legal case: facts, documents, federation rules, procedure, and a request that the competent body provide an assessment.
At first glance, this is a story about gymnastics. To me, it is much more than that. It tests whether Ukraine is capable of moving from the model of “we object your decision” to a different one: “here are your rules, here are the actions of your member — explain whether the two are consistent.” And it brings us back to a broader question: why has Ukraine still not built a systematic legal mechanism for protecting its interests in international sport?
Several years ago, we already proposed a different approach: not to wait for an unfavorable decision and not to start looking for lawyers after the problem has already emerged, but to work proactively — through statutes, regulations, disciplinary procedures, the rights of national federations, and, when necessary, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).
In 2023, after the Ms.Olga Kharlan case, Mr.Taras Samborskyi said it directly: the rules of international federations must be worked with before a conflict, not after one. In December of that same year, the NGO Sports Context presented the Office of the President and the Ministry of Youth and Sports(Ministry) with a concept for reforming the system: the state should stop merely reacting to consequences and instead create mechanisms that function regardless of who happens to occupy the minister’s office.
The problem was visible, and an alternative was proposed, but it never became a system. That is why the principle we proposed to the state of Ukraine is now being implemented, together with the lawyers and experts of Sports Context, in our work with Ms.Stella Zakharova. There is a concrete case, a procedure, and eventually there shodw be a result.
The State and International Sport Use Different Tools
The state operates through diplomacy, political statements, sanctions, intergovernmental relations, and decisions by public authorities. International sport operates through its own statutes, disciplinary codes, ethical rules, appeals procedures, membership rules, and dispute-resolution mechanisms.
Even if Ukraine is one hundred percent right politically, an international federation is not legally obligated to act the way we demand. A minister of Youth and Sports can make a statement, the Foreign Ministry can send a diplomatic note, partners can support Ukraine — but in the end, the federation will open its own statute. If we do not speak the language of that statute, political legitimacy risks remaining nothing more than a statement.
A Different Strategy Could Have Been Chosen Earlier
After the start of the full-scale invasion, the focus on the political and diplomatic isolation of Russian sport was logical and produced results. But over time, the limitations of that strategy became clear: “neutral status,” the return of Russian athletes, and the gradual rollback of restrictions. And each time, Ukraine was reacting to a decision that had already been made.
Mr.Matvii Bidnyi has been part of the leadership of the Ministry of Youth and Sports since 2020 — long enough to see the weak points of the existing strategy and to hear an alternative. That alternative existed: move from a reactive model to a systemic one — work through law, procedures, the internal mechanisms of international federations, and support Ukrainian national federations as full-fledged actors in international sport.
That transition never happened. First, an international institution makes a decision; then Ukraine looks for a way to stop it, change it, or appeal it. At this point, the problem is no longer a single decision. It is the architecture of the policy itself.
The Difference Between Protest and a Legal Problem
A political statement can be ignored. A properly framed legal question is much harder to ignore.
“Do not allow Russian athletes to compete because Russia is waging a war” is a strong moral and political position, but it still leaves a federation room to choose. A very different question is: “Do the actions of your member comply with your own rules?” At that point, the federation no longer has to be persuaded to support Ukraine; it has to explain how it applies its own rules.
That is the logic behind Ms.Zakharova’s case: not “support us,” but “here is the fact, here is the document, here is the action of your member, here is the relevant rule — now provide an answer.” Political volume is replaced by a legally structured contradiction.
And This Is Where Sports Context Has to Be Mentioned
The evidentiary and strategic architecture of this case is being developed with the participation of experts from the NGO Sports Context — the same organization that previously proposed this kind of work to the Ministry.
In January 2025, as head of the NGO, I signed a memorandum of cooperation with Mr.Matvii Bidnyi. We saw it as an opportunity to move from conversations about reform to joint professional work. A permanent mechanism for that cooperation never took shape.
We were ready to cooperate, but not to serve as expert decoration, not to endorse decisions that had already been made, and not to participate in a process where an expert is expected to agree rather than maintain an independent position. We were ready to work on changing the rules. That model turned out not to be needed.
The work moved outside the Ministry. We are now implementing the same approach directly within sport. Ms.Stella Zakharova’s case is one example — and, at the same time, an experiment: political reaction after a problem emerges versus a legal sequence of fact, evidence, rule, and procedure.
What a “ Legal Approach” Means in Practice
First, the fact is established. The evidence is verified. The applicable rule is identified, along with the competent body, the applicant’s procedural standing, and the relevant procedure. Only then does political and diplomatic support come into play.
If a Russian sports structure is operating in occupied Ukrainian territory, the first question should not be, “What statement will the Ministry make?” It should be: what rule may have been violated, who has standing to submit a complaint, to which body, within what deadline, under what standard of proof, and with what documents?
That is when politics strengthens the law instead of replacing it.
The State Should Not Do the Federation ’ s Job
This should be part of the state’s sports infrastructure. Today, we see two extremes: either the state treats federations as if they were its own administrative departments, or it suddenly remembers the autonomy of sport and says, “that is your problem.” Both approaches are wrong.
The state should not draft an appeal to an international federation on behalf of a national federation. It should provide access to sports lawyers, an evidence base, systematic monitoring, diplomatic support, and, where necessary, funding for complex international proceedings. Its role is not to manage the federation, but to strengthen its capacity.
The responsibility of the relevant minister is not to produce the best statement after the latest decision by World Gymnastics, the IOC, or another international federation. It is to make sure the system is working before that decision is made.
Developments should be monitored continuously, documents should be collected, and a legal team should immediately determine whether there is a potential violation, whether a procedure exists, who has standing, and what further action is available. A national federation should not have to start from scratch every single time.
That is exactly what we proposed. So the question is not whether the minister knew about another approach. He did: there were meetings, proposals, a concept, and even a memorandum of cooperation.
Why did this approach never become part of state sports policy?
It should monitor not only the eligibility of Russian athletes, but deeper processes as well: which Russian sports federations incorporate organizations from occupied territories into their structures; where Crimea, Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, or Kherson regions appear in official Russian sports documents; who participates in competitions; who is included on judging lists; which regional organizations are recognized; which appointments are made; and what changes are introduced into statutes.
Every fact should pass through a legal filter: what is legally significant here, what rule may have been violated, which body has jurisdiction, and what procedure is available? That is what professional policy looks like.
We are Not Saying the Ministry and the NOC Did Nothing
There were statements, diplomatic efforts, and legal steps. The question is why they never became a permanent system. Why does law usually appear only after a crisis? Why is there no unified evidence infrastructure? Why are Ukrainean national sports federations so often left alone with the problem? Why were the experts who proposed such a model several years ago never integrated into a permanent mechanism?
Against that background, Ms.Zakharova’s case is particularly revealing: a concrete legal process is now being prepared with the same expert team whose potential for systematic cooperation the Ministry failed to recognize.
The NOC Could Also Play a Different Role
The National Olympic Committee of Ukraine can be an important institution precisely because it is not a government body, yet it operates inside the international Olympic movement. It could accumulate legal practice across sport federations, maintain expertise in international procedures, and create an early-response mechanism. But the Ukrainean NOC should not turn into a second Ministry. Its strength lies in its autonomy.
A Strong Sport Federation Is a Resource, Not a Problem
The state does not need a weak sport federation that is easy to control. It needs a strong one — one that knows its rights, has the necessary expertise, and is capable of acting within its international federation.
A government official often has no procedural standing there, while a national federation does. A minister can send a letter; a federation, under certain conditions, can initiate a procedure. That is why sports autonomy is not a threat to the state, but an additional channel for protecting the national interest.
The Most Important Part of Ms.Zakharova ’ s Story Is Still Ahead
I do not know what decision the GEF will make, and no one has the right to guarantee the outcome: legal results are not announced in advance.
But already today, a small team of athletes, lawyers, and experts is doing what we proposed several years ago should become part of a state system: gathering evidence, verifying facts, identifying rules, determining procedures, working with a person inside the sports system who has the appropriate standing, and building a legal case instead of merely creating a media event. To a significant extent, this is happening outside the state system.
So my question to the Ministry — and personally to Mr.Matvii Bidnyi — is not whether they support Ms.Stella Zakharova’s report. That is secondary. The real question is why an expert resource capable of building cases like this never became part of the system for protecting Ukrainian sports interests, especially when this very approach had been proposed to the Ministry in advance.
From Asking for Support to Becoming a Legal Actor
Ukraine has already learned how to explain to international sport why its decisions are unfair. The next step is to learn how to work with the system itself: its statutes, regulations, procedures, competencies, disciplinary bodies, and CAS.
“ Here is the fact. Here is the evidence. Here is your rule. Here is the procedure you created. Now apply your own rules.”
For the Ukrainian state, the principle is simple: do not manage sport in place of sports institutions; create the conditions in which those institutions are capable of professionally defending both their own rights and Ukraine’s national interests.
This is the logic we have been advancing for several years at Sports Context. The Ministry had the opportunity to use this expertise; at one point, we even formalized our cooperation, but no lasting working relationship emerged. The expertise did not disappear. It simply began to be implemented directly through actors within sport.
After the Ms.Stella Zakharova case, I would leave two questions.
First: what is more effective for the state — to control an independent expert community, to distance itself from it, or to learn how to use it as a normal part of a modern sports ecosystem?
And second: if the approach we proposed to the Ministry several years ago is now beginning to work without the Ministry, perhaps it is finally time to look not at who proposed it, but at the approach itself.

title: Enugu police arrest 182 suspects, rescue 31 kidnap victims
body: By Alumona Ukwueze ENUGU — The Enugu State Police Command says it has arrested 182 suspects, rescued 31 kidnapped victims and recovered 57 firearms, including 13 AK-47 rifles, since the establishment of its Violent Crime Response Unit (VCRU) in April 2026. The Commissioner of Police, Mamman Bitrus Giwa, disclosed this on Wednesday while presenting the unit’s operational scorecard during its formal launch by the Inspector-General of Police, Olatunji Rilwan Disu, at the VCRU headquarters in Golf Estate, Enugu. Giwa said the suspects were arrested for offences including armed robbery, kidnapping, unlawful possession of firearms and ammunition, cultism, and drug and substance trafficking. He added that many of the suspects had been prosecuted. The police commissioner said the unit also recovered 669 rounds of assorted live ammunition and 44 vehicles, comprising cars, tricycles and motorcycles, alongside other exhibits. The Inspector-General of Police, represented by the Assistant Inspector-General of Police in charge of Zone 13, Miller Gajere Dantawaye, described the establishment of the VCRU as a strategic initiative to strengthen intelligence-driven policing, prevent violent crime and protect lives and property. Disu charged personnel of the unit to uphold professionalism, discipline, accountability and respect for human rights in the discharge of their duties. He also commended Enugu State Governor, Peter Mbah, for providing vehicles and supporting security infrastructure across the state. Giwa explained that the VCRU comprised specialised sections responsible for tackling armed robbery, terrorism and related offences, kidnapping, cultism and drug trafficking. He said other sections handled operational monitoring, professional conduct oversight and media liaison. The commissioner reaffirmed the command’s commitment to combating violent crime and safeguarding lives and property, while acknowledging the state government’s continued support for security operations. Speaking on behalf of the VCRU State Civilian Oversight Board, a representative of civil society organisations, Larry Ogwuego, commended the Inspector-General for establishing the unit and promoting intelligence-led operations and respect for human rights. Ogwuego assured that the board would discharge its oversight responsibilities to promote accountability and incorporate community feedback into the unit’s activities. The launch, held at the VCRU headquarters in Golf Estate, Enugu, was attended by senior police officers, Vincent Onyeabor, Special Assistant to the Governor, and members of the State Civilian Oversight Board representing traditional institutions, the legal profession, the Police Community Relations Committee, the media and youth groups. The post Enugu police arrest 182 suspects, rescue 31 kidnap victims appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Fuel market situation improving, Novak says
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. The situation on the domestic fuel market is now much better than one month before, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters on the sidelines of the Russian Energy Week forum.
"The situation is improving. Yesterday we had the ordinary staff meeting together with the regions, the Energy Ministry, and the federal executive authorities. Certain our refiners returned to work after turnarounds and the situation is today much better than one month ago, a fortnight ago," Novak said.
This is related in particular to strengthened protection of facilities, the official noted. "Let’s hope the situation will continue improving. Certainly, much depends on further development of the situation with attacks against the energy infrastructure, although our refineries defend themselves - we are strengthening this defense. This is one of the venues for improvement of the situation in this sense," he added.

title: IDF Manpower Directorate head recounts former hostage's story of abuse in Gaza at memorial event
body: IDF Manpower Directorate head Maj.-Gen. Dado Bar Kalifa recounted former hostage Avinatan Or's testimony of how a three-year-old boy was instructed to spit on him by a Hamas terrorist during his captivity in Gaza, speaking before thousands of soldiers at a battle heritage and fallen soldiers' memorial event in the Negev on Tuesday.Bar Kalifa, who fought in the Gaza Strip as commander of the 36th Division following the October 7 attacks, addressed the soldiers at the Southern Command event."I wasn't going to miss this opportunity to speak to you here at Southern Command, fighters, commanders, female and male soldiers. I feel it is a great privilege to be here with you and to tell you that we must not give up, and that we must make sure that what happened will never happen again," he said.He added that he feared the memory of October 7 would fade."I'm afraid we'll forget what happened, that we'll forget that perhaps we are a complicated people. We are not an easy people, but we are a people of heroes, a wonderful people. I'm afraid we'll be overwhelmed by the fractures, that we'll grow weary of learning, and that we won't understand that they are part of who we are, part of what we are building."October 7 not just another day on the calendar, Bar Kalifa saysBar Kalifa went on to speak about October 7, saying it was not just another day on the calendar."It is a long, momentous journey between devastation and hope, between defeat and rebirth," he said.He then introduced the participants in the event's panel discussion.Among them was Avinatan Or, "who returned from Hamas captivity after more than 700 days," and Roy Benjamin Roko, "a company commander who rushed from his home into the terrible inferno, a true hero."He also introduced Mazi Ayalon, the widow of a community security coordinator who fought heroically, "and who is herself now safeguarding our recovery," and Rabbi Shmuel Slotki, "whose two wonderful sons sought out the enemy on October 7 and fought to their last drop of blood.""I want to tell you what I learned from this incredible encounter with these people," the Manpower Directorate chief said."I learned one small story from Avinatan Or. What is the difference between us and those on the other side of the fence? Those who came here to murder us on October 7? Where does the difference begin? Probably in kindergarten."Bar Kalifa then described what Or had told him about the moments before his girlfriend was abducted.According to Bar Kalifa, Or said his captors beat him over the head with a club and rocks."He was covered in blood, his undershirt was soaked, and blood had congealed with mud on his face. He had just arrived inside the Strip, spending a few brief minutes above ground before descending into the dark tunnels for two years."Bar Kalifa said Or had been certain he was about to be lynched, particularly when a terrorist entered carrying a large kitchen knife.Palestinian child pushed into spitting on Israel hostageOr believed that was the moment he would be killed."This vile, cursed, despicable terrorist picks up a three-year-old child and brings him up to face level, lifting him by the waist, and tells him, 'Spit on him.' And the child spits, too weakly for the liking of those around him."They tell him, 'Spit again.' And the child spits, and this time he enthusiastically improves his performance. Everyone around him applauds and tells him, 'Good boy, good boy.'""These are the people we fought against," Bar Kalifa concluded. "These are the people we will not return until we have destroyed them all. This is how a generation of murderers is educated and raised."

title: Flood: Senate directs emergency interventions in Anambra, Imo, others
body: The Senate has urged the Federal Government to deploy urgent emergency interventions across flood- and erosion-ravaged communities in Anambra, Imo, Ebonyi, and neighboring states. The red chamber’s action followed joint motions sponsored by Senator Victor Umeh (NDC, Anambra Central), Senator Anthony Ani (APC, Ebonyi South), and Senator Osita Izunaso (APC, Imo West), detailing the ongoing ecological disaster gripping their respective constituencies. Leading the debate, Senator Victor Umeh highlighted the humanitarian and environmental crises unfolding in Ogidi, Obosi, and Oko. He revealed that heavy torrents had caused catastrophic flooding and expanding gully erosion, resulting in at least four casualties—including a pregnant woman and a six-year-old child—alongside the mass displacement of families. Ekiti, Osun polls: Votes sold for N50,000, says EU observer group Retirees now receive benefit within 48hrs – PenCom Umeh warned that rapidly expanding gullies are threatening major transport arteries, including vital sections of the strategic Onitsha-Owerri Expressway, threatening to paralyze interstate commerce and daily livelihoods. Supporting the motion, Senator Anthony Ani emphasized the devastating economic toll on Ebonyi South, where overflowing waters have swallowed farmland, destroyed livestock, and wiped out family valuables, further worsening local economic hardship. Ani called on the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security to urgently assess crop damage and deliver immediate relief to affected farmers. Senator Osita Izunaso highlighted that flooding and severe gully erosion continue to threaten numerous communities and roadways across Imo West—a persistent disaster he previously brought to the Senate floor in 2023. He stressed that without coordinated drainage works and road rehabilitation, motorists and pedestrians remain in constant danger. Following extensive contributions, the Senate adopted all prayers directed the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) to immediately deliver food, medical supplies, and relief materials to displaced residents. The Senate also directed the Federal Ministries of Works and Environment to conduct rapid assessments, restore blocked access routes, and deploy long-term ecological control measures. The Upper Chamber mandated the Senate committees on Environment, Works, Ecology, and Climate Change to conduct joint field inspections of the damaged areas and submit a comprehensive report within 30 days. Our correspondent reports that the lawmakers stood to observe a minute of silence in memory of victims who lost their lives to the natural disasters.

title: Aoun reports of phone call with FM Araghchi
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 14 (MNA) – Lebanese President Joseph Aoun announced his telephone conversation with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and support for a diplomatic solution for the region.
The Lebanese presidency announced: Aoun received a call from the Iranian Foreign Minister, during which they discussed the current situation in the region.

title: LGA Chair Seeks FG Intervention As East-West Road Erosion Claims Two Lives
body: The Chairman of Tai Local Government Area of Rivers State, Mbakpone Okpe, has called on the Federal Ministry of Works to urgently repair an erosion-damaged section of the East-West Road in the Kira-Ogoni axis, attributing the damage to heavy flooding that has swept through the area. Okpe, alongside residents of the community, says the heavy flooding has caused severe erosion along the road, forcing motorists to navigate a single lane and exposing road users to danger. The chairman disclosed that more than six accidents had occurred around the affected section, with two persons reportedly killed and several others taken to hospital. “Two persons have died. A lot were taken to hospital,” Okpe said, recalling an accident he witnessed and immediately reported to the ministry’s controller. He explained that the situation had become so concerning that members of the community planned to block the road in protest last week, but he appealed to them to exercise restraint. Speaking during a meeting with a representative of the Federal Ministry of Works, Okpe said the local government had written to relevant authorities, including the federal and state ministries of works and the deputy governor, who oversees the state flood committee. He said the responses received indicated that intervention would follow once the rains stopped completely, but expressed concern over the risks posed by the continuing deterioration of the road. The chairman also spoke about discussions involving construction company RCC, which he said had initially offered to carry out repairs as a goodwill gesture using available materials, but later indicated that it was waiting for the Federal Government to settle outstanding payments before mobilising to the site. Okpe maintained that the damaged section was separate from RCC’s previous expressway project and insisted that the Federal Ministry of Works should take responsibility for the emergency repairs. “This section of the road has nothing to do with RCC. This is the entire responsibility of the Federal Ministry of Works,” he said. He urged the ministry to assess the damage, prepare a bill of quantities and engage a contractor to undertake the repairs without further delay. “The processes and procedures people are talking about have nothing to do with this. It is an emergency job,” the chairman said, warning that further erosion could cause the road to collapse completely. President of the Movement for the Survival of Ogoni People (MOSOP), Olu Angah Wai-Ogosu, has also called for urgent intervention, raising concerns about possible environmental factors behind the road damage. Wai-Ogosu suspects that sand mining activities around the area may have weakened the soil, making it more vulnerable to erosion during heavy flooding. His suspicion has not been independently confirmed. He urged the Rivers State Government to intervene quickly, suggesting that it could undertake the repairs and subsequently seek reimbursement from the Federal Government. The East-West Road is a major transport corridor connecting Rivers State with Akwa Ibom, Cross River and other parts of the country. The damage has raised concerns about road safety, the movement of goods and passengers, and the economic impact on communities and businesses that depend on the route. Residents are calling on the relevant authorities to prioritise emergency repairs to prevent further damage and protect road users. The post LGA Chair Seeks FG Intervention As East-West Road Erosion Claims Two Lives appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Sanwo-Olu promotes Ogunbanwo, five others as perm secs
body: New appointees to be inaugurated Thursday By Olasunkanmi Akoni LAGOS — Lagos State Governor, Babajide Sanwo-Olu, has approved the appointment of Olatunbosun Sunday Ogunbanwo and five others as permanent secretaries in the state civil service. Ogunbanwo, a media relations and public communication professional, was until his elevation the Director of Public Affairs at the Lagos State Ministry of Health. The appointments were announced in a circular dated October 13, 2026, with reference number CIR/HOS/’26/071, signed by the Head of Service, Bode Agoro. According to Agoro, the appointments take immediate effect. He said the appointments were part of the state government’s efforts to strengthen its policy implementation machinery. The newly appointed permanent secretaries are scheduled to be inaugurated by Sanwo-Olu on Thursday at Lagos House, Alausa, Ikeja. title: UN Secretary General Guterres Presents $14bn Budget To Ibrahim-Led Committee
body: United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres has presented a proposed $14 billion budget for the 2027 fiscal year to the General Assembly’s budget committee, chaired by Nigeria’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Senator Jimoh Ibrahim. Presenting the proposal in New York, Guterres said the budget was designed to strengthen the United Nations’ capacity to deliver on its core mandates of international peace and security, sustainable development and human rights, while advancing reforms to improve efficiency and accountability. Receiving the proposal, Ibrahim described the proposal as a budget for a sustainable United Nations and assured that the committee would commence deliberations and consultations on the budget. The General Assembly’s budget committee is chaired by Nigeria’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Senator Jimoh Ibrahim. He assured the secretary-general of the committee’s cooperation and commitment to a constructive budget review process. Guterres, who is presenting the proposed budget for the final time during his tenure, said the estimates reflect the organisation’s continuing reform agenda under the UN80 Initiative, which seeks to make the Secretariat more efficient, effective and responsive to emerging global challenges. He said the proposal includes 11,150 posts and provides $423 million for the continued operation of special political missions in 2027. According to the Secretary-General, the approach will give member states a clearer picture of the organisation’s financial requirements earlier in the budget process. Guterres also highlighted proposed investments in sustainable development, including an additional one million dollars each for the regular programme of technical cooperation and the Development Account. United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said the proposal includes 11,150 posts and provides $423 million for the continued operation of special political missions in 2027. The budget further proposes $2.7 million to support the United Nations Sustainable Development Group System-wide Evaluation Office, as well as $3.7 million to advance the implementation of the organisation’s disability-inclusion strategy. Other allocations include $1.7 million for work on mandate implementation review, $3.2 million for the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Afghanistan and $2.1 million for the next-generation upgrade of Umoja, the United Nations’ enterprise resource planning system. An additional $22 million is proposed to meet rising costs associated with after-service health insurance for retirees. The Secretary-General said the proposals followed a review of existing resources and opportunities for savings, adding that new and expanded mandates had been considered alongside the need to maintain effective programme delivery. Ibrahim described the proposal as a budget for a sustainable United Nations and assured that the committee would commence deliberations and consultations on the budget. On organisational reforms, Guterres outlined plans to expand common administrative platforms across Geneva, Nairobi, Vienna and Addis Ababa, relocate additional functions to lower-cost duty stations and reduce duplication across the Secretariat. He also highlighted measures to streamline senior management structures and improve the alignment of resources with the organisation’s priorities. Despite the proposed savings, Guterres warned that efficiency measures alone would not resolve the United Nations’ financial difficulties without predictable funding and the timely payment of assessed contributions by member states. He urged countries to fulfil their financial obligations in full and on time, in accordance with the UN Charter, noting that liquidity challenges could undermine the effective implementation of approved mandates. The proposed 2027 programme budget will now be subjected to consideration and deliberation by the General Assembly’s Fifth Committee, which is responsible for administrative and budgetary matters, before the Assembly takes the necessary decisions. The post UN Secretary General Guterres Presents $14bn Budget To Ibrahim-Led Committee appeared first on Channels Television .

title: ‘Agbara Nla: The Return’ remake records biggest non-December Nollywood opening
body:
Nollywood faith-based film ‘Agbara Nla: The Return’ recorded the biggest non-December opening for a Nigerian film, earning about N170.6 million across its preview screenings and first weekend in cinemas.
The film generated about N71.4 million from preview screenings ending on 1 October and added approximately N99.2 million between Friday, 2 October, and Sunday, 4 October.
The performance also makes it the highest-grossing October opening for a Nigerian film and the strongest opening recorded by a faith-based Nollywood production.
This non-December distinction matters because Nigerian cinemas usually record their strongest traffic during the festive season. Major Nollywood productions are often scheduled for December to benefit from public holidays, family outings, increased consumer spending, and the “Detty December” entertainment rush.
As a result, many of Nollywood’s biggest opening records belong to December releases, including Funke Akindele’s ‘ Everybody Loves Jenifa’ (2024) and ‘ Behind the Scenes’ (2025).
By earning N170.6 million in October, ‘Agbara Nla: The Return’ achieved blockbuster-level numbers without the advantage of the Christmas holiday season.
In this context, the “biggest non-December opening” refers to the highest opening gross recorded by a Nollywood film released between January and November, based on available Nigerian box-office figures.
‘Agbara Nla’ was originally produced by Mike Bamiloye in 1993. The story returned to cinemas on 1 October 2026 as ‘Agbara Nla: The Return’, directed by his sons, Damilola Mike-Bamiloye and Joshua “Jay Mikee” Mike-Bamiloye.
Before its first full weekend, ‘Agbara Nla: The Return’ generated approximately N71.4 million from 12,134 admissions during its preview screenings.
The film then recorded about N99.2 million from 16,223 admissions between 2 and 4 October, bringing its four-day gross to about N170.6 million.
The opening places the faith-based production among Nollywood’s strongest cinema debuts, although Funke Akindele’s December releases remain ahead in the overall opening-weekend rankings.
‘Everybody Loves Jenifa’ recorded an opening-weekend total of approximately N206 million, while ‘Behind the Scenes’ earned about N205.5 million.
Speaking in a video about the film’s history, Mike Bamiloye recalled that production of the original Agbara Nla began in 1993 with only N5,000.
“In 1993, we wanted to shoot Agbara Nla. We started the film with N5,000. People were bringing yam and corn; we were eating corn in the forest just to shoot Agbara Nla,” he said.
The filmmaker said the production had neither a manager nor a promotional team when it was completed, although several marketers later competed to distribute it. He recalled that the filmmakers continued to struggle financially even as the film became popular across Nigeria.
“We were hungry, we were suffering, we had no food to eat, but our name was everywhere,” he said.
Mr Bamiloye also recounted approaching a marketer for financial assistance after the production, “We approached one marketer and said, ‘Give us money, please give us money, even if it is N10,’ and the marketer said, ‘Mount Zion people, you are becoming lovers of money; you are pursuing money.’
“But he is the one advertising the thing and selling. You can take all the money; you can’t take the anointing. You can take all the money; you can dupe us, but you can’t carry the grace. If you steal our movie, another one will rise from inside.”
The filmmaker said the difficult experience eventually shaped his understanding of the film’s impact, “I went to God and said, ‘Lord, we are suffering.’ You know what God said? He said, ‘I never told you that I would make you rich through Agbara Nla, but I will give you a name through the movie,’” he recalled.
Mr Bamiloye said the promise became evident as the film attracted a following and audiences increasingly associated him and his colleagues with Mount Zion Faith Ministries.
Although the film became widely known through television broadcasts and home-video circulation in the 1990s, Mr Bamiloye traced the story’s origin to the National Festival of Christian Drama, HARVEST ’87.
Mount Zion Faith Ministries organised the festival at the GOFAMINT International Gospel Centre in Ojoo, Ibadan.
The project was initially titled Agbara To Ju Agbara Lo. It involved drama ministers from churches and tertiary institutions, including the University of Lagos, University of Ibadan, Ogun State University and the College of Education, Ilesa.
The first production attempt collapsed after filming at Apete Village in Ibadan. According to Mr Bamiloye, the cameraman disappeared with the recorded tapes, and repeated attempts to find him failed.
The project was subsequently abandoned before Mr Bamiloye rewrote the script and restarted production at Badeku Village in Ibadan.
Members of the Christian community helped to keep the production alive. A Foursquare Gospel Church pastor contributed N5,000 toward a camera deposit, while the late Idowu Animashawun of World Hope Mission accommodated crew members.
The completed film was eventually broadcast on television, introducing the story to audiences across the country.
An English-language adaptation, ‘The Ultimate Power ‘, followed in 1994, extending its reach beyond the predominantly Yoruba-speaking audience of the original production.
The story is set in Muwonleru, a village dominated by Isawuru, a powerful herbalist whose spiritual influence keeps the community in fear.
It centres on the confrontation between Christian faith and traditional spiritual power after evangelists attempt to take the gospel to the village.
Isawuru, portrayed by Mr Bamiloye in the original production, became one of the filmmaker’s most recognisable characters.
The film’s treatment of spiritual warfare, deliverance, faith and the triumph of divine power over evil also became a defining feature of subsequent Mount Zion productions.
More than three decades later, the story has been reimagined for a new generation in Agbara Nla: The Return, with Mr Bamiloye reprising his role as Isawuru.
Damilola Mike-Bamiloye , Joshua “Jay Mikee” Mike-Bamiloye, and Chris Odeh produced it. Mohammed Sedik and Damilola Mike-Bamiloye are credited as co-producers.
Mount Zion Film Productions, Circuits, and Sozo Films produced it, while Nile Entertainment handles distribution.
The cast includes Philip Olubakin as Olaboye, Damilola Mike-Bamiloye as Kola, and Aanu Kolade Abiodun as Bose. Gloria Mike-Bamiloye, Remilekun Mosiko, and David Kola Okeowo also feature in the film.

title: Russian, US energy authorities discussing diesel supplies — Novak
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. The Russian Ministry of Energy and the US Department of Energy are holding talks on contracts for Russian diesel fuel supplies, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters on the sidelines of the Russian Energy Week forum.
"Talks on making contracts are now underway between the Russian Energy Ministry and the US Department of Energy. An instrument will be found there that will make it possible to support supplies," Novak said.
The Russian Energy Week forum is being held in Moscow on October 14-16. Roscongress Foundation is the forum organizer. TASS is the information partner of the forum.

title: Amupitan: AI won’t decide 2027 election but could influence voters’ choices
body: The Chairman of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), Prof. Joash O. Amupitan, has declared that algorithms will not decide the outcome of the 2027 general elections, insisting that the choice of Nigeria’s leaders rests exclusively with the electorate. Amupitan said artificial intelligence (AI) could influence the information available to voters and shape their political choices, but maintained that technology must remain a tool for strengthening democracy rather than determining electoral outcomes. He spoke on Wednesday in Abuja at the Artificial Intelligence and Democracy Forum, where he delivered a keynote address on safeguarding the 2027 general elections in the age of AI organized by Yiaga Africa. “Algorithms will not, and must never, decide the 2027 vote. Algorithms will not decide the vote, because the choice of who leads Nigeria belongs exclusively to the Nigerian people,” he said. Ekiti, Osun polls: Votes sold for N50,000, says EU observer group Retirees now receive benefit within 48hrs – PenCom The INEC chairman explained that sovereignty in a constitutional democracy rests with the people, who exercise their will through ballots cast at polling units across the country. He, however, warned that dismissing the influence of artificial intelligence would be naive, noting that the technology could shape the information environment in which citizens make electoral choices, influence election logistics and alter the strategies of political actors. “While algorithms will not decide the vote, AI will undeniably shape the information environment in which citizens form their choices, influence the speed and security of electoral logistics, and alter the tactics of both democratic actors and anti-democratic disruptors,” he said. Amupitan said the commission had a responsibility to ensure that AI was deployed to strengthen electoral integrity while protecting the process against manipulation and other emerging technological threats. He identified deepfakes, synthetic media, targeted disinformation, automated social media accounts and cyberattacks as potential threats to the credibility of the 2027 elections. According to him, advances in generative AI have made it easier to produce convincing fake videos, audio recordings and images capable of misleading voters, impersonating election officials and spreading false information about electoral procedures. He warned that such content could be used to falsely announce the withdrawal of candidates, circulate fake election postponement notices or make inflammatory statements capable of provoking ethnic and religious tensions. “The greatest threat we face is not the hacking of a ballot box, but the hacking of the voter’s mind,” he said. The INEC chairman also cautioned that AI-powered platforms could exploit voters’ personal preferences and vulnerabilities to circulate targeted political messages, manipulate public opinion and discourage particular groups from participating in elections. He said the commission was developing a digital strategy to monitor the information environment and was partnering with technology platforms to facilitate the rapid debunking of false information and the identification of AI-generated content relating to electoral processes. Amupitan disclosed that INEC had established a specialised AI unit within its Information and Communication Technology Directorate to monitor digital threats, detect deepfakes and track attempts to manipulate electoral information. He stressed that critical electoral decisions, including voter accreditation, result collation and candidate qualification, would not be fully automated or delegated to autonomous systems. “No critical electoral decision, result collation, voter accreditation, or candidate qualification will ever be fully automated or delegated to an autonomous system,” he said, adding that human accountability, statutory oversight and judicial review would remain central to the electoral process. He also urged political parties and candidates to commit to ethical use of AI by refraining from deploying deepfakes, synthetic impersonation, deceptive political advertisements and automated accounts to mislead voters or discredit opponents. The chairman called on technology companies to strengthen measures against the spread of fabricated electoral content and ensure greater transparency in political advertising, particularly where algorithmic targeting could exploit sensitive characteristics such as ethnicity and religion. He further urged media organisations to strengthen fact-checking and digital verification mechanisms, warning that the speed of information dissemination must not take precedence over accuracy. According to him, INEC would work with the National Orientation Agency, civil society organisations and media partners to incorporate AI media literacy into voter education programmes, encouraging citizens to verify sensational online content before sharing it. Amupitan said the 2027 general elections would involve more than 103 million registered voters across 176,846 polling units in the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory. He added that the commission had completed 10 of the 14 major operational milestones for the elections, while continuing to modernise its systems and strengthen preparations. He maintained that technology could improve election administration through better logistics planning, biometric database management, anomaly detection and cybersecurity, provided its use remained transparent and subject to human oversight. “The 2027 vote will be decided, as it must always be, by the sovereign people of the Federal Republic of Nigeria,” he said. Amupitan added that INEC’s responsibility was to ensure that technological tools supported the credibility of the electoral process and did not undermine the will of voters.

title: Thales quadruples Belfast missile output for Ukraine
body: Thales is now building Lightweight Multirole Missiles at its Belfast site at four times the rate it managed in 2022, and has committed £100 million to expanding that capacity further, the company told the UK Defence Journal after the Prime Minister announced accelerated deliveries of the weapon to Ukraine. Phil Siveter, chief executive of Thales in the UK, said: “We are proud that the Prime Minister continues to see Thales in the UK as a trusted partner of the UK Government. Our Lightweight Multirole Missiles are designed and built at our site in Belfast, which has been supplying complex weapons to the UK for more than 70 years. With the support from Government, we have been able to quadruple our production to meet the global demand, and we are committed to investing £100m to expand this capacity further. “The work carried out in Northern Ireland helps to sustain 1,100 direct jobs and supports around 700 more across our UK supply chain, giving the UK a sovereign capability it can rely on when it matters.” Andy Burnham hosted Volodymyr Zelensky in Downing Street on Wednesday, pledging faster deliveries of air defence missiles alongside further military aid and tighter sanctions on Russia, with Britain pressing international partners to restrict Russian liquefied natural gas exports and to lean harder on Moscow over its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. The Prime Minister said: “Our rock-solid support to Ukraine is vital for keeping us safe here in the UK and ensuring those on the frontlines have the equipment they need to push back Russia.” All of that rests on a single production line in Belfast, a site that has built complex weapons for Britain for more than seventy years, through Shorts and then Thales, and it is the home of the Starstreak family from which LMM descends. Starstreak and LMM share the launcher and much of the surrounding equipment, which is part of why the line has been able to grow quickly. LMM is a laser beam riding missile weighing around thirteen kilograms, with a range of about six kilometres. It is fired from shoulder launchers, from lightweight multiple launchers on vehicles, and from the Royal Navy’s Wildcat helicopters, where it carries the name Martlet. Against drones it is substantially cheaper than the surface to air missiles that would otherwise be expended on them, which is the characteristic that has driven demand since 2022. The Belfast expansion is the kind of industrial response the Strategic Defence Review and the Defence Investment Plan have both called for, with onshore capacity that can be surged when a war consumes stock faster than peacetime contracts replace it. The post Thales quadruples Belfast missile output for Ukraine first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: 1,125 Kyiv residents injured in Russian attacks since the start of 2026, more than a third of them in five weeks from late August, Kyiv health chief says
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Russian attacks have injured 1,125 Kyiv residents since the start of 2026. Of these, 379 people, or nearly 34%, were injured in just five weeks, from 27 August to 7 October, Tetiana Mostepan, director of the Kyiv City State Administration’s Department of Health, said in an interview published on 13 October. Russian air attacks on Kyiv have intensified since late August. Air attacks occur both day and night, and Russian drones target not only military facilities but also civilian buildings, including apartments. As a result, the number of casualties is also increasing. More than 40% of emergency medical responses to attacks this year occurred between late August and early October, Mostepan noted. During this period, the capital’s emergency medical teams responded to 782 calls related to the attacks, the department director said. She also released data showing that 138 medical facilities in Kyiv have been damaged since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, including 47 this year. “And when we talk about statistics, I always emphasize that behind every number is a human life. These are people who have been injured, as well as medical workers who respond to attack sites to save them,” Mostepan said. People giving first aid to two women injured in the Russian drone strike, Kyiv, 8 September 2026. Photo: Zelenskyy's Telegram Russian attacks on Kyiv have become more frequent Russia attacked Kyiv with drones throughout the day, Suspilne Kyiv reported on 27 August. Air raid alerts were issued 12 times in the capital, drone debris was found in five districts, and at least four people were injured, the report said. Russian forces used about 140 attack drones against Ukraine throughout the day, more than 100 of them jet-powered, the Ukrainian Air Force reported at the time. At least 38 people were killed and dozens injured in a Russian drone strike on an ammunition depot in the Bucha district near Kyiv, triggering a massive fire and hours of explosions in a residential area, CNN reported . The attack in the Bucha district came amid near-constant Russian airstrikes, which continued into Sunday, the outlet reported. Russian forces were likely seeking to exhaust Ukraine’s air defenses, disrupt civilians’ daily lives, and increase the scale of destruction, analysts at the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said , citing CNN’s reporting. On 8 September, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte stressed the urgent need to strengthen support for Ukraine, particularly by providing air defense systems. Delays in delivering assistance cost human lives, he said. On 1 October, a Russian drone struck a school in Kyiv’s Solomianskyi district while 104 children were inside, Suspilne reported . The evening and morning strikes killed four people in Kyiv, three of them women in a high-rise in Desnianskyi district, Kyiv prosecutors said . Aftermath of the attack on Kyiv on the night of 14 October 2026. title: Kazakhstan Economic Growth Hits 4.2% Despite Decline in Oil Production
body: Kazakhstan’s economy grew by 4.2% in the first nine months of 2026, despite an 8.3% drop in oil production. Growth in construction, manufacturing, transportation, and trade helped offset the decline in the country’s main export industry, although real household incomes have barely risen. According to figures presented on October 13 by Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin, Kazakhstan produced 69.4 million metric tons of oil between January and September. GDP growth accelerated slightly from 4.1% in the first eight months of the year. Kazakhstan is Central Asia’s largest economy and a significant supplier of oil to the global market. Most of its oil exports pass through Russia, including via the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) pipeline system to a terminal on the Black Sea. Disruptions along these routes can force producers to cut output. The Times of Central Asia previously examined why even high global oil prices do not always translate into the expected revenues for Kazakhstan. According to government estimates, the non-resource sector expanded by 5.4%. Manufacturing, construction, transportation, and trade accounted for more than three-quarters of GDP growth. Manufacturing output rose by 8.6%, with machinery production increasing by 22.8%. Over the nine-month period, automobile production increased by nearly 30%, while electrical equipment output rose by approximately 21%. Production of fabricated metal products, food, chemicals, and pharmaceuticals also increased. Investment in fixed assets, including buildings and equipment, rose by 7% between January and September, reaching 16.1 trillion tenge (approximately $35.7 billion). Private investment accounted for 85.7% of the total and increased by 18.2%, with particularly strong growth in manufacturing and construction. At the same time, the strengthening of the tenge, Kazakhstan’s national currency, has put pressure on exporters when dollar-denominated earnings are converted into local currency. Consumer lending has also slowed: annual growth in consumer loans fell from 26.4% in August 2025 to 10.4% in August 2026. Annual inflation stood at 9.3% in September, down from 9.8% in August. Prices are still rising, although somewhat more slowly. In the second quarter, real household incomes per person, adjusted for inflation, grew by just 0.7% compared with the same period last year, following an increase of just 0.1% in the first quarter.

title: Zelensky Arrives in UK to Meet King Charles and Burnham
body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in Britain with his team on Wednesday, Oct. 14, ahead of an audience with King Charles III and security talks with Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
“We will discuss a broad range of security issues. We are preparing decisions that will strengthen us,” Zelensky wrote on his official Telegram channel .
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The president thanked the king, the prime minister and Britain for their support. He did not specify the decisions being prepared or identify the members of his delegation.
Ahead of the visit, Britain announced £45 million ($59 million) in surface-to-air missile deliveries , with £10 million ($13 million) fast-tracked for Ukraine’s urgent winter needs.
The deliveries include British Lightweight Multirole Missiles, which the UK government says have proved effective against Russia’s jet-powered drones.
Burnham has also instructed ministers to prepare further sanctions, military assistance and financial support for Ukraine in the coming weeks.
“We are with you for as long as it takes,” the prime minister said ahead of the meeting.
Zelensky’s arrival follows an overnight Russian attack involving 39 missiles and 128 drones . The president said the barrage damaged energy infrastructure and left at least 600,000 people without electricity.
Kyiv authorities also reported water supply issues after the attack, as Kyiv’s CHP-4 power plant was targeted , along with other facilities.
He called for stronger sanctions against Moscow and additional Patriot interceptor missiles to help Ukraine defend against Russian ballistic missiles.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Why Canada’s caregivers say their retirement plans are being ‘decimated’
body:
When Tracy Slaney imagined her life after retirement, she says she pictured travelling the world with her husband. But like many caregivers in Canada, the cost of looking after her loved ones means she had to put her plans on hold.
“Those retirement plans that I once had are gone. They are decimated,” she said.
In 2014, she became a caregiver for her father after he was diagnosed with terminal cancer. Within days of his passing, her mother received a dementia diagnosis. Slaney then stepped into a caregiver role for her until she died in 2019.
On Valentine’s Day 2020, she found her husband had been diagnosed with stage four colorectal cancer. She spent most of her time, energy and finances caring for him, until he passed away in April this year.
“I’ve been caregiving for 12 years, back-to-back,” she said.
Canada’s caregivers are feeling the squeeze financially, a new report by financial firm Edward Jones has found. More than seven in 10 Canadians who care for loved ones over the age of 65 are also financial caregivers, spending thousands of dollars on the care.
These caregivers say they “may reduce or stop their savings or tap into their non-retirement savings,” the report says.
“They may also reduce retirement contributions, and some even borrow from or draw on their retirement accounts,” it adds.
More than nine in 10 said they’re spending their own money, out of pocket, to care for their loved ones, said Tracey McLennan, a director and financial planner at Edward Jones and a caregiver.
“Even more compelling is about 83 per cent of them are telling us that they have at least one impact on their lifestyle. They’re either moving, they’re relocating those that they’re caring for, they are changing their own expenses, they’re impacting their lifestyle,” she said.
More than half (54 per cent) of caregivers surveyed said are “sandwiched” between two generations, meaning they have children they are supporting in addition to caring for another loved one.
Most often (63 per cent of the time), the recipient of the care is a parent. But they can also be grandparents (10 per cent), spouses (nine per cent), parents-in-law (nine per cent) or a friend, sibling or other relative (nine per cent).
In cases when the recipient of the care cannot reimburse the caregiver, they end up spending an average of $10,190 a year.
Even with health insurance, the costs add up, Slaney said.
“There were drugs that were not covered, even with an insurance plan. There were medical supplies that were not covered. There’s travel cost. We had to have a care support worker at times when I couldn’t be there. That is expensive,” she said.
Slaney was 38 when her father was diagnosed with cancer and the decade that followed saw her pass up promotions, miss time at work and spend time with her loved ones who needed care.
“I was in the prime of my career at that point,” she said.
“We’ve lost basically everything. We had two cars, we had the savings, we had everything. Unfortunately, no one is prepared for that type of scenario – to go down to one income, as well as take time off work myself,” Slaney added.
Canadians who take time off work to care for loved ones “get punished twice” for it, said Liv Mendelsohn, CEO of the Canadian Centre for Caregiving Excellence.
“You get punished for leaving the workforce, you miss out on advancement, but you get punish come time to collect your CPP (Canada Pension Plan) because you haven’t paid in at the full capacity that you would have,” she said.
Slaney has felt the cascading effects of the financial loss.
“Over the course of the last six years, we have lost over $100,000 in earnings, savings, RRSPs. Everything is gone in the caregiving journey,” she said.
Those who are caring for younger family members between the ages of 18 to 64 have to be caregivers for much longer, McLennan said.
“They are more likely to put in their own financial resources, and it is much more likely to impact their health physically,” she said.
Caregivers are also ageing as they spend money, time and energy caring for someone else. The average age of the caregiver is 49, with the average caregiving tenure lasting seven years, the Edward Jones report said.
This is typically the age when many Canadians hit their peak earning years, and when financial experts say when you should be saving aggressively. For many, this is also when they have to ramp up spending on sending their kids to college.
According to the Canadian Centre for Caregiving Excellence, one in five caregivers is already over the age of 65.
“We’re seeing more and more caregivers who themselves are one fall or one hospital visit away from needing care,” Mendelsohn said.
“If mom is looking after dad and mom has a fall, then their children, if they have children, are immediately thrust into a double caregiving role.”
The “sandwich generation” is turning into a “club sandwich” in Canada, said Laura Tamblyn Watts, CEO of the nonprofit advocacy group CanAge.
“We don’t just have a sandwich generation anymore. We’ve got a club sandwich,” she said.
“Someone who is 90 might be receiving care from someone who’s 68 and still working full-time. While the 68-year-old next door is receiving care from younger family members,” Watts added.
Nearly half (49 per cent) of caregivers surveyed for Edward Jones found that their own health was being negatively affected as they cut back on expenses for their own medical care.
Money is a hard subject to talk about when a loved one is dealing with a debilitating illness, Mendelsohn said.
“People feel terrible guilt when they’re making those choices between putting food on the table for their family and caring for dad in the way that they want to,” she said.
But getting past the initial awkwardness can help in the long term, McLennan said.
“There’s certain taboo topics that we were told don’t talk about around the dinner table. We don’t about death. We don’t talk about money,” she said.
Asking your parents about how they want to age and making sure you speak with your siblings about responsibilities ahead of time can help, she said.
“We have to have a conversation about roles. We know from this study that typically, caregiving falls on one individual, and quite frequently it falls on a female in the family,” McLennan said.
Having a caregiving role thrust on you doesn’t have to mean your plans have to be abandoned entirely, McLennan said.
“It doesn’t mean giving up all your plans, but it may mean amending them,” she said, adding that this could include working with a financial planner to figure out what your trade-offs could be and how you can keep squirreling money away into your RRSP.
Once Slaney retires from her government job in five years, she won’t have her husband by her side. But she hopes to still travel with her two children.
When asked what her top three bucket list destinations are, she doesn’t miss a beat when she says, “Hawaii. Hawaii. Hawaii.”
“That was on my husband’s bucket list, and we are going to fulfill that wish,” she says.

title: Russian attack on Lutsk kills five, injures 10
body:
According to Ukrinform, the Volyn Regional Police reported this.
“Police officers are working at the sites of the strikes in Lutsk. Five fatalities have been confirmed,” the statement said.
Law enforcement officers are assisting those affected, maintaining public order and documenting the aftermath of the Russian attack.
Police have also set up tents to provide immediate assistance to residents.
According to police, during another Russian drone attack on the Volyn region, a grocery store in Lutsk caught fire. Five people were killed and 10 injured.
A building on Sobornosti Avenue was also damaged. Two people, including a child, were preliminarily reported injured.
Acting Head of the Volyn Regional Military Administration Roman Romaniuk said that debris from a Russian drone struck the EuroHurt wholesale store. Two people were found dead at the scene, while another person died in hospital.
According to Romaniuk, the fire has been contained. Rescue workers are continuing to clear the rubble and deal with the aftermath.
According to the official, two people, including one child, were injured in a nine-story apartment building.
As reported, Russian forces attacked civilian infrastructure in Lutsk with a jet-powered drone, leaving six people injured.

title: The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is almost the Android tablet we needed
body:
We have to talk about this screen. It’s the first thing you notice, and maybe the only thing that matters, about the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro. It’s a 12-inch, 2800 x 1840 panel with a new technology Amazon calls “Nanomatte” that is meant to decrease glare and increase the feeling that you can reach out and touch the things you see onscreen. When Amazon set out to build the best tablet the company has ever shipped, it started with this screen.
The $549.99 device I’ve been testing is one of four new models in the Alexa Tablet lineup, which ranges from a $229.99 8-inch model up to a $679.99 12 Pro with this Nanomatte coating and some extra RAM you don’t really need. The pitch for all those devices is the same: They’re well-made, midrange tablets that can access the full universe of Android apps through the Play Store and come with a whole bunch of Amazon bloatware whether you want it or not. I haven’t tested those other devices, but I’m glad they exist — cheap, good Android tablets are too hard to come by.
[Product: Amazon Alexa Tablet 12 Pro | https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0FMS8C99W?tag=theverge02-20]
But the Nanomatte. The Nanomatte! The etching on the display, which Amazon says it partnered with Corning to do at a sub-pixel level to reduce glare without causing the slight rainbow-shimmering effect you can get on other matte screens, absolutely does its job. When I use my iPad outdoors, I can often see what’s behind me like I’m staring into a mirror; the 12 Pro reflects only a small sheen of light, and does it without losing any sharpness. The viewing angles are incredible, too. I’d like the display to be a little brighter, but since the main reason to crank the brightness is to fight glare, it hasn’t really been a problem.
The screen is not perfect. The anti-glare texture gives the Alexa Tablet a bit of shimmer, especially when you’re looking at light text on a black background. And the iPad’s blacks are still blacker; watching a movie, the letterboxes above and below are still slightly lit on the Alexa Tablet’s LCD, and they’re just flat-out off on the iPad’s OLED panel. Some of this you can fix: The 12 Pro has specific modes that automatically tweak tone and color to make reading more pleasant, and you can even control the overall picture through a few presets like the ones you’d find on your TV. My review unit came with “Boosted” mode turned on, which made every color just a smidge too colorful. I turned it to “Natural” and immediately liked the picture better.
[Image: This is as nice a reading tablet as you’ll find anywhere. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Alexa-Tablet-reading.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
I’m not sure this screen counts as some revolution in display technology, but then again, I did reflexively say “whoa” the first second I turned it on, and all that was showing was the Amazon logo. I like this display for everything. The 120Hz refresh rate looks great when running Star Wars: Galactic Racer, and the 3:2 aspect ratio feels right for web browsing and side-by-side work. The more muted display modes even make reading more pleasant than your average giant screen, though it’s lame that they only work in the Kindle app. After a few days of using the tablet indoors and out, I prefer the 12 Pro’s screen to any iPad I’ve tried. (Unfortunately, I don’t have an iPad Pro with the nano-texture glass to compare it to, but that’s a $2,200 tablet. I doubt anyone’s debating between the two.)
All that display tech in a $549.99 device requires tradeoffs basically everywhere else, and Amazon makes lots of them. The MediaTek Dimensity 8400 processor benchmarks somewhere between a flagship high-end Android phone from last year and a flagship phone from two years ago, and gets absolutely lapped by practically every current iPad. In one graphics-heavy benchmark, the current 13-inch iPad Pro scored about nine times higher.
I’d like more horsepower here, but in my day-to-day use there’s plenty of power in this tablet. In several days of playing games, doing work, and watching a lot of NFL RedZone, the only slowness I’ve detected has been little niggling things in the Android experience. The app switcher sometimes stutters when it loads. I suppose I worry a little about how this tablet will age, given that it doesn’t share the iPad’s preposterous oversupply of processing power, but for now it’s fine.
Come to think of it, “it’s fine” explains most of the 12 Pro’s hardware. The four speakers are a little thin and muddy, but loud and clear enough. The cameras wash out some colors, but they work for video calls. The $149.99 keyboard case is nice to type on, but a little awkward to detach and manipulate. The $89.99 pen is smooth and responsive, but not many Android apps support a stylus. The battery lasts me about eight hours of screen time, which is a little less than I’d like and less than Amazon advertises. Nothing here is a deal-breaker, it’s just a lot of fine.
[Image: The Play Store immediately makes this an improvement on Fire tablets. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Alexa-Tablet-Android.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
The software, on the other hand, is all extremes. The great news: The Alexa Tablets run full Android, not the weird off-brand operating system Amazon’s Fire tablets have used for the last 15 years. That means you get all the apps in the Play Store, a vastly improved interface, and access to things like Google’s Gemini assistant. All by itself, that change makes these the most functional Amazon tablets ever.
Unfortunately, Amazon did to Android exactly what you’d fear — and maybe expect. It Amazon-ed the crap out of things. I’m fine with the slide-over panel to the left of the homescreen filled with content recommendations; the overlap of Alexa Tablet owners and Prime subscribers / Kindle readers is probably pretty high, and at least that screen isn’t staring you in the face every time you unlock your tablet. I can even live with Amazon preloading its own browser, photos, and music apps, none of which are better than their competition. But it is frankly outrageous that Amazon thinks it can get away with adding two separate, non-removable homescreen widgets that serve no purpose other than advertising Amazon’s products.
If you’re going to say you “obsess over customers,” you don’t get to borrow the top left corner of my homescreen and then use that space to show me an ad vaguely offering to “Cook with premium ingredients” that launches an also unhideable Alexa chat window in the bottom right corner of my homescreen.
Luckily, this is Android, and installing a new launcher takes 30 seconds. If you buy an Alexa Tablet, I recommend doing so immediately.
[Image: I do not need Alexa this front and center on my tablet. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Alexa-Tablet-Alexa.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
I would be less annoyed by Alexa’s overbearing presence on this tablet if Alexa Plus were actually useful, which it mostly is not. If you’re looking to buy whatever’s on your screen, Alexa’s your bot: You can invoke the assistant in any app, and it’ll almost always assume your goal is to shop for whatever you’re currently looking at. If you want, well, anything else, you’re probably out of luck. Almost a year after its launch, Alexa Plus is not a very good assistant. It’s slow, it gets lost in back-and-forth conversations, and it still doesn’t have enough access to my apps and data to be useful. You can switch to Gemini in the device’s settings, and you should.
Once you de-Amazon the tablet, you’re left with a pretty useful Android device. And this is where the Alexa Tablet gets tricky to evaluate. I wouldn’t recommend using it as a primary computer, given the still sorry state of large-screen Android apps. (Between this and the ongoing Googlebook fiasco, I really hope Google is learning a lesson about incentivizing developers to care about big screens and keyboards.) But between the Kindle-specific display mode, all the streaming and reading apps in the Play Store, and this terrific screen, this is immediately one of the best tablets-for-tablet-things you can buy.
Realistically, you’re probably debating whether to buy the Alexa Tablet or an iPad. (Apologies to the Samsung Galaxy Tab shoppers out there, but this one’s a way better buy for almost everybody.) For the same $550 you’ll drop on the 12 Pro, you can get a base-model iPad with 256GB of storage. I’d probably tell you to buy the iPad; it has much better tablet software and much better big-screen apps, and Apple has a much better track record in tablets.
And yet for the last few days, I’ve had an iPad and an Alexa Tablet sitting on my desk, and every time I want to watch or read something I’ve found myself gravitating to Amazon’s device. It is really nice to look at.

title: The Ocarina of Time remake feels remarkably modern — and surprisingly terrifying
body:
With its upcoming remake for the Switch 2, Nintendo might have nailed the best thing about The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time: its timelessness. The 1998 3D action adventure game for the Nintendo 64 that pioneered so much — 3D graphics, movement, exploration, openness — has been reengineered with changes that make it feel more modern, and surprisingly terrifying at times. Based on my early hands-on time with the game, it’s shaping up to be the best-looking, best-playing version of the game that addresses the most frustrating aspects of playing the original.
More than just sanding off its roughest edges, Nintendo also fitted Ocarina of Time with modern trappings to make it more welcoming to those who were introduced to Zelda through more modern releases, like Breath of the Wild. The remake has a new progression marker, called Threads of Time, that’s viewable when you pause. It also has Zelda Notes integration within the Nintendo Switch app to let you view game maps and other info on your phone. Oh, it also has a dedicated jump button.
I spent around 90 minutes during a recent preview event in New York City playing through some chunks of the game, including when you first take control of Child Link, and later on after you yank the Master Sword in the Temple of Time to become Adult Link. Its story still makes it a standout Zelda title, and the improvements make it even easier to get immersed in.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Switch2_ZeldaOoT_MedaiBroll_SCRN_14.png?quality=90&strip=all]
In some ways, the remake feels similar to modern Zelda games. Link is snappy to control, and lock-on combat is engaging. Swapping between items and weapons no longer requires hopping into the pause menu, as it did in the original. Holding a shoulder button halts the action, and you can navigate with an analog stick to find what you want in near-realtime. However, it’s an adventure on a much smaller scale; the complexity of your quests, and the tools at your disposal for combat and getting around are simpler, but no less fun.
All of the sections I played were truncated, though I left feeling confident that Nintendo nailed this remake. My favorite section was the Forest Temple, which really shows off the more realistic art style. It can finally portray the game’s horror themes in ways that weren’t possible 28 years ago. For example, Link traverses rooms in the dungeon that have red stained glass windows, and as he passes through beams of light, he is cast in the color of blood. It really looks and feels like he’s on an adventure to stave off cataclysm, and the visual evolution frequently made me stop playing for a second while I took in the changes. Also, being able to use the right stick to control the camera lets you create cinematic moments on-the-fly, which is great if, like me, you like taking a lot of screenshots.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/oot.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-13-112347.png?quality=90&strip=all]
Ocarina of Time is one of Nintendo’s most influential games, and playing it is a rite of passage for any Zelda fan, but it can be tough to go back to the original. As accessible as it is considering it was one of Nintendo’s earliest fully-3D titles, the remake makes it so much easier to get into. And it’s launching at a time when the Zelda franchise is bigger than ever. Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom were big sellers, and they continue to attract new players years after launch, while fans will be able to dig into the live-action movie in April 2027. Even sooner, though, Switch 2 owners will get to feast on the best way to play through a defining Zelda classic.
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time launches for the Nintendo Switch 2 on Thursday, November 5th.
