title: Only youths ignorant of Atiku’s history can be hoodwinked – Keyamo
body: By Nwafor Sunday Polycarp Minister of Aviation, Festus Keyamo, SAN, has criticised former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar over his comments on the economic hardship and insecurity in the country, accusing him of hypocrisy and saying only younger Nigerians unfamiliar with his record could be misled by his claims. Keyamo, who made the remarks in a post on his X account on Wednesday, challenged Atiku’s criticism of President Bola Tinubu’s administration, citing the liquidation of Nigeria Airways in September 2004 and the alleged failure to pay the pensions and gratuities of its former workers. The minister argued that the Tinubu administration was addressing the outstanding entitlements of the airline’s former workers, claiming that the President had approved and released N36 billion to provide relief to affected families. According to Keyamo, some of the beneficiaries had begun receiving payment notifications, while the workers’ union had also recognised Tinubu for the intervention. He said it was hypocritical for Atiku to criticise the current administration over hardship without addressing issues arising from decisions taken when he served as vice-president under former President Olusegun Obasanjo. “It’s only the younger ones who don’t know your history you can attempt to hoodwink, but we will expose you to them,” Keyamo wrote. The minister also accused Atiku of taking credit for the achievements of the Obasanjo administration when convenient while distancing himself from its decisions at other times. “When it is convenient for you, you claim some credit of the Obasanjo-Atiku government and when not convenient, you say Obasanjo was in charge and not you as Vice-President,” he said. Keyamo’s comments followed Atiku’s appeal to Nigerians over the rising cost of living and insecurity, in which the former vice-president said families were struggling to afford food, healthcare, transportation and other basic necessities. In his message, Atiku expressed concern about the difficulties confronting pensioners, young workers and parents, as well as the fear experienced by families amid reports of kidnappings and attacks across the country. He said no Nigerian family should have to contend with hunger and insecurity simultaneously, warning against allowing the prevailing conditions to become the future inherited by the next generation. Atiku also urged registered voters to collect their Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs), describing them as instruments through which Nigerians could peacefully demand change. “Bola made life expensive. I will work to make life affordable again and restore the security every Nigerian deserves,” he said, calling on citizens across generations to support his vision of a country where families could live with dignity, safety and hope. The exchange comes amid growing political mobilisation ahead of the 2027 general elections, with political leaders increasingly using public statements and social media to criticise their opponents and promote their policy positions. The post Only youths ignorant of Atiku’s history can be hoodwinked – Keyamo appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: CONAA Mobilises Artisans Nationwide for Tinubu’s Re-election, Targets 15m Votes
body: Funmi Ogundare The Coalition of Nigerian Artisan Associations (CONAA) has pledged to mobilise artisans across the 36 states of the federation to secure 15 million votes for President Bola Tinubu and Vice-President Kashim Shettima in the 2027 presidential election. The coalition, which acknowledged the economic hardship confronting Nigerians, said it believed the economic reforms introduced by the Tinubu administration would yield long-term benefits for the country. Speaking at a press conference on the 2027 elections and the role of artisans in electoral politics in Lagos, the Director-General of CONAA, Chief Segun Ajibulu, announced plans for a nationwide mobilisation campaign to sensitise artisans and secure support for the president and his deputy ahead of the election. He said the campaign would involve the production of 10 million educational pamphlets, internet radio broadcasts and social media campaigns, supported by coordinating units established across the six geopolitical zones. Ajibulu noted that the coalition would also embark on a nationwide tour beginning October 15 to educate and mobilise artisans for the 2027 elections. Describing the election as significant to Nigeria and the international community, the DG said the country’s position as Africa’s largest democracy and home to more than 200 million people made the electoral process important beyond its borders. The coalition comprises several artisan associations, including mechanics, carpenters, welders, aluminium workers, iron benders and bricklayers. Explaining its decision to support the Tinubu administration, he acknowledged that Nigeria continued to grapple with longstanding challenges, including poverty, unemployment, corruption, inadequate housing, terrorism and questions surrounding national cohesion. He, however, argued that the challenges were deeply rooted in the country’s history and could not be resolved within three or four years. According to him, “The administration has recorded progress in some areas, including security, education financing, infrastructure development and foreign reserves, which has justified our support for Tinubu and Shettima.” On security, CONAA cited reported military operations against terrorist groups, including the killing of terrorists in Borno State and the reported elimination of an Islamic state West Africa province commander, Abdussamad Ohida, in Ondo State. Ajibulu said the reported gains had helped restore confidence in the Federal Government’s capacity to address insecurity, adding that a more stable environment was necessary for artisans and small businesses to thrive. The DG also expressed support for the proposed establishment of state police, describing it as a significant step towards restructuring Nigeria’s security architecture. He argued that decentralising policing would help address security challenges that continued to discourage local and foreign investment. On education, he commended the establishment of the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND), describing it as an important intervention to expand access to tertiary education. He claimed that the programme had recorded between 1.5 million and 1.6 million direct student beneficiaries as of mid-2026, with more than N282 billion disbursed in loans to students. On the economy, Ajibulu cited improvements in remittances by the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC), arguing that increased contributions to the federation account could strengthen government revenue and support economic growth. He contrasted the corporation’s reported remittances under the current administration with the zero remittance recorded in 2022, despite NNPC declaring a profit of N2.52 trillion in its 2022 audited financial statement. The DG also endorsed the Lagos-Calabar Coastal highway and proposed additional highway projects, including the Lagos-Sokoto and Calabar-Enugu routes, saying the projects would improve connectivity and stimulate economic activities when completed. He further said Nigeria’s foreign reserves had risen above $55 billion, noting that this is the highest level in more than 18 years, with an increase of over $12.7 billion in the preceding year. He expressed optimism that sustained economic improvements would strengthen the informal sector and improve the livelihoods of artisans across the country. Ajibulu was accompanied at the press conference by the General Secretary of the Nigerian Automobile Technicians Association, Mr David Ajitumobi; the Vice-President of the Arewa Youth Consultative Forum; and the Chairman of the South-East Artisan Coalition, Mr. Fred Ojinika.

title: Airbus and SIIT Partner to Advance Indigenous Aerospace Training
body: Airbus Helicopters in Canada is supporting the development of advanced aerospace training opportunities for Indigenous communities through a partnership with the Saskatchewan Indian Institute of Technologies (SIIT) . Airbus Helicopters and Saskatchewan Indian Institute of Technologies partner to advance Indigenous aerospace training capabilities in Canada Airbus will provide SIIT instructors and students with access to leading-edge helicopter maintenance training tools and technologies, while supporting the continued development of its Aircraft Maintenance Engineer (AME) program. “Access to this equipment means our students can build their skills with technology connected to the aircraft they may encounter in the industry,” said Riel Bellegarde, President and CEO of SIIT. “We are grateful to Airbus for investing in Indigenous learners with this state-of-the-art technology and helping SIIT create more pathways into aviation careers.” “This partnership is about creating lasting capability and opening more pathways into Canada’s aerospace industry,” said Dwayne Charette, President, Airbus Helicopters in Canada. “SIIT is doing important work to equip Indigenous learners with the skills and opportunities they need to build successful careers in aerospace, and we are proud to support that work. By bringing H135 training capability to SIIT, we are investing not only in students today, but in the strength and growth of Canada’s aerospace workforce for years to come.” The donation supports the objectives of the Government of Canada’s Industrial and Technological Benefits (ITB) program, which encourages investments that strengthen Canadian industry, skills, and capabilities. The donated equipment, initially used to support technician training associated with the FAcT program, includes H135 flight control, fuel system, main gearbox and tail unit training equipment, as well as Helionix Advanced Tool Simulator (HATS). HATS is a portable, simulator-based system designed for realistic avionics and cockpit training. The Saskatchewan Indian Institute of Technologies (SIIT) is Canada’s largest credit-granting Indigenous post-secondary institution, and Saskatchewan’s exclusive provider of Aircraft Maintenance Engineer training. The Airbus H135 was selected for Canada’s Future Aircrew Training program, with 19 aircraft to be delivered to the Royal Canadian Air Force and designated the CT-153 Juno . The program will support the training of the next generation of RCAF aircrew while generating broader benefits for Canada’s aerospace and defence sector. title: WHO calls for urgent health action across the Eastern Mediterranean
body:
The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) has called for promoting, providing and protecting health in the Eastern Mediterranean region, home to some of the world’s top humanitarian crises such as Sudan, Yemen and the Occupied Palestinian Territory.
Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus was speaking on Wednesday to health leaders and senior officials attending the WHO regional committee meeting underway in Cairo, Egypt.
“Over the past year, Member States have continued to advance the health and wellbeing of their people, often under the most difficult circumstances,” he said in remarks on the annual report for the region, which spans 22 countries and territories.
He highlighted numerous achievements, including strengthened response to noncommunicable diseases – such as cardiovascular disease, cancer and diabetes –which account for roughly two thirds of all deaths in the region, with more than 2.8 million lives lost every year.
Yet, the report was also a reminder that the Eastern Mediterranean continues to face a multitude of challenges.
“This region remains the epicentre of global humanitarian need, with more than 117 million people in need of humanitarian assistance,” he said. It is also home to some of the world’s largest displacement crises.
“Conflict continues to affect millions of people across several countries and territories,” he said.
“We continue to see an appalling number of attacks on healthcare and climate-related shocks continue to place additional pressure on already fragile health systems.”
These developments are unfolding amid a sharp fall in international funding for both healthcare and humanitarian operations and increasing fiscal constraints at the national level.
“At the very moment when needs are increasing, resources are declining,” he said.
Tedros urged leaders to continue measures that promote health, such as reducing tobacco use and other risk factors for noncommunicable diseases and ensuring that all children are vaccinated.
Governments should also continue to invest in strong, equitable and resilient health systems and in health workers.
“Make every primary healthcare facility a place where a woman can receive quality care during pregnancy, where every newborn and child can get a healthy start in life and where hypertension, diabetes and cancer can be detected and managed early,” he said.
The WHO chief called for protecting health by strengthening preparedness, security and resilience.
“The threats facing this region are evolving,” he warned, noting that conflicts and outbreaks continue while climate risks continue to grow.
“Preparedness cannot be an afterthought. Preparedness saves lives before emergencies begin,” he said, underlining the need for continued investment in surveillance, laboratories, emergency workforces, resilient health facilities and supply chains.
Repeated delays in bringing lifesaving medicines, prosthetics and more from Israel into Gaza risk having devastating consequences on Palestinians who urgently need them in the war-torn enclave, the UN World Health Organization (WHO) said on Friday.

title: Yemen: WFP warns of potential ‘humanitarian catastrophe’ as fighting blocks aid delivery
body:
Intensifying fighting in Yemen has cut off life-saving assistance to 800,000 people as shifting frontlines, blocked roads and growing insecurity severely restrict access to the city of Taiz and other conflict zones, the UN World Food Programme (WFP) said on Wednesday.
“We are critically concerned about the escalating conflict, but even more so about the growing number of people we can no longer reach because of it,” said El-Khidir Daloum, WFP country director in Yemen.
He noted that many of the affected families have been displaced multiple times and were already struggling to afford even basic food items.
“This is the kind of situation that can rapidly spiral into a humanitarian catastrophe if assistance cannot move safely and reach those who need it most,” he warned.
Taiz is Yemen’s third largest city and capital of an eponymous governorate in which some districts have hosted the largest numbers of people displaced by the mounting violence between Saudi-supported Government troops and Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
Many of the displaced are now inaccessible due to ongoing fighting and imminent road closures around the governorate.
WFP said the situation is especially alarming as Taiz has some of the highest levels of food insecurity, with 10 out of 16 districts already classified at emergency levels.
The latest monitoring indicates that wheat flour stocks are nearly depleted while local markets are running out of food, according to the UN agency.
WFP and partners cannot access more than 600,000 people in Taiz who depend on humanitarian assistance, including more than 200,000 women and children.
Some 800,000 people are now out of reach nationwide, taking into account communities affected by access losses on the West Coast.
The UN continues to sound the alarm over the crisis in Yemen, where more than 18 million people face acute food insecurity. Some 2.2 million children under five are acutely malnourished, including 500,000 suffering from severe acute malnutrition, the most life-threatening form of the condition.
Recent WFP monitoring in accessible areas found that nearly 75 per cent of households were unable to meet their basic food needs – a record number for this year and a sign that food security is significantly deteriorating.
WFP said the escalation has also severely disrupted its operations, with offices breached, assets and food stocks lost and critical supply chain routes cut off.
Meanwhile, 37 of its staff are among 72 UN personnel who remain detained by Houthi de facto authorities. WFP has joined UN Secretary-General António Guterres in repeatedly calling for their immediate and unconditional release.
The agency continues to uphold the critical need for safe and sustained humanitarian access in Yemen along with immediate funding. Teams have provided emergency assistance to more than 115,000 newly displaced people are preparing to expand to include 1.5 million people when access is restored.
WFP stressed that it requires $268 million to sustain operations through 2027, which include emergency food assistance, nutrition programmes, school meals, resilience activities and critical humanitarian logistics services.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres has condemned a Houthi missile attack on Riyadh’s main airport that Saudi authorities say killed 12 people and wounded more than 300.
Yemen’s southwestern city of Taiz is facing a “devastating” humanitarian crisis as escalating tensions are dramatically driving up food prices and causing shortages of supplies, the UN Spokesperson said on Tuesday.

title: 5 Fun Projects for LLM Inference Engineering
body:
Want to understand what makes LLMs fast? Build the systems yourself.
Training large language models gets most of the attention, but once a model is trained, another engineering problem begins: how do you serve it quickly and efficiently?
LLM inference engineering focuses on reducing latency, increasing throughput, lowering memory consumption, and getting more useful work from the available hardware. This involves techniques such as KV caching, continuous batching, quantization, prefix caching, speculative decoding, optimized attention kernels, and distributed inference. The best way to learn these concepts is not by reading about them individually — it is by building something and seeing what happens. In this article, we will look at 5 projects that progressively introduce the most important ideas behind modern LLM inference systems .
If you want one project that exposes you to almost the entire inference stack, this is probably the best place to start. Nano-vLLM is a small educational implementation of a vLLM -style inference engine, with its core implementation small enough to actually read. It includes scheduling, KV-cache block management, prefix caching, tensor parallelism, CUDA graphs, and other optimizations while using a real Qwen model. Instead of simply cloning it and running the example, rebuild one component at a time: first perform normal autoregressive generation, then add KV caching, then batching, then block-based KV-cache allocation. Benchmark tokens per second after every addition. By the end, you will understand concepts like PagedAttention and continuous batching in a much better way.
A normal attention implementation uses large matrices and repeatedly moves data between GPU memory and fast on-chip memory. FlashAttention restructures the computation to reduce that memory traffic. Triton's official tutorial provides an implementation of a FlashAttention-style fused attention kernel, making it a great starting point for learning kernel-level optimization. This video also builds FlashAttention from scratch while explaining HBM versus SRAM, arithmetic intensity, tiling, online softmax, benchmarking, and finally integrating the kernel into an inference engine. I would recommend it to those who prefer video-based learning. This project teaches you that making an LLM faster is not always about doing fewer mathematical operations. Sometimes it is about moving less data .
Take one small open model and run several versions — for example FP16, INT8, and 4-bit. Measure model size, peak memory, model-load time, time to first token (TTFT), tokens per second, and quality on a small evaluation set. Hugging Face supports multiple quantization approaches, including AWQ, GPTQ, bitsandbytes-based 8-bit and 4-bit loading, and several newer formats. llama.cpp also supports a wide range of low-bit quantization formats and runs across CPUs, Apple Silicon, NVIDIA GPUs, and several other hardware backends. For an extra challenge, quantize both the weights and KV cache and see whether using fewer bits always improves latency or not.
Speculative decoding is one of the most enjoyable inference optimizations to implement. Instead of asking the expensive target model to generate every token sequentially, a smaller draft model proposes several candidate tokens. The target model then verifies those candidates together. Choose a small target/draft pair, implement normal autoregressive decoding as the baseline, and then build the draft-and-verify loop. Track not only tokens per second but also acceptance rate — which is the percentage of draft tokens accepted by the target model. Then experiment with drafting 2, 4, 6, or 8 tokens at a time. The Columbia high-performance machine learning project experiments with both speculative decoding and quantization using the Llama model family while evaluating latency, throughput, perplexity, and code-generation quality. An interesting extension is to test different workloads. Code, repetitive text, factual question-answering, and creative writing can produce very different draft acceptance behavior.
The final project is a capstone where we combine KV caching, quantization, batching, and benchmarking into a single system. Start with a basic OpenAI-compatible inference endpoint. Deploy it on a GPU. Add streaming. Add load testing. Instrument TTFT and token-generation latency. Introduce quantization. Experiment with speculative decoding. Add prefix caching. Push concurrency higher and identify what breaks first. The Time to First Token project provides an interesting structure for doing this. Its roadmap revolves around continuously improving one inference service rather than completing disconnected exercises. It covers deployment, instrumentation, heavy concurrency testing, quantization, speculative decoding, routing, and reproducible benchmarking. For an even harder extension, add a request router that decides which model or GPU should process each request based on queue length, expected generation length, or latency requirements.
You need enough machine learning knowledge to understand transformers and attention, but many of the hardest problems have surprisingly little to do with training models. They involve memory allocation, scheduling, batching, caching, kernel optimization, networking, load testing, and figuring out how to keep very expensive hardware busy.
This is why building projects is such a good way to learn the field.
Start by generating one token inefficiently. Add a KV cache. Batch several users together. Break the cache into pages. Quantize the weights. Let a smaller model speculate about future tokens. Write a GPU kernel. Then put everything behind an API and bombard it with requests. By the time you finish, tools such as vLLM and SGLang will no longer feel like black boxes. You will have built smaller versions of many of the ideas that make them fast.
Kanwal Mehreen is a machine learning engineer and a technical writer with a profound passion for data science and the intersection of AI with medicine. She co-authored the ebook "Maximizing Productivity with ChatGPT". As a Google Generation Scholar 2022 for APAC, she champions diversity and academic excellence. She's also recognized as a Teradata Diversity in Tech Scholar, Mitacs Globalink Research Scholar, and Harvard WeCode Scholar. Kanwal is an ardent advocate for change, having founded FEMCodes to empower women in STEM fields.

title: F-35C fighter lands on Ford-class aircraft carrier for the first time
body:
A Lockheed Martin F-35C Lightning II stealth fighter landed aboard the future USS John F. Kennedy (CVN 79) on October 13, becoming the first aircraft of its type to land on a Gerald R. Ford-class aircraft carrier.
The aircraft belonged to Air Test and Evaluation Squadron 23 (VX-23), known as the Salty Dogs, a U.S. Navy test unit based at Naval Air Station Patuxent River in Maryland.
Follow Air Data News: WhatsApp | Instagram | LinkedIn | Twitter | Facebook
The landing was conducted as part of aircraft compatibility testing aboard Kennedy, the second carrier of the Ford class, which is currently undergoing trials ahead of its formal delivery to the Navy in 2027.
The event is particularly significant because the first ship of the class, USS Gerald R. Ford (CVN 78) , entered service in July 2017 but has yet to deploy with the F-35C, despite being designed to accommodate the fifth-generation fighter.
Although Gerald R. Ford is capable of launching and recovering the F-35C, it has not received all the modifications required to support the aircraft during extended operational deployments.
The distinction involves more than the carrier's electromagnetic catapults and arresting equipment. The F-35C requires additional infrastructure to support maintenance, logistics and other aspects of operating the stealth fighter at sea.
According to previous U.S. Navy explanations, the modifications include reinforced jet blast deflectors and specialized spaces and equipment associated with F-35C operations.
Without these upgrades, the carrier can accommodate the fighter for limited periods but cannot routinely sustain an embarked F-35C squadron throughout a deployment.
Gerald R. Ford has consequently continued operating with Boeing F/A-18E/F Super Hornets as its principal strike fighters.
Kennedy followed a different construction approach. The Navy originally intended to install the necessary F-35C modifications after delivery, as planned for the first carrier.
However, the service changed its strategy in 2020, incorporating the upgrades into the construction program so that Kennedy could deploy with the F-35C from the beginning of its operational career.
The decision contributed to the carrier's extended construction schedule, alongside difficulties involving its Advanced Arresting Gear (AAG) and Advanced Weapons Elevators (AWE).
The first F-35C landing occurred just two weeks after the Navy took preliminary acceptance of Kennedy on September 29 .
Under that arrangement, the ship and its crew can conduct operations and testing at sea even though Newport News Shipbuilding has not completed all contractual work.
The Navy reported that Kennedy was approximately 99% complete at the time of preliminary acceptance. Four of its 11 advanced weapons elevators still required final testing, although the seven completed units already provided access to the ship's ammunition magazines.
The carrier's formal delivery is scheduled for spring 2027, following several postponements from earlier targets.
Kennedy is expected to replace USS Nimitz (CVN 68) in the Pacific Fleet and will eventually be based at Naval Base Kitsap-Bremerton in Washington state.
The Navy has not yet announced which carrier air wing or F-35C squadron will make the ship's first operational deployment.

title: INEC Commences PVC Collection, Display Of Voter Register In FCT
body: The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) has commenced the display of the Register of Voters and collection of Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs) across the territory. According to a public notice signed by Mrs. Abimbola Oladunjoye, on behalf of the FCT Resident Electoral Commissioner, the exercise is being held in all 62 Registration Area Centres (RACs) in the FCT and will end on Thursday, October 15, 2026. The commission, however, said that the exercise would continue at the six area 2council offices from October 16, 2026. It urged all registrants in the FCT to take advantage of the exercise to check the correctness of their names on the register, confirm and identify their Polling Units, raise objections to the inclusion of ineligible persons, and collect their PVCs if they registered, transferred, or updated their records before 2026 and are yet to collect their cards. The commission clarified that PVCs for the 2026 Continuous Voter Registration exercise were currently not available, adding that voters would be duly notified as soon as the cards were ready for collection. INEC FCT advised members of the public to call 0700 225 5634 632 or 0701 578 0499 for further enquiries. INEC ‎Chairman Joash Amupitan, during a strategic engagement meeting with journalists in Abuja, announced that the cards would be distributed from October 9, 2026. Amupitan also said that the Commission was strengthening the use of technology to ensure that stolen, lost, or compromised voter cards cannot be used by unauthorised persons to interfere with the electoral process. According to him, Nigeria now has 103 million registered voters , with Lagos, Kano and Kaduna having the highest number of voters. He disclosed that the FCT has 1,772,043 voters. The chairman also said that the national voter register showed that male voters account for 53,528,218, representing 51.75 per cent, while female voters number 49,900,497, representing 48.25 per cent. He added that the age profile revealed that the register is dominated by voters between the ages of 35 and 49, who account for 43,265,946 voters, or 41.83 per cent of the total. title: SEC to develop Social Bond Guidelines; over half of listed firms report on ESG indicators
body: The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is in the process of developing Social Bond Guidelines aligned with the International Capital Market Association’s ICMA Social Bond Principles (SBP). According to the SEC, the guidelines would aim to encourage the development of a credible and transparent social bond market, promote financing for projects that deliver positive social outcomes while ensuring integrity, transparency, and accountability in the issuance and reporting of social bonds. Eligible uses of proceeds will include affordable basic infrastructure, essential services such as healthcare and education, affordable housing, employment and Small and Medium Enterprises support, food security, and the empowerment of vulnerable populations. Overall, the SEC’s approach is explicit about aligning capital market development with national and global sustainability goals. The SEC adopted a structured approach to integrating sustainable finance into the domestic capital market under the Capital Market Master Plan (2020–2029). Its strategy rests on three mutually reinforcing pillars: Standardised Disclosure, Credible Green Finance Instruments, and Strong Governance and Enforcement. These measures aim to enhance transparency, improve disclosure quality, protect investors, reduce greenwashing risks, and mobilise private capital for environmentally and socially beneficial projects. To this end, SEC approved the Ghana Stock Exchange (GSE)’s ESG Disclosure Guidance Manual in 2022, which adopts the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) Standards as the common ESG reporting framework for listed companies. The manual guides materiality, sector-specific disclosures, and the integration of ESG into corporate strategy and reporting. By promoting a single internationally recognised framework, the SEC seeks to improve comparability, strengthen disclosure quality, and boost investor confidence. More than half of the 39 listed companies now report on ESG indicators, reflecting progress while highlighting the need for continued capacity building.

title: US makes no official statements on slowdown in Starlink service for Ukraine — Kremlin
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. There has been no official statement from the US on the slowdown of the Starlink service for the Ukrainian armed forces, so it is too early to jump to conclusions, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
"How do we know this? This is just completely scattered information. 'What if…' Indeed, there is a lot of information suggesting that there are some restrictions on the provision of intelligence and early warning information about our missile launches," the spokesman said, commenting on the slowdown in Starlink services. "But, on the other hand, there have also been statements from Washington that the assistance is continuing," the spokesman pointed out.
"We need to wait for some more or less specific information here," Peskov stressed.
"We don’t know what the US has done. How can we speculate about what it can or cannot do?" he noted, responding to a question about whether Washington could do more than just slow down Starlink. "We haven’t heard any official statements from representatives of [Elon] Musk’s company [which owns the service], nor have we heard any official statements from representatives of the Kiev regime on this matter," the spokesman stressed.
"We’ve heard statements from [US President Donald] Trump that aid is continuing. Let’s analyze the information as it comes in and not rush to conclusions," Peskov concluded.

title: Georgian opposition leader Japaridze detained at Turkish airport
body: Georgian opposition politician Zurab Japaridze has been detained at an airport in Turkey while travelling to Brussels. The Alliance of Liberals and Democrats for Europe (ALDE) reported that Japaridze was held in a cell and had his passport and luggage confiscated. The organisation added that he would be returned to Georgia on Thursday. The document shared by Japaridze on Facebook states that Turkey has imposed a five-year entry ban on him, from 20 November 2025 to 20 November 2030, under code G-87. It also states that the ban could be extended to 10 years. Japaridze leads Girchi — More Freedom, a member party of ALDE. He was travelling to Brussels via Turkey to attend the Renew Europe Leaders’ Summit, scheduled for Thursday.Renew Europe is a liberal political group in the EU Parliament. In a statement published on X, ALDE expressed concern over Japaridze’s detention, saying it regretted that he would be unable to attend the summit. We're concerned to learn that @Zuraja, leader of ALDE member party @GIRCHIMF has been detained at the airport in Turkey, held in a cell with his passport and luggage confiscated and will be sent back to Georgia tomorrow. He was transiting en route to Brussels where he was invited and was due to participate in the @RenewEurope Leaders’ Summit. We regret that he will not be able to participate and lament that such pressures continue to be placed on the work and movements of opposition parties who seek a pro-European and democratic future for their country. — ALDE Party (@ALDEParty) October 14, 2026 ‘We lament that such pressures continue to be placed on the work and movements of opposition parties who seek a pro-European and democratic future for their country’, the organisation wrote. Japaridze also posted about the incident on Facebook, saying he had been changing flights in Turkey when he was detained at the airport. ‘As they explain it to me, I have been banned from entering Turkey since November 2025. They have apparently received some information about me from official Georgian institutions’, Japaridze wrote. He added that he would be returned to Tbilisi the following morning and had consequently lost the opportunity to attend important meetings. He said there was nothing else to worry about. ‘Sabotage’ case against Georgian opposition politicians moves forward Some of the politicians involved in the case are already serving sentences in other cases. OC Media Mikheil Gvadzabia OC Media has asked Georgia’s Interior Ministry whether it shared information about Japaridze with Turkish authorities. In 2025, Japaridze served a seven-month sentence for failing to appear before a temporary parliamentary investigative commission. He was released in December of that year. Whilst in prison, in November 2025, the authorities brought additional charges against him, including sabotage and assisting a foreign country in hostile activities. Japaridze is among a number of opposition politicians in Georgia, who have been accused of treason. As he is still facing these charges, Japardize requires the Prosecutor General’s Office’s permission to leave Georgia. On 20 September, he wrote on Facebook that he had been granted permission to travel to Vilnius.

title: Putin Convenes Top Russian Officials to Discuss Cybersecurity
body:
Russia n President Vladimir Putin will discuss cybersecurity with top officials on Wednesday, the Kremlin said, describing it as an increasingly pressing issue but denying the meeting was prompted by a spate of Ukrainian drone attacks on Russia n data centers.
"Artificial intelligence technologies bring many benefits and advantages, boosting efficiency. But at the same time, of course, attempts by various states to weaponize these new technologies... pose threats to entire sectors of any country's economy," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
"Naturally, we are no exception, and we must be prepared for these challenges. That is why the president is holding this meeting today."
Peskov said the meeting was not connected with Ukrainian drone strikes in the past week on four Russia n data centers — three belonging to tech group Yandex and one to Sberbank.
"No, this is a much more systemic meeting. It is not connected to those specific, isolated attacks," he said.
The participants will include government ministers, top security officials, the head of Sberbank and Central Bank Governor Elvira Nabiullina, Peskov added.

title: Kyiv city energy grid strikes up 2.6-fold in 2026 – mayor
body:
The city of Kyiv's energy supply facilities have been hit by nearly 50 missile and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) strikes so far in 2026, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said while addressing the Verkhovna Rada on Wednesday.
"In 2022, 12 missiles and UAVs struck Thermal Power Plants 5 and 6. In 2023, there were seven; in 2024, zero; and in 2025, 19. This year, there have already been nearly 50 missile and UAV strikes on our energy supply systems. Throughout this time, specialists have been working, restoring equipment and preparing facilities for winter every year, and Kyiv has stood firm," he said.
According to the mayor, the capital is under constant enemy attacks targeting its infrastructure, energy sector, industry and businesses, but the city is trying to maintain essential services under martial law.
At the same time, Klitschko emphasized that the overnight attack on October 14 struck several key energy facilities in the city and the surrounding region, causing fairly serious damage.
The mayor also sharply criticized the central government, saying that funds had been blocked and payments suspended, freezing energy resilience projects not only in the capital but also in other territorial communities.
"You could even blame Klitschko for World War III, but this is not just a question I have. Each of you has the same question: Where is the air defense protecting the capital of Ukraine? Where is the protection for Ukrenergo's facilities? title: Griko language: Is this Italian dialect Magna Graecia’s last echo?
body: LECCE, October 2026 — The Griko language of southern Italy became a talking point on X on Tuesday 13 October 2026. A widely shared thread asked whether the dialect is the last living link to Magna Graecia. Why the Griko language is trending The interest began with a thread by X user Iain Cameron , posted on 13 October. It opened with a bold claim. “In a handful of villages in southern Italy, people still speak what may be the last surviving linguistic descendant of ‘Magna Graecia’.” By the morning of Wednesday 14 October, the post had passed 112,000 views and almost 2,000 likes on X. As a result, the platform turned the conversation into a trending story about the Griko language and its ancient roots. Oxford classicist Armand D’Angour shared the thread with his own followers. He also linked the name of the Calabrian mafia, ’Ndrangheta, to the Greek word “andragathia” , which he glossed as “men of honour” . However, many replies challenged the headline idea. Some users said the dialect owes more to Byzantine Greek than to the ancient colonists. Others pointed out that Salento and Calabria each have their own variety. Grecanico and the Calabrian villages Strictly speaking, the Griko language belongs to Salento, in the province of Lecce in Apulia. Its sister variety, Grecanico, survives in the Bovesia area around Bova, in the Aspromonte mountains of Reggio Calabria. Linguists group the two as Italiot Greek. Even so, several speakers on X stressed that they differ in sound and vocabulary. In Bova, a museum named after the German scholar Gerhard Rohlfs is dedicated to the Calabrian Greek dialect. Unlike Salento, the Calabrian area is small and remote, and its villages sit high in the mountains. Greek City Times has followed both communities, from its report on Grecanico in Calabria to Ambassador Sourani’s visit to the Calabrian villages in August 2026. Still, the speaker figures behind the trend deserve a closer look. According to a study by Angeliki Douri and Dario De Santis , the Grecìa Salentina enclave covers nine villages. About 41,500 people live there. Specifically, the list includes Calimera, Castrignano dei Greci, Corigliano d’Otranto, Martano, Martignano, Melpignano, Soleto, Sternatia and Zollino. The authors put Griko language speakers at about 20,500, nearly half the population. Most of them are elderly. They also found that the dialect has already died out in Melpignano and Soleto. Other researchers say fewer than 20,000 people speak it natively, mostly people over 60. They also treat that figure as likely too high. A debate over origins Arguments on X mirror a scholarly dispute that is more than 150 years old. In 1870, the Italian linguist Giuseppe Morosi traced the dialect to Byzantine-era Greek. In his view, waves of settlers brought it around 1000 AD. Later, Rohlfs took a different view. Following the Greek linguist Georgios Hatzidakis, he argued that the Griko language grew directly from the speech of Magna Graecia. The Greek colonisation of southern Italy began in the 8th century BC. Still, many linguists now take a middle view. They see Griko as largely based on Koine Greek. At the same time, it keeps some older Doric features. Because of this, both camps in the online debate can point to evidence for their case. Unlike other Greek dialects, the Griko language uses the Latin alphabet. In addition, speakers of Modern Greek understand it only in part. Centuries of contact with Italian have shaped its words and sounds. Laws, songs and the next generation Italy gave the communities legal protection in 1999. Law 482 of 15 December 1999 lists Greek among the historic minority languages that Italy protects. Albanian, Catalan and Slovene sit on the same list. At the same time, international bodies list the dialect as at risk. The Endangered Languages Project rates the Griko language as severely endangered. UNESCO gives both Italiot Greek varieties the same status, and speaker numbers are falling fast. Music has done much to keep the dialect in public view. Salento groups such as Ghetonia and Canzoniere Grecanico Salentino perform in Griko, while local associations run courses and festivals. Greek City Times has also profiled the villages of Grecìa Salentina . There, road signs still greet visitors in the dialect. Overall, the 13 October thread gave a centuries-old Griko language debate a new global audience. Whether its roots lie in Magna Graecia or Byzantium, its future depends on younger residents. Unless they speak it, the dialect will fade. Source: X The post Griko language: Is this Italian dialect Magna Graecia’s last echo? appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: UBEC: $552m World Bank grant targets 29m Nigerian children, 500,000 teachers
body: …13,000 classrooms planned as agency warns states over 2027 budget provisions By Joseph Erunke, Abuja The Universal Basic Education Commission, UBEC, has unveiled an ambitious plan to reach 29 million Nigerian children with improved basic education under a $552.18 million World Bank-supported programme, warning state governments that failure to provide the required funding could jeopardise its implementation. The Human Capital Opportunities for Prosperity and Equity in Education (HOPE-EDU) programme is also targeting 500,000 teachers, 65,000 public schools and 10,000 non-formal learning centres nationwide, alongside the construction of 13,000 new classrooms. But the Federal Government’s ambition to expand access to quality education now faces a critical test at the state level, with UBEC insisting that governors must demonstrate the political will and financial commitment required to unlock the programme’s benefits. The Executive Secretary of UBEC, Dr Aisha Garba, raised the concern on Tuesday in Abuja at a two-day meeting with chairmen of State Universal Basic Education Boards (SUBEBs) on implementation readiness. Garba disclosed that the programme became effective on February 27, 2026, and had entered its implementation phase, stressing that states must act swiftly to incorporate relevant activities and funding provisions into their 2027 budgets. According to her, several of the programme’s disbursement-linked indicators depend on states making adequate budgetary allocations, warning that failure to meet the requirements could affect their ability to access the corresponding funds. She said: “A lot of the deliverables for Year 1 will require provisions in the states’ 2027 budget.” The UBEC boss, therefore, directed SUBEB chairmen to take the programme’s implementation report to their respective state executives, secure their commitment and ensure that the necessary financial provisions were made in good time. The warning places state governments at the centre of the initiative, which is designed to improve learning outcomes, reduce inequalities in access to education and strengthen accountability in the delivery of basic education across Nigeria. Garba explained that HOPE-EDU adopts a results-based financing model under which disbursements are tied to the achievement of agreed targets and performance indicators. Under its funding structure, $262.239 million has been earmarked for improving the quality of basic education, $123.9 million for expanding access, while $133.611 million is allocated to strengthening key systems. The three result areas are designed to address persistent challenges in the basic education sector, including poor learning outcomes, inadequate educational access and weaknesses in institutional capacity and accountability. Garba said the quality component would focus on improving teaching standards, providing essential learning resources and raising pupils’ achievement levels in participating states. A key intervention under this component is the adoption of the Structured Pedagogy Programme (SPP), which is intended to strengthen the teaching of literacy and numeracy in primary schools. She said the programme would build on existing Universal Basic Education interventions while complementing other government initiatives in governance and primary healthcare. The UBEC executive secretary disclosed that the programme’s three result areas have different participation requirements. According to her, the first result area, which focuses on improving education quality, is open to 33 states, with participation potentially extending to all 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, subject to involvement in the HOPE-GOV operations. The second result area, which targets increased access to education, is designed for 15 states with the highest populations of out-of-school children that also satisfy other eligibility requirements. The third component, focused on strengthening key systems, is open to all 36 states and the FCT. The varying eligibility conditions mean that states must understand the requirements attached to each component and ensure they meet the relevant benchmarks to benefit from the programme. Garba said successful implementation would require close coordination among state ministries of education, SUBEBs, Local Education Authorities, schools and School-Based Management Committees. She urged SUBEB chairmen, whom she described as key drivers of basic education implementation at the state level, to take ownership of the programme and ensure that their states meet the agreed targets and verification requirements. Garba said the initiative, introduced under President Bola Tinubu’s administration, was intended to ensure that every Nigerian child, particularly those in rural communities, marginalised populations and out-of-school groups, had equitable opportunities to access quality education. However, she emphasised that achieving this objective would depend on translating policy commitments into concrete action, particularly through adequate budgetary provisions and effective coordination at the state level. “The success of HOPE-EDU rests on your shoulders. Let us work together to ensure that no state is left behind,” she told the SUBEB chairmen. She urged participants to engage actively during the meeting, seek clarification on implementation requirements and return to their respective states as advocates for the programme. Garba also commended the National Programme Coordinator, the Programme Manager and the HOPE-EDU team for organising the meeting, while acknowledging the support of the Federal Ministry of Education, the World Bank and other technical partners. Earlier, the Programme Manager of HOPE-EDU, Mr Olumayowa Aleshin, presented an overview of the initiative, outlining its funding arrangements, implementation targets and key milestones. The programme’s framework requires participating states to meet specified performance targets and verification requirements before qualifying for the corresponding disbursements. With 29 million children, 500,000 teachers, thousands of schools and non-formal learning centres covered by its targets, HOPE-EDU represents a major intervention in Nigeria’s basic education sector. Its ultimate impact, however, will depend on whether federal and state authorities can convert the funding commitments into classrooms, better teaching, improved learning outcomes and wider access to education for millions of children. title: Elbit Systems to Produce Laser Warning Systems in Sweden
body:
Israeli defence company Elbit Systems plans to establish its first European production and maintenance centre for Laser Warning Systems (LWS) in Sweden. Scheduled to become operational in 2027, the facility will provide local assembly, integration, maintenance and lifecycle support for European customers. The investment is intended to strengthen the company’s industrial presence in Europe while reducing dependence on production and support facilities outside the region. Elbit Systems is expanding its European industrial footprint through a new facility dedicated to laser warning technology. The planned centre, to be established by Elbit Systems Sweden, will become the company’s first European production and maintenance facility specifically for Laser Warning Systems. According to the company, the centre is expected to begin operations in 2027. It will undertake local production-related activities, including assembly and integration, as well as maintenance and lifecycle support for systems operated by European armed forces. The initiative forms part of Elbit Systems’ strategy to expand its industrial presence in Europe and develop local technological capabilities. By transferring selected production and support activities to Sweden, the company aims to improve system availability, shorten delivery times and provide European customers with more direct access to technical support. The facility is also intended to contribute to European defence industrial resilience by establishing additional capabilities within the region. Passive Detection of Laser Threats The new centre will focus on the next generation of Elbit Systems’ passive Laser Warning Systems. These systems are designed to detect and locate laser emissions directed towards a protected military platform, providing its crew or protection systems with information about a potential threat. Laser warning receivers are an important component of modern platform self-protection architectures. Laser emissions may indicate that a vehicle or other military asset is being observed, its range is being measured or it is being designated as a target for a laser-guided weapon. By detecting such emissions, a laser warning system can provide an early indication of possible hostile activity. Depending on the platform and its equipment, the warning may allow the crew to take evasive action, deploy obscurants or initiate other protective measures. Unlike active sensors, passive laser warning systems do not need to emit their own signals to detect incoming laser radiation. This enables them to monitor the surrounding environment without revealing their position through their own laser emissions. According to Elbit Systems, its next-generation LWS is designed to detect and localise laser threats rapidly, giving operators additional time to assess the situation and respond. Decentralised Architecture for Easier Integration A central feature of the new system generation is its decentralised architecture. According to Elbit Systems, this reduces the number of components required for installation and limits the modifications needed to integrate the system into existing military platforms. The design is also intended to simplify integration with existing command-and-control systems, allowing laser threat information to be incorporated into a wider situational awareness and self-protection architecture. This is particularly relevant when upgrading vehicles and other military equipment already in service. Retrofitting additional protection systems can require modifications to vehicle structures, electrical installations and onboard electronics. A system designed to minimise these changes may therefore simplify integration and reduce the effort associated with modernisation programmes. Elbit Systems states that its laser warning technology is already deployed by armed forces internationally as part of integrated platform self-protection suites. The company has not identified which customers or platforms will receive systems manufactured or assembled at the planned Swedish facility. Sweden as a Northern European Industrial Hub Elbit Systems Sweden was established in 2020 and has since expanded to more than 100 employees across the country. The subsidiary serves as a regional hub for the group’s activities in Northern Europe and cooperates with Sweden’s defence industry and military organisations. In recent years, the Swedish subsidiary has participated in defence and digitalisation programmes supporting the Swedish Armed Forces. The planned LWS centre would extend these activities into local production and maintenance of specialised protection equipment, adding industrial capabilities to the company’s existing regional presence. Elbit Systems also intends to transfer relevant technologies to support the new operation. According to the company, this is designed to strengthen local expertise and establish more resilient supply and support arrangements for European and NATO customers. The Swedish location is significant in the context of Europe’s wider efforts to strengthen defence production and reduce vulnerabilities in military supply chains. Local manufacturing and maintenance capacity can provide additional flexibility in responding to changing procurement requirements and sustaining equipment already in service. However, the extent to which the new facility will independently manufacture components, rather than assemble and integrate systems supplied from elsewhere, has not yet been specified. Local Support and European Supply Chains Beyond initial production, the planned centre is intended to provide long-term maintenance and lifecycle support. For military customers, these activities can be as important as the original delivery of a system. Access to regional maintenance facilities may reduce the need to return equipment to manufacturers outside Europe and could help shorten repair and turnaround times. Elbit Systems expects the Swedish centre to improve availability and delivery schedules while strengthening its ability to support European armed forces over the service life of their equipment. “This initiative represents an important step for us and reflects our commitment to strengthening our capabilities to develop, deliver and produce locally,” said Tobias Wennberg, CEO of Elbit Systems Sweden. “It also aligns well with our core technologies and enables us to expand our scope going forward. Through the establishment of this centre and the transfer of advanced technologies, we aim to support Swedish, European and NATO customers with reliable, long-term and locally supported self-protection solutions with secure and sovereign supply chains.” The announcement reflects the increasing importance of regional industrial capabilities in European defence procurement. While the underlying laser warning technology remains part of Elbit Systems’ portfolio, the new Swedish centre is intended to bring production-related activities and long-term support closer to the armed forces that operate the equipment. If the facility becomes operational as planned in 2027, it will represent a further expansion of the Israeli company’s European manufacturing and support network. Elbit Systems expects the Swedish centre to improve availability and delivery schedules while strengthening its ability to support European armed forces over the service life of their equipment. “This initiative represents an important step for us and reflects our commitment to strengthening our capabilities to develop, deliver and produce locally,” said Tobias Wennberg, CEO of Elbit Systems Sweden. “It also aligns well with our core technologies and enables us to expand our scope going forward. Through the establishment of this centre and the transfer of advanced technologies, we aim to support Swedish, European and NATO customers with reliable, long-term and locally supported self-protection solutions with secure and sovereign supply chains.” The announcement reflects the increasing importance of regional industrial capabilities in European defence procurement. While the underlying laser warning technology remains part of Elbit Systems’ portfolio, the new Swedish centre is intended to bring production-related activities and long-term support closer to the armed forces that operate the equipment. If the facility becomes operational as planned in 2027, it will represent a further expansion of the Israeli company’s European manufacturing and support network. Laser warning receivers are an important component of modern platform self-protection architectures. Laser emissions may indicate that a vehicle or other military asset is being observed, its range is being measured or it is being designated as a target for a laser-guided weapon. By detecting such emissions, a laser warning system can provide an early indication of possible hostile activity. Depending on the platform and its equipment, the warning may allow the crew to take evasive action, deploy obscurants or initiate other protective measures. Unlike active sensors, passive laser warning systems do not need to emit their own signals to detect incoming laser radiation. This enables them to monitor the surrounding environment without revealing their position through their own laser emissions. According to Elbit Systems, its next-generation LWS is designed to detect and localise laser threats rapidly, giving operators additional time to assess the situation and respond. Decentralised Architecture for Easier Integration A central feature of the new system generation is its decentralised architecture. According to Elbit Systems, this reduces the number of components required for installation and limits the modifications needed to integrate the system into existing military platforms. The design is also intended to simplify integration with existing command-and-control systems, allowing laser threat information to be incorporated into a wider situational awareness and self-protection architecture. This is particularly relevant when upgrading vehicles and other military equipment already in service. Retrofitting additional protection systems can require modifications to vehicle structures, electrical installations and onboard electronics. A system designed to minimise these changes may therefore simplify integration and reduce the effort associated with modernisation programmes. Elbit Systems states that its laser warning technology is already deployed by armed forces internationally as part of integrated platform self-protection suites. The company has not identified which customers or platforms will receive systems manufactured or assembled at the planned Swedish facility. Sweden as a Northern European Industrial Hub Elbit Systems Sweden was established in 2020 and has since expanded to more than 100 employees across the country. The subsidiary serves as a regional hub for the group’s activities in Northern Europe and cooperates with Sweden’s defence industry and military organisations. In recent years, the Swedish subsidiary has participated in defence and digitalisation programmes supporting the Swedish Armed Forces. The planned LWS centre would extend these activities into local production and maintenance of specialised protection equipment, adding industrial capabilities to the company’s existing regional presence. Elbit Systems also intends to transfer relevant technologies to support the new operation. title: Insurance firms have up till January 2027 to incorporate ESG in financial reporting
body: Beginning January 2027, all insurance companies will have to incorporate Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) in their financial reporting or face sanctions. This follows the integration of ESG principles within the insurance industry in 2023 by the National Insurance Commission (NIC). In partnership with the German Development Agency for International Cooperation (GIZ) and Financial Sector Deepening (FSD) Africa, the NIC conducted a comprehensive diagnostic study to evaluate ESG integration across the sector, aimed at identifying key gaps, opportunities, and areas for further advancement. It then set a voluntary deadline for January 2026. The move is part of Sustainable Finance Roadmap led by the Bank of Ghana and with support from the other financial regulators. The NIC initiated its integration of ESG principles within the insurance industry in 2023. A targeted survey was implemented to collect data from industry stakeholders. This allowed the NIC to assess the market’s adoption of ESG principles and ESG-related risks and opportunities, as well as to gauge the extent of ESG integration within company operations. Based on the survey findings, the NIC developed and issued an industry guideline in December 2024, outlining general and specific requirements for regulated entities on ESG integration across the insurance value chain. To facilitate industry compliance with these guidelines, the NIC introduced a suite of toolkits designed for self-assessment. These resources enable insurers to evaluate their current position regarding ESG and lay the groundwork for establishing a comprehensive Roadmap. Subsequently, the NIC undertook several capacity-building initiatives addressing persons in charge of governance on the relevance of institutionalising ESG principles across their operations. Other training sessions were delivered to the senior management and persons designated as ESG-responsible officers across the sector. The training emphasised the importance of integrating ESG into core business processes, highlighting that such integration extends beyond regulatory compliance and represents a strategic step towards long-term sustainability.

title: State Street plans 100 jobs for Emiratis at Al Ain hub as it aims for July 2027 opening
body: US financial services group State Street plans to employ about 100 Emiratis at its Al Ain operating centre as it targets a July 2027 opening date. The new centre is expected to have 300 staff by 2030, with technology, artificial intelligence, operations and client services among its main areas. About a third of the workforce will come from State Street’s global centres, another third will be recruited from the UAE talent pool and a third will be Emiratis, said Jack Keshishian, State Street’s head of Middle East and North Africa (excluding Saudi Arabia and Bahrain). Preparations are under way, including arranging links with UAE universities through its partnership with the Abu Dhabi Investment Office. “We are looking at the go date of the first of July,” Mr Keshishian said. This is earlier than the “end of next year” start date outlined at the Al Ain Future Business Forum in September. State Street announced the centre in January. Mr Keshishian said the current focus was on building a workforce of 300 over three years to 2030, with the possibility of future expansion if there was sufficient demand. “Obviously, we have ambitions to grow because [the] Middle East is a growth market for us, and we take a long-term view,” he said. Opportunities for graduates The company expects to identify potential graduate recruits in the first quarter of next year. The “talent pool” in Al Ain is a key reason the company chose to set up there, alongside the potential to sustain and grow the business, Mr Keshishian said. AI and technology will help automate work and improve the use of data, while employees will also provide operational and client services. Mr Keshishian said technology and staff would work together to improve efficiency for clients. He did not provide an investment figure for the centre and said spending would continue over the coming three years. Why Al Ain? State Street’s decision is based on its assessment of the available workforce and the potential to sustain and expand an operation in the city, Mr Keshishian said. The company has had a presence in Abu Dhabi since 2018. Its new centre will broaden that operation beyond the capital and support clients across several markets. “I think despite the tension in the region, we are seeing global institutions establishing their presence here in the UAE and the wider region, and we haven't seen any sort of a change in that,” he said. The company has also submitted an application to expand the services it can offer at Abu Dhabi’s financial centre ADGM. Subject to approval, these would include safeguarding clients’ financial assets and providing administrative services for investment funds.

title: Russia to decide on talks with US, Ukraine based on Moscow’s interests — Kremlin
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Moscow will decide whether to resume trilateral consultations on the Ukrainian settlement with Kiev and Washington at a later date and strictly in accordance with Russia’s national interests, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
"After Ukraine tried to disrupt our elections, we will now consider when to resume the trilateral talks," he said, reiterating Moscow’s principled position.
"We will do so strictly in accordance with our national interests," Peskov emphasized.

title: Novak outlines factors behind future easing of sanctions on Russian energy sector
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Any further easing of sanctions against the Russian fuel and energy sector will depend on the current market situation and the state of relations, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters on the sidelines of Russian Energy Week.
"We cannot predict things in advance. It will all depend on the current market situation and relations [with the US - TASS]," he said.
On October 9, Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump held a telephone conversation, during which they discussed, among other topics, the supply of petroleum products. The Russian leader stated that Moscow had confirmed its readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US and global markets. According to Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, Russia is beginning to lift its ban on diesel fuel exports ahead of schedule; it is prepared to supply 300,000 tonnes of diesel in October, 500,000 tonnes in November, and 1 million tonnes in December, with the aim of eventually increasing this volume to 3 million tonnes per month. Meanwhile, the US administration is exempting shipments of Russian diesel fuel to global markets from US sanctions until April 7, 2027.
The Russian Energy Week international forum is taking place in Moscow from October 14 to 16, supported by the Russian government, the Ministry of Energy, and the Moscow government. The forum is organized by the Roscongress Foundation. TASS is an information partner of the event.
