NOTE: Some of the photos are taken from the Prusa official guides and belong to them.
In the last couple of weeks I’ve been working on upgrading my 3d printer. I have a Core One that I assembled from a kit, and I got an upgrade kit that includes the INDX and Gen2 upgrades. This hardware is new (I preordered it), so it contains a wonderland of undiscovered problems.
Gen2 involved some quality-of-life upgrades for the printer itself - finer gear bands (more teeth, allowing for more accurate movement), different bed spacers (shorter bed heat time). INDX involved replacing the print head completely. The head is in charge of drawing in the filament, heating it, pushing the melted filament onto the bed, then cooling it a little. The INDX head is composed of a single “active” part (that contains the motors, heater, sensors, fans), and 8 “passive” parts that only have the filament passing through them and are grabbed by the active part. I think about it like a hand and multiple pens - the printer only has one complex part, but can quickly grab a pen, write with it, then put it back.
My INDX printing, alternating between pink and black
This is in contrast to the MMU units, where there was a single head that unloaded one filament and loaded another. The unloading part was a new process for the printer and had its own failure modes (e.g. hotend generates a blob too thick for the gears).
The two upgrades can be installed sequentially, but they both involve taking the printer apart to a certain degree, so Prusa created a meta-guide. It’s a single page guiding you on how to hop between the Gen2 guide and the INDX guide (“start from step 2.40, get back here after 2.76”) to do both at the same time. This made the upgrade even more complicated, which it already was as it involved taking working things apart and not just greenfield construction.
I recently had a positive experience with applying LLMs to non-programming, yes-engineering tasks. I decided to test it by having it:
I tried having it create its own version of the meta guide that is less confusing, but it didn’t work very well. The result wasn’t bad, it just wasn’t that much better than the original.
I found it knowing the guide useful for other reasons:
Some of the instructions referred to screws “you removed earlier”. How earlier? Unclear. When I remove a screw, do I keep it or does it go to the big-bag-of-screws never to be seen again?
indx 4.3 - do I keep the nextruder holder screws?
indx 4.15. “Ensure that the four highlighted holes are empty…” keep screws I find there?
Being a smarty-pants, I sometimes wanted to do things not in the way the guide instructed because it made more sense to me.
indx 4.35. when do I connect the x,y motors I disconnected in gen2 upgrade? can I do it now?
can I move the dockside fan installation forward? or should I do electronics first?
Since the LLM held the whole guide in the context window, it could answer whether reordering the stages would make things easier or more complex for me.
After the assembly was complete, the time came to actually test and use it. Since the LLM already had context, I used it for troubleshooting the calibration and testing process. I then added a new layer by having it clone the printer’s firmware ( Prusa-Firmware-Buddy ) so it can authoritatively answer where errors come from and what the printer is trying to do.
Some things were not interesting, but some were very much so.
One of the hardest parts in the Prusa Core One printer is attaching the belts to the head carriage. It involves grabbing 4 belt ends, inserting each one through two holes, then screwing the carriage to another piece in a way that squashes the belt ends, holding them in place. Turns out that although I did this part in the Core One assembly 5 times, I didn’t learn enough for this to go smoothly.
The printer has a new “squareness” test, where it checks that moving between all of the head’s range (back-left to back-right to forward-right to forward-left) generates a shape of a square. This test failed, hinting at “something wrong with the belts”. I told the LLM about the error message, and it went looking for what the squareness check actually does, and what I could have done to fail it. After ensuring there are no twists, I told the LLM that it has to be my fault somehow, and is it possible I did the holder wrong. It replied that unevenness in the teeth grabbed in the holder can manifest exactly like that, and suggested I take the holder apart. Turns out that on one side, the bottom belt had 5 teeth inserted, and the top one had 6 . The guide doesn’t mention the “equality” part at all. Obviously that was the problem, and after meticulously ensuring 5 teeth in every part of the holder, squareness passed great.
Before a print starts, the printer checks the height of the bed (the printing surface) on several points. Usually it’s something like a grid of 7 * 7 points under the printed object. It does so because the bed is not absolutely flat due to minute imperfections, dust trapped beneath the printing sheet etc, and knowing how the bed curves lets the printer compensate for that during the print itself. One of my prints failed on this leveling check. The middle check came out 0.5mm taller than one of the edges (which is a lot for this kind of an engineered flat surface), and the contact was “soft”, which in human speak means the surface had some yield to it. Since this worked before my meddling, I had the LLM identify screws that I worked on during the upgrade. Using its knowledge of what I did, it directed me to specific screws and how tight they need to be (based on what they actually do).
If you have a sharp eye (I didn’t at the time) you could see that the black disk on the top is not fully adhering to the rest of the black mass. That disk keeps the front-left side from moving upwards, and without the screws holding it in place, the bed did indeed escape upwards. After tightening them, the bed worked perfectly with both the textured sheets, and the smooth ones too.
In 3d-printing there’s a concept of “first layer offset”, which is the initial distance of the print head (that extrudes the material) to the bed (where the object is being printed). Just like when writing with a brush, you can’t be so far that the paint just falls off and drips, but you also can’t be so close that you’ll smear the paint. You need a sort of light touch, and in the first 3d-printers the tuning was more of an art than a science. The newer Prusa printers come with a “loadcell”, which measures how much force is applied on the head from the bottom, indicating how hard it’s “touching” the bed. Using this device, the printer can self-calibrate at the start of each print, for each of the tools (as I have 8 of those “pens” now, each with its own tiny difference in shape and alignment), to find the ideal distance from the bed.
I had a weird problem where printer calibrations done outside of a print would complete successfully. The bed would get closer and closer to the head (in my printer it’s the bed that goes up, not the head that goes down) until it’s just-touching, then move on to the next tool or conclude happily. When actually starting a print and doing the exact same procedure, the printer would stop the bed when it’s a big distance (3cm) from the head, hesitate, try a bit lower, rethink its life choices, then often fail. The failure was justified as the printer got multiple results indicating wildly different heights (expected variance between checks is under 1mm), so something’s obviously wrong. Sometimes it’d retry, sometimes I’d have it retry, and overall most of the prints failed several times on this. The LLM enabled some diagnostic output on the printer (which required me to connect it over ethernet to its OctoPi companion) and confirmed the loadcell is getting crazy readings. Its initial assumption was that during printing the printer is quicker to act after picking up the tools, causing “ringing” (vibrations from the pickup that disturbed the electronics), and it suggested waiting a bit more with more retries. It generated a custom firmware we flashed to the printer and we tried again. It worked a bit better, but mostly because there was more retrying, so better chance of randomly getting a good result. I wasn’t happy with this solution and wanted to continue troubleshooting. “If ringing is the problem, we can wait for 30 seconds after a tool change and it’ll settle”, I suggested. We tested it and the ringing theory didn’t hold. After that, the LLM wanted to run convoluted tests on the printer that involved picking up, returning, waiting on the printer via its usb connection. It was thwarted by the printer itself getting bored after 5 seconds of not getting instructions, and treating it as a “printing finished”, cleaning the nozzle and putting it away, which ruined the testing. Reading the firmware, the LLM had me disable “serial printing screen” (which is a spooky internal setting), which means the printer didn’t have the concept of cleanup anymore, so the LLM could send whatever it wanted. We couldn’t reproduce the problem anymore, and the LLM suggested “the printer is warmed up after all the testing, so no ringing and you can print what you want”, so I did and it worked. The main downside was that because the printer didn’t treat this like a print, it didn’t turn on all of its lights so I couldn’t really see what’s going on.
After 2 successful prints, and now knowing that a warm printer is a happy printer, I turned the “serial printing screen” on again to print something AND see what’s going on. The loadcell calibration failed. I was pulling my hair out when the LLM said that the exact same print succeeded with the serial printing screen off, so we should try that, which made things work again. I then had it analyze the firmware to see what actually changes with and without serial printing, aside from the printer lighting. The answer was very little, nothing it could suspect, so it said that the LEDs could be a problem. Being a smart guy overall, I knew this was folly, but had no better lead so I had it flash a custom firmware with the LEDs disabled. It printed perfectly. We proceeded to separate the different LEDs (4 of them) and try a calibration with every possible permutation (16). The raw result is here (p2p is the peak-to-peak noise the firmware reports on the loadcell while it waits for the reading to settle, OK/NOK are the probes accepted and rejected during the tool offset calibration):
From reading the table, one can see that whenever the bed LEDs are used:
Any run without the bed LEDs is as pure as snow.
I’m not smart enough with electronics to know exactly how the bed LEDs are affecting the loadcell’s readings, but I reported it to Prusa ( prusa3d/Prusa-Firmware-Buddy#5526 ) and they’ll probably figure it out.
To the best of my knowledge, the LEDs are PWM-operated, meaning that their intensity (and intensity of each color) is controlled by what percent of the time their power is on. Think of it like sending a few hundred pulses a second, where if 80% of those pulses are “1” compared to “0”, the LED is on in 80% intensity. This means that theoretically, these pulses can manifest as noise in another wire or component nearby, and if there’s a component measuring the signal strength in that vicinity, those pulses might affect that measurement.
Those LEDs are not very important - they change their color to indicate what the printer is up to right now, and a quick workaround was to completely disable them during the print. A quick followup was a custom firmware that disabled the LEDs just for the moments the loadcell was in use.
No. I’m a somewhat intelligent, highly motivated, overfocused, tech-savvy person. Given enough time (and help from Prusa support), I would have tackled all of these successfully. However, having the ability to query against the guide and the firmware effortlessly, asking garden variety questions about electronic components, and being able to quickly churn out new firmware versions and testing scripts provided a lot of utility and shortened the time for me to get to a working printer.

title: Spices, shipwrecks and ancient trade routes: Louvre Abu Dhabi explores 1,000 years of Indian Ocean history
body: Visitors to Louvre Abu Dhabi's latest exhibition begin their journey in darkness, lights above mimicking a star-filled sky. It's a reminder of a time when sailors relied on the heavens to navigate the Indian Ocean, carrying spices, precious stones and textiles between distant civilisations. Such voyages connected communities from East Africa and the Arabian Peninsula to India, China and South-East Asia, establishing commercial and cultural relationships that developed over centuries. Their history is explored in Spices and Wonders: Sailing the Indian Ocean, opening at Louvre Abu Dhabi on Wednesday, October 14, and running until February 14, 2027. Organised in partnership with the Guimet National Museum of Asian Arts in Paris, the exhibition brings together about 240 artworks and historical objects from 24 lenders, covering maritime exchange from antiquity to the 17th century. Among them are archaeological discoveries, jewellery, religious artefacts and objects recovered from shipwrecks. Six detailed models of historic vessels and specially created maps illustrate how sailors crossed vast waters and transported goods between continents. The exhibition places the Arabian Gulf at the centre of its narrative, examining the region's historical role in these networks. “The story is told from here, and that is something we consider very important at Louvre Abu Dhabi: telling the story from the region,” says Guilhem Andre, the museum's director of scientific, curatorial and collections management “This has never really been done on this scale before.” The exhibition features loans from institutions including the Asian Civilisations Museum in Singapore, the National Museum of the Philippines and the Al Sabah Collection in Kuwait . Pierre Baptiste, director of collections and curatorial staff at the Guimet in Paris, says the exhibition explores how people established relationships through commerce and spiritual exchange. The Arabian Gulf's pearl industry provides a significant regional example. Pearls harvested from its waters travelled to markets in India and beyond, while materials such as carnelian were traded across the ocean from ancient times. Later networks expanded the circulation of gemstones, jewellery , furniture and textiles. Andre said the objects revealed how discoveries of new sources of gold, spinels, rubies and emeralds influenced jewellery production. Diplomatic gifts also feature, demonstrating how valuable objects helped establish relationships between rulers and communities. Beyond the goods themselves, the exhibition examines the techniques that made these journeys possible. Its opening gallery recreates the darkness experienced by ancient navigators, who relied on stars and coastal landmarks to determine their position. “The main idea was to give visitors a sense of what people at the time experienced,” Baptiste says. Subsequent galleries explore navigational instruments, including the kamal, used in Arab and Indian maritime traditions, and the astrolabe. Twenty-four maps created specifically for the exhibition trace the routes connecting ports across the ocean. Six large ship models represent Arabian, South-East Asian, Chinese, Portuguese and Spanish maritime traditions. Andre says they were constructed in South Africa over the course of a year, drawing on extensive historical research. The models are accompanied by objects recovered from shipwrecks, offering evidence of the cargo these vessels carried. Baptiste says advances in underwater archaeology since the 1990s have enabled researchers to recover significant quantities of material from sunken ships, including objects originating in China, India, Spain and Mexico. Among the most valuable commodities were spices, which commanded high prices alongside luxury products such as jewellery and textiles. Cultural exchange is another central theme. A Buddha sculpture from present-day Pakistan, loaned by the Guimet, reflects the influence of ancient Greek and Roman artistic traditions on Buddhist sculpture. The final gallery examines four religious traditions that spread across the Indian Ocean, showing how beliefs travelled along the same routes as commercial goods. Andre says merchants and pilgrims often crossed these waters for different purposes, carrying objects and practices that became part of life in distant communities. “Religion was not separate from trade,” he says. “They were all part of the same relationships and exchanges.” The exhibition also offers a perspective on maritime history that predates the expansion of European influence in Indian Ocean commerce during the 17th and 18th centuries. Baptiste says the decision to conclude the historical narrative in the 17th century was deliberate, allowing visitors to understand the networks that existed long before European powers became prominent in the region. These earlier connections, he says, laid the foundations for the expansion of international commerce in subsequent centuries. “We wanted to approach the history of commercial relationships from a multicultural perspective,” he says. “Europe was only one part of this story.” Spices and Wonders: Sailing the Indian Ocean runs at Louvre Abu Dhabi from October 14, 2026, until February 14, 2027. The exhibition will subsequently travel to the Guimet in Paris, where it will be presented from May 12 to September 6, 2027.

title: Watch the B.C. election provincial leaders’ debate live
body:
The only scheduled leaders’ debate leading up to the B.C. provincial election on Oct. 24 was held on Wednesday night, with many topics covered, discussed and debated.
BC NDP leader David Eby, BC Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson and BC Green Party leader Emily Lowan took part.
After opening remarks, debate moderator Shachi Kurl turned the conversation to topics that are likely top of voters’ minds.
Eby was asked if calling this snap election was anything other than an opportunistic power grab. He said now is the time for British Columbians to have their say so they can move forward.
“Our province, our country, is facing an existential moment,” Eby said.
“And I know for your families at home, you’re feeling it, too. There’s a crucial moment for you. You want government to take action to make sure your job is protected, that we’re growing the economy. You’re supported with costs like gas and groceries… We need a government with representatives from every part of the province that are focused on your priorities, not on culture wars, not on repealing the Human Rights Code, but on the real issues that matter to you and your family.”
Doerkson, who admitted he was a little nervous ahead of the debate, said this election is about Eby’s record in the past 10 years in the legislature.
“I will lead my caucus with a great amount of dignity to all British Columbians. I am absolutely committed to unifying and bringing our team together, which we have done, and I’m committed to doing that for British Columbians as well.”
Lowan, the only woman in the debate and the youngest, said that while she is relatively new to politics, she is the only leader on the stage who is a renter.
“I’m the only leader on this stage who has worked a minimum wage job in the last decade, which means that I am the only leader on this stage that feels the decisions being made in the legislature, especially as it relates to the cost of living crisis and the climate crisis,” she said.
“You know, the B.C. Greens are building a formidable movement to reclaim our economy for everyday people. This means that we have a credible plan to deliver a life you can afford, care you can count on, and a fair economy. I think my youth is an asset. I think I am bringing bold ideas to the stage, and I am proud of what the BC Greens have to offer.”
B.C. is facing a record never seen before $13.8 billion deficit.
Doerkson has criticized Eby’s government for its spending and for promising a $1,000 rebate for all residents, which was then reversed due to budget constraints.
“I have made it clear that we are going to cut through red tape in this province and all of the bureaucracy that is holding us back so badly,” he said.
“The reality is we have to grow our economy in this province. It’s absolutely fundamentally the case.”
Doerkson said the government needs to support the forestry industry, LNG and the liquor industry.
Lowan said we are seeing the Eby government pour billions of dollars into gas projects and the resource extraction industry, but there is no path forward.
“We aren’t seeing a path forward from these parties on sustainable forestry,” she said.
“We know that we can keep more jobs and more profits in B.C. if we actually have communities take the reins and build value-added products here in B.C. Instead, these raw logs are being shipped abroad for the profit of foreign shareholders.
“So the BC Greens plan looks at how we can build a stable, sustainable industry right here in B.C., from green manufacturing to forestry to service.”
Eby acknowledged that his government has spent more, but they have built schools, hospitals and will balance the budget not on the backs of British Columbians.
“I’ll make sure that we grow the economy,” he said.
“We address wasteful spending. But I have to say, to show up to the leaders’ debate after making $5 billion in promises, for the Conservative leader to be here without explaining, without giving British Columbians the dignity you at home to know where that $5 billion is going to come from.”
Eby said British Columbians need an explanation.
While government spending was an important topic, the everyday cost of living is on voters’ minds.
Lowan said they are proposing a one-time tax on B.C.’s ultra-wealthy, meaning households with net wealth over $50 million.
She said they would follow that with a marginal annual tax.
“That would generate $5.4 billion a year,” Lowan said.
“You know, this is the kind of ambition that we need… this is exactly what we need to rein in B.C.’s deficit to reduce wealth inequality and to ensure that we can actually bring in universal childcare, fast, free and frequent transit, and the social housing we so desperately need.”
Eby, who has been criticized in recent days for having a child in the $10-a-day daycare program, said his government has created 60,000 daycare spaces across B.C., but added that is not enough and more needs to be done to convert them to the $10-a-day model.
“To expand it, we’ll have an announcement about how we’re going to add thousands and thousands of new spaces across the province – before and after school care. But Mr. Doerkson and his team are unable to explain how they’re going to fund the $5 billion in promises that will be coming for childcare.”
The BC Conservatives have pledged to replace ICBC’s no-fault system with a hybrid model, which has some drivers worried that insurance premiums will go up.
“I am committed to keeping our rates very competitive in British Columbia,” Doerkson said.
“British Columbians of course want that. But on the other side of that, when you speak with a woman in the Kootenays who has lost her daughter and two of her grandchildren in a car accident that had simply a tire blow on the front end of a logging truck, and that there has been no compensation for supports for that family, no compensation for those children going forward, at this point, for the children that survived the accident.
“It’s shocking to me that we’re having this debate.”
Doerkson said they would put caps in place on what lawyers can charge clients, but he said the no-fault plan is not working.
Eby said he knows the no-fault system is not perfect.
“But the idea that you’re going to open up the doors to personal injury lawyers, again, I want to take British Columbians back to the dumpster fire of ICBC losing $1 billion a year, 30 per cent rate increases slated for British Columbians in a single year, some of the most expensive insurance,” he added.
The BC NDP is promising a three-year freeze to any increase in ICBC rates.
Lowan pointed to Eby’s promise two years ago to connect every B.C. resident with a family doctor, but said he has failed to deliver on that promise.
“The BC Greens are the only party with a credible plan to bring community-based, team-based, preventative health care into every riding in this province,” she said.
“It is in our platform that we would bring in community health care centres into every riding. And that would mean that you could walk into your neighbourhood and you would have access to a physician, a nurse practitioner, and imaging all under the same roof.”
Eby said if there is one issue that keeps him awake at night, it is health care.
“People are showing up at emergency rooms sicker than ever. We have a growing population. And the miraculous cures that are being offered are wildly expensive.. the big challenge we face is the shortage of health-care workers.”
Eby said they have to recruit more doctors, including from the U.S., and he is promising to triple that recruitment.
Doerkson said there are things that can be done in B.C. to help alleviate the stress on the health-care system.
He pointed to nurses who are afraid to work because they don’t feel safe in hospitals due to being attacked by strangers.
Doerkson said they have committed to making sure there will be security in emergency rooms and in hospitals.
“We will also commit a $50 million fund to bolster our ERs that are closing right now,” he added.
“There are hospitals in this province that have been closed every night for ages… It’s shocking to me to see what’s happening… British Columbians are up at night worried that their hospital is closed when they need it most.”
Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA)
Eby acknowledged this is a crucial issue in B.C. and one that has some residents concerned about property rights.
“There are two cornerstones to our success as a province,” he said.
“One is if we want to be successful, if we want to take advantage of the incredible prosperity out there, there’s only one path forward and that’s in partnership with the Indigenous people in this province. The reason why we’re leading Canada and major projects at the Major Projects Office, the reason why we’ve been able to open so many minds, the reasons why we were able to do LNG Canada Phase II, all of these projects, the reason why these things are happening is because we have entered into those partnerships that are enabled by this law.”
Eby said they are appealing recent court decisions to ensure that private property in B.C. is protected.
Doerkson said if the BC Conservatives are elected, they will repeal DRIPA.
“I’m committed to doing that for a number of reasons,” he said.
“First off, it has not helped. British Columbia has created more division on the landscape than I have ever seen in my life and this legislation is not that old.
“The reality is, is that we are more divided on this topic than ever before. There has to be a better path forward and that is through respect and relations and certainly partnerships with First Nations in this province.”
Lowan said that First Nations have been unequivocal in saying that the government must do the work to implement DRIPA.
“Frankly, when we talk about certainty, the uncertainty that has been sown over the last year has been from a premier who can’t seem to make up his mind, and it’s been from a Conservative party that is constantly pushing misinformation and blatant fearmongering,” she said.
“You know, we’ve seen from both parties, you know, just a willingness to engage on this bad-faith argument has no bearing on private property. It sets out the rules for government to go ahead, do their homework and bring up our legislation in alignment with B.C. laws, and the minimum standards set out by the UN on human rights of Indigenous people.”
This debate came at a crucial time in the campaign.
An exclusive Ipsos poll, conducted with Global BC, showed that the BC Conservatives have now gained a five-point lead over the BC NDP.
“David Eby has two tasks in the leaders’ debate,” Kyle Braid, senior vice president of Ipsos, said on Tuesday morning.
“One is to create some sense of risk for people for electing a BC Conservative government. And the other is to try to persuade some of those voters who are considering either the NDP or the Greens that a vote for the NDP is the correct choice.
“Lorne Doerkson’s main thing is simply to introduce himself to voters in the province. Most people don’t know him. The other thing is quite simply just to stand up and look like a premier. That’s it.”

title: FCT judicial committee flouted procurement law, financial regulations in N866.5m contract awards – Audit report
body:
The latest federal audit has revealed a series of infractions by the Judicial Service Committee of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT JSC), Abuja, in awarding contracts worth about N866.5 million in 2023.
The report revealed the FCT JSC’s rampant disregard for procurement law, financial regulations and federal government’s policy directives.
According to the just released 2024 report of the Office of the Auditor-General of the Federation (OAuGF), the infractions stemmed from weaknesses in the judicial committee’s internal control system.
In some instances, the auditor general found no evidence of work done for the payments the FCT JSC made to contractors. In other cases, there were no documents to show that the committee awarded contracts to qualified contractors.
According to the report, many of the flagged infractions possibly resulted in the loss or diversion of public funds channelled into the contracts.
The FCT JSC is an institution of the judiciary established by the Nigerian constitution, to oversee judicial appointments, promotion, and discipline, as well as safeguard both the independence of the judiciary and the administration of justice in FCT courts.
One of its key responsibilities is recommending qualified lawyers for appointment to the bench, after conducting, what it called , rigorous evaluation of professional qualifications and experience, background and integrity checks, and consultation with relevant stakeholders.
The body, which its equivalent exists across Nigeria’s 36 states and at the federal level as the Federal Judicial Service Commission, is also mandated to ensure “high standards of ethical conduct and professional integrity.”
But the new 2024 audit report on the 2023 finances of federal ministries, departments and agencies revealed that the FCT JSC, statutorily chaired by the Chief Judge of the FCT High Court and run day-to-day by an executive secretary, hardly played by the rules in a series of contract awards. Justice Husseini Baba-Yusuf, the incumbent chief judge of the FCT High Court and chair of the FCT JSC, has served in those roles since 2021.
The audit report identified five contracts aggregately worth N866.5 million with their litany of issues and the risks they pose to public funds.
The issues include award of a contract worth N302.3 million to non-accredited local manufacturers or assemblers, irregularities in the award of contracts valued at N192.1 million, and infractions in the award of renovation contracts worth N174.2 million.
The two other issues are award of N144.2 million worth of contract and payment to inactive companies without due diligence and splitting of N57.3 million contracts to circumvent procurement/ approval threshold.
The queried contracts summed up to N866.5 million in monetary value. The auditor general’said their handlings by the JSC raised concerns of possible supply of substandard products, diversion of public funds, loss of public funds, award of contracts to unqualified contractors, possible insider dealing and payments for fictitious transactions.
Meanwhile, this amount does not include the N112.6 million in salary vouchers flagged by the audit report as the sixth issue uncovered in the JSC’s financial records for 2023.
All told, the N866.5 million in questionable contract disbursements, coupled with N112.6 million in queried payroll entries, brings the total unaccounted sum at the FCT JSC to roughly N979.1 million for 2023.
The report, titled Annual Report on Non-Compliance/Internal Control Weaknesses in Ministries, Departments and Agencies of the Federal Government of Nigeria for 2024, was submitted by Auditor-General of the Federation (AuGF) Shaakaa Chira to the National Assembly on 17 July.
Volume II of the report covers a section on judiciary institutions, presenting findings on the infractions by the JSC of the FCT for the period between 1 January and 31 December 2023. The Code of Conduct Tribunal is the only other body whose infractions for the year under reference were captured in the section.
The report revealed that the FCT JSC failed to respond to queries on the issues raised.
The audit report flagged a purchase of “motor vehicle” for N302.3 million by the JSC in 2023. The type or the make of the vehicle was not disclosed in the report.
However, it revealed that the committee procured and made payment for the supply of the motor vehicle to contractors “who were not among the list of accredited local manufacturers/assemblers in Nigeria for the procurement of federal government vehicles.”
This action, according to the report, flouted the provisions of the Financial Regulations 2009 and “does not encourage local manufacturer/industrialisation in Nigeria.”
Paragraph 2305 of the Financial Regulations (2009) referenced in the report states, “As much as it is practicable, goods must be purchased from reputable manufacturers or their accredited agents. When goods are obtained through an agent, the procuring officer will satisfy himself that the goods are authentic.”
The report added that JSC’s action infringed on paragraph 1 of the Executive Order No. 3 (2017) which states, “All Ministries Department and Agencies (MDAs) of the FGN shall grant preference to local manufacturers of goods and service providers in their procurement of goods and services.”
It similarly cited paragraph 1 of the Establishment Circular Ref. No. NADDC.NAIDP/S.137/1/36 dated 17 March 2023, which provided an updated list of accredited local manufacturers/assemblers in Nigeria, for the procurement of federal government vehicles.
The report regarded the flouting of the financial regulations and policy documents as “anomalies” that possibly arose from the “weaknesses in the internal control system” at the JSC of the FCT.
These, according to the report, exposed the government to the risks of “supply of sub-standard vehicles” and “diversion of public funds.”
The report also revealed a payment of over N192 million to companies without supporting documents showing the contractors’ qualifications.
The report found that seven vouchers totalling over N192 million were raised and the money was paid in favour of different companies for the provision of services and supply of goods to the JSC.
But the JSC failed to present any documentary evidence such as tax clearance certificate, Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) certificate of registration, PenCom certificate, Industrial Training Fund certificate, Nigeria Social Industrial Trust Fund certificate, among others, to show that the contractors were qualified bidders.
This lack of compliance, according to the audit report, contravenes Section 16(7) of the Public Procurement Act 2007, which states that “The procuring entity may require a bidder to provide documentary evidence or other information it considers necessary as proof that the bidder is qualified in accordance with this Act and the solicitation documents and for this purpose any such requirements shall apply equally to all bidders.”
Similarly, the JSC awarded contracts worth over N174.2 million to four contractors for renovations and rehabilitation without any advertisements, bid documents submitted, or a detailed bid evaluation report, said the account general of the federation’s report.
Also according to the report, the contractors’ files lacked information about the contractors, pictorial evidence of the work done, or proof that the contractors had been filing their annual tax returns with the Federal Inland Revenue Service (now the National Revenue Service) and that “the company was inactive on the CAC dashboard.”
There was also no evidence of procurement due process as the JSC could not produce relevant documents such as advertisements carried out in two national dailies, bid documents submitted, and detailed bid evaluation report.
The committee, by its actions or omissions, the audit report said, violated section 24(1) of the Public Procurement Act 2007 and paragraph 2907 (i) of the Financial Regulations.
Section 24(1) of the Public Procurement Act provides that “Except as provided by this Act, all procurements of goods and works by all procuring entities shall be by way of open competitive bidding.”
Paragraph 2907(i) of the Financial Regulations (FR) (2009), which the audit report said the JSC also flouted, states, “To ensure transparency and accountability, achievement of value for money, economy and efficiency, and equity and fairness, all procurements falling within the Bureau’s thresholds shall be by way of Open Competitive Bidding.”
The report again attributed the anomalies to weaknesses in the internal control system at the JSC.
It added that these pose the risks possible of insider dealing – using internal information to unfairly win public contracts. It also said the funds meant for the contracts could be diverted.
Award of N144 million to companies with inactive CAC and FIRS status
The report also flagged the JSC’s contracts worth over N144 million awarded to eight companies with inactive status on both CAC and FIRS portals.
This violates Section 16(5) and (6) of the PPA, which stipulate that “A supplier, contractor or service provider may be a natural person, a legal person or a combination of the two….”
The audit report also referenced Section 16(6) of the PPA (2007) states, “All bidders in addition to requirements contained in any solicitation documents shall (b) possess the legal capacity to enter into the procurement contract: (c) not be in receivership, the subject of any form of insolvency or bankruptcy proceedings or the subject of any form of winding up petition proceedings; (d) not have fulfilled all its obligations to pay taxes, pensions and social security contributions.”
The auditor general said the infractions, attributable to weak internal control, posed the risk of loss of public funds and diversion of public funds.
The audit also found that the JSC unduly split a N53.6 million worth contract for the supply of computers and laptops into six units.
It observed that the contract was for the supply of the same products and ought to have been awarded as a single contract, but was rather split into six at a price that fell within the approval threshold of the executive secretary.
It added that all six smaller contracts were awarded about the same period in 2023, pointing out that the splitting enabled the secretary to circumvent tenders’ procedures.
Also, the JSC failed to provide documents showing the distribution of the computers/laptops, records of officers to whom they were issued, and details of their respective locations or user departments.
Section 20(2) of the PPA cited as a legal provision the transactions breached, states, “The accounting officer of every procuring entity shall have overall responsibility for the planning of, organisation of tenders, evaluation of tenders and execution of all procurements and in particular shall be responsible for… (e) ensuring that no reduction of values or splitting of procurements is carried out such as to evade the use of the appropriate procurement method.”
The report said the “anomalies could be attributed to weaknesses in the internal control system.”
It added that these transactions posed the risks of payments for “fictitious transactions” and diversion of public funds.
The report also faulted the committee for failing to present 93 salary vouchers totalling over N112.6 million, creating the risk of payments to non-existent staff members and a contravention of paragraph 601 of the Financial Regulations.
This provision mandates that “All payment entries in the cash book/accounts shall be vouched for on one of the prescribed treasury forms. Vouchers shall be made out in favour of the person or persons to whom the money is actually due. Under no circumstances shall a cheque be raised or cash paid for services for which a voucher has not been raised.”
According to the audit report, the committee failed to respond to queries on any of the six infractions.
Therefore, the auditor general recommended that the Secretary of the FCT JSC, Omolola Akindele, account for all the funds, recover and remit them to the treasury and forward the evidence to the Public Accounts Committees of the National Assembly.
Failure to comply attracts sanctions, the report stated.

title: Iran executes Kerman terror suspect convicted of enemy ties
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 14 (MNA) – Iran’s Judiciary says an armed terrorist, convicted of wounding several civilians, including a minor girl, in shooting during the 40-day US-Israeli war of aggression has been hanged.
In a statement, the Judiciary said Ali Sina Mostafavi, who was working as an “agent of the American-Zionist enemy”, was hanged in Kerman on Wednesday morning, following legal procedures and confirmation of the verdict by the Supreme Court.
It noted that the convict had launched several armed operations in the southern city during the 40-day war, Known as the Ramadan War.
In his first armed attack on March 24, Mostafavi carried out a shooting in Azadi Square in Kerman that injured a citizen and a young girl. On April 21, he opened fire on conscripts and passing vehicles, injuring several citizens.
According to the Judiciary’s Media Center, technical investigations and the case documents revealed that Mostafavi had been operating as an active member of a "monarchist terrorist" organization inside Iran and had extensive connections to hostile media outlets.
Inquiries revealed communications on his mobile phone with the convict was also active during the foreign-backed riots of early January, and that he sent images and videos to hostile media. Furthermore, Mostafavi had filmed sites hit by enemy projectiles and sent the footage to anti-Iranian networks, the Judiciary went on to say.
Documents, the court said, on Mostafavi's phone also revealed that the convict had expressed, through the messages he had sent to Persian-language hostile media, his readiness to carry out terrorist operations inside Ayatollah Hashemi Rafsanjani Airport in Kerman.
Mostafavi had also sent many messages to Israel's Persian-language Instagram account, according to Press TV.
The case documents further showed two earlier unsuccessful shootings at the Kerman-Mahan traffic police.

title: Lockstep to pipeline in almost one line
body:
In the previous post I talked about some of the benefits of a discrete time (tick) based system . In this post I'm going to cover one of the other boons of a simple lockstep tick system. It's easy to change it into a pipelining tick system.
Note: all my public writing and code is handcrafted by me.
Game loops are normally lockstep because it makes sense to do your updates and then render. It makes it easy to define your game (or app) as a sequence of phases which greatly simplifies reasoning about things like concurrency. Most of the time this is enough. However, even though single writer systems can scale incredibly well you ideally want to be writing all the time. In a lockstep system you are by definition not writing when you are rendering. With a single writer that also means you only have one core doing work while you're writing.
Pipelining is when you move phases to run in parallel instead of in sequence. Haven't we basically gone back to an event based continuous time system? No, not quite, the phases are still running on their own cores/threads in batches. They also cannot race ahead of each other, they all wait at a barrier before the next tick. This means we still have back pressure, and we can still track tick overruns as normal.
A synchronization aid that allows a set of threads to all wait for each other to reach a common barrier point. CyclicBarriers are useful in programs involving a fixed sized party of threads that must occasionally wait for each other. The barrier is called cyclic because it can be re-used after the waiting threads are released. If you need support for variable numbers of parties per cycle, alternate actions on exceptions, termination control, contention control, or status monitoring, use the more flexible Phaser class.
Note: you know it's good when you start reaching for concurrency tools that sound like they are out of StarTrek (CyclicBarrier, Phaser and Disruptor)
So if tick-time was 100 and write-time was 90 and read-time was 100. A tick would take 190:
So if tick-time was 100 and write-time was 90 and read-time was 100. A tick would take 100:
With a pipeline read batch and write batches overlap. That's why they must be wrapped in transactions, so the reads don't see future writes until the next tick (or use the same basis-t if you're using a datomic-like).
But, you still have a tick barrier so that both must complete before the next tick. This gives you the same back pressure and the same overrun tracking as the lockstep model.
Yeah, that's it. We move the done-barrier and kick it off with a (.await ^CyclicBarrier start-barrier) outside the while loop.
We open up 1000 SSE read connections to the server and keep them open. We then simulate a sequence of slow write transactions.
In the lockstep system. This leads to lots of overruns.
The pipelining system is almost completely unaffected:
We are now writing at the same time as reading. What about read consistency? Thankfully each of our render batches is wrapped in a read transaction, so the whole batch sees a consistent view. All the batches start before the write batch completes so there's no read skew (this can be strictly enforced by adding a third barrier if desired). For a given tick everyone is still seeing the same view of the database.
Hopefully, this post shows you some of the benefits of modelling your system as separate phases coordinated around discrete time barriers.
Thanks to Everyone on the Datastar discord who read drafts of this and gave me feedback.

title: From Saddam Hussein to Israel: How Iran's wars have divided a nation - analysis
body: On September 22, 1980, as Iraqi warplanes bombed Iranian airfields and Saddam Hussein's tanks crossed the Iranian border, Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini appeared remarkably unconcerned by what was unfolding in the fledgling Islamic Republic.Iraq's attack, he told the Iranian people, was little more than “a thief throwing a stone” before running away. There was no reason to panic, he insisted, and certainly no reason to believe that Iran had entered a major war. The country's armed forces were perfectly capable of dealing with the threat.History, of course, would prove him spectacularly wrong as the war dragged on for eight long years and left an estimated half a million people dead.Saddam's invasion brought together a deeply fractured Iranian nationHowever, for all the destruction that followed, Saddam's invasion also achieved something that the Islamic Republic, barely a year and a half old, could scarcely have accomplished on its own. It brought together a deeply fractured Iranian nation, many of whose people had little affection for Khomeini or the clerical establishment that had seized power in Tehran.Nearly half a century later, with Iran engaging twice in the space of one year against Israel and the United States, the question of how Iranians respond to an external enemy has returned to the fore. And while Iran's leaders have spent much of the past year insisting that the country stands united behind them, the events unfolding inside Iran tell a considerably more complicated story.When Saddam launched his invasion, Iran was still struggling to come to terms with the revolution that had overthrown Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi in February 1979. The revolutionary government had barely established control over the country, while competing political factions were fighting for influence, and the military, once among the most powerful in the Middle East, had been weakened by purges of officers associated with the former monarchy.There was unrest in the provinces and among different ethnic groups, opposition to clerical rule was growing, and the new Islamic Republic was still engaged in the bloody business of eliminating its political rivals.From Baghdad, Hussein believed he had found his moment to strike and take, among other things, the Shatt al-Arab waterway and its key oil installations.The Iraqi dictator calculated that Iran's internal turmoil would make a swift military victory possible, particularly if he could exploit the country's ethnic divisions. Hussein hoped that the Sunni-majority Arab population of Khuzestan, the oil-rich Iranian province bordering Iraq, would welcome his troops as liberators against their Shi'a oppressors.. He was very much mistaken.Rather than embracing the invading Iraqi army, many Iranian Arabs joined their compatriots in defending their homeland. Political opponents of Khomeini, including supporters of the ousted monarchy, similarly recognized that whatever their differences with the new government, the country's territorial integrity was at stake. Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi, a trained fighter pilot and son of the exiled Shah, even extended an offer to his country's new rulers to return and fight for Iran.Iranian patriotism, it turned out, extended considerably further than loyalty to the Islamic Republic."We are ready to send all our children to battle the thugs,” Khomeini stated just days after the invasion.For Khomeini, the war provided an opportunity to harness that patriotism and place the defense of the nation at the center of his revolutionary government's struggle for survival. As the fighting dragged on, the regime more and more associated resistance to the Iraqis and Hussein with support for the Islamic Republic itself, while the demands of wartime offered further opportunities to silence domestic opposition and consolidate clerical rule. This was also the period of massive expansion in the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps - originally formed to safeguard the revolution domestically.By the time the guns finally stopped  in August 1988, the Islamic Republic had survived its greatest external challenge and emerged with a far stronger grip on power than it had possessed when Iraqi troops first crossed the border.If the 1980-88 war, however, was relatively successful in its ability to get Iranians to “rally around the flag,” the wars of 2025 and 2026 proved more difficult for the Iranian regime to succeed in garnering nationalist fervor.  Unlike Iraq, American and Israeli military campaigns were conducted from the airUnlike Saddam's invasion, which involved Iraqi ground forces attempting to capture and occupy Iranian territory, the American and Israeli military campaigns were conducted overwhelmingly from the air, targeting nuclear facilities, missile installations, military infrastructure, and senior figures within the Islamic Republic's security establishment.Neither the US nor Israel attempted a comparable occupation of Iranian territory, and both countries repeatedly presented their military operations as directed against the regime and the threat posed by its military capabilities, rather than against the Iranian people themselves.The reaction this time around, from Iranians, was very different.There were, of course, civilian casualties, and considerable anger at the attacks, including among Iranians who have little sympathy for the government. The bombing of one's country by foreign powers is hardly a straightforward proposition, regardless of how deeply one despises those who govern it.But Iran in 2026 is also a country that has endured almost five decades of Islamic Republic rule, successive waves of protests, deteriorating economic conditions, and increasingly brutal attempts by the authorities to suppress opposition.The nationwide uprising that began in December 2025, and the massacres that followed in January, which left an estimated 40,000 people killed in two days, added another devastating chapter to that history. Security forces sought to crush demonstrations that had spread across the country, leaving families mourning their dead and an already profound divide between the population and the political establishment even deeper.It is against this background that Iranians' response is even more powerful.During Iraq's invasion, Iranians from across the political spectrum rallied to defend their country against a foreign army. In 2026, footage emerging from inside Iran has shown people thanking the leaders of the very countries carrying out strikes against the Islamic Republic.Graffiti appealing directly to US President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu began appearing during the January uprising, including messages pleading with them to intervene as protesters faced the security forces. Following the American and Israeli military operations, other messages went considerably further, thanking Trump and Netanyahu for their actions.In Karaj, west of Tehran, graffiti reading "We love you BB," a reference to Netanyahu, appeared on a wall, while videos circulated by Iran International showed Iranians expressing gratitude toward both leaders.The sight of Iranians publicly thanking an Israeli prime minister and an American president for military action against targets inside their own country would have been almost inconceivable during the Iran-Iraq War.Such expressions are not representative of the entire population, but the fact they are seen and they are there is crucial in understanding the standing of the Islamic Republic currently. Many Iranians oppose foreign military intervention, including those who are bitterly opposed to the Islamic Republic, and the continued appearance of pro-government rallies (however falsified their attendance numbers) demonstrates that the authorities retain a constituency prepared to mobilize in their support.Nevertheless, the messages of gratitude, particularly those directed toward Netanyahu, offer an astonishing illustration of how far relations between sections of Iranian society and their rulers have deteriorated.The Islamic Republic, meanwhile, sought to portray the wars as further proof of the country's enduring national unity.Following the Twelve-Day War in June 2025, senior military and political officials repeatedly praised the solidarity of the Iranian people, with IRGC spokesman Brigadier-General Ali Mohammad Naeini declaring that Israel had encountered the "ironclad unity of the Iranian people."Similar declarations accompanied the renewed conflict in 2026. In September, IRGC Aerospace Force commander Brigadier-General Majid Mousavi praised the nightly pro-government gatherings, describing them as a demonstration of the Iranian people's commitment to defending their country's identity, independence, and very existence, while urging continued support for the Islamic Republic and its armed forces. Later that month, President Masoud Pezeshkian accused the US and Israel of attempting to sow divisions within Iranian society, insisting that the country was experiencing "unprecedented unity and cohesion."Such language would have been familiar to Khomeini, who spent much of the Iran-Iraq War portraying the sacrifices of ordinary Iranians as evidence of the nation's commitment to the revolution. But to proclaim national unity is one thing. Demonstrating that the population remains united behind those making the proclamations is quite another.An incident in Tehran last Friday evening provided a particularly interesting example.Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei, one of the Islamic Republic's most recognizable diplomatic voices throughout the conflict, was booed by members of an audience attending a performance of Arash, an orchestral theatrical production based on the legendary Iranian archer who sacrificed himself to protect his homeland.Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei was booed by audience members after being invited to the podium for a short speech during a performance of the orchestral production “Arash” in Tehran on Friday, according to footage circulating on social media. https://t.co/6HPxlFYrn9— Iran International English (@IranIntl_En) October 10, 2026According to footage circulated by Iranian media, Baghaei had taken a microphone to address the audience when some spectators began booing him.Arash occupies a special place in Iranian mythology, a patriotic figure immersed in the defense of the nation's territorial integrity. That a senior representative of the Islamic Republic should encounter such a hostile reception at a production celebrating one of Iran's most enduring national heroes speaks to the complicated relationship between Iranian national identity and the clerical government that claims to represent it.It also lets us see into a small window of the current feelings of the Iranian people compared to 1980.Hussein invaded an Iran was still coming to terms with the upheaval of revolutionSaddam Hussein invaded a country that was bitterly divided, politically unstable, and still coming to terms with the upheaval of revolution. His expectation that those divisions would make Iran easy prey proved disastrous, as Iranians who disagreed profoundly about their country's future nevertheless found common cause in defending its borders.Khomeini was able to capitalize on that national resistance, using the war to strengthen the very political system whose future had appeared so uncertain when the fighting began.The Islamic Republic's present leadership has sought to draw upon much the same sentiment, invoking the nationalistic language of sacrifice, sovereignty, and resistance, while insisting that the nation stands firmly behind its armed forces. For those who know Iranians, love of their homeland is one thing that can bring them together.But the Iran of 2026 is a very different country from the one Saddam invaded. Its people have lived under the Islamic Republic for almost half a century, and for a substantial section of the population, the government itself has become inseparable from the grievances that have repeatedly brought Iranians onto the streets.Forty-six years ago, Saddam discovered that Iranians were prepared to put aside their differences to defend their country, allowing Khomeini to transform a war for national survival into a foundation for the Islamic Republic's consolidation. Today, the same government continues to invoke the patriotism of the Iranian people, but after decades of repression, revolution, and economic uncertainty, it can no longer assume that those who love their country are still loyal to those who rule it.

title: Indonesia seeks Nigerian investors, eyes stronger trade ties
body: By Favour Ulebor, Jakarta Indonesia is seeking increased investment from Nigerian businesses and stronger bilateral cooperation in renewable energy, waste management, manufacturing and agriculture, while expressing willingness to invest in Nigeria, and expand trade, industrial partnerships between both countries. Speaking to Nigerian journalists ahead of the 41st Trade Expo Indonesia on Tuesday in Jakarta, Senior Trade Analyst at Indonesia’s Ministry of Trade, Iska Huberta Sinural, said bilateral trade should go beyond Nigeria importing Indonesian products to include Nigerian exports, investments and business partnerships in Indonesia. Sinural said the country was targeting $17.5 billion in transactions at the exhibition, which would bring together more than 600 exhibitors to showcase products and explore business opportunities with international buyers and investors. She said Indonesia was particularly interested in attracting buyers from Africa and expanding its business networks beyond traditional markets, while encouraging Nigerian investors to explore opportunities in the Indonesian economy. The analyst said Nigeria had remained among the leading countries in terms of buyers attending the Indonesian trade exhibition, ranking third in 2024 and fourth in 2025, according to figures she presented during the interview. Sinural said the two countries could achieve more through stronger government engagement, noting that trade agreements needed to translate into practical business transactions and investment commitments. She explained that Indonesia wanted officials from partner countries to deepen communication and hold more meetings to implement existing agreements. Sinural said attracting buyers had become increasingly challenging because of geopolitical tensions, global economic conditions and the financial demands on exhibitors. She added that the organisers were focusing on sectors with export potential and seeking reliable exhibitors capable of meeting buyers’ requirements. According to her, the exhibition will feature five broad areas, including food, beverages and agricultural products; manufactured goods; industrial estates and services; fashion and handicrafts; and furniture and home decoration. Also speaking, a member of the Export Enhancement Division of the Indonesian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Muhammad Alpvy, said there were significant untapped opportunities for trade and investment between Indonesia and African countries, including Nigeria. Alpvy said Indonesian businesses were interested in expanding cooperation beyond existing commodity transactions to include manufacturing, renewable energy, waste management and the establishment of factories in Nigeria and Indonesia. He identified palm oil, rubber products, food ingredients and healthcare manufacturing as areas with opportunities for expanded trade, adding that both countries could also explore ways to process raw materials into finished products. Alpvy said high shipping costs and trade barriers remained major challenges to trade between Nigeria and Indonesia, noting that the distance between the two countries increased transportation expenses. He called for further discussions on trade arrangements that would reduce these costs and make it easier for businesses to establish long-term commercial relationships. On investment, Alpvy said Nigerian businesses had expressed interest in renewable energy and waste management, including partnerships that could support the establishment of production facilities. He explained that businesses needed clear arrangements on investment structures, tariffs, shipping costs and other operating conditions to make cross-border investments sustainable. Alpvy also urged Nigerian businesses to introduce local food and beverages to Indonesian consumers, saying greater awareness of Nigerian products and culture could open new markets for both countries. He said Nigerian businesses could adapt their products to Indonesian tastes and consumer preferences, while exploring opportunities to establish Nigerian restaurants and introduce local food products to the market. Alpvy further highlighted opportunities in renewable energy and waste management, including the production of alternative fuel from agricultural and animal waste. He said stronger cooperation in these sectors could create long-term benefits beyond immediate import and export transactions. Separately, Head of International Trade Division at the Regional Office of Industry and Trade of West Java Province, Moch. Lukmanul Hakim, presented data showing growth in the province’s exports to countries within the jurisdiction of the Indonesian Embassy in Abuja, with Nigeria accounting for the largest share of exports recorded during the first eight months of 2026. According to the presentation, West Java’s total exports to the eight countries covered by the Abuja office rose from $275.78 million in 2024 to $383.61 million in 2025. The data further showed that exports to the eight countries amounted to $160.17 million between January and August 2026, of which Nigeria accounted for $109.36 million, representing 68.28 per cent of the total. Other destinations included Ghana, which accounted for $21.85 million, Benin with $9.59 million, Liberia with $3.48 million, Niger with $2.94 million, Togo with $14.96 million and Burkina Faso with $930,000. The presentation also highlighted West Java’s major export commodities, including processed food products, motor vehicles and parts, paper and paperboard, electrical equipment, pharmaceutical products, vegetable oils, beverages and machinery. The figures underscored Nigeria’s importance as a destination for West Java’s exports and the scope for both countries to explore further trade and investment opportunities. The presentation also identified potential Nigerian products for export to Indonesia, including cocoa beans, soybean oilcake, soya beans, sesame seeds, cashew nuts, groundnuts, cotton, cocoa paste, aluminium alloys, lead, rubber-related products and glass containers. Other products highlighted on the export potential map included electrical energy, insecticides, leather products, ethylene polymers and waste and scrap aluminium, pointing to opportunities for Nigeria to diversify its exports to Indonesia beyond crude oil. The Indonesian side also identified challenges associated with Nigeria’s banking system, particularly the difficulties foreign investors may encounter when seeking to open bank accounts to facilitate business transactions. The officials expressed hope that the Nigerian government would look into the concerns to make it easier for foreign businesses to establish operations and sustain commercial relationships in the country. The 41st Trade Expo Indonesia is scheduled to hold from October 14 to 18, 2026, bringing together exporters, buyers, manufacturers and investors to explore trade and investment opportunities. The post Indonesia seeks Nigerian investors, eyes stronger trade ties appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: The mysterious mission of a Ukrainian plane in the Middle East. Another military transport
body:
A Ukrainian military Il-76MD was recorded on 12 October on a route from Sharurah in Saudi Arabia to Istanbul. While the route itself is significant for military transport, the context is even more important; for months, Ukraine has been developing defence cooperation with Riyadh and Arabian Peninsula states in the areas of drones, air defence, and electronic warfare.
On this occasion, a military Il-76MD of the Ukrainian Air Force was observed. This same aircraft has previously been seen on routes connecting Ukraine, Turkey, and Saudi Arabia. Therefore, the flight from Sharurah is part of the ongoing military-logistical cooperation between Kyiv and Riyadh.
Sharurah is located right on the border with Yemen, a key area for the Saudi armed forces in the context of the Houthi threat. In September, the Houthis claimed to have attacked the base there with ballistic missiles and drones. A month later, a Ukrainian heavy military transport aircraft took off from the same area.
It is worth noting that Ukraine is no longer just a state requesting assistance. Kyiv is beginning to export its own wartime experience. Ukrainian specialists have already worked in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Qatar on countering Shahed drones and providing air defence consultancy. This is complemented by a ten-year „Drone Deal”, which includes interceptor drones, air defence systems, electronic warfare, and the transfer of Ukrainian weaponry and know-how.
Ukraine provides its partners on the Arabian Peninsula not only with the political experience of the war with Russia but also with highly practical solutions—namely, how to detect, combat, and neutralise drones as well as missile and UAV attacks. For Saudi Arabia, which is once again facing Houthi strikes, this is a necessary defence partnership.
The observed flight aligns perfectly with the strengthening military cooperation between Ukraine, Saudi Arabia, and key states on the Arabian Peninsula. Although there are doubts regarding „Ukrainian drone technologies”, it must be emphasised that more countries are seeking to cooperate with Kyiv.

title: Russian Supreme Court Bans Ingush Sufi Muslim Order as ‘Extremist’
body:
Russia’s Supreme Court on Wednesday outlawed the Batal Hajji brotherhood , a closed Sufi Muslim order originating from the North Caucasus republic of Ingushetia.
The court granted a request from state prosecutors to designate the order as an “extremist” organization for “providing material support for bandit insurgents of the North Caucasus.”
The Prosecutor General’s Office said Batal Hajji members were linked to numerous attacks on Russian police and military in the North Caucasus and orchestrated the deadly 2009 Nevsky Express train bombing claimed by Chechen rebel leader Doku Umarov.
The prosecutor also said that Batal Hajji affiliates aided the deadly March 2024 attack on the Crocus City Hall concert venue near Moscow and the assassination of Lieutenant General Igor Kirillov the same year by selling weapons and ammunition to the perpetrators.
“More than 100 members of the order have been convicted of the illicit trafficking of means for committing acts of terror. Leaders and members of the community organized illegal channels to supply foreign-made firearms from abroad,” the prosecutor’s office said in a statement published Wednesday.
Russian authorities designated the brotherhood’s so-called “military wing” a “terrorist” organization in 2023.
The Batal Hajji brotherhood was founded in the 19th century by Ingush Sheikh Batal Hajji Belkhoroev, a pupil of the Chechen Muslim mystic Kunta-Hajji (Kunta Kishiev).
Membership in the closed order, which numbers around 20,000 members, is passed down strictly by birthright.
The order’s members held a handful of key government roles and a near monopoly on Ingushetia’s construction industry in the 1990s and early 2000s before a clash with the republic’s new Kremlin-appointed leadership led to their fall from power.
Around 100 of its members allegedly joined the Russian military in 2022 as part of the Batal Hajji Rapid Response Unit, a part of Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov's Akhmat military unit within the Russian army, according to the exiled news website Meduza.

title: High Court throws out Afenyo-Markin’s GH¢15m defamation suit against Sammy Gyamfi
body: The High Court’s General Jurisdiction 1 has thrown out Minority Leader Alexander Afenyo-Markin’s GH¢15 million defamation suit against Ghana Gold Board Chief Executive Officer, Sammy Gyamfi. The court found the writ incurably defective and incompetent, ruling that it could not properly invoke the court’s jurisdiction. In reaching its decision, the court relied on Coleman v Newmont on the applicable procedural rule and Owusu Domena on the requirement to raise objections promptly. The ruling ends the proceedings under the defective writ. It concerns the procedural validity of the action rather than a determination of whether the statements complained of were defamatory. Mr Afenyo-Markin announced the legal action in Parliament on 24 August 2026, saying it followed allegations of extortion made against him amid a dispute over GoldBod and the Bank of Ghana’s Domestic Gold Purchase Programme. The High Court suit also named Multimedia Group Limited as a defendant. The Minority Leader maintained that the allegations were false and intended to damage his reputation. The case subsequently generated disagreement over service of the writ. Mr Gyamfi authorised his lawyers, Ayine & Partners, to accept the court documents, while Mr Afenyo-Markin’s lawyers later said service had been completed and rejected claims that their client was avoiding it.

title: Authorities Find Young Man Dead at Stegna Beach in Rhodes
body: RHODES, October 2026 — A 25-year-old man died at Stegna beach in Rhodes on Wednesday after floodwaters swept his car into the sea during a severe storm on the island. Authorities raised the alarm after they found the man unconscious on the beach, near the village of Archangelos on the east coast of Rhodes, in the Dodecanese. The Hellenic Coast Guard and the Fire Service then responded to the scene. Rushing water from a nearby stream carried a total of four vehicles into the sea at Stegna beach, local reports said. Authorities have not officially released the man’s name, and it remains unclear exactly how he came to be caught in the floodwaters. Stegna beach storm response Heavy rain hit Rhodes from the early hours of Wednesday 14 October, turning roads into rivers in several parts of the island. As a result, authorities sent a warning through the 112 emergency number at 10:44am local time, urging residents of the Rhodes regional unit to limit their movements. In addition, the Municipality of Rhodes closed part of the road from Archangelos to Malona for safety reasons. Bus services on the Faliraki route also stopped. Lightning struck the Rhodes station of public broadcaster ERT South Aegean, damaging its electrical system and taking its radio program off the air. Weather across the Dodecanese Before the storm peaked, the Hellenic National Meteorological Service issued an emergency bulletin that forecast locally heavy rain and thunderstorms across the Dodecanese until Wednesday afternoon. Severe weather has also hit other Greek islands this month. Greek City Times reported on 4 October on flooding and rescues in Ierapetra, Crete . Live rainfall readings for Rhodes are available from the National Observatory of Athens weather network . So far, officials have not said when they will release further details about the man’s death. Source: AMNA The post Authorities Find Young Man Dead at Stegna Beach in Rhodes appeared first on Greek City Times .

Andy Lord, Interim Chair of the NAD Group Advisory Board
Andy Lord has been appointed Interim Chair of the National Armaments Director (NAD) Group Advisory Board.
Andy is currently Commissioner of Transport for London, responsible for the delivery of safe and reliable transport services across the capital.
He joined TfL in 2019 as Managing Director of London Underground, subsequently becoming Chief Operating Officer before his appointment as Commissioner. Throughout his career, he has held several senior engineering, operational and customer-service roles.
Andy also served as a Non-Executive Director and Board member for Defence Equipment & Support from 2018 until March this year.
Andy has been appointed by Luke Pollard, Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, until April 30, 2027.
The appointment comes as the NAD Group continues to establish a simpler, more integrated governance model designed to support effective decision-making, clearer accountability and stronger management of performance and risk across the Group.
National Armaments Director Rupert Pearce said of the appointment:
I am delighted to welcome Andy as Interim Chair of the NAD Group Advisory Board. Andy brings extensive experience both within our organisation, having served as a DE&S Board member and trusted critical friend for eight years, and in leading large, complex organisations.
His insight, challenge and independent perspective will be invaluable as we continue to build the NAD Group into an integrated, mission-focused organisation.
The new Advisory Board’s role is to provide independent support and challenge to the NAD and senior leadership, helping to ensure that the Group is well run and manages its strategy, performance and risks effectively.
I am delighted to be appointed the Interim Advisory Board Chair. I have seen first-hand the expertise and commitment that exists across the organisations that now make up the NAD Group, and the vital contribution they make to Defence.
The opportunity now is to build on those strengths, bringing together expertise from across the Group to deliver even greater impact. I look forward to supporting the leadership team as it continues to drive integration, transformation and operational excellence in support of its mission.
The Board provides a strategic, Group-wide perspective, testing whether the organisation is moving in the right direction and identifying where further support, challenge or intervention may be valuable.
These contributions support the NAD Group’s ambition to create a high-support, high-challenge environment, in which leaders are empowered to deliver while remaining accountable for results.
Alongside Andy, the NAD Group’s Non-Executive Members (NEMs) are Robert MacLeod, Tony Meggs, Tracy Sheedy, Carolyn Battersby, Claire Hawkings and Sarah Albon (Safety & Security Committee only).
NEMs are not part of the NAD Group’s executive management structure. Their value comes from their independence and the breadth of experience they bring.
The Board will be supported by three specialist committees covering nominations and remuneration; audit and risk assurance; and safety and security.
Biographies of the NEMs can be found here: NAD Group Non-Executive Members biographies 2026-27 ( PDF , 192 KB , 3 pages )
