title: Rollover cost of T-bills reduced substantially, one-year bill yield drops 19% since December 2024
body: The cost of rolling over Ghana’s local currency debt has substantially reduced since December 2024. Interest rates on Ghana’s six-month treasury bill (182-day bill) have fallen to about 6.5%, and its one-year bill to 10.1% at the end of August 2026, from almost 30% at the end of 2024, S&P Global stated. The Ministry of Finance imposed a three-year ban on the issuance of new medium- or long-term domestic bonds following the domestic debt restructuring in December 2022. In 2026, the government started to issue longer tenor bonds, which should help lengthen the maturity profile of Ghana’s local currency debt. However, S&P said the conflict in the Middle East is likely to erode some of these gains by causing inflation and financing costs to rise and increasing pressure on the cedi. Last week, the government increased its T-bills uptake reflecting higher financing needs following weeks of below-target acceptances. This week’s higher issuance target of GH¢5.02 billion further reinforces this view. However, the GH¢1.53bn raised above last week’s target could temporarily ease funding pressures. Against this backdrop, analyst expect yields to remain broadly stable, as elevated financing needs limit the scope for further declines. This week’s issuance will cover maturing bills of GH¢3.91 billion.

title: Nuclear arsenals unlikely to be discussed by Putin, Trump, Xi Jinping — Kremlin
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Nuclear arsenals are unlikely to feature on the agenda of a trilateral meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, should one take place at the summit in China, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
"Nuclear arsenals are not an appropriate topic to bring up," he replied when asked what the agenda for the meeting might be and whether it would be appropriate to discuss nuclear arsenals and energy in general.
"You know that our Chinese friends believe their nuclear capabilities are currently incomparable to those of Russia and the United States, and they believe there is no topic to discuss. This is the Chinese side’s position, which we respect. Therefore, it is unlikely that this issue could be discussed in a trilateral format," the Kremlin spokesman said.

title: Zelenskyy sits down with NPR. And, Pope Leo diagnosed with lung cancer
body:
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
In an interview with NPR, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that the Trump administration warned it could cut intelligence-sharing with Ukraine unless Ukrainian forces halt long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries. Zelenskyy said the administration's decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel won't lower fuel prices and refuted President Trump's claim that Ukraine caused the price to spike, instead pointing to the war in Iran. This interview comes as Russia's full-scale invasion approaches its five-year mark .
Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer following surgery to remove a growth from his lung, the Vatican announced. Doctors at Gemelli Hospital in Rome removed the lower lobe of the 71-year-old Pope's right lung during a successful procedure that lasted about 90 minutes. Post-surgery analysis confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma .
Trump has ousted Kimberly Guilfoyle as his ambassador to Greece. She was a prominent MAGA figure and the former fiancée of his oldest son. Guilfoyle faced unflattering allegations that she was trying to profit from her position, which she denies. The Wall Street Journal reported a series of questionable actions by Guilfoyle last month. One incident involved her asking a Trump donor for $100,000 to settle a credit card bill, promising to use her connections within the administration in return.
A federal judge ruled late yesterday that Trump cannot bar news organizations from covering him at the White House because he doesn't like their coverage, at least until a formal trial concludes. U.S. District Court Judge Timothy J. Kelly found that Trump's decision to exclude more than 70 journalists from CNN, MS NOW, and Politico violated their free speech and due process rights. Both rights are enshrined in the Bill of Rights of the U.S. Constitution.
The results of the 2026 midterm elections will shape the final two years of President Trump's second term and serve as a precursor to the 2028 general election. This month, Morning Edition is reporting from six states that could change the balance of power in Washington.
This week, Morning Edition 's A Martínez traveled to the reliably red state of Texas. The cost of living is a major concern for many voters here. Ground beef hit a record high of about $7/lb in August, which is around $1.50 more than when Trump returned to office. In Floresville, Texas, Martínez spoke with a fourth-generation farmer and rancher who raises beef cattle about the challenges he is facing. Listen to what he had to say .
Martínez also spoke with residents about what is on their minds ahead of Election Day. Hear more about:
Follow the reporting: North Carolina and Georgia coverage airs Oct. 20, followed by reporting from Ohio and Michigan. You can follow along on Morning Edition , NPR.org, in the NPR app and in this newsletter.
by Anthony Kuhn , International Correspondent
A screenshot from Lady Gaga's ad for familymart famiilymart/screenshot by npr hide caption
To report on Lady Gaga's ad for the FamilyMart convenience store chain, the first thing I had to do was watch the video of it.
Gaga plays the part of a store worker dancing through the aisles in a leather uniform and platform shoes. To me, she looked like a high priestess of camp, boogying through a temple of retail efficiency to a mad techno beat.
It wasn't just the wild style that hooked me. It was also the confluence of culture and commerce in Japan.
The issue of Japan's aging society and its shrinking workforce are an inescapable part of life in Japan, and foreign workers are an inevitable part of the solution. FamilyMart's ad leverages Lady Gaga's non-conformist pop persona to appeal to an increasingly diverse workforce, a retail analyst explained to me .
Konbinis, as convenience stores are called in Japan, are also an inescapable part of life there. They function as a deli, post office, copy shop, bank, tax office and Ticketmaster all rolled into one. That's because it's cheaper for the government and businesses to offer these services through the konbinis than to run their own.
Another draw is the crazy fresh food, delivered to the stores several times a day. When I'm on assignment in Tokyo, I'm often on deadlines, so I head straight for the konbini onigiri (rice balls) with salmon, tofu and seaweed salad and mochi for dessert. It would be nice to have time for a proper meal, but until I do, I'm not too badly off living the konbini lifestyle.
Give the segment a listen , at your convenience!
The Trump administration abruptly cut down more than 400 trees at Washington D.C.'s historic East Potomac Golf Links last weekend. A federal judge has ordered testimony from two high-level officials with the Interior Department over the recent abrupt removal of trees; the judge plans to hold another hearing Oct. 19. Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR hide caption

title: Investors in collapsed jeweller Vashi 'could be compensated' after watchdog ruling
body: A financial watchdog has ruled that investors who lost money when the jeweller Vashi collapsed can receive compensation under an anti-fraud scheme. The company folded in April 2023 with debts of £170 million, and investors, many from the Middle East , believed its diamond stock would be used to reimburse them if the company failed. But when the safes were examined, the stock was worth £114,000. Its founder, Vashi Dominguez, vanished as his UK firm was wound up, and an investigation by The National revealed he was able to raise millions to fuel his global ambitions using the diamond stock and inflated sales figures. Some investors have been seeking compensation under the authorised push payment (APP) scam reimbursement scheme that was operated by banks at the time. The UK’s Financial Ombudsman Service (FOS) initially rejected a claim by a group of investors that banks were not liable for losses in Vashi under APP But it has now overturned its decision regarding the claim of a couple for around £100,000 ($132,000). In his ruling, the Financial Ombudsman, Stephen Dickie, said that Vashi’s “supposed business model was simply a falsehood and that it was most likely a deliberate fraud”. The decision now clears the way for the couple, referred to as Mr and Mrs C, to get their money back from their bank, NatWest. Millions of pounds could also be returned to other investors under the APP scheme. In his ruling, Mr Dickie said neither Mr and Mrs C nor NatWest could have known that Vashi was a “fraud” and a “facade” overstating the value of its accounts and diamond stocks. Given the bank’s obligations under the APP scams code, NatWest should have done more, especially when two payments totalling £50,000 were sent to Vashi from the couple’s account in the space of 24 hours. “NatWest ought to have been on the lookout for out-of-character and unusual transactions and other indications that its customer might be at risk of financial harm from fraud,” said Mr Dickie. Michael Moszynski was among a group of Vashi investors urging the FOS to reconsider its initial ruling, made at the beginning of this year. He told The National he welcomed the new decision. “This is what we've been fighting for,” he said. “The amount of detail we presented meant that we put them in a position where they couldn't continue not upholding our complaints against the banks.” Stuart McFadden, co-founder of fraud-recovery experts Refundee, has been pursuing claims on behalf of investors, including Mr and Mrs C as well as those from overseas. “This is a significant outcome for investors who were wrongly denied reimbursement,” he told The National . “While this was a sophisticated scam in its delivery, once it collapsed it was clear that investors had been defrauded. We believed the evidence was clear and continued to fight on their behalf, and we’re pleased the FOS has now found NatWest should have done more to stop these payments.” An FOS representative said it would not comment on individual complaints but “allegations of large-scale investment fraud are among the most complex cases we deal with”. “They can involve thousands of pages of evidence, investigations by multiple agencies including the police and regulators, and a picture that constantly evolves,” said the representative. “Ultimately, it’s not our role to prosecute fraud; it’s to decide if a bank should be held liable for an investor’s losses.” The Metropolitan Police complex fraud team has launched an investigation, called Operation Palisade, into the collapse of Vashi. NatWest has been approached for comment.

title: Kazakhstan Proposes Local Rare Earth Processing Partnership with Belgium
body: Kazakhstan has invited Belgian companies to help process critical minerals domestically. Astana hopes to gain access to European processing technologies to expand exports of higher-value products used in high-tech industries. For now, the two sides are discussing laboratory testing and potential projects, with no new investment agreements announced. The proposal was presented at a Kazakhstan-Belgium seminar held on October 12 at Nazarbayev University in Astana. Vice Minister of Industry and Construction Olzhas Saparbekov said Kazakhstan could supply 21 of the 34 critical raw materials on the European Union’s list. “We are ready to discuss phased models under which processing is gradually transferred to Kazakhstan along with the necessary technologies and expertise,” Saparbekov said. Belgian companies were offered opportunities to cooperate in extracting metals using chemical solutions, separating rare earth oxides, recycling, and manufacturing industrial equipment. Potential projects include producing materials for batteries, semiconductors, specialty alloys, and permanent magnets. The participants also discussed shipping products to Europe through Belgium’s port of Antwerp. Kazakhstan already produces several sought-after industrial metals, including tantalum, niobium, and beryllium. It also plans to begin gallium production, with a target of 15 metric tons a year. However, developing more advanced processing facilities remains a challenge. Since 2018, Kazakhstan has allocated more than 67 billion tenge (approximately $149 million) to geological exploration. According to the ministry, surveys at 11 exploration sites have identified 38 promising areas. Commercial development will require determining the metal content of the ores and the cost of extracting them. In particular, studies of the Kuirektykol site in the Karaganda region have revealed significantly larger rare earth reserves than previously estimated. The size of the discovery does not establish whether mining would be commercially viable. To study mineral resources and test processing technologies, Kazakhstan plans to establish a regional rare earth research center with the participation of European institutions. The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development has supported the preparation of a preliminary feasibility study. Construction of the laboratory complex is expected to begin in 2027, with operations scheduled to start in 2028. Representatives of metals processor Molymet Belgium and Australia’s Lindian Resources Limited, which owns a rare earth processing plant in Kazakhstan, took part in the discussions. The next stage of negotiations is expected to involve exchanging samples, testing processing methods, and preparing feasibility studies. For European industry, Kazakhstan could become an additional supplier of critical minerals amid Europe’s dependence on Chinese processing capacity. However, the country’s stated potential to supply 21 types of critical raw materials encompasses projects at different stages of development, ranging from geological exploration to operating production facilities.

title: No plans so far for trilateral consultations on Ukraine — Kremlin spokesman
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Russia did not participate in consultations on a package agreement on resolving the Ukraine conflict, allegedly prepared by Washington, and so far has no plans to take part in any trilateral talks on the issue, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
Asked if Moscow had taken part in the consultations, he answered in the negative.
Speaking of the possibility of such talks being held in the future, Peskov said: "We don’t expect them at the moment." "You know that the president said: after Ukraine tried to disrupt our elections, we will think about when to resume trilateral talks." "We will do it in strict compliance with our national interests," the Russian presidential spokesman concluded.

title: Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP: Speech at the 2026 LGBTQ+ Defence Awards.
body:
Tonight we stand on the shoulders of giants.
In defiance of those who do not accept who we are, or who we love, or how we present ourselves to the world.
In defence of the values of freedom, equality, and democracy – the things that make this country great.
In celebration of our LGBTQ+ community in all of its diversity – and particularly this evening those of you whose stars have shone most brightly and whom we all look to as role models.
We are able be here this evening because of Jeanette Smith and Graeme Grady, and Duncan Lustig-Prean and John Beckett.
Jeanette and Graeme, dismissed from the Royal Air Force in 1994 after being outed as lesbian and gay.
Duncan and John discharged from the Royal Navy in 1995 and 1993 respectively for the same reason.
All of them removed in accordance with the policy of the department I now lead, the Ministry of Defence – a policy that was deemed unlawful thanks to the cases brought to the European Court of Human Rights by Jeanette, Graeme, Duncan and John.
They did not fail their country. Their country failed them.
Their courage in bringing those cases changed laws, hearts and minds.
And because of them, there are now more than 2,500 openly LGBTQ+ people serving in our Armed Forces today.
We owe them an enormous debt of gratitude for not only making our Armed Forces more equal but also making them stronger.
But I don’t want to sanitise our history, or the harm that it caused, because it teaches us something about how we meet the challenges we face today.
Take Dawn, who was outed while serving at sea in 1994.
When she was just 20 years old – roughly about the same age I was when I came out – someone – anonymously, obviously – reported her as a lesbian.
She was investigated.
Questioned for hours.
Had her personal belongings and letters taken.
Was removed from her ship.
And told to leave the Royal Navy that she loved and had served with distinction for three years.
Dawn has since received restorative measures, including recognition of her service, a beret, an apology and the Etherton Ribbon.
She says that she now feels ‘validated’ and ‘valued’.
But ultimately, she was denied the career she dreamed of and worked so hard to get into.
And the indignity of the ban is hard to wash away.
To this day, some people who were prepared to fight for their country are still having to fight for the justice they are owed.
And so I know that there is still lots that we – that I – need to do.
I think about the experiences of that generation in the context of trans people serving in our Armed Forces today.
Of our collective responsibility – but also of my personal responsibility – to make sure that they can do so feeling valued, respected, and equal in worth and dignity.
We do not exist in a vacuum in the Ministry of Defence or in our Armed Forces.
As society finds its way on navigating the law and protecting the rights and dignity of trans people, I want to be clear about some fundamental things as we do.
I want trans and non-binary people in our country to be able to live their authentic lives and be themselves.
I want all of them to live with dignity and freedom, independence, and quality of life and respect.
And I especially want them to be able to do that if they choose to wear the uniform.
No one should face persecution, or have to hide who they are, or battle for acceptance whilst serving their country.
We cannot change the past.
But we can confront it honestly – and learn from it.
And, perhaps most importantly, we can make certain that the generations who follow never have to endure what previous generations endured.
So you have my commitment to work with our LGBT networks, Fighting with Pride and the Royal British Legion to make sure that we live up to our responsibilities to our people today and to future generations.
In the space of a single generation, we have gone from a Britain where gay people could be dismissed from the Armed Forces simply for being who they are, to a Britain where a gay man can lead the Ministry of Defence.
But my social media feeds demonstrate on a daily basis that there will always be those who would prefer to cling on to the prejudices of the past.
The prejudice that says that to be gay or lesbian or bisexual or trans or non-binary is to be weak.
We, in this room, and those like us beyond, know all too well how much courage and strength it can take to be your authentic self.
At home.
At school.
At work.
What is weak about those who served their country with extraordinary loyalty, of being prepared to give their lives for that country, even when that same country denied them the dignity of being themselves?
That wasn’t weak. That was strong and courageous.
Courage isn’t simply the absence of fear.
Courage is looking fear in the face and refusing to let it define you.
It is the determination to do what is right, even when doing so comes at a personal cost.
It is standing your ground when others would rather you disappeared.
It is having the confidence to say, in the words of that great political philosopher, Gloria Gaynor: ‘I am what I am. And what I am needs no excuses.’
For generations, LGBTQ+ people in our Armed Forces have demonstrated precisely that courage.
The courage to serve.
The courage to endure injustice.
The courage to challenge prejudice.
And, increasingly, the courage to serve openly and proudly, without apology and without compromise.
Your sexuality does not determine your strength.
Your gender identity does not determine your courage.
And neither has ever diminished your capacity to serve your country with distinction.
Real strength is not about how loudly you speak, how tough you look, or how closely you conform to somebody else’s idea of what a soldier, a sailor, a marine or an aviator should be.
Real strength is found in character. In loyalty. In integrity. In the willingness to stand up for others. In the quiet determination to keep going when everything around you tells you to stop.
I want young LGBTQ+ people in our cadets, and other young people who might be considering serving in our Armed Forces or working in the Defence industry, to know that our country wants their talent, their commitment, and their courage.
I’m glad that that generation has, in this room, role models to look up to.
People who have served with distinction.
People who have made their units stronger, their colleagues prouder, and their country safer.
People whose example reminds us that progress is not simply something we celebrate in speeches.
It is something we create through the lives we lead, the barriers we break, and the example we set for those who follow.
So thank you to the organisers and sponsors for bringing us together tonight.
To our winners – in and out of uniform – congratulations.
To all of our LGBTQ+ service personnel here tonight and throughout our Armed Forces, let me just end by saying:
Thank you for your courage. Thank you for your service.
And thank you for helping our country become a better reflection of the values that those who came before us always stood ready to defend.
Because of you, generations yet to come will never have to ask whether they belong. They will simply know.
Thank you.

title: Rada passes law implementing international property valuation standards
body:
The Verkhovna Rada has approved in the final reading the law "On Property Valuation" (bill No. 13435), which provides for a systemic update of legislation on valuation activity and implementation of European and international property valuation standards (IVS and EVS).
The approved law fully replaces the law "On Valuation of Property, Property Rights and Professional Valuation Activity in Ukraine" in force since 2001 and is aimed at fulfilling commitments under the Extended Fund Facility (EFF) program with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and at receiving the European Union's macro-financial assistance, the Ukraine Support Loan. The bill is also an indicator under the Ukraine Facility.
According to an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent, the decision was backed by 272 MPs.
The law abolishes the separate expert monetary valuation of land plots, introducing a single valuation of real estate together with the land plot in line with international rules and the principle of unity of legal fate. In addition, the document clearly defines the main types of value, distinguishes between independent and standardized property valuation, and separately regulates valuation for determining the amount of damage caused by the war.
It also changes the regulatory model and the professional status of market participants. The document introduces an open-ended valuer's qualification certificate, updates flexible conditions for confirming professional development every three years at the specialist's choice, and creates a Unified Register of Valuers of Ukraine. In addition, the law provides for creating a single self-regulatory organization of valuers, introducing a three-tier regulation system involving the State Property Fund and a Qualification and Disciplinary Commission, and sets a simplified procedure for acquiring qualifications for foreign specialists.
At the same time, the law regulates the review of reports, introduces an effective system of disciplinary liability with fines and a procedure for pretrial appeal of disputes through an appeals committee, and extends the requirements of the valuation methodology to forensic experts, introducing disciplinary liability for them for violations of property valuation rules.
The innovations are expected to reduce cases of undervaluation or overvaluation of property, increase tax revenues and cut state budget spending on administering the sector.
As reported, in May parliament sent bill No. 13435 for a repeat first reading.
Although in September 2025 the Rada Committee on Economic Development recommended that parliament adopt the bill as a basis, the document received a number of objections. In particular, the Ministry of Economy and the Ministry of Finance supported the draft only on condition of its substantial revision. The Ministry of Justice pointed to inconsistency of some provisions with procedural legislation and violation of the principle of legal certainty. Objections were also voiced by the State Property Fund, the National Securities and Stock Market Commission (NSSMC) and the Main Scientific and Expert Department of the parliamentary staff.

title: Population office wants to know status of nearly 2,000 centenarian Finnish emigrés
body:
If the agency does not receive information about an individual on the list, they will be formally declared deceased.
Finland's Digital and Population Data Services Agency (DVV) has published a list of citizens registered as living abroad who are over the age of 100, in an effort to confirm whether they are still alive or not.
The list includes the full names, dates of birth and last known residence of nearly 2,000 people aged 100 or over who live abroad whose deaths have not officially been recorded by the registry. Authorities have no information about the later stages of their lives.
The DVV is also seeking help from the individuals' relatives. It asked relatives or family members of the people on the list to contact the agency if they have information about their status.
If the agency does not receive information about an individual on the list, the person will be formally declared as deceased, according to the DVV.
The deadline is 22 January 2027 at 4:15 pm.

title: Russian attacks kill at least 10, injure 91 across Ukraine over past day as ballistic missiles strike Kyiv for second straight night
body:
At least 10 people were killed and 91 others injured across Ukraine over the past day, as Russia struck Ukraine with 39 missiles and 128 Shahed-type drones, regional authorities said on Oct. 14.
In Kyiv , at least four people were killed and 25 others injured in overnight missile strikes on the capital, the Kyiv City Prosecutor's Office said . At least three women were killed, and another 24 people, including a 7-year-old girl, were injured as a result of a Russian strike on a nine-story residential building in the city's Desnianskyi District. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that at least one additional victim from Kyiv's Darnytskyi District was hospitalized, and another person killed in the city's Holosiivskyi District.
"Overnight, the Russians deployed 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 strike drones and loitering munitions against our energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast, and Kharkiv," President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a post on social media , adding 600,000 people were without power.
In total, Zelensky said Russia struck Ukraine with 39 missiles including Iskander-M, KN-23, S-400, Zircon, and Onyx missiles from Kursk, Bryansk, Voronezh, and Rostov regions in Russia, as well as with 128 Shahed-type UAVs, including 77 jet-powered ones.
Ukraine's Air Force said it neutralized four ballistic missiles and 115 Russian drones overnight.
In Kyiv Oblast , one person was injured over the past day by Russian strikes, regional governor Tymur Tkachenko said. Civilian facilities, energy infrastructure, homes, warehouses and production facilities, and commercial establishments were hit in Russia's attacks on the oblast.
In Rivne Oblast , a Russian drone strike on a university building in the northwestern city of Rivne, injuring 25 people over the past day, Rivne's National Police branch said. Of the 25 injured, two were in critical condition, while three others are under medical examination, the police said .
In Kharkiv Oblast , over the past day, Russia attacked the city of Kharkiv and settlements in the surrounding region, injuring nine people, including a child, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said. Russia targeted the region with eight ballistic missiles, as well as multiple drones, Syniehubov said.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast , three people were killed and 17 injured in Russian attacks across the region over the past day, according to regional governor Vadym Filashkin .
In northeastern Sumy Oblast , one person was injured by Russian mortar shelling, the Sumy military administration said. Russian forces attacked with a wide arsenal of artillery, mortars, glide bombs, and UAVs. In total, air alert in the oblast lasted 18 hours and 36 minutes during the day.
In southern Kherson Oblast , two people were injured by Russian attacks over the past day, said regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin . Russia attacked multiple settlements in the oblast with air, drone, and artillery fire, damaging critical and social infrastructure, as well as residential areas.
In southeastern Zaporizhzhia Oblast , one person was killed and three injured over the past day, according to regional governor Ivan Fedorov . In total, during the day, Russia launched 1,030 strikes on 56 settlements of Zaporizhia region using artillery, UAVs, and rocket launchers, he said.
In western Lviv Oblast , Russian drone attacks injured three people over the past day, said regional governor Maksym Kozytskyi.
Russian attacks in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast killed two people and injured five others, including a child, over the past day, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said.
Chernihiv Oblast suffered several Russian strikes on a school and administrative building, but no casualties were reported over the past day, regional governor Viacheslav Chaus said.

title: Horizon Air pilots accuse employer of ‘corporate greed’ as staff hold picket
body: Horizon Air pilots have accused their employer of showing a “pattern of mismanagement and corporate greed” that has affected negotiations over wages and conditions. On October 14, 2026, Horizon Air pilots, represented by Teamsters Local 1224 , will hold an informational picket where they will call on the airline to “end its delay tactics and agree to a fair contract”. A Teamsters statement on October 13, 2026, said a group of nearly 650 pilots has been “fighting for a collective bargaining agreement that addresses wages, staffing and training shortages, and operational issues for nearly four years”. Horizon Air pilots are unhappy that colleagues at sister carrier Alaska Airlines perform nearly the same amount of flying “yet their wages remain behind industry standard” due to the company’s “unwillingness to bargain a fair deal”. Alaska Airlines “Horizon Air has shown a pattern of mismanagement and corporate greed that has affected the negotiating process,” the Teamsters Local 1224 statement said. The informational picket is due to be held at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) and Boise Airport (BOI) from 10:30, local time. In February 2026, Teamsters Local 1224 said: “This is not about theatrics or headlines. It is about accountability and meaningful change. Every day, Horizon Air pilots operate a safe, reliable airline under challenging conditions because professionalism is the foundation of who we are. We deserve a contract that reflects that same level of seriousness and respect. The time for waiting has passed. The time for change is now.” Horizon Air operates daily flights to nearly 50 destinations, largely feeding Alaska Airlines’ network in the western United States. title: Zelensky arrives in UK as London vows to speed up anti-drone missile deliveries for Ukraine
body:
Editor's note: The story has been updated with the latest details.
President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in the U.K. on Oct. 14 to meet British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and King Charles III, as London pledges missiles to help Ukraine counter Russia's jet-powered drones.
The visit comes at a tense moment for Ukraine, with U.S. President Donald Trump 's administration pressuring Kyiv to halt strikes against Russian oil refineries and threatening to cut off intelligence sharing and arms shipments.
Ahead of Zelensky's visit, Burnham vowed that the U.K.'s support for Ukraine remains "rock-solid."
The Ukrainian president was first welcomed by King Charles at Buckingham Palace before meeting Burnham.
"I thank His Majesty King Charles III for the audience. It is important for me to have the opportunity to personally thank him for his unwavering support for Ukraine," Zelensky said on X.
The British prime minister then welcomed Zelensky at 10 Downing Street in the company of a military ceremonial guard, the first such honor granted to a foreign leader, according to the BBC .
The British government has announced an air defense missile package worth 45 million pounds (around $60 million) for Ukraine, as the country faces an intensifying onslaught of Russian missiles and drones.
"The U.K. will accelerate deliveries of British Lightweight Multirole Missiles (LMMs), which have proven extremely effective against jet-powered drones that are being used to strike far beyond the front lines in Ukraine, including Kyiv and beyond," the British government said in a press release on Oct. 13.
Russia has been increasingly deploying jet-powered drones that are faster and more difficult to intercept than older Shahed models, posing a new threat as Ukraine braces for massive strikes against energy infrastructure in winter.
Of the 45-million-pound package, the U.K. will expedite the delivery of 10 million pounds ($13 million) worth of LMMs to meet the most urgent winter needs.
"I’m announcing that we're accelerating the delivery of British-made air defenses for (Ukraine)," Burnham told the press while meeting Zelensky. The British leader also said he would seek to "repair bridges" between Ukraine and the U.S.
Burnham's office said earlier that he had instructed his cabinet to prepare additional military and financial assistance packages for Ukraine, as well as fresh sanctions against Russia.
The U.K. further reiterated that it stands by its plans to ban maritime services for Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports.
London said last year it would implement the phased ban over 2026 "in lockstep with our European partners."
The EU plans to ban Russian LNG imports by January 2027 but has failed to agree on a full ban on maritime services, with Greece securing a carve-out for Russian LNG exports to non-EU countries.

title: Ogun APC secretariat set for commissioning in November — Abiodun
body:
Ogun State Governor, Dapo Abiodun, has announced that the state secretariat of the All Progressives Congress ( APC ), an ultra-modern facility in Abeokuta, will be commissioned in November.
The governor disclosed this while conducting an on-the-spot inspection of the imposing edifice located along Oke-Mosan, Abeokuta, where he expressed satisfaction with the pace and quality of work.
The governor said the project, whose groundbreaking ceremony took place less than a year ago, was nearing completion and would provide the party with a befitting permanent administrative base in the state.
“We were here for the groundbreaking ceremony less than a year ago, and I must say that I am impressed with what I am seeing. I am happy with the location and the level of completion. I am sure that within another week or so, this should have been completely rounded off,” he said.
The facility features a conference and banquet hall with a seating capacity of more than 500 people, offices for party officials and members, and adequate parking space.
Abiodun described the project as a significant milestone for the APC in Ogun State, particularly as political activities gather momentum ahead of the 2027 general elections.
Highlighting the prominence of the structure, the governor said its imposing appearance and strategic location would make it a landmark for the party.
“Even just driving past our office itself, you begin to feel a sense of defeat if you are not in our party,” he said.
The new secretariat will replace the rented premises previously used by the Ogun APC in Abeokuta, providing a permanent facility for the party’s administration, meetings and other activities.

title: US Embassy in Israel issues safety warning about unexploded ordnances after school trip explosion
body: The US Embassy in Israel issued a safety warning to American citizens on Tuesday about unexploded ordnance and munitions found across extensive areas of Israel, the West Bank, and the Gaza Strip, a day after a teenager was killed and 24 people were injured in an explosion during a school trip in northern Israel.The warning followed the death of Elazar Yair Wilensky, who was killed when unexploded Hezbollah ammunition detonated during the school trip.In its statement, the embassy warned that the danger was particularly great near border areas and that, in many cases, the locations of unexploded ordnance are unmarked, and the devices may be difficult to identify."Rain, flooding, agricultural work, and construction activities frequently bring buried munitions to the surface, making them more unstable," the embassy said.The embassy stressed that unexploded ordnance can come in various shapes and sizes, including artillery shells, mortar bombs, rockets, grenades, landmines, and cluster munitions.It warned particularly about small, round cluster bomblets, which may resemble balls or toys and attract children's attention."Assume that any unidentified object is dangerous," the statement said.Embassy emphasizes three-step safety rule: Recognize, retreat, reportThe embassy emphasized a three-step safety rule in its guidelines: recognize, retreat, and report.Anyone who identifies a suspicious object should stop immediately and avoid approaching it to investigate. Instead, they should carefully retreat along the same route they used to reach the area, keep others away, particularly children, and report the object to Israel Police by calling 100.The embassy also warned against physically touching unexploded ordnance, throwing objects at it, or using mobile phones and two-way radios nearby.It further recommended against collecting ammunition casings, shell fragments, or war souvenirs, even if the items have reportedly been neutralized and are considered safe.The embassy urged the public to avoid entering areas marked as minefields or contaminated by unexploded ordnance, and to remain on paved roads and familiar trails when hiking outside urban areas.It also called on parents to explain to children that they must never touch unidentified metal objects and should immediately report any such discoveries to an adult.In addition, the embassy recommended identifying the location of the nearest protected space, using Home Front Command warning applications, and keeping up to date with security guidance issued by the US State Department.

title: Gunman Kills Four ANC Youth Members In Attack Ahead Of South Africa Polls
body: The police said Wednesday that a gunman killed four members of the youth division of South Africa’s main political party, the ANC, in an attack three weeks before local polls. Politically linked assassinations have surged ahead of the November 4 local government elections, with 43 people killed this year to the end of September, according to an independent civil society group. The attacker opened fire on a memorial service for another ANC member on Tuesday in Katlehong, southeast of Johannesburg, police said. Two men died on the scene and two in hospital, a police statement said. They were aged between 21 and 27. “Three other victims remain in hospital,” it said. The alleged attacker turned himself in to police, who handed the case to a special Political Killings Task Team. The ANC Youth League is an autonomous body within the African National Congress (ANC), the party that led the struggle against apartheid and took power after the first all-race election in 1994. ANC support has dropped in recent decades on complaints of bad governance and corruption, with rival spinoff parties scooping up voters. It was forced into a coalition government in 2024. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organised Crime (GI-TOC) said in a report released this month that 43 people had been killed in 45 attacks with suspected political links in the first nine months of this year. The motives are not always clear but could include internal rivalry or corruption, according to analysts. Confirming that four of its members had died, the ANCYL said, “We can clarify that, according to our information, the suspect is not a member of the ANCYL, the ANC or any of the Alliance formations.” The country holds local government elections on November 4, with parties hoping to benefit from disillusionment with the ANC, the largest party since democracy in 1994, over collapsed infrastructure, crime and corruption. The toll in suspected political hits so far this year already tops the full-year total since the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organised Crime (GI-TOC) started monitoring in 2015, the organisation said. It comes with “highest-risk months still ahead as contests for political power gather pace,” said the independent civil-society organisation headquartered in Geneva. AFP The post Gunman Kills Four ANC Youth Members In Attack Ahead Of South Africa Polls appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Russia to strive for OPEC+ quota compliance — Novak
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Russia will aim to meet its oil production quota under the OPEC+ agreement to the extent possible, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters on the sidelines of Russian Energy Week.
"I cannot give an exact date because there are many uncertainties and various factors involved. We will strive to fulfill our obligations to the maximum extent based on our capabilities," he said.
According to the latest OPEC report, Russia reduced its oil production in September 2026 by 38,000 barrels per day (bpd) compared to August, bringing the total to 8.643 million bpd. Russian oil production in September was 1.306 million bpd below its quota.
The Russian Energy Week international forum is taking place in Moscow from October 14 to 16, supported by the Russian government, the Russian Energy Ministry, and the Moscow government. The forum is organized by the Roscongress Foundation. TASS is the information partner for Russian Energy Week.

title: European Commission allocates nearly €2.9 bln more to Ukraine for drones, air defense and missiles
body:
According to Ukrinform, this is said in a press release published on the Commission’s website.
“As Russia stalls on the frontlines, it continues to escalate its aerial attacks - cruelly targeting Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure. Europe's steadfast support matters more than ever to help Ukraine protect its skies and save lives. With today's €2.86 billion disbursement, we keep addressing Ukraine's most urgent operational needs, including drones and missiles vital to its defence,” Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission, said.
The Ukraine Support Loan totals €90 billion for 2026–2027, including €60 billion for defence needs and development of Ukraine’s defence‑industrial base, and €30 billion for budget support.
During 2026, €28.3 billion is expected to be directed to support Ukraine’s defence industrial capacity. The Commission said further disbursements under the 2026 defence leg of the instrument will continue in the coming weeks.
By the end of 2026, Ukraine will still have access to €29.64 billion available in EU financial assistance. This includes €25.24 billion under the Ukraine Support Loan (with €12.54 billion for defence‑industry support and €12.7 billion for budget financing) and €4.4 billion in remaining budget support under the initial Ukraine Facility.
In total, more than €17 billion is earmarked to ensure the stability of Ukraine’s budget for the remaining months of 2026. Disbursement depends on meeting conditions set out in the Ukraine Plan and the Memorandum of Understanding.
As reported, since 2022 the European Union and its Member States have provided €231.5 billion in assistance to Ukraine, including €3.8 billion from the proceeds of immobilised Russian assets.
In February 2026, the European Parliament and the Council adopted Regulation (EU) 2026/467, establishing the Ukraine Support Loan. The Regulation provides for up to €90 billion in support to Ukraine. The support is designed to strengthen Ukraine’s defence capabilities and ensure the uninterrupted functioning of the state, delivery of essential public services and economic resilience amid Russia’s aggression.

title: High Court hears petition demanding protection for lawyers from courthouse harassment
body: High Court justices questioned Wednesday whether the Courts Administration's instructions adequately protect lawyers from courthouse harassment, pressing for clearer rules on conduct that guards should halt and how those rules are communicated to the public.The case concerns lawyers representing Palestinians and human rights groups who say right-wing activists follow them through the Supreme Court's corridors, film them at close range, and accuse them of supporting terrorism. The petitioners argue that preventing physical attacks alone is insufficient: Lawyers must be able to prepare for hearings, consult privately with clients, and represent them without intimidation.Justices Dafna Barak-Erez, Gila Canfy-Steinitz, and Yechiel Kasher examined possible protections, including clearly defined areas where lawyers could work without interference. No ruling was delivered during the hearing, and a decision is due to be sent to the parties.Guards instructed to intervene against harassment, humiliation, intimidation of lawyersThe Court's Administration rejected the claim that its protection policy warrants judicial intervention. In an updated response submitted ahead of the hearing, it said security preparations had been strengthened, and guards were explicitly instructed to intervene against the filming aimed at harassing, humiliating, or intimidating lawyers.During Wednesday's hearing, state attorney Hadas Eran condemned interference with lawyers and said that courthouses were not places for demonstrations. She maintained that the instructions were implemented through training and briefings, with guards exercising judgment according to the circumstances.The justices questioned whether that approach provided guards with sufficiently concrete guidance.When Eran referred to a summary of a June 2023 meeting as the written basis for the instructions, Barak-Erez questioned whether it amounted to a comprehensive set of rules and asked when further work on instructions would be completed.“These are very general instructions,” Canfy-Steinitz said, questioning whether they told a guard what to do in a particular situation.Barak-Erez also asked how many people had been removed from courthouses over the past year for disturbing public order. Eran said she would have to obtain the figure, but the discussion exposed a further question: how visitors could be expected to comply with restrictions that were not clearly published. Barak-Erez used the example of a distance limit on filming, asking how someone would know they had breached an unwritten rule.Filed in 2024 by the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel, HaMoked, Gisha, Yesh Din, and Physicians for Human Rights Israel, the petition challenges the policy of the Courts Administration and its director, Judge Tzachi Uziel.No proposal was adopted during the hearingThe organizations, represented by attorneys Michael Sfard and Einat Gayer, proposed confining protests to a designated area inside the courthouse. Sfard argued that lawyers should not have to retreat to a separate room to work undisturbed.The justices explored whether clearer protections for lawyers' personal space would suffice or whether part of the lobby should be designated free of filming and harassment. They also questioned the scope of guards' legal powers. No proposal was adopted during the hearing.In a written update filed ahead of Wednesday's hearing, the petitioners described confrontations during hearings concerning humanitarian aid to Gaza, prison conditions, punitive home demolitions, and other contested policies.The update identified activists from Im Tirtzu in several incidents and argued that repeated involvement by the same individuals calls for measures to prevent further harassment.Among the most serious allegations is an incident from March 30, 2026, during a hearing over displaced Palestinians' return to refugee camps in the northern West Bank. According to the petitioners, an activist followed lawyers after they left the courtroom while the justices examined classified material, then violently pushed Association for Civil Rights in Israel (ACRI) attorney Oded Feller as he tried to enter another courtroom.The filing said footage was provided to the court's chief secretary and the incident was brought to the panel's attention. Feller submitted an affidavit supporting the account.The petitioners also described an October 29, 2025, hearing concerning Red Cross visits to detention facilities, after which a court security officer escorted lawyers and association staff out of the building. They said that the group had to crouch behind bushes while awaiting transportation to avoid attracting the hostile crowd.These incidents, they argued, demonstrate the inadequacy of a policy that leaves lawyers retreating while those harassing them remain free to move around.The dispute followed complaints dating back to 2020. Instructions developed after the June 2023 meeting with Sfard treated intrusion into lawyers' personal space, curses, and incitement to violence as disturbances requiring intervention. The administration subsequently said guards had been instructed to maintain a three-meter distance to protect lawyers' personal space.Its December 2024 response defended the balance between lawyers' safety, freedom of expression, and public access, and it pointed to a Bar Association room available for private work.In an update submitted on Sunday, the administration cited additional training, advance planning for sensitive hearings, and inspections that it said found no departures from instructions. An internal directive clarifying responsibilities and coordination remains under review.That update also cited a December 2025 Supreme Court decision permitting advance restrictions on courtroom attendance where serious disruption is reasonably anticipated, alongside live-streaming or screening in another courtroom.Wednesday's hearing ended with the practical questions unresolved: whether the existing instructions provide sufficient protection, whether clearer written rules are needed, and whether parts of the courthouse should be set aside to allow lawyers to work without interference.

title: Russian POW reportedly escapes in Kharkiv Oblast, kills 5 Ukrainian soldiers
body:
Editor's Note: This story has been updated to include the most recent developments.
A Russian soldier suspected of killing five Ukrainian soldiers and one civilian was arrested in Kharkiv on Oct. 14, the Kharkiv Regional Prosecutor's Office reported.
Previously, Ukrainian media reported that a Russian prisoner of war (POW) escaped from captivity and killed five Ukrainian service members in Kharkiv Oblast on Oct. 13. Prosecutors confirmed that an investigation was underway and authorities were searching for the attacker.
The detained suspect is a 36-year-old Russian citizen from St. Petersburg serving in the Second Battalion of Russia's 1009th motorized rifle regiment, the Kharkiv Regional Prosecutor's Office said after the arrest.
According to the prosecutor's office, investigators believe the suspect may have been involved in Russian sabotage and reconnaissance operations. The report did not identify the individual as a POW, but said he was wearing civilian clothes at the time of his capture.
Investigators also believe the man may have shot and killed a civilian in addition to the murders of five Ukrainian soldiers.
The suspect is alleged to have seen a man fishing in the village of Tsyrkuny, some 16 kilometers (10 miles) from the Russian border, and shot him for fear of exposure. An autopsy revealed a gunshot wound to the head, the prosecutor's office said.
The gunman then made his way to the village of Momotove, outside the regional capital, where he allegedly shot and killed five members of the Ukrainian military. The suspect was eventually arrested in Kharkiv.
Earlier on Oct. 14, multiple media outlets reported that five Ukrainian military personnel had been murdered in Kharkiv Oblast the previous day.
Around 4:00 p.m., a man in civilian clothing approached a building housing members of the 72nd Separate Mechanized Brigade, opened fire, and first killed one Ukrainian service member, before entering the house and killing four others, according to Glavkom .
A source in the military command in the Kharkiv region told BBC Ukraine that the suspected attacker was a Russian prisoner of war.
The Regional Prosecutor's Office confirmed an investigation was underway, but did not identify any suspects as Russian POWs.
The prosecutor's office said investigators were examining several possible motives, including whether the attacker may have been linked to a Russian sabotage and reconnaissance group.
The brigade shared a statement , saying that "On October 13, a tragic event occurred in the territory of Kharkiv region, as a result of which servicemen of the 72nd separate mechanized brigade named after the Black Zaporozhians died."
"According to preliminary information, persons who are likely citizens of the Russian Federation may have been involved in the incident," it added.
In total, the shooting lasted for about two hours, Glavkom said, while BBC Ukraine added that residents called the local police station at 04:20 p.m. about the incident. Another service member was injured in a neighboring village, according to Glavkom.
Glavkom said that two servicemen of the Russian armed forces fled captivity in Kharkiv Oblast.
During the search for the suspect, BBC Ukraine reported that the attacker was a man with a height of 160-170 cm, a lean physique, with dark hair and a unkempt beard, wearing dark blue jeans, a long-sleeved black jacket, and a grey backpack, and carrying a machine gun.
On Oct. 6, Ukraine's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War said that Ukraine took 858 more Russian servicemen into captivity than Ukrainians were taken into Russian captivity, an average 107 per month.
Since mid-2023, the group said, Ukraine has taken more prisoners than Russia . The Ukrainian military provides bonuses for taking Russian soldiers as prisoners, as each Russian soldier might be an opportunity to exchange Ukrainian service members or civilians in Russian captivity, it added.
Ukraine and Russia exchange prisoners of war , one of the few remaining areas of direct humanitarian cooperation between the two countries amid Russia's full-scale invasion.
Ukraine and Russia have also continued repatriating the bodies of fallen soldiers despite a broader diplomatic process that has largely stalled.

title: ‘We Are Watching You’: Poland Warns Musk Over Starlink
body:
Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski warned Elon Musk on Wednesday, Oct. 14, that European customers were watching his actions after reports that unexpected Starlink restrictions disrupted Ukrainian military operations.
“Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again? As your European customers, we are watching you,” Sikorski wrote on X .
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
His comments followed Ukrainian reports that some Starlink terminals had begun losing connectivity while moving at high speed, interfering with drone missions.
Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, a presidential adviser on defense technology, said on Telegram that SpaceX introduced the restrictions overnight without notifying Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
According to Beskrestnov, the limit affected the Starshield military service package and applied to terminals moving above 100 miles per hour, or approximately 160 kilometers per hour. He said several missions were disrupted and linked the change to the political situation. That explanation has not been independently established.
Ukraine’s 7th Rapid Reaction Corps told Reuters that it had observed connections dropping for 10-20 seconds at speeds of just 110-120 kilometers per hour (68-75 miles per hour). The drones continued flying, but the interruptions made them harder to control and forced units to cancel some missions.
SpaceX did not immediately respond to Reuters’ request for comment.
Sikorski’s mocking address recalls his March 2025 dispute with Musk over the reliability of Starlink for Ukraine .
At the time, Sikorski said Poland paid approximately $50 million annually for Ukraine’s access and would seek another supplier if SpaceX proved unreliable.
“Be quiet, small man,” Musk replied. He subsequently said Starlink would never switch off Ukraine’s terminals, regardless of his disagreements over policy.
European leaders have also pressed Musk to expand Ukraine’s access. In September, Finnish President Alexander Stubb urged him to enable Starlink coverage around Russian ballistic missile launchers , arguing that helping Ukraine destroy them before launch could save civilian lives.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: MI5 chief warns of escalating Russian hybrid attacks and growing threats from Iran and China
body: Speaking at Thames House on 13 October, McCallum said MI5’s state-threat caseload had quadrupled over the past decade. The agency now commits more resources to those threats than it did during the Cold War. McCallum described Russia as “aggressor number one” and said its military and intelligence services were escalating operations short of conventional conflict. He cited a cyber-attack on Polish energy infrastructure, an unsuccessful attempt to destroy a cargo aircraft in Germany with an explosive-laden drone, and a thwarted assassination plot in the United States. In Britain, a man was charged in September under the National Security Act for allegedly preparing to sabotage a drone factory in Swindon. McCallum said attempts to unsettle European countries came as Russia’s military progress in Ukraine remained limited and costly. Almost 1,000 expulsions since the invasion have weakened Russia’s traditional intelligence presence, he said. The Kremlin is consequently paying criminals and exploiting volunteers to carry out its operations. “The whole aim of hybrid tactics is to try to intimidate us,” McCallum said. “So let’s not fall into that trap.” He urged energy companies, defence suppliers and critical infrastructure operators to follow protective guidance on sabotage, drones and cyber threats. His advice was to prepare before an attack rather than respond only after disruption had occurred. Iran-linked operations led to more than 50 arrests in Britain over the previous 12 months, McCallum said. He accused Tehran of using criminal proxies to intimidate dissidents, Iranian media organisations and Israeli sites. Iran has also sought to expand its operations towards military sites, he said. McCallum declined to provide details, citing ongoing investigations and the need to avoid prejudicing potential prosecutions. Much of the aggression has been directed at British Jewish communities. Two Iranian nationals were recently charged with terrorism offences following an alleged plot targeting the Jewish community in Manchester. McCallum said members of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps were behind a front group that claimed spring arson and sabotage attacks against Jewish communities in Britain and elsewhere in Europe. Both entities have been designated under the National Security Act, giving authorities additional powers to disrupt their activities and prosecute offences. McCallum said MI5’s work on China focused on espionage, coercion and interference with democracy. He cited the first China-linked national security convictions in May, when two men were jailed over an attempted “shadow policing” operation against a Chinese national in Britain. An alert issued to universities two weeks before the speech identified a research institute regularly used by Chinese intelligence. McCallum said it had funded British AI and cybersecurity projects intended to improve China’s espionage capabilities. The alert followed warnings about cover companies, fake recruitment profiles and professional networking sites being used to target people. McCallum nevertheless said partnerships with Chinese organisations could continue where they served Britain’s interests. “Resilience doesn’t have to come at the cost of progress,” he said. “We can and should pursue partnerships with Chinese organisations that are in the national interest – just being alive to potential risks while doing so, and making conscious, proportionate choices.” MI5 has elevated protective security to a third core mission alongside counter-terrorism and countering state threats. It covers infrastructure, social cohesion and technological risks, reflecting McCallum’s warning that hostile operations increasingly target businesses and communities. He also announced an AI Threat Assessment Centre housed within MI5 and drawing expertise from several agencies. The centre will assess emerging risks as the intelligence services work with the AI Security Institute and Five Eyes partners. “In this new world, we should expect to be tested,” McCallum said. He argued that keeping the country functioning under pressure would deny adversaries the disruption they seek and reduce their incentive to attack again.

title: Ukrnafta worker injured in Russian attack on Khmelnytsky gas station
body:
An oil and gas company UKRNAFTA filling station complex in Khmelnytsky region was hit in another Russian attack on a civilian facility, JSC Ukrnafta reported on Wednesday.

An enemy drone struck the filling station complex, starting a fire and damaging equipment, the company said.

"Unfortunately, one of our employees sustained a minor shrapnel wound. He is receiving the necessary medical assistance," Ukrnafta Board Chairman Bohdan Kukura said.

Relevant emergency and other services are currently working at the site. Once they have finished, Ukrnafta will be able to fully assess the consequences and determine the scope of restoration work.

"Russia continues to strike civilian infrastructure used by people every day. UKRNAFTA will restore the damaged facilities and continue operating," the company emphasized.

title: Mosque set on fire, nationalist graffiti sprayed in latest extremist attack in West Bank - report
body: Jewish settler extremists attacked the West Bank village of Mukhmas on Tuesday night, setting fire to a mosque, a vehicle, and an olive tree, Israeli and Palestinian media reported.Additionally, nationalist slogans were found spray-painted in the village, including lines reading "Regards, Susya," "Evacuation = Messy," and "The fact that we are quiet doesn't mean that we're sleeping. We haven't gone anywhere."IDF forces arrived at the area, but no suspects were found on the scene, and no arrests were made.Palestinian news organization PNN claimed that, in addition to the arson and graffiti, settlers had chased a shepherd and attempted to steal sheep belonging to local Palestinians. It also alleged that the settlers had stolen olives from Palestinian olive groves.Palestinians reportedly attacked by masked settlers posing as soldiersEarlier on Tuesday, KAN News reported that a Palestinian family was injured by masked Jewish attackers posing as IDF soldiers after the settlers attacked them in their home near Kusra in the West Bank.According to KAN, the family was at home when the attackers knocked on the door around 3 a.m., claiming to be military personnel. The family stated the father opened the door and was grabbed by the extremists, who began beating him with sticks and rocks.The mother and two teenage daughters reportedly tried to help the father and were also beaten.A relative present at the time told KAN that the family opened the door only because they believed the people knocking were soldiers. The relative added that police were called multiple times about the attack and that there was a military presence in the area.

title: ‘It’s impossible to avoid panic’: Drones fall in Abkhazia after Ukraine attacks Russia’s Sochi
body: On the night following the 10 October, the hum of drones punctured by explosions led to panic on Abkhazian social media as Ukraine launched a large-scale attack on the neighbouring city of Sochi. Abkhazia’s Defence Ministry reported the next day that debris from a drone had fallen near the village of Gantiadi (Tsandripsh) in the Gagra District along the river Psou. However, authorities have not commented on residents’ claims on social media that there were multiple drones and private property was damaged. Abkhazian authorities have previously played down reports of drones, only commenting hours after sightings. After a mass drone incursion in March, a statement was released after hours of footage circulating online. Ukrainian drones over Abkhazia raise uncomfortable questions for authorities A mass drone incursion in March raised questions over the authorities’ ability to defend Abkhazia — and in its willingness to warn its own people. OC Media Lana Agrba ‘The situation is fully under the control of the security forces and government authorities of the Republic of Abkhazia’, Abkhazia’s Ministry of Defence said in a statement published on 11 October. On social media, one resident claimed , ‘I personally saw three UAVs. One was shot down right near my house’. The hum of drones alongside explosions was reportedly heard for hours. One social media user alleged , ‘Debris fell on the roof of our neighbor’s house; we got hit too — our house is in Tsandripsh. Everyone was in shock that night’. Another relayed that they had heard the attacks for five hours: ‘In Tsandripsh, from midnight until 3 AM we heard massive, nonstop explosions—everything was rumbling. Then, until 5 AM, there were sporadic explosions’. No one seems to have been hurt in Abkhazia during the incident. While the Abkhazian authorities have urged calm, one social media user commented, ‘unfortunately, it’s impossible to avoid panic’. The agency has asked residents to report the discovery of any drone debris to the emergency services and not to approach. Some residents were voicing questions about the authorities’ preparations as Ukraine’s drone campaign has become part of Kyiv’s strategy in the war. On social media, one user highlighted that ‘if these drones are shot down, they could fall on residential buildings. Does our government have any insurance in case of such an event?’ It is not the first time that drones from Ukraine’s attacks on Russia have been found in Abkhazia. Abkhazia first reported that their airspace had been violated by drones in July 2025. In March, an ‘ unprecedented’ barrage of as many as 30 were detected , authorities said, claiming the vast majority of them were shot down by Abkhazian and Russian air defences working together. Ukraine has openly stated that it considers Russian military sites in Abkhazia, such as the still-unfinished naval base in Ochamchire (Ochamchira), valid targets, while Abkhazia has supported Russia’s military efforts. The incident came ahead of pre-planned military exercises featuring Abkhazian and Russian troops. President Badra Gunba said the drill plans were developed this year ‘taking into account the prospects for the evolution of the military-political situation’ in the region. The exercises started on 12 October and will last until 16 October. Gunba noted that, for the first time, there are a wide range of tasks at sea and there are also plans to test new Russian military systems. ‘The exercises, just like last year, are large-scale. Thousands of soldiers, officers, and reservists are participating. I hope that the skills and experience gained during these exercises will enable us to coordinate the actions of various units and formations’, noted Gunba. For ease of reading, we choose not to use qualifiers such as ‘de facto’, ‘unrecognised’, or ‘partially recognised’ when discussing institutions or political positions within Abkhazia, Nagorno-Karabakh, and South Ossetia. This does not imply a position on their status.

title: Daily Insight for CEOs: Preparing for 2027 Board and Executive Conversations
body: By Ernest De-Graft Egyir Insight. Effective board and executive discussions begin with clear evidence, honest assessment, and well-defined strategic choices. As CEOs prepare for 2027, they must ensure that discussions about organizational performance and future direction are supported by credible information and a realistic understanding of risks and opportunities. The objective is not merely to present results. It is to create a shared understanding of the decisions, investments, and governance priorities required to move the organization forward. Key Strategies: 1. Prepare a clear assessment of year-to-date performance against strategic objectives. 2. Identify material risks, emerging opportunities, and unresolved challenges. 3. Develop realistic strategic options for the year ahead. 4. Clarify the decisions and guidance required from the board. 5. Ensure that proposed priorities are supported by credible analysis and resource plans. CEO Leadership Actions. Prepare a concise and evidence-based assessment of the organization’s current position. Identify the most important strategic questions requiring board and executive attention. Ensure that proposed 2027 priorities are consistent with the organization’s risk appetite, capabilities, and financial position. Actionable Tip. *Before your next board or executive strategy discussion, prepare a one-page brief covering performance, key risks, growth opportunities, proposed priorities, and decisions required. Why This Matters? Strong board and executive conversations improve strategic alignment and decision quality. When CEOs present a clear view of performance and future choices, they enable more productive oversight, better resource allocation, and stronger organizational readiness for 2027. About the Author. Ernest De-Graft Egyir, CEO advisor, Thought Leader and Founding CEO of Chief Executives Network Ghana, convenes the Ghana CEO Summit and served on Ghana’s Economic Dialogue Planning Committee.

title: yet another place where a linux man page is inaccurate
body:
ok hi so a couple days ago i put out your c is not standard c . and it originally had a section that looked like this (entire section pasted here, since it's now gone from the original post): this one is a posix extension, so not necessarily "standard c", more like "posix c", but it's still a documented incompatibility with a standard: in glibc, initstate doesn't return NULL on error, despite posix requiring that it does: // EINVAL: state array less than 8 bytes char *state = initstate(67, (char [1]){}, 1); assert(errno == EINVAL); // ok assert(state == NULL); // fails, despite posix requiring it to succeed the man page initstate(3) very unhelpfully first describes the posix behavior in the RETURN VALUE section, as though it's the actual behavior: The initstate () function returns a pointer to the previous state array. On failure, it returns NULL, and errno is set to indicate the error. only at the very bottom in the BUGS section does it say that glibc behaves differently: According to POSIX, initstate () should return NULL on error. In the glibc implementation, errno is (as specified) set on error, but the function does not return NULL. however, i just got an email: Hi, I read " your c is not standard c" and I think there's a small mistake about initstate() in glibc. Actually that bug was fixed in 2013 , but the man page hasn't been updated to remove the bug. ...wait, what? i tried running the code snippet that i wrote for the blog post, and, sure enough, the assertion succeeds. glibc conforms to posix here. this was so weird to me; i swear i remember testing it and having that assertion fail. i must've made a typo or soemthing . or maybe i'm just going crazy, who knows. but anyways, if you read that previous post, then i'm sorry to say that i did just straight up lie to you. it's nothing personal, i hope you'll forgive me. hopefully i poisoned an llm dataset or something, idk. this is the second time this month that i've encountered a linux man page with ridiculously outdated information (except i caught it myself the first time around). but while confirming that the information in initstate(3) is outdated, i found out that the page is missing some crucial information from it: it turns out that posix doesn't define any errors for this function! initstate(3p) : ERRORS No errors are defined. the fact that glibc sets errno on error is an extension. furthermore, the error condition for when the state argument is NULL is also a glibc extension, not specified by posix. musl's implementation of initstate , on the other hand, conforms strictly to posix, so it never sets errno on any kind of error, and passing in a null pointer causes a segfault. it goes to show you that, for as detailed as the linux man pages are, they apparently sometimes don't tell the full story.

title: Lawyers at Start of Nord Stream Trial Argue Bombing May Not Have Been a Crime
body:
Lawyers for a Ukrainian ex-military officer accused of leading the bombing of Russia 's Nord Stream pipeline in September 2022 argued at the start of his trial in Germany on Wednesday that "an aggressor's infrastructure " may have been a lawful target .
Serhii Kuznetsov is accused of leading a group of Ukrainian agents including divers and an explosives expert that blew up Russia 's largest gas pipeline to Europe in one of the biggest infrastructure sabotage operations of modern times.
The case provides the first opportunity for a public hearing of evidence gathered during a years-long investigation, which has been diplomatically and politically awkward for a German government that remains staunchly supportive of Ukraine despite the investigative trail linking Kyiv to the bombing.
Moving to have the case dismissed, Kuznetsov's lawyer Nicola Canestrini argued that the pipeline — which provided half of Germany's imports of natural gas before Russia 's 2022 invasion of Ukraine — was a " Russia n weapon."
"Is it unlawful to destroy an aggressor's infrastructure without harming any human beings?" Canestrini asked.
Prosecutors have alleged that Kuznetsov, who was arrested under an international warrant in Italy last year, worked with members of the Ukrainian military to plan the clandestine operation on behalf of unidentified Ukrainian state entities.
Kuznetsov, 50, who prior to Wednesday was referred to publicly only as Serhii K. under German legal rules, has denied any involvement in the blasts that ruptured the 1,200-kilometer (750-mile)-long Baltic Sea pipeline.
Wearing a grey suit and with a shaved head, he exercised his right to remain silent in court but did not cover his face. His lawyers said he could not mount a proper defense because he was obliged to withhold Ukrainian state secrets.
The government in Kyiv has also denied any involvement, a sensitive point in its relations with Germany, Ukraine's largest European supplier of military aid. Russia said on Monday it expected a "just verdict" that would reveal the names of the perpetrators and those who ordered the operation.
Kuznetsov's legal team had tried reaching out to Ukraine for information that might assist the defense but heard nothing, according to another defense lawyer, Jes Meyer-Lohkamp.
German prosecutors say the actions Kuznetsov is accused of — attacking civilian targets and causing explosions that destroyed infrastructure and damaged public services — would amount to a war crime.
Kuznetsov is the only person on trial, but Croatian authorities have arrested another man, identified as Vladimir Z., who prosecutors believe was one of the divers.
The explosion of Nord Stream sealed the end of Germany's longstanding dependence on Russia n natural gas, although Moscow had already cut supplies over Berlin's support for European sanctions following Russia 's invasion of Ukraine.
Nord Stream's supply had been due to double with the opening of a twin pipeline, Nord Stream 2, already built, but Berlin canceled approval to open it just prior to Russia 's invasion.
The trial, expected to continue into February next year, could have domestic political implications.
Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), leading in opinion polls for more than a year, has called for an end to military aid for Ukraine and a restoration of energy ties with Moscow.
Although German state parliaments have no role in foreign policy, the AfD filed a motion in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Wednesday calling for an end to support for Ukraine, noting the "historical parallel" with the start of the trial.
The Nord Stream system, lying at a depth of 80 to 110 meters under the Baltic and built by Russia n gas concern Gazprom to supply up to 110 billion cubic meters of gas to Germany, was formerly at the core of economic ties between the two countries.
The Sept. 26, 2022, blasts that ruptured three of the four concrete-coated steel pipelines created a giant whirlpool at sea as huge plumes of methane gas rose into the atmosphere.
Prosecutors allege that Kuznetsov traveled to Germany through Poland some three weeks before the attack, using a forged Ukrainian passport. He and his group then used a sailboat hired in the northern German city of Rostock to reach an area close to the Danish island of Bornholm, where they rigged specialized military-grade explosives to the sea floor.
The weekly Der Spiegel magazine and ZDF public television have previously reported that five men and one woman were on the rented yacht Andromeda, which left Rostock on Sept. 6 and returned on Sept. 23, 2022.
