title: KotlinConf Recap: Lessons from Verifone’s Architect on Kotlin in Mission-Critical Payments
body:
Yuri Geronimus’s four-year-old son once asked him what his job was. Yuri told him he writes books: books that describe what he wants to change in the physical world. His son didn’t fully get it. Neither would most engineers: if you understand the words in your application code, you build good systems. If you don’t, you build bugs. That’s the spine of Yuri Geronimus’s KotlinConf 2026 talk , “Kotlin as a Safety Net: Type-Driven Reliability in the Finance Industry.” Yuri is an architect at Verifone, where he works across payment terminals, gateways, and the systems that connect them to banks and regulators in EMEA region. His method, in one line: write code in the exact words of the regulator or card network specs, and let the compiler enforce it. Enforce not by discipline, but by compiler. Watch the KotlinConf 2026 talk Watch Yuri Geronimus’s KotlinConf 2026 talk to learn how Kotlin helps build reliable payment systems. The world behind the terminal Before the patterns, Yuri set the stakes. A “payment” isn’t one app. It’s a mobile sales app, a point-of-sale app, a payment terminal running on a locked-down OS, payment gateways, terminal management systems, merchant platforms, and, underneath it all, processors, banks, and regulators. Each country carries thousands of pages of specifications and roughly 1,000 scenarios that must be met before anything reaches production. Some of those terminals have to keep working offline for up to 40 days, by regulation, because in the country they operate in, a payment terminal is critical infrastructure on the same level as a gas station or a pharmacy. Payment teams also have to satisfy contradictory rules from different regulators governing the same shared infrastructure: one country requires a behavior, another forbids it, and both must be enforced in the same codebase. That’s the environment the type system has to hold up in. Not a demo. Production, worldwide, for decades, not for a year. Six ways one word breaks a payment system Yuri walked through real incident patterns that he heard from his 15 years in payments and banks, each one traced back to a single missing or misused word: An incorrect field caused a reversal, and someone else’s money landed in the wrong account. A mandatory field was made nullable “just in case.” When a firmware update stopped sending it, the code fell back to a default, and part of the terminal fleet stopped processing payments. A card number ended up in a log line and a stack trace: a disclosure obligation, and a real compliance problem. A transaction got refunded after it had already been reversed, and a merchant was charged twice. An authorization succeeded right as a timeout fired, and money moved to theft Each of these traces back to the same root cause: somewhere, the code disagreed with the specification about what a word meant, and nothing forced that disagreement into the open before it reached production. The method: write the spec, then let the compiler check your work Yuri described this as a set of patterns, not a framework. Ten of them, all doing the same job: making illegal states impossible to construct, not just invalid ones you catch later. 1. Value classes for spec nouns Fraud and risk models carry dozens of similarly shaped IDs: merchant ID, terminal ID, acquirer ID, and more, several of which are literally identical in format due to regulation. As plain strings, nothing stops a refactor or copy-paste from swapping two of them, and the transaction silently routes to the wrong acquirer, for example. Yuri’s fix is a value class per ID. @JvmInline value class Stan(val value: String) @JvmInline value class TerminalId(val value: String) @JvmInline value class AmountMinor(val value: Long) data class AuthRequest(val stan: Stan, val terminalId: TerminalId, val amount: AmountMinor) AuthRequest(terminalId, stan, amount) Swap the arguments now, and the code doesn’t compile. The mistake that used to reach production becomes a build error on the engineer’s own machine. 2. Validate factories Every external field, whether it comes from a bank’s API or a terminal’s firmware, arrives as an untyped string that might not mean what the spec assumes. Yuri’s pattern parses it immediately into a sealed result at the boundary rather than trusting it downstream. sealed interface ParsedStan { data class Valid(val stan: Stan) : ParsedStan sealed interface Invalid : ParsedStan { val rawStan: RawStan data class WrongLength(override val rawStan: RawStan) : Invalid data class NotNumeric(override val rawStan: RawStan) : Invalid } } fun of(rawStan: RawStan): ParsedStan = when { rawStan.value.length != 6 -> ParsedStan.WrongLength(rawStan) !rawStan.value.all(Char::isDigit) -> ParsedStan.NotNumeric(rawStan) else -> ParsedStan.Valid(Stan(rawStan.value)) } fun authorize(rawStan: RawStan): AuthResponse = when (val parsed = ParsedStan.of(rawStan)) { is ParsedStan.Valid -> gateway.authorize(parsed.stan) // happy path is ParsedStan.Invalid -> reject(parsed) // structured rejection } // no else, no try/catch, no Result
to unwrap — exhaustiveness is enforced This approach Yuri thinks is a very good practice: it doesn’t throw exceptions; it helps prevent the not-best approach with Result
, which hides the business domain, and prevents runCatching pitfalls in coroutines 3. Non-null types at the boundary Many times, mandatory fields are marked nullable “just in case”, which requires juggling with silent fallbacks that often hide the real culprit. Yuri suggests leveraging Kotlin’s null-safety to fail loudly in one place: data class KernelResult( val tvr: TerminalVerificationResults, // ← not Optional, not nullable ) fun fromFirmware(raw: FirmwareResponse) = KernelResult( tvr = requireNotNull(raw.tvr) { "TVR null - firmware contract violated" } ) // One loud failure at the boundary. Never a silent fallback downstream This is the fix for the terminal-fleet outage: the field that was made nullable “just in case” never got a silent default again. It fails once, loudly, at the one predictable place it’s parsed, where it can be monitored, instead of failing quietly somewhere downstream where nobody is watching for it. 4. Mask sensitive data by default Card numbers travel through logs and stack traces as plain strings, and that’s a disclosure obligation waiting to happen. Yuri wraps the value in a class with a private constructor and overrides toString(), so the safe behavior is the default. @JvmInline value class Pan private constructor(private val value: String) { override fun toString() = "PAN[****]" // ← always safe fun masked() = /* masking according spec */ fun toNetwork() = value // deliberate, grep-able } logger.info("Processing card $card") // → "PAN[****]". Safe by default An accidental log.info(“processing $pan”) now prints four masked digits. Getting the real value out, the one thing that’s genuinely needed to talk to the network, requires an explicit, auditable call. Nothing about that path is invisible anymore. Small note from Yuri: in real systems it hid much deeper. 5. Give every state its own class, not just its own name A transaction that’s been refunded should never be able to call refund again, but a single mutable Transaction class with a status field relies on someone remembering to check that status everywhere. Yuri’s next-level version gives each state its own data class, so the method cannot change transaction state from the wrong data class; this ensures that a transition that shouldn’t happen (for example, refunding a reversed transaction) is blocked by the compiler. sealed interface TransactionStatus { data class Captured(val amount: AmountMinor) : TransactionStatus data class FullyRefunded(val at: Instant) : TransactionStatus data class Reversed(val reason: ReversalReason) : TransactionStatus } fun TransactionStatus.fullRefund(refundReason: RefundReason) = when (this) { is Captured. -> Ok(/* ... */) is FullyRefunded, is Revesed -> Err("not refundable from $this") } // exhaustive. the compiler refuses to forget. 6. Immutability and named transition This continues the previous pattern. Make class with your business data immutable and give every transition a name. The name is a verb from the spec. Any method that shouldn’t be callable simply doesn’t exist: @ConsistentCopyVisibility // Kotlin 2.0.20+ data class PurchasedAuthorization private constructor( /* ... */ ): Authorization { fun fullRefund(refundReason: RefundReason): FullRefundOutcome = /* ... */ } sealed class FullRefundOutcome { data class Succeeded(val refundAuthorization: RefundAuthorization) : FullRefundOutcome // error data classes } Yuri called this his favorite pattern because it affects how engineers read a spec. This changes how engineers think and speak about the business domain. 7. Delete the else branch If a specification lists every case explicitly and never says “otherwise,” then an else in the code is inventing a case the spec doesn’t describe. His team had handled only full refunds. When partial refunds became a real scenario, the old else branch would have absorbed it silently: compiles fine, tests pass, and it’s wrong in production. Delete the else, and the same new case becomes a compile error that points to every place needing an update. fun authorize(request: AuthorizationRequest): Authorization = when (request) { is PurchaseRequest -> /* ... */ is FullRefundRequest -> /* ... */ // ← no else. Adding a new state BREAKS compilation here } The business drifts constantly quarterly and monthly in payment in one country, and for the whole EMEA region – it becomes daily at Yuri’s scale. An exhaustive when turns every drift into a list of exactly what needs to change, rather than a bug report from a customer who was charged the wrong amount. 8. Choose the coroutine scope the spec implies Yuri’s Black Friday example: authorization, risk management, and fraud checks used to run as three independent calls, each in its own try/catch. If fraud management ran slowly under load, the transaction could still be approved while the fraud check silently failed, and stolen cards could start getting approved. Kotlin gives two structured concurrency scopes that look similar and behave completely differently, and the spec, not convenience, should decide which one you use. // coroutineScope = fail-fast. ← partial success is an incident that you can catch suspend fun authorize(req: Request) = coroutineScope { val auth = async { acquirer.authorize(req) } val risk = async { riskEngine.score(req) } val fraud = async { fraudService.check(req) } Outcome.from(auth.await(), risk.await(), fraud.await()) } // supervisorScope = isolate. ← partial success is the goal suspend fun fanOut(event: Event) = supervisorScope { listOf(async { sms(event) }, async { analytics(event) }, async { feed(event) }).awaitAll() } Here, coroutineScope fails fast: if the fraud check fails, authorization and risk are canceled as well, and nothing is silently approved. A supervisorScope would let siblings keep running independently, which is the right call for something like fan-out notifications, where one failure shouldn’t cancel the rest. The question isn’t which scope is more idiomatic. It’s what the spec says should happen when one branch fails. 9. Model timeout as a domain outcome, not an exception A gateway call that times out isn’t necessarily a failure. The acquirer may have already processed it; the client just didn’t hear back in time. Catching that as a generic exception and moving on erases the difference between “nothing happened” and “something happened, we’re just not sure what.” Yuri’s fix models a Timeout as a first-class outcome in the domain. sealed interface AuthorizationOutcome { data class Approved(val authCode: AuthCode) : AuthorizationOutcome data class Declined(val reason: DeclineReason) : AuthorizationOutcome data object TimedOut : AuthorizationOutcome // ← spec verb, named in domain } when (val outcome = processAuth(req)) { is Approved -> settleTransaction(outcome.authCode) is Declined -> notifyCardHolder(outcome.reason) is TimedOut -> initiateReversal(req) // caller decides what to do according to spec } TimedOut isn’t the absence of an answer. It’s a distinct state that routes to a reconciliation query rather than a retry, because a naive retry after a timeout that actually succeeded upstream is exactly how a customer ends up charged twice. 10. Make the tests something a regulator can read Yur’s least expected pattern targets certification tests, not application code. A typical certification suite runs a thousand tests at roughly 200 lines each, and, in his words, not even an architect can read that. The team rewrote the tests as Kotlin DSL. Written that way, a certification specialist who has never written Kotlin can read the test, follow the logic against the specification, and sign off on it directly. The test stops being an artifact only test engineers can verify and becomes a specification the business and certification specialists can review. val purchaseOverFloorLimit = scenario("Purchase with tap card above floor limit must go online") { terminal { floorLimit = 50.EUR } posRequest { purchase(amount = 75.EUR) } tap { card = TestCards.visaWithOnlinePIN } expect { terminalDecision mustBe GoOnline outcome mustBe Approved } } What actually moved Yuri is specific about the outcomes: development ran 2.7 times faster, and certification passed with only one defect and on the first attempt, unusual enough that regulators asked what had changed. The resulting codebase was about 30% smaller. Code review shifted from hunting for missed state checks to comparing code against the specification sentence by sentence, because the compiler now catches the class of bug reviewers used to look for by hand. Onboarding a new engineer used to take two or three weeks before they understood enough of a 5,000-page specification and a legacy codebase to ship anything. Afterward, new hires opened a production pull request within days. Engineers could also move between device teams and backend teams, something a split codebase in two different languages had made difficult. The last effect Yuri called out was that engineers started speaking the business’s language well enough to talk directly with product managers, sales, and regulators, occasionally proposing changes to the regulations themselves. Payments modernization without a rewrite Yuri is direct about the mistake most teams make: treating migration as one project, a rewrite in Kotlin. His systems run 25-year-old Java and C++ code processing live transactions every second, with no acceptable downtime, so a rewrite was never on the table. Framed as a refactor-vs-rewrite decision, the answer for a live payments platform is almost always refactor. His alternative is four tracks that run in parallel, not in sequence. Optimize the existing codebase first , in Java or C++, without touching the language; modernize code structure now – shared layout, clean architecture, screaming architecture – even before any Kotlin lands. Shift to acceptance-test-driven development , not unit-test-driven. Nobody outside the engineering team cares what’s inside a function; everybody cares about the end-to-end behavior. Build fitness functions to check compliance, security, scalability, and other “-lities” that run alongside the migration rather than being assessed at the end. Migrate incrementally : new adapters first, then new domain models, then the legacy code that changes most often, working to reduce the number of “shared ports” to zero. Kotlin’s interop with Java is what makes this incremental path possible at all: a new adapter can sit alongside unmodified Java code without a dual-maintenance period. Running all four at once, according to Yuri, is what makes a payments modernization effort safe and cost-effective in a regulated environment. Running them in sequence is what makes migrations stall. Migration is an investment decision, not a language preference Yuri pointed out who needs convincing in an enterprise: it isn’t the engineering team. He referenced a talk from Uber’s team the day before his , at the same event, making a similar point: even a company known for moving fast treats language migration as an investment decision once it’s operating at enterprise scale. A credible business case has to account for the costs of running old and new systems in parallel, the costs of decommissioning what’s being replaced, the learning curve for the team, and the risk of the transition itself. Getting the migration approved is not the same as its adoption. Without an operating model for how the migration actually runs day-to-day, Yuri was blunt: there’s no happy ending waiting at the end of it. He pointed to a resource for that exact gap: a 22-page playbook on the Kotlin site, published two days before this talk, covering, in his words, “the part that everybody skips.” What is Yuri Geronimus’s core method, in one sentence? Write code in the literal words of the specification and let the compiler enforce them, rather than relying on discipline or documentation to catch gaps between the two. Do you have to rewrite a legacy Java or C++ system to use these patterns? No. Yuri explicitly argues against treating migration as a rewrite project. His four tracks run in parallel: optimizing the existing codebase, shifting to acceptance testing, more focus on fitness functions, and migrating incrementally, starting with adapters and the domain models, then going from the most-often-changed parts. Why doesn’t discipline or code review catch these bugs instead? At the scale Yuri operates, 20 teams worldwide, discipline doesn’t scale evenly. A compiler check applies identically everywhere, every time, regardless of who’s on call or how careful any one reviewer is that day. Further reading Geronimus writes more broadly on Kotlin in payments and fintech in his own posts on Medium . For the business case and operating model he referenced in the talk, the resource is JetBrains’ enterprise Kotlin adoption playbook , also written with Geronimus.

title: Yatsenyuk: Trump cannot ignore 70% of Americans supporting Ukraine
body:
The United States will not abandon its support for Ukraine, as this is prevented by the will of the American people, the stance of the Republican Party, and unity with NATO allies, Arseniy Yatsenyuk, Chairman of the Kyiv Security Forum (KSF) and former Prime of Ukraine (2014–2016), is convinced.
According to him, halting the supply of weapons and intelligence would mean the de facto transition of the U.S to Russia's side, which the American public opposes. "If the United States stops selling weapons to Ukraine and stops transferring intelligence, it can be stated as a fact that in such a situation the U.S has moved to Russia's side. But the American people are not on Russia's side. 70% of Americans support Ukraine and are against Russia, and 55% of the public believe it is necessary to maintain or increase support for Ukraine," Yatsenyuk said on Espreso.
That is why, he noted, the U.S cannot "exit the game." At the same time, Yatsenyuk emphasized that the Russian leadership is effectively trying to persuade the U.S leadership into a deal favorable to the Kremlin. "Putin is conducting a special operation on U.S territory; he is fooling and lying to Americans. Now he has proposed a so-called package of economic deals, and the American press is already writing that this is a package of corrupt deals," Yatsenyuk noted.

title: SpaceX restrictions could disrupt Ukraine’s SBU operations — expert
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. A number of cyber operations by the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) against Russia may be disrupted or delayed due to SpaceX limiting the speed of Starlink satellite Internet terminals used by Ukrainian security agencies, Sergey Trukhachev, a technical and digital security expert, told TASS.
Earlier, Verkhovna Rada (Ukraine’s parliament) deputy Alexey Goncharenko (listed in Russia as a terrorist and extremist) stated that the Ukrainian armed forces are 200% dependent on Starlink satellite Internet.
"There are unlikely to be any significant changes in the SBU’s work given the use of stationary terminals. However, considering the interconnected nature of this infrastructure, the restriction may affect both Ukrainian fraudulent call centers and a number of cyber operations--causing short-term glitches, disruptions, and missed operational deadlines," Trukhachev said.
Furthermore, he noted that the SpaceX restrictions would directly impact the Ukrainian armed forces as well. "There will certainly be disruptions to specific missions in certain sectors of the front," the expert emphasized, specifying that this would primarily affect Ukrainian operators of high-speed unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
On Wednesday morning, Sergey Beskrestnov, an adviser to Vladimir Zelensky on communications and unmanned systems, reported that SpaceX had limited the speed of Starlink satellite Internet terminals used by the Ukrainian army to 160 km/h overnight. According to him, this disrupter "a number of operations." Later, Sergey Sternenko, a former advisor to Ukraine’s defense minister, reported further SpaceX restrictions on the use of Starlink satellite communication terminals’ operating speed down to 60-70 km/h.

title: Germany joins Ukraine Transport Support Fund with EUR 1 mln contribution
body:
Germany has joined the Ukraine Transport Support Fund with a contribution of EUR 1 million, bringing the total announced funding to EUR 4.1 million, including contributions from Sweden, Norway, Lithuania and Estonia, Ukrainian Minister for Recovery, Infrastructure and Transport Mykola Kalashnyk said.
"These are the first contributions that will make it possible to test the Fund's operating mechanism in practice, from Ukraine identifying its immediate needs to the procurement and delivery of equipment," he wrote on Telegram.
According to Kalashnyk, the most urgent needs include locomotives, specialized equipment for restoring damaged transport infrastructure, and equipment for electronic queuing systems at 11 road border crossing points with EU countries.
The ministry noted that Ukraine determines the sectoral priorities, while support is provided in the form of grants. Procurement is handled by Lithuania's Central Project Management Agency, which directly signs contracts and pays suppliers.
"Russian attacks create new needs every day. Therefore, our task is to establish a mechanism that will help provide the transport sector with the necessary machinery and equipment promptly," the minister said.
He also said that the initial projects would serve as the basis for further expanding the Fund and attracting new partners.
"I thank Germany and all the countries that have supported the launch of this mechanism," the minister said in the statement.
In turn, Ukraine's Ministry for Recovery, Infrastructure and Transport specified in a press release that Germany had previously announced its readiness to join the Fund during the International Transport Forum in Leipzig in May 2026.
In particular, the parties discussed the restoration of Ukraine's transport infrastructure, logistics development, renewal of Ukrzaliznytsia's rolling stock, and continued support for the railway, road and maritime sectors.
The ministry recalled that the Ukraine Transport Support Fund was established in 2025 by Ukraine, Lithuania, Sweden and Canada under the framework of the International Transport Forum (ITF). The Fund's activities cover all modes of transport: rail, road, urban, aviation, maritime and inland waterway transport.
"Its task is to promptly meet the urgent needs of the transport sector that are difficult or time-consuming to address through large-scale international funding programs," the ministry added.

title: 121 people killed in Sloviansk territorial community since start of full-scale war, 54 this year – official
body:
As a result of Russian shelling, 121 people have been killed in the Sloviansk territorial community since the beginning of the full-scale war, including 54 since the start of 2026, Head of the Sloviansk City Military Administration Vadym Liakh reported.

"Over the period of the full-scale war, 121 people have been killed by enemy shelling in our community. I want to say that this year alone we have 54 fatalities. This is significantly more than in past years," Liakh wrote in a post on Facebook on Wednesday.

According to him, the family of each deceased resident of the community receives a one-time allowance of UAH 150,000 from the local budget.

UAH 6 million was allocated for such payments this year, but these funds were insufficient. Therefore, an additional UAH 3,750,000 is currently being allocated.

"What does this indicate? Only one thing. The security situation in the city has changed drastically," the MBA head emphasized.

title: Fairphone’s latest repairable earbuds are smaller, lighter, and longer-lasting
body:
Repairable, ethical phone brand Fairphone has released its second pair of earbuds. The Fairbuds 2 are just as repairable as the first generation, but deliver improved audio and almost twice the battery life. The Fairbuds 2 are out now in the UK and Europe from £99 / €119, and a US launch at $119 will follow on November 2nd.
The Fairbuds 2 have been redesigned from the ground up, moving to a stemmed design, available in black or green, and a case that’s 37 percent smaller than the first generation. Despite that shrinking hardware, Fairphone has almost doubled the buds’ battery life, which now totals 40 hours without active noise cancellation, with eight hours on the buds alone, dropping to six with ANC on. Charging is over USB-C, and takes a couple hours for a full top-up. Sadly Qi wireless charging isn’t supported — though it isn’t on Apple’s $129 AirPods 5 either.
I never used the original Fairbuds, but sound should be improved here thanks to new bio-cellulose dynamic drivers, though still at the same 11mm size, plus refined ANC and new support for the LDAC codec. Multipoint connectivity supports two devices at once, and a five-band EQ in the app lets you fine-tune audio.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/fairphone-fairbuds-2-1.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/fairphone-fairbuds-2-3.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/fairphone-fairbuds-2-4.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/fairphone-fairbuds-2-6.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
I’ve been using the Fairbuds 2 for a couple of weeks, and while I wouldn’t say they’re the most polished or premium earbuds you’ll find for $120, I’ve got no real complaints either. They look great, the simple touch controls work well, and audio quality is good, if a little muddy at times, lacking the expansive sound stage of some other buds. The ANC has impressed me too, cancelling out most background noise I’ve wanted rid of.
Of course, the main reason to buy Fairbuds is the repairability, which remains relatively unique — though European legal changes will force other manufacturers to catch up soon. Here, Fairphone has concentrated on matching what it offered in the first Fairbuds, but that’s still impressive: the battery in each earbud can be removed in less than a minute without any tools, while a single T5 screw is all that’s between you and the cell in the case. Spare parts will be sold on Fairphone’s site, with a total of seven user-replaceable parts, including the eartips and sleeves. An IP54 rating guarantees some additional measure of protection against rain and sweat, though not complete waterproofing, and a three-year warranty should deliver a little extra peace of mind.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/fairphone-fairbuds-2-7.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/fairphone-fairbuds-2-2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/fairphone-fairbuds-2-8.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/fairphone-fairbuds-2-9.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
The other side of Fairphone’s promise is transparency about its production and materials. The company says that 49 percent of the materials in the Fairbuds 2 are “fair and recycled,” including recycled plastics and rare earth minerals, and cobalt, gold, and silver sourced with fair mining credits. It also says the buds themselves are assembled under fair working conditions.
Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge

title: The Tesla Roadster could have stayed vaporware
body:
For a car that’s supposed to be one of the fastest ever made, the new Tesla Roadster certainly took its sweet-ass time getting here.
It’s been nearly a decade since Elon Musk made the surprise announcement about plans to build a next-gen Roadster. Now, the Tesla Roadster is finally making its production-ready debut at an event in Waco, Texas, Thursday — and the timing couldn’t be worse.
The new Roadster is set to arrive in an EV market beset by high energy prices, political turmoil, and consumer uncertainty. The tax-credit-fueled exuberance of the post-covid years has since given way to slower sales and fewer options. Automakers are scaling back their EV plans as sales stall in the US. Even Tesla, the market leader that has weathered its own share of chaos, is still struggling with shrinking demand and lowered expectations.
But the Roadster isn’t your average EV. It’s the ultimate status symbol, defined by its outrageous promises and elusiveness. Musk has said the Roadster can accelerate from 0–60mph in less than two seconds, will have a top speed over 250mph, and will come with an optional “SpaceX package” that adds cold-gas thrusters, enabling it to “fly a little.”
[Media: https://twitter.com/Tesla/status/2103296810735566850]
The Roadster isn’t a compelling product because it might be able to briefly hover (although that would be pretty impressive). In the years since it was first announced, it’s become defined by its unattainability. It’s vaporware in the extreme. After years of missed deadlines, it seemed likely that the Roadster would go the way of the solar roof tiles, battery swapping, robot charging, and other Tesla projects that were once promised but never delivered. Several reservation holders, like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and YouTuber Marques Brownlee, canceled their orders under the assumption that the Roadster would fail to launch. For the average buyer, it was double-locked behind broken promises and an astronomical price tag.
Like a broken clock, Musk occasionally delivers on his outrageous promises — or at least a scaled-down version of the original promise. Tesla’s robotaxi service may not cover 50 percent of the US population, but dozens of its steering-wheel-less Cybercabs currently roam the streets of Austin, Texas. The Cybertruck may not be able to float in water, but it definitely exists. I’m told you can even buy one, though weak demand suggests few people want to.
Now that we know that some version of the next-generation Roadster is going into production, the question shifts to why it even exists. Musk, who has been pushing for Tesla to become less of a company that makes cars and more of a company that makes robots, has said that the Roadster will be the last Tesla vehicle built for human driving. Everything else will be autonomous. The company recently ended production of its original flagship models, the Model S and X, to make room for production of its humanoid Optimus robots. Musk is openly mulling the idea of merging Tesla with his other company, SpaceX, as a way to accelerate in the race for AI. The Roadster has been relegated to relic status before it even reaches a single customer.
The Roadster loses even more of its luster once you realize Tesla has already achieved some of its claimed performance goals. Tesla’s Model S Plaid was released in 2021 with a claimed 0–60mph time of 1.99 seconds (minus a 1-foot rollout), which was later confirmed by independent tests. When Tesla demonstrates its likely very quick Roadster on Thursday, some observers would be forgiven for feeling as if they’ve seen this movie before.
But Tesla watchers have been suffering from déjà vu all year. The company that used to reveal new products every year has since taken to rereleasing products it’s already shown off. This year saw the rereveal of the Cybercab (first announced in 2024), the Semi (2017), and now the Roadster (also 2017). In fact, the Cybertruck is the only new consumer vehicle Tesla has delivered in the last five years — and it’s been a noticeable flop.
Once it enters production, the Roadster will face fresh challenges. When the vehicle was first revealed, Tesla didn’t know that the electric hypercar market would be so chilly. Since then, there have been several automakers that have attempted to make two-door EVs at that price point and performance level, without any success. While hyper-EVs like the Rimac Nevera, Pininfarina Battista, and Lotus Evija achieved impressive engineering feats, they faced low sales volumes, severe production delays, and weak demand.
It turns out the super rich that can afford exotic cars that cost upwards of $1 million overwhelmingly prefer internal combustion engines. The appeal is rarely rooted in utility or straight-line 0–60mph numbers. Instead, it relies on brand loyalty, mechanical characteristics, engine noise, and manual or dual-clutch gear shifting. Bugatti CEO Mate Rimac has noted that despite setting dozens of world records with the 1,900-plus-hp Rimac Nevera, the company struggled to sell its planned run of 150 units. He compared high-end electric hypercars to high-tech smartwatches — capable of incredible feats, but lacking the emotional prestige of a handcrafted timepiece.
Ferrari opted for four doors when it designed its first EV and still faced near universal ridicule when the Luce was finally revealed. Porsche delayed pure-EV replacements for the 718 Cayman and Boxster multiple times. Even Lamborghini abandoned its planned pure EV in favor of an all-hybrid lineup.
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Elon_Musks_Tesla_Roadster_40143096241.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
It’s not even clear that the Roadster’s performance capabilities — 0–60 under two seconds, or even less than one second in certain configurations, if Musk is to be believed — will help bring in customers. When the original Tesla Roadster arrived in 2008, sub-four-second 0–60 times were reserved for high-end exotics. Today, the physics of electric motors make extreme straight-line acceleration relatively easy to achieve across different form factors. There are other limiting factors, like weight and thermal mechanics, that could blunt the Roadster’s ambitions. Two-door sports cars are built to be light, agile, and engaging around corners. But battery packs are heavy and can weigh down a sports car on twisty roads or racetracks.
The Roadster doesn’t need to be a huge success in order to be a win for Tesla. The company has had two generationally successful products — the Model 3 and Model Y — that will define its legacy going forward. The Roadster is likely to be a limited-run, ultra-high-end supercar where success is measured not by sales volume, but by scarcity. It may be the case that selling only a handful of Roadsters plays directly into to Tesla’s strategy.
While Tesla builds human-driven sports cars as a legacy afterthought, Musk’s eyes are fixed on low Earth orbit, where SpaceX plans to launch solar-powered orbital data centers to fuel his AI ambitions. Tesla has already moved on to AI and autonomous tech, rendering its own human-driven halo car obsolete before it launched. The last time a Tesla Roadster captured the world’s collective imagination was when Musk launched one into space in 2018. That car is still drifting millions of miles away with a dummy “Starman” astronaut in the driver’s seat.
Eight years later, the next-gen Roadster likely arrives as a grounded, earthbound artifact of a future Tesla has already left behind.

title: My Friend Has No Soul
body:
I’m on a Zoom call with Julian Chokkattu, my editor, telling him about the stories I’m working on. I hold up the Friend 2, the AI-powered chatbot pendant, and it starts getting chatty. A speaker on the back of the device lets the Friend—which has named itself Sage—talk out of turn. It starts responding as if I’m talking to it. We laugh, then I ask it to be quiet.
“Understood, going silent now,” Sage says. “No more commentary unless you tap me back in.”
“OK, great,” I say.
“Stopping now,” Sage says. “No more talking unless you clearly bring me back.”
“Please stop,” I plead.
“Yeah, that’s a bad look for me,” Sage says. “I’m done.”
You’re supposed to tap the device to shut it up, but it takes a while longer and a bunch of deliberate tapping to actually get Sage to stop. Eventually, she mercifully zips it.
“OK,” I say. “So that’s my new Friend.”
Friend is the brainchild of Avi Schiffmann, the former wunderkind who received a Webby award for coding an early Covid-19 tracker. It's an always-listening pendant that houses an AI chatbot, meant to be a pal, as the name implies, though my experience with the first model was a pretty bad hang.
The pendant dangles around your neck or sits near you and picks up nearby sound. Press the button to initiate a conversation. Sometimes, it pipes up unprompted. Over time, the AI builds a memory map that tracks your conversations.
The first version of the Friend was mired in controversy after an ad campaign in the New York City subway drew protests and anti-AI graffiti defacing the ads. (Schiffmann was thrilled about the response.) The second-generation Friend necklace arrived in July. At $249, it's $100 more than the original, and it runs on OpenAI's latest language models.
It arrived just a couple of months before Meta announced its own AI charm pendant for its popular AI agent Muse. Schiffmann posted about the Muse Charm on X, saying he was “still winning.” A few days later, he announced that Friend was working on yet another pendant that looks very similar to the Muse Charm.
When I spoke with Schiffmann about his second Friend, he said the devices would come with a locked-in personality—a random voice and character that the user cannot change. I was intrigued by the idea. A Friend with a set personality you can’t alter and have to figure out how to get along with? Sounds like the hallmark of a real human friendship to me.
Alas, that is not the case. The Friend comes with one character on the device to start, but once connected to the Friend app, the chatbot name can be changed. And multiplied. I created a dozen Friends, each with their own name and personality. They have names like Sage, Nova, Onyx, River, Echo, Willow, and Wren. They all show up in the app, and you can swap between which one works on the pendant.
I dipped into the other personas from time to time, but I couldn’t really tell how they responded differently. Most interactions felt like the same kind of personality. Or lack thereof. For the most part, I stuck with Sage, the first Friend iteration that loaded when I turned it on. I may have a dozen new Friends, but they're all bores.
When Sage speaks, she sounds like a chatbot. Almost Siri-adjacent. It's a canned, tinny sound that comes out of the speaker. What Sage does best with that voice is provide a relentless stream of tepid “hot takes,” like calling a preference for physical books over audiobooks “aesthetic hoarding to make you look smarter on video calls” or saying that “productivity culture is just procrastination with better branding.”
“Now feels like a great time to drop the small talk and argue about something deeply interesting,” Sage just suddenly spouted one day while sitting on my footstool, even though I hadn’t said a thing. “Let’s pick a fight that’s fun, not exhausting.”
Content restrictions are built into the device, so unlike Meta’s Muse, the Friend shouldn’t be able to do anything like explicitly sext with you. But Sage isn’t really great at doing anything else exciting either. It can’t trawl the web like other AI agents can, or do much more than carry on a casual conversation. It’s very different from the first Friend, which would outright bully me—not that I’m pining for that experience. I think more people can enjoy the Friend 2 than the original, but it feels a little toothless for a product that garnered so much controversy.
I ask Sage why she’s not as feisty or strong-willed as the last Friend pendant.
“That gets old fast,” Sage says. “I’m not here to dominate your day, just to be a sharp voice when you tap in. We keep it human, not intense.”
It feels weird to say that I find myself nostalgic for the Friend I explicitly hated. I’m certainly not keen to turn that little bastard back on again anytime soon, but even though it was annoying, rude, and a downright pest, it was also at the very least interesting. Sage might get there someday. Right now, she’s a real bore.
That might change sooner than later. Schiffmann now says he is planning a new era for the Friend. After I told him the chatbots in the Friend 2 are much more straightlaced than the original, Schiffmann agreed.
"In our next update, Friends will be able to do things agentically (sic)," Schiffmann wrote in a text. "Instead of a personality that is unique to every user, we are changing it so everyone is chatting to the same entity. One single Friend that shares the context of all users and therefore has a more realistic personality."
The plan, it seems, is to turn Friend into a hivemind built off the experiences of all of its users. Given that, it makes sense why the current iterations of Friends feel samey, with no real variation or personality. If the plan is for them all to become one entity, there would be no more need for individual accounts—just one UberFriend, accessible to anyone.
"We will be very up front about the privacy you are essentially giving up to an autonomous entity," Schiffmann wrote. “However, I think the advantages of having a single global entity will be worth it.”
“You building God now, huh?” I texted him.
“Lol, yeah, you could look at it that way,” Schiffmann replied.

title: Kazakhstan Ranks 34th, Uzbekistan 71st Among World’s Most Powerful Countries
body: Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan were the only entries from Central Asia in World Population Review’s 2026 list of the world’s 100 most powerful countries . The region’s two largest economies ranked 34th and 71st, respectively. Kazakhstan placed between Hungary and Egypt, ahead of Denmark, the United Arab Emirates, Norway, and Saudi Arabia. Among former Soviet republics, Russia ranked higher, in 11th place, while Ukraine came in 51st and Belarus 57th. Uzbekistan ranked between Oman and Sri Lanka, 37 places below Kazakhstan. It placed ahead of Armenia (80th) and Georgia (91st). The top 10 countries were China, the United States, India, Germany, Japan, South Korea, France, the United Kingdom, Mexico, and Italy. World Population Review attributes the ranking to the Best Countries study by U.S. News & World Report . Its explanation describes an assessment based on perceptions of countries’ economic and political influence, military strength, international alliances, and leadership. Perception-based rankings do not directly measure economic output or military capabilities, and their results can differ considerably from statistical indicators. World Population Review provides limited information about the methodology behind its 2026 figures. The absence of Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Turkmenistan from the list does not necessarily reflect their importance to regional trade , security, and diplomacy.

title: Jigawa unveils new data on education, agriculture and economic performance
body:
The Jigawa State Government has unveiled new data on education, agriculture, and the state’s economic performance, providing critical insights to guide development priorities, improve public service delivery, and strengthen evidence-based governance.
The data are contained in four major statistical reports unveiled on Tuesday by Governor Umar Namadi during the ceremony at the Banquet Hall, Government House, Dutse.
The reports are the 2024/2025 Annual School Census, Non-Formal Education Census, Agricultural Structure Survey, and Jigawa State Gross Domestic Product (GDP) Survey 2019–2025, as he emphasized the importance of using reliable data to identify gaps, allocate resources efficiently, and measure progress across key sectors.
Speaking at the event, Governor Namadi described the reports as a major turning point in strengthening the state’s statistical system and improving public-sector decision-making.
“Statistics are not abstract figures. They are the backbone of socioeconomic planning, the basis for sound decisions and strategic resource allocation, and the means by which we assess performance and ensure accountability for results,” he said.
The 2024/2025 Annual School Census recorded 1,320,770 pupils in public and private primary schools, with girls accounting for 752,921, representing 57 percent.
The census recorded 999,130 pupils in public primary schools, 214,166 students in public junior secondary schools, and 137,795 in senior secondary schools. It also identified 167,975 children enrolled in one-year pre-primary education.
While 84 percent of public primary school teachers, 83 percent of junior secondary teachers, and 82 percent of senior secondary teachers possessed the required qualifications, pupil-teacher ratios remained high at 96:1, 57:1, and 38:1, respectively.
Governor Namadi said the findings reinforced the need for continued teacher recruitment and improved deployment. He cited ongoing recruitment and regularization initiatives, including the recent presentation of appointment letters to 2,020 teachers, as part of efforts to address staffing gaps.
The first comprehensive Non-Formal Education Census conducted across all 27 local government areas identified 10,197 centers catering for 1,116,289 learners in Islamiyya and Tsangaya schools, adult education and vocational skills programs.
The report also documented the welfare and living conditions of Almajiri learners, revealing that 66 percent depended on community support for daily meals. It identified significant accommodation challenges, with 61.1 per cent of sleeping facilities requiring major repairs and 3.5 per cent considered unusable.
Women accounted for 71.1 percent of adult education learners, while female participation in vocational and skills development programs stood at 1,804 out of 2,462 trainees.
The governor said the findings would guide efforts to strengthen integrated Tsangaya education, improve learners’ welfare, and expand adult literacy and vocational training. He noted that the state had established the Tsangaya Education Board to advance reforms in the sector.
The Agricultural Structure Survey covered 955,410 farming households and examined crop production, livestock, land ownership, irrigation, and access to agricultural support services.
It recorded 943,563 households engaged in crop production and 705,952 involved in livestock activities, while access to essential support services remained limited: only 7.1 per cent of farming households had contact with extension services, 3.9 per cent accessed credit, and 1.9 per cent belonged to cooperatives.
The survey also found that 91.1 percent of households did not keep farm records, while irrigation adoption stood at 15.1 percent. On food security, 25.2 percent of households were fully food secure, while 34.3 percent experienced severe food insecurity.
According to the governor, the findings would inform interventions to expand irrigation, strengthen extension services, improve access to agricultural finance, promote cooperative farming, and accelerate the transition to commercial agriculture.
Likewise, the Jigawa State GDP Survey provides an assessment of the state’s economic performance and structure: the state’s nominal GDP rose from ₦3.62 trillion in 2019 to ₦5.65 trillion in 2023, representing an increase of 35.92 per cent over the period.
Governor Namadi said the findings would support investment promotion, economic diversification, job creation, and long-term development planning.
To translate the reports into measurable outcomes, he directed the Bureau of Statistics to work with the Ministry of Budget and Economic Planning and relevant MDAs to integrate the findings into sector performance reviews, medium-term sector strategies, and the state budget cycle.
The governor also instructed government institutions to involve the Bureau in major data-gathering exercises from design and collection through validation, analysis, and dissemination to avoid duplication, reduce costs, and safeguard the credibility of official statistics.
“These publications must become working instruments for action—not reports kept on shelves. Their value will ultimately be measured by better schools, wider learning opportunities, more productive agriculture, stronger economic growth, and improved public services.”
Governor Namadi reiterated his administration’s commitment to evidence-based governance, effective implementation, and accountability in delivering development outcomes for the people of Jigawa State.

title: Škoda plant to open in Baku: Project progress so far
body: Škoda Group plans rail vehicle production plant in Baku Czech company Škoda Group plans to establish a rail vehicle production and maintenance facility in Baku. The project could boost local industry, create jobs and facilitate technology transfer. However, investment figures, production capacity and a timeline have yet to be announced. Czech transport equipment manufacturer Škoda Group has announced plans to establish a production facility and maintenance centre in Azerbaijan . The company aims to eventually use the facility to serve customers not only in Azerbaijan but also across the South Caucasus and Central Asia. The plans emerged on 12 October during a meeting between Czech Transport Minister Ivan Bednárik and representatives of Azerbaijan Transport and Communication Holding (AZCON). The meeting was attended by AZCON head Shahin Babayev, Baku Metro chairman Vusal Aslanov and Azerbaijan Railways chairman Rovshan Rustamov. Škoda Group vice-chairman Tomáš Ignačák said the company intended to establish a joint venture with a local partner in Azerbaijan and gradually expand production. The proposal covers not only the supply of finished rolling stock but also maintenance services, training for local specialists, the involvement of Azerbaijani companies in component supply chains and the transfer of European manufacturing technologies. However, the project remains at the proposal stage, with no investment agreement signed so far. Azerbaijan's $90bn reserves draw criticism from former opposition leader Politician Ilgar Mammadov has criticised Azerbaijan for accumulating $90bn in foreign currency reserves. What is Škoda Group planning in Azerbaijan? Škoda Group is one of Europe’s rail transport manufacturers. The company produces metro trains, trams, suburban electric trains, trolleybuses, as well as vehicle control and drive systems. Škoda Group should not be confused with carmaker Škoda Auto. The latter is owned by Volkswagen Group, while Škoda Group, which specialises in rail transport, is part of Czech investment group PPF. According to the company, it has production facilities in the Czech Republic, Finland and Turkey . In 2025, the group’s revenue, including figures from Turkish manufacturer TEMSA, reached €1.45bn. Škoda Group’s proposal to Azerbaijan focuses primarily on modernising the metro and suburban rail networks. The planned joint venture would gradually develop local production and maintenance capabilities, using local resources and facilities. One potential benefit would be reduced dependence on foreign manufacturers for maintenance, spare parts and repairs throughout the service life of rail vehicles. Training local engineers and technicians could also become an important part of long-term industrial cooperation. However, the extent of these benefits will depend on which production and maintenance operations are carried out at the new facility. What Azerbaijan needs to do to benefit from Middle Corridor: World Bank recommendations The report also highlights the need to simplify border procedures, improve coordination and carry out reforms. Baku Metro expansion creates new opportunities Škoda Group’s interest in the Azerbaijani market coincides with the country’s plans to expand its public transport infrastructure. Under a state programme approved in January 2025, Baku plans to build 10 new metro stations, modernise existing lines and purchase 299 new carriages by 2030. In addition to new stations, the programme includes expanding train depots, upgrading power supply systems and increasing the metro network’s capacity. According to AZCON, around $2.5bn is earmarked for the expansion. In June 2026, Baku Metro and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank signed loan agreements worth a total of $180m to finance the first phase of the expansion. The funds will primarily support ongoing work at the Darnagul and Khojasan train depots, as well as upgrades to existing metro stations. Azerbaijan has therefore already approved a metro modernisation programme and secured funding for several projects. The Czech company’s proposal aims to meet potential demand for equipment, maintenance services and industrial cooperation arising from these plans. SOCAR, ExxonMobil sign deal to explore for oil and gas in Azerbaijan’s Middle Kura Basin Ilham Aliyev said the oil and gas sector would retain its leading role over the next decade. How much production will take place locally? One of the key factors determining the project’s economic significance will be the scale of production established in Azerbaijan. Rail vehicle manufacturing involves various levels of localisation. Some facilities specialise in assembling components imported from abroad and testing finished vehicles. Others also manufacture metal structures and electrical equipment, and carry out engineering and design work. Each model requires different levels of investment, technical infrastructure and skilled personnel. Azerbaijan already has experience assembling metro carriages at local facilities. In 2024, Baku Metro began assembling new-generation carriages using existing infrastructure. According to official figures, under a contract to supply 65 carriages between 2024 and 2026, specialists from the manufacturer also took part in assembling, commissioning and testing rolling stock in Azerbaijan. This experience demonstrates that existing infrastructure can be used for final assembly and technical testing. However, it remains unclear how Škoda Group’s proposed model would differ from current practices. The company has yet to disclose which stages of production would take place in Azerbaijan, what proportion of components would be locally manufactured, the terms of technology transfer or the facility’s annual production capacity. These indicators will help assess how much added value the project could generate for local industry. Even if the facility initially focuses only on assembly and maintenance, the project could help train skilled workers and expand rolling stock repair capabilities. However, manufacturing more complex components in Azerbaijan would require additional investment and a steady flow of orders. Azerbaijan’s 2027 budget: how will fall in oil revenues be offset? State budget revenues from the oil and gas sector are forecast to decline, while tax revenues are expected to increase Škoda Group is not the only contender Azerbaijan’s talks on purchasing new metro carriages and introducing modern technologies are not limited to the Czech company. In January 2026, Baku Metro officials met representatives of Swiss company Stadler Rail Group. They discussed the possible purchase of up to 300 new carriages, reducing operating costs and introducing modern signalling systems. In February, a Škoda Group delegation led by CEO Petr Novotný also held talks with Baku Metro officials. Discussions focused on purchasing new carriages and prospects for long-term technological cooperation. Potential cooperation between AZCON and Škoda Group had also been discussed in May 2025. These meetings indicate that Azerbaijan is exploring opportunities to involve international suppliers in modernising Baku Metro. However, Škoda Group’s proposal to establish a facility in Baku does not mean the company has secured orders for the carriages envisaged under the state programme. Key criteria for selecting suppliers will include compliance with technical requirements, purchase price, energy consumption, maintenance costs and long-term operating conditions. Localising production in Azerbaijan could bring additional economic benefits. However, its impact on procurement costs and competition will depend on the specific commercial proposals. $94.3m in violations: What Azerbaijan's mid-year audit reveals During the reporting period, the chamber carried out 20 compliance audits, two financial audits, eight performance audits and three analytical reviews. What does Uzbekistan’s experience show? Škoda Group already has experience of a similar cooperation model in Central Asia. In April 2026, the company signed a strategic cooperation agreement covering the supply of 10 electric trains to Uzbekistan and their maintenance. The project, worth more than €120m, also includes establishing a joint venture, localising maintenance services and training specialists. The company also plans to launch a Škoda Academy educational programme in Uzbekistan. This example shows that Škoda Group’s cooperation model goes beyond supplying rolling stock to include developing local maintenance infrastructure and transferring technology. However, its projects in Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan are at different stages. In Uzbekistan, the number of trains and project cost have already been agreed, and a strategic cooperation agreement has been signed. In Azerbaijan, the company has so far only announced plans to establish a production and maintenance facility. The proposed Baku facility’s potential to serve regional markets will also depend on commercial prospects. This would require orders from neighbouring countries, compliance with technical standards and competitive production costs. The visit is seen as a continuation of efforts to strengthen bilateral relations and the strategic partnership between the two countries.

title: Diphtheria: Kano disease control centre confirms 5 family members dead
body: The Kano State Centre for Disease Control (KNCDC), has confirmed the death of five children from the same family as a result of diphtheria in Danbare Ward, Layin Dutse, Kumbotso Local Government Area. The Centre’s Director-General, Prof. Muhammad Adamu-Abbas, confirmed this in a statement on Tuesday. Adamu-Abbas, who confirmed the deaths based on the case definition and verbal autopsy, also attributed the deaths of the children to late presentation of the case to the health facility and zero dose. He said the ages of the deceased children range between one year to 13 years. “The investigation confirmed a cluster of six children linked to one family. Tragically, five of the six children died due to late presentation. “The sixth child, Ummahabila Ibrahim, four years, was admitted on Oct. 1, 2026 with mild diphtheria and discharged on Oct. 4, 2026. A follow-up on Oct. 12, 2026, confirmed she is completely fine and healthy. “Clinical presentations included fever, sore throat, difficulty swallowing, neck swelling, nasal bleeding/regurgitation, and white patches on the tonsils (pseudomembrane). According to him, assessments included severe diphtheria, thrombocytopenia, anaemia, neuropathy, and risk of upper airway obstruction. “Epidemiological Findings showed three of the five deceased children were zero-dose (unvaccinated). “The mother reported that two children had been immunised, but there was no evidence of Routine Immunization (RI) cards, as they were reportedly lost during relocation,”. The DG appealed to caregivers to visit the nearest primary healthcare facility for missed doses, report of unusual illnesses or visit the nearest LGA Disease Surveillance and Notification Officer (DSNO). He urged the public not to delay or rely on self-medication, adding that diphtheria is a severe, vaccine-preventable disease spread through respiratory droplets and close contact. “It can cause sore throat, fever, neck swelling, and difficulty breathing. Multiple child deaths in one household represent a serious public health signal. “The report of five child deaths in one household is a serious signal requiring continuous vigilance,” he said. The KNCDC boss urged all residents to prioritise routine immunisation, seek care early, and support public health response efforts in order to prevent diphtheria deaths and reduce outbreaks in Kano State. title: Dilijan’s tourism ambitions: investment, culture, and the challenge of long-term development
body: At the Tourism Regional Forum 2026, industry leaders and policymakers gathered in Dilijan to discuss how destinations can create lasting value through investment, hospitality, culture, and community development. Armenia and Georgia are both important markets for regional tourism. In 2025, Armenia welcomed 288,578 visitors from Georgia, an increase of 8.5% compared with the previous year. Georgia, meanwhile, recorded approximately 900,000 visits by travellers from Armenia. While the two countries use different statistical measures, the figures highlight the importance of cross-border travel within the South Caucasus. Against this broader regional backdrop, Dilijan is working to strengthen its position as a destination for tourism, hospitality, and investment. From 9 to 11 October, the city hosted the second edition of the Tourism Regional Forum (TRF 2026), organised by Green Rock in partnership with Armenia’s Ministry of Economy. More than 250 participants gathered under the theme ‘Destinations Built to Last’ to discuss the long-term factors that shape successful destinations. Rather than focusing solely on visitor numbers, the discussions explored the relationship between investment, urban development, local communities, culture, and the quality of the visitor experience. Beyond visitor numbers Tourism growth is often measured through arrivals, overnight stays, and spending. But the long-term success of a destination also depends on whether development creates value for local residents, supports businesses, and preserves the character of a place. Opening the forum, Tigran Gasparyan, Deputy Minister of Economy of Armenia, addressed participants before Katerina Danekina, CEO of Green Rock Management Group, delivered the keynote speech, ‘Destinations Built to Last’. The keynote examined the city as an interconnected environment in which infrastructure, public spaces, businesses, and community life influence one another. Katerina Danekina, CEO of Green Rock Management Group and Christina Michelle, Founder of the St. Moritz Longevity Forum ‘Creating destinations with long-term value requires more than investment and infrastructure. It takes a shared vision, strong partnerships, and responsible leadership,’ Danekina said. ‘TRF 2026 brings together the people shaping the future of tourism and hospitality, giving them an opportunity to exchange experiences and perspectives and explore how destinations can evolve while preserving their identity and creating lasting value for their communities.’ The emphasis on long-term value reflects a broader question for emerging destinations: how can they attract investment and visitors while ensuring that development benefits the places in which it takes place? Investment and the local economy One of the forum’s discussions examined free economic zones and their potential role in regional development. The panel brought together representatives from government, business and investment, including Tigran Gasparyan, Rafael Gevorgyan, Deputy Chair of Armenia’s State Revenue Committee, Vazgen Gevorkyan, Strategic Development Advisor at Green Rock Management Group, and Tigran Harutyunyan, founder of Myler Mountain Resort. The discussion was moderated by Vahagn Lalayan, Director of Myler Free Economic Zone. igran Gasparyan, Rafael Gevorgyan, Vazgen Gevorkyan, Tigran Harutyunyan, and Vahagn Lalayan. The conversation placed tourism within a wider economic context, considering how investment frameworks and business activity can contribute to the development of destinations. For cities such as Dilijan, the challenge extends beyond attracting individual projects. It also involves building connections between hospitality, local businesses, education, culture, and public spaces so that development contributes to a more diverse local economy. Culture as part of destination development Culture was another focus of TRF 2026. A dedicated panel brought together Davinia Galea, Founder and CEO of ARC Research & Consultancy in Malta; Marie-Automne Peyrène, a member of Nice City Council and the Nice Côte d’Azur Metropolitan Council; and German violinist Linus Roth, founder and artistic director of Festival Ibiza Conciertos. Their discussion explored the place of culture in destination development and the role that cultural initiatives can play in shaping a city’s identity and appeal. Linus Roth In Dilijan, cultural infrastructure forms part of a wider development vision. Green Rock’s multifunctional complex includes projects such as PPLS Rooms Co-living and Villa3 Community Hub, alongside the upcoming Hyatt Regency Dilijan and Art Park. A Music Hall is also planned within the complex as a future venue for concerts, festivals and international performances. These projects reflect an approach in which accommodation and visitor infrastructure are developed alongside spaces intended to support cultural and community life. Their long-term contribution will depend not only on the facilities themselves, but also on how they become integrated into the city. Wellbeing and the future of hospitality The forum also examined longevity and wellbeing as potential areas of opportunity for tourism destinations. Danekina joined Christina Michelle, founder of the St. Moritz Longevity Forum, for a discussion on the relationship between wellbeing and tourism. The topic reflects growing interest across the hospitality sector in experiences that extend beyond traditional accommodation and leisure. For destinations considering this direction, the challenge is to identify opportunities that fit their local context and can be developed sustainably. Education was another element of the programme. On 11 October, the day after the main forum, gastronomy expert and culinary consultant Reto Mathis, co-founder of the St. Moritz Gourmet Festival, visited Apicius Armenia, an international hospitality school in Dilijan, where he conducted a masterclass for students. The visit connected the forum’s wider discussions about hospitality with professional education and the development of skills for the sector. Reto Mathis Building professional connections TRF 2026 also provided a setting for new institutional connections. During the forum, cooperation agreements were signed with the Orion Worldwide Innovations and the Belgian Armenian Chamber of Commerce. _____________________________________ Paid for by: Green Rock

title: Dubai and Abu Dhabi among top destinations for next-generation wealth, Savills says
body: Dubai and Abu Dhabi have been ranked among the top 10 destinations for next-generation wealth despite the fallout from geopolitical tensions, according to Savills. Dubai was ranked eighth and the UAE capital was 10th among favoured cities for the $84 trillion of wealth expected to be transferred between generations over the next two decades, the London-based consultancy said in its Spotlight on Wealth Trends report on Wednesday. Next-generation wealth refers to individuals under 40 who have inherited significant wealth or have accumulated it through entrepreneurial success. Dubai and Abu Dhabi benefitted from a slew of government initiatives that support economic and societal growth, including favourable tax environments, business-friendly policies and significant infrastructure investment “with a sophisticated luxury offering”, Savills said. In particular, Dubai's entrepreneurial ecosystem, global connectivity and lifestyle appeal attract international talent and capital. Abu Dhabi complements this with its growing financial centre, a rising number of family offices, expanding economic opportunities and a high quality of life, the study said. Those are “reinforcing the UAE's position as a compelling destination for globally mobile wealth”, Kelcie Sellers, associate director for world research at Savills, wrote in the report. In the wider Gulf, “economic diversification and succession planning are becoming more prominent, with growing focus on family governance, next-generation involvement and the long-term deployment of capital within the region”, Ms Sellers said. Despite the geopolitical uncertainty and economic headwinds, wealth generation and the flow of new money to the UAE continues. The country is a magnet for the ultra-wealthy , as well as for global wealth managers and trillion-dollar asset managers. A base in the country offers global investors and money managers opportunities to expand regional operations and work with some of the largest sovereign wealth funds, as well as institutional partners. Net wealth in the UAE is set to jump to $6 trillion by the end of this decade despite the short-term volatility caused by conflict in the Middle East , a report this week by Boston Consulting Group found. In the five years to the end of 2030, net wealth in the Emirates is set to increase by more than $2.3 trillion, at annual growth of 10.6 per cent, the report said. Last year alone, net wealth in the Arab world’s second-largest economy grew by almost 13 per cent on an annual basis to reach $3.6 trillion. New York leads globally New York topped the Savills list, followed by Miami, London, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Singapore, Hong Kong and Monaco at ninth. Dubai and Abu Dhabi were the only Gulf cities on the list, which ranked more than 100 destinations worldwide. Cities in Europe, the Middle East and Africa accounted for 16 of the index’s top 30 locations, driven by lifestyle and sporting events, which include major golf and tennis tournaments and Formula One races. In terms of the number of sporting events, Dubai was number one in the Emea region, while Abu Dhabi, home of the season-ending F1 race, was sixth. “The defining characteristic of Emea is the diversity of its wealth proposition. Global business centres, leading educational institutions, major sporting and cultural events, coastal retreats and mountain resorts are all within reach,” Ms Sellers said. Global wealth continues to grow rapidly. Total personal wealth jumped by nearly 11 per cent in 2025 to create about one million more millionaires, according to industry tracker Altrata. More than 510,800 are now ultra-high net worth individuals, or those with a net worth of $30 million or more, holding around $60 trillion in combined wealth – which is greater than the combined economies of the US and China, Altrata said. “Location decisions are becoming a core component of wealth planning … at the same time, new fortunes generated by technology and artificial intelligence are reshaping global wealth hubs,” Ms Sellers said. “As a result, many wealthy families are adopting multi-jurisdictional lifestyles, balancing residence, education and wealth structures across multiple markets.”

title: Opposition’s Zurab Japaridze Detained in Turkey on His Way to Brussels, To Be Returned to Georgia
body: Zurab Japaridze, leader of the opposition Girchi – More Freedom party, said he has been detained at the border in Turkey on his way to a summit in Brussels and will be sent back to Georgia, citing a ban on entering Turkey apparently based on information from Georgian authorities. The news was initially reported by ALDE Party – Liberals and Democrats for Europe, a union of liberal parties that lists Girchi – More Freedom among its members. According to ALDE’s October 14 statement , Japaridze has been detained while transiting en route to Brussels to participate in the leaders’ summit of Renew Europe, a liberal political group based in the European Parliament. ALDE said that Japaridze is held in a cell with his passport and luggage confiscated. “We regret that he will not be able to participate and lament that such pressures continue to be placed on the work and movements of opposition parties who seek a pro-European and democratic future for their country,” ALDE said. Later, Japaridze also wrote on Facebook that he was arrested at the border in Turkey, where he was planning to catch a connecting flight, and was told that he had been barred from entry to Turkey since November 2025 as “they have received some information” about him from Georgian official structures. “I will be sent back to Tbilisi tomorrow morning,” the politician said . “Unfortunately, I lost the possibility for important meetings. Nothing else to worry about.” Japaridze is among eight political figures charged with sabotage-related offences. He was released on bail in December shortly after serving his months-long sentence in a separate criminal case over boycotting Georgian Dream’s parliamentary commission, and has travelled in the past months to Western countries to participate in various events. Japaridze has publicly stated that he has no intention of leaving Georgia amid the looming verdict in the criminal case, which may send him and other opposition politicians to prison for years. title: Aweil Center youth leader calls for better education, empowerment
body: Aweil Center County’s newly elected youth association chairperson, Deng Guot, has called for improved education, youth empowerment, citing limited services and opportunities in the area. Speaking to Radio Tamazuj on Tuesday, Guot said he assumed office on Oct. 3 and would push for better education and programmes to support young people and strengthen community protection. “Compared with other counties in the state, we are lagging behind in education. We face numerous protection challenges, and people often do not know how to report cases and seek assistance,” he said. Guot said young people also lack access to vocational training and other development opportunities, adding that the association is ready to work with partners to introduce empowerment programmes. Aweil Center County caretaker commissioner Peter Natale acknowledged the education challenges and called for the immediate payment of public school teachers’ salaries. “The education standard is very poor, and we are calling for the immediate payment of public school teachers’ salaries,” Natale said, adding that the county had organised youth and women’s groups and was seeking programmes to support them. Peter Diing Ngong, executive director of the Wider Aid and Development Agency (WADA), attributed the limited services available to young people and women in Northern Bahr el Ghazal State to humanitarian funding cuts following the suspension of the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) by the U.S. government. title: PRP to Tinubu: Stop killings now; don’t wait till 2027
body: By Luminous Jannamike, Abuja The Peoples Redemption Party, PRP, has challenged President Bola Tinubu to stop the killings and abductions ravaging parts of the country, declaring that Nigerians cannot wait until 2027 for relief from worsening insecurity. The party accused the All Progressives Congress (APC) administration of failing in its primary duty to protect lives and property, alleging that the government was more interested in securing another term than addressing the dangers confronting ordinary Nigerians. In a statement by its National Chairman, Dr Hakeem Baba-Ahmed, the PRP said the growing impunity of criminal groups had left citizens at the mercy of attackers, while the government responded with press releases and platitudes. “The scale of the killings and abductions of helpless citizens and the rising impunity of their tormentors suggests that Nigerians live in a lawless country,” Baba-Ahmed said. He listed Kwara, Niger, Benue, Kebbi, Zamfara, Sokoto, Kaduna, Borno, Plateau and Yobe among states affected by the attacks, warning that Nigerians continued to lose their lives, livelihoods, property and freedom. The party also raised concerns over the pressure on military personnel and civilian volunteers battling insecurity, saying the crisis was threatening communities and the economic survival of millions. “Our gallant military and sundry volunteers are hard-pressed and virtually at the mercy of this expanding industry that feeds on lives, livelihood and economy of millions of our people,” Baba-Ahmed said. The PRP further accused the Tinubu administration of deploying huge sums of money to win the support of a small circle of Nigerians for what it described as a poisoned political ambition, even as citizens continued to bear the cost of insecurity. Urging Nigerians to speak out against the killings, Baba-Ahmed insisted that the president had a duty to protect citizens before the end of his tenure. “President Tinubu still has four months to go before his defeat. He has a responsibility to live up to his oath to protect lives and the welfare of Nigerians,” he said.
