title: Peller announces planned livestream with Nobel Laureate Wole Soyinka
body: Popular Nigerian streamer and content creator, Habeeb Hamzat, popularly known as Peller, has announced plans to host Nobel laureate Professor Wole Soyinka on his livestream, promising viewers a session filled with “proper English” and “grammar.” Peller disclosed the plan during a livestream on Tuesday, saying he would announce further details about the proposed session at a later date. “I want to do a stream with Mr. Wole Soyinka. I will announce it soon and tell you guys what the plan is. It will be a proper English day on that day. You will hear some ‘grammar’ that day,” he said. The proposed collaboration has drawn attention because of the contrast between Peller’s humorous, informal streaming style and Soyinka’s reputation as one of Africa’s most distinguished literary figures. Peller has built a large following through his livestreams, which often feature spontaneous conversations, humour and interactions with celebrities and other content creators. Soyinka, meanwhile, is a renowned Nigerian playwright, poet and novelist who became the first African to win the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1986. The prospect of bringing the two personalities together has generated interest online, with the anticipated session expected to offer a different experience from Peller’s usual livestreams. Although Peller said he would provide more information about the plan, no date for the proposed session was announced in his remarks. It is also unclear whether Soyinka has accepted the invitation. The post Peller announces planned livestream with Nobel Laureate Wole Soyinka appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Israel seeks urgent NIS 1b. purchase of Apache helicopters, diverting Arab sector funds
body: Israel's Defense Ministry confirmed Wednesday that it has purchased 12 Apache attack helicopters from Boeing. Ministry Director General Maj.-Gen. (res.) Amir Baram instructed the ministry's delegation in Washington to sign the agreement with the Pentagon.“The helicopters, scheduled for delivery at the beginning of the next decade, are of the Echo variant, the newest and most advanced model of the helicopter,” the Defense Ministry said.“The procurement of the Apache helicopters is a critical step in the IDF's force buildup, one that will strengthen its operational capabilities against a wide range of threats and contribute to the security of the State of Israel in the years to come,” Defense Minister Israel Katz said.“The Israeli defense establishment invested considerable effort and acted with determination to overcome the challenges and complete this agreement out of a deep understanding of its importance in ensuring the IDF's strength and readiness for future challenges,” he noted.“I thank our partners in the US administration and the Pentagon for their steadfast commitment to Israel's security, and for the cooperation and flexibility that made this agreement possible. Thank you to all those involved, led by Baram, for their professional and dedicated work, and for the perseverance that led to the completion of this important procurement,” Katz said.“The execution of the Apache agreement was made possible thanks to creative solutions we developed together with our American partners, without compromising operational needs,” Baram said.“This professional work with the US administration reflects the depth of our strategic relationship and the mutual commitment to Israel's security.“The Defense Ministry will continue to work at full pace to sign additional critical agreements, including the acquisition of additional platforms, munitions, interceptors, and more. This is to ensure immediate readiness for any scenario, alongside the implementation of the decade-long force buildup plan as part of the Defense Ministry's strategy in the face of emerging challenges,” he added.“Boeing has been a trusted partner of Israel's in building and advancing the country's national defense capabilities since its earliest days, and we are proud to continue serving as a leading supplier of fighter aircraft, helicopters, munitions and other equipment in the future,” Boeing Israel President Maj.-Gen. (res.) Ido Nehushtan said.“The IDF's selection of the Apache Echo, following its selection of the world's most advanced refueling aircraft, the KC-46A, and the decision to procure a second squadron of the world's most advanced fighter jets, the F-15IA, is compelling proof of its proven operational capabilities on the battlefield and its continued relevance in addressing evolving threats and future operational challenges.“Boeing will work in close cooperation with the Government of Israel to provide the Israel Air Force with the world's most advanced and capable attack helicopters,” Nehushtan added. He served as IAF chief from 2008 until 2012 before leaving the military.Arab sector funding diverted to Apache purchaseThe government was preparing to allocate NIS 3.5 billion on Wednesday for urgent defense procurement, including a roughly NIS 1 billion deal to purchase Apache helicopters, The Jerusalem Post confirmed earlier on Wednesday.The Finance Ministry told the Post that close to NIS 1 billion used for the Apache helicopter purchase would be diverted from funds earmarked for a five-year plan to develop Israel's Arab sector. The remaining NIS 68 million would come from the 2026 state budget.Government ministers were asked to approve the purchase via an urgent telephone vote, according to Israeli media.The decision comes two weeks before the elections, a period during which the government must generally exercise restraint and avoid actions that are not particularly urgent.A legal opinion attached to the government decision reportedly raised two main concerns: creating a situation in which the incoming government is faced with an irreversible situation, as well as risking prioritization of party interests over the public interest.However, the document added that after examining the necessity and urgency of the decision to advance the procurement, bringing forward the procurement would be necessary for security reasons.Shir Perets contributed to this report.

title: Ukraine warns of “a new type of humanitarian crisis” as Russia aims at its biggest cities
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine is drafting crisis scenarios for November to March as Russian strikes target the country’s biggest cities, Head of the Presidential Office Kyrylo Budanov said on 13 October after chairing a meeting with donor-country diplomats and humanitarian organizations. His deputy Iryna Vereshchuk warned the same day that this winter may bring a new type of humanitarian crisis. She asked donors to be ready with fast extra funding. Russia has struck Ukraine’s grid deep into winter before: last February, it launched more than 500 missiles and drones as temperatures fell below −20°C. Strikes have continued despite a US-announced energy truce Moscow has not confirmed . Kyiv now wants donors ready to pay for the humanitarian fallout in advance. Crisis scenarios for November to March The core task is clear crisis scenarios and synchronized response plans for that period, Budanov wrote. The government is building a baseline threat scenario through the State Emergency Service, while the military and intelligence will provide a risk assessment. “The available resource must be concentrated where people will have the hardest time,” Budanov wrote. Ukraine, he added, must hold its rear as reliably as the Defense Forces hold the front line. What officials mean by a new type of crisis A war of rear areas is underway, Vereshchuk wrote. Russia is changing tactics in an attempt to deepen the humanitarian crisis, especially in Kyiv, Kharkiv, Odesa, and Dnipro, she added. Vereshchuk did not define what makes the crisis new, but she tied her warning to the big cities. “This winter, it is the big cities that may become the testing ground of our national resilience,” she wrote. Humanitarian organizations must adapt their plans to protect and support civilians, Vereshchuk wrote. Donors, she said, must be ready to provide additional crisis-response funding quickly. The capital lags behind Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on 13 October that even border and frontline oblasts were ahead of Kyiv on resilience plans as of mid-October. Even single hits by Shahed attack drones can cut power and water across much of the capital, he noted. He also began consultations on urgent security and management steps to fix the situation in the city. Explore further Three days after Washington announced an energy ceasefire, Russia fires 39 ballistic missiles at Ukraine’s grid Russia carried out more than 200 strikes on Ukraine’s power generation and transmission in the week to 11 October, Zelenskyy said . Overnight on 14 October, Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones at energy and critical infrastructure. The barrage left at least 600,000 people without power, Zelenskyy said . title: ‘Massive’ Oil, Gas, Mineral Exploration To Begin In Greenland, Says Trump
body: US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that oil, gas and mineral exploration was preparing to begin in Greenland, and hailed the Arctic island’s position for US and European security. Washington signed a security deal with the leaders of Greenland and Denmark after Trump threatened to take Copenhagen’s strategically important Arctic Circle territory by force. A photo taken on September 6, 2026 shows houses and other buildings in Nuuk, Greenland. Photo by MADS CLAUS RASMUSSEN / RITZAU SCANPIX / AFP Greenland, which lies on the shortest route for missiles between Russia and the United States, represents a highly strategic location for Trump’s desired “Golden Dome” defence shield. It also has untapped rare earth deposits and could be a critical player as melting polar ice opens up new shipping routes. “Massive Oil, Gas, and Mineral Exploration is getting ready to begin in our new and beautiful Greenland!” Trump said in a post on Truth Social. Citing experts, Trump said “the amount of easily available oil is far greater than that of almost… anywhere in the world.” He did not give details of prospective American involvement. In August, media reports of a US oil company’s preparatory operations in a remote region of eastern Greenland left locals and authorities on the island uneasy. In the same message on Truth Social, Trump hailed Greenland’s position as “second to none” for US and European security. “Any future attack on the United States will have to come across Greenland, where our Defense will routinely knock down drones, missiles, or any other form of weapon not yet even conceived,” Trump said. “It gives us time, location, and sightline, like nowhere else in the World!” he added. Trump signed a security deal with the leaders of Greenland and Denmark in September. Under the 10-page pact, the US will build two military bases in southern and eastern Greenland. These will be established in Narsarsuaq in the south of the island and Mestersvig in the east, in addition to the Pituffik base it already operates in the north. AFP The post ‘Massive’ Oil, Gas, Mineral Exploration To Begin In Greenland, Says Trump appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Ukraine says Starlink limits threaten defense against jet-powered Shaheds
body: SpaceX’s new restrictions on Starlink satellite communications threaten Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russia’s increasingly fast jet-powered Shahed drones, a presidential adviser warned on October 14, 2026, as Ukrainian military units reported canceled drone missions and communications failures at speeds well below the initially reported limit. Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on defense technology, said the restrictions could undermine what he described as Ukraine’s most effective current solution for intercepting jet-powered Shaheds. “Starlink is used in what is currently the most effective solution (interceptors) for protecting our skies from jet-powered Shaheds,” Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram . He said the decision was effectively depriving Ukraine of one of its few available means of countering the faster Russian drones. The warning followed the introduction of a speed restriction on Starshield, the military-oriented version of SpaceX’s Starlink service, overnight on October 13–14. According to Beskrestnov, the limit was set at 100 miles per hour (160 kilometers per hour), without advance warning to Ukrainian forces. Ukrainian units report canceled drone missions Ukrainian military personnel prepare a fixed-wing attack drone for a nighttime mission. (Credit: 9th Separate Brigade of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces) Ukraine’s 7th Rapid Reaction Corps, operating in the Huliaipole sector of Zaporizhzhia, told Ukrainian outlet NV that drones were experiencing Starlink interruptions lasting 10 to 20 seconds at speeds of just 110–120 kilometers per hour (68–75 miles per hour). The aircraft continued flying during the interruptions, but operators struggled to maintain control. One unmanned systems unit had already canceled several missions because of the problems, the corps said. The disruption was particularly serious for intermediate-range strike drones, which must accelerate during launch. Flying more slowly to preserve connectivity would also make the aircraft more vulnerable to Russian defenses. Separately, Ukrainian volunteer and former defense ministry adviser Serhii Sternenko reported that some military personnel were experiencing dropouts at speeds as low as 60–70 kilometers per hour (37–43 miles per hour). That lower threshold has not been independently established. A new problem for Ukraine’s jet-powered Shahed defenses A Ukrainian serviceman installs a Starlink satellite communications terminal. (Credit: Support Forces of Ukraine Command) The restrictions come as Russia increasingly deploys jet-powered variants of its Shahed-derived Geran attack drones, forcing Ukraine to develop faster interceptors. The Geran-4, for example, typically flies at 300–400 kilometers per hour (185–250 miles per hour), according to Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence. Ukrainian manufacturers have responded with new interceptor designs, including models capable of reaching speeds above 600 kilometers per hour (375 miles per hour). A Starlink connection restricted to 160 kilometers per hour would therefore be insufficient for high-speed interception if the drone depends on the satellite link throughout its flight. The impact on individual interceptor types will depend on their communication architecture and degree of onboard autonomy. The restrictions also mark a reversal of the circumstances that originally prompted Ukraine to seek tighter Starlink controls. In January 2026, Ukrainian officials discovered Russian drones using Starlink terminals to maintain communications beyond the reach of conventional radio links. On January 29, 2026, then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov announced that Kyiv was working with SpaceX on countermeasures. On February 2, 2026, Ukraine introduced a terminal whitelist intended to prevent Russian forces from accessing the network while preserving legitimate Ukrainian access. The measures also included restrictions on operating terminals in motion. The latest change appears to have extended speed restrictions to Starshield services previously used for higher-speed operations. Poland challenges Musk as SpaceX remains silent A Starlink terminal loaded on a Ukrainian military pickup truck alongside equipment used for drone operations (Credit: Ukraine’s 45th Artillery Brigade) The restrictions have also prompted a diplomatic reaction. Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski publicly challenged SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk on October 14, 2026, asking whether he was “playing politics” with his products again. He added that European customers were watching. Poland helps finance Ukraine’s Starlink connectivity, making Warsaw a significant stakeholder in the service. Beskrestnov suggested that the sudden restrictions were connected to the current political situation, while Sternenko speculated that SpaceX had acted at the request of US President Donald Trump’s administration. The changes come amid US pressure on Kyiv to halt strikes against Russian oil refineries. However, the drones used for those attacks reportedly rely on other communications systems. As of early afternoon on October 14, 2026, SpaceX had not publicly explained the restrictions. The post Ukraine says Starlink limits threaten defense against jet-powered Shaheds appeared first on AeroTime .

title: Ministry urges next government to tackle transport tax reform without delay
body:
Proposed reforms could mean stricter taxation for electric vehicles, new congestion charges, and road tolls.
The Ministry of Transport and Communications is urging the incoming government to implement a reform of transport taxation, warning in a new statement that further delay is no longer an option.
Transport tax revenues are set to fall sharply over the next decade as vehicles become increasingly battery-powered. The ministry also points to mounting pressure to raise transport taxation given the state of public finances.
Olli-Pekka Rantala , Head of Department at the Ministry of Transport and Communications, says current emission-based taxation is working as intended, but that very success is eroding the funding base.
The ministry’s statement follows a similar one issued by the Ministry of Finance last week.
To secure sufficient funding for basic road maintenance, the ministry proposes linking vehicle tax to road maintenance costs. Currently, a significant portion of vehicle tax is based on a car's carbon dioxide emissions, while the state also levies a seperate fuel tax on vehicles that do not run on petrol.
"It is likely that taxation of electric vehicles would become stricter as a result. In that case, it will be essential to ensure through other means that road traffic emissions are reduced in line with Finland's international commitments," Rantala says.
Under the ministry's policy, tax revenue collected from transport should continue to cover at least the costs and nuisances caused by it.
The finer details of any tax changes, Rantala notes, will need to be worked out together with the Ministry of Finance.
Even if the focus of vehicle taxation shifts, the ministry stresses that emission targets must still be met through a broad set of tools — including transport emissions trading, energy taxation, distribution obligations and other EU legislation.
The EU's new road transport emissions trading system (ETS2), takes effect in 2028 and will impact fuel prices, according to Rantala.
The ministry also ties the shift away from fossil fuels directly to national security.
"It is also a security measure. Giving up fossil fuels strengthens Finland's strategic independence, since we won't be dependent on oil imports," Rantala says.
With public finances under strain, the ministry has also been exploring new ways to fund major road and rail projects — including new user fees and cost-sharing arrangements among those who benefit from them.
This approach, they argue, would help guide the selection of economically efficient projects. In practice, this could mean collecting separate user fees from those who use a major new road or railway line.
The ministry also wants regional congestion charges introduced in large urban areas, with revenue from such charges planned and agreed jointly with the cities concerned.
The ministry's statement also flags the poor condition of Finland's road and rail network. With funding already insufficient to repair anything beyond the busiest routes, the backlog of repairs — now at 4.3 billion euros including railways — is set to keep growing.
Sabina Lindström , Head of Department at the Ministry of Transport and Communications, says maintaining existing infrastructure — basic road upkeep in particular — remains the top priority.
Without confirmed funding, the current savings trajectory will have to tighten further, with direct consequences for provisional and lower-tier roads.
"In practice, this means that we can maintain these busiest routes, but unfortunately, all those that fall into a lower category will continue to receive too little maintenance," Lindström says.
Some in the public debate have occasionally floated the idea of stripping asphalt from roads in poor condition and converting them to gravel. Lindström says this offers little relief.
"Removing the surface is already part of the solution, and it's done every year. Unfortunately, it doesn't solve the problem. It's costly in itself, and maintaining a gravel road isn't cheap either. It's done on an appropriate scale," Lindström says.

title: Hellenic Navy Tests SARONIC’s Corsair USV Ahead of Major Order
body: The Hellenic Navy is currently testing a number of Corsair autonomous unmanned surface vessels (USVs) and has submitted a Letter of Request (LOR) to the United States for the procurement of at least 30 vessels to expand its unmanned maritime capabilities. On Tuesday, October 13, 2026, Greek Minister of National Defence Nikos Dendias attended the inauguration of the Joint Unmanned and Autonomous Maritime Systems Training Centre at the Palaskas Training Centre (KEPAL), part of the Hellenic Navy’s Naval Training Command. The facility is located at the Kanellopoulos Naval Base in Skaramagas, west of Athens. Photo taken during the inauguration of the Joint Unmanned and Autonomous Maritime Systems Training Centre at the Palaskas Training Centre, showing a Corsair USV (left) and the Hellenic Navy-developed Pyrpolitis USV (right). Photo: www.mod.mil.gr The event showcased several domestically developed systems that Greece is currently testing, supporting its ambition to become a European leader in autonomous platform development by 2030, as stated by the Minister of National Defence. However, the most notable highlight was a Corsair autonomous unmanned surface vehicle (USV) developed by US company Saronic . According to a video released by the Ministry of National Defence (screenshots below), at least two Corsair USVs are currently in Greece undergoing trials with the Hellenic Navy. The trials involved several Fleet units, with the fleet support ships HS Perseas (A377) and possibly HS Aias (A473) serving as motherships for transporting the unmanned vessels. The trials also demonstrated the vessel’s ability to cooperate tactically with several warships. Operating from HS Perseas Corsair USV and HS Perseas Corsair USV and HS Aias On the deck of HS Perseas The Ministry of National Defence stated that the Corsair USVs had undergone extensive trials and had been successfully evaluated by the Hellenic Navy. A Letter of Request (LOR) has also been submitted to the United States for the procurement of an unspecified number of vessels through the government-to-government Foreign Military Sales (FMS) programme. Separately, George Sideris of Hellas Journal reports that the Hellenic Navy plans to acquire at least 30 such vessels. The reported procurement would form part of Greece’s ambition to significantly expand its USV capabilities in the near future. Corsair USV Specifications The Corsair USV is capable of operating at ranges over 1,000 nautical miles and can support 1,000-pound payloads. Saronic picture. The Corsair is a 7-meter ASV capable of carrying payloads of up to 1,000 lbs (approximately 454 kg) over distances exceeding 1,000 nautical miles. Designed for rapid deployment and scalable operations worldwide, it offers a versatile platform for a broad range of missions. The vessel carries electro-optical systems, advanced communications equipment, and a range of sensors tailored to each mission. A key capability is collaborative autonomous operation, or swarming, which enables multiple vessels to coordinate their actions and execute complex missions autonomously. Corsair can perform a wide variety of missions, including Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance (ISR), Anti-Surface Warfare (ASuW), one-way attack (OWA) missions, including kamikaze-style attacks, and Search and Rescue (SAR). Its advanced artificial intelligence and open architecture enable further upgrades and integration of additional capabilities, expanding its operational versatility. The US Navy has brought Corsair USVs into operational service and deployed them in real-world missions. Their operational use in the Persian Gulf region came to light in June 2026, when a Corsair USV reportedly played a key role in rescuing the two crew members of a downed AH-64E Apache attack helicopter . In July 2026, three Corsair USVs reportedly struck the port at Bandar Abbas Naval Base, marking the first use of US unmanned surface vessels in American combat operations. The post Hellenic Navy Tests SARONIC’s Corsair USV Ahead of Major Order appeared first on Naval News .

title: Sybiha: Putin must face consequences for rejecting peace, not incentives to continue war
body:
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha called on international partners to increase pressure on Russia through sanctions and provide Ukraine with additional air defense systems, stressing that Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin must be held accountable for rejecting peace.
“Putin has delivered yet another negative “response” to the proposal of an energy ceasefire announced by President Trump and supported by President Zelenskyy. Instead of one “yes” to peace efforts — 39 missiles and more than 120 drones,” Sybiha said on X on Wednesday, commenting on Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities.
He said energy infrastructure facilities were the main targets of the strikes. At least three people were killed in Kyiv and more than 20 others were injured. Kyiv and Kharkiv came under massive attacks, while rescue and repair crews across Ukraine were dealing with the aftermath.
Sybiha said Russia was not only attacking Ukraine but was also openly challenging the United States and showing contempt for every effort to stop the war.
“There can be no economic rewards for aggression. No sanctions relief. No concessions that allow Russia to finance its next wave of terror,” Sybiha said.
He said every dollar flowing into Russia’s war budget becomes an additional resource for attacks on Ukrainian civilians and poses a threat to transatlantic security.
Sybiha called on partners to respond to the Russian attacks by tightening sanctions, strengthening enforcement and immediately providing Ukraine with additional air defense systems.
“Putin must face consequences for rejecting peace, not receive incentives to continue the war,” the minister said.

title: Aldar's international unit plans to deliver 9,000 homes in next five years
body: London Square, which is part of Abu Dhabi’s Aldar Properties , plans to deliver about 9,000 homes in the next five years in the UK capital with a total development value of £5 billion ($6.6 billion), as demand remains resilient. The homes will be built across about 30 sites, with the company targeting buyers in the affordable segment as well as international investors. More than 3,600 homes will be for sale, 1,538 will be for build-to-rent and another 3,575 will be sold in the affordable segment, in which government support helps people to buy a home. London Square plans to start work on 12 sites this year with 65 per cent of those affordable, said chief executive Adam Lawrence. “There's always demand for affordable housing, it is a huge market and a huge need,” he told The National. There is also international demand from buyers in Turkey, Hong Kong and Middle East countries, he added. “Turkey is really strong at the moment. We've opened an office in Turkey, in Istanbul, recently, and we're seeing, within days of opening, we're into double-digit sales there. Hong Kong's been very quiet, but that looks like it's coming back.” The company, which was acquired by Aldar in 2023, has delivered 5,000 homes across 46 sites with a development value of £2.9 billion ($3.8 billion) since London Square was founded in 2010. “Under the Aldar banner, our sales have actually been better than they were historically and in the current market have been outperforming all of our peers,” said Scott Brown, chief financial officer of London Square. “Through our involvement with Aldar, we've not only been able to drive the capital but we've also been able to drive our sales.” London Square, which regenerates former industrial sites, is behind projects such as the Nine Elms development, which features more than 750 residential homes and 21,500 square feet of commercial and retail space. It is also transforming the former headquarters of Surrey County Council into a premium 292-home development, which includes the restoration of old structures. The company aims to complete 600 homes this year, up from 398 last year, with sales backlog to reach £1 billion by the end of 2026. “Most of this year will be on the affordable market rather than the build-to-sell market … about 30 per cent of what we're building is affordable,” Mr Brown told The National in London. He did not provide details on the total sales the company expects this year. London Square reported sales of £251 million for the first half of 2026, up 236 per cent year-on-year on the back of three new projects – Bermondsey Phase 3, Wimbledon Bridge House and Ransome’s Wharf. Sales from the Middle East account for 10 to 15 per cent of total international sales, with UAE buyers dominating sales activity, says Naomi Minegishi, London Square international sales director. “International demand is being driven by investment opportunity, safe haven of their capital and a strong legal framework,” Ms Minegishi said. “Families also want to have a second home to spend time in summer, as well as to have a home to support their children as they enrol them in school or universities to study in London.” London's property market has been affected by geopolitical uncertainty that is pushing inflation higher. In the third quarter, the average home price in London grew modestly by 0.4 per cent annually to £529,720, as demand remained subdued amid higher borrowing costs, according to the Nationwide Building Society. However, fundamentals remain strong on higher investment activity, lifestyle vibrancy and a diverse population, said Sharief Ibrahim, executive director and head of residential agency at CBRE. “There is real cause for optimism. There are countless examples of schemes that are performing really well, many in the London Square portfolio in terms of the volume of apartments being sold and the value being achieved,” he said. “London is a resilient place. It's been through economic downturns, shocks to the economy and the system and the appeal of London has endured throughout that period. It's a global powerhouse and one of the, if not the most, successful city in terms of inward investment globally.” It projects home transaction volumes to be around 6,000 to 7,000 this year and 7,500 to 8,000 next year.

title: Pulsar at ESUG 2026 (new Smalltalk IDE)
body:
At ESUG 2026 I presented Pulsar, a new coding-first IDE for Pharo. The talk explores why staying close to the code still matters in the age of generative agents—and where Pulsar is heading next.
At ESUG this year —2026, for those reading this from the future— I presented Pulsar , a new IDE for Pharo, with a strong focus on coding.
That may sound like an obvious thing for an IDE to focus on. But in these days of RAD reborn in the form of generative agents, perhaps it is not so obvious after all.
Pulsar comes from a fairly simple idea: programming tools should help programmers understand the system, navigate it, change it, and stay close to the code while doing so. Generative tools can certainly help, but I do not think they make those capabilities less important. If anything, they make them more important.
The ESUG talk was my attempt to explain that direction, show where Pulsar is today, and give a glimpse of where I would like to take it.
Slides: Pulsar: A New Pharo IDE — Growing the Power User in You
And, of course, you can find Pulsar itself here:
Pulsar is still very much a work in progress, but it is already usable, and feedback is more than welcome.

title: AI Laser Locking for Quantum Computers: How QuEra Automates It
body:
Phone: +1 617-588-7207 Email: info@quera.com
1380 Soldiers Field Road, Boston, MA 02135, USA
QuEra's quantum computers run on lasers held at exact frequencies, a precision no eye can see and only the atoms can distinguish. Keeping a laser there is a continuous act: temperature, vibration, and pressure push it off target all day, and layered feedback pushes it back. When the feedback loop fails, the lock breaks and the machine stops. Bringing it back has historically taken one specific expert: someone who knows the lasers intuitively and has experience with the exact recovery sequence required to return it to the right state. If the lock broke in the middle of the night, that person had to drive to the lab and fix it.
This is not a new problem, and QuEra has built automatic relocking for common disturbances. Aquila, our production QPU available through Amazon Braket, already runs with excellent uptime exceeding 99%. But the team knew that the level of human involvement in relocking, particularly for the less frequent but more severe disturbances, was not scalable. As a result, this spring QuEra deployed the Model Hardware Standard (MHS), a standard that started as a collaboration between Anthropic and HHMI Janelia Research Campus. A cross-functional task force took relocking to another level: the level that scalable deployment of logical QPUs will demand. Working through MHS on a dedicated testbed, with an AI agent in operational control of roughly $0.7M of precision hardware inside human-set safety bounds, the lock now comes back in seconds: verified, on target, with no one in the building. And then the same approach went one step further. It tuned the lock itself, to a quality level it can prove, and carried that new ability to a second operating wavelength in a single run.
The results are promising and are just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to QuEra's plans for layering AI, at a foundational level, across our quantum computers.
Picturing a ball on a see-saw is a useful visual analogy for the problem our AI agent was solving. In this simplified analogy, the ball's position is the laser's frequency. If we can hold it in a specific location (in this example, inside the green region), we can successfully control the atomic qubits.
In QuEra's systems, the lasers that drive logical qubits must hold within ±1 kHz or better, about ±0.000000001 nm (illustrative values, for education). The infrared laser here is invisible to the eye, shown in false color. The ball swings; no eye could ever tell. Only atoms can tell the difference.
The see-saws in the diagram are analogous to actuators within our system. But the challenge is that the required precision is so high that no single actuator can do it alone. Multiple actuators are stacked together. A big, slow layer takes the wide drift; progressively faster layers take the finer jitter. Together, the ball never leaves the zone.
But there is a twist. A real tuning knob is not smooth. The laser prefers certain wavelengths, shaped by its internal filters (etalon, birefringent filter). In this example, each dip is a fixed mode the ball can settle into. And here is the trap: after a disturbance, bringing the knob back to level does not bring the ball home. It sits stably in the wrong mode, looking locked.
A big enough perturbation throws the ball clear out of the fine layers' reach, into a competing mode. No matter how far you tune the smaller layer, the ball remains stuck in the wrong lock. The recovery requires a sweep of the coarse, wide-range knob beyond the threshold to carry the ball home and then quickly ease off to capture the target mode. Finally, the lock has to be verified against an absolute wavelength reference so a wrong mode is never mistaken for success. This process is known as a Ti:sapphire mode-hop recovery. This is the judgment the MHS auto-relock controller was built to perform on its own.
In the real laser system, all of the layers coexist. The birefringent filter is the coarse, widest-range layer: its landscape has a few widely spaced modes. The etalon sits on it with a finer comb. And the piezo (smooth, continuous, fastest) rides on top doing the rapid final trim. Working gracefully means each coarse element stays seated in the right dip of its own landscape while the fine one glides, and the ball never leaves the zone.
The recovery process described above traditionally has been the craft of a small team of highly skilled experts. Automating it is not a one-person job either: it takes a laser-systems engineer who understands how and why the lock fails, a software engineer to command the instruments, an algorithms designer for the recovery logic, and a tester to pit that logic against the many ways a real lock breaks. A QuEra team of exactly that shape spent roughly two to three weeks building our earlier hand-written recovery script, and its limits were the limits of any fixed script: it could only handle the failures its authors thought to enumerate.
The task force then handed the same problem to a single AI agent, Claude, working through MHS against the live testbed. MHS let the agent run its own experiments: propose a recovery, try it on the hardware, read what happened, refine. It is the same loop the human team runs, but continuously, at machine speed, and overnight. The agent did nothing a person fundamentally could not do; it watched the same instruments and learned only what they revealed. The difference was scale: enumerating and hardening against hundreds of edge cases, every neighboring mode the laser can fall into, every stale calibration, every wrong-mode grab, is unreasonable by hand, and the agent reached corners of the problem no team would have the bandwidth to. The humans stayed in the orchestrator's seat: setting scope, reviewing every step, deciding what counts as proof. That role became more important, not less. Tight oversight from Evgeny Ostroumov, the laser-side technical champion, provided the physical reality check, more than once catching the agent before it spent its effort on things that looked right and were not.
Given no information about what disturbed the lock (a blocked beam, mechanical vibration, electrical noise that disrupts the tuning configuration, a frequency hop small or large), the controller reads the live instrument state, classifies the disturbance, runs the correct recovery, and declares success only when the cavity signal confirms a lock and the absolute wavelength matches the target. The agent's code runs at native speed and supervises from above the microsecond servo loop, rather than within it. In validation it recovered on target 695 of 700 times: 99.3% across seven disturbance classes, one hundred timed trials each. Recovery took 0.9 to 5.4 seconds for wavelength-preserving faults and roughly 10 to 14 seconds for the hardest ones, where the laser's color has hopped far away, against 5 to 10 minutes for a human expert. Four qualities were proven together: correctness (never a wrong-mode lock reported as success), autonomy (no operator, no fault information), speed (seconds, not minutes), and predictability (tight, repeatable recovery times, which for unattended operation matters as much as the average). The five misses shared one rig-condition cause, not a control-logic one; in each the controller correctly declined to claim success, and the lock was back on target before the next trial. No failure left the system dark.
The validation was not confined to injected faults. The testbed lives in a working lab with realistic foot traffic, a deliberate choice, and over the weeks of the pilot the laser hopped modes on its own 43 times. All 43 were caught and recovered automatically.
One distinction matters and we will keep making it: MHS is the environment in which Claude designed, wrote, and validated this controller. What runs on the bench is a deterministic, fully inspectable program: AI-driven in development, human-orchestrated, autonomous in operation. And that autonomy is bounded by design: MHS enforces device-declared bounds, interlocks, and emergency stops at the hardware interface, independent of the model.
So the team pointed the same approach at the quality of the lock itself. That quality is set by a tuning process: twelve interdependent feedback parameters, adjusted within a continuously running control loop. Done well, tuning removes residual noise from the lock, which directly improves the performance of the computer's quantum gates and makes the lock drop less often. There is no closed-form optimum: a specialist tunes by eye, and can quiet the band they are watching while missing a resonance somewhere else. The agent instead recomputed the full noise spectrum after every adjustment, thousands of times, across far more of the space than a person could reach. Working inside a hard safety envelope (every candidate setting that dropped the lock was detected and reverted, and not one of roughly 12,500 evaluations caused the laser to hop modes), it mapped which parameters matter, searched the space, and converged on a configuration it then confirmed by running unattended overnight. The result was residual frequency noise cut by a factor of five, and a lock that simply stopped dropping: zero unattended lock drops in a roughly 19-hour soak test, against 1.6 per hour before.
Then came the test that matters most: an independent, out-of-loop measurement, the noise the qubits actually see, on an instrument the optimization could not touch. It compared the agent's configuration against a manual tune by an experienced specialist. Across the measured band, the two were indistinguishable: the agent matched the expert everywhere the expert was right. But the manual tune had left behind a hidden resonance near 220 kHz, invisible on the instruments a human tune normally watches, where the loop was quietly adding noise, worse than no lock at all. The agent's configuration suppressed it roughly a thousandfold, and a linewidth-type metric improved from 58 to 21 kHz. The point is not that the specialist erred; it is that the automated procedure scores the entire spectrum on every tune, so it cannot overlook a defect the way a hand tune can. It delivers its optimum every single time.
And the capability travels. Pointed at a second operating wavelength, one directly relevant to the gates our machines run, the agent worked out the new operating parameters from scratch in a single unattended overnight run, leaving that lock roughly ten times quieter than it was found and passing every acceptance test. It took weeks to bring up the pilot, and one night to bring it up at a new wavelength. That is what it looks like when the understanding gained in one campaign carries to the next: the sensitivity maps, the safety envelope, the calibrations.
One status distinction, for precision: the auto-relock controller is a standalone production script, with the AI out of the loop at runtime. The tuning workflow still runs with the AI in the loop, and packaging it as a standalone tool is next on the engineering list. Read more about MHS and see QuEra's case study on Anthropic's blog .
In machines running short, discrete jobs, a laser fault is downtime: the queue stalls until the lock returns. In a system like Libra, a machine class capable of running logical-qubit programs for hours or days, a laser that falls out of state mid-run can corrupt a result that quantum error correction can no longer salvage. From a customer's seat, two error rates carry equal weight, two LERs as our team puts it: the Logical Error Rate, and the Laser Error Rate. A failed result looks the same whichever LER caused it.
Fast, verified, autonomous recovery, validated on our testbed and headed for live machines next, is how the second LER is held down. But the deeper story is what this does to the economics of deploying quantum computers. Every stabilized laser in a machine used to carry a standing claim on scarce expert time: 5 to 10 minutes of attended recovery per lock loss, at any hour; 15 to 30 minutes per tune, on a specialist's calendar; a new operating point commissioned over weeks of hands-on work. Each generation of machine carries more lasers than the last, and a fleet in the field multiplies all of it, in places where there is no laser physicist down the hall. After the pilot, the same functions run in seconds, unattended, verified, and commissioning a new wavelength costs one overnight run. Recovery becomes predictable, far less subject to human variance, and runs with a frugal human footprint. That is the shape of a quantum computer that can be deployed: at QuEra, and anywhere a machine has to stand on its own.
This is not, in the end, a laser story. It is a story about an AI model developing control logic a quantum computer depends on, doing it at expert level, and proving it against independent measurement. The pilot's single biggest enabler was a physical training ground: a live testbed the agent could act on, a reality engine. And what the pilot banked is more than two results. It is the measured understanding, the safety practices, and the calibrations that made the second campaign overnight where the first took weeks. Each subsystem this approach touches makes the next one cheaper to reach.
A QPU contains many subsystems that differ in detail but match the same pattern as the MHS pilot: precise, fragile, and hungry for scarce expert attention. The laser is the first proof point, and we expect it not to be the boundary. For QuEra, the pattern is a path to machines that stay up (today's job queues moving, tomorrow's logical computations alive) and to machines that can be built, commissioned, and operated with a fraction of the specialist hours they demand today. For the field, it reaches further: the laser at the center of this work has carried atomic physics for more than twenty years on know-how passed from student to student, and that know-how can now live in a controller any lab can build the same way.
At QuEra, the late-night drive to bring a laser back may no longer be a rite of passage for system operators.
QuEra's quantum computers run on lasers held at exact frequencies, a precision no eye can see and only the atoms can distinguish. Keeping a laser there is a continuous act: temperature, vibration, and pressure push it off target all day, and layered feedback pushes it back. When the feedback loop fails, the lock breaks and the machine stops. Bringing it back has historically taken one specific expert: someone who knows the lasers intuitively and has experience with the exact recovery sequence required to return it to the right state. If the lock broke in the middle of the night, that person had to drive to the lab and fix it.
This is not a new problem, and QuEra has built automatic relocking for common disturbances. Aquila, our production QPU available through Amazon Braket, already runs with excellent uptime exceeding 99%. But the team knew that the level of human involvement in relocking, particularly for the less frequent but more severe disturbances, was not scalable. As a result, this spring QuEra deployed the Model Hardware Standard (MHS), a standard that started as a collaboration between Anthropic and HHMI Janelia Research Campus. A cross-functional task force took relocking to another level: the level that scalable deployment of logical QPUs will demand. Working through MHS on a dedicated testbed, with an AI agent in operational control of roughly $0.7M of precision hardware inside human-set safety bounds, the lock now comes back in seconds: verified, on target, with no one in the building. And then the same approach went one step further. It tuned the lock itself, to a quality level it can prove, and carried that new ability to a second operating wavelength in a single run.
The results are promising and are just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to QuEra's plans for layering AI, at a foundational level, across our quantum computers.
Picturing a ball on a see-saw is a useful visual analogy for the problem our AI agent was solving. In this simplified analogy, the ball's position is the laser's frequency. If we can hold it in a specific location (in this example, inside the green region), we can successfully control the atomic qubits.
In QuEra's systems, the lasers that drive logical qubits must hold within ±1 kHz or better, about ±0.000000001 nm (illustrative values, for education). The infrared laser here is invisible to the eye, shown in false color. The ball swings; no eye could ever tell. Only atoms can tell the difference.
The see-saws in the diagram are analogous to actuators within our system. But the challenge is that the required precision is so high that no single actuator can do it alone. Multiple actuators are stacked together. A big, slow layer takes the wide drift; progressively faster layers take the finer jitter. Together, the ball never leaves the zone.
But there is a twist. A real tuning knob is not smooth. The laser prefers certain wavelengths, shaped by its internal filters (etalon, birefringent filter). In this example, each dip is a fixed mode the ball can settle into. And here is the trap: after a disturbance, bringing the knob back to level does not bring the ball home. It sits stably in the wrong mode, looking locked.
A big enough perturbation throws the ball clear out of the fine layers' reach, into a competing mode. No matter how far you tune the smaller layer, the ball remains stuck in the wrong lock. The recovery requires a sweep of the coarse, wide-range knob beyond the threshold to carry the ball home and then quickly ease off to capture the target mode. Finally, the lock has to be verified against an absolute wavelength reference so a wrong mode is never mistaken for success. This process is known as a Ti:sapphire mode-hop recovery. This is the judgment the MHS auto-relock controller was built to perform on its own.
In the real laser system, all of the layers coexist. The birefringent filter is the coarse, widest-range layer: its landscape has a few widely spaced modes. The etalon sits on it with a finer comb. And the piezo (smooth, continuous, fastest) rides on top doing the rapid final trim. Working gracefully means each coarse element stays seated in the right dip of its own landscape while the fine one glides, and the ball never leaves the zone.
The recovery process described above traditionally has been the craft of a small team of highly skilled experts. Automating it is not a one-person job either: it takes a laser-systems engineer who understands how and why the lock fails, a software engineer to command the instruments, an algorithms designer for the recovery logic, and a tester to pit that logic against the many ways a real lock breaks. A QuEra team of exactly that shape spent roughly two to three weeks building our earlier hand-written recovery script, and its limits were the limits of any fixed script: it could only handle the failures its authors thought to enumerate.
The task force then handed the same problem to a single AI agent, Claude, working through MHS against the live testbed. MHS let the agent run its own experiments: propose a recovery, try it on the hardware, read what happened, refine. It is the same loop the human team runs, but continuously, at machine speed, and overnight. The agent did nothing a person fundamentally could not do; it watched the same instruments and learned only what they revealed. The difference was scale: enumerating and hardening against hundreds of edge cases, every neighboring mode the laser can fall into, every stale calibration, every wrong-mode grab, is unreasonable by hand, and the agent reached corners of the problem no team would have the bandwidth to. The humans stayed in the orchestrator's seat: setting scope, reviewing every step, deciding what counts as proof. That role became more important, not less. Tight oversight from Evgeny Ostroumov, the laser-side technical champion, provided the physical reality check, more than once catching the agent before it spent its effort on things that looked right and were not.
Given no information about what disturbed the lock (a blocked beam, mechanical vibration, electrical noise that disrupts the tuning configuration, a frequency hop small or large), the controller reads the live instrument state, classifies the disturbance, runs the correct recovery, and declares success only when the cavity signal confirms a lock and the absolute wavelength matches the target. The agent's code runs at native speed and supervises from above the microsecond servo loop, rather than within it. In validation it recovered on target 695 of 700 times: 99.3% across seven disturbance classes, one hundred timed trials each. Recovery took 0.9 to 5.4 seconds for wavelength-preserving faults and roughly 10 to 14 seconds for the hardest ones, where the laser's color has hopped far away, against 5 to 10 minutes for a human expert. Four qualities were proven together: correctness (never a wrong-mode lock reported as success), autonomy (no operator, no fault information), speed (seconds, not minutes), and predictability (tight, repeatable recovery times, which for unattended operation matters as much as the average). The five misses shared one rig-condition cause, not a control-logic one; in each the controller correctly declined to claim success, and the lock was back on target before the next trial. No failure left the system dark.
The validation was not confined to injected faults. The testbed lives in a working lab with realistic foot traffic, a deliberate choice, and over the weeks of the pilot the laser hopped modes on its own 43 times. All 43 were caught and recovered automatically.
One distinction matters and we will keep making it: MHS is the environment in which Claude designed, wrote, and validated this controller. What runs on the bench is a deterministic, fully inspectable program: AI-driven in development, human-orchestrated, autonomous in operation. And that autonomy is bounded by design: MHS enforces device-declared bounds, interlocks, and emergency stops at the hardware interface, independent of the model.
So the team pointed the same approach at the quality of the lock itself. That quality is set by a tuning process: twelve interdependent feedback parameters, adjusted within a continuously running control loop. Done well, tuning removes residual noise from the lock, which directly improves the performance of the computer's quantum gates and makes the lock drop less often. There is no closed-form optimum: a specialist tunes by eye, and can quiet the band they are watching while missing a resonance somewhere else. The agent instead recomputed the full noise spectrum after every adjustment, thousands of times, across far more of the space than a person could reach. Working inside a hard safety envelope (every candidate setting that dropped the lock was detected and reverted, and not one of roughly 12,500 evaluations caused the laser to hop modes), it mapped which parameters matter, searched the space, and converged on a configuration it then confirmed by running unattended overnight. The result was residual frequency noise cut by a factor of five, and a lock that simply stopped dropping: zero unattended lock drops in a roughly 19-hour soak test, against 1.6 per hour before.
Then came the test that matters most: an independent, out-of-loop measurement, the noise the qubits actually see, on an instrument the optimization could not touch. It compared the agent's configuration against a manual tune by an experienced specialist. Across the measured band, the two were indistinguishable: the agent matched the expert everywhere the expert was right. But the manual tune had left behind a hidden resonance near 220 kHz, invisible on the instruments a human tune normally watches, where the loop was quietly adding noise, worse than no lock at all. The agent's configuration suppressed it roughly a thousandfold, and a linewidth-type metric improved from 58 to 21 kHz. The point is not that the specialist erred; it is that the automated procedure scores the entire spectrum on every tune, so it cannot overlook a defect the way a hand tune can. It delivers its optimum every single time.
And the capability travels. Pointed at a second operating wavelength, one directly relevant to the gates our machines run, the agent worked out the new operating parameters from scratch in a single unattended overnight run, leaving that lock roughly ten times quieter than it was found and passing every acceptance test. It took weeks to bring up the pilot, and one night to bring it up at a new wavelength. That is what it looks like when the understanding gained in one campaign carries to the next: the sensitivity maps, the safety envelope, the calibrations.
One status distinction, for precision: the auto-relock controller is a standalone production script, with the AI out of the loop at runtime. The tuning workflow still runs with the AI in the loop, and packaging it as a standalone tool is next on the engineering list. Read more about MHS and see QuEra's case study on Anthropic's blog .
In machines running short, discrete jobs, a laser fault is downtime: the queue stalls until the lock returns. In a system like Libra, a machine class capable of running logical-qubit programs for hours or days, a laser that falls out of state mid-run can corrupt a result that quantum error correction can no longer salvage. From a customer's seat, two error rates carry equal weight, two LERs as our team puts it: the Logical Error Rate, and the Laser Error Rate. A failed result looks the same whichever LER caused it.
Fast, verified, autonomous recovery, validated on our testbed and headed for live machines next, is how the second LER is held down. But the deeper story is what this does to the economics of deploying quantum computers. Every stabilized laser in a machine used to carry a standing claim on scarce expert time: 5 to 10 minutes of attended recovery per lock loss, at any hour; 15 to 30 minutes per tune, on a specialist's calendar; a new operating point commissioned over weeks of hands-on work. title: I let an AI run my startup for a week
body:
I completely missed the OpenClaw hype - I actually thought it looked kind of dumb at the time.
But the past week or so I've been quite enjoying using Grok Bot - which is very similar (and like OpenAI dots I guess).
It's basically a mini team of agent/bots that run on a Linux server somewhere that you can assign jobs to.
Eg, I have a support bot that uses my Gmail to answer emails, an engineer bot that writes code, and a security bot that monitors my Cloudflare and server logs for suspicious things.
I don't want to delve into the weeds of it too much here but I thought it would be cool to jot down why I'm quite intrigued by this as a solo entrepreneur/developer.
Grok Bot clicked for me when they worked together and fixed a bug for a customer without me (texts to my bro):
Having these bots interact with each other like this is really cool - this is the most interesting thing for me. Trivial things that you sometimes put off (e.g. fixing small bugs, or following up an email) become automatable so you can focus on bigger stuff.
The idea of coding/working from my phone seemed awful to me. I dislike my phone in general. But last week on a 5 hour hike in the middle of nowhere in Wales, I was communicating with these bots to do stuff for me.
I had a really enjoyable day, and got more work done than some days where I'm sat in front of my laptop for 9 hours.
It made me realise how effort-in does not correlate to output, and made me think what work might be like when you don't have to "work" as much in a weird AI future.
As a 1 man startup - I've always been limited with what I can do. Things like content marketing & trying paid ads have always seemed out of reach because I don't have enough time.
I now have a marketing bot whose sole goal is to grow PromptBase's social reach 2% per week.
It's started a TikTok profile, YouTube shorts channel and more. I've told it to experiment and double down on what works. It seems to kinda be working!
I would never have time in my day for this usually, and it makes me want to try more creative things like startup vlogs alongside this blog.
It's made me actually believe for the first time that a 1-man startup could actually compete with a much bigger one (not just hype). And being a 1-man startup might actually be an advantage because there's less human overhead.
A few nights ago I instructed my project manager bot to ship one secret feature to PromptBase at 4am and deploy it whilst I was asleep - it just had to benefit the site in some way.
I wanted to see what this felt like - which sounds weird - I know.
It decided to ship a feature that alerts users before their account is about to get timed out from too many declined submissions - a pretty useful idea based on a lot of emails from support.
It went well, and worked! - waking up and seeing it felt very cool, but also a bit strange, like PromptBase could just be run by an AI agent if I really wanted.
So far Grok Bot has been pretty good, the main downsides I've found are:
- It takes a while to set up and connect everything - and I'm quite locked in and have handed over a lot of data; I think that's why these AI labs are pushing these products so hard right now.
- I was hoping these bots would have some crazy moonshot ideas on how to grow PromptBase given all the context they have - so far that has not really happened - you still need to come up with ideas.
- It can sometimes feel as a human you lose understanding of what's going on in your business, you need to be careful to stay on top of this so the bots don't start running you.
This is a long post, my hand hurts from writing. I'd definitely recommend experimenting with this if you've not tried these kind of products before.
If anything, it's maybe given me a bit of an insight into the hype around always-on Agents and where things are going.
Get in touch via email: tinyprojectsdev@gmail.com

title: Keanu Al Azhari to represent UAE with 'immense pride' after landing F3 contract for 2027
body: Keanu Al Azhari says he can't wait to test himself in Formula 3 after being named in Hitech's three-man line-up for the 2027 championship. The 18-year-old racer joins as a rookie alongside the returning Kanato Le and Michael Shin, having progressed through the ranks with the team. After two years in Formula 4, in which he finished runner-up in the Spanish F4 championship, Al Azhari joined Hitech’s GB3 team in 2025, claiming one victory, six podiums and three pole positions to finish sixth in the championship. Al Azhari, a member of the Alpine Academy since March 2025, said he was proud to represent the UAE on the F1 support programme. No Emirati driver has ever raced in F3 before. He said: “I am proud and honoured to continue my journey with my family at Hitech as we step up together into the 2027 FIA Formula 3 Championship. “To become the first driver from the UAE to compete in FIA F3 is a milestone I carry with immense pride. “Representing my nation at this level is the greatest honour, and I’m humbled by the support of the UAE behind me. I hope this journey inspires the next generation of drivers across our region to dream without limits.” BREAKING: Keanu Al Azhari steps up to Formula 3! 🪜 The Emirati driver becomes Hitech’s first confirmed signing for 2027 ✍️ More info ℹ️👉 https://t.co/UdJpr1zsXM #F3 #RoadToF1 pic.twitter.com/e2JCybXrxj — Formula 3 (@Formula3) October 6, 2026 Paul Bellringer, Hitech’s F3 team manager, said: “We’ve worked closely with [Keanu] over the last two seasons and have seen first-hand how much he has developed in that time.” Al Azhari is the son of Karim Al Azhari , a German-Emirati businessman and multiple UAE karting champion. He is the older brother of Adam Al Azhari , who he raced against in Spanish F4. After some success in karting, Al Azhari began his racing career in the 2023 Formula 4 UAE Championship for Yas Heat Racing Academy before moving up through the ranks. Last season, he competed in Eurocup 3, winning the Spanish Winter Championship title. He is currently third overall in the Eurocup-3 standings.

title: Russia bombs Sloviansk’s warming center as the day’s attacks wound four Red Cross workers
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); A Russian attack on Sloviansk on 13 October wounded members of a Ukrainian Red Cross team, the Ukrainian Red Cross Society reported . The same day, a Russian bomb hit the city’s invincibility point, one of the state-run hubs where residents warm up and charge phones when power goes out. Help is getting harder to reach in Sloviansk. Public transport stopped after a Russian strike on two buses in nearby Kramatorsk killed 30 people on 8 October. From 1 November, a curfew from 16:00 to 11:00 will cover nearly all of Donetsk Oblast’s free territory. The people providing help are hit too. Russian drones struck three ambulances in Kramatorsk on 5 October. In August, a Russian strike destroyed a World Health Organization humanitarian warehouse in Dnipro. Team had moved from Lyman Three members of the society’s Lyman city branch were hurt. The branch had moved to Sloviansk because of the security situation and kept working there. All three were hospitalized with shrapnel wounds and burns. The building where the team worked took heavy damage, and a fire caused by the attack damaged the organization’s property. The society’s Donetsk Oblast branch later added that a fourth person suffered a concussion, and that all four were hospitalized. The Red Cross condemned attacks on civilian infrastructure and humanitarian workers. Bomb hit the warming center The strike came at 12:45 in the Lisnyi microdistrict, Sloviansk city military administration head Vadym Liakh wrote . He later identified the weapon as a FAB-250, a 250-kg air-dropped bomb. Eight people were injured, and five apartment blocks were damaged, Liakh said. He described the warming center’s building as damaged, while Suspilne Donbas reported it destroyed. The aftermath of the Russian attack on Sloviansk, Donetsk Oblast, 13 October 2026. Photo: Donetsk Regional Organization of the Ukrainian Red Cross Society/Facebook Two Russian strikes on Sloviansk that day killed at least one person, Donetsk Oblast head Vadym Filashkin wrote . Liakh said a Russian attack on the Semenivka neighborhood killed a 55-year-old woman. On 14 October, Filashkin reported that Russian attacks killed three people across Donetsk Oblast on 13 October, in Sloviansk, Druzhkivka, and Starovarvarivka.
