title: Nigerian government introduces ‘five big fiscal reforms’ to woo investors, engender growth
body:
Nigeria’s Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, on Wednesday unveiled five fiscal reforms he said the Nigerian government will introduce to create a conducive business environment, engender growth and boost investments.
The minister spoke at the Nigerian Investors’ Forum held on the sidelines of the World Bank/IMF annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand.
The forum, attended by corporate investors, bankers, government officials and others, was put together to showcase Nigeria’s bankable opportunities and strategic investor conversations in Bangkok.
Speaking at the event, Mr Oyedele said Nigeria plans to introduce “five big reforms” in the fiscal space as part of its efforts to attract the right investment and engender development. He listed the key reform areas to include agriculture and food security, power, regulation, inflation and data management.
“I’ll give you some of the five big issues, big reforms, to expect from the government,” the minister said at the forum.
“One of it is agric reform. One of the drivers of inflation is food. So we are trying to now piece this together to find where these problems are coming from. One thing that we’ve seen recently is that when analysts go on TV, economists talk about why there is inflation; they will talk about bad roads, they will tell you insecurity, and I say yes to some extent.
“If roads are bad, they shouldn’t create inflation unless the roads are worse this year than they were last year. So, the data we have shows that roads are better generally than previously.”
“So, we know where the inflation and the pressure for it is coming from. We’re going to tackle it there, not only just to bring it down to a single digit, but to leave it there.”
Mr Oyedele said the second significant reform to expect is power.
“You cannot power a one trillion-dollar economy in darkness,” the minister said.
“It’s impossible. So we’re looking at strategies to address the issues; whether it’s market-reflective pricing, dealing with issues around transmission, how do you drive efficiency, which is not there currently.”
The minister said inflation management remains another major reform target.
“So there is a dedicated focus on what we want to do, particularly from the fiscal side, to rein in inflation. And we’re working with sub-nationals. So everybody has their role.
“And this is not just to say something that’s nice, it’s a plan with assigned roles and responsibilities with timelines. So, my role is just to coordinate all of that together.”
Another pain point identified by the government, the minister said, was in the area of regulations.
He said: “We estimate that over-regulation, regulatory burden, lack of clarity, a number of those excessive burdens that we impose on businesses actually are costing us more than the combined revenue from corporate tax, personal income tax, and VAT combined.
“And you can ask me, what is the best example of a win-win outcome? Where the government wins, private sector wins even more. So we have started by developing a framework for economic policy for Nigeria.”
The minister explained further that data management remains key.
“People say, and we agree with them, that it’s difficult to find data about Nigeria, especially from the fiscal side. Something as important as our tax-to-GDP ratio, you can’t find it easily. The World Bank in their NDU quoted an amount of tax-to-GDP ratio that is much lower than it is actually.
“If you go to the IMF today, their numbers are different. Within government, depending on who is saying it and when they are saying it, they quote different numbers. Now, we said, ‘not anymore’.
“So we are currently finalising all of that and it will be available on the website of the Ministry of Finance, finance.gov.ng . It will be updated timely, it will be accessible, it will be credible. We are playing now on visibility and elevating credibility.”
Oladeinde Olawoyin reports Business & Economy, Development and Lagos Metro at PREMIUM TIMES. A First Class graduate of Mass Communication from the University of Ilorin, Ilorin, he was nominated in the journalism category of The Future Awards Africa in 2017. Aside maintaining a column titled ‘SATURDAY SATIRE’, he also writes art and culture pieces on weekends. Twitter : @Ola_deinde

title: 2026 Ballon d’Or: How voting system works
body: The 2026 Ballon d’Or ceremony will hold in London on October 26, with an international jury of journalists set to determine the winners of the prestigious football awards. According to the Ballon d’Or website, the jury for the men’s award comprises journalists from the top 100 countries in the FIFA rankings, while representatives from the top 50 nations will vote for the women’s award. The rankings in effect when the nominees were announced on September 8, 2026, will determine the countries represented on the jury. Each juror will select 10 players from a 30-man shortlist, ranking them in order of merit. The players will receive points based on their positions, with 15 points awarded to the first choice, followed by 12, 10, eight, seven, five, four, three, two and one point. The player with the highest overall score will win the award. In the event of a tie, the winner will be determined by the number of first-place votes received. If the tie persists, second-place votes and subsequent rankings will be considered. The organisers added that any other disputes arising from the voting process would be resolved by the editor-in-chief of France Football, the award’s organiser. The October 26 ceremony will mark the 70th edition of the Ballon d’Or. The post 2026 Ballon d’Or: How voting system works appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Kiev to fail to counter Russian jet-powered drones without Starlink — Zelensky’s adviser
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. The Ukrainian army will no longer be able to counter Russian jet-powered drones due to the slower operation of the US Starlink satellite Internet service, Vladimir Zelensky’s external adviser, communications and unmanned systems expert Sergey Beskrestnov said.
"All say that Starlink restrictions have affected long-range missions and frontline logistics but there is another big problem for us," he wrote on his Telegram channel.
As the adviser pointed out, Kiev uses Starlink to counter jet-powered drones but now the Ukrainian military will be unable to do that due to restrictions in its operation. Beskrestnov said that by their actions Ukraine’s partners "actually deprive" Kiev of one of few chances to intercept such drones.
Earlier, Beskrestnov reported that SpaceX had restricted overnight the operating speed of Starlink satellite Internet terminals used by the Ukrainian army to 160 km/h. Later, Sergey Sternenko, a former adviser to the country’s defense minister, said that SpaceX had further restricted the terminals’ operating speed to 60-70 kilometers per hour that morning.

title: Gbenga Adeyinka to end Laffmattazz tour in Lagos
body:
Nigerian comedian Gbenga Adeyinka will end his 2026 Laffmattazz comedy tour in Lagos on 15 November. The tour has held shows in Nigeria, Canada and the United Kingdom.
The grand finale, tagged Lagos Gets the Last Laugh, will take place at the Balmoral Convention Centre, Federal Palace Hotel, Victoria Island, Lagos. The event will begin at 3 p.m.
According to a statement by the organisers, Laughter Incorporated Ventures, the show will feature comedy, music, culture and fashion. It will also mark the end of the tour’s 15th anniversary year and celebrate more than 30 years of Mr Adeyinka’s career in entertainment.
The event’s theme is The Next Chapter: A New Season of Laughter.
For Mr Adeyinka, also known as Gbenga Adeyinka 1st, the Lagos show is a return to a city that helped build his career. The organisers said Lagos provided stages where he performed and audiences who supported his work more than 30 years ago.
The 2026 tour has held shows in Ibadan, Akure, Calgary, London, Ontario, Toronto and Abeokuta. The Lagos event will be the final show of the tour.
FirstBank is the lead sponsor and official tour partner. The organisers thanked the bank for supporting the tour in Nigeria and Canada.
They are also seeking more sponsors and brand partners for the Lagos event. According to the statement, brands can support the show through promotions, audience activities and hospitality services.
The organisers said the event would give brands a chance to connect with people through comedy and other cultural activities.
More information about the performers and tickets will be shared through the tour’s official channels.

title: COCOBOD raises GH¢3.4bn as Cocoa Capital PLC lists inaugural commercial paper on GFIM
body: The Ghana Cocoa Board (COCOBOD) has raised GH¢3.396 billion from domestic institutional investors through its inaugural commercial paper issuance, as the cocoa regulator moves to diversify its financing sources and reduce reliance on external borrowing. The funds were raised through Cocoa Capital PLC, a wholly owned subsidiary of COCOBOD, under a GH¢16.3 billion Domestic Cocoa Notes Programme, comprising GH¢14 billion in commercial paper to finance cocoa purchases and GH¢2.3 billion in bonds to refinance existing cocoa-sector debt. The inaugural issuance, known as Series 1 (Tranche 1), has been admitted to the Ghana Fixed Income Market (GFIM) of the Ghana Stock Exchange, marking a significant step in the development of a domestic financing framework for the cocoa industry. Speaking at the official commercial paper listing ceremony, COCOBOD Chief Executive, Dr Randy Abbey, described the transaction as an important milestone in the evolution of Ghana’s cocoa financing framework. He said the listing demonstrated the potential of domestic capital markets to mobilise resources for strategic sectors of the economy while strengthening the financial foundations of the cocoa industry. “Today’s ceremony is more than the listing of a financial instrument. It represents an important milestone in the evolution of Ghana’s cocoa-financing framework and demonstrates what can be achieved when public institutions, regulators, capital-market participants, professional advisers and domestic investors work together towards a shared national objective,” he said. The issuance attracted total bids of approximately GH¢3.586 billion from 38 institutional investors, with 36 successful bids amounting to GH¢3.396 billion accepted at a clearing yield of 11 per cent. Dr Abbey said the level of demand reflected confidence in the cocoa sector and the transaction structure, as well as the capacity of Ghana’s domestic investment community to support large-scale financing initiatives. “The breadth of participation and the level of demand recorded are particularly encouraging for an inaugural issuance under a newly established financing framework,” he said. He added that the successful listing should encourage more domestic institutional investors to participate in subsequent issuances under the programme. Financing cocoa purchases The proceeds from the inaugural commercial paper issuance will provide working capital to support cocoa purchases during the 2026/27 crop season. Dr Abbey said the financing was ultimately intended to ensure that funds were available to purchase cocoa beans from farmers across the country. “At its heart, therefore, this transaction is about the cocoa farmer. It is about ensuring that adequate funding is available to purchase cocoa beans produced through the hard work of farmers across the country,” he said. The COCOBOD Chief Executive noted that the financing arrangement was part of broader efforts to safeguard farmer incomes, facilitate timely payments and place the cocoa industry on a more sustainable financial footing. For the 2026/27 season, the producer price has been set at GH¢42,400 per tonne, equivalent to GH¢2,650 per 64-kilogramme bag. This represents 71.18 per cent of the realised gross free-on-board (FOB) value, according to Dr Abbey. He said the pricing arrangement was consistent with the framework under the Ghana Cocoa Board Act, 2026, which guarantees cocoa farmers at least 70 per cent of the realised gross FOB price. Shift towards domestic financing For years, Ghana’s cocoa purchases have relied substantially on external financing arrangements. However, changing market conditions and the need to strengthen COCOBOD’s financial resilience have prompted efforts to diversify the sources of funding. Dr Abbey said the Domestic Cocoa Notes Programme represented a deliberate move towards mobilising domestic savings to finance cocoa purchases and meet other funding requirements within the sector. “The Domestic Cocoa Notes Programme represents a deliberate transition towards a cedi-denominated financing model that mobilizes domestic liquidity, reduces reliance on offshore borrowing and establishes a stronger connection between Ghana’s capital market and one of the country’s most important productive sectors,” he said. He explained that the programme was designed not merely to replace one source of funding with another, but also to broaden COCOBOD’s financing options, diversify funding risks and provide a flexible platform for meeting the seasonal and longer-term needs of the industry. Cocoa Capital PLC was established as a dedicated financing vehicle wholly owned by COCOBOD to raise funds through the domestic capital market for approved cocoa-sector financing and refinancing purposes. Under the programme, the commercial paper component will provide short-term liquidity for cocoa purchases, while the bond component is intended to refinance designated legacy obligations. Transaction structure and investor confidence The programme incorporates arrangements intended to strengthen transparency and discipline in the management of funds and repayment obligations. Under the structure, selected receivables from executed cocoa forward-sales contracts have been assigned to Cocoa Capital PLC. Collections from these receivables are channelled through designated ring-fenced accounts and applied according to an agreed payment waterfall. Dr Abbey said the arrangements were intended to improve cash-flow management and provide investors with greater visibility over repayment. He, however, clarified that the commercial paper remained a senior unsecured obligation of Cocoa Capital PLC, with the assigned receivables and supporting cash-management arrangements forming part of the broader transaction structure. He said maintaining investor confidence would require strong governance, transparent reporting and the consistent fulfilment of financial obligations. “Ghana Cocoa Board and Cocoa Capital PLC remain fully committed to these principles,” he said. Boost for Ghana’s capital market The listing also expands the range of fixed-income instruments available to investors on the Ghana Fixed Income Market. Dr Abbey said the ability to mobilise approximately GH¢3.4 billion for the inaugural issuance demonstrated the capacity of Ghana’s domestic capital market to support transactions linked to productive sectors of the economy. He expressed hope that the transaction would encourage other Ghanaian companies and public-sector institutions to explore capital-market financing as a credible and sustainable funding option. For domestic investors, the programme provides an opportunity to invest in a cedi-denominated instrument linked to the cocoa value chain, while the broader financing framework is intended to strengthen the relationship between domestic savings and local production. Dr Abbey stressed that the long-term success of the programme would depend on effective governance, financial discipline and the productive use of funds raised from investors. Institutions behind the transaction The issuance involved several financial institutions, regulators and professional advisers. The Securities and Exchange Commission provided regulatory oversight, while the Ghana Stock Exchange facilitated the admission and listing of the commercial paper on the Ghana Fixed Income Market. The Central Securities Depository supported the issuance, settlement and depository arrangements. SEM Capital served as transaction adviser, while Absa Bank Ghana, CalBank, Fincap Securities, GCB Bank, One Africa Securities and Stanbic Bank Ghana acted as joint lead managers and bookrunners. Sory@Law served as transaction counsel, KPMG as the special-purpose vehicle manager, PwC as reporting accountant and Beacon Ratings as the ratings agency. Dr Abbey commended the institutions and the wider transaction team for their contributions to the structuring, regulatory engagement, investor education and execution of the programme. He said the listing marked the beginning of a broader responsibility to manage the financing arrangement transparently, meet debt-service obligations and ensure that the benefits of the funds raised were felt across the cocoa value chain. “The long-term strength of the platform will depend on our continued commitment to sound financial management, effective governance and the productive use of the funds entrusted to us,” he said. The successful admission of Series 1 (Tranche 1) to the Ghana Fixed Income Market marks the first step in implementing the GH¢16.3 billion Domestic Cocoa Notes Programme, which seeks to connect Ghana’s domestic capital market with the financing needs of its cocoa industry.

title: Georgian judge resigns after being asked to rule in opposition ban
body: Manana Kobakhidze has resigned as a judge of Georgia’s Constitutional Court, the court announced on Tuesday, a day after her colleagues rejected her request to recuse herself from a controversial case seeking to ban five of the country’s main opposition parties. The departure of Kobakhidze (no relation to Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze) comes as the Constitutional Court prepares to hear a lawsuit filed by the ruling Georgian Dream party seeking to ban five opposition parties. The court said Kobakhidze’s judicial powers had been terminated early at her own request. ‘The Constitutional Court of Georgia wishes her success in her future activities’, the court’s statement read . On Monday, it emerged that Kobakhidze had requested to recuse herself from the case. However, the court’s plenary panel rejected her motion. In her request, Kobakhidze acknowledged that the public was aware of her political background, including her role as a founding member and chair of Georgian Dream and her tenure as a member of parliament. She also noted that, before entering judicial service, she had publicly criticised the United National Movement (UNM) and individual members who are now affiliated with other parties named in the lawsuit. Kobakhidze argued that she had called for those responsible to be held accountable for actions cited in the constitutional complaint as grounds for declaring the parties unconstitutional and banning them. ‘Moreover, during one of the plenary sessions of parliament, which was broadcast publicly, she directly called on members of UNM to dissolve their party and leave the political arena altogether’, the document published by the court stated . Kobakhidze maintained that, since becoming a judge, she had acted solely in accordance with the Georgian Constitution and her judicial responsibilities, and that there were no grounds to question her impartiality. However, she argued that her past political activities could nevertheless raise doubts about her independence and impartiality, potentially undermining public trust in the court. The plenary panel rejected her motion, arguing that her previous political statements amounted to general criticism and did not provide sufficient grounds to presume that she would decide the case impartially. The court also said her statements did not correspond in substance to the claims made in the lawsuit. ‘The criticism voiced by Judge Manana Kobakhidze was directed specifically at [the UNM] during her political activities, a considerable time ago’, the court’s ruling stated, describing the remarks as reflecting the political confrontation of the time and containing harsh but general criticism. The court further stated that it disagreed with Kobakhidze’s assessment and considered that her participation in the proceedings could not give the parties to the case, the public, or an objective observer grounds to doubt her impartiality. Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze commented on the recusal request, responding to a question from an opposition leaning TV Pirveli journalist. ‘As a lawyer, I will tell you that being a founding member of a party is not grounds for recusal. In that case, Ms Manana would not be able to hear any case at all. […] She was a founding member of a particular party at the time, and this is her 10th year as a judge’, he said. He added that she had no connection to any particular political party and that nobody prevented her from adopting a new position towards other parties or acting differently. Manana Kobakhidze was one of the founders of Georgian Dream and chaired the party from 2012 to 2013. From 2012 to 2016, she served as First Deputy Chair of Parliament. She was re-elected to parliament in 2016 and became a Constitutional Court judge in 2017. Parliament elected Manana Kobakhidze to the court on 8 February 2017, following Georgian Dream’s nomination, with 101 votes in favour and 10 against. Manana Kobakhidze has not publicly commented on her decision to resign. She did not answer OC Media ’s calls. The opposition party ban case On Tuesday, it became known that the Constitutional Court had admitted Georgian Dream’s lawsuit seeking to ban five opposition parties for consideration on the merits. The parties targeted by the lawsuit are: UNM; Coalition for Change; Strong Georgia – Lelo; the Federalists; Gakharia’s For Georgia. The European Parliament condemned Georgian Dream’s efforts to ban opposition parties in a resolution adopted on 8 October. Georgian Dream officials criticised the resolution, with Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze comparing the European Parliament to the Soviet Union’s Supreme Soviet. EU Parliament condemns Georgia’s attempts to ban opposition, Azerbaijan’s treatment of critics The resolution called for the release of those detained for political reasons in both countries. OC Media Rafig Shahbazov Opposition politicians have said that hearings in the party ban case are scheduled to begin on 21 October. A procedural notice published on the Constitutional Court’s website on Tuesday states that the case will be heard by the plenary panel, comprising seven judges, chaired by Revaz Nadaraia. The other judges on the panel are Eva Gotsiridze, Giorgi Tevdorashvili, Goga Kikilashvili, Sergo Metopishvili, Giorgi Modebadze, and Vasil Roinishvili, who is the reporting judge. Darejan Chaligava will serve as the secretary of the hearing. Under Georgian law, the Constitutional Court has nine months from the filing of a complaint to decide cases concerning the prohibition of political parties.

title: India Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh Visits Greece and Cyprus to Boost IMEC and Maritime Security
body: IMEC bypasses Turkish territory entirely. Ankara is pursuing alternative routes. India’s gateway to Europe runs through Greece. India’s Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh is in Athens (14–15 October 2026) after his official visit to Cyprus on 12–13 October. The trip focuses on maritime security and defence industrial cooperation, linking defence ties to the economic security of the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC). It builds on the elevation of India-Cyprus relations to a Strategic Partnership after President Nikos Christodoulides’s visit to India in May 2026 and the adoption of a 2026–2031 Defence Cooperation Roadmap. In Cyprus, Singh met Defence Minister Vasilis Palmas, the Chief of the National Guard, the Naval Commander at Mari Base, and industry representatives. Discussions covered naval engagement, joint training, port calls, capacity building, and cooperation in emerging domains such as AI, cyber and electronic warfare. India also reaffirmed its long-standing support for Cyprus’s sovereignty and UN peacekeeping efforts. In Greece, the visit follows the Greek Defence Minister’s trip to India in February 2026 and talks with Defence Minister Rajnath Singh. Singh is meeting senior Greek defence and military leadership. The sequence underscores the growing India-Greece-Cyprus alignment in the Eastern Mediterranean and supports India’s wider security partnership with the EU. Hellenic Ports formally joined the “IMEC Ports Club” at its founding meeting in New Delhi earlier in October, with Thessaloniki positioned as a key gateway to Southeast and Central Europe. Greek shipyards (including Salamis) are already collaborating with Indian partners on shipbuilding and repair, and further opportunities to service Indian vessels are under discussion. Greece and Cyprus have both expressed interest in deeper involvement in IMEC, which routes through the Mediterranean rather than Turkish territory. Together, these steps place Greece and Cyprus at the centre of India’s Eastern Mediterranean strategy, combining defence industrial cooperation with the economic and connectivity goals of IMEC. The post India Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh Visits Greece and Cyprus to Boost IMEC and Maritime Security appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: No Party Card, just a Party Microphone! A Ghanaian story of Elections, Referees and Convenient Amnesia
body: By Jimmy Aglah In a certain Ghanaian town, two football clubs quarrelled over the appointment of a referee. The lady chosen was an accomplished professional who had recently travelled with one team, explained its tactics and encouraged supporters to believe in victory. The club chairman dismissed the protests: the referee had never possessed an official membership card. Surely the spectators could now go home satisfied. What more convincing evidence of neutrality could anyone demand? If this sounds like village comedy, replace football with elections and the pitch with Ghana. On 12 October, President John Dramani Mahama swore in Emelia Afi Agbenyo as Deputy Chairperson of the Electoral Commission, alongside Dr Joseph Kwaku Asamoah. He urged them to serve without favour. Excellent advice. Unfortunately, Ghana, that hardworking factory of political contradictions, has noticed a complication in the packaging. In August 2024, the NDC officially listed Agbenyo among the spokespersons for the governance section of its election manifesto. This is documentary evidence, not WhatsApp archaeology. Presidential staffer Beatrice Annan explains that Agbenyo has never been a card-bearing NDC member and that her campaign engagement reflected longstanding advocacy for women’s representation. Her explanation and Agbenyo’s professional credentials deserve consideration. But the public may still reasonably ask whether speaking for a party’s election manifesto creates an appearance of political affinity. The membership card has apparently become Ghana’s newest miracle-working object. You may carry a party’s microphone, explain its promises and help persuade the electorate, but if no card emerges from your handbag, every hint of association vanishes. The mouth that has tasted pepper may now swear the tongue knows nothing of heat. Perhaps our political scientists should stop studying institutions and begin studying handbags. The NPP has greeted the appointment with thunder. Its communications director, Dennis Miracles Aboagye, questions the wisdom of placing a former NDC manifesto spokesperson in electoral leadership. It is a question worth asking. But memory, that inconvenient village elder, has arrived carrying a stool from 2023. Under President Akufo-Addo, appointments of Peter Appiahene and Salima Ahmed Tijani to the Commission provoked objections over alleged NPP affiliations. CODEO and other civil society organisations warned that even the appearance of partisanship could damage public confidence. Their protest did not produce the resignations they sought. The NDC now offers a familiar defence. Rashid Tanko-Computer recalls how concerns about earlier appointments were dismissed. But when your neighbour’s goat destroys your cassava, you do not repair the injustice by releasing yours into his maize. Two farms ruined do not make a bumper harvest. If the previous government set a poor example, why must its successor treat the mistake as an heirloom? Let us be fair to Agbenyo. Earlier advocacy does not establish future dishonesty. A citizen can publicly support particular policies and later perform a national duty impartially. Equally, a fine curriculum vitae cannot by itself settle questions of public trust. The Electoral Commission is not a family funeral committee where the chairman may award his cousins the best seats. It administers elections whose losers must trust the arithmetic as much as the winners. Our Constitution allows the President, acting on the advice of the Council of State, to appoint the Commission’s leadership while requiring the institution to remain independent. There lies the puzzle: the political executive helps select the referee and then asks the crowd to forget who handed over the whistle. Proposals for a more transparent appointment process already exist. Why prefer elaborate assurances to stronger safeguards? Perhaps the real scandal is not the appointment itself but our national talent for manufacturing principles that expire whenever governments change. In opposition, politicians become fierce defenders of institutional independence, quoting the Constitution with the solemnity of a chief priest consulting the oracle. Once in government, yesterday’s outrage mysteriously becomes today’s administrative wisdom. The same mouths change their sermons without changing their congregations. As our elders warn, the crab cannot give birth to a bird. Yet Ghanaian politics has perfected the art of laying political eggs and announcing that the chicks are completely independent of their parents. Agbenyo deserves the opportunity to demonstrate impartiality through her conduct. But Ghana deserves something greater than assurances that the referee will behave. We deserve institutions whose credibility does not depend on which political party last occupied Jubilee House. For when citizens begin to suspect the referee before the match has even started, every whistle becomes a controversy, every decision a conspiracy and every defeat a potential national crisis. And therein lies the question our politicians would rather we did not ask: *If the NDC and NPP can recognise the dangers of partisan appointments so clearly when they are in opposition, why do those dangers suddenly disappear when they enter government?* Perhaps the answer is painfully simple. In Ghana, we do not appear to object to the referee wearing party colours. We object only when the colours are not our own.

title: Combined Russian attack: Five killed, 36 injured in Kyiv since last evening
body:
Ukrinform reports this, citing the Kyiv police in a Telegram post.
Law enforcement officers continue working at sites across the city to deal with the aftermath of the attack.
The largest number of casualties occurred in an apartment building in the Desnianskyi district, which was hit by Russian forces yesterday evening. Three women, aged 35, 58, and 84, were killed there. Another 25 people, including a young child, were injured.
A Russian ballistic missile struck a residential building in Kyiv. / Photo: Danylo Antoniuk, Ukrinform
Police have set up a mobile tent where investigators have already received approximately 80 reports from residents about property damage. They continue to document the consequences of what they describe as a war crime.
Two other people were killed in the Holosiivskyi district.
In total, five people have been killed and 36 injured in Kyiv since yesterday evening.
The aftermath of Russia’s attack on Kyiv. / Photo: Oleksandr Klymenko, Ukrinform
As Ukrinform previously reported, Ukrainian air defence forces neutralized four ballistic missiles and 115 drones launched by Russian forces against Ukraine beginning on the evening of October 13.

title: Ukrainian Ex-Officer Stands Trial in Germany Over Nord Stream Bombing
body:
Lawyers for a Ukrainian ex-military officer accused of leading the bombing of Russia 's Nord Stream pipeline in September 2022 argued at the start of his trial in Germany on Wednesday that "an aggressor's infrastructure " may have been a lawful target .
Serhii Kuznetsov is accused of leading a group of Ukrainian agents including divers and an explosives expert that blew up Russia 's largest gas pipeline to Europe in one of the biggest infrastructure sabotage operations of modern times.
The case provides the first opportunity for a public hearing of evidence gathered during a years-long investigation, which has been diplomatically and politically awkward for a German government that remains staunchly supportive of Ukraine despite the investigative trail linking Kyiv to the bombing.
Moving to have the case dismissed, Kuznetsov's lawyer Nicola Canestrini argued that the pipeline — which provided half of Germany's imports of natural gas before Russia 's 2022 invasion of Ukraine — was a " Russia n weapon."
"Is it unlawful to destroy an aggressor's infrastructure without harming any human beings?" Canestrini asked.
Prosecutors have alleged that Kuznetsov, who was arrested under an international warrant in Italy last year, worked with members of the Ukrainian military to plan the clandestine operation on behalf of unidentified Ukrainian state entities.
Kuznetsov, 50, who prior to Wednesday was referred to publicly only as Serhii K. under German legal rules, has denied any involvement in the blasts that ruptured the 1,200-kilometer (750-mile)-long Baltic Sea pipeline.
Wearing a grey suit and with a shaved head, he exercised his right to remain silent in court but did not cover his face. His lawyers said he could not mount a proper defense because he was obliged to withhold Ukrainian state secrets.
The government in Kyiv has also denied any involvement, a sensitive point in its relations with Germany, Ukraine's largest European supplier of military aid. Russia said on Monday it expected a "just verdict" that would reveal the names of the perpetrators and those who ordered the operation.
Kuznetsov's legal team had tried reaching out to Ukraine for information that might assist the defense but heard nothing, according to another defense lawyer, Jes Meyer-Lohkamp.
German prosecutors say the actions Kuznetsov is accused of — attacking civilian targets and causing explosions that destroyed infrastructure and damaged public services — would amount to a war crime.
Kuznetsov is the only person on trial, but Croatian authorities have arrested another man, identified as Vladimir Z., who prosecutors believe was one of the divers.
The explosion of Nord Stream sealed the end of Germany's longstanding dependence on Russia n natural gas, although Moscow had already cut supplies over Berlin's support for European sanctions following Russia 's invasion of Ukraine.
Nord Stream's supply had been due to double with the opening of a twin pipeline, Nord Stream 2, already built, but Berlin canceled approval to open it just prior to Russia 's invasion.
The trial, expected to continue into February next year, could have domestic political implications.
Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), leading in opinion polls for more than a year, has called for an end to military aid for Ukraine and a restoration of energy ties with Moscow.
Although German state parliaments have no role in foreign policy, the AfD filed a motion in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Wednesday calling for an end to support for Ukraine, noting the "historical parallel" with the start of the trial.
The Nord Stream system, lying at a depth of 80 to 110 meters under the Baltic and built by Russia n gas concern Gazprom to supply up to 110 billion cubic meters of gas to Germany, was formerly at the core of economic ties between the two countries.
The Sept. 26, 2022, blasts that ruptured three of the four concrete-coated steel pipelines created a giant whirlpool at sea as huge plumes of methane gas rose into the atmosphere.
Prosecutors allege that Kuznetsov traveled to Germany through Poland some three weeks before the attack, using a forged Ukrainian passport. He and his group then used a sailboat hired in the northern German city of Rostock to reach an area close to the Danish island of Bornholm, where they rigged specialized military-grade explosives to the sea floor.
The weekly Der Spiegel magazine and ZDF public television have previously reported that five men and one woman were on the rented yacht Andromeda, which left Rostock on Sept. 6 and returned on Sept. 23, 2022.

title: Moroccan Navy orders fishing vessels to violate Spain’s territorial waters — newspaper
body:
MADRID, October 14. /TASS/. Spanish military authorities intercepted direct orders from the Royal Moroccan Navy instructing fishing vessels flying the Moroccan flag to violate Spain’s territorial waters, the ABC newspaper reported.
According to the newspaper, this coincided with the unauthorized entry of Royal Moroccan Navy vessels into the waters off Spanish Ceuta at the height of the migration crisis in the city in late July and early August. The Spanish Defense Ministry immediately responded by deploying naval forces, including the Rayo patrol ship and two frigates, to the area to maintain a show of force and deterrence until Morocco ceased such actions. ABC noted that Spanish Armed Forces’ Chief of Defense Staff Admiral General Teodoro Lopez Calderon also held talks with the Moroccan high command, demanding an end to the provocations.
Earlier, the El Pais reported, citing sources, that at least one Moroccan frigate and several patrol vessels had entered Spanish territorial waters. These actions were described as deliberate and repeated violations of territorial waters. The incidents occurred in early August and nearly led to a clash between the two countries' vessels. The situation around the waters off Ceuta is particularly sensitive because Spain considers its 12-nautical-mile territorial waters to be part of its territory, the newspaper pointed out. However, Morocco does not recognize Spain’s sovereignty over Ceuta and Melilla, nor over their waters.
In late July, tens of thousands of undocumented migrants reached Ceuta by swimming or wading across the breakwater separating the city from Morocco. Due to the crisis, Madrid decided to deploy the military to ensure the city's security. According to official estimates, up to 80,000 people may have entered the city, though it is believed that most of the undocumented migrants have already returned to Morocco.

title: Jo Bonfrere: 30 years after Atlanta ’96, I still haven’t received Olympic Gold Medal
body: Former Super Eagles coach Jo Bonfrere has said he is yet to receive his Olympic gold medal or promised reward, 30 years after guiding Nigeria to victory in the men’s football event at the 1996 Atlanta Olympic Games. The Dutch tactician made the disclosure during an interview with CreativeLordTV in Ebonyi State, where he attended the opening of Chief Agueze’s country home on Saturday, October 10, 2026. Asked whether the promises made to him following Nigeria’s historic triumph had been fulfilled, the 80-year-old coach, speaking through an interpreter, said he had never received the medal and had no idea what it looked like. “I have never seen the gold. That’s the problem, so I don’t know how it looks. I don’t know how the gold medal looks because I have never received it,” he said. Bonfrere’s account, as relayed by the interpreter, suggested that while members of the victorious team and other officials had received their rewards, he was yet to be compensated for his contribution to the achievement. “Every player has received, even the reward, every player and official. So after 30 years, I have never received my reward,” the interpreter said while conveying the coach’s account. The claim raises questions about whether the promises made to the coach after Nigeria’s historic Olympic football victory were fulfilled. Bonfrere was at the helm when Nigeria’s Under-23 team made history at the Atlanta Games, defeating Argentina 3-2 in the final to become the first African nation to win the Olympic gold medal in men’s football. The Nigerian side’s campaign remains one of the country’s most celebrated football achievements, with the team overcoming strong opposition to secure the title against a star-studded Argentine squad. Beyond the outstanding performance on the pitch, Bonfrere also recalled the challenges he faced in selecting the team that eventually won the tournament. According to the interpreter, the coach faced repeated pressure from a minister to include certain players in the squad. However, Bonfrere reportedly insisted on making his own selection, maintaining that he needed to choose the players he believed could deliver victory for Nigeria. The interpreter said the minister repeatedly urged the coach to field particular players, but Bonfrere stood by his judgment and the team he considered capable of winning the competition. Despite the reported disagreements surrounding team selection, Nigeria went on to defeat Argentina 3-2 in the final, securing a landmark victory that elevated the country’s standing in international football. Thirty years later, Bonfrere’s assertion that he has neither received his Olympic gold medal nor his promised reward has brought renewed attention to his personal account of the historic achievement. The claim, however, has not been independently verified.

title: Minority welcomes suspension of teachers’ strike, demands timely payment of promotion arrears
body: The Minority Caucus in Parliament has welcomed the suspension of the nationwide teachers’ strike by the Ghana National Association of Teachers (GNAT), the National Association of Graduate Teachers (NAGRAT) and the Pre-Tertiary Teachers Association of Ghana (PRETAG), while urging the government to honour its commitments to the unions. In a statement issued on Wednesday, October 14, 2026, the Minority commended teachers for returning to the classroom despite their outstanding grievances, saying they had prioritised the education of Ghanaian children. “Their return is an act of patriotism and good faith,” the statement said. The caucus also commended the union leadership, parents and the National Council of Parent-Teacher Associations, and acknowledged the roles of the Council of State and the Fair Wages and Salaries Commission in facilitating discussions. The Minority argued that the strike could have been prevented if the government had implemented previously agreed conditions of service, including the placement of promoted teachers on their new salary grades, payment of the 20 per cent Deprived Area Allowance and negotiations towards a new collective agreement. It said that although the government and the unions agreed on a process for placing promoted teachers on their new grades on August 31, only 6,079 of the 58,620 promoted teachers had their documents received by the Controller and Accountant-General’s Department as of September 22. According to the statement, the government missed the unions’ September 24 deadline, leading to the withdrawal of teachers’ services on September 25. The Minority said the resulting disruption affected pupils across the country, particularly candidates preparing for the Basic Education Certificate Examination (BECE) and the West African Senior School Certificate Examination (WASSCE), as well as children in deprived communities. The caucus said the government had made commitments to address the outstanding issues within specific timelines. It cited October 16, 2026, as the deadline for promotion arrears for the first batch of 51,000 teachers, and October 31 for the placement and arrears of the remaining promoted teachers. It also listed November 2026 for payment of the Digital Instruction Support Allowance, December for the Continuous Professional Development Allowance, and January 2027 for the rollout of the Deprived Area Allowance. The conclusion of a new collective agreement remains subject to a timeline to be agreed with the unions. “The unions have made clear that the strike will resume if any of these dates is missed,” the statement said, urging the government to meet the commitments in full and on time. The caucus has called for the prompt placement of all promoted teachers on their correct salary grades and payment of arrears dating from January 1, 2026. It also wants the government to reconcile the union’s figure of more than 80,000 promoted teachers with the official figure of 58,620 and publish a verified list to ensure that no eligible teacher is excluded. Other demands include digitising the promotion-to-payroll process, briefing Parliament’s Education Committee on progress, agreeing on a firm timeline for a new collective agreement, and developing a learning recovery plan for BECE and WASSCE candidates and pupils in deprived communities. The Minority said it would monitor the government’s performance against each deadline and report to the public. “The 2024 Collective Agreement already provides the framework to resolve these matters. What is needed now is implementation, not more promises,” the statement said. The suspension of the strike follows engagements between the government and the unions over delayed promotions, allowances and negotiations on a new collective agreement. The next key deadline identified by the Minority is October 16, when the first batch of 51,000 teachers is expected to receive their promotion arrears.

title: Plateau police arrest suspects, recover locally made guns
body:
The police have arrested several suspects and recovered locally fabricated firearms and ammunition in separate operations in Plateau State .
The Commissioner of Police, Ayodeji Faniyan, disclosed this on Tuesday at the Inspector-General of Police’s conference in Abuja.
Mr Faniyan, said the command was strengthened intelligence-led operations and community policing to prevent crime and deny criminal elements safe havens.
“Plateau State will be too hot for them to operate,” Mr Faniyan warned, adding that the command had reviewed its crime prevention strategies in response to security challenges across the state.
He said officers had been directed to uphold professionalism, discipline, integrity and transparency in their duties, warning them against corruption and illegal operations.
Mr Faniyan said the command was also strengthening collaboration with residents and other security agencies to improve intelligence gathering and facilitate the arrest of criminal suspects.
According to him, a joint security operation involving the police, military, State Security Services, Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps, National Drug Law Enforcement Agency and other agencies was conducted in parts of the state following recent security incidents in Mangu, Barkin Ladi, Riyom and Bokkos local government areas.
He said the operation, which included a show of force, covered vulnerable communities, flashpoints and suburban areas to reassure residents and reinforce security presence.
The commissioner added that the command had launched a statewide community engagement initiative to appreciate residents for their cooperation and rebuild public confidence in the police.
He said the command remained committed to citizens’ welfare, prompt responses to complaints and respect for human rights.
Mr Faniyan said police operatives had arrested suspects in separate operations across the state, including a 24-year-old man in Jos South Local Government Area from whom officers allegedly recovered a locally fabricated Beretta pistol, two rounds of 9mm ammunition and two double-edged daggers.
He also said operatives of the Violent Crime Response Unit arrested two suspects during a routine patrol along the Anguldi-Vom Road and recovered locally fabricated firearms.
In another operation, the commissioner said a 24-year-old suspect was arrested in Bokkos over the alleged sexual assault of a 23-year-old woman while she was working on a farm.
He added that detectives arrested a 40-year-old man over the alleged rape of a nine-year-old girl.
The commissioner said police operatives also arrested a 23-year-old suspect at a hotel in Bassa Local Government Area following intelligence gathering.
He disclosed that four suspects were arrested during a raid in Angwan Rogo, where officers recovered a large quantity of dried leaves suspected to be cannabis and other substances suspected to be illicit drugs.
According to him, the command has sustained surveillance and raids on identified criminal hideouts and security flashpoints.
Mr Faniyan further said mobile police officers operating in Barkin Ladi engaged suspected bandits in a gunfight during an intelligence-led operation in the Kafi Abu area.
He added that police tactical operatives in Barkin Ladi sighted suspected illegal miners who abandoned their activities and fled into nearby bushes.
The commissioner said some of the arrested suspects had been charged to court, while investigations into other cases were ongoing.
He did not provide a breakdown of the arrests or specify how many suspects had been charged.
Police disburse ₦25.8 million to families of deceased officers Mr Faniyan said the command had disbursed ₦25.82 million to 22 families of police officers who died in the line of duty.
He described the payment as part of efforts to support families of officers who died while serving the country.
The commissioner attributed the state’s security efforts to cooperation between residents, security agencies and the Plateau State Government.
He said he had also engaged traditional rulers to strengthen collaboration between communities and security agencies.
Mr Faniyan reaffirmed the command’s commitment to protecting residents and visitors, adding that officers had been directed to respect citizens’ rights and uphold the rule of law.

title: Customary ownership accounts for 80% of land; it complicates land administration – Lands Commission
body: The Lands Commission says family disputes, multiple sales of the same plots and inadequate planning on customary lands remain major obstacles to effective land administration in Ghana. Its Deputy Executive Secretary in charge of Operations, Surveyor Raphael Hokey, said an estimated 80% of the country’s land falls under customary ownership, leaving about 20% classified as public land. He explained that this ownership structure complicates efforts to manage land and ensure orderly development. “It’s been roughly estimated that about 80% of the land is customary land. Only 20% are public lands,” he said in an interview with Citi FM. Mr Hokey explained that public lands include state and vested lands. For vested lands, customary owners retain the beneficial interest, while the legal interest rests with the state. He said these arrangements present difficulties for institutions tasked with administering land, particularly where they lack full control over the property concerned. “You are trying to manage what you don’t own and control properly,” he stated. Mr Hokey identified disagreements within landowning families and disputes over traditional leadership as recurring problems affecting transactions. He explained that competing claims over who is authorised to represent a family or community can lead to litigation and uncertainty for prospective buyers. The sale of a single parcel to different purchasers, he added, continues to create ownership disputes and undermine land administration. Beyond ownership conflicts, Mr Hokey expressed concern about the lack of planning and infrastructure on some customary lands. He said plots are often sold without access roads, essential services or clearly marked boundaries, leaving buyers to contend with difficulties when developing their properties. This, he noted, also raises questions about whether landowning families or the State should provide the infrastructure needed to support those developments. On enforcement, Mr Hokey said stronger cooperation among public institutions was necessary to address unauthorised construction and other land-related challenges. He explained that local assemblies could seek Police assistance to deal with unauthorised development and pursue court orders where cases require judicial intervention.

title: JV Ejercito flags ‘major changes’ in House-approved 2027 budget bill
body: MANILA, Philippines – Senate finance committee chairperson JV Ejercito on Wednesday, October 14, flagged billions of pesos in reductions to preventive health programs and infrastructure projects in the House-approved version of the P7.2-trillion 2027 general appropriations bill (GAB). Ejercito said in a news briefing that the House version of the budget bill, which the Senate formally received on Tuesday, had major changes compared to the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP), including a P130-billion reduction in foreign-assisted projects, a P9.5-billion cut in calamity funds, and billions of pesos in reductions to health programs. The “major changes” include a P4-billion reduction in the Department of Health’s (DOH) immunization program and a P4.5-billion cut in the DOH-Health Facilities Enhancement Program (HFEP), which funds the improvement and expansion of government health facilities. He also cited a P2.6-billion reduction in right-of-way funding and a P4.6-billion cut in funding for flood mitigation structures within major river basins. The House version of the budget bill increased funding for the DOH’s Medical Assistance to Indigent and Financially Incapacitated Patients (MAIFIP) by P23.9 billion, allocated P10 billion for a new Presidential Assistance to Farmers and Fisherfolk program under the Department of Agriculture, and added P8.04 billion for flood mitigation structures under the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH). “The cuts to preventive health programs are substantial, while medical assistance has increased. This is a puzzle for me because one of the key factors of Universal Health Care (UHC) is strengthening preventive care, yet that is what they reduced,” Ejercito said in Filipino. “What are we supposed to do with this? Remove funding for immunization and health promotion, then provide medical assistance when people get sick?” he added. Ejercito said the Senate received the House-approved GAB late Tuesday afternoon, and that copies have been distributed to the senators. An October 23 deadline was set for the Senate finance committee vice chairpersons to submit their committee reports. The Senate temporarily paused from its impeachment court duties starting October 14 in view of the ongoing committee hearings for the proposed 2027 national budget. Ejercito said the chamber is targeting to finish all budget-related committee hearings by October 23 before it goes on a brief recess. The senator also said he is eyeing to sponsor the 2027 budget bill in the Senate plenary by November 23, and have it approved by the second week of December. “We are also planning to continue what Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian did when he was the finance chairperson — livestream the bicameral conference committee to ensure transparency. We are also keeping in touch with CSOs, the academe, and other watchdogs and will meet them to hear their observations on October 26,” said Ejercito. The House of Representatives approved the proposed 2027 budget on Monday amid concerns from some lawmakers and civil society organizations (CSOs) that the spending plan is riddled with pork barrel allocations. – Rappler.com

title: Nord Stream bombing suspect acted on orders from Ukrainian state agencies — prosecution
body:
HAMBURG, October 14. /TASS/. Sergey Kuznetsov, the suspect in the case involving the bombings of the Nord Stream and Nord Stream 2 gas pipelines, acted alongside his accomplices on orders from Ukrainian state agencies, a prosecution representative said at a court hearing in Hamburg, a TASS correspondent reported.
According to the prosecution representative, Kuznetsov and his accomplices, who were fellow servicemen, acted "on orders from Ukrainian state agencies."

title: Ukraine ‘blind,’ ‘deaf’ without Western intelligence — Hero of Russia
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Without Western intelligence, the Kiev regime is effectively "blind" and "deaf," Sergey Lipovoy, Hero of Russia and the chairman of the presidium of the Officers of Russia public organization, told TASS.
In the early morning hours of October 14, the Ukrainian Air Force confirmed that the West had failed to warn Ukraine about ballistic missile launches for the second night in a row.
"Ukraine has never had its own intelligence and has always relied on NATO and US satellite systems. Ceasing intelligence sharing with the Ukrainian armed forces and the Kiev regime is tantamount to rendering them blind and deaf," Lipovoy emphasized.
Earlier, an air raid alert was declared in Kiev almost simultaneously with a reported series of strikes. According to Politico, the US informed Kiev that no warning about the recent strikes on Ukrainian territory had been received due to adverse weather conditions. On October 13, US President Donald Trump stated that his administration had not stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine and was helping the country, including by assisting it in reaching a final settlement of the conflict.

title: Greece Advances Co-Production Talks on Israeli LORA Ballistic Missiles as Range Hits 500+ km
body: Discussions on the Israeli LORA ballistic missile produced by Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) are advancing, with strong interest from the Greek side. According to NemesisHD, the focus of recent contacts has shifted toward co-production of the system in Greece—a goal that sits at the center of planning by the Ministry of National Defense and the joint staffs. This development comes as the missile’s profile itself is evolving. Following the German Navy’s successful operational test of the Naval LORA under the OPEX program in early September 2026, official reports now place its potential range at 500 kilometers and above, compared with the up to 430 km figure IAI had previously indicated for the existing version. The difference suggests either a newer extended-range configuration or earlier conservative figures. For Greece, the updated range would give Army artillery an organic deep-strike category it currently lacks. NemesisHD has followed the LORA topic closely for years. Reporting around the parliamentary approval of the PULS multiple-launch rocket systems already flagged LORA as a deeper interest. A subsequent technical analysis, based on discussions with IAI officials, highlighted lesser-known advantages. In January 2026, during the visit of Israel’s Defense Minister to Athens, LORA was a central point of talks. Israel appeared open to broad cooperation, including co-production, provided Greece committed to a sufficient number of missiles, and proposed systems carried at least 25 percent domestic participation. By September, well-informed sources indicated LORA was likely the next choice to strengthen the Hellenic Army’s deep-strike capability, particularly for artillery. The LORA is a solid-fuel ballistic missile designed for precision strikes at operational and strategic depth. As detailed in earlier Nemesis reporting and consistent with IAI data, it measures roughly 5.2 meters in length and 624 millimeters in diameter, with a launch weight of about 1,600 kilograms. Range spans 90 to more than 500 kilometers, accuracy is on the order of 10 meters CEP, and guidance combines INS/GNSS with a terminal TV seeker according to unofficial information. The warhead can reach approximately 600 kilograms depending on configuration, and the impact angle runs from 60 to 90 degrees. In land configuration it carries four missiles in sealed canisters on a vehicle of around 16 tons. It is intended for high-value targets such as command centers, air bases, air-defense batteries, missile systems, infrastructure, and hardened sites. Its high speed and shaped ballistic trajectory sharply reduce reaction time for opposing air defenses. A standout feature emphasized in IAI briefings covered by Nemesis is the hermetically sealed Transport-and-Launch Canister, or TPK. It creates a stable micro-environment of controlled temperature, pressure, and humidity that protects the solid propellant and electronics. This “wooden round” concept allows the missile to remain fully ready for years without preventive maintenance. Electric actuators, with no hydraulics, further simplify logistics. According to the manufacturer, a battalion-level package carries 48 ready missiles and can deliver a mass salvo in under two minutes, with reload in about 60 minutes, full 360-degree coverage, ten minutes into action, and three minutes to displace. Such a salvo could saturate even modern AESA-equipped air defenses that possess anti-ballistic capability. Naval launch has been demonstrated since at least 2017 and was confirmed operationally by the German Navy in 2026. Because the missile stays inert yet permanently ready inside the canister, minimal preparation is required and the system can be activated from a command console in minutes. Integration on low-signature platforms, including auxiliary or commercial-type vessels, would allow power projection beyond coastal A2/AD zones while creating uncertainty for an adversary about which platforms actually carry operational missiles. Co-production remains the central issue, as Nemesis has reported. The national goal at Ministry and staff level is for Greece to move beyond being a simple buyer of defense systems and become a co-producer of defense technologies. For a system like LORA this could mean domestic manufacture of subsystems, technology transfer, and meaningful participation by the Greek defense industry in a strategically important capability. The existing framework already includes at least 25 percent local content, with scope for further co-production and know-how transfer; according to the latest information, negotiations are now concentrating on this point. Completion of talks and a final price are still required before any purchase proceeds. For Greek deterrence doctrine, which has long rested on air superiority, naval flexibility, and dispersed power across the island complex, LORA would add a fourth independent axis: immediate, deep, high-precision strikes from land or sea platforms without lengthy force deployment or exposure of aircraft. In an environment of rapidly improving air-defense umbrellas, a weapon that strikes targets while keeping aircraft out of harm’s way has clear value. The ability to place canisters on commercial-type ships, already proven in tests, adds strategic ambiguity. LORA is classified as a precision tactical ballistic missile rather than a long-range strategic system. It offers theater-level strike options—up to 430 km in the current version and over 500 km in the newer one—against time-sensitive and hardened targets. Its sealed canisters, electric actuation, and multi-platform flexibility make it particularly suited to Greek operational needs in the Aegean and Eastern Mediterranean. title: US judge backs CNN, MS Now, Politico access to White House
body: A federal judge blocked on Tuesday the White House from banning CNN, MS Now and Politico journalists, following President Donald Trump’s decision to ban the news outlets last month. District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that the Trump administration must grant the journalists access to the White House while the lawsuit filed by the three outlets against the ban proceeds. Kelly said the outlets were “likely to succeed not only on their due process claim, but also on their two First Amendment claims.” The First Amendment upholds the right to a free press. Trump barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House on September 18 for distributing what he called “fake news” and “fiction and lies.” The three outlets filed a joint lawsuit seeking a preliminary injunction against the ban. A court order temporarily restored the White House credentials of the journalists. That ban was set to expire Tuesday. “The Court will extend the relief it already ordered, which will continue to preserve the status quo while this case proceeds,” Kelly wrote in an opinion accompanying Tuesday’s order. “President Trump likely banned Plaintiffs from the White House because he believes that their reporting is generally inaccurate and biased against him,” Kelly added. Trump has long attacked media that have aired critical coverage of him, repeatedly blasting the press as the “enemy of the people.” AFP The post US judge backs CNN, MS Now, Politico access to White House appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Western sanctions increase risk of satellite collisions — expert
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. The sanctions regime imposed by the European Union and the United States on Russia and other nations is increasing the risk of spacecraft collisions as satellite constellations expand, Yelena Pavlova, Chief Designer of a component of the Russian Automated Warning System on Hazardous Situations in Outer Space (ASPOS OKP), told TASS.
"Large low-Earth orbit satellite constellations are being expanded primarily by the Americans and the Chinese. While the Americans ensure collision safety for their own and European spacecraft (Starlink performed over 350,000 collision-avoidance maneuvers last year), they do not coordinate satellite trajectories with the Chinese or with the operators of the Rassvet satellites. This is a direct result of the sanctions policy pursued by the US and EU against 'unfriendly' Eastern states. Consequently, the simultaneous growth of these constellations significantly raises the probability of collisions due to the absence of universally accepted space traffic management rules," Pavlova noted.
According to her, the "layers" of the US military constellations Starshield and SDA pose a distinct threat. The US Space Command does not publish their orbital data, which also creates conditions for potential collisions with other space objects, the expert believes.

title: Poroshenko named opposition leader, European Solidarity rated least negatively among Rada factions – KMIS poll
body:
The European Solidarity party faction in the current 9th convocation of the Verkhovna Rada holds the highest public performance ratings among Ukrainians, although negative evaluations outweigh positive ones across all parliamentary political forces, according to the results of a nationwide public opinion poll conducted by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KMIS) between September 12 and 21. Commissioned by Forum NGO, the survey included questions assessing the performance of parliamentary factions and identifying perceived opposition leaders.
Some 38% of respondents believe the European Solidarity faction's activities benefit Ukraine, compared to 43% who believe they hinder development. In September 2025, 38% considered the faction's activities beneficial and 36% viewed them as a hindrance.
The Holos party faction follows in the rankings: 30% of respondents consider its activities beneficial to Ukraine, while 31% hold the opposite view. Ratings have slightly worsened compared to September 2025, when 33% noted benefits and 27% cited hindrances.
Meanwhile, 22% of respondents consider the Servant of the People faction's activities beneficial, while 66% believe its actions hinder state development (compared to 52% last year).
Similar negative trends are evident for the Batkivshchyna All-Ukrainian Union faction, whose activities are deemed beneficial by 21%, while 68% view them as hindering state development (up from 48% in September 2025).
Regarding Platform for Life and Peace group, 16% believe its activities benefit Ukraine, while 43% disagree. This represents no significant change compared to September 2025.
Overall, a majority of respondents (64%) positively evaluate the performance of at least one faction from the list, up from 59% in September 2025.
Respondents were also asked to identify the leader of the opposition in Ukraine; a majority (68%) were able to select a public figure from a list of six politicians. The largest relative share pointed to European Solidarity leader and MP Petro Poroshenko (30%). He is followed by MP Dmytro Razumkov (11%), volunteer and public figure Serhiy Prytula (8%), and Batkivshchyna leader and MP Yulia Tymoshenko (6%). MPs Yuriy Boiko and former Presidential Office advisor Oleksiy Arestovych were each named by 3% of respondents.
An additional 11% believe there is no genuine opposition in Ukraine (down from 16% in February). Compared to February, the shares of respondents naming Poroshenko (previously 24%) and Razumkov (previously 7%) increased, while metrics for other figures remained unchanged.
Commenting on the survey results, KMIS Executive Director Anton Hrushetsky noted that the crisis of trust in parliament among Ukrainians persists. "In effect, Ukrainians believe the parliament is more of a hindrance than a contributor to the country's development. Naturally, the critical attitude of Ukrainians toward the Verkhovna Rada and parliamentary political forces is not new... But during wartime, this situation is particularly alarming. It is especially critical that in the case of the Servant of the People faction—which forms the basis of the coalition and the current government—those who believe its actions hinder development outnumber those who see it as contributing by a factor of three," he stated.
Hrushetsky emphasized that the Verkhovna Rada is expected to pass necessary legislation to secure funding from Western partners and demonstrate Ukraine's fulfillment of European integration obligations, noting that opposition MPs must also demonstrate their responsibility.
The survey was conducted via telephone interviews (CATI) using a random sample of mobile phone numbers across all government-controlled regions among 1,002 respondents aged 18 and older. Under normal conditions, the formal statistical margin of error for such a sample (with a 0.95 probability and design effect of 1.3) does not exceed 4.1% for indicators near 50% and 1.8% for indicators near 5%, though wartime conditions introduce additional systematic deviation.

title: Gaza committee signs recovery assistance deal with Germany’s GIZ in Cairo
body: The Palestinian committee set up to administer Gaza has signed an agreement with Germany’s international development agency GIZ to support the coastal strip's postwar recovery and reconstruction, although Israeli objections continue to prevent the body from entering the territory. The pact, signed on Tuesday at the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza’s temporary headquarters in Cairo , establishes a framework for technical assistance on reconstruction, public institutions and essential services, the committee said. It was formed in January under US President Donald Trump's peace plan and UN Security Council Resolution 2803. Mr Trump's plan brought about a shaky ceasefire between Israel and Hamas last October after two years of fighting and also established a Board of Peace to oversee its implementation. Led by Ali Shaath, a former Palestinian Authority deputy minister, the committee is intended to restore public services and oversee civilian administration and reconstruction under the supervision of the Board of Peace. Mr Shaath and GIZ country director Alexander Zschocke signed the agreement at the committee’s temporary headquarters in Cairo. Bulgarian diplomat Nikolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace’s high representative, attended alongside German officials. Under the agreement, GIZ will provide technical expertise, advisory services, needs assessments and training to strengthen the committee’s planning and implementation capabilities. Co-operation will cover municipal services, social protection, education, employment, water, agriculture and energy. The statement did not mention a funding commitment, specific projects or a timetable for implementation. Mr Shaath called for the agreement to be translated into practical measures that improve living conditions. He said the committee would lead its implementation according to Gaza’s urgent needs and in co-ordination with Palestinian institutions. However, Israel refuses to allow the committee to enter Gaza or to proceed with the second stage of Mr Trump's peace plan until Hezbollah disarms. Its restrictions on the entry of equipment and supplies are also hampering recovery efforts. Gaza needs extensive reconstruction of homes and infrastructure. A European Union and UN assessment released in April estimated the cost of recovery and rebuilding at $71.4 billion over the next decade.

title: EIB plans to increase financial support for Ukraine – deputy secretary general
body:
EIB Deputy Secretary General Mikołaj Dowgielewicz said this in comments to an Ukrinform correspondent on the sidelines of the Warsaw Security Forum.
“We are working very actively in Ukraine. For us, it has been one of the most important areas of activity for more than five years. Above all, we support critical infrastructure so that what has been destroyed can be rebuilt. We also support local communities, cities and infrastructure recovery to help society and the country function as normally as possible,” Dowgielewicz said.
He said supporting Ukraine through the winter remains a constant priority for the EIB: “We will do everything in our power to help Ukraine protect its critical infrastructure so it can get through this winter in the best possible condition.”
According to Dowgielewicz, the EIB works closely with the government, local authorities across Ukraine and financial institutions.
“We have signed agreements with many Ukrainian banks to support entrepreneurs. We lend to Ukrainian financial institutions so they, in turn, can provide credit to businesses. This is essential for sustaining economic activity, because the economy must function as much as possible,” he said.
He recalled that since the start of the full‑scale war, the EIB has allocated €4.5 billion to Ukraine, including €1.5 billion in 2025, as well as an additional support package of nearly €500 million announced in June 2026 for the housing sector, infrastructure and support for Ukrainian businesses.
Dowgielewicz expressed hope that the EU’s new multi‑year budget will include solid guarantees for continued financial support for Ukraine.
“We are working to convince EU governments to provide the necessary financing. If negotiations on the EU budget conclude successfully in the near future, we will make every effort to increase our support for Ukraine in the coming years,” he said.
As reported, the Cabinet of Ministers will allocate more than UAH 4.9 billion in EIB funds for community‑level recovery projects.
