title: NRSA to auction vehicles of non-subscribers who fail to pay towing charges within 21 days
body: The Director-General of the National Road Safety Authority (NRSA), Abraham Amaliba, has warned that vehicles belonging to drivers who fail to subscribe to the mandatory towing service could be auctioned if the Authority removes them from the road and the owners fail to pay the resulting charges. Speaking in an interview on Joy FM’s Super Morning Show on Wednesday, October 14, Mr Amaliba explained that the Authority would remove vehicles that break down in dangerous locations and pose a risk to other road users, regardless of whether their owners had subscribed to the towing service. He said the owners would be surcharged for the removal and could lose their vehicles if they failed to settle the charges after being contacted through the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Authority (DVLA). “If you don’t subscribe, and we find that your car is stationary and will cause an accident, we’ll come and remove it, and we’ll surcharge you,” he said. Mr Amaliba added that the Authority would use vehicle registration records to trace owners who fail to pay. “If you don’t pay the surcharge, we will find you through your registration processes at DVLA. We will contact you within 21 days. If you don’t come, we will gazette the sale of the car, and then auction it,” he stated. His comments come as the government prepares to implement a new road safety policy expected to accompany the Road Traffic (Amendment) Bill, 2025, which seeks to address the dangers posed by broken-down vehicles on Ghana’s roads. Mr Amaliba also announced plans to develop a mobile application that would connect motorists whose vehicles break down with the nearest available towing company. When asked what a driver who had subscribed to a towing service in Accra should do if their vehicle broke down in Wenchi, Mr Amaliba said the proposed application would allow motorists to request assistance from a nearby towing operator rather than wait for their registered company to travel a long distance. “We are going to develop an app. We know your towing company could be far away from where you are, and so calling the towing company to come may take time as well. And the law says that you must remove the car immediately,” he explained. He said the application would work in a similar way to ride-hailing services, matching motorists with the nearest available towing company. “We are going to develop an app where you can, just like Uber, have the nearest available towing company come and remove you,” he said. Mr Amaliba added that towing companies would be responsible for resolving payment arrangements among themselves when a company other than the motorist’s subscribed provider responded to a call. “The towing companies will now deal with how to exchange their money,” he said. According to him, the application would also provide a practical way of demonstrating that the required notification had been made promptly. During the Joy FM interview, concerns were raised about whether towing companies would be able to respond quickly enough, even when drivers notified them immediately. The host pointed to the NRSA’s indication that stationary vehicles contribute to between 10 and 12 per cent of fatal accidents and asked how quickly towing companies were expected to arrive after being informed of a breakdown. Mr Amaliba said the proposed application was intended to address that concern by identifying the nearest available operator. “That’s why we are supporting with an app,” he said. “When you go on your Uber app, you find the nearest Uber car. You don’t wait for the Uber car that is coming from Tema to you when there is one in Kokomlemle. So that’s how we are going to deal with it,” he said. This comes after the National Road Safety Authority revealed that drivers whose vehicles break down in major city centres will be required to arrange towing within 30 minutes under a new road safety policy expected to accompany the implementation of the Road Traffic (Amendment) Bill, 2025. The policy is aimed at preventing broken-down vehicles from causing traffic congestion and road hazards, particularly in busy urban areas.

title: Singapore Airlines introduces new range of in-flight amenities across all Cabin Classes
body:
Suites and First Class customers will receive SISLEY amenity kits featuring products from the Sisleÿa and Sisleÿum ranges, as well as new 100% cotton sleeper suits

 	
Business Class customers will receive sleeper suits for the first time, alongside BYREDO amenity kits with the signature Blanche Eau de Parfum fragrance spray

 	
New Premium Economy Class zip pouch features SIA’s signature batik motif, and include INK & WATER lip balm, eyeshades, socks, and a dental kit

 	
Economy Class customers will receive a bespoke drawstring pouch featuring the SIA batik motif, together with a selection of travel essentials

 	
The new amenities form part of SIA’s elevated end-to-end travel experience, which will be unveiled in November 2026


New Delhi, Oct 14. Singapore Airlines (SIA) is introducing a new range of in-flight amenities across all cabin classes to support the comfort and well-being of its customers, helping them arrive at their destination feeling even more refreshed and relaxed.



Yeoh Phee Teik, Senior Vice President Customer Experience, Singapore Airlines, said: “Singapore Airlines is continuously finding ways to elevate the moments that matter to our customers in every cabin class. This is why we have carefully curated our new range of amenities, from skincare and personal care products to sleepwear and travel essentials, to support the enhanced comfort, rest, and wellbeing of our customers during their journeys with us.”

The Airline has partnered with SISLEY, the renowned French luxury cosmetics maison, to offer men’s and women’s amenity kits to Suites and First Class customers. These will include products from its premium anti-aging Sisleÿa and Sisleÿum ranges.

First Class and Suites customers will also enjoy new 100% cotton sleeper suits that are designed for greater breathability and comfort, and coral fleece slippers.

Business Class customers will be offered sleeper suits for the first time. These relaxed-fit poly-cotton sleepwear come in two sizes, enhancing customer comfort during flights.

Customers will also receive BYREDO amenity kits featuring products from the Stockholm-founded brand’s iconic Blanche Eau de Parfum, as well as hand cream and a lip balm. SIA will be the first airline to offer BYREDO’s Blanche range of products.

Premium Economy Class customers will receive new SIA-designed zip pouches with a hand strap that are embossed with the Airline’s signature batik motif. Each kit will include a white tea-scented lip balm from INK & WATER, the Australian personal-care brand, that is exclusively available for SIA customers. The kit will also contain other travel essentials, including eyeshades, socks, and a dental kit.

Customers in Economy Class will receive a collectible drawstring pouch featuring SIA’s batik motif. It will contain travel essentials including eyeshades, socks, and a dental kit.

All new amenity kits will be progressively introduced from November 2026 on flights above six hours. The sleeper suits will be available on selected mediumhaul overnight flights of more than six hours and on all long-haul flights.

The amenities form part of SIA’s broader elevated end-to-end travel experience, alongside next-generation cabin products, refreshed food and beverage offerings, the new KrisWorld in-flight entertainment system, and high-speed internet connectivity. The experience will be unveiled in Singapore in November 2026.

title: First African Maritime Security Forum getting underway in Ghana
body:
The inaugural African Maritime Security Forum is getting underway at the Kofi Annan International Peacekeeping Training Centre in Ghana from Wednesday, focussing on maritime security threats across Africa in a time of geopolitical uncertainty, and examining strategies to address current and future challenges.
The Forum is organised by the Royal Danish Defence College (RDDC), the Kofi Annan International Peacekeeping Training Centre (KAIPTC), and the Security Institute for Governance and Leadership in Africa (SIGLA) at Stellenbosch University.
In a concept note giving background on the event, the organisers explained that since 2022, they have collaborated to present an annual conference on maritime security in the Gulf of Guinea. Last year’s conference took place in Stellenbosch, South Africa, to highlight and tackle the recent developments in the Red Sea and its repercussions for the littoral countries in southern and western Africa. “To elevate the discussion to the next phase, the institutions have agreed to rename the conference the African Maritime Security Forum. The parties wish to create a stand-out name, more effectively promoting the shared goal of safer seas and a prosperous blue economy in littoral Africa.”
The African Maritime Security Forum, under the theme ‘The African Maritime Security Landscape in Times of Geopolitical Uncertainty in 2026 and Beyond,’ aims to highlight various maritime security threats across Africa; present high-level, key maritime stakeholders, researchers, practitioners, and industry players from the West, South, and East with a platform to share perspectives and insights; and foster greater mutual comprehension on strategies to address maritime security challenges and capacity-building to address the challenges of the present and tomorrow.
The forum comes amid intensifying strategic competition, shifting alliances, and conflicts in Europe and the Middle East that are creating direct and indirect consequences for African states and economies. Similarly, the maritime domain is consequently becoming an increasingly important arena in wider geopolitical competition, the organisers noted.
“Strategic sea lanes, ports, offshore resources and maritime infrastructure are gaining significance, while maritime chokepoints can exert influence well beyond their immediate geographical surroundings. For African states, this creates both opportunities and vulnerabilities. Limited maritime domain awareness (MDA) and uneven capacity to monitor and secure territorial waters increase exposure to geopolitical spillovers, alongside more established threats such as piracy, trafficking and illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing. At the same time, autonomous systems and other emerging technologies are transforming approaches to maritime domain awareness,” they noted.
West, South and East African coasts face a shared, albeit uneven, set of maritime security challenges, the briefing note emphasised. “In the Gulf of Guinea, piracy and armed robbery at sea have declined markedly from the period when the region accounted for the overwhelming majority of global maritime crimes. This has been as a result of the initiation of frameworks such as the Yaoundé Architecture, Djibouti Code of Conduct, and other regional and national initiatives to sustain naval patrols and exercises. Nonetheless, the underlying drivers of maritime insecurity, including limited naval patrol capacities, weak coastal governance, youth unemployment and pollution of toxic chemicals into river bodies as a result of misguided surface mining for mineral resources particularly across West Africa, persist, underscoring that the threats remain adaptive.
“Along the eastern coast, littoral states continue to contend with the piracy risk emanating from the wider Western Indian Ocean and Somali basin, alongside smuggling, trafficking, and IUU fishing that erodes coastal economies.
“Southern Africa, meanwhile, sits at the crossroads of major global shipping lanes and is increasingly exposed to spillover effects from crises far beyond its own waters,” the organisers stated.
They pointed to this shared exposure, combined with the divergence in capacity and resourcing between the three coasts, that makes a single, cross-regional forum a valuable platform for comparing experiences and building common solutions.
Recent developments around the Bab el-Mandeb, Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz have further heightened the debate around maritime security.
“These developments have demonstrated how insecurity around a single chokepoint can alter global shipping patterns and generate wider economic and security repercussions for littoral states,” the briefing note said. “The growing importance of these chokepoints introduces increased vulnerabilities or perceptions thereof that generate ripple effects across multiple security, economic and political domains. Competition over access, control, and security around strategic sea passages have now increasingly become part of wider geopolitical contestation, while disruptions are placing additional pressure on already limited maritime security capacities in general and navies in particular. Thus, understanding the rapidly emerging politics of maritime chokepoints will be essential.”
Both the risks and opportunities, such as reinforcing security and access to the Cape Sea Route, must be considered to shift perceptions from a convenient once in a while crisis-management route to a normalised route, the briefing note emphasised. “Similarly, the debate must shift to reinforce opportunities, risk mitigation, and the route’s status as an African and globally important trade route. It requires a stronger maritime domain awareness framework, greater (inter)regional cooperation, enhanced national commitment to enforcing regional and international agreements and closer attention to developments beyond national waters, particularly where disruptions in one maritime theatre can generate spillover effects across the wider African maritime landscape.”
As these developments escalate naval involvement and potential clashes or skirmishes between naval forces, the relevance of the San Remo Manual on the Law of Armed Conflict at Sea becomes relevant, the Forum organisers emphasised. The Forum offers leeway to expose delegates to selected aspects of the Manual’s progress by one of the representatives from Africa on the Working Group.
Lastly, autonomous systems are emerging as valuable force multipliers for maritime security, the briefing note stated. Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), Unmanned Surface Vessels (USVs), and other autonomous sensors can provide persistent surveillance, enhance maritime domain awareness, and extend the reach of limited maritime forces.
“Operating at relatively lower cost and risk than traditional platforms, these technologies enable security agencies to monitor remote areas, detect suspicious activities, and support law enforcement and search-and-rescue operations more effectively. However, the adoption of autonomous technologies is not without challenges. Criminal and terrorist organisations are increasingly exploiting drones and other unmanned platforms for illicit activities, creating new security risks that maritime agencies must be prepared to counter. In addition, operational constraints such as limited endurance, communications requirements, maintenance demands, and shortages of skilled personnel continue to affect deployment and sustainability.”
At the Forum, discussions are set to focus on lessons from existing deployments, emerging technologies, regulatory requirements, capacity-building needs, and opportunities for regional cooperation.
Beyond the exchange of perspectives among panellists and delegates, the Forum is intended to produce concrete, lasting value for maritime stakeholders across the African continent. Key expected outcomes include strengthened professional networks and dialogue channels between West, South, and East African maritime stakeholders; a shared, cross-regional understanding of how geopolitical shocks, criminal adaptation, and emerging technologies are reshaping the threat picture; awareness of ways and means to promote awareness, information fusion and progress on the Law of Armed Conflict at Sea, and; and practical recommendations that regional bodies, national authorities, and industry can draw on to inform their own strategies and capacity-building programmes.
The organisers plan on releasing an official communiqué along with one or two policy briefs directed at national and regional decision-makers and identify further research activities aimed at deepening the outcome of the deliberations through the generation of additional evidence-based knowledge.

title: The Mother of All Cutters
body:
The United States Navy seeks to prevail over a potential Chinese military threat before 2027 as the naval component of a joint force. 1 Passing through the “Davidson Window” of China’s maximum military threat without China initiating a war could be interpreted as a victory of deterrence. 2 The reality could be that the Navy focused on the expanding People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) instead of China’s actions to relentlessly expand its influence and control in the South China Sea through non-military means. To halt China’s subliminal war through use of non-military, civilian entities, the United States Coast Guard (USCG) should build the Mother of All Cutters (MOAC) based on a container ship with deck-mounted mission modules in standard shipping containers. MOAC will function as a very large cutter and power projection platform, adding joint, interagency, and allied and partner capabilities to U.S. Pacific Command (PACOM) for a full range of law enforcement missions.
This article will discuss China’s territorial claims and the problematic nature they pose; America’s objectives in the region; the nature of China’s subliminal war relying on the China Coast Guard (CCG) and the China Maritime Militia (CMM); military activities that have failed to halt China’s gradual advances; the risk of relying on military power to stop China; and how the USCG can use MOAC to contribute to PACOM plans and exercises in the non-military realm.
The South China Sea Tinderbox and China’s Dashed-Line Sparks
America does not recognize China’s “dashed line” which is China’s claim of territorial ownership and encompasses most of the South China Sea. 4 China uses its dashed line to justify its subliminal war to challenge the U.S. principles of freedom of the seas and settling territorial disputes between parties “without coercion and on the basis of international law.” 5 America rejects excessive maritime territorial claims that are “unlawful and sweeping” or that advance “incoherent legal theories of maritime entitlement” undermining the rules-based international system. 6
China distorts the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) provisions to justify treating the internationally recognized sea as an internal issue for China to define and resolve. 7 Notably, China rejected a 2016 international tribunal ruling in favor of the Philippines seeking relief under UNCLOS from China’s illegitimate territorial claims. 8
China asserts core interests—so vital that they are “not subject to negotiations or compromise”—in the South China Sea, as well as for Taiwan and territory administered by Japan and India. 9 Although the Philippines bears the brunt of China’s aggression, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Vietnam increasingly defy China by asserting their own South China Sea territorial claims. 10
The National Security Strategy declares America’s commitment to “preserving freedom of navigation in all crucial sea lanes” as “ core, vital national interests”. 11 The National Defense Strategy declares America’s commitment to “a decent peace in the Indo-Pacific, where trade flows openly and fairly.” 12 On the ten-year anniversary of the international tribunal ruling, the Philippines was joined by the U.S., Japan, and 11 other countries to affirm the ruling as “final, legally binding, and definitive between China and the Philippines.” 13
The South China Sea is “an arena of U.S.-China strategic competition.” 14 Admiral Samuel J. Paparo, commander of PACOM, stated to Congress that “our strategy is clear: we must deny China the ability to achieve its objectives through military aggression while strengthening the network of alliances and partnerships that constitute our greatest asymmetric advantage.” 15 Admiral John Aquilino, then commander of Indo-Pacific Command (now PACOM), told a U.S. House of Representatives committee that if China’s aggression “resulted in the death of a Philippine service member”—even with water cannons used by the CCG—the Philippines could trigger the U.S.-Philippines mutual defense treaty. 16 China warned America to keep out of the dispute and refrain from “stirring up trouble.” 17
If China controls the South China Sea, America’s military deployments in the western Pacific will be constrained. American allies and partners might then “reexamine their own defense programs and foreign policies” that support the U.S. in ways that weaken America’s security network and accelerate China’s goal of regional hegemony. 18
China’s Subliminal War: “Fishermen” Versus FONOPs
Admiral Paparo stated that his command embraces the need to address “a broad range of factors outside of the military realm” in its plans and exercises, including a “broader group of interagency partners.” 19 Without addressing the perils of over-analyzing the useful shorthand term “DIME” (diplomatic, information, military, and economic), 20 PACOM would benefit from other instruments to more effectively resist China’s subliminal war that relies on non-military means to methodically expand and entrench its unlawful South China Sea territorial claims. 21
To reinforce international norms the U.S. conducts Freedom of Navigation Operations (FONOPs) through international waters and air space that China unlawfully claims. 22 These overt actions are part of information operations through military means within the current DIME strategy. China’s subliminal war continues despite more countries deploying military forces to signal their rejection of China’s claims. 23 China typically advances South China Sea objectives by using its CCG to confront foreign vessels, purportedly for “law enforcement” while the PLAN provides overwatch, deterring foreign military escalation. 24
China’s naval strength includes the PLAN, the CCG, and the CMM. China has expanded the PLAN massively in size and sophistication. It is the largest navy measured by numbers and deploys modern multi-mission ships. 25 The non-PLAN component of China’s naval strength includes the CCG and CMM. 26 The CCG is the largest coast guard and includes newer ships with better armament and longer endurance than most CCG ships, plus numerous regional patrol combatants and coastal patrol craft. 27 The CMM standing force mobilizes civilian fishing vessels that can be massed for months-long deployments, and trains with and supports the PLAN and CCG. China may have 1,000 fishing vessels available in the South China Sea alone, in addition to the standing component of the CMM. 28
China employs DIME means to assert control in the South China Sea. 29 While its military supports the effort, China keeps its actions “below the threshold of open warfare” but beyond the “boundaries of normal diplomatic and economic interaction.” 30 The most innovative line of attack has been creating islands in the South China Sea from sea features that do not confer territorial claims. China describes its island-building as “routine domestic governance.” 31 Admiral Paparo stated that China “uses coercive behavior and overt aggression to exert its excessive claims, including harassing the Philippines, Japan, and other Southeast Asian partners.” 32
The CCG and CMM exploit “China’s significant maritime force advantage” to intimidate its targets in territorial disputes. 33 Using non-PLAN ships for overt aggression makes it difficult for targeted states to define effective rules of engagement without giving the appearance of escalation. 34 Advancing slowly spreads out the harm in small doses, none of which seems worthy of escalation by targets. 35 China’s framing of their actions as its internal affairs promotes a favorable narrative about any clashes. 36 China has focused on the Philippines to erode their ability to exercise sovereignty in its South China Sea territory and EEZ. The CCG has a massive ship that overpowers what the Philippines can deploy. 37 In a trend already evident with its “monster ships” with superior crew size, weapons, and fuel capacity that dwarf USCG cutters, China decided to build a CCG mothership that may carry aircraft or drones. 38
America and its allies resist China’s subliminal war
Over the past few years, the U.S. and it’s allies have taken deliberate actions to counter the Chinese narrative and reaffirm the legal precedents. These include:
Yet China has not restrained its claims or behavior:
The U.S., Japan, and the Philippines view China’s actions with concern. 50 U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called China’s actions inconsistent with international law, accusing China of undermining regional peace and stability. 51 The American and Philippines defense secretaries jointly reaffirmed the importance of the U.S.-Philippines alliance “for upholding a free and open Indo-Pacific region.” 52 Because even a victory through a traditional military war could be ruinously costly, PACOM’s focus has been deterring China’s growing military power in the western Pacific. 53 In this environment, China’s subliminal war raises the risk of Great Power War.
The U.S. seeks to deter aggression and ensure that force or coercion are not used to settle territorial disputes. America needs to “draw a balance between doing nothing and doing too much.” 54 America is seemingly trapped between risking war by using military power to directly confront China’s civilian-led advances or seeing U.S. alliances fray as China advances without overt military aggression. The U.S. clarified the broad extent of its defense pact with the Philippines, but noted it has options short of shooting under the treaty. 55 The missing piece in PACOM’s DIME effort is strengthening the capacity of the Philippines and other targets of China’s subliminal offensive to exercise sovereignty over their territory with civilian regulatory and law enforcement agencies. Recent expansion of USCG presence begins to provide the means to accomplish that.
The USCG is “a more relevant model for partner nation maritime forces than any [Department of Defense] branch and more effective than them in executing a host of international missions.” 56 The service has the appropriate power and authority to defy China’s efforts to expand de facto control of the South China Sea to match its unlawful claims. The USCG seeks to be “bold, innovative, collaborative, and willing to act in new ways” to overcome challenges. 57 A USCG line in the South China Sea would give America more options below the Navy threshold. Just as the PLAN provides overwatch for the CCG and CMM, PACOM’s objective of denying China escalation options could keep PACOM’s DIME campaign in the sub-military realm. The USCG remains ready for evolving missions, recognizing that it may need to develop new assets. 58 MOAC can be the critical force multiplier for USCG and allied civilian agencies to exercise administrative and law enforcement powers in their recognized South China Sea territory.
MOAC, the Missing Piece of America’s Line in the Sea
The USCG must strengthen its primary lines of effort of “persistent presence, meaningful engagements, and maritime governance” in the Indo-Pacific. 59 The USCG describes itself as America’s only multi-mission, military maritime service, bridging gaps between law enforcement, diplomacy, and defense capabilities. It provides a full spectrum of options in the gray zone world of China’s subliminal war. 60 The USCG is the best service for employing non-shooting options in the broad spectrum between doing nothing and doing too much. In May 2026, the USCG cutter Midgett joined a maritime cooperative activity with the Philippine navy and coast guard. That joint patrol near Scarborough Shoal moved beyond mere presence or FONOP to active “law enforcement activities, including maritime interdiction of vessels and boarding actions.” 61
Without sufficient USCG assets in the Western Pacific, instead of being a non-military force multiplier, the USCG could remain insignificant or even counter-productive if China’s subliminal war persists. 62 A MOAC flagship would support formalizing persistent USCG deployments for law enforcement activities. 63 Such a strengthened USCG would, as one analyst explained, “allow the U.S. to play on a broader spectrum” than the Navy can. 64 By complementing fleeting FONOPs and military exercises, the USCG would establish itself as the “Global Coast Guard” it seeks to be. 65
MOAC is modeled on the modularized auxiliary cruiser described in Military Review . 66 Such a ship relies on a modified civilian container ship hull equipped with weapons and systems in standard shipping containers mounted on the deck. MOAC would require a flight deck for manned and unmanned operations. It would have flexibility in the design to allow capabilities to be added or removed as the mission and scenario dictates. MOAC would resupply and provide overwatch for smaller USCG patrol boats and cutters which have difficulty operating far from support infrastructure in America. 67 Unmanned surface vessels (USVs) could be deployed and sustained from MOAC using containerized systems, building on Navy experience integrating a Medium USV into a Carrier Strike Group. 68 Joint and interagency vessels and aircraft plus allied and partner law enforcement assets could be sustained and supported by MOAC.
MOAC’s very size will convey power to reassure allies and partners who routinely face “monster” CCG vessels, and could sail alongside allies and partners in the South China Sea to bolster the rules-based international order founded on freedom of the seas. 69 The following missions will strengthen capacity to assert sovereign maritime governance while raising the price China would pay for escalating to force with the CCG and CMM:
Humanitarian first responders . When natural disaster strikes, MOAC could initiate relief operations using onboard supplies and UAVs providing intelligence on devastated areas. It would conduct rescue missions, deliver supplies, and evacuate the injured.
Safety of life at sea . MOAC would conduct rescues at sea with helicopters or forward-deployed USCG vessels. Onboard medical facilities could provide emergency care.
Environmental stewards . Surveillance would identify and record evidence of actors threatening the sea environment. MOAC personnel could intervene alongside regional allies and partners.
Protecting natural resources . MOAC would help regional states protect their EEZs from poaching or illegal resource extraction. One mission could be to support the Philippine Kadiwa initiative to escort and resupply their fishermen operating near the Scarborough and Salina shoals. 70 Whether the offender is a state or non-state actor, MOAC could support prompt diplomatic, law enforcement, or armed responses.
Law enforcement . Piracy, other crimes, or state interference in international maritime trade and civil air traffic would be more difficult with a well-armed MOAC “cop on the beat” identifying threats. 71 Increasing the capabilities of other nations to police their own waters strengthens maritime governance. 72 The USCG has established a precedent away from the South China Sea. 73
Securing maritime borders . International law provides standards to define maritime boundaries. Powers like China can ignore them if unopposed. MOAC would work with regional states to protect allied and partner territorial integrity, including support for outpost resupply missions. One PACOM commander stated that escorting supply ships is “an entirely reasonable option” under the U.S.-Philippines defense treaty. 74
Promoting rule of law . MOAC would exercise with allies and partners to build collective law enforcement capacity that promotes a “free and open Indo-Pacific.” 75 Allied law enforcement agencies deployed on MOAC could conduct “visit, board, search, and seizure operations” against what could be deemed privateers doing China’s bidding behind a façade of civilian status. 76
Preventing terrorism . Terrorists threatening life and property from the sea may be thwarted with a persistent USCG armed presence, including its planned special operation organization, Special Missions Command. 77 MOAC could be bolstered by intelligence personnel, regional assets, and other American military forces, including Marine Corps and Special Operations Command detachments.
Enhancing cyber and critical infrastructure security . MOAC could host training that shares best practices with regional partners and allies to harden defenses and preempt malign actors in the maritime domain.
Military force . As an armed service, the USCG would be the first line of defense if a crisis escalates beyond water cannons. MOAC would act as a deterrent to all but the most deliberate armed escalation.
Intelligence gathering and sharing . The USCG is an intelligence partner with other American armed services and friendly nations. All of the missions would be assisted by and contribute to joint and international intelligence on regional threats to the rules-based order.
These missions—and more as the USCG evolves to meet new challenges—will strengthen alliances and partnerships to defend the principles of freedom of the seas and settling territorial disputes without use of force or coercion.
A White Hull Line in International Waters
The USCG’s value was validated with a nearly $25 billion “historic investment” that then-Acting Commandant, Admiral Kevin Lunday, said “marks a new era for the Coast Guard.” 78 Defending a “white hull” line in the South China Sea will be a bold demonstration of the U.S.’s “commitment to a free and open Indo-Pacific” and will protect the U.S.’s “powerful ties of commerce, culture, technology, and defense.” 79 To hold the line against and roll back China’s subliminal DIME war before United States Navy “gray hulls” must intervene, the United States Coast Guard must build and deploy to the South China Sea the Mother of All Cutters to embark on its new era in PACOM. 80
Brian J. Dunn holds an AB in political science and history from the University of Michigan and a MA in history from Eastern Michigan University. He retired from his job as a nonpartisan research analyst for the Michigan State Legislature, and served in the Michigan Army National Guard for six years. He has written articles for publications such as Proceedings , Army , Military Review , and Joint Force Quarterly, and writes about defense and national security issues on Substack in The Dignified Rant: Evolved .

title: Show HN: A guided 3D Leonardo da Vinci museum, built in code
body:
We mark what is known and what is guessed.
The label names what you see. The drawer explains the evidence. The record gives the full sources, measurements and licences. Certainty words distinguish documented, reconstructed, conjectural and not known. The museum labels the reproduction, not the painting.
The past rebuilt in 3D. We mark what is known and what is guessed.

title: Denel says it is on a “good trajectory” despite ninth straight audit disclaimer
body:
Despite an annual revenue increase of some 15.8 per cent in the 2025/26 financial year, persistent operating losses, liquidity pressures, and unresolved financial reporting deficiencies continue to drive concern over the long-struggling state-owned defence company’s eventual turnaround.
While Denel Group Chief Executive Officer Tsepo Monaheng did acknowledge the continued challenges faced by the company, he used the opportunity of his presentation of the company’s 2025/26 annual report to Parliament’s Portfolio Committee on Defence and Military Veterans on 9 October to present an overall positive picture.
“Although there are challenges as we navigate the growth journey of Denel, the company is in a good trajectory for growth, stability, and doing good for the country,” Monaheng said.
He began Denel’s presentation cautioning that the company’s importance and mandate should not be narrowly linked to its finances, stating that “Financial performance is secondary to us delivering and strengthening a sovereign capability,” explaining that this view serves to ground the company as it continues on its recovery journey.
“And so, we do say that Denel’s mandate is to safeguard and strengthen South Africa’s sovereign defence capabilities, in a financially sustainable environment,” he added.
“Denel’s turnaround is a journey that requires discipline, accountability and sustained execution. We are under no illusion about the challenges that remain, particularly around liquidity, financial controls and operational sustainability. At the same time, we have made important progress in stabilising the organisation and rebuilding the foundations for a stronger Denel,” Monaheng emphasised in a subsequent press release.
According to Denel’s annual report, Group revenue rose from R1.272 billion to R1.473 billion, returning to 2023 financial year levels. Denel Aerospace contributed more than half of the revenue generated, at R880 million, followed by Denel Land Systems at R478 million, Denel Dynamics at R84 million, and Denel Integrated Systems Solutions at R29 million.
On the positive side, Denel pointed to an improved gross profit, growing from 11 percent in 2024/25 to 24 percent, or R361 million, in 2025/26, as well as a 74 percent (R305 million) increase in its “share of profit in associate companies.” Net profit stood at R156 million.
Despite these positives, the Denel Group continued to make an operating loss of R364 million, slightly less than the loss of R370 million reported last year. Denel attributed the continued losses to a higher-than-planned cost base, alongside the execution of legacy contracts, payments for which had been received and spent in previous years.
Monaheng also provided an overview of Denel’s progress towards meeting the company’s shareholder compact targets, with the Denel presentation indicating that the company only managed to achieve 41 percent of the targets set.
Key achievements included improved liquidity from cash generated from operations, which rose from a loss of R122 million in the 2024 financial year to R261 million (largely thanks to the RDM dividends, payments received from customers, and the SAAF settling outstanding debt). Additionally, the G6 upgrade export contract is understood to be ahead of schedule, while both the gross and net profit margins saw growth.
However, Monaheng’s presentation also indicated that a number of targets were either only partially met or missed entirely. Revenue growth was well below the set target of 25 percent per annum, at 15 percent, just one percent above the 2024 financial year. The company’s operating expenses as a percentage of revenue worsened from 43 percent in the 2024/25 financial year to 55 percent in 2025/26, against a target of equal to or less than 30 percent.
On Denel PMP (Pretoria Metal Pressings), he explained that, at R157 million, PMP failed to reach its revenue target of R235 million as a result of remaining legacy contracts that the recovery plan did not account for, among other reasons. In addition, Monaheng noted that good progress had been made on phase one of Project Hoefyster, with only mine blast testing being delayed to the 2026/2027 financial year.
Notably, Monaheng also addressed the company’s continued failure to improve the employee turnover rate, which stands at 11.4 percent, with 186 employees having left. While acknowledging that this has meant a substantial loss in terms of skills and experience, he did preface this by noting that the figures included retirements.
“We have a lot of people in Denel who are on the higher end of the age and they are going to exit and then we have an opportunity to replace them with younger people,” he said, adding that Denel is not overly worried about this, as it presents an opportunity to bring in more young people who are more adaptable to technological and operational changes, thus better enabling the company to more easily modernise its technology.
However, Denel’s “going concern” picture is starker than some of the headline numbers may suggest. Denel’s own figures show that its continued operating losses have deepened the company’s liquidity challenges, with the company indicating its liquidity position would turn negative in September 2026, though the company assured the Committee that interventions were underway. Notably, of the R3.378 billion recapitalisation received since 2023, just R81 million remained as of 30 April.
Denel’s presentation concluded with closing remarks proffered by the company’s interim board chair, Tshidi Mokgabudi. She chose to focus on the Auditor-General of South Africa’s (AGSA) audit outcomes, particularly the fact that this is the ninth year that there has been a disclaimer attached to the audit report, alongside a finding declaring the company’s financial statements “not credible.”
“The board is now doing a deep-dive into the supporting documentation and evidence to actually establish what makes our financial statements to be termed as not credible,” she said.
Subsequently, she also indicated that the board had taken a decision to evaluate more closely a number of other areas related to the company as a “going concern”, such as why Denel, despite having a number of orders and contracts, continues to fail to execute these orders and thereby generate new revenue.
Mokgabudi insisted that the board would do all it could to ensure that the next annual report would show significant improvements as part of what she termed an “exiting disclaimer project.”

title: OPP yet to launch formal probe into alleged ‘egregious’ OSAP use at career colleges
body:
As the Ford government faces increasing scrutiny over how a handful of private career colleges tapped into the OSAP system, Ontario’s provincial police say they are reviewing the allegations but have yet to decide on whether to launch a formal criminal probe.
In early October, the Ministry of Colleges and Universities sounded the alarm about six private career colleges that were engaged in “egregious use of taxpayer dollars” and accused them of criminality by taking advantage of the student assistance program.
Nolan Quinn said an internal investigation found “unusually high concentrations of OSAP applications submitted from the same geographic locations” and also pointed to the involvement of “immigration services firms” being directly tied to or co-owned by some career colleges in question.
After referring the findings to auditing firm KPMG for a deeper dive, Quinn said the government had also “reported it to the OPP and the Auditor General.”
The OPP confirmed that it “received a referral from the Ontario government and that the allegations are “currently under review.”
“I am not able to provide an estimated timeline for the review,” an OPP spokesperson said in a statement. “As the matter remains under review, we are unable to provide any further detail or comment.”
Ontario’s Auditor General, however, said the office only received a “notification” from the government, but that the province stopped short of requesting a formal value-for-money audit.
“A statement was made by Minister Quinn on October 6 that states “As a result, the government notified the Auditor General last week and has also referred this matter to the Ontario Provincial Police,” the auditor’s office said in an email.
“We can confirm that the Office of the Auditor General received a notification from the government last week. This was separate from the request for an audit received from MPP Tyler Watt.”
While the minister has the power to request a “special assignment,” it’s unclear why the government chose to only notify the auditor as opposed to request a performance audit – similar to Liberal MPP Tyler Watt’s request.
The auditor’s office added that the office has been notified about similar issues in the past and stressed that it’s their “expectation that the government would inform us, as we are its independent auditor of the public accounts of Ontario.”
While the investigations remain in question, the Ford government continues to face calls to prevent the problem from spilling over into other institutions.
There are currently 242 career colleges that are eligible to receive OSAP in Ontario, all of which have now been cut off from the provincial program as the province examines the scope of the problem.
Career Colleges Ontario, the association representing hundreds of institutions, is urging the Ford government to reinstate student financial aid for career college students who were already approved for funds and are actively attending in-person classes.
The association, which had been warning the government about possible misuse of OSAP since 2023, says the government should be taking targeted action to address those concerns, not disrupting the education of students who have followed the rules.
The minister has only indicated that the pause in OSAP grants will remain in effect until the government’s third-party auditors can complete a wider probe.
“The auditors, the third-party auditors, haven’t given us assurances yet, and I will respect the experts. And whenever they give me assurance to be able to release all of the institutions,” Quinn said on Oct. 2.
“That’s when we’ll move forward with OSAP for career colleges.”

title: Operation Vivaldi's 'Fourth Season' — Ukraine retakes another 101 square kilometers on Lyman front, Biletskyi says
body:
Ukraine's Third Army Corps, together with its attached units, has retaken another 101 square kilometers during the fourth stage of Operation Vivaldi on the Lyman sector in Donetsk Oblast, the corps announced on Oct. 14.
Ukraine liberated the villages of Zelena Dolyna, Lypove, and Kolodiazi, while Russia lost about 3,000 of its soldiers in the fourth stage of the operation, the corps reported on Telegram .
"The enemy was unable to cut the key logistics artery of our group in the Donbas. We thwarted the offensive of the group 'Zapad' and forced it to transfer part of the units of the 1st Tank Army, which weakened the pressure on Kupiansk-Vuzlovyi," corps commander Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi said.
In total, Operation Vivaldi saw the liberation and return of 16 settlements and 277 square kilometers (106 square miles) to Ukraine, the corps said. "Four seasons of 'Vivaldi' are over, but the music continues."
On Sept. 15, Biletskyi confirmed that Ukrainian forces under the command of the 3rd Army Corps were conducting a series of counterattacks north of the front-line city of Lyman in Donetsk Oblast.
The operation dealt "a heavy blow to the combat capabilities of Russia's 20th and 25th Combined Arms Armies," Biletskyi said then, adding that Ukrainian drone strikes had pushed Russian supply hubs across the state border.
The fight for the heart of the so-called Donbas fortress belt — Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, Druzhkivka, and Kostiantynivka — is crucial going into the winter months, when Russia will look to maximize its foothold in urban areas to prepare for a 2027 offensive campaign.

title: Press review: Zelensky-Trump bad blood threatens US support and IMF updates GDP outlook
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Zelensky’s latest conflict with US President Donald Trump puts Ukraine at risk of losing American support; the IMF adjusts its 2027 economic outlook as the global situation is better than expected; and NATO's nuclear drills are causing tension on the European continent. These stories topped Wednesday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Although Vladimir Zelensky’s latest conflict with US President Donald Trump has European leaders feeling a little on edge, experts believe they are simply banking on waiting out the current Washington administration. Should the Republicans lose Congress in the midterm elections, it will make that strategy much more tenable, with Trump's powers potentially limited for the remainder of his current term. However, as long as Trump remains in power, Ukraine could lose US support: the White House has all the leverage it needs to cut off Kiev from intelligence, block arms deliveries via European funds, and even shut down Starlink satellite communications. Meanwhile, the UK and the European Commission are trying to derail the diesel agreement between Moscow and Washington.
Dmitry Suslov, deputy director of the Center for Comprehensive European and International Studies at the Russian National Research University Higher School of Economics, told Vedomosti that Trump's goal is not to force Kiev into a crushing defeat, so he is advocating a conflict settlement that makes both sides look like winners. The White House believes that "certain incentives" will persuade Russia to agree to a conflict freeze along the lines of engagement. The expert noted that the recently announced diesel deal is not an isolated instance of Russian-American cooperation, but rather a step toward Russia, in exchange for which Washington expects concessions from Moscow. "Russia should not agree to this framing of the issue. It should not be viewed as a precursor to mutual concessions or a settlement on Trump’s terms, but rather as practical, mutually beneficial cooperation between the two countries," Suslov pointed out.
According to expert Dmitry Novikov, Washington remains convinced that it can use economic incentives to persuade Moscow to make territorial concessions. "At the same time, the US aims to strengthen its influence here, since, for example, it could gain direct access to the gas transportation system. The plan is this: economics in exchange for politics, but the economics are controlled by the Americans," the expert said.
In turn, Bogdan Bezpalko, a member of the Russian Presidential Council for Interethnic Relations, told Izvestia that the White House could now announce new sanctions relief for Moscow that would benefit the US economy. Such a move would also put pressure on Zelensky and Kiev’s European allies, he stressed.
For now, however, European countries will try to push Ukraine toward steps that would derail the implementation of the Russian-American agreements on diesel fuel, Russian Foreign Ministry’s Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik stated. According to him, the UK and the European Commission, led by Ursula von der Leyen, will be the main drivers of this push.
In 2026, global economic growth will be about 3.1%, while in 2027, that number is expected to rise to 3.4%, the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) World Economic Outlook report said. The organization has moderately raised its 2027 forecasts compared to its April projections, citing the world economy's better-than-expected ability to withstand the consequences of the Middle East war and other destabilizing factors. Nevertheless, the medium-term outlook for economic growth is disappointing compared to previous periods, the report noted. Key risks include the energy crisis, the AI bubble, and rising public debt in countries around the world.
According to the IMF, the secret to resilience lies in two key factors, economy expert Ksenia Bondarenko told Vedomosti. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz caused serious supply disruptions by cutting off the transit route through which nearly 20 million barrels of oil, or roughly a quarter of global maritime traffic, were transported daily prior to the war. The flexibility of the energy market made it possible to quickly reroute supplies and increase production outside the Persian Gulf. Thanks to countries such as the US, Brazil, Kazakhstan, and several others, production increased by up to two million barrels per day, the report pointed out.
Moving on to the second factor, Bondarenko stressed that global reserves were depleted in an effort to combat the energy crisis. This included the emergency release of strategic reserves under the auspices of the International Energy Agency, as well as the large-scale use of domestic reserves. These measures provided an additional four million barrels per day. Thanks to all of this, the shock caused by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz did not lead to a spike in oil prices to 110 dollars per barrel or a 0.9 percentage point decline in global growth. The net negative impact on global growth in 2026 was only about 0.3 percentage points. In addition, the investment boom around AI continued to support growth in business activity and trade, the expert emphasized.
For Russia, the IMF revised its GDP forecast to a growth rate of 0.9% for both 2026 and 2027, down from 1.1% previously. Rising commodity prices are supporting economic activity in Russia to some extent, despite a decline in total oil exports due to infrastructure damage, the IMF noted. The downward revision of the Russian forecast may be linked to a more cautious assessment of investment prospects, financial expert Alexander Abramov stressed. An unbalanced budget and increased spending amid the geopolitical situation could fuel high inflation, he emphasized. In this case, the Russian Central Bank’s key rate will also remain high, curbing investment and hindering economic growth, the expert concluded.
Large-scale NATO nuclear exercises have begun in Italy, with 17 countries participating. Thousands of servicemen and dozens of aircraft capable of carrying nuclear weapons are involved. Russia has stated that these drills will not reduce regional tensions. The exercises are taking place at a time when the US seeks to deploy tactical weapons near Russia’s borders, and the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START) has yet to be signed.
NATO troops are rehearsing scenarios involving dual-use aircraft: jets capable of carrying both conventional and nuclear weapons. According to military expert Dmitry Kornev, a key element of the Steadfast Noon drill is the practical testing of the Nuclear Sharing program for the use of American tactical thermonuclear bombs. "These special munitions are carried by specific types of aircraft, such as the German Tornado or the new-generation F-35 fighter jets used by the Netherlands, Denmark, Norway, Poland, Italy, and Finland," the expert told Izvestia.
Moscow’s official position on these exercises was articulated by the Russian embassy in Belgium, which maintains contact with NATO leadership. "We take note of statements by NATO officials that the drills are routine in nature and pose no threat to Russia. However, at a time when NATO is portraying our country as the main security threat, these exercises do not help reduce tensions on the continent and are part of the alliance’s nuclear policy, which is notoriously negative towards Moscow," the diplomats noted.
The New START Treaty officially expired on February 5, 2026. No new agreement was signed. For the first time since 1972, Moscow and Washington are not bound by a legal framework for controlling their nuclear arsenals. It is precisely in the absence of these deterrent mechanisms that the current drills are taking place. The expired START Treaty limited the delivery systems and nuclear warheads of Russia and the US, but it did not prohibit such exercises, Vasily Klimov, a senior research fellow at the International Security Center at the World Economy and International Relations Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences, emphasized.
The leaders of Germany, Italy, and Belgium have called for a new mechanism to be introduced among EU member states. The idea is to allow European governments to suspend laws adopted by Brussels if they deem the laws to be burdensome. According to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, and her Belgian counterpart Bart De Wever, the new mechanism would benefit small and medium-sized European businesses the most. The new initiative aims to ensure greater independence from Brussels and prevent unnecessary regulatory burdens, which could lead to irreversible losses of Europe’s industrial potential and further weaken investment and competitiveness.
It would be wrong to suggest that the initiative will weaken EU bodies. Germany, Italy, and Belgium have all benefited from European integration, and they have no interest in causing division at this time, Artyom Sokolov, a senior research fellow at the MGIMO Institute of International Studies, told Vedomosti. Rather, this is about rebalancing the EU as a possible way out of the current tense situation. This indicates that current EU leaders recognize the organization's problems with expansion, the expert noted.
For now, the mechanism mentioned by Merz, Meloni, and De Wever is "nothing but propaganda," Vadim Trukhachev, an associate professor at the Russian Financial University, pointed out. Such statements are made for domestic political purposes: Merz is concerned about his extremely low approval rating, Meloni faces elections next year, and De Wever is also trying to consolidate his position within Belgium. According to the expert, what’s more important is the ongoing debate within the EU over abolishing the veto and replacing it with the double-majority principle, when decisions are adopted if approved by 55% of member states (15 out of 27), representing 65% of the EU’s population, provided there is no blocking minority consisting of at least four countries.
Given that the EU is going through difficult times, leaders fear the collapse of consensus. Therefore, by transferring some powers to national capitals, they are trying to save the bloc, not dismantle it, political scientist Alexander Kamkin emphasized. If there is indeed a threat to Brussels in the form of the creation of some kind of parallel structure, the European Commission and its President Ursula von der Leyen may try to thwart the initiative of the three countries, the expert noted.
The UK’s Labour Party will release evidence that Moscow allegedly interfered in British politics, Minister of State for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard told a media outlet. However, it is unclear exactly when this will happen. In this way, the Cabinet has backed Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s virtually unsubstantiated accusation that Moscow attempted to influence the 2016 referendum on the UK’s exit from the EU. Burnham is now counting on a rapprochement with the EU. He even named the exact date when the groundwork for the country’s future reintegration will be laid: November 20, the date of the UK-EU summit.
"So far, Brussels’ reaction to the possibility of the UK’s return to the EU remains unclear. In theory, the EU return should please officials," political expert Alexander Tevdoy-Burmuli told Nezavisimaya Gazeta. He emphasized that London’s rapprochement with Brussels is driven by US President Donald Trump’s policies. "As one of the largest economies, as well as a country with nuclear weapons and permanent membership in the UN Security Council, the UK could once again become a welcome partner for the EU in this difficult situation," the expert explained.
However, it is true that reintegration is a complex process under current circumstances. "The UK has always been divided on the issue of EU membership. Brexit was an expression of this persistent division. In theory, the Burnham government could initiate talks on joining the EU. But that would require securing a majority in favor of reintegration within the country," Tevdoi-Burmuli emphasized.
This will not be easy. The British public associates the pro-European stance with failed immigration policies, which have become one of the country's central problems. "The UK has received a huge number of migrants, who are now a source of conflict. In addition, far-right forces advocating an end to migration are gaining ground in the country. In this context, joining the EU, where a left-liberal agenda is being implemented, could prove problematic," the expert noted.
TASS is not responsible for the material quoted in these press reviews

title: [Be The Good] Help youth leaders, students attend Social Good Summit 2026
body: Hello! In about a month, Rappler will be holding Social Good Summit 2026 , which will be all about upskilling people to survive and thrive amid artificial intelligence — the risks it poses, and the opportunities it presents. That’s why we’ve entitled the summit, WE, THE HUMANS: Reclaim Our Future . More than an event, it’s a resounding declaration for the need to put humans at the center of any technology, most especially generative AI. (READ: Scientists call for international body to oversee advanced AI ) It’s also our biggest yearly fund-raising event. Proceeds will go to our investigative journalism and AI literacy initiatives. But we also want to ensure the people most vulnerable to AI threats and those most in need of skills and know-how to navigate the AI era are also in the room. So, this week, we’re launching MAKE ROOM , a way for individuals with more resources to sponsor a summit ticket for students, educators, community leaders, youth leaders, and student journalists. You can also sponsor a ticket for a specific person or beneficiary. If you want to leave it up to us, just let us know how many people you would want to sponsor and we’ll give the tickets to students, educators, community leaders, youth leaders, and student journalists we’ve worked with and supported. What’s in store for them at the summit? They get to attend two mini masterclasses (out of six options) , each designed to give them new skills for navigating AI. The workshops cover vibe coding, data storytelling, personal safety and data protection, how to deal with AI-fueled disinformation, and more. The panel discussions will feature global expertise on AI and human rights , with speakers like Amnesty International secretary-general and former UN rapporteur Agnés Callamard , AI Singapore’s Leslie Teo , 2021 Nobel laureate and Rappler CEO Maria Ressa , Nobel Committee leaders Jorgen Watne Frydnes and Kristian Berg Harpviken , Forbes 30 Under 30 Lister and Empath CEO Steph Naval , actress and advocate Iza Calzado , and a pre-recorded conversation between Maria and historian and bestselling author Yuval Noah Harari . Attendees will thus get both an upskilling experience and exposure to new ideas about AI policy-making shaping the world. They’ll be taking part in one of the most urgent conversations of our time: how to protect human values, human creativity, and human communities from the threat of unregulated and abused AI. The summit will take place on November 21, a Saturday, at Shangri-La The Fort Manila in Taguig City. To sponsor a ticket for a specific person or beneficiary, you can buy the tickets from here , and input their names in the ticket holder field during the purchasing process. If you want us to be the one to choose the beneficiaries, just email us at socialgood@rappler.com. If you know someone who would be interested in this initiative, I hope you can forward them this email. With your support, you help keep our newsroom independent and ensure more voices and perspectives are represented at Social Good Summit. NBI files complaints vs Davao contractor linked to Dutertes The company, Genesis88, owned by a known friend and associate of former president Rodrigo Duterte, won one out of four flood control projects in Davao City, according to our investigation. Four years on, Marcos’ door for comms chiefs still revolving Bea Cupin explains the dynamics behind the constant changes in President Marcos’ presidential communications secretary appointments, most recently given to Lino Cayetano, the younger brother of minority senators Pia and Alan Peter. DOE: Visayas may face more red alerts in 2027 without sufficient backup systems Energy Secretary Sharon Garin also lays out steps the government is taking to address the power crisis in the Visayas.
