We deliver updates straight to your inbox on how journalism and communities can work together for impact. To subscribe, follow the #FactsFirstPH movement or visit rappler.com/newsletters .

title: ‘You can’t swim’: The rejection that fuelled Maha Al Shehhi’s Olympic journey
body: Maha Al Shehhi was only 13 when she realised there was no established pathway for an Emirati girl who desired to swim competitively. But being told she was unable to train and swim lit a fire inside her that ultimately led her to the Olympics. “When I found out that I couldn’t swim in the first three years because I was a female, that hit me really hard. They were like, 'You can’t swim. We won’t give you a pool; it’s impossible'. I was like, 'What do you mean? I can'.” Her family searched for a pool that would allow her and her sisters to swim and train alongside boys. The absence of a clear pathway became the reason for her determination to create one. “I feel like that was the time when it hit me. I should be a change,” the 20-year-old told The National in an interview at Middlesex University's 'Dubai Women in Sport' series. In 2024, Al Shehhi represented the UAE at the Paris Olympics , where she swam a personal best time of 2:17.17 in the 200 metres freestyle. For her, progress is about removing that sense of novelty surrounding female athletes. “The way we talk about females is always a surprise. We never say, 'Great, she’s a female; she did it like how a man would do it',” she says. Instead, she argues, there’s so much surprise when a woman competes. “My goal is to make it normal. For everyone,” she adds. For Al Shehhi, normalising female athletes participating in all disciplines is the only way to ensure progress. View this post on Instagram Family backing Maha’s family encouraged her and her two sisters to pursue whatever made them happy. “They always told me that whatever you’re going to pursue, make sure you finish it. You can’t start something without finishing it,” she says. And so she, alongside her twin sister Mahra and their younger sister Mira, took up the sport together. They became known as 'M3', the three Al Shehhis. All of them went on to represent the UAE. Sport runs in the family. Born to a Polish mother and an Emirati father, Maha’s mother had once participated in athletics in her youth. Their father initially needed time to adjust to the idea of his daughters training in an environment he had largely associated with men. However, their commitment to the sport eventually won him over. “He did have a rough time trying to understand but then he saw the 4am training and the 5pm training and he saw how dedicated we were so he was like, ‘You know what, I’ll always support you. I’m your father. I’m here for you. Just know I’ll be the backbone of everything’,” says Al Shehhi. “Our mother is the support system. She makes sure that every training session I go to, I smile. Everyone has this thing with me that if you don’t see Maha smiling, it’s a bad thing; it’s the end of the world. “She always makes sure I’m happy. She makes sure that I’m doing it for myself and if I feel low, she's like do it for me and it motivates me. “She always reminds me that I’m also doing it for the younger generation; that's my priority and I really want to just make a clear path.” That’s not to say there haven't been times when she didn’t contemplate walking away. Having a strong support system was key to keeping her on track, as is her fierce competitive nature and the desire to rebel against those who tell her 'no', something she attributes to her heritage. “When it comes to swimming and when it comes to fighting in the pool or racing, it’s the Polish blood coming out,” she says. View this post on Instagram Forging a path Emiratis often speak with pride of Eyal Zayed, the sons of Zayed, named after the nation’s founding father. Al Shehhi wants the same reverence for ‘Banat Zayed’, his daughters. She wants future generations to find it easier to access pools, sponsorship and equipment. “My goal is to make sure the girls that are coming right after me or in any other sport feel like they shouldn’t go through the challenges I went through because I would never wish that on my worst enemy, honestly,” she says. Al Shehhi estimates that 90 per cent of parents she meets still discourage their daughters from entering the sport, whether it be on account of wearing a swimsuit, mixed training, or the belief that sport is simply a distraction from studies. Al Shehhi says she often offers to speak to parents to ease their concerns. “Let her enjoy what she wants to do. You can't force her to just study and then spend the day doing nothing. If she feels like she wants to do a sport, let her. Let her run, let her jog, let her do anything. But let her experience what she wants to experience,” she says.

title: Olympic Qualifier: Eguavoen speaks on Ajibade’s injury, hails Okpe after big win
body:
Super Falcons captain Rasheedat Ajibade will undergo an MRI scan to determine the extent of the injury she sustained during Nigeria’s emphatic 5-0 victory over Comoros in the second leg of their 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games qualifying tie.
The midfielder was forced off in the 23rd minute following a collision with a Comoros defender at the Remo Stars Stadium in Ikenne, Ogun State, on Tuesday. Visibly in pain, Ajibade received medical attention before being stretchered off, with Folashade Ijamilusi coming on as her replacement.
The injury cast a shadow over an otherwise dominant evening for the Super Falcons, who secured a 7-0 aggregate victory to advance to the third round of the qualifiers, where they will face Morocco’s Atlas Lionesses.
Toni Payne and Uchenna Kanu both scored braces, while Christy Ucheibe converted a penalty as Nigeria completed the rout and strengthened their hopes of progressing further in the race for a place at the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles.
However, the immediate concern after the final whistle was the condition of Ajibade, with interim coach Augustine Eguavoen confirming that the medical team would conduct further examinations before providing an official update on the Captain’s injury.
Speaking at his post-match press conference, Eguavoen admitted that he was yet to receive a definitive diagnosis but expressed hope that the injury would not be serious.
“On Ajibade, I have not heard anything,” he said.
“I was with the medical team, and they said they are taking her to a hospital for an MRI to ascertain the degree of the injury.
“Hopefully, before we get back to the hotel, we will know. As soon as we have information, I am not the one to give it.
“The medical team will contact the head of media, and then you will get an update on Ajibade’s injury. Unfortunately, we lost Ajibade early in the game, but I think, and I hope and I pray, that the injury is very minute.”
Ajibade’s fitness will be a major concern for Nigeria as they prepare for a more demanding encounter against Morocco. The captain is an influential figure in the Super Falcons setup, and her availability could prove important as the team attempts to navigate the next stage of the Olympic qualifying campaign.
Beyond the concern surrounding Ajibade, Eguavoen expressed satisfaction with the team’s performance, praising the players for translating their work on the training ground into an emphatic victory.
The Super Falcons had taken a 2-0 advantage into the second leg and completed the job with five unanswered goals, demonstrating their attacking quality and ability to maintain control of the tie.
For Eguavoen, who is currently serving as interim coach, the performance was particularly encouraging as he continues to work with the squad and establish his methods.
“The game today, I’m very pleased. I’m very, very happy. Congratulations to the girls; they made my day. I remember I kept begging them because I’m in a new terrain.
“We need everybody’s support. The response in training showed in the game.”
The coach also acknowledged the improvement shown by Comoros despite the heavy defeat, suggesting that the visitors approached the second leg with a different mentality after losing the first encounter 2-0.
“Yes, 5-0 today, the first leg was 0-2. I would say the Comoros team improved. Today, they improved and were beaten 5-0, so it’s a little bit tricky,” he added.
“I’m 100 per cent sure that they knew today they had nothing to lose, so they had to play. Congratulations to us, like I said, I’m very impressed with the team.”
Nigeria’s victory ensured a comfortable passage into the next round, but Eguavoen will know that the performance against Comoros is only one step in a longer qualifying campaign. Morocco are expected to provide a sterner test, making the Super Falcons’ preparations and the fitness of key players even more important.
Eguavoen also reserved praise for Blessing Okpe, whose performance strengthened her case for a more prominent role in the national team after earning a late invitation to the squad.
The coach revealed that Okpe was initially left out of the 28-player selection but was eventually called up after another player withdrew. He said he had questioned the omission of a forward who had been scoring regularly in the Belarusian league.
According to Eguavoen, a recommendation from someone who contacted him helped draw his attention to the player’s situation.
“On Okpe, I want to say a very big thank you to someone who called me. I got a call from—I won’t mention the name,” he said.
“Okpe was a late invitee. I was like, somebody scoring a lot of goals in the Belarus league and then she is not in the 28. I was like, that means you didn’t take your time.”
The coach added that even if he does not remain in charge of the Super Falcons, he intends to recommend Okpe to whoever takes over the team, citing the forward’s ability to make an impression despite her late arrival.
“Next game, hopefully, I am here. I know I am the Technical Director. If I don’t continue in this job, I will go back to my office.
“Then whoever becomes the coach, I will recommend Okpe. But luckily for Okpe, a player pulled out and she had a chance to come. I think she has proven that her late call-up was worth it.”
Okpe’s display will be encouraging for the forward, who has taken advantage of the opportunity to show what she can offer at senior international level. Her performance also gives Eguavoen another attacking option to consider as Nigeria prepare for the challenge of Morocco.
While the Super Falcons can celebrate a convincing aggregate victory and the emergence of additional attacking options, Ajibade’s injury remains the biggest concern from Tuesday’s encounter. The results of her MRI scan will determine the next steps as Nigeria turn their attention to the third round of the Olympic qualifiers.

title: WAFU B U17: Black Starlets target AFCON slot after booking semi-final place
body: Ghana’s U17 side, the Black Starlets, have turned their attention to securing a place at next year’s Africa Cup of Nations after reaching the semi-finals of the ongoing WAFU Zone B tournament. The Starlets secured back-to-back wins over Togo and Benin to qualify for the last four with a game to spare in the group stage. The two teams that reach the final will seal qualification for next year’s AFCON. “Coming here [Ouagadougou], we had three targets; to qualify for the semi-final, to qualify for the AFCON by being finalists and to lift the trophy,” head coach Kassim Ocansey said after the 3-1 win over Benin. “So far, the first target of making it to the semi-final has been achieved. We have two more to chase and In Sha Allah we will achieve,” he added. The U-17 Africa Cup of Nations will take place in April and May 2027 in Morocco. Ghana will face Burkina Faso in their final group game of the WAFU B tournament on October 16 before the semi-finals kick off.

title: South Sudanese diplomat Dominic Jok dies in Cairo
body: Dominic Jok Deng Majak, South Sudan’s deputy head of mission to Rwanda, died in Cairo, Egypt, on Tuesday night after battling a heart condition for nearly two years, a family member said. Mustafa Biong, a relative, told Radio Tamazuj that Majak had suffered from the heart condition for almost two years. “Dominic had a heart problem over the past two years. He was posted to Japan, but because of his heart condition, he preferred to work in the region to be close to home. That is why he was posted to Rwanda,” Biong said. Biong said Majak had spent some time in Nairobi before collapsing there about two months ago because of his heart condition. He was later taken to Cairo because the doctor who had performed his heart surgery was based there. “He was admitted to hospital in Cairo and, after diagnosis, the doctor said everything was fine and he could travel and come back after three months. But after some days, he underwent more tests. After the tests, he collapsed and was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) on Sept. 25. Last night, he died,” Biong said. Majak graduated with a law degree from the University of Cairo and worked as an administrative officer before joining Sudan’s foreign service following the signing of the 2005 Comprehensive Peace Agreement. He also served as office manager in the office of Deng Alor Kuol, who was then Sudan’s foreign affairs minister. After South Sudan gained independence in 2011, Majak served as a diplomat in several countries, including Syria and South Africa. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs had not issued a statement on his death by the time of publication. The post South Sudanese diplomat Dominic Jok dies in Cairo appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Building under reconstruction collapses in Tel Aviv, none injured as workers escape unharmed
body: A building in Tel Aviv collapsed on Wednesday morning, Israel Police announced.The Tel Aviv-Jaffa Municipality said the building, on Nahalat Binyamin Street, was slated for demolition before its unexpected collapse. Residents were told to stay away from the scene.The Fire and Rescue Authority said it was conducting searches at the site alongside police and Magen David Adom (MDA) paramedics to rule out the possibility of anyone trapped under the rubble. It added that five construction workers inside the building were able to escape moments before it came down.Footage from the scene shows people running from the site as the building came down, sending dust billowing across the busy street. Police closed several roads in the area.In 2021, a residential building in Holon collapsed after authorities evacuated 16 families due to safety concerns. The evacuation was carried out after reports that there had been an explosion in the building on Serlin Street.When firefighters and rescue workers arrived at the scene, they observed cracks in the building. Some residents who tried to leave their homes said they could not open doors because the building's infrastructure had shifted, police said.Some 80,000 buildings in Israel in danger of collapseFollowing the 2021 incident, the Israel Builders Association warned that as many as 80,000 buildings in Israel, with about 300,000 apartments, are in danger of collapsing and must be reconstructed in the coming years to avoid calamity.“We published this in a report that we submitted to the government in 2017, but this is something we have been saying for years,” the association's then-deputy director-general Shay Pauzner said.“The message is that Israel needs to start thinking strategically about this because we are in the danger zone.”Police announced that, due to the collapse, several roads in the area had been closed.

title: Ukraine strikes a Sberbank data center in Russia. Meanwhile, Kyiv isn’t getting crucial missile warnings from the U.S., and SpaceX is restricting Starlink.
body: A fire in a residential building in Kyiv after a Russian attack on October 13 Russia Ukrainian drones struck a data center operated by Sberbank in the city of Balakovo in the Saratov region overnight on October 14. Ukrainian monitoring channels were the first to report the attack. Saratov Governor Roman Busargin said the strike damaged residential buildings in Balakovo and killed one person. He said all infrastructure facilities in the city are “operating normally.” A few hours later, Sberbank First Deputy Chairman Alexander Vedyakhin confirmed the attack on the data center, saying all the bank’s systems and services are “operating normally.” The bank’s press service said no employees were injured. This is the first Ukrainian attack on Sberbank data centers. Last week, Ukrainian drones struck data centers belonging to Yandex in the Ryazan and Vladimir regions, as well as in Kaluga. Sberbank announced plans to build a data center in the Saratov region in 2020 and began construction the following year. The facility is expected to cover almost 60,000 square meters (about 646,000 square feet). Authorities said it would be the largest data center in Europe, and one of Sberbank’s supercomputers is being built at the Balakovo site. Ukraine Ukraine’s Western partners once again failed to warn Kyiv that Russia was preparing a ballistic missile strike on the capital, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on the evening of October 13. He said the missiles were detected only as they approached Kyiv. The main target was the CHP-4 power plant, one of Kyiv’s major energy facilities. Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said partners did not warn Ukraine ahead of the first ballistic missile strike during the overnight attack on October 14, but did send notifications ahead of the three subsequent waves of strikes. A day earlier, Zelensky had said Ukraine had received no intelligence from Western partners about the Russian missile strike on Kyiv on October 12. “Intelligence about the launch of Russian ballistic missiles helps save people’s lives, and this is one of the most critical issues. This is exactly what helps prevent killings when there is a warning about ballistic missiles,” he said. According to Politico , the United States told Ukraine it had withheld intelligence about the missile strike on Kyiv on the evening of October 12 because of poor weather conditions. Ukrainian authorities fear “this might not have been the case.” U.S. President Donald Trump, asked directly by a journalist whether Washington had stopped sharing intelligence with Kyiv, answered: “No.” Earlier, the Financial Times reported that the United States had threatened to cut off intelligence sharing with Ukraine unless Kyiv stopped striking Russian oil refineries. On the morning of October 14, Ukrainian military personnel began reporting that SpaceX had restricted the operation of Starlink satellite terminals used by Ukrainian forces at the front. The restrictions affect Starshield, the military version of Starlink, and limit the speed of drones that rely on satellite communications. Starshield is faster and necessary for drone operators, a source in the Ukrainian military told Ukrainska Pravda, a Ukrainian news outlet. Regular Starlink, installed on drones, supports speeds of up to 160 kilometers per hour (99 mph), which is not enough for some missions. One commander sent the outlet a video showing two Ukrainian drones climbing into the sky and then “lose” their connection, unable to continue the mission. “Our defense forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and that led to the failure of a number of missions. It’s obvious that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation,” said Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to the Ukrainian president. SpaceX has not yet commented on the Ukrainian military’s statements. The war in photos. The aftermath of the missile strike on Kyiv Russian forces struck Kyiv overnight on October 14, killing three people and injuring 21, according to the latest data. A strike hit a multistory residential building in the Desnianskyi district. Among the injured is a child. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication. title: The West continues to warn Ukraine about missile attacks. Just not about all of them
body:
During the recent Russian ballistic missile attack on Ukraine, Kyiv did not receive a warning from its partners regarding the first wave of strikes. However, the first wave was followed by three subsequent ones, about which Ukraine was informed sufficiently in advance.
On the night between Tuesday and Wednesday, another Russian attack on Ukraine took place using ballistic missiles. The targets were energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, the Kyiv region, and Kharkiv. Russian forces deployed 39 ballistic missiles and over 120 drones . It was specifically the attack on the capital that Western partners failed to provide information about.
“The situation is similar to yesterday – we did not receive information from partners regarding the launch of missiles from enemy territory. The reasons are being established,” the Ukrainian Air Force reported via the Telegram messaging app. Yesterday’s situation refers to the attack on Monday at 22:10 local time. Russia used five missiles flying on ballistic trajectories at that time. The lack of warning was addressed yesterday by the Ukrainian Minister of Foreign Affairs, Andrii Sybiha, while participating in the Warsaw Security Forum conference. When asked about the overnight attacks, he confirmed that there were delays in the operation of the warning system. In his view, this was caused by the type of weaponry utilised by the Russians .
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy commented on the latest attack. He pointed out that Russia had targeted energy infrastructure – “ the very infrastructure covered by the ceasefire announced by the American President ” a few days ago. The American side must understand that Moscow will not adhere to a ceasefire, as has been proven many times already. The current shift in the Trump administration’s policy towards Russia may lead to the end of the war, but it will not be a favourable conclusion for Ukraine and Europe.
Overnight, the Russians used 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions against our energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, the Kyiv region, and Kharkiv. A targeted Russian ballistic missile strike specifically against energy infrastructure – the very infrastructure covered by the ceasefire announced by the American President. The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States. Russia does not consider the American President’s statements strong. Unfortunately, at least 600,000 people are now without power. Outages could become even more widespread. Unfortunately, there is significant damage to facilities and equipment – at 26 facilities of our power system and four facilities in the oil and gas sector. I am grateful to the repair crews, all Ukrainian energy workers, and the personnel of the State Emergency Service of Ukraine for all their efforts to address the aftermath of this Russian strike. Tragically, there have been fatalities and injuries. We ask America and EVERYONE in the world who does not turn a blind eye to reality to respond – and to respond forcefully. Russia has squandered the opportunity for de-escalation and has clearly chosen to continue its insane war of annihilation. We ask President Trump to impose STRONG sanctions on Russia, especially since the Lindsey Graham bill, which was recently passed and signed into law, authorizes and regulates such measures. The American President has all the effective and necessary tools to bring peace closer through strength, justice, and pressure on the aggressor. We ask for additional packages of Patriot missile interceptors for Ukraine. It is entirely fair for us to tell the United States, Europe, and all our partners that no country in the world should be left alone to face such a deranged and pro-war actor as Russia. I am grateful to everyone who helps Ukraine! Peace can only come through strength, and we ask America to remember this principle of Reagan’s. Glory to Ukraine!

title: Ambassador Alison Duncan Receives Prestigious Orthodox Honour in Athens
body: ATHENS, October 2026 — Archbishop Makarios of Australia has invested Australian Ambassador to Greece Alison Duncan with the Order of the Christ Loving. The ceremony took place at the Australian Residence in Athens. Ambassador Alison Duncan in Athens. Photo: Supplied The Order of the Christ Loving recognises Duncan’s distinguished service and generosity, the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia said. In addition, it honours her commitment to strengthening the longstanding relationship between Greece and Australia. It also acknowledges her support for the Greek Australian community and its efforts to preserve its cultural heritage. Guests at the Order of the Christ Loving ceremony Senior Greek government officials, Orthodox Church leaders and members of the diplomatic community attended the ceremony. Among the guests were Bishop Athinagoras of Canberra, Bishop Evmenios of Chora and Rev. Deacon Timothy Mavromatis. Guests at the Australian Residence, Athens. Minister of State Akis Skertsos and Deputy Foreign Minister Alexandra Papadopoulou also attended. This bond is shaped by diplomatic cooperation, shared values and the contributions of the Greek Australian community. title: Ambassador Alison Duncan Receives Prestigious Orthodox Honour in Athens
body: Australian Ambassador Alison Duncan has been invested with the Order of the Christ Loving by His Eminence Archbishop Makarios of Australia during a solemn ceremony at the Australian Residence in Athens. The honour recognises Ambassador Duncan’s distinguished service, generosity and commitment to strengthening the longstanding relationship between Greece and Australia, including her support for the Greek Australian community and its efforts to preserve its cultural heritage. The ceremony brought together senior Greek government officials, Orthodox Church leaders and members of the diplomatic community. Among the distinguished guests were His Grace Bishop Athinagoras of Canberra, His Grace Bishop Evmenios of Chora and Rev. Deacon Timothy Mavromatis. Greek government representatives included Deputy Prime Minister Kostis Hatzidakis, Minister of Education and Religious Affairs Sofia Zacharaki, Minister of State Akis Skertsos and Deputy Foreign Minister Alexandra Papadopoulou. Teresa Angelatou, Secretary General of the Greek Ministry of Foreign Affairs, also attended, alongside German Ambassador Andreas Kindl, Women Act co-founder May Zanni and Alice Kokodis. The occasion celebrated the enduring relationship between Greece and Australia, shaped by diplomatic cooperation, shared values and the contributions of the Greek Australian community. For generations, Greek Australians have helped maintain the cultural, linguistic and religious connections between the two countries, strengthening the bonds between their communities. The recognition of Ambassador Duncan highlights the importance of continued cooperation in preserving this shared heritage and fostering closer ties between Greece and Australia. Source: Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia The post Ambassador Alison Duncan Receives Prestigious Orthodox Honour in Athens appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: JAL orders up to 26 Embraer E190-E2 jets to replace J-AIR’s E170 and E190 fleets
body: Japan Airlines (JAL) announced on October 14, 2026, that it has ordered up to 26 Embraer E190-E2 aircraft to replace the regional jet fleet of its subsidiary J-AIR. The order includes 16 firm aircraft and 10 options, with deliveries scheduled to begin in fiscal year 2029. The E190-E2s will succeed J-AIR’s current Embraer E170 and E190 aircraft. From its main hub at Osaka International Airport (ITM), the regional carrier operates jet flights across Japan, from Memanbetsu in Hokkaido in the north to the Amami Islands in Kagoshima Prefecture in the south. Fleet renewal comes as Japan’s domestic market faces falling business demand and rising costs JAL said the decision is part of wider changes to its domestic operations. The market has been under pressure from declining business travel, Japan’s long-term population changes, and higher costs driven by inflation and the weak yen. Under its long-term strategy, the “JAL Group Management Vision 2035,” the airline aims to keep its domestic network sustainable, describing it as essential infrastructure for Japan. JAL called the E190-E2 a core part of that plan for J-AIR, saying the aircraft is suited to future demand and environmental goals and will support regional economies. JAL CEO says the E190-E2 will help sustain Japan’s regional air network for the next generation Mitsuko Tottori, JAL’s President and group CEO, said the domestic network supports local economies and daily life across Japan. She said the new aircraft, with its environmental performance and economic efficiency, would help the group maintain and develop a sustainable air network for the next generation while offering passengers a more comfortable experience. E190-E2 promises lower fuel burn, emissions, noise and maintenance costs According to JAL, the E190-E2’s new-generation engines and redesigned wing deliver significant gains in fuel efficiency and a substantial reduction in carbon emissions compared with previous-generation aircraft. The jet is also much quieter, which reduces the impact on communities near airports, and its reliability and durable components are expected to lower maintenance costs. The E190-E2 is powered by Pratt & Whitney PW1900G engines and typically seats between 97 and 114 passengers. It has a range of 5,463 kilometers (2,950 nautical miles), a length of 36.3 meters, a wingspan of 33.7 meters and a height of 10.7 meters. title: Allies Warn Ukraine of Delayed Missile Waves, Air Force Says
body:
Ukraine’s partners warned it about three waves of Russian ballistic missile attacks overnight, although no warning arrived before the first wave, Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said on Wednesday, Oct. 14.
Speaking during the national telethon, Ihnat clarified the sequence after earlier military statements and comments by President Volodymyr Zelensky raised questions about missing launch notifications.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“We gave our first report at around 10:40 p.m. that there had been no warnings from our partners about ballistics,” Ihnat said, according to RBC-Ukraine .
Warnings about the use of ballistic missiles did arrive during the following three waves, he added. Ihnat did not identify which partners provided them or explain why the initial warning was missing.
The clarification follows two consecutive evenings when Ukraine reported receiving no advance warning before Russian ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv.
Discussing the Monday, Oct. 12 attack in his Tuesday evening address, Zelensky said five missiles had been detected only seconds before impact.
“Normally, we receive advance warning from our partners, which are crucial for our defense,” he said.
After another strike on Tuesday evening, Zelensky again said there had been no advance warning. That attack hit Kyiv’s CHP-4 power plant and a residential building.
Ihnat’s Wednesday account confirms the absence of an initial alert while establishing that warnings were received later in the overnight attack.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha offered a different explanation for the delayed alert during Monday’s attack, attributing it to the type of weapon Russia used.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum on Tuesday, he confirmed that Ukraine continued receiving US intelligence . He did not disclose whether the scope of that cooperation had changed.
Trump also denied that Washington had stopped sharing intelligence .
“No, we haven’t,” he said when asked on Tuesday, adding: “We are helping them.” Neither statement explained why the missile-launch warnings had been missing.
Concerns intensified after reports that US envoys threatened to restrict intelligence sharing unless Ukraine stopped attacking Russian oil refineries.
Axios cited a Ukrainian official who said Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner conveyed that warning during talks in Miami. A US official disputed that an explicit threat had been made.
Zelensky subsequently told NPR that Washington had warned about a possible suspension of intelligence cooperation over refinery strikes, according to RBC-Ukraine’s account of the interview . The White House referred NPR to Trump’s remarks that intelligence sharing continued.
Officials have not publicly established a connection between those warnings and the missing missile alerts. Ihnat’s latest statement confirms that partners supplied information during the subsequent waves, but leaves the failure before the first strike unexplained.

title: Dubai launches literacy platform to help parents guide children on safe use of AI
body: Dubai has launched a digital platform designed to help parents guide their children in using artificial intelligence safely and responsibly. The Dubai Centre for Artificial Intelligence announced GenDubAI in collaboration with the Community Development Authority and Dubai Future Foundation, state news agency Wam reported on Wednesday. The platform aims to nurture creativity, protect privacy and strengthen family engagement, supporting the objectives of the Dubai Social Agenda 33 and the UAE's Year of the Family. Available in Arabic and English, GenDubAI is designed for families with children aged 8 to 15 and is accessible through a dedicated mobile-friendly version. The platform offers interactive content rooted in UAE values and culture, addressing key questions around AI use while helping children develop critical thinking and creativity. It also introduces parents to the fundamentals and tools of AI, highlighting its opportunities and challenges. Hessa bint Essa Buhumaid, director general of the CDA in Dubai, said the platform placed families at the heart of AI learning. "This initiative reflects Dubai's commitment to preparing future-ready generations by empowering young people to embrace technology with confidence and responsibility while preserving their values and identity," she said. Khalfan Belhoul, chief executive of Dubai Future Foundation, said the UAE was among the world's leading countries in AI adoption, and smart-device use among children continues to rise. "Knowledge of safe and responsible AI use is one of the greatest gifts parents can give their children to help them thrive in the age of AI," Mr Belhoul said. Saeed Al Falasi, executive director of the DCAI, said the platform was built around the concept of "family moments", offering content that can be integrated into everyday life and encouraging meaningful conversations about AI within the home. Mr Al Falasi added that GenDubAI will evolve continuously through new content, tools and educational pathways to keep pace with rapid advances in AI and the changing needs of families.

title: Residential buildings and agricultural enterprises hit in Rivne region, eight people injured
body:
The Rivne Regional Military Administration's press service stated this in a comment to Ukrinform.
"Following the morning attack on Rivne, five people were injured. Another three were injured at one of the agricultural enterprises," the press service said.

title: F-35C fighters complete landing and takeoff trials aboard aircraft carrier John F. Kennedy
body: The fighters belong to Air Test and Evaluation Squadron 23, known as VX-23. They took part in testing as the carrier approaches its formal entry into service. John F. Kennedy, designated CVN-79, left the shipyard on September 29 and moved to Norfolk after receiving preliminary technical acceptance. That acceptance cleared the way for military sea trials and checks of onboard systems. The ship is equipped with electromagnetic catapults, known as EMALS, and the Advanced Arresting Gear system for recovering aircraft. The F-35C tests covered launches and landings aboard the carrier. USS Gerald R. Ford, the first ship of the class, entered service in 2017. Its operational deployments to date have used air wings whose fighter squadrons operate Boeing F/A-18E/F Super Hornets. Plans for U.S. naval aviation call for 413 F-35Cs, with 140 destined for the Marine Corps and 273 for the Navy. Aircraft already delivered have been used extensively in combat, including operations against Iran.

title: Azerbaijan’s top cleric claims no hijab ban in schools
body: Azerbaijan’s top Muslim cleric has rejected claims that the country has banned the hijab in schools, as protests over school dress code restrictions have spread to Azerbaijani diplomatic missions in Turkey. Sheikh-ul-Islam Allahshukur Pashazadeh, head of the Caucasus Muslims Board, said on Tuesday the school uniform rules do not explicitly mention the hijab and accused unnamed forces of using religion to turn people against the state. The dispute has also sparked demonstrations in Ankara and Istanbul, where protesters have criticised Azerbaijan’s school dress code rules and its relations with Israel. Pashazadeh also claimed that protests against school dress code restrictions are being deliberately organised. Speaking to local media, Pashazadeh said that some people were using religion and spirituality to turn citizens against the state. ‘Who is inciting them to say these things? We know. The Azerbaijani people know, too. There are people who use their religion and spirituality to turn them against the state. I trust my state. If there is a problem […] This is not a problem. I do not even see it as a problem. It will be resolved’, Pashazadeh said. According to Pashazadeh, the decision introducing a uniform school dress code does not mention the hijab, and he claimed that presenting the issue as a hijab ban was a deliberate attempt to make it more contentious. ‘They call it a hijab issue. But the decision that was adopted does not mention the hijab; it refers to a uniform school dress code. They call it a hijab issue to make it more effective and influence Muslims’, he said. Pashazadeh also claimed that the protests had moved beyond religious concerns and had become a political campaign directed against the state. ‘We, as religious people, stand with our state today. All religious people should support our state and statehood. This state has been entrusted to us by the martyrs and the mothers of martyrs’, he added. The cleric further alleged that some families of soldiers killed in service had been drawn into the protests. He said he believed the issue would be resolved through the Ministry of Science and Education. Protests outside Azerbaijani diplomatic missions in Turkey The dispute has also prompted protests in Turkey. In Ankara, members of the Köklü Değişim movement gathered outside the Azerbaijani Embassy to protest restrictions related to wearing the hijab in schools. A large number of police officers were deployed to the area. The protesters criticised the school dress code rules, while the demonstrations have also featured accusations concerning Azerbaijan’s relations with Israel. A similar protest was held outside Azerbaijan’s Consulate General in Istanbul on 3 October. At the time, demonstrators also voiced criticism of Azerbaijan’s relations with Israel, and attempted to connect the two issues. Turkey has a contentious relationship with Israel, and Turkish society and officials across the political spectrum have long had issues with Azerbaijan’s close ties with the country.

title: Dispatch from Killhouse: Ukraine’s Lessons for US Army Drone Training
body:
Jordan Bower , Nico Martire and James L. Andreasen | 10.14.26
Inside a bunker, a pilot operates a first-person-view drone, unable to see the aircraft directly. A navigator plots a grid and helps search a degraded video feed. Somewhere in the cluttered environment the drone navigates is the target the operator seeks. But finding it is only the first task. To destroy the target, the pilot must have the skill to place the drone within a few feet for five seconds.
The drone crashes. This is not a mission failure, however. It is a learning opportunity—because the pilot and navigator are at a training site. The target they sought was a twelve-inch designator, affixed to a room, a vehicle, a culvert, a tree, or any other object depending on the training iteration. Finding the target demonstrates an important capability. So does the hover. And after the crash, the team recovers the aircraft, diagnoses the problem, repairs or replaces what is needed, and flies again.
This is Killhouse. And the training it delivers holds lessons for the US Army as it seeks to develop the skills its formations will need on tomorrow’s battlefield.
We had the opportunity recently to visit the Killhouse training site and document the training delivered during the site’s six-day First-Person-View (FPV) Pro Course. Its sixteen students demonstrated simulator proficiency before beginning repeated live flights built around crew coordination, degraded video, cluttered terrain, payload effects, maintenance, and increasingly complex tactical tasks. The key lesson for the US Army is to protect advanced-course time for skills that require specialized facilities and instructors. Basic aircraft control should be learned before arrival.
The Army is already moving in that direction. In July 2026, Fort Rucker’s Unmanned Advanced Lethality Course (UALC) reported increasing kinetic engagements from five to twelve and announced a culminating exercise at a new drone training facility incorporating close-quarters battle training. The facility opened in April with an indoor drone flying course, classrooms, and labs. UALC leaders said they would use it to progress soldiers from basic flight skills toward lethality.
The new facility is the Army aviation branch’s effort to re-create the Killhouse training model using lessons from the course in Ukraine. But to do that requires first answering a fundamental question: What should advanced FPV training actually produce?
Advanced training should produce a crew that can employ the system when the video degrades, the terrain closes in, the aircraft carries mission-representative weight, and components begin to fail. The crew must still navigate, communicate, troubleshoot, and complete a tactical task. Sustained practice beyond that proficiency standard develops expertise.
The first thing Killhouse got right was the entrance standard. Students were tested immediately on the Liftoff simulator and had to demonstrate stable hovering, controlled yaw without drift, and precision landings before moving to live aircraft. Instructors could then move directly to the harder skills that justify scarce range time and specialized cadre.
Students should establish simulator proficiency before entering advanced FPV courses. Units can build basic stick skills at home station with commercially available simulators, controllers, and a published performance standard. The advanced course can validate that baseline on arrival. Regardless of simulator choice, students must demonstrate controlled manual flight, commonly called acro mode, before beginning advanced training.
That division of labor creates a training pipeline the Army can sustain. Home stations develop basic pilots. Institutional and specialized courses develop tactical crews and instructors. Units then sustain those skills through repetition. Prerequisites keep advanced-course time focused on advanced tasks.
At Killhouse, students operated in pilot-navigator teams. Each team worked from a bunker-based ground control station while launch and recovery occurred outside. The navigator helped plot grids, coordinated launch and recovery, supported target search, and maintained the crew’s broader picture. The pilot concentrated on aircraft control and interpreting the video feed. That structure forced communication and division of labor from the beginning.
The target set reinforced the same logic. Dozens of small numbered placards were placed in rooms, vehicles, culverts, vegetation, and behind concrete or other obstructions that degraded the signal and complicated target acquisition. Students had to search, orient, associate the video with the terrain, and hold a stable hover near the target before receiving the next task. The standard required precise control as the crew’s view deteriorated, a skill that gives operators time to identify a target before committing to an engagement.
The course also treated sustainment as part of employment. Crashes were expected. Students managed batteries, tightened components, identified faults, and remained accountable for the condition of their aircraft. Engineers supported repairs while operators remained responsible for resolving faults. Students often ran to recover crashed drones and disconnect their batteries to prevent further damage. Recovery, repair, and after-action review returned the crew to another flight quickly.
FPV capability depends on the crew, controller, video link, batteries, antennas, navigation, launch and recovery procedures, spectrum management, repair, and tactical integration. As the Army builds out its drone training enterprise, that effort must reflect the reality that evaluating only whether an individual can fly leaves most of the overall system untested.
Killhouse introduced signal degradation and visual clutter early in the course. Beginning on the second day, aircraft carried added weight that changed handling and endurance. Controlled training also exposed students to imperfect but serviceable equipment, forcing them to recognize the difference between a nuisance, a developing fault, and a condition that required repair.
That approach built a useful habit: Students continued to think while the aircraft became harder to fly. They learned to slow down, search deliberately, use terrain association, and preserve control as the video degraded. The final progression included dynamic targets and a tightly controlled terminal-effects block, connecting piloting to tactical employment.
The Army should not copy Ukrainian wartime risk tolerance or assume every Ukrainian practice belongs on an American range. Airspace, safety authorities, equipment, force structure, and mission profiles differ. However, Killhouse provides a benchmark for training standards and practices, and from there FPV training can be adapted to US requirements. Its prerequisites, crew training, demanding range design, and emphasis on sustainment can inform American courses without importing every wartime practice.
The Army’s Progress Needs a Common Standard
Army programs now address several parts of this requirement. In February 2026, the Maneuver Center of Excellence launched a pilot of the Robotic Autonomous Systems Leader Tactics Course to teach leaders how to integrate those systems into tactical planning. At Fort Indiantown Gap, the Unmanned Aircraft System Training and Innovation Facility began training instructors on the Neros Archer FPV system . The Joint Multinational Readiness Center’s Drone Validation Course trains opposing-force soldiers to employ FPV and other small drones in demanding terrain. These programs demonstrate progress toward different objectives and must be assessed against their respective training purposes.
As those programs expand, the Army needs a common understanding of what advanced FPV crews must be able to do. Otherwise, courses can carry the same label while training students to different standards. Killhouse demonstrates a training progression in which crews build on basic aircraft control to employ the system under representative constraints.
Training quality also affects acquisition decisions. In June 2026, priority transformation-in-contact units received hands-on training on multiple Group 2 medium-range reconnaissance drones before selecting systems through the Army’s Unmanned Aircraft Systems Marketplace. In August, that storefront became the air domain of the Department of Defense’s broader Drone Marketplace . The purchases involved reconnaissance platforms, but the same evaluation problem applies to FPV aircraft. User feedback is useful only when evaluators can distinguish a platform limitation from a training, communications, or employment problem. Evaluators must test systems under representative contested conditions to assess operational suitability.
The Army can carry these lessons into its expanding training system doing three things. First, the service should establish a performance-based simulator gate for advanced FPV courses. Students should demonstrate controlled manual flight, stable hover, deliberate yaw, and precision landing before using specialized facilities and instructor time. Those who do not meet the standard should complete additional home-station preparation.
Second, the Army should require installations to make representative FPV training routine. That requires approved areas for beyond-visual-line-of-sight training, varied terrain, crew operations, realistic communications constraints, payload-representative configurations, repair support, and safe terminal-effects training where authorized. Federal Aviation Administration and military airspace authorization processes already exist; installations must coordinate the applicable airspace, range, safety, and spectrum requirements to provide predictable access. As Charlie Phelps argued in a 2025 article , installations must supply the airspace and infrastructure for drone readiness. Once soldiers have a place to fly, the course must make them solve demanding problems there.
Third, the Army should develop instructors and evaluators who combine tactical experience with technical competence. Selected operators, maintainers, communications specialists, software and hardware experts, and acquisition personnel should observe mature partner training, compare it with US practice, and bring those lessons back into schoolhouses and field evaluations. Recurring exposure to current equipment and employment methods would help keep courses and requirements aligned with a capability area that changes faster than normal institutional cycles.
Graduation should depend on what a crew can repeatedly demonstrate. A useful standard would require tactical navigation and target-search tasks in both pilot and navigator roles, operation through degraded video, control of a payload-representative aircraft, recovery from common faults, and compliance with safety and crew-coordination standards. Courses should document performance against those tasks so that a qualification means the same thing when a soldier returns to a unit.
The Army is expanding drone courses, facilities, and acquisition pathways. These are important steps. But to maximize capability across its formations, it should establish common performance standards now, before programs settle on different definitions of proficiency. FPV capability requires crews that can employ the system through degraded video, difficult terrain, and imperfect equipment while completing tactical tasks.
These are the lessons we witnessed firsthand at Killhouse.
Warrant Officer 1 Jordan Bower is a US Army warrant officer who served with an operational data team supporting Ukraine. His work there included observation and analysis of FPV training and employment.
Master Sergeant Nico Martire serves with I Corps on an operational data team. He previously served with an operational data team supporting Ukraine.
Chief Warrant Officer 3 James L. Andreasen is an AH-64E Apache instructor pilot and aviation mission survivability officer at Fort Rucker, Alabama. Following a six-month assignment with Security Assistance Group–Ukraine, he contributes to the Unmanned Advanced Lethality Course and Army aviation modernization efforts focused on unmanned systems integration.

title: Russia Fumes as Top Gymnasts Blocked From World Championships in Netherlands
body:
Russia has accused Dutch authorities of denying visas to three of Russia’s leading female gymnasts for the World Championships in Rotterdam, which kick off this weekend, and jeopardizing their qualification path for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Reigning world all-around champion Angelina Melnikova, Tokyo 2020 team Olympic champion Viktoria Listunova and 2026 European silver medalist Anna Kalmykova have all reportedly been refused visas, the Russian Gymnastics Federation said Tuesday, citing the Dutch Embassy in Moscow.
The refusal notices apparently expressed diplomatic concerns, stating that “one or several Schengen member states consider the athletes a threat to their international relations.”
“We view the actions of the Dutch authorities as a deliberate elimination of the strongest gymnasts from competition for world medals and Olympic quotas,” the Russian Gymnastics Federation said.
The Dutch foreign and sports ministries declined to comment on individual visa applications, but clarified to local media that the refusals were unrelated to athletic performance.
The three denied athletes have faced scrutiny from Ukrainian sports authorities over their ties to the Russian military and public displays supporting the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Melnikova represents the military-affiliated CSKA sports club and has previously posted social media photographs featuring the pro-war “Z” symbol.
Listunova took part in a March 2022 pro-war rally with President Vladimir Putin and was previously denied neutral status by World Gymnastics over pro-military social media posts.
Kalmykova holds a sports contract with the Russian National Guard, according to Ukrainian officials.
Russia’s Ambassador to the Netherlands Vladimir Tarabrin said he personally visited the Dutch Foreign Ministry to demand visas, but was presented with “utterly unconvincing arguments that defy any reasonable criticism.”
Russian Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyaryov said the Russian Olympic Committee will lobby to strip the Rotterdam championship of its official Olympic qualifying status.
The Oct. 17-25 World Artistic Gymnastics Championships in Rotterdam serve as the opening team qualifier for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games.
Out of 61 members of the Russian delegation, 47 were granted Dutch visas, including five male and three female gymnasts.
World Gymnastics and European Gymnastics lifted restrictions on Russian and Belarusian gymnasts after the International Olympic Committee provisionally lifted its ban on the countries’ Olympic committees in July.

title: Ghana faces $6.1bn debt-service burden from 2027 to 2029 due to Akufo-Addo’s DDEP – Haruna Iddrisu
body: Education Minister Haruna Iddrisu says Ghana is expected to face approximately US$6.1 billion in debt-service obligations between 2027 and 2029, which he attributes to debt restructuring and Eurobond negotiations concluded under the erstwhile Akufo-Addo administration. Speaking on Joy FM’s Super Morning Show on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, the Tamale South Member of Parliament warned that the obligations would continue to put pressure on public finances and constrain resources available for national development. Mr Iddrisu cited an assessment reportedly by the World Bank, which indicates that Ghana faces substantial debt-service payments over the next three years. He said the financial commitments could narrow the fiscal space available to President John Dramani Mahama’s administration to finance major infrastructure projects, invest in education and implement its broader development agenda. The Education Minister questioned how much public revenue would remain for critical national priorities when significant resources had to be committed to servicing inherited debt. He also challenged the New Patriotic Party’s claims of superior economic management, arguing that the consequences of borrowing and the subsequent debt restructuring under the previous administration would continue to affect the country beyond its tenure. Mr Iddrisu maintained that the current government’s fiscal challenges must be considered in the context of the debt obligations it inherited. He said the government would have to balance debt servicing with investment in essential public services and measures to support economic growth.

title: EU disburses close to 3 billion euros of defense money to Ukraine ahead of leaders summit
body:
The EU disbursed 2.86 billion euros ($3.2 billion) in military support to Ukraine on Oct. 14 as part of the bloc's 90 billion-euro ($100 billion) support loan for Kyiv.
"With today's 2.86 billion euro disbursement, we keep addressing Ukraine's most urgent operational needs," said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
The funding will go towards drones, air defense systems, missiles, radars, electronic warfare systems, and ammunition, reads a European Commission press statement.
"As Russia stalls on the front lines, it continues to escalate its aerial attacks — cruelly targeting Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure. Europe's steadfast support matters more than ever to help Ukraine protect its skies," von der Leyen said.
The disbursement lands one day before EU leaders are set to meet for a two-day summit, which President Volodymyr Zelensky is also expected to attend.
"Ukraine will be front and center at this week's European Council," von der Leyen said after an Oct. 11 call with Zelensky.
The latest disbursement was also previewed as a result of that call, with Zelensky thanking von der Leyen for the payment in a Telegram post .
"These funds will strengthen us," Zelensky said.
The latest announcement follows a previous disbursement of 1.24 billion euros ($1.4 billion) in defense support on Oct. 7, and further disbursements from the EU are expected until the end of the year.
Within the EU's 90 billion euro loan, 28.3 billion euros ($31.7 billion) were earmarked for Ukraine's defense needs in 2026, of which 18.26 billion euros ($20.44 billion) have now been disbursed.
Ukraine's plans for how to spend the remaining 10 billion euros ($11.2 billion) have already been approved by the EU; all that is required is for Kyiv to send the receipts for sign-off by Brussels.

title: Licences of 17 Sanad services cancelled
body:
MUSCAT: The Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Investment Promotion (MOCIIP) has announced the cancellation of licences of 17 Sanad Services Centres for violating the provisions of the regulations governing their operations. The ministry said the action was taken in accordance with Regulation No 244/2022 as part of its regular monitoring efforts to ensure service quality and compliance with applicable regulations. The affected establishments include 15 in the Wilayat of Salalah, one in the Wilayat of Sohar and one in the Wilayat of Thamrait. The ministry reaffirmed the importance of ensuring that all Sanad Services Centres comply with the approved regulations and guidelines governing their operations.

title: Container ship sinks after hitting mine in Strait of Hormuz — IRGC
body:
TEHRAN, October 14. /TASS/. A container ship attempting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz along a route not agreed upon with the Iranian authorities has sunk after striking a mine, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said.
The incident occurred in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday morning, the Mehr news agency reported, citing the IRGC. An explosion caused the vessel to catch fire and sink.
The ship was carrying about 2,500 containers.
The report did not specify the ship’s owner or provide information about the fate of its crew.

title: Pro-Iran hackers claim responsibility for cyberattack on Azerbaijan, citing hijab ban
body: In a statement released on Wednesday, Azerbaijani authorities announced that they were experiencing ‘intensive cyberattacks’ against ‘state information infrastructures’. A pro-Iranian hacker group has claimed responsibility for the attack, while Azerbaijan has blamed a ‘foreign hacker group’. Azerbaijan’s State Service for Special Communications and Information Security said that the attacks were recorded ‘starting at around 22:00 on 13 October 2026'. ‘The attack was carried out by a foreign hacker group, targeting more than 100 state domains on the state information infrastructure of the Republic of Azerbaijan.’ Azerbaijan has not specified which country they are blaming for the attack, but the ‘313 Team,’ a pro-Iranian hacker group believed to be operating out of Iraq, has claimed responsibility, In a Telegram statement on Tuesday at 21:00 Baku time, the group said they had ‘launched a massive, sophisticated cyberattack targeting 47 key IP ranges belonging to the Republic of Azerbaijan’s government digital infrastructure.’ The group named Azerbaijan’s ban on hijabs in schools as motivation and said the attack would last 24 hours. ‘We have received numerous complaints against the government of the Republic of Azerbaijan regarding the ban on female students wearing the hijab in schools and universities. Given the significant size of the Shia community in Azerbaijan, we will take firm action against the state: we will completely destroy its government digital infrastructure.’ The 313 Team claimed that the cyberattack’s intensity exceeded ‘2.5 terabits per second’ and ‘caused a complete paralysis of all Azerbaijani government websites—including the official state portal, as well as the sites of the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Interior’. They said 1,825 government websites were offline. Azerbaijani authorities have said 100 domains were affected. While the agency claimed that ‘the effects of the cyberattack were limited and the continuity of the sites' activities was ensured,’ OC Media journalists were unable to access many Azerbaijani government websites at the time of reporting: including domains for the Ministry of Defense, Ministry of Science and Education, Ministry of Emergency Situations, and Ministry of Health. Other domains, such as for the State Security Service, appear to be working but at a slower pace. The cyberattack comes after several social media sites, including Instagram and TikTok, were blocked in Azerbaijan on 12 October as the country experiences growing protests against a ban on students and teachers wearing hijab in public schools. The social media blackout seems to have lifted as of this morning, with social media users in Baku claiming that they no longer have to use a VPN. Explainer | Why are schoolchildren protesting a hijab ban in Azerbaijan? The protests against the hijab ban in schools appear to be some of the largest public demonstrations in years. OC Media Rafig Shahbazov The cyberattack comes as tensions between Iran and Azerbaijan have intensified since Baku implemented a ban on wearing hijabs in schools for students and teachers. Iran and Azerbaijan’s relationship has been historically highly fractious but with a larger ethnic Azerbaijani population than the entire population of the Republic of Azerbaijan, Tehran has historically approached its policies cautiously, as missteps could alienate the country’s largest ethnic minority. What recent Baku–Tehran tensions reveal about Iranian Azerbaijan Tehran is cautious of alienating its largest ethnic minority, leaving Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in crisis mode. OC Media Nigar Hasanova Baku has historically closely watched Tehran’s policies towards Azerbaijanis, especially during periods of political tension between the two countries. However, relations seem to have gone into freefall during the recent hijab protests, with Azerbaijani authorities accusing Iranian outlets and figures of inflating the situation. On Wednesday, Azerbaijan’s media council claimed that Iran’s Saher TV channel was deliberately spreading misinformation around the protests – claiming that the state channel was presenting footage of an event from Turkey as ‘a protest organised in our country to support individuals wearing hijabs’. The council has also claimed that ‘public figures, politicians, and even officials’ from multiple foreign countries were ‘actively participating in targeted information campaigns against Azerbaijan’, specifically saying there had been an ‘intensification’ in attacks from Iran and Turkey. This is a developing story.

title: Bauchi records 70 human trafficking cases, three convictions – NAPTIP
body:
The National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons (NAPTIP) recorded 70 human trafficking cases in Bauchi State between January and October 2026, securing three convictions during the period.
The agency also rescued 25 indigenes of the state who were trafficked to North Africa, according to the state coordinator, Aliyun Kalli.
Mr Kalli disclosed the figures on Tuesday during a two-day review workshop on the Bauchi State Youth Policy Development Framework, organised by the state’s Sustainable Development Goals office with support from the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA).
He said most of the victims were young people lured abroad with false promises of better opportunities.
Mr Kalli urged young people to take advantage of local skills acquisition programmes and other economic opportunities rather than risk dangerous journeys that could expose them to trafficking and exploitation.
He said three convictions had been secured from the 70 cases recorded during the period, while other cases remained before the courts.
The coordinator did not provide details of the convictions or specify how many of the remaining cases had been charged in court.
He added that NAPTIP was profiling returned migrants and working to reintegrate them into their communities.
Mr Kalli also disclosed that the agency was investigating local agents allegedly involved in recruiting young girls from rural communities for exploitation in urban centres.
He did not provide details of the alleged recruitment activities or disclose whether arrests had been made in connection with the investigations.
The coordinator said NAPTIP’s anti-trafficking efforts were built around five strategic pillars: prevention, protection, prosecution, partnership and policy.
He added that the agency had conducted awareness campaigns in more than 50 communities, motor parks and schools across Bauchi State in 2026.
The campaigns also included radio and television engagements, as well as outreach programmes targeting women’s groups.
Mr Kalli urged young people to remain patient and engage in productive activities, expressing optimism that ongoing government reforms would create more opportunities for them within the country.

title: Raytheon Wins 8B U S Air Force Contract for Nuclear Communications Modernization
body:
The U.S. Air Force has awarded Raytheon an $8 billion contract to modernize Strategic Communications Terminals supporting the United States’ Nuclear Command, Control and Communications (NC3) architecture.
According today’s U.S. Department of War announcement, the contract covers terminal developmental modernization, production restart services and technical studies. Work will take place in Marlborough, Massachusetts, and Largo, Florida, through October 12, 2036. The contract is administered by the Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center (AFNWC) at Hanscom Air Force Base, Massachusetts.
NC3 architecture and strategic terminals
The AFNWC manages secure, survivable and jam-resistant networks connecting nuclear command authorities, command centres and operational forces. These systems are designed to preserve critical communications during electronic jamming and high-altitude electromagnetic pulse (HEMP) events. The AFNWC Integration Directorate oversees the AN/USQ-225 weapon system, the overarching framework for the Air Force’s contribution to the U.S. NC3 architecture.
The broader terminal portfolio supports satellite, ground-based, mobile and airborne communications, including the Advanced Extremely High Frequency (AEHF) and legacy Milstar satellite networks.
Global Aircrew Strategic Network Terminal (Global ASNT)
Managed by the AFNWC Nuclear Networks Division, Global ASNT distributes emergency action messages and aircrew alerts to strategic bomber, missile-related and supporting aircraft crews. The programme comprises 90 terminals: 45 fixed and 45 transportable. It uses extremely high frequency (EHF) waveforms and an Equipment Control Unit capable of simultaneous encryption and decryption.
Its three development increments provide:
Increment 1: Compatibility with Milstar and AEHF satellite constellations.
Increment 2: High-frequency (HF) communications and local message distribution through pagers, radios and base klaxons.
Increment 3: Redundant message reception using very low frequency (VLF) waveforms.
Family of Advanced Beyond Line-of-Sight Terminals (FAB-T)
FAB-T provides protected, high-bandwidth satellite communications for airborne command posts and strategic aircraft. It interfaces with the AEHF constellation and supports extended data rate (XDR) signals of up to 8.192 Mbps, offering higher throughput than legacy Milstar systems.
Associated platforms include the B-2 Spirit, B-52 Stratofortress, RC-135, E-4B National Airborne Operations Center and E-6B Mercury.
SMART-T (Secure Mobile Anti-jam Reliable Tactical-Terminal): Transportable satellite communications supporting tactical and strategic forces in electronically contested environments.
SCAMP (Single-Channel Antijam Man-Portable Terminal): A portable EHF terminal providing secure communications for personnel in remote locations.
Common Very Low Frequency Receiver (CVR): Hardened receiver equipment designed to capture low-data-rate strategic instructions under severely disrupted communications conditions.
Together, these systems provide alternative communications pathways across ground, mobile and airborne platforms.
