title: AI isn't just a tool and it might be dangerous
body:
Published on 14/10/2026 Updated on 19/10/2026
I've seen many people claim that AI is just another tool that boosts our productivity and we should embrace it. They say that AI will not only fail to make us obsolete but will also create new jobs. But is this the case and are the people, who think otherwise, paranoid?
It seems reasonable to think that AI is just another tool, since any historical discovery and advancement didn't make us jobless. Calculators and even computers didn't make accountants and mathematicians obsolete, similarly, feller bunchers didn't do the same to human loggers.
And it seems this will be true forever. I'd love to think this way, but there is a problem, AI has one crucial difference: unlike any other tool, it doesn't just solve or automate some narrow problem, it also constantly learns, improves and adapts like us. And once AI does something faster, cheaper and with higher quality than an average person, that average person will be replaced. Nowadays, a non artist can quickly (often under a minute) generate a good image that an average artist could produce only in several hours if not days. A couple of years ago, such images were that artist's bread and butter... The same thing is happening in many other professions. A lot of things, including intelligence or uncommon skills, are starting to turn into commodities.
Being average, let alone below average / disabled, is becoming more of a disadvantage. And that's the problem. Most people are average , they are not gifted or some kind of genius, they are AVERAGE . And sooner or later, AI is likely to outperform them in many domains. Meanwhile, for people with jobs the rat race wheel spins even faster by creating more workload, more pressure, more expectations, more anxiety, more detachment and more burnout.
For now, manual labor and other professions requiring interaction with the physical world seem safe. But once AI agents acquire robotic bodies, workers in these fields will also become vulnerable.
The most horrifying thing is that modern AI can rival even the most gifted people. For example, AI models can be so capable that they can solve math problems so complex that even the best mathematicians have been struggling to solve them for decades, if not centuries. Don't you believe? Just watch this video:
The guy in the video is Terence Tao, who is called the "Mozart of Math" and is considered to be one of the greatest mathematicians in the human history. This means that AI is beginning to challenge one of the things we traditionally considered the pinnacle of human intelligence: the ability to reason about extremely abstract problems that require extraordinary creativity, intuition, and intellectual sophistication.
And this touches one important problem related to capitalism. Capitalism has been remarkably successful at incentivizing innovation, increasing productivity, and organizing complex economic activity. But it doesn't necessarily optimize for human well being. It mostly rewards things that generate profit.
For much of industrial history, those goals overlapped sufficiently: businesses needed productive workers, workers earned wages, and wages allowed them to consume what businesses produced. And capitalism has a fundamental problem. If AI allows companies to produce the same output with 90% fewer employees, adopting AI may be the economically rational decision. But if every company does the same thing, an economy organized around employment income faces a problem. The tension is that what is rational for an individual company can be harmful for society. This is especially awkward when scarcity is no longer a major issue.
In recent years Universal basic income (UBI) is being discussed largely because of the concerns about unemployment caused by AI. UBI is a minimum income that people (even unemployed) receive unconditionally. So, UBI might be the solution to this awful situation.
How much UBI is feasible, is debatable, but at least it could help to cover food / bills and reduce income insecurity. UBI still doesn't necessarily mean a completely fulfilling life and might be insufficient to sustain a family and to have many other optional joys of life. It just guarantees a life without starvation, homelessness and income insecurity. Although, with the right governmental incentives and the future AI / automation increase, UBI might become less taxing, thus it can increase.
In any case, UBI might be the only viable option for some people. Time will tell whether we will have a universal basic income. See you later.

title: New Starlink restrictions disrupt Ukrainian drone missions. Kyiv adviser says move is tied to “political situation”
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine’s presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said SpaceX had imposed a 100 mph (160 km/h) speed limit on its military Starshield service overnight into 14 October, disrupting several missions without warning Ukraine’s defense forces. Ukraine’s forces use Starlink-connected drones to strike Russian positions and logistics, including targets behind the front line. Unlike earlier restrictions introduced at Kyiv’s request to stop Russian forces from exploiting Starlink, the latest change reportedly targets the military Starshield service and was imposed without warning Ukraine’s military. What the new restriction covers Beskrestnov wrote that the restriction applies to the “military package” of Starshield services. He said the move “obviously cannot be a coincidence” and was connected with the “current political situation,” but did not explain what he meant. Activist Serhii Sternenko, a former adviser to Ukraine’s defense minister, reported that connections began disappearing at speeds above 160 km/h. He suggested SpaceX had acted at the Trump administration’s request but provided no evidence. Starlink does not work inside Russia, and the drones hitting Russia’s oil industry use other means of communication, Reuters noted . Sternenko added that the ordinary satellite terminals were still working. Later on 14 October, Sternenko wrote that, according to military reports, restrictions had been tightened further, with connections starting to drop at 60–70 km/h. Beskrestnov later warned that the restriction also hits Starlink-linked interceptor drones, which he called Ukraine’s most effective current defense against jet-powered Shaheds. Front-line units report dropped connections Ukraine’s 7th Rapid Reaction Corps confirmed the disruptions in a statement to Reuters. The corps’ press service told Novynarnia that its units on the Huliaipole front began experiencing problems overnight. The corps said the change affected drones controlled through Starlink in flight and concerned Starshield’s data-transmission speed, which it said had previously been unrestricted. The corps said connections could disappear for 10–20 seconds at movement speeds of 110–120 km/h, complicating drone control. Flying slower creates its own risk, it said, because “slower targets become more vulnerable to being hit by the enemy.” Some high-speed drones, particularly mid-range strike models, must reach high speed quickly, the corps said. An unstable connection “will make it impossible to launch such aircraft or use them as intended.” Since the start of the day, one unmanned systems unit on the Huliaipole front had to cancel some missions because of connection problems, the corps said. Earlier limits came at Kyiv’s request In late January, SpaceX began restricting Starlink in Ukraine at Kyiv’s request after Russian forces started mounting terminals on strike drones. After Russian drones struck a passenger train in Kharkiv Oblast on 27 January, Beskrestnov, then an adviser to the defense minister, suggested one of them may have been controlled via Starlink. In early February, Ukraine introduced a whitelist under which only registered terminals could continue operating. Beskrestnov called the earlier countermeasures “temporary” and “emergency.” SpaceX had not publicly commented on the restriction, and Ukraine’s Defense Ministry was looking into its cause, Radio Svoboda reported . Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski asked Elon Musk on X whether he was “playing politics with your products again,” adding: “As your European customers, we are watching you.” Read also Can Starlink block Russian drones? Yes — but the devil’s in the details SpaceX begins blocking Russian drones exploiting Starlink over Ukraine Fears that Ukraine will lose Starlink are back after Musk backed Trump against Zelenskyy. Adviser says profit makes cutoff unlikely

title: Nigerian man, Adebayo arrested in Canada after exposing self to three victims
body: A Nigerian man has been arrested in Canada after allegedly exposing himself to three victims in separate incidents aboard Toronto’s public transit system. The suspect, identified as Adebayo Maoli, 28, of Toronto, is facing one count of sexual assault and two counts of indecent act, according to the Toronto Police Service. Police said the first incident occurred on September 1 at about 3 p.m. aboard a southbound Toronto Transit Commission (TTC) subway train at King Station. The suspect allegedly exposed himself to two victims before leaving the train after they activated the security alarm. In a separate incident on October 3, at approximately 12:10 a.m., the accused allegedly followed a person who had alighted from a subway train at College Station. Investigators said both individuals boarded an escalator, where the suspect allegedly exposed himself to the victim. “The victim verbally confronted the accused, who fled the area,” the Toronto Police Service said in a news release. Maoli was subsequently arrested and charged in connection with the incidents. He was scheduled to appear in bail court on October 9. Police said they believe there may be additional victims and urged anyone with relevant information to contact the Toronto Police Service or Crime Stoppers anonymously. The investigation is ongoing, and the allegations against the accused have not been tested in court. title: These workers help train robots who could one day steal their jobs
body:
KARUR, India — Three men stride across a cavernous textile factory floor of Texworth in the southern Indian city of Karur, handing GoPros and smart glasses to workers, including 40-year-old Shoba Kirubakaran. She's packing yellow aprons decorated with chickens into plastic wrapping for the brand Designs By Danica . It's the third time Kirubakaran says she's been told to don a GoPro.
It's recording her every hand gesture, to train AI robots to take over this job — a fact that she says the company did not share with her. NPR informed her when they interviewed her on a recent day. "Nobody told me anything about it," she says.
Kirubakaran has worked in the factory for 10 years, six days a week, from around 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. She makes $90 a month. With that money, she's helped her husband, a rickshaw driver, raise their two sons. And she adds, "I only know how to do this job."
Scenes like these shook the Indian public in April after a video went viral showing rows of textile factory workers wearing these headsets. "This is not a scene from a science fiction film," warned one news anchor from outlet News9Live. "That is happening right now on factory floors across India." Another outlet, AsiaNet News warned: "Indian workers are training AI robots to take their jobs."
India is emerging as one key place to record this kind of footage because of its large population, relatively low wages and relative openness to new tech. And developers need millions of hours of this footage, what the industry calls egocentric data — data gathered from the perspective of a human with a camera to train AI robots.
"That can be obtained only by emulating or collecting data from real human beings that does the job," says Prathosh A.P. , a professor at the Indian Institute of Science in Bengaluru . Like many other Indians, he uses initials to refer to his family name. "Think of today's AIs as brains without a body," he says. "Now you have to give them all motor skills ... to do all kinds of intricate motions that we do using a physical body."
Some workers are signing up because they're paid by the hour for the data. But it appears many others, like Kirubakaran, are simply made to record herself working without any explanation. "Call it what it is, which is exploitation of labor," says Astha Kapoor, co-founder of the Aapti Institute, which studies the impact of technology on people.
What will the impact be for India's workforce — the world's second largest, with 600 million people working or seeking work? "Training workers, retraining workers, absorbing them into new occupations," says Amit Basole , economics professor at Azim Premji University. "Do we have the policy agility to do that? I doubt it."
But that vision of a future full of factory and domestic robots isn't exactly around the corner, say some experts. AI robots are unlikely to be deployed at scale in India — in the near future at least — because they cost a lot of money and consume a lot of power, which is both unreliable and costly across parts of India. "We may be able to make the robots, but they're bloody expensive to run, right?" says Kapoor of the Aapti Institute. "Humans are cheaper to run than robots."
That power crisis is evident even in Karur, where an Indian tech company, Objectways, gathers egocentric data to sell onto AI developers. Massive generators loudly rumble to ensure seamless electricity in the buildings it powers. The company appears to be one of the town's biggest white-collar employers, occupying at least four building blocks in the town.
The CEO, Ravi Shankar, is a Karur native who migrated to Arizona decades ago. He's in perhaps unlikely agreement with Kapoor about the deployment of AI robots in India. "I think it will be more expensive," he says of AI robots, in comparison to human labor. "I don't think it's going to be cheaper."
He says his Indian clients want help designing AI robots for jobs that they can't find people to do, like tapping rubber from rubber trees; jobs that are geographically isolated, like dusting off solar panels in rural areas, and jobs that are physically grueling, like destemming chiles for processing.
Inside Objectways, employee Rajeshkumar Ramaswamy shows us how they are training other robots to do repetitive industrial jobs for foreign clients, through what he calls collecting exocentric data — that's data collected from the point of view of a robot. Instead of filming hands of actual workers, young men with GoPro cameras strapped to their heads record themselves doing jobs while holding and manipulating what look like grippy robot claws. One man records himself using the claws to screw bottle lids off and on.
There are dozens of bottles — big, small, plastic, metallic. Ramaswamy says it's to teach robots how to identify all the different shapes and sizes of this thing called a water bottle. The "robot needs to learn what is [a] water bottle," he says.
Ramaswamy says they'll repeat this process of screwing bottle tops about 100 times and feed that data into an AI robot, so it can see for itself how to use its own grippy hands to do the job.
"The robot is like a child," Ramaswamy says. "We are the humans. We are teaching the robots what needs to be done."
The company also trains robots to do household tasks — like folding towels, putting away books and unpacking bags. It sells that data to AI companies hoping to create domestic robots — there's already a few on the market, including one prominent model that looks like a faceless servant and retails for $20,000 .
Up a few flights of stairs, Ramaswamy shows us where they have humans recording themselves doing domestic jobs, on a floor kitted out to look like an Ikea-style three-bedroom house. In a fake kitchen, a woman, Rani N., records herself chopping onions.
Most clients who want first-person recordings of domestic chores are in the U.S., so Ramaswamy says they also pay Americans to record themselves doing housework — so their clients can train AI robots on American-specific data.
For instance, in India, many folks use stainless steel plates to eat. A robot trained to pick up a stainless steel plate could use a lot of pressure to grip it, and could drop it — no harm done. But if the same robot tried to pick up a ceramic plate, which is what many Americans use, the same pressure would cause it to "be separated into minute particles," Ramaswamy says — that is, smashed to bits.
And to amass recordings of humans doing work with their hands for clients who request ecocentric data, Ramaswamy says, they pay hundreds of people across India to undertake domestic jobs, like Sneha Jegadish, a 24-year-old who lives on the edge of town.
Jegadish clipped her smart phone to a headset and began chopping a carrot, her phone recording her every hand movement.
She records herself doing housework for a few hours a day, for about $2.60 an hour, and makes around $120 a month. Jegadish folds clothes, wipes the floor, does the dishes — jobs she was never expected to do growing up, because her mother wanted her to focus on her studies. So when she got this gig a few months ago, "my mother had to show me how to do those jobs," she smiles.
Money or not, it's still drudgery, says Jegadish. One day, she hopes, she'll have a robot to do her housework. "The work we are doing now is going to be done by robots in the future," she says.
That's the same conclusion that 42-year-old textile worker Kannagi Periyasaamy has come to.
At the textile factory, Periyasaamy was folding and packing aprons with a GoPro fastened to her head.
She's one of the few workers who is paid about $2.60 an hour to record herself, and she's been told why. She explains: "We are training them [the robots] on how to package the aprons, how to do a quality check, how to fold the aprons."
Periyasaamy says she's been doing this for the past three months, enough for her to be convinced that someday, a robot will take over her job. When that day comes, she says, "I'm thinking about taking up farming" — the family owns a scrap of land where she could raise cattle. Meanwhile, Periyasaamy thinks of AI robots as her students and says, "I'm proud I can teach it to do a good job."
With additional reporting by Vinodh Arulappan

title: EU Accelerates Break from China with 46 Strategic Projects, Three in Greece
body: Exactly one year after China imposed export restrictions on rare earths that threatened to disrupt European industrial chains—from automotive manufacturing to wind-turbine production—the European Union is moving to turn a temporary easing of tensions with Beijing into lasting supply security. According to Kathimerini, the European Commission has selected 46 new strategic projects across 16 member states, three of them in Greece, as it accelerates efforts to curb dependence on China and other dominant suppliers of critical raw materials. Commission Vice-President Stéphane Séjourné underscored the stakes: “The battle for industrial sovereignty and competitiveness depends on our resilience in critical raw materials.” He recalled that on 9 October 2025 China announced rare-earth export curbs. Although some measures have been suspended and dialogue with China continues, he said, “we must now turn this temporary respite into permanent security.” The 46 projects, chosen from 102 applications, are expected to require €21.1 billion in capital. They comprise eight mining projects, 11 processing projects, 19 recycling projects and eight integrated projects that combine stages of the value chain. Together they cover 15 of the 17 strategic raw materials identified by the EU, with particular emphasis on lithium, nickel, cobalt and graphite for batteries, as well as magnesium, tungsten and rare earths essential for the defence and aerospace industries. Kathimerini notes that, with this latest selection, the number of strategic projects inside the Union rises to 93, while another 13 have already been designated in third countries and overseas territories. According to the Commission, the full set of investments could fully meet the EU’s 2030 extraction-capacity targets for lithium, nickel, rare earths, magnesium and tungsten, and its processing targets for lithium and rare earths. These benchmarks stem from the Critical Raw Materials Act, which aims for the EU to extract at least 10 % of its annual consumption, process 40 % and recycle 25 % by the end of the decade, while limiting dependence on any single third country to no more than 65 % of processing needs for each strategic material. Three new projects in Greece The new list includes three Greek investments—two in recycling and one in mining. ElvalHalcor’s ETEOCLES project will develop a hub for recycling low-grade copper scrap, while the company’s New Aluminium Recycling Hub in Greece focuses on aluminium recycling. The third is the Skouries mining project of Hellenic Gold (Hellas Gold), listed as a strategic copper-mining operation. Séjourné also singled out Greece’s Metlen, whose mine he has visited, noting that the company is already producing gallium “for the first time in Europe.” The metal’s output is significant for Europe’s diversification efforts, given its use in advanced technologies and the Union’s heavy reliance on imports. “This is what our sovereignty policy means in practice,” he said. European Centre and financing tools Beyond project selection, the Commission is preparing a European Centre for Critical Raw Materials to serve as the operational arm of the strategy. The Centre will monitor international markets, guide investments, support strategic projects and connect producers with buyers. Its planned functions also include organising joint European purchases of critical materials and building strategic stocks so the Union can respond more effectively to supply disruptions. In parallel, the European Critical Raw Materials Company, previously announced by Ursula von der Leyen, is intended to mobilise public and private capital through grants, loans, guarantees and equity stakes, working with the European Investment Bank and member states. Under the RESourceEU initiative, more than €2 billion in public financial support has already been mobilised. Of the projects selected in 2025, 25 have completed environmental-impact assessments and 17 have received construction permits. The next challenge Séjourné’s sharpest warning concerned economic viability. Securing financing and permits is not enough if European companies continue to buy cheaper materials from third countries. “We can finance a mine. We can accelerate a permit. We can build a factory. But if no one buys what it produces, it will close,” he cautioned. Several European projects face unfair competition, he said, with some market actors suppressing prices to prevent new competitors from emerging. He called on European industry to share responsibility for diversification: “Buy European when a European alternative exists. And when that is not possible, diversify your purchases.” The Commission is now urging legislative changes to the Critical Raw Materials Act and the Industrial Accelerator Act to encourage procurement of European products. It is also preparing a new diversification instrument by the end of the year and expects to announce additional strategic projects outside the EU shortly. title: Amazon pushes up prices across the Internet
body:
Not-Ship turns one next week!! To mark it, I'll be kicking off a campaign for new members. I won't spam you; free subscribers will only get three extra emails on top of the weekly edition.
But first, can I ask for a small birthday present? Hit reply and finish this: I read Not-Ship because...
Last week I wrote about how Amazon's search page is designed to screw you over : the top row trap, the swamp of ads, the discount-washing. Today, I'll explain what's going on behind the scenes, and how Amazon's rules make sure prices stay high not just at Amazon, but everywhere you shop.
This isn't just my theory. This system is at the heart of the US Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) upcoming antitrust case against Amazon.
Amazon relies on independent sellers to populate its online marketplace, and it charges them to be on the site. Amazon takes a big cut. In 2014, this was about 19% of sales . But today, many sellers hand close to half of every sale to Amazon. Half!
Amazon's basic commission (15% of the sale price in most categories) is in line with what eBay and Walmart charge. What pushes Amazon's cut higher are the other fees stacked on top.
Based on an apparel seller that opts for Amazon fulfillment, storage, returns and advertising.
There's the referral fee, which is the commission Amazon takes on every sale. The fulfillment fee is the cost to have Amazon pack and ship items from its warehouses. Then there's advertising: those sponsored spots in the top row we saw in last week's article.
Of these costs, only the referral fee is mandatory. Sellers can choose to ship orders themselves, for example, or forgo advertising. But in practice, the choice isn't actually much of a choice.
Here's what it looks like for a seller considering these so-called options:
In other words, the real choice for sellers isn't between paying for extras or not; it's between making sales or not. The FTC calls Prime eligibility, which effectively requires Amazon's fulfillment service, "a virtual necessity for doing business on Amazon." It says the same of advertising.
Here's where the fees are passed on to us consumers. When sellers give roughly half of their sales to Amazon, the other half isn't profit. That money has to cover making the product, shipping it to Amazon's warehouses, paying staff and everything else. So even if they wanted to absorb Amazon's fees on your behalf, most companies can't afford to. They have to raise their prices.
Don't forget, Amazon's biggest single fee — the referral fee — is a percentage of the price. So when prices go up, Amazon's cut goes up, too.
Now here's where it gets really crazy. Amazon's Fair Pricing Policy lets it remove the Buy Box (the "Add to Cart" button), or even suspend a seller , if they're offering their item cheaper elsewhere. So, a seller who raises prices on Amazon to cover the fees has to raise them everywhere else too — even on their own website! — or risk losing their Amazon sales.
The consequence is clear: We pay Amazon prices, even when we're not shopping on Amazon.
It's been documented again and again. In 2024, Amazon sellers told CNBC they lost the Buy Box after Target put their products on sale. In an ongoing lawsuit , California's attorney general alleges Amazon pushed brands to get Walmart, Target and other retailers to raise their prices. And when progressive media outlet More Perfect Union reported on this, they even found an Amazon seller who was suspended over a one-cent price gap with Target.
Ideally, market competition would sort this out. High prices send shoppers elsewhere and force fees down. But when sellers can't charge less anywhere else, there's nowhere cheaper to go.
For sellers, this is frustrating. So, why don't they just leave? Because Amazon is where the shoppers are: it accounts for about 40% of all US online retail sales . For many sellers, not being on Amazon isn't an option.
At least regulators have noticed. In 2023, the FTC and 17 US states sued Amazon, arguing that it illegally maintains its monopoly power by, among other things, punishing sellers who offer lower prices elsewhere, effectively forcing them to use its warehouses and charging ever-higher fees. Amazon denies any wrongdoing, and the case is set to go to trial next year. In Europe, Germany ordered Amazon to stop controlling its sellers' prices earlier this year, though the decision isn't yet final.
After last week's piece , a Not-Ship reader wrote to say none of this is new: plenty of online stores push ads and fake discounts. That is true. But what's different about Amazon is its reach. When prices increase on Amazon, they tend to increase elsewhere too. You can, of course, choose not to shop on Amazon. But if the FTC is right, you may be paying Amazon's prices anyway.
Not-Ship's data dispatch. In your inbox, weekly.
No spam. Just lots of charts. Unsubscribe anytime.
I spent two years working at the Washington Post, which Amazon founder Jeff Bezos owns. During that time, he was busy dismantling the publication , so he wasn't well loved in the newsroom.
In August, I saw Cory Doctorow speak at the Edinburgh International Book Festival. His enshittification concept — the process by which online platforms shift from serving their users to squeezing them — inspired this two-part series on Amazon. If you want to understand it all a lot better, I highly recommend his book Enshittification: Why Everything Suddenly Got Worse and What to Do About It. Somehow it makes antitrust issues both accessible and entertaining!
Here's what I found interesting, important or delightful this week:
Life after death? Alvin Chang's latest masterpiece has dropped! It’s about what people around the world believe happens after we die, drawn from surveys of nearly 130,000 people in 23 countries. (Proud to count Alvin as a Not-Ship subscriber 💙.)
Stunning embroidery. If you haven't seen the work of Irene Saputra, get yourself over to Instagram . Endlessly inspirational.
Instant knowledge. The Ars Notoria was a medieval magic book that promised scholars university learning through prayers, rituals and diagrams. No studying required!

title: Russia-India relations remain unchanged amid global turmoil — foreign minister
body:
NEW DELHI, October 14. /TASS/. Relations between Russia and India remain unchanged despite major shifts in the world, Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar said.
India has maintained good relations with Russia since the early years of its independence, and these ties have remained stable. "We (India) are a natural partner for Russia because we have had very good relations with Russia practically from the very beginning," the Indian foreign minister said in a conversation with John Micklethwait, editor-in-chief of the Bloomberg New Economy Forum, at a business forum in New Delhi.
"We assure Russia that, despite all the changes in the world, New Delhi’s relations with Moscow, which have been built over the past 75 to 80 years, remain unchanged, helping improve the balance of power and the overall status quo in Asia. We consider this a good sign," he added.
According to Jaishankar, India is becoming a genuine partner for Russia as Moscow increasingly develops ties with Asian countries. "As a result of the war in Ukraine, Russia has become much more focused on Asia. Apart from India, China is a major part of that picture in Asia. But I believe it is in our interests and in the interests of the world as a whole for Russia to have a choice and other important and meaningful relationships in Asia," the foreign minister noted.

title: Latvia notifies Russian journalist Leonid Ragozin of his expulsion
body: Latvia has officially notified Russian journalist Leonid Ragozin that it is expelling him from the country, he said on social media. “I can now confirm that yesterday I was notified of my expulsion from Latvia where I lived for 12 years,” Ragozin wrote. The notice did not specify “any specific misdemeanors or statements which prompted the decision,” according to Ragozin. He added that he had been declared persona non grata, a status intended “for diplomats who enjoy immunity from prosecution, not for ordinary people.” Ragozin considers his expulsion political persecution, saying it stemmed from “long-brewing revenge” by far-right politicians over his investigation into their ties to Russian neo-Nazis who have taken refuge in Kyiv. “It is also a punishment for my commentary on the Russian aggression in Ukraine and for Pavel Sheremet investigation,” he wrote. Latvian outlets reported in early October that the country’s Foreign Ministry had begun the process of declaring “another Russian citizen” persona non grata. Foreign Minister Baiba Braže said the decision was based on information “from the competent authorities” following consultations with the interior minister and the prime minister. The identity of the person being expelled was not officially disclosed, but Delfi reported it was Ragozin. In Russia, Ragozin worked as a correspondent and producer for BBC Russia from 1998 to 2103 and as an editor at the magazine Russian Newsweek, and he also collaborated with Lonely Planet. He moved to Latvia after Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014. More recently, he has worked with Al Jazeera, Jacobin, and The American Conservative. title: Yemeni army targets Aramco, King Khalid Airport in Riyadh
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 14 (MNA) – Yemeni Army Spokesman Brigadier General Yahya Saree said on Wednesday that the Armed Forces of the country targeted Aramco sites and King Khalid Airport in Riyadh with missiles and drones.
Yemeni Armed Forces vowed further strikes on Saudi airports, oil facilities, he pointed out.
Several Saudi positions have been targeted by the Yemen Armed Forces in retaliatory strikes, General Saree underlined.

title: Container carrier sinks in Strait of Hormuz after explosion
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 14 (MNA) – A container carrier vessel carrying more than 2,500 containers sank in waters south of the Strait of Hormuz this morning after hitting a naval mine and catching fire, the Islamic Revolution Guard Corps Navy said.
The Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said the container carrier struck a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz, caught fire and sank Wednesday morning in waters south of the strait. The vessel had attempted to cross an unauthorized and high-risk route through the strait when it hit the mine and caught a severe fire after the explosion, according to the IRGC Navy's public relations office. The vessel sank in the southern waters of the Strait of Hormuz as a result of the fire. The IRGC Navy cautioned local vessels and fishermen over colliding with containers floating on the water's surface while transiting the area. MNA

title: Alleged Attack: Sowore Files N5bn Damages Suit against AGF, DSS
body: The presidential candidate of the African Action Congress (AAC), Omoyele Sowore, has instituted a N5 billion fundamental rights enforcement suit against the Department of State Services (DSS), its Director-General, Tosin Ajayi, the Attorney-General of the Federation (AGF), and a Deputy Director of the DSS, Benjamin Bulus, over an alleged violent attack and abduction carried out by armed, hooded DSS operatives within the premises of the Federal High Court in Abuja on 22 June 2026. The suit, filed on October 13, 2026 and marked: FHC/ABJ/CS/2480/2026, challenges the legality of the DSS operation and seeks judicial redress for violations of Sowore’s constitutionally guaranteed rights to human dignity and personal liberty. The legal action was based on the plaintiff’s claim that DSS operatives, acting outside the scope of a judicial remand order, violently attacked him within the Federal High Court complex and forcibly transported him in elevators reserved for Federal High Court judges to the basement of the building against his will, injuring him in the process of the violent attack. According to a statement by Sowore’s lawyer, Mr Peter Femi Joseph, following an order by Justice Mohammed Umar of the Federal High Court, on June 22, 2026, directing Sowore’s remand at the Kuje Correctional Centre pending the hearing and determination of his application seeking a stay of the order revoking his bail and the bench warrant issued against him, operatives of the agency including armed men and women wearing hoods, stormed the fourth floor of the Federal High Court building in a bid to arrest him. The statement further claimed that operatives descended on Sowore, physically assaulted him, and forcibly removed him from the area before transporting him against his will to the basement of the court complex. Sowore maintained that he had committed no offence warranting such an operation and that the DSS had no lawful authority to assault, abduct, intimidate, or subject him to degrading treatment within the premises of a court of law. He further contended that the operation was intended to intimidate and harm him, notwithstanding the existence of a judicial order specifying the lawful process for his remand. The suit identifies Tosin Ajayi, the DG of the DSS and Benjamin Bulus, a Deputy Director and operative of the DSS, as the officer who led the operation. Meanwhile, video evidence of the alleged attack, which the plaintiff disclosed was captured with Ray-Ban Meta Smart Glasses, forms part of evidence to be presented as evidence in proof of Sowore’s case. The suit invokes Sections 34 and 35 of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (as amended), which guarantee the rights to dignity of the human person and personal liberty. The Applicant contended that the alleged physical assault, forcible removal, intimidation, and false detention constituted violations of these fundamental rights. He also seeks to establish the respective legal responsibilities of the DSS, its Director-General, the Attorney-General of the Federation, and Benjamin Bulus for the misconduct. Sowore is asking the Federal High Court to award him N5 billion in aggravated damages over the alleged assault, abduction, humiliation, intimidation, and infringement of his constitutionally protected rights. He is also seeking declarations concerning the alleged unlawfulness of the conduct complained of, appropriate injunctive and consequential orders, and any further relief the court considers justified. Kano Committed to High-impact Health Research, Says KIRCT Ahmad Sorondinki in Kano The Kano Independent Research Centre Trust (KIRCT) has disclosed that it will continue to provide high-impact services and cutting-edge research outcomes capable of addressing existing and emerging health challenges in Kano, Nigeria, and beyond. The Chairman, Board of Trustees (BoT) of the Centre, Prof. Aliyu Abdu, disclosed this at the opening ceremony of the Advanced Bioinformatics Workshop organised by KIRCT in Kano yesterday. He said KIRCT is equipped with state-of-the-art facilities to enable scientists to conduct advanced research locally without travelling abroad, adding that its researchers are currently working on several health areas, including genomics, breast cancer, antimicrobial resistance, vaccines and others. Prof. Abdu noted that the Centre has also established mutually beneficial collaborations with research institutions within and outside the region, with plans to expand globally. According to him, the training covered young scientists to conduct impactful research,s which is one of the mandates of the Centre. He commended the diversity of the workshop participants, especially with regard to gender distribution, and urged the participants to apply the knowledge to be gained from the workshop for the benefit of humanity. He thanked the funders of the Centre, Pfizer Inc. and the Kano State Government, for their support, and lauded the board and management of the Centre for the progress it recorded. In his remarks, the Special Adviser to the Kano State Governor on Health Services and member of the Board of Trustees, Dr. Ibrahim Musa Idris, reaffirmed the state government’s support for the Centre. He said the administration of Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf is pleased with the Centre’s impressive progress, expressing optimism that the Centre will soon be on the global map for providing innovative health solutions.

title: Palestinian faction leaders gather in Cairo to renew bid for long-elusive reconciliation
body: Leaders of Palestinian factions were gathering in Egypt on Wednesday for a renewed bid for reconciliation, after legislative elections scheduled for next month were postponed by President Mahmoud Abbas , sources told The National. They said the talks were scheduled to begin Thursday and will continue until the end of the month, but not necessarily at leadership level. The gathering in Egypt represents eight factions, including Hamas, Islamic Jihad, a pro-reform faction of Fatah, and the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine. The talks will be the latest in a long-running series of attempts to narrow the gap between Palestinian factions divided over policies, ideology and the way forward for Palestine. Egypt has been trying to reconcile Palestinian factions for years, without success. Officials from its spy agency have led efforts, taking responsibility for key foreign policy files traditionally handled by the Foreign Ministry. The sources said Khalil Al Hayya, the political leader of Hamas, and Mohammed Dahlan, who leads the pro-reform faction within Fatah, were among those taking part in the talks. Also participating are Jebril Rajoub, a top official of the Palestine Liberation Organisation, and Mohammed Ashtiyah, a former Palestinian prime minister and top Fatah official. Among the main topics to be discussed are how to narrow ideological gaps between their factions, the inclusion of Hamas and Islamic Jihad in the Palestine Liberation Organisation, and charting a political role for armed groups like Hamas and Islamic Jihad. “These are preliminary contacts that will precede negotiations that bring together everyone in the same room, which is expected to happen towards the end of the month,” said one source. The talks in Egypt will take place at a time when prospects for the Palestinian cause are looking dimmer than at any time perhaps since the mass displacement of Palestinians around the time of Israel's creation in 1948. A year since a US-sponsored Gaza ceasefire was announced to pause two years of fighting, the strip lies in ruins, Israel's military controls more than 60 per cent of the enclave and shows no intention of withdrawing as provided by American President Donald Trump's peace plan. Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank are facing frequent violent attacks on their homes and farmland in what increasingly looks like a concerted, state-backed campaign to displace them. Mr Abbas, head of the Palestinian Authority, announced last weekend that the legislative vote would be postponed until next September next, when the presidential election is also due to take place. Sources from various factions have told The National the delay was primarily intended to address what has been described as “Palestinian divisions” before the elections take place. The executive committee of the Palestine Liberation Organisation has approved the postponement. It said the delay was due to the lack of security in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank. The last election for the Palestinian Legislative Council, or parliament, was held in 2006 and won by Hamas , triggering a split between the group and Fatah, the dominant faction in the Palestinian Authority. Mr Abbas, 90, who is also Fatah's leader, has remained in office 17 years beyond the end of his original term. The deeply unpopular president, according to recent polls, has been ruling by decree amid growing discontent over his policies and reports of widespread corruption. An opinion poll run by the Palestinian Centre for Policy and Survey Research in August found 79 per cent of the 1,270 people surveyed wanted him to step down. Hamas described the postponement as a “step in the right direction,” saying political and security conditions were not suitable for holding a free election. The delay, its statement said, “must lead to a serious, fruitful and comprehensive national dialogue”. However, Mr Dahlan's pro-reform faction responded to Mr Abbas's decision in markedly different terms. It said the postponement was an “attack on democracy” and a threat to younger generations of Palestinians, who have been deprived of their right to choose their representatives. “The absence of elections deepens the crisis of legitimacy and weakens the Palestinian domestic front,” it explained in a statement on Saturday. “The leadership [Mr Abbas] is enshrining fiscal, political and administrative corruption, and pushes institutions away from the national track.” The group also called for broad dialogue between Palestinian factions to establish a “popular front” capable of exerting pressure.

title: Kuwait’s Jazeera Airways Eyes Resumption of Direct Flights to Kazakhstan
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. ASTANA – Kuwait’s airline Jazeera Airways is interested in resuming direct flights to Kazakhstan once regional conditions stabilize, potentially restoring a route suspended after its launch in 2021. Kazakhstan’s Ambassador to Kuwait Yerzhan Yelekeyev discussed restoring direct air connectivity with Jazeera Airways CEO Barathan Pasupathi, the Kazakh Foreign Ministry reported on Oct. 13. The officials explored opportunities to expand cooperation in civil aviation, tourism and trade. Yelekeyev emphasized that resuming flights would boost tourist flows, strengthen business ties and facilitate exports of Kazakh products to Kuwait. Jazeera Airways reaffirmed its interest in the Kazakh market, saying it would consider resuming flights when the regional situation stabilizes and operating conditions become favorable. The airline launched direct flights between Kuwait City and Almaty in 2021, but suspended the service later due to the regional situation. The post Kuwait’s Jazeera Airways Eyes Resumption of Direct Flights to Kazakhstan appeared first on The Astana Times .

title: Kano Committed to High-impact Health Research, Says KIRCT
body: Ahmad Sorondinki in Kano The Kano Independent Research Centre Trust (KIRCT) has disclosed that it will continue to provide high-impact services and cutting-edge research outcomes capable of addressing existing and emerging health challenges in Kano, Nigeria, and beyond. The Chairman, Board of Trustees (BoT) of the Centre, Prof. Aliyu Abdu, disclosed this at the opening ceremony of the Advanced Bioinformatics Workshop organised by KIRCT in Kano yesterday. He said KIRCT is equipped with state-of-the-art facilities to enable scientists to conduct advanced research locally without travelling abroad, adding that its researchers are currently working on several health areas, including genomics, breast cancer, antimicrobial resistance, vaccines and others. Prof. Abdu noted that the Centre has also established mutually beneficial collaborations with research institutions within and outside the region, with plans to expand globally. According to him, the training covered young scientists to conduct impactful research,s which is one of the mandates of the Centre. He commended the diversity of the workshop participants, especially with regard to gender distribution, and urged the participants to apply the knowledge to be gained from the workshop for the benefit of humanity. He thanked the funders of the Centre, Pfizer Inc. and the Kano State Government, for their support, and lauded the board and management of the Centre for the progress it recorded. In his remarks, the Special Adviser to the Kano State Governor on Health Services and member of the Board of Trustees, Dr. Ibrahim Musa Idris, reaffirmed the state government’s support for the Centre. He said the administration of Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf is pleased with the Centre’s impressive progress, expressing optimism that the Centre will soon be on the global map for providing innovative health solutions.

title: Russia Arrests Japanese Journalist on Suspicion of Spying
body:
Russia said on Tuesday it had detained a Japanese journalist on suspicion of espionage and accused Tokyo of using media correspondents to gather intelligence, marking a new low in bilateral relations that have deteriorated sharply in recent months.
Russia's Foreign Ministry identified the journalist as Yuki Imai and the FSB security agency said he worked for the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, which is a regional newspaper for Japan's northern island.
He was detained in the far eastern Sakhalin region the day before he planned to leave the country, the FSB said without specifying the date. It accused him of collecting and storing information on Russia's defense capabilities for intelligence purposes that it said could be used against Russian security.
The Hokkaido Shimbun did not confirm the journalist's identity, saying only that it was still confirming details and that the reporter's safety was its top priority.
Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said on Wednesday that Tokyo had asked Russian authorities for information and called for fair treatment and humanitarian consideration for the national.
Kihara stopped short of condemning Moscow, saying only that Tokyo would take appropriate action.
Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said on Wednesday that Tokyo had asked Russian authorities for information and called for fair treatment and humanitarian consideration for the national.
A senior official of the Japanese Foreign Ministry later summoned the Russian ambassador to Japan and lodged a protest for detaining the Japanese national and unilaterally issuing statements regarding the matter without providing an explanation to Tokyo, the ministry said in a statement.
The director-general of the Foreign Ministry's European Affairs Bureau, Kimitake Nakamura, also asked the ambassador, Nikolay Nozdrev, to set up an opportunity swiftly to meet the detained journalist, the ministry said.
In a Russian state TV video report, three masked men in black uniforms handcuffed a man lying on the ground as a voice off camera said he was suspected of spying.
The video showed the man being accompanied by two FSB servicemen onto a plane, then in a cage in a Moscow court, which ordered him detained for nearly two months.
It is the most high-profile detainment of a foreign journalist since the 2023 detention of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich.
Gershkovich, who says his arrest was a carefully planned FSB sting, was found guilty of espionage by a Russian court, sentenced to 16 years and then freed in an East-West prisoner swap in August 2024.
The case adds to long-running tensions between Russia and Japan, which have yet to sign a formal World War II peace treaty due to a territorial dispute over the Kuril Islands, known in Japan as the Northern Territories.
Those tensions heightened when Japan joined Western sanctions against Moscow over the war in Ukraine, with Russia regarding Japan as an "unfriendly" country. But business ties remain with Japan a purchaser of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG).
Then in August, Russian President Vladimir Putin visited one of the disputed islands, causing an uproar in Japan. On Tuesday, a delegation from a Chinese province visited the same island, in what appeared to signal closer coordination between Moscow and Beijing in their criticism of Tokyo.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said on Tuesday that Japan had refused to consider Moscow's concerns about what she called Tokyo's "remilitarization." She criticized Japan's alleged use of accredited journalists in Russia to gather information that could undermine Russian security.
"We have to note that what has occurred will become an additional factor clouding the atmosphere of Russian-Japanese relations," Zakharova said.
Asked whether improving relations between Russia and the U.S. and Japan's purchases of LNG from Russia made it difficult for Tokyo to take countermeasures, Kihara said: "It is true that there are many issues between Japan and Russia.
"From Japan's perspective, despite the difficult situation in Japan-Russia relations, Japan has taken resolute measures based on its position. At the same time, Russia is a neighboring country to Japan, and communication is necessary to resolve these issues."
