title: Starlink slowdown makes it impossible to launch medium-range UAVs — Ukrainian army
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. A slowdown in Starlink service is making it virtually impossible to launch medium-range drones, some missions involving them have already been cancelled since the start of the day, the 7th Corps of the Ukrainian airborne assault troops reported on Telegram.
"The problem is particularly acute when launching high-speed drones. At takeoff, certain devices, such as the Middle Strike, must reach very high speeds. Consequently, unstable connectivity makes it impossible to launch such aircraft or use them for their intended purpose. The consequences are already being felt in practice. Since the start of the day alone, one unmanned systems unit operating within the 7th Corps' area of responsibility, in the Gulyaipole sector, has had to cancel some missions due to these issues," the statement reads.
Earlier, Sergey Beskrestnov, an adviser to Vladimir Zelensky on communications and unmanned systems, reported that SpaceX had restricted the operating speed of Starlink satellite Internet terminals used by the Ukrainian army overnight.

title: 115 families still living in tents in Negros Occidental nearly a year after Tino
body: NEGROS OCCIDENTAL, Philippines – Nearly a year after Typhoon Tino (Kalmaegi) battered the Visayas , including southern Negros Occidental, over 100 displaced families in La Castellana town are still living in tents, with no clear timeline for their transfer to a permanent relocation site. For mothers Anna Fernandez, 35, of Lapak-Duldol, and Dorelyn Dagang, 32, of Igpanulong, both in Barangay Robles, the November 4 anniversary of the devastation is a reminder that their ordeal is far from over. Their families are among 115 displaced households staying in tents provided by the Office of Civil Defense (OCD) on the grounds of Colegio de La Castellana in Barangay Robles. MAKESHIFT. Anna Fernandez stands in front of her family’s makeshift shelter for nearly a year after Typhoon Tino. Ambo Delilan/Rappler In an interview with Rappler on Monday, October 12, Fernandez said living in a tent for nearly a year had taken a toll on her family. “Kainit, kaging-ot, kag tulo sang ulan ang amon gina-antus sa masami,” she said in Hiligaynon. (We often endure the heat, stuffiness and leaking rain.) Even meeting their basic sanitation needs has been difficult, she added. Fernandez has two children, and her husband relies on daily odd jobs as a cement hauler to support the family. Dagang, meanwhile, gave birth to her youngest child in a tent last May after losing her home and belongings to Tino while she was three months pregnant. Now a mother of three with an unemployed husband, she said her greatest wish was for her family to have a permanent home. “Diyos ko, san-o pa ayhan?” she asked in Hiligaynon . (My God, when will it be?) The municipal government has purchased a six-hectare property in Barangay Robles for a relocation site, but the transfer of the families, comprising 423 people, cannot proceed until the land is developed and the necessary permits are secured, La Castellana Vice Mayor Alme Rhummyla Nicor-Mangilimutan said. “We need time. We need money. We need help from the national government,” said Mangilimutan, who also heads the town’s Incident Management Team. Tino displaced about 1,600 families across La Castellana alone, including 600 from Barangay Robles. “Wala na gid sila sang puli-an. Kalulu-oy gid sila, actually,” Mangilimutan said. (They really have no home to return to. They are truly in a pitiful state.) The municipal government spends about P30,000 daily to feed the families in the tent community, Mangilimutan said. “It’s financially draining, really,” she said. “But we have no choice; we have to face this as a daily challenge.” To sustain assistance for the displaced residents, the municipality has been realigning its Maintenance, Operating and Other Expenses (MOOE) budget to cover educational allowances for schoolchildren, as well as burial and medical assistance for affected families. Despite efforts to secure national government funding, Mangilimutan said the municipality was still waiting for assistance. La Castellana, one of the localities hardest hit by Tino in the province, has submitted a P300-million recovery proposal, said Donato Sermeno III, director of the Office of Civil Defense in Negros Island Region. The proposal has been included in the OCD-NIR’s post-disaster needs assessment, which Sermeno said had been submitted to the OCD’s central office in Manila for possible funding through the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Fund (NDRRMF). Civil Defense Undersecretary Harold Cabreros pledged to prioritize the endorsement of the OCD-NIR’s assessment for funding through the OCD and the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC). Sermeno has yet to disclose the total amount proposed under the assessment for the entire Negros Island Region. Other local governments seeking assistance for Tino victims through the PDNA include the cities of Bago, La Carlota and Himamaylan; the towns of Moises Padilla, Isabela, Binalbagan, Hinigaran and Pontevedra in Negros Occidental; and Canlaon City in Negros Oriental. – Rappler.com

title: Chelsea’s defensive crisis: Alonso’s system, missing pieces, or individual errors?
body: Twelve goals conceded in five Premier League games have left Chelsea with the Premier League’s worst defensive record. Is Xabi Alonso’s system being exposed, are key absences destabilizing the side, or are too many players simply making costly mistakes? There is a clear contradiction at the heart of Chelsea’s start to the Premier League season. Xabi Alonso arrived at Stamford Bridge with a reputation for structure, control, and sophisticated positional football. His Chelsea side have already shown flashes of the attacking ambition expected of one of Europe’s most highly regarded young coaches. Yet defensively, they have looked anything but controlled. After five Premier League matches, Chelsea have conceded 12 goals and are still waiting for their first league clean sheet of the season. The 3–0 defeat at Brentford was merely the latest and most damaging example in what is appearing to be an endless list. It also extended Chelsea’s sequence without a Premier League clean sheet to more than 20 matches. The immediate temptation is to look at Alonso. Chelsea are playing a new system under a new manager. Their defensive line can be aggressive, their wing-backs advance high up the pitch placing significant responsibility on the midfield to protect the spaces created when possession is lost. But that explanation alone is too convenient. Alonso did not build a defensively reckless team at Bayer Leverkusen. Quite the opposite. His unbeaten Bundesliga champions of 2023–24 conceded just 24 goals in 34 league matches , a club record and an average of approximately 0.7 per game. Neither did his early work at Real Madrid suggest a coach unconcerned by defensive control. Under Alonso, Madrid initially reduced the number of counter-attacks they faced from 1.47 per match the previous season to 0.83, while pressing more aggressively and winning possession higher up the pitch. How then has a coach noted for control inherited a Chelsea side that currently looks so vulnerable? The answer is probably less satisfying than blaming one man or one tactical idea. Chelsea’s defensive problems appear to be a combination of missing personnel, an unfinished tactical structure, and repeated individual errors . Caicedo’s Absence is Not Simply About Losing a Midfielder The significance of Moises Caicedo is perhaps clearest when he is not playing. Caicedo has yet to have a premier league start barring the 22 minutes he had as a substitute in the 4:3 win over Brighton due to injury. His absence was particularly conspicuous in the Brentford defeat, when Jordan Henderson started in midfield in his place alongside valentin Barco. To describe Caicedo merely as Chelsea’s defensive midfielder understates his importance. In Alonso’s system, the player at the base of midfield is one of the central components of the team’s ‘ Rest Defence’ — the structure left behind the ball while Chelsea attack. When the wing-backs push forward and Chelsea commit numbers around the opposition penalty area, somebody must protect against the first pass of a counter-attack. Caicedo is exceptionally suited to that task. He anticipates danger, covers ground quickly, wins second balls, and can defend both centrally and towards the touchline. Perhaps most importantly, his positioning allows defenders behind him to remain compact rather than being dragged forward into midfield. A simplified version looks something like this: When Chelsea loses possession, Caicedo can occupy the area opponents would ideally use to launch the counter. He does not necessarily have to win the ball. Sometimes his value is simply forcing an opponent sideways, slowing the transition by two or three seconds and allowing Chelsea’s wing-backs and attacking midfielders to recover. Without that protection, Chelsea can instead resemble this: Those few meters matter enormously. A center-back who should be concentrating on the striker can suddenly be forced forward to confront a midfielder running at him. The outside center-back then moves across; thus, the opposite side becomes vulnerable. One missing player can therefore alter the responsibilities of four or five others. That does not mean Caicedo’s return will automatically repair Chelsea. But it helps explain why a team trying to play aggressively without one of its best transition defenders can suddenly look significantly less secure. Palestra May Be the Less Obvious Missing Piece If Caicedo’s absence was always likely to attract attention, Marco Palestra’s importance would be easier to overlook. The Italian had barely begun his competitive Chelsea career before injury intervened, but his pre-season form offered important clues about Alonso’s plans. Palestra impressed repeatedly during the summer and was used on both sides of the pitch. After Chelsea’s 3–0 pre-season victory against AC Milan, Alonso praised his impact, hunger, adaptability, and ability to perform in different positions. Chelsea’s manager said the youngster was getting “better and better” with every game. His profile is particularly relevant. Alonso’s wing-backs are not traditional full-backs. They are expected to provide attacking width, arrive high in possession, participate in the press, and still possess enough athleticism to recover when the ball is lost. That creates a demanding tactical equation. If the wing-back stays too deep, Chelsea can lack width. If he goes forward but cannot recover quickly enough, Chelsea leaves the channel behind him exposed. Palestra looked capable of performing both jobs. Consider the responsibility placed on the right wing-back: If possession is lost, the chain must reverse almost immediately: One delayed recovery can create a domino effect; The right center-back gets dragged towards the touchline. The central defender moves across. Suddenly the far side of the penalty area is available for a late runner. A late recovery run from Morgan Rogers almost leads to a goal This is why Palestra’s absence matters beyond the loss of one promising young player. Chelsea is missing somebody who appeared unusually well suited to one of Alonso’s most specialized roles. But injuries alone cannot explain 12 Goals There is an obvious danger here; once important players are injured, almost every poor performance can be explained through their absence. Chelsea cannot allow that to happen. They have conceded at least twice in each of Alonso’s first five Premier League matches. Hull City scored twice at Stamford Bridge, Arsenal scored twice, and Brentford scored three. Even Chelsea’s victories contained defensive warning signs. That is too consistent a pattern to attribute solely to Caicedo and Palestra. The more uncomfortable question is whether Chelsea currently understands Alonso’s defensive system well enough to execute it. The Problem with Alonso’s Football When One Player Arrives Late Alonso’s football is highly dependent on relationships between players. A wing-back can attack because a midfielder moves across. A center-back can step forward because another defender covers behind him. The front line can press aggressively because the midfield squeezes upwards at exactly the same moment. When those actions are synchronized, the pitch becomes small. When they are not, the pitch becomes enormous; that may explain some of Chelsea’s current difficulties. Imagine Chelsea initiating a high press: A high press where distance between attack and midfield is tight The above scenario is manageable; the attacking and midfield lines move together. The opponent has limited time and limited space. Now consider what happens if Chelsea’s forwards press but the midfield hesitates, as shown below: At that point Chelsea has a problem. The press has effectively removed their own forwards from the defensive phase while giving the opposition midfielder time to turn. The center backs then face a difficult decision. Step forward and risk space behind, stay deep, and allow the ball-carrier to advance. Neither option is particularly attractive. This is where judging defenders purely on the final moment of an attack can become misleading. A center-back may appear responsible for allowing an attacker into the penalty area, but the tactical breakdown may have occurred several seconds earlier when Chelsea’s first and second defensive lines became disconnected. That is fundamentally a coaching issue, and it is an area Alonso must fix. This is what makes his Leverkusen record especially interesting. The strongest argument against the suggestion that Chelsea’s current defensive chaos is simply an inevitable consequence of Alonso’s philosophy is Bayer Leverkusen. His 2023–24 side did not win the Bundesliga unbeaten by accepting defensive vulnerability in exchange for attacking freedom. They defended exceptionally well. Leverkusen conceded only 24 goals across 34 league matches—their best defensive record in a Bundesliga season. Their back three were protected by excellent spacing ahead of them. Granit Xhaka particularly brought positional intelligence. Exequiel Palacios offered mobility while Jeremie Frimpong and Alejandro Grimaldo pushed extremely high from wing-back, yet the defenders behind them were rarely left completely abandoned. The important concept was not the formation; it was the rest defense. When Leverkusen attacked, Alonso wanted enough players behind or around the ball to deal with a turnover immediately. A simplified version looked like this: The aggressive positions of the wing-backs appear risky, but the central structure underneath them gives the system its security. Chelsea currently appears to possess the attacking ambition of that system without consistently reproducing its defensive insurance. That distinction is crucial. Real Madrid provides another clue. Alonso’s brief Real Madrid tenure also undermines the idea that his football is naturally vulnerable to counter-attacks. Early in the 2025–26 campaign, Madrid were allowing only 0.83 counter-attacks per game, compared with 1.47 the previous season. Their PPDA—a measure often used to indicate pressing intensity—fell from 12.1 to 10.8, suggesting Alonso was asking Madrid to engage opponents more aggressively. They were also winning possession significantly more often near the opposition goal. The tactical principle was revealing. Alonso wanted Madrid to defend with the ball. Rather than attack as quickly as possible every time possession was recovered, an additional pass could allow the defensive structure behind the attack to settle. The opponent might then have fewer opportunities to counter. Chelsea have not consistently reached that stage. Their matches frequently become stretched. And once stretched, a young and still-developing defensive unit is being asked to defend situations that Alonso’s system is designed to prevent in the first place. Then Come the Individual Mistakes There is another side to Chelsea’s defensive problems that tactical diagrams cannot fully explain. Sometimes a defender simply has to defend. Hull’s 2–2 draw at Stamford Bridge included an error from Jorrel Hato that contributed to Chelsea conceding. Against Brentford, Chelsea were repeatedly punished by basic failures to win first contacts, track runners, and defend the far post. Most significantly, Chelsea have already conceded four goals from set pieces in five Premier League games. Since the beginning of last season, they have conceded 23 goals from set-piece situations, joint-worst among Premier League clubs over that period. That cannot simply be blamed on Alonso’s open-play tactics. A corner removes most of the debate about ‘Rest Defence’. There is no midfield transition to blame. The players know where the ball is coming from. They know which opponents they are supposed to track, and yet Chelsea continue to concede. Brentford even acknowledged that they deliberately targeted space at Chelsea’s back post after identifying the weakness. That raises questions about concentration, communication, and physical competitiveness. Levi Colwill admitted after the Brentford defeat that Chelsea had been “bullied” at times. That is not language associated with tactical complexity. It is about duels. Structure Versus Execution Is the Wrong Debate Football analysis often attempts to separate goals into neat categories. Managerial error, individual error, and system failure; in reality, they overlap. Consider a common Chelsea transition. Wing-back attacks ↓ Chelsea loses possession ↓ Midfielder fails to stop counter ↓ The center-back must defend wider area ↓ Defender mistimes challenge ↓ Goal: Who is responsible? The manager for committing the wingback? The midfielder for allowing the pass? Or the defender for losing the duel? Potentially all three. That is probably the most useful way of understanding Chelsea’s defensive start. The structure is allowing too many difficult situations to develop, and individual players are then failing to solve enough of those situations. Fixing only one part may therefore be insufficient. Chelsea are also losing control after setbacks; another worrying feature of Chelsea’s early season has been their response to conceding. The Brentford game was particularly revealing. Chelsea were relatively competitive before the opening goal. Afterwards, their defensive structure deteriorated, and Brentford scored twice more. Alonso subsequently questioned his players’ ability to maintain their level and competitive focus throughout a full match. That points towards a different sort of defensive weakness: game management. The best possession teams understand that conceding does not require an immediate emotional response. Sometimes the correct reaction is five minutes of safe possession. Recycle the ball. Slow the tempo. Re-establish territory, and force the opposition backwards again. Chelsea currently have a tendency for matches to become even more open once they fall behind. As more players advance, distances increase. The urgency to equalize creates another transition; then another. A 1–0 deficit becomes 2–0. At Brentford it eventually became three. Alonso therefore faces a psychological challenge as well as a tactical one. So is Alonso responsible? Partly. That is the unavoidable conclusion. A coach cannot be given credit when a structure works and absolved whenever it fails. Chelsea’s spacing is sometimes poor. Their press can become disconnected. Their defensive transitions are too easy to play through, and the team is yet to establish the collective automatisms associated with Alonso’s best Leverkusen side. Those issues belong on the training ground. But there is an equally important distinction between saying Alonso has tactical problems to solve and saying Alonso’s tactics are the fundamental problem. His previous teams provide little support for the latter argument. Leverkusen were defensively excellent. His early Madrid side reduced counter-attacking opportunities rather than increasing them. The philosophy itself can produce control; Chelsea simply are not producing enough of it yet. The return of Caicedo could tell us much more; that is why the next phase of Chelsea’s season should be illuminating. Caicedo’s eventual return would restore arguably the squad’s most important transition defender. Palestra would give Alonso another natural option in a demanding wing-back role that appeared tailored to his qualities during pre-season. If their presence makes Chelsea dramatically more compact, the first five games may ultimately be viewed as the difficult installation phase of a new system deprived of two important components. The manager is still trying to create the compact distances and collective pressing that characterized his Leverkusen side. And when Chelsea’s structure has broken down, individual players have too often compounded the problem with poor decisions. But Alonso’s history provides Chelsea with at least one reason for patience. A coach whose Leverkusen side conceded only 24 goals across an entire unbeaten Bundesliga campaign has already demonstrated that he can construct an elite defensive structure. The question at Stamford Bridge is whether he can build one again—with different players, in a different league, and under considerably greater scrutiny. For now, Chelsea’s defense does not look fundamentally doomed. It looks unfinished. And the Premier League is an unforgiving place to finish building it.

title: Russian Overnight Strikes Target Kyiv CHP Plants and Kill Civilians Across Ukraine
body:
Russian forces targeted all three of Kyiv ’s municipal combined heat and power (CHP) plants in an overnight attack on Oct. 13-14, Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi reported on Wednesday. Strikes across Ukraine killed civilians and damaged civilian infrastructure.
Russian ballistic missiles targeted energy infrastructure in Kyiv, Kharkiv and surrounding regions, Koretskyi said on Telegram . In the Kyiv region, Russian forces also struck critical infrastructure supplying electricity to the capital and central regions.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Energy workers and emergency responders began working at the affected sites early in the morning, conducting firefighting and debris-clearing operations. Specialists have also started priority restoration work at the targeted facilities, according to the prime minister.
The attacks followed an evening strike on a high-rise residential building in Kyiv that killed two people and injured 25. Another person was killed and one injured in a separate morning attack on the capital, Koretskyi said.
Railway infrastructure was also targeted in five regions. No casualties were reported at the railway facilities, as timely evacuations helped protect workers and others at the sites. Restoration work is ongoing.
In the Khmelnytskyi region, Russian drone attacks sparked fires at industrial sites in the Khmelnytskyi and Shepetivka districts, the State Emergency Service (DSNS) reported on Telegram.
Falling drone debris also caused a fire at a gas station in Khmelnytskyi district, injuring two people. In the city of Khmelnytskyi, drone debris ignited fires at two private homes in a residential neighborhood. No casualties were reported there.
Emergency crews were repeatedly forced to leave their work sites because of renewed Russian attacks. Eighty rescuers and 22 pieces of equipment were deployed to extinguish a fire at one of the industrial facilities in Khmelnytskyi District.
In the Dnipropetrovsk region, Russian attacks killed two people and injured six others, including a child, according to the DSNS. In Pavlohrad, a strike on an open area killed one person and injured four others, including a child. In Nikopol district, attacks on the district center and the Myrivka community killed another person.
Russian forces also struck an enterprise in Dnipro overnight, injuring a man and triggering a large-scale fire. In Synelnykove district, attacks on the Yavornytske and Mykolaivka communities injured a woman and damaged a private house. Emergency responders extinguished all fires caused by the attacks, the DSNS said.
In the Donetsk region, a Russian airstrike on a residential area in Sloviansk wounded seven people and damaged five apartment buildings. A fire broke out in a non-residential building and was later extinguished.
A car also caught fire following a Russian attack in Bylbasivka. Firefighters had to suspend their work because of the continuing threat posed by Russian drones.
In Ternopil, a Russian drone strike damaged an administrative building and sparked a fire on the second floor. Rescuers extinguished the blaze, and no casualties were reported.
Russian forces also attacked a railway infrastructure facility in the Vinnytsia region, causing a large fire. Emergency crews had to interrupt their work because of the threat of follow-up attacks involving drones and ballistic missiles. Responders eventually extinguished all remaining hotspots, and explosives experts inspected the site for unexploded ordnance. No fatalities or injuries were reported.
In the Kharkiv region, five people were injured in a Russian attack on the city of Derhachi, as per DSNS. A first person-view (FPV) drone struck a garage at a civilian enterprise, sparking a fire that spread across 200 square meters and engulfed trucks inside the building. Emergency crews extinguished the blaze.
Koretskyi thanked rescuers, police officers, medics, energy workers and others involved in responding to the attacks and helping affected residents.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Crunch SPL fixture involving Cristiano Ronaldo’s Al Nassr postponed due to ‘logistical considerations’
body: The Saudi Pro League clash between Cristiano Ronaldo’s Al Nassr and Asian champions Al Ahli has been postponed. The fixture, which was due to be played on Thursday, is one of three SPL games that have been rearranged. The league cited “logistical considerations” related to rest period for players, rather than the security situation in Riyadh . Alerts were sounded in the Saudi capital on Wednesday, as fighting intensified between the kingdom and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels. An SPL fixture in Abha that was due to be played on Sunday had been postponed, as a direct consequence of the situation. It was the day after 12 people died and more that 300 were wounded in an attack on the main international airport in Riyadh. Abha is around 200 kms from the Yemen border. Matches in Riyadh did go ahead. Each of Nassr , who were playing at home, and Ahli were in Asian Champions League action on Monday night. While Ahli’s fixture in Dubai against Al Wasl went ahead as planned, Nassr’s game in Riyadh was delayed for an hour because of an alert. 🚨Le match entre Al Nassr et Neftchi Ferghana 🇺🇿 en phase de groupes de ligue des champions asiatique a été retardé en raison d’une alerte ! 🎤 Le speaker du stade a annoncé : « Chers spectateurs, en raison d’une alerte signalée par la Protection civile, nous vous prions de… — SPL 🇸🇦 (@ActuSPL) October 12, 2026 In postponing three matches planned for this week, though, the league said the reasons were related to “the mandatory minimum rest period between matches”. The three matches all involve sides who were involved in the Champions League. That is Al Hilal and Nassr, who are based in Riyadh, and the Jeddah teams Ahli and Al Ittihad. “The [SPL] has rescheduled three Roshn Saudi League Matchweek 9 fixtures for logistical considerations, taking into account the mandatory minimum rest period between matches” the league wrote in a statement. “Two fixtures; Al Riyadh against Al Hilal and Al Ittihad against Al Shabab will now be played on Saturday, December 19, 2026, while Al Ahli versus Al Nassr will be played on Saturday, March 6, 2027. “The remaining games in Matchweek 9 will be played according to the previously announced schedule with no changes. “In making the decision, the SPL took into consideration the mandatory minimum rest period between matches in addition to organisational and operational requirements for the matches. “The changes are made in accordance with approved regulatory procedures for managing the competition's schedule, factoring in clubs' various logistical considerations for matches.” The Ahli-Nassr clash, in particular, was keenly anticipated. It was to be the first meeting between the sides since their acrimonious clash at Al Awwal Park last season. There, Nassr refused to give a guard of honour to their visitors, just days after Ahli had secured a second successive AFC Champions League title. Tempers boiled over in the game, with Ronaldo pointing out he has won five (Uefa) Champions League titles to goading Ahli fans. Merih Demiral, the Ahli centre back, also brought along his Champions League winner’s medal, and used it to taunt Nassr with in the melee which followed the game.

title: Pashinyan says Armenia and Azerbaijan should have ‘no enclaves or exclaves’
body: Explaining how he imagines the peace agreement with Azerbaijan, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said that he believes there should be ‘no enclaves or exclaves on either side of the border’ as part of the peace agreement with Azerbaijan, and that the two countries should exchange territories of corresponding sizes. Armenia and Azerbaijan have four enclave and exclave clusters that have become the subject of political controversy in the process of demarcation and delimitation between the two countries. Karki, Barkhudarlyu and Yukhari Askipara — Yukhari and Askipara are two separate villages that form a single cluster — are located in Armenia but are part of Azerbaijan according to the Almaty Declaration of 1991. Artsvashen, which is currently under Azerbaijani control, is considered to be part of Armenia. The enclaves were created in the 1920s when Soviet authorities drew internal borders within the Transcaucasian Federation based on their demographic makeup, rather than geography. Consequently, a cluster of Azerbaijani villages could legally become part of Azerbaijan while surrounded by Armenia, and Armenia’s Artsvashen village could end up cut off inside Azerbaijani territory. Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev has previously demanded the return of Armenian exclaves that were Azerbaijani territory during the Soviet Union. Pashinyan says his vision for peace with Azerbaijan includes Armenia with a territory of 29,743 square kilometres, with borders as defined in the Alma-Ata Declaration. He added that the transit between the two countries should not be limited to the Trump Route (TRIPP) under any agreement. ‘Now, the next and perhaps most important question is whether there is a real possibility of giving peace this form. Based on the results of my engagements with the President of Azerbaijan in Turkmenistan, I have the preliminary impression that we have an opportunity to give peace such a form, and in the coming period we will be engaged in realising this opportunity, turning this possibility into reality’, said Pashinyan. Pashinyan and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev did not have an official meeting in Turkmenistan, where they both attended the Caspian Environmental Summit on 9 October. Russian media had reported that Pashinyan met with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Aliyev on the sidelines of the event, but Pashinyan’s office denied the reports on Monday. The Armenia–Azerbaijan peace process entered a new stage after the 2025 US-mediated Washington summit, which brought together Pashinyan, Aliyev, and US President Donald Trump, and resulted in the initialling — but not the signing — of a peace treaty. The border delimitation, enclaves, and exclaves remain some of the most important steps on the way to signing a peace agreement .

title: Cornell University faculty to begin debating no-confidence resolution
body:
Approximately 150 faculty members are said to be in support of the resolution.
Cornell University’s faculty senate on Wednesday will begin deliberating a no-confidence resolution to condemn the school’s response to sexual violence on campus.
One month after allegations of a “gang rape” at a campus fraternity shook the Ivy League school, the resolution, if adopted, could mark the clearest repudiation of Cornell’s leadership since the controversy began.
“We're saying we have no confidence in how the administration has handled this. It is a crisis. It's a long-term systemic problem. Jane Doe's case is significant, but it is not nearly the only case like this,” Iris Packman, a faculty senator, told ABC News.
Cornell University’s president and provost are scheduled to address the faculty senate and take questions before the debate begins, and the formal vote on the resolution is set to take place later this month.
“What we are wanting is real effective leadership, not just reactive responses by the central administration,” said Professor Risa Lieberwitz, another member of the faculty senate.
Cornell’s faculty senate is debating adopting a one-sentence resolution that reads, “The Faculty Senate has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University.”
“The key point to understand is that scores of students, staff, faculty and alumni have approached the sponsors of the resolution to emphasize to us that the Jane Doe case is but the tip of the iceberg,” Professor Paul Ortiz, the lead sponsor for the resolution, told ABC News via email.
According to Packman, approximately 150 faculty members have signaled their support for the resolution, and the measure was co-sponsored by a dozen members of the faculty senate. For the resolution to pass, the measure would need support from a majority of the faculty senate.
Cornell’s faculty senate is a “governing body that supports faculty communication toward successful management of objectives for the University,” according to the school. Academic titleholders at Cornell -- including professors, senior lecturers, librarians, archivists and others -- are eligible to be senators, who serve three-year terms.
The resolution itself does not call for specific action -- such as demanding resignations or forcing policy changes -- and instead offers a broad condemnation of the school’s response.
“I think it's important that we did not specifically call for [the] resignations of anybody. We are not saying XYZ administrators need to leave, but these ones are okay. We're saying we don't have confidence in the way that they are handling this, and we don't have confidence that they are going to effectively address it going forward,” said Packman, one of the co-sponsors of the resolution.
What is scheduled to take place on Wednesday?
The bulk of Wednesday’s meeting is centered on remarks and presentations from Cornell’s leadership, according to the meeting agenda.
Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff and Provost Kavita Bala are scheduled to deliver remarks and answer questions before members of the school’s Sexual Assault Task Force address the group. Cornell’s director of sexual harassment and assault response is also set to address the senators before taking questions. The final 30 minutes of the 90-minute meeting is scheduled to begin debate of the resolution.
Cornell’s dean of faculty is also set to address the body to read an “expressive activity statement.” Past faculty senate meetings have not begun with that kind of statement, according to Professor Lieberwitz, and the purpose and content of those remarks are not clear.
Cornell finalized its “expressive activity policy” last year in the aftermath of campus protests. It allows the school to restrict speech if it “disrupts essential operations necessary for the teaching, research, patient care, or residential campus missions of the university.”
“A zealous commitment to freedom of expression does not mean that anyone can say anything they like, whenever and however they like,” the policy says.
Packman argued that the statement may have a “chilling effect on faculty speech” by discouraging some speakers, particularly senators who do not have the protections afforded by tenure.
“If we're having a statement read telling us what we can and can't say and how we can and can't say it before we even engage in that debate, that is a significant overstep and restriction on our speech,” she said.
When is the vote scheduled to take place?
Deliberations over the resolution are set to take place on Wednesday, as well as a meeting on Oct. 28, according to the resolution.
Voting on the resolution is scheduled to take place after the October 28 meeting and last for five days. The voting will take place online, according to organizers.
Cornell University is prohibiting photography or video recording of Wednesday's meeting. Only individuals with Cornell ID will be allowed to enter the auditorium where the meeting will take place.
According to organizers, a recording of the meeting will be released by Cornell later this week.
What measures did Cornell announce on Tuesday?
Wednesday’s meeting comes on the heels of an announcement by President Kotlikoff about measures to “strengthen campus safety, better support survivors, and begin addressing the social context of sexual violence at Cornell.”
Cornell suspended all social events and parties held by fraternities while the school conducts a “review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue.”
The school also vowed to add more staff to its Office of Civil Rights -- which conducts Title IX investigations -- as well as report allegations of sexual assault to the New York State Police during the school’s review of its policies.
“We are working with the New York State Police to allow their experienced, trauma-informed criminal investigators, who are independent of Cornell University, to investigate allegations of sexual assault on campus. These individuals will interview survivors who elect to pursue criminal charges and will prepare comprehensive investigative summaries for the appropriate law enforcement agency,” the statement said.
Kotlikoff also vowed to implement changes proposed by Cornell’s Presidential Task Force on Sexual Assault, as well as “re-form and re-focus” that entity to examine “opportunities for safe and healthy social engagement and further ways to reduce risks.”

title: Ukraine Says SpaceX Limits Starlink Operations, Disrupting Military
body:
Ukraine accused Elon Musk's SpaceX on Wednesday of limiting Starlink services, crippling its drones, as Russia n missiles knocked out power stations in attacks President Volodymyr Zelensky called "ostentatious disrespect" to Donald Trump.
Kyiv's relationship with Washington has taken a sharp turn for the worse since U.S. President Trump abruptly lifted sanctions on Russia n diesel last week and publicly turned on Zelensky.
Trump, under political pressure to lower fuel prices that have soared since he launched a war against Iran, has called on Kyiv to halt attacks on Russia n refineries, and said Ukrainians should replace their wartime leader.
The U.S. president also announced that Ukraine and Russia had both agreed to halt attacks on energy targets, although neither side confirmed this and the past two days have seen intensive Russia n bombing, including of Ukrainian power stations.
Ukrainian military officials said Musk's SpaceX had without warning interrupted functioning of military-grade Starlink terminals moving at high speed, effectively preventing Kyiv from using them as onboard guides for drones.
"Our defense forces did not receive a warning about this limitation, and this led to the disruption of several missions," presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram.
The apparent suggestion that Musk's company might limit Ukrainian military capabilities drew a sharp response from Poland, which pays for Ukrainian Starlink subscriptions on Kyiv's behalf.
"Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you ​playing politics with your products again?" Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski asked Musk on X. "As your European customers, we are watching you."
There was no immediate response from Musk, who in the past has called Sikorski a "small man." SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside of U.S. business hours.
Musk is a close political ally of Trump, and the suggestion that SpaceX might limit Ukrainian capabilities reinforced wider Ukrainian concerns that Washington could withhold battlefield support to compel its onetime ally to make concessions.
Sources have told Reuters and other news organizations that the U.S. has threatened to cut off intelligence for early warning of missile strikes on Ukraine, to press Kyiv to suspend attacks on Russia n oil refineries.
Rescue workers in Kyiv were stretchering the injured from the wreckage of a blasted-out residential building overnight, while firefighters battled a huge blaze in the darkness. Officials said 2 people were killed and 21 wounded at the site.
Some 600,000 people were left without power as Russia n missiles careened into power stations during hours of attacks that primarily targeted Kyiv and Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city. Russia 's Defense Ministry confirmed it had struck four power plants in and around Kyiv and two in Kharkiv, among other targets. Zelenskiy said more than 30 power stations were damaged.
Ukrainian officials said late on Tuesday they had received no warnings from Western partners for a second day before the massive Russia n attacks on the capital. Trump had insisted on Tuesday that Washington was still sharing intelligence.
Zelensky cast the latest attacks as a deliberate snub to Trump's declaration of a ceasefire on energy targets.
" Russia does not consider the American President's statements strong," Zelensky wrote on X. "The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States."
Zelensky has said Ukraine is willing to observe an energy ceasefire and has not targeted Russia n refineries since Trump announced it, but will not continue to hold back if Russia ignores the purported truce. The Kremlin said on Tuesday that contacts were continuing about an energy truce.
Ukraine reported downing just four out of 39 Russia n missiles, reflecting Kyiv's weakened air defenses against fast-moving ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones amid a shortage of weapons.
Starlink does not work inside Russia , and Ukrainian drones hitting Russia 's oil industry use other means of communication, but Ukraine uses Musk's system to guide drones over its own territory, including parts of Ukraine occupied by Russia .
"According to our observations, during flights, the connection could drop for 10-20 seconds at speeds of just 110-120 km/h [68-75 mph]. The drones kept moving, but these interruptions made them harder to control," Ukraine's 7th Rapid Reaction Corps, deployed in the southeast, said in a statement to Reuters.
A source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry said the limitations significantly complicate logistics and some drone operations.
Since being turned on over Ukraine in the early days of Russia 's invasion in 2022, Starlink has been the lifeblood of Ukrainian battlefield communications.
Its resistance to electronic signal jamming has made it a crucial tool for flying long-range attack drones and drones used to drop supplies to frontline troops.

title: India’s Defence Secretary Deepens Strategic Partnership During Cyprus Visit
body: India’s Defence Secretary, Rajesh Kumar Singh, has completed an official two-day visit to Cyprus (12–13 October 2026) focused on expanding cooperation in maritime security and the defence industry. The visit forms the first leg of a wider tour that continues to Greece until 15 October. According to the Indian Ministry of Defence, the trip builds on the fresh momentum created by the elevation of bilateral relations to a Strategic Partnership following the state visit of President Nikos Christodoulides to India in May 2026. The engagements aim to translate political commitments into practical outcomes under the Roadmap for Bilateral Defence Cooperation 2026–2031 and the broader India–EU Security and Defence Partnership. High-Level Meetings in Nicosia On 13 October, Singh met Defence Minister Vasilis Palmas. The two sides reviewed progress under the Bilateral Defence Cooperation Programme for 2026 and set priorities for 2027, including joint exercises, naval visits and military training. They discussed the possible establishment of a regular security dialogue between the defence ministries to address shared concerns and guide future cooperation. Discussions also covered defence-industry partnerships, cybersecurity, emerging technologies and maritime security. Singh extended an invitation to Palmas to visit India in early 2027. Singh separately met Permanent Secretary Stelios Kountouris and officials of the Armament Directorate. India offered capacity-building support, expert exchanges and technical assistance in maritime security, drawing on its coastal-security experience. He also held talks with the Chief of the National Guard, Lieutenant General Emmanouel Theodorou, on bilateral defence cooperation and regional security developments. Naval Engagement at Mari At the Evangelos Florakis Naval Base in Mari, Singh met the Commander of the Cyprus Naval Command, Commodore Nicolaos Luca. Talks centred on strengthening navy-to-navy links through leadership exchanges, maritime domain awareness, search-and-rescue coordination, joint training, professional exchanges and potential port calls by Indian naval vessels. India offered training, capacity building and technical assistance to the Cypriot Navy. The Indian delegation boarded the offshore patrol vessel Commodore Andreas Ioannides (P61). These discussions form part of the practical implementation of the 2026–2031 defence roadmap. Defence Industry and Innovation Singh engaged with the Cyprus Chamber of Commerce and Industry, led by President Stavros Stavrou, and representatives of the Cyprus Association of Research and Innovation Enterprises (CARIE), as well as the Cyprus Defence and Space Industry Cluster. Talks focused on translating the May 2026 Strategic Partnership into concrete industrial and R&D cooperation in drones, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, space and dual-use technologies. Both sides explored business-to-business partnerships and collaboration between defence start-ups. Singh invited Cypriot industry representatives to India and encouraged participation in Aero India 2027 in Bengaluru to facilitate matchmaking and commercial partnerships. Additional Engagements Singh met UNFICYP leadership, including Special Representative Khassim Diagne and Force Commander Major General Mohammad Asadullah Minhazul Alam, to discuss the mission’s mandate and India’s longstanding contribution to UN peacekeeping. He paid tribute by laying a wreath at the Makedonitissa Military Cemetery in Nicosia, honouring Greek and Cypriot servicemen who died in 1974, and at the Commonwealth War Memorial in the Buffer Zone, which commemorates Indian soldiers who fell in the Second World War. Broader Context The visit underscores Cyprus’s growing importance as an EU partner for India in the Eastern Mediterranean, particularly in maritime security. It follows other recent steps, including progress on the India–Cyprus Action Plan 2025–2029 and earlier maritime committee meetings. Singh is now proceeding to Greece for meetings with senior political and military leaders. The Greek Minister of National Defence visited India in February 2026 and held talks with Defence Minister Rajnath Singh. The Cyprus and Greece stops form part of India’s wider effort to deepen defence and strategic relations with EU member states. The engagements highlight the expanding scope of the India-Cyprus partnership across defence, naval cooperation, industry and innovation. title: Digital VAT collection to cover mobile payments, not just bank cards – GRA
body: The Commissioner-General of the Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA), Anthony Kwasi Sarpong, says the digital Value Added Tax (VAT) collection system will cover qualifying payments made through mobile and other digital payment platforms, beyond transactions involving bank cards. Speaking on Joy FM’s Super Morning Show on Wednesday, 14th October, he explained that the collection mechanism would capture payments for qualifying foreign digital services routed through the banking and other digital payment systems. His clarification came during a discussion on the 20% tax applicable to services such as Netflix, Spotify and other online subscription platforms. “So it’s not only for a card. Assuming you are also using your mobile to pay, that will also be captured,” he said. Mr Sarpong was responding to a question about whether consumers who pay through standing orders or direct debits, rather than bank cards, would still fall within the collection system. He explained that the system would separate the tax component from the provider’s share when a qualifying payment is processed. “So any other digital payment platform you are using, at the point of payment, the system will split the value into two,” he stated. The tax component would be transferred to a government account, while the remaining amount would go to the merchant or service provider. Mr Sarpong said the arrangement would improve the GRA’s ability to track transactions and collect taxes that foreign providers currently remit themselves. Using Netflix as an example, he explained that the Authority presently relies on the company to declare the number of transactions and the corresponding VAT due. The new system, he said, would give the GRA an independent record of the number and value of payments, alongside the applicable tax. He stressed that the change in collection would not impose an additional 20% on subscriptions whose prices already include the tax. “So this system is not adding another 20 per cent to what you already pay. It is already embedded, and consumers are paying,” he said. According to him, about 92 foreign companies currently remit VAT to the Authority, and the collection reform would not change their pricing. However, the GRA has identified about 100 additional providers that are not charging VAT and intends to bring them into the system gradually. READ ALSO: Banks to charge 20% VAT on payments for Netflix, Zoom, TikTok and others The Real-Time VAT framework covers electronically supplied services from non-resident providers paid for through Ghana-issued payment instruments, including cards, mobile money accounts and digital wallets. In an earlier explanation, the Commissioner-General’s Technical Advisor, Elsie Appau-Klu, said participating financial institutions would collect and remit the tax at the point of payment. The effective 20% charge comprises 15% VAT, a 2.5% National Health Insurance Levy and a 2.5% GETFund Levy. Services covered include streaming subscriptions, cloud computing, online gaming and digital advertising. Mr Sarpong also clarified that the initial rollout applies to services rather than physical goods purchased from foreign online platforms. He said imported goods already attract applicable duties and VAT when they enter Ghana through its borders. “So it is not going to affect goods or products, tangible products at the moment,” he stated.

title: Ukrainian Defence Forces strike Russian drone storage and launch site near Donetsk
body:
Ukrinform reports this, citing the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine in a Telegram post.
On October 13 and during the night of October 14, Ukraine's Defence Forces struck several Russian military targets.
In the Donetsk area, they hit a site used to store, prepare, and launch attack drones.
Systematic strikes against such facilities are intended to reduce Russia's ability to attack civilian infrastructure across Ukraine.
In addition, Russian military logistics depots were struck near Popova Balka and Hirnyk in the Donetsk region.
As Ukrinform previously reported, Ukraine's Defence Forces struck a maintenance base in Russia's Kursk region for self-propelled launchers and transport-loading vehicles belonging to the Iskander-M tactical ballistic missile system.

title: Nigerian newspapers review: APC drafts Accord, APGA, PDP men into Tinubu’s campaign
body: In today’s Nigerian newspapers review programme, Today in the News, Vanguard leads with the Presidency and the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) including leading opposition figures and governors in President Bola Tinubu’s re-election council, in spite of strong pushback from sections of the party. Another headline features the International Monetary Fund (IMF) saying that despite Nigeria’s economic growth and status as an energy exporter, the cost of living remained high, leaving many Nigerians struggling to meet their basic needs. Vanguard reports that the House of Representatives Committee on Host Communities recommended the dismissal of a petition against Pipeline Infrastructure Nigeria Limited (PINL), citing the failure of the petitioners to provide evidence to substantiate their allegations. Moving to another newspaper, The Guardian reports that President Tinubu urged the judiciary to close procedural loopholes exploited by politically exposed persons and organised criminal networks to delay or frustrate corruption trials, and called for reforms to strengthen the prosecution of financial and economic crimes. The Punch reports that nine days after a Nigerian Air Force aircraft crashed in Igbokoda, Ilaje Local Government Area of Ondo State, the wreckage and bodies of the 25 victims remain unrecovered, raising fears of a public health crisis as residents complain of an increasingly offensive stench from the crash site. Lastly, The Nation reports that politicians under the aegis of Arewa for Asiwaju (A4A) said Tinubu’s performance in the last three years would earn him massive votes in the North in the 2027 general election. title: Business association Delovaya Rossiya proposes partially scrapping simplified tax system, taxing Russians’ passive income
body: The business association Delovaya Rossiya has drafted proposals to overhaul the Russian economy, the Russian business news outlet RBC reported. Some of the proposed measures would significantly tighten conditions for small and medium-sized businesses, while others target citizens’ passive income. The draft document, which RBC reviewed, includes 52 proposals covering a wide range of topics. Among other things, the organization proposes the following: Eliminate the tax regime known as the “Income” version of the simplified tax system (USN), which carries a 6% rate. The Bell explains that this would mean “primarily an increase in the tax base for entrepreneurs who earn income through their own skilled labor.” Lower the threshold for applying VAT under the auto-USN regime from 60 million to 20 million rubles (matching the current threshold for the “standard” USN). Eliminate the patent-based tax system, which The Bell says is widely used by microbusinesses. Introduce social security contributions for citizens whose income mainly comes from interest or dividends. Introduce an inheritance and gift tax on amounts exceeding 50 million rubles. Restrict imports of “strategic innovative products.” The Bell calls the proposal “a blow to small business” and says it “looks very bad” for medium-sized businesses too.
