title: U.S. Army receives first VAMPIRE counter-drone systems from L3Harris
body: VAMPIRE is a self-contained weapons system that provides reconnaissance and precision strike capabilities against drones and other remotely piloted aircraft. The Army ordered it to meet an urgent counter-drone requirement. “From day one, our team has worked side-by-side with the Army to rapidly field VAMPIRE systems,” said Chris Aebli, president of Communications & Spectrum Dominance at L3Harris. “U.S. armed forces are now equipped to reliably defend personnel and vital assets against drone threats.” L3Harris announced high-volume VAMPIRE production at its dedicated Huntsville, Alabama, facility in March 2026, ahead of the Army order. The company established the line to meet U.S. and allied demand for protection against drone threats to troops and infrastructure. The facility combines assembly, testing and installation space for fitting VAMPIRE onto ground vehicles and containerized weapon systems. Its flexible production line can increase output as demand changes. L3Harris developed and invested in VAMPIRE at the beginning of the war in Ukraine to provide a low-cost means of defeating Russian drones. The company said military forces have used the technology extensively in European combat operations, logging more than 350,000 operational hours since 2023. The initial Army deliveries follow that operational use and the start of high-volume production in Huntsville. L3Harris did not disclose how many systems it has delivered or when the order will be completed.

title: Analysis: What the Denel and Armscor BRRR presentations revealed – and what they left unsaid
body:
On Friday, 9 October 2026, the Portfolio Committee on Defence and Military Veterans received the Annual Report presentations of Denel SOC Ltd and Armscor SOC Ltd as part of the Budgetary Review and Recommendation Report (BRRR) process. What emerged was not the rigorous examination these entities require. It was another compressed exercise in which two organisations charged with equipping the South African National Defence Force (SANDF) were permitted to place selective narratives before members inside a sitting of roughly three hours.
I have raised the inadequacy of the BRRR process in the Portfolio Committee on Defence and Military Veterans (PCDMV) before, and on Friday I placed it on the record again. Members of Parliament are handed documents of substantial length, annual reports that contain the detailed financial and operational record of entities in serious difficulty, and are expected to analyze them, test them, and respond to them under constant pressure to speed up because of time constraints. That is not a reasonable expectation. It compresses oversight into a short presentation and a short response. It turns Parliament into a rubber stamp. If the BRRRs are reduced to that, the process is a farce. The same rushed treatment is applied to the annual reports of the SANDF, the Department of Military Veterans and, more broadly, the reports of other departments and entities. The entire manner in which Parliament deals with these reports is highly unsatisfactory. It is urgently necessary that the time allocated, the depth of prior research required, and the willingness of committees to insist on complete information rather than polished PowerPoint slides be addressed. The hardware needed to equip the SANDF, and the sovereignty that hardware is meant to protect, cannot be treated as a box-ticking exercise.
Denel’s presentation contained some facts that should be acknowledged. Revenue rose to R1.473 billion and gross profit to R361 million. Group executive posts have been filled. The company returned to the Department of Defence on 1 April 2025. On 10 July 2025 the Armaments Acquisition Council confirmed that the Badger infantry combat vehicle remains necessary and that Project Hoefyster should continue. Those are facts. They are not a turnaround. The Corporate Plan had budgeted revenue of R1.956 billion and an operating loss of R168 million. Actual revenue missed that target by almost half a billion rand. The operating loss was R364 million — more than double what Denel itself had budgeted. The entity remains significantly loss-making. Any figure that rests on associate accounting, particularly dividends received from Rheinmetall Denel Munition, rather than cash generated from operations, cannot be allowed to dress up that result. Denel’s own PowerPoint presentation indicated that cash in September 2026 was negative. Liquidity ratios sit below benchmark. Legacy debt is not fully paid. Hoefyster advances are not supported by cash on hand. The escrow balance is a meagre R169 million.
Of the roughly R3.297 billion drawn under the turnaround framework, more than 80 per cent — about R2.757 billion — went to legacy obligations. Only about R178 million reached the growth allocation. The R1.8 billion expected from non-core asset disposals has not materialised. Public money has continued to fund the past. It has not funded a future. The audit remains the central and most serious fact: a ninth consecutive disclaimer. The Auditor-General could not obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence across 34 areas of the financial statements. Prior-period errors were still open at 31 March 2026. Material irregularities included misuse of a public resource, statements that were not credible, data loss, customer advances used for other purposes, R14.7 million in tax penalties and interest, and R2.5 million paid for services not received. Denel has also lost significant numbers of engineers, technologists, scientists and technicians. Recruitment has resumed in some areas, but the skills base required for a sovereign defence industry has been hollowed out. The interim board chair offered a somewhat more realistic assessment than the Group CEO, whose presentation struck me as a forced and outdated recovery narrative that did not match the reality before the Committee. Members of Parliament should not be asked to applaud a recovery that the numbers do not support.
Project Hoefyster remains the wound that will not close. It was meant to replace the Ratel, which has been in service since about 1976. It is more than ten years late because of capacity constraints at Denel. The revised Phase 1 baselines required the Section variant at Denel by 31 May 2025 and the Fire Support variant by 31 July 2025. The Annual Report gives no performance against those dates. Armscor indicated that Denel has gone out on a Request for Information to find a partner for Phase 2. An entity that must advertise for a partner to finish a project it has held for more than a decade has not demonstrated that it can deliver. There is consistent procrastination. There are no delivery dates that can be held. Increasingly ageing and outdated equipment sits stored away in warehouses — some of it was seen during oversight visits — while the Ratel remains in the field. Nobody has told Parliament whether the technology already paid for is obsolete. The question Denel must answer is when it will bite the bullet and take a decision on Hoefyster. That decision may be to close the project, with all the financial losses that follow. Hard as that is, a decision must be taken. No decision, and simply allowing the disaster to drag on, is the worst possible situation. The dragging-on is itself the damage. Because Hoefyster is a gaping wound that keeps bleeding, it is also a major reason Denel cannot address its liquidity problems and cannot obtain finance or credit. It drains cash, it sits on the balance sheet as an unresolved obligation, and it scares away possible financiers. No lender will fund an entity that will not decide whether this project continues or stops.
Armscor is not Denel and should not be treated as if it were. It again received an unqualified audit opinion, which is better than a disclaimer and should be recorded. Some work is moving. Inshore patrol vessel support is described as near finalisation. The Dockyard remains a strategic facility, though it is poorly managed. These are limited positives. They do not excuse what sits underneath the opinion. The financial statements submitted for audit were not fully prepared under section 55 of the Public Finance Management Act. Material misstatements were corrected before the opinion was signed. Irregular expenditure rose by a further R19.15 million to a cumulative R51.4 million. Fruitless and wasteful expenditure rose by R1.614 million to R7.4 million. Subsistence and travel rose from R35 million to R64.2 million. Non-executive fees rose from R8.1 million to R15.2 million, with about 70 per cent of that classified as ad hoc. These are red flags that cannot be waved away.
The same pattern of delay and incomplete accountability is visible in Project Hotel, the acquisition of a new hydrographic survey vessel — the SAS Nelson Mandela — intended to replace the ageing SAS Protea and restore the South African Navy’s ability to chart its waters, meet international maritime obligations, and support safe navigation and naval operations. The contract became effective in December 2017, with delivery first promised for May 2021. Repeated extensions followed. By April 2026, when the Portfolio Committee conducted an oversight visit to the Sandock Austral shipyard in Durban, there was still no firm handover date, earlier completion percentages had become unreliable, and more than R2 billion had already been spent. The hull remains unfinished. The same yard is also late on the SAS Isandlwana refit. Armscor’s slides list Hoefyster among the projects where Denel’s failures are hitting prime-mission equipment, but Project Hotel is an Armscor-managed acquisition whose slippage cannot be blamed solely on others. Oryx and Rooivalk continue to be kept alive by cannibalisation. A decade of such slippage is also a failure of contract management.
What makes Project Hotel particularly troubling is the manner in which the tender was handled. The previous Chief of Materiel of the SANDF, Dr Mthobisi Clyde Zondi, played a central role in the adjudication process that awarded the contract to Southern African Shipyards, which later became Sandock Austral. Shortly afterwards, in an extraordinary revolving-door move, he joined the successful bidder as an executive. This sequence raises the clearest possible appearance of a conflict of interest: an official responsible for awarding a major public contract moves directly into senior employment with the company that received it. The irregularities in the tender process, the subsequent delays, the absence of a credible completion date, and this post-award transition have never been properly accounted for to Parliament. During the April oversight visit the unfinished vessel stood as a concrete reminder of what happens when procurement decisions are not subjected to rigorous, independent scrutiny.
Two further procurement matters illustrate the same problem of incomplete information. Tender ELWS/2024/71 for 462 border-patrol vehicles — 210 section, 144 command and 108 ambulance — was issued on 23 July 2024 to replace the Land Cruiser troop packs used on Operation Corona. A field evaluation set for March 2025 was cancelled after compliant bidders had mobilised. Milkor did not take part in that process. In October 2025 Milkor was confirmed as the winning bidder. On 18 March 2026 the matter was taken to court, with the Minister and Armscor as respondents. Both the award and the litigation fall inside the 2025/26 financial year. Yet the Annual Report does not account for the cancelled evaluation, the award or the case. Silence in an annual report on a tender already before the courts is itself a reporting failure. The R500 million figure cited in Parliament is an allocation, not a contract value. Armscor has still not placed the value or the full evaluation record on the table.
The second matter is the soldier’s rifle. Armscor issued Request for Information 02061-900-013 for self-loading automatic rifle systems. It closed on 30 September 2026. Officially it is not a bid. Officially it is a study into a possible replacement of the Vektor R4 and R5. It was issued after year-end, so it is not a line in these accounts. It is, however, the live test of the same procurement culture. The study is being read, reasonably, against a Kalashnikov-pattern pitch, the AK201 in 5.56 mm. Questions have been put to the Minister about information indicating that 300 such rifles were already bought for trials and have not been delivered, and that local content would be assembly rather than manufacture. These claims require confirmation or denial. A study that looks like a corridor is not oversight. The R4 and R5 are a locally designed and supported family. They can be improved. They are not to be replaced in a side room without Parliament being told whether a decision to leave that family has already been taken.
During the Committee meeting I put five questions to each entity for answer that afternoon. For Denel they concerned the concrete corrective actions taken after a ninth disclaimer, the status of every Hoefyster variant against the stated baselines and whether a binding go or no-go decision has actually been taken, the cash versus accounting nature of any bottom-line improvement given the negative cash position, the status of the non-core disposal programme, and the basis for a Corporate Plan revenue path toward R3 billion when the entity missed its own target by R483 million. For Armscor they concerned progress on the instruction arising from the April oversight visit on the future of Project Hotel, the absence of Hoefyster delivery figures and any consequence applied to Denel, the full story of tender ELWS/2024/71 including why the March evaluation was cancelled and why the Annual Report is silent, the rifle Request for Information and any prior orders of AK201 rifles, and the named control that will stop further material misstatements and rising irregular expenditure.
It was critical that the committee should not be left with another undertaking. It should receive dates with names and with decisions. What the committee must insist on is that Denel must be required to produce a time-bound plan to exit the disclaimer, report quarterly to the committee and to SCOPA, put the independent turnaround review on the table, make a decision on Project Hoefyster within sixty days — either a ring-fenced, performance-bonded delivery schedule or closure with the losses quantified, because no decision is the worst possible situation — and produce a cash-flow statement before any further recapitalisation is entertained.
What Armscor must be required to produce is a joint accountability matrix with Denel on the shared projects so the two entities can no longer point at each other; monthly reporting on flagship projects with dates, spend and a responsible official; a full report on ELWS/2024/71; a written answer on the rifle Request for Information; and Budgetary Review and Recommendation Reports that tie the next allocation to delivery milestones and the closing of audit findings, not to the repetition of an unqualified opinion with findings. Project Hotel requires the same treatment: a clear statement of the revised cost, the revised date, the capacity of Sandock Austral to finish both the hydrographic vessel and the Isandlwana refit, and a full accounting of the tender process and the revolving-door transition of the former Chief of Materiel.
What we learned on 9 October is that both entities remain in serious difficulty and that the soldier is still waiting for the vehicle Hoefyster was meant to provide, while the Navy is still waiting for the hydrographic vessel that was supposed to restore its ability to chart its own waters. What we did not learn is equally important, and more alarming. We did not learn the true cash position of Denel in a form that can sustain a going-concern claim without associate income. We did not learn whether a binding decision on Hoefyster has been taken or what the cost of cancellation versus continued obsolescence would be. We did not learn the full evaluation record or contract value of the border-patrol vehicle tender now before the courts. We did not learn whether a decision to replace the R4 and R5 has already been taken, whether any Kalashnikov-pattern rifles have been ordered and paid for, or what local content is actually proposed. We did not learn a credible completion date or full cost for the SAS Nelson Mandela, nor a proper explanation of the circumstances in which the tender was awarded and the former Chief of Materiel moved into the successful bidder. Presentations that omit these facts raise legitimate questions about whether they reflect the true reality inside Denel and Armscor.
Denel’s disclaimer is now a governance failure, not a bookkeeping failure. Armscor’s unqualified opinion is being asked to carry a capital programme it is not delivering, a border-vehicle tender that is in court, a rifle process that Parliament was not told about, and a hydrographic vessel whose tender process and revolving-door transition have never been properly scrutinised. Project Hoefyster is where the failures of the two entities meet. The SANDF cannot defend the sovereignty of the nation with ageing equipment, cannibalised aircraft, delayed ships, an unfinished hydrographic vessel, and an unresolved infantry combat vehicle project. The BRRR process itself must cease to be a rushed rubber stamp and become the rigorous oversight the Constitution requires. Anything less is a failure of Parliament’s duty to the soldiers and sailors who are expected to defend this country, and to the sovereignty they are meant to protect.
* Ambassador Carl Niehaus is an EFF member of Parliament, and the EFF’s permanent representative on the Portfolio Committee on Defence and Military Veterans, and the Joint Stsnding Committee on Defence.

title: Greek Police Bust Network Smuggling Chinese Migrants via Albania and Athens Safehouses
body: Athens police have dismantled a criminal network that facilitated the illegal movement of foreign nationals—primarily from China—into Greece via Albania and onward to other European Union countries. Following coordinated raids in the eastern Athens suburb of Vyronas (Byronas) and central Athens, officers arrested a 39-year-old man alleged to have played an active role in the group. He is accused of managing temporary accommodation facilities and assisting with the illegal entry, stay, and exit of migrants. Authorities identified four apartments in the same building in Vyronas that served as “safehouses” for short-term stays. Inside them, police found 21 foreign nationals aged 22 to 58 who lacked the required documents to remain in Greece. The arrested man is believed to have overseen the apartments and the temporary housing arrangements. According to the Hellenic Police, the network had been operating since at least late July. Migrants reportedly flew from China to Albania, then crossed the Greek-Albanian border on foot through remote, unguarded stretches. Once inside Greece, they were transported by car or bus to the Vyronas apartments, where they stayed temporarily while the next stage of their journey was organized—typically toward other EU destinations. The group is also accused of producing and supplying forged travel and identification documents, including passports, residence permits, and identity cards of questionable authenticity. These were used to help the migrants leave Greece and travel to countries such as Italy and Spain. The fee charged per person for the full illegal transport and relocation package reportedly ranged from €6,500 to €7,000. During searches of the 39-year-old’s residence and the four apartments, police seized passports, residence permits, and identity documents of dubious authenticity; 10 boarding-pass stubs; photocopies of airline tickets; small quantities of narcotics; a large number of keys; three surveillance cameras; counterfeit clothing items; 28 mobile phones; and one vehicle allegedly used by the group. The arrested man faces charges including participation in a criminal organization, forgery, facilitating illegal entry and exit from the country, illegal possession of travel documents, and violations of immigration and narcotics laws. The 21 individuals found in the apartments face charges of illegal residence. Those detained were brought before the competent prosecutor. title: airBaltic sends A220 pilots to Air Niugini amid financial restructuring
body:
Latvian carrier airBaltic has begun sending Airbus A220 pilots to Air Niugini under a 12-month agreement aimed at supporting the Papua New Guinea airline as it expands its fleet of the commercial jet.
The first two airBaltic captains have arrived in Port Moresby, with a total of 30 pilots expected to participate in the program, Air Niugini said. Around 15 will be in Papua New Guinea at any given time, working on 28-day rotations.
Follow Air Data News: WhatsApp | Instagram | LinkedIn | Twitter | Facebook
Additional pilots are expected to arrive progressively over the next two months. The airBaltic crews will fly alongside Air Niugini pilots and support the development of local captains and first officers as the airline introduces more A220s.
The arrangement provides Air Niugini with pilots already experienced on the aircraft without involving the provision of airBaltic jets. The Latvian airline was the launch operator of the A220-300 in 2016 and has since built one of the world's largest fleets of the type.
Air Niugini is introducing the A220 as a central element of its fleet renewal and expansion. The airline currently operates three A220-300s and has eight smaller A220-100s on order.
The carrier has acknowledged that its fleet growth is creating additional demand for trained crews. Chief Executive Officer Alan Milne said in September that Air Niugini could require around 100 additional pilots to support its expansion plans.
The agreement with airBaltic provides an interim source of experienced A220 crews as Air Niugini trains more of its own pilots.
Earlier discussions indicated that as many as 45 airBaltic pilots could become available for the program. Air Niugini's latest announcement confirms 30 pilots under the 12-month arrangement.
The deployment comes as airBaltic undergoes a financial restructuring after seeking Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States in September.
The Latvian airline continues to operate but is considering measures to reduce costs, with reports indicating that hundreds of jobs could be affected by its restructuring plans.
The pilot agreement gives airBaltic an opportunity to deploy experienced A220 crews with another operator during that process. Neither airline has said that the 30 pilots involved would otherwise face redundancy.
The Latvian Aviation Union has sought clarification over employment conditions for airBaltic pilots assigned to Papua New Guinea, including how their contracts and working arrangements will be handled during the deployment.

title: “We can never get to a situation where we allow AI to run away with us”
body:
The world is on an exponentially accelerating timeline towards Artificial General Intelligence but there is not enough debate about the inherent dangers of that, according to Wayne Dalton, Senior AI officer at the Cyber Security Institute.
“We can never get to a situation where we allow Artificial Intelligence (AI) to run away with us,” he said at the Future of Warfare Symposium on the first day of the Africa Aerospace and Defence (AAD) 2026 Conference at Air Force Base Waterkloof.
The development of AI has occurred in three waves with the first wave being classical AI, using machine learning, while the second wave was a narrow application blending supervised and unsupervised learning and the third type is reinforcement learning, the most powerful form of AI.
“The world was underestimating the scope, scale and speed of AI evolution,” said Dalton adding, “this is the time we should be talking about what it means when we talk about human control.”
The Global Commission on Responsible Artificial Intelligence in the Military Domain (GC REAIM) on which Dalton served, came up with four variations on the meaning of human control that goes beyond humans mechanically approving what is happening to human agency.
“If you want human control, you need human agency, you need legal accountability and you need moral responsibility.”
Meaningful human control can be divided up into four different situations of human agency: human in the loop (low autonomy), human on the loop (active supervisor), human in command (preset parameters managing risk) and finally human out of the loop where AI is fully autonomous.
It was vital, he said, to distinguish between AI capability and use cases and to help do this, he and his team came up with Military AI Responsibility Contextualisation (MARC) framework to create the context to allow for responsible use.
The context looks at three axes; the spectrum of conflict (peace, war or grey area), the type of war (offensive kinetic or non-kinetic, defensive kinetic or non-kinetic or service and support) and finally the domain (sea, air, land or cyber) to properly define the problem and its responsible solution.
The GC REAIM had come up with five core recommendations. These include the enforcement of strict guardrails prohibiting AI from autonomously selecting and engaging targets; banning AI from nuclear command and control; the implementation of responsibility by design; embedding legal and ethical safeguards; and the standardisation of testing, evaluation, verification and validation.
“We have to invest in our defence colleges and the military academy. We should be investing in data literacy and AI literacy for our tactical components, not just our technical teams,” he concluded.

title: Linux Lockdown and Hibernation (again)
body:
(This is an updated version of an older post - the introduction remains the same, the technical details are different)
Linux draws a distinction between code running in kernel (kernel space) and applications running in userland (user space). This is enforced at the hardware level - in x86-speak 1 , kernel space code runs in ring 0 and user space code runs in ring 3 2 . If you’re running in ring 3 and you attempt to touch memory that’s only accessible in ring 0, the hardware will raise a fault. No matter how privileged your ring 3 code, you don’t get to touch ring 0.
Kind of. In theory. Traditionally this wasn’t well enforced. At the most basic level, since root can load kernel modules, you could just build a kernel module that performed any kernel modifications you wanted and then have root load it. Technically user space code wasn’t modifying kernel space code, but the difference was pretty semantic rather than useful. But it got worse - root could also map memory ranges belonging to PCI devices 3 , and if the device could perform DMA you could just ask the device to overwrite bits of the kernel 4 . Or root could modify special CPU registers (“Model Specific Registers”, or MSRs) that alter CPU behaviour via the /dev/msr interface, and compromise the kernel boundary that way.
It turns out that there were a number of ways root was effectively equivalent to ring 0, and the boundary was more about reliability (ie, a process running as root that ends up misbehaving should still only be able to crash itself rather than taking down the kernel with it) than security. After all, if you were root you could just replace the on-disk kernel with a backdoored one and reboot. Going deeper, you could replace the bootloader with one that automatically injected backdoors into a legitimate kernel image. We didn’t have any way to prevent this sort of thing, so attempting to harden the root/kernel boundary wasn’t especially interesting.
In 2012 Microsoft started requiring vendors ship systems with UEFI Secure Boot, a firmware feature that allowed 5 systems to refuse to boot anything without an appropriate signature. This not only enabled the creation of a system that drew a strong boundary between root and kernel, it arguably required one - what’s the point of restricting what the firmware will stick in ring 0 if root can just throw more code in there afterwards? What ended up as the Lockdown Linux Security Module provides the tooling for this, blocking userspace interfaces that can be used to modify the kernel and enforcing that any modules have a trusted signature.
But that comes at something of a cost. Most of the features that Lockdown blocks are fairly niche, so the direct impact of having it enabled is small. Except that it also blocks hibernation 6 , and it turns out some people were using that. The obvious question is “what does hibernation have to do with keeping root out of kernel space”, and the answer is a little convoluted and is tied into how Linux implements hibernation. Basically, Linux saves system state into the swap partition and modifies the header to indicate that there’s a hibernation image there instead of swap. On the next boot, the kernel sees the header indicating that it’s a hibernation image, copies the contents of the swap partition back into RAM, and then jumps back into the old kernel code. What ensures that the hibernation image was actually written out by the kernel? Absolutely nothing, which means a motivated attacker with root access could turn off swap, write a hibernation image to the swap partition themselves, and then reboot. The kernel would happily resume into the attacker’s image, giving the attacker control over what gets copied back into kernel space.
This is annoying, because normally when we think about attacks on swap we mitigate it by requiring an encrypted swap partition. But in this case, our attacker is root, and so already has access to the plaintext version of the swap partition. Disk encryption doesn’t save us here. We need some way to verify that the hibernation image was written out by the kernel, not by root. And thankfully we have some tools for that.
Trusted Platform Modules (TPMs) are cryptographic coprocessors 7 capable of doing things like generating encryption keys and then encrypting things with them. You can ask a TPM to encrypt something with a key that’s tied to that specific TPM - the OS has no access to the decryption key, and nor does any other TPM. So we can have the kernel generate an encryption key, encrypt part of the hibernation image with it, and then have the TPM encrypt it. We store the encrypted copy of the key in the hibernation image as well. On resume, the kernel reads the encrypted copy of the key, passes it to the TPM, gets the decrypted copy back and is able to verify the hibernation image.
That’s great! Except root can do exactly the same thing. This tells us the hibernation image was generated on this machine, but doesn’t tell us that it was done by the kernel. We need some way to be able to differentiate between keys that were generated in kernel and ones that were generated in userland. TPMs have the concept of “localities” (effectively privilege levels) that would be perfect for this. Userland is only able to access locality 0, so the kernel could simply use locality 1 to encrypt the key. Unfortunately, localities are typically only available on systems that implement a Dynamic Root of Trust Measurement like Intel’s TXT, and most consumer systems have no support for this. So, we need another approach.
TPMs have a set of Platform Configuration Registers (PCRs), intended for keeping a record of system state. The OS isn’t able to modify the PCRs directly. Instead, the OS provides a cryptographic hash of some material to the TPM. The TPM takes the existing PCR value, appends the new hash to that, and then stores the hash of the combination in the PCR - a process called “extension”. This means that the new value of the TPM depends not only on the value of the new data, it depends on the previous value of the PCR - and, in turn, that previous value depended on its previous value, and so on. The only way to get to a specific PCR value is to either (a) break the hash algorithm, or (b) perform exactly the same sequence of writes. On system reset the PCRs go back to a known value, and the entire process starts again.
Some PCRs are different. PCR 23, for example, can be reset back to its original value without resetting the system. We can make use of that. The first thing we need to do is to prevent userland from being able to reset or extend PCR 23 itself. All TPM accesses go through the kernel, so this is a simple matter of parsing the write before it’s sent to the TPM and returning an error if it’s a sensitive command that would touch PCR 23. We now know that any change in PCR 23’s state will be restricted to the kernel.
When we encrypt material with the TPM, we can ask it to record the PCR state. This is given back to us as metadata accompanying the encrypted secret. Along with the metadata is an additional signature created by the TPM, which can be used to prove that the metadata is both legitimate and associated with this specific encrypted data. In our case, that means we know what the value of PCR 23 was when we encrypted the key. That means that if we simply extend PCR 23 with a known value in-kernel before encrypting our key, we can look at the value of PCR 23 in the metadata. If it matches, the key was encrypted by the kernel - userland can create its own key, but it has no way to extend PCR 23 to the appropriate value first. We now know that the key was generated by the kernel.
Unfortunately it turns out that some people actually make use of PCR 23, and restricting it to the kernel makes them sad. There are other resettable PCRs, but only in non-0 localities, so (a) we can’t reset them on most systems and (b) we’ll just find someone who uses them anyway and run into the same problem. We need a different approach.
Thankfully TPMs have a small chunk of non-volatile RAM that can be used for storing things, and by “storing” I mean they can be used in a range of different ways. One of these is effectively as additional PCRs. These values can be configured such that they work the same way as PCRs, with the only way to modify them being to append a new hash to their existing value and update the new value to the hash of that merged value. We can allocate one of these for in-kernel use and reject any access from userspace, and also there are officially allocated ranges (so people shouldn’t be using random values) and the namespace is large enough anyway that w eshouldn’t collide with anyone, so we can carve one of those out and use it for this purpose.
Unfortunately, though, these NV indexes aren’t included in the creation data we get when we create a key, so we need another approach. TPMs have the concept of sessions, a series of commands executed in sequence. A flag allows these sessions to be “audited”, with the TPM keeping a running track of the hash of the commands executed and the results returned. At the end of the session you can ask for a signed copy of this hash, and if you’ve kept a log of all the commands then you can verify that they match that signed hash and know that this log represents a real communication with the TPM. If we read the NV index and generate the key inside the same session, we can verify that the key we’re looking at was created while the NV index had a specific value, and if only the kernel can set that value then we know that the key was generated by the kernel.
Or, well, can we? Only new kernels would impose the restriction on modifying that NV index. An attacker could boot an old kernel, generate a key there in userland, sign a hibernation image with it, and then reboot into a new kernel. The new kernel would see a valid signature with a valid NV index associated with it and have no way to know it was generated from userland rather than the kernel. We need to be able to tell the difference between kernels that implement this feature and ones that don’t, and we need to do that without being able to go back in time to change old kernel behaviour. We can extend a PCR to indicate we implement the new functionality, but so can an attacker running an old kernel.
The normal approach to determining whether an event occurred in a specific phase of the boot process is to “cap” the PCRs - extend them with a known value that indicates a transition between stages of the boot process. Any events that occur before the cap event must have occurred in the previous stage of boot, and since the final PCR value depends on the order of measurements and not just the contents of those measurements, if a PCR is capped before userland runs, userland can’t fake the same PCR value afterwards. If Linux capped the PCRs before userland started running, we’d be able to place a measurement there before the cap occurred and then prove that that extension occurred before userland had the opportunity to interfere. We could simply place a statement that the kernel supported the NV index restrictions there, and we’d be fine.
Unfortunately Linux doesn’t currently do this, and adding support for doing so doesn’t fix the problem - if an attacker boots a kernel that doesn’t cap a PCR, they can just cap it themselves from userland. So, we’re faced with the same problem: booting an older kernel allows the system to be placed in an identical state to the current kernel, and a fake hibernation image can be written out. Solving this requires a PCR that was being modified after kernel code was running, but before userland was started, even with existing kernels.
Thankfully, there is one! PCR 5 is defined as containing measurements related to boot management configuration and data. One of the measurements it contains is the result of the UEFI ExitBootServices() call. ExitBootServices() is called at the transition from the UEFI boot environment to the running OS, and the kernel contains code that executes before it. So, if we measure an assertion regarding whether or not we support restricted access to NV indexes into PCR 5 before we call ExitBootServices(), this will prevent userspace from spoofing us (because userspace will only be able to extend PCR 5 after the firmware extended PCR 5 in response to ExitBootServices() being called). Obviously this depends on the firmware actually performing the PCR 5 extension when ExitBootServices() is called, but if firmware’s out of spec then I don’t think there’s any real expectation of it being secure enough for any of this to buy you anything anyway.
That’s what this patchset does. Review feedback so far seems positive, although James Bottomley suggested a design improvement. My approach of using an NV index as a PCR and generating a signing key made sense as a consequence of my original approach involving PCR 23, which had been to use the key creation data and not use audit sessions at all. But the goal isn’t to use a key - it’s to prove that hibernation occurred in-kernel, and while signing is one way of doing that, there are others. His suggestion is to simply record the hash of the hibernation image into the NV index and then read that back as part of the audit session. On resume we verify the audit session log is legitimate, read the hibernation image, and compare the hash of the hibernation image against the hash in the log. If it matches, and if the PCR 5 value matches, we know the audit session happened in kernel and that the hibernation image hasn’t been modified.
It still seems like we’re missing something, though. If we’re not storing a key anywhere, how do we verify the audit session? To explain this we’re going to need to go into some details about how TPM keys work in the first place. TPMs can produce a special kind of key called an Attestation Key, or AK. Attestation keys are used to sign attestation statements from the TPM, such as PCR quotes or audit logs. We need a separate key type for this in order to prove that the signature was generated as part of an attestation - normal TPM signing keys are fundamentally designed to sign arbitrary material, and so can be used by userland to sign something that looks identical to an attestation record. By being able to distinguish the types of key the TPM uses, we can prove that a signature was generated using an AK, and so know that it’s a real TPM attestation (because nothing other than the TPM can sign stuff with an AK).
But even beyond this distinction, TPMs have different key types. Ordinary keys are generated using an RNG and will be unique. Primary keys are generated using a seed that is used as an input into a key derivation function. For a given TPM, using the same seed to generate the same type of primary key will always generate the same primary key 8 . We can have the kernel deterministically generate an AK during suspend in order to sign the audit log, and then generate the same key again on resume to validate it. This means we don’t need any other form of trusted storage for the AK - the TPM already provides that functionality.
This is all rather complicated but I’ve been thinking about this for some time now and I haven’t come up with a cleaner solution. The only real open issue is the degree to which machines actually perform the PCR 5 extension. If it turns out there’s a bunch that don’t we’ll need to come up with some alternative approach to identifying whether the kernel supports this functionality, but the design is such that that should be invisible to userspace so adding alternatives later shouldn’t be an issue. Filtering accesses to the NV index is also not super clean, and depends on there not being alternative mechanisms to get at the TPM by sending raw commands. Again, this is intended to be opaque to userland and can be improved if we come up with something better later on (such as a secure way to pass a secret to the kernel on boot that can be used as an auth value for acess to the NV index).
Anyway. Time to go and fix the next thing.
Other architectures use different terminology here, such as “supervisor” and “user” mode, but it’s broadly equivalent ↩︎
In theory rings 1 and 2 would allow you to run drivers with privileges somewhere between full kernel access and userland applications, but in reality we just don’t talk about them in polite company ↩︎
This is how graphics worked in Linux before kernel modesetting turned up. XFree86 would just map your GPU’s registers into userland and poke them directly. This was not a huge win for stability ↩︎
IOMMUs can help you here, by restricting the memory PCI devices can DMA to or from. The kernel then gets to allocate ranges for device buffers and configure the IOMMU such that the device can’t DMA to anything else. Except that region of memory may still contain sensitive material such as function pointers, and attacks like this can still cause you problems as a result. ↩︎
This describes why I’m using “allowed” rather than “required” here ↩︎
Saving the system state to disk and powering down the platform entirely - significantly slower than suspending the system while keeping state in RAM, but also resilient against the system losing power. ↩︎
With some handwaving around “coprocessor”. TPMs can’t be part of the OS or the system firmware, but they don’t technically need to be an independent component. Intel have a TPM implementation that runs on the Management Engine, a separate processor built into the motherboard chipset. AMD have one that runs on the Platform Security Processor, a small ARM core built into their CPU. Various ARM implementations run a TPM in Trustzone, a special CPU mode that (in theory) is able to access resources that are entirely blocked off from anything running in the OS, kernel or otherwise. ↩︎
Unless the TPM is cleared, in which case it’ll generate a new internal seed and now the keys will be different to before the clear ↩︎

title: Lebanon ambassador to US receives complaint for asking Israeli ambassador about his son
body: The US State Department strongly condemned a complaint filed against Lebanon's Ambassador to Washington, Nada Hamadeh Moawad, after reports that she contacted Israeli Ambassador to the US Yechiel Leiter to ask about his son, who was wounded in a terrorist attack.In a sharply worded statement, a State Department spokesperson said the US was aware of the complaint, which was filed by a lawyer affiliated with Hezbollah."It is embarrassing that a military court is handling a complaint against Lebanon's ambassador in Washington simply because she was implementing her legitimate government's policy and participating in US-led negotiations," the statement said.The State Department added that Lebanon's military justice system should use its limited resources to prosecute Hezbollah operatives planning to act against the Lebanese government and its citizens, "rather than those acting on their behalf."The department also called on Lebanon to repeal laws and procedures that, it said, enable the "political persecution of citizens and diplomats," while Hezbollah operatives systematically receive protection."We have no patience for obstruction," the statement said.The complaint was filed by Lebanese lawyer Hassan Adel Bazzi following an article published in September by Beirut Review.According to the report, Moawad contacted Israeli Ambassador to the US Yechiel Leiter to inquire about the condition of his son, who had been wounded in a terrorist attack.The report said Lebanon's attorney-general referred the complaint to the government commissioner at the military court to examine possible legal action.It remains unclear whether the complaint will lead to legal proceedings or be dismissed and closed.The affair has raised concerns that the complaint represents an attempt to deter officials involved in negotiations between Lebanon and Israel.Such a move could complicate diplomatic efforts between the two countries amid political and security tensions in Lebanon.Lebanon concerned over Hezbollah's strengtheningThe development comes amid growing concerns in Lebanon over Hezbollah's conduct and its strengthening position.The organization recently announced it had funds at its disposal, a claim the United States rejected. The State Department maintained that the funds purportedly received from Iran do not exist.Meanwhile, Lebanese authorities reported intercepting a shipment of explosives.According to reports, two suspects affiliated with Hezbollah smuggled the explosives in a truck from eastern Lebanon toward Beirut's southern suburbs.The incidents illustrate the challenges facing the Lebanese government as it seeks to strengthen state authority while simultaneously confronting political and security pressure from Hezbollah.

title: SA and autonomous weapons: Regulating risk without surrendering technological sovereignty
body:
The international debate over lethal autonomous weapons systems (LAWS) is entering an important phase. For South Africa, this debate should not be viewed only through the lens of arms control, international humanitarian law or the ethics of machines making decisions about the use of force. It is also a debate about defence innovation, industrial capability and, increasingly, technological sovereignty.
The question confronting South Africa is therefore more complex than whether autonomous weapons should be permitted or prohibited.
It is also about whether South Africa will retain the technological knowledge and industrial capability necessary to understand, develop, test, assure and defend against the autonomous systems that will increasingly shape the future security environment.
The United Nations Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) Group of Governmental Experts on emerging technologies in the area of lethal autonomous weapons systems has been working on the issue for more than a decade. In 2026, the process has moved towards formulating elements of a possible international instrument, without prejudging whether that instrument will ultimately be legally binding or take another form. The 2026 discussions have also brought together legal, military and technological considerations.
This makes the current period particularly important for South Africa.
The dilemma is not simply regulation versus no regulation
There are legitimate reasons for international concern about autonomous weapons.
Military systems capable of operating with limited human intervention raise questions about civilian protection, accountability, predictability, escalation and compliance with international humanitarian law. South Africa has itself supported continued work in the CCW process and has emphasised the humanitarian implications of emerging weapons technologies. In its 2024 submission, South Africa reaffirmed its commitment to the CCW, the protection of civilians and the development of international norms around emerging weapons technologies.
South Africa has also stressed the importance of clarity around the definition of LAWS and human involvement. During the 2025 GGE discussions, South Africa called for a clear characterisation of LAWS and highlighted the importance of explicitly addressing human involvement where this is intended to be a requirement.
There is therefore a legitimate case for international governance.
But there is another side to the equation.
Autonomy is not a single technology. It is an aggregation of technologies including artificial intelligence, machine learning, robotics, computer vision, sensor fusion, autonomous navigation, communications, edge computing and human-machine interfaces.
These technologies are increasingly dual-use.
The same computer-vision capability can support agricultural automation, medical imaging, border surveillance or military reconnaissance. Robotics can support mining and manufacturing as well as explosive ordnance disposal and military logistics. Autonomous navigation can support civilian transport and unmanned military systems.
A regulatory approach that fails to distinguish between a specific unacceptable weapon function and the underlying technologies could therefore have consequences far beyond the LAWS issue itself.
South Africa should avoid becoming a technology rule-taker
This is where the debate becomes particularly important for South Africa.
The country does not have the technological scale of the world’s largest military and commercial technology powers. It has important pockets of competence across defence research, development and innovation (RDI), aerospace, electronic systems, land and maritime technologies, AI, cybersecurity, advanced manufacturing and systems engineering, but it also has significant dependencies on foreign technologies, components, software and intellectual property.
A technologically advanced country entering an international restriction regime may already possess decades of accumulated knowledge, intellectual property, industrial infrastructure, operational experience and skilled personnel.
A technology-developing country may still be building those capabilities.
The same international rule can therefore have very different consequences for the two countries.
This does not mean South Africa should oppose international regulation. It means that the consequences of regulation must be considered from the perspective of both humanitarian responsibility and technological development.
The central question should be: does a proposed restriction regulate an unacceptable weapon capability, or does it unintentionally constrain the development of the wider technology base from which legitimate future capabilities may emerge?
Military autonomy should not be understood as a simple choice between human control and completely independent machines.
There is a spectrum ranging from systems directly controlled by humans, through systems that assist human decision-making, to systems operating under human supervision and systems capable of increasingly independent mission functions.
This matters because autonomy in one part of a system does not necessarily mean autonomy in the use of lethal force.
An unmanned system may navigate autonomously while its employment decisions remain under human control. Another system may use AI to classify objects while a human makes the engagement decision. A defensive system may need to respond extremely quickly to an incoming threat while operating within tightly defined parameters.
Consequently, the policy question should not simply be whether a system is “autonomous”.
It should ask what function is autonomous, under what circumstances, within what constraints, and with what human responsibility and control?
This functional approach would allow the international community to address genuinely unacceptable risks without inadvertently treating all autonomy-related technologies as equivalent.
Technology sovereignty is becoming a defence requirement
For South Africa, perhaps the most important issue is technological sovereignty.
Technology sovereignty does not mean producing every component domestically. No modern defence industry can realistically operate without international technology partnerships and global supply chains.
It means retaining sufficient national capability to understand and manage strategically important dependencies.
Consider an autonomous military system acquired from abroad.
South Africa may own the platform. But does it own the software? Can it inspect the algorithms?
Does it control the data? Can it independently test the AI model? Can it determine what happens when communications are lost? Can it modify the system? Who controls software updates? Can the system be independently maintained if the supplier withdraws support?
And, perhaps most importantly, can South Africa reconstruct what happened if an autonomous system behaves unexpectedly during an operation?
These are not merely procurement questions. They are sovereignty questions.
A country that owns a defence platform but cannot independently understand or assure the technology governing its critical behaviour may have physical possession without full technological sovereignty.
This leads to a concept that deserves greater attention in the South African debate: sovereign assurance.
South Africa should be able to establish, particularly for strategically important systems, what the system can do, what it cannot do, how it behaves under different conditions, what its failure modes are and whether meaningful human intervention is possible.
This requires more than buying equipment.
It requires national competence in testing, verification and validation, AI assurance, cybersecurity, human factors, systems engineering and operational experimentation.
It also requires access to appropriate test infrastructure and secure environments in which autonomous systems can be evaluated under realistic conditions.
This is important for the LAWS debate because responsible regulation depends upon technological understanding.
A country cannot meaningfully assure the behaviour of a system it cannot independently test.
Nor can it establish meaningful human control if it does not understand the system’s limitations, operating envelope and response to intervention.
The defence industry has a stake in this debate
The implications extend directly into South Africa’s defence industrialisation agenda.
Future defence value will increasingly reside not only in platforms, but in software, AI, sensors, data, communications, autonomy, cybersecurity and systems integration.
This creates opportunities for South African companies, universities, research institutions and SMMEs.
If the domestic industry becomes primarily an importer and integrator of foreign autonomous technologies, South Africa may acquire increasingly sophisticated systems without developing the underlying technological competence.
The objective should therefore be to move beyond local assembly towards meaningful participation in the technology value chain.
For selected critical technologies, South Africa should seek the ability to develop, integrate, test, maintain and modify systems domestically.
This does not mean attempting to reproduce every foreign technology.
It means identifying the technology layers where dependence would create unacceptable strategic vulnerability.
There is another issue that deserves attention in the international discussion: what happens if other states develop and deploy increasingly autonomous military systems?
South Africa will need to be able to detect, understand and defend against them.
Counter-autonomy will itself require advanced technologies.
These could include AI-enabled detection, electronic warfare, cyber resilience, autonomous interception, navigation resilience, sensor deception detection and other defensive capabilities.
A regulatory framework that inadvertently prevents a country from developing defensive technologies needed to protect its forces against autonomous threats could produce an unintended security consequence.
The distinction between offensive autonomous weapons and defensive autonomous technologies therefore deserves careful consideration.
Regulation must not close South Africa’s technology window
Emerging technologies provide a limited opportunity for countries to build technological competence before the technology ecosystem becomes dominated by established players.
The earlier South Africa develops knowledge, experiments with technologies, builds prototypes, establishes testing capability and develops industrial competence, the greater its ability to make informed decisions later.
If the country waits until technologies are mature elsewhere before developing national expertise, it may find that the cost of entry has become substantially higher.
This is why the LAWS debate should not be separated from South Africa’s broader defence RDI strategy.
The country needs enough capability to understand emerging autonomy even if it ultimately decides that particular applications should be restricted or prohibited.
Indeed, technological understanding strengthens rather than weakens responsible regulation.
There are consequently two strategic risks for South Africa.
Poorly governed autonomous weapons could create humanitarian consequences, accountability gaps, unsafe deployment, escalation risks and legal uncertainty.
The second is premature or excessively broad regulation.
Poorly defined restrictions could constrain legitimate RDI, weaken defence-industrial competitiveness, increase foreign technology dependence, reduce access to emerging technologies and limit South Africa’s ability to develop countermeasures.
There is also a third risk: regulatory fragmentation.
If different groups of states adopt fundamentally different definitions, standards and restrictions, the result could be an increasingly fragmented technology and defence market, creating additional challenges for interoperability, acquisition, industrial cooperation and international technology partnerships.
South Africa therefore has an interest in international rules that are clear, practical and technologically informed.
The current LAWS process provides South Africa with an opportunity to bring a perspective that goes beyond the traditional divide between advocates of prohibition and advocates of technological freedom.
South Africa can support strong adherence to international humanitarian law and human responsibility while also making the case that responsible international governance should not unintentionally deprive technology-developing states of legitimate opportunities to build scientific, engineering and industrial capability.
The country can support rigorous testing, assurance, human judgement, accountability and appropriate constraints while retaining the ability to develop defensive technologies and counter-autonomy capabilities.
And it can support international cooperation without abandoning the principle that strategically important national capabilities require a degree of sovereign technological competence.
This is particularly relevant as the 2026 CCW process moves towards the November Review Conference, where states are expected to consider the next phase of work on LAWS. The 2026 GGE has been tasked with developing elements of a possible instrument without prejudging its nature, while incorporating legal, military and technological expertise.
A South African question for the LAWS debate
The question for South Africa should therefore not simply be:
“Do we support or oppose autonomous weapons?”
The more strategically useful questions are:
· What autonomous functions present unacceptable humanitarian or legal risks?
· What forms of human responsibility and control are required?
· Which technologies should be regulated, and which should remain available for legitimate research and development?
· What capabilities must South Africa retain to defend itself against autonomous systems developed elsewhere?
· Which technology dependencies could compromise sovereign decision-making?
· What RDI and industrial capabilities must South Africa develop now to remain technologically relevant in the future?
How can South Africa contribute to responsible international governance without surrendering the technological options required for its future defence and national security?
These questions place the LAWS debate where it arguably belongs: not simply in the domain of weapons regulation, but at the intersection of international humanitarian law, national security, defence innovation, industrialisation and technological sovereignty.
For South Africa, responsible participation in the international LAWS process should therefore mean more than deciding what technologies may or may not be used.
It should also mean ensuring that the country retains enough technological understanding and sovereign capability to make that decision intelligently, independently and in the national interest.

title: Montenegrin citizens to be required to obtain visas to enter Russia — diplomat
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Montenegrin citizens will need to obtain visas to enter Russia due to Podgorica’s decision to abolish the visa-free regime for Russian citizens, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said.
"Consequently, Montenegrin citizens will also have to obtain visas to travel to Russia. This decision by Podgorica clearly harms Montenegrin interests," the diplomat told Izvestia, commenting on the country’s introduction of a visa regime for Russians from November 1.
According to the diplomat, "In pursuit of European aspirations, long-standing achievements in Russian-Montenegrin relations are being systematically undermined, and insufficient attention is being paid to the economic consequences of such steps." She noted that Podgorica’s new measures will reduce tourist traffic from Russia, hurt Montenegrin businesses, and lead to a deterioration of the investment climate in the country. "At the same time, of course, it is pointless for the Montenegrin authorities to count on compensation from Brussels for the inevitable losses," Zakharova pointed out.
According to the spokeswoman, the process of EU integration, which led Montenegro to impose visa requirements on Russians, "no longer in any way implies the possibility of new members retaining neutral status." "We hope that the countries of the Western Balkans are observing and analyzing these changes in the EU and clearly understanding the consequences of European integration for their own national interests and the well-being of their citizens," she concluded.
