title: What agents mean for Rust (and vice versa)
body:
This blog is where I post up various half-baked ideas that I have.
As someone who has made a career of programming language design, I definitely have moments of existential dread about the rise of LLMs. I started coding in 5th grade on an x86 1 that ran at 5MHz, had something like a 5MB hard-disk and 512K of RAM 2 . Computers were really, really different back then. But honestly, programming wasn’t. For all the advances in IDEs and programming languages and so forth, the basic act of entering code into a file has remained surprisingly constant 3 – right up until a few years ago, when everything kinda turned on its head. That’s been exciting and empowering at times 4 but also scary and disorienting. Will my skills in programming matter? What about my skills in programming language design (such as they are)? This blog post is my attempt to answer those questions.
So as not to keep you in suspense, let me just give you the conclusion. In short, yes, I believe there will still be a role for humans in programming . And yes, I think that programming language design is still relevant . And, naturally, I also happen to think Rust is a really good fit for agentic development – but that’s not to say we can’t make it a better fit . And that’s what this post is ultimately about: what makes Rust and agentic development work well, and where we could double down on those strengths.
This is a kind of “blog post companion version” of a talk I gave this week at REBASE, part of SPLASH . You might also enjoy the slides from the talk I gave at IWACO, IWACO and Rust: hidden links revealed , which was a bit more of a retrospective (no soundtrack for those, though). In any case, this turned out to be a great conference! Jack Huey presented on the Rust Vision Doc and, quite to my surprise, Steve Klabnik and Dorian Scheidt presented “LLMs as Collaborators in Language Specification and Design” , talking about their process in building out Rue . It was fun to see Steve again. On top of that, there was a ton of great research presented at IWACO in particular. I was particularly taken by the work on Reachability Types and Information Borrowing . I also really liked learning about Hylo Lang , particularly their approach to projections. Clever and cool.
Rust is popular right now. Very popular:
Stratospheric among the breakout languages is TypeScript, cropped from the chart and sitting currently at +1200% growth from the prior year. [..]
The second most rapid recent growth is in Rust. Meta engineers have written twice as much first-party Rust code so far this year than in the previous 9 years combined.
Some of that is because agents make it very easy to try out new things. And some of that is because Rust has a reputation for being performant and, if it’s just as easy to pick any language, why not pick one that will yield faster execution times?
But I think Rust is popular for another reason: because Rust happens to be a really good fit for agentic coding 6 . Of course, I would, wouldn’t I? The point of this post is (1) to argue for why that is and then (2) to discuss what we might change about Rust to make it work even better.
It seems to me that an effective “software factory” will have three pillars:
None of these pillars are solved, but some have made more progress than others.
Rust is designed to give “good performance by default”, making the idiomatic thing typically also be the fastest thing. But another key part of Rust is that you have the knobs to eke out better performance when you need it. You control when something is stack- or heap-allocated and where pointer indirection occurs. If you want to, you can force the layout of your structs to be done in a particular way, or decide where to introduce boxing into your async stack frames. In the limit, you can put in inline assembly.
In the past, learning how to “tune the performance knobs” could be a bit of a black art: but agents are making that much easier. 7 It turns out that agents are really good at fine-tuning the performance of existing code. For example, people who work on super high-performance cryptographic algorithms used to do so by hand-tuning assembly code. But those people tell me that they are now turning to agents for that same job. More prosaicly, a lot of people building network services are finding that, using a profiler like dial9 , agents can quite effectively diagnose async performance pitfalls, like long polls or blocking.
Therefore, I think the task for Rust is clear. We keep on with our goal of “low-level enough for a kernel, high level enough for a GUI” . If anything, I think the shift around agents means we can tolerate a bit more “noise” in the form of explicit calls to clone() or share() – but not too much, since we still want the “happy path” of the code to be clear and evident 8 , even as we surface details that are important in specific scenarios (like tracking precisely how many clones you have of a channel endpoint). Combined with a profiler, you get an effective feedback loop to get your code running fast:
As usual though, while a reputation for good performance is what brings people to Rust, what makes them want to stay is a sense that using Rust “just seems to work better”. The basic theory is that Rust’s type system and guardrails help keep agents on track :
rust is a perfect language for agents, given that if it compiles it's ~correct
I think there’s truth in that: languages like Rust, Ocaml, or Haskell all share this “if it compiles, it works” feeling, and I think that agents will benefit from that.
Testing can show the presence of bugs, but not their absence.
Writing tests has never been enough to show that your program is correct – but, with agents, it’s not even close. It happens so often that my first few tests seem great and then the next one goes completely bonkers. Usually bonkers in a way where I cannot even imagine how that bug could have come about. Then I dig in and I realize the agent completely missed the boat on the logic I was trying to express. 9
This is where a type systems really shines – particularly an advanced one like Rust. Type systems give you some guardrails that keep the agent on track. In Rust, those guardrails extend beyond simple stuff like “do all fields have the correct names” and to stuff like never having to close a socket .
Type systems can show the absence of bugs, but not the presence of correctness.
— Me, failing to coin a phrase of equal eloquence 10 , 2026
So yeah, type systems are helpful! But they have inherent limits. A type system is a simple set of rules that, if you follow them, make sure that you avoid (certain kinds of) mistakes. But they don’t tell you that you do the right thing – only that you don’t do (certain kinds of) wrong things . If you want to go further, you need a proof system – something that will let you show that richer properties are actively true, not just that you’re avoiding bugs.
As it happens, there are a lot of interesting proof tools for Rust, like Verus , Creusot , Aeneas , and Kani . As a starting point, you can prove that your code is panic-free, which will eliminate a lot of bugs, though it is still fundamentally a “type-checker-like” property (i.e., you avoid doing things wrong). But you can also go further and add assertions that show your code is computing the results you expect.
Deplying proofs is not just good for getting code right – it’s good for getting code fast . This is somewhat counterintuitive, but it’s true. Earlier I mentioned how optimized cryptographic algorithms were now being written by agents . Part of what makes that possible is that cryptographic algorithms have a very clear mathematical definition. This means that you can basically tell the agent “do whatever you want, as long as you can prove that the code still computes the correct result”. These proofs can be done with theorem provers like Lean or Rocq . The blog post “Why Lean is faster than Rust” makes the point quite well.
For Rust, a good example of this would be around unsafe code. Right now, people are sometimes reluctant to deploy unsafe code even if it might make their code faster because it’s not worth the risk of getting it wrong. And I applaud that effort. But what if you could use a prover to show that your unsafe code is, in fact, safe (i.e., incapable of causing undefined behavior)? Then you’d be free to optimize to your heart’s content.
You might wonder: if we’re deploying a proof system on our code, do we still need type systems? I think the answer is definitely yes. Type systems are infinitely simpler to work with, which is why they are much more popular. Using a type system lets you rule out all kinds of annoying bugs so that you can focus your “proof energy” only on the important stuff.
As a simple example of this, consider the following Java code:
Without seeing more code, it is impossible to prove whether this assertion is true or not! This is because there could be any number of other threads running around mutating this . In contrast, the following Rust code must be true (at least, so long as the Eq operator is reflexive for Bar ):
We know this because the type system of Rust guarantees that &mut self implies a unique reference.
This is in fact exactly how Verus works. By trusting the Rust borrow checker to track uniqueness etc, it simplifies the job of the SMT solver, making proof checking must faster and more reliable than it would be otherwise.
So my take is that Rust should double down on if it compiles, it works . As expressive as Rust’s type system is, there are plenty of things that it cannot capture. This includes fairly common things, like this method only reads one particular field or internal references , but also fancy things like “no logging of personally identifiable information”. We should work to lift those limits, giving agents room to prove more complex properties.
We also need to improve the experience of integrating a proof tool by working towards an extensible compiler . As cool as the existing Rust-based proof tools are, using them is a janky experience involing annoying macros and pinned compiler versions. We can do better.
I’d like to propose a north star for Rust: no more unsafe code . By that, I don’t mean that we never use the unsafe keyword . Rather, I mean that we have the power to prove that all the unsafe code we write is correct and cannot cause undefined behavior. Don’t get me wrong: knowing exactly what code needs to be vetted is a huge step forward, as is normalizing the idea that libraries need to be responsible for protecting their users from undefined behavior via safe API boundaries 11 . But given agents’ ability to find vulnerabilities, I think we need to up-our-game if we want to stop the steady stream of CVEs. 12
But before you go about proving things or optimizing them, you need to have a clear idea of what you are building. As far as I can tell the state of the art here is basically variations on “markdown-driven-development”, developing docs and hoping that agents pay attention.
I don’t know how much of a role for Rust there is in this space. I think there are some steps we might wind up taking that could be helpful here – for example, having ways to separate out interface from implementation so that it’s easier to review the interface in isolation or to see when the agent made changes there. 13 Or perhaps just providing betters tools to review that.
I also think there’s space for dedicated “modeling languages”, something that let you iterate quickly with agents on the high-level designs and invariants without having to get into the weeds and read the code. I have more thoughts on this but it merits many blog posts all of its own. For the moment, I’ll start by pointing you all at this post by Kari Wilhelm, “Principles of Anchor Engineering” , which I think does a nice job of describing what it means to pull out the key elements of a design and drive the coding from there.
We covered a lot of ground here, so let me put this all together. What makes Rust a good choice for developing with agents?
And what could make it better, from a language design perspective? Overall, I think it’s very similar to what we were doing, except that the way we weight the tradeoffs is tweaked to account for agents doing the code authoring, and humans focused more on code comprehension:
As a final close, let me point you at this interesting article by Marc Brooker, “What’s easy now? What’s hard now?” . He posits that the more it is possible to clearly specify success criteria for a task, the easier it is, and that we may find that tasks we traditionally think of as ‘hard’ (e.g., building out an efficient implementation of a cryptographic algorithm) may soon become automated, whereas tasks that we have thoght of as ’easy’ (e.g., making a unique, compelling website) may become more valued.
Looking at it from a PL point-of-view, I think Marc’s point reinforces my sense that the biggest action is going to come from design languages , things that let you capture the architecture and intended behavior at a very high-level. The goal would be to let humans intuitively specify a design that gets translated into effective guardrails, whether that’s type system checks, lints, or theorems to be proven. Agents would then take on the task of translating the design into code written in a traditional PL like Rust, with humans looking at it only rarely. This doesn’t make the design of traditional PLs less interesting, but it definitely makes the tradeoffs very different than they were before.
Secretly I have always been jealous of people that coded using punchcards and stored things on gigantic rolls of tape or whatever. I just want to be world weary so badly! I am kinda delighted that I’m finally old enough that I can say things like “I remember when we had to edit CONFIG.SYS before we could play a computer game!” and younger programmers will gasp in horror. 5 But I still feel like I must sound like a silly kid to folks who were around “back in the day”. ↩︎
I still remember when my dad told me he had bought me a 10MB disk and secretly he had bought a 40MB disk to surprise me. It seemed absurdly large. “I’ll never need a new disk again!” ↩︎
I mean my god, we’re even using vi again! My first editor! ↩︎
I built an electron app! And it was so easy to do! And reading weird papers and things is so much more accessible now that I can ask an LLM to translate all the math jargon for me. ↩︎
I remember once trying to tell Alex Crichton how I used to “order shareware from a paper catalog by putting a check in the mail” and he was like “I do not understand any of the nouns in that sentence”. Highlight of my life, right after Rust 1.0. Oh, and maybe the birth of my child and getting married. I guess. ↩︎
I’m not saying Rust is the only language that’s a good fit. I’m not even saying that the way that Rust is a good fit is the only way to be a good fit. I have heard for example that Go is a really good fit for agentic coding and I believe it: I think it hits a different sweet spot, one that helps agents iterate quickly (although I do suspect agents will let data races and subtle bugs slip through that Rust would have prevented). ↩︎
The fact that agentic development makes more room for knobs is good for Rust performance, but it is quite likely an even better fit for performance in other languages. Tuning a GC has traditionally been a job that really requires a GC expert, but agents can likely fill that role pretty well these days. ↩︎
On this pont, I’m even more convinced of the importance of ergonomic RC now that I work with agents. Agents are good at introducing the extra clones and things you need to deal with capturing around async tasks, but the resulting code is so annoying to read, it really hides what’s going on. ↩︎
“Claude, this is not what we talked about!” – me, all too often. ↩︎
So close though, right? I just .. couldn’t land the plane. ↩︎
All too often, C++ libraries consider it adequate to tell users “you’re holding it wrong” – i.e., that they are responsible for causing undefined behavior by misusing the API. Rust takes a clear position that a safe API has to protect its users, no matter how much they abuse it. ↩︎
To be fair, if Rust is encountering a stream of CVEs, other languages like C++ and Java are encountering a veritable flood, since they lack the protection of Rust’s type system. st takes a clear position that a safe API has to protect its users, no matter how much they abuse it. ↩︎

title: IMF warns against blanket petrol subsidies, suggests targeted support for poor, vulnerable people
body:
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) on Wednesday warned against blanket subsidies, saying targeted support for vulnerable and poor people provides better results.
Rodrigo Valdés, Director of the IMF’s Fiscal Affairs Department, spoke during a press briefing on the fund’s fiscal monitor at the 2026 annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok, Thailand.
The fund said that, beyond being expensive, blanket petrol subsidies often benefit higher-income consumers disproportionately and could worsen fiscal pressures amid rising debt and borrowing costs.
“Protecting people is not the same as protecting the price of fuels,” Mr Valdés said.
“It’s first fiscally very costly, and second, if you look at the pattern of consumption, it’s easy to see that that subsidy is readily regressive in many places.”
Mr Valdes spoke in response to a question on how the IMF could recommend energy prices to reflect scarcity when higher fuel prices in Nigeria and some other countries have led to higher cost of living, increased transport costs, worsening inflation, and poverty.
The IMF official said fuel subsidies or measures preventing prices from adjusting fully to an energy shock had cost countries between 1 per cent and 1.5 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 2026.
He called on governments across the world to instead use social safety nets and household data to identify people who need assistance.
“There are better tools to deal with this,” he said.
The fund’s intervention is in line with its long-standing position on subsidy, as recently canvassed in a recent report.
“ Targeted and temporary transfers are the most effective and cost-efficient way to protect poorer households when prices for basics spike,” fund said in its report.
“This approach directly supports those who need it most, preserves scarce fiscal space, and allows high market prices to continue signalling scarcity, encouraging consumers to reduce consumption if they can.”
Debates over the propriety of fuel subsidy has been at the centre of discussions in Nigeria in recent weeks, ahead of a crucial election slated for January.
While the Nigerian government, led by President Bola Tinubu, has defended its economic policy of subsidy removal as critical to the nation’s fiscal survival, opposition politicians—such as Atiku Abubakar of the ADC and Peter Obi of the NDC—have canvassed for and promised a return to different subsidy arrangements if elected into power.
Oladeinde Olawoyin reports Business & Economy, Development and Lagos Metro at PREMIUM TIMES. A First Class graduate of Mass Communication from the University of Ilorin, Ilorin, he was nominated in the journalism category of The Future Awards Africa in 2017. Aside maintaining a column titled ‘SATURDAY SATIRE’, he also writes art and culture pieces on weekends. Twitter : @Ola_deinde

title: Overnight Russian attack on railway spans 5 regions, no casualties, workers restoring service – board chairman
body:
A massive overnight Russian attack on railway infrastructure affected Kharkiv, Kyiv, Vinnytsia, Khmelnytskyi, and Ternopil regions, resulting in no casualties but significant material damage, while railway workers are already working to restore operations, Chairman of the Board of JSC Ukrzaliznytsia Oleksandr Pertsovsky reported.
"Another night of dense strikes on railway facilities. The enemy is trying to destroy everything it can reach: locomotive and wagon depots, repair facilities, stations and stops, not to mention rolling stock," Pertsovsky wrote on Facebook on Wednesday.
According to him, the attack knocked out power infrastructure, which railway specialists promptly restored. Key routes were blocked due to clearance obstacles, leading railway staff to organize alternative routes and ensure continued movement.
Regarding the capital's railway hub, where movement was temporarily suspended due to a ballistic threat, Pertsovsky noted that trains delayed for security reasons are now gradually departing.
"Most importantly, everyone was warned in advance, evacuated in an orderly manner, and made it through the night without casualties or loss of life. Material losses are significant; we have been working on recovery since morning. Deep respect and credit to every railway worker for keeping traffic moving under such conditions," the board chairman emphasized.

title: The Ballot, The Breadline And The Battle For 2027
body: As Nigeria moves closer to the 2027 elections, three contests are unfolding simultaneously: a legal battle over who gets on the ballot, an economic argument over whether reforms are delivering relief, and a growing test of public confidence in the institutions that will oversee the vote. There is a curious contradiction at the heart of Nigerian politics today. The country is preparing for an election in which the candidates are increasingly visible, but the rules governing their participation are still being contested. The economy is showing signs of improvement, yet millions of households continue to struggle with the cost of everyday living. And while politicians are busy calculating their electoral fortunes, Nigerians are asking a rather more immediate question: when will things get better? These are not separate stories. They are becoming the defining issues of the 2027 election. And this Tuesday, the signals are getting clearer. The Ballot Before The Battle An election is supposed to offer voters a choice. But what happens when the argument over who qualifies to contest threatens to overshadow the contest itself? Today, the Federal High Court in Abuja fixed November 20 to rule on an application by Atiku Abubakar and the African Democratic Congress to amend their suit challenging President Bola Tinubu’s eligibility to participate in the 2027 presidential election. The case centres on allegations concerning the authenticity of the President’s National Youth Service Corps discharge certificate submitted in support of his nomination. Tinubu and the APC oppose the proposed amendment. The allegations remain contested, and the court has made no determination on their merits. The political significance extends beyond the courtroom. At a time when Nigerians should be comparing candidates’ programmes for the economy, security and national development, considerable attention is being directed towards legal eligibility. There is nothing inherently improper about challenging a nomination in court. Indeed, judicial scrutiny is an important safeguard in a constitutional democracy. But the increasing prominence of pre-election litigation raises a broader question: will the 2027 election be defined primarily by the choices voters make, or by the decisions courts must first resolve? That question becomes even more pressing when we turn to the Independent National Electoral Commission. INEC And The Credibility question The controversy surrounding INEC’s candidate lists is no longer confined to one state. In Gombe, former Communications Minister Isa Pantami and the PDP have given the commission until Wednesday, October 14, to include his name on the governorship candidates’ list, following a disputed nomination process and a court-ordered rerun. Pantami’s lawyers maintain that INEC has no authority to exclude him after the rerun. The commission has yet to publicly resolve the dispute. Meanwhile, in Edo State, two candidates have reportedly appeared on the final House of Assembly list under both the PDP and the Allied Peoples Movement. INEC’s state office has acknowledged the duplication and referred the matter to its headquarters. These are distinct disputes, with different legal and administrative circumstances. They should not be treated as evidence of a single coordinated problem. Nevertheless, together they underline the importance of accurate nomination records, timely corrections and transparent explanations. For INEC, credibility is not something that can be established only on election day. It begins with the register of voters, the nomination process, the publication of candidates’ names and the consistent application of electoral rules. Every unresolved dispute consumes time, invites litigation and potentially weakens public confidence. The commission must demonstrate not merely that it can conduct an election, but that it can administer the processes leading to it with transparency and consistency. The signal here is straightforward: confidence in the ballot begins long before the first vote is cast. The Economy: Good Numbers, Difficult Realities If the courtroom is shaping the legal contest, the economy is shaping the political conversation. The World Bank’s latest Nigeria Development Update offers the Tinubu administration grounds for optimism. According to the report, Nigeria’s economy grew by 4.2 per cent in the first half of 2026, compared with 3.9 per cent in the corresponding period last year. The Bank projects average annual growth of 4.4 per cent between 2026 and 2028, provided reforms continue and public service delivery improves. The Presidency has welcomed these findings as evidence that its economic reforms are producing results. But there is another side to the story. The Central Bank’s September survey showed business activity expanding for the fourth consecutive month, even as households expressed growing pessimism about their finances and economic conditions. There, in a single contrast, lies one of the central political questions of 2027. Can an economy be improving while the people living in it feel worse off? Of course it can. Economic recovery does not automatically translate into immediate improvements in purchasing power. And macroeconomic stability, however necessary, does not put food on the table unless its benefits reach households. The government can legitimately point to growth, improved fiscal conditions and the prospect of lower inflation. But voters will also be looking at food prices, transport fares, wages and the cost of running small businesses. The political debate, therefore, is moving beyond whether reforms are necessary to whether their benefits are sufficiently visible. Petrol, Wages And The Politics Of Relief The Federal Government’s temporary petrol discount has added another dimension to that debate. Under the arrangement announced last week, NNPC Retail is foregoing its profit margin for a limited period, with the government insisting that the intervention does not amount to restoring the petrol subsidy removed in 2023. The measure is intended to provide some relief from the sharp increase in international energy prices. Yet it has also raised difficult questions. If the intervention is temporary, what happens when it ends? Will lower pump prices translate into lower transport fares? And can relief at selected retail outlets meaningfully change the cost-of-living pressures facing households nationwide? These questions are especially relevant following the Nigeria Labour Congress’s two-week ultimatum, effective October 9, demanding lower petrol prices and negotiations over a new national minimum wage. Labour argues that the purchasing power of the current ₦70,000 minimum wage has been severely eroded. The government faces competing pressures: preserving fiscal discipline, maintaining market confidence and responding to immediate hardship. The opposition, meanwhile, has an opportunity to scrutinise the intervention’s effectiveness. But criticism alone is not an economic programme. Alternative proposals must also explain how relief would be financed and sustained. The deeper signal is that the economic argument is becoming less about the direction of reform and more about the distribution of its benefits. That distinction could become increasingly important as the campaign develops. Nigeria 2027 Election Watch: A crowded field, unresolved questions The publication of INEC’s final list of presidential candidates has brought greater clarity to the electoral field. Eighteen presidential candidates are listed, including President Tinubu of the APC, Atiku Abubakar of the ADC, Peter Obi of the Nigeria Democratic Congress and Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde of the Allied Peoples Movement. The emergence of these candidacies changes the focus of political analysis. It is no longer sufficient to speak generally about opposition unity or fragmentation. The relevant questions now concern actual candidates, party organisations, campaign programmes and the coalitions they are attempting to build. For the APC, the central task is to explain the administration’s record and the benefits it expects Nigerians to derive from its policies. For opposition parties, the challenge is to articulate credible alternatives on the economy, insecurity and governance while building effective electoral structures across the states And for voters, the task is to distinguish between campaign promises and proposals that can realistically be implemented. One constituency deserves particular attention: younger Nigerians. Youth participation cannot simply be measured by social media enthusiasm, large rallies or online criticism. The meaningful indicators will be voter registration, collection of permanent voter cards, turnout and the capacity of parties to engage young people beyond campaign events. The same applies to state-level contests. Governorship races, local party structures and the mobilisation of communities may reveal political dynamics that national campaign rhetoric cannot capture. As January approaches, the contest deserves to be examined not only through the personalities seeking office, but also through the policies, institutions and voters that will shape the outcome. Three developments deserve close attention over the coming days: Wednesday, October 14: INEC’s response to the Pantami ultimatum and whether the dispute moves further into litigation. October 23: The expiry of Labour’s two-week ultimatum and whether negotiations produce an agreement or lead to industrial action. November 20: The Federal High Court’s ruling on Atiku and the ADC’s application to amend their eligibility suit against Tinubu and the APC. Beyond these dates, the most important economic indicator may not be another growth projection, but evidence that inflation is easing in ways households can actually feel. There is an old temptation in politics to mistake activity for progress. A crowded courtroom is not necessarily evidence of a stronger democracy. A growing economy does not automatically mean rising living standards. And a crowded ballot paper does not, by itself, guarantee a meaningful electoral choice. Nigeria’s political institutions are approaching another important test. The courts must adjudicate disputes according to law. INEC must administer the electoral process transparently. Political parties must present credible alternatives. And those in government must demonstrate how economic progress can translate into tangible improvements in everyday life. For Nigerians, the questions are becoming increasingly practical. Will the electoral process be fair? Will the economy provide greater opportunity? Will communities become safer? And will the next government, whoever leads it, be accountable for the promises made during the campaign? These are the questions that deserve to dominate the road to 2027. Because elections are not simply contests between politicians. They are opportunities for citizens to determine the direction of their country. And perhaps that is today’s most important signal: Nigeria’s political future will be shaped not only by who appears on the ballot, but by the credibility of the process and the choices offered to the people. That’s The Signal for Tuesday, October 13, 2026. The post The Ballot, The Breadline And The Battle For 2027 appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Champions League: Can Anyone Stop PSG From Winning Three in a Row?
body: Winning the Champions League requires an outstanding team, excellent coaching and a little luck at the right moments. Winning it twice? That proves the first victory was no accident. Winning it three times in a row? Paris Saint-Germain would instantly have a claim to be one of the greatest teams in the competition’s modern history. Is PSG Still the Standard? There’s a reason that PSG are one of the favourites to win the Champions League at 6.50 with BetKing; they’re the consensus pick to retain their UCL title with only Barcelona (5.00) ranked above them. Those odds reflect how close the leading contenders appear to be, but PSG still have the most important advantage: they know how to win the competition. Their recent success was built on overall team quality, but their attack separated them from everyone else. Last season, PSG created chances in different ways, could score from a variety of sources and introduce match-winners from the bench at will. With an attacking core of Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, Ousmane Dembele, Desire Doue and the recently signed trio of Mika Godts, Ferran Torres and Maghnes Akliouche, they have enough firepower to outscore just about anyone as they look to become just the second team to win the Champions League three times in a row. Arsenal’s Missing Marquee Attacker The Gunners are one of PSG’s closest challengers, but their summer business will be examined carefully if they fall short again. With Leandro Trossard and Gabriel Martinelli departing the Emirates, the North Londoners had a three-man shortlist of marquee attackers they hoped to sign. Vinicius Jr. (who resigned with Real Madrid), Morgan Rodgers (who opted to join Chelsea) and Julian Alvarez (who Atleti simply refused to let go) were all admired by Mikel Arteta but couldn’t land. That decision may prove sensible if their existing forwards continue to deliver. If the goals start to dry up however, the chance to upgrade their attack could prove costly Arsenal already possess the defence, midfield control, tactical organization and squad cohesion required to win the Champions League. Whether they have enough match-winners in attack remains the unresolved part of the equation. Real Madrid’s European Heritage & Barcelona’s Firepower Real Madrid can never be dismissed from this competition. Other clubs may arrive in better form or with more balanced teams, but Madrid possess a relationship with the Champions League that regularly defies conventional analysis. Kylian Mbappe, Jude Bellingham and Vinicius Jr are household names who guarantee goals, while Jose Mourinho has been brought in to manage this star-studded squad. Can the Portuguese legend refind his old magic? We’ll see. Elsewhere in Spain, Barcelona are chomping at the bit to win a sixth UCL title and will believe that this is their season after an electric start to the season. Despite missing out on primary attacking target, Julian Alvarez, the Catalan side has faced few issues in attack with 31 goals scored in the La Liga and just seven conceded (in 7 games). The UCL is a different proposition than the La Liga, but Real Madrid and Barcelona are priced at 8.00 and 5.00 respectively to win the coveted trophy with BetKing. The Difficulty of Winning Three PSG began the campaign as favourites, but winning three consecutive Champions Leagues is extraordinarily difficult. title: Kazakhstan Claims Two Golds at U23 World Wrestling Championships in Las Vegas
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Greco-Roman wrestlers have secured two gold medals at the U23 World Wrestling Championships on Oct. 14 in Las Vegas, with Aibek Aitbekov and Yusuf Ashrapov winning their finals and Temirlan Turdakyn advancing to the title bout. Photo credit: kazwrestling_official Aitbekov claimed the title in the 60-kilogram category, defeating Azerbaijan’s Elmir Aliyev, the reigning U23 world champion, in the final. En route to gold, the Kazakh wrestler also defeated Russia’s Alibek Amirov, Japan’s Seima Tokuharu, and Ukraine’s Yevhen Pokovba. The victory adds to Aitbekov’s achievements this year, having previously won the U23 Asian Championship, according to the National Olympic Committee. Ashrapov secured Kazakhstan’s second gold medal in the 72-kilogram category, defeating Armenia’s Gaspar Terteryan in the final. The two victories have strengthened Kazakhstan’s Greco-Roman wrestling performance at the United States competition. Turdakyn advances to gold medal bout Turdakyn reached the final in the 87-kilogram category after defeating Russia’s Alexander Krikukha in the semifinals. He will face Iran’s Yasin Ali Yazdi for the gold medal. With Turdakyn through to the final, Kazakhstan can add another title to its two gold medals at the U23 world championships. title: Diplomacy's changing footprint as told by mission openings and closures
body: Over the past few years, global politics have been reshaped by sudden shifts in power. The Taliban retook control in Afghanistan in August 2021 after US-led forces withdrew, and rebel forces in Syria toppled the Assad regime in December 2024. Those shifts are being reflected in diplomatic networks, and our latest chart of the week shows this clearly. Some cities are gaining missions as countries deepen or restore ties. Others have lost posts amid conflicts, political upheaval or isolation. The number of missions a country sends or hosts offers a glimpse of its diplomatic reach and priorities. But a reopening does not, on its own, prove that relations have fundamentally changed — or that the change will last. “Reopening an embassy is a political signal, but it does not necessarily indicate a lasting shift,” says Jasmine El Gamal, founder and CEO of Averos Strategies, a think tank focused on diplomacy and geopolitics. “A reopening is therefore better understood as a sign of renewed engagement than a guarantee of lasting alignment.” The reverse can also happen: a mission may remain open, close or move even after the political circumstances that prompted the decision have changed. As El Gamal says, such decisions “can outlast the administrations that made them even when the original intent does not necessarily apply”. Syria has seen one of the biggest changes. After the fall of the Assad regime, several countries reopened embassies in Damascus that had been closed for years. Turkey and Qatar resumed operations in December 2024, followed by Spain in January 2025 and Germany in March 2025. Damascus recorded 12 openings between December 2024 and December 2025. Embassies returned to Pyongyang after pandemic-era closures. From 2024 onwards, Reuters reported that many European countries began sending delegations and missions back to North Korea. Brazil, Sweden, Poland, India and Nigeria were among the countries to resume operations, while Ukraine opened a series of new missions in African cities in 2024, including Kinshasa, Abidjan, Maputo and Kigali. Closures have been concentrated in a smaller number of cities. Kabul lost 19 diplomatic posts between 2017 and 2025, many after the Taliban returned to power in 2021. Governments evacuated staff and suspended operations amid the security crisis following the takeover, and others left due to uncertainty over how to engage with the new authorities' policies. The Taliban’s restrictions on women and girls have since further complicated diplomatic relations. Khartoum had the second-largest loss, with 14 diplomatic posts closing in the eight years to 2025. Most closures followed the outbreak of Sudan's civil war in April 2023, with governments evacuating staff and suspending operations amid security fears. Despite the closures, the figures suggest an expanding diplomatic footprint across more regions overall. The Middle East and Africa have seen the biggest net gains, as many Western countries shift their attention toward resoutowardsch, people-power countries.

title: Hamburg rally calls for investigation into Nord Stream blasts
body:
HAMBURG, October 14. /TASS/. A rally calling for an investigation into the sabotage of the Nord Stream gas pipelines is taking place in Hamburg, Germany, ahead of the start of the trial in the blast case, a TASS correspondent reports.
The rally is organized by the BSW party. One of the banners calls for "a political investigation" into the terrorist attack and the creation of a commission to look into the incident. Pro-Ukrainian activists are also holding a rally nearby.
The first trial in the Nord Stream blasts case is set to begin at the Hamburg Higher Regional Court later on Wednesday. Ukrainian national Sergey Kuznetsov is the defendant in the case. The court has scheduled 24 hearings before the end of the year. Besides, additional hearings are planned for February but they have yet to be finalized. More than 100 journalists have been accredited to cover the trial.
On September 26, 2022, unprecedented damage was recorded on three strings of the Nord Stream pipelines and the never-commissioned Nord Stream 2 pipeline. The Russian Prosecutor General’s Office opened a criminal case over an act of international terrorism.

title: House control all but gone, top Republicans privately concede
body: Some top congressional Republicans have privately concluded that it is likely impossible for them to keep control of the House of Representatives in the midterm elections, and they are now focused on limiting the scale of the defeat and salvaging the party’s Senate majority. Five senior Republican lawmakers, all granted anonymity to speak candidly about their party’s dire position, told POLITICO the House had all but slipped away. One senior House Republican said the GOP’s goal at this point was to “save as many Republican seats as we can.” The president, this person said, was not helping. “President Trump has made this election all about himself,” the lawmaker said. “Now we have to survive that political storm.” A second Republican member of Congress said the movement of campaign advertising made plain which side was in control of the midterms. This lawmaker predicted Democrats would pick up about 10 seats, more than enough to take control of the chamber. Even in newly redistricted red states like Florida and Texas, this person said, Republican candidates were “hanging on with their fingernails.” Republicans have already fallen back from several contested House districts that they feel are no longer winnable, including those held by Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa and Tom Kean Jr. of New Jersey. Trump carried their districts just two years ago. The party last week gave up on an Omaha-based district held by retiring Rep. Don Bacon. Trump officials and other top GOP operatives say more candidates may be cut off in the coming days, in order to shift advertising money to races where it can make more of a difference. Republican groups have already given up on multiple races where they once hoped to unseat Democratic lawmakers. The Republican Party is under extreme pressure across the Midwest, where it is now spending heavily to defend Senate seats in once-reliably MAGA states like Iowa, Nebraska and Kansas. Bacon, a maverick often at odds with the White House, said there was no mystery in his party’s political tribulations. “I’ve talked to some who are making these decisions: The biggest problem is the president’s polling numbers and unfavorables,” Bacon said. White House officials insist they’re not giving up on either chamber of Congress. In a statement, White House spokeswoman Liz Huston said Trump remained “committed to maintaining Republican majorities in both the House and Senate.” As he departed on Tuesday to campaign in Alaska for embattled GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan, Trump professed optimism about the midterms but acknowledged that sitting presidents typically see their party lose seats in the off year. “But I'm doing a tour right now and I'm doing rallies,” Trump added. “The level of enthusiasm for the Republican Party is way up.” House Speaker Mike Johnson went even further, flatly declaring during a campaign stop in deep-red Texas that “the polling is wrong” in showing his party on the brink of a broad defeat. Yet at a tactical level, the Republican Party’s shift in focus away from defending the House and toward saving the Senate is clear enough. In recent days, the Congressional Leadership Fund, the top super PAC for House Republicans, canceled advertising for key House candidates in Nebraska and Iowa to move that money to other House races. That allowed the Senate Leadership Fund – a Republican group focused on the upper chamber – to swoop in and claim the airtime to support Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts and Rep. Ashley Hinson, who is running for Senate in Iowa. “These are not the moves of a party that’s going to keep the House,” a third Republican lawmaker said. In statements to POLITICO, both CLF and the National Republican Congressional Committee said they had no intention of giving up on the fight for control of the House. NRCC spokesperson Mike Marinella said districts are won "one by one," and that the GOP has "the financial firepower and ground game needed to win." Chris Winkelman, president of CLF, said his group would keep moving money around to maximize the impact nationally. The goal, he said, was to “keep the pressure on the most vulnerable Democrats and preserve a path to 218 seats.” Former Rep. Carlos Curbelo, a Florida Republican who lost his swing seat in Trump’s first midterm election eight years ago, said his former colleagues were clear-eyed about where the election seemed to be headed. “The environment is about as tough as one could expect,” Curbelo said. “There is no one who has privately stated that they believe Republicans can hold the House — not in recent weeks, anyway.” Megan Messerly, Lauren Fedor, Lisa Kashinsky and Myah Ward contributed to this report. CLARIFICATION: This article has been updated to make clearer the CLF's ad reservation changes in Iowa and Nebraska.

title: Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda plan joint visa for AFCON 2027 fans
body:
Tanzania, Kenya and Uganda said they are working on a joint visa scheme to ease travel for football fans during the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON), an official said.
Rebecca Alitwala Kadaga, Chairperson of the East African Community (EAC) Council of Ministers, announced the plan on Tuesday during an inspection of the Arusha Pamoja AFCON Stadium by members of the East African Legislative Assembly (EALA).
Ms Kadaga, who is also Uganda’s First Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for EAC Affairs, said the three host countries were developing a special visa framework to facilitate the movement of supporters across their borders during the tournament.
She said the proposed arrangement would enable fans to attend matches in different countries and visit tourist attractions, while creating business opportunities for hotels, tour operators, transport providers and other service businesses.
An EALA member, Abdullah Makame, said the scheme’s impact would depend on the final visa requirements and how effectively they were implemented at border crossings.
During the inspection, the delegation was informed that construction of the Arusha Pamoja AFCON Stadium, which is designed to accommodate about 32,500 spectators, had reached 95 per cent completion.
The 36th edition of AFCON will be co-hosted by Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda from 19 June to 17 July, 2027, marking the first time the tournament will take place across three countries.

title: OpenAI says Saudi citizen arrested over hidden recording device in office
body: An OpenAI employee has been arrested and charged with using a hidden recording device in a San Francisco office, according to the artificial intelligence company and the US Justice Department. Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi citizen, was arrested on October 9, more than a week after staff at OpenAI discovered an audio recording device in the back of a television in an executive conference room, the Justice Department said on Tuesday. Mr Alfozan, who is accused of planting the device, is currently in custody having appeared in court in San Francisco on Tuesday. Mr Alfozan had started working at OpenAI in July last year and worked on its product team. He was fired on the same day as his arrest, the company said. The incident is poised to heighten concerns about security at top technology companies at a moment when nations are competing aggressively to develop more powerful AI systems. “At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” the company posted on social platform X on Tuesday. OpenAI said one of its security teams discovered the device on September 30 during a sweep of a company conference room. According to details and images released by the Justice Departmen t, the device was plugged into a USB port in the back of a TV in the room and covered with toilet paper to disguise it. An image released by the Justice Department showed a small, black device with the text “Seeed Studio” on it. The agency said OpenAI determined it was planted around September 28. OpenAI said it used its AI models to understand more about the device and identify who placed it. Mr Alfozan did not have approval to access the conference room, which typically hosted meetings involving “highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information”, according to the complaint, which references an unnamed AI company with offices in San Francisco. The company said it uncovered evidence that Mr Alfozan had planned to use other recording devices to secretly record meetings in other parts of the office. Early this month, according to the Justice Department, OpenAI security employees found a similar recording device in a bag he had left inside one of its corporate buildings. According to a LinkedIn profile connected to Mr Alfozan, he worked as an engineering lead at OpenAI on AI agent software. The profile says he has worked part-time as a partner at Saudi Arabia-based venture capital firm Raed Ventures since 2025, and previously as a senior systems engineer at Meta Platforms. Mr Alfozan attended the Massachusetts Institute of Technology from 2011 to 2016 where he studied computer science and engineering, and the University of California, Berkeley, from 2023 to 2025 to study for a master’s degree in data science, the profile states. OpenAI said it has alerted the FBI and that the investigation is continuing. According to the FBI’s criminal complaint, the device was a Seeed Xiao ESP32-S3 Sense, which was described as a “thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone and microSD storage”. A device by that name and description appeared to be for sale for $14 from the website seeedstudio.com as of Tuesday. Lennart Koopmann, founder of cyber security firm Nzyme, said the device Mr Alfozan allegedly used appears to be built on “a hobbyist circuit board”, and noted features such as the microphone, and the ability to save recordings to a memory card and send audio wirelessly over short distances via Wi-Fi. “That makes it cheap and easy to hide, and catching one takes either equipment that watches the airwaves for unfamiliar devices or, if its wireless is switched off, someone physically searching the rooms,” Mr Koopmann said. Mr Alfozan is scheduled to appear before Magistrate Judge Alex G. Tse in federal court in San Francisco on October 19.

title: Pope Leo has lung cancer, the Vatican says
body:
Pope Leo XIV arrives at the Gemelli University Hospital in Rome for an operation to remove a lump from his lung. Alberto Pizzoli/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
While Pope Leo's lung cancer diagnosis may have come as a shock to Catholics this week, the prognosis is likely a lot less scary.
The cancer, adenocarcinoma, is a common one, and while worrisome if caught late, has a track record of high rates of survival with early intervention.
"The fact that surgery was the first tool that they utilized is a really good sign," says Dr. Vin Gupta, a pulmonologist and board member of the American Lung Association. "It suggests that they think this is early stage."
Leo underwent surgery in Rome on Tuesday, which he announced over the weekend. But while he mentioned a "nodule" would be the target, the 90-minute operation resulted in a larger part of his right lung being removed. Still, Gupta says that isn't inherently a bad sign.
"People have parts of their lungs removed all the time for all sorts of reasons, and they recover just fine," says Gupta. "And in his case, he's pretty robust at baseline from a health standpoint."
At 71, Leo still exercises regularly, including a weekly tennis game, which will help with his road to recovery.
"He had a minimally invasive surgery," says Dr. Jonathan Villena Vargas, a cardiothoracic surgeon at Weill Cornell Medical Center in New York City. "When we do this, because we do this all the time, most patients are allowed to travel about two weeks after the surgery."
That outlook bodes well for the pope's calendar, which has only been cleared of events until Oct. 20. After that, barring any updates from the Vatican, he's expected to travel to South America in November, visiting a number of countries including Peru, where he lived for decades.

title: Turkish Media Highlight Christodoulides’ First Turkey Visit in a Decade for COP31
body: Several Turkish media outlets are highlighting the planned presence of Republic of Cyprus President Nikos Christodoulides at the COP31 UN climate conference in Antalya in November. Coverage frames the trip as a notable development after a 10-year gap, while largely avoiding any linkage to the Cyprus problem or possible bilateral contacts with Turkish leaders. Pro-government site Haber7 ran the headline “First visit after ten years: The Greek Cypriot leader is coming to Turkey,” focusing on the historical angle. It referenced the 2016 visit by then-President Nikos Anastasiades to Istanbul, creating an implicit comparison without assessing any potential shift in Turkish-Cypriot relations. Similarly, the pro-government newspaper Yeni Akit used the title “For the first time after ten years: The Greek Cypriot leader is coming to Turkey,” again emphasizing the decade-long absence as the main point. Opposition-leaning OdaTV, under the headline “Christodoulides is coming to Turkey,” limited itself to announcing his participation and noting the preceding diplomatic efforts that secured the invitation. It offered no evaluation of Turkey-Cyprus relations or the prospect of meetings with Turkish leadership. Yeni Şafak, another pro-government paper, headlined “The Greek Cypriot leader Christodoulides is coming to Turkey: His program has been announced.” It stressed the upcoming arrival but did not detail any specific bilateral meetings. Overall, Turkish reporting treats the visit primarily as a historical first rather than a signal of progress on the Cyprus issue. Christodoulides has confirmed he will attend, stating that the Republic of Cyprus consistently participates in such summits and that the invitation followed diplomatic efforts with EU partners. Turkey, as co-host with Australia, initially faced EU pressure over selective invitations before extending one to the Cypriot president. title: John Darko denies role in SIC settlement after EOCO interrogation
body: Suame Member of Parliament John Darko has denied any involvement in a post-judgment settlement between SIC Savings and Loans Company Limited and Equity Savings and Loans Limited that allegedly resulted in financial losses to SIC. The denial follows his appearance before investigators of the Economic and Organised Crime Office (EOCO) on Tuesday, October 13, to assist with ongoing investigations into the matter. In a statement dated Wednesday, October 14, his lawyers, Darko, Keli-Delataa & Co, said the interrogation focused on his role as legal counsel for Equity during its litigation with SIC over a matured but unpaid investment, as well as his membership of Equity’s board between 2015 and 2023. According to the law firm, Mr Darko assured investigators that his legal involvement was limited to the litigation and the recovery of part of the judgment awards in favour of SIC. It maintained that the firm played no further role in any subsequent settlement between the parties. The statement also said the firm was unaware of Equity’s decision to dispose of land that was the subject of a judicial attachment to a third party, Eco Swiss Investment Limited. It added that the firm had already terminated its legal services to Equity over non-payment of fees before the post-judgment developments occurred. “Our client had ceased to be a board member of Equity by September 2023 and was certainly not a participant in any decision to compromise a court judgment in a conspiratorial scheme to deny SIC the benefits of its judicial awards,” the statement said. The clarification comes amid EOCO’s investigation into an alleged criminal conspiracy involving SIC Savings and Loans. The case concerns a July 2024 settlement involving SIC, Equity and Eco Swiss Investment Limited, under which SIC agreed to accept GH¢5 million in full and final settlement of a revised judgment debt of GH¢14.85 million. EOCO has put the estimated financial loss arising from the alleged conspiracy at approximately GH¢27 million. The investigation has also involved Manhyia South MP Nana Agyei Baffour Awuah, who has been charged with conspiracy to commit a crime, intentionally causing financial loss to a public body and money laundering. Mr Darko’s lawyers said their client remained committed to the investigation and was prepared to provide any further assistance required by EOCO. They also commended the EOCO investigators for their professionalism and the courtesies extended to him during the interrogation. The firm insisted that Mr Darko and his legal practice had acted ethically and professionally throughout their engagement with Equity, adding that their conduct had always been guided by the principles of professional responsibility.

title: NAF Air Crash: Aiyedatiwa Orders Fumigation Of Igbokoda River To Avert Outbreak Of Diseases
body: Following complaints from Igbokoda residents about the strong stench emanating from the river where the Nigerian Air Force aircraft crashed last week, Ondo State Governor Lucky Aiyedatiwa has directed the ministries of environment and health to begin extensive fumigation of the river. The directive aims to prevent a possible outbreak of diseases, as the river is a major source of livelihood for residents of Igbokoda and neighbouring communities. The governor also directed the authorities of Ilaje Local Government to arrange water tankers for the continuous distribution of potable water to residents if the river is found to be severely polluted and unsuitable for use. Governor Lucky Aiyedatiwa and other state government officials paddle their way to the crash site. The arrangement, according to a statement signed by the Commissioner for Information and Orientation, Idowu Ajanaku, is to remain in place pending a lasting intervention to address the pollution. In addition, Governor Aiyedatiwa directed the ministries to provide nose masks and other essential health kits to residents to protect them from potential health hazards. The governor reiterated the state government’s commitment to providing all necessary support to the Nigerian Air Force in its ongoing evacuation efforts, as well as ensuring the welfare and safety of residents of the affected community. The NAF ATR-42 aircraft (NAF 931) crashed on October 5, 2026, with 25 people, comprising five crew members and 20 passengers. The aircraft was said to be on a routine mission from Benin City in Edo State to Lagos when the accident occurred. Although search-and-rescue procedures were immediately activated by relevant authorities, the passengers and crew have yet to be located. The Nigerian Air Force on Tuesday set up a 12-member board to investigate the crash. The Service said that the board would establish the circumstances and causes of the crash and recommend measures to prevent similar incidents. The Chief of the Air Staff, Air Marshal Sunday Aneke, ordered sustained search and recovery operations alongside a comprehensive investigation into the accident. Air Vice Marshal FO Ankeli will head the investigation board, while Air Vice Marshal EOE Ebiowe, head of the Investigation and Recovery Team, will coordinate the wider response. The board comprises specialists in aviation operations, flight safety, piloting, air traffic control, aircraft engineering, maintenance, medical services and other technical fields. It also has representatives of the Nigerian Civil Aviation Authority and the Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau to provide civilian aviation expertise. The NAF said the investigation would cover operational, technical, environmental, human, and organisational factors that may have contributed to the crash. title: Interception rate for Russian jet-powered drones rises to 76% — Ihnat
body:
Yurii Ihnat, spokesperson for the Ukrainian Air Force, made the announcement during a televised broadcast, according to Ukrinform.
"Today, 128 UAVs of various types were deployed. These included Gerbera, Parody, and jet-powered UAVs. Of the 128 drones, 77 were jet-powered. That is a fairly large number. Naturally, the enemy is increasing the proportion of jet-powered UAVs in every attack. At the same time, the overall interception rate across all types of UAVs is 90%. In other words, 115 were shot down or suppressed, including 59 jet-powered drones. The figures are improving. I would emphasize that last month the interception rate for jet-powered UAVs was still around 60%; today, it has risen to 76%, based on the latest attack," he said.
Ihnat noted that it is impossible to intercept every drone.
The spokesperson also explained that jet-powered UAVs are relatively expensive to manufacture. According to him, a single engine costs approximately $40,000. Ihnat stressed the need to impose sanctions on Russia to reduce its capacity to manufacture such weapons.
As Ukrinform previously reported, Ukrainian air defence forces neutralized four ballistic missiles and 115 drones used by Russian forces to attack Ukraine beginning on the evening of October 13.

title: Russia’s Krasnodar Region Raises Alert as Oil Washes Ashore on Black Sea Coast
body:
Authorities in Russia’s southern Krasnodar region have raised the alert level in Gelendzhik and Novorossiysk over an oil spill after fuel oil washed ashore and satellite images showed pollution spreading along the Black Sea coast.
Governor Veniamin Kondratyev issued an order warning of a potential emergency in the two cities. He attributed the spill to “accidents” involving vessels targeted by Ukrainian naval drones on Oct. 6.
The order calls for increased environmental monitoring and surveillance of potential industrial hazards. It also recommends that the regional branch of Russia’s Marine Rescue Service take measures to prevent oil from reaching the shoreline.
Fuel oil has already been found along roughly 500 meters of coastline near Novorossiysk, the city’s chief rescue official, Alexei Oderov, said .
Local residents have also reported pollution on the shore. Olga Kotlyar, head of the Abrau-Dyurso rural district, appealed for volunteers to help municipal workers clean up a beach.
Birds with reported chemical burns from petroleum products have been found in Gelendzhik and the nearby resort village of Arkhipo-Osipovka.
The satellite monitoring project Transparent World earlier reported that an image taken overnight on Oct. 10 showed a large oil slick between Arkhipo-Osipovka and Novorossiysk.
Over the following two days, the slick broke into smaller patches and spread as far as Anapa, the project said. It also identified oil traces near Novorossiysk Bay and the Caspian Pipeline Consortium’s offshore loading facilities.
Transparent World linked the pollution to the Oct. 6 naval drone attack on the tanker Aframax Rio off Sochi. The vessel can carry up to 100,000 metric tons of oil, though its cargo at the time of the attack has not been independently confirmed.
The Mash Telegram channel, citing unnamed sources, reported that the tanker was fully loaded.
The attack triggered a major fire that blanketed Sochi in black smoke. The blaze was extinguished the following day.
Authorities closed beaches in Sochi and the neighboring federal territory of Sirius after the attack, but reopened them on Oct. 8, saying tests had found no oil contamination in local waters.
Russia’s consumer protection watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said seawater samples from all districts of Sochi met sanitary standards.
