title: Kazakhstan, Belgium Expand Academic Cooperation at Rectors’ Forum Attended by Tokayev and Royal Couple
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Belgium agreed to expand academic mobility, joint research and artificial intelligence cooperation as President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, King Philippe and Queen Mathilde attended a bilateral Rectors’ Forum on Oct. 13, bringing together leaders of 29 universities and research organizations. Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, King Philippe and Queen Mathilde of Belgium attended the Rectors’ Forum in Astana on Oct. 12. Photo credit: Akorda Held at the Alem.ai International Center during the Belgian royal couple’s state visit, the forum focused on the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on higher education and scientific research. Kazakh and Belgian universities signed more than 20 agreements and memorandums of understanding, Akorda reported. AI in education and research Discussions focused on integrating AI into teaching, research and university management, adapting curricula to emerging technologies and strengthening digital competencies among students and faculty. Participants also explored AI applications in language education, translation and multilingual academic communication, as well as the role of human expertise and trust in digital tools. Kazakhstan highlighted its AI-Sana initiative, which aims to develop students’ AI skills, entrepreneurship and deep-tech startups. According to Deputy Minister of Science and Higher Education Gulzat Kobenova, the country plans to increase the share of universities incorporating AI courses into their curricula to 60% by 2029, according to the ministry’s press service. The forum also discussed opportunities for Kazakh researchers to participate in European research programs, including Horizon Europe, and for universities to strengthen industry links. Universities sign cooperation agreements Al-Farabi Kazakh National University signed memorandums with Ghent University, KU Leuven and the University of Mons. The agreements provide for academic exchanges, joint educational initiatives and research cooperation. KazNU and Ghent University plan to develop exchanges in linguistics and a dual-degree program for doctoral students. L.N. Gumilyov Eurasian National University signed three agreements with the same Belgian institutions, covering student and faculty mobility, joint educational programs, research projects and internships. Serikbayev East Kazakhstan Technical University signed an agreement with KU Leuven and its SIM² research institute to establish a joint center focused on critical materials, including rare and rare-earth materials. The initiative is intended to combine research activities with specialist training. Another initiative will advance the Mirror Lab, a joint Kazakhstan-Ghent University laboratory focused on mathematics, AI, modeling and engineering computations. It is expected to operate at the Institute of Mathematics and Mathematical Modeling and the Alem.ai International Center. Building Kazakhstan’s AI ecosystem The forum presented Alem.ai’s ecosystem development model, linking school education, universities, research laboratories and technology companies. Its annual targets include training 1,000 AI specialists, supporting 100 startups and developing 10 research projects. Minister of Science and Higher Education Sayasat Nurbek said the high-level participation underscored the strategic importance of education and science in bilateral relations The forum concluded with the signing of cooperation documents and the Belgian royal couple’s signing of the digital guestbook, marking another step toward expanding academic and research ties between Kazakhstan and Belgium. The post Kazakhstan, Belgium Expand Academic Cooperation at Rectors’ Forum Attended by Tokayev and Royal Couple appeared first on The Astana Times .

title: US Supreme Court to hear case of Nigerian deported over cooking for terrorists
body: Does cooking for members of a Nigerian separatist group amount to providing “material support” for terrorism? That’s the thorny question facing the conservative-majority US Supreme Court. In a brief order Tuesday, the Supreme Court agreed to hear the Trump administration’s bid to reinstate the ruling that denied asylum to a Nigerian man who was deported for having provided material support to a terrorist group. The case will be considered during the Court’s current term, which began October 5 and runs through late June. Beyond Izuchukwu Ozurumba’s case, the ruling could have far-reaching implications for asylum seekers, depending largely on how the nine justices — six conservatives and three liberals — interpret the concept of “material support.” Izuchukwu Ozurumba says he was forced to cook for about six months at a separatist group’s camp in southern Nigeria beginning in 2022. He then fled to Venezuela and from there crossed the US-Mexico border illegally in the summer of 2023. In 2024, a US immigration judge denied Ozurumba’s asylum claim and ordered him deported citing a provision of US immigration law that bars foreign nationals who provide “material support” to a terrorist organization from receiving asylum. The decision was later upheld on appeal. Ozurumba was deported to Nigeria in April 2025, according to his lawyers. But a federal appeals court later overturned the earlier decisions and sent the case back to the immigration court for reconsideration. “Cooking meals using food and supplies purchased by the organization may have ‘sustained’ the organization in the broadest possible sense…but provided nothing that the organization could use or readily divert to plan or carry out its terrorist activities,” the appeals court wrote. “As far as the record shows, Ozurumba was simply a captive laborer whose work had nothing to do with those activities.” The Trump administration, as part of its sweeping campaign of deportations of undocumented immigrants, is asking the Supreme Court to overturn the appeals court ruling. The post US Supreme Court to hear case of Nigerian deported over cooking for terrorists appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Pope Leo recovering in Rome hospital after cancer diagnosis
body: Pope Leo XIV spent a peaceful night in hospital after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, the Vatican said Wednesday, adding that further information about the 71-year-old pontiff's condition would be released later in the day.  Leo was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer, after doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung during an operation Tuesday at Rome's Gemelli Hospital. The diagnosis, suspected during preliminary examinations, was confirmed through tissue analysis performed during surgery.   The operation lasted approximately 90 minutes and was completed without complications, according to a statement issued by Stefano Margaritora, the surgeon who led the procedure, and Luigi Carbone, the pope's personal physician. Leo spent about three hours in the operating room before regaining consciousness and returning to his hospital room. Doctors removed the entire lower lobe of the right lung in an effort to eliminate the cancerous tissue. The human lungs have five lobes, three on the right and two on the left. The Vatican has not disclosed the tumor's precise size or whether cancer cells were found in nearby lymph nodes, factors that could influence the pontiff's prognosis and any need for additional treatment. Leo was admitted to the hospital Tuesday after a small, localized growth was discovered during routine medical examinations. He had publicly disclosed the finding Sunday, saying doctors believed it was best to remove the nodule because of its early detection. The Vatican previously said the pope was expected to remain hospitalized for approximately one week. All his public engagements have been canceled through October 20. Elected in May 2025, Leo is relatively young for a pontiff and has generally maintained an active lifestyle, including playing tennis. He is not known to smoke and had no previously disclosed major health problems during his papacy.

title: Greece and UNESCO Cooperate on Cultural Heritage and Tourism
body: Greece and UNESCO are exploring ways to strengthen cooperation on sustainable cultural tourism, protect cultural heritage and develop cultural routes, following meetings between Greek Tourism Minister Olga Kefalogianni and the organisation’s leadership in Paris. Kefalogianni met UNESCO Director-General Khaled El-Enany, Egypt’s former Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, and Assistant Director-General for Culture Nayef Al-Fayez, Jordan’s former Minister of Tourism and Antiquities. Greece’s Permanent Representative to UNESCO, George Koumoutsakos, also attended the meetings, while Secretary-General for Tourism Policy and Development Vasiliki Koutsoukou accompanied the minister. The discussions highlighted culture as more than a motivation for travel, identifying it as a cornerstone of a high-quality, sustainable and resilient tourism model. Greece promotes an approach that showcases not only monuments and archaeological sites but also intangible cultural heritage, local traditions, gastronomy and the creativity of local communities. This strategy aims to extend the tourist season and distribute tourism benefits across more regions of the country. Protecting cultural heritage through sustainable tourism The meetings placed particular emphasis on linking tourism development with the protection and preservation of cultural heritage for future generations. Participants highlighted responsible visitor management, strengthening the resilience of cultural sites against climate change and ensuring the active participation of local communities as key priorities. According to an official announcement, UNESCO recognises the importance of connecting culture and tourism. The organisation promotes approaches that combine heritage protection with sustainable tourism development, community participation and intercultural dialogue. Through its work on World Heritage Site management, intangible cultural heritage and the exchange of expertise, UNESCO supports responsible tourism practices that protect cultural identity and strengthen the sustainability of destinations. Greece and UNESCO also examined opportunities for joint initiatives on sustainable cultural tourism, knowledge-sharing and the development of cultural routes. Their shared objective is to establish a tourism model that does more than benefit from cultural heritage: it must actively safeguard, showcase and pass that heritage on to future generations. Greece proposes closer cooperation between UNESCO and UN Tourism Kefalogianni specifically stressed the importance of strengthening cooperation between UNESCO and the United Nations World Tourism Organization (UN Tourism). She proposed joint initiatives to highlight the connection between culture and tourism and promote a sustainable, responsible and inclusive model of tourism development. The initiative aims to encourage international dialogue, facilitate the exchange of expertise and advance practices that ensure tourism contributes meaningfully to cultural heritage protection and supports local communities. It also seeks to promote the cultural wealth of individual countries as a bridge between societies and cultures. title: What African countries, others can learn from Nigeria’s economic reforms – Minister
body:
The Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, on Tuesday highlighted key lessons African countries and the rest of the world can learn from Nigeria’s economic reform experience.
Mr Oyedele spoke at the Africa’s Golden Future Forum, held on the sidelines of the World Bank /IMF meetings in Bangkok, Thailand.
The minister said that proper sequencing, consistent communication and public trust were critical to successful reforms. He also identified fuel subsidy removal, foreign exchange liberalisation and tax reform as Nigeria’s major economic reforms in recent years.
“My experience is for reforms to build resilience, growth, we have to start with the end in mind, like I said. Think about what can go wrong, perhaps, in relation to scenario planning and how you respond to that. And while you’re at it, keep communicating with clarity to build trust,” Mr Oyedele said.
He explained that one of the things that worked for Nigeria with the reforms is presentation of the counterfactual realities.
“People can easily tell that because of the reform, life is harder. But you need to show them without the reform, it will be hardest,” he said.
“And it doesn’t mean they will believe you the first time, but you keep saying it. Second thing, sequencing matters. So a lot of the reforms were price correction issues. So you do price correction to bring volatility, then you focus on stabilising the system, and then you scale. But most importantly, think about how do you make it sustainable. And that’s by putting it into institutions and putting it into law.”
Nigeria has introduced a series of reforms the government said were focused on fixing the structure of the economy, although the impact has been enormous for many Nigerians grappling with cost-of-living crisis.
The government introduced reforms in the foreign exchange market, abolished what it termed a wasteful, corruption-ridden subsidy regime amid fiscal pressures, and institutionalised tax reforms.
While the reforms have been hailed as positive for the nation’s fiscal health by global development and financial institutions, many Nigerians have expressed frustrations over their impact on the domestic front amid skyrocketed energy prices, high cost of living and sundry inflationary pressures.
The minister explained that the right deployment of the law and the need to institutionalise reforms also mattered and helped with consolidation.
“So most of the reforms we did in Nigeria are either enacted into law or embedded into institutions. Because you need to be able to do that for sustainability. And the last one is you must stay the course.
“Policy consistency is important. Capital follows trust before it follows returns. They need to be able to plan and predict what you’re going to do.”
Mr Oyedele added, however, that the peculiarity of African economies and the population should also be considered in sequencing and communication.
“But while you’re at it, bear in mind, particularly in Africa, many of our citizens live in poverty. Many of them are not well educated. When people are hungry and they are angry, they cannot be rational,” he said.
“So how do you keep these people being able to survive? Because for them, they have to be alive to see tomorrow that they are promising. And this is when the support system becomes very important. Cash transfer funds.
“In Nigeria, we’ve done over 10 million households. We also did education funds to our… students, enabling not only for them to continue with their education, but for their parents and their guardians to have the sources of funds for other important things that they have to do. So at the end of the day, we need to ensure that we have clarity.”
The minister also lauded the political leadership for its tenacity, adding that it helped in maintaining policy consistency.
“I have to also say that we’re very lucky with the political leadership at the very top to be able to see these reforms through. So if it was possible in Nigeria, it’s possible elsewhere,” Mr Oyedele said.
Oladeinde Olawoyin reports Business & Economy, Development and Lagos Metro at PREMIUM TIMES. A First Class graduate of Mass Communication from the University of Ilorin, Ilorin, he was nominated in the journalism category of The Future Awards Africa in 2017. Aside maintaining a column titled ‘SATURDAY SATIRE’, he also writes art and culture pieces on weekends. Twitter : @Ola_deinde

title: INEC explains exclusion of Pantami, Adebutu from 2027 governorship candidates’ list
body:
The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) has explained its decision to exclude the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) candidates in Gombe, Isa Pantami, and in Ogun State, Ladi Adebutu, from its final list of candidates for the 6 February 2027 governorship elections.
In a statement by its spokesperson, Mohammed Haruna, INEC said the decision stemmed from their political parties’ failure to comply with the membership register requirements under Section 77(5)-(7) of the Electoral Act, 2026, and were ineligible to sponsor candidates in the elections.
INEC said it applied the sections of the law after it won the case challenging the application of the sections of the Electoral Act at the Supreme Court, following a suit by the Zenith Labour Party (ZLP) challenging it.
“In particular, the court upheld the constitutionality of Item No. 2 of INEC’s Timetable and Schedule of Activities, which mandated political parties to submit their membership registers between 21st April and 10th May, 2026,” the statement reads in part.
INEC’s exclusion of Messrs Pantami and Adebutu in the governorship election and the inclusion of Kingsley Chinda of the All Progressives Congress (APC) have also sparked conversation as to the application of the law.
Mr Chinda registered with the APC on 27 April 2026 and formally announced his defection from the PDP to the APC on 2 June, after the APC had conducted its governorship primary on 21 May.
The sequence has raised questions about whether he was a registered APC member when the party held its primary and whether his name appeared on the membership register submitted to INEC within the required period.
The governorship election has been scheduled to hold on 6 February 2027, while the presidential and National Assembly elections will hold on 16 January 2027.
INEC said the final list of presidential and National Assembly candidates had been published on 12 September, 13 days before the Supreme Court delivered its judgment.
Under Section 32(2) of the Electoral Act, 2026, political parties that believe their candidates were wrongly omitted from the list have 14 days from the date of publication to notify the commission.
The deadline for such notifications is 24 October, the commission said.
“Under Section 32(2) of the Electoral Act, 2026, political parties that believe their candidates were wrongly left off the list have 14 days from the date of publication to notify the Commission. The deadline is 24th October, 2026,” it added.
“The commission assures the public of its commitment to transparency, the rule of law and the credibility of the electoral process.”
On 24 September, the Supreme Court ruled in a case between the Zenith Labour Party (ZLP) and the electoral commission, INEC, about the submission of party registers and their use to determine who contests elections under each political party.
The court nullified the earlier decision of a Court of Appeal to nullify Sections 77(5)-(7) of the Electoral Act, 2026, which require political parties to submit their membership registers to INEC before conducting valid primaries.
The supreme court said the provisions were constitutional and mandatory for all political parties as included in the Electoral Act 2026.
The apex court also upheld the INEC timetable requiring parties to submit their membership registers between 21 April and 10 May, ruling that parties that failed to submit their registers within the stipulated period were ineligible to sponsor candidates, INEC said.
The commission said it relied on Section 287(1) of the 1999 Constitution, which requires authorities to enforce decisions of the courts, in applying the judgment to the final list of governorship candidates.

title: Nigeria ​‌‍‍‍‍⁠⁠‍​‍‍​‌‍​‌‌​condemns attacks on fellow Africans, demands action against xenophobia
body: Nigeria has condemned rising xenophobic attacks against Africans in other African countries, warning that discrimination threatens continental solidarity, integration and peaceful coexistence. The Federal Government expressed its concern during the United Nations General Assembly’s adoption of a new political declaration against racism and racial discrimination. Speaking in Nigeria’s national capacity, Amb. Bola Asaju urged African governments to confront growing hostility against migrants and foreign nationals within their territories. The delegation warned that economic hardship, unemployment and social challenges could never justify violence, persecution or discrimination against people because of their nationality. Nigeria maintained that African countries could not credibly champion Pan-Africanism and continental integration while tolerating attacks against fellow Africans. Asaju expressed particular concern about incidents of hostility and violence targeting Africans living outside their countries of origin. According to the delegation, such developments threaten the historical bonds of solidarity that supported Africa’s struggles against colonialism and racial oppression. Nigeria stressed that the sacrifices made during the continent’s liberation movements should inspire greater unity rather than division among African populations. The country maintained that governments had a responsibility to protect everyone within their territories, irrespective of nationality or immigration background. It also called for accountability for individuals and groups responsible for xenophobic violence, intimidation and discrimination. Nigeria urged African governments to strengthen national legislation, improve regional cooperation and intensify public education against xenophobia. The delegation also recommended addressing underlying socioeconomic conditions that could be exploited to incite hostility against migrants and foreign nationals. It warned against collective blame, particularly where economic difficulties were used to portray foreign nationals as responsible for domestic challenges. Nigeria reaffirmed its commitment to the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, the international framework adopted in South Africa in 2001 to combat racism. Asaju said Nigeria supported the latest political declaration and voted in favour of its adoption. The General Assembly adopted the declaration by 95 votes in favour, five against and 37 abstentions. The declaration commemorates the 25th anniversary of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action and renews international commitments to eliminating racial discrimination. It recognises the enduring consequences of slavery, the transatlantic slave trade, colonialism and apartheid, while calling for stronger measures against contemporary discrimination. The declaration also addresses racial profiling, hate speech, unequal access to justice and discriminatory practices associated with emerging digital technologies. Nigeria said international commitments against racism must produce practical improvements in people’s lives rather than remain declarations of political intention. The country urged governments to demonstrate greater political will in confronting racism and xenophobia, including discriminatory practices occurring within their own societies. Nigeria maintained that protecting human dignity and strengthening solidarity among Africans remained essential to the continent’s integration and development aspirations. South Africa supported the declaration, while the European Union raised reservations concerning certain provisions relating to neocolonialism and reparatory justice. title: IMF/World Bank Annual Meetings: Africa must help shape global AI rules – BoG Governor
body: Bank of Ghana (BoG) Governor, Dr Johnson Asiama, has urged the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to strengthen its support for Africa’s digital transformation and help secure a stronger voice for the continent in shaping global digital rules. He said countries needed practical assistance to develop systems for artificial intelligence (AI) governance, supervisory technology, cybersecurity and digital risk management. “This will allow Africa not only to harness AI, but to adapt, govern, and innovate with it for resilience and inclusive growth,” he said during the African Caucus Meeting today. Dr Asiama made the call during the second round of a governors’ meeting on Africa’s digital sovereignty and AI for structural transformation, held on the sidelines of the IMF/World Bank Annual Meetings. He urged the IMF to deepen its analysis of the links between AI, digital transformation and macro-financial stability. This, he said, should include integrating relevant AI issues into the Fund’s surveillance work and Financial Sector Assessment Programmes (FSAPs), while examining their implications for productivity, employment, financial resilience and inclusive growth. The Governor also called for greater policy coordination on data governance, digital trade and cross-border AI regulation. He urged the IMF to help mobilise affordable financing for secure digital public infrastructure and efforts to narrow the digital divide. Dr Asiama stressed that the responsible use of AI was essential to advancing Africa’s structural transformation, economic resilience and long-term development. “AI is already reshaping productivity, competitiveness, governance, and finance. Africa has taken giant leaps in digital payments, ID systems, AI-enabled financial services, and fintech,” he said. However, he cautioned that gaps in regulatory capacity, cybersecurity, infrastructure and financing continued to limit the safe and inclusive use of these technologies. He warned that Africa risked falling further behind without urgent, coordinated action, making a stronger partnership with the IMF essential.

title: Finland's new baby box has 14 more items than last year
body:
The value of the maternity grant increased from 170 to 210 euros this year, allowing Kela to include more items in the box.
Finland's new maternity package, often called 'the baby box', was unveiled on Wednesday with more products than last year.
Distribution of the new box has begun, according to the Social Insurance Institution of Finland, Kela. As in the past, it contains a range of clothes, accessories and other essentials for babies.
"This year's box contains 52 products, compared with 38 last year," Kela coordinator for family benefits, Anniina Kuokka told Yle's morning programme.
The package also includes several muslin cloths, a blanket, a sleeping bag, a book, nail scissors and a toothbrush.
Lubricant and a pack of condoms have also returned to the box after being left out of last year’s version .
The box, designed by illustrator Eveliina Muotkavaara , features a peach-coloured space-themed pattern.
The latest maternity package includes a ball, as promised by Prime Minister Petteri Orpo’s (NCP) government.
The plan to include a ball was written into the government programme in 2023 as part of its "Finland on the Move" initiative, which aims to increase physical activity across all age groups.
Kela says the ball is intended to support interaction between parents and babies and encourage families to spend time doing things together.
Kela draws on customer surveys and feedback when deciding what to include in the maternity package.
Colour is a subject that generates considerable feedback, Kuokka said.
"Some people want colourful products, while the majority prefer neutral shades."
According to Kela's surveys, some of the most popular baby box items include the merino wool suit, nail scissors, outdoor suit, sleeping bag and towel.
Kuokka said many parents report continuing to use the nail scissors for years after receiving them in the package.

title: Google Opens Advanced AI Systems to 200 European Scientists
body: Google will give 200 European researchers access to its most advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models and systems to support scientific research, the US technology giant announced on Wednesday. The European Commission will select the researchers from among beneficiaries of the European RAISE programme, Google told Agence France-Presse (AFP). The company announced the initiative ahead of an AI summit scheduled to take place in Dublin on Wednesday. The selected researchers will gain direct access to advanced scientific tools from Google DeepMind and Google Cloud, including AlphaFold 3, which specialises in protein research, AlphaGenome and WeatherNext, a system for weather forecasting. “By providing critical computing power and cutting-edge tools, this initiative aims to accelerate innovation in Europe and strengthen the competitiveness of the continent’s researchers,” Google said. The announcement comes as artificial intelligence increasingly transforms scientific research, from mathematics to the biological sciences. title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico prevail against White House — for now
body:
WASHINGTON, DC - SEPTEMBER 19: CNN signage on the network's booth in the press area of the White House after journalists with the network were earlier denied entry to the White House grounds, on September 19, 2026 in Washington, DC. Graeme Sloan/Getty Images hide caption
A federal judge ruled late Tuesday that President Trump cannot ban news organizations from covering him at the White House because he does not like the nature of their coverage — at least, not until the matter goes to a formal trial.
U.S. District Court Judge Timothy J. Kelly found that Trump's decision to bar more than 70 journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico violated their fundamental free speech in two separate ways as well as their due process rights. Both rights are enshrined in the Bill of Rights to the U.S. Constitution.
The news organizations sued last month after the Trump administration denied them access. The judge granted a temporary restraining order to CNN, MS NOW and Politico on Sept. 24.
Kelly pointed repeatedly to Trump's own public statements and social media posts to construct his conclusion that Trump was not responding to national security concerns. Instead, he wrote, Trump sought to pressure news outlets to cover him more favorably by stripping them of press credentials to gain access to the White House.
"President Trump's own comments suggest that he intended the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes to alter their reporting on him, bolstering the case that his action here is sufficient to deter a reporter of ordinary firmness from reporting in the same way she had before," Kelly wrote in the opinion.
He later continued, "[T]he ban threatens to cut off all Plaintiffs' access to the White House press area — a space open to many of their competitors — thereby restricting their ability to observe happenings there firsthand, immediately report on those activities, and try to engage with government officials."
WASHINGTON, DC - OCTOBER 08: Lawyer for CNN, MS Now and Politico Ted Boutrous leaves the E. Barrett Prettyman United States Court House on October 08, 2026 in Washington, DC. Finn Gomez/Getty Images hide caption
Theodore J. Boutrous, the noted First Amendment attorney representing the three U.S. news outlets, had argued in court last week that Trump was the best witness his clients could offer for their case — because the president was so blatant about not liking the tenor of their coverage. Late Tuesday, after the release of Kelly's ruling, he hailed the judge's words.
"When the President issued his 'ban on the free press,' he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment," Boutrous said in a statement shared with NPR.
"Since then, the President has repeatedly, candidly, and consistently admitted in public that he banned our clients from the White House to punish reporting he doesn't like and to try to force journalists to cover him in ways he prefers," Boutrous wrote. "The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound."
On Wednesday afternoon, the Justice Department notified the court that it would appeal Judge Kelly's ruling.
"The Fake News has no place demanding a spot in the President's Oval Office," the White House said in a statement shared with NPR. "The lies they smear are a disservice to the American public and tear at the very fabric of our Democracy. They're completely capable of reporting from directly outside. We intend to appeal this misguided decision."
Kelly, a Trump appointee, turned aside the U.S. Justice Department's arguments invoking national security concerns and the objections the White House took with their reporting. Trump has said coverage is framed in a way to drag him down and make his Democratic critics look good.
The judge also rejected the department's claims that the court should not weigh in on such matters. Kelly had ruled against the Trump administration during the president's first term in office on a related matter involving efforts to bar then CNN White House correspondent Jim Acosta. And Kelly pointed to other precedents that he said must guide his conclusions, even as the Justice Department argued in court they were wrongly decided.
Even so, Kelly took pains to note that he did not utterly dismiss those as valid governmental concerns.
"No one should interpret the Court's decision to suggest that President Trump's concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media's reporting are unfounded," Kelly wrote, "or that the government is powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed."
Even so, Kelly found that the White House's actions to put the president's words into practice had caused a kind of irreparable harm. Trump was not required to admit the reporters to the White House. Once they were credentialed to do so, under earlier court rulings, those credentials could not be stripped away simply because the president or other administration officials do not like their coverage.
The Justice Department invoked national security only in court filings days after the White House acted against the reporters. And the news outlets were neither given fair warning of what was ahead nor a means to object ahead of time. The White House communications office sent letters expressing concern over accuracy and what it said were national security disclosures days later and gave the journalists several days to respond and appeal.
Kelly wrote that the Justice Department's presentation was inadequate to make a compelling case. And he said that after-the-fact notification did not constitute an adequate process to be warned about consequences and to appeal the punishment.
"It is not hard to conclude that President Trump likely banned Plaintiffs from the White House because he believes that their reporting is generally inaccurate and biased against him," Kelly wrote. And that, he wrote, represents a form of unlawful retaliation.
WASHINGTON, DC - SEPTEMBER 19: A CNN sign hangs on the wall behind the broadcast area in the White House briefing room, on September 19, 2026 in Washington, DC. Graeme Sloan/Getty Images hide caption
The ruling did not, however, address the question of the administration's periodic refusal since the ban to permit CNN's journalists into smaller spaces where the full press corps cannot fit simultaneously, such as Air Force One or the Oval Office.
That has made it impossible for CNN to serve as the designated representative of the video pool.
The pool - made up of CNN and four competitors (ABC, CBS, Fox and NBC) - share costs and logistical obligations to capture video of Trump at every public appearance, even in tightly held locations.
Even after Kelly earlier issued a temporary restraining order compelling the administration to allow the reporters back into the White House, the order was observed unevenly. CNN was periodically blocked by the administration from representing the pool either generally or in tight spaces. In one recent instance, CNN was blocked from accompanying Trump aboard Air Force One on a trip to Tennessee.
The three major U.S. news organizations sued shortly after reporters for the outlets reported their credentials, which give them daily access to the White House, were confiscated.
The administration has waged a multi-front battle against the press, including an early review of the broadcast licenses for ABC's local TV stations that could lead to them being revoked. It also forced news outlets out from the Pentagon when they did not agree to withhold any reports that had not been authorized for release ahead of time. The administration has launched investigations of all major networks — including NPR — except Fox, which is controlled by Rupert Murdoch, the president's ally, and successfully pressured the Republican leaders of Congress to pull back all federal funds for public media.
Last week, the Department of Justice said it was investigating five major television networks - CNN, ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News, alleging that they have broken antitrust laws when they decided to stick together after the president banned CNN.
As a private citizen, Trump has sued the New York Times , CNN, the Des Moines Register, the BBC, and Wall Street Journal (also owned by Murdoch). ABC settled a Trump lawsuit ahead of his return to office and CBS settled days before its corporate owner received the green light from Trump's pick as the nation's chief broadcast regulator to sell itself to its new owners, allies of the president.
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

title: Daniel’s GFF Sponsors 754 Patients for Free Surgeries
body: James Sowole in Abeokuta No fewer than 754 patients have been scheduled to benefit from free surgeries and medical treatments from October 9 to October 24, 2026, and are sponsored by Gateway Front Foundation (GFF). The GFF, which is celebrating its 25th anniversary, is being sponsored by the Senator representing Ogun East in the Senate, Otunba Gbenga Daniel, covering nine local government areas of Ogun State. The programme was organised in conjunction with Sharing Hope Medical Mission, USA; Redeemed Medical Village (RMV), and Eye Foundation Hospital. While the surgical aspects, which cover major and minor surgeries of the eye, orthopedics, gynaecological surgeries, plastic surgeries and medical treatment, will take place at the Redeemed Medical Village in the Redeemed Christian Church of God (RCCG) City, Ogun State, other medical services will take place in other 12 centres within the Ogun East senatorial district. Speaking at the commencement of the programme at the RMV, the Chief Medical Consultant to the Gateway Front Foundation, Dr Bankole Osisanya, said the foundation had conducted prescreening exercises at 12 centres to identify patients requiring surgical procedures, adding that the exercise was still ongoing and the number of beneficiaries could increase. According to him, the programme also provides free medical consultations, diagnostic assessments and medications to patients attending the various centres. He explained that the surgical component was designed to address conditions requiring operations, while the general medical outreach would ensure that residents who needed routine examinations and treatment could also benefit from the initiative. Osisanya said the foundation was collaborating with Sharing Hope Medical Mission, USA, and the Redeemer’s Health Village to deliver the programme, with the objective of surpassing the achievements of previous medical missions organised by Sharing Hope International. He added that the Eye Foundation was also participating in the initiative, providing free eyeglasses and eye drops to beneficiaries through teams visiting the various outreach centres. The medical consultant said doctors, nurses and other paramedics from the United States were participating in the programme, with most of the visiting medical personnel deployed to the surgical centre to support the operations. At The Ark, one of the 13 medical outreach locations, Osisanya said three doctors, including two family physicians from the United States, were attending to patients, supported by interpreters to facilitate communication between the medical personnel and beneficiaries. He said approximately eight nurses were also conducting preliminary assessments, including checks on patients’ blood pressure, random blood sugar levels, weight, temperature and hepatitis B status, before they proceeded to consultations with doctors and received prescribed medications free of charge. Patients identified during the consultations as requiring surgical interventions, he explained, were referred to the designated hospital, where the free operations were scheduled to commence the following day. Osisanya attributed the medical mission to the 25th anniversary of the Gateway Front Foundation, established in 2001, saying the initiative was sponsored by former Ogun State Governor, Senator Otunba Gbenga Daniel. He described the sponsorship as a humanitarian intervention driven by Daniel’s concern for the welfare of the people, insisting that the programme was non-political and intended to provide healthcare support to those who might otherwise struggle to access medical services. The consultant said he had personally worked with Daniel on medical outreaches over the past three years, travelling to different communities to provide treatment and support to people in need. On arrangements for beneficiaries after the exercise, Osisanya said the foundation’s direct follow-up activities during the mission were generally limited to about 48 hours, after which patients were expected to continue their care with their regular healthcare providers. He advised beneficiaries who underwent surgery or received medical treatment to return to their regular doctors for necessary follow-up consultations, adding that they could also benefit from subsequent outreach programmes when organised. One of the beneficiaries, Joseph Akpan, expressed appreciation to the organisers, saying the medical team had been attending to patients, conducting examinations and providing treatment since last Friday. Akpan said he had received medications and undergone medical tests during the outreach, adding that medical personnel discovered that his blood pressure was very high and provided medication to help manage the condition. He thanked the organisers for bringing free healthcare services to the community, and prayed for their continued wellbeing.

title: Turkish Police Raid TV Channel Aligned to Opposition Party
body: Turkish police have raided the headquarters of opposition-aligned broadcaster Halk TV in Istanbul, halted its live broadcasts and prevented employees from entering the building, according to the channel and Turkish media reports. Halk TV announced on Wednesday morning that police had entered its headquarters and appointed a new manager to take control of the station. “Police are inside the Halk TV building. A supervisor has been appointed to take control of the station. Live broadcasts have been interrupted,” the broadcaster said in a statement posted on X. Turkish media reports said financial crimes police were searching the premises and authorities had issued 17 arrest warrants in an operation linked to the channel’s owner. Halk TV has close ties to the opposition Republican People’s Party (CHP) and regularly criticises President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AK Party). The raid comes amid mounting pressure on Turkey’s main opposition. In May, a Turkish court removed the CHP leadership from running the party in a legal move that the opposition said further strengthened Erdoğan’s grip on power. Meanwhile, Istanbul Mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu, widely regarded as Erdoğan’s most prominent political rival, has spent more than a year in prison over corruption allegations. He denies all the charges. The post Turkish Police Raid TV Channel Aligned to Opposition Party appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Netherlands denies visas to three Russian gymnasts for world championships, including Olympic champion Angelina Melnikova
body: Dutch authorities denied visas to Russian artistic gymnasts Angelina Melnikova, Viktoria Listunova, and Anna Kalmykova, barring them from traveling to the world championships in Rotterdam, Netherlands. The Russian Gymnastics Federation said the denial came because “one or several Schengen Area member states consider the athletes a threat to their international relations.” The federation said it viewed the Dutch authorities’ actions as “a deliberate elimination of the strongest gymnasts from contention for world championship medals and Olympic quota spots.” The federation said it plans to appeal to the International Olympic Committee (IOC) and World Gymnastics to “assess the situation and its impact on ensuring equal conditions for Olympic qualification.” Five other Russian athletes received visas: Ilya Zaika, Saveliy Syedin, Lyudmila Roshchina, Milana Kayumova, and Elizaveta Us. The Russian Gymnastics Federation said Dutch authorities issued visas to 47 of the 61 members of the Russian delegation. The world artistic gymnastics championships will take place in Rotterdam from October 17–25, marking the first stage of team qualification for the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles. The top three men’s and top three women’s teams will earn Olympic quota spots as a result. Angelina Melnikova is the 2020 Olympic champion in the team all-around and a multiple world and European champion. In August 2026, Russian gymnasts competed in international competitions for the first time in five years — at the European Championships in Zagreb, Croatia. At that tournament, Melnikova won gold in the vault and became the all-around champion for the first time in her career. Kalmykova took second place in the all-around. Croatia did not issue visas to the Russian athletes on the first attempt — they were initially denied, but the decision was reversed a few days before the competition. All the gymnasts competed in the tournament under neutral status. At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication. title: INEC in the Eye of the Storm
body: The Independent National Electoral Commission has the authority to enforce electoral rules, but that authority carries an obligation to explain consequential decisions and demonstrate consistency. What precisely disqualified the affected candidates, and have the relevant legal provisions been applied uniformly? Who, ultimately, should be held accountable when the right to appear on the ballot becomes a matter of dispute. Jonathan Eze writes. Democracy begins long before voters approach the ballot box. It begins with the rules governing who may contest, the institutions entrusted with enforcing those rules and the confidence citizens place in the fairness of the process. Against this backdrop, the omission of Ladi Adebutu, Isa Ali Pantami and other candidates from INEC’s published lists for the 2027 governorship elections raises questions that reach beyond party politics into the foundations of electoral legitimacy. While no candidate is above the law, no electoral institution should be beyond scrutiny when its decisions determine who can participate in a democratic contest. Are the omissions the necessary consequences of statutory violations, or do they reveal procedural weaknesses requiring urgent redress? And can an election command enduring legitimacy if the process determining access to the ballot is itself a subject of controversy? That is the controversy confronting the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) following the publication of its governorship candidates’ lists for the February 6, 2027 elections. Among the prominent omissions are Ladi Adebutu, the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) candidate in Ogun State, and Professor Isa Ali Pantami, the party’s candidate in Gombe State. Aminu Abdussalam Gwarzo, the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) candidate in Kano State, is also reportedly missing from the list. In Bauchi State, candidates of the Social Democratic Party (SDP), New Nigeria Peoples Party (NNPP), Action Alliance (AA) and Accord Party were reportedly omitted. The development raises questions that extend beyond the fortunes of individual politicians. Was INEC enforcing the Electoral Act, responding to specific legal impediments or correcting nomination irregularities? Were the same standards applied consistently across parties? And has the commission adequately explained its decisions? These are questions of electoral accountability that demand evidence-based answers rather than partisan conjecture. The law behind the omissions The legal context is central to understanding the controversy. On September 24, 2026, the Supreme Court restored Sections 77(5), 77(6), 77(7) and 84(2) of the Electoral Act 2026, provisions concerning political party membership registers and participation in party primaries, congresses and conventions. Section 77(5) restricts participation in party primaries to members whose names appear in the membership register submitted to INEC within the prescribed period. Section 77(6) requires parties to use the relevant register for their primaries, while Section 77(7) stipulates consequences for failure to submit the register within the statutory timeframe. The ruling provides a legal basis for enforcing membership and nomination requirements. It would therefore be premature to conclude that every omission reflects political interference. Equally, citing the law does not, by itself, establish that every individual decision was correctly made. In Adebutu’s case, questions have arisen over whether his name appeared in the PDP membership register submitted to INEC. The Ogun PDP has rejected allegations of non-compliance, maintaining that Adebutu registered within the stipulated period and that the relevant documentation was submitted. Adebutu has similarly maintained that he remains a duly registered member of the party. Pantami’s case presents a different complication. A Federal High Court in Gombe nullified his initial emergence as the PDP candidate and ordered a fresh primary. He subsequently won another primary on September 29, 2026. His camp maintains that the exercise complied with the court’s directive and that the omission is being addressed through legal and administrative channels. These cases should not be conflated. A dispute over membership registration is distinct from one concerning compliance with a court-ordered primary. INEC must explain the specific legal and factual grounds applicable to each candidate. Political intrigue or administrative failure? The omissions have inevitably generated suspicion. The Ogun PDP has alleged that pressure from the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) contributed to Adebutu’s exclusion. Such allegations are serious, but they remain claims by an interested political party and should not be treated as established evidence of interference. Nevertheless, unexplained decisions involving prominent candidates create fertile ground for speculation. The appropriate response is neither to presume a conspiracy nor to grant INEC unquestioning immunity from scrutiny. Did the commission identify specific statutory violations in each case? Were the affected parties notified of deficiencies? Were comparable cases treated consistently? Were relevant court orders properly considered? If the omissions resulted from administrative errors, what lawful mechanism exists to correct them? These questions are essential to determining whether the commission’s decisions rest on verifiable facts and applicable law. The scrutiny must also extend to the political parties. Parties cannot demand strict compliance from INEC while treating membership registers, nomination procedures and statutory deadlines casually. Where a party fails to meet legal requirements, its candidates may suffer the consequences regardless of their popularity or political standing. Conversely, a party’s insistence that it complied with the law cannot substitute for documentary verification. Accountability must apply to both the electoral regulator and the organisations it regulates. Is INEC truly independent? The controversy also raises a broader question about the meaning of electoral independence. Under Section 153 of the 1999 Constitution, INEC is established as an independent electoral commission. But institutional independence is demonstrated not merely by constitutional provisions; it is sustained through impartial decisions, consistent procedures and transparent explanations. An unpopular decision does not automatically establish political compromise, just as an institution’s claim to independence does not place its decisions beyond scrutiny. The controversy surrounding Kingsley Chinda, listed as the APC governorship candidate in Rivers State, further illustrates the importance of consistency. Reports have raised questions about the timing of his party registration relative to the APC primary. The Rivers APC has defended his candidacy. Whether the circumstances amount to a violation must be determined by the applicable law and verified facts. The public is entitled to understand how membership and nomination requirements are applied across comparable cases. This is not a demand that INEC exclude additional candidates; it is a demand for equal treatment under the law. Parties’ responses and narrowing window The PDP has said it is engaging INEC to resolve the omissions in accordance with the law and established electoral guidelines. Its spokesperson, Jungudo Mohammed, urged affected candidates and supporters to remain calm while discussions continue. Pantami’s camp has expressed confidence that its legal and liaison teams can address the matter. The NDC has maintained that Gwarzo remains its candidate, while the Kwankwasiyya Movement has called on INEC to explain the exclusion. In Bauchi, the reported omission of candidates from four parties raises additional concerns about smaller political organisations’ ability to secure representation on the ballot. These reactions reflect the affected parties’ positions, not definitive legal findings. The precise grounds for each omission, and the availability of remedies, must be established from official records and any subsequent court decisions. The approaching election makes a prompt resolution imperative. Uncertainty can disrupt campaign planning, weaken party structures and leave supporters unsure whether their preferred candidates will appear on the ballot. Smaller parties may be particularly disadvantaged by the financial and logistical demands of prolonged litigation. Affected parties may seek administrative clarification or pursue appropriate legal remedies, subject to statutory deadlines and the circumstances of each case. However, neither the candidates nor the public should assume that every omission is reversible or that every legal challenge will succeed. What is at stake? If the omissions stand, the affected parties could enter the elections without the candidates they intended to present in Ogun, Gombe, Kano and Bauchi. Their supporters could consequently lose the opportunity to vote for those candidates, unless a lawful remedy becomes available. The wider danger is the erosion of public confidence. When consequential electoral decisions are inadequately explained, citizens may begin to suspect that access to the ballot depends on considerations beyond the law. Such perceptions can weaken institutional credibility even where a decision is legally defensible. INEC must therefore publish clear explanations of the grounds for the omissions, identify the relevant statutory provisions and clarify whether administrative corrections are legally permissible. Where disputes are before the courts, it should distinguish established facts from matters awaiting judicial determination. The commission must resist political pressure to reverse lawful decisions, but it must equally demonstrate that its authority is exercised consistently and transparently. Ultimately, the controversy is larger than the political fortunes of Adebutu, Pantami, Gwarzo or the affected Bauchi candidates. It concerns whether Nigerians can trust that access to the ballot is governed by clear rules, impartially administered and open to lawful scrutiny. Political prominence cannot confer immunity from electoral law. Equally, electoral administration must not become so opaque that parties and voters are left to speculate about the reasons candidates have disappeared from official lists. As the 2027 elections approach, INEC has an opportunity to replace suspicion with evidence and uncertainty with clarity. The credibility of the electoral process will depend not only on whether its decisions withstand legal scrutiny, but also on whether the commission can convincingly demonstrate that those decisions were made fairly. In a democracy, the ballot is the instrument through which citizens choose their leaders. The process determining who may appear on that ballot must command no less confidence than the vote itself.

title: Pope passed a ‘calm’ night after lung operation: Vatican
body: Pope Leo XIV spent a calm night in hospital in Rome after having a cancerous tumour removed from his right lung in a 90-minute operation, the Vatican said Wednesday. “The pope passed a calm night,” the Vatican said, without providing any more details on the 71-year-old, who underwent surgery at the Gemelli hospital on Tuesday.
