title: 'This cannot be a coincidence' — Ukraine's Starlink access restricted without warning, Zelensky adviser says
body:
Ukraine's Starlink access has been restricted without warning, severely disrupting "several" military missions, presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said on Oct. 14.
The speed restrictions were accompanied by signal disruptions and instability, even at lower speeds. Military personnel from mulitple units reported serious issues with Starlink throughout the day.
"I confirm that (Starlink owner) SpaceX implemented speed restrictions on Starlink terminals while in motion last night. Currently, the restriction applies to the Starshield 'military service package' and limits speed to 100 miles per hour (160 kilometers per hour)," Beskrestnov said in a post on social media.
Ukraine's Defense Ministry later told journalists that the actual speeds available during the day were even lower than the 160 kph limit. By the end of the day, service was reportedly stabilized, but the restriction remained in place.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said only U.S. President Donald Trump had the power to determine the speed restrictions for Starshield systems.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately (the president). .... Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action," he said .
Ukraine relies on Starlink for several military applications including operating its "middle strike" campaign in Russian-occupied Ukraine, as well as interceptor drones that defend against Russia's new jet-powered attack drones.
This mid-range strike campaign this year has allowed Ukraine to strangle Russian logistics , hampering its ability to fight on the front lines.
A source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry confirmed to the Kyiv Independent that speed limitations had been discovered and the cause was being investigated.
"This complicates drone missions —specifically those involving interceptors and mid-range strike drones — and hampers capabilities for frontline logistics, reconnaissance, and signal relay," the source added.
A soldier working on mid-range strike drone operations, who requested anonymity, confirmed that "certain issues are being observed" but declined to elaborate, citing operational security.
Two other commanders — both from elite drone units working on the eastern and southern front lines — reported issues with Starlink terminals on "middle strike" drones flying at higher speeds over the last 24 hours.
Both likewise requested to remain anonymous, and declined to describe the problems in more detail, so as to not assist the enemy.
During the day, Ukraine's 7th Air Assault Corps said on social media that it was experiencing a "throttling" of its Starlink connectivity.
"The consequences are already being felt in the field. Since the start of the day alone, a drone unit operating within the 7th Corps' area of ​​responsibility in the Huliaipole sector has had to cancel a number of missions due to these connectivity issues," the corps said.
Later in the evening of Oct. 14, ex-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov — who famously negotiated with Musk to cut off Russian forces from Starlink while in office — announced that service was being restored, with the speed limit in place.
"Attack drones and interceptor drones should be operational again," he wrote. "Now, the focus should be on completely removing the speed limit for Starshield."
Fedorov, who no longer holds a position in the Ukrainian government after being dismissed by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July, did not provide evidence for his claims or explain where he got his information, though he thanked Musk in his post on X.
The Defense Ministry confirmed that service had been stabilized at a speed of 160 kilometers per hour.
"SpaceX continues to maintain the 161 km/h limit. Throughout the day, the actual limits were significantly lower. However, as of now, we observe that connection quality has improved at speeds up to 160 km/h," the ministry said in a comment to reporters.
The Defense Ministry is currently negotiating with partners and with SpaceX "regarding stable service conditions and the prevention of sudden restrictions."
But Musk's response was not encouraging — particularly for Ukraine's middle-strike campaign.
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government," he wrote in response to Fedorov.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately (the president). .... Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."
Musk comments point to a link between the Starlink disruption and Kyiv's deteriorating relationship with the White House — a fear voiced earlier in the day by Beskrestnov.
"Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is associated with the current political situation," he said.
As reported by the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 12, U.S. President Donald Trump has threatened Ukraine with the withholding of intelligence and other assistance in a bid to protect Russian oil refineries.
Beskrestnov did not provide evidence that the Starlink restriction was connected to U.S. pressure on Ukraine, and the White House has not commented on the issue.
Serhii Sternenko , an activist and former advisor to Fedorov, also reported the restriction of access, saying "SpaceX likely took these measures at the request of the Trump administration."
The development comes after Ukraine worked with SpaceX earlier this year to deactivate unauthorized Starlink terminals being used by Russian forces. Starlink has played a critical role in Ukrainian military communications throughout the full-scale war.
The threats came after a confusing 48 hours during whichTrump announced a controversial "deal" with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel, followed by repeated demands that Ukraine replace Zelensky as president, followed by Trump announcing a unilateral " energy ceasefire " between Russia and Ukraine, which blindsided both Moscow and Kyiv.
Ukraine has since refrained from attacking Russian oil refineries but Russia has continued its blitz on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, most recently overnight on Oct. 14 when "several" power plants in Kyiv were hit. Trump has refused to accuse Russia of breaking the ceasefire.
The reported Starlink restrictions come as questions have been raised about U.S. intelligence sharing in relation to Russian ballistic missile launches, following two straight nights of attack on Kyiv with little to no warning.
Five Russian S-400 missiles struck the Ukrainian capital shortly after 10 p.m. local time on Oct. 12, causing "massive explosions," Kyiv Independent journalists reported. Air raid sirens and mobile alerts sounded only after the attack.
Zelensky described the strike as "particularly vile," saying Kyiv "received no early warning from our partners about this strike." His remarks raised questions about whether Washington had suspended intelligence assistance to Ukraine.
Despite the failure of Kyiv's early warning system and threats to halt U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukraine, Washington made no such decision, Ukrainian and American sources told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 13.
But later that day, around 10:30 p.m. another wave of ballistic missiles hit Kyiv, again without the usual warning.
At least three women were killed, and another 24 people, including a 7-year-old girl, were injured as a result of a hit on a residential building in the Desnianskyi District. Three more waves of ballistic missiles struck Kyiv throughout the night.
Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat told Ukrainian TV that Ukraine received no warnings from its partners about the first wave, though it did for the following three.
"Ukraine did not attack Russian oil refineries, yet Trump has already begun imposing sanctions on my country. Meanwhile, sanctions against Russia have been eased," Sternenko said.

title: Legarda extends medical leave until October 13
body: MANILA, Philippines — Senator Loren Legarda has again extended her medical leave, this time until October 13, Senate Secretary Renato Bantug Jr. confirmed. This is the latest medical leave filed by Legarda, who first left the country with her son, Batangas 1st District Representative Leandro Leviste , on August 2. This was days after plunder and graft complaints were announced against them by the Office of the Ombudsman over the latter’s solar energy projects. Legarda first filed for medical leave from August 3 to 5, and has been extending it since then. The senator previously confirmed that she had filed for medical leave with the Senate and asked the public “not to draw unwarranted conclusions from my travel or link it to the recent false and baseless allegations, which undeservedly besmirch a reputation that I have built over decades of public service.” Legarda and three other senators — Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta who are detained over plunder charges, and Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa who is in hiding over an International Criminal Court warrant of arrest — have stopped receiving salaries as they remain absent from plenary sessions of the Senate and the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte. – Rappler.com

title: Houthis strike Aramco headquarters; report: Chinese components used in missile production
body: Air raid sirens sounded Wednesday morning in Riyadh and the nearby city of Al-Kharj, a day after Yemen's Houthi rebels struck the headquarters of Saudi oil giant Aramco in Dhahran, eastern Saudi Arabia. The Saudi Energy Ministry confirmed that an administrative building at the company's headquarters was hit, causing what it described as a limited fire. There were no casualties, while international media reported that it remained unclear whether the building had been struck directly by a missile or damaged by interception debris or shrapnel.  The attack followed Saudi airstrikes on oil facilities in Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen. Before the strikes, Saudi authorities issued an evacuation warning for facilities belonging to the Yemeni Oil Company, particularly the al-Sabaha station in the capital, Sanaa. The Houthis subsequently issued their own warnings to Aramco employees, identifying the company's headquarters in Dhahran, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Aramco's Riyadh refinery as potential targets. Like the Saudis, the Houthis included precise locations of the threatened facilities in their announcements.    The exchange came after a devastating Houthi attack on Riyadh's international airport on Saturday, which killed at least 13 people and wounded 309. A regional official familiar with the details told the Associated Press that the missile struck an area containing passenger terminals 3 and 4, which serve domestic flights. According to the Saudi aviation authority, the dead included foreign nationals from the United States, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, the Palestinian territories, Sudan and Bangladesh, as well as Saudi citizens. Reports said the airport was evacuated and numerous ambulances were dispatched to the scene. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio subsequently confirmed that an American citizen had been killed and strongly condemned the attack, calling for an immediate end to strikes that endangered innocent civilians. Saudi authorities deployed heavy security around the airport and warned against distributing footage of the Houthi attacks. Saturday's strike came just two days after another deadly Houthi assault on the same airport, Riyadh's main international aviation hub. During the earlier attack, at least one passenger aircraft, reportedly empty at the time, was damaged, and three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, were killed. Three additional people were killed in previous attacks on airports in Riyadh and Abha last week.   The strikes mark a significant escalation in the long-running conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis. Fighting has continued inside Yemen between the Iran-backed rebels and forces loyal to the internationally recognized Yemeni government, which receives Saudi military support, including extensive airstrikes. The growing ability of the Houthis to disrupt Saudi aviation represents an especially serious challenge for Riyadh, exposing vulnerabilities in its defenses and undermining confidence in the kingdom's ability to protect vital infrastructure. Repeated missile attacks have also severely disrupted international aviation, effectively restricting access to Saudi airspace and putting additional pressure on airlines already struggling with the effects of regional wars and soaring fuel prices. The damage to airports, combined with the threat to energy infrastructure, has heightened concerns about how long the kingdom can sustain such disruptions. The Chinese connection Meanwhile, a report published Wednesday by The Wall Street Journal revealed that the Houthis had obtained a range of components from Chinese suppliers to develop their own version of Iran's Kheibar Shekan ballistic missile. The findings, based on research by Conflict Armament Research, suggest that the rebels are working to manufacture more advanced weapons domestically rather than relying exclusively on complete missile systems smuggled from abroad.  The Iranian missile, which has reportedly been used against US military targets during the war with Iran, is designed to maneuver toward its target and potentially evade air defense systems. According to US assessments cited in the report, certain versions feature a warhead that separates during the final phase of flight and uses a small propulsion system to adjust its trajectory. The technology could make interception considerably more difficult.   The Conflict Armament Research report described two shipments intercepted by Yemeni authorities in 2025, with missile-related equipment concealed among other goods. The seized material reportedly included metal components for missile bodies and engines, stabilizing fins, solid-fuel rocket motor components and heat-resistant materials designed to protect parts of the missile during launch. According to UN reports cited by The Wall Street Journal, Chinese companies have become the largest source of goods destined for the Houthis. Beijing, however, maintains that it complies with restrictions on arms sales to the rebel group. The findings raise concerns about the Houthis' growing manufacturing capabilities and their ability to acquire increasingly sophisticated missile technology despite international restrictions. The latest escalation is also raising fears of wider economic consequences for Saudi Arabia. The kingdom's real GDP is projected to contract by 3.6% this year, reflecting several factors, including declining oil activity. The attacks have added pressure ahead of major international gatherings scheduled for Riyadh this month, including the kingdom's flagship investment conference and the World Petroleum Council's energy congress. Several senior executives have reportedly canceled plans to attend. The impact is extending beyond the suspension of operations at Riyadh's airport. Employees in the capital's financial district were instructed to work from home Wednesday amid continuing security concerns, illustrating how the Houthi campaign is increasingly disrupting the kingdom's economic and commercial life.

title: Citi and Credendo Announce Landmark USD 328 Million
body:
Transaction marks the world’s first-ever Credendo-insured aviation financing and first Export Credit Agency (ECA)-backed aircraft financing structured through GIFT IFSC, in line with Government of India’s vision to make India a global aircraft leasing hub

Bangalore. Citi and Credendo, Belgium’s export credit agency, on Oct 13, 2026 announced the successful closing of a USD 328 million financing for eight Airbus aircraft (six A321s and two A320s) for IndiGo, India’s largest airline by network and fleet size and one of the fastest growing carriers in the world. Under the structure, Citi acted as Sole Mandated Arranger, ECA Coordinator and Sole Lender, with the financing backed by Credendo’s credit insurance.



Executed through IndiGo’s subsidiary, InterGlobe Aviation Financial Services IFSC Private Limited, the transaction marks the first-ever Credendo-insured aviation financing globally and the first ECA-backed aircraft financing through a GIFT IFSC leasing structure, setting an important milestone in India in aviation finance.

The bespoke financing solution was jointly conceptualized, structured and developed by Citi and Credendo in close partnership with IndiGo and Airbus, leveraging Citi’s market-leading expertise in ECA structuring and aviation finance together with Credendo’s credit insurance capabilities to deliver a tailored funding solution that supports IndiGo’s ambitious fleet expansion plans through the GIFT IFSC platform. Airbus played a key role in supporting this pioneering financing, working closely with Citi, Credendo and IndiGo throughout the process. The transaction further underscores Airbus' commitment to developing innovative financing solutions that enhance funding access and support the growth ambitions of its airline customers.

This landmark transaction reflects the growing importance of access to innovative international capital and export credit support in meeting the financing needs of India's rapidly expanding aviation sector and reinforcing its position as a global aviation hub. For IndiGo, the facility provides a competitive and diversified source of long-term funding for fleet and network growth. It also demonstrates the strong collaboration between Citi, Credendo, IndiGo and Airbus in delivering a first-of-its-kind financing and broadening the range of funding solutions available to the Indian aviation market.

K Balasubramanian, India CEO and Banking Head and Indian Subcontinent Sub-Cluster Head, Citi, commented: “The Government of India has made aircraft leasing through GIFT City a clear policy priority, and the incentives introduced have helped position India as an attractive destination for aircraft leasing. This transaction is a strong example of that vision in action. By combining Citi’s cross-border aviation and ECA financing expertise with Credendo’s credit insurance and IndiGo’s GIFT IFSC platform, we have delivered a first-of-its-kind solution that opens a vital new pathway connecting Indian aviation with the deep pool of ECA-backed international liquidity and supports the next phase of India’s aviation growth. Citi is proud to have led this landmark facility as Sole Mandated Lead Arranger, ECA Coordinator and Sole Lender. We also thank Airbus for its partnership and support in making this transaction possible.”

Frank Vanwingh, Group Deputy CEO, Vice Chairman of the Executive Committee, Credendo – Export Credit Agency stated:“This transaction is a significant milestone for Credendo and the first step in a broader initiative aimed at enhancing support for the Belgian aviation industry. As our inaugural aircraft finance transaction, it demonstrates our ambition to become a long-term partner for Belgian aviation stakeholders seeking access to international opportunities and innovative financing structures. The transaction also showcases the value that Belgian export credit support can bring to the aviation sector through bespoke risk mitigation solutions. We are proud to have worked alongside Airbus, Citi and IndiGo in delivering this landmark transaction through GIFT IFSC and look forward to supporting further aviation finance projects worldwide.”

Riyaz Peermohamed, Chief Aircraft Acquisition & Financing Officer, IndiGo said, “We are pleased to partner with Citi, Credendo and Airbus on this landmark financing, which offers IndiGo a competitive source of liquidity for our growing Airbus fleet. The transaction demonstrates the potential of GIFT IFSC to bring together international banks and export credit agencies and create innovative financing solutions for Indian aviation.”

title: APC announces Kano campaign council
body:
The Kano State chapter of the All Progressives Congress (APC) on Tuesday unveiled a 155-member Campaign Advisory Council for the 2027 presidential and governorship elections in the state.
The council, which will serve as the apex body overseeing campaign activities, will be chaired by Governor Abba Yusuf.
Its high-profile members include former Governors Ibrahim Shekarau and Abdullahi Ganduje, alongside three former military administrators from the state: Habibu Shuaibu, Lawan Jafaru-Isa, andYakubu Bako.
The Kano State APC Chairman, Umar Doguwa, noted that the advisory body also features Deputy President of the Senate, Barau Jibrin, Senators Kawu Sumaila and Rufa’i Hanga, as well as all APC candidates and members of the House of Representatives from Kano State.
The Advisory Council will provide strategic oversight for the operational 2027 Campaign Directorate, which will be constituted and announced at a later date.
The announcement comes barely three days after Governor Yusuf and 16 others made the final list of governorship candidates in the state, which was released by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) on Saturday.
Meanwhile, opposition parties—including the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) and the African Democratic Congress (ADC)—have yet to announce their campaign councils.
The NDC is currently struggling to address the omission of its governorship candidate, Aminu Abdulsalam, from the INEC’s list.
His exclusion has sent shockwaves through the state’s political arena, leaving the NDC scrambling for legal and administrative remedies to salvage its position in the crucial gubernatorial contest.

title: Europe Must Switch Arms Production to ‘War Mode’ to Match Russia, Polish Defense Minister Says
body:
Europe should move into “war mode” in terms of arms production to keep up with Russia, Poland’s defense minister has said.
Russia is already producing arms in war mode, and Europe cannot “stay asleep” at a time when the period of peace has ended and the continent must “prepare to defend our civilization,” Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said on the sidelines of the Warsaw Security Forum on Tuesday.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Russia spent an estimated 7.5% of its GDP on military expenditure in 2025, according to an analysis by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, and produced around seven million artillery, mortar, tank and rocket munitions, data from the Estonian Foreign Intelligence Service show.
By contrast, the total defense spending of all EU member states last year was estimated at 2.2% of combined GDP, according to a leaked EU report cited by Euronews.
The same report puts expected ammunition production by all 27 EU member states plus Norway at two million artillery shells this year.
European defense spending has “grown radically” under EU Commissioner for Defense Andrius Kubilius (in photo), Poland’s defense minister said. (PAP) Other Topics of Interest Russia Innovates for War, Not Prosperity Putin inherited a country with scientific talent and industrial capacity. He has squandered that inheritance.
European defense spending has “grown radically” under EU Commissioner for Defense Andrius Kubilius (in photo), Poland’s defense minister said. (PAP)
Speaking at a joint press conference with EU Commissioner for Defense and Space Andrius Kubilius , Kosiniak-Kamysz made the case for ramping up Europe’s defense industry capacity now to prevent greater costs later.
The defense minister said Warsaw is pushing for increased defense and security spending in the EU budget, describing current proposals by the Irish presidency as “unacceptable” to Poland.
“I understand that Ireland is a neutral country, situated far away on an island, and does not feel these threats [from Russia], but the role of the presidency is to hear the voice of those who do feel the threats, and our strong voice,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said, adding that the issue had formed the starting point of his talks with Kubilius.
Ireland, which holds the rotating six-month presidency of the Council of the EU, presented a budget proposal for 2028–2034 on Saturday that foresees an 8% cut in expenditure compared with the European Commission’s plan and trims the broader competitiveness, prosperity and security budget heading by around 13%.
Kosiniak-Kamysz pointed out that under Kubilius, EU-level defense financing had “grown radically,” but said it must be increased further, arguing that the “time has come” for Europe to multiply its defense production, as failure to do so would not only cost more in the future but also affect the prospects of future generations.
“Poland has already been through this,” he said. “So we know what we’re talking about.”

title: Kenya and India extends naval ties after frigate visit to Mombasa
body: An Indian Navy delegation led by Commodore Kartik Srimal paid a courtesy call on Commander Kenya Navy, Major General Paul Otieno, at Kenya Navy Headquarters on 5 October 2026, days after an Indian frigate concluded a four-day stop in Mombasa. The visit followed the arrival of INS Tarkash, a Talwar-class guided-missile frigate, which docked in Mombasa from 29 September to 2 October for what the Indian Navy called an operational turnaround, a routine stop for crew rest, resupply and maintenance between deployments. During the port call, Indian and Kenyan sailors held professional exchanges and joint activities meant to sharpen coordination between the two navies. Commodore Srimal’s delegation included India’s Defence Attache to Kenya, Captain Arjit Pandey, and other officials. The sides reviewed shared maritime interests and looked at ways to widen cooperation between the Kenya Navy and the Indian Navy, according to a statement from Kenya’s Ministry of Defence. Major General Otieno said sustained professional interaction helps strengthen bilateral defence ties and improves partner navies’ ability to respond to threats in the maritime domain. He added that the engagements open room for knowledge exchange, professional development and sharing of operational experience, while building institutional links between the two forces. An Indian delegation led by Commodore Kartik Srimal paid a courtesy call on the Commander Kenya Navy, Maj Gen Paul Otieno, at the Kenya Navy Headquarters with the engagement providing an opportunity to review areas of mutual interest. INS Tarkash is one of six Talwar-class frigates built around a modified Krivak III design from Russia, displacing roughly 4,000 tonnes fully loaded and carrying BrahMos supersonic anti-ship cruise missiles, a surface-to-air missile system and a medium-range naval gun. The class has a top speed near 30 knots and can operate for about 30 days without resupply, which suits the kind of long-endurance patrol and escort work India has leaned on it for in the Western Indian Ocean. Tarkash itself has recent operational credentials; it took part in an anti-piracy interception off the Horn of Africa in March 2024. The courtesy call and frigate visit are the latest in a run of naval engagements that has picked up pace since late 2023. INS Sumedha, a Saryu-class patrol vessel, made the f irst-ever visit by an Indian warship to Kenya’s port of Lamu on 9 December 2023, the same month Presidents William Ruto and Narendra Modi issued a joint maritime vision known as BAHARI. That same year, Goa Shipyard Limited and Kenya Shipyards Limited signed a memorandum of understanding on ship design, construction and wider defence industrial cooperation, part of Kenya’s push to build a shipbuilding and repair base on the East African coast. The cooperation has since broadened beyond port calls. In April 2025, India hosted the first Africa-India Key Maritime Engagement exercise off Tanzania, bringing in nine African navies including Kenya’s. Major General Otieno travelled to India in September 2025 for high-level talks, and the fourth Joint Defence Cooperation Committee session between the two countries met in Nairobi from 24 to 26 February 2026. In April 2026, the frigate INS Trikand called at Mombasa for a four-day visit, and Indian officials handed over 100 INSAS rifles and 50,000 rounds of ammunition to the Kenya Defence Forces on 8 April that year. For Kenya, the relationship offers access to training support, simulators and shipyard expertise as the navy works to expand its long courses and reposition itself as what officials have called a maritime centre of excellence. For India, the steady cadence of port calls, exercises and committee meetings forms part of a broader push, branded MAHASAGAR, to deepen naval diplomacy with Indian Ocean littoral states and maintain an operational presence along trade routes that run past the Horn of Africa. Analysts tracking India’s Africa posture have also linked the push to concerns in New Delhi about China’s growing footprint on the continent, a dynamic not stated in Kenyan or Indian official statements but widely discussed in regional security literature. The Indian Ocean carries a large share of the world’s seaborne trade, and both Nairobi and New Delhi have framed naval cooperation there as a shared interest rather than a response to any single threat. Kenya’s statement on the latest courtesy call cast it as part of continued naval diplomacy aimed at building institutional capacity and contributing to peace and stability across the region.

title: Trade between Russia and China up by 30.6% to $214.3 bln in January-September
body:
BEIJING, October 14. /TASS/. Trade between China and Russia rose by 30.6% year-on-year to $214.3 billion in January-September, according to the General Administration of Customs of China (GACC).
In the reporting period, Chinese exports to Russia grew by 33.1% to $98.06 billion, while imports of Russian products into China increased by 28.6% to $116.24 billion.
In January-September, Russia’s trade surplus with China reached $18.16 billion, which is 10.1% up year-on-year.
According to the GACC statistics, Chinese-Russian trade turnover in September rose by 13.5% compared to August, reaching $29.06 billion. In particular, Chinese exports to Russia totaled $13.39 billion (up 12.9%), while shipments from Russia to China increased by 13.9% to $15.67 billion.
In terms of value, the bulk of Russian goods supplied to China consists of oil, natural gas, and coal. Other key items include copper and copper ore, timber, fuel, seafood, and agricultural products. China exports automobiles, tractors, computers, smartphones, industrial and specialized equipment, and a wide range of consumer and industrial goods to Russia. Authorities in both countries are working to optimize the structure of bilateral trade, including through the development of e-commerce and primary processing projects.
In 2024, Chinese-Russian trade turnover reached a record high, exceeding $244 billion, but contracted by 6.9% to $228.1 billion in 2025. As Russian Ambassador to China Igor Morgulov said earlier, this annual figure could soon rise to $300 billion.

title: Indian Navy commissions third Mahe-class ASW-SWC
body:
The Indian Navy commissioned INS Mangrol (P82), the third Mahe-class anti-submarine warfare shallow water craft (ASW-SWC), at the Naval Dockyard, Mumbai, on October 12, 2026.
The commissioning ceremony was attended by senior officers of the Defense Forces, representatives of the Ministry of Defense, Cochin Shipyard Limited (CSL), industry partners and others.
INS Mangrol was designed and built by CSL with more than 80 percent indigenous content. Its construction involved Indian defense industries and Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) as part of the Make in India program.
Designed for operations in coastal and shallow waters, INS Mangrol is equipped to undertake anti-Submarine warfare (ASW), underwater surveillance and low-intensity maritime operations (LIMO), along with mine warfare-related tasks. Its sensors, sonar and weapon systems serve to detect, track and counter underwater threats in the challenging littoral environment.
Powered by three diesel engine-driven waterjet propulsion units, the ship offers high manoeuvrability and rapid response, essential for operations in shallow and confined waters, according to the navy.
Sanjay Vatsayan , Flag Officer Commanding-in-Chief, Western Naval Command, highlighted the importance of indigenous warships in strengthening India's maritime surveillance and anti-submarine warfare capabilities, particularly in the evolving maritime security environment.
He also emphasized the growing capabilities of India's indigenous shipbuilding industry and the Indian Navy's continued commitment to technological advancement, operational preparedness and self-reliance in defence manufacturing.
INS Mangrol derives its name from the coastal town and prominent fishing harbour of Mangrol in Junagadh district of Gujarat. The ship also carries forward the legacy of the erstwhile INS Mangrol (M85), a minesweeper that served the Indian Navy until April 2004, continuing the naval tradition of preserving the names of distinguished warships.
To remind, the first Mahe-class ASW-SWC, INS Mahe, was commissioned in November last year, while the second unit in this class entered service in July this year.

title: Iran Air to launch direct flight btw Zahedan, Quetta
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 14 (MNA) – Iran’s National Flag Carrier [Iran Air] has announced that it will launch a direct flight between Iran’s Zahedan and Pakistan’s Quetta for the first time.
In continuation of the development of its flight network to the neighboring Pakistan, Iran Air is launching a flight route between Zahedan and Quetta for the first time, the launch of this route brings the airline's total number of active flights to Pakistan to three.
The first flight of the route Zahedan - Quetta, bearing No. 826, will take place at 10:10 a.m. from Zahedan Airport to the destination of Quetta on Wednesday October 14.
Additionally, the return flight for this route will be operated on the same day at 14:25 from Quetta to the destination of Zahedan, bearing Flight No. 827.
According to the scheduled program, flights on Zahedan-Quetta route will be operated weekly on Wednesdays.

title: Q3: Dangote Refinery Posts $22.5bn Revenue, Records $4.7bn Profit
body: Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals has recorded a remarkable turnaround in its financial performance, posting $22.5 billion in revenue and $4.7 billion in net profit for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, compared with a loss of $117.2 million in the corresponding period of 2025. The development comes as the African industrial giant consolidates its transition into a major profit-generating industrial enterprise. The unaudited financial results, released in Lagos on Tuesday, reveal that revenue surged by 144 per cent from $9.2 billion in the first nine months of 2025, while earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) jumped nearly ninefold to $5.5 billion, reflecting higher refining throughput, improved operational reliability and stronger refining margins. The performance represents a significant financial milestone for the 700,000 barrels per day refinery, which is currently undertaking a landmark Initial Public Offering (IPO) aimed at broadening African ownership of the industrial complex. According to the results, net income rose to $4.73 billion from a loss of $117.2 million a year earlier, while EBITDA margin expanded to 24.56 per cent from 6.83 per cent, reflecting a marked improvement in the economics of its refining operations. Operating cash flow also increased more than tenfold to $3.68 billion, compared with $364.7 million in the corresponding period of 2025, demonstrating the refinery’s growing capacity to generate cash from its core business. The company’s cash balances climbed to $6.69 billion from $809.5 million, while its balance sheet moved from a net debt position of $1.73 billion in September 2025 to net cash of $650.8 million by September 2026. The transition to a net cash position indicates that the refinery’s cash holdings now exceed its reported debt obligations on a net basis, a development that strengthens its financial flexibility as it pursues further expansion. Revenue increased from $13.91 billion at the end of June to $22.48 billion by September, implying third-quarter revenue of approximately $8.57 billion. Similarly, EBITDA rose from $2.60 billion in the first half of the year to $5.52 billion at the end of September, indicating that the refinery generated approximately $2.92 billion in EBITDA during the third quarter alone. Net profit also increased from $1.82 billion at the half-year mark to $4.73 billion by September, representing an additional $2.90 billion in the three months to September. Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals, David Bird, attributed the strong results to higher throughput, greater operational stability and improved refining margins. “Our third-quarter performance demonstrates the successful transition from commissioning and ramp-up activities to sustainable commercial operations,” Bird said. “Revenue increased to US$22.5 billion from US$9.2 billion in the corresponding period of 2025, while EBITDA rose to US$5.5 billion from US$627.6 million, reflecting higher throughput, improved operational reliability and stronger gross refining margins.” Bird said the results validated the strength of the refinery’s integrated business model and provided a solid foundation for the company’s next phase of growth. “These results reflect the strength of our integrated business model and provide a solid foundation as we progress through our IPO and execute our Vision 2030 growth strategy,” he stated. “With our expansion programme already underway, we remain focused on increasing refining capacity and broadening our product portfolio. We will continue to strengthen our distribution network across Africa and support energy security across the continent, while creating long-term value for stakeholders.” The financial performance comes at a defining moment for Dangote Petroleum Refinery, whose IPO is seeking to bring a broader cross-section of Africans into the ownership of one of the continent’s most significant industrial investments. The company recently secured approval from the Securities and Exchange Commission to extend the closing date of the offer from October 13 to October 27, 2026, to accommodate growing investor interest across Africa and facilitate wider cross-border participation. The IPO comprises 4.1 billion ordinary shares at ₦525 per share, representing an offering valued at approximately ₦2.15 trillion. President/Chief Executive of Dangote Industries Limited, Aliko Dangote, had disclosed that subscriptions to the offer had already exceeded the company’s original fundraising target, stressing that the overriding objective was to enable more Africans to participate in the refinery’s ownership rather than merely raise additional capital. Located in the Lekki Free Zone, Lagos, Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals operates an integrated refining and petrochemical complex with a crude distillation capacity of 700,000 barrels per day. The facility, built to international environmental, safety and product quality standards, is among the world’s most modern large-scale refining complexes and represents a major investment in Africa’s energy and industrial infrastructure The post Q3: Dangote Refinery Posts $22.5bn Revenue, Records $4.7bn Profit appeared first on Channels Television .

title: ‘Blatant Disrespect Toward America’: Zelensky Slams Russia’s Strike on Ukraine’s Energy Sector
body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky urged US President Donald Trump to impose strong sanctions on Russia after a massive overnight Russian attack on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure left at least 600,000 people without electricity.
In a Telegram post on Wednesday, Oct. 14, Zelensky said Russia had launched 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions against energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv region, and Kharkiv.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
He described the ballistic strike on Ukraine’s energy sector as deliberate and said its scale demonstrated Russia’s disregard for Washington’s calls for a ceasefire.
“Russia does not view the US President’s statements as strong,” Zelensky said, calling on the US and others to respond firmly to Moscow’s actions.
He urged Trump to impose “STRONG sanctions” on Russia, referring to legislation introduced by US Senator Lindsey Graham that Zelensky said provided the necessary tools to increase pressure on Moscow. He also called for additional interceptor missiles for Ukraine’s Patriot air defense systems.
“Peace can only be achieved through strength,” Zelensky said, invoking a principle associated with former US President Ronald Reagan.
The president added that further power outages were possible as Ukrainian crews worked to repair the damage. According to him, the attack damaged facilities and equipment at 26 sites in Ukraine’s electric power system and four facilities in the oil and gas sector. He also reported casualties and injuries but did not provide figures.
According to Ukraine’s Air Force , Russia began the combined attack at 6 p.m. on Tuesday, Oct. 13, launching 167 aerial weapons, including 39 missiles and 128 attack drones of various types.
The missiles included Iskander-M, North Korean KN-23, S-400, Zircon, and Onyx types. The drones included Shahed-type weapons, among them 77 jet-powered drones, as well as Banderol, Dan-T, Gerbera, Italmas, and Parodiya-type drones.
Ukraine’s Air Force said aviation, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare systems, unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups were involved in repelling the attack.
As of 9 a.m. on Wednesday, Oct. 14, Ukrainian air defenses had shot down or suppressed 119 targets: four missiles and 115 drones. The intercepted drones included 59 jet-powered ones.
The Air Force reported missile and drone impacts at 22 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at eight locations. Some Russian missiles failed to reach their intended targets.
Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv’s CHP-4 power plant and a nine-story residential building late on Tuesday, Oct. 13, killing at least three people and injuring 21, including an eight-year-old child, Ukrainian officials reported.
The attack hit the capital at around 10:40 p.m., sparking fires across several districts. In the Desnianskyi district, a fire spread across apartments on the first through eighth floors before firefighters extinguished it.
Rescuers recovered two bodies from the building and evacuated 16 residents, while other strikes caused fires and casualties in the Holosiivskyi, Dniprovskyi, Darnytskyi, and Shevchenkivskyi districts.
Zelensky said CHP-4 was a main target and that Ukraine had received no advance warning from Western partners about the incoming ballistic missiles for the second consecutive night.
The Ukrainian Air Force confirmed that no warning had come through the usual channels, while presidential adviser Dmytro Lytvyn said military and intelligence services were investigating the missing notifications.
Notably, President Donald Trump said Washington continues to share intelligence with Ukraine , rejecting suggestions that the US had halted cooperation.
However, his administration has yet to explain why Ukraine received no early missile warnings for two consecutive nights.
Asked by Fox News correspondent whether the US had stopped sharing intelligence with Kyiv, newly appointed White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said Tuesday, Oct. 13: “I’ll have to get back to you on that.”
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: GMTF takes fight against crippling treatment costs to Volta Region
body: The Ghana Medical Trust Fund (GMTF) has taken its nationwide public education campaign to the Volta Region, calling for stronger collaboration to ensure that financial hardship does not prevent patients with chronic diseases from accessing life-saving treatment. At a town hall meeting in Ho, the Fund brought together traditional authorities, faith-based organisations, health professionals, students and community members to explain its mandate, the support available to eligible patients and how to access assistance. The engagement focused on helping people living with cancer and other chronic non-communicable diseases understand the support available to ease the financial burden of treatment. The Chancellor of the University of Health and Allied Sciences (UHAS), Professor Lydia Aziator, described the Fund as a significant intervention for patients and families struggling with the high cost of managing chronic illnesses. She said treatment costs could discourage patients from seeking timely medical attention, making the Fund’s support particularly important for households in need. Prof. Aziator called for greater awareness of early detection, particularly for breast cancer, and urged women to seek medical attention promptly when they noticed unusual symptoms. She also encouraged women diagnosed with cancer to seek treatment without allowing stigma, fear or public perception to discourage them. The Volta Regional Minister, James Gunu, said the sensitisation exercise offered an opportunity to educate residents about the Fund’s purpose and how eligible patients could benefit. He said the initiative would help households overwhelmed by the cost of treating chronic diseases and improve access to quality healthcare. Mr Gunu noted that the region’s diverse healthcare needs required coordinated action by government institutions, health professionals and community stakeholders. He called on Metropolitan, Municipal and District Chief Executives (MMDCEs), civil society organisations and the media to spread the message across the region. He also urged healthcare professionals to help patients understand and navigate the procedures for accessing support. The minister emphasised the need for transparency and accountability in managing the Fund, saying financial openness was essential to sustaining public confidence. He assured the delegation of the Volta Regional Coordinating Council’s support for the public education campaign. The Administrator of the GMTF, Adjoa Obuobia Darko-Opoku, said the visit aimed to bring the Fund closer to communities and provide accurate information about its mandate and access procedures. She explained that the Fund was established to support households facing financial difficulties in caring for relatives with chronic non-communicable diseases. However, she cautioned that financial assistance must be backed by adequately equipped healthcare facilities. “Even if people receive financial support, it will come to nothing if the health facilities do not have the needed equipment and infrastructure,” she said. Ms Darko-Opoku stressed the need to strengthen the capacity of the Ho Teaching Hospital and UHAS to support specialised healthcare delivery in the region. She said access to treatment depended on both patients’ ability to afford care and the availability of facilities and equipment to provide the required services. She appealed to political leaders, health professionals and other stakeholders to work with the Fund to identify and reach families in need of assistance. The Volta Region engagement forms part of the GMTF’s nationwide campaign to raise awareness of specialised healthcare support, strengthen partnerships and improve access to treatment for people living with chronic non-communicable diseases.

title: Nearly 200 Ukrainian drones flew toward Moscow, while a Sberbank data center came under attack in Russia’s Saratov region
body: A total of 493 Ukrainian drones flew toward the Moscow region from the evening of October 13 through the morning of October 14, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said. Air defense forces intercepted most of the drones at distant approaches, Sobyanin said, and destroyed 180 more as they neared Moscow. No damage or casualties were reported. Ukrainian Telegram channels have published footage purportedly filmed in the Moscow region showing a “Pantsir” air defense system firing at targets directly from a highway. Drones also struck the Saratov region. Saratov Governor Roman Busargin said several residential buildings in Balakovo were damaged and that, according to preliminary information, one person was killed. He later clarified that “all infrastructure facilities in Balakovo are operating normally.” Monitoring Telegram channels claim the strikes in the Saratov region hit the MegaCOD data center belonging to Sberbank. Construction of the data center in Balakovo began in 2021, and Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Chernyshenko promised it would become the largest in Russia. The independent Russian investigative outlet Agentstvo examined photos from the Telegram channels and confirmed they show a damaged Sberbank data center. Fire Point, a Ukrainian manufacturer of drones and missiles, also reported the strike on the Sberbank data center. The Telegram channel Exilenova+ also confirmed a strike on the industrial zone of the “MZ Balakovo” metallurgical plant, which produces steel and rolled metal products. title: Lagos orders registration of pregnant women turned away at hospital
body: …Management denies 45-patient cap as staff blame workforce shortage By Florencemary Nwabueze LAGOS — More than 30 pregnant women seeking antenatal care at the Mother and Child Hospital, Ogombo Road, Lekki, were left stranded on Tuesday over an alleged policy limiting registrations to 45 patients, prompting the Lagos State Commissioner for Health, Professor Akin Abayomi, to intervene and order the registration of all affected women. The women, some of whom said they had visited the government-owned facility several times without success, expressed frustration after arriving early in the morning only to be told that the registration quota had been exhausted. Some hospital administrative staff reportedly told the women that the practice had been in place for more than a year, explaining that even if 100 pregnant women arrived as early as 6 a.m., only 45 would be attended to while the others would be turned away. The situation triggered protests, with some of the women leaving the hospital in frustration while others remained, pleading to be registered. One of the pregnant women said, “This is my third time coming here, and they will tell me that the number has reached 45 and I should go home.” Another patient said she had arrived early as instructed but was still turned away. “I am tired of coming here. They ask me to come early. I got here at 6:40 a.m., and they are telling me the number is finished,” she said. The incident attracted the attention of Abayomi, who reportedly contacted the hospital’s Managing Director, Dr Femi Aletan, to address the complaints. Aletan apologised and summoned the hospital management to resolve the situation. Following a meeting with the affected women, the management apologised for the incident and said it was unaware of any policy restricting antenatal registration to 45 patients per week. A hospital official told the women: “We are very sorry for what happened here today. “We only ask our women to come early so we can finish early. We didn’t say we will only attend to 45 people. Everyone here today will be registered.” Nurses were subsequently directed to register all the women, although the process continued into the afternoon, with some patients still waiting as of 4 p.m. Workforce Shortage Blamed A doctor at the hospital, identified as Dr Sariki, attributed the situation to a shortage of healthcare workers, saying the limited workforce was placing considerable pressure on available staff. “Our biggest problem is workforce. I have to come all the way from the mainland every day. There are no healthcare workers living on the island. Accommodation is very expensive. If the government can provide us with accommodation within the hospital, maybe build housing for us, it will ease the stress. We are only a few workers here,” he said. The doctor also disclosed that he had recently declined a job offer from Saudi Arabia, expressing hope that he would not regret the decision. He called for reforms in medical education to increase the number of healthcare professionals trained in Nigeria. “The cut-off mark to admit students to study medicine in the university is too much. Schools need to create room to train more healthcare workers,” he said. A nurse who exchanged words with the pregnant women defended the reported limit, citing the hospital’s staffing capacity. “Do you know our workforce capacity? Do you know our strength? We take 45 because that is what we can attend to,” the nurse said. Hospital MD Cites Japa Syndrome The hospital’s Managing Director, Aletan, also blamed the shortage of healthcare workers on the migration of Nigerian medical professionals to other countries, saying the trend was affecting service delivery. “Our biggest problem is the mass exodus of healthcare workers from Nigeria to other countries. We have only a few healthcare workers left in Nigeria. It is seriously affecting our working system,” he said. He attributed the migration partly to better salaries and employment benefits offered abroad. “The salary they are being offered outside the country and the workers’ benefits are pushing them out. If the government can make the same offer here, I believe they will stay,” Aletan added. The Mother and Child Hospital, located along Ogombo Road in Lekki, was established by the Lagos State Government to provide maternal and infant healthcare services, including specialist gynaecological care and emergency services. The facility has attracted patients seeking maternal healthcare because of its facilities and range of services. Tuesday’s incident, however, highlighted concerns over access to antenatal care, communication between hospital staff and patients, and the capacity of healthcare facilities to manage demand amid reported staffing shortages. Although the hospital management directed that all the affected women be registered, the episode raised questions about how antenatal services are scheduled and whether staffing constraints are preventing pregnant women from accessing timely care. The post Lagos orders registration of pregnant women turned away at hospital appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Russia-linked bot networks kept their weekly rhythm after drone strikes on three Yandex data centers—disinformation monitor LetsData
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); The claim that strikes on Russian tech giant Yandex thinned out social media bots finds no support in the networks tracked by Ukrainian disinformation-monitoring company LetsData, co-founder Ksenia Iliuk told Euromaidan Press on 13 October. She cautioned that the strikes may still have affected networks outside the company’s view. At the Warsaw Security Forum, Lithuania’s prime minister suggested allies should ask Ukraine to strike more Russian data centers because that might help protect European elections from foreign interference. Bot networks are one tool of that interference, so whether the strikes mute them carries weight well beyond Ukraine. No drop in the networks LetsData tracks Drones hit Yandex data centers in Sasovo and Vladimir between 8 and 11 October. Ukrainian drone maker Fire Point said its FP-1 drones struck Yandex’s Kaluga site in between. On 12 October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the Warsaw Security Forum that once Ukraine’s response reached Yandex, social media had fewer bots. Explore further More than 500 drones by Moscow’s count: Kh-101 fuel plant, second Yandex data center, and a far-north refinery hit LetsData checked X and Facebook, where bot networks usually stand out clearly, Iliuk said. Its analysts looked at networks attributed to Russia’s influence ecosystem. Among them are groups of X accounts spreading domains from what she called a new wave of Doppelgänger , a Russian campaign that clones real news sites. Those networks look unaffected, Iliuk said. None of them has stopped posting or broken its usual rhythm, she added. Some are slightly less active, but LetsData’s analysts say that is typical for them. The networks run on a weekly cycle, and the check fell in the part of the week when they post less. A network that jumped from Germany to Ukraine LetsData worked with two samples. One covers accounts that systematically target Ukraine, Moldova, and Armenia. The other covers bot networks the company has followed for some time that keep changing their target audience, so they have no fixed country. Explore further Ukrainian drones hit three of Russian tech giant Yandex’s data centers in four days. Ukraine’s president says the bots thinned out too About two weeks ago, one network from that second sample wrote about elections in Germany and spread fake Die Welt sites, she said. It now posts about mobilization in Ukraine and shares a fake site of Ukrinform, Ukraine’s state news agency. What the check can’t see The company can compare only within networks whose usual behavior it knows, Iliuk said. Checking the whole internet is impossible because the scale is colossal, she said. A Cloudflare chart that circulated as evidence counted automated web requests from Yandex’s network, including its search crawlers, not social media posts, Cybernews reported . So the networks LetsData follows show no impact, Iliuk said. That does not mean the strikes had no effect at all, she noted. They may have shown up in networks the company isn’t tracking now. LetsData will keep watching and report other signals if they appear. title: Argentina allows JetSmart Chile to operate domestic flights
body:
Argentina has authorized JetSmart Airlines SpA, the Chilean airline of the JetSmart group, to operate domestic passenger and cargo flights in the country under ninth-freedom traffic rights.
The authorization was granted by Argentina's Subsecretaría de Transporte Aéreo through Disposición 27/2026, dated October 7 and published in the country's official gazette on October 14.
The measure grants JetSmart Chile traffic rights ranging from the third through the ninth freedoms of the air for scheduled passenger and cargo services.
Ninth-freedom rights, also known as stand-alone cabotage, allow a foreign airline to carry passengers between two points within another country without the flight being connected to a service originating or terminating in the carrier's home country.
Follow Air Data News: WhatsApp | Instagram | LinkedIn | Twitter | Facebook
This means JetSmart Chile could, for example, operate a Buenos Aires-Córdoba flight independently, rather than as an extension of a service from Santiago.
The authorization is unusual in JetSmart's case because the airline already operates domestic services through JetSmart Airlines S.A., its locally registered Argentine subsidiary.
The new approval potentially gives the group greater flexibility to deploy aircraft from its Chilean operation on domestic Argentine routes. However, JetSmart has not announced routes or a date for beginning services under the new authorization.
The regulatory approval alone does not mean that Chilean-registered aircraft will immediately replace or supplement aircraft operated by the Argentine subsidiary.
JetSmart has been expanding rapidly in Argentina. The airline carried 442,347 domestic passengers in September and accounted for around 31% of the country's domestic market.
The company previously announced plans to increase the number of aircraft based in Argentina to 23 by the 2027 summer season.
The approval comes amid problems at rival low-cost carrier Flybondi, which has sharply reduced the supply of domestic flights in Argentina and has not operated commercial services since August.
Flybondi filed for creditor protection earlier this month after returning most of its aircraft to lessors. Court documents subsequently revealed liabilities of ARS 609.6 billion (US$396 million), compared with assets of ARS 176.1 billion (US$114 million).
The carrier's retreat has opened additional space in a domestic market dominated by Aerolíneas Argentinas and increasingly contested by JetSmart.
Argentina has gradually expanded traffic rights for foreign airlines as part of changes to its commercial aviation regulatory framework.
LATAM Airlines Group previously received authorization covering traffic rights through the ninth freedom, allowing its foreign operators to perform domestic services in Argentina. Ethiopian Airlines has also received ninth-freedom authorization for cargo operations.
The distinction between eighth- and ninth-freedom rights is significant. Eighth-freedom cabotage allows a foreign airline to carry domestic traffic as part of an international service, while ninth freedom permits a completely independent domestic operation.

title: African Lion 2027: US and Morocco commence planning
body: U.S. Army Southern European Task Force, Africa (SETAF-AF) and the Royal Moroccan Armed Forces (Forces Armées Royales, or FAR) opened planning for African Lion 2027 in Agadir, Morocco, with a five-day event that ran from 21 to 25 September 2026. African Lion is the largest multinational military exercise on the African continent. Morocco and the United States have run it together since 2004, and the 2027 edition will coincide with the 250th anniversary of Morocco’s recognition of the United States in 1777. Planners met at the FAR Southern Zone headquarters to set goals, fix timelines and name possible training sites. Smaller working groups used space at the joint task force headquarters to work through organization and logistics. U.S. Army Colonel Benjamin Roark, director of training and exercises for the SETAF-AF G7 (the staff section that runs training), described the week as a starting point. “This initial planning event is where we begin laying the groundwork for African Lion 2027,” Colonel Roark said. Planners expect more than 45 nations across land, sea, air, space, cyber and intelligence domains. U.S. Africa Command (AFRICOM) put the 2026 edition at more than 5,600 personnel from over 40 nations, spread across Morocco, Ghana, Senegal and Tunisia. The 2025 edition drew about 10,000 troops. No personnel total has been published for 2027. The planning sequence, known as the glide path, includes a main planning event in December 2026 and a final event in February 2027. “African Lion remains focussed on building combined joint force readiness. The exercise enables us to work with our multinational partners to ensure that, when asked, we are able to deploy forward and operate as a multinational force,” US Army Lieutenant Colonel Corbett Baxter, branch chief and lead planner for African Lion, SETAF-AF G7, is reported as saying. The cycle follows the pattern of the last edition. For African Lion 2025 , planners held an initial event in Agadir in September 2024 and a main event there on 18 to 22 November 2024, and they have said preparation needs to start about two years ahead. The 2027 initial event falls about seven months before the planned start, a similar gap. The start date for execution is unsettled. The U.S. Army account of the Agadir event gives 19 April 2027. Moroccan press reports citing the FAR give 25 April to 7 May 2027, with activity in Agadir, Tan-Tan, Guelmim, Benguerir, Kenitra and Dakhla. This report checked both on 9 October 2026 and found no source that reconciles them. The gap could reflect separate phases, but no source says so. What the planners are weighing Planners are considering combined-arms maneuvers, in which infantry, armor, artillery and aviation operate together, along with live-fire events and maritime and air operations. A command field exercise (CFX), in which headquarters staffs direct units in the field, is the centerpiece. Other proposals include special operations training at Cap Draa and possible training against weapons of mass destruction, meaning chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear threats, in Agadir. Humanitarian civic assistance projects are also on the list. SETAF-AF says all of these remain under review while teams refine concepts of operations, logistics and site surveys. The CFX is built to bring vendors and industry partners directly into training, so new technology is tested alongside military units in realistic scenarios. U.S. Army Lieutenant Colonel Corbett Baxter, branch chief and lead planner for African Lion at the SETAF-AF G7, tied the exercise to a practical goal. “African Lion remains focused on building combined joint force readiness,” Lieutenant Colonel Baxter said. Mixing commercial equipment with multinational units carries a cost. Vendors need controlled conditions and safe ranges, while units need their own training objectives met. Planners will have to balance the two. The Army says the exercise offers venues for safe industry participation; how that works at the scale of 45 nations is not yet public. An academic program is also under review. Courses cover joint operations planning, intelligence operations, cybersecurity, electronic warfare and noncommissioned officer development. These sessions target staff skills and doctrine rather than hardware. Cyber may move into the field Cyber training could shift from the classroom to the exercise itself. At a working group in Bedford, Massachusetts, from 27 to 31 July 2026, Moroccan representatives asked U.S. specialists whether National Guard exercises such as Cyber Shield and Wolverine could validate the cyber protection teams the FAR is forming. The U.S. Army published its account on 29 September 2026. Moroccan personnel had already observed Utah cyber teams at Wolverine in April. U.S. Air Force Captain Robert Matheny, who directs the Utah National Guard’s state partnership program, said the Moroccan side wants cyber activity inside African Lion and not only in training. He said the Utah Guard plans cyber-focused expert exchanges in next year’s program and expects to plan a cyberattack scenario for future editions. Utah and Morocco have worked together through the U.S. State Partnership Program since 2003. This is a proposal, not a scheduled event. The Army has not announced that a cyberattack scenario will run in the 2027 field phase. Morocco World News also reported that, before the 2026 field phase, U.S. and Moroccan forces completed a first test linking Moroccan equipment to the U.S. Link 16 network, a secure tactical data link that shares position and track data between aircraft, ships and ground units. This report could not confirm that test from a primary source. What it means For the FAR, the cyber requests and the industry track point the same way: more testing of new capability under realistic conditions, with U.S. help. For the United States, the exercise stays a place to trial technology and practice running a multinational headquarters on partner territory. Whether cyber remains a classroom subject or becomes a live scenario depends on decisions not yet made. The same goes for how far industry testing reaches into the field phase. The next marker is the main planning event in December 2026, which should settle the start date, the site list and how much of the industry and cyber agenda becomes a plan. Alongside field training, African Lion planners are developing an academic programme. Courses under review include joint operations planning, intelligence operations, cybersecurity, electronic warfare and non-commissioned officer development. These sessions intend to build doctrinal knowledge and staff skills in support of operational objectives. The 250th anniversary commemoration marks Morocco’s recognition of the US as a nation and, according to Beagle, ushers in a new era of partnership, readiness and innovation, setting the stage for emerging technologies and multinational co-operation across the African theatre. US-Moroccan relations are being highlighted as well at the 2026 Marrakech Airshow (MAS) at the Marrakech Royal Moroccan Air Force Base taking place from 7 to 10 October. The highlight of the American Airpower portion will be a dynamic F-35A Lightning II stealth fighter flyby, demonstrating the unmatched, integrated capabilities of the US–Moroccan security partnership in North Africa, Africom said.

title: How to be more ambitious when using AI
body:
I work on Claude. It's an interesting experience: Every day I learn about yet another feat accomplished with or by Claude that I hadn't considered, didn't think possible, or simply lacked the curiosity and time to try. This month, it may have helped discover a new planet , I've seen the first AI music video that I really like , and we are discussing a new era of math .
Model capabilities don't grow uniformly. Models are, as Terence Tao puts it, "astounding in some directions, while inadequate in others". Some people manage to pilot the astounding capabilities and seem to be flying - it's addicting to watch people reach incredible heights with the products I've built. Many others are still struggling to get their new wings to work, wondering what they're good for beyond asking "What is the capital of France" or "Can you make this email sound less angry".
I frequently proclaim (together with other people working on AI) that we ought to be more ambitious when using it. It's become a rallying cry. Whenever we see something impressive, we repost and write "we're not ambitious enough". I understand how tricky it is to follow that advice, so here's a tutorial on being more ambitious.
I think of ambition in four types: Speed, Altitude, Depth, and Range.
I primarily use Claude (duh) but my advice is not model-specific.
We often flippantly call this "letting the model operate at a higher abstraction". When you give the model a task, it's executing your best guess at how to get the outcome you want. To be more ambitious in altitude, ask yourself - what do you want to happen next? What's the goal beyond the goal? At the beginning of last year, I still asked Claude to fix individual crashes for me. Eventually I asked Claude to simply keep our apps crash-free.
Let's consider an everyday (dare I say mundane?) office task. You're at Acme Inc, an imagined company, where you need to put together a deck for the quarterly business review (QBR). Given a bunch of data, Claude will happily make you some slides. Maybe you even have a template and it just needs to fill it in. That's hardly comparable to finding a new planet, so let's look at some concrete steps to make our approach more ambitious. We'll start basic and get a little bit more ambitious with each step:
The altitude approach works best if you really are after some ultimate outcome; it works less well for creative endeavors. A good tell-tale sign that ambition in altitude is a good idea is if you're going to have meetings to discuss whatever you're working on. There are currently limits ("Claude, go make money" doesn't seem to work for most businesses by itself in 2026), but I generally see that models seem to be able to operate at higher levels of abstraction the more capable they become.
Altitude is also where people find durable workflows that take the human out of the loop, making it less necessary for you to constantly update the model with task after task. Doing this well often involves changing your workflow - in order to let Claude make sure our app is crash-free, I first had to make sure it can easily fetch crash reports, understand which app version maps to what git commit, and give it access to Windows, macOS, and Linux computers so it can actually independently reproduce and verify fixes.
Sometimes, you just want a task executed really well. Being ambitious in depth means pushing the model to use the tools, techniques, media, and knowledge employed by the best professionals in the field - and to keep pushing until even those people might learn something new from your work.
Let's continue with our Acme Inc example of a quarterly business review deck. Assume for a second that Acme Inc struggles with some user churn (customer loss over time). I've found a mix of the following techniques useful:
In short, being ambitious in range means that we consider our work from the perspective of different fields - more fields than would have been economical in the past. This isn't a particularly unique insight, every single heist movie spends the first 30 minutes assembling a diverse cast of characters and talents. As AI products make it easier and easier to run multi-agent systems (with multiple threads, orchestrators, or simply subagents), I've seen really interesting results by imploring Claude to bring in additional fields.
Putting this into practice isn't easy; it requires you to be creative. Until I saw my colleague Alex Albert use Blender to render interior designs, I never considered using Claude for 3D environments for my homepage - even though I've previously made video games! However, this is easily where I see the most magic happen.
So, how do we do this? I use the following techniques:
All the ways in which I describe ambition require the model to have a computer with the ability to install software and access to all kinds of relevant data (either using MCP connectors or other means). Plenty of tools make this possible and I recommend that you use one.
That's my concrete advice for how to be more ambitious. If you're willing to stick around for a minute, I'd like to tell you why I think this is even necessary in the first place.
We humans have always been held back by what we believe possible - and what's worse, we usually trust ourselves only in very narrow disciplines. Michelangelo famously didn't want to paint the Sistine Chapel - you see, he was a sculptor, not a painter.
While researching the problem of ambition, I learned that psychology has a name for this: self-efficacy . In short, people with high self-efficacy believe in their own abilities more, and in turn actually accomplish more. There's evidence that self-efficacy can be hacked: Locke and Latham pored over 35 years of goal-setting research to confidently proclaim that humans who are given specific hard goals perform better than those who are simply told to try their best . Stripe founder Patrick Collison maintains a "Fast" list , chronicling the many things humans have accomplished when given both audacious goals and tight deadlines. Some hacks that are well documented:
Self-efficacy isn't a new problem, but it is a more powerful one now. In a world where our abilities make leaps every couple of weeks, we need techniques that allow us to do things we didn't really consider or believe possible. If you find more techniques that allow you to be more ambitious, please let me know!

Felix Rieseberg I'm an EM at Anthropic, where I've so far led engineering for Claude.ai, Cowork, and Claude Code Desktop. I'm co-maintainer of Electron and various other open source projects. I've previously worked on and for Notion, Stripe, Slack, and Microsoft.
