title: US may halt intel sharing over refinery strikes - Zelenskyy
body:
The administration of U.S. President Donald Trump warned that it could halt intelligence sharing with Ukraine if Ukraine does not stop strikes on Russian oil refineries, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an interview with NPR.

Zelenskyy also rejected Trump’s claim that Ukraine was allegedly responsible for rising diesel fuel prices. He said the increase was due to the war involving Iran.

“Mostly people in the world know why their prices on any kind of energy, including diesel, raised up, why they increased. Because of Hormuz. Yes. Because of blocking the Strait of Hormuz,” Zelenskyy said in the interview.

He said Ukraine strikes Russian energy and logistics facilities in order to weaken the Kremlin’s ability to wage war.

Zelenskyy said Ukraine wants to end the war but will not stop these strikes until Russia stops attacking Ukrainian energy facilities.

title: ‘Napatawad ko na’: Scam victims move on and leave fraud cases hanging
body: Naka-move on na po ako eh. Okay na po, napatawad ko na. (I’ve already moved one. It’s okay, I’ve forgiven them.) It’s a prosecutor’s nightmare to hear those words from a scam victim. Yet that’s exactly the predicament Department of Justice (DOJ) Office of Cybercrime Assistant Director Chris Jark Ace Maño has faced, recalling how complainants would often lose interest just as prosecutors were ready to bring their scammers to court. “If we’re to change one characteristic of Filipinos, it’s the ningas kugon mentality in the sense that when we try to file cases, report cases, we have to see it through,” Maño said at an anti-scam forum hosted by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas on Monday, October 12. He had a rather blunt reaction to those who suddenly had a change of heart. “ Eh paano naman ‘yung [kaso?] Marupok nga (Then what happens now to the [case]? Too softhearted).“ It’s a problem investigators know all too well since pursuing fraud charges needs victims to help establish what happened and, in some cases, testify against the people who scammed them. For instance, National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Financial Intelligence Unit Chief Minerva Sobreviga-Retanal recounted how even successful raids of scam hubs didn’t always end with fraud charges against the perpetrators. Sobreviga-Retanal cited one operation in which authorities shut down suspected scamming activities but ended up prosecuting the operators for qualified trafficking in persons instead. “Technically, we need victims. If it’s a scam, there should be damage caused,” she told Rappler on the sidelines of the event. “When you prosecute, the court would require the damaged party to appear as witnesses.” But persuading victims to come forward is not always easy. Some may be reluctant to disclose that they were deceived, while others do not want to commit to a lengthy investigation and court proceedings. “It’s discouraging when you do the investigations because it’s evidence-based, and some would not like to be involved in that,” Sobreviga-Retanal said. Must Read Scam or legit? Banks launch checker website, Google-backed game to learn That doesn’t even consider the vast majority of victims that never report the crime in the first place. A 2026 survey by the Global Anti-Scam Alliance (GASA) found that 15% of the 1,160 Filipino adults surveyed suffered financial losses from scams, but only 29% of those who lost money reported the incidents to authorities. But Sobreviga-Retanal also warned victims against trying to play detective themselves, as this wastes precious time that authorities could use to trace funds and identify suspects. (READ: A failed scam attempt gave BPI a glimpse into how fraudsters take your money ) “Transfers are made in milliseconds because virtual assets are available, cryptocurrency is availabale, so it’s just a matter of time,” she said. But with scammers becoming more and more sophisticated, experts warn that no one should consider themselves immune, especially younger, tech-savvy Filipinos who may assume that they are less likely to fall victim to fraud. “Before it was the titos, titas, lolos, lolas (uncles, aunts, grandgathers, grandmothers) that were victims. Now, it’s the young,” Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) Executive Director Renato Paraiso said on Monday. “It’s rising — the numbers of victims of the Gen Zs, the Millennials, Gen Alphas. It’s because of overconfidence.” Case in point: even Google Philippines country manager Prep Palacios admitted once losing P90,000 to an online seller who immediately disappeared after receiving her payment. “I’m a tech executive, and I was still fooled,” she told the same forum. – Rappler.com Must Read Stay alert online: Join anti-scam community forum in Laguna

title: ASC extends HIFraser partnership for Collins-class sub support
body:
Australia’s ASC has signed a six-year contract with engineering and manufacturing specialist HIFraser to extend their partnership supporting the Royal Australian Navy’s Collins-class submarine program beyond 40 years.
The nearly $40 million contract covers HIFraser’s continued provision of valves and maintenance services for Australia’s Collins-class submarines. The company has supported ASC and the Royal Australian Navy’s Collins-class submarines since 1992. It will continue delivering high- and low-pressure valves and on-board maintenance services that are critical to helping sustain the operational readiness of the fleet.
ASC Chief Operating Officer – Multi-Class Sustainment Rebecca Brickhill said the agreement recognised the important role trusted Australian suppliers play in sustaining one of the nation’s most important Defence capabilities.
“ASC’s ability to deliver safe, reliable and effective sustainment outcomes for the Collins Class submarine fleet relies on strong partnerships with highly capable Australian suppliers such as HIFraser,” she added.
HIFraser Group Chief Operating Officer Peter Andrews stated the new agreement marked another significant milestone in the company’s long-standing relationship with ASC.
“Operating for more than 40 years, HIFraser has developed a reputation for highly specialised capabilities in advanced manufacturing, engineering and ongoing sustainment services. These skills are critical to supporting Australia’s submarine fleet and position us strongly to meet future defence industry requirements," he noted.
HIFraser is an Australian component manufacturer and an approved subcontractor to Australia’s Collins Class fleet through-life sustainment activities. Established by the Australian Submarine Agency (ASA) in partnership with the US Government, the Defence Industry Vendor Qualification (DIVQ) Program, delivered by ASC, helps Australian industry lift its systems, processes and technical capability to meet US submarine requirements.
HIFraser has been qualified to manufacture and supply specialised valves, fittings and other components for the Virginia-class submarines.
ASC is Australia’s Sovereign Submarine Sustainment Partner and is responsible for ensuring the ongoing availability of the Collins-class submarine fleet through sustainment and Life of Type Extension activities.

title: 'Ostentatious disrespect' — Zelensky says Russia defied Trump's energy ceasefire with latest missile strike
body:
Russia demonstrated its disregard for U.S. President Donald Trump's proposed energy ceasefire by launching drones and missiles against Ukraine's power grid overnight, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 14.
Moscow's forces deployed 39 ballistic missiles and over 120 drones against energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast, and Kharkiv, Zelensky said , calling it "ostentatious disrespect toward the United States."
At least three people were killed, and another 22 were injured as a result of the Russian strike that hit a residential building in the Desnianskyi district and power plants elsewhere in the city, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Russia has ramped up aerial strikes against Ukrainian energy sites as winter nears, despite Trump's unexpected and unilateral announcement on Oct. 11 that both Kyiv and Moscow agreed to halt attacks against each other's energy infrastructure.
Even as Kyiv said it had halted attacks against Russian oil refineries since Trump's ceasefire announcement, Trump declined to blame the Kremlin for breaking the truce when asked by a reporter on Oct. 13.
"The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale," Zelensky noted, adding that at least 600,000 people are without power and reporting damage to 26 power facilities, as well as four oil and gas sites.
"Russia does not consider the American President 's statements strong," the Ukrainian leader added.
The comments come as Washington piles on pressure on Kyiv to halt its aerial campaign against Russian refineries, which he linked to rising global fuel prices — a claim disputed by experts.
The Kyiv Independent has previously learned that the Trump administration threatened senior Ukrainian military and government officials with cutting intelligence sharing and arms sales unless it stopped attacking Russian refineries.
While Ukrainian and U.S. sources told the Kyiv Independent earlier this week that Washington has not yet stopped intelligence support, questions about the early warning provided by partners are mounting as strikes now hit Kyiv even before the alarm sounds.
Presidential Advisor Serhii " Flash " Beskretnov and Serhii Sternenko , an activist and former advisor to ex-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, claimed on Oct. 14 that Elon Musk's SpaceX has limited the speed of Starlink terminals in Ukraine, causing disruption to "a number of critical missions."
"The American President has all the effective and necessary tools to bring peace closer through strength, justice, and pressure on the aggressor," Zelensky noted, urging Washington to impose sanctions on Russia under late Senator Lindsey Graham's sanctions bill and calling for additional supplies of Patriot interceptors.

title: Russian strike on Kyiv kills three, injures over 20; parts of city lose power
body: Russian forces struck Kyiv overnight on October 14, killing three people and injuring 21, according to data from Ukraine’s State Emergency Service. A strike hit a multistory apartment building in Kyiv’s Desnianskyi district late on October 13, sparking a fire. The bodies of two people killed in the blaze were found. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said an 8-year-old child was among those injured. Sixteen people were hospitalized, four of them in serious condition. In Kyiv’s Holosiivskyi district, a strike on a non-residential building killed one person and injured another, the State Emergency Service said. Klitschko also said a massive ballistic missile strike had hit energy facilities in Kyiv and the Kyiv region, triggering power outages in the capital. Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine’s Western partners again failed to warn it that Russia would launch another ballistic missile strike on Kyiv on the evening of October 13. He said the main target was the city’s energy infrastructure, specifically the CHPP-4 power plant, one of Kyiv’s main energy facilities. Russia’s Defense Ministry said on the morning of October 14 that the Russian Armed Forces had carried out a massive strike on communications and energy infrastructure facilities in Kyiv, the Kyiv region, and the Kharkiv region, which it said served the military-industrial complex and the Ukrainian Armed Forces. Donald Trump announced on October 11 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to a ceasefire in the energy sector. Volodymyr Zelensky said the Ukrainian Armed Forces had “received all the relevant orders” in connection with this. The Kremlin said on October 13 that contacts on the energy ceasefire were continuing, but there had been no changes so far. title: Ukraine downs four ballistic missiles, 115 drones in massive Russian overnight attack
body:
According to Ukrinform, the Ukrainian Air Force reported this on Telegram .
Starting at 18:00 on Tuesday, October 13, Russia launched a massive combined attack on Ukraine using attack drones and 39 missiles of various types following ballistic trajectories toward their targets.
The main targets were Kyiv, Kyiv region and Kharkiv region.
The attack was notable for the simultaneous use of different types of aerial weapons launched from multiple directions, as well as the large number of ballistic missiles aimed at energy facilities.
In total, the Air Force’s radio-technical troops detected 167 aerial attack assets: 39 missiles and 128 drones of various types:
39 Iskander-M/KN-23/S-400/Zircon/Oniks anti-ship missiles launched from Russia’s Kursk, Bryansk, Voronezh and Rostov regions;
128 attack drones, including Shahed drones (77 of them jet-powered), Banderol/Dan-T, Gerbera and Italmas drones, as well as Parodiya decoy drones. They were launched from the directions of Millerovo, Oryol, temporarily occupied Donetsk, Hvardiiske in temporarily occupied Crimea, and the Sea of Azov.
The aerial attack was repelled by aircraft, surface-to-air missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 9:00 on Wednesday, October 14, air defense had shot down or suppressed 119 targets:
Four Iskander-M/KN-23/S-400/Zircon/Oniks ballistic missiles;
115 drones of various types, including 59 jet-powered drones, accounting for 90% of all attack drones deployed.
Preliminary reports indicate that missile and attack drone strikes were recorded at 22 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at eight locations as of 9:00. Some of the Russian missiles failed to reach their targets.
As Ukrinform reported, four people were killed in a combined Russian attack on Kyiv.

title: Ukraine once again receives no intelligence warning from US overnight — Zelensky
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Ukraine once again received no intelligence warning from its Western partners last night, Vladimir Zelensky said.
"There was no warning from our partners about a ballistic missile launch. This is the second time Ukraine has not received a warning," he wrote on Telegram.
The US warned Ukraine that it could suspend intelligence sharing, Zelensky said in an interview with NPR. According to him, Ukrainian generals reported that they had been informed of such a possibility at the military level.
Politico reported on October 13 that US President Donald Trump could cut off US intelligence support for Kiev or pressure Elon Musk to disable SpaceX’s Starlink internet service, on which Ukraine’s military heavily relies. Zelensky said the same day that the US had not warned Ukraine about Russian missile launches the previous night.

title: 600,000 without power in Ukraine as Russia launches aerial attack, Zelenskyy says
body:
The outages could become more widespread, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
LONDON -- At least 600,000 people were without power early Wednesday in Ukraine, after Russia launched an aerial attack that struck energy infrastructure, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
"A targeted Russian ballistic missile strike specifically against energy infrastructure -- the very infrastructure covered by the ceasefire announced by the American President," the Ukrainian president said on social media.
President Donald Trump said on Sunday that both sides had agreed to an "energy ceasefire."
The outages on Wednesday may become more widespread, the president said, as there is "significant" damage to at least 26 power facilities and four others in the gas and oil sector.
The attack included some 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones, officials said, with many targeted Kyiv and its surrounding area.
Russia's Ministry of Defense said in it carried out a "massive strike by ground-launched high-precision weapons and long-range drones against communication and energy infrastructure facilities" in Kyiv and Kharkiv.
Katarina Mathernova, the European Union's ambassador to Ukraine, said more than a dozen explosions were heard before dawn in the Kyiv.
"A nine-storey apartment building was hit in the capital. Fire spread through people’s homes," Mathernova said early on Wednesday. "Rescuers helped residents down ladders while others stood outside, watching their building burn."
Mathernova and Ukrainian officials said an early warning system, which detects aerial attacks and allows for better defense, appeared to not have worked for a second night in a row.
"That missing warning means missing time," Mathernova said. "Time to wake a child. To get downstairs. To reach a shelter."
Kyiv's mayor, Vitali Klitschko, described the overnight strike on Kyiv as "massive," saying at least one person had been killed in the capital.
Ukrainian also struck Russian military overnight, according to the Ukrainian General Staff, which said it targeted sites that Russia was known to use to launch drones.
"In the area of Donetsk, a site used by the enemy for the storage, preparation and launch of attack UAVs was hit," Ukraine said . "Systematic strikes against such sites are aimed at reducing the russian aggressor’s ability to strike civilian infrastructure across Ukraine."

title: Russian forces strike ATM Ukrsibbank data center used by Ukrainian military in Kiev
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Russian forces have struck the ATM Ukrsibbank data center in Kiev, which was facilitating Internet traffic exchange for gathering intelligence about the Russian army, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"The strike hit in Kiev <…>: the ATM Ukrsibbank data center, which was facilitating the exchange of Internet traffic to gather intelligence about the Russian Armed Forces," the ministry said in a statement.

title: ‘It’s regressive’ – IMF warns Nigeria against restoring petrol subsidy
body: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has advised Nigeria against restoring broad petrol subsidies, recommending targeted financial assistance and social protection programmes to cushion vulnerable households against rising energy costs. The fund said blanket fuel subsidies were fiscally expensive, disproportionately benefited higher-income consumers and could worsen pressure on public finances amid rising borrowing costs. Rodrigo Valdés, director of the IMF’s Fiscal Affairs Department, gave the advice during a press briefing on the fund’s Fiscal Monitor at the 2026 annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok, Thailand, on Wednesday. Valdés was responding to a question on the impact of allowing energy prices to reflect scarcity, particularly in Nigeria, where rising petrol prices could increase transportation costs, fuel inflation and deepen poverty amid calls for the restoration of petrol subsidies ahead of the 2027 general elections. “Protecting people is not the same as protecting the price of fuels,” Valdés said. He said fuel subsidies and other measures preventing energy prices from adjusting fully to supply shocks had cost countries between one and 1.5 per cent of gross domestic product in 2026. “It’s first fiscally very costly, and second, if you look at the pattern of consumption, it’s easy to see that that subsidy is readily regressive in many places,” he said. The IMF official urged governments to use social safety nets and household data to identify people who needed assistance rather than subsidise fuel prices across the board. “There are better tools to deal with this,” he said. The Federal Government recently announced a 30-day petrol discount at Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC) retail stations, with priority for public transport operators, to cushion the impact of rising fuel prices. The Minister of Finance, Taiwo Oyedele, said NNPC retail outlets would sell petrol at cost by foregoing their retail profit margins, describing the initiative as temporary relief rather than a return to petrol subsidy. The government also proposed negotiating a ceiling of N1,350 per litre on petrol’s ex-gantry or landing cost, subject to monthly reviews. IMF Advocates Targeted Support for Vulnerable Households The IMF also called for targeted interventions to cushion the impact of higher fuel prices on transportation and other essential household expenses. Davide Furceri, a division chief in the fund’s Fiscal Affairs Department, said governments could redirect some of the resources spent on blanket subsidies towards vulnerable consumers. He cited transportation support as one alternative, suggesting that governments could subsidise bus fares rather than reduce fuel prices for all consumers. “For example, you mentioned transportation costs. Yeah, gasoline could go up, and perhaps bus fees may be subsidised in a way that is a much better policy at the end of the day than just a blanket subsidy for everybody,” Furceri said. He also identified school feeding programmes, geographical targeting and assistance for vulnerable farmers as possible measures to protect households from rising living costs. Furceri acknowledged that some countries lacked comprehensive household registries and digital payment systems needed to identify beneficiaries and deliver targeted assistance efficiently. However, he said governments could adopt alternative arrangements in the short term while developing stronger systems for delivering social support. He stressed that such interventions should be limited, targeted and temporary. Subsidies Could Worsen Global Energy Pressures Valdés also warned that fuel subsidies could intensify global energy pressures by preventing consumers from adjusting their demand when supplies were constrained. According to him, keeping fuel prices artificially low encourages consumption even when less fuel is available in the global economy, forcing prices to rise further as the market adjusts. “When you subsidise, you don’t allow, at the end of the day, demand to adjust,” he said. “And reality is that we have less fuels in the world economy. That means that someone else has to adjust more, and the market produces a higher price for that.” The IMF official maintained that broad fuel subsidies were not only costly and regressive but could also generate spillover effects across the global economy. The fund’s position places emphasis on targeted social protection measures that directly assist vulnerable households while allowing energy prices to reflect market conditions. title: W/Bank mobilises $5.79bn private capital for Nigeria
body: By Emma Ujah, Abuja Bureau Chief The World Bank Group has said it is helping to mobilise $5.79 billion in private capital for investment in Nigeria’s agriculture, telecommunications and micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), in a major push to expand private-sector participation in the economy. The financing drive is being supported by policy reforms, investment platforms, risk-sharing mechanisms and commercial financing aimed at removing barriers to investment and unlocking opportunities across critical sectors. The initiative is also expected to strengthen food security, improve access to finance for small businesses, expand digital connectivity and create jobs, as the Federal Government intensifies efforts to improve the business environment and attract private investment. “The World Bank supports reforms and projects that improve the investment environment and create viable opportunities. IFC complements this work by structuring investments, deploying its own capital, and bringing commercial lenders and institutional investors into those opportunities,” the institution said. In agriculture, the World Bank Group highlighted financing arrangements for Dangote Industries Limited fertilizer production and Indorama Fertilizer, which it said were helping to expand domestic fertiliser production and improve access to agricultural inputs for more than 10 million smallholder farmers. According to the institution, IFC helped mobilise $1.02 billion for Dangote through refinancing and financing from development institutions and commercial lenders, while $282.5 million was mobilised for Indorama through syndicated financing. The two projects have a combined production capacity of 6.8 million metric tonnes annually, a development the bank said could reduce Nigeria’s dependence on imported inputs, improve affordability and strengthen food security. $1.89bn for small businesses The World Bank Group said its Fostering Inclusive Finance for MSMEs in Nigeria programme, known as FINCLUDE, was designed to improve the availability and quality of financing for more than 250,000 micro, small and medium enterprises operating in job-intensive sectors. Thirty per cent of the financing is targeted at women-led businesses, reflecting efforts to broaden access to credit among enterprises that often struggle to secure affordable funding. The programme is backed by a $500 million package from the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the International Development Association, combining financing and risk-sharing instruments to encourage financial institutions and other investors to extend additional capital to underserved businesses. The bank said FINCLUDE was expected to mobilise nearly $1.89 billion in private financing and support an estimated 850,000 direct and indirect jobs. The initiative is particularly significant for Nigeria, where access to affordable credit remains a major constraint on the ability of small businesses to expand operations, invest in equipment and generate employment. Telecoms attract $1.1bn In the telecommunications sector, IFC acted as an anchor investor in a $1.2 billion bond issuance by IHS Towers, helping to mobilise more than $1.1 billion from private investors and broaden participation in the transaction. The World Bank Group said the transaction demonstrated investor confidence in Nigeria’s digital infrastructure sector and its capital markets. It noted that the tower-sharing model adopted by IHS Towers enables mobile network operators to expand connectivity more quickly and at lower cost while reducing the environmental footprint of network deployment.Beyond telecommunications, the institution said its Building Resilient Digital Infrastructure for Growth (BRIDGE) Project would introduce a new model for developing Nigeria’s digital infrastructure through public-private partnerships. Under the arrangement, a nationwide open-access fibre-optic network will be built, owned and operated through private-sector participation rather than relying exclusively on public financing. The first round of investor selection is expected to mobilise at least $156 million in private equity, while subsequent financing rounds could unlock up to $1.1 billion in private investment by 2030. The project is expected to extend affordable broadband access to an additional 58 million people, increasing coverage from 92 million people in 2025 to 150 million by 2030. Its beneficiaries are projected to include an additional 42 million young people and 15 million women. The project will also connect millions of households, 38,800 public schools, 16,900 health facilities and 3,400 local government offices to high-speed broadband internet. According to the bank, the expanded connectivity would bring digital services closer to communities, improve access to education and healthcare, facilitate public service delivery and create new opportunities for businesses and livelihoods. The World Bank Group attributed the growing opportunities for private capital, in part, to reforms undertaken by the Federal Government to improve foreign exchange management, strengthen public finances, reform fuel subsidies and establish more predictable conditions for investors. title: Russian strikes hit Epicentr malls in Chernihiv, Dnipro, destroy Khmelnytsky logistics hub
body:
On Tuesday evening, Russia struck the logistics center of Epicentr K LLC in Khmelnytsky 10 times. It was the company's last major logistics center, Yulia Chudnovets, head of Epicentr's public relations department, said.
"Our last major logistics complex in Khmelnytsky region. 10 hits. Five fires. One after another. Throughout the day… This was the company's last major logistics complex. The other two in the city of Kyiv and Kyiv region have already been destroyed by the Russians," Chudnovets wrote on Facebook.
According to the company, 10 hits were recorded throughout the day during the attack on the logistics complex in Khmelnytsky region, triggering five fires. Rescue workers' efforts to extinguish the fires were complicated by the presence of another 30 enemy drones in the sky. Epicentr said that this facility had remained the group's last major logistics complex after Russian shelling had previously destroyed two other logistics centers in Kyiv and Kyiv region.
As a result of enemy attacks over the course of a week, the new Epicentr shopping center in Chernihiv was effectively destroyed. The company had rebuilt it in a larger, more modern format after it was completely destroyed in 2022. A strike was also recorded on a shopping center in Dnipro that had been operating in the city for nearly 20 years.
As reported, the Epicentr group of companies is a leader in Ukraine's retail market for home improvement and construction goods. Before Russia's full-scale invasion, the chain comprised more than 70 shopping centers across Ukraine. However, as a result of hostilities and regular missile and drone attacks, some facilities in various regions were destroyed or sustained significant damage.

title: Shelling of Kharkiv region injures 9, including child, in past day – official
body:
Over the past day, the Russian Armed Forces launched missile and drone strikes of various types against Kharkiv and 18 settlements in the region, leaving nine people injured, Head of the Regional Military Administration Oleh Synehubov reported.

"In the city of Kharkiv, 76- and 77-year-old women were injured; in Derhachi, 40- and 55-year-old men were injured; in the urban-type settlement of Pokotylivka in the Vysochanske community, a 15-year-old girl was wounded; in Liubotyn, a 68-year-old man was injured; in the urban-type settlement of Blyzniuky, a 36-year-old man was wounded; in Izium, a 72-year-old woman and a 68-year-old man suffered acute stress reactions," Synehubov wrote in his Telegram channel.

title: Uganda host first African Chiefs of Defence Forces Conference on non-combat operations
body: Uganda hosted the first African Chiefs of Defence Forces Conference on Military Operations Other Than War (MOOTW) from October 5 to 8, 2026, bringing defence chiefs from 18 African countries to Speke Resort Munyonyo in Kampala. The four-day meeting was organised by Uganda’s Ministry of Defence and Veteran Affairs and the Uganda Peoples’ Defence Forces (UPDF). Its theme, “Strengthening Adaptive Noncombatant Military Response to Emerging Complex Security Threats in Africa,” set the agenda for four days of closed sessions and bilateral talks closing in a session where Museveni said Africa cannot effectively address emerging security threats without confronting the economic, political and geopolitical factors that determine the strength and stability of nations. The conference brings together participants from more than 18 countries, African Union regional bodies, and Force Commanders from United Nations and African Union peace support missions. Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, Uganda’s Chief of Defence Forces and Senior Presidential Advisor for Special Operations, hosted the gathering. Alongside national defence chiefs, the conference drew commanders of the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO), the United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA) and the United Nations Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS), along with representatives of the African Union, the African Peace and Security Architecture (APSA), and regional blocs including the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), the East African Community (EAC) and the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS). Opening the conference, UPDF Chief of Joint Staff Lt Gen Jack Bakasumba framed the gathering as a response to a security picture that no longer fits the old template of state-on-state war. “Across Africa and the wider global arena, the security landscape has evolved away from interstate warfare, shifting instead toward a challenging matrix of interstate conflict and complex non-traditional threats,” he said. He pointed to terrorism, organised crime, cyber warfare, public health emergencies and climate related crises as the threats now dominating planning, and said forces across the continent are often short on training, specialised equipment and functional early warning systems to meet them. Bakasumba pressed delegates to move past communique language and into shared procedure. “We must establish mechanisms that extend beyond discussions and conferences and can be translated into concrete standard operating procedures, training, early-warning systems, joint communications, information sharing and deployable capabilities,” he said. His emphasis on standardised SOPs and rapidly deployable capability echoed through the week, including from Uganda’s Deputy Chief of Defence Forces, Lt Gen Sam Okiding, who told the Chiefs of Defence Intelligence and Security session that the point was not to introduce new concepts but to redefine how existing operations are run. He argued for intelligence-led planning across humanitarian crises, terrorism, transnational organised crime, irregular migration and climate related displacement. For a semi-technical audience, MOOTW is worth defining precisely. It covers the set of military tasks that fall short of conventional combat: peace support and stabilisation operations, disaster and pandemic response, counter-terrorism and counter-insurgency support, protection of critical infrastructure, maritime and border security, and military assistance to civil authorities during emergencies. NATO and several Western militaries have used variants of the term for decades; Uganda’s pitch in Kampala was to build an African-owned version of the doctrine, shaped by its own record in Somalia , South Sudan and the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo rather than imported from outside. The conference agenda, as laid out by Uganda’s Ministry of Defence, ran wide: cybersecurity and artificial intelligence, unmanned aerial systems, gender mainstreaming, natural resource management, space and environmental security, disease pandemics, external influence operations and legal and ethical accountability for military forces operating in civilian spaces. That breadth reflects a genuine operational problem. African militaries are increasingly tasked with civil support missions, from Ebola and COVID-19 response to flood relief, without a shared framework for command, funding or legal mandate when troops operate outside a declared conflict. Gen Muhoozi used the platform to advance his own formulation of the doctrine, describing it in UPDF materials as “Military Support to Peace and Security” and citing the army’s role in Uganda’s Ebola and COVID-19 responses, maritime patrols and humanitarian logistics as a working model other states could adapt. General Salim Saleh, addressing delegates virtually, argued that wealth creation is itself a pillar of peace. Closing the conference on October 8, President Yoweri Museveni tied the whole exercise back to economics. “A country cannot have a strong and safe defence force without a strong economy,” he said, urging delegates to pursue wealth creation through commercial agriculture, manufacturing, services and ICT, and to widen markets through the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) and deeper regional integration. “Security and prosperity go together,” he told the assembled chiefs, thanking them for taking part in what organisers billed as the first conference of its kind at the level of African defence chiefs. Whether Kampala’s conference produces anything beyond a communique will depend on follow through that conference organisers themselves flagged as the hard part: converting discussion into standard operating procedures, interoperable communications and pooled early warning systems that can survive a change of government or a budget cycle. Uganda’s defence ministry has not yet announced a secretariat, working group structure or date for a follow-up conference. What is clear is that 18 African states have now put MOOTW on their agenda as a named doctrine rather than an ad hoc practice, setting up a test of whether the next deployment, whether to a flood zone, a disease outbreak or a counter-terrorism operation, looks any different on the ground.

title: The fear of institutional independence by our strong politicians; Another opportunity for governance reset duly deferred
body: The Electoral Commission (EC) under the Fourth Republic initially enjoyed a relatively high level of public confidence under the leadership of Kwadwo Afari-Gyan, who served from 1993 to 2015. Although political parties occasionally challenged election results and aspects of electoral administration, criticisms were generally directed at specific electoral processes rather than at the legitimacy of the EC Chairperson’s appointment. Afari-Gyan’s long tenure contributed to the perception of institutional continuity and stability, and despite occasional electoral disputes, party politics had not significantly intruded into debates over the occupancy of the office itself. A noticeable shift emerged in 2015 with the appointment of Charlotte Osei by President John Dramani Mahama following the retirement of Afari-Gyan. As the first transition from the Commission’s founding Chairperson in the Fourth Republic, her appointment attracted heightened political interest and scrutiny. While her appointment itself was historic, the EC leadership increasingly became a subject of partisan commentary, with political actors paying closer attention to the perceived political implications of appointments to the Commission. The intrusion of partisan politics into EC leadership became most evident during and after the events leading to the removal of Charlotte Osei in 2018. The circumstances surrounding her dismissal generated intense political debate, with competing narratives emerging from the major political parties regarding the independence of the Commission and the appropriateness of the constitutional processes employed. What had previously been largely administrative and institutional discussions evolved into highly polarized political contests, drawing the EC leadership directly into partisan discourse. The appointment of Jean Adukwei Mensa later in 2018 further deepened the politicization of discussions surrounding EC leadership. Opposition parties questioned the transition and raised concerns about neutrality and public trust, while supporters maintained that the constitutional requirements for appointment had been fully respected. Since then, debates concerning the Electoral Commission have increasingly focused not only on electoral administration but also on the perceived political affiliations, independence, and legitimacy of its leadership. This development marks a significant departure from the earlier period when the EC was largely viewed as an institution operating above overt partisan contestation. Thus, while electoral disputes existed during the tenure of Afari-Gyan, the politicization of the office of the EC Chairperson itself became more pronounced from 2015 onward and intensified considerably following the 2018 removal of Charlotte Osei and the appointment of Jean Adukwei Mensa. The recent appointments to Ghana’s Electoral Commission (EC) have once again ignited a familiar political debate. The opposition has accused the government of appointing individuals with perceived partisan connections into positions that ought to be fiercely independent, while government supporters have responded by reminding the public that similar appointments were made by previous administrations. Both arguments may contain elements of truth. Yet both miss a more important point. The real issue is not who made the appointments. The real issue is why Ghana’s political leaders, regardless of ideology or party affiliation, remain unwilling to reform a system that repeatedly generates controversy and undermines public confidence in critical democratic institutions. The current debate exposes a deeper and more troubling reality about Ghanaian politics: politicians often defend principles only when those principles serve their political interests. When in opposition, political parties become passionate advocates of institutional independence, transparency, and accountability. When in government, however, many of the same principles suddenly become negotiable. What was once portrayed as a threat to democracy becomes a constitutional prerogative. What was condemned as political interference becomes a lawful exercise of executive authority. This hypocrisy is not unique to one political party. It has become a recurring feature of Ghana’s political landscape. The opposition’s concerns about perceived partisan appointments to the Electoral Commission are understandable. The EC occupies a critical place in Ghana’s constitutional order. It is the institution responsible for administering elections and safeguarding one of the most fundamental pillars of democracy: the will of the people. For this reason, appointments to the Commission should not only be fair but should also be seen to be fair. Public confidence in electoral outcomes depends largely on public confidence in the institution conducting those elections. However, the opposition’s criticism is weakened by the reality that when it had the opportunity to reform the system, it defended the same constitutional arrangements it now questions. The standards appear to change depending on whether a party is in government or opposition. Similarly, the government’s justification that previous administrations engaged in similar practices is equally problematic. The argument that “they did it too” is not a defense of principle. It is simply an admission that Ghana’s political class has become comfortable perpetuating practices it once condemned. A nation cannot progress by benchmarking its governance standards against yesterday’s mistakes. What makes the present situation particularly disappointing is that it comes against the backdrop of the much-publicized Reset Agenda. One of the earliest and most commendable actions of President Mahama’s administration was the establishment of a Constitutional Review Committee (CRC). The decision was widely welcomed because it demonstrated a willingness to examine structural weaknesses within Ghana’s governance system and identify reforms that could strengthen democratic institutions. The committee undertook consultations across the country and submitted its report to government last year. Many Ghanaians expected the exercise to produce meaningful reforms capable of addressing longstanding concerns about excessive executive influence over public institutions. This year, Cabinet announced its decisions on the CRC recommendations. While several proposals were accepted, many others were reportedly rejected. Significantly, a considerable number of the rejected recommendations sought to transfer key governance functions from political discretion to more transparent and independent institutional processes. Among these were proposals relating to the appointment of Electoral Commission officials and other constitutional office holders. The recommendations sought to make appointments more transparent, merit-based, and less susceptible to perceptions of political influence. The underlying principle was simple. The legitimacy of democratic institutions should not depend primarily on the preferences of political leaders but on systems and procedures that command broad public trust. Ironically, many of the reforms that would have most effectively advanced the objectives of the Reset Agenda were those that required politicians to relinquish some degree of control. This is where Ghana’s democracy confronts one of its greatest challenges. Politicians readily support institutional reforms when those reforms constrain their opponents. They become far less enthusiastic when those same reforms require them to surrender power themselves. The reluctance to implement recommendations that would reduce executive influence raises legitimate questions about the political commitment to institutional transformation. If political leaders genuinely believe that perceptions of partisan influence undermine confidence in institutions such as the Electoral Commission, then one would expect them to embrace reforms that reduce such perceptions. Instead, what emerges is the age-old instinct of political self-preservation. Across successive governments, leaders have demonstrated a remarkable unwillingness to cede powers that could prove politically advantageous in the future. The fear of losing office often translates into a determination to retain as much influence as possible over key institutions of state. Consequently, constitutional reform becomes an attractive campaign promise but an uncomfortable governing reality. This continuous cycle has serious implications for Ghana’s democracy. It breeds public cynicism and reinforces the perception that political principles are merely instruments of convenience. Citizens increasingly view institutions through partisan lenses because political actors themselves encourage such perceptions through their inconsistent positions. Over time, trust in public institutions declines. Confidence in governance weakens. Democratic legitimacy suffers. The irony is that Ghana possesses the expertise, experience, and democratic maturity necessary to build stronger institutions. Numerous commissions, expert panels, civil society organizations, and governance scholars have identified practical reforms capable of enhancing institutional independence and public confidence. The obstacle is not knowledge. The obstacle is political will. Indeed, the true test of leadership is not the willingness to establish committees or commission reports. It is the courage to implement recommendations that may reduce the power of those currently in office while strengthening the Republic for future generations. President Mahama deserves recognition for initiating the Constitutional Review process. However, the ultimate measure of success will not be the establishment of the CRC or the quality of its report. It will be the extent to which government embraces reforms that place strong institutions above political interests. The ongoing controversy over Electoral Commission appointments should therefore serve as more than a partisan dispute. It should spark a national conversation about whether Ghana genuinely wants independent institutions or merely independent institutions when our preferred party is not in power. Until politicians are prepared to subject themselves to the same standards they demand of their opponents, accusations of hypocrisy will continue to define our political discourse. The debate is therefore not about the Electoral Commission alone. It is about whether Ghana wishes to build a democracy founded on strong institutions or one perpetually dependent on the discretion of strong politicians. So far, the evidence suggests that while many politicians speak passionately about reform, far fewer are willing to surrender power in order to achieve it. And therein lies the unfinished business of Ghana’s democratic reset. Business-as-usual continues. By

title: HII nets deal for AUKUS engineering and design work
body:
HII's Newport News Shipbuilding (NNS) division was awarded a $56 million contract by the US Navy for shipbuilding engineering and design in support of the trilateral Australia, United Kingdom, and United States (AUKUS) partnership.
Under the contract, as part of Foreign Military Sales (FMS) requirements, NNS will continue supporting the United Kingdom and Australia, including technology insertion, engineering, supply chain and workforce development support, and digital transformation.
The award also includes the United States Industry Support (USIS) effort, wherein NNS engineers and designers will support the design of the SSN-AUKUS nuclear-powered submarine to be built by the United Kingdom and Australia.
The contract includes an option that, if exercised, would bring the cumulative value of this contract to $91 million. HII continues to take a whole-company approach to support the AUKUS agreement, providing services and support for AUKUS across its business divisions.
“Our longstanding nuclear experience at NNS directly benefits the AUKUS mission to support shared security objectives,” said Bryan Caccavale , NNS vice president of program management.
“We are honored to leverage that experience and contribute even more to the AUKUS partnership.”
The contract award is the latest in a range of initiatives HII is actively engaged in to advance the AUKUS partnership. HII’s Mission Technologies division in Australia was awarded the contract to deliver the Australian Submarine Supplier Qualification (AUSSQ) Program, which accelerates the identification, development and qualification of Australian suppliers for integration into the United States submarine industrial base.
Furthermore, HII is working with Australian industry and academia in Australia to develop the skilled workforce needed to support Australia’s nuclear-powered submarine enterprise. This includes educating and training thousands of engineers, maritime specialists, nuclear tradespeople and other professionals to support the enterprise across its full lifecycle.
The company was also awarded the Australian Submarine Agency’s Nuclear Capability Advisory Services (ANCAS) contract in December 2025 to support development of Australia’s Nuclear Power Submarine (NPS) programs through nuclear program management and technical support services.
To remind, in September 2021, leaders of Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States announced the creation of an enhanced trilateral security partnership called AUKUS.
This announcement began the trilateral consultation period with two related lines of effort. The first initiative under AUKUS is a commitment to support Australia in acquiring nuclear-powered submarines for the Royal Australian Navy. The second initiative intends to enhance joint capabilities and interoperability, focusing on cyber capabilities, artificial intelligence, quantum technologies and additional undersea capabilities.

title: 2 terrorists killed in joint operation in NW Pakistan
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 14 (MNA) – Two terrorists were killed in a joint intelligence-based operation by security forces and police in Pakistan's northwest Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Tuesday, the Counter Terrorism Department (CTD) said Wednesday.
The operation was conducted in Bannu district following intelligence reports that terrorists were planning a major attack, the CTD said in a statement, Xinhua reported. One of the killed terrorists, identified as Muhib Khan, was wanted in 22 cases, including those related to target killings, attacks on security personnel and kidnappings. Authorities are working to identify the second terrorist, the statement added. The CTD said intelligence-based operations would continue to eliminate terrorism in the province. MNA

title: Russian drone debris sparks fire at gas station in Khmelnytskyi region, two injured
body:
According to Ukrinform, the State Emergency Service of Ukraine reported this on Telegram .
Rescuers are continuing to deal with the aftermath of the Russian drone attack.
Drone debris sparked a fire at a gas station in the Khmelnytskyi district. Two people sustained minor injuries.
In one of Khmelnytskyi’s neighborhoods, drone debris caused fires at two private properties. No injuries were reported.
Rescuers were repeatedly forced to leave the sites where they were working because of renewed strikes.
Firefighting operations are also ongoing at an enterprise in the Khmelnytskyi district. A total of 80 rescuers and 22 pieces of equipment have been deployed to put out the fire.
As Ukrinform reported, fires broke out at industrial facilities in the Khmelnytskyi and Shepetivka districts following Russian attacks in the evening of October 13.

title: IRGC chief hails defense industry experts during imposed wars
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 14 (MNA) – The chief Commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) has praised the unsparing efforts of the specialists in the defense industry of the country during the two wars imposed by US and Israel against the country.
Speaking at his meeting with the newly-appointed Minister of Defense Mehrdad Akhlaghi on Wednesday, Chief Commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) Major General Ahmad Vahidi hailed the industrious and unflinching endeavors of specialist in the defense industry of the country, especially during the two wars [12- (June 13), and 40-day (February 28)] imposed by the United States and Zionist regime against Iran.
During the meeting, the two senior commanders exchanged their views on host of issues, including the role of the defense industry in supporting the Armed Forces, continuity in production of defense equipment and weaponry at the wartime conditions, strategies for cooperating and establishing synergy between industrial entities of the Ministry of Defense and IRGC.
General Vahidi pointed to the significance of endeavors of specialists and staffers in the defense industry of the country during the 12-day and also 40-day war [Ramadan War] imposed against the country, and emphasized the strategic role of the indigenized capabilities in meeting the demands of the country’s defense industry.
He said that Iran’s defense readiness depends on domestic capabilities, sustained production and the development of strategic technologies.
Regarding the necessity of bolstering industrial and technological activities at the current situation, IRGC chief stated, “Relying upon the indigenous knowledge and technical knowhow, the determination of specialists, and continuity of the defense equipment production chain are key factors in maintaining readiness of the Armed Forces and countering potential threats from adversaries.”
He emphasized the importance of maximum use of the domestic capabilities, identifying the development of cooperation between operational and industrial sectors of the Armed Forces as a means to enhance combat capabilities, boost defense readiness, and strengthen the country's deterrence.
The newly-appointed defense minister, for his part, voiced readiness of the Defense Ministry to support the Armed Forces of the country in producing and promoting the technology, especially the strategic weaponry.
Highlighting the capabilities and readiness of the defense industry sector to expand cooperation and interaction with the corresponding branches of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Akhlaghi emphasized the development of joint collaborations regarding the design, production, procurement, and support of defense equipment.

title: SpaceX limits Starlink terminal speed in Ukraine overnight without warning – presidential adviser
body:
Presidential Advisor Serhiy Flash Beskrestnov reported that SpaceX restricted the operational speed of its Starlink satellite communication terminals in motion overnight, leading to the disruption of a number of missions.
"I confirm that tonight SpaceX introduced speed restrictions on Starlink terminals while in motion. Currently, the restriction applies to the 'military package' of StarShield services and is set at a speed of 100 miles per hour [160 kilometres per hour]. Our defense forces received no prior warning of such a restriction, which led to the disruption of several missions," he wrote on Telegram.
Beskrestnov called it obvious that this restriction could not be a coincidence and is linked "to the current political situation."
As reported, American billionaire and SpaceX owner Elon Musk previously denied Ukraine the ability to use Starlink satellite internet for strikes on Russian territory, expressing the view that it was time for Ukraine to reach a peace agreement with Russia.
At the same time, a bipartisan delegation from the U.S Congress visiting Kyiv in October advocated for expanding Ukraine's access to Starlink to counter Russian aggression.
Prior to this, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported that work was underway on a satellite system similar to Starlink.

title: 'We're going to hit them hard': Trump threatens Iran as Tehran escalates shipping attacks
body: US President Donald Trump threatened further military action against Iran on Tuesday during a campaign rally in Wasilla, Alaska, where he was campaigning for Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan."Wait and see what we do to Iran. We're going to hit them hard. Wait and see what we do to Iran, because we've had enough," Trump said.The remarks followed a series of shifting statements about Washington's next steps against Tehran. Trump initially indicated on Wednesday that he would not launch further strikes before the November midterm elections, but appeared to leave the possibility open the following day, warning during an October 9 campaign rally in New York that he could "finish it off" if Iran failed to reach a deal.During Tuesday's rally, Trump also claimed that Iran's nuclear facilities remained buried beneath "thousands of tons of rock" and that Tehran had been just two weeks away from developing a nuclear weapon, accusing his predecessor, former president Barack Obama, of failing to stop the program."They were the bullies of the Middle East, but they are the bullies of the Middle East no longer," Trump said, adding, "It's going to end very soon."Trump's renewed threats come as Tehran reportedly seeks to increase pressure on Washington through attacks on maritime traffic and disruptions to global energy markets ahead of the US midterm elections.Iran is deploying new tactics to target ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz in an effort to keep oil prices high and influence the US midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters.Iran targets Strait of Hormuz shipping to pressure US ahead of midtermsTehran has tried to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz since the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran on February 28. It has restricted passage through the waterway, which carried about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade before the war, to gain leverage over Washington.Its threats and attacks have severely curtailed traffic through the strait, driving up oil prices, though some oil has continued to transit.The two officials declined to provide details of the new strategy, but one said Iran began using different offensive tactics against vessels it considered in violation of its restrictions about 10 days ago, adding that this led to more attacks on such ships.Iran changes attack tactics to keep global oil prices high The strategy included a change in the type as well as the pace of attacks, with one goal being to influence the outcome of the US vote, they said."The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices," one of the two officials said.The decision to adopt the new strategy had been taken at the highest levels of Iran's leadership and was fully coordinated across the country's ruling system, the officials said.

title: NAF Plane Crash: Igbokoda residents lament stench, fear disease outbreak, as body parts float
body: By Dayo Johnson, Akure More than a week after a Nigerian Air Force, NAF, aircraft crashed in Igbokoda, Ondo State, residents said they are battling offensive odour, polluted water and fear for disease outbreak. Read Also: NAF PLANE CRASH: How hero pilot died saving town The NAF ATR-42, which was flying from Benin City to Lagos, crashed into a swamp near the Air Force Forward Operating Base in Igbokoda on October 5, killing all 25 persons on board. They appealed to the Federal Government, Ondo State government and the Nigerian Air Force to urgently evacuate the human remains, clean up the environment and provide safe drinking water for the community. The aircraft was on a routine operation when it crashed on Monday, October 5, killing all 25 persons on board, comprising five crew members and 20 passengers. It submerged into the swamp, prompting a joint search and recovery operation by the Air Force, other security agencies and emergency responders. More than a week after, locals say the operation is yet to be fully concluded. Community leaders and residents told Vanguard that the decomposing bodies and spillage of aviation fuel have left the entire area polluted. Body parts float The Olu of Igbokoda, Oba Afolabi Odidiomo, said the stench from the crash site has spread to residential areas, making life unbearable for residents. He said body parts were still seen floating on the river, while traces of fuel could be observed some distance from the wreckage site. “The odour is extremely offensive and unbearable. So many parts of human bodies are floating around in the river. Some of the bodies have not been recovered, they have decomposed and it is affecting everything,” the monarch said. According to him, the development has raised serious concerns over contamination of the river, which serves as a major source of water for domestic use. “People are worried about cooking, bathing and other domestic uses. We are appealing to government to urgently remove the remaining bodies and debris, contain any fuel spillage and carry out full environmental remediation,” Oba Odidiomo said. He also called for immediate provision of potable water for residents pending conclusion of recovery and clean-up operations, stressing that the welfare of the host community should not be overlooked. Smell For residents living near the river, the experience has been distressing. Omogbemi Damola, a resident, said she has been perceiving the foul odour in her upstairs apartment for days. “What happened in Igbokoda is a very sad experience. Since the accident occurred, different kinds of unpleasant odours have been carried by the breeze into our homes. “I live upstairs and I have been perceiving the smell for at least four days now,” she said. She appealed to the state government to expedite action on the recovery of bodies and measures to control the stench, noting that the community has already suffered enough trauma from the incident. Another resident, Oroyo Levy, said the situation has gone beyond discomfort to a public health concern. “We are appealing to government to act swiftly to contain the odour and prevent it from posing further health risks. “The smell suggests air pollution and we are worried about its effect, especially on children,” Levy said. He described the crash as an unusual and painful experience for the riverine community, and urged authorities to investigate the environmental impact of the incident to avert another crisis. Levy added that more than a week after the tragedy, uncertainty over water safety has heightened anxiety among residents who depend on the river. Residents therefore urged the National Emergency Management Agency, NEMA; State Emergency Management Agency, SEMA, and relevant environmental agencies to intervene and ensure that the aftermath of the crash does not trigger an outbreak of waterborne diseases. Govt reacts Reacting, the State Commissioner for Environment, Tob Loko, said the state government was collaborating with the Federal Government to ensure maximum recovery. “The state government is collaborating with the Federal Government to ensure that we carry out as much recovery as possible. “But you know that despite the number of days the recovery effort has been ongoing, no meaningful recovery has been made. None of the corpses has been recovered. “Shortly afterwards, concerns about pollution were raised. What we are trying to do is make a holistic assessment of the level of public health impact and determine how we can embark on decontamination efforts because the surrounding area is surely contaminated. “So, there is a case of pollution. But we are not resting on our laurels. As I have said, we are carefully undertaking holistic assessments of the environmental impact and the public health impact of what has happened there to ensure that we address it as quickly as possible,” he said. ‘They have drinking water’ On claims of drinking water pollution, the commissioner said the complaint was not entirely correct. “That is not the water they drink. There are boreholes around. So, the claim that the water is no longer useful is not entirely correct. “Let me also say this: Some people insinuate that the site of the crash is close to the metropolis. Of course, the crash site is at least 500 metres away from the bulk of the metropolis. So, the issue of not having water to drink and other associated concerns is not there. “We are not ruling out the fact that there may be cases of pollution. But to say that the people do not have water to drink as a result of the crash is not a sustainable argument or concern, so to speak,” Loko added. title: Nigerians warned against relocating to Indonesia without business plans
body: Nigerians seeking greener pastures in Indonesia have been advised to invest in their home country rather than relocate without viable business plans, as employment opportunities for foreigners are limited and setting up businesses requires substantial capital. The Charge d’Affaires ad interim of the Nigerian Embassy in Jakarta, Eze Nduka, gave the advice while speaking to journalists at the embassy on Tuesday. Nduka said many Nigerians had spent between 10 and 15 years in Indonesia without meaningful employment, while some had become stranded and were seeking assistance from the embassy to return home. He urged Nigerian youths to verify claims about opportunities in Indonesia and avoid travelling based on promises made online, particularly those linked to drug trafficking, cybercrime and other criminal activities. According to him, some Nigerians have also spent years in the country without valid immigration documents, restricting their freedom of movement and access to opportunities. He advised prospective migrants to develop clear plans before travelling, including identifying whom they intend to meet, the business they hope to establish and how they would sustain themselves. “Many of them are here, they have spent 10-15 years doing nothing. Some of them are coming to the embassy crying, asking us that they want to go home. They don’t have transportation, that we should find a means of repatriation and all that,” he said. Nduka urged Nigerians to consider the four Ws and other essential questions before relocating, including who they were going to meet, what business they intended to pursue, where and when they would operate, and how they would survive. “The only advice I have for them is this: you must employ those four Ws in everything you are going to do. Who you are coming to meet, what business you are coming to do, and where and when and how you will survive in Indonesia, because there’s no job here in Indonesia, there’s no job for foreigners,” he said. The envoy said establishing a business in Indonesia was expensive, requiring significant financial resources to meet the country’s business and residence requirements. He advised Nigerians with the financial capacity to establish businesses abroad to consider investing at home, where their investments could contribute to economic growth and job creation. “In terms of business, to set up a business here in Indonesia is quite expensive. Even to set up a business, you must have some deposit of millions of naira, so if you are bringing in that money here, why not invest home?” he asked. Nduka also warned Nigerians against engaging in drug trafficking and cybercrime, saying Indonesia had strengthened its cybersecurity systems and enforcement of laws against such offences. He said the country had introduced stricter policies, making it increasingly difficult for offenders to evade law enforcement. “Indonesia has really improved in terms of cybersecurity and other technologies. Before, Indonesia used to be a kind of endpoint that any money you wanted to move out, or that you must have made from any part of the world, you could come here and clear it. “But there are new governments, there are new policies. It’s no longer business as usual. Many of them are still in detention. Many of them are on life sentence. Many of them are on death sentence. Many of them are on long-term prison,” he said. The envoy said the Nigerian population in Indonesia had declined significantly compared with previous decades, partly because of stricter enforcement against drug-related offences and cybercrime. He added that some Nigerians had encountered difficulties accessing vocational training and employment, making it more challenging for them to establish themselves in the country. Nduka, however, encouraged Nigerian investors to explore legitimate business opportunities in Indonesia, describing the country as a market with considerable potential for bilateral trade and investment. He said Indonesian companies had established businesses in Nigeria across several sectors, including manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, oil and gas, petrochemicals, consumer goods and healthcare. Among the Indonesian-linked companies operating in Nigeria, he listed Indorama, Primera Food, Wing Group and Orange Group. The envoy urged Nigerian investors to study Indonesia’s business environment and establish credible partnerships with local companies, noting that previous cases of fraud had undermined Indonesian suppliers’ confidence in Nigerian businesses. He called on Nigerian companies to demonstrate their credibility through verifiable registration documents and transparent business dealings. “Tell our investors that they should utilise this government-to-government trade expo and prove to them that their company is duly registered with the CAC,” he said. On bilateral relations, Nduka said trade between Nigeria and Indonesia had continued to expand, with opportunities for both countries to strengthen cooperation in manufacturing, renewable energy, agriculture, pharmaceuticals and waste management. He encouraged Nigerians attending the trade expo in Indonesia to use the platform to establish genuine business relationships and explore investment opportunities. The envoy also said Nigeria could benefit from studying Indonesia’s approach to infrastructure development, particularly its use of public-private partnerships to finance roads, railways and other major projects. He explained that such arrangements could enable private companies to finance and maintain infrastructure in exchange for revenue generated over an agreed period, thereby reducing the immediate financial burden on government. On the welfare of Nigerians in Indonesia, Nduka disclosed that six Nigerians died in the country between January and August 2026. He said the embassy was working with relevant authorities to establish the circumstances surrounding some of the deaths and provide consular assistance to affected families. According to him, the mission had visited detention facilities, supported burial arrangements, communicated with families in Nigeria and assisted with the repatriation of deceased citizens. He added that the embassy was following up on cases involving Nigerians detained over criminal offences and those requiring assistance to return home. Nduka urged Nigerians in Indonesia to report emergencies and other serious incidents to the embassy promptly to enable the mission to engage the appropriate authorities. He also called for stronger coordination among Nigerian community groups in Indonesia, saying a more unified approach would help the embassy communicate with citizens and address their concerns effectively.
