title: Exercise Vuk’uhlome V Underway at Lohathla Training Centre
body: The South African Army is putting its training to the test in the arid Northern Cape, where Exercise Vuk’uhlome V is under way at the Combat Training Centre (CTC) at Lohathla. The exercise began on 19 September and is scheduled to run until 5 December, according to the SA National Defence Force (SANDF) Directorate Corporate Communication (DCC), as reported by DefenceWeb . Lieutenant General Lawrence Mbatha’s Army is the main player, but elements of the SA Air Force (SAAF) and the SA Military Health Service (SAMHS) are also involved, and SA Police Service (SAPS) participation is expected again. Vuk’uhlome is an isiZulu phrase meaning “arise and arm yourself.” This is the fifth exercise in the series, and the DCC says it will again run at “division minus level.” The directorate gave no personnel numbers and did not say which units are taking part. Who Is Taking Part Five of what the Army calls its “modern brigades” (airborne, light, mechanised, motorised and reserve) will take part alongside the specialist medical brigade. They will move across the 158,000-hectare Lohathla CTC, carrying out manoeuvres and tasks with other elements of the force so that combat readiness can be evaluated. As in earlier editions, the exercise also covers continuation training, division-level planning, brigade planning cycles, tactical-level planning, and command and control. Defence Intelligence, the Military Police, Legal Services and Logistics divisions of the Department of Defence (DoD) are contributing as well. The modern brigade structure was visible when the series began. Military Africa’s coverage of the first exercise in 2022 recorded how the brigades were assembled for the exercise. The motorised brigade was built around Headquarters 46 SA Brigade with 7 and 14 South African Infantry (SAI) battalions and General Botha Regiment. The airborne brigade drew on 6 and 9 SAI, 44 Parachute Brigade and 101 Air Supply Unit. The light brigade included the SA Army Specialist Infantry Capability, the Andrew Mlangeni Regiment and a quick response force. The DCC has not said whether the same allocations apply this year. Personnel numbers are not normally published. DefenceWeb reported that earlier Vuk’uhlome exercises involved between 7,000 and 9,000 military personnel. That range is not an official figure, and the DCC has not confirmed a number for this year. What “Division Minus” Means In standard military usage, a minus sign after a formation’s level means it is operating below its full establishment, for example a division headquarters controlling fewer brigades than a full division would. The DCC did not define the term, and without unit lists it is not possible to say how much of a division is on the ground. The label marks a change in emphasis. Vuk’uhlome I was billed as the first division-level exercise since the SA Army was formed in 1994. Military Africa reported in December 2025 that the fourth edition concentrated on brigade-level operations, using the Lohathla area to simulate a “hot war” against a fictional destabiliser force. That report described the brigade as the largest independent manoeuvre unit the Army can sustain, and said the exercise was validating its prime mission equipment and its command and control structures. Soldiers and Police Together Police are expected to take part again. Earlier Vuk’uhlome scenarios included crowd and riot control, with soldiers and SAPS personnel working in tandem. In 2025, Military Africa’s reporting recorded the Light Modern Brigade training with SAPS mounted units, K9 teams and motorcycles. The SAPS role this year has not been confirmed. Observers From the Region The 16-member Southern African Development Community (SADC) has been invited to send observers, which the DCC says adds to the exercise’s “collaborative dimension.” The DCC did not say which member states have accepted. The invitation comes after the end of the SADC Mission in the Democratic Republic of Congo (SAMIDRC) in mid-March 2025. Military Africa reported that critics called the mission set up for failure because of insufficient troop numbers, poor planning and exposed base locations, while the Chief of the SANDF said it had contributed to peace efforts. The DCC has not linked the two events. Lohathla has hosted regional exercises before. It staged the African Union’s Amani Africa 2 field exercise in 2015 to demonstrate the AU’s rapid deployment capability. Readiness in Context The run-up gave some indication of the Army’s condition. On 15 September, Mbatha oversaw a stabling parade of mission equipment at the CTC, including infantry fighting vehicles, an armoured car, tanks, field ambulances and trucks. DefenceWeb reported that he described the parade as part of building a better Army, one capable of working with partners in joint missions . The same report covered preparatory retraining in Limpopo, where 15 SAI catering personnel cooked on firewood and light workshop mechanics returned unserviceable vehicles to service with limited resources. That points to the logistics and maintenance pressures behind the exercise. Military Africa reported in 2023 that more than R277 million had been spent repairing and preserving military vehicles, with Cuban technicians helping refurbish more than 10,000 Samil and similar vehicles, according to that report. Vuk’uhlome also serves the defence industry. During preparations for the 2025 exercise, Exercise Chief of Staff Brigadier General Leon Puckree called it a chance to showcase capabilities and market modernised equipment , and for the South African defence industry to network with the DoD. In 2023, Military Africa reported that companies bidding for army armoured vehicle tenders would be invited to display at the exercise . No industry component has been announced for this year. What Has Not Been Announced Several details are still unavailable: the numbers and units involved, the scenario, which SADC states will observe, the SAPS role, and the date of any distinguished visitors’ day. Last year’s was expected in late November. Until the DCC releases more, Vuk’uhlome V can be described only by its dates, its structure and its stated purpose: a test of whether the SA Army’s planning, command and logistics hold up when its brigades work together.

title: GMTF targets Volta healthcare gaps with equipment, specialist training and patient support
body: The Ghana Medical Trust Fund (GMTF) is prioritising medical equipment, specialist training and financial support for patients as it works to close gaps in specialised healthcare in the Volta Region. The Fund’s Administrator, Adjoa Obuobia Darko-Opoku, said improving access to care required a comprehensive approach that combined financial assistance with investment in diagnostic equipment, specialist expertise and effective referral systems. She was speaking at an engagement with medical professionals and healthcare stakeholders in Ho as part of the Fund’s first-anniversary activities and nationwide sensitisation tour. The event, dubbed “One Year On – An Evening of Reflection”, brought together the Volta Regional Minister, James Gunu, medical directors, specialists, other healthcare professionals and representatives of Roche Ghana. Ms Darko-Opoku urged health professionals to identify and document equipment shortages, inadequate diagnostic capacity, referral challenges and gaps in specialist services. She called for evidence-based recommendations to guide the Fund’s interventions and improve patient outcomes. She explained that the GMTF’s four pillars—financial support for eligible patients, medical equipment and infrastructure, specialist training, and research and innovation—were designed to address both treatment costs and the capacity of health facilities to deliver quality care. Speaking on behalf of the Chief Executive Officer of Ho Teaching Hospital, the Medical Director, Dr Emmanuel Kasu, urged the Fund to prioritise the early identification and enrolment of eligible patients, better referral coordination, support to help patients navigate the care process and faster provision of medical equipment. He said the Fund’s impact should be measured beyond patient enrolment to include timely access to treatment, improved clinical outcomes and reduced financial hardship for patients and their families. Reflecting on the Fund’s first year, Ms Darko-Opoku said its patient-support programme began with a pilot involving 50 patients nationwide. The exercise helped management assess procedures, identify implementation challenges and improve systems ahead of expanding assistance. She also highlighted the development of the Fund’s Medicines List and Tariff Manual, prepared with input from specialists and subject-matter experts to guide decisions on eligible treatments, procedures and costs. On infrastructure, she cited the restoration of the Cardiac Catheterisation Laboratory at Korle Bu Teaching Hospital and the development of cardiology centres at Komfo Anokye Teaching Hospital and Tamale Teaching Hospital. She also highlighted a partnership with KGL Group to support a US$10 million diagnostic and imaging centre at the Greater Accra Regional Hospital. Ms Darko-Opoku stressed that investment in modern equipment must be accompanied by specialist training to ensure its effective use and improve patient outcomes. She acknowledged challenges encountered during patient onboarding and said the GMTF Care digital platform was operational, with ongoing improvements to simplify applications, strengthen communication and reduce delays. She urged healthcare professionals to educate patients about the Fund’s mandate and application procedures, particularly those living far from major urban centres who might otherwise miss out on available support. Ms Darko-Opoku reaffirmed the Fund’s commitment to working with health institutions and other stakeholders to close gaps in specialised healthcare, reduce the financial burden of treatment and improve access to quality care. She commended Mr Gunu for his support and thanked Roche Ghana for sponsoring the engagement.

title: How Israel votes: a guide to the Knesset, political parties and coalition governments
body: In Israel, voters do not directly elect their prime minister or individual members of parliament. Instead, each voter chooses a single list of candidates, usually representing a political party or an alliance of parties. The votes determine how the 120 seats in the Knesset, Israel’s parliament, are distributed. What happens after the election can be just as important as the vote itself. Parties negotiate alliances, agree on policies and divide government responsibilities. The leader of the largest party does not automatically become prime minister, and a smaller party can sometimes determine who governs.   Israel uses a system called proportional representation, which helps explain its many political parties, complicated coalition negotiations and frequent early elections. Why does Israel have so many political parties? Unlike the United States, where two major parties dominate national elections, Israel has a multiparty system. Its parties represent a broad range of political, religious, ethnic and social interests. Some focus on security, diplomacy and economic policy. Others represent particular communities, including ultra-Orthodox Jews, religious Zionists and Arab citizens of Israel. Parties also differ over relations with the Palestinians, religion’s role in public life and the balance between government authority and judicial power. The Knesset has 120 seats, a number inspired by the Great Assembly, a council of Jewish religious leaders and sages traditionally associated with the period following the return from the Babylonian exile in the fifth century BCE. Unlike the US Congress, the Knesset has only one chamber. The entire country is treated as a single electoral district, meaning there are no separate parliamentary constituencies for Jerusalem, Tel Aviv or other cities. Parties win seats according to their share of the nationwide vote, provided they receive enough votes to qualify. How do Israelis vote? Israeli citizens who are at least 18 years old are generally eligible to vote. Citizens can run for the Knesset beginning at age 21, although certain restrictions apply. The president, judges, the state comptroller, the military chief of staff, the two chief rabbis and certain senior civil servants, military officers, police officers and prison officials cannot run while holding their positions. Depending on their position, some must resign well before an election. Certain criminal convictions can also disqualify candidates. Knesset terms are legally set at four years, but the interval between elections can be longer. Regular elections are scheduled for a Tuesday in the Hebrew month of Heshvan, which falls in October or November. The precise Tuesday depends on whether the preceding Hebrew year was a leap year. Following an early election, the next regular election is scheduled for Heshvan after four years have elapsed, potentially extending the interval beyond four years. Early elections are also common, and the Knesset can postpone elections in exceptional circumstances with the support of at least 80 of its 120 members. At polling stations, voters select a paper slip bearing the name and identifying letters of their preferred electoral list, printed in Hebrew and sometimes also in Arabic, place it in an official envelope and deposit it in a ballot box. Each voter chooses one list. There is no separate vote for prime minister, no vote for a local representative and no ranking of individual candidates. Every list presents its candidates in a predetermined order. If a list wins 15 seats, its first 15 candidates enter the Knesset. Parties use different methods to select and rank candidates, including primary elections, party committees and decisions by party leaders. A list can represent one party or several parties running together. Voters selecting a joint list vote for the combined slate, not its individual components. What is the electoral threshold? To enter the Knesset, an electoral list must receive at least 3.25% of all valid votes cast nationwide. This is known as the electoral threshold. If 4 million valid votes are cast, for example, a list needs at least 130,000 votes to qualify. A list receiving 3.24% wins nothing, while one receiving 3.25% would ordinarily receive about four seats, depending on the overall results. The threshold was originally 1%, increased to 1.5% before the 1992 election, rose to 2% in 2004 and reached 3.25% in 2014. The increases were intended to reduce parliamentary fragmentation and encourage smaller parties to run together. Votes cast for lists that fail to cross the threshold are excluded when distributing the 120 seats. Suppose three parties each receive 3% of the vote. Together, they attract 9% of voters, but none enters the Knesset because each ran separately and fell below the threshold. Their votes are not transferred to any other party. Instead, all 120 seats are divided among the qualifying lists, increasing those parties’ proportional shares. This can alter the balance of power between political blocs and helps explain why parties with similar positions sometimes run on joint lists. How are Knesset seats distributed? After excluding votes for lists that fail to cross the threshold, election officials add the votes received by all qualifying lists and divide the total by 120. The result is an initial electoral quota representing the approximate number of votes needed for one seat. Each list’s vote total is divided by this quota, with the whole-number result determining its initial allocation. For example, if qualifying lists receive 3.6 million votes altogether, the quota is 30,000 votes per seat. A list with 310,000 votes initially receives 10 seats, with 10,000 votes left over. Because this calculation normally leaves some seats unassigned, Israel uses a mathematical formula known as the Bader-Ofer method, named after former Knesset members Yohanan Bader and Avraham Ofer, to distribute the remaining seats. Rather than simply awarding these seats to parties with the largest number of leftover votes, the formula divides each list’s vote total by the number of seats it has already received, plus one. The list with the highest resulting figure receives the next seat, and the calculation is repeated until all 120 seats have been assigned. Suppose Party A receives 310,000 votes and has 10 seats. Its figure for an 11th seat is 310,000 divided by 11, or approximately 28,182. Party B receives 205,000 votes and has six seats. Its figure for a seventh seat is 205,000 divided by seven, or approximately 29,286. Party B would have priority for the next seat, despite receiving fewer votes overall. The complete calculation also accounts for agreements between parties over their excess votes. What are excess-vote agreements? Before an election, two lists can sign an excess-vote agreement, sometimes called a surplus-vote agreement. This allows their votes to be combined when calculating eligibility for the remaining seats under the Bader-Ofer method. If their combined votes qualify them for an additional seat, a further calculation determines which partner receives it. The agreement can improve the chances of one partner gaining another seat, although it does not guarantee one. Both lists must independently cross the 3.25% electoral threshold for the agreement to take effect. If either fails, the agreement cannot save its votes or transfer them to its partner. These arrangements differ from joint electoral lists. Parties running together on one list combine their votes before the threshold is applied. Parties signing an excess-vote agreement remain separate, appear independently on the ballot and receive their own Knesset seats. An excess-vote agreement also does not require its participants to cooperate in forming a government. Its immediate purpose is mathematical, not political. Why doesn’t the largest party automatically form the government? Once the seats have been allocated, the next challenge is forming a government. A party needs 61 of the Knesset’s 120 seats to hold an outright parliamentary majority. Because no single party has won such a majority in modern Israeli elections, governments generally depend on coalitions involving several parties. A coalition is an agreement among parties to govern together, usually involving compromises over policy, government ministries, budgets, and legislation. Consider an election in which Party A wins 35 seats, Party B wins 30, Party C wins 18, Party D wins 15, Party E wins 12, and Party F wins 10. Although Party A is the largest, Parties B, C and D could form a coalition with 63 seats, giving them a majority. This also gives smaller parties considerable bargaining power. A party holding just five or six seats can sometimes determine whether a prospective coalition reaches the 61-seat mark. In exchange for joining, it may demand cabinet positions or commitments on policies important to its voters. However, coalition partners must also make compromises, and disagreements can eventually threaten the government’s survival. Relatively small shifts in voting can dramatically change the outcome of an Israeli election. The balance between right-wing and center-left blocs may come down to just a handful of Knesset seats. A party gaining or losing one or two seats, or narrowly crossing or missing the electoral threshold, can determine which bloc has enough support to form a government. The outcome also depends on parties that do not fit neatly into either bloc. Some centrist, religious or other parties may be willing to join coalitions led by different political camps, depending on their priorities and the agreements they can negotiate. As a result, even when the overall vote changes only slightly, the composition of the next government can be very different. What does Israel’s president do after the election? Israel’s president is the head of state, with mainly ceremonial and representative responsibilities, while the prime minister leads the government. After an election, the president plays a central role in deciding who gets the first opportunity to form a government. Once the official results are published, the president consults representatives of the newly elected parliamentary factions. Each can recommend a Knesset member to form a government. The president considers these recommendations and assigns the task to a willing Knesset member, generally choosing someone who appears capable of assembling sufficient parliamentary support. The president is not legally required to choose the leader of the largest party or even the candidate receiving the most recommendations. The assignment must be made within seven days of the official publication of the election results. How is a government formed? The candidate selected by the president receives 28 days to negotiate a governing coalition. The president may grant extensions totaling up to 14 additional days, allowing a maximum of 42 days. Negotiations typically cover coalition policies, government ministries, budgets, legislation and arrangements for resolving disputes. Once an agreement is reached, the candidate informs the president and the Knesset speaker that a government has been formed. The proposed government is presented to the Knesset, including its policy guidelines, ministers and their responsibilities. Lawmakers then vote on whether to express confidence in it. Although a coalition normally seeks the support of at least 61 members, an initial confidence vote requires a majority of those voting, not necessarily 61 affirmative votes. This means Israel can have a minority government if enough lawmakers outside the coalition support it or abstain. Such governments, however, can have difficulty passing budgets and legislation. If the confidence vote succeeds, the new government takes office, and the person who formed it becomes prime minister. What happens if the first candidate fails? If the first candidate cannot form a government within the allotted time, or the proposed government fails to win the Knesset’s confidence, another election does not automatically follow. Within three days, the president can assign the task to another willing Knesset member, who receives 28 days without an extension. Alternatively, the president can inform the Knesset speaker that there appears to be no possibility of forming a government. If the second attempt fails, or the president has declared that no government appears possible, Knesset members have 21 days to propose their own solution. During that period, at least 61 lawmakers can submit a written request asking the president to assign the task to a particular willing Knesset member. That candidate then receives 14 days to form a government. If no candidate receives 61 signatures during the 21-day period, or the final candidate fails, the Knesset is considered dissolved, and new elections must be held within 90 days. The outgoing government remains in office until a new one takes over. Can a government fall before the next election? Yes. Coalition partners can withdraw their support, a prime minister can resign, or the Knesset can dissolve itself and call early elections. Israel also uses a system known as constructive no-confidence. Rather than simply voting to remove a government, at least 61 Knesset members must vote to express confidence in a specific alternative government that is ready to take office. This prevents lawmakers from dismissing a government through a no-confidence vote without agreeing on its replacement. A failure to pass the state budget within the legally required period can also trigger early elections. Between April 2019 and November 2022, Israel held five general elections, largely because of repeated difficulties forming and maintaining governing coalitions. The combination of proportional representation, multiple parties, and coalition politics means election night rarely settles every question about who will govern. Voters determine which parties enter the Knesset and how many seats they receive. The government that emerges depends on which parties can assemble enough parliamentary support to take office and remain there.

title: UK loses 'leverage' to prevent atrocities in global wars
body: Cuts to the UK’s foreign aid and diplomatic arms are hampering Britain's ability to prevent atrocities as global conflicts increase, experts have warned. Yasmine Ahmed, senior director at Amnesty International , said the UK government was not acting fast enough to prevent war crimes, such as those allegedly committed in Sudan and Gaza . “Often atrocity prevention is not prioritised sufficiently in terms of a whole of government policy response,” Ms Ahmed told The National. Last year, Britain’s overseas aid budget was slashed from 0.5 per cent of its gross national income to 0.3 per cent, at a time when conflicts are increasing worldwide. These cuts were issued by former prime minister Keir Starmer in January last year and Britain's spending on overseas aid is expected to fall by 42 per cent, or £6.5 billion ($8.6 billion), over four years, according to the Independent Commission for Aid Impact. One of the first Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office units to feel the impact of the cuts was international humanitarian law cell monitoring war crimes in Gaza. The FCDO has insisted these aid cuts would not affect the department’s ability to conduct human rights assessments of a conflict – but Ms Ahmed was sceptical. “If you’ve got a huge percentage – 20 per cent of the Foreign Office being cut – there’s no doubt this is going to have a significant impact across the board,” she said. “The question is how well will the Foreign Office continue to be equipped to conduct these assessments.” In the past few weeks there has been an escalation of conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen, and the possibility of all-out war between Eritrea and Ethiopia has developed. Will we continue to respond to atrocity crimes only after they have shocked our conscience, or will we build a serious system to predict and prevent them? Gordon Brown Yet the UK's ability to enforce the laws of war and human rights on the world stage was dwindling. “What we’re finding now is that the UK and certainly other European states and other western states don’t have as much leverage as they used to,” Ms Ahmed said. This was leading to a visible decline in the protection of civilians in conflict. “They [the UK and European governments] are operating in an increasingly volatile political world and it’s increasingly transactional,” she said. “There is less space to be values driven.” On Tuesday, a group of British human rights lawyers and experts in global conflict called on the UK to loosen jurisdiction rules, so British courts can prosecute on a wider range of war crimes as well going after as companies accused of involvement. The group warned that the UK was currently “ill-equipped to identify and respond effectively to the warning signs of genocide and other atrocity crimes”, and that this had “serious implications” for “national security, stability and economic prosperity”. The Atrocities Standing Group, which includes Nobel Peace Prize laureate Oleksandra Matviichuk and Baroness Helena Kennedy, published the results of its 18 months of inquiry and parliamentary hearings on Tuesday in a report. It called for a tougher global policing role by using more “Magnitsky-style sanctions”, targeted punitive measures. Frozen sovereign assets from such sanctions could be repurposed to compensate victims of war crimes, by introducing relevant laws to do so, the report suggested. The UK government is seeking to re-establish Britain’s role in the world as conflicts escalate globally. “As the international rules-based order is facing fragmentation and significant challenges, it is key that the UK uses its global position to lead and support efforts to secure justice and accountability for international crimes,” the report said. Former British prime minister Gordon Brown, who has endorsed the report, said the UK needed to take serious foreign policy steps that go well beyond “condemnation” and “sympathy”. “Sympathy is not prevention, condemnation is not policy,” he said ahead of the report's launch. “The question before the United Kingdom and other democratic states is simple and grave. “Will we continue to respond to atrocity crimes only after they have shocked our conscience, or will we build a serious system to predict and prevent them, and respond to them lawfully and in time?” The upholding of human rights risks being further eroded by the US decision to sanction the International Criminal Court in The Hague. While the UK has made “strong statements” of their continued support for the court, their next step could be putting in place a “blocking statute” that would make the sanctions unenforceable in the UK, Ms Ahmed said. The wars in Sudan and in Gaza have featured clear examples of the UK government’s inability to intervene in time, Ms Ahmed said. She questioned why it had taken the UK months to apply a partial suspension of around 30 out of about 350 arms export licences to Israel for military use in Gaza, which the British government eventually announced in September 2024. Export licensing was one area in which the government could act quickly, by referring to its own criteria and the Arms Trade Treaty, she said. “They have the duty to prevent genocide and other crimes, but that’s very hard to enforce. But when you have the export-licensing criteria, that’s where we find there’s a space where the government themselves has processes to evaluate. “I was going in on a weekly basis with either ministers or high-level officials and sometimes middle-ranked officials. We were presenting the evidence. It certainly took longer than it should have,” she said. “It did so on the basis that Israel couldn’t be found to have a commitment to comply with international law because it was restricting aid.” Likewise, the UK’s response to the Sudanese civil war had failed to activate “the full plethora of government machinery”, despite its key resolutions on Sudan at the UN Security Council. With cuts to overseas aid anticipated for the long term, Ms Ahmed – who previously worked as a legal adviser to the FCDO – outlined options that would reinforce the role of human rights in UK foreign policy. The units involved in human rights and atrocity prevention needed to be “supported at the highest-ministerial level, prioritised, given resources and given the power within the bureaucratic system to have a say when policy decisions are being made,” she said. Instead, government advisers on human rights policy were often sidelined. “So often, what I have found, is that the human rights directorate aren't key stakeholders in key political decisions,” Ms Ahmed said. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's declaration last month that settler “terrorists” were responsible for “ethnic cleansing” in the West Bank was a major step, Ms Ahmed said. “That was a really huge development and important to note because it's the first time the government has ever made any such determination and it's clear, given the magnitude of the forced displacement of Palestinians from their land in the West Bank,” she said. Questions remain about how the UK will implement its most significant foreign policy shift in months – the move to impose sanctions on the expansion of illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank. Foreign Office officials have suggested a six to nine month time frame for initial measures to be implemented but campaigners including Ms Ahmed say this is too long. “As I understand it, there is a commitment to implementing it in a way that’s effective,” she said. “The devil will be in the detail to ensure that they in fact do that.” Amnesty International and other organisations are calling on the government to make sure the ban extends to banks and financial services that work with companies involved in illegal settlements. “It’s not just about goods and services to settlements. It’s also about the financial enabling of the occupation … which are involved in continuing the financial stability of the settlements,” Ms Ahmed said.

title: IMF: Nigeria’s banks need stronger safeguards after recapitalisation
body: *Flags sovereign debt exposure as banking sector risk *Calls for adequate capital, liquidity buffers, timely recognition of bad loans *Warns AI market correction could trigger wider global financial instability By Babajide Komolafe, Economy Editor, in Bangkok, Thailand The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has urged Nigerian authorities to strengthen regulatory safeguards in the banking sector following recapitalisation, warning that “the sovereign and bank nexus is also an important area” of concern for African economies. Read Also: Nigerians still suffer high cost of living, despite economic growth — IMF •PRESS BRIEFING: From left – Director of the Research Department, Silvana Tenreyro; Deputy Director, Research Department, Petya Koeva-Brooks, and Division Chief, Research Department, Deniz Igan, all of International Monetary Fund, IMF, at the press briefing on the Fund’s World Economic Outlook, WEO, report, released at the ongoing annual meetings of the World Bank/IMF in Bangkok, Thailand. Photo by Babajide Komolafe. Assistant Director, Monetary and Capital Markets Department, IMF, Jason Wu, gave this recommendation at a press briefing on the release of its Global Financial Stability Report, during the ongoing World Bank/IMF annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, stressing that stronger capital bases must be complemented by adequate liquidity requirements, timely recognition of bad loans and effective monitoring of banks’ exposure to government debt to build resilience against financial shocks. Wu said: “What we often see in emerging economies is that, after recapitalisation, there is a need to impose appropriate regulations to prevent risks from building up in the future.” He added: “These include adequate capital and liquidity requirements as well as timely recognition of credit losses and bad loans.” Highlighting the relationship between banks and governments as a critical area requiring closer attention in Africa, Wu said, “In Africa in particular, I think the sovereign, bank nexus is also an important area. So is understanding the exposure to sovereign risks.” He stressed that these measures were essential to strengthening the banking system, stating: “So I think those are critical elements to building further resilience in the banking sector.” Monetary policy outlook Commenting on the recent decision of the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) to reduce its Monetary Policy Rate, MPR, by 350 basis points to 23 per cent, following the three consecutive months decline in the country’s inflation rate to 15.39 per cent in August from 15.93 in May 2026, Wu noted that Nigeria’s improving inflation outlook could create room for a less restrictive stance, while emphasising the need for credible, data-driven decisions by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN). “We have seen improvements on the inflation front, which suggests that perhaps a not-as-tight monetary policy stance would be appropriate,” Wu stated, stressing that the CBN must sustain confidence in its policy decisions. “I think what’s important is credibility. The central bank has to be data-driven and has to be able to explain the decisions clearly. So far, based on what we have seen, it seems like the news is on the good front,” he said. Wu further emphasised the importance of communication in managing inflation, saying: “Further data dependence, clear, transparent monetary policy communications give a key to containing this wave of inflation shocks.” AI boom poses global financial risks Beyond Nigeria, the IMF, in its Global Financial Stability, GFS Report, warned that the growing concentration of investments in artificial intelligence (AI), coupled with ambitious earnings expectations, could expose global financial markets to a potentially destabilising correction. The GFS report, among other things, highlighted financing arrangements involving AI companies, including equity investments, debt and commitments linked to future revenues. Explaining the findings from the report, Deputy Director, Monetary and Capital Markets Department, IMF, Athanasios Vamvakidisan, said: “We looked at 14 public transactions and what we found is about $300 billion in equity investments and $650 billion in debt investments.” Vamvakidisan explained that the transactions involved “$1.4 trillion of future revenue commitments,” adding that the future revenue component made the arrangements unusual. He warned that the structure could amplify losses if AI companies failed to deliver expected returns. “If there are questions about the monetisation in AI, the equity investments will deplete the value, the debt may be difficult to service and the revenue commitments in the future may not materialise,” he said. The GFS report also questioned whether the strong earnings performance that has supported market optimism could continue indefinitely. “In recent quarters, the actual earnings beat these expectations and the market upgraded the forecast even higher,” Vamvakidisan said, describing a cycle in which positive earnings surprises fuel increasingly ambitious expectations. He warned that sustaining the trend could become more difficult as expectations rise and market exposures become concentrated. Vanguard News The post IMF: Nigeria’s banks need stronger safeguards after recapitalisation appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Judge extends White House access for CNN, MS NOW, Politico amid legal fight
body: WASHINGTON, USA – A federal judge extended access to the White House for CNN, MS NOW, and Politico journalists, deciding on Tuesday, October 13, that President Donald Trump likely broke the law when he tried to ban them, in the latest ruling against him in the press freedom dispute. US District Judge Timothy Kelly issued a written decision that elaborated on his September 24 emergency order that reinstated access for the journalists. The news organizations and press freedom groups have accused Trump of unconstitutional retaliation against journalists for coverage he does not like. Kelly’s order last month gave the CNN, MS NOW, and Politico journalists access to the White House grounds on a temporary basis. The judge issued a ruling called a preliminary injunction on Tuesday that will remain in effect until he makes a final judgment in the lawsuit brought by the news organizations, unless an appeals court lifts his order. Kelly wrote that Trump’s public remarks made clear that he banned the news outlets because he considered their reporting biased and inaccurate, and not because of national security concerns as government lawyers later asserted in court. “Simply put, that is unlawful viewpoint discrimination,” the judge wrote, adding that “no one should read this decision as suggesting that President Trump’s complaints are meritless.” Trump appointed Kelly in 2017 during his first presidential term. Campaign against media Past presidents have battled with the press, but Trump’s campaign against the media has been unprecedented. He has upended decades of tradition by ​denying basic access to many major news organizations, launching personal attacks on journalists for their reporting and elevating media outlets seen as more sympathetic to the administration. He also has filed lawsuits against multiple news outlets. Trump announced the ban in September on his social ​media platform, saying CNN, Politico, and MS NOW “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States.” The Justice Department has emphasized ​Trump’s contention that the ban is legally justified on national security grounds. The outlets have said the revocation of their White House passes was unlawful retaliation for their news coverage and accused the Trump administration of manufacturing meritless national security concerns to justify the ban. The outlets said in a lawsuit that the ban violated the US ⁠Constitution’s First Amendment protections for freedom of speech and a free press, as well as their rights to due process, meaning fair treatment from the government. The White House on September 24 reinstated the CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists after Kelly decided the ban “likely violated their constitutional due process rights,” and ordered their access immediately restored. ‘Coerce better coverage’ The judge held a hearing on October 8 to hear arguments by the news outlets and the Justice Department over whether to extend the protection for the journalists against being barred from the White House. The Justice Department defended the bans as fair and justified. “Here we have the unusual situation where the president himself has said he wants to chill speech. He wants to coerce better coverage,” Theodore Boutrous, an attorney for the outlets, told Kelly during the hearing. “CNN, MS NOW, and Politico engaged in apparently indefensible conduct,” Justice Department lawyer Michael Velchik said. The legal battle is being waged just weeks before the November 3 US midterm elections in which Trump’s ‌fellow Republicans ⁠are fighting to retain control of Congress. Trump’s job approval ratings are at record lows in opinion polls amid concerns over issues such as inflation and the Iran war. – Rappler.com

title: Water After Glaciers: Preparing Kazakhstan for Different Water Future
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s water future may depend less on how much water reaches its rivers than on when it arrives. Climate change is shifting snowmelt, glacier runoff and river-flow peaks across Central Asia, forcing the country to rethink how it stores, forecasts and uses water. A view of the Tian Shan mountain peaks near Almaty, Kazakhstan. Photo credit: Reuters For centuries, Central Asia’s mountains have acted as a natural water-storage system. Snow accumulates in winter, glaciers store water as ice, and meltwater feeds rivers during the warmer months. But that seasonal balance is changing. Central Asian glaciers experienced their most severe year of ice loss on record in 2025, losing an estimated 30 cubic kilometers of ice, equivalent to nearly 2% of the region’s remaining glacier volume, according to a study published in Environmental Research Letters in May. Kazakhstan has more than 2,400 glaciers covering approximately 930 square kilometers, according to data maintained by the Central Asian Regional Glaciological Center. Earlier estimates recorded 2,724 glaciers nationwide. In the Ile Alatau, the glacierized area declined by 47.4% between 1955 and 2021. The changes have implications for regional water security: glacier melt accounted for approximately 25% of annual river discharge in the northern Tien Shan during 1991-2021, while 44.3% of Kazakhstan’s average annual surface-water resources originate beyond its borders. When the water arrives matters Tomas Saks, a senior researcher at the Department of Geosciences at the University of Fribourg, said snow cover remains the dominant source of river runoff in Central Asia, accounting for around 70-80% of total runoff. Glaciers provide a smaller share annually, around 6-10% for the Syr Darya and Amu Darya. Their importance rises sharply during dry summer months, when most seasonal snow has already melted. “In the dry summer seasons, when most of the snow has already melted, glaciers contribute up to 80%, making them a crucial water resource for the dry summer months,” Saks told The Astana Times. This means glacier retreat is not simply a matter of declining annual water volumes. One of the first major changes is seasonality. Saks expects the Syr Darya’s peak runoff to shift from roughly July-August towards May-June as snow melts earlier. Summer runoff is then expected to decline as glacier volumes decrease. The Amu Darya is also projected to reach its peak earlier, although its larger, higher-elevation glaciers are expected to continue supplying significant summer meltwater for longer. Planning for a changing water calendar Kazakhstan is adapting its water policy to this shift. The country’s Water Code , adopted in 2025, incorporates climate adaptation into water-sector management. The Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation told The Astana Times that it is now assessing long-term water availability at the basin level. The ministry expects to complete eight basin plans by the end of this year. The Balkhash-Alakol, Aral-Syr Darya and Shu-Talas basins have been identified among the most climate-sensitive because of high water demand, snow- and glacier-fed rivers and dependence on transboundary flows. For Saks, this basin-level approach is important because climate change will not affect every river in the same way. Storage can buy time Kazakhstan plans to build 42 new reservoirs, adding 2.6 billion cubic meters of storage, while modernizing existing reservoirs and irrigation infrastructure. However, reservoirs cannot create water; they can only store it when it is available. That makes efficiency increasingly important. The ministry plans to reconstruct or modernize more than 4,600 kilometers of irrigation canals. This year alone, 962 kilometers are expected to be upgraded, improving water supply to around 200,000 hectares of irrigated land. As Saks’s projections suggest, the challenge is not simply to store more water, but to capture it when it arrives and use it efficiently when it is needed. Data is part of the solution Saks also stressed the importance of turning scientific knowledge into timely decisions. Central Asia has substantial research on glacier and snow-cover changes. But if snowmelt and river-flow peaks are moving earlier, governments need better forecasts of when water will arrive in each basin. Kazakhstan is developing a National Information System of Water Resources to integrate information on water bodies, infrastructure, water users and water availability, strengthening monitoring and forecasting. Warning signs may appear long before glaciers disappear: earlier snowmelt, lower late-summer river flows, changes in smaller glacier-fed catchments, and growing pressure on irrigation systems. A regional water system Kazakhstan alone cannot manage the changes that Saks describes. Water resources are concentrated mainly in the Kyrgyz Republic and Tajikistan, while major demand is downstream in Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan. Changes in snow and glacier melt therefore affect the entire regional system. As water flows become less predictable, Saks said, cooperation between upstream and downstream countries will become increasingly important. For Kazakhstan, stronger data-sharing, forecasting and agreements over transboundary rivers will be essential. Preparing for a different future A “post-glacier” water system does not mean a future without glaciers or rivers. It means a future in which glaciers can no longer be assumed to provide the same seasonal buffer they have provided for generations. Kazakhstan is responding with new reservoirs, modernized irrigation, basin-level planning and better forecasting. The real test will be whether these measures allow the country to anticipate changes rather than react to shortages. In 2030 and onward, water security may depend not only on how much water Kazakhstan has, but on how accurately it can predict when that water will arrive and how efficiently it can use every drop. The post Water After Glaciers: Preparing Kazakhstan for Different Water Future appeared first on The Astana Times .

title: Fancy Curl Sites
body:
So a good while ago I added a fun curl version of my site, meant for viewing in the terminal. Try running these commands!
(sorry Windows users, not my fault that ANSI escape codes are disabled-by-default in cmd.exe . And not my fault that in Powershell you have to use curl.exe instead of curl because Powershell inexplicably aliases that to Invoke-WebRequest .)
I posted about it a bit on the Fediverse, but otherwise didn't elaborate much on it becuase I figured it was fairly self-explanatory. But I've had a handful of people ask me how I did it, so I decided it might actually be worth it to write a post about how I did it (…like seven months late).
I should note this idea came from trinkey's ( curl trinkey.com ) and strongsand's ( curl proot.party ) curl sites, I didn't come up with it myself. Even though I did go about it quite a bit differently from them, all credit for the very cool idea goes to them. (UPDATE: unfortunately neither of their curl versions are functional anymore as of 2026-10-14.)
First, since it's the more interesting part, actually generating the ANSI-marked-up files to send to the clients. I entirely hand-wrote the index page and about page .
Note that I believe trinkey and strongsand generate theirs on-the-fly with the ratatui library (or similar), which is probably more convenient; hand-writing it seemed more expedient to me though.
I had the main escape code— ESC[ , i.e. \x1b[ — 1 in a Vim register to easily paste when needed, and then the Wikipedia page for the main graphics codes open to reference the specific escape codes. And, yeah, that's about it. I experimented to decide on consistent styling I liked, and just referenced the Gopher version of my pages when crafting the marked-up curl pages.
Now, the notable thing about my version is that I have curl versions of the entirety of my blog, rather than just one or two pages being available. This is entirely due to a convenient coincidence: over four years ago I implemented outputting ANSI-marked-up plaintext in my custom markup language I use for my blog, Gemroff . Originally it was just to allow convenient previewing of drafts in the terminal while writing; but it was trivial to plug into my static site generator to immediately get Curl versions generated.
I did manually write a wrapper template for blog posts , as well as a template for the index page listing posts , but that plus a few extra lines in my static site generator was all that was needed to wire it up.
This is the main thing that makes it hard to say it's easy! since it was only easy for me because I use an entirely custom markup language and static site generator and I happened to make the right design choices years ago—e.g. my SSG also happened to already have support for multiple, modular output formats instead of solely HTML like other SSGs, since I tri-host my site on HTTP, Gemini, and Gopher.
However, offering nothing but a few hand-written pages for fun is a completely acceptable way to set up a site like this anyways, since it's just a neat gimmick and no one's likely to actually use it more than a few minutes of browsing.
Finally, the last step is actually presenting the Curl version of your site to any user agent containing curl , which for me was just a few changes to my Nginx config , with other servers it'd presumably be equivalently simple. The main feature I wanted was an override header ( X-Original: true ) so you could still get an unmodified HTTP response like someone casually running Curl likely wanted, and I wanted everything to be served statically still.
And… that's really it! As I said, when I first set it up it seemed fairly self-explanatory to me, but it is very non-orthogonal to what people normally do with either web servers or ANSI escape codes so I can see where people's curiosity/confusion came from. It would be neat to see more sites doing this trick around!
EMDASH! AI-GENERATED! acksually I'll have you know that my markup language has had an explicit markup element for emdashes since November 2022 . And believe it nor not: LLMs are trained on shit copied from actual authors, so LLMs wouldn't be using emdashes if they weren't already used in human-written works.
And what, am I supposed to avoid having twenty parentheticals a paragraph, to where I feel the need to use emdashes to vary it up? Unthinkable! ↩︎

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,557,350 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
body:
Russia has lost 1,557,350 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 14.
The number includes 1,650 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,414 tanks, 25,535 armored combat vehicles, 162,789 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,195 artillery systems, 2,212 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,704 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,951 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1." A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action. While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action. The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: Russia launches 39 missiles, 128 UAVs at Ukraine; 4 missiles, 115 drones downed or suppressed – Air Force
body:
Russian forces on Wednesday overnight deployed 39 missiles and 128 drones of various types against Ukraine, of which air defense forces shot down or suppressed four missiles and 115 UAVs, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
"On the night of October 14 (from 18:00 on October 13), the enemy launched a massive combined strike against Ukraine using strike UAVs and 39 missiles of various types approaching targets on a ballistic trajectory," the Air Force said in a message on Telegram.
In total, the radio-technical troops of the Air Force recorded 167 air attack weapons – 39 missiles and 128 drones of various types.
According to preliminary data as of 09:00, air defense shot down or suppressed four missiles and 115 enemy UAVs, including 59 jet-powered drones. According to the Air Force, this accounts for 90% of the total number of strike UAVs.
Russian forces used Iskander-M, KN-23, S-400, Zircon, and Oniks missiles, as well as Shahed strike drones, including jet-powered ones, Banderol/Dan-T, Gerbera, Italmas, and Parodiya-type decoy drones.
The main directions of the strike were Kyiv, Kyiv region, and Kharkiv region. According to the Air Force, a key feature of the attack was the simultaneous deployment of various air attack weapons from multiple directions, along with a large number of ballistic missiles targeting energy infrastructure facilities.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, as well as mobile fire groups of the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
According to preliminary information as of 09:00, impacts of missiles and strike UAVs were recorded at 22 locations, with falling debris from intercepted targets recorded at eight locations. Some Russian missiles failed to reach their targets.
As of the time of publication, the attack was ongoing, with Russian strike drones remaining in Ukrainian airspace.

title: DRDO to lead thematic session on ‘Semiconductors & Next-Gen Chips’ at ESTIC-2026
body:
By R Anil Kumar

Bengaluru, Oct 13, 2026. Defence Research & Development Organisation (DRDO) will spearhead a thematic session on ‘Semiconductors and Next-Gen Chips’ during Emerging Science, Technology & Innovation Conclave (ESTIC-2026) scheduled to be held at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi from October 27 to 29, 2026. The conclave is being jointly organised by 12 ministries/departments under the guidance of the Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India. It is a significant national initiative aimed at advancing the vision of Viksit Bharat @ 2047 and strengthening Aatmanirbharta through science, technology and innovation.



The DRDO session will bring together eminent leaders from the industry, academia, indigenous chip-development ecosystem and defence electronics. It will feature a keynote address by VP & MD, Micron India followed by talks by CEO, Bharat Semi, CEO, Netrasemi and Director, IIT Madras. The talks will explore key developments in semiconductor technologies, purpose-built AI system-on-chips, intelligence at the silicon edge and the evolving microprocessor landscape.

The speakers with diverse expertise will enable a substantive dialogue on semiconductor fabrication, chip design, AI computing, indigenous semiconductor platforms, research and development, and strategic and defence applications. The session is expected to foster stronger collaboration among industry, academia and strategic stakeholders, identify emerging technological opportunities and contribute to the development of a robust domestic semiconductor ecosystem, with emphasis on indigenous capabilities for critical and next-generation applications.

The Outreach Stall at ESTIC 2026 will provide a platform to showcase the Ministry’s key initiatives, achievements, research programmes, and contributions to science, technology, and innovation. The stall will feature a diverse range of indigenous technologies developed by DRDO laboratories, including advanced communication systems, quantum technology prototypes, extreme-cold-weather clothing, the PRABALA female full-body protector, passive and powered exoskeletons, portable hybrid energy management systems, high-power pulse laser diodes, and scramjet engine technology.

The exhibits will highlight ongoing efforts to strengthen indigenous R&D, promote technology development and self-reliance, and address critical requirements in defence and other strategic sectors. The stall will also foster collaboration among academia, industry, start-ups, and research institutions while enhancing public awareness of the Ministry’s role in advancing India’s scientific and technological capabilities.

Presiding over the curtain-raiser event organised by DRDO in Bengaluru, Karnataka on October 13, 2026, Distinguished Scientist and Director General (Electronics and Communication Systems) Dr BK Das underscored the importance of semiconductors and next-gen chips for economic competitiveness, digital sovereignty and national security. He stressed that building an end-to-end, resilient microelectronics ecosystem is essential to powering telecommunications, automotive systems, industrial automation, AI hardware and strategic defence platforms as India advances towards Viksit Bharat.

Dr Das added that strengthening domestic capabilities is critical to protecting the national economy from global supply-chain disruptions, geopolitical volatility and international technology export controls. He underlined India's aim to emerge as a global semiconductor powerhouse, advancing strategic autonomy and high-value exports across the microelectronics value chain.

Distinguished Scientist and Director General (Technology Management) Dr Anupam Sharma highlighted the critical role of semiconductors in modern warfare, stating that these technologies are integral to virtually every aspect of military operations. He added that business in the semiconductor-related segment is expected to rise to 200 billion dollars by 2035.

Director, Directorate of Extramural Research & Intellectual Property Rights, Director, Solid State Physics Laboratory, Director, Electronics and Radar Development Establishment and Center Head, Combat Aircraft Systems Development & Integration Centre were among those present on the occasion.

title: Court Jails Man Six Months For Forcefully Evicting Wife, Destroying House
body: An Iboko High Court sitting in Abakaliki, the Ebonyi State capital, has sentenced a 39-year-old man, Chituru Mbam, to six months’ imprisonment without the option of a fine for forcefully evicting his wife, Mbam Ozoemena, from their matrimonial home and subsequently destroying the property. The couple, who married in 2009 and share five children, had been experiencing marital conflicts for several years, ultimately culminating in the forced eviction. Court proceedings revealed that at midnight on January 6, 2026, Mbam, accompanied by two unidentified men, invaded the family residence and evicted his wife shortly after he relocated to a newly completed building. Following the eviction, he caused her arrest and detention at the Police Headquarters in Abakaliki. While she was held in police custody, Mbam allegedly invaded the property again, removing the roof, doors, windows, and other valuable fittings to render the building completely uninhabitable. The incident sparked swift intervention from a local human rights organization, the Rose Foundation for the Protection of Women and Children. The organisation’s Executive Secretary, Professor Mike Ajanwachukwu, submitted a formal petition to the Ebonyi State Commissioner of Police, leading to Mbam’s arrest and prosecution. Delivering the judgment on Monday, the presiding judge, Justice Ruth Okeh, found the defendant guilty of the charges. In addition to the six-month custodial sentence, the court ordered Mbam to pay his wife ₦500,000 in damages and directed him to secure a befitting shelter for her. Reacting to the verdict, counsel to the complainant, Mrs. Ijeoma Mike-Ajanwachukwu, commended the judiciary for upholding justice, emphasizing that no spouse has the legal right to eject another from a shared home. “The defendant committed an offence punishable under Section 6 (1) of the Violence Against Persons Prohibition (VAPP) Law of Ebonyi State (2018), which strictly prohibits a spouse from forcefully evicting another,” Mrs. Mike-Ajanwachukwu stated. “He evicted his wife from her matrimonial home, destroyed the building, and moved into a new residence with another woman.” “He effectively rendered her homeless by deploying police officers and thugs to drive her out.” The post Court Jails Man Six Months For Forcefully Evicting Wife, Destroying House appeared first on Channels Television .
