title: UAE weather: Rainy weekend expected in east of country
body: Rain is expected in parts of the UAE across much of the weekend, according to the latest update from the National Centre of Meteorology (NCM). Wet weather is forecast in the south-east of the country on Wednesday, with winds reaching up to 50kph. On Friday and Saturday, clouds in the east are likely to bring rain, while wet weather is forecast in the north-east. The NCM's website says rain is expected on Wednesday in Fujairah and in Al Ain on Thursday. At the weekend, the highest temperature in the country will be 41°C in Sweihan on Saturday. The temperature will reach 39°C in Abu Dhabi on Saturday, with Dubai's temperature cooling slightly from 37°C on Wednesday and Thursday to 35°C on Saturday and Sunday.

title: Russian combined attack on Kyiv kills four, injures 27
body:
According to Ukrinform, the Kyiv City Prosecutor’s Office reported this on Facebook .
As of 8:50 on Wednesday, October 14, three women had been killed and 19 people injured in Russia’s overnight attack on the Desnianskyi district. The injured included a seven-year-old girl who sustained cuts and burns to her arm.
The fire damaged apartments on the first through eighth floors of a nine-story residential building. Windows were also blown out in a nearby building, injuring five people.
Russian forces continued striking the capital overnight and in the morning of October 14. One person was killed in the Holosiivskyi district, and another was injured.
The final number of casualties is being established.
Under the procedural supervision of the Kyiv City Prosecutor’s Office, a pre-trial investigation has been launched into another alleged war crime committed by Russian military personnel under Part 2 of Article 438 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine.
Earlier, Kyiv police reported three fatalities.
Law enforcement officers are documenting damage to private houses and apartment buildings, cars, an office building, a coffee shop, a library, a stadium and a school.
More than 100 police officers have been deployed to deal with the aftermath of the attack. They continue working at the sites alongside rescuers, medical personnel and other emergency services.
As Ukrinform reported, the Russian attack caused emergency power outages in Kyiv’s Darnytskyi, Dniprovskyi, Pecherskyi and Solomianskyi districts, as well as part of the Holosiivskyi district.

title: Zayed National Museum's first temporary exhibition to explore 7,000 years of camel history
body: Zayed National Museum has announced its first temporary exhibition, exploring more than 7,000 years of camel history and the animal's significance in Emirati culture. Tracks Through Time: The Camel in Society, Trade and Art will open in early December, coinciding with the Abu Dhabi museum's first anniversary. The exhibition will trace the camel's role in trade, society and artistic expression, from its presence in the region thousands of years ago to contemporary traditions such as racing and beauty competitions. Among the highlights will be the first public display of archaeological evidence of an extinct wild camel species. These include bones discovered in Baynunah in Abu Dhabi, from between 4500 and 4000BC, and Bronze Age remains from Al Sufouh in Dubai, dating to between 2000 and 1300BC. Domesticated camel bones from Saruq Al Hadid in Dubai will also be displayed, offering some of the world's earliest evidence of the transition from wild camels to domesticated animals. The artefacts are on loan from the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi, and the Dubai Culture and Arts Authority. “We are excited to present our first temporary exhibition, which celebrates the camel's profound significance in Emirati culture and the broader story of the UAE,” says Peter Magee, director of the Zayed National Museum . He says the exhibition draws on archaeological research to explore the relationship between humans and camels, from early domestication to the prestige of Al Hejin racing and Mazayna beauty competitions. Other objects include camel rock artwork from Fujairah dating back 3,000 years, a rare children's book from the 1840s detailing camel species and their uses and UAE postage stamps featuring the animal. Archival photographs, film footage and oral testimonies from camel herders will offer further insight into the animal's place in daily life. Recordings of Taghrooda, a form of Bedouin poetry, and Alheda'a , the traditional practice of camel calling, will also feature. Both are recognised by Unesco as intangible cultural heritage. The exhibition will be accompanied by workshops, guided tours and activities as part of the museum's first anniversary celebrations, alongside a dedicated retail offering inspired by the exhibition's themes. Tracks Through Time: The Camel in Society, Trade and Art opens at Zayed National Museum in Abu Dhabi in early December

title: Netanyahu says he didn't meet Egyptian spy chief during pre-Oct. 7 visit to Israel. So who did?
body: "Egypt's intelligence minister was here. He spent 59 minutes on the ground. I'm turning to the security and law enforcement authorities. I want to know whom he met. Someone who met with him is trying to pin this on me." With those remarks Tuesday evening, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu confirmed that Abbas Kamel, Egypt's former intelligence chief, had visited Israel shortly before the October 7, 2023 massacre. According to reports, Kamel had arrived with a warning that Hamas was preparing a major attack. Netanyahu's acknowledgment, delivered during an interview with Channel 14, has raised more questions than answers. On Wednesday morning, Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana told Kan public radio that Kamel had arrived in Israel 11 days before the massacre and had apparently met a senior security official. "He met someone here. The question is whom," Ohana said. "My assessment is that he met one of the heads of the security establishment. The prime minister is calling for an investigation, and so am I. We have no answer to that question."   The reported Egyptian warning is not new. Just two days after the massacre, ynet's Smadar Perry reported, following an Associated Press report about an Egyptian warning, that Kamel had conveyed a message to Netanyahu's office concerning "something unusual, a massive operation" that was being prepared in Gaza. The Prime Minister's Office denied receiving such a warning. Yet three years later, it remains unclear whether any serious effort was made to establish whether Egyptian officials had delivered information to Israel's security establishment, even if it had not reached Netanyahu personally. According to previously published flight records, an aircraft associated with Egyptian intelligence landed at Ben Gurion Airport shortly before 10 a.m. on September 26, 2023. It departed for Cairo 67 minutes later. Netanyahu insists that he neither spoke with nor met Kamel during the visit. But identifying who did meet him would appear to offer a relatively straightforward starting point for an investigation. The prime minister could, for example, ask Transportation Minister Miri Regev to have airport officials examine any available security camera footage or records from that day. Whether he has taken such a step remains unclear. The episode also raises a broader question about Netanyahu's oversight of the security establishment. If Egypt's intelligence chief held a meeting with senior Israeli security officials less than two weeks before the massacre, how could the prime minister have been unaware of it? At the very least, the possibility of such an encounter taking place without his knowledge raises questions about the management of sensitive security and intelligence matters. Netanyahu also offered an explanation for why he would not have met Kamel himself. "He didn't speak to me. Since when does an intelligence chief speak to a head of state? It's never happened to me. There's no such thing. He would always come with someone," he said. Yet just two years earlier, Netanyahu had hosted Kamel at the prime minister's residence in Jerusalem. Footage released by the Prime Minister's Office in 2021 showed the two shaking hands and speaking during a visit by a delegation of senior Egyptian officials led by Kamel. While that meeting does not establish that Netanyahu met him in September 2023, it contradicts his broader claim that such encounters do not take place. For now, Netanyahu's demand for answers has been made publicly on television. On previous occasions, the prime minister has issued formal announcements stating that he instructed security agencies to investigate particular matters. This time, however, it remains unclear whether he has issued such instructions or sought to examine the airport's security records. 'We do not underestimate any threat' The controversy resurfaced last month when The Atlantic published an investigation revealing details of Kamel's brief September 26, 2023 visit. According to the magazine, the Egyptian intelligence chief warned Israeli officials that Hamas appeared to be preparing a major attack and urged Israel to introduce economic concessions in Gaza to prevent an escalation. The warning did not specify a date or provide detailed operational information. Flight records cited in the investigation showed that the aircraft carrying Kamel remained in Israel for just 67 minutes before returning to Cairo. A former Israeli official interviewed by The Atlantic said the extraordinary nature of the visit should itself have made the urgency of Kamel's message clear. The fact that the head of Egyptian intelligence had traveled to Israel for such a brief meeting was significant. "The messenger was the message," the official said. About two hours after the Egyptian aircraft landed, Netanyahu attended a ceremony in Jerusalem marking the 50th anniversary of the Yom Kippur War. Reflecting on the lessons of that surprise attack, he declared: "We do not underestimate any threat." The Wall Street Journal separately reported that Kamel called Netanyahu in early October 2023 to warn him of an impending attack from Gaza, after two earlier Egyptian warnings had reportedly gone unheeded. According to the newspaper, Kamel was growing increasingly anxious about the situation. The report reinforced the account first published by Smadar Perry in ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth in the days following the massacre. Netanyahu continues to deny that he spoke with Kamel or personally received the reported warning.

title: G-24: Nigeria, other developing nations need cheaper financing — Oyedele
body: By Babajide Komolafe, Economy Editor, in Bangkok, Thailand The Intergovernmental Group of Twenty-Four on International Monetary Affairs and Development, G-24, has called for improved financing conditions, faster debt restructuring and stronger international financial cooperation to support Nigeria and other developing economies facing mounting debt and development financing challenges. Read Also: Nigerians still suffer high cost of living, despite economic growth — IMF Nigeria’s Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Mr Taiwo Oyedele, who is Chairman of the Intergovernmental Group of Twenty-Four on International Monetary Affairs and Development, G-24, made the call at a press conference on the outcome of the meeting of the Group, during the ongoing International Monetary Fund (IMF)/World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand. He said developing countries needed a more responsive international financial system capable of addressing their economic vulnerabilities, supporting growth and ensuring that debt obligations did not undermine development priorities. “Debt vulnerability is a major obstacle to growth in many developing countries,” Oyedele said, highlighting the need for predictable and coordinated approaches to resolving sovereign debt problems. “We call for predictable, timely and coordinated sovereign debt treatments,” he said, stressing the importance of cooperation between creditors and debtors in resolving debt difficulties. The G-24 chairman said the growing financing challenges confronting developing economies required collective action by governments, multilateral development institutions and other international stakeholders. His position reflects concerns that high borrowing costs and debt-service obligations are limiting the fiscal space available to developing countries to finance infrastructure, healthcare, education and other development priorities. Oyedele said the international community must also strengthen the voice and representation of developing economies, particularly vulnerable countries, in global financial institutions. He called for reforms that would make the international financial architecture more responsive to the changing structure of the global economy and the needs of developing countries. “We emphasised the importance of strengthening the voice and representation of developing countries, particularly the most vulnerable economies, in international financial institutions,” he said. According to him, a more representative multilateral system is essential to restoring confidence in the global economy and ensuring that international economic decisions take account of the circumstances of developing nations. “Restoring confidence in the global economy requires a multilateral system grounded in respect for national sovereignty and the principles of the United Nations Charter,” he said. Climate financing Oyedele also called for increased climate financing for developing countries, arguing that efforts to address climate change must take account of the economic and social challenges facing vulnerable populations. He said climate action should not undermine the livelihoods of people in developing countries, particularly those struggling with poverty, food insecurity and inadequate access to essential services. The G-24 chairman stressed the importance of international cooperation in mobilising the resources required to support climate adaptation and sustainable development. “We also stressed the importance of expanding access to climate finance, guided by the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities,” he said. He urged multilateral development banks and other stakeholders to meet their financing commitments. “We expect the World Bank Group, multilateral development banks and other stakeholders to deliver on the target of mobilising at least $300 billion annually by 2035, as established at COP29,” Oyedele said. He also called for international tax reforms to address tax avoidance, profit shifting and illicit financial flows, which reduce the resources available to governments for development. “On international taxation, we called for reforms to address profit shifting, tax avoidance and illicit financial flows,” he said. Oyedele welcomed progress under the United Nations Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)/G20 Inclusive Framework. Growth must create jobs Director of the G-24 Secretariat, Iyabo Masha, said economic growth must translate into jobs, better living standards and improved opportunities for citizens rather than being measured solely by macroeconomic indicators. “The objective is to create a more liveable environment for our people, irrespective of their circumstances,” Masha said. She stressed that growth must be inclusive and provide tangible benefits for households, particularly young people seeking employment and economic opportunities. “Economic growth must create jobs, provide opportunities for young people and improve living standards,” she said. Masha added that the quality of growth was as important as the pace of expansion. “Growth should be inclusive and translate into tangible benefits for households,” she said. Oyedele, however, emphasised that macroeconomic stability remained a necessary foundation for achieving these development objectives. “Macroeconomic stability is not a bad policy objective. It is actually the foundation of economic growth,” he said. “If a country does not have a stable macroeconomic environment, it becomes difficult to implement structural reforms, employment-generating policies, infrastructure development and other measures needed to support growth,” he added. According to him, macroeconomic stability should complement policies designed to promote productive investment, employment and inclusive development. “The ultimate objective is to ensure that economic growth improves the living standards of our people,” he said. The G-24 also called for reforms to the IMF quota system to reflect changes in the global economy and improve developing countries’ representation in the institution’s decision-making processes. The group argued that the quota framework should recognise the growing importance of emerging markets and developing economies while protecting the interests of smaller and poorer members. It also stressed the need for stronger coordination among creditors, greater transparency in sovereign debt negotiations and more effective participation by private creditors in debt restructuring. The G-24 said these measures would help improve the international debt resolution framework, reduce prolonged uncertainty for countries facing debt distress and create better conditions for sustainable economic growth. Oyedele said restoring confidence in the global economy would require a multilateral system that respects national sovereignty while responding more effectively to the financing and development needs of vulnerable economies. Vanguard News The post G-24: Nigeria, other developing nations need cheaper financing — Oyedele appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: NAFDAC Bursts Over 20 Fake Alcoholic Drink Factories At Lagos Trade Fair Complex
body: Operatives of the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC), on Tuesday, uncovered a large-scale counterfeit alcoholic beverage operation at the Zamfara Plaza, BBA Trade Fair Complex, along the Badagry Expressway, Ojo, Lagos State. A statement by the Agency noted that the feat was achieved by its Investigation & Enforcement (I&E) Directorate, which raided the facility. Operatives of the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC) during the operation at the Zamfara Plaza, BBA Trade Fair Complex, along the Badagry Expressway, Ojo, Lagos State, on Tuesday, October 13, 2026. According to NAFDAC, the fake alcoholic beverage operation concealed within makeshift parking stores on the premises was executed based on credible intelligence and resulted in the discovery of more than 20 illegal stores engaged in criminal operations within the complex. NAFDAC noted that its officers found suspects in the process of blending and counterfeiting popular alcoholic beverage brands, revalidating expired and unsafe beverages for resale, and stockpiling banned imported products. Two suspects were apprehended during the operations, while products seized and evacuated are valued at over ₦2 billion. The Agency urged members of the public to remain vigilant and report any suspicious manufacturing, revalidation, or sales activity through NAFDAC’s official complaints line: 0800-1-NAFDAC (0800-1-623322). title: 'Blown out of proportion' — Domestic politics at the core of South Korea's rift with Ukraine
body:
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung listens to a journalist during a news conference at the presidential Blue House in Seoul, South Korea, on Sept. 18, 2026. (SeongJoon Cho/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Seoul's diplomatic spat with Kyiv continues to deepen, but experts say it is less about Ukraine than about South Korea's own politics.
The East Asian country, traditionally counted among Ukraine 's partners in the region, announced on Oct. 8 that it is recalling its ambassador from Kyiv amid a dispute over North Korean prisoners of war (POWs).
The rift started on Sept. 23 with President Volodymyr Zelensky telling the U.N. General Assembly that Kyiv had transferred two North Korean POWs, captured while fighting on Russia's side, to Seoul.
The move angered South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who accused Ukraine of violating a confidentiality agreement. Ukraine initially claimed that there was no such deal, with Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha later downplaying the situation as a "diplomatic misunderstanding."
In a matter of days, the row turned into a never-ending tit-for-tat war of words: on Oct. 6, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said that Ukraine had privately apologized for the incident but that the apology was, apparently, "insufficient."
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry responded that Sybiha had merely expressed regret that the situation had escalated to this level, noting that diplomatic correspondence should remain confidential.
While there is no end in sight to the diplomatic stand-off, experts who spoke to the Kyiv Independent argued that none of this was likely to affect the strategic side of relations between Ukraine and South Korea.
“Even now, (South Korea’s) Foreign Ministry says cooperation with Ukraine will continue, so hopefully a cooling-down period will come, and both countries can get back to what is really important.”
Instead, the feud says more about the politically tense situation of President Lee — and about South Korea's piling geopolitical challenges.
After the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, South Korea has officially joined Western-led anti-Russian sanctions, notably by restricting strategic exports and helping cut Moscow off from the international financial system.
In practice, the sanctions regime is not fully respected. For instance, the Guardian has found that Seoul is now exporting diesel by sea to Russia , after heavy Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries caused shortages across the country.
"South Korea joined the sanctions, but is partially circumventing them, and is not ready to openly supply Ukraine with weapons," explained Leonid Petrov, a Korea researcher at the Australian National University.
Seoul maintains this ambivalent approach because authorities want to be able to normalize ties with Moscow if the war in Ukraine ends, said Sydney Seiler, a researcher and former U.S. national intelligence officer for North Korea.
On the other hand, South Korea remains a donor — albeit a relatively minor one — of humanitarian and non-lethal military aid to Ukraine, with commitments totaling approximately $627 million since 2022, according to the Kiel Institute.
"And when it comes to arms deliveries, South Korea doesn't support Ukraine openly, but it can do this indirectly, for instance, by selling arms to (an intermediary like) Poland," explained Chun In-Bum, a retired South Korean lieutenant general and expert affiliated with the Institute for Security and Development Policy, a Stockholm-based think tank.
Another issue is intelligence cooperation, where South Korea is seriously interested in learning from Ukraine's wartime experience, Chun said.
"Even now, (South Korea's) Foreign Ministry says cooperation with Ukraine will continue, so hopefully a cooling-down period will come, and both countries can get back to what is really important," he added.
Ultimately, the Ukraine-South Korea feud was mainly about Kyiv's announcement seemingly getting in the way of potential talks between Seoul and Pyongyang, according to Seiler.
"Lee is interested in warming up relations with North Korea and ultimately in holding a summit with (North Korean dictator) Kim Jong Un," noted Fyodor Tertitskiy, an international relations scholar at Korea University in Seoul.
On the North Korean side, though, there is absolutely no interest in rapprochement with Seoul, experts who spoke to the Kyiv Independent agreed. In any case, Seiler doubts the POW transfer would have much bearing on whether Kim decides to engage.
But since Lee cares deeply about this initiative, his administration is particularly sensitive to it, Chun explained.
On top of the diplomatic issues, Zelensky's announcement also raised some worry about the security of the transferred North Korean soldiers.
"It's quite well-known that South Korea is full of North Korean spies, many of whom disguise (themselves) as people who defected from the North," Petrov explained. "So, it makes sense that these kinds of exchanges should be done quietly."
But Chun believes that Zelensky's announcement at the U.N. General Assembly did not change much in terms of the soldiers' safety, as North Korea would have found out about the exchange anyway.
The development came at a particularly sensitive time for Lee, whose ratings fell for a second week in a row to 35.2%, an Oct. 12 poll showed .
According to Petrov, these ratings were also one of the reasons why Zelensky's move became "a scandal deliberately blown out of proportion" by Seoul.
Finally, South Korea's changing geopolitical situation also plays a role. With China, Russia, and North Korea in the immediate vicinity, authorities in Seoul are increasingly wary of the strengthening alliance of the three countries.
"Lee Jae Myung is mainly just trying not to irritate any of these countries," Petrov said.
But Lee's administration might not be "fully comprehending" the geopolitical shifts going on in the region, Seiler said, by insisting on attempts to appease North Korea, which "aren’t working," rather than prioritizing cooperation with partners like Ukraine and the U.S.
"In any case, Zelensky did the right thing" by transferring the North Korean soldiers to Seoul, Chun said.
"This was a courageous move, especially (since) they could have just sent them back to Russia — as a Korean, I am just personally thankful to Ukraine that they did not."
Karol Łuczka is a freelance journalist focused on Ukraine and Russia. He also works as Eastern Europe Advocacy Lead at the Vienna-based International Press Institute (IPI). Karol holds an MA in International Security from Sciences Po Paris.

title: TCab Tech and SIDEC sign MOU to advance E20 eVTOL commercialization in Malaysia
body: On October 9, 2026, the “Malaysian Engineers, Global Impact: TCab Tech E20 eVTOL Showcase”, jointly organized by the Selangor Information Technology and Digital Economy Corporation (SIDEC), TCab Tech, and IOI City Mall, officially opened at IOI City Mall in Putrajaya, Malaysia. Featuring the Malaysian debut of TCab Tech’s independently developed five-seat tilt-rotor E20 eVTOL, the month-long showcase marks the company’s formal entry into the Malaysian market and a new milestone in its Southeast Asia expansion. During the opening ceremony, TCab Tech Founder and CEO Mr Ng Yon Wui and SIDEC CEO Mr Yong Kai Ping exchanged the Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to explore E20 eVTOL commercialization pathways and advance the development of Malaysia’s Low Altitude Economy ecosystem. The exchange of the MOU was witnessed by YAB Dato’ Seri Amirudin Shari, Menteri Besar of Selangor, YB Mr Ng Sze Han, Selangor State Executive Councillor for Investment, Trade and Mobility, together with Mr Wilfred Vui Hiung Wong, General Manager of IOI City Mall, and other invited guests. TCab Tech is an aviation technology company specializing in the research, development, and commercialization of electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft (eVTOL). Its independently developed five-seat E20 eVTOL adopts a tilt-rotor configuration and is designed around safety, efficiency, convenience, and affordability, targeting applications including tourist routes, intercity travel, and intracity travel. The Selangor Information Technology and Digital Economy Corporation (SIDEC) is a key state-backed organization within the Selangor ecosystem, supporting technology innovation, digital economy development, and industry ecosystem growth. SIDEC focuses on connecting innovation resources, facilitating collaboration among industry stakeholders, and supporting the development of technology-driven initiatives in Selangor. Under the MOU, TCab Tech will contribute its expertise in eVTOL research, development, and manufacturing, while SIDEC will leverage its local innovation ecosystem, industry networks, and coordination capabilities to support TCab Tech’s engagement with relevant government agencies, the Civil Aviation Authority of Malaysia (CAAM), and industry stakeholders, advancing both the certification pathway and future commercialization of the E20 eVTOL in Malaysia. As part of TCab Tech’s Southeast Asia strategy, the company will establish its regional business center in Malaysia to support commercial development, industry collaboration, and long-term engagement with the local ecosystem, while providing an important base for broader regional expansion. The showcase, themed “Malaysian Engineers, Global Impact,” was conceived around the journey of TCab Tech Founder and CEO Ng Yon Wui, a Malaysian engineer with more than two decades of international aviation experience across China, Australia, and Europe. His career has spanned aircraft design and manufacturing, engineering and project leadership, supply chain development, airworthiness, and eVTOL research and development. Drawing on this experience, Ng Yon Wui noted that the development of the Low Altitude Economy depends not only on aircraft technologies, but also on the coordinated development of certification, regulation, infrastructure, industrial capabilities, and practical applications. Malaysia’s capabilities in aerospace manufacturing, Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO), engineering services, and aviation talent development provide a strong industrial foundation for the adoption and development of emerging aviation technologies. Its diverse geography, tourism resources, and growing demand for regional connectivity also create favorable conditions for Low Altitude Economy applications. Building on these conditions, TCab Tech will explore potential applications of the E20 eVTOL in Malaysia across tourist routes, intercity travel, and intracity travel, including connections between transportation hubs and tourism destinations, point-to-point travel between nearby cities, and new mobility options between key urban locations. As part of the broader collaboration between TCab Tech and SIDEC, Ng Yon Wui was appointed as Industry Advisor to SIDEC, in recognition of his extensive experience in aircraft design, eVTOL technology, aviation certification, and the global advanced air mobility ecosystem. In this advisory role, Ng Yon Wui will provide strategic industry perspectives to SIDEC on the development of high-technology industries in Selangor, particularly in aerospace, advanced air mobility, autonomous technologies, and emerging innovation sectors. He will also support deeper connections between Selangor’s local innovation ecosystem and the global aviation industry, including engagement with regulators, industry leaders, strategic investors, and other key stakeholders. The appointment broadens the scope of cooperation between TCab Tech and SIDEC beyond E20 eVTOL commercialization, creating further opportunities for industry exchange, ecosystem development, and longer-term collaboration in advanced technology sectors. The E20 eVTOL is currently progressing through its Type Certification (TC) process with the Civil Aviation Administration of China (CAAC). TCab Tech has completed key certification milestones, including the signing of the Certification Basis (G-1), Means of Compliance (G-2), and Certification Plan (CP), and is progressing toward Type Certification (TC) according to its established roadmap. At the same time, TCab Tech has been actively advancing the regulatory and technical preparations required for the E20 eVTOL’s future entry into overseas markets, including Malaysia, with continued engagement on applicable airworthiness requirements and certification pathways. On September 21, 2026, the Civil Aviation Authority of Malaysia (CAAM) and the Civil Aviation Administration of China (CAAC) signed an aviation safety cooperation Memorandum of Understanding (MOU), further strengthening bilateral cooperation between the two civil aviation authorities. The agreement covers areas including airworthiness, aviation organization certification, personnel licensing, operational oversight, and the mutual recognition of compliance findings and certificates. Malaysia is also continuing to develop the regulatory environment required to support Advanced Air Mobility (AAM). CAAM has initiated preparations including the establishment of an AAM Technical Working Group, advancement of the AAM Concept of Operations (ConOps), exploration of regulatory sandbox mechanisms, and development of a national AAM roadmap. Together, these developments provide a stronger regulatory and institutional foundation for the future introduction of eVTOL aircraft in Malaysia. TCab Tech will continue to advance the certification and commercialization preparations for the E20 eVTOL in the market, while deepening engagement with relevant authorities, industry partners, and ecosystem stakeholders. With Malaysia serving as an important regional base, TCab Tech aims to strengthen its long-term presence in the local market and extend its eVTOL commercialization and industry partnerships across Southeast Asia. The post TCab Tech and SIDEC sign MOU to advance E20 eVTOL commercialization in Malaysia appeared first on AeroTime .

title: ESTIC 2026: India’s Defence Technology Roadmap and Semiconductor Self-Reliance
body:
By R Anil Kumar

Bengaluru, Oct 13, 2026. The address at Emerging Science Technology and Innovation Conclave (ESTIC 2026) Curtain Raiser Event held in Bengaluru,called for end-to-end Indian ownership of defence technologies, especially semiconductors, as a foundation for Viksit Bharat and global leadership.



The presentation framed semiconductor capability as strategic infrastructure for Viksit Bharat 2047 and outlined India’s gaps, priority technologies, and staged goals for building a resilient domestic ecosystem.

The presentation outlines a future-oriented national science and technology conclave, its 12 thematic areas, government-wide organization, three-day program, and prominent speakers.

Delivering the Keynote address at the Curtain Raiser event on the upcoming ESTIC 2026, to be inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi, on October 27, Dr. B K  Das, Distinguished Scientist and Director General Electronics and Communication Systems, Defence Research and Development Organisation ( DRDO), on the role of the defence technology ecosystem, he acknowledged DRDO leaders, researchers, technology developers, defence-system users, financial support, and the press, emphasizing collaboration from initial vision through production and deployment.

SSPL was recognized for developing semiconductor building blocks used in systems such as LRB radars and CASI jammers and electronic warfare systems.

ESTIC 2026 Das presented as a national effort supported by government leadership and intended to advance India’s transition from Atmanirbhar Bharat to Viksit Bharat.

Defence self-reliance as a foundation for peace

India’s goal, as described by Das, is to fight with systems designed, developed, trusted, and deployed by India rather than relying on imported weapons.

Das cited Operation Sindoor, saying it concluded in 72 hours and demonstrated the use of Indian systems, including Akash and BrahMos.

A strong domestic technology base was framed as essential to protecting peace: technological capability earns international respect and strengthens India’s ability to advocate for peace, he said.

Das urged scientists, engineers, designers, developers, and manufacturers to innovate and bring products through to deployment.

“Last-mile” indigenization and technology freedom

A product should not be considered fully indigenous if a critical component—such as its core chip, software, or algorithm—depends on imports, even when that component represents only 5% of the product.

The target should be 100% domestic control of critical technology, rather than meeting a particular indigenization percentage such as 60%, 70%, or 80%, Das stated.

Drawing on experience in India’s missile program, the Das recalled that imported systems had been withdrawn when India pursued missile development, and argued that this made technological independence imperative.

Technology freedom was described as the ability to think, design, manufacture, and deploy systems domestically, extending beyond political and economic independence.

From Atmanirbhar Bharat to Viksit Bharat

Comparing 2006 with 2026, Das pointed to India’s shift from importing many weapon systems to developing domestic capabilities and inviting countries to cooperate and invest rather than simply sell products or designs.

The audience was challenged to consider what India could achieve over the next 20 years, with 2047 and the goal of Viksit Bharat as the horizon.

Growth alone was deemed insufficient: reaching that goal requires planning, execution, commitment, and a roadmap, he said.

Self-reliance can reduce imports, but global leadership also requires systems that other countries want to acquire.

Export growth should rely on strong Indian design and avoid critical foreign dependencies that could constrain exports or system availability, Das stated.

Semiconductors, design capability, and the next 20-year roadmap

Das said the semiconductor market was estimated at $600 billion today and $1.5 trillion by 2047, with $200 billion of that future market expected to be served by work from India.

He urged that India should become a global technology-design hub as well as a production hub, attracting Indian-origin talent with opportunities, advanced semiconductor design, and next-generation challenges.

Domestic chip design was presented as critical to future warfare and defence systems; he called for Indian designs tailored to Indian applications and weapon systems, down to the core chip level.

ESTIC was described as a catalyst for identifying priorities, not a complete solution in itself. The work requires DRDO, academia, startups, MSMEs, industries, and incubation and information centres acting as a national ecosystem.

Das urged every stake holder to treat the conference as a starting point and develop a roadmap for the next 20 years, identifying priority technologies and critical building blocks.

India’s semiconductor ambitions include progressing from the cited 100-nanometer, 28-nanometer, and 14-nanometer scales toward 2-nanometer technology by 2047, he said.

Das noted that 6 to 8 fab labs had come up, and said that the Prime Minister was encouraging them.

ESTIC’s three days Conclave with its 1,800 attendees were expected to help shape and spread a shared national message about designing, developing, and delivering defence technology in India.

India’s Semiconductor Self-Reliance Roadmap to Viksit Bharat 2047

Semiconductors as strategic infrastructure

National priorities:Telecommunications, automotive, industrial automation, AI, defence, and aerospace depend on a resilient semiconductor ecosystem that protects digital sovereignty and national security.

Foreign dependence:India relies on foreign sources for more than 90% of semiconductor-related needs, including critical IP and manufacturing inputs.

Design versus ownership:Although India has 20% of the global chip-design workforce, its role has historically centered on design services rather than owning IP.

Imported inputs:More than 90% of required chemicals, pure gases, wafers, machines, and fabrication tools are imported.

Global concentration and India’s capability gaps

Global specialization: The United States is concentrated in electronic design automation, system architectures, advanced chip design, and IP; Taiwan and South Korea lead advanced fabrication; Japan, Europe, and the Netherlands supply key wafers, photoresists, chemicals, and production infrastructure; China has mature capabilities in several fabrication nodes.

Six connected stages:A national capability needs domestic design and EDA, IP, materials and equipment, front-end fabrication, and back-end packaging, supported by security, substrates, high-purity gases, raw materials, and metals.

Manufacturing transition:India is moving from design services toward manufacturing, with Semicon 1 and Semicon 2 initiatives, plants targeting 28-nanometer fabrication, and foundry, ATMP, and OSAT activity. Startups and MSMEs are contributing.

Structural weaknesses:Domestic ownership of IP and local content in chemicals and devices remain low.

Research base:Existing strategic capabilities include DRDO laboratories, the Solid State Laboratory, the Gallium Technology Center in Hyderabad, Star-C in Bengaluru, and Chandigarh Silicon, Sunny Verma Complex Limited. Universities and national laboratories also contribute to compound semiconductors and sensors.

Commercialization gap: India lacks large-scale technology production centers linking manufacturing with R&D. Needed foundations include pilot lines, shared clean rooms, process engineering, and common IP infrastructure for civil, defence, and space applications.

Staged goals and enabling conditions

By 2030:Achieve self-reliance in strategic mature nodes such as 28 nanometers and produce 10% of domestic chip demand in India.

By 2035:Develop accelerators and AI high-bandwidth devices, build export potential, and meet domestic value-addition goals.

Longer-term leadership:Lead in selected domains, including 3D structures and 3-nanometer technologies; establish at least two world-class foundries among the global top 10; and contribute at least 20% in high-cost niche technologies.

Investment and partnerships: Semiconductor manufacturing requires substantial upfront CapEx and long payback periods. Progress also depends on domestic IP, commercialization pathways, resilient supply chains, and partnerships—not a single organization acting alone.

Materials resilience:Domestic supply of chemicals, gases, and other production materials is essential to reduce supply-chain vulnerability.

Differentiated opportunities:Open silicon and AI ecosystems could support high-bandwidth modules for edge devices and data centers. India generates 20% of global data, but has capacity for only 3% of data centers that can store it, indicating a need to expand data-center infrastructure.

Priority technologies and strategic applications

Compound semiconductors:Potential uses include renewable energy, radar, and power-conversion devices; indium phosphide was identified for terahertz applications.

Advanced packaging:2.5D and 3D packaging, compound-semiconductor packaging, and specialized packaging are needed to meet domestic requirements and support frontier technologies.

Emerging computing:Quantum, neuromorphic, and molecular computing are cited as important future technology areas.

Trusted fabrication: Domestic IP, open architectures, mainstream CMOS, and a trusted silicon-based foundry are needed for strategic assurance and a pathway toward more advanced fabrication.

Strategic sensors: IR detectors and focal-plane arrays should be built domestically because access to these technologies can be denied by other countries. Supporting needs include high-vacuum facilities, wafer-level encapsulation, and glass-to-silicon cavity interposers.

Applications and infrastructure: Inertial navigation, defence timing, and IoT sensor hubs require expansion of commercial MEMS and specialized wafer-level packaging.

Potential IP leadership:Quantum and photonic ICs, neuromorphic computing, and CMOS-compatible design kits were identified as promising areas. The technologies should be energy-efficient and support AI at the edge, data-center interfaces, and other AI hardware.

Overall direction:Front-end fabs, packaging scale-up, and R&D must advance together to support the stated ambition of reaching third place in semiconductor technology.

Future-Focused Science and Technology Conclave: Themes, Organization, and Program

ESTIC-2026-A future-focused national conclave

The conclave is framed around future technologies and possibilities, rather than past achievements.

Unlike established conferences such as the Indian Science Congress, the conclave uses a distinct, forward-looking format aligned with India’s ambition to become a developed nation by 2047.

Its theme is “Creative Minds, Catalyzing Science and Empowering Technologies.”

The approach is described as “whole of government, whole of the nation,” with participation intended from across India and from technology-related fields.

Organization and thematic areas

The overall vision is attributed to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, with Minister of Science and Technology Dr. Jitendra Singh steering the conclave and the Principal Scientific Adviser providing guidance.

Scientific ministries and departments, including the Ministry of Education, are involved as co-organizers. CSIR holds primary organizing responsibility this year; that responsibility is expected to rotate to another department in future years, with DRDO given as an example.

The program includes 12 thematic areas, reflecting major technology and emerging fields.

The session areas and coordinating bodies:

Advanced manufacturing — CSIR

Energy technologies — Department of Atomic Energy

Systems and synthetic biology — Department of Biotechnology

Ocean science and maritime technologies — Ministry of Earth Sciences

Intelligent networks and quantum communication — Department of Telecommunications

Semiconductors and “Naxal Chips” — DRDO (

AgriTech, food systems and nutrition — ICAR

Generative and autonomous AI — MeitY

Autonomous systems, physical AI and robotics — Department of Science and Technology

Preventive medicine and advanced healthcare — ICMR and AYUSH

Immersive technology, generative XR and spatial computing 

Space science — Department of Space

The 7 plenary speakers, 6 panelists in a presenter's category, 26 invited speakers, 72 panelists, and 12 keynote speakers.

Three-day program and expected outcomes

Day 1: An inaugural session, followed by a 60-minute plenary panel chaired by the Principal Scientific Adviser, two plenary talks, and three technical sessions; a cultural program is planned for the evening.

Day 2: Three plenary talks and six parallel sessions, split between morning and afternoon. A networking dinner and an evening program associated with the Ministry of Finance.

Day 3: A panel talk and three technical or panel sessions precede the concluding program. Recommendations from speakers across the thematic areas are to be consolidated into a document and presented to the minister; awards are also planned.

Featured speakers and panel

The speaker lineup is said to include three Nobel laureates and other prominent academics.

The plenary panel after the inauguration is described as lasting about an hour and chaired by Principal Scientific Adviser Professor Ajay Sood.

title: Telecel Ghana wins 2 awards at the CCIFG Gala and Awards 2026
body: Telecel Ghana has been recognised for its commitment to innovation and responsible business, securing two of six major honours at the Chamber of Commerce and Industry France-Ghana (CCIFG) Awards 2026: Digital Transformation & Innovation Excellence and Sustainability & ESG Impact. Organised by the CCIFG, the awards celebrate organisations that demonstrate exceptional business leadership, innovation and impact. The 2026 awards attracted nominations from leading businesses across multiple sectors, all of which were evaluated by an independent multi-sectoral jury comprising industry leaders, consultants and diplomats. Entries underwent a detailed review and validation process, with submissions assessed against clearly defined benchmarks to determine the most deserving winners. The transparency and depth of the evaluation underscore the significance of Telecel Ghana’s victory in two highly contested categories. The event brought together key stakeholders from Ghana’s business community and was attended by distinguished guests including the French Ambassador to Ghana, Her Excellency Diarra Dime-Labille; the Economic Adviser to the President of Ghana and former Finance Minister, Seth Terkper; and the President of the Board of CCI France Ghana, Guillaume Valence. Telecel Ghana’s recognition in the Digital Transformation & Innovation Excellence category reflects the company’s strategic investment in technology solutions that are transforming the experiences of customers, businesses and communities. Over the past year, Telecel has accelerated its digital agenda by building an integrated ecosystem that extends beyond traditional connectivity to enable secure digital transactions, e-commerce, customer engagement, and financial inclusion. Equally significant was Telecel Ghana’s win in the Sustainability & ESG Impact category, recognising its commitment to creating long-term value through environmental stewardship, social impact and strong governance practices. The award acknowledges Telecel’s conviction that business growth must be accompanied by responsible action that benefits communities and contributes to national development. Telecel has embedded ESG principles into both its operations and corporate culture. On the environmental front, the company has planted 43,000 trees over the past five years and expanded its use of renewable energy through 16 solar-powered network exchanges nationwide, helping reduce its environmental footprint while improving operational efficiency. Through the Telecel Ghana Foundation’s Connected for Good agenda, the company has continued to invest in education, digital inclusion, STEM development, and health and community empowerment programmes, positively impacting more than 6,000 beneficiaries in the year under review. Internally, Telecel has championed diversity and inclusion through strong female representation and initiatives that support financial and digital literacy among women entrepreneurs. These efforts are complemented by a governance framework that emphasises ethical business conduct, transparency, regulatory compliance, data protection and accountability. Winning both awards demonstrates that innovation and sustainability are not separate ambitions for Telecel Ghana, but complementary pillars of its business strategy. The recognition affirms the company’s ability to deliver commercially impactful solutions while simultaneously making meaningful contributions to society and the environment. It also serves as a validation of the investments, partnerships and long-term initiatives that continue to position Telecel as a responsible technology leader in Ghana’s digital economy. Komla Buami, External Affairs Director, speaking on what the recognition means to the business, shared that “These awards are a strong endorsement of the work Telecel Ghana is doing to drive meaningful digital transformation while creating lasting value for society. “They recognise the passion, commitment and purpose behind initiatives that expand financial inclusion, strengthen digital access, support communities and advance sustainability. We are honoured by these awards, which reinforce our belief that innovation and responsible business must go hand in hand.”

title: Nigeria’s private capital inflows hit $6bn as reforms gather pace — W/Bank
body: •Tax-to-GDP ratio rises to 12.5% from 7% — Oyedele By Emma Ujah, Abuja Bureau Chief Nigeria’s private capital inflows have surged nearly 20-fold to almost $6 billion in 2026 from about $300 million in 2023, President of the World Bank Group, Mr. Ajay Banga, has said, just as the Federal Government (FG) said it has intensified efforts to translate economic reforms into faster growth, job creation and improved living standards. Banga spoke on Monday during a meeting with the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Mr. Taiwo Oyedele, and the Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria, Mr. Olayemi Cardoso, on the sidelines of the 2026 International Monetary Fund, IMF, and World Bank Group Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand. The meeting reviewed Nigeria’s progress in implementing economic reforms and explored strategies to move the economy from macroeconomic stability to sustained growth, increased private investment and stronger domestic revenue generation. According to a statement, yesterday, by Efe Oviakporie, Head of Information and Public relations of the Federal Ministry of Finance, Banga highlighted the significant increase in private capital inflows as evidence of growing investor interest in the Nigerian economy. Oyedele, in his remarks, disclosed that Nigeria’s tax-to-Gross Domestic Product, GDP, ratio had risen from about seven per cent to 12.5 per cent over the same period, strengthening the government’s capacity to finance public investment without resorting to deficit monetisation. The development comes as the FG seeks to consolidate the gains of its economic reforms and create the conditions for increased investment in productive sectors of the economy. According to the Minister, improved domestic revenue mobilisation would provide greater fiscal space for the government to fund critical infrastructure and development priorities. The discussions also focused on how Nigeria could make greater use of World Bank guarantee instruments to unlock financing for infrastructure projects and attract additional private capital into the domestic economy. Such guarantees could help mobilise funding for projects that might otherwise struggle to attract investors, while reducing some of the risks associated with long-term infrastructure investments. Power infrastructure and human capital development were identified as key priorities for sustained public investment, given their implications for business competitiveness, productivity and employment generation. title: Nearly 500 Drones Head Toward Moscow as Russian Data Centers and Oil Facilities Face Attacks
body:
Nearly 500 drones headed toward Moscow overnight, disrupting operations at four airports, while a reported Ukrainian drone attack killed one person in Balakovo and an oil terminal fire continued in Rostov-on-Don.
According to Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin, 493 drones headed toward the Russian capital from the evening of Oct. 13 into the morning of Oct. 14. He said 180 were destroyed as they approached the city.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Moscow’s Sheremetyevo, Domodedovo, Vnukovo, and Zhukovsky airports suspended operations amid the drone threat. Vnukovo remained closed for more than eight hours, and passengers were reportedly asked to leave their aircraft.
The Russian Defense Ministry said 902 Ukrainian drones were shot down over Russian regions overnight.
One person was killed and several residential buildings were damaged in Balakovo, Saratov Oblast, following an overnight drone attack, Oblast Governor Roman Busargin reported.
On Oct. 14, Russia’s Defense Ministry warned of a Ukrainian drone attack on the city. Busargin later said the attack had damaged several residential buildings and caused one death.
According to an OSINT analysis by the Russian outlet Astra , one of the damaged buildings is located at 9 Titova Street, approximately three kilometers from the Balakovo combined heat and power plant (CHPP-4), a major source of heat for the city.
Astra identified the building’s location using footage published by eyewitnesses.
Meanwhile, the Ukrainian OSINT Telegram channel Exilenova+ reported that local residents had heard dozens of explosions overnight. Footage shared by the channel shows an apparent impact followed by a fire.
Exilenova+ also reported fires in the Balakovo industrial zone, citing data from NASA’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS).
The area includes a Sberbank data center and a metallurgical plant, although the specific sites affected have not been independently confirmed.
One possible target identified by monitoring channels was Sberbank’s large data center complex in Balakovo. Construction of the facility is ongoing, with sections being commissioned in stages, meaning parts of the complex may already be operational.
The project, valued at 122.2 billion rubles (more than $1 billion), is intended to become one of Russia’s largest data centers. It is designed to accommodate around 3,000 server racks and up to 120,000 servers, with a planned power capacity of 82 megawatts. The facility was also expected to host services for the Russian government’s GosTech digital platform.
Shortly before 7 a.m., Exilenova+ published footage it described as evidence of an attack on the data center.
“There is confirmation of the attack on the Sberbank mega-data center in the Saratov region. We are showing you exclusive footage from Balakovo,” the channel wrote.
Exilenova+ also reported a possible strike on the industrial zone of the Balakovo Metallurgical Plant, known as MZ Balakovo, in a post published at 7:13 a.m.
The plant specializes in steel and rolled metal products, including reinforcing bars and merchant bars. It has its own steelmaking facilities and produces more than 1 million tons of rolled steel annually.
Russian authorities have not publicly confirmed damage to either the data center or the metallurgical plant, and Ukraine has not commented on the reported attack.
The reported incident in Balakovo follows other drone attacks that have allegedly disrupted Russian data center operations.
On Oct. 11, drones reportedly forced a Yandex data center in Vladimir Oblast to suspend operations, taking dozens of the company’s services offline across Russia. Yandex acknowledged that the facility had been disabled.
On Oct. 8, another attack struck Yandex’s largest data center in Ryazan Oblast, reportedly triggering a major fire. The same day, the company removed the locations of its data centers in four Russian Oblasts from online maps.
Separately, Astra reported that a fire at the NZNP oil terminal in Rostov-on-Don had continued for four days following an attack early on Oct. 10.
The terminal belongs to the Novoshakhtinsk Petroleum Products Plant and was formerly known as Yug Rusi.
According to Astra’s analysis of eyewitness footage, at least eight of the facility’s 12 storage tanks had been damaged by Oct. 14. An earlier analysis of footage recorded before the latest update indicated that seven tanks had been damaged.
Astra reported on Oct. 12 that the fire was still burning, although no open flames were visible in the footage at that time. New footage published early on Oct. 14 indicated that the fire was continuing.
The terminal handles the transfer of petroleum products for export, generating revenue for Russia, and supplies fuel to the Russian military, according to the report. Its annual handling capacity is estimated at 2.5 million to 3.5 million tons of petroleum products.
Julia is a Deputy Head of News and correspondent for Kyiv Post who has previously worked as a parliamentary editor, journalist, and news editor. She has specialized in covering the work of the Ukrainian parliament, government, and law enforcement agencies.

title: Zelenskyy: Russian attack on energy grid leaves 600,000 without power, damages 30 facilities
body:
A massive overnight Russian strike on critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv region, and Kharkiv damaged 26 electric power elements and four oil and gas facilities, leaving at least 600,000 consumers without electricity supply, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported on Wednesday.
"A targeted Russian ballistic strike specifically against energy infrastructure, regarding which the President of America defined a ceasefire. The strike was absolutely deliberate and demonstrative in scale – there has never been such a show of disrespect from Russia toward America," the head of state wrote on his Telegram channel.
According to the president, overnight Wednesday Russian forces deployed 39 ballistic missiles and over 120 strike drones and loitering munitions against Ukrainian energy and critical infrastructure. The attack resulted in dead and wounded, and the scale of power outages may increase. Energy repair crews and units of the State Emergency Service are working at the impact sites.
Zelenskyy emphasized that with this attack Russia rejected the possibility of de-escalation and demonstrated contempt for U.S statements regarding an energy truce. In this regard, the Ukrainian head of state called on U.S President Donald Trump to introduce tough sanctions against the Russian Federation provided for in the recently passed and signed law by Senator Lindsey Graham, as well as to provide Ukraine with additional missile packages for Patriot air defense systems.

title: LCCI proposes 20% petrol price cut in 6-month programme
body: By Yinka Kolawole The Lagos Chamber of Commerce and Industry (LCCI) has proposed a six-month petrol price reduction programme targeting a 15 to 20 per cent cut in pump prices to ease the burden of high energy and transportation costs on Nigerian businesses and households. In a statement, Director-General of LCCI, Dr. Chinyere Almona, said the Federal Government should work with domestic refiners, petroleum marketers, regulators and other stakeholders to achieve progressive, measurable and sustainable reductions in petrol prices. Almona, while commending the Federal Government’s proposed petrol price-stabilisation mechanism, said the initiative was timely, given the pressure of rising energy and transportation costs on business operations, household purchasing power and the competitiveness of Nigerian enterprises. LCCI welcomed the proposed ceiling of N1,350 per litre on the ex-gantry or landing cost of petrol, subject to monthly reviews and public disclosure, describing it as recognition of the economic consequences of excessive volatility in energy prices. However, Almona warned that stabilising petrol prices at elevated levels would not provide sufficient relief to businesses already grappling with high electricity tariffs, alternative power costs, expensive financing and rising logistics expenses. She said the proposed mechanism could cushion businesses against sudden price increases but would not necessarily guarantee reductions in pump prices. According to her, the government should assess the initiative not only by its ability to moderate price volatility but also by its capacity to lower operating costs and improve economic welfare. The LCCI chief also cautioned that requiring refiners and importers to absorb temporary cost increases and recover them when market conditions improve could create deferred obligations that might eventually push prices upwards if not transparently managed. To support the proposed six-month programme, the Chamber recommended that the government ensure predictable and commercially viable crude oil supplies to domestic refineries to reduce procurement uncertainties, foreign exchange exposure and avoidable logistics costs. title: Nigerians still suffer high cost of living, despite economic growth — IMF
body: *Advocates cash transfers to cushion hardship in Nigeria *Urges FG to cut debt without worsening hardship IMF upgrades forecast for Nigeria’s economic growth to 4.2% *Warns of tougher times as global growth slows to 3.1% *Says AI boom, energy shocks threaten global economic outlook By Babajide Komolafe, Economy Editor The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has said that despite Nigeria’s economic growth and status as an energy exporter, the cost of living remained high, leaving many Nigerians struggling to meet their basic needs. The fund advocated targeted cash transfers and temporary income support for vulnerable households in Nigeria to cushion the impact of high living costs, reduce poverty and improve food security. The IMF, also warned of tougher times as global growth slows to 3.1%, even as it upgraded its forecast for Nigeria’s economic growth for 2026 to 4.2 per cent but warned that rising energy and food prices, geopolitical tensions and potential market corrections linked to artificial intelligence (AI) threaten the global economic outlook. The new forecast was contained in the IMF World Economic Outlook report October 2026, titled Resilience Under Strain, Urgent Choices,” released yesterday during the ongoing annual meetings of the IMF/World Bank in Bangkok, Thailand. Furthermore, the new forecast represents a one percentage points above the 4.1 per cent, earlier projects by the IMF in the July 2026 edition of its WEO. According to the IMF, “Growth in sub-Saharan Africa is expected to remain stable at 4.5 percent in 2026, though this masks substantial divergence across countries, reflecting differences in policy space, reform implementation, commodity exposure, climate shocks, and access to external financing. “Oil-importing, non-resource-intensive economies are more adversely affected by higher energy and food prices, whereas some larger economies continue to benefit from earlier stabilization and reform efforts, even though they are largely absent from the AI-driven global technology upswing and face headwinds from declines in official development assistance. “Nigeria is supported by improved macroeconomic stability and favorable terms-of-trade effects, though higher prices for essentials are expected to further aggravate poverty and food insecurity.” Global growth under pressure However, the IMF warned that the global economy’s resilience was under increasing pressure, with growth projected to slow from 3.5 per cent in 2025 to 3.1 per cent in 2026, before recovering to 3.4 per cent in 2027. Speaking at the press briefing on the WEO report Sylvana Tenreyro, the IMF’s Economic Counsellor and Director of the Research Department, said: “The global economy has been resilient, but that resilience is under strain, with risks tilted to the downside.” She added: “The task ahead is to move from coping to rebuilding,” stressing the need to restore fiscal space, strengthen supply-side resilience and improve countries’ capacity to withstand future economic shocks. Explaining the global outlook, Tenreyro identified energy and commodity price increases as major factors weighing on economic activity, while investment associated with artificial intelligence had provided support for growth.” The IMF report noted that the global economy had withstood repeated shocks, including geopolitical conflicts and trade tensions, but cautioned that “these margins of adjustment are not unlimited.” According to the IMF, the interaction between geopolitical tensions and technological investment has created divergent growth outcomes across countries. While economies benefiting from technology-related investment and favourable commodity trade conditions have received some support, others face higher import bills, exchange-rate pressures and weaker real incomes. The Fund warned that prolonged geopolitical tensions could keep energy and food prices elevated, revive inflationary pressures, worsen fiscal and external balances, and weigh on economic growth. Global headline inflation is projected to rise from 4.1 per cent in 2025 to 4.7 per cent in 2026 before easing to 4.1 per cent in 2027, with higher energy and food prices driving the temporary increase. AI boom raises fresh risks The IMF also cautioned that the technology investment boom, particularly in artificial intelligence, could become a source of financial instability. Although AI-related investment has supported economic activity and international trade, the Fund warned that investment gains were concentrated in a relatively small number of firms, sectors and economies. It cautioned that “a reassessment of AI-related profitability and productivity prospects could sharply reduce investment, trigger equity market corrections, and tighten financial conditions.” Such a correction, the report said, could spill over into economies integrated into technology supply chains and markets with significant exposure to technology stocks. Urges fiscal discipline Against this backdrop, Tenreyro called on governments to rebuild fiscal buffers, safeguard financial stability and strengthen private-sector dynamism. “Fiscal policy must be restrained and help contain demand pressures at a time of heightened inflationary risks,” the IMF chief economist said in the report. The Fund also stressed the importance of monetary policy focused on price stability, adding that “central bank independence is instrumental in achieving that goal.” Advocates cash transfers to cushion hardship in Nigeria The Fund advocated targeted cash transfers and temporary income support for vulnerable households in Nigeria to cushion the impact of high living costs, reduce poverty and improve food security. The Fund said the intervention should be accompanied by improved public expenditure quality and stronger revenue collection to help the Federal Government achieve fiscal consolidation and put public debt on a sustainable downward path without worsening the hardship faced by ordinary Nigerians. Chief of the IMF Research Department’s World Economic Studies Division, Deniz Igan, stated this during a press briefing on the Fund’s World Economic Outlook at the ongoing IMF/World Bank Annual Meetings in Thailand. Igan said that despite Nigeria’s economic growth and status as an energy exporter, the cost of living remained high, leaving many Nigerians struggling to meet their basic needs. “Although economic growth has held up in Nigeria, given that it is an energy exporter, living costs are still very high, and we are very mindful that the population is suffering,” she said. She noted that the pressures were particularly severe because of the rising cost of essential goods, especially food and energy, which account for a significant proportion of household consumption. “In our chapter on fiscal policy, we also examine the pressures countries are facing from the rising cost of living, particularly increases in the prices of essential goods, which account for a significant proportion of the consumption basket,” Igan said. Against this backdrop, she said the IMF was advocating targeted and temporary support for the most vulnerable households to cushion the impact of risingprices. “In this environment, we advocate cash transfers and targeted, temporary income support for the most vulnerable households in Nigeria,” she said. According to her, the intervention would help address the immediate effects of economic hardship on poor households. “Such transfers can help reduce poverty and improve food security,” she said. However, Igan stressed that social protection measures must be accompanied by fiscal reforms to ensure that governments can sustainably finance public spending and gradually reduce their debt burden. “This should be accompanied by a credible medium-term fiscal framework. That framework should focus on improving the quality of public expenditure and strengthening revenue collection,” she said. Responding to the broader policy challenge, specifically how fiscal and monetary policies could be better positioned to ensure that the burden of economic stabilisation did not fall disproportionately on ordinary citizens while preserving price stability and investor confidence, Igan explained that monetary authorities must also balance the need to control inflation against the effects of policy measures on economic activity, particularly when economies face supply-side shocks. On how central banks should respond to an oil price shock that pushes up inflation without a corresponding increase in demand, she said: “This is a classic case of a policy trade-off. Inflation is high, but economic activity is being constrained or reduced by the shock. This is where the central bank needs to manage the trade-off.” She explained that such a situation differs from one in which inflation is driven by strong demand, requiring policymakers to consider the underlying causes of price increases before deciding on the appropriate response. “This is a different situation from what we see in economies experiencing a demand-driven shock,” she said. Central banks’ focus According to Igan, central banks must nevertheless maintain their focus on price stability and ensure that inflation returns to target within the policy horizon. “It must ensure that inflation returns to target within the policy horizon, which we typically consider to be two to three years,” she said. She added that monetary policy should remain sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation back to target, while policymakers take account of the implications for economic activity. “In such circumstances, the central bank must continue to focus on price stability and ensure that its monetary policy stance remains sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation back to target, while also taking account of the effects on economic activity,” Igan said. She noted that the appropriate policy response would depend on the nature of the shock and the circumstances of each economy, including labour-market conditions, the initial level of inflation and the economy’s exposure to the shock. For Nigeria, the IMF’s recommendations underscore the need to combine measures to restore fiscal sustainability and maintain price stability with targeted interventions to protect vulnerable households from rising living costs. The approach, as outlined by Igan, would require improved public spending efficiency, stronger revenue mobilisation and temporary income support for households most affected by economic pressures. title: Why is every rationalist blog post way too long?
body:
For my piece on Catholic miracle apologetics , I read (correction: skimmed) a 25,000-word post by rationalist blogger Scott Alexander. My piece, which cited (but does not focus on) his, ended up being a cool 2,700 words. I don't think it would benefit from being longer, and it was the result of me cutting around 70% of the text I initially wrote.
Rationalist bloggers do not generally appear to have this impulse. Eliezer Yudkowsky's "sequences" are over one million words long . Nearly every blog post I have read in this ecosystem, even the rare one that contains some good ideas, is painfully long and extremely tedious. These bloggers tend to spend their time on precisely the wrong things, i.e. adding layers of detail and nuance rather than interrogating the one or two assumptions they make at the start or broadening their philosophical background beyond the collection of texts popular within their subculture.
It seems to me that, in this community, verbosity is a substitute for thoroughness: surely, if someone wrote a lot about something, and is able to demonstrate that by producing a large volume of text, they must have something worthwhile to say about it? Consider when blogger Gwern explained that nicotine, actually, is not addictive, and is good for you, as long as you don't smoke it, over the course of 9,000 words, with over 100 references. It turns out, actually, nicotine is addictive, and is bad for you even if you don't smoke it, as you probably already obviously knew.
In any case, what is missing from this endlessly verbose rationalist writing style is wisdom . Wisdom involves discretion: an intuition for what ideas are and are not worth seriously pursuing, and the ability to determine what does and does not need to be said. This community, broadly speaking, does not seem to value wisdom as a trait at all; the idea that something may be true, valuable, or good merely because it is common sense or inherited tradition is anathema to them. Instead, there is a heavy bias towards that which is unconventional and counterculture, with the amount of ink spilled for heterodox ideas taken as evidence in itself that these ideas are worth taking seriously.

title: European Cities Deploy NVIDIA-Powered AI Agents to Run Smarter Urban Operations
