title: Pope Leo has lung cancer, the Vatican announces after surgery
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 14 (MNA) – Pope Leo XIV had surgery on Tuesday to remove a cancerous growth in his lung, the Vatican announced.
The surgery, performed at Gemelli Hospital in Rome, involved removing the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung, according to a statement by Leo's doctors released by the church. Lung tissue examined after the surgery confirmed a previous test that revealed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said. Adenocarcinoma of the lung is the most common form of lung cancer in the United States, representing about 40% of all lung cancers, according to the Lung Cancer Foundation of America. MNA

title: The US trains Libya while Russia builds six bases
body:
US Marines have trained with Libyan naval special forces during Phoenix Express 2026 in Tunisia. The headline may suggest that Washington is suddenly conducting exercises with forces closely connected to Russia, but the reality is more complicated. Official US military material identifies the Libyan participants as Navy Special Forces personnel from Tripoli, not forces controlled by Khalifa Haftar. The more important story is that the United States is trying to engage both sides of divided Libya while Russia is simultaneously consolidating a permanent military presence in the country.
Phoenix Express should also not be presented as an exercise against one specific “common enemy”. The 12-day multinational exercise brought together 13 countries and focused on maritime security, including visit, board, search and seizure operations and wider cooperation in the southern Mediterranean. US Force Reconnaissance Marines trained directly with Libyan personnel from Tripoli in Bizerte.
However, Washington’s policy towards Libya in 2026 goes much further. In April, Libya, Italy and the United States jointly organised part of Flintlock 2026 in Sirte, bringing together Libyan joint forces and international partners. AFRICOM explicitly presented the exercise as supporting the development of a more unified Libyan military.
The next step came in August. Security leaders from eastern and western Libya travelled together to Ramstein Air Base, where the US Air Force presented C-130J operations, maintenance, air mobility planning and the structures required to build an integrated air command. This is important because Washington is not simply choosing Tripoli against Haftar. It is trying to connect military structures from both sides and gradually bring them into a system of cooperation with the West.
At the same time, Russia is building something much more physical. The US National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency’s Tearline project identified Africa Corps-linked activity at six Libyan air bases: Al-Khadim, Al-Jufra, Tamanhint, Matan al-Sarra, Al-Qardabiyah and Brak al-Shati. Since 2024, satellite imagery has shown construction and renovation of hangars, barracks, aprons and runways. This network gives Russia military access across eastern, central and southern Libya and provides an important logistical bridge towards the Sahel.
Al-Khadim is particularly important as a transit point between Libya and the Sahel, while Matan al-Sarra extends Russian access deep into the Sahara, close to Chad and Sudan. Russia therefore does not need to transform Libya into a formal ally or establish officially recognised bases. Access to airfields, personnel, logistics and infrastructure already gives Moscow a durable military position on NATO’s southern flank.
There is also a paradox around Haftar. His forces remain closely connected to Moscow and control territory hosting much of Russia’s military infrastructure, but they are not isolated from Washington. In August 2026, Haftar’s forces played an important role in the release of American hostage Kevin Rideout, while US contacts with eastern Libyan military structures continued. At the same time, Reuters reported that Haftar’s forces had acquired Chinese and Turkish combat drones despite the UN arms embargo.
Libya therefore cannot be divided neatly into an American camp and a Russian camp. Washington is trying to work with Tripoli while also opening channels to eastern forces and promoting military integration between the two sides. Moscow is pursuing a different objective: permanent access, infrastructure and a logistical corridor towards Africa. The competition is therefore not simply about who supports whom, but it is about who will have access to Libyan territory, military structures and infrastructure when the country eventually becomes more unified – if that ever happens.

title: Von der Leyen Outlines Five Priorities for EU Migration Policy
body: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has set out five key priorities for EU migration management in a letter to leaders ahead of this week’s Brussels summit. Irregular crossings of EU external borders have dropped 55% in two years to their lowest level since 2021. Asylum applications and secondary movements are also falling, while returns are rising. Von der Leyen warned, however, that sudden mass arrivals can still rapidly strain borders, citing the recent Ceuta crisis as an example. The priorities are: Full implementation of the Pact on Migration and Asylum and restoration of full Schengen functioning Strengthening Frontex and external border controls, including a new rapid reaction force and Return Coordination Centre A more flexible emergency framework for exceptional migratory pressure Faster returns of those with no right to stay (currently only 32%), including possible return hubs in third countries Closer partnerships with origin and transit countries, with particular focus on Libya The Entry-Exit System has already logged more than 204 million border crossings. Additional EU funding has been allocated for cooperation in eastern Libya. Source: APE-MPA, 13 October 2026 The post Von der Leyen Outlines Five Priorities for EU Migration Policy appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Field trip tragedy shows Israel needs answers, not a blame game - editorial
body: Numerous questions must be asked following the tragic death on Monday of 14-year-old Elazar Yair Wilensky during a school field trip to the Naftali Mountains Forest near the Lebanon border.Wilensky was killed, and 24 others were wounded, when one of the students picked up an unexploded Hezbollah bomb and put it in his backpack.Among the questions that must be asked: Why did the Education Ministry approve a hike in an area that Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael said was closed to hikers? Did the approved route pass through that area? Why did the KKL warning signs at the site not explicitly explain that there was lethal unexploded ordnance in the area?And if, as Education Minister Yoav Kisch suggested in an interview, the group strayed from the approved route, who made that decision, and why?These questions need an investigation, not a round of competing statements where each body explains why responsibility lies elsewhere: Who knew what, which instructions were issued, were the crystal clear, and were they followed? That is what a probe must ascertain.Three years of war have left remnants of rockets, drones, unexploded munitions everywhereResponsibility matters because rules that are written down on paper offer no protection if nobody ensures that they are followed.But the response cannot end with determining responsibility for this particular trip. There is also a wider danger that will linger long after the immediate headlines fade.Three years of war have left remnants of rockets, drones, and interceptors, along with unexploded munitions littered around the country. Some objects may look harmless; some may arouse the curiosity of children.Clearing forests and open spaces will require years of work, substantial resources, and sustained attention. The necessary budgets must be allocated. Areas known to be particularly dangerous must be clearly marked and access restricted, and routes opened to hikers must undergo thorough checks.Even then, nobody can honestly promise that every dangerous object will be found.That is not an argument for accepting a child's death as inevitable. It is an argument for taking the remaining danger seriously and making sure the public also understands it.Despite lurking dangers – and Israel has more than its fair share – normal life needs to continue. Children must be able to take field trips, and families need to be able to hike. But returning to these activities requires precautions suited to the landscape the war has left behind.Israel is experienced in protecting children from war-related hazardsAuthorities approving outings must establish that the routes are safe. Organizers must follow those routes and keep their groups together. And hikers must know what to do if they encounter an unfamiliar object: Do not touch it, keep others away, and notify the police.Israel has experience conveying such warnings.In the 1970s, 1980s, and 1990s, when terrorist bombs were exploding in cities, public campaigns repeatedly warned Israelis about suspicious objects. Children learned not to touch abandoned items. Adults knew that an unattended bag or briefcase warranted attention. Traffic stopping while police sappers dealt with a suspicious object became a familiar sight.The message became part of the country's everyday awareness.A similar effort is needed now, adapted to a danger that may be lying beside a forest path rather than under a bus-stop bench.Public service announcements should be at the heart of that effort. A warning issued after a tragedy and then forgotten will not do. All Israelis must hear this message repeatedly: on the radio while driving, on television at home, and on their phones. It must be drummed in. It must reach parents planning a family outing, teachers preparing a field trip, and the children themselves.Radio and television advertisements, billboards, school briefings, and prominent signs at trail entrances should convey this simple warning: Unexploded ordnance can kill. Do not touch unknown objects.Those approving and leading trips need clear instructions as well. A general reference to “war damage” is not enough to explain that a possibly innocent-looking but unknown object on the ground can be deadly.The country owes the Wilensky family answers. It also owes the public action. Investigating Monday's tragedy and launching a sustained awareness campaign should proceed together. Neither should wait for the other; both need to start at once.

title: War update: 229 clashes along front line over past day, Pokrovsk sector sees fiercest fighting
body:
According to Ukrinform, this was reported by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine in a Facebook post on the situation as of 08:00 on Wednesday, October 14.
Russian forces launched one missile strike and 87 airstrikes, dropping 283 guided aerial bombs. They also deployed 9,393 kamikaze drones and carried out 2,780 shelling attacks.
In the Sumy region, the settlements of Ulanove, Pysarivka, Korenok, Fotovyzh, Khotin, Sadky, Mala Korchakivka, Ivolzhanske, Yunakivka, Khrapivshchyna, and Mohrytsia came under Russian artillery fire. The area around Vasylivka was hit by an airstrike.
Ukraine’s Air Force, missile forces and artillery struck two Russian artillery systems and two unmanned aerial vehicle command posts.
In the Northern Slobozhanshchyna sector , Russian forces launched six attacks near Sukhodil, Tovstodubove, Mala Slobidka, Ryzhivka, Mala Korchakivka, and Volfyne.
In the Southern Slobozhanshchyna sector , Ukrainian units repelled 16 attacks. Russian troops attempted to advance near Izbytske, Vovchanski Khutory, Volokhivka, Vilkhuvatka, and Rybalchyne.
In the Lyman sector , Ukraine’s Defense Forces repelled seven Russian attacks near Dibrova, Lyman, and Zarichne.
In the Sloviansk sector , Russian forces launched eight attacks near Kryva Luka, Yampil, and Mykolaivka.
In the Kramatorsk sector , Russian forces conducted no assault operations.
In the Kostiantynivka sector , 12 Russian attacks were recorded. Russian troops conducted assault operations near Kostiantynivka, Rozkishne, Novoselivka, Osykove, Illinivka, Mykolaipillia, and Dovha Balka.
In the Pokrovsk sector , Ukraine’s Defense Forces stopped 39 Russian attacks. Russian troops attacked near Serhiivka and Molodetske as well as toward Vilne, Kucheriv Yar, Sofiivka, Petrivka, Zolotyi Kolodiaz, Dobropillia, Novyi Donbas, Chernihivka, Rodynske, Novooleksandrivka, Myrne, Udachne, and Muravka.
In the Huliaipole sector , Ukrainian forces repelled 10 Russian attacks near Dolynka, Rizdvianka, and Hirke.
In the Kupiansk, Oleksandrivka, Orikhiv, and Prydniprovske sectors , Russian forces conducted no offensive operations over the past 24 hours.
In the Volyn and Polissia sectors , the situation remained largely unchanged. No signs of Russian forces forming offensive groupings were detected.
As Ukrinform reported, Russia’s total combat losses since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, reached approximately 1,557,350 personnel as of October 14, 2026.

title: Four Syrian troops killed in ambush on Hama motorway
body: Four Syrian security personnel were killed when two patrols were ambushed in the countryside of Hama province on Tuesday night. Nour Al Baba, spokesman for Syria's Interior Ministry, condemned the attacks on the Salamiya-Athriya motorway and said authorities would pursue those responsible. “With deep sorrow and grief, we mourn the loss of four of our brothers – road security personnel – who were killed when two of their patrols were targeted in the Hama countryside,” he said. “The crime will not deter us from continuing to pursue the perpetrators and bring them to justice,” Mr Al Baba said, adding that the incident would strengthen the security forces’ resolve to protect civilians and safeguard lives. Internal security forces said they were continuing efforts to track down those involved. The attack took place on the road linking Salamiya, east of Hama city, with Athriya, an area farther east on the route towards the Syrian desert. The motorway forms part of a transport corridor connecting central Syria with the country’s eastern regions. The area is on the edge of the Syrian desert, where armed groups and ISIS militants have carried out attacks. The ministry did not provide further details about the circumstances of the attack, including the weapons used.

title: Petrol, diesel prices set to fall from Oct. 16 as LPG faces 18.5% hike
body: Petrol and diesel prices are expected to fall marginally at the pumps from Friday, October 16, 2026, while liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) could see an 18.5% increase per kilogram. This is according to the Chamber of Oil Marketing Companies’ pricing outlook for the next pricing window. Breakdown Petrol is projected to decline by almost 2% to GH¢17.67 per litre, while diesel could fall by 3.32% to GH¢19.30 per litre. LPG, however, is expected to rise by 18.5% to GH¢20.60 per kilogram. During the October 1 pricing window, most oil marketing companies maintained their prices following a GH¢2 levy on diesel and a government intervention in which Tema Oil Refinery and Sentuo Oil supplied refined products to the companies at previous prices. Reasons for the price changes The Chamber attributed the projected adjustments to developments on the international market and recent government subsidy measures. In its report, the Chamber said average crude oil prices rose by 2.03% to US$126.73 per barrel for the October 16 pricing window. It attributed the increase to renewed supply concerns, as Ukraine questioned a proposed US-backed energy ceasefire and Saudi Arabia faced fresh attacks amid the war with Iran. Prices of refined petroleum products, however, recorded mixed movements. LPG rose by 7.77%, while diesel fell by 6.68% and petrol declined by 3.93%. Meanwhile, the Ghana cedi depreciated by 1.61% to GH¢11.8222 to the US dollar, based on average bank rates between September 26 and October 11, 2026. The Chamber said the cedi had lost more than 11% against the dollar so far this year, with seasonal import demand and higher energy costs continuing to put pressure on the currency. Despite these developments, petrol and diesel prices are expected to see only modest reductions at the pumps, in line with projections from several analysts earlier this month. NPA lowers petrol and diesel price floors The National Petroleum Authority (NPA) has also reduced the minimum prices for petrol and diesel for the October 16 pricing window. Market data sighted by Joy Business shows that the petrol price floor has been lowered from GH¢16.45 to GH¢16.09 per litre. The diesel price floor has also been reduced from GH¢17.97 to GH¢17.09 per litre. The LPG price floor, however, has increased from GH¢11.10 to GH¢13.87 per kilogram. The NPA said these price floors exclude premiums charged by International Oil Trading Companies (IOTCs), operating margins of Bulk Import, Distribution and Export Companies (BIDECs), and margins charged by Oil Marketing Companies and LPG Marketing Companies. Those charges will be determined independently by the respective companies in accordance with the prescribed Petroleum Products Pricing Formula.

title: Mehmedi bags Iran 1st gold medal at GR Wrestling C’ship in US
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 14 (MNA) –Abolfazl Mehmedi of the Islamic Republic of Iran has secured the country's first coveted gold medal at the World Junior Greco-Roman Wrestling Championships in the United States, defeating his Armenian opponent 2–1 in the final.
Earlier, Iran’s national Greco-Roman wrestling team had discovered their opponents for the U23 World Wrestling Championships in Las Vegas, United States.

title: People of Israel candidate quits Ofer Winter's party amid mounting pressure from right-wing rivals
body: Davidi Ben Zion, a candidate on Ofer Winter's People of Israel party list, announced his withdrawal from the race on Tuesday, two weeks before the elections, following an intensive campaign urging him to step aside over concerns that the party could endanger the right-wing bloc's electoral prospects.The campaign against Ben Zion had called on him to withdraw, arguing that the party's participation in the elections posed a risk to the right-wing bloc.In his resignation statement, Ben Zion wrote: "A month and a half ago, I joined People of Israel out of a sense of mission and humility. Ofer Winter is a true right-winger, a fighter and a commander who has dedicated his life to Israel's security and does not apologize for what he believes in.""I believe in him and in his path, and I thank him for his trust and for the journey we have shared. A mission is measured in moments when you have to choose between what is good for you and what is right. Two weeks before the elections, based on the emerging picture, it appears that the risk of failing to cross the electoral threshold is high, and I am not prepared to let the votes of people who believed in this path go to waste," he added.Ben Zion concluded his statement by referring to his military service following the October 7 attacks.Ben Zion cites military service and responsibility in withdrawal"On October 7, I rushed with my battalion to Kfar Aza because I will always be there for my brothers. Since then, I have served hundreds of days in the reserves, and that is where I learned that the mission comes before everything else. I believe in this path, and out of a sense of responsibility, I have decided to withdraw from the list. With God's help, I will continue to serve the residents of Samaria, the State of Israel and the people of Israel, as always, on every front."In a message sent to members of People of Israel immediately after his withdrawal, Ben Zion wrote: "Friends, I love you. My family and my wife come before everything else. Every single one of you is dear to me, and may you continue to succeed, God willing."Ofer Winter condemns campaign against party candidatesPeople of Israel chairman Ofer Winter responded to the announcement on Tuesday evening during a campaign event in Eilat, sharply criticizing the campaign against members of his party."This evening, Davidi Ben Zion, one of the candidates on my list, asked me to withdraw. I tell you: Jerusalem was destroyed because of baseless hatred. The inconceivable campaign, which descended to personal attacks against people in our party by various elements on the right, is a disgraceful, low campaign. Truly low," Winter said."They hung signs near the children's transportation, yesterday near their homes. I mean, what did Dudi do? What did Dudi Ben Zion do? What did Lali Deri, a bereaved mother, do? Just withdraw, withdraw. For what? What did they do? They wanted to join a new, clean party, something that has not existed in Israeli politics. To lead a genuine, clean path, and they went after them with everything they had, relentlessly, without limits," he added.He went on to condemn those responsible for the campaign, accusing them of putting candidates and their families under relentless pressure."Now I say to those who did this: They should be ashamed of themselves. Instead of being good, they trample others. Tell us what you are good at. And I say one more thing: I understand Davidi. I understand that he could not withstand the pressure, that his wife could not withstand it, with all the signs they hung near their home and the number of times they threatened him and told him, withdraw, withdraw. By the way, it is not as though we accidentally went with Mansour Abbas. It is simply because we decided to lead a new path. That is the story. So I say that whoever did this should be ashamed. This is not the way of the right. This is not how people should behave," Winter pointed out."I tell you, we came to lead a new, clean path, with people of integrity. It is time to put an end to this petty, disgraceful politics. I say this to you from the bottom of my heart. And to all those who are worried, I say: We are strong. We will go all the way now. We do not surrender in battle. Sometimes there are casualties. There is nothing to be done. I have experienced such things several times in my public life, as a fighter and as a commander who has led enough soldiers. There are casualties. We will win and bring a different message to the people of Israel."Netanyahu and Smotrich welcome withdrawal, urge others to followPrime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu welcomed Ben Zion's decision and called on other candidates on Winter's list to withdraw as well."I commend Davidi Ben Zion for his important decision to withdraw from Winter's party after realizing that Winter's candidacy endangers the right-wing bloc and will lead to the establishment of a left-wing government of Eisenkot, Yair Golan, Liberman, Bennett and the Arab parties. I call on the other members of the list to act similarly to ensure a victory for the right," Netanyahu said.אני מחזק את דוידי בן ציון על החלטתו החשובה לפרוש ממפלגתו של וינטר לאחר שהבין שהריצה של וינטר מסכנת את גוש הימין, ותוביל להקמת ממשלת שמאל של איזנקוט, יאיר גולן, ליברמן, בנט והמפלגות הערביות. אני קורא לשאר חברי הרשימה לנהוג באופן דומה כדי להבטיח את ניצחון הימין.— Benjamin Netanyahu - בנימין נתניהו (@netanyahu) October 13, 2026Religious Zionist Party chairman and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich also issued a statement praising Ben Zion's decision."I would like to congratulate my friend, Maj. (res.) Davidi Ben Zion, on a courageous and difficult step of national responsibility. Over the past three years, Davidi has demonstrated military courage, reporting again and again for reserve duty as a fighter and commander on every front. This is a direct continuation of many years of public service in education, settlement, and social affairs. This evening, Davidi is demonstrating civilian courage, taking responsibility and acting to save the State of Israel from the loss of power by the national camp and the rise of the left because of votes being wasted below the electoral threshold," Smotrich wrote.He also called on Winter and the remaining candidates to follow Ben Zion's example, warning of what he described as the consequences of a left-wing government coming to power."With his courageous step, Davidi is acting to save the State of Israel from the clear and immediate danger of the establishment of a Palestinian state, a devastating blow to the Jewish identity of the state and damage to democracy. I call on Ofer Winter, who demonstrated military courage for many years, to demonstrate civilian courage as well, to take the right and necessary step in light of a series of polls showing that he is not crossing the electoral threshold, and to announce his withdrawal. I call on attorney Eran Ben Ari and Lali Deri: You are people of the national camp. Take responsibility and follow Davidi's example. Do not take upon yourselves responsibility for a left-wing government that will cause enormous damage to the State of Israel. We do not gamble with Israel's security!" Smotrich added.Party candidates previously expressed openness to coalition with EisenkotJust a week earlier, during a preelection gathering at a private home, People of Israel candidates attorney Eran Ben Ari and Davidi Ben Zion said they were entirely open to joining a broad unity government that would also include Gadi Eisenkot.When asked whether they would sit with Eisenkot or bring him into the coalition, Ben Zion replied: "Why shouldn't Eisenkot join? I wish he would. On the contrary, let there be a broad government here. Excellent."Ben Ari reinforced those remarks, explaining that a strong showing for their party would force political figures in the center-left to compromise and join a Netanyahu-led coalition."Our strength, when it becomes significant, will mean that Liberman will have to decide whether he is joining the government ... that Eisenkot will have to decide whether he wants to join the government," he said.Yoseph Haddad vows party will continue despite pressureYoseph Haddad addressed party members following Ben Zion's withdrawal, accusing political rivals on the right of financing an aggressive campaign intended to destroy People of Israel."We are facing an ugly campaign funded by enormous budgets, whose sole purpose is to crush us as though we are the enemy. And this is coming from the right, from within our own home, so to speak. And yes, the political pressure is heavy. They are using disgusting methods, and not everyone is capable of withstanding them, especially when it reaches their families. Our foundations are stronger than any pressure. We are moving forward with full force," Haddad said.

title: Bank of Ghana engages stakeholders in Techiman
body: The Bank of Ghana (BoG) has held a day’s stakeholder engagement forum at Techiman in the Bono East Region, to strengthen stakeholder collaboration towards deepening public understanding of the mandate of the central bank and its policy development. The forum, the central bank said, further sought to maintain financial stability and to create value for money. It was on the theme: “Strengthening stakeholder relations through dialogue and engagement” and attended by traditional authorities, religious leaders, traders and market women, transport unions, Small and Medium Enterprises, community banks and microfinance institutions. The stakeholders were taken through the mandate of the BoG, as well as microfinance sector reforms, responsible borrowing and consumer protection, currency education and identification, and proper handling of banknotes among others. Addressing the stakeholders, Mr Bernard Otabil, the Director of Communications at the BoG, said the engagement was part of the BoG nationwide drive to deepen public understanding and to strengthen the nation’s financial sector. He explained that the engagement was designed to enable the BoG to access feedback from the public towards policy development and unlicensed financial schemes and currency abuses. Mr Otabil emphasised that the central bank remained dedicated to the public and strengthened public trust and confidence in the Ghana cedi. “The Cedi is not just a paper or coin, but it’s trust and we can’t formulate the best monetary policy, if the trader in Techiman market does not understand or trust the cedi,” he stated, adding: “That is why we are here, to listen, to dialogue, and to partner for financial reforms and stability.” Mr Otabil reiterated the BoG commitment to sustaining open dialogue with stakeholders across the regions and to promote financial literacy and financial inclusion. He urged members of the public to report suspected activities of unlicensed financial institutions to the bank. Mr Abdulai Lawal Abubakar, the Regional Director, Sunyani office of the BoG noted that the central bank remained committed to engaging stakeholders and to gather information that would foster the development of the bank. “Our engagement is meant to interact with and engage stakeholders to improve the total development of our operations that would enhance the BoG’s policy,” he added. Some of the stakeholders commended the central bank, describing the engagement as an eye opener and insightful. They expressed concern about high lending rates as well as activities of unregulated lenders and called on the BoG to do more to tackle those challenges.

title: Severe Weather Across Greece: Storms and Winds Up to 10 Beaufort
body: Authorities are on high alert as severe weather hits much of Greece, bringing floods, property damage and transport disruptions. In Skiathos , floodwaters swept away two parked cars. Heavy rain and traffic problems were reported in Attica. Schools in the Aegean islands and parts of Evia are closed today. Eight areas are under Red Code alert. The National Meteorological Service (EMY) warns of heavy rain, storms and gale-force winds continuing into Wednesday, with improvement expected from Thursday night. Areas of greatest concern: Evia (Red warning): heavy rain and storms until late afternoon Orange alert: Northeastern Peloponnese, eastern Central Greece, Attica, Cyclades, Halkidiki, Sporades, eastern Thessaly, Dodecanese and Crete Northeasterly winds of 8–9 Beaufort, temporarily reaching 10, will affect the northern and central Aegean until late Wednesday night. There is also an increased risk of hail in the Aegean, especially the Dodecanese and Crete. Attica can expect rain and possible storms, with winds of 6–8 Beaufort. Temperatures will drop further nationwide, with possible light snow on the highest peaks of Central Greece, Thessaly and the north. Source: EMY / General Secretariat for Civil Protection, 14 October 2026 The post Severe Weather Across Greece: Storms and Winds Up to 10 Beaufort appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: PIAC unable to verify GH¢21m petroleum-funded projects in Ayawaso West
body: The Public Interest and Accountability Committee (PIAC) has been unable to verify four petroleum revenue-funded projects valued at about GH¢21 million in the Ayawaso West Municipality because of inadequate information and vague project descriptions. ‎The projects could not be identified during a field inspection to assess the use of petroleum revenues between 2012 and 2024. ‎Mr Isaac Dwamena, Executive Secretary of PIAC, said the Committee had written to the Ministry of Roads and Highways three weeks before the inspection to request additional information but had not received a response by the time of the visit. ‎The inspection team, led by Nana Soglo Alloh IV, a PIAC member and Paramount Chief of the Likpe Traditional Area, identified three road projects and a Community-based Health Planning and Services (CHPS) compound with assistance from officials of the Assembly. ‎The road projects were the surfacing of Mega Link Road at Mempeasem, valued at GH¢178,170.13; construction of a 0.45-metre U-drain along Nii Sai Road, costing GH¢130,114.85; and surfacing of Nii Sai Road, valued at GH¢131,923.65. ‎The three projects were implemented by the Ministry of Special Initiatives. ‎The team also identified a CHPS compound at Mempeasem, which received GH¢657,395.99 in 2020 and was implemented by the Ministry of Health. ‎The four projects that remained unlocated included the construction of a concrete drain at East Legon, valued at GH¢3.35 million, and emergency road rehabilitation works costing GH¢3.9 million. ‎The rehabilitation works involved the upgrading of Spintex Road and roads and culverts in the East Legon area. ‎The other projects were the resealing of selected roads in Ayawaso West and Ga Central, valued at GH¢1.5 million, and the Boundary Road and Motorway Slip Road projects, estimated at GH¢12 million. ‎The projects were attributed to the Ministry of Water Resources, Works and Housing and the Ministry of Roads and Highways as implementing agencies. ‎Mr Dwamena said the information requested from the Ministry of Roads and Highways included the names and contact details of the contractors who executed the projects. ‎“When you go to the field armed with relevant information, it positions you better to carry out the exercise and get the results you want,” he said. ‎Mr Dwamena said PIAC could not conclude that the projects did not exist because it lacked the information needed to locate them. ‎“We would not say categorically that the projects do not exist. The information that would have enabled us to find the project, we didn’t get from the Ministry of Roads and Highways,” he said. ‎At a post-inspection meeting, Mr Gordon Domayele, Municipal Coordinating Director of the Ayawaso West Municipal Assembly, said information-sharing on centrally implemented projects was necessary to improve monitoring and accountability. ‎He called on the Central Government to involve the assemblies in projects undertaken within their jurisdictions. ‎“Sometimes, when people come from the national to ask certain questions, they think that some of us are not on top of the issue. It is not our fault,” he said. ‎The inspection formed part of PIAC’s mandate to collect data from stakeholder institutions and conduct physical visits to projects funded with petroleum revenues to assess value for money and promote transparency and accountability in the management of the revenues.

title: Former Malawi President Chakwera arrives for historic Assemblies of God congress in Accra
body: Former President of Malawi, Dr Lazarus Chakwera, has arrived in Accra to participate in the 10th Triennial World Congress of the World Assemblies of God Fellowship. He is accompanied by his wife, Mrs Monica Chakwera. They were received at the Accra International Airport by the Minister for Foreign Affairs, Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa; the Minister for Gender, Children and Social Protection, Dr Agnes Naa Momo Lartey; and officers of the Executive Presbytery of Assemblies of God, Ghana, led by the General Superintendent, Rev Stephen Yenusom Wengam. Mr Ablakwa expressed the government’s delight at Dr Chakwera’s visit to Ghana for the World Congress. The Foreign Affairs Minister commended the World Assemblies of God Fellowship for choosing Ghana, and Africa, to host the global event. He assured the Church of the government’s support to ensure the successful organisation of the congress. Rev Wengam thanked former President Chakwera for accepting the invitation to attend the historic global gathering. Dr Chakwera, on his part, expressed confidence in Ghana’s ability to host the important event. The former Malawian President, who previously served as General Superintendent of Assemblies of God, Malawi, expressed optimism that the congress would usher in a spiritual revival. “There would be a great revival afterwards,” he said. The World Congress, which runs from Wednesday to Friday, will feature morning conference sessions, followed by gospel revival rallies at the Accra Sports Stadium. The evening rallies are open to people of all denominations, and attendance is free.

title: Russian Energy Week forum kicks off in Moscow
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. The Russian Energy Week (REW) International Forum starts in Moscow on Wednesday. Against the backdrop of a protracted global energy crisis, participants will discuss existing challenges and barriers, examples of cooperation, and opportunities to pool efforts to stabilize the global market, as well as ways to strengthen Russia’s position and potential.
The forum will take place from October 14 to 16 at two venues: business program events will be held at the Manege Central Exhibition Hall, while an exhibition of equipment and technologies for the fuel and energy sector will be organized in the Gostiny Dvor Atrium.
The main events of this year’s REW business program will take place on October 15 and 16. The business program features more than 30 panel sessions and discussions with the involvement of over 100 speakers split into seven thematic tracks: 'Transformation of the Oil Market,' 'Developing the Gas Market,' 'Investment in the Electric Power Industry,' 'The New Energy,' 'Ecology and Energy Efficiency,' 'The Energy of International Cooperation,' and 'Education and Human Resources'.
The agenda of this year’s forum reflects the most relevant industry trends, with participants to discuss current challenges and barriers, as well as the best practices for collaboration, according to Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak. Russian Energy Week participants will discuss global shifts in the oil and gas markets, the development of international energy cooperation, investment and modernization in the electric power industry, and the emergence of new players such as energy storage systems and data centers. Particular attention will be paid to energy supply for the Arctic and remote regions, robotization and the development of small-scale distributed generation, the environmental and climate agenda, and issues of engineering sovereignty and personnel security in the fuel and energy sector.
The key event of the business program is the plenary session. Russian Energy Week is being held with the support of the Government of the Russian Federation, the Ministry of Energy of the Russian Federation, and the Government of Moscow. The Roscongress Foundation organizes the forum. TASS is the information partner of Russian Energy Week.

title: Ketu North MP led delegation petitions government over deteriorating Weta Irrigation Scheme
body: Eric Edem Agbana, Member of Parliament (MP) for Ketu North, has led a delegation of chiefs, rice farmers and concerned youth from Weta to petition the Ministry of Food and Agriculture for urgent rehabilitation of the deteriorating Weta Irrigation Scheme. The petition, presented on Monday, was received on behalf of the Minister by Mr John Dumelo, Deputy Minister of Food and Agriculture, who assured the delegation of the government’s commitment to rehabilitating the scheme and supporting farmers to revive the agricultural facility. The delegation called for immediate intervention to restore the irrigation infrastructure and reclaim farmlands severely damaged by years of operational challenges. The farmers said more than 1,200 families had been affected by the situation and appealed for appropriate compensation to help them recover their livelihoods. They also called for a thorough investigation into the utilisation of World Bank funds released for the redevelopment of the scheme to ensure accountability and transparency in the implementation of the project. Mr Agbana described the scheme as a critical agricultural asset with significant potential to boost rice production, create employment and strengthen Ghana’s food security. He said the continued deterioration of the facility had imposed considerable hardship on farmers and their families, stressing the need for urgent and decisive government intervention. The MP assured the delegation that he would continue to engage the relevant authorities to secure concrete action towards rehabilitating the scheme and addressing the concerns of affected farmers. He said the intervention should result in a clear rehabilitation plan, accountability for funds committed to the project and a credible strategy to restore the livelihoods of farmers. Mr Agbana reaffirmed his commitment to ensuring that the concerns of the people of Weta remained on the national agenda until meaningful progress was achieved.

title: 'You live from one deployment to the next': Israeli reservists struggle to rebuild their lives
body: On October 6, 2023, after 21 consecutive days on base, Gleb and his soldiers headed home for the weekend. The next day, just two days before he was due to begin his pre-discharge leave, his phone rang. It was his commanding officer: "Get here." Three years later, Gleb has never really left military life behind. Although he officially completed his mandatory service in December 2023, he has since been called up for six rounds of reserve duty. His next deployment is already scheduled for January.   Noam, who completed his mandatory service almost a year after Gleb, has also been caught in the same cycle. He has already served more than 260 days in the reserves. Both belong to a generation of young combat soldiers caught between military service and civilian life. They were discharged in the midst of the longest war in Israel's history, with no smooth transition or period of respite. As the reserve system struggles under an unprecedented burden, they are repeatedly called back to fight in the north and south, while their education, careers and personal lives remain on hold.   The two discussed the friends they have lost, the psychological toll they continue to endure and a discharge that exists largely on paper. "I avoided starting school, taking a new job or getting involved in a project because I knew I'd be called back to reserve duty," Gleb says. "So why even start?" 'A zombie horror movie' The two men came to the military from different backgrounds. Noam gave up a potential career as a professional soccer player and consulted his rabbi and father before enlisting. "We concluded that I would find a way to combine military service with my religious lifestyle." In March 2022, he enlisted in the Givati Brigade's Tomer Company, a unit for ultra-Orthodox soldiers. Gleb enlisted a year earlier, in March 2021, joining the Paratroopers Brigade. He completed his mandatory service as a commander in the combat platoon at Havat Hashomer, an IDF training base. "I started my military journey at Havat Hashomer, so I went back there to come full circle," he explains.   After receiving that phone call, Gleb rushed to his base to collect equipment, then headed to the Jordan Valley to prepare his battalion. "We stocked up on as much ammunition and water as we could, then headed into the unknown," he recalls. From the Jordan Valley, his unit was sent directly south to Kfar Aza, Be'eri and Sderot. "It was a shock," Gleb says. "The roads around Gaza looked like something out of a zombie horror movie. It was hard to believe this was happening, especially here, in our own home. "The first week was one shock after another, mission after mission, and we still hadn't grasped the magnitude of what had happened. Then we started hearing about the soldiers killed in our battalion, in our team. The first friends we had lost. Only then did we understand that we were going to war and that we would be entering Gaza. This wasn't an operation in Nablus or a firefight in a refugee camp. This was about taking back control." Noam: "Say you start studying. Then what? Before you know it, you're back in Lebanon with no reception, trying to connect to Zoom and falling behind. It just won't work." Noam and his team were training at the Tsnobar military outpost in northern Israel on Oct. 7, where they were serving as the area's quick-reaction force. "You don't even feel like you're part of what's happening. You're in shock," he recalls. He describes how, the moment they learned of the attack on the Gaza border communities, the commanders and soldiers quickly gathered their equipment and boarded buses that took them south, to the front lines. In those early days, when the full picture was still unclear, devastating messages began appearing in their WhatsApp groups. "One of the guys I went through basic training with wrote, ‘Our unit is gone. Our team is gone.’" Noam says. "You read that and can't process the fact that it's happening so close to you."   Discharged from the military, called straight back to the reserves The war made it clear to both men that completing their mandatory service was far from the end of their military obligations. Gleb's mandatory service was extended by three months. Just six months after it ended, he was called up for his first reserve deployment. "You never get your reserve call-up notice six weeks in advance, the way you're supposed to," Gleb says. "It's always just a few days beforehand. Once, I got a message from one of my officers at 4:30 a.m.: 'Report to the base in the north on Friday. We're entering Lebanon on Sunday.'" Noam was discharged in November 2024, and just a month later he was back in uniform. "The soldier I trained to replace me was killed," he says. "At that moment, I realized I had to find a way to go back and train someone else. I returned to my unit as a reservist, and this time I trained five soldiers instead of one." Another emergency reserve call-up order, known in Israel as a Tzav 8, is already awaiting him in November. For both men, every attempt to build a civilian life has been thwarted by the knowledge that another call-up is just around the corner. "It's constant exhaustion, a steady downward spiral," Noam says. "You remain in the same place you were when you were discharged, living from one deployment to the next. In between, you start thinking about civilian life and realize it's not really possible. "Say you start studying. Then what? Before you know it, you're back in Lebanon with no reception, trying to connect to Zoom and falling behind. It just won't work."   He was forced to postpone plans to improve his high school exam scores and register for the psychometric  exam, Israel's standardized test for university admission, after realizing he would be called up for another deployment midway through his first semester. "Since my discharge, for two years and eight months now, I've been stuck in the same place: working in security, going on a reserve deployment, returning to security work and then another deployment," Gleb says. "There's this feeling of being stuck that affects almost everything. I avoided starting school, taking a new job or getting involved in a project because I knew I'd be called up for reserve duty and wouldn't really be able to devote myself to it. So why even start?" 'Everyone I know is struggling emotionally' But the deepest wounds do not appear on a resume, and recognizing the need to address them is only half the battle. "There's a huge and difficult gap between understanding what needs to be done and actually doing it," Gleb says. "I realized during the first months of the war that I would need to process what I'd been through, but I didn't actually start until six months after completing my mandatory service." Members of his team organized their own sessions to process their experiences. Every two or three days, they would sit together without professional guidance, simply to make sure no one was left behind. "It gives me the feeling that I'm not alone. There are difficult moments, and I know who to turn to. My friends always keep an eye on anyone who's struggling, and I do the same." Gleb: "The state and the Defense Ministry must pay much more attention to the mental health of discharged combat soldiers because what's being done today simply isn't enough. Everyone close to me has been affected psychologically." But not everyone can talk about their distress or ask for help, and in the most extreme cases, the consequences can be devastating. "When you don't process what you've been through, it can reach the point where a combat soldier takes his own life," Gleb warns. "Sadly, I lost one of my soldiers and a friend who couldn't cope with what they'd been through. May his memory be a blessing. That's the price of failing to address these issues. The state and the Defense Ministry must pay much more attention to the mental health of discharged combat soldiers because what's being done today simply isn't enough. "Everyone close to me has been affected psychologically, and there's no shame in that. We do difficult work that not everyone is willing to take on and not everyone is capable of handling. It comes at a cost, and that cost needs to be acknowledged. "At the same time, treatment is available, and people must get help. Responsibility is shared by the state, the Defense Ministry and the military, but some of it also rests with the combat soldier himself." Noam points to another failure: The system relies entirely on soldiers seeking help themselves. "Some guys just can't bring themselves to ask for help. All they have are their friends, who come and sit with them, but we're not professionals. A mental health professional needs to reach out to them and provide ongoing support." He believes friends and relatives should also be able to report when a soldier is in distress, rather than waiting until it is too late.   Alongside their psychological struggles, Noam and Gleb discovered that taking their first steps into civilian life was far from straightforward. Both turned to Gav LaLochem ("Support for the Fighter"), a nonprofit organization founded in 2019 by Oria Isaak and Itamar Israelit that has helped approximately 2,000 discharged combat soldiers to date. Through a series of meetings, the organization provides practical tools for managing finances, entrepreneurship and career development, as well as job placement assistance, a personal mentor and access to an alumni community. "Combat soldiers think they'll be welcomed with a red carpet when they leave the military, but that's not how it works at all," Noam says. "You get out and you're in shock. At Gav LaLochem, there are mentors who guide you every step of the way." "That transition is critical," Gleb explains, "because discharged combat soldiers don't have a sufficient safety net to ease their transition to civilian life, something to help them make sense of civilian life, even when it comes to the simplest things."

title: Compiler bootstrapping depends on more than you might think
body:
You're probably reading this page because you've attempted to access some part of my blog (Wandering Thoughts) or CSpace , the wiki thing it's part of. Unfortunately you're using a browser version that my anti-crawler precautions consider suspicious, most often because it's too old (most often this applies to versions of Chrome). Unfortunately, as of early 2025 there's a plague of high volume crawlers (apparently in part to gather data for LLM training) that use a variety of old browser user agents, especially Chrome user agents. To reduce the load on Wandering Thoughts I'm experimenting with (attempting to) block all of them, and you've run into this.
If this is in error and you're using a current version of your browser of choice, you can contact me at my current place at the university (you should be able to work out the email address from that). If possible, please let me know what browser you're using and so on, ideally with its exact User-Agent string.
I am not blocking Inoreader's feed fetcher or considering it to be too old, and it routinely fetches feeds from me. I don't know why Inoreader is showing you this page. It is possible that they're periodically trying to fetch feeds or pages with an old browser HTTP User-Agent (or an actual old browser) and taking the results of that fetch (this page) as what they should show people instead of the results of their syndication feed fetcher agents. This is a bad mistake today; the results of modern HTTP fetches depend partly on the HTTP User-Agent used .
Much like Inoreader, Feedly is periodically fetching my syndication feeds with a fake, old browser HTTP User-Agent header, which fails, and is then grimly latching on to the results for their actual feed fetching with their regular Feedly HTTP User-Agent. There is nothing I can do about this; you should contact Feedly support, if you can find them. See this comment of mine in Wandering Thoughts for more details.
Due to an ongoing attack, you may need to change the "User Agent Brand Masking" setting so that your Vivaldi identifies itself as Vivaldi, instead of Google Chrome. This applies to even the current version of Vivaldi.
You may be seeing this through archive.today, archive.ph, archive.is, and so on. Unfortunately, archive.* crawls pages to archive in a way that is impossible to distinguish from malicious actors. They use old Chrome User-Agent values, crawl from IP address blocks that are widely distributed and not clearly identified as theirs, and some of their IP addresses have falsified reverse DNS entries that claim they are googlebot IP addresses (which is something that is normally done only by quite bad actors). I suggest that you use archive.org, which is a better behaved archival crawler and can crawl my blog (Wandering Thoughts) .

title: Video: Peek inside Turku's new music centre
body:
Fuuga opens to the public in late October, bringing a new concert venue and public space to the banks of the Aura River.
Fuuga, Turku's new, sprawling music centre along the Aura River is opening on 26 October.
The 90-million-euro project was approved back in 2020, and the facility is preparing to welcome its first visitors.
The name Fuuga is the Finnish term for ‘fugue’ - a musical composition in which different voices weave around a central melody.
At the heart of the building is the main concert hall, which seats around 1,300 people. A second smaller hall, Ateljee, can accommodate another 300.
Fuuga will become the home of the Turku Philharmonic Orchestra, but the centre is intended to be more than just a concert venue. Its restaurant and roof terrace offer views over the Aura River, while visitors can enter the building without buying a concert ticket or visiting the restaurant.
According to Turku Mayor Piia Elo , the space is meant for all of the city's residents, rather than a venue exclusively reserved for concertgoers.
Interest in the new venue is strong, with more than 80 percent of tickets for the autumn programme already sold.

title: Unpaid contractor delays KATH Mother and Baby Unit as materials deteriorate
body: The stalled Mother and Baby Unit project at the Komfo Anokye Teaching Hospital (KATH) is facing further setbacks, with its consultant project manager warning that construction materials procured for the facility are deteriorating, and some have already become defective or expired due to prolonged delays. Consultant Project Manager Emmanuel Fobi Asabere disclosed this during a visit by Parliament’s Select Committee on Health to the abandoned facility in Kumasi to assess the project’s status and challenges. He said the contractor had been unable to resume full-scale construction because payments for work already undertaken remained outstanding, leading to repeated suspensions. Mr Asabere said the project had been suspended for about 14 months, following an earlier period of reduced activity due to payment delays. He explained that although the contractor had continued to maintain the site during the suspension, the prolonged inactivity was putting the procured materials and their warranty protections at risk. “The suspension is as a result of non-payment to the contractor,” he said, adding that the contractor was awaiting payment before returning to work. The project began in November 2019 as an effort to complete an existing hospital structure planned to accommodate about 850 beds. However, assessments conducted after the contractor took over revealed serious structural defects. Three other firms and the Ghana Institution of Engineers were subsequently engaged to evaluate the building, and their assessment concluded that repairing it would not be economically advisable. The project was therefore redesigned as a 509-bed hospital, involving the demolition of the old structure and construction of a new facility. Mr Asabere said the project initially cost €138.5M, but repeated suspensions led to additional expenses. He put physical construction progress at approximately 56 per cent and procurement at 75 per cent, while confirming that the design work and demolition of the previous structure had been completed. The outstanding payments, he warned, remain a major obstacle to resuming construction and completing the facility.

title: Russia Innovates for War, Not Prosperity
body:
Russia excels at making things that destroy – at the expense of its own future.
Since Vladimir Putin launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia has concentrated its technological expertise, dwindling human capital, and oil-and-gas revenues on war, rather than on its people’s well-being.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
It has sharply increased production of missiles, glide bombs, and attack drones. Russian forces have improved their electronic warfare capabilities, learned to modify Iranian-designed Shahed drones, and incorporated Chinese jet engines into Banderol quasi-cruise missiles. Cheap first-person-view drones saturate the battlefield, and Russian engineers have devised increasingly sophisticated decoys to overwhelm Ukrainian air defenses.
Russia’s war machine is inflicting ever-greater death and devastation on Ukraine.
Four and a half years of war have created a war economy in which the Kremlin can concentrate money, engineers, imported components, and industrial capacity on its military priorities. That concentration of resources has imposed mounting costs that are becoming harder to conceal.
In September, the Bank of Russia kept its benchmark interest rate at 14 percent and forecast inflation of 6 to 7 percent for 2026. Russia is no longer experiencing the apparent wartime boom that followed the invasion. High interest rates make investment and modernization expensive, while military factories compete with civilian companies for engineers, machinists, capital and materials.
In an article entitled “The Coming Crisis in Russia’s Political Economy,” published in May, Nigel Gould-Davies of the International Institute for Strategic Studies argues that Russia is approaching the limits of its productive capacity. Labor is an even tighter constraint. Oil-and-gas revenue can finance government spending but it cannot manufacture skilled workers or create factories, industrial equipment, and technological knowledge. As more resources are pushed into the military economy, each additional increment produces less.
Nowhere is Russia’s predicament clearer than in semiconductors. Mikron, part of the Rostec- and Sberbank-controlled Element Group, is a leading Russian chip manufacturer. It advertises production technologies ranging down to 90 nanometers; such mature semiconductors remain essential for automobiles, industrial equipment and many military systems.
By contrast, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) began volume production of its 2-nanometer technology late last year. Russia lacks the advanced chip-design capabilities, fabrication capacity, high-bandwidth memory, packaging, interconnects, cooling systems, and sophisticated software needed to manufacture processors competitive with those produced by TSMC and other leading semiconductor companies.
This matters because technological backwardness is not measured against where competitors stood five or ten years ago but where they are today. A Russian company that replaces an unavailable Western component may keep a factory operating but it has not narrowed the technological gap – it has merely reconstructed yesterday’s technology at considerable expense.
The pace outside Russia is accelerating further. On Sept. 30, 2026, OpenAI and Synopsys announced GPT-Synopsys, an artificial intelligence (AI) system being developed specifically to help design semiconductors. AI is increasingly being applied to the process of designing the next generation of technology itself.
Russian engineers, meanwhile, have a very different assignment – finding substitutes for unavailable software, maintaining aging equipment, and solving compatibility problems caused by sanctions. Russia calls this “technological sovereignty.”
One of its own most prominent businessmen has inadvertently exposed the weakness of that claim. In May, Sberbank CEO German Gref said Russia’s largest bank hoped eventually to operate its GigaChat AI system using Chinese processors. One of Russia’s showcase AI projects may depend on sophisticated chips Russia cannot competitively manufacture itself.
According to Bloomberg , citing people familiar with official assessments, more than 90 percent of Russia’s imports of sanctioned technology were coming through China by 2026. Before the war, Russian companies could participate, however imperfectly, in a diversified international technology economy. Putin has replaced much of that relationship with dependence on a single, more powerful neighbor whose interests do not necessarily align.
The deeper damage from this process is cumulative because industrial equipment and information systems require replacement parts, software updates, firmware, calibration, technical documentation and continuing support. A machine does not stop operating the morning its foreign manufacturer leaves Russia. It becomes progressively more difficult to maintain.
The results of Russia’s import-substitution campaign point in that direction. In a May 2026 study based on official documents, statistical data, and company surveys, Heli Simola of the Bank of Finland Institute for Emerging Economies (BOFIT) found that heavy investment in priority industries had produced only limited import substitution. In many sectors, output has declined and dependence on foreign inputs has increased.
The same problem appears in information technology. Russian technology company K2Tech reported this year that 70 percent of companies it examined remained dependent on Western backup systems. Russian replacements exist, but companies have been reluctant to abandon established foreign systems for critical operations.
Industrial deterioration is rarely instantaneous, but Ukraine has found a way to accelerate that process. Its deep drone strikes against Russian refineries and industrial facilities amount to what Ukrainians have aptly called “long-range sanctions.” Destroying a piece of equipment matters more when replacing it is difficult.
The Aug. 11, 2026 strike against the Orsk refinery illustrates the point. The refinery was forced to shut after a Ukrainian drone attack, and according to Orenburg Oblast Governor Yevgeny Solntsev, repairs are expected to take as long as six months because sanctions complicated the replacement of imported equipment.
Damage to one industrial facility consequently spreads outward – to fuel availability, transportation, military logistics, export revenues, and, ultimately, prices paid by Russian consumers.
None of the above makes Russia less dangerous. Russia has repeatedly demonstrated its ability to improvise, cannibalize commercial technologies, and solve particular military problems. This, however, is precisely the distinction that matters. A country can become exceptionally good at concentrating declining resources on weapons without becoming technologically stronger as a whole.
Putin inherited a country with considerable scientific talent, engineering traditions and industrial capacity. He has squandered that inheritance. Engineers are diverted toward weapons, civilian investment is crowded out, and Russian companies spend money reproducing technologies already available elsewhere. Dependence on Western technology has increasingly become dependence on Chinese technology. With every additional year of war, Russia risks becoming less capable of designing, building, and maintaining the technologies on which its future will depend.
Steven Fisher served as CEO of Citibank Ukraine from 2010 to 2018. He and Georgetown University’s Harley Balzer coedited Failure: Russia Under Putin (Brookings Institution Press, 2025). This op-ed was prompted in part by Balzer’s unpublished manuscript, “Technocide: How Putin’s Regime Stole Russia’s Future.”
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.
