title: NASFAT agency inaugurates new council in FCT zone
body: The NASFAT Agency for Zakat and Sadaqat (NAZAS), FCT Zone, has inaugurated a new council comprising 12 members to steer the affairs of the agency and strengthen its commitment to effective Zakat and Sadaqat administration. The inauguration ceremony, held recently at NASFAT Utako, Abuja, was attended by the past NAZAS council members, prominent NASFAT leaders and other well-wishers. The outgoing chairman of the council, Alhaji Isiaq Ajibola, administered the oath of office to the 12 newly inaugurated council members. In his presentation, he highlighted some of the agency’s achievements and charged the new council to uphold the principles of transparency, fairness, and accountability in the discharge of their responsibilities. He emphasised the importance of adhering to NAZAS’ operational principles, particularly the first-come, first-served approach, while explaining the agency’s mission and vision. He also clarified that NAZAS is an independent organisation limited by guarantee, underscoring its distinct organisational status and commitment to its objectives. In another presentation, Dr. Nasir Raji-Mustapha, an outgoing council member, provided valuable insights into strategies for mobilising Zakat and Sadaqat for the agency. He highlighted avenues through which the organisation could strengthen resource mobilisation and expand its reach to more beneficiaries. Similarly, the outgoing Head of the Finance and General Purpose Committee, Alhaji Adebayo Kilani, spoke on the impact of the NASFAT Zone on NAZAS. His presentation highlighted the contributions of the Zone to the agency’s growth and operations, providing the incoming Council with useful perspectives for sustaining and improving the existing achievements. Speaking on behalf of the newly inaugurated council, the chairman, Alhaji Abdulganiyu T. Balogun, expressed gratitude to the outgoing administration for the confidence reposed in him to lead the new team. Having served during the previous Council’s tenure, he acknowledged the foundation laid by his predecessors and pledged to build on their achievements. He further assured stakeholders of the new Council’s commitment to introducing beneficial initiatives that would enhance the agency’s operations, strengthen its impact, and advance its mission of effective Zakat and Sadaqat administration. The event was graced by the Chairman of the NASFAT Board of Trustees, Alhaji Abdulateef Wale Olasupo, and his wife; the NASFAT Zonal Chairman; the Women Secretary; the Zonal Missioner; and other distinguished guests and well-wishers. Also in attendance were outgoing NAZAS Council members, including Dr Mrs. Maryam Sheihu and Barrister S. O. Q. Giwa, among others. The inauguration marked a new chapter in the leadership of NAZAS in the FCT Zone, with renewed expectations for stronger institutional development, effective resource mobilisation, and improved service delivery to eligible beneficiaries of Zakat and Sadaqat.

title: Yobe distributes 160 motorcycles, other items to forest guards
body: The Yobe State Government has distributed 160 motorcycles and other operational items to 886 forest guards deployed to support security operations across the state. The Secretary to the State Government (SSG), Dr Muhammad Goje, announced the distribution on Tuesday, saying the items were intended to improve the working conditions and operational capacity of the personnel. The items include 900 raincoats, 900 pairs of rain boots, 900 blankets, 900 torchlights and 900 mosquito nets. Goje said the intervention was made on behalf of Governor Mai Mala Buni to provide additional security support and strengthen the protection of lives and property in the state. The Commander of the 27 Task Force Brigade, Buni-Gari, Brigadier General M.S. Mukhtar, described the donation as a force multiplier that would enhance the operational effectiveness of the forest guards. He said the motorcycles would improve mobility, extend patrol coverage and strengthen rapid response to security threats, particularly terrorism, banditry and other criminal activities in the state. He urged the forest guards to make judicious use of the equipment, particularly the motorcycles, in line with the purposes for which they were provided. The brigade commander assured residents that the military and other security agencies were working to improve security across the state. He also appealed for additional support to strengthen operations and enable residents to carry out their daily activities without fear. Earlier, the governor’s Security Adviser, Brigadier General Dahiru Abdulsalam (rtd), said Yobe was allocated an initial batch of 1,000 forest guards under a Federal Government pilot scheme. He said the recruits were drawn from seven frontline local government areas: Gulani, Gujba, Damaturu, Tarmuwa, Bursari, Yunusari and Geidam. According to him, 886 personnel successfully completed their training in December 2025 before undergoing further training under the Nigerian Army. Abdulsalam said the personnel were deployed to various locations in March 2026 under the mentorship of the military, particularly the 27 Task Force Brigade. He explained that the forest guards were established to help security agencies tackle criminal activities in forested areas and ungoverned spaces used by insurgents, kidnappers and other criminals. The security adviser commended Governor Buni for the support but appealed for additional communication equipment, surveillance devices for intelligence gathering and reconnaissance, and vehicles for administrative duties and patrols. He also called on the governor to approve the recruitment of another 1,000 forest guards to strengthen the force and extend its operations to other parts of the state.

title: Ekiti, Osun polls: Votes sold for N50,000, says EU observer group
body: The European Union Support to Democratic Governance in Nigeria (EU-SDGN) Election Observation Hub has said vote trading during the Ekiti and Osun states governorship elections was rampant, with voters rewarded heavily for selling their votes. The Hub, established for election monitoring, is made up of the Kukah Centre (TKC), TAF Africa, Nigerian Women Trust Fund (NWTF), Yiaga Africa, International Press Centre (IPC) and Centre for Media and Society (CEMESO). Speaking at the presentation and dissemination of the report on the Ekiti and Osun Off-cycle Elections (which took place in June and August, 2026, respectively) in Abuja on Tuesday, Prof. Bolade Eyinla, who read the findings of the Hub, said voters got up to N50,000 for selling their votes. “The scourge of vote trading is becoming a pandemic,” he said, adding that, “if we don’t do anything about it, the sanctity of the vote and freedom of choice is beginning to come under severe threat and pressure.” Prof. Eyinla lamented that vote trading has become extremely well organised and standardised, stressing that offenders remain unpunished. “Maybe the IG (Inspector-General of Police) will tell us if they are arrested. And the result of that is that everybody has assumed a sense of impunity. “The data shows us that 77% of the 84 verified incidents were vote trading, and party agents were the main actors in at least 90% of these cases. “In Osun, it was 69%, and as I said, we still have not heard of any reported arrests, investigations, or prosecutions, given the magnitude of vote trading that went on in both elections.” Describing how it was carried out, he said the voter marks the ballot paper to show his preference, but he then brings it up to show the people who are making the tally. “And of course, once the agent confirms ‘he has done what we demanded’, payment follows. “Originally, I was thinking payment was within the range of 10,000 or thereabouts, but the report from Osun even told me that people got N50,000. If you divide N50,000 by the number of voters in Osun, how much that will amount to in terms of the volume of money involved,” he said. The Hub also called for the presentation of results from the ward level, noting that most of the irregularities are done at that level. “I think for the presidential election, it’s 8,809 (wards). We want to see the results of the ward level uploaded. If you can upload polling units, then you should be able to upload ward-level results,” he argued. However, the Hub commended the Independent Electoral Commission for organising a near-perfect election, noting that the election started early and the results were almost the same as those independently compiled. It also commended the security agencies for ensuring a peaceful poll in Ekiti and Osun. Dr Akin Akingbulu, the Executive Director, Centre for Media and Society (CEMESO), in his remarks, said the Hub deployed 598 observers across all 16 Local Government Areas in Ekiti on 20 June, and 823 observers across all 30 LGAs in Osun on 15 August. “That is more than 1,400 trained Nigerians who watched, counted, verified and reported, polling unit by polling unit, so that the conversation we have today rests on facts and not on sentiment,” he said.

title: Catholic diocese shuts Benue institutions after attacks
body: The Catholic Diocese of Gboko has ordered the indefinite closure of all its institutions in Ihugh town of Vandeikya Local Government Area of Benue State, following repeated arson attacks on school hostels and other church properties. Our correspondent reports that the decision, which also involves the withdrawal of all priests, religious workers, teachers and medical personnel serving in the community, followed the latest fire outbreak at St. Winifred Girls Secondary School on Sunday, October 11, 2026. The fire, which gutted a hostel block at the all-girls school, was the fourth such incident at the institution since October 2025 and the third in four months, raising fresh concerns over the safety of students and the security of church-owned facilities in the community. In a pastoral letter and decree dated October 12, 2026, the Bishop of Gboko Diocese, Most Rev. William Avenya, said the decision followed years of hostility, including repeated fires at the school, persistent burglary at St. Winifred Parish and criminal attacks on St. Thomas Hospital. The Bishop also cited an incident during the reopening of the hospital on June 21, 2024, when some persons allegedly declared that they no longer wanted Reverend Sisters to work in the community. He said that the diocese had made several attempts to resolve the situation through dialogue with traditional rulers, community elders, civil authorities and security agencies but had yet to obtain lasting peace and credible guarantees of safety. Consequently, the diocese ordered the closure of St. Winifred Girls Secondary School, St. Thomas Hospital, Salus Mind Care Centre, Hospital Chaplaincy, St. Winifred Nursery and Primary School, and St. Winifred Parish, all in Ihugh. Avenya also directed the withdrawal of all priests, consecrated persons, catechists, teachers, medical personnel and administrative staff serving under the diocese in the community. He said arrangements would be made for affected students to continue their education in other Catholic schools, while patients receiving care at St. Thomas Hospital would be referred to other health facilities. Earlier, some parents threatened to withdraw children after the latest fire outbreak on Sunday heightened fears among them about the students safety. A parent, Paul Tikyaa, who has two children in the school, told journalists in Makurdi by telephone that he had decided to withdraw them. “I have made up my mind to take my two children out of that school. One day, it will be the children that will be set ablaze. Enough is enough,” he said. Another parent, Mrs Dooshima Agande, said parents had appealed to the Bishop to relocate the school outside Vandeikya LGA. “This is the fourth time fire has gutted a hostel in that school and we, parents, have now appealed to the Bishop to relocate the school to another local government, not even within Vandeikya,” she said. Our correspondent gathered that the hostel gutted in Sunday’s fire had reportedly been renovated by members of the Ihugh community following an earlier incident in which another hostel block was completely razed. After that incident, Avenya had threatened to relocate the school but reconsidered following appeals from community members. A business mogul and politician, Dr Livinus Tsar, had also reportedly undertaken the construction of a new hostel block, donated N20 million and installed closed-circuit television cameras on the school premises in an effort to prevent further incidents. However, the latest outbreak has renewed concerns about the effectiveness of measures taken to protect the institution as the cause of the fire had yet to be established as of the time of filing this report, Police Public Relations Officer (PPRO) for Benue command, DSP Peter Aondongu, also confirmed the fire incident, saying no life was lost. “Yes, there was a fire incident, but no life was lost. The police are currently investigating the incident,” the PPRO said.

title: Kofi Adams says Ghanaians ignored warnings over World Cup visa payments
body: Minister for Sports and Recreation Kofi Adams says some Ghanaians disregarded repeated warnings against paying intermediaries who promised to secure United States and Canadian visas for the 2026 FIFA World Cup, with post-tournament information suggesting that money changed hands without the Ministry’s knowledge. He said prospective travellers had been cautioned against trusting individuals who claimed they could influence visa decisions through personal connections with government officials or members of the World Cup oversight committee. Mr Adams urged Ghanaians seeking travel assistance to use registered travel and tour companies with clear procedures and contractual obligations. He said some of the individuals allegedly demanded money by presenting themselves as friends of the Minister or people with access to the oversight committee. He warned that such claims should not be treated as a guarantee of visa approval, stressing that the Ministry had not authorised individuals to collect money on its behalf to influence visa applications. Speaking to Channel One TV on Tuesday, October 13, Mr Adams said he had issued several public warnings before the tournament. However, information gathered afterwards indicated that some people still paid intermediaries, including individuals allegedly holding official positions. “Before the World Cup, as Minister, on several occasions I had cause to warn Ghanaians and advise Ghanaians not to give money out to anybody in the name of going to offer you a visa to go to the US or Canada,” he said. The comments come amid scrutiny of alleged visa facilitation arrangements involving the Ghana Tourism Authority and the National Sports Authority. The Minority in Parliament has raised concerns over claims that some applicants were charged between US$7,000 and US$14,000 for visa assistance. President John Dramani Mahama has directed Yaw Ampofo Ankrah to step aside as Director-General of the National Sports Authority as police investigate the allegations.

title: Over 1.2m complaints received, 700 resolved in 2 years – PPC
body: The Public Complaints Commission (PPC) has said it received over 1.2 million cases in the past two years, with over 700 of them resolved. The Chief Commissioner of the PPC, Hon. Bashir Abubakar, disclosed this on Tuesday while addressing the media ahead of the Commission’s anniversary conference slated for Thursday, 15 October, 2026. He said that since the establishment of the Commission over 50 years ago, up to 2025, it has recorded around 1.8 million complaints, with about 1.4 million of them resolved. He said the recent surge showed greater awareness and confidence of the public in the activities of the Commission. He also said the Commission had ensured industrial harmony between the management and all the unions, creating an improved working environment, including equipping the generality of staff with modern technologies best suitable in modern times. “There is a surge in complaint index statistics and data in recent times more than ever before as follows: 1,281,984 cases received,716,688 cases resolved, leaving behind 562,296 cases, “ he said. “Recall that in the year 2025 the Nigerian Ombudsman celebrated her golden jubilee, and the dividend of that public outing was highly rewarding to the commission in terms of effective partnership from all relevant stakeholders to date.” Hon. Abubakar said it was based on some identified challenges and the giant strides recorded that the Commission had decided to organise its 1st Nigerian Ombudsman Conference scheduled to take place tomorrow, “to put on the front burner importance and comparative analysis between a strong system and a weak institution.

title: Iran's nuclear tech. potentials 'par with advanced nations'
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 14 (MNA) – The head of Atomic Energy Organization of Iran (AEOI) says that the country’s capabilities in nuclear science and technology are rival to those of the developed countries, showing Iran’s eye-catching progress in this field.
Opposing the country’s possession of peaceful nuclear technology cannot change the reality of its scientific achievements, AEOI Chief Mohammad Eslami stated, emphasizing that Iran stands on a par with developed countries in nuclear science and technology.
Speaking at a ceremony marking National Standard Day in Tehran on Tuesday, the country's atomic chief highlighted that the country’s intellectual resources, technological expertise, and the resourcefulness of its younger generation qualified it to achieve the highest levels of scientific and technological advancement.
“We are on a par with the developed and advanced countries in nuclear science and technology, and that is a reality.
Opposition and refusal to accept Iran’s possession of nuclear technology does not change the reality of the country’s scientific capabilities,” he opined.
“We have done nothing wrong,” he asserted, adding that Iran’s adversaries would have no other grounds to target the country if they stopped trying to tarnish its nuclear energy sector.
Addressing Iran’s industrial capabilities, Eslami said nuclear technology had become integrated into major industrial sectors, including refineries, petrochemical plants, and steel production.
He noted how industrial facilities across the country were targeted during unprovoked American-Israeli aggression in order to try to afflict damage to components involved in maintaining the stability of industrial processes.

title: Court fixes Nov 20 for ruling on Atiku’s forgery suit against Tinubu
body: A Federal High Court sitting in Abuja, on Tuesday, fixed November 20, 2026, to rule on whether the former Vice President, Atiku Abubakar, can be permitted to amend his suit against the President, Bola Tinubu, over alleged certificate forgery. The judge fixed the date following the insistence of the presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) to alter his claims against Tinubu, claiming the president forged his National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) certificate. Daily Trust reports that Atiku and the ADC had filed the main suit seeking the disqualification of Tinubu and the APC from the 2027 presidential election over the President’s National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) discharge certificate submitted to the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC). They alleged that the APC submitted a forged NYSC discharge certificate to INEC and asked the court to order the electoral commission to remove Tinubu and the APC from the list of candidates and parties for the election. The main grouse of Atiku and ADC was that the NYSC discharge certificate presented by Tinubu bears Bola Adekunle as against the well known of his name as Bola Tinubu. Tinubu and the APC have denied the allegation and asked the court to dismiss the suit. The President opposed the application, arguing that the proposed amendments went beyond correcting errors and would introduce new reliefs, documents and facts into the case. INEC also opposed the amendment, arguing that it would introduce a new cause of action and seek to cure defects in the original suit after the constitutional deadline for filing pre-election cases had lapsed On September 10, Atiku and the ADC filed the application, seeking leave to amend their originating summons and have the proposed amended process deemed properly filed. They said they discovered errors in the original suit, including referring to an INEC form as Form CF001 instead of Form EC9A. However, Wole Olanipekun, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria, who represented Tinubu, kicked against Atiku’s application, adding that since both parties have joined issues with each other, the former Vice President cannot shift the goalpost in the middle of the game. At Tuesday’s proceedings, Joseph Silas Onu, who stood for Atiku, adopted his application praying for permission of the court to amend the originating summons against Tinubu and APC to accommodate more allegations. Justice Inyang Ekwo announced November 20 to make his decision known in his ruling on the application.

title: US lawmakers press Pentagon over civilian deaths in Iran
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 14 (MNA) – A group of 77 US Congress members is “demanding answers” from the Pentagon on the protection of civilians after two deadly US strikes in Iran this year.
On September 1, a US air strike killed five civilians, including two children, at a wedding in Kuhestak, Hormozgan province.
In a post on X, Democratic Congresswoman Yassamin Ansari said it was “the latest in a horrifying pattern of civilian casualties” resulting from Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s “disastrous and illegal war” in Iran.
She also highlighted a February 28 strike on a school in Minab, Hormozgan province, which killed 120 children.

title: Climate change: Expert urges media to tell Africa’s stories
body: Africa has been urged to move beyond climate commitments and translate them into tangible results through stronger collaboration, private investors and development institutions. George Nwangwu, Convener of the Africa Climate Forum, made the call in his welcome address at the fourth edition of the forum held in Abuja on Tuesday. He noted that the continent continued to face flooding, drought, food insecurity and environmental degradation despite commitments to address climate change. Nwangwu added that the media also has a role to play in climate action by telling stories that highlight the impact of climate change on livelihoods, as well as the resilience and innovations of African communities. He said climate reporting should go beyond statistics to reflect the experiences of farmers affected by flooding, families facing drought and young entrepreneurs developing solutions to environmental challenges. According to him, Africa must not be seen merely as a recipient of climate solutions developed elsewhere. He stated, “We are also a source of knowledge, creativity and innovation. Our entrepreneurs understand the realities of our markets and communities.”

title: Christa Pike survives two doses of lethal injection drug: can Tennessee try to execute her again?
body: How could a death row inmate survive two doses of a lethal drug and regain consciousness? The extraordinary case of Christa Pike has thrust the death penalty in the United States back into headlines around the world in recent days, reigniting debate over how executions are carried out. Pike was sentenced to death for murdering a female friend at age 18 because she suspected the victim was trying to "steal" her boyfriend. On September 30, more than 30 years after the murder, the state of Tennessee attempted to execute her.   Pike received two doses of a drug that, in high concentrations, is supposed to stop breathing and heart function. But then something highly unusual happened: She did not die. Pike was taken to a hospital, recovered quickly and in recent days has begun walking and even speaking. Death row inmates surviving execution attempts is uncommon, but not unprecedented. In almost every previous case, it happened because the procedure was halted midway, either because an electric chair malfunctioned or because the execution team was unable to find a suitable vein and insert an IV. Pike's case, however, is particularly extraordinary. As far as is known, she is the first person in U.S. history to survive an execution attempt after the lethal drug had already been injected into her body. Pike's was not even the only botched execution attempt in Tennessee this year. In May, the state attempted to execute Tony Carruthers, who had been sentenced to death for kidnapping and murder, at the same prison. The execution team spent about an hour and a half trying to insert an IV but failed, and the procedure was called off. Pike's case, however, proved to be the final straw for Tennessee. In its wake, the governor suspended all executions through the end of the year, and the state's corrections commissioner resigned. The injection designed to be 'humane' has the highest failure rate But what happened in Tennessee was not merely an isolated failure. A study by Professor Austin Sarat, which examined nearly 8,800 executions in the United States between 1890 and 2010, found that the very method intended to make executions more efficient and less gruesome has an exceptionally high rate of complications. According to the study, 7.2% of the 1,054 executions carried out by lethal injection since 1982 were botched. That is a higher failure rate than any other execution method and more than twice the overall average. There are three main reasons for this. The first is physiological: The injection works only if the drug enters the bloodstream directly. But for some inmates, including older people and those with a history of drug use, finding a suitable vein can be extremely difficult. When the IV is not properly inserted, the drug may fail to reach its intended destination.   The second problem is a lack of properly trained personnel. According to research by Professor Corinna Lain of the University of Richmond, very few doctors across the United States participate in executions. Many physicians refuse to take part in the procedure on ethical grounds. The result is a paradox: The procedure looks entirely medical, with syringes, IV lines and monitors, but those carrying it out do not necessarily have the necessary medical training or experience. The third problem is the drugs themselves. Many pharmaceutical companies do not want their products used in executions and therefore refuse to sell them to states for that purpose. As a result, states are forced to obtain the drugs from small pharmacies and suppliers whose identities are sometimes kept secret. Under these circumstances, it is difficult to know who manufactured the drugs, how they were stored and how reliable they are. This is where the economic absurdity comes in. Because almost no one is willing to supply the drugs, states pay exorbitant prices for them. Tennessee, for example, paid an average of approximately $95,000 for the drugs needed for each execution between 2017 and 2020, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Even so, the drugs account for only a small portion of the overall cost. The common assumption is that the death penalty is cheaper than life imprisonment, but in many cases the opposite is true. A University of Denver study found that cases in which prosecutors seek the death penalty take more than five years on average to reach sentencing, compared with less than a year and a half for cases involving life imprisonment without parole. The real costs come afterward, during the appeals process, which lasts nearly 20 years on average. According to the Death Penalty Information Center, in some states a death penalty case costs $1 million to $3 million more than a case that ends in a life sentence. Can Pike be executed a second time? Despite the failed attempt, Pike's story is not over. Her death sentence remains in effect, and at least in theory, Tennessee could attempt to carry it out again. But her case differs from previous botched executions. In Pike's case, the lethal drug had already been injected into her body. Her case could therefore present the courts with an unusual legal question: Would a second attempt to execute someone violate the Eighth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, which prohibits "cruel and unusual punishments"? Another possibility is that Tennessee's governor could decide to commute her sentence to life imprisonment. As of October 2026, the death penalty remains legal in 27 US states. Another 23 states have abolished it, while executions are effectively suspended by governors' orders in several states, including California. Tennessee tried to close the case of Christa Gail Pike, but instead reopened the broader debate over the death penalty. Her case raises a question that is difficult to ignore: If the state cannot reliably carry out an execution, how much can it be trusted to decide who should be put to death?

title: Banks to charge 20% VAT on payments for Netflix, Zoom, TikTok and others
body: Commercial banks are preparing to apply 20 per cent Value Added Tax (VAT) to payments for cross-border digital services and e-commerce transactions made with cards issued in Ghana, according to information gathered by Joy Business. The banks say they are implementing a directive from the Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA). However, Joy Business has yet to establish the details of the directive or whether any banks have already begun applying the tax. Standard Chartered Bank has notified its customers by email that it will begin applying the 20 per cent VAT to payments for cross-border digital services made with its Ghana-issued cards from October 15, 2026. According to the bank, the move is in line with GRA requirements. Transactions expected to be affected Information gathered by Joy Business suggests that the tax could cover payments across the following categories. The full scope and treatment of individual services are yet to be confirmed: Digital media and entertainment: Services such as Netflix, Spotify, Disney+, Showmax and beIN Sports. Software and software as a service: Products and subscriptions from Microsoft, Adobe, Zoom, Salesforce and Google Workspace. Cloud and hosting services: Platforms such as Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, DigitalOcean and SiteGround. Digital gaming and betting: Payments to platforms such as Steam, Blizzard, Roblox, DraftKings and Betway Ghana. Education and subscriptions: Services such as Coursera, Udemy, MasterClass and Cambridge University Press. Digital advertising: Payments for Google Ads, Meta Ads, TikTok Ads and LinkedIn advertising. Social media and communication: Paid services offered by platforms such as TikTok, LinkedIn, X and WhatsApp Business. Online travel and hospitality: Payments through platforms such as Booking.com, Agoda, Hotels.com, Uber and Bolt. Computer and IT services: Payments to providers such as Groundhog Tech and Neris Analytics. Security and VPN services: Subscriptions to services such as McAfee, NordVPN and ExpressVPN. What it means for customers Customers paying for affected services with debit or credit cards issued in Ghana should expect the 20 per cent VAT to be added to the amount payable. Some commercial banks have stressed that the additional cost is a tax imposed under GRA requirements, rather than a fee introduced by the banks. For affected transactions, customers could therefore pay the service price, the applicable VAT and any existing bank transaction charges.

title: AREWA24 launches new programme to promote maternal, newborn health
body: AREWA24, a Hausa-language family entertainment and lifestyle television network, has launched a new show “Uwa Da Da” dedicated to mothers, babies and the journey from pregnancy through childbirth and early childhood. The show premieres every Saturday primetime (7 pm – 7:30 pm) on the AREWA24 television network. The show comes at a time when maternal, newborn and child survival remains a major public health challenge in Nigeria, particularly in northern communities where health outcomes are lagging. According to the 2023–24 Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey (NDHS), Nigeria recorded an infant mortality rate of 63 deaths per 1,000 live births, while neonatal mortality stood at 41 deaths per 1,000 live births. Earlier NDHS data showed an under-five mortality rate of 187 deaths per 1,000 live births in the Northwest, compared with 62 per 1,000 in the Southwest. Aisha Lawal, AREWA24’s Director of Studio Production, said: “For many women, pregnancy and motherhood can be accompanied by uncertainty, fear and misinformation. “Uwa Da Da places particular emphasis on supporting first-time mothers by providing clear, practical and culturally relevant information to help them understand what to expect before, during and after childbirth. “The show will create a platform where mothers can hear directly from qualified health professionals and other mothers, while learning about important issues including pregnancy nutrition, antenatal care, birth preparedness, breastfeeding, newborn danger signs, immunisation and postnatal wellbeing.” A central objective of Uwa Da Da is to encourage pregnant women, particularly expectant and first-time mothers, to seek appropriate antenatal care (ANC) early in pregnancy and maintain regular contact with qualified healthcare professionals. The Chief Executive Officer of AREWA24 TV Network, Celestine Umeibe, affirmed that “Uwa Da Da (“Mother and Child”), reflects AREWA24’s commitment to producing content that informs, educates and entertains while addressing issues that directly affect families and communities across Northern Nigeria and beyond. “The program combines human-interest stories, expert advice, practical demonstrations and conversations with mothers and families to make maternal and newborn health information engaging, relatable and actionable. The goal of the “Uwa Da” is not to replace professional healthcare, but to encourage mothers and families to seek, understand and use available healthcare services at the right time,” he said.

title: West Africa must build competitive regional industries, not just expand trade — Benedicta Lasi
body: African Trade Chamber Chair calls for greater investment in productive industries, stronger African enterprises and regional integration that supports industrial transformation. Lomé, Togo — The Executive Chair of the African Trade Chamber (ATC), H.E. Benedicta Lasi, has called for a more ambitious approach to West Africa’s economic transformation, urging governments, regional institutions and development finance organisations to prioritise competitive industrial production, technological capabilities and the development of integrated regional value chains. Speaking at the media launch of the ECOWAS Investment Forum (EIF) 2027, organised by the ECOWAS Bank for Investment and Development (EBID), Ms. Lasi argued that West Africa’s continued vulnerability to global economic disruptions reflects structural weaknesses that require sustained investment in productive capabilities, diversified industries and competitive African enterprises. She observed that the region’s dependence on primary commodity exports, limited industrial diversification and relatively weak production linkages constrain its ability to retain economic value, generate productive employment and withstand external shocks. She maintained that regional resilience must increasingly be measured by the capacity of African economies to produce competitively, develop technological capabilities, accumulate capital and participate in higher-value segments of regional and global industries. Regional Integration Must Extend to Industrial Production Addressing the region’s low levels of intra-regional trade, Ms. Lasi drew attention to EBID’s West African Development Outlook 2025, which estimated intra-ECOWAS trade at approximately 7 per cent in 2024, down from around 10 per cent in 2023. The figures underscore the need to strengthen economic integration, although recorded trade statistics do not fully capture informal cross-border commerce. She acknowledged the institutional foundations established through ECOWAS, while arguing that the next phase of integration must combine trade facilitation with deliberate efforts to develop diversified and complementary production capabilities across West African economies. “We continually ask how West African countries can trade more with one another. We must now ask how West African countries can produce more with one another,” she stated. Ms. Lasi advocated the development of commercially viable regional production networks that build on the comparative advantages, industrial capabilities and infrastructure of participating economies. She explained that regional industrialisation should enable countries to specialise in different stages of production where such arrangements improve productivity, competitiveness and access to markets, rather than encouraging the unnecessary duplication of industries across national economies. Using cocoa as an illustration, she argued that West Africa’s substantial contribution to global production should support greater participation in commercially competitive segments of the industry’s value chain, including specialised processing, industrial ingredients, product development, packaging, branding and distribution. Similar opportunities, she observed, exist in agro-processing, pharmaceuticals, fertilisers, energy and aluminium, provided investments are supported by credible demand, competitive infrastructure and appropriate industrial capabilities. Africa Must Build Productive and Competitive Enterprises Turning to inclusive entrepreneurship, Ms. Lasi urged governments and development partners to place greater emphasis on enterprise productivity, technological upgrading and the ability of commercially viable businesses to expand beyond their domestic markets. She cited World Bank estimates indicating that 10–12 million young Africans enter the labour force annually, while approximately three million formal jobs are created, highlighting the importance of building productive enterprises capable of generating employment at scale. “Perhaps one measure of a successful SME policy should be how many enterprises eventually cease to qualify as SMEs,” she remarked. Ms. Lasi argued that entrepreneurship policies must distinguish between support for livelihoods and targeted interventions that enable high-potential enterprises to become competitive medium-sized and large firms. She emphasised that access to finance must be accompanied by investments in technology, skills, management capabilities, infrastructure and market access. She also called for greater African participation in productive investment and enterprise ownership, alongside international partnerships that strengthen domestic suppliers, facilitate technological learning and support long-term capital formation. According to her, industrial transformation should be assessed not simply through the volume of goods processed or manufactured locally, but through improvements in productivity, technological sophistication and the capacity of African companies to compete sustainably. AfCFTA and Development Finance Must Deliver Measurable Industrial Outcomes On the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), Ms. Lasi described the agreement as an important opportunity to overcome market fragmentation and improve the commercial viability of industrial investment. She emphasised that its economic significance lies in converting fragmented national markets into increasingly accessible regional and continental markets, allowing firms to achieve economies of scale and develop stronger production networks. She referenced World Bank modelling indicating that full implementation of AfCFTA could increase Africa’s income by approximately US$450 billion by 2035, with around US$292 billion of those potential gains arising from trade facilitation measures, including reduced administrative barriers and lower trade costs. She noted that these estimates demonstrate the economic importance of implementation, although the projected benefits depend on sustained reforms. Ms. Lasi stressed that the success of AfCFTA must ultimately be reflected in the ability of businesses to invest, source inputs, access financing and expand across borders, rather than being measured exclusively through the adoption of trade agreements and regulatory instruments. Welcoming EBID’s 2026–2030 Growth, Resilience and Optimisation Strategy, she commended the Bank’s increased emphasis on private-sector development, infrastructure and regional economic integration. EBID has indicated that 63 per cent of its new commitments are directed towards the private sector, including a dedicated allocation to SMEs. She encouraged development finance institutions to assess their investments not only by financing volumes, but by their additional contribution to productive capacity, private capital mobilisation, technological upgrading and regional enterprise growth. Ms. Lasi further proposed that EIF 2027 identify a limited number of commercially promising regional production systems and develop coordinated investment pipelines around them, bringing together industrial projects, supporting infrastructure, enterprise development and financing arrangements. She argued that the Forum’s investment Deal Rooms could provide an important mechanism for addressing specific regulatory, infrastructure and financing constraints, while establishing clearer responsibilities for project implementation. She also underscored the importance of mobilising African institutional capital through appropriately structured investments, guarantees and risk-sharing arrangements capable of attracting pension funds, insurance assets and private investors without compromising their prudential obligations. From Economic Potential to Productive Transformation Ms. Lasi concluded by urging African governments and regional institutions to place greater emphasis on the execution of industrial strategies and the development of institutions capable of coordinating investment, infrastructure, finance and enterprise development. She maintained that West Africa’s economic transformation should ultimately be measured by the productive capabilities it develops, the competitiveness of its industries, the expansion of its enterprises and the value it creates through regional economic cooperation. “Resilience must become less about West Africa’s capacity to endure the consequences of economic decisions made elsewhere and more about our capacity to build productive power here,” she stated. The ECOWAS Investment Forum 2027 is scheduled for 7–8 April 2027 in Lomé, Togo, bringing together governments, investors, development finance institutions and private-sector leaders to advance investment opportunities supporting regional economic transformation.

title: Social media bans are no cure-all, but governments may still find them necessary
body: BALI, Indonesia – Restricting access to online platforms cannot address all the factors that contribute to the radicalization of young people, but governments have “valid” reasons for imposing bans, said I Gusti Agung Wesaka Puja, executive director of the ASEAN Institute for Peace and Reconciliation (ASEAN-IPR). “There is no perfect solution, especially when we are encountering this new kind of threat, a new kind of non-traditional security issue,” Puja told Rappler in an interview on October 12. Puja maintained that while governments may find it necessary to step in and implement social media bans to protect children from harmful content, these measures still require careful assessment. “The government in this respect has the responsibility to consider the safety and well-being of young people because they are our future leaders, particularly as digital platforms continue to evolve and continue to provide a threat to them,” said Puja. “However, whether restrictions on social media access will produce positive long-term outcomes, certainly this needs careful assessment,” he added. Puja leads ASEAN’s think tank on peace and conflict. A recent study by ASEAN-IPR found that traditional security responses are insufficient to prevent violence as young people in Southeast Asia gain greater access to it. The Philippine Senate has approved Senate Bill 2424 that restricts social media access of children under 16. The House of Representatives approved a similar measure or House Bill 11566. These legislative developments follow three school shootings in the country that occurred this year. (READ: Why Congress should think twice about banning under-18s from social media ) Indonesia also started implementing the ban early this year, and countries across the world are considering social media legislation, following the likes of Australia, the United Kingdom, and Brazil. “Maybe putting some bans on the use of social media, it could be effective,” Bora Park, security and terrorism expert from Seoul-based Institute for National Security Strategy, told Rappler in a separate interview. “But in the long term, it might also have a side effect,” Bora said, adding that young people may find ways to circumvent the regulations and create new slang, making it “much harder to detect which one is radicalized and how dangerous that individual would be.” Proposal to create tiered restrictions Skeptics of such measures cite their potential effects on young people’s access to information, education and opportunities, as well as their social interactions. Implementation of the regulation remains uncertain, as it relies heavily on the cooperation of private technology companies. Senator Risa Hontiveros , the sole Philippine lawmaker who voted against the bill on social media ban for kids, said the priority is how to effectively protect children. Hontiveros advocates for “tiered restrictions for adolescents.” In her statement , Hontiveros said younger adolescents should have tighter restrictions. As kids age and mature, she proposed they be given “autonomy while protections remain against abuse, exploitation, and harmful content.” “Taking it away from them all of a sudden without providing adequate ways for them to cope with its absence is not the answer to their needs and it is not the answer to our collective fears,” Hontiveros said. title: Ban on Departures from Piraeus and Lavrio Due to Strong Aegean Winds
body: A ban on sailings from the ports of Piraeus and Lavrio is in effect until 3 pm because of strong winds reaching force 9 and temporarily 10 Beaufort in parts of the Aegean, according to the National Meteorological Service (EMY). The passenger ferry Blue Star Delos departed Piraeus normally at 7:20 am on its scheduled route to Paros, Naxos, Thira and Ios. In the Argosaronic Gulf, only certain conventional passenger-cargo routes are operating; no hydrofoil services are running. Morning departures from Rafina are expected to proceed normally. The Agia Marina–Nea Stira and Arkitsa–Edipsos routes are suspended due to adverse weather. Passengers planning to travel today are advised to check with local port authorities or travel agents for any changes or cancellations. Latest updates: Hellenic Coast Guard – https://www.hcg.gr | EMY – https://www.emy.gr The post Ban on Departures from Piraeus and Lavrio Due to Strong Aegean Winds appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Judge grants preliminary injunction continuing to block Trump's White House media ban
body:
Trump had tried to bar CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House.
A federal judge continued to block the Trump administration's move to bar CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House.
U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly's preliminary injunction orders the defendants to continue to preserve the status quo while the case proceeds.
The preliminary injunction was sought by the media organizations.
It follows a temporary restraining order the same judge issued last month blocking Trump's attempt to ban the news organizations from the White House.
"We are grateful that the Court ruled in favor of our clients CNN, MS NOW and POLITICO and secured access to the White House for these news media organizations and their journalists,” Theodore J. Boutrous, Jr., attorney for CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO, said in a statement obtained by ABC News.
“When the President issued his ‘ban on the free press,’ he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment. Since then, the President has repeatedly, candidly, and consistently admitted in public that he banned our clients from the White House to punish reporting he doesn’t like and to try to force journalists to cover him in ways he prefers,” Boutros Jr. added.
“The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound. The Court was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this ‘unconstitutional ban on the free press’ for the foreseeable future," said Boutrous Jr.
Last month, CNN, MSNOW and Politico requested a temporary restraining order to restore their reporters' access to the White House complex after Trump instituted the ban. In the lawsuit, the news organizations called Trump's decision at "direct assault on the First Amendment" and a "blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles."
Trump said in a social media post in September that the "Media Outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America."
The Department of Justice defended the ban , citing specific stories from each outlet that it claimed violated "standards of professionalism and decorum" by “trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information."
Justice Department lawyer Michael Velchik last month argued that President Trump has broad authority to remove outlets based on national security determinations and the letters sent to the media organizations provided sufficient due process to justify revoking their passes.
"Access to the White House is a privilege, not a right," Velchik said.

title: Attempt to smuggle snakes foiled at Muscat Airport
body:
Muscat: Several royal pythons were seized at Muscat International Airport after a traveller attempted to bring the snakes into Oman. It considers a violation to wildlife trade regulations. The Environment Authority (EA), in cooperation with the Royal Oman Police (ROP) and the Directorate General of Customs, apprehended the individual during an attempted import of the snakes through the airport. The royal pythons are listed in Appendix II of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), which regulates international trade in listed wildlife species. The attempted import violated Oman’s Wildlife Trade Regulation Law, and the necessary legal procedures have been taken against the violator, the EA said.
