title: Greece Offers €10,000 to Move to Remote Areas – Applications Now Open
body: The platform for Greece’s expanded Relocation Program opens today, offering €10,000 to up to 1,000 households that permanently move to remote areas. The scheme aims to address demographic decline and urban concentration. Applications remain open until 31 December 2028 or until the 1,000-household limit is reached. Eligible areas include municipalities in Evros, Drama , Florina, Kilkis, Serres, Pella, Kastoria, Kozani, Grevena, Ioannina and Thesprotia. Greek residents of other EU countries may also apply if they can prove prior residence abroad. Recent university graduates with ties to the relevant regional unit are likewise eligible. Applicants cannot come from Epirus, Western Macedonia, Eastern Macedonia and Thrace, or the Northern and Southern Aegean, as these are already considered remote. There are no income or employment requirements. A tax return for the previous three years is needed, and minor children must complete compulsory education. The residence may be owned or rented. Applications are submitted online at https://relocation.vouchers.gov.gr using Taxis codes. Required documents include AMKA, ID or passport, Greek IBAN and proof of residence or tax filings where applicable. After document checks and municipal verification of the move, €5,000 is paid as an advance. The remaining €5,000 is released after one year of confirmed residence. Source: Chrysostomos Tsoufis, SKAI.gr The post Greece Offers €10,000 to Move to Remote Areas – Applications Now Open appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: NATO no longer constrained. Gen. Nowak: New air defence rules in Poland [INTERVIEW]
body:
A special, sterile prohibited area, designated “P”, will be established in Polish airspace to facilitate operations by ground-based air defence systems in the east of the country. In an interview with Defence24, Armed Forces Operational Commander Maj. Gen. Ireneusz Nowak explained that the change is intended to give operators confidence and certainty about targets crossing the border.
Maciej Szopa: An Air Force officer and pilot has become the Operational Commander. Does this reflect Poland’s current situation? Do we regard an air attack as the greatest threat?
Maj. Gen., Pilot Ireneusz Nowak, PhD : I would not want to link my professional background as a pilot to my appointment as Operational Commander. I hope someone recognised my experience and my vision for developing the armed forces and considered them the best fit for the threats we currently face.
Leaving my own appointment aside, it is encouraging that genuine “jointness” is developing within the Operational Command. Maj. Gen. Maciej Jabłoński has become my first deputy. He is an Army officer with extensive experience who recently served as deputy commander of the US Army’s V Corps. There, he worked directly with the part of the US Army that would assist us during a crisis or war. My second deputy is Vice Adm. Piotr Sikora, another highly experienced officer, from the Navy. We communicate well as a team. These are constructive discussions that produce something worthwhile.
Both the Operational Command and the General Command now have this “joint” character. Our commanders have different backgrounds. Each of us is different, and each brings something unique to the organisation. This is a modern approach for these difficult times.
How are you developing a multidomain approach within the Armed Forces?
We are developing it continuously, and it is a long-term process. It involves changing organisational culture and ways of thinking, while constantly monitoring trends. Russia’s war against Ukraine also gives us food for thought, although we must avoid certain conceptual traps. As we have repeatedly said, we do not want to fight that way. We do not want a static, frozen, attritional conflict lasting many years. We must find a different model for how the armed forces operate and boldly address the challenges emerging before us.
A multidomain approach is not easy. It requires broad awareness, beginning with an officer’s education at a military academy. Officers should then encounter it at successive stages of their professional development.
Someone who is closed-minded, stands still, and refuses to accept change will never be a good soldier capable of being creative and responding to new challenges. In our reality, those challenges sometimes change from week to week.
Are you starting from scratch, or has Poland already achieved something in this area?
There are areas where the multidomain approach is strong and has become firmly established. One example is what we call air-land integration.
This began with the JTAC programme, Joint Terminal Attack Controllers, but is evolving much more broadly. It has found fertile ground, for example, in cooperation between aviation and Army artillery.
So there are centres from which this way of thinking can spread. One is the Missile and Artillery Forces Training Centre in Toruń. It is a place where people from different domains will meet, learn to communicate, and learn how to make the most of their respective services’ strengths. They will also conduct joint exercises, including joint fires training.
Who will the artillery personnel be meeting there?
They already work with military aviation, and we want to expand this considerably, extending cooperation beyond the Air Force and, eventually, to all the other services. Artillery is very strong in terms of command and control and network-centric capabilities.
The people there are very open-minded and willing to cooperate. Col. Będkowski recently became the centre’s commandant. He is a living legend when it comes to establishing the JTAC programme in Poland. These are people for whom working together, cooperating, and avoiding silos are second nature.
Technology has reached a point where artillery can even help aviation gain air superiority over a designated area. For example, surface-to-surface missiles can destroy air defence systems…
The ranges we are now acquiring, including in the artillery component, have already completely changed the geometry of the battlefield. These are operations beyond visual range, at very long distances. One could also say that artillery is beginning to have more and more in common with helicopter aviation. If our Apaches are equipped with weapons such as Spike NLOS (with a range of 50 km – Eds.), they will move from tactical-level missions to at least the operational level. And who knows: when suppressing certain elements of an adversary’s air defences, they may operate at the strategic level.
The F-35 has not yet reached operational readiness, but can you already see how it will connect these domains? Will it also serve as a catalyst?
Yes, our experience only confirms what we have said since the very beginning of the F-35 programme. However, I would still caution against excessive optimism. First and foremost, I see the F-35 supporting the air defence system as quickly as possible. These aircraft are critically needed there because of their sensors, information-processing capabilities, and combat capabilities.
Later, of course, they will help build that multidomain capability and cooperate with other services. For now, however, several details still need to be addressed. Certain software elements and databases must be loaded. This is a newly introduced aircraft that has only just landed in Poland.
The introduction process is moving quickly, and personnel are learning quickly, but it will still take some time. I am sorry to say this, but there will be neither a honeymoon month nor a honeymoon year for the F-35. Given the current situation and our needs, these aircraft will enter the air defence system much sooner than the F-16 did.
Changes have recently been introduced to the legal framework and decision-making process for threats to Polish airspace. What exactly has changed, and what has improved?
The main driver is to enable ground-based air defence systems deployed in eastern Poland to operate more effectively. These are not the optimal systems, because they are either short-range or very-short-range systems, such as the SA-8 Osa or Poprad. For now, this is the segment we have developed most extensively. Narew would be the best solution for the task I have to carry out every night, but we do not have it yet and probably will not see it for some time.
We therefore wanted to make the systems we already possess more effective and create the best possible operating conditions for them. The key is to establish a special, segregated, sterile volume of airspace. This airspace will be established within days, probably before this interview is published, through a Council of Ministers regulation.
It will receive “P”, or “prohibited”, status, making it a no-fly zone. This will give ground-based air defence operators confidence. Once several other procedural requirements have also been met, they will be certain that an object they can engage without visual contact is, beyond any doubt, an airspace intruder originating from the Russian Federation.
Anything that is not engaged, or cannot be engaged, by ground-based air defence systems will continue to be engaged by aircraft. Aviation is also receiving new authorities under the procedures.
Will visual identification of the target no longer be required?
Of course, when conditions permit, such identification will still be possible. For example, during the day, when an interception can even involve the use of the cannon.
However, at night, in cloudy conditions, when only radar contact is available and several other conditions for positive identification have been met, it will also be possible to engage such an object with AMRAAM missiles beyond visual range.
When a Kh-101 missile came down in a field in August… were you concerned that it might be a Ukrainian fighter that had strayed off course?
That was a real concern, because a Ukrainian fighter was operating in the area. It was, in fact, close to that cruise missile.
Naturally, it was more visible on radar and was practically on the national border. Only when it made a sharp manoeuvre eastward could we stop tasking one of our F-16s to monitor it, because we were then certain it was a Ukrainian fighter. We had not known that earlier because our neighbours had not notified us.
After that incident, we asked the Ukrainian side to inform us about their fighters’ movements, particularly when operating so close to the border with Poland.
Last year, you said that 2025–2026 would be the most dangerous period for Poland, with gaps in our capabilities. After that, this window would begin to close. Do you stand by that assessment?
Yes, I do. Equipment deliveries will increase very substantially beginning in 2027, including the FA-50PL. Nine aircraft should be delivered between July and the end of December next year. As with the F-35, this system will need several months for personnel to familiarise themselves with the new technology. These aircraft are, of course, similar to the GF version, and the pilots are trained, but the technical differences may require some time.
So 2027 will probably not be the year when we see a step change in capabilities. In 2028, however, we should expect that to happen in aviation. Right now, though, the ground-based air defence component is the most exposed to these threats.
As Operational Commander, I have many questions and expectations in this area. What about the Narew batteries, additional Patriot batteries, and PAC-3 missiles? There is considerable uncertainty and a risk of delays. It is clear that the conflict in the Middle East, in short, US involvement in Iran, will also affect delivery schedules.
But that should probably not have much of an impact on Narew?
I hope not. I also hope San delivers, and I am keeping my fingers crossed for those 18 batteries. They would help us the most in countering a broad spectrum of aerial threats. However, I am a realist and know the industry’s problems. I know that things are not proceeding smoothly and that there is currently no modernisation programme running on schedule without significant delays. Except one.
Delivery of the two MQ-9Bs is on schedule. They should arrive in January next year, and there do not appear to be any major risks there.
The FA-50GFs are to begin quick reaction alert duty early next year. How much will that ease the burden on the F-16 squadrons?
Not very much. The idea is for FA-50GFs to provide additional assistance to our F-16s on air defence missions, in other words, support them. Their main task will be to engage Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered drones, if necessary.
Pilica, Pilica Plus, and even Poprad are not systems that add much qualitatively to national air defence in terms of area coverage. These are short-range systems intended for point defence, and unfortunately, from a defender’s perspective, Poland’s eastern border is very, very long, and the airspace is extensive.
There are assessments that Russia’s ground forces have replenished their equipment. Drone and counter-drone capabilities have also expanded, but Russia is likely to economise on its air force and navy for the foreseeable future, as their capabilities are questionable anyway. Is that a correct interpretation of the situation?
I disagree that the Russians will allow any of the traditional armed services to atrophy. I fully agree that there has been a step change in unmanned capabilities, because they are experimenting not only with aerial platforms but also with ground, surface, and underwater systems. What is happening there concerns us. The Rubikon concept (establishing a personnel training centre that also develops doctrines for employing unmanned systems) demonstrates their considerable ability to adapt.
At the same time, I see absolutely no deliberate constraints on their air and space forces. Any constraints stem solely from the fact that their industry, partly because of sanctions, is currently unable to move into mass production.
That is what is happening with the various Geran models, for which new factories have been built. There is large-scale mass production: thousands of drones produced weekly and tens of thousands monthly.
The same will happen with the air force. For now, the Russians cannot accelerate production there. They have only tiny numbers of Su-57s and Su-35s, but they are not abandoning production. Note that they are systematically replacing the losses they sustain in this segment.
Fortunately for us, they cannot produce strategic bombers, because that would really hurt us. The same applies to modern hypersonic missiles and cruise missiles. Production remains relatively constrained by costs and sanctions. But that does not mean Russian industry would not increase its production rate if those sanctions were suddenly lifted.
We continually observe Russian tactical aviation operating along the front line every day. Among other weapons, it drops glide bombs fitted with UMPK kits. There is no indication that the Russians are moving away from the traditional employment of airpower.
During exercises recently held at the centre, alongside robots, there were also traditional weapons: heavy, effective aerial bombs. The Russians assume that at some point they will be able to gain local air superiority and drop weapons of this kind.
At present, I consider the very rapid progress in the production of unmanned systems, concepts for their employment, and the development of doctrine and tactics to be deeply concerning. Very concerning for us.
There now appears to be a Russian trend away from inexpensive piston-powered Shaheds and Gerans towards fewer jet-powered designs that are much harder to destroy. Is that really the trend?
Absolutely. Jet-powered drones already account for at least 50 per cent, and sometimes 70 per cent, of daily strikes. They use inexpensive Chinese engines, so with mass production, the unit cost of such a drone is not that high. It is clearly higher than for piston-powered models, but their survivability and effectiveness are also greater.
It is concerning that the Russian Federation has also mastered networked drone operations. It can navigate precisely during the terminal phase of flight, effectively turning these drones into deep precision strike weapons. Ukraine’s air defence system was briefly caught off guard. Over time, it began adapting, as always happens in war. There is action, and there is reaction. When a new, effective solution appears, the other side immediately seeks ways to neutralise it.
So the Russian Federation will not return to those mass-produced propeller-driven drones?
They will continue to be used to saturate the air defence system and supplement strikes. The acoustic detection system for piston-powered drones introduced in Ukraine, which we wanted to introduce as well, is already becoming outdated. That gives us a great deal to think about. The threats have changed, and things will no longer be as they were.
Then perhaps the San concept, with its many different sensors and effectors, is not such a bad approach in this situation? We do not know how the threats will evolve, but at least we have a foundation for the future, a range of solutions.
Above all, the system must be adaptable. That means an open architecture that can be easily reconfigured.
The US B-21 Raider bomber is a good example. It looks like the B-2. So why develop a new design? Because the B-2 has a closed architecture, leaving virtually no scope for further development or fundamental changes. A new concept was needed: an “open” bomber with a completely different internal philosophy. We must take a similar approach with San, making it as open and flexible as possible, so that it can be broken down into elements and combined with other components.
The Russian Federation is very good at analysing developments on our side. If it finds a gap in our capabilities, it will certainly exploit it.
Substantial Army forces remain deployed along the border. Will this continue for a long time, and how does it affect the armed forces’ readiness?
The Chief of the General Staff has already issued an official decision to reduce that presence. It will happen gradually. We will withdraw personnel from the immediate front line and replace soldiers with Border Guard personnel, because that service has also matured and strengthened sufficiently. Fortification of the border is also having an effect, particularly the barrier – the sensors are doing an excellent job. We know where crossings or attempted crossings are no longer taking place, and we know where they have shifted.
We are therefore scaling down, because this costs money, and the military also keeps track of costs. Since it began, our military presence on the eastern border has already cost more than PLN 3 billion. It is time to consider where those funds should be redirected, for example, to counter-drone systems.
We can already say that the border operation has been scaled down from division level to brigade-plus level, and we are now reducing it further to brigade level.
What about the maritime border? We are seeing provocations over the Baltic: for example, escorted Tu-22M3s practising missile launches against Poland from the north. Does this change the missions as well, requiring closer protection of that direction?
Yes, we must protect the maritime border, and there is an awareness of that. Developments in naval modernisation show that decision-makers have understood that we have substantial critical infrastructure along our maritime border and must protect it. It is very good that this has happened, because as military personnel, we advocate a holistic approach to developing the armed forces. That means more than focusing exclusively on expanding capabilities in the land domain. Other services have their own requirements and cannot be excluded from the modernisation programme. That happened to the Navy, but now absolutely no one disputes its needs.
The LNG terminal, Baltic Pipe, fuel terminals, cargo terminals that would also be used in a NATO logistics operation, telecommunications and IT infrastructure running along the Baltic seabed, wind farms: all of this makes it clear that the maritime border must be protected. That includes the air domain.
In the face of growing threats, is cooperation with our allies improving? Can we say anything about that?
First and foremost, in NATO operational planning, an operational plan for the Central and Eastern European theatre has been signed. It provides for specific responses to various situations above and below the Article 5 threshold.
That is a major development, because it required consensus among all the countries contributing forces to this process. They have committed to providing resources on time. Much has also improved since the Ankara summit. Standing Defence Plan 12000, or SDP 12000, is an air defence plan that eliminated the previous narrowly defined missions, such as Baltic Air Policing and Air Shielding. This is now an air defence mission that provides for countering violations of NATO airspace.
So no more sorties with a cannon and two Sidewinders?
All allied aircraft have been carrying AMRAAMs and operating in full combat configuration for a long time. The change is that it is now easier to employ these aircraft across the theatre.
There are no longer bilateral arrangements imposing restrictions under which a particular pair of armed aircraft can operate over one area but not another. Resources, including fighters, can now be allocated flexibly.
And something entirely new is that Swedish, Czech, and even Hungarian Gripens can assist us in Polish airspace. This shows that NATO has adapted to the new situation. Until now, it had enormous military potential and substantial capabilities, particularly in the air domain, but was constrained by restrictions. Now we defend the Alliance’s entire airspace. This is very important for us. We have a fairly small F-16 fleet that flies almost every night. We are stretched thin, and any outside assistance is critically important.
I would add that Sweden has presented a very interesting concept. It has pledged the presence and assistance of its Gripen fighters. They will take off from an airfield in Sweden and, if necessary, land at Mińsk Mazowiecki after completing their mission in Polish airspace. There, they will be turned around for another sortie, even with their engines running, and then return to Sweden or continue operating over Poland.
That is precisely ACE (Agile Combat Employment). The flexible employment of aircraft from different airfields and locations. It is something we also need. With these Gripens landing here, our technicians will also have an opportunity to learn rapid Gripen turnaround procedures through Aircraft Cross Servicing. This is a practice that had been somewhat forgotten within the Alliance, and now there is an opportunity to train technical personnel in it.
So, overall, all of this is moving towards NATO forces cooperating like the armed forces of one large country.
Yes. You could say that we treat the Alliance’s airspace as allied airspace, without national barriers or restrictions. SACEUR (the Supreme Allied Commander Europe, NATO’s commander in Europe, as the editor notes, Gen. Grynkewich) has also received significantly expanded authority.

title: S’ Court ruling: INEC gives Oct. 24 deadline for parties to submit omitted candidates
body: By Omeiza Ajayi ABUJA: The Independent National Electoral Commission INEC has given political parties that believe their candidates were wrongly left off the final list for the 2027 governorship election until 24th October, 2026 to notify it. The deadline follows a Supreme Court ruling that bars parties which failed to submit membership registers from sponsoring candidates. National Commissioner and Chairman, Information and Voter Education Committee, Mohammed Kudu Haruna, said in a statement in the wee hours of Tuesday said the Commission applied the apex court’s decision in finalising the governorship list. “The Commission, while finalizing the list of candidates for the Governorship election applied the above decision of the Supreme Court and excluded political parties that failed to comply with Section 77(5)-(7) of the Electoral Act, 2026, in relation to fielding of candidates,” Haruna said. The judgement, in INEC v. Zenith Labour Party, Appeal No. SC/CV/495/2026, was delivered on 24th September, 2026. It arose from INEC’s appeal against a Court of Appeal decision which “nullified the provisions of Section 77(5)-(7) of the Electoral Act, 2026 requiring the submission of membership registers as a prerequisite for the conduct of valid party primaries.” The Supreme Court overturned that position. It held that the provisions “are constitutional and mandatory for all political parties.” The Court also upheld the constitutionality of Item No. 2 of INEC’s Timetable and Schedule of Activities, which required political parties to submit their membership registers between 21st April and 10th May, 2026. According to the statement, “failure to comply with the provisions of Section 77 (5)-(7), renders the defaulting political parties ineligible to sponsor any candidate for the election.” Haruna said the Commission acted “in accordance with Section 287(1) of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (as amended).” He noted that the final list of Presidential and National Assembly candidates “had already been published on 12th September, 2026, thirteen days before the Supreme Court delivered its judgement.” On the window for complaints, the statement said: “Under Section 32(2) of the Electoral Act, 2026, political parties that believe their candidates were wrongly left off the list have 14 days from the date of publication to notify the Commission. The deadline is 24th October, 2026. “The Commission assures the public of its commitment to transparency, the rule of law and the credibility of the electoral process.” The post S’ Court ruling: INEC gives Oct. 24 deadline for parties to submit omitted candidates appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Greek Health Minister Rejects Anti-Israel Protests as Antisemitic Propaganda
body: Greek Health Minister Adonis Georgiadis has strongly backed growing ties with Israel, labelling recent anti-Israel protests “antisemitic propaganda” with little impact on the government or the wider public. His comments, made ahead of the launch of an Israel Allies Caucus in the Greek parliament, follow official condemnation of an anti-Israel rally held on the anniversary of the 7 October Hamas attack. “Our public opinion has shifted dramatically to pro-Israel. We are almost an exception within the EU,” Georgiadis told JNS. He said demonstrations by leftist groups and migrants were rejected by most Greeks. “As a government we resist antisemitism, and as a society we resist antisemitism. Their propaganda does not influence us.” Migration Minister Thanos Plevris added that Israel’s fight against terrorism was also a fight for the West. The statements reflect deepening strategic cooperation between Israel, Greece and Cyprus on energy, defence and regional security, including a $3.5 billion air-defence agreement. Former Prime Minister Antonis Samaras and Israeli Ambassador Pninat Yanay also underscored the partnership. Source: Etgar Lefkovits, JNS The post Greek Health Minister Rejects Anti-Israel Protests as Antisemitic Propaganda appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Jewish extremist attacks surge in West Bank: officials accuse ministers of backing rioters
body: While Palestinian terrorism has declined significantly, Israel's security establishment is expressing deep concern over a dangerous trend in the opposite direction: a sharp and sustained rise in incidents of nationalist violence in the West Bank. "We are not talking about a handful of people, and anyone who says it is just a handful simply does not want to solve the problem, just like those who claim the entire settlement movement behaves this way," a security official said. "We are talking about a hard core of approximately 300 to 500 teenagers who are completely out of control."   According to security establishment figures published here for the first time, the number of incidents has risen dramatically since the start of the war. While approximately 800 incidents were recorded in 2025, the total had already exceeded 950 by early October 2026, approaching the record of 980 incidents recorded throughout 2023, the year the war began. Security officials point to February 28, when Operation Roaring Lion began, as a major turning point, with another sharp increase in both the number and severity of incidents. "These are criminals in every sense of the word, lawless thugs who set fire to homes with people inside," the security official said. "In the past, they would justify their actions as responses to terrorist attacks, something along the lines of 'price tag' attacks. Today, their entire approach has changed. These are now deliberate incursions intended to drive Palestinians out." Last month, ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth revealed that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had ordered the evacuation of all outposts located in Areas A and B of the West Bank. However, military officials say the extremists are acting in direct defiance of that directive, establishing illegal outposts in those areas.   More seriously, the security establishment has sharply criticized the political support the extremists receive. "There are Knesset members and government ministers who visit illegal outposts and give them their full backing," the official said. The IDF stresses that the main difficulty in confronting the phenomenon stems from the stark differences in the tools available to security forces. "It is important to understand that when dealing with Palestinian terrorists, we use every tool available, from M16 rifles to F16 fighter jets, and gather extensive intelligence," the security official explained. "By contrast, the IDF is prohibited from gathering intelligence on the 'blue side' [Israeli civilians], and the range of tools at our disposal is far more limited." Despite these restrictions, security officials insist they are making full use of the tools at their disposal. However, they say tackling the problem requires action in several areas, including education, tougher penalties, public outreach, financial sanctions and legal measures. Security officials say authorities should make greater use of existing regulations to confiscate vehicles used by extremists and require illegal outpost owners to cover the costs of evacuating their outposts. They are also calling for more vehicle confiscation orders, stronger financial penalties and more effective legal enforcement.   A central part of the problem involves ensuring that suspects arrested during enforcement operations are held accountable. Security agencies have also criticized the judiciary. "Some judges fail to grasp the seriousness of the situation and release rioters accused of serious offenses, including assaulting security forces or violating court orders," officials said. "Others, however, take a much tougher approach." The IDF is calling for additional dedicated forces to handle this complex mission. Military officials also say the Shin Bet, Israel's domestic security agency, is now employing methods that were not previously available. "The head of the Shin Bet is operating very creatively and achieving significant successes in preventing attacks, using methods we have not seen before and cannot elaborate on," military officials said. At the same time, they are questioning how the extremists raise money and why authorities are not taking legal action against their fundraising activities. "These young extremists are raising money. Why isn't their fundraising being treated as illegal?" they asked. The IDF would also like to see stronger public condemnation from regional council heads and senior settlement leaders. "Two council heads are not afraid to speak out openly and honestly, but where are the rest?" security officials said. "When they need something from the military, they make sure their voices are heard. They clearly know how to speak up and exert pressure when they want to."   Addressing the issue of administrative detention, which allows suspects to be held without trial under certain circumstances, a senior security official said: "I am not going to get into whether it is good or bad. There are directives, and we follow them. But on the ground, the feeling right now is that these teenagers believe they are untouchable." The official added that "attempts were also made to revoke administrative detention orders, but ultimately that did not happen, despite heavy pressure." The security establishment warns that the true cost of nationalist violence could be far greater, potentially causing severe strategic damage to Israel and the settlement movement as a whole. "Because of their actions, we could lose all the security achievements we have made," the official warned. "Beyond that, we are losing valuable assets. In the United States, voices critical of Israel that we had not heard before are now emerging because of these incidents. "In fact, because of American pressure, the settlement movement could lose gains it has made in recent years that have changed the reality on the ground. And there are people who do not understand that." Regional council heads, some of whom are working behind the scenes to combat extremist violence, are aware of the criticism directed at them. However, they insist that they have been demanding that law enforcement authorities take action against the rioters and remove them from the West Bank. The incidents come as settlement activity reaches new heights. Regional council heads also fear that nationalist violence could fuel efforts to delegitimize Israel and jeopardize the gains the settlement movement has made in recent years.

title: Crete Fertility Clinic Loses Melbourne Woman’s Four Embryos Ahead of Major Trial
body: A Melbourne woman has lost four embryos after the Mediterranean Fertility Institute in Chania, Crete, was raided by Greek police three years ago. The woman, identified as Maggie, had stored embryos created with her own eggs and donor sperm at the clinic. When she later requested their return from Chania hospital, staff told her none of her material had been found. The clinic had been heavily promoted in Melbourne and Italy. Maggie had travelled to Crete, made multiple payments and was told her first two embryo transfers had failed. She now questions whether the embryos were sold to other clients. On Wednesday, 33 defendants—including clinic founder Ioannis Giakoumakis, 76, and chief embryologist Diamantis “Danny” Dafnis, 47—begin a year-long trial in Chania. They face charges including facilitating a criminal organisation, fraud, human trafficking, illegal sale of genetic material, fake embryo transplants and forging medical documents. Dozens of Australians are among the alleged victims. Maggie later had a second child via surrogacy in Africa using a donor egg. She said she would not have used the Crete clinic if she had known of the alleged deceit. Name changed to protect identity. Source: Jacquelin Magnay, The Australian The post Crete Fertility Clinic Loses Melbourne Woman’s Four Embryos Ahead of Major Trial appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Russian forces strike Epicentr’s logistics hub in Khmelnytskyi 10 times in one day
body:
According to Ukrinform, Epicentr said in a Facebook post that Russian forces struck the facility 10 times in a single day, triggering five large-scale fires.
“Eventually, the enemy achieved its goal – the fire destroyed about 85% of the goods stored inside. Nearly 30 drones in the sky prevented firefighters from putting out the blaze,” the company said.
No employees were injured, but Epicentr described the attack as a devastating blow to the company.
The company noted that Russian forces had previously completely destroyed its two largest logistics complexes in Kyiv and Kyiv region. The Khmelnytskyi distribution center was effectively the company’s only major warehouse complex that remained intact.
“This was where goods were shipped to our stores. This was where people worked every day so that millions of Ukrainians could buy what they needed. Today, the enemy struck it 10 times in one day. This is not simply lost merchandise. It is destroyed logistics, enormous financial losses, and months and years of work by thousands of people,” Epicentr said.
As Ukrinform reported, Russian attacks on October 13 caused fires at enterprises in two districts of the Khmelnytskyi region.

title: Judge extends White House access for CNN, MS NOW, Politico amid legal fight
body: A federal judge extended access to the White House for CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists, ruling on Tuesday that President Donald Trump likely broke the law when he tried to ban them, in the latest ruling against him in the press freedom dispute. US District Judge Timothy Kelly issued a written decision elaborating on his September 24 emergency order reinstating access for the journalists. The news organisations and press freedom groups have accused Trump of unconstitutional retaliation against journalists for coverage he does not ​like. Kelly’s order last month gave CNN, MS NOW, and Politico journalists temporary access to the White House grounds. The judge ​issued a preliminary injunction on Tuesday that will remain in effect until he issues a final judgment in the lawsuit brought by the news organisations, unless an appeals court lifts it. Past presidents have battled with the press, but Trump’s campaign against ​the media has been unprecedented. He has upended decades of tradition by denying basic access to many major news organisations, launching personal attacks on journalists for their ​reporting and elevating media outlets seen as more sympathetic to the administration. He has also filed lawsuits against multiple news outlets. Trump announced the ban in September on his social media platform, saying those news organisations “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States.” The Justice Department has emphasised Trump’s ​contention that the ban is legally justified on national security grounds. The outlets have said the revocation of their White House passes was unlawful retaliation for ​their news coverage and accused the Trump administration of manufacturing meritless national security concerns to justify the ban. The outlets said in a lawsuit that the ban violated the US Constitution’s First Amendment protections for freedom of speech and a free press, as well as their rights to due process, meaning fair treatment by the government. The White House on September 24 reinstated the CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists after the judge decided the ban “likely violated their constitutional due process rights,” and ordered their access immediately restored. The judge, who Trump appointed in 2017 during his first presidential term, also raised doubts about the US Justice Department’s national security arguments to justify the ban, noting that Trump himself had said the action was due to what the president alleged was false or negative coverage. Justice Department lawyers have said the outlets endangered national security by publishing classified information, citing stories about US missile stockpiles, construction of Trump’s White House ballroom and turnout at the recent Republican ​midterm convention. ‘COERCE BETTER COVERAGE’ The judge held a hearing on October 8 to hear arguments from the news outlets and the Justice Department over whether to extend protection for journalists against being barred from the White House. The Justice Department defended the bans as fair and justified. “Here we have the unusual situation where the president himself has said he wants to chill speech. He wants to coerce better coverage,” Theodore Boutrous, an attorney for the outlets, told ⁠Kelly during ​the hearing. “CNN, MS NOW and Politico engaged in apparently indefensible conduct,” Justice Department lawyer Michael Velchik ​said. The legal battle is being waged just weeks before the November 3 US midterm elections in which Trump’s fellow Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress. Trump’s job approval ratings are ​at record lows in opinion polls amid concerns over issues such as inflation and the Iran war.

title: UK to accelerate deliveries of LMM missiles to Kiev — PM’s office
body:
LONDON, October 14. /TASS/. The UK will accelerate deliveries of Lightweight Multirole Missiles (LMMs) to Ukraine, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s office said in a statement.
"The UK doubles down on support for Ukraine, including delivering 45 million pound sterling ($60 mln - TASS) of surface-to-air missiles," the statement reads.
"The UK has already committed 1.6 billion pounds to deliver more than 5000 LMMs to Ukraine over the next four years and will accelerate 10 million pounds of the 45 million pounds package of missiles <…> to meet Ukraine’s most urgent winter requirements," the office said.
The statement from Burnham’s office has been published ahead of his meeting with Vladimir Zelensky in London scheduled for October 14.

title: EU expands migration cooperation with eastern Libya through new funding
body: The European Union has signed an additional €25 million ($29 million) in funding to expand migration cooperation into eastern Libya, according to a letter from European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to EU leaders, seen by Reuters. The funding will support border management, search-and-rescue and anti-smuggling activities in eastern Libya. It is a further sign of deepening EU engagement with the region controlled by military commander Khalifa Haftar ​, as Brussels seeks to curb irregular migration across the Mediterranean. Libya, ⁠where control is split between rival western and eastern administrations, has ​been a major transit route for migrants attempting the dangerous sea crossing ​to Europe since the 2011 NATO-backed uprising that toppled Muammar Gaddafi . The EU and its member states have long supported and trained the Libyan coast guard, which intercepts migrants at sea. While the EU formally recognises only the Tripoli-based government, ​it has stepped up contacts with authorities in eastern Libya since last year ‌as ⁠migrant departures from areas controlled by Haftar in eastern Libya have risen. The move follows the EU’s July announcement that it would establish a Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre in the eastern Libyan city of Benghazi, further expanding cooperation with authorities in the east. “Libya remains the top country of departure for illegal crossings to the EU,” von der ​Leyen wrote, describing an upcoming EU-Libya meeting as a ​way ⁠to keep cooperation going. She said the EU and the International Organisation for Migration were supporting voluntary returns from Libya to countries of origin. “We are ⁠equally ​focused on reducing the number of migrants ​arriving in Libya with the sole intention of crossing illegally into the EU,” she ​added.

title: Man United ratings vs Atletico Madrid: Yoro off and Baleba promising on another tough night for Carrick
body: Atletico Madrid needed only 50 seconds ​to punish Manchester United's high defensive line on their way to a 2-0 victory in the Spanish capital on Tuesday night. Alex Baena broke clear down the left before squaring for Pablo Barrios ​to finish and it looked like being a long night for the visitors. United threatened through ‌ Bryan Mbeumo , who shot narrowly wide and later forced a close-range save from Jan Oblak, while Marcus Rashford also squandered an opportunity. Atletico had a Johnny Cardoso ⁠effort disallowed for a Marcos Llorente handball before the break and Julian Alvarez volleyed against the post early in the second ⁠half. United's task became harder when Leny Yoro was sent off in the 74th minute for denying Jonathan David a goalscoring opportunity. Five minutes later, Ademola Lookman tapped into an empty net after David's shot was saved. "I don't see it being a red card, I have to say. I really don't agree with the decision," said United boss Michael Carrick. "I don't know whether I'm allowed to say or not, but I just don't agree with the decision. "He wasn't really moving in a quick direction to goal. Whether it was or wasn't a foul, or not a foul, it was very soft and slow and [to get] a red card for that, especially to be taken to VAR. I just don't understand it." Man United ratings Senne Lammens – 6: Awful start, not that he was at fault, as he conceded to the excellent Barrios after 50 seconds. Then beaten by a Cardoso shot which Atleti thought was a goal, but it was handball. Good save from David before the second. One clean sheet in eight games. Ayden Heaven – 6: Nightmare start for the makeshift left-back despite his best efforts as a simple ball over United’s defence split it. Actually unlucky not to block Barrios’ shot. Some nice turns. Grew in confidence. Lovely ball towards the corner as United attacked on 79 minutes. Lisandro Martinez – 6: Left centre-back and drifted a lovely ball towards Rashford on 14 minutes. Clumsy challenge on Barrios conceded a free-kick. His post-match criticisms of Manchester United will be headline news. Lisandro Martínez did NOT hold back after United's loss to Atletico 😬👀 pic.twitter.com/OGo25Pzd30 — Prime Video Sport UK (@primevideosport) October 13, 2026 Leny Yoro – 6: Right centre-back after playing well on Saturday at right-back. Didn’t realise how much time he had on the ball at times as he ballooned it back towards Atletico or gave up possession. Started second-half well but sent off after 74 minutes – he was the last line of defence. But it was harsh, especially as the referee was so close. It was not a clear and obvious error. Diogo Dalot – 5: Right-back and kept very busy by the excellent Baena and Grimaldo on that flank. Poor on goal as Baena caught him out as the ball came over. He was up against better players. Andrey Santos – 6: First start since the opening day of the season and steady in the middle alongside Baleba. Found his feet, played deeper and played the full 90. There might be something there with him and Baleba. Carlos Baleba – 7: Tame header from an unmarked position eight yards out went straight at Oblak. Beaten by Barrios who then crossed for Alvarez in a superb bit of Atletico play. Otherwise good energy and decent passing in his first United start. Youri Tielemans – 6: Played higher – at least in theory – up behind Mbeumo, whom he played a smart one-two with on 24 minutes, but barely featured in first half. More advanced in second and brilliant vision for a ball to Fernandes. Bruno Fernandes – 5: On the right and less of an impact on the game. Stunning turn to beat Grimaldo – three times in total – as United pushed to equalise on 39 minutes but he didn’t cross. He did at the start of the second – and nearly equalised on 57 minutes as his volley bounced just wide of the post. Moved into his usual role after the subs and was better. Hit crossbar on 70 minutes with a right-foot shot. Michael gives his assessment of Tuesday's game 💬 — Manchester United (@ManUtd) October 13, 2026 Bryan Mbeumo – 6: Swept a deflected shot wide in United’s first attack on 11 minutes after he took out two defenders and did a number on Romero. Came close again on 23 minutes – well saved by Oblak. Marcus Rashford – 5: Scored against Atletico last season. Good duels against Llorente. Made a run on goal but couldn’t get on the ball enough before he switched right. Didn’t really get in the game. Ineffective. Booked. United Subs Joshua Zirkzee (for Tielemans, 65') – 5: Should have scored in stoppage time when he had time. Floats around. Frustrating. Mason Mount (for Baleba, 65') – 5: No impact Amad Diallo (for Rashford, 65') – 5: See above Matheus Cunha (for Fernandes, 80') – N/A: Outrageously pulled back in a yellow card incident. Shot was well-saved by Oblak. Harry Maguire (for Heaven, 80) – N/A: Late sub.

title: Trump's 'Shield of the Americas' is more fragile than it seems
body:
Populations in Latin America aren't exactly thrilled with the right-wing governments the US is allied with
President Donald Trump likes to say he is " nine for nine " with the candidates he has backed in Latin America and the Caribbean, and Brazil's Oct. 25 runoff could make it ten. Senator Flávio Bolsonaro led the first round on Oct. 4, and Brazil under his leadership could seek to join the Shield of the Americas, the security coalition Washington launched in March and now presents as proof that the hemisphere has turned its way.
How much support do the coalition's current members have at home? Less than Trump's scorecard suggests. In eight of the 11 Shield countries measured by the 2026 round of LAPOP's AmericasBarometer , fielded between October 2025 and June 2026, more respondents would vote for an opposition party than for the president's party or candidate, and in seven of them the gap reached 20 points or more.
Survey results indicate that voters grade governments on crime and the cost of living, and the lukewarm voters who once stayed with incumbents have stopped doing so. El Salvador and Costa Rica, where voters have rewarded hard-line security policies, are the clear exceptions, along with Honduras, surveyed in President Nasry Asfura's first months in office.
What does a government do when its voters are walking away? Across the coalition, the answer has been to build up the security apparatus, with more military operations, more prisons and wider emergency powers.
Washington is covering the bill. On Sept. 15, the State Department told Congress it would shift $52 million in foreign military financing — money budgeted for allies in Europe and the Middle East — to Colombia, Ecuador, Panama and Peru to fight what it called "narcoterrorism in our backyard." Washington had announced plans in August for $1 billion in security assistance to Colombia's new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, whom Trump calls a " worthy champion ." U.S. forces also began supporting Ecuadorian military operations in March against groups Washington designates as terrorist organizations.
Voters did ask for tougher policing, and these governments are supplying it in the form El Salvador made famous, with mass prisons and emergency law. Costa Rica opens a maximum-security prison for 5,100 inmates on Oct. 14, built at a cost of $35 million on the pattern of Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele's CECOT ; Bukele himself helped lay its first stone in January. Honduras's Congress approved El Salvador-style prison measures in September at Asfura's request, including isolation for high-risk prisoners. In Chile, José Antonio Kast sent Congress a reform in August that would create a new state of exception for "grave alterations to public security," letting the armed forces deploy in affected zones, along with separate prison regimes for organized crime, but withdrew it in October after it failed to secure enough votes in the Senate.
In Ecuador, Daniel Noboa has governed under an "internal armed conflict" declaration since 2024, and on Sept. 16 he decreed another 60-day state of exception across eight provinces, suspending the inviolability of the home and imposing the year's third curfew. Of the 5,023 people arrested during the May curfew, only 717, about 14%, had ties to organized crime, according to Ecuador’s own interior minister . Judging by the survey, two years of emergency rule have bought neither security nor support: 35% of Ecuadorians said they had been crime victims in the past year, the highest rate in the coalition, and 63% felt unsafe in their own neighborhoods. Only 17% said they would vote for Noboa's side.
Five of the eight flagging presidents — those in Panama, Guatemala, Paraguay, Chile, and the Dominican Republic — are barred from consecutive terms, so what they entrench is a set of institutions that their successors will inherit. Paraguay's Congress ratified a status-of-forces agreement in March that places U.S. military personnel under U.S. criminal jurisdiction. In January, Guatemala's Bernardo Arévalo declared a 30-day state of siege that suspended the right to protest and allowed detentions without a judicial order.
Only Bukele has entrenched himself personally. He secured an indefinite reelection in 2025 after running for a second term despite a constitutional ban, and his state of exception has resulted in about 92,000 arrests without judicial warrants since 2022.
Washington's own standing has slid along with its partners'. LAPOP has asked about the trustworthiness of the U.S. government in nine Shield countries every year since 2012, and the answers have risen and fallen with the occupant of the White House. In 2012, an average of 72% called the U.S. government very or somewhat trustworthy. The share fell to 45% during Trump's first term, recovered to 60% under Joe Biden , and has dropped back to 45% in the latest round.
Some of the steepest declines since 2012 have come among Washington's most dependable partners, from 87% to 40% in Panama and from 71% to 36% in El Salvador. In Panama, an 18.5-point drop in popularity since 2023 is specific to Washington. Over the same period, trust in the National Assembly, the presidency, the Supreme Court, and elections held steady or rose slightly, while only the police lost ground by about 6 points.
The decline also cuts across political lines, from 57% to 34% among Panamanians on the left, from 62% to 43% on the right, and from 66% to 44% among those who approve of President José Raúl Mulino. In Argentina, Chile, and Bolivia, 60% to 69% of those who approve of the president trust Washington, compared to about 10% of those who disapprove. Across the 16 Latin American countries surveyed in 2026, 40% consider the U.S. government trustworthy. The administration reads its partners' election wins as a mandate at a moment when the publics in those countries trust Washington as little as they did at the low point of Trump's first term.
In most of these countries, the next government will be chosen by voters who distrust Washington and are already looking past the incumbent. When Noboa asked Ecuadorians in November 2025 to allow foreign military bases, about 61% said no . Emergency decrees also expand the armed forces' role in policing, and militaries rarely relinquish prerogatives once civilian governments have granted them.
Successors may try to unwind what they inherit, or they may keep the prisons and emergency powers for their own purposes — the more dangerous of the two outcomes in a model that treats the state of exception as ordinary government. Washington, in either case, is tying its hemispheric strategy to commitments made by governments that their own citizens are preparing to replace, and millions of Latin Americans will live inside the security apparatus those governments leave behind.
Note: Vote-intention figures cover the 11 Shield governments that LAPOP surveyed under their current administrations; Peru and Colombia were surveyed under earlier governments and are excluded. Trust figures average the nine Shield members surveyed in every round since 2012: Colombia, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Panama, Paraguay and Peru. AmericasBarometer estimates are weighted and exclude "don't know" and "no answer."

title: Why the US will never give up Diego Garcia
body:
How the island became central to America’s maritime posture in the Indian Ocean is a complicated story that one author is eager to tell
Writing for the Daily Mail in 2023, Former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson sardonically argued , “The Americans don't give us crucial nuclear secrets because they love little old England. They don’t share intelligence because they adore our quaint accents. We have a great and indispensable relationship because we have important things to offer – including Diego Garcia.”
In March, during the ongoing war, Iran launched two missiles at Diego Garcia, which houses a joint UK-American base in the Indian Ocean. While both missiles missed their target, the attack provided the first operational demonstration of Iran’s intermediate-range ballistic missile capability. It also offered a reminder that security in the Indian Ocean is inextricably linked with the larger Middle East . Or, as a senior American naval official put it decades earlier, the Indian Ocean was the “backdoor” to the Middle East and Russia and China’s “soft underbelly.”
To understand why Iran targeted an island 2,500 miles from its shores, turn to Samuel Bashfield’s new and well-drawn history of the U.S. and U.K.’s Cold War adventures in the Indian Ocean, entitled simply “The British Indian Ocean Territory.” As Bashfield effectively demonstrates, the island is central to America’s maritime posture in the Indian Ocean. It has been so since the Second World War.
Today, Diego Garcia is crucial for naval logistics, air power facilitation, military supply prepositioning, and intelligence gathering. It is also a key node for operations across the Indian Ocean, Middle East, South Asia, and Africa . In Bashfield’s words, it is “a coveted lily pad.” For Washington’s strategy, Diego Garcia is to the Indian Ocean as Guam is to the Pacific.
For this work, Bashfield has accessed materials from relevant archives in the U.S., U.K., and Australia. While some documents still remain confidential due to government regulations, the ones used to piece this volume together show a clear pattern.
Bashfield, who holds a doctorate in maritime history and national security policy, begins his book by recounting the importance of Diego Garcia to the Allied war effort during the Second World War. Back then, Japan’s rapid advances in Southeast Asia threatened British Singapore. In 1941, the British decided to use Diego Garcia as a naval logistics base to cover the Indian Ocean.
However, it was only during the early Cold War, amid rapid decolonization in parts of Asia and Africa, that British and American military planners grasped the value of Diego Garcia and the entire Chagos Archipelago’s strategic real estate. Successive policy measures like the Indian Ocean Task Force (1959), America’s Strategic Island Concept (1960), and Britain’s Island Strategy (1963) outlined this thinking.
Bashfield goes into rich detail about U.S. and British negotiations over the Chagos Islands and Diego Garcia and their “detachment” from colonial Mauritius and Seychelles. He further shows how, during the late 1960s, London and Washington wanted to entrench each other’s position in the Indian Ocean. Couched within this larger history of the British Indian Ocean Territory, there is also an interesting story about the lesser-known Aldabra Island, which captivated British planners as a potential military facility.
Over the years, the United States and Britain negotiated three quid pro quo deals that linked expanded American access to Diego Garcia with the British nuclear deterrent. In exchange for an expanded American presence on Diego Garcia, Britain secured American assistance in three successive submarine-launched ballistic missile programs: Polaris, Super Antelope and Trident. These capabilities allowed London to stay comfortably in the nuclear club, possess a second strike capability and enhance undersea deterrence. In this manner, Bashfield’s work on maritime history also makes useful forays into nuclear history. As then-British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher said, her decisions on nuclear technology came with “the greatest long-term consequences for Britain.”
In the latter half of his book, Bashfield deals with the “coming of age” of Diego Garcia. Given the expansion of American military infrastructure over decades, the author argues that the British Indian Ocean Territory has become a “de facto American territory,” despite occasional hand-wringing about sovereignty from London. Diego Garcia’s strategic value was burnished when it was used as a key logistics node and airbase during Operations Desert Shield and Desert Storm, after Saddam Hussein’s unprovoked invasion of Kuwait in 1990.
One aspect I would have liked to know more about was the international scene, especially the view of other major actors, while the crucial negotiations between British and American officials proceeded. To be sure, the author touches upon the role of the Soviet Union, India, and some other littoral states in the context of these negotiations. However, these are not fully fleshed out.
In our time, Britain is caught in a muddle trying to dissolve the British Indian Ocean Territory and help ease Mauritian sovereignty over the Chagos archipelago. In his customary style, President Donald Trump has induced unpredictability into this dynamic. He enjoys haranguing British officials for signing a “stupid” deal to return the island chain to Mauritius. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, on the other hand, has called the deal “historic” in his remarks and has supported both Britain and Mauritius in their negotiations.
In exchange for Mauritian sovereignty over the entire Chagos archipelago, the United Kingdom can operate the Diego Garcia base – through the U.S. – initially for 99 years, with a potential 40-year extension. The agreement also entails a payment of £3.4 billion ($4.5 billion) from London to Port Louis, divided over the next few years. Starting in the late 1960s, the native Chagossians were forcibly displaced to secure military sites in the British Indian Ocean Territory. Legal battles, starting in the early 1970s, are still ongoing in British courts.
From the perspective of the British and American military establishments, the base on Diego Garcia is crucial. Given the chilly winds of naval rivalry in the Indian Ocean and China’s expansion in those waters, losing access to the territory could have long-term consequences. At the same time, the question of Mauritian sovereignty and territorial integrity is urgent, as is dealing with the claims of the exiled Chagossians. As Bashfield hints, these two objectives do not diverge. Yet, the conundrum persists. Such is the knot of Diego Garcia in the heart of the Indian Ocean.

title: High on wins in Tigray, Ethiopia now has Eritrea in its crosshairs
body:
Addis Ababa has long wanted access to the Red Sea. Now, it may have an opportunity to seize it.
On Friday, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos wrote to the U.N. Security Council, citing Article 51 of the U.N. Charter, to say Eritrean troops had advanced up to 38 miles into Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region and that Ethiopia would defend itself against the incursion.
On Saturday, Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh wrote a separate letter to the Security Council, calling Ethiopia’s accusations a “declaration of war.” Saleh cited a statement he attributed to Ethiopia’s deputy chief of staff, Gen. Abebaw Tadesse, who, according to the letter, said on September 27 that the “ultimate objective of the war [in Tigray] was to invade Assab,” a city on Eritrea’s Red Sea coast.
Ethiopian forces, meanwhile, reportedly struck Eritrean forces near Adirgat, in Ethiopia's Tigray region, with drones on Wednesday and Thursday. An unnamed security source told AFP that between 5,000 and 8,000 Eritrean troops are deployed in Tigray.
To understand why Ethiopian and Eritrean troops are now clashing, one must look back at 2020, when Ethiopia’s federal government under Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed fought the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF).
The TPLF dominated Ethiopia for nearly three decades before Abiy came to power in 2018, after which it retreated to its stronghold in the Tigray region, where it escalated tensions by refusing to join Abiy’s new ruling party, defiantly holding regional elections, and according to Abiy, attacking a federal army base. Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian forces in the first Tigray war, which ended in 2022 with the Pretoria agreement, a ceasefire that left the hardest questions unresolved: disarmament, disputed territory and the withdrawal of non-federal forces. Eritrea was not party to the deal.
Since then, the trust that existed briefly between the two neighbors has withered. Ethiopia lost access to the sea when Eritrea became independent in 1993, and Abiy has spoken of the loss of the Eritrean port of Assab as a mistake “that will be corrected tomorrow.” Ethiopian officials often clarify that they seek access through peace and dialogue. But Eritrea feels its bigger neighbor intends to use force, as it highlighted in its recent letter to the United Nations.
As tensions between Asmara and Addis Ababa rise, Ethiopia is struggling to contain an internal rebellion that took shape on September 20, when the TPLF and six other armed groups announced the Ethiopian Peoples’ Alliance for Survival, with the stated aim of removing Abiy and installing a transitional government. Its members include the Amhara region’s Fano militias and the Oromo Liberation army, the groups behind the insurgencies in Ethiopia’s two largest and most populous regions.
Addis Ababa says Eritrea finances and directs the rebels. Asmara says Ethiopia has been planning to invade it for three years. The public evidence supports both accounts.
Because of its suspicions toward Ethiopia, Eritrea has started to open channels and coordinate with the TPLF, a surprising move given that this is the same movement it fought in the first Tigray war and, before that, during a devastating border war in 1998-2000, when the TPLF still dominated Ethiopian politics. A small state facing a much larger one needs a buffer, and Eritrea is trying to ensure the TPLF fills that role. As long as the TPLF remains armed, Ethiopia’s army cannot cleanly deploy to the border with Eritrea.
Eritrea also cultivated Egypt and Sudan’s army as allies. They have their own grievances with Ethiopia over its construction of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam and its alleged support for the Rapid Support Forces fighting Sudan’s military.
For Addis Ababa, these moves look like encirclement. An armed and hostile TPLF, an Eritrean patron and Egyptian and Sudanese alignment pose a clear danger—one that Abiy, however, recently brushed aside, claiming his government doesn’t have “an iota of fear” regarding the threat they pose.
Moreover, the Eritrean presence on Ethiopian soil was never new. The Pretoria agreement and its follow-up Nairobi declaration tied disarmament of Tigrayan forces to the withdrawal of “foreign and non-ENDF [Ethiopian National Defense Force] forces.” Eritrean troops left the larger towns but remained in contested border pockets. When asked about it in 2023, Eritrea’s president, Isaias Afwerki, called the question “nonsense.”
The reported advance now is deepening that presence, and Addis Ababa has been handed a casus belli it lacked before: that Eritrean forces are deep inside Ethiopia, and Ethiopia must fight back to defend itself.
On the diplomatic side, the walls have closed in. Ethiopia and Eritrea severed relations on October 1. Ethiopia and Egypt expelled each other’s diplomats, and Ethiopia’s military chief of staff, Field Marshal Birhanu Jula, expressly pointed the finger at “Shaebia” — the widely used term that refers to Eritrea’s government — as well as “Sudan, Egypt, and powers beyond” for supporting the TPLF’s renewed military insurgency.
On October 4, Egypt hosted the leaders of Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan at El Alamein on Egypt’s Mediterranean coast, where they declared that Red Sea governance belongs to coastal states — a blatant swipe at landlocked Ethiopia. Reuters, citing Egyptian security officials, reported that the four nations agreed to coordinate military and intelligence efforts if the conflict spills over Ethiopia’s borders. In short, a full-on war between Asmara and Addis Ababa would not necessarily remain bilateral for very long.
The most worrying signal is that Ethiopia’s military advantage may make escalation with Eritrea more tempting, not less. Ethiopian government forces have momentum. Government-allied units recaptured Mekelle, the capital of the Tigray region, on October 4, and Ethiopian airlines resumed flights to the city on Sunday.
Getachew Reda, a former Tigray leader now advising Abiy, greeted supporters at the airport on Sunday and promised the people “visible change.” Buoyed by this victory, Addis Ababa may calculate that it can resolve its long-standing security dilemma with Eritrea and its lack of a coastline in one stroke, by taking the fight north.
Yet, there are also strong reasons for restraint. The TPLF may look subdued for now, but other members of the rebel alliance, such as the Fano in Amhara and the Oromo Liberation Army in Oromio, remain committed to the fight. It is also crucial to note that the TPLF merely withdrew from Mekelle; its command remains intact and has not collapsed.
Compounding these security threats is the fact that most of Ethiopia’s imports travel along a single highway to Djibouti. The TPLF’s recent push into the Afar region, where this corridor lies, proved just how exposed the critical highway is and how much leverage the rebels stand to gain against the federal government.
Consequently, marching north into Eritrea and attempting regime change, or annexation, with half the country in revolt would be a gamble of the highest order for Ethiopia.
The international community meanwhile is not absent, but is thus far unconvincing. The African Union (AU) is headquartered in Addis Ababa. The organization has long been accused of going soft on its landlord, and much of the blame for the unresolved issues of the Pretoria agreement can be attributed to the AU's lethargy and systemic inaction.
Washington is better placed to mediate, given that Ethiopia has long been regarded as America’s most important partner in the Horn of Africa , and Washington is now warming to Eritrea. Ambassador Ervin Massinga had also shuttled between Mekelle and Addis Ababa and engaged the TPLF, yet as the insurgency in Tigray accelerated he blamed the TPLF’s “poor decision to launch a large-scale offensive."
Whether the U.S. can still help between Ethiopia and Eritrea is an open question, and so far it looks unprepared for what may come. Days before fighting resumed, the U.S. let the sanctions regime tied to the last Tigray war lapse, removing Eritrean officials and entities from the list, and it had already eased restrictions on arms sales to Addis Ababa.
On September 30, with fighting under way, Boeing signed a $5 billion aircraft deal with Ethiopian Airlines. Washington likes the story Abiy tells, of an Addis Ababa that becomes Africa’s Dubai, a $12.5 billion airport at Bishoftu meant to be among the largest in the world, and a country keen to do business with Washington as it undergoes an ambitious economic transformation. But a state sliding into a civil war and a simultaneous interstate war with its northern neighbor could soon have little to buy or build.
