title: Pensioners, military board faceoff
body: T he meeting between the management of the Military Pension Board (MPB) and the retired officers of the Nigerian Armed Forces to resolve the disagreement on the monthly pension ended in a stalemate yesterday as the veterans insisted that their newly approved monthly pay should be re-calculated. The deadlocked meeting came after the retired officers had shut down the main entrance of the board’s headquarters located in Dutse-Alhaji/Kubwa area of Abuja in protest over what they described as the board’s ‘miscalculation’ of their new monthly take-home and other entitlements. The protesters, led by one Innocent Azubuike, a retired Lieutenant-Colonel, arrived in their numbers as early as 8:30am, saying their action became imperative after they observed that the Board was trying to create unnecessary disparities in the pension structures and payments. Daily Trust reports that the military veterans were on Friday engaged by the Board chaired by Mikail Abdulraheem, an Air Vice Marshal, to clarify issues surrounding the implementation of the newly approved pension rates. El-Rufai’s case on alleged funds misappropriation adjourned to Nov 30 Strike: FCT council chairman begs teachers to resume work The new rates came into existence after the retired military officers carried out a series of protests to press home their demands over what they called the stagnant nature of their monthly pay amid rising cost of living occasioned by inflation in the country. The spokesman of the MPB, Aliyu Mohammed, a Squadron Leader, had told journalists via a statement that the engagement provided an opportunity for the board to explain the implementation process. Mohammed noted that the board also addressed concerns raised by the representatives during the meeting, saying the gathering promoted a shared understanding of the new pension rates. “During the meeting, the representatives expressed their understanding of the explanations provided by the board and appreciated the opportunity to engage directly with them. “The discussions also reinforced the importance of continued dialogue, mutual understanding and the use of established communication channels to address pension-related concerns,” Mohammed said. Daily Trust reports that there was back and forth between the management of the board and the protesters’ representatives on Tuesday when the two parties met at a roundtable to resolve the issues. After several hours of dialogue, both parties stuck to their guns as the MPB urged them to show understanding. But the retired officers said they would not back down and might continue the protest if their demands are not met. Military retirees, yesterday, blocked entrance to the Military Pensions Board office in Dutse Alhaji, Abuja, over unpaid entitlements. The issues Prior to the Tuesday protest, checks by our correspondent showed that the main issue borders on consequential adjustment implementation of retired military officers’ pensions. The protesting veterans argued that there were two germane issues that must be resolved immediately, which include re-computation of their monthly pay in line with retirees’ equal ranks and number of years in the service. They are also demanding a forensic audit of the MPB to ascertain what was released and what was actually utilised in the payment of the consequential adjustment. In August, the protesters laid siege to the headquarters of the Federal Ministry of Defence in Abuja for days to demand immediate implementation of consequential adjustments to their pensions. The protesters, who retired on the rank of Colonel and below, demanded the inclusion of retired personnel in the consequential adjustment arising from recent salary increases for serving military personnel. President Bola Tinubu had in August approved a new salary scale for military men and officers, effective from September 2026, to bolster their performance across all theatres of operations in the country. The retired military officers said they should benefit from the increment, having served the country for 35 years. During the August protest, armed police officers and soldiers were drawn from the Guards Brigade, leading to a confrontation between the protesters and the security operatives attached to the ministry. The operatives prevented protesting retired military personnel from converging on the entrance of the ministry. The security operatives were heard threatening to open fire if the protesting officers crossed the line, saying they were acting on orders. Despite the threat, the protest went on for days before the minister finally brokered a truce. Similarly, in 2024, scores of retired military personnel stormed the headquarters of the Federal Ministry of Finance and shut down the place over non-payment of their entitlements by the government. The retirees, who arrived the protesting ground as early as 7:30am with sleeping mats, chairs and canopies, accused the federal government of not paying them a 20% to 28% salary increment from January to November 2024. The fresh protest came less than 12 hours after another group of retired military personnel under the aegis of Ex-Service Men and Family Welfare Association of Nigeria, held a rally to demand payment of pension arrears. What transpired on protest ground Speaking to journalists before the meeting with the MPB commenced, Azubuike alleged underpayment of their pensions, accusing the board of using a pension computation formula that allegedly reduced the percentage increases approved for retired personnel. Azubuike, who is the coordinator of the Veterans Association of Nigeria, demanded an urgent re-calculation of their entitlements in line with approved adjustments to the salaries of serving military personnel. According to him, the approved adjustments provided for an 80 per cent increase for personnel from the rank of private to staff sergeant, 50 per cent for warrant officers to colonels, and 30 per cent for brigadier generals and higher ranks. He alleged that the Board failed to apply the approved percentages directly to the pension veterans were already receiving, instead using a calculation method that reduced their entitlements. “We have gotten presidential approval for the consequential allowance on the percentages allotted to various rank categories. Now, in paying us this consequential adjustment, the Military Pension Board did not pay this very approved percentage”, he said. He explained that the veterans had earlier approached the Ministry of Defence in August to demand the inclusion of retired personnel in the salary-related adjustments after discovering that they had initially been excluded. According to him, the ministry acknowledged the omission and subsequently included them in the approved adjustments. He, however, accused the Military Pensions Board of introducing a calculation method that allegedly undermined the approved increases, despite the fact that the pension rates of retirees had already been determined by their ranks and years of service at retirement. The protesters argued that the approved percentage should apply to the pension each retiree was receiving before the adjustment, rather than being subjected to another calculation based on the conditions under which the individual retired. To illustrate his concern, Azubuike cited a retired soldier entitled to an 80 per cent increase, arguing that the board’s alleged approach could leave the pensioner receiving less than the approved adjustment. He also alleged that the computation method had not been applied uniformly, leaving some veterans with payments below what they believed they were entitled to receive. The veterans further claimed that some pensioners received only part of their expected adjustments and had to complain before the outstanding amounts were paid. Azubuike stated that the board could release the remaining arrears within days after receiving complaints, a practice he said raised questions about the consistency and transparency of its payment procedures. “We are about 100,000 military veterans,” he said, adding that he had records to support the allegations of discrepancies in pension payments. Another protester, Master Warrant Officer Duru Augustine, said the alleged underpayment had left retired personnel feeling betrayed after years of service to the country. He maintained that the dispute concerned the implementation of approved pension adjustments, which he said veterans had fought to secure after discovering that retired personnel were initially excluded. Augustine recalled that the veterans protested on August 19, after which, according to him, the Minister of Defence, Christopher Musa, acknowledged their concerns and supported their inclusion in the adjustment. He said the National Salaries, Incomes and Wages Commission had also provided a chart explaining the calculations, arguing that the board should implement the approved percentages rather than introduce a different method. “It’s an insult to the president of the Federal Republic of Nigeria. It’s an insult to the capacity of the commander-in-chief of the armed forces, for him (the minister) to go back and do whatever he feels like doing,” he said, referring to the alleged departure from the approved adjustment framework. Augustine argued that applying the approved percentages to existing pensions should be straightforward. “For whatever he (Azubuike) is taking every month as his pension, 50 per cent of that thing added to what he’s taking now is his actual pension now. What is the big deal?” he asked. He also expressed concern about the impact of the dispute on veterans’ health and their ability to meet basic needs, including the cost of medication. “Many of them are sick. They can’t afford medicine,” he said, describing the hardship among the protesters. Augustine said he travelled from Owerri, Imo State, overnight to join the protest and draw public attention to the veterans’ complaints. He appealed to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and the defence minister to intervene, insisting that many retired personnel depended entirely on their pensions for survival. “Some of us are not well. The government should look into our plight and help us,” he said. Explaining the computations Pensioners’ calculation: For instance, if a Private had retired in 2025 having served for 35 years on a salary of N100,000, he would have been receiving 90% of his last salary – N90,000 – as monthly pension. Based on Consequential Adjustment (CA), they argued that the approved increase for his rank category is 80%. This means 80% of his N90,000 pension, which amounts to N72,000 that will then be added to make his new monthly pension N162,000. If a Private whose current salary is N180,000, following the 80% increment, retires in October 2026, his pension would be calculated as 90% of his last salary (N180,000), which amounts to N162,000 per month. This brings the pension for both old and new retired privates to par. MPB calculation: But based on the Military Pension Board (MPB) calculation, the 2025 retired Private can only get 90% of the approved increase. To such a retiree, an 80% increase means N72,000. But to MPB, it has to be 90% of N72,000, which amounts to N64,800. The MPB says it is N64,800 that will then be added to the retiree’s N90,000 pension to arrive at a new monthly pension of N154,800. Commenting on the board’s computation, the retirees said such calculation promotes disparity in the pension of retirees of equal ranks and number of years of service. They said the implication is that both soldiers, who served for 35 years and retired on the same rank, would be earning different pay. “The one that retired in 2025 is on a N154,800 monthly pension, while the one that retired this year is on a N162,000 pension. This is just for the lowest paid; the disparity increases with higher ranks. This is not the spirit and letter of the Constitution for consequential adjustment to the pension of retirees any time there is an increase in the salary of workers. “It’s also not the intent of the circular from NSIWC for pension purposes. And that conflated form of computation by MPB becomes more complex in computing for retirees of lesser number of years of service, and provides good room for sharp practices of short-payment,” they added. We’re transparent – Military Pension Board chair Speaking after the meeting, the chairman of the Board said the legal framework and salary structure used in computing retirees’ pensions have been transparent following complaints about the consequential adjustment. Abdulraheem said the board was committed to administering pensions in accordance with the applicable laws and salary structures issued by the NSIWC. He explained that the commission provided a revised salary structure for pension and gratuity purposes following the salary review for serving military personnel, effective September 1, 2026. According to him, the structure incorporates the approved adjustments and provides the basis for calculating pension entitlements across ranks and years of service. He said the board did not independently determine the salary rates but applied the approved structure in line with the relevant pension regulations. Abdulraheem explained that pension computation followed a graduated formula based on years of service, with entitlements increasing from the prescribed minimum to a maximum of 90 per cent of the applicable final emolument after 35 years of service. He said applying a common framework was essential to maintaining consistency between existing pensioners and personnel who would retire in the future. The chairman urged veterans to submit their calculations and supporting pension records so the board can examine differences between the amounts expected and those received. He said the board was willing to explain its computation and work with the relevant authorities to clarify the issues raised. “We want everyone to see the applicable documents and understand the computation rather than rely on assumptions,” he said. Abdulraheem said the NSIWC had also been invited to provide clarification on the revised salary structure and the basis for the figures used in the computation. He emphasised that individual complaints would be more effectively addressed through the examination of pension records and supporting documents. The chairman also urged veterans’ organisations to adopt a coordinated approach to engage the board, saying a recognised channel would facilitate communication and help prevent the fragmentation of complaints.

title: SPECIAL REPORT: Insecurity exposes Zamfara communities to recurring cholera outbreaks
body:
It started with a sharp pain in Musa Saidu’s stomach.
The 20-year-old initially thought little of it. But the pain was soon followed by fever, vomiting and frequent watery stools. Within hours, his condition had deteriorated.
This was August 2025, during a cholera outbreak in Bukkuyum Local Government Area of Zamfara State, where Mr Saidu and his family were living after fleeing their home in Dan Bago village following attacks by bandits.
Like thousands of people displaced by years of insecurity in the state, the family had already lost the stability of home. Now, as Mr Saidu became increasingly ill, they faced another problem: getting medical care.
His parents first tried what they could afford. They gave him some medicines and mixed a local herbal remedy with water, hoping his condition would improve. But i t did not.
With the health facility serving their community no longer functional, the family eventually took Musa to the Orphan and Less Privileged Clinic (OLPC) in Bukkuyum town, where he was diagnosed with cholera.
But reaching a health facility did not immediately end their difficulties.
The clinic was struggling with an influx of cholera patients. Only three health workers were on duty, while essential medicines were unavailable.
Many residents affected by the outbreak were brought to the same facility, while some had to seek treatment elsewhere because of shortages of staff, medicines and space.
For displaced families such as Mr Saidu’s, the outbreak exposed a problem that went beyond cholera.
Years of insecurity have displaced many communities across Zamfara, forced health workers away from some rural areas and disrupted access to healthcare, safe water and disease surveillance. These are services that become particularly important during an outbreak of a disease that can kill within hours if severe dehydration is not treated.
Zamfara is one of the states hardest hit by the insecurity that has spread across north-western Nigeria over the past decade.
What began largely as cattle rustling has evolved into organised violence by armed groups commonly referred to as bandits. Communities have been attacked, residents killed or abducted and thousands forced from their homes.
The armed groups have also imposed levies on some farming communities, stolen livestock and harvests and carried out kidnappings for ransom.
Data obtained from the Mass Atrocities Tracker show that 28,974 people were killed across Nigeria between 2021 and 2025. Borno recorded the highest number, with 4,539 deaths, followed by Zamfara with 3,936 and Kaduna with 2,811.
Zamfara recorded the highest number of abductions during the same period, with 5,447 people kidnapped. Kaduna recorded 4,050 and Niger 3,331.
But deaths, abductions and displacement are only some of the consequences.
In Bukkuyum LGA, residents and health workers told The ICIR that insecurity has also weakened access to healthcare. Some communities have been deserted, while health workers have stopped providing services in areas they consider unsafe.
Reports in 2025 indicated that only about 200 of Zamfara’s more than 700 Primary Healthcare Centres (PHCs) were functional, with persistent insecurity blamed for the closure or abandonment of many facilities.
For residents of affected rural communities, the closures mean illness can require travelling several kilometres, sometimes through unsafe areas, before reaching a health worker.
For people displaced by violence, the risks are compounded by overcrowding, poor sanitation, poverty and limited access to safe water.
During a cholera outbreak, those conditions can become deadly.
Buba Muhammad had already fled his home in Sadawa with his family because of repeated bandit attacks when his son began vomiting and passing frequent watery stools.
The 40-year-old farmer and his family were living as displaced persons in Bukkuyum, where several families shared limited space and sanitation facilities.
Mr Muhammad immediately tried to find medical help.
There was no functioning health facility close to where they were staying.
“My first attempt when my son was affected was to go to a hospital, but there was no facility nearby,” he said. “I had to take him to a medicine shop.”
The medicines he obtained there did little to improve the boy’s condition.
As the vomiting and diarrhoea continued, Mr Muhammad decided to take him to General Hospital Bukkuyum, the nearest facility where he believed the child could receive appropriate treatment.
The hospital was struggling with patients arriving from communities affected by the outbreak.
“We didn’t receive the proper care we expected immediately because there were not enough staff,” he recalled.
“There was no bed space. We even kept our patient on the floor before a staff member later found us a bed.”
The illness also placed a financial burden on a family already displaced by insecurity.
Mr Muhammad said they spent heavily on transportation and medicines, including drugs they had to buy outside the hospital after receiving prescriptions.
“The only solution to ease the hardship of such unwanted incidents or outbreaks is to provide facilities in our local communities,” he said.
But he said restoring healthcare without addressing insecurity would leave another part of the problem unresolved.
“We need security in our locations because we are not safe; there are attacks every day and night in our locations. The government needs to double its efforts to end the problem.”
Cholera is an acute diarrhoeal disease caused by consuming food or water contaminated with the bacterium Vibrio cholerae. Without prompt treatment, severe cases can lead to rapid dehydration and death.
It is also largely preventable through access to safe water, adequate sanitation and good hygiene, while prompt administration of oral rehydration solution and other appropriate treatment can substantially reduce deaths.
Yet cholera has repeatedly affected communities in Zamfara State.
In 2023, a World Health Organisation (WHO) report recorded 907 suspected cholera cases in the state, representing about 28 per cent of Nigeria’s suspected cases during the period covered.
The state was affected again in 2024. WHO reported more than 700 cases and over 30 deaths across Zamfara and neighbouring Sokoto during the period covered by its report.
By 9 July 2025, Zamfara had recorded 1,619 suspected cases, six confirmed cases and 31 deaths across 12 of its 14 local government areas, according to a UNICEF situation report.
UNICEF said suspected cases increased by 30 per cent within one week, with children and young people accounting for 62 per cent of reported cases.
In August 2025, an outbreak in communities in Bukkuyum LGA killed at least eight people and affected more than 200 across 11 communities, according to residents and local officials cited by Reuters .
For residents already dealing with displacement, unsafe water and weakened healthcare services, the outbreak exposed how insecurity can magnify an otherwise preventable public health emergency.
The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) identifies unsafe water, inadequate sanitation and poor hygiene as major factors driving cholera transmission.
In parts of Bukkuyum LGA, insecurity has made addressing those risks more difficult. Residents have been displaced into congested settlements, some health facilities are non-functional, and health workers say reaching remote communities for surveillance and other services can be dangerous.
For some patients, simply reaching treatment presents another risk.
In Masu community, Salihu Bello returned home one afternoon to find his two sisters seriously ill.
“They had stomach pain, and became very weak,” he recalled. “Later we realised it was cholera.”
With no health facility in the community, the family initially relied on local remedies.
But the sisters’ condition continued to worsen. Seeking treatment meant undertaking a difficult journey to Bukkuyum town. Before reaching the town, they had to cross a river, a challenge that has become even more dangerous since insecurity forced many healthcare workers to stop visiting remote communities.
“Sometimes health workers used to come to our community, but because of security problems they stopped,” Mr Bello said.
As night fell, the family began the trip. Fear of bandits lingered throughout the journey, but Mr Bello said concern for his sisters outweighed every other worry.
“At that moment, we were not thinking about insecurity. We only wanted to save them. It took about three hours before we received attention because we arrived very late at night,” he said.
When a health worker eventually prescribed medicines, he had to wake a medicine vendor before dawn to obtain them.
His sisters remained under observation for about 24 hours before their conditions improved.
For Mr Bello, the experience showed the cost of having no functioning healthcare facility nearby.
“If we have a health facility in our community, things will be easier, considering how quickly the disease can affect the human body,” he said.
“Before a patient from our community gets to the hospital, they suffer a lot. Having our own health facility would make access to treatment much easier.”
But the health facility is only part of what residents say they need.
In Masu and other communities around Bukkuyum, preventing cholera begins with something even more basic: clean water.
In communities around Bukkuyum, residents said access to clean water remains a major challenge.
Some depend on streams for drinking, cooking and other household needs. In Dan Bago, residents said people and cattle sometimes rely on the same water sources.
For a community already vulnerable to cholera, such conditions increase the risk of transmission.
Nigeria’s 2021 Water, Sanitation and Hygiene National Outcome Routine Mapping (WASHNORM) report highlighted the scale of the country’s water and sanitation challenge.
The report, based on a survey of more than 24,600 households, estimated that approximately 179 million Nigerians, about 87 per cent of the population, lacked access to safely managed drinking-water services.
The situation was particularly difficult in northern Nigeria. The Northeast had the lowest access rate at just two per cent, compared with 29 per cent in the Southwest.
Although 67 per cent of the population had access to basic water supply services, about a quarter of Nigerians still relied on unimproved or surface water sources.
Muhammadu Sadawa, a community leader, said insecurity has made the situation worse by forcing residents from their homes and concentrating displaced families in already strained settlements.
“Another major challenge we have in our community now is insecurity,” he said. “Most of our people left the community because of banditry. Where we are now living is too congested and very dirty. That congestion helped the disease spread among us.”
Mr Sadawa said access to healthcare had also deteriorated.
Although there is a health facility in his community, he said it is no longer functional.
“We have a facility, but it is not in existence. There are no staff, no drugs. The building is dilapidated and almost collapsing,” he said.
During the cholera outbreak, residents therefore had to look elsewhere for treatment.
He said some families struggled to obtain care before outside assistance arrived, while others faced delays because of distance and the cost of treatment.
“Many people died, and it took a long time before we received any intervention. Some people were treated, some were not. I have a relative who spent over N50,000 on treatment. Many families went through the same thing,” he said.
For critically ill residents, reaching another health facility can itself be difficult.
Mr Sadawa said residents must cross a river to reach Bukkuyum town, where they can get more comprehensive medical care.
“When someone is sick, we have to cross a river before reaching the hospital. We need the facility renovated, and we also need a bridge or canoes to help us cross,” he said.
He estimated that more than 50 people in and around his community were affected during the outbreak, with some becoming ill in displacement settlements before being taken to Bukkuyum town for treatment.
At General Hospital Bukkuyum, Abdullahi Salihu remembers the pressure as cholera patients arrived from communities across the local government area.
“At the time of the outbreak, it was very tense and hectic considering how patients were being brought to the hospital,” he said.
“Some survived, some were quarantined, and unfortunately some died.”
According to Mr Salihu, insecurity complicated the response.
Patients who could leave affected communities were brought to the hospital. But health workers had limited options for people trapped in settlements that were difficult or unsafe to reach.
“As health workers, we faced a lot of challenges because of insecurity,” he said.
“Some people managed to bring patients from their communities because they had no other option. But for those who could not come out, there was little we could do for them.”
Mr Salihu said government officials, politicians and humanitarian organisations provided intravenous fluids, antibiotics, rehydration supplies and other support during the outbreak.
But insecurity was not the only challenge.
Many of the patients were displaced people who had lost livelihoods and struggled to afford transportation, food and other necessities.
“Most of them were displaced from their communities with nothing to eat,” he said. “Then the outbreak added another difficulty to their lives.”
Zaharadeen Abdullahi, a health worker at the Women and Children Welfare Clinic in Bukkuyum, also described insecurity as a major obstacle to preventing and responding to outbreaks.
“Insecurity is a major contributing factor to outbreaks like this,” he said.
“We have services, vaccinations and awareness programmes, but because of security challenges many health workers cannot reach vulnerable communities.”
Some affected settlements are more than 10 kilometres from health facilities, Mr Abdullahi said. In some areas, insecurity has also limited the transportation options residents can use.
“Some communities cannot use motorcycles because of security threats,” he said. “People have to walk long distances or use donkeys. Because cholera requires urgent treatment, these delays can lead to deaths.”
He said displacement had created additional risks.
“Most of the affected people are internally displaced persons living in congested conditions,” Mr Abdullahi said. “Many rely on unsafe water sources, and stagnant water is still being used for drinking and household activities.”
He acknowledged support from the Zamfara State government, UNICEF and other organisations during the outbreak but said greater investment was needed in health facilities, medical supplies and outreach to vulnerable communities.
Shakir Balogun, an epidemiologist, said recurring cholera outbreaks in conflict-affected parts of Zamfara should not be viewed simply as a disease problem.
He said they also expose weaknesses in healthcare access and disease surveillance created or worsened by years of insecurity.
Mr Balogun said insecurity had affected the health system’s ability to reach some communities even before recent cholera outbreaks.
“When insecurity makes communities difficult to reach, children can be missed by immunisation programmes, cases of Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) can escape surveillance, and cases of acute watery diarrhoea can similarly go undetected or reach treatment late,” he said.
“The pathogen changes; the health-system vulnerability does not.”
Mr Balogun said these weaknesses became particularly evident during the 2025 cholera outbreak.
According to him, the African Field Epidemiology Network (AFENET), with technical and financial support from the US Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, deployed eight Field Epidemiology Training Programme residents and a graduate to support Zamfara’s response between 11 September and 2 October 2025.
The team worked with state authorities in four high-burden local government areas.
Mr Balogun said the response identified cases in inaccessible and insecure settlements. It also identified under-reporting linked partly to weak active case searches and insecurity, as well as delayed reporting and incomplete records.
Other challenges included transporting stool samples to the state reference laboratory, shortages of essential supplies outside initially prioritised LGAs and inadequate personnel in some health facilities.
The findings suggest that insecurity can affect almost every stage of outbreak control, from identifying a sick person and reporting a suspected case to testing samples and getting treatment to patients.
Mr Balogun said strengthening community-based surveillance could help close some of those gaps.
Trusted residents and community structures, he said, can help identify and report suspected cases when conventional health teams cannot safely reach affected settlements.
Treatment also needs to be brought closer to vulnerable communities.
“If insecurity means a severely ill patient has to travel several hours or cross an unsafe area before receiving ORS or intravenous fluids, geographical access itself becomes a determinant of survival,” he said.
He recommended establishing oral rehydration points and treatment units close to vulnerable communities, backed by reliable referral systems for patients who develop severe disease.
Authorities should also use surveillance and previous outbreak data to identify communities repeatedly affected by cholera and position essential supplies there before outbreaks escalate, he said.
“You do not want to begin moving ORS, IV fluids, chlorine and other essential supplies into a hard-to-reach community only after an outbreak has accelerated,” Mr Balogun said.
“We should use surveillance and historical data to identify recurrent hotspots and position supplies before the rainy season.”
Bringing treatment closer to affected communities could save lives, but Mr Balogun said it would not eliminate the conditions that allow cholera to return.
He said safe water and sanitation remain fundamental.
Vaccination and effective case management can reduce infections and deaths during outbreaks, he said, but communities will remain vulnerable if they continue to depend on unsafe water and inadequate sanitation.
Mr Balogun recommended strategic use of oral cholera vaccines among high-risk populations and in communities with recurring outbreaks, particularly where insecurity makes immediate improvements to water and sanitation infrastructure difficult.
But he cautioned against treating vaccination as a replacement for those investments.
“Vaccination is an additional layer of protection, not a substitute for water, sanitation, surveillance and access to treatment,” he said.
The Zamfara State government said it has adopted community-based measures to maintain disease surveillance and provide basic cholera support in areas where insecurity makes conventional healthcare difficult.
The state Ministry of Health, working with the World Health Organisation (WHO) and other partners, has also begun developing a Multi-Hazard Incident Action Plan to strengthen preparedness and response to public health emergencies, including cholera.
Ahmad Muhammad, the Zamfara State epidemiologist, acknowledged the difficulty of reaching communities affected by insecurity.
He said one strategy has been to identify community health workers from insecure areas, bring them to safer locations for training and then send them back to support residents.
“We train them, particularly the community health workers there. So we train them and then allow them to go back to their community and support them,” he said.
Mr Muhammad said trained workers are provided with available medical supplies and asked to report suspected cases so health officials can track whether infections are increasing or declining.
He said the approach forms part of the state’s risk communication and community engagement strategy, under which people with health-related roles in affected communities are trained to support local outbreak response.
Patients who can safely be evacuated are moved to accessible areas for further treatment, including general hospitals and the treatment centre at the Infectious Disease Hospital in Gusau, he said.
He attributed the state’s reduced cholera burden this year, compared with the previous year, to interventions including community sensitisation, improved hygiene, and oral cholera vaccination.
“Community sensitisation and improvement of hygiene, oral cholera vaccination campaign last time. The burden of the disease has reduced this year compared to last year,” he said.
He said the government had also intensified water, sanitation and hygiene interventions, including measures aimed at reducing open defecation.
“So I think those strategies have really gone a long way in mitigating the impact,” he said.
But for residents of communities where health facilities remain closed or poorly equipped and safe water remains difficult to obtain, the conditions that make cholera dangerous have not disappeared.

title: Britain must settle its Brexit argument before seeking an EU return
body: Confusion reigns where the UK and EU is concerned. Having been dormant for so long, avoided and ducked by successive recent prime ministers, Britain’s future relations with the EU has suddenly become a major political and diplomatic issue. The uncertainty stems from how far Andy Burnham wants to go and at what speed. He gives every impression of wishing the UK to rejoin and quickly. But then he will say in the next breath that the British public must decide. That raises the possibility, make it probability, of a bitter, protracted Brexit battle all over again. He is pinning much on the forthcoming UK-EU Summit, scheduled for November 20, and has set out his wish-list of what he would like that meeting to achieve – including free trade of food and drink products, greater movement of young people – while giving the impression of this only being the first step. That in itself, though, is radical compared with where the UK and EU were. And, as Leader of the Opposition Kemi Badenoch has rightly observed, it’s a curious way to proceed into a negotiation, showing your hand at one go. It is clear to everyone, not least the EU that he sees this as merely the beginning not the end. How though, can he get there, without resurrecting the old battle-lines and splitting the country? He began by being inflammatory, by suggesting the referendum verdict was improperly obtained. No sooner did Mr Burnham signal his desire for the UK to form closer ties with the EU, with a view possibly to rejoining, than the Prime Minister appeared on a podcast saying there was incontrovertible evidence that Russia interfered in the referendum campaign . Bearing in mind the decision to leave was won by just 2 per cent of the vote, the suggestion that it was some way Russian influenced has the ability to invalidate Brexit, to throw the authenticity of the UK’s departure into doubt (Remainers would argue it was already questionable as part of the Brexiteers’ campaign was based on hyperbole and falsehood). So, we actually didn’t choose to exit after all, which could help our efforts to gain readmission. Except Mr Burnham’s was not a new claim. It had been made repeatedly in the past and had always been denied by government ministers and security officials. Nevertheless, here was Mr Burnham maintaining that upon arriving in No 10 he asked about possible Russian interference in the 2016 ballot and stating: “I’ve had the clear answer that, yes, there was.” Fine, if he has the proof. At the time of writing, none is forthcoming. Indeed, well after Mr Burnham made his comment, Stephen Doughty, the Foreign Office minister, was challenged by the BBC to produce it, and replied he wouldn’t “get into specifics”. Instead, Mr Doughty resorted to vague accusations that “Russia clearly has attempted to interfere on a number of our democratic processes. They’re engaged in information warfare, they’re spending £1.5 billion [almost $2 billion] this year alone on disinformation and propaganda”. Cue Nigel Farage, the Brexit architect, denouncing Mr Burnham as “a liar”. Cue too, a feeling of deja vu, that we’ve been here before, many times, that nothing has really changed, that the old wounds have never healed, but still exist, waiting to be reopened. All this row – and it quickly erupted into a war of words, with Mr Farage, who has been accused in the past of enjoying close ties with Russia, sensing his honour and reputation had been impugned sounding most indignant – served to show was that the UK is nowhere near ready to rejoin, not collectively with a consensus, that EU leaders starting to take Mr Burnham at his word might wish to reconsider. The question they should ask themselves is, does Mr Burnham speak for the nation? He may wish to come back but does the electorate, how certain can they be that the same mixture of disregard, often tipping into open contempt, for the EU and its ideals, won’t simply rear its head again? It’s true that a majority of the British people, far greater than the percentage who chose to quit, now believe Brexit was a mistake . The polls put the figure slightly above 70 per cent. In democratic terms, that’s substantial. But it’s an opinion poll, not the real thing, and however the cake is cut, a significant portion of the populace still argue we were right to go. That slice is inspired by committed and noisy agitators. Mr Farage has already said Mr Burnham’s public ambition has regalvanised his Reform UK party’s support base. Until the senior pro-Brexit players in the epic drama of a decade ago come out and admit they were wrong, those of a suspicious nature in the EU are fully entitled to worry the UK would become the renegade member it was before – harrying, obstructing and yes, insulting, at every turn. It would require former prime minister Boris Johnson to recant, and ideally, Mr Farage. Even better still, for the pair of them together to fall on their anti-EU swords. Well, that will never occur . Rather, what will happen is that they will unpick the scars and a whole new anti-EU front will erupt. In the same way that Britain withdrew by the thinnest of margins, this perception matters. Because should we pursue readmittance, we must clear several hurdles, any one of which could block our path. Mr Burnham clearly would like to make it an election issue, to be included in the Labour manifesto. If he wins that popular mandate, in theory, there ought to be no requirement for a re-run of a separate EU vote. That is the view of the mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, among others. But the EU is likely to insist upon a second referendum as a precursor to commencing membership negotiations. Their argument is that they would want to be persuaded the decision is non-party political, and that a vote for a manifesto covers all manner of issues, only one of which is the EU. A re-run could make the case that recommencing membership would last beyond the lifetime of the newly elected government and extend across successive governments. Virtually all countries joining have done so only after holding a public ballot. So, the UK could not realistically seek special dispensation. The European Commission, which would lead the process, would also need to vote its agreement. So too would a majority of the members of European Parliament. Critically, as well, the 27 member countries would have a say and it is by no means guaranteed they would approve the UK resuming. Traditional anti-Britishness could re-surface and they could have agendas of their own – skilful diplomacy by the UK government and Foreign Office would have to be deployed. That said, British diplomats are indicating privately they think simply going back in and taking up where we left off is a tall, if not impossible, order. The EU too would be right to examine Britain’s motives – why now, why the sudden change of heart, why after all this time, 10 years and counting, do we wish to return? The answer, and one Mr Burnham is correct to proclaim, is because Brexit has not delivered . At a stroke, we ditched a free trade bloc of 450 million people. British businesses too found themselves bereft of skilled EU labour. Nothing we’ve done since has come remotely close to replacing what was lost. The Bank of England estimates a loss to our gross domestic product of 6 per cent to 8 per cent – this at a time of increased global competitiveness, rising protectiveness and sovereignty, energy crisis, supply chain difficulties, rising cost of living, threat of AI to jobs, when just adding 1 per cent is a tough bar. Here was the UK saying goodbye to 6 per cent. Just like that. As welcome as they are, trade deals have helped plug the gap, but they only go so far. We had a huge customs-free market on our doorstep, and we blew it. Business investment post-Brexit also fell, down, according to estimates, by 12 per cent to 18 per cent. That’s what we’d like again and if not through full membership, through a much greater rapprochement, possibly through the Customs Union. We’d love also to be able to stem the tide of illegal immigration, which we have failed to do on our own. But the EU is aware of our need and it realises too, that is a prize worth having and is not something to be awarded easily. Not if it comes with the baggage of anti-EU rhetoric and the likelihood that at any moment, a new administration, one led by Mr Farage, say, could again up sticks. That said, there are those in the EU who would like to see Britain’s return in some form. We bring with us 69.5 million people and we could provide an economic as well as political fillip. In a world dominated by two superpowers, a united EU would be a match for them. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s speech to Davos earlier this year, in which he called for the “middle powers” to combine, continues to resonate loudly. The fact Mr Carney has followed that up with a suggestion of “associate membership” of the EU has met with a warm response. Mr Carney and Canada, they can do business with. Are they able to say the same with certainty for an unclear, impatient Mr Burnham and his Perfidious Albion? Therein lies the rub.

title: Zelensky, Carney discuss U.S. contacts and upcoming diplomatic events
body:
As reported by Ukrinform, Zelensky said this in a Telegram post .
“I spoke with Prime Minister Mark Carney. Thank you, Canada! I briefed him on the latest Russian strike on Kyiv and no advance warning from our partners about the ballistic missile launch. This is the second time Ukraine has received no warning this week,” Zelensky said.
He said a rescue operation was underway following the strike, which damaged a residential building and set apartments on fire from the first through the eighth floors.
“All emergency services are on the scene, and residents are being evacuated. So far, one person has been reported killed and six injured. My condolences to their families and loved ones,” the president wrote.
He added that another strike hit the premises of one of Kyiv’s main power plants. Ukraine is counting on support from its partners in this situation.
Zelensky and Carney also discussed contacts with the United States and diplomatic events that could take place this week.
“It is important that the world clearly supports an end to this war and real steps toward de-escalation – genuine steps that Russia will actually take to bring its war and its killings to an end,” the President of Ukraine stressed.
As Ukrinform reported, Zelensky said that Ukraine again received no information from its partners about missile launches ahead of the ballistic attack in the evening of October 13.

title: Shell to sell Nigeria’s domestic gas business to Vaaris Energy
body:
British energy giant Shell has signed an agreement to sell its full interest in Shell Nigeria Gas Group to indigenous energy firm Vaaris Energy Limited, marking its planned exit from Nigeria’s domestic gas distribution business.
Shell announced the deal in a statement on Tuesday, noting the transaction forms part of the strategy to simplify its portfolio and concentrate investments on areas of competitive strength.
“Shell Nigeria Gas has served industrial and commercial customers in Nigeria for more than 25 years, supported by the commitment and expertise of its people,” Elohor Aiboni, Shell’s country chair in Nigeria, said.
“We believe this agreement provides a much stronger platform for the business’ next chapter under new ownership. Shell continues to focus on strategic Deepwater and Integrated Gas positions in Nigeria.”
The companies did not disclose the financial terms of the transaction.
The deal is subject to regulatory conditions and approvals, and covers Shell Nigeria Gas Holding B.V., established in 2019, which holds all but one share in Shell Nigeria Gas Limited.
Until the transaction is completed, Shell Nigeria Gas Group will remain part of Shell and continue to serve its customers, while operating as usual.
Established in 1998, Shell Nigeria Gas supplies natural gas to industrial and commercial customers and runs about 170 kilometres of pipeline infrastructure across Ogun, Abia and Rivers states.
The company serves more than 130 connected customers, but is not involved in upstream gas production, liquefied natural gas (LNG) operations or international gas trading.
Vaaris Energy is a privately held Nigerian energy company with interests across the oil and gas value chain.
The divestment reflects Shell’s broader efforts to streamline its global portfolio under Chief Executive Officer Wael Sawan, and focus on businesses and projects offering competitive returns.
In Nigeria, the company said it would continue to prioritise deepwater operations and integrated gas, including its interest in Nigeria LNG.
Last week, Shell reportedly raised its forecast for third-quarter integrated gas production to between 740,000 and 780,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, up from its previous estimate of 570,000 to 630,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day.

title: 2027 Presidential Poll: Atiku Brings Tinubu into Policy Debate, Obi Missing
body: Olawale Olaleye With 13 weeks and three days to the January 16, 2027 presidential election, candidate of the Africa Democratic Congress (ADC), Alhaji Atiku Abubakar, has intensified his policy exchanges with the administration of President Bola Tinubu, particularly on petrol pricing, fiscal accountability and the cost of living. This gradually evolving debate, and the Presidency’s sometimes elaborate responses, have begun to change the character of the campaign conversation as the nation counts down to the election next January. Curiously, however, the presidential standard beaer of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), Mr. Peter Obi, appears to be missing in the emerging debate, albeit not totally in the wider conversation. Beyond the customary political intrigues, partisan recriminations, alliances and campaign rhetoric, an increasingly substantive argument about the direction of the country’s economy is beginning to take shape with the duo constantly sparring. The recurring disagreement between APC’s Bola Ahmed Tinubu and ADC’s Atiku Abubakar, is neither new nor particularly surprising. What is noteworthy, however, is the increasing specificity of the questions and policy alternatives being advanced by Atiku, and the detailed responses these have elicited from the Presidency. And, coming from Tinubu, who is naturally not disposed to a debate as evident during the 2023 presidential election, Atiku might have subtly forced the president and his government into interesting policy debate, and inadvertently changing the tenor of campaigns, based on issues. From the removal of petrol subsidy to the management of the exchange rate, public borrowing, taxation, government expenditure and the affordability of basic necessities, Atiku has repeatedly challenged the administration to explain not merely why its economic reforms were necessary, but how their benefits are reaching ordinary Nigerians. In doing so, the former vice-president has sought to shift the political conversation from personalities and partisan loyalties to the actual consequences of public policy. The government, on its part, has not allowed the arguments to go unanswered. Its statements, campaign interventions and direct responses have defended the logic of Tinubu’s reforms, challenged the financial sustainability of Atiku’s alternatives and questioned whether his proposals are compatible with existing legislation. This exchange has produced an interesting feature of the emerging presidential contest: a government defending the economic decisions it has already taken and an opposition candidate being pressed to explain the practical implications of the decisions he proposes to take. Yet, amid this increasingly sustained encounter, another major presidential candidate, Peter Obi of the NDC, has not occupied the same place in the particular exchange between Atiku and the Presidency. Obi has certainly not been silent on national issues. He has articulated positions on economic production, petroleum subsidy, corruption, electricity and public accountability. Indeed, his party recently criticised the government’s petrol discount. The distinction is that the recent sequence of proposals, presidential responses, counterproposals and fiscal arguments has developed principally around Atiku’s intervention. That development offers a useful window into the changing character of the 2027 contest. From Political Rhetoric to Policy Alternatives For much of Nigeria’s Fourth Republic, presidential campaigns have frequently been shaped by questions of ethnicity, religion, zoning, personalities and political alignments. Although economic policy has never been entirely absent, the technical details of proposed reforms have not always received the sustained public interrogation that a country facing serious structural economic challenges requires. The present circumstances make such an interrogation particularly relevant. When President Tinubu assumed office on May 29, 2023, he announced the removal of petrol subsidy, setting in motion one of the most consequential economic decisions of his administration. Changes in the foreign exchange system followed, while the government subsequently introduced far-reaching tax and fiscal reforms. The administration has maintained that these decisions were necessary to correct distortions, improve government finances, encourage investment and place Nigeria on a more sustainable economic footing. Atiku’s central objection is solely about the implementation of those reforms, the social protection available to vulnerable citizens and the accountability mechanisms governing the resources released. The argument became particularly pronounced in August 2026, when the ADC presidential candidate publicly pledged to restore petrol subsidy if elected. His declaration attracted immediate criticism, partly because Atiku had previously supported subsidy removal and downstream petroleum deregulation. But as the debate developed, his campaign clarified that the proposed arrangement would not simply revive the old system of subsidising imported petrol. Instead, Atiku advocated a capped, budgeted production subsidy directed at petroleum products refined within Nigeria, including those produced by modular refineries. According to his campaign, the proposed programme would be linked to verified domestic production, monitored independently and designed to ensure that the benefits reached consumers through lower pump prices. The distinction is consequential. Under the former arrangement, public resources were used extensively to compensate for differences between regulated domestic petrol prices and the cost of supply, much of which involved imported products. Under Atiku’s proposal, government support would be tied principally to domestic refining, potentially through crude oil supplied to qualifying refineries at preferential prices. The argument, therefore, concerns whether public intervention in the petroleum market should be eliminated, temporarily permitted or deliberately redesigned to support domestic production and consumer affordability. It is a question with substantial consequences for government revenue, investment, industrial development and household expenditure. How Tinubu Entered the Argument However, the government’s responses have demonstrated how closely the issue has become associated with the presidential campaign. On August 2, 2026, the Presidency published a detailed response to Atiku’s criticisms of the administration’s economic management. The statement addressed his concerns about public borrowing, the 2024 budget, subsidy removal, tax reforms and the utilisation of oil revenue. It argued that Atiku’s criticisms placed insufficient emphasis on the economy’s subsequent performance, pointing to improvements in macroeconomic conditions, government revenue and investment confidence. The government also defended the removal of subsidy as a structural correction that had improved allocations to states and local governments. The debate intensified the following month. On September 20, the APC Presidential Campaign Council publicly challenged Atiku to explain the legal, financial and operational implications of his proposed production subsidy. Among the questions raised were the subsidy rate, annual expenditure ceiling, eligible crude volumes, funding sources, pricing arrangements, safeguards against diversion and possible amendments to the Petroleum Industry Act. The council estimated that the proposal could cost between 17 trillion and N21 trillion annually, depending on its design and implementation. Importantly, those figures were APC’s projections, not an independently established cost of Atiku’s programme. The detailed assumptions necessary to reproduce the estimates have not been fully published. Nevertheless, the questions themselves were substantial. They required the opposition candidate to move beyond the broad promise of cheaper petrol and explain how the intended intervention would be financed, regulated and monitored. Atiku’s campaign subsequently maintained that the proposal would be capped, budgeted and independently audited. It also indicated that amendments to existing petroleum legislation could be pursued if necessary. However, the actual proposed discount rate, annual funding requirement and complete mechanism for passing savings to consumers remain outstanding. This is precisely the kind of practical policy interrogation that should accompany presidential proposals involving potentially significant public resources. The presidency’s engagement has not been confined to technical arguments. Some responses have included strong personal and political criticisms of Atiku. Yet, underneath the political language, questions of subsidy design, market pricing, public expenditure and the legal authority of government intervention have remained central. October 1: A Clash of Economic Narratives The exchange acquired additional significance during Nigeria’s 66th Independence anniversary. In his October 1 national address, President Tinubu declared that the country was transitioning from economic stabilisation towards what he described as an era of shared prosperity. The President defended the removal of subsidy and foreign exchange reforms, insisting that they had helped repair structural weaknesses inherited by his administration. He cited improved economic growth, rising foreign reserves, stronger non-oil exports and moderating inflation. According to Tinubu, the economy had expanded by more than four per cent during the year, while non-oil exports exceeded $6 billion in 2025. He also outlined priorities involving agricultural mechanisation, industrial production, transportation infrastructure, power supply, employment and access to finance. Significantly, the president criticised those advocating a return to subsidies, arguing that the country should not abandon reforms simply because their initial effects had been painful. Although the statement did not expressly identify Atiku, the timing and substance placed the issue of subsidy at the centre of the president’s economic argument. Atiku responded that same day with an extensive address disputing the administration’s assessment of national conditions. His criticism revolved around the difference between improvements in macroeconomic indicators and the purchasing power of ordinary households. He questioned whether economic growth, higher government revenue and reduced inflation could legitimately be described as prosperity when many citizens continued to struggle with food, transport, electricity, education and healthcare costs. He also offered specific illustrations. For instance, Atiku argued that the N30,000 minimum wage in April 2023 could purchase approximately 118 litres of petrol, whereas the current N70,000 minimum wage would purchase only about 50 litres at prevailing prices. The comparison is instructive, though it depends on the petrol prices and locations used. It illustrates how a nominal increase in wages can coexist with a decline in purchasing power. The statutory minimum wage has risen by approximately 133 per cent, from N30,000 to N70,000. But if petrol costs approximately N1,400 per litre, the newer wage purchases substantially less fuel than the older wage did at prices prevailing before subsidy removal. Atiku also raised questions about the administration’s budgeting arrangements, public debt, social intervention programmes and the extent to which increased government resources had translated into tangible improvements in living standards. In effect, the exchange highlighted two different measurements of economic progress. Tinubu’s emphasis was on macroeconomic stabilisation, structural reforms and the conditions necessary for future growth. Atiku’s emphasis was on immediate affordability, household welfare and the distribution of the gains arising from those reforms. These are not mutually exclusive economic objectives. Indeed, a sustainable recovery ultimately requires both. The disagreement concerns the pace, sequencing and effectiveness of the policies intended to achieve them. The Petrol Discount That Reopened the Controversy Perhaps the most revealing chapter of the argument emerged between October 8 and 11. Against the backdrop of higher international oil prices, the federal government announced measures intended to moderate petrol costs. The Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited extended a N66-per-litre discount introduced on October 1 at its retail stations, with the arrangement scheduled to continue until October 31. The Minister of Finance, Taiwo Oyedele, explained that NNPC Retail would forgo part of its profit margin and sell petrol at cost to provide temporary relief to consumers. The government also outlined a proposed framework involving a negotiated ceiling of approximately N1,350 per litre on petrol supply costs, with provisions for smoothing temporary price increases. The N1,350 figure was not a uniform nationwide pump price. It related to proposed supply-cost arrangements, with the eventual price paid by motorists still affected by distribution and retail costs. NNPC subsequently insisted that the discount did not constitute a restoration of the former petroleum subsidy regime. But Atiku disagreed with the political and economic presentation of the policy. His campaign questioned why the administration, having consistently defended subsidy removal and criticised government intervention in petrol pricing, was now supporting a temporary discount. At the October 9 inauguration of the ADC Presidential Campaign Council in Abuja, Atiku accused Tinubu of borrowing from his production-subsidy proposal without adopting its essential features. The former vice-president, who constantly referred to the president as “Bola” in his speech, a disposition the presidency considers disrespectful, argued that a short-term retail discount could not substitute for a properly structured arrangement intended to lower the cost of domestically refined petroleum products. He went on to challenge the government to explain what would happen when the discount expires. The Presidency answered. On October 11, presidential adviser, Sunday Dare, issued a detailed rebuttal defending the discount as a temporary market intervention rather than an abandonment of deregulation. The statement argued that Atiku’s production-subsidy proposal underestimated the commercial and contractual complexities of Nigeria’s petroleum industry. It maintained that the government could not simply distribute crude oil at discounted prices without considering production-sharing contracts, joint ventures, contractual obligations and the revenue implications for the Federation. The Presidency also pointed to compressed natural gas, domestic refining arrangements and alternative transportation initiatives as components of its broader response to the cost-of-living crisis. This was a clear example of the debate moving beyond generic campaign accusations. Atiku had questioned the adequacy, duration and financial transparency of the government’s relief arrangement. The administration, on its part, challenged the legality, affordability and sustainability of Atiku’s proposed alternative. Unfortunately, neither argument can be resolved by political rhetoric alone as they both require published figures, transparent implementation arrangements and evidence of benefits to consumers. The Arithmetic Behind the Argument A closer examination of the numbers demonstrates why the ongoing debate matters. According to the National Bureau of Statistics, Nigeria’s economy expanded by 4.43 per cent in real terms in the second quarter of 2026, compared with 3.89 per cent in the first quarter. This is evidence of economic expansion and provides a factual basis for the administration’s argument that macroeconomic conditions have improved. Inflation has also moderated considerably from the exceptionally high levels experienced during the earlier stages of the reform programme. The NBS reported headline inflation of 15.39 per cent in August 2026, slightly below the 15.43 per cent recorded in July and substantially below the 23.14 per cent recorded in August 2025. But a decline in inflation does not ordinarily mean that prices have returned to earlier levels. It means that the general price level is increasing more slowly. Indeed, the consumer price index rose from 145.3 in July to 146.3 in August, confirming that prices continued to increase despite the moderation in the annual inflation rate. This distinction explains an important part of the disagreement between the government and its critics. The administration can point to lower inflation and faster growth but the households continue to experience pressure from accumulated price increases. The International Monetary Fund acknowledged both sides of this reality in its June 2026 assessment of Nigeria. The Fund credited reforms with improving macroeconomic conditions and strengthening resilience. However, it also estimated that poverty had reached 63 per cent of the population, measured against the national poverty line, while approximately 27 million Nigerians faced food insecurity in the latter part of 2025. Those estimates described specific earlier periods and should not be presented as fresh October 2026 measurements. Nevertheless, they demonstrate that improvements in macroeconomic indicators had not eliminated widespread economic vulnerability. Yet, government finances present another area requiring scrutiny. The Debt Management Office reported that Nigeria’s total public debt reached N166.79 trillion at the end of June 2026, compared with N159.35 trillion at the end of March. That represented an increase of approximately N7.44 trillion, or 4.7 per cent, within three months. Domestic debt accounted for approximately N91.59 trillion, while external obligations stood at about N75.20 trillion. The administration argued that borrowing should be assessed against economic output, government revenue, debt-servicing obligations and the purposes for which the borrowed funds are used. Atiku’s criticism focuses more directly on fiscal discipline, expenditure accountability and the measurable benefits of public borrowing. Both considerations are however relevant. Debt stock alone does not establish whether an economy faces an unsustainable fiscal position. Equally, an improving debt-to-GDP ratio does not remove the need to account for the cost, utilisation and returns on borrowed resources. The same scrutiny applies to petrol subsidy. Regulatory data for August 2026 indicated average daily petrol receipts of approximately 50.5 million litres, of which around 35.9 million litres came from domestic sources and 14.6 million litres from imports. Dangote Refinery accounted for approximately 35.87 million litres of the daily domestic receipts. This means the refinery supplied roughly 71 per cent of the total daily petrol receipts recorded during that period. The figure raises important questions about competition, market concentration and the effectiveness of any production-linked subsidy. If the government supplies discounted crude to domestic refiners, how much of the financial benefit will reach consumers? What arrangements would prevent the benefits from being retained entirely within the refining and distribution chain? Conversely, the current government’s temporary discount also requires scrutiny. Oyedele disclosed that NNPC Retail sells approximately 70 million litres of petrol monthly. At a discount of N66 per litre, applying the reduction to that entire volume would amount to approximately N4.62 billion in reduced gross sales revenue over one month. That is an illustrative calculation, not an established fiscal cost or profit loss. Actual figures would depend on the volume qualifying for the discount and the company’s sales margins. The government says the discount is financed through NNPC’s retail margin rather than direct budgetary expenditure. But the wider implications for company earnings, the number of beneficiaries and the actual effect on transport fares remain important matters for public disclosure. These figures demonstrate why subsidy policy cannot be reduced to a simple argument between compassion and deregulation. The relevant questions concern the fiscal cost, commercial incentives, distribution of benefits and long-term sustainability of whichever arrangement is adopted. Beyond Petrol: Budgets, Taxes and Accountability Although petrol pricing has attracted considerable attention, the Atiku–Tinubu exchange has further expanded into other areas of economic governance. Atiku has questioned the administration’s budget implementation, including the continued operation of earlier appropriations alongside newer budgets. His October 1 address specifically criticised the extension of the 2025 budget’s implementation period towards the end of 2026. His broader concern was that overlapping budget arrangements complicated public scrutiny of expenditure, completed projects and outstanding obligations. The administration, meanwhile, defended its broader fiscal reform programme as part of efforts to improve efficiency and government revenue. Taxation has produced another disagreement. The Presidency argued that its reforms were intended to protect lower-income earners and small businesses while strengthening compliance among those with greater taxable capacity. In an August response to Atiku, the government highlighted protections for individuals earning no more than N1 million annually and smaller businesses with turnover not exceeding N100 million. Atiku’s criticism has concentrated on the wider effects of government economic policy on household finances and private enterprise. The substantive public-policy question is whether higher government revenue is accompanied by more equitable taxation, transparent spending and sufficiently visible improvements in public services. Similarly, the two camps have disagreed over the assessment of social intervention programmes, infrastructure investment and the benefits of subsidy savings. These questions are especially important in a federation where increased allocations to states and local governments can create additional opportunities for development, but where actual outcomes depend substantially on spending decisions and institutional accountability at different levels of government. Consequently, the responsibility for translating fiscal improvements into public welfare cannot be examined solely at the federal level. Governors, local governments, spending agencies and public institutions also have responsibilities that should form part of the broader debate. Where Is Peter Obi in This Exchange? The growing prominence of the Atiku–Tinubu policy exchanges inevitably raises questions about Peter Obi’s place in the presidential conversation. Obi emerged from the 2023 presidential election with considerable electoral support. According to the Independent National Electoral Commission, Tinubu received 8,794,726 votes, Atiku secured 6,984,520, while Obi obtained 6,101,533 votes on the Labour Party platform. Those figures explain why the three politicians remain central to discussions about the forthcoming presidential election. However, their approaches to the current policy conversation are not identical. Obi has consistently emphasised the need to transform Nigeria from an economy heavily dependent on consumption and imports into one that prioritises domestic production, agriculture, manufacturing, investment and human capital development. His 2027 campaign programme includes proposals to improve agricultural productivity, strengthen industrial capacity, expand infrastructure and address insecurity. He has also pledged to increase electricity generation and distribution by at least 10,000 megawatts within four years and to improve healthcare financing and access. On petroleum policy, Obi recently entered the subsidy discussion more directly. In a BBC interview on October 6, he said he would retain a form of subsidy while removing the corruption associated with the previous arrangement. That position attracted attention because he had earlier supported subsidy removal, arguing that resources committed to the programme could instead be invested in education, healthcare and other productive sectors. This was after his running matter, Rabiu Kwankwaso has held a different view on the subject. His supporters subsequently maintained that the proposal did not amount to a return to the former subsidy system. Furthermore, on October 9, the NDC publicly criticised the federal government’s 30-day petrol discount, describing the intervention as inadequate to resolve the underlying affordability crisis. Therefore, while it may not be entirely accurate to suggest that Obi has offered no policy alternatives or has been entirely absent from the conversation, the fact that he never really offers clear thought on issues remains concerning. But the more precise observation is that he is not seriously sold on any idea in particular, often lacking the kind of depth required of a presidential hopeful on issues and policies. Not only is he shifty on policies as if on default mode, he hardly sounds convincing about his own propositions, largely superficial and often citing quite unrelated instances drawn from other parts of the world. This is why the sustained sequence of direct challenges and detailed presidential rebuttals have been from Atiku’s proposals. That difference is relevant to understanding the changing public conversation, establishing the relative merit of either opposition candidate’s programme. Many a time, Obi’s proposals present their own questions requiring clarification, which he hardly explains with lucidity. Take for instance, his idea on fighting corruption. When asked how he planned to tackle the scourge, his submission that once his family refuses to indulge in corruption, the scourge is half-defeated is disappointing to many. That response is not only considered shallow in many quarters, it shows his limitation in the understanding of issues and evident inability to sell them, even when they emanate from him. In another example, Obi was asked how he intended to achieve his proposed 10 megawatts of electricity generation and his response to such a critical question that’s central to many things, the economy especially is: “We are gonna do it”. This seemingly elusive disposition to leadership, seeking perhaps automatic coronation, is deemed the reason Obi might have consciously elected to be absent in the serious debate on issues and policies in the countdown to 2027, counting strongly on his arguably organic and obviously fanatical support base. Taken together, if a future administration intends to retain petrol subsidy while eliminating corruption, what specific form would the subsidy take? Who would receive it? How would eligibility be determined, what would it cost annually, and how would the government ensure that consumers actually received the intended benefit? His electricity target equally invites examination of the generation capacity, transmission infrastructure, distribution investment and financing required to achieve it. These are questions of policy implementation rather than campaign personality. They, too, deserve the same scrutiny being applied to Atiku’s proposed production subsidy and Tinubu’s existing economic reforms. Yet, Obi never gives clarity about the workings. A Different Conversation Ahead of 2027 The emerging policy argument reflects a broader development in the presidential campaign. Nigeria’s major political actors are increasingly being required to distinguish between announcing desirable outcomes and explaining the practical arrangements for achieving them. For Tinubu, the challenge is to demonstrate how the fiscal and macroeconomic gains recorded under his administration are translating into improvements in purchasing power, employment, public services and household welfare. For Atiku, the challenge is to establish that his proposed alternatives are legally workable, financially sustainable and capable of producing the benefits he promises. For Obi, the challenge is to translate his emphasis on production, transparency and human capital into fully specified implementation programmes, with financing arrangements, timelines and measurable targets. These are distinct but equally legitimate areas of public scrutiny. The petroleum debate offers a particularly useful example because it exposes both the attractions and limitations of different forms of government interventions. A temporary retail discount can provide immediate relief to eligible consumers without necessarily changing the underlying structure of the market. A production subsidy may seek to support domestic refiners and reduce input costs, but its success depends on financing, competition and the extent to which savings reach the public. A transparent subsidy regime, as proposed by Obi, equally requires a design capable of preventing abuse while preserving affordability. None of these outcomes follows automatically from a campaign declaration. Each requires clear legal authority, credible financial calculations, competent implementation and independent monitoring. The Larger Significance Perhaps the most interesting aspect of the recent exchanges is that the arguments have begun to move away from the familiar question of who should occupy the presidency towards the more demanding question of how the presidency should manage the economy. The difference is substantial. A government seeking another mandate must account for its record. Opposition candidates seeking the same office must explain their alternatives. Atiku’s recent interventions have created repeated occasions for that comparison, particularly by challenging the government on the relationship between macroeconomic reform and the daily cost of living. The Presidency’s responses have, in turn, subjected his proposals to questions about law, economics and fiscal sustainability. That is a legitimate function of competitive democratic politics. It is also a reminder that policy debates are not determined simply by the frequency of official statements or the sharpness of political exchanges. Their public value depends on whether the competing arguments produce sufficient information for citizens to understand the choices before them. Thus, as the January 27, 2027 presidential bout approaches, the relevant questions should become more specific. How much will the different petroleum-pricing proposals cost?
