What proportion of public resources will be committed to education, healthcare and infrastructure? What measurable improvements in electricity, transportation and security are promised? How will government borrowing be managed, and how will citizens assess implementation? These are the questions that turn campaign promises into propositions capable of serious examination. For now, the sustained exchange between Atiku and the Tinubu administration has placed several of those issues more firmly in public discussion. Obi has not been absent from the wider policy conversation, but the recent direct argument has been particularly shaped by Atiku’s interventions and the government’s responses. Whether the broader campaign subsequently develops into an even more extensive debate among all 18 presidential candidates remains to be seen. Ultimately, the importance of the emerging conversation is not which politician makes the most persuasive accusation or issues the most elaborate rebuttal. It is whether Nigerians are presented with sufficiently detailed, credible and measurable policy programmes to judge what each candidate proposes to do with the responsibilities and resources of the presidency. That would be a meaningful development in the country’s electoral politics. Therefore, as the 2027 contest moves deeper into its campaign phase, the debate over what Nigeria’s economic future should look like is becoming as significant as the contest over who should preside over it.

title: Trump’s remarks about Tehran destroying LA election rhetoric
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 14 (MNA) – Iranian Ambassador to Russia Kazem Jalali has slammed US President Donald Trump’s allegations that Iran can destroy Los Angeles and San Diego as a figment and campaign rhetoric.
"Mr. Trump’s allegations about the possible destruction of American cities are completely unfounded, unrealistic, and amount to nothing more than campaign rhetoric. Iran’s military doctrine is absolutely clear, responsible, and based on defense and deterrence. We have never been the initiators of any wars. However, Iran’s capabilities and missile power are an indisputable, undeniable, and frightening fact," he told TASS.
"Mr. Trump seems to be trying to shirk responsibility during his election campaign and intending to use this real deterrent as a pretext for resolving domestic political issues and settling scores with his Democratic rivals in California," the diplomat added.

title: Lagos-Calabar Coastal Road: Presidency Disowns Plan to Bypass Some States
body: Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja The Presidency yesterday dismissed suggestions that President Bola Tinubu had ordered the abandonment of parts of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway to route the project through the existing East-West Road, insisting that the entire 750-kilometre coastal highway would be constructed as originally planned. The clarification followed public controversy over the proposed use of the East-West Road corridor in parts of the Niger Delta, with concerns that the decision could leave some states and coastal communities outside the original alignment of the flagship infrastructure project. In a statement posted on the Presidency’s official X handle, the government declared that at no time did the President direct that the 750km dualised Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway be discontinued to East-West Road from Edo State. Instead, it said the proposed reconstruction of 400 kilometres of the East-West Road, from Edo State to Cross River State, was an additional project to be executed alongside the coastal highway. “This additional project, which is the reconstruction of East-West Road, is presently below flood level due to climate change and whose pavement is badly damaged, will not affect the complete construction of the entire 750km dualised Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway as initially proposed,” the statement said. The statement, issued following a directive by the Minister of Works, David Umahi, sought to clarify the government’s position amid mounting questions over the route of the coastal highway and the implications of the proposed changes for states along the corridor. Umahi had earlier said Tinubu directed that the continuation of the coastal highway should use the existing East-West Road in parts of the Niger Delta rather than create an entirely new alignment. The comments generated controversy, with critics demanding clarification on whether the original route had been altered and which communities would benefit from the project. The latest statement, however, maintained that the original alignment remained intact and that work was progressing on several sections of the highway. It identified five sections where work was ongoing in the Niger Delta and adjoining areas, including Sections 3A and 3B in Cross River and Akwa Ibom states, covering 75 kilometres of dual carriageway; Sections 4A and 4B in Ogun and Ondo states, covering 65 kilometres; and Section Five in Akwa Ibom State, covering 62 kilometres. The government said surveying and design work was continuing on the outstanding portions of the highway, extending from the end of the Ondo section through Edo, Delta, Bayelsa and Rivers states before connecting with Section Five in Akwa Ibom. It added that procurement and construction of the remaining sections would commence after the survey and design work had been completed. “As soon as the survey and design of the remaining sections of the 750km of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway are completed, procurement and construction will commence starting from the end of Ondo axis,” the statement said. The Presidency also cited the additional route approved for the Akwanga-Jos-Bauchi-Gombe-Biu-Maiduguri highway to explain why the East-West Road reconstruction would not mean the abandonment or alteration of the coastal highway. According to the statement, Tinubu approved an additional 410-kilometre Wukari-Langtang route under the fourth legacy road project, expanding the planned dual carriageway from 700 kilometres to 1,100 kilometres. It said the additional route had not affected the original alignment of the project, adding that the same principle applied to the coastal highway and the East-West Road reconstruction. “All sections of the legacy projects are ongoing as proposed, and the additional projects will not affect the performance of the original alignment nor will it change it,” the statement added. The Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway is one of the federal government’s major infrastructure projects, designed to link Lagos with Calabar through Ogun, Ondo, Edo, Delta, Bayelsa, Rivers and Akwa Ibom states. The controversy over its alignment intensified after Umahi’s comments that the existing East-West Road would be incorporated into the route in parts of the Niger Delta. The minister cited flooding, climate change and the condition of the existing road as reasons for the proposed reconstruction. However, the reported changes prompted questions about the project’s original objectives, particularly its promise of improved connectivity for coastal communities and economic centres across the southern corridor. But the latest clarification did not provide a detailed map of the final alignment or explain precisely how the coastal highway and the reconstructed East-West Road would connect along the affected stretches. The Presidency urged Nigerians to disregard what it described as misinformation about the administration’s commitment to delivering the projects as planned.

title: Actress Selma Blair faces charges for kicking nurse and officer after plane incident
body: US actress Selma Blair has been charged with two additional assault counts over allegedly kicking an officer and a nurse after being removed from a flight. Blair was arrested late Sunday in New York after she allegedly attacked flight attendants on a Delta plane travelling from Los Angeles to New York. The FBI issued her a federal summons accusing her of assault on board. While appearing in court over the additional charges, the Legally Blonde star’s attorney asked the judge to consider the actress’s “body of work”, and called Blair the “gold standard.” The judge said she should not “get special treatment”. Blair has pleaded not guilty. She has since been released on bail. She was taken to hospital after the incident on the flight. Her representatives have told the BBC that she had “experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct”. As the flight landed in New York on Sunday evening, airport officials responded to a call about “a physically abusive passenger” on the flight. Two flight attendants were hurt, and one was taken to hospital, the New York Port Authority said. Audio recorded on air traffic control details a pilot asking for medical help, describing “a bloody nose” and “some bite marks”, according to CBS News, BBC’s US News partner. Blair, 54, who also starred in Cruel Intentions and Hellboy, was arrested and taken to hospital. She was issued a federal summons for a charge of assault within the special maritime and territorial jurisdiction of the US. The two additional charges of assault, filed in state court, came after she was taken off the plane. One of the alleged assaults happened when she was being transported in an ambulance, where she allegedly kicked a police officer. Once at the hospital, prosecutors allege that she also assaulted a nurse. At her arraignment in Queens, Blair’s attorney Shawn Barnes asked the judge for leniency. He said that “violence” is “not who she is” and asked for the judge to consider her body of work. The actress is somebody that people look up to, he said, referring to her as “the gold standard”. The judge denied his request, saying she “should not get special treatment…because she is a celebrity”. The judge set her bail at $20,000 cash or $60,000 bond, with the next hearing scheduled for 19 January. It is unclear when a date will be set for the federal case against her, which concerns the allegations of assault aboard the aircraft.

title: Oil Surveillance: Reps Panel Clears PINL, Okunbo, Petitioners Fail to Provide Evidence
body: A subcommittee of the House of Representatives has found no evidence to support allegations against Pipeline Infrastructure Nigeria Limited (PINL) and its Executive Director, Dr. Osahon Okunbo, and has recommended that the petition against them be thrown out. Constituted under the House Committee on Host Communities, the panel was set up to examine a petition dated September 5, 2026 from the Niger Delta Oil-Producing Communities Reform Movement (ND-OCRIM), which challenged PINL’s pipeline surveillance contract. The petitioners made five claims, including that the contract was not properly executed; that contract funds were mismanaged, that PINL’s finances required a forensic review and that the executive director spent money on personal matters. Besides, the petitioner alleged that the welfare of field workers had been neglected. However, no documents or proof of any kind accompanied them. The Committee nonetheless referred the petition for a proper hearing. Proceedings followed the rules of the House and the principle of fair hearing, with the Committee’s Deputy Clerk serving as secretary. ND-OCRIM was invited three times, on September 14; September 22 and October 5, 2026, and failed to turn up on each occasion. It sent no one in its place, gave no reason and brought no evidence. No other stakeholder appeared. However, PINL did appear. Its representative submitted a written document: “The Impact of PINL Operations on Oil Production and Stability of the Niger Delta,” supported by location-tagged photographs. Nobody challenged it. Hearings closed on October 7, 2026. The submission set out the conditions PINL met on arrival. By May 2022, according to the company, 97 of every 100 barrels of crude pumped into the Trans Niger Pipeline (TNP) were being lost. Force majeure had been declared, and national output had fallen below 900,000 barrels per day. PINL, engaged in August 2022, said it now works across all 215 host communities and engages more than 35,600 community members. Its operations are supported by 28 forward bases, 130 boats, 175 vehicles, 25 drones and 454 personnel from government security agencies. The company reported that the share of crude reaching the Bonny Terminal through the TNP rose from 3 per cent in May 2022 to 98 per cent in September 2026. It said the OML 11 field was restarted within 90 days after an 18-month shut-in, that 2,049 illegal connections were repaired and that 1,010 illegal refinery clusters were destroyed. It also pointed to its work in host communities, citing more than 5,000 scholarships, skills training for over 4,000 women and girls, and flood relief for more than 10 communities in Rivers State. In its findings, the panel said PINL’s submission directly answered the claims about how the work was done. It also admitted a gap: the submission did not address the claims about contract funds or personal spending. On those two matters, its findings rest on the petitioners’ failure to bring any evidence. On welfare, members noted PINL’s palliative and food bank support and found no sign of neglect. They described PINL as a well-organised company with a strong structure, well regarded in its host communities, and said no evidence backs any claim against Okunbo. Twelve recommendations followed. The panel asked the full Committee to dismiss the petition, end any further investigation, and record the claims against PINL and Dr. Okunbo as unproven, while noting that affected parties keep their legal rights. Also, it asked the Committee to acknowledge PINL’s work in protecting pipelines and its programmes in host communities, urged the company to sustain that work and look after its field staff, and recommended that the federal government extend PINL’s contract. Commendation was also sought for President Bola Tinubu, for sustaining security reforms in the oil and gas industry; the National Security Adviser (NSA), for coordinating the protection of pipelines as well as the management of NNPC Limited. They also lauded the pipeline security firms including PINL and Tantita Security Services Nigeria Limited and further asked the Committee to pass a vote of confidence in all of them. But the report is not yet final. Dated October 7, 2026, it has been submitted to the full Committee for consideration and adoption, and the signature lines for the Chairman, four members and the Secretary were blank in the copy seen.

title: Aramco building attacked after Saudi-led coalition hits Houthi site
body: An administrative building of Saudi Arabia's state oil company Aramco was attacked by a missile on Tuesday night, causing a fire but no casualties, as fighting intensifies between the kingdom and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The kingdom's Energy Ministry said the missile strike happened in Dhahran, in the Eastern Province. Authorities responded to the attack, with no deaths or injuries reported, the Saudi Press Agency reported. People living near the Aramco compound described terror as a powerful explosion shook the area. “This was the loudest explosion I have ever heard in my life,” one woman told The National . Another resident said relatives living closer to the site had reported seeing smoke and flames rising from the area. “They couldn't go outside to check what had happened because the smoke was everywhere,” she said. Debris from two cruise missiles intercepted and destroyed over the capital Riyadh injured four people – two women, a man and a child – state television quoted the Saudi Civil Defence as saying. A Civil Defence representative said the falling debris also damaged 15 residential homes in the Saudi capital. Authorities implemented established procedures in response. Bloomberg reported that the site was Aramco’s executive headquarters, while a company source quoted by Reuters identified the target as an Aramco headquarters complex. Neither Aramco nor Saudi authorities had officially confirmed which building was hit. The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen separately said it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched towards Dhahran, with debris falling in a residential area. It also reported intercepting a missile targeting Haradh and three drones north of the capital, Riyadh. The coalition said late on Tuesday that it had carried out an operation against energy sites in Houthi-held areas of Yemen, including the Al Sabahah station in Yemen's capital, Sanaa, and piers used for loading fuel at the Red Sea port of Hodeidah. Coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malki accused the Houthis of using civilian infrastructure to support their military operations and supply their arsenals. Coalition hits Sanaa “It has been established that the Houthi terrorist militia uses civilian objects and vital resources to sustain its war effort," he said on X. "These include the Al Sabaha central station in Sanaa, underground strategic fuel reserves and storage facilities and fuel and dedicated fuel-loading and unloading berths in Hodeidah, Sanaa and Dhamar.” Video posted on social media appeared to show a huge orange fireball erupting above Sanaa, followed by a towering column of thick black smoke. The strikes came after the coalition had warned civilians near the oil facility to leave “for their safety”. The scale of the damage to the site and the impact on fuel supplies were not immediately clear. The Houthis said fuel reserves had been dispersed before the attack, a claim that has not been independently verified. Saudi energy infrastructure has been been hit before. A refinery in Jazan, in the kingdom's west, was shut after a strike, and a key oil export port on the Red Sea coast was also targeted. A cross-country pipeline used by Aramco to transport crude to export markets was temporarily shut in September following an attack launched from Iraq. The pipeline is strategically important because it offers an alternative route for Saudi oil exports when shipping through the Gulf faces disruption. Oil prices rose on Wednesday after news of the attack on the Aramco building, as traders weighed the risk of further disruption to regional energy supplies. It is unclear how the latest incidents could affect production, refining or exports. Dhahran lies at the centre of Saudi Arabia’s oil industry, close to major oil fields in Eastern Province and the Gulf.

title: Donald Duke Canvasses Two-Party Political Blocs for Effective Presidential System
body: • Warns opposition division could hand incumbents electoral advantage Sunday Ehigiator The presidential candidate of the Peoples Redemption Party (PRP) and former governor of Cross River State, Donald Duke, has advocated an emergence of two dominant political blocs in Nigeria, arguing that a fragmented opposition could give incumbents an electoral advantage under the country’s presidential system. Duke also called for a review of Nigeria’s constitutional requirements for electing a president, saying the existing electoral framework could produce a winner without the support of a majority of voters. Speaking in an interview yesterday, the former governor said Nigeria needed to understand the differences between presidential and parliamentary systems and structure its political competition accordingly. “Those of us in the democratic space in Nigeria today really don’t understand how it works. There are different ways of expressing yourselves democratically. But for the system we run, the presidential, the avenue towards success is different from that of Westminster, for instance. “The Westminster system, you can have several parties. The ability to form government is, if you’re a minority, if you don’t have all the required number of seats in parliament, you can cobble together an opposition. The presidential is different,” he said. Duke maintained that a presidential system would function more effectively with two major political blocs representing the incumbent and the opposition, warning that the division of opposition votes among several parties could weaken the chances of challenging an incumbent. “The important thing is that if you want a proper presidential system of government, you ought to have only two major parties, right? An incumbent and an opposition. Once you, like I said, balkanise or fractionise the opposition, you will lose your ball. The incumbent will always have it,” he said. Citing the 2023 presidential election, Duke argued that the existing constitutional provisions could allow a candidate to win without securing an absolute majority of votes cast nationally. “It will still be a minority government. It won’t get the majority of the votes cast on election day. Last time we had about 36–37 per cent,” he said. He warned that the same scenario could recur in the 2027 general election if opposition parties failed to overcome their divisions. “So that scenario may replay itself. It may even be less. It may get maybe 25 and all that. But because they are fractured, all you would strive to do is get 25 per cent in two-thirds of the states and a simple majority. “It doesn’t need to get eight million votes. It could just get 10 votes more, five votes more than every other person. And that is one of the faults with the electoral system. It’s not designed for a presidential system.” Under Section 134 of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, a presidential candidate must secure the highest number of votes cast and satisfy the prescribed geographical spread requirements. The Constitution does not generally require a candidate to obtain more than 50 per cent of all valid votes cast nationally. Duke called for a review of the constitutional framework, arguing that Nigeria needed electoral rules that better reflected the principles and workings of its presidential system. “This is why we really need to revisit the constitution, because those who put it together probably didn’t understand these fundamentals,” he said. He also criticised the absence of clear ideological distinctions among political parties, saying this had encouraged politicians to move between platforms without firmly established philosophical commitments. “We don’t have any ideological stance in our politics. They’re just platforms. We have not developed to the point where we stand for certain ideologies. So, these platforms are not ideologically based. And that’s why you have people swarming back and forth,” he said. Reflecting on the political arrangement of the aborted Third Republic, Duke said there was some merit in the attempt to establish two broad political platforms through the Social Democratic Party and the National Republican Convention, although he questioned the process through which the military government created them. “Normally, parties form governments. But in this case, the government formed the party,” he said. Beyond electoral reform, Duke argued that Nigeria needed to redefine the purpose of government by prioritising citizens’ productivity, economic opportunities and security. “What I find, the synergy I find with PRP, is it articulates something I always believed in, that the main essence, the main function of government is the optimal productivity of our citizens within a safe and orderly environment. “I think that’s what the government is all about. Not just for people to administer or supervise over people, but to ensure that they are productive within a safe and orderly environment,” he said. He said education, healthcare and infrastructure should be viewed as investments in the productive capacity of citizens. “That’s why we send kids to school. That’s why we send them to hospitals. We build infrastructure. All towards the productivity of our citizens. That is the mission statement of the government. It changes the way we see the dynamics of government.” The former governor also called for Nigeria’s 36 states to develop sustainable economic bases by identifying and exploiting their comparative advantages, rather than functioning primarily as administrative units. Recalling his tenure as Cross River governor from 1999 to 2007, he said his administration sought to demonstrate that every federating unit could become an economic centre through agriculture, tourism and other viable sectors. “We wanted to prove a point that it could happen. We wanted to prove that every federating unit in this country could also be an economic unit. “So, we took our strengths, right? Agriculture, we have incredible land mass. But beyond that, we took a low-hanging fruit like tourism, which everyone thought wouldn’t work. And it worked spectacularly. It can be done. That can-do spirit has been proven before,” he said. Duke cited Tinapa, the business and tourism project established during his administration, as part of the effort to expand Cross River’s economic opportunities. “Tinapa was one thing that we built in Cross River. It was a dream. To the extent that it was commissioned a month before I left office, it was successful,” he said. He maintained that electoral reforms, viable political competition and economic development should ultimately serve the purpose of improving citizens’ living standards. “Government is to ensure that they are productive within a safe and orderly environment,” Duke said.

title: Speaker Abbas Unveils 100-Day Legislative Plan
body: •Warns lawmakers against abandoning duties for 2027 campaigns Juliet Akoje in Abuja Speaker of the House of Representatives, Hon. Tajudeen Abbas, has proposed a 100-day legislative programme to accelerate pending bills, clear outstanding committee reports and strengthen oversight, warning lawmakers against abandoning their constitutional responsibilities for the 2027 election campaigns. Abbas who announced the plan on Tuesday while addressing members at the resumption of plenary after the 2026 annual recess, said the remaining months of the 10th House must be devoted to completing priority legislation and delivering measurable results for Nigerians. He also proposed that Tuesdays and Thursdays be dedicated to major bills and urgent national issues, alongside stricter attendance at plenary and committee sittings. Committees are expected to clear outstanding reports within defined timelines, while the House plans to publish a comprehensive legislative scorecard and legacy report before the end of its tenure. “Our constituents elected us for a full term, and they deserve a full term of service,” the Speaker said, stressing that political activities must not take precedence over legislation and oversight. Abbas said the House had received 2,747 bills and passed 363 as of mid-June 2026, with its bill passage rate rising from approximately seven per cent in the first session to about 26 per cent in the third. The House also processed hundreds of motions and public petitions during the period. He disclosed that an internal assessment showed the House had completed between 65 and 70 per cent of the principal milestones in its legislative agenda, but cautioned that the number of bills passed was not, by itself, a sufficient measure of legislative performance. According to him, the effectiveness of the National Assembly must be judged by whether laws resolve public problems, motions lead to action, investigations protect the public interest and oversight improves the management of public resources. The Speaker identified the conclusion of the constitutional review process as one of the House’s immediate priorities, naming the State Police Bill, the Reserved Seats for Women Bill and other outstanding constitutional alteration bills as proposals requiring sustained engagement with the Senate and state Houses of Assembly. He also urged the Executive to submit the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework promptly to allow the legislature sufficient time to scrutinise the 2027 budget and facilitate the timely passage of the Appropriation Bill. Abbas said the House would give prompt consideration to bills and requests transmitted by President Bola Tinubu, including the National Research Development Fund Bill and a request received on Tuesday for the domestication of the Geneva Conventions and their relevant protocols. He described the Geneva Conventions request as nationally and diplomatically significant, saying its approval would strengthen protections for civilians, wounded persons and prisoners during armed conflicts. On preparations for the 2027 general elections, the Speaker called for strict adherence to the Electoral Act and adequate lawful support for the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to discharge its responsibilities. He said all public institutions involved in the electoral process must demonstrate neutrality, competence and restraint, while lawmakers must ensure that political competition does not undermine their constitutional obligations. Acknowledging the defections and political realignments recorded across party lines, Abbas said such developments were part of an active democracy but should not distract members from their shared responsibilities. “Whatever our political affiliations or personal ambitions, we remain members of one House. We are bound by one Constitution and one oath. The campaign must never become more important than the country,” he said. The Speaker also called for the completion of outstanding committee reports and bills awaiting legislative action, warning that important proposals should not expire simply because they had remained unattended. Reflecting on developments since the House adjourned on July 23, Abbas acknowledged improvements in key economic indicators but said the gains must translate into better living conditions for Nigerians. He cited economic growth of more than four per cent, a decline in inflation to 15.39 per cent in August from 23.14 per cent in the corresponding period of 2025, and external reserves of $54.7 billion in September, the highest level since 2009. He also said Nigeria recorded a trade surplus exceeding N20 trillion in the first half of 2026, almost twice the figure recorded during the same period in 2025. While describing the figures as encouraging, Abbas said the priority should be to convert economic stability into affordable food, productive employment, accessible credit and reliable public services. He noted that investor confidence was improving, with new commitments emerging in ports, power, agriculture and industry. Among the projects he cited was the proposed $7 billion Gateway Deep Seaport and Blue Marine Economic Zone, which he said could create jobs, expand exports and strengthen Nigeria’s position in African trade. The Speaker further observed that increased public revenues had expanded the financial capacity of federal, state and local governments, placing a greater responsibility on them to demonstrate accountability, particularly at the subnational level. He said higher revenues should result in better roads, stronger schools, safer communities and more effective healthcare. Abbas, however, drew attention to security challenges and natural disasters reported during the recess, including the abduction of schoolchildren in Borno State, attacks and displacement in parts of Ondo State, and destructive flooding and erosion in Enugu and Abia states. He expressed solidarity with families who had lost loved ones, homes and livelihoods, calling for prompt relief and lasting protection for affected communities. He said security agencies would continue to receive the support required to perform their duties but maintained that they must remain accountable for the resources and authority entrusted to them. On budget implementation, Abbas recalled that the House, on September 29, extended the capital component of the 2025 Appropriation Act to December 31 to protect ongoing projects and prevent public investment from going to waste. He said the extension must lead to faster implementation and measurable results, adding that it would not justify further delays. The House, he said, would continue to scrutinise fund releases, project timelines and performance. The Speaker said the 10th Assembly had entered its fourth and final phase, making it necessary for lawmakers to assess their achievements and concentrate on unfinished business. He acknowledged that the House had experienced disagreements, intense debates and considerable political pressure but said members had preserved the institution’s unity and repeatedly found common ground on issues of national importance. Abbas commended Deputy Speaker Benjamin Kalu, the Majority Leader, other principal officers, committee chairmen and members for their contributions, while acknowledging the Minority Caucus for what he described as a robust and responsible opposition. He also praised the Clerk to the National Assembly and legislative staff for sustaining the institution, and thanked the media for keeping Nigerians informed. The Speaker called for continued cooperation among the Executive, the Judiciary and the legislature, in line with the constitutional independence of each arm of government. He also urged civil society organisations, professional bodies, the media and constituents to continue holding the House accountable. He said the final months of the Assembly would test lawmakers’ commitment as political interests intensified and attention shifted towards the elections. Abbas urged members to remain focused until the end of their mandate, expressing the expectation that the House would complete its priority legislation, strengthen oversight and maintain its service to Nigerians. The plenary resumed following the annual recess and rehabilitation of the House chamber. However, Abbas thanked members for their patience during the break and commended the Chairman of the Committee on House Services, Hon.Daniel Amos, the Clerk and technical teams involved in restoring the chamber.

title: Appeal Court Quashes Free Speech Case Against Saraki
body: Hammed Shittu in Ilorin The Court of Appeal sitting in Ilorin, the Kwara State capital, yesterday, dismissed the criminal defamation and cyberbullying case filed by Kwara State Government against former Senate President, Dr. Bukola Saraki. The court, in its unanimous decision, also declared that the charge and the evidence produced disclosed no offence committed by Saraki. In a judgement read by Hon. Justice Ridwan Maiwada Abdullahi on behalf of two other judges, Hon. Justice Gabriel Omoniyi Kolawole and Hon. Justice Abdu Dogo, the appellate court held that there was nothing in the statement by Saraki being complained of by Mr. Abdulrahman Abdulrazaq, Governor of Kwara State, capable of inciting violence in any part of Kwara State or moving anybody to resort to the breakdown of law and order The judge stated that all the evidence and witnesses’ statements supplied in support of the charge did not disclose that Saraki’s statement led to any breach of the peace in the state; rather, they merely showed that those who testified felt dissatisfied with the statement. He added that the Administration of Criminal Justice Act, the Penal Code Law of Kwara State, and the Cybercrime and Cyberbullying law were not enacted for the purpose of protecting individuals against statements that they were uncomfortable with. He added that while the attorney general of a state and that of the federation had wide powers to institute criminal cases, such powers could not be exercised in a manner prejudicial and oppressive of any individual or to violate the fundamental human rights of citizens. The judge, therefore, ordered that the case instituted at the Kwara State High Court against Saraki over his statement in which he alleged that Abdulrazaq did not complete secondary education and that his level of education was affecting his judgment, could not be sustained, having not disclosed any offence or included any statutory ingredient of the offence he was being charged for. In his reaction to the judgement, Saraki’s Press Officer on Local Matters, Abdulganiyu Abdulqadir, quoted his principal as stating that he had once again been vindicated in his unflinching belief that nobody, no matter how powerful, can successfully muffle the voice of dissent, particularly, when those in government fail in their responsibility to the people. Saraki also expressed his gratitude to the judiciary for once again standing for the truth and defending the cause of justice. He said he wanted his supporters to know that Abdulrazaq’s oppressive tendencies were mere inconveniences that would soon blow away. The former senate president stated, “This is because the administration has only seven months to stay in office, and the tendency that it represents will be totally eradicated in Kwara State by the people. “If the need arises, he will not hesitate to reiterate his position on the level of education of Governor Abdulrazaq and that he will not keep quiet when there are issues of public interest that deserve his comment.”

title: IMF Warns Poverty Remains High in Nigeria Despite Economic Growth
body: Raises 2026 growth forecast to 4.2%, retains 4.3% for 2027 •Backs CBN’s data-driven inflation fight, urges stronger banking sector safeguards Oyedele cautions against higher taxes on vulnerable households, calls for policy alignment to unlock AfCFTA Nume Ekeghe in Bangkok, Thailand The International Monetary Fund (IMF) yesterday warned that poverty remains high in Nigeria despite resilient economic growth, urging the federal government to provide targeted, temporary support to vulnerable households as rising food and energy costs continue to undermine living standards. The Fund, however, raised Nigeria’s economic growth forecast for 2026 by 0.1 percentage point to 4.2 per cent, while retaining its projection of 4.3 per cent for 2027, reflecting expectations of continued economic expansion despite persistent domestic and external challenges. The IMF’s assessment came as the Group of 24 (G-24), chaired by Nigeria’s Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, called on the IMF and the World Bank to make development financing more affordable, warning that developing countries pay an estimated $500 billion more in borrowing costs than developed economies. At the ongoing IMF/World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, Oyedele urged African countries to improve policy coordination, remove barriers to intra-African trade and mobilise private capital to accelerate economic transformation through the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). The Fund also acknowledged improvements in Nigeria’s inflation outlook, supporting a data-driven approach by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), while emphasising the need for stronger capital and liquidity buffers, effective banking supervision and timely recognition of bad loans. IMF: Poverty Remains High Despite Growth The IMF’s projections were presented in its 2026 World Economic Outlook, titled Resilience Under Strain, Urgent Choices, released during the Annual Meetings. Speaking on fiscal policy responses to rising living costs in Africa, the Fund’s Research Department Division Chief, Deniz Igan, said policymakers needed to balance immediate household needs with medium-term fiscal stability. She explained that the disproportionate rise in food and energy prices had intensified the cost-of-living crisis, making it necessary for governments to protect vulnerable citizens without undermining the sustainability of public finances. “What we are advocating for is for policymakers to balance the near-term needs of the population, and that involves food security. “That involves energy security. Given that the prices of food and energy are increasing disproportionately, while also keeping in mind medium-term stability, how to do that is, of course, a great question,” she said. Igan noted that the IMF had examined fiscal policy responses capable of addressing situations in which essential goods become more expensive faster than the broader consumption basket. Using Nigeria as an example, she said the economy had demonstrated resilience, partly reflecting its position as an energy exporter, but the benefits of growth had yet to sufficiently address widespread poverty and household hardship. “While growth held up in Nigeria, given that it is an energy exporter, poverty rates are still very high, and we are very mindful that the population is suffering, especially when it comes to food security, with risks also arising from El Niño,” she said. The IMF therefore recommended targeted and temporary income support, including cash transfers, to cushion the effects of higher living costs on the most vulnerable households. According to Igan, such interventions could alleviate poverty and improve food security, provided they were consistent with a credible medium-term fiscal framework. She said governments also needed to improve the quality of public expenditure and strengthen revenue collection to ensure that social protection measures remained sustainable. IMF Backs CBN’s Inflation Fight, Urges Banking Sector Vigilance Separately, the IMF acknowledged improvements in Nigeria’s inflation outlook, suggesting that a less restrictive monetary policy stance could eventually become appropriate, provided incoming economic data continued to support such a decision. The Fund’s Assistant Director in the Monetary and Capital Markets Department, Jason Wu, made the assessment at the launch of the Global Financial Stability Report, titled Resilience, Risk, and Transformation, during the Annual Meetings. Wu stressed that the progress recorded on inflation made monetary policy credibility, data dependence and transparent communication particularly important as the CBN assessed the appropriate direction of policy. “We have seen improvements on the inflation front, which suggests that a perhaps not as tight monetary policy stance would be appropriate,” he said. He cautioned, however, that central banks needed to remain responsive to changing economic conditions and clearly explain the rationale behind their decisions, particularly as renewed inflationary pressures and uncertainty continued to shape the global outlook. “I think what’s important is credibility. In other words, the central bank has to be data-driven and has to be able to explain the decisions clearly. And so far, based on what we have seen, it seems like the news is on the good front,” he added. According to him, continued reliance on economic data and clear policy communication would be essential to containing further inflationary shocks. Beyond monetary policy, the IMF urged regulators to strengthen banking sector oversight, noting that recapitalisation alone would not guarantee financial stability without effective supervision and appropriate prudential safeguards. Wu said emerging economies needed to ensure that stronger capital positions were accompanied by adequate liquidity requirements and timely recognition of credit losses and non-performing loans. “On strengthening the banking sector, I think often what we see in emerging economies is, after recapitalisation, starting to impose appropriate regulations to prevent risks from building up in the future,” he said. He also identified the relationship between sovereign and banking sector risks as a critical concern for African economies, urging regulators to understand financial institutions’ exposure to government debt and related vulnerabilities. The IMF official said these measures would help strengthen banks’ resilience and reduce the likelihood that emerging risks would undermine financial stability. His comments come amid efforts by Nigeria’s banking industry to strengthen capital positions following the CBN’s recapitalisation exercise. Meanwhile, the IMF’s Deputy Director in the Monetary and Capital Markets Department, Athanasios Vamvakidis, said emerging markets had remained resilient despite elevated global bond yields, supported by stronger domestic fundamentals, sound policies and investor appetite for risk. However, he warned that the combination of high yields and historically narrow credit spreads could leave developing economies exposed if global financial conditions deteriorated. He said developments in advanced economies and renewed energy price shocks could widen spreads, raising borrowing costs even for countries with relatively strong economic fundamentals. Vamvakidis urged emerging economies to strengthen financial buffers in anticipation of adverse scenarios, adding that transparency was essential to sustaining investor confidence and access to international capital markets. He said clear information about countries’ financial obligations could reassure investors and preserve financing opportunities, particularly for African economies that depend on international borrowing. G-24 Seeks Cheaper Financing for Developing Countries The G-24 called on the IMF and the World Bank to expand access to affordable concessional financing and accelerate sovereign debt restructuring, warning that high borrowing costs are constraining developing countries’ ability to finance infrastructure, social services and job creation. Oyedele, who chairs the group, made the appeal at its press briefing during the Annual Meetings, arguing that developing economies faced a disproportionate financing burden estimated at about $500 billion compared with developed countries. He said borrowing remained necessary to finance development and stimulate investment, but the cost of debt was increasingly limiting governments’ capacity to deliver inclusive growth. “What we have seen by members of the G-24 and across, particularly the developing countries, such as those in Africa, is the increasing burden of not just high debts or high costs of debts. To the extent that we have some estimates indicating that these developing countries are paying in the region of about $500 billion more than they should be paying compared to developed countries,” he said. The group urged the Bretton Woods institutions to make short-term concessional borrowing more affordable, particularly for vulnerable countries facing mounting fiscal pressures, while developing frameworks that would attract more private investment over the longer term. Oyedele said greater access to affordable financing would help governments direct limited public resources towards areas where they were most needed, including healthcare, education and social protection. The G-24’s intervention comes as developing economies contend with debt vulnerabilities and competing expenditure demands, with debt-servicing obligations threatening to crowd out investments that could support economic growth and improve living standards. The group also called for more predictable, timely, orderly and coordinated sovereign debt treatment, alongside greater transparency and improvements in credit-rating assessments. The Director of the G-24 Secretariat, Iyabo Masha, said progress had been made in strengthening the international debt-resolution architecture, including updates to debt sustainability assessments and restructuring procedures. She cited improvements to the IMF’s debt sustainability framework and developments under the Global Sovereign Debt Roundtable and the Common Framework, which are intended to facilitate more effective responses when countries face unsustainable debt burdens. However, Masha said further reforms were necessary, particularly to ensure that private creditors participated more effectively in debt-resolution initiatives. Countries with substantial exposure to privately held bonds, she noted, might not benefit fully from existing arrangements. She also called on advanced economies to support improvements in credit-rating methodologies, arguing that developing countries should not be unfairly penalised when their debt sustainability and financing risks are assessed. Masha cited the experience of countries such as Sri Lanka as evidence of the weaknesses exposed by previous debt crises, adding that the Borrowers’ Platform, spearheaded by the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), could strengthen cooperation among debtor countries and improve knowledge-sharing on sustainable borrowing. Oyedele Warns Against Taxing Vulnerable Households Beyond the cost of borrowing, Oyedele cautioned governments against responding to fiscal pressures by imposing additional taxes on vulnerable households and productive sectors of their economies. He argued that governments needed to improve domestic revenue mobilisation and identify inefficient expenditure while ensuring that fiscal measures did not deepen hardship or weaken economic activity. According to him, taxation and borrowing both have economic and social consequences and should be assessed according to their implications for household welfare, investment and long-term development. He noted that higher taxes could deprive low-income households of resources needed for food, healthcare and education, while excessive taxation of businesses could undermine productive activity and employment. “The way I like to put it is: if you collect taxes, you raise the money now, and that itself has a lot of trade-offs. What taxes are you collecting? Are you collecting taxes from the most vulnerable, and this will deprive them of money to provide food, health, education? They have to be mindful of tax, and debts is future taxes,” he said. He added that the choice was not simply between taxation and borrowing, but about striking a balance that supported sustainable public finances without undermining citizens’ welfare. “So it’s not one or the other. It’s to strike a balance, bearing in mind ultimately that the essence of tax and of debts is to cater for the people. If you put people always at the centre of your policies, you will not be perfect, but you are likely to strike a balance that works and is sustainable,” he said. His remarks highlighted the dilemma facing developing economies as governments seek to raise revenue, contain debt and meet rising demands for public services. Oyedele also stressed that economic growth needed to create employment and improve living standards rather than be judged solely by headline macroeconomic indicators. He warned that the adoption of artificial intelligence could complicate employment prospects if governments failed to make deliberate policy choices on its deployment and regulation. “It’s not only just the World Bank and the IMF. This is a collective responsibility for all of us to ensure that growth is not just for the sake of growth. It has to be job-rich. It has to be inclusive, and at the end of the day, must be able to translate to better living standards for our people,” he said. Masha, however, maintained that macroeconomic stability remained essential to achieving these objectives, arguing that governments needed a stable economic environment to implement structural reforms, employment policies and infrastructure programmes. Oyedele agreed, describing stability as the foundation for sustainable growth and prosperity. “The stability itself is the foundation upon which you can build the growth and the prosperity that you want for your people,” he said. Oyedele: Africa Needs Policy Alignment to Unlock AfCFTA On regional economic integration, Oyedele called for stronger policy coordination among African countries, arguing that the AfCFTA could transform the continent’s economic prospects if governments removed trade barriers and established consistent rules and standards. Speaking at the Africa’s Golden Future panel during the Annual Meetings, he said the agreement offered an opportunity to turn Africa’s fragmented national markets into a larger, more competitive continental market capable of supporting production, investment and trade. “So we have a lot of small countries, and what AfCFTA is trying to do is to turn 54 countries into one market, so that way it’s easy for us to scale. But that will not happen until we remove the barriers, and many of them are actually non-tariff,” he said. He explained that effective implementation would require clear standards, predictable regulations and supporting infrastructure, noting that non-tariff barriers remained a major impediment to intra-African commerce. Oyedele cited Nigeria’s National Single Window initiative as an effort to streamline border processes and improve trade facilitation, adding that technology was being deployed to make the process more efficient. He also disclosed that Nigeria was developing an economic policy framework incorporating its international commitments, including regional treaties. According to him, economic integration would remain difficult if countries failed to align their trade, fiscal and monetary policies, even within their own borders. “If you have trade policies, fiscal policies, monetary policies, and they’re not speaking together even within the same country, you can imagine the nightmare dealing with 54 or 53 other countries,” he said. The minister also emphasised that policy consistency, institutional strength and public trust were critical to attracting private capital, which Africa needs to close its development financing gap. “Capital follows trust before it follows returns. They need to be able to plan and predict what you are going to do,” he said. Reflecting on Nigeria’s economic reforms, Oyedele said governments needed to communicate the reasons for policy changes clearly, demonstrate the consequences of failing to implement them and ensure that reforms were properly sequenced. He explained that price corrections should be followed by efforts to stabilise the economy before policies to expand growth were pursued. Institutionalising reforms through legislation and strong institutions, he added, would help ensure that they survived changes in political leadership. “But most importantly, think about how do you make it sustainable, and that’s by putting it into institutions and putting it into law. So, most of the reforms we did in Nigeria are either enacted into law or embedded into institutions, because you need to be able to do that for sustainability,” he said. He also cautioned that reform implementation needed to account for the circumstances of vulnerable citizens, particularly in African countries where poverty and limited access to education remained widespread. Oyedele said governments had to ensure that people could withstand the immediate effects of economic adjustment while waiting for the benefits of reform to materialise. He cited cash transfers to more than 10 million households in Nigeria and education funding supporting more than 1.5 million students as examples of social protection measures intended to cushion the impact of reforms, according to his remarks. The minister maintained that Nigeria’s experience demonstrated the possibility of implementing difficult economic reforms, provided governments remained committed to policy consistency, institutional development and measures to protect vulnerable populations. His position reinforced the broader message from the meetings: economic stability, affordable development financing and regional integration must work together to generate investment, create jobs and deliver tangible improvements in citizens’ living standards.

title: Alleged Forgery: Court to Decide If Atiku Can Amend His Suit against Tinubu Nov 20
body: Alex Enumah in Abuja Justice Inyang Ekwo of the Federal High Court, Abuja, yesterday, adjourned till November 20 for ruling in a motion by former Vice President Atiku Abubakar requesting to amend his suit challenging the eligibility of President Bola Tinubu for the 2027 presidential election. Ekwo adjourned to the said date after listening to Atiku and Tinubu’s lawyers argue for and against the granting of the motion. At yesterday’s proceedings, Joseph Onu, who stood for Atiku, adopted his application, praying for permission of the court to amend the originating summons against Tinubu and his party, All Progressives Congress (APC), to accommodate more allegations. Onu explained that the amendment being sought was to allow the plaintiff to produce more evidence against Tinubu and his party in the certificate forgery allegations. Atiku and his party, African Democratic Congress (ADC), had on September 10 brought an application seeking leave to amend their originating summons and have the proposed amended process deemed properly filed. They said they discovered errors in the original suit, including referring to a form of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) as Form CF001 instead of Form EC9A. The plaintiffs added that the amendment was necessary to set out the particulars of the alleged fraud, include a written deposition by Atiku, and attach clearer copies of exhibits that were unavailable when the suit was filed. However, Chief Wole Olanipekun, SAN, who represented Tinubu, opposed the request for amendment, arguing that since both parties have joined issues in the matter, Atiku cannot shift the goal post in the middle of the game. Similarly, APC, represented by former Attorney General of the Federation (AGF) and Minister of Justice, Akin Olujimi, SAN, opposed Atiku on the same ground and urged the judge to reject the bid. Counsel to INEC, Dr Alex Izinyon, SAN, also urged the court to reject the amendment request and proceed to the substantive matter. Ekwo after listening to all sides announced November 20, to rule on the application. The plaintiffs in the main suit are seeking the disqualification of Tinubu and APC from the 2027 presidential election, over the president’s National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) discharge certificate submitted to INEC for purposes of the presidential poll. They alleged that APC submitted a forged NYSC discharge certificate to INEC and asked the court to order the electoral commission to remove Tinubu and APC from the list of candidates and parties for the election. The main grouse of Atiku and ADC was that the NYSC discharge certificate presented by Tinubu bore Bola Adekunle as against the well-known name Bola Tinubu. Tinubu and APC denied the allegation and asked the court to dismiss the suit. Tinubu opposed the application, arguing that the proposed amendments went beyond correcting errors and would introduce new reliefs, documents, and facts into the case. The president’s legal team also argued that the substantive suit was statute-barred, contending that the cause of action arose when Tinubu’s name was submitted to INEC on July 11, while the suit was filed on August 14. INEC also opposed the amendment, arguing that it would introduce a new cause of action and seek to cure defects in the original suit after the constitutional deadline for filing pre-election cases had lapsed.

title: APC Appoints Wike, Adeleke, Soludo Campaign Managers for FCT, Osun, Anambra
body: • Ruling party publishes revised presidential campaign council list •Umahi: why Tinubu deserves a second term Yinka Kolawole in Osogbo, Adedayo Akinwale in Abuja and Laleye Dipo in Minna All Progressives Congress (APC) has appointed Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, Governor of Osun State, Senator Ademola Adeleke, and his Anambra State counterpart, Professor Chukwuma Soludo, as campaign coordinators for the FCT, Osun, and Anambra states in the revised Presidential Campaign Council (PCC) list. According to a notice by National Secretary of APC, Senator Ajibola Basiru, the inauguration of the council is scheduled for tomorrow, Wednesday, at the Banquet Hall, Presidential Villa, Abuja by 11am. Adeleke, a member of Accord Party in Osun State, was preferred to the president’s cousin and Minister of Marine and Blue Economy, Gboyega Oyetola, who is the leader of APC in the state. Soludo, also a member of the opposition All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA), had never hidden his desire to work for the re-election of President Bola Tinubu in the January 16, 2027 presidential election. Even before the ruling party released the revised campaign list, Wike, a member of Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), had named himself the field operations commander for the FCT. Vice President Kashim Shettima would serve as Vice Chairman I, while National Chairman of APC, Professor Nentawe Yilwatda, is Vice Chairman II. Senate President Godswill Akpabio, House Speaker Tajudeen Abbas, and Kwara Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq are Deputy Vice Chairmen of the presidential campaign council. Former Zamfara State Governor, Senator Abdulaziz Yari, remains Director-General of the campaign council. Deputy Director-Generals of the PCC are: Yobe State Governor, Mai Mala Buni (North I), Senator Opeyemi Bamidele (South I), Deputy Senate President Barau Jibrin (North II), Deputy Speaker Benjamin Kalu (South II), while Senator Adams Oshiomhole will head mobilisation. Equally on the list is Chief of Staff to the President, Hon. Femi Gbajabiamila, who will serve as Head of Administration, while Hon. James Faleke is Deputy Director-General in charge of Election Planning. Hon. Ibrahim Masari is in charge of Logistics and Operations, Hon. Aminu Masari heads Parliamentary Mobilisation, and Minister of Works, David Umahi, heads Infrastructure Mobilisation and Sensitisation. Imo State Governor, Hope Uzodimma, is Secretary of the Council, while Basiru is Deputy Secretary, and Hadiza Bala Usman is Assistant Secretary. Zonal Campaign Coordinators include Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu for South-west, Governor Peter Mbah for South-east, Senator Bassey Otu for South-south, Governor Umar Bago for North-central, Governor Uba Sani for North-west, and Senator Ali Modu Sheriff for North-east. The list also shows state coordinators, comprising serving APC governors, past governors, National and State Assembly members, and other critical stakeholders. Key directorates in the council are: Finance/Treasury to be led by Delta State Governor Sheriff Oborevwori; Fund Raising by Ogun State Governor, Dapo Abiodun; Policy and Manifesto by Minister of Budget and Economic Planning, Atiku Bagudu; and Legal Directorate by Dr. Muiz Banire, SAN. Directorate of Media and Strategic Communications has Minister of Information, Idris Malagi as Coordinating Director I, while Dele Alake is Presidential Campaign Spokesperson I. Other spokespersons include Bayo Onanuga, Lere Olayinka, Ajuri Ngelale, Ayobami Oyalowo, Kemi Asekun-Shitu, Bala Ibrahim, Hon. Adamu Fanda, and Mohammed Garba. Directorate of Security and Intelligence would be headed by Gen. Sarki Yaki, Data Management by Dr. Bisoye Coker, while Directorate of Support Groups is headed by H.E. Silas Agara. The party said all members were expected to be present at the inauguration. In the same vein, Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives, Hon. Benjamin Kalu; Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Festus Keyamo; and Dr. Maryam Shetty have also been included in the revised list. The inclusion of Kalu who represents Bende Federal Constituency in Abia State, is viewed as an effort to shore up the party’s support base in the South-east, a region where the APC has historically struggled to gain traction. For Shetty, her appointment, according to party insiders, was a well-deserved recognition of years of quiet but substantial investment in the party and the Tinubu administration. A medical doctor by training and a politician of considerable grassroots influence in Kano State, Shetty has long been regarded within APC circles as one of the party’s most committed loyalists, a lady who has consistently put her resources, time, and network at the disposal of the party, often without seeking the spotlight. Umahi: Why Tinubu Deserves a Second Term Minister of Works, Senator David Umahi, said President Bola Tinubu deserved a second term because of the tremendous work he had to do all over Nigeria, which would further improve the condition of living of the ordinary person. Umahi said Tinubu had commenced the construction of 5,100 kilometres of road across the country, which would be completed in his second term in office Speaking at the flag-off of the reconstruction and dualisation of the Lambata-Bida-Mokwa-Makera-Kontagora Federal Highway in Bida, Niger State, yesterday, Umahi said the administration was committed to improving road infrastructure in all the geopolitical zones. He said the president had constructed several kilometres of roads in Adamawa and Anambra states, which the ADC presidential candidate, Alhaji Atiku Abubakar, and the NDC candidate, Mr Peter Obi, could not construct when they were Vice President of Nigeria and Governor of Anambra State, respectively. Umahi said the president needed another four years to complete the numerous road projects initiated across the country, adding that the administration is committed to improving road infrastructure in all geopolitical zones. He described the Niger highway project as a potential fifth legacy road project of the Tinubu administration, citing its scale, the use of reinforced concrete pavement, and the involvement of Dangote Group under the federal government’s infrastructure tax-credit scheme, which will make funding of the project seamless. According to the minister, the president’s ongoing infrastructure programme covers several states, with Niger benefiting from a substantial share of the road construction projects. He added that so far 162 kilometres of roads and 115 metres of bridges had been completed in the North-central region of the country alone. Umahi commended Governor Mohammed Bago for his investments in infrastructure, pointing out that the governor has constructed more than 300 kilometres of roads, and over five flyovers and underpasses. He said Bago’s approach to road construction demonstrated his commitment to development, regardless of whether a road fell under federal or state government jurisdiction. Special Adviser to the President of Dangote Group, Alhaji Mondir Ahmed, said the company was pleased to participate in the project through the infrastructure tax-credit scheme, describing the highway as a strategic corridor for Nigeria’s economy. Ahmed said the road would be constructed with concrete pavement rather than conventional asphalt and that work would commence from four locations to accelerate delivery. Bago, for his part, described the highway project as a major intervention in a strategic transportation corridor linking communities and facilitating the movement of people and goods between different parts of the country. Bago pledged to deliver the highest number of votes for Tinubu in the next election, citing federal government’s infrastructure investments in the state. He expressed gratitude to the president for approving major road projects expected to improve transportation and economic activities across Niger State.

title: Greece Issues Emergency Weather Alert for Aegean Islands
body: Greece’s 112 emergency alert system has urged people in Evia, Skyros and the Sporades to limit travel to essential journeys from Tuesday until Wednesday afternoon, October 14, as severe weather threatens the areas. The warning advises residents and visitors to follow instructions from the authorities as intense weather conditions affect the islands and surrounding regions. The emergency message states: “Severe weather conditions are expected in Evia, Skyros and the Sporades from Tuesday afternoon, October 13, until Wednesday afternoon, October 14. Limit your movements to those that are absolutely necessary. Follow the instructions of the authorities.” Heavy rain and thunderstorms expected across Greece According to the Emergency Bulletin of Dangerous Weather Phenomena issued by the Hellenic National Meteorological Service (HNMS) on Tuesday, October 13, heavy rain and thunderstorms, with the possibility of local hailstorms, are expected across most of Greece on Tuesday and Wednesday. The most severe conditions are forecast for marine and coastal areas. The HNMS also forecasts locally very strong northeasterly winds in the northern Aegean from Tuesday evening, October 13. The post Greece Issues Emergency Weather Alert for Aegean Islands appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: 2027: Why APC opted for ‘Rainbow campaign council’
body: By Hussein Yahaya (Abuja), Sani Ibrahim Paki (Kano) & Mumini Abdulkareem (Ilorin) The revised list of the All Progressives Congress (APC) 2027 Presidential Campaign Council signals a strategic shift in Nigeria’s political landscape, with the ruling party seeking to build an all-inclusive “Rainbow Coalition” ahead of the general elections. Beyond its role as an electioneering structure, the expanded council reflects the APC’s efforts to transcend traditional party boundaries, incorporate influential opposition figures and consolidate support for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s re-election bid. The most striking feature of the revised list is the inclusion of prominent politicians from opposition parties. Leading the initiative is the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, who has been named campaign coordinator for Tinubu in Rivers State and the FCT. Osun State Governor Ademola Adeleke, a member of the Accord Party, has also been appointed campaign coordinator for his state. Similarly, former Gombe State Governor and serving Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) senator Ibrahim Dankwambo has been named an adviser to the campaign council, alongside Obafemi George. Political analysts said the appointments suggest that the APC is seeking to weaken opposition strongholds in the South-South, South-West and North-East by bringing influential politicians from rival parties into its campaign structure. NRS boss, Adedeji retained, Betta Edu, Ngozi Olejeme missing Despite the strategic ambition of the “Rainbow Coalition,” the composition of the revised council did not address the debate over the inclusion of some individuals such as Zacch Adedeji (Chairman, National Revenue Service – NRS). Appointed as Deputy Director of Fundraising, Adedeji’s inclusion has raised questions regarding institutional neutrality. Critics have argued that placing the head of the country’s tax authority in charge of campaign fundraising could create a potential conflict of interest between tax administration and partisan political activities. A careful review of the new list shows that neither Dr Betta Edu nor Ngozi Olejeme is included. Dr Betta Edu, former Minister of Humanitarian Affairs, was initially named Director of Women Mobilisation. Edu’s inclusion comes after her suspension in January 2024 following an investigation into an alleged N585 million financial impropriety. Though she was subsequently replaced by Prof. Nentawe Yilwatda, the public absence of a final report from the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) drew scrutiny from transparency advocacy groups. Also, Ngozi Olejeme, a former board chairperson of the NSITF, was earlier appointed as South-South Zonal Director for Election Planning, Coordination, and Mobilisation. Her inclusion had similarly drawn questions due to past anti-graft inquiries concerning her tenure at the Nigeria Social Insurance Trust Fund. Irony in Wike, Adeleke’s appointments The appointments of Wike and Adeleke have raised questions about the implications for their respective political parties, particularly as both parties have presidential ambitions of their own. Although Wike and Adeleke have been associated with Tinubu’s re-election bid, their inclusion in the APC campaign council presents a political contradiction: the PDP and the Accord Party, to which they belong, also have presidential candidates. Our correspondent reports that the PDP is fielding Prof Sandy Onor as its presidential candidate while the court has ordered the Accord Party to recognise Gbenga Olawepo-Hashim as its presidential candidate. What this implies for the PDP on the surface is that while the party would be campaigning to win the presidential election, the leader of the party, Wike, by virtue of his appointment to the APC presidential campaign, would be directly working against the party without fear of any likely consequence. Political analysts note that, under stricter party discipline, such an arrangement could have been regarded as anti-party activity. But beyond the surface, many are of the view that the PDP only presented a presidential candidate who is loyal to Wike in order not to allow a vacancy for others to take the position and work against his interest. It is not clear how the party would react, but it is not likely that the party would frown on it. Despite remaining a PDP member, the former Rivers State governor has been one of Tinubu’s most consequential political allies outside the ruling party since the 2023 election. Speaking on Tuesday, Wike said the president’s approach was to accommodate people outside the APC who were willing to contribute to his re-election. He argued that people who wanted Tinubu to continue in office should be allowed to contribute regardless of their party affiliations. His position, however, comes against the backdrop of disagreements within the ruling party over his proposed Rainbow Coalition and the extent to which non-APC politicians should influence the president’s re-election machinery. Some APC state chapters have questioned the arrangement, insisting that those genuinely committed to Tinubu should formally join the party. Adeleke’s appointment presents a similar dilemma. The Osun governor, who secured re-election on the platform of the Accord Party, has been tasked with mobilising support for a presidential candidate whose party is a political rival of his own party. After months of litigation, a court reportedly ordered the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to recognise Olawepo-Hashim as the Accord Party’s presidential candidate. However, it was unclear at press time whether the commission had uploaded his name to its portal. If the court’s order is implemented, Adeleke’s appointment could create further questions about the Accord Party’s presidential campaign, particularly given that he is the party’s only governor. The arrangement could help the APC extend its reach beyond its established political network in Osun State. However, it also raises questions about how support for Tinubu at the presidential level will coexist with competition for governorship and legislative seats. The APGA, meanwhile, has publicly endorsed Soludo’s inclusion in the campaign council. The party said the arrangement reflected its position that Tinubu should be supported for president while APGA maintained its independent identity and pursued other elective offices. The appointments suggest that the APC is seeking to build a broader electoral support base around Tinubu. With opposition parties and political blocs yet to establish a united front against the ruling party, Tinubu’s camp appears to have an opportunity to cultivate alliances across party lines. How revised council reshapes APC’s internal structure The revised campaign council list also appears to have altered aspects of the ruling party’s internal command structure. Senate President Godswill Akpabio and Speaker of the House of Representatives Tajudeen Abbas have been elevated to deputy vice-chairmen, while Kwara State Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq occupies another deputy vice-chairmanship position. Senator Abdulaziz Yari remains director-general of the campaign council, with other senior party and government figures assigned responsibilities across its various directorates. Former Kwara senator Gbemisola Saraki is among the new entrants. She has been listed as zonal secretary in the Contact and Mobilisation Directorate for the North-Central. However, not all prominent figures appearing in the revised document are new entrants. Delta State Governor Sheriff Oborevwori, for instance, was previously listed as director of finance and treasury. He retains that responsibility while also serving as Delta State campaign coordinator. Former Lagos State Governor Babatunde Fashola had earlier been assigned to South-West stakeholders’ mobilisation, while Aviation Minister Festus Keyamo was already part of the media and strategic communications structure. Inclusion threatens multi-party democracy – Analyst A professor of Political Science at North West University, Kano, Murtala Muhammad, has warned that the inclusion of opposition leaders in the APC Presidential Campaign Council poses grave risks to Nigeria’s multiparty democracy. He described the development as “unprecedented and disheartening.” “This is the first time in Nigeria’s history that major opposition leaders are openly campaigning for a ruling party’s presidential candidate. “It raises fundamental questions about ideological consistency, political accountability, and the future of Nigeria’s multiparty democracy,” he said. The professor argued that opposition parties exist to scrutinise government policies and present credible alternatives, not to “negotiate access to power.” He warned that the blurring of party identities risks deepening political cynicism and weakening democratic accountability. “We are in a serious mess. Every serious political party should have a distinct manifesto and ideological orientation. “When opposition leaders abandon this role, Nigeria’s political system becomes directionless,” Muhammad stressed. He further questioned whether the cooperation was based on any transparent, written agreement serving national interest, saying the absence of such clarity suggests self-interest rather than patriotism. Muhammad cautioned that the trend could slide Nigeria toward “political disorder and ideological backwardness,” adding that alliances without principles or clear commitments reduce multiparty politics to “a marketplace of elite interests rather than an instrument of democratic representation.” ‘Tinubu made right decision’ Professor Hassan Saliu, Interim President of the Nigerian Society of International Affairs (NSIA) and professor of Political Science and International Relations at the University of Ilorin, said no political party could confidently win the 2027 presidential election by relying solely on its members, warning that cross-party alliances could determine the outcome. Saliu described the All Progressives Congress (APC)’s decision to include politicians from opposition parties and the broader coalition in its presidential campaign structure as a strategic move to expand its support base beyond its traditional constituencies. “The environment, the electoral environment confronting us, does not suggest that one party alone and its members can win,” he said. He added that candidates would need to reach voters outside their established political bases to improve their chances. According to him, the arrangement reflects the realities of Nigerian politics, where party affiliation alone may no longer guarantee sufficient support to win a presidential election.

title: Private political loyalties deserve scrutiny too in EC appointments – Osae-Kwapong
body: CDD-Ghana Fellow Dr John Osae-Kwapong has questioned whether public scrutiny of Electoral Commission (EC) appointments gives sufficient attention to people whose political loyalties remain private. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, he said an appointee could hold strong partisan sympathies without openly displaying them. “The second point for me then becomes this idea of the open partisan being appointed to an independent constitutional body versus the person who could be just as partisan but is more private about his or her partisanship.” He argued that public discomfort often centres on visible political affiliations.
