He described his father as a cerebral, versatile traditional ruler, and a strong advocate for balancing tradition with modernity. “We pledge our commitment once again to walk in his footsteps of progress and meaningful impact,” Oba Ewuare stated at the lecture, themed, “Oba Erediauwa’s Voice in Discourse: Defining His Intellectual Legacy.” The monarch stated, “As a former ambassador to many countries, these values cherished and instilled in us by our father of blessed memory, remind us constantly of our heritage within our spheres to be committed as one of the shakers and movers of modern African history and civilisation.” Ahead of the inaugural edition of the Oba Erediauwa Memorial Lecture scheduled for March 23, 2027- marking the exact date month of Oba Erediauwa’s coronation held in 1979 – Oba Ewuare announced the dissolution of the planning committee set up nine years ago, led by Prof. Sam Guobadia and Prince Aghatise Erediauwa, citing lethargy in discharging their royal assignments. Consequently, Oba Ewuare announced the immediate appointment of Professor Osarhiemen Benson Osadolor, a professor of history at the University of Benin and keynote speaker at the event, as the new chairman of the Oba Erediauwa Memorial Lecture Series Committee. Earlier, in his welcome address, Vice Chancellor of the University of Benin, Prof. Edoba Omoregie, SAN, described Oba Erediauwa as an erudite scholar, a moral compass, and a monarch who combined intellectual depth and integrity that brought prestige to the Benin monarchy. He listed key milestones of his reign, commending him for his fatherly leadership and acknowledging his support for the university’s endowment, research, arts, technology, and environmental conservation initiatives. In his keynote presentation, Osadolor described Oba Erediauwa as a monarch with an outstanding reputation. He recalled scholarly works conveyed through the Oba’s books and articles that shaped government policies even before his reign in Benin, citing publications, such as, I Remain, Sir, Your Obedient Servant, and The Cradle of Ideas. Earlier, Mr. Lucky Imasuen, a former deputy governor of Edo State and chairman of the 10th Coronation Anniversary Committee, outlined activities planned for the anniversary. Imasuen commended the management of the University of Benin for its support. The convergence of academia, royalty, and governance underscores the enduring influence of the Benin throne, setting a high intellectual tone for the roadmap leading up to Oba Erediauwa memorial grand launch in March 2027.

title: Nigeria Ramps Up Crude Output, Meets OPEC Quota for Five Straight Months
body: • Oil, condensate production rise 2.34% to 1.72 million bpd •Forcados, Bonny lead terminal output Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja and Peter Uzoho in Lagos Nigeria sustained its recovery in crude oil production in September, meeting its Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) quota for the fifth consecutive month. A statement in Abuja by the spokesman of the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC), Eniola Akinkuotu, said daily output also peaked at 1.84 million barrels, including condensates. The country recorded an average daily production of 1,717,030 barrels of crude oil and condensate during the month, representing a 2.34 per cent increase over August, according to the data released by the NUPRC. The September performance further consolidated Nigeria’s position as Africa’s largest crude oil producer, with production reaching 1.84 million barrels on the highest-output day and falling to a low of 1.68 million barrels during the period. Excluding condensates, Nigeria produced an average of 1.53 million barrels of crude oil per day, exceeding its OPEC-assigned quota of 1.5 million barrels per day by approximately 2 per cent. The latest figures mean Nigeria has now met its crude oil production quota for five consecutive months, sustaining output above or at the assigned threshold despite the operational challenges that have historically constrained production in the country. Crude oil production stood at 1.53 million barrels per day in May before rising to 1.55 million barrels per day in June. Output subsequently moderated to 1.51 million barrels per day in July and 1.5 million barrels per day in August before recovering to 1.53 million barrels per day in September. The improvement in September was attributed to stable operations across most producing assets and the absence of major pipeline outages during the month. According to the commission, the relative stability enhanced production uptime and improved the efficiency of crude oil evacuation, helping operators sustain output across the upstream petroleum sector. The commission said the sustained growth reflected the commitment of operators and other industry stakeholders to improving operational efficiency, maintaining asset integrity and strengthening production reliability. Nigeria has faced persistent difficulties in achieving its production potential, including crude oil theft, pipeline vandalism, ageing infrastructure and disruptions to production and evacuation. Sustaining output above the OPEC quota could therefore help strengthen crude oil export volumes and government revenue, provided the improved performance is maintained. A breakdown of production by terminals and streams showed that Forcados Terminal recorded the highest average daily output in September, accounting for 320,320 barrels per day. Bonny Terminal followed with 303,270 barrels per day, according to the NUPRC data. The September figures highlighted the steady return of operational stability and uninterrupted evacuation infrastructure in sustaining Nigeria’s recent production gains. Nigeria has set an ambitious target of raising crude oil production to 2 million barrels per day by 2027 and 3 million barrels per day by 2030 as part of efforts to maximise its petroleum resources, boost foreign exchange earnings and strengthen government revenue. Despite the recent improvement, achieving the targets will require a significant increase in production capacity. September’s average crude oil output of 1.53 million barrels per day, excluding condensates, remains about 470,000 barrels short of the two million-barrel target and 1.47 million barrels below the 3 million barrel ambition.

title: DICON Gray Lauds Army for Promoting Local Defence Manufacturing
body: • Seeks sustained military-industry collaboration Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja DICON Gray Insignia (DGI), a Nigerian defence manufacturing company, has hailed the Nigerian Army for opening up opportunities for indigenous defence manufacturers to test and demonstrate their products under practical field conditions. The organisation, in a statement in Abuja, described the initiative as a significant step towards building the country’s domestic defence industry, calling for sustained military-industry collaboration and greater opportunities for local manufacturers to supply equipment to the armed forces. Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of DGI, Bem Garba, specifically noted the role played by the Chief of Army Staff, Lt. Gen. Waidi Shaibu, and the military leadership in providing Nigerian technology companies with the opportunity to demonstrate their capabilities and receive feedback from military end users. Garba said the exercise provided a practical platform for manufacturers to understand operational requirements, assess their technologies and identify areas for improvement, stressing that closer engagement between the military and local industry was essential to developing a sustainable domestic defence manufacturing sector. “We sincerely commend the Chief of Army Staff and the Nigerian Army leadership for this important initiative. At Jaji, we experienced a genuine willingness to engage Nigerian companies, understand their capabilities, and provide an opportunity for practical evaluation,” he said. During the Nigerian Army’s field evaluation of military equipment prototypes in Kaduna, DGI presented its tactical shotgun platforms and DGI100 portable intelligent live-fire target system for assessment. Other participating indigenous companies included Proforce, PRIMETEK and Tera Haptic Industries. The company also acknowledged the contribution of Terra Industries, which provided its KAMA drone for a counter-unmanned aerial vehicle demonstration involving DGI’s tactical shotgun platforms. Garba said field evaluations went beyond assessing individual products, providing an opportunity for the armed forces to help local manufacturers develop technologies that respond to Nigeria’s security needs. “A defence manufacturing industry cannot develop in isolation from the institutions it is established to serve. Manufacturers need access to end users, an understanding of operational requirements, opportunities to test their products, and professional feedback to help them improve. “This is why the Nigerian Army’s initiative is so important. It takes the conversation about indigenous defence manufacturing beyond policy statements and product presentations into practical engagement and field evaluation,” he said. He added that sustained military engagement could help domestic manufacturers improve their technologies, strengthen technical capabilities, attract investment and establish viable production operations. DGI also commended the Minister of State for Defence, Bello Matawalle, for his oversight and support for the Defence Industries Corporation of Nigeria (DICON) and efforts to strengthen indigenous defence manufacturing. The company equally praised the Director General of DICON, Maj. Gen. B. I. Alaya, for his efforts to develop Nigerian companies operating under the DICON Related Industries (DRIs) framework. Garba said building a viable defence industrial base required more than establishing factories, noting that manufacturers needed skilled personnel, reliable supply chains, technology transfer, quality assurance and sustained institutional support. The company stressed that Nigeria’s ambition to develop a stronger domestic defence industry would depend on sustained cooperation among the federal government, the armed forces, indigenous manufacturers, research institutions, investors and international technical partners. It said expanding local production could reduce dependence on imported military equipment, create skilled jobs, promote technology transfer, strengthen domestic supply chains and retain more economic value within the country. However, it emphasised that local production must be backed by rigorous testing, dependable manufacturing standards, transparent procurement processes and predictable demand from government institutions. “Local manufacturing should never mean compromising quality, safety or operational standards. Our Armed Forces deserve equipment that meets their requirements, and indigenous manufacturers must be prepared to demonstrate that capability. “However, companies also need a credible pathway from research and development to evaluation, product improvement and, where appropriate, procurement. Without that pathway, it becomes difficult to justify the substantial investment required to establish and sustain local manufacturing operations,” Garba said. He urged the Chief of Army Staff to sustain and expand the field evaluation initiative, while encouraging other military, security and government institutions to establish similar platforms for engaging indigenous technology companies. “We may not manufacture everything Nigeria requires today, but we must create the conditions that will enable us to manufacture much more tomorrow,” he added.

title: Iran, Oman FMs discuss regional developments
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 14 (MNA) – Iran and Oman's foreign ministers held a phone call early Wednesday to discuss Yemen and other regional developments.
Iranian Foreign Minister Seyyed Abbas Araghchi and Omani Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr al-Busaidi discussed the latest regional developments, including Yemen, in a phone call early Wednesday.
The two ministers reviewed ways to achieve peace and stability in the region.
No further details were immediately available.

title: Roma v Real Madrid: Mourinho struggles to solve Vinicius Jr conundrum amid Bernabeu chaos
body: The idea that Jose Mourinho was the man to restore order to the mayhem that is Real Madrid and prevent a third successive campaign without a major trophy appears to be unravelling fast. Last season was a turbulent one for Los Blancos that saw managers sacked, players jeered by their own fans, teammates fighting each other, all topped off by bitter rivals Barcelona securing a second successive La Liga title. To control a dressing room of rampant egos, Madrid president Florentino Perez turned to the biggest coaching ego of them all, brining Mourinho back for his second stint at a club who sacked him back in 2013. But just nine matches into the new season, all is not well in the Spanish capital. On Saturday at the Bernabeu, Madrid were labouring towards a 1-0 win over Villarreal – courtesy of teenager Yan Diomande's first goal for the club – when Vinicius Junior scored with a clinical first-time finish. It sparked ferocious celebrations from the attacker, with Mourinho sprinting across the pitch to join in. But the joyous scenes were cut short when referee Isidro Diaz de Mera Escuderos was asked to view the pitchside monitor by VAR, where he saw Vinicius clearly pulling the hair of Nathan Saliba in the build-up to the goal. 💥 | Diaz de Mera Escuderos acude a la pantalla del VAR en el Santiago Bernabéu. ⚪️🇪🇸 📌 Vinicius Junior le tira del pelo a Nathan Saliba sin disputar el balón, ES ROJA Y NO ES GOL ✅ Acierto del conjunto arbitral 🏟️ Real Madrid - Villarreal pic.twitter.com/kLzNsU1eOr — Laliga News (@laligaa_neews) October 10, 2026 Just 20 minutes after coming off the bench to replace Trent Alexander-Arnold, Vinicius was shown a red card and the scene quickly descended into chaos as furious Madrid players surrounded the referee, while the Brazilian had to be dragged away by teammates. An incandescent Mourinho, who had already spent the entire game berating officials, earned himself a yellow card, then refused to appear for the post-match press conference. The player himself has since issued a brief apology on social media – saying “sorry to the team and the fans” – but could now receive a three-match ban that would see him miss the Clasico on October 25 against a table-topping Barca team that has won eight from eight in La Liga so far. While Mourinho continues to rant and rave about perceived refereeing agendas against his team, the fact remains they are not playing well. They find themselves in fourth place, six points shy of Barca, having lost to Real Betis and the derby against Atletico Madrid, where Mourinho was again left bemoaning refereeing decisions . And the biggest puzzle facing the veteran Portuguese is coaxing Vinicius – who signed a bumper new six-year contract extension over the summer – back into top form. The 26-year-old has managed just one goal in 672 minutes of action this season prompting questions as to why Mourinho has not turned to other attacking options in his squad. “Some players need time to get back to their usual level … and I’m not going to hide from that,” he insisted ahead of the Villarreal game. “I never criticise the Madrid fan base; I only respect it. It breaks my heart to see a boy like him suffer. He wants to become that Vinicius again who wins matches and makes the difference … Vini deserves support.” Mourinho has also found himself defending top-scorer Kylian Mbappe – who has eight goals in nine games, taking his Madrid career tally to 94 in 112 matches – after the French attacker was criticised for making trips to Paris and Switzerland while still recovering from a minor knee injury picked up on international duty. “What I can promise is when a Real Madrid player doesn't behave the way a Real Madrid player is supposed to … They won't have the chance to whistle, because they'll be at home,” said the 63-year-old, who dismissed the criticism as “ridiculous” while also accusing the media of trying to turn Madrid fans against Mbappe. After starting their Uefa Champions League campaign with a 2-1 win over Inter Milan – with Mbappe and Federico Valverde on target – they now face another of Mourinho's former clubs in Roma at the Stadio Olympico on Wednesday. The Italian side are currently third in Serie A after drawing 0-0 at Como on Sunday, when they had top-scorer Donyell Malen shown a straight red card for a reckless tackle on home defender Kaiki. The Giallorossi's opening European game saw them draw with Fenerbahce in Turkey. Mourinho's three-year spell in the Italian capital was a trademark mix of success and controversy that ended in the sack. He guided Roma to their first major European crown when they defeated Feyenoord 1-0 in 2022's inaugural Europa Conference League final, which also meant Mourinho became the first manager to win all four major European trophies, having previously lifted the Uefa Cup, Champions League and Europa League. “I knew the moment I arrived what it meant to the people,” said Mourinho after the match in Tirana. “They had been waiting for something like this. This was not work tonight, this was history. We had to write history. We wrote it.” But 12 months later, Mourinho was once again left ranting at officials after Roma were beaten by Sevilla on penalties in a Europa League final that witnessed a tournament record 13 yellow cards. His infamous foul-mouthed tirade at referee Anthony Taylor in the car park after the game earned him a four-match ban. The following season, Mourinho was sacked after a poor run of results, but the Portuguese insists his love for the club remains intact. “I think the bond between me and the Roma fans was created by the fact … they understood that for me there was only Roma and the Roma fans. I fought for them, I gave everything,” he said last week in an interview with Corriere dello Sport. “What do I expect from the Olimpico? I do not expect banners. I do not expect anything. I expect respect. ”

title: Netanyahu, Eisenkot blocs struggle to secure majority, raising fears of another election deadlock
body: With just two weeks to go before Israel's election, the political chessboard is set, and there is little indication that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has found a winning move.Israel's voters do not elect the prime minister directly; instead, the prime minister must assemble a coalition commanding a majority of the Knesset's 120 seats. That means Benjamin Netanyahu's chances of retaining power depend in part on how well his smaller political allies perform at the polls.There are 38 parties running in these elections, although no more than 15 will meet the 3.25% vote threshold - the percentage of the total vote that a party needs to clear to gain any seats in the Knesset. The parties that will be left standing after the Oct. 27 vote will likely include three or four on the right, led by Netanyahu's Likud list; four or five on the center-left, with polling showing the new Yashar party led by Gadi Eizenkot, a former military chief of staff, leading them; two Haredi Orthodox parties; and two predominantly Arab parties.Unfortunately for Netanyahu, several right-wing parties didn't merge as he had hoped. Religious Zionism, the ultra-nationalist party led by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, did not join forces with National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit or Amcha Yisrael, led by retired Brig.-Gen. Ofer Winter.As a result, both Smotrich's party and Winter's party remain close to Israel's electoral threshold, raising the possibility that one or both could fail to win enough votes to enter the Knesset—meaning their votes, which could have strengthened Netanyahu's bloc, would be wasted. With the 3.25% threshold, the equivalent of four Knesset seats, the wasted vote could be substantial.Netanyahu's political magic faces test as right-wing parties remain divided“Netanyahu has been considered Israel's political magician for many years — the man who managed in 2022 to bring Ben-Gvir and Smotrich together on a joint list,” said Dr. Gayil Talshir, a political scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.Ahead of that election, Netanyahu publicly urged the two parties to merge, warning that the right-wing bloc “can't take the risk” of either party falling below the electoral threshold. Days later, the two leaders reached a deal following a meeting with Netanyahu, who had pressed for the merger.“We haven't seen that happen in this election,” Talshir continued. “Netanyahu is entering this election in the weakest position we have seen him in over the past decade in terms of the parties running.”The right-wing parties' decisions to run separately reflected a combination of personal animosity and ideological differences. Winter emphasized the need to bring new faces into politics, arguing that those tainted by the failures behind Hamas' invasion of southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, should make way for new leadership. Smotrich and Ben-Gvir, meanwhile, remained divided by personal tensions and the belief that each appeals to a somewhat different segment of Israel's ultranationalist right.Electoral threshold threatens Netanyahu's path to 61 seatsVeteran pollster Shmuel Rosner believes Winter's new party risks falling below the threshold. It currently polls at around four to five seats, but support for new parties has traditionally declined as the initial excitement around their launch fades. Smotrich's Religious Zionism, which is polling at roughly five to six seats, is also vulnerable. The party has spent much of recent months below the threshold in polling.“The party lineup is more challenging for Netanyahu than for his opponents,” Rosner said. “In the anti-Netanyahu camp, there is currently no party that is at risk of falling below the electoral threshold, while in the bloc that leans toward Netanyahu, there is at least one - and potentially another - party in that position.”Even if both parties clear the threshold, however, current polling suggests that Netanyahu remains well short of the 61 seats needed to form a governing coalition. Most polls put his bloc at around 52-53 seats.Arab parties emerge as potential kingmakers amid election deadlockBut the picture is not entirely bleak for Netanyahu. The opposition-aligned bloc, currently led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, is also not projected to reach 61 seats. In recent weeks, its numbers have fallen sharply, from roughly 58-59 seats to around 52-53. The balance of the seats goes to Arab-led parties.Yashar party chairman Gadi Eisenkot speaks during the “Game-Changing Generation” National Youth Conference at the International Convention Center in Jerusalem, October 11, 2026. (Yonatan Sindel/Flash90)Talshir attributes the decline not necessarily to a loss of support for the bloc itself, but to shifts elsewhere on the electoral map. Three Arab parties have joined forces to make up a unified Joint List party, strengthening the Arab political bloc and helping one of the parties avoid falling below the electoral threshold. The merger could also increase turnout among Arab voters.Both major political camps have pledged not to include the Arab parties in a governing coalition. However, the anti-Netanyahu bloc is in a better position here, too.Joint List and Ra'am are projected to win roughly 14 seats. And the leader of Balad, one of the parties making up the Joint List, withdrew from the race late last month after the Supreme Court signaled that his candidacy would be disqualified. The impact of his forced withdrawal remains unclear, but some analysts suggest it could further boost turnout among Arab voters, who may cast protest votes against those who prevented him from running.Netanyahu's potential coalition partners adamantly oppose including any Arab parties and have made the possibility of a coalition that includes an Arab party a line of attack against the opposition bloc. The previous government, formed by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid in 2021, brought Ra'am into its coalition to secure a parliamentary majority, a historic first.But key figures in the current opposition camp have pledged not to repeat that arrangement this time, saying that emotions remain too raw in the Jewish public three years after the Oct. 7, 2023 deadly Hamas raids inside Israel. Those ruling out another partnership with Arab parties include Gadi Eisenkot, the current leader of the opposition camp in the polls; Lapid, who helped engineer the previous coalition; and Avigdor Lieberman, the hawkish former finance minister.Talshir nevertheless believes that those commitments could ultimately be tested if the election produces another deadlock. She points to a possible scenario in which Eisenkot and Ra'am could cooperate to form a minority government, with Ra'am voting to install an Eisenkot-led list while remaining outside the coalition to prevent Netanyahu from remaining prime minister.Abbas told Channel 12 in an August interview that his top priority was replacing Netanyahu's current government. On Saturday, Joint List chairman Youssef Jabareen said his party would support any government that ends Netanyahu's rule, subject to conditions he did not specify.Leader of the Arab Israeli party Ra'am (United Arab List), Mansour Abbas speaks during an election campaign event, ahead of Israel's legislative elections, in the Arab town of Ka'abiyye-Tabbash-Hajajre in Israel's Northern District on September 26, 2026. If neither bloc can assemble a coalition, Israel could once again head toward another election, as happened during the two-year political crisis that began in 2019 and led to five subsequent elections, while Netanyahu would remain in office as caretaker prime minister.“Looking at the scenarios and the polls we are seeing right now, we see a very small chance that either bloc will be able to reach 61 seats,” Rosner said.Smaller parties could determine Israel's next governing coalitionOne of the biggest wild cards is the handful of parties currently polling below the electoral threshold that have nevertheless decided to remain in the race. Rosner points to three notable parties in that position: the Reservists-Economic Party, led by Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha; the Haredi-oriented party, led by Moti Leitner; and Benny Gantz's Blue and White.Rosner said the most significant of the three is the Hendel-Zelekha party, which is hovering around the electoral threshold and could either cross it or fall short. “It is on the edge of the threshold,” Rosner said. “It could pass or fall with four seats.”He added that the party is difficult to place politically. “It doesn't really say what it will do, and it is made up of people who have different interests and different desires,” Rosner said. Still, he estimates it would be easier for the party to join the opposition-aligned bloc than Netanyahu's coalition, partly because of the coalition's partnership with the Haredi parties. Military reservists deeply resent Haredi men who avoid serving in the military and want the next government to end the practice.Gantz's Blue and White, which once led the opposition camp but lost much of its popularity after Gantz joined Netanyahu's government, is still running despite remaining well below the threshold. It is currently polling at around 1%. Gantz has made clear that if his party clears the electoral threshold, he would seek to form a unity government that includes both Netanyahu and parties from the opposition's change bloc.The new Haredi party, HaTzibbur HaHaredi, is polling similarly. It could draw one or two seats away from the established ultra-Orthodox parties, potentially weakening Netanyahu's bloc. The party has said it would support a “broad national government,” without specifying which political camp it would join.For now, the key question is not so much whether voters will switch sides, but whether each bloc can mobilize its existing supporters to turn out on election day.“The struggle right now is much less about moving voters from one side to the other and much more about making sure voters leave their homes and vote,” Rosner said. “And I estimate that the more difficult test will be for the right-wing bloc.”

title: TIMELINE: Changes in AFP’s structure since revised modernization law
body: It has been nearly 14 years since then-president Benigno Aquino III signed the Revised Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) Modernization Act, a landmark law that enabled the military not only to acquire modern assets but also to review its structure and personnel. Many of the adjustments reflect the Philippines’ goal of shifting its focus from internal security operations to territorial defense. Here’s a breakdown of how the AFP’s organizational structure has shifted since then: February 23, 1995 The first AFP Modernization Act is signed. Aside from acquisition of assets, the plan includes components on force restructuring and organizational development as well as human resource development. The latter puts emphasis on the need for the AFP to transition from an internal security-oriented force to a primarily external security-oriented force. But reluctance from Congress to fund it, as well as the 1997 Asian financial crisis, prevented the plan from taking off, a 2005 paper by defense expert Renato de Castro said. The law’s implementation period lapsed 15 years later in February 2010 . January 1, 2011 The AFP’s six-year Internal Peace and Security Plan — more commonly known as Oplan Bayanihan — takes effect. It aims to eventually allow the AFP to transition into a territorial defense-focused force. From 2011 to 2013, the AFP continued its primary task of fighting internal armed threats. The remaining years — 2014 to 2016 — were focused on handing over the lead role in internal peace and security to appropriate civilian agencies. October 2011 The Defense Planning Guidance (2013–2018) is released, according to a 2016 study by De Castro . It restructures the AFP into a “lean but fully capable” military to confront the challenges to the country’s territorial integrity and maritime security. The guide emphasizes the importance of naval assets. The guide also includes the reduction of infantry and marine battalions so limited financial resources could be redirected to key priorities. These reductions would take effect in 2012. May 4, 2012 The military’s development arm and anti-insurgency unit , the National Development Support Command, is abolished . It was first formed in 2006 under the Arroyo government to handle the military’s development programs in far-flung areas and address insurgency. July 12, 2012 The AFP National Capital Region Command (NCRCOM) is deactivated . It had mainly served as an anti-coup unit in the capital region. A smaller joint military task force for Metro Manila is activated to take NCRCOM’s place, called the Joint Task Force (JTF) NCR . December 11, 2012 Aquino signs the Revised AFP Modernization Act . It effectively restarts the clock on the modernization program, but also amends the language used to describe the components on force restructuring and human resource development. The revised law says the AFP should be transformed into a “multi-mission oriented force” that has the shifting capability to meet internal and external threats. February 2014 Responsibility for Bajo de Masinloc (Scarborough Shoal), a high-tide elevation some 120 nautical miles off Zambales, is transferred from the Tarlac-based Northern Luzon Command (Nolcom) to the Palawan-based Western Command (Wescom). The move is meant to put the country’s external defense efforts under one commander. Wescom also has more ships and aircraft capable of monitoring the shoal. March 16, 2016 The Philippine Navy activates its Submarine Group to “lay the groundwork for undersea warfare.” April 6, 2018 Special operations are effectively unified under one command, after then-president Rodrigo Duterte deactivated the Army Special Operations Command and transferred its personnel to the newly activated AFP Special Operations Command (AFPSOCOM). The AFPSOCOM is tasked with commanding all the military’s elite units: the Special Operations Wing of the Air Force, Naval Special Operations Group of the Navy, Scout Ranger Regiment, Special Forces Regiment (Airborne) and Light Reaction Regiment of the Army, and Joint Special Operations Group of the General Headquarters. June 2018 The AFP activates the AFP Cyber Group (AFPCyG). April 13, 2022 Duterte signs Republic Act No. 11709 , which sets a fixed three-year term for high-ranking AFP officers, including the chief of staff. The law is said to end a “revolving door” policy that gave rise to military chiefs serving for only a few months before mandatory retirement. Other provisions in the law intend to strengthen the merit system of the AFP and ensure continuity of programs and policies. September to November 2022 The 4th Marine Brigade transfers from Sulu to Ilocos Norte. It is now under the command of Nolcom, which means it is also responsible for Scarborough Shoal and the Philippine Rise, key features in the West Philippine Sea. (READ: From Sulu to Burgos, the Marines’ Fourth Brigade comes home ) May 17, 2023 President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. amends the law fixing high-ranking AFP officers’ terms to three years. The AFP chief is given a “maximum tour of duty” of three consecutive years, instead of the “fixed tour of duty” in the previous law. The maximum tour of duty of the commanding generals of the Army, Navy, and Air Force are also set to two years instead of the three stipulated in the law Duterte signed. January 11, 2024 The AFP reactivates its counterintelligence group that is tasked with protecting the military against espionage, sabotage, and other intelligence activities. The unit was first organized in 1989 and disbanded in 1995 to create a presidential task force on intelligence and counterintelligence instead. (READ: Why did the Philippines reactivate its military counterintelligence group? ) January 24, 2024 Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. announces that the AFP is embarking on a “comprehensive archipelagic defense concept.” It is the country’s strategy to secure its vast maritime areas. August 21, 2024 A new AFP Intelligence Command is activated “to enhance the nation’s intelligence capabilities in response to evolving security challenges,” according to AFP spokesperson Colonel Francel Margareth Padilla. Late 2024 The AFPCyG becomes the AFP Cyber Command sometime in late 2024 . Expanding the group into a command allows it to have more personnel and equipment. (READ: AFP chief Brawner eyes ‘Cyber Command’ ) February 28, 2025 JTF NCR once again becomes the NCRCOM. March 31, 2025 The reorganization of the Naval Forces West to the Western Naval Command and the Naval Forces Northern Luzon to the Northern Luzon Naval Command is approved . (READ: Presence is deterrence: The Philippine Navy’s pivot ) May 28, 2025 The AFP reorganizes special operations again, deactivating the AFPSOCOM and simultaneously reactivating the Special Operations Command of the Philippine Army and creating the Joint Special Operations Command of the AFP. October 27, 2025 The AFP officially activates the AFP Strategic Command. It is described as a “strategic hub where intelligence, operations, and civil-military functions converge,” and is tasked with overseeing and synchronizing joint exercises and engagements with allies and partners. July 2026 The AFP announces plans for a space force or a space command by 2028. – Rappler.com

title: APC drafts PDP, Accord, APGA into Tinubu’s campaign council
body: ***Why Tinubu pushed for Wike, Soludo, Adeleke despite internal push-backs ***Rainbow Coalition has come to stay, Wike tells APC govs By Omeiza Ajayi ABUJA — To ensure a smooth sail for President Bola Tinubu in the January 16, 2027 presidential poll, the Presidency and ruling All Progressive Congress, APC, have included leading opposition figures and governors in Tinubu’s re-election council, in spite of strong push-backs from sections of the party. In its expanded Presidential Campaign Council, PCC, that will be inaugurated today in Abuja, the APC included Minister of Federal Capital Territory, FCT; Nyesom Wike of the Peoples Democratic Party, PDP; Governor of Osun State, Ademola Adeleke of Accord; and his counterpart in Anambra State, Chukwuma Soludo of the All Progressives Grand Alliance, APGA. Wike was appointed coordinator of the party’s campaign in Rivers and the FCT, Soludo coordinator for Anambra, while Adeleke was named coordinator for Osun. The revised list also incorporated former Gombe State governor and serving PDP Senator, Ibrahim Dankwambo, who was appointed as adviser to the Campaign Council alongside Obafemi George, who will also advise on media strategy. Key leadership positions within the campaign hierarchy were also confirmed in the updated release. Senator Abdulaziz Yari retained his position as Director-General of the re-election campaign. Former Edo State Governor, Senator Adams Oshiomhole, serves as Deputy Director-General for Mobilization, while Chief of Staff to the President, Femi Gbajabiamila, takes on the role of Deputy Director-General for Administration. Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives, Benjamin Kalu, was named Deputy D-G South II, while the Speaker of the Rivers State House of Assembly, Martin Amaewhule, will serve as South-South Deputy Coordinator for State Assemblies Mobilization. Minister of Works, David Umahi, was appointed Deputy D-G for Infrastructure and Sensitization. Delta State Governor, Sheriff Oborevwori, has been named Director of Finance, while Ogun State Governor, Dapo Abiodun, and Chairman of the Nigeria Revenue Service, NRS, Zacch Adedeji, will jointly coordinate fund-raising operations. Former Kano State Governor, Abdullahi Ganduje, was named Director for Stakeholder Mobilization, while former Lagos State Governor, Babatunde Fashola, serves as the South-West Zonal Coordinator for Stakeholders’ Mobilization. Chief Ayiri Emami was named Director for Special Duties, while former Super Eagles captain, Joseph Yobo was appointed Deputy Director for Sports Sector Mobilization. A notable difference in the new list is the appointment of all 32 APC governors as campaign coordinators for their respective states, while Sharafadeen Alli, the party’s governorship candidate in Oyo, was appointed coordinator for the state. For Bauchi, Mohammed Abubakar, the APC governorship candidate, was appointed campaign coordinator, while Chijioke Chukwu, the party’s flagbearer in Abia, is coordinator for the state. Minister of Solid Minerals, Dele Alake, continues his role as Official Spokesman for the Campaign Council. Joining the media communications team are Minister of Aviation, Festus Keyamo, Abdulmumin Jibrin, Lere Olayinka (media aide to FCT Minister Wike), and Segun Sowunmi. In administrative and operational roles, Imo State Governor, Hope Uzodimma, continues as Secretary of the Campaign Council, supported by APC National Secretary, Senator Ajibola Bashiru, and Hadiza Bala-Usman as Deputy and Assistant Secretaries, respectively. Representative James Faleke will serve as Deputy Director-General for Election Planning, Coordination, and Monitoring. Unlike the first list, the new one contains 14 advisers, including Chief Bisi Akande, Aremo Segun Osoba, Secretary to the Government of the Federation, SGF, George Akume, former Cross-River south senator; Florence Ita-Giwa, former governor of Ogun State, Ibikunle Amosun, former APC national secretary, Iyiola Omisore, and former Coordinating Finance Minister, Wale Edun, among others. The expansion of the campaign structure underlines the ruling party’s strategy to build a broad-based political coalition as momentum builds toward the 2027 general elections. A statement by the APC National Secretary, Senator Ajibola Bashiru, said the campaign council will be inaugurated today. Why Tinubu pushed for Wike, Soludo, Adeleke despite internal push-backs Last night, details emerged on the strategic calculations behind President Tinubu’s decision to formally include non-APC political heavyweights, despite internal push-backs from key party stakeholders. The move followed concerns raised by a section of APC loyalists who privately urged the President to allow the trio operate and campaign for his re-election bid from outside the formal council structure. Party sources said opponents of the inclusion argued that integrating non-card-carrying members into official campaign structures could displace dedicated party loyalists, dilute party identity and trigger local friction in states such as Osun, Rivers and Anambra. Presidency sources and campaign strategists revealed that President Tinubu remained firm on their formal inclusion to ensure an all-inclusive campaign structure and to establish a unified management of campaign resources across non-APC controlled strongholds. According to insider accounts, the President’s decision was finalised only after receiving firm assurances of direct support and alignment from Wike, Soludo and Adeleke, with the agreement to trade off or retain other positions in their states. Rather than relying on informal or parallel external support groups, President Tinubu prioritised a consolidated command centre. “By formally designating the trio as state and regional campaign coordinators, the campaign administration aims to optimise resource allocation by consolidating campaign funding, logistics and grassroots mobilisation under single state-level coordinators to eliminate duplicated efforts and conflicting campaign machineries. “Furthermore, this approach builds a genuine coalition that transcends traditional party lines, while bringing influential allies into an accountable structure directly overseen by the President and the campaign directorate,” said the party source. Addressing resistance within APC ranks, party insiders noted that President Tinubu recognised the apprehensions of party stalwarts but viewed the broader electoral arithmetic as the over-arching priority. “By securing solid guarantees of commitment from Wike coordinating Rivers and the FCT, Governor Soludo coordinating Anambra, and Governor Adeleke coordinating Osun, the Presidency believes that pooling political weight directly within the official campaign council offers a far more effective electoral advantage than managing disconnected outside support movements,” another source added. President Tinubu is set to officially inaugurate the unified Presidential Campaign Council, PCC, at the Presidential Villa in Abuja today, signaling a firm push towards a broad, cross-party campaign structure. Why I’m leading Tinubu’s campaign in Rivers, FCT – Wike Speaking on the issue, during a media chat in Abuja yesterday, Wike said the decision was based on the need to accommodate people outside the APC who are willing to contribute to Tinubu’s re-election bid. “My thinking is that the president, in his wisdom, said there are those who are not members of our political parties but have something to offer to his re-election, and it’s proper to accommodate them,” he said. He added that the campaign should bring together people willing to support Tinubu’s continuation in office, regardless of their party affiliations. Rainbow Coalition has come to stay, Wike tells APC govs Wike also declared that his Rainbow Coalition backing President Bola Tinubu’s re-election has come to stay, saying there was “nothing anybody can do about it.” Asked if his inclusion in the APC PCC had silenced his critics, who were mainly APC governors, he said: “I don’t know where you are getting all these from. Problem that does not exist. I don’t know what concerns there are. As far as I am concerned, there is no problem.” Speaking in his monthly media chat, he dismissed suggestions that the coalition had unsettled APC governors or could encourage defections from the ruling party, and challenged anyone unhappy with the arrangement to take the matter up with him directly. “If you have any problem against me, come out and face Wike. Don’t go under the Rainbow Coalition. For Rainbow Coalition, it has come. It will stay. There is nothing anybody can do about it,” he said. Wike, who coordinates the coalition’s activities in Rivers State and the FCT, said the initiative puts APC members and Tinubu’s supporters in other parties on one platform. “If you see that word, PBAT/APC, it means those who are supporting the president who are not members of the party, together with the party, are working together to achieve that purpose,” he said. He cited Governors Soludo and Adeleke, as political figures associated with the coalition’s state-level coordination. The minister, who noted that the coalition was not meant to displace APC, said the party remains the platform on which the president will seek re-election, while supporters outside it could work towards the same goal. “The major thing is Mr President. Whatever we are going to do, whoever has any idea or anything to contribute is to the success of Mr President. That is the whole thing,” he said. He pointed to the FCT as proof that the arrangement works, adding that “we are going to vote for Mr. President, and the National Assembly candidates are for APC. Why would anybody say there is a problem there?” Wike also rejected the idea that the arrangement is new in Nigerian politics, adding that such backing existed before without being formalised. “But this time, it came out because of the period we are in,” he said. He accused opposition politicians of misleading Nigerians about Tinubu’s performance, saying “whether anybody likes it or not, Mr President has done well.” To show that praise for the president could come from outside the APC, he pointed to remarks attributed to the governor of Bauchi State, Bala Mohammed, of the Allied Peoples Movement, APM, acknowledging aspects of Tinubu’s performance. “Politics must not be played as a do-or-die affair,” Wike said, adding that he had never hidden where he stood. Only baby politicians’re kicking against Rainbow Coalition Wike also said only baby politicians were kicking against the Rainbow Coalition, citing Edo State, where he said a similar cross-party alliance defeated the then governor’s preferred successor. He dismissed claims that backing President Bola Tinubu through the coalition would confuse supporters of other parties. He said he had told his supporters to back the president, while also telling them their own National Assembly candidates mattered. “Anybody who says he does not recognise the importance of rainbow coalition is not a politician. Anybody who said that is a baby politician. Is there any conflict? There is no conflict. How does it confuse people?” he queried. Wike then turned to Edo, where, he said, the then governor, Godwin Obaseki, was determined to install a successor. He said he supported the APC, though he belonged to the PDP, adding “I did not support Obaseki, even though I was and still a member of PDP.” He said a PDP faction known as the Legacy group led by the late Chief Dan Orbih had joined hands with APC. “That legacy group and APC now met to work together, and that was how they defeated Obaseki’s successor. If we did not do that, it would have been difficult for APC to defeat Obaseki,” he explained. Tinubu will win on first ballot The minister equally declared that President Tinubu will win the 2027 presidential election on the first ballot, ruling out the possibility of a run-off. “I have not seen any likelihood of a run-off,” he said. Asked about the legacy Tinubu will be leaving behind should he lose re-election, Wike said: “It will be wrong for me to even answer that kind of question. He will be returned. Nigerians will return him.” Wike also denied working against three governors of the APC, including Hope Uzodimma of Imo State; AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq of Kwara State; and Inuwa Yahaya of Gombe State. According to him, it will be wrong to accuse him of sponsoring candidates against the governors. “It is very much unfair,” he said. Wike, who insisted his party is entitled to field candidates, said further: “I am not in their party. So you can’t tell me my party cannot have candidates.” He said backing the president did not stop him from doing that. “The mere fact I supported President Tinubu, which I did in 2023, and I am still doing does not mean we cannot field candidates at other levels,” he said. Wike said he made no deal with the governors, citing Uzodimma as proof of his good faith and invited the governor to say whether he had backed him in his second-term bid. “Ask Governor Hope. If he is a sincere person, he will tell you the role I played in his re-election,” Wike said. He said politicians commonly hope their rivals would stumble, adding that every person prayed for his opponent to make a mistake. “So, I have no hand”, he said of the situation in Kwara between the governor and former Senate President, Bukola Saraki. Why Fubara isn’t coordinating Tinubu’s campaign in Rivers The minister said he is coordinating President Tinubu’s re-election campaign in Rivers State because the situation there is peculiar. Rivers is the only state the campaign is not coordinated by a sitting APC governor, Siminalayi Fubara, adding that the job called for a particular kind of leadership. “Look, in an election, it takes a lot of leadership, there are a lot of things that are involved. You require somebody who has a buy-in,” Wike said. Describing the situation in Rivers as “peculiar,” Wike rejected the suggestion that Governor Fubara had been sidelined. “No, he has not been pushed aside,” he said. Asked whether Fubara would be involved in the campaign, he replied: “Of course,”, adding that the governor will take part at every level, from the state to the national. Wike, who noted that Fubara is not an unwilling participant in the president’s campaign, said: “He is happy with the role we are giving him. If he is not happy, why would you hold a meeting in his house? “Do you know what it takes to hold a meeting in his house for everybody to be there? Fubara is fully a member, fully plays his part. What is of concern to Fubara, whether he is running or not, is to keep his political family intact.” Wike blames ‘some govs’ for rift with Fubara The minister blamed some governors for the rift between him and Fubara, saying they are now working together and that Fubara is happily working for PresidentTinubu. He said people who never meant well for the governor were behind the trouble. “We are all one, we have forgiven each other, we have come together but the truth still remains the evil works of some Nigerians is the cause,” he said. Asked whether he was positioning Fubara for a ministerial role when he leaves office next year, Wike said the decision is not his. “I am not the president to choose who will be a minister. I don’t have right to nominate,” he stressed.. The post APC drafts PDP, Accord, APGA into Tinubu’s campaign council appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: In Philippines’ external defense push, resilience boils down to logistics
body:
As the Revised AFP Modernization Act approaches the end of its 15-year horizon, what upgrades are in store for the Philippine military?
MODERN FLEET. The BRP Tarlac (LD-601) sails in waters close to Bajo de Masinloc (Scarborough Shoal) alongside partner navies for an ADMM-Plus joint sail in September 2026.
PART 1: Of drones, dreams, and endless possibilities for the Philippine Navy
SUBIC, Philippines â When visiting the Philippine Navyâs newest warships at the Naval Operating Base (NOB) in Subic, most people â including military personnel â go through at least three gates. The long wait at the first gate speaks volumes of how the vision of a modern armed forces turns into reality.
Despite its ambitions, the Navy does not have its own docking facility to accommodate its brand-new frigates and offshore patrol vessels (OPVs). The big shipyard here that holds the countryâs finest warships is owned by private firm Agila Subic Compass, which assigns its own civilian security at the first two gates that visitors enter.
Yet, what a sight to behold â a fleet of six modern gray ships now owned by a navy of an archipelago that had, for decades, had to make do with hand-me-downs from its allies.
In August when we paid a visit one damp and humid evening, we saw the BRP Diego Silang (FFG-07) berth at the shipyard after almost a week out at sea for a maritime patrol and joint drills with Australia and the United States. Already docked beside the spot allocated for her was a fleet of the Navyâs pride â modern frigates that were acquired, in relative rapid succession, under the Revised Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) Modernization Act.
Silang docked beside her sister ship, the BRP Miguel Malvar , which was commissioned in the summer of 2025. With them were two similar ships, BRP Jose Rizal and BRP Antonio Luna , the first brand-new frigates that the Navy acquired in 2020 and 2021 after a long wait. Before this, the Navy had to live with old ships from other countries which it would refurbish.
Flanking the frigates were the modern fleetâs first and latest acquisitions.
The BRP Tarlac , an Indonesia-made landing platform dock, was the first major vessel to be delivered in 2016 under the new modernization program. Beside it stood a similar ship, the BRP Davao del Sur . Both Tarlac and Davao del Sur are the largest of the Navyâs vessels that perform a wide array of tasks â humanitarian and disaster response, as well as resupply missions for features in the West Philippine Sea.
Beside Tarlac was the BRP Ramon Alcaraz , a US coast guard cutter commissioned to the Philippines in 2013. Sheâs a senior citizen in human years, but remains a steady and reliable workhorse for the fleet, especially for maritime patrols in all fronts of the countryâs maritime spaces.
On the other side of the lineup was the freshly commissioned BRP Rajah Lakandula , an OPV. It was the first to berth at the Naval Station Jose Andrada in Manila, after dredging work in the area.
That the Philippine Navyâs newest and most modern platforms are docked in a private facility in Subic, where the government must pay fees for usage, illustrates the difficulties the AFP continues to face despite strides in modernization since 2012.
The privately owned NOB-Subic is still the largest port facility for the Navy. The waters off the Naval Station Heracleo Alano in Cavite (popularly known as Sangley Point) are far too shallow for the newest assets of the Philippine Fleet.
This is why the defense department is looking to finally acquire and convert some 300 hectares of the state-owned Philippine Veterans Investment Development Corporation (Phividec) Industrial Estate in Tagoloan, Misamis Oriental, into a naval base that will include drydock facilities. However, over a year since Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. confirmed that the department was proceeding with the planned acquisition, talks have yet to wrap up.
Things were vastly different a dozen years ago.
Then-military chief Gregorio Catapang Jr. recalled that in one naval gunfire exercise, rust icicles would fall on the beddings of sailors inside a hand-me-down battleship. At the time, the Navyâs newest vessel was the BRP Conrado Yap , a secondhand corvette from the South Korean Navy. Before her were the secondhand vessels from the US, the Del Pilar class.
Today, more vessels are coming â mostly brand-new ones, although both Japan and South Korea are also set to transfer their existing five and two warships each.
The Indonesia-made BRP Tarlac and BRP Davao del Sur , named after the home provinces of the presidents under whom they were commissioned, will soon be joined by the BRP Ilocos Norte and the BRP Leyte . At least four more OPVs of the BRP Rajah Sulayman class will be delivered to the Philippines, and the BRP Diego Silang will eventually be joined by two more sister ships.
Senior officers of the military are not one to take for granted the relative speed at which modernization has taken place.
At the end of a maritime drill in August 2026, Captain John Percie Alcos was asked about the strides the Navy has made in its modernization plan in over a decade. Alcos was the last commander of the first BRP Miguel Malvar (PS-19) before it was decommissioned in 2021. The first Malvar was a US warship that was transferred to Vietnam before eventually finding her way to the Philippine Navy. Alcos also commanded the BRP Andres Bonifacio (PS-42) of the Del Pilar class, before being appointed Navy spokesperson and eventually, the first commanding officer of the new Silang .
âWe have always been able to perform our mandate with the limited assets that we used to have. Now, with the assets in our inventory, we can do more and perform our mandate,â he told reporters.
But where do they go? Where would they be serviced?
SILANGâS CHIEF. Captain John Percie Alcos is the first commanding officer of the BRP Diego Silang.
The AFPâs long-overdue modernization, to a large extent, was spurred by China.
In 2012 , the Philippine Navy was in a brief standoff with Chinese maritime forces in Bajo de Masinloc (Scarborough Shoal).
By June that year, the Philippines eventually withdrew the white-hulled Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) vessel , expecting China to do the same under a deal supposedly brokered by the United States. Beijing stayed.
To this day, at least one China Coast Guard (CCG) ship is stationed at the opening of the shoal, with at least one or two more roving within its vicinity. Chinese Maritime Militia serve as force multipliers in Beijingâs sovereignty claim over the shoal.
In early December 2012, the Philippine Congress passed Republic Act No. 10349 or the Revised Armed Forces of the Philippines Modernization Program Act, a 15-year plan divided into three horizons.
Chinaâs actions and apparent aspirations in the West Philippine Sea, an area that includes the Philippinesâ exclusive economic zone (EEZ) and features where it has sovereignty claims, is the most obvious priority in the military and the reason for the Navyâs shift in focus to external defense .
But the western front is only one of five critical spots that the Navy must cover, through its fleet, the Marines, and other units that monitor and detect potential threats.
To the east is the Pacific Ocean, with the yet-to-be-tapped Philippine Rise in the northeastern part of the countryâs vast maritime area. The âbigger domainâ east to the Philippines is where the military must âstart building infrastructure and logistical bases,â said Teodoro in an August 2026 budget hearing.
Down south are both sea-lanes and porous borders between the southernmost Philippines and neighbors Malaysia and Indonesia.
Between the major island groups are archipelagic sea-lanes that are vital not only for domestic use but also for international trade and freedom of navigation. The Philippine Archipelagic Sea Lanes Act codified the 2016 Arbitral Award by identifying where foreign vessels, including the military kind, may pass.
Up north is where the AFP, non-uniformed experts, and pundits may feel the most anxious. Taiwan, an issue that for China is even touchier than the South China Sea, is a flashpoint for tensions not only between independently governed Taipei and Beijing, but the rest of the region.
Self-proclaimed Chinese scholars have claimed that the northernmost Batanes province is part of Taiwan and therefore, also Chinaâs. The Chinese embassy in Manila, in September 2026, claimed âsovereign rightsâ over waters between Batanes and Taiwan.
Tensions over northernmost features started after the Philippines and Japan announced maritime delimitation talks .
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has ruled out offensive attacks from the Philippines, even in the event of a Taiwan conflict. But the sheer proximity of the countryâs northern provinces to Taiwan is also why Marcos has said that Manila would be dragged into the conflict âkicking and screaming.â
All of those potential flashpoints and weakpoints are where the Navy â the fleet, the Marines, and special units like the elite Special Warfare Force â is expected to always be on the frontlines and in the forefront.
Itâs a tall order when budgets are perennially tight, assets remain limited to serve a vast archipelago, and resource gaps exist.
But as one officer once put it, the Navy and the rest of the armed forces have always managed to do the most with even the barest of means.
On most days, Ulugan Bay in Palawan is a picture of calm.
Tucked in the middle of Palawan island, the bay is close to the Western Command (Wescom) in Puerto Princesa City, the site of an air base where American troops may preposition assets under the bilateral Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement. Itâs the center of West Philippine Sea operations for the Philippine military.
From Ulugan Bay, Pag-asa (Thitu) Island, the Philippinesâ farthest civilian-populated island in the west, is just around a dayâs sail away. It takes under two hours by military cargo plane to fly from Wescomâs Antonio Bautista Air Base to Rancudo Airfield in the remote island.
On a rainy June afternoon in 2024, the three vessels of the Del Pilar class â the BRP Gregorio del Pilar , the BRP Ramon Alcaraz , and the BRP Andres Bonifacio â were all moored in the middle of the bay as inclement weather slowly creeped into the Palawan mainland from the West Philippine Sea.
The Bonifacio had just narrowly missed bad weather in the West Philippine Sea after a weeklong Maritime Domain Awareness mission with reporters on board. The same weather conditions would cause a Chinese fishing vessel to run aground near Pag-asa (Thitu) Island.
The Del Pilar , former US Coast Guard cutters that were launched in the 1960s and commissioned into the Philippine Navy as frigates in 2011, 2013, and 2016, are the senior citizens of the Philippine Fleet.
They have since been upgraded beginning in the 2020s to more modern systems, as the South Korea-made frigates started arriving and the Del Pilar ships were reclassified as OPVs.
Dotting the shoreline of Ulugan Bay are private and public resorts and secluded homes â that is, until you get closer to Naval Detachment Oyster Bay, where smaller patrol ships, attack craft, and the Navyâs supply vessels are usually docked.
The detachment itself is surrounded by vast greenery.
In 2002, then-president Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo declared at least 1,838 hectares of land as part of the Ulugan Bay Naval Reservation, with most of it dedicated for what was then the proposed Naval Operating Base Ulugan.
More than two decades later, Oyster Bay is the site of major upgrades, thanks in part to the United States, treaty-ally of the Philippines. In 2025, the US announced several plans for the bay â a boat repair and maintenance facility , a fast boat base , and maintenance facility for unmanned surface vessels .
These planned upgrades are a huge boost to the capabilities of the Wescom, whose area of operation includes most of the West Philippine Sea â from the BRP Sierra Madre in Ayungin Shoal to Pag-asa (Thitu) Island, located beyond the countryâs EEZ.
Theyâre part of the Navyâs âbroader effort to strengthen the Armed Forces of the Philippinesâ external defense capabilities, particularly its ability to sustain maritime operations in the West Philippine Sea,â said Navy public affairs chief Captain Marie Angelica Sisican in a message to Rappler.
Sisican, citing Teodoroâs earlier statements from 2024, said naval facilities on the western side of Palawan would âreduce the distance that naval assets would otherwise have to cover in conducting operations.â
US-funded projects, including the boat maintenance facilities, are âintended to enhance the [Philippine Navyâs] repair and maintenance capabilities for watercraft, including unmanned surface vessels, while improving existing infrastructure.â
The facility will cater to both the AFP and the PCG for âcapabilities related to maritime security, maritime domain awareness, interoperability, and infrastructure development.â
Indeed, itâs the Wescom in Palawan and the Northern Command up north that have become the focus of US assistance.
Americaâs âonce-in-a-generation investmentâ was first announced in 2024, a total of $500 million in foreign military financing for the Philippines. This has since grown to a $2.5-billion commitment in military aid over five years, from 2026 to 2030, under the US 2026 National Defense Authorization Act signed in December 2025.
The support for the US-Philippine alliance is one of the bipartisan issues in a deeply divided Washington, an indication not just of shared values but of common strategic interests. Even as US President Donald Trump has signaled a âstrategic stabilityâ with China, America still wants a âfavorable, but durable, balance of power in which no state â including China â can impose its hegemony and hold the security or prosperity of our nation and our allies in question,â said US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore in May 2026.
But even with bipartisan support for aid to fund the Philippinesâ military upgrades, the White Houseâs message for partners and especially allies is clear: burdens must be shared. âAlliances only work when they are true partnerships. It is a two-way street. You don't have a strong alliance unless everyone has skin in the game. No freeloading,â said Hegseth in Singapore.
At the bridge of the BRP Diego Silang , a junior officer was calm as she pored over the lines that she would repeat many times over in the coming hour or so.
It was August 22, 2026, and a Chinese navy ship sailed nearby, some 7 nautical miles away, as the Silang headed to a point in Escoda (Sabina) Shoal for a maritime patrol and a joint sail with Australia and the United States. The Peopleâs Liberation Army (PLA) Navy ship had been trailing the Silang since the day prior.
It was her turn, as the junior officer on duty, to issue Silang's challenge to the interloper.
Before she could settle into her station, the speakers crackled. From it, the bridge heard the slow and deliberate voice of a Chinese sailor claiming Beijingâs "indisputable sovereigntyâ over Escoda Shoal, a low-tide feature where sovereignty cannot be claimed.
It was the Chinese warshipâs first response to the Silang after previous challenges went unanswered.
The junior officer and the rest of the crew were unperturbed. She picked up a phone handset and spoke deliberately. It was her voice that the bridge over at the Chinese navy ship heard. âPLA Navy 536, this is Philippine Navy warship 7. You are a state party to UNCLOS. You are endangering our security. Leave the vicinity immediately â over.â
The August 2026 exercise was just one of many the Silang has been part of since its commissioning in December 2025. There has been little rest â after its first exercise in Philippine waters was a long sojourn to Australia for the multilateral naval exercise Kakadu. Between drills with allied and partner navies, it spent a few weeks out at sea to safeguard a regional meeting.
Alcos, during the five-day mission at sea, showed some signs of tiredness, even as he was quick to say the pace of engagements is one that he welcomes. The Silangâs crew, especially its officers, are young and eager to learn.
Some had been assigned to older warships, a few more to the Rizal or the Malvar . Other personnel of the Silang may soon man the newly arrived OPVs. From her crew could be the future commanding officers of modern platforms â frigates, landing platform docks, or OPVs that are forthcoming.
At around 6:30 in the evening, the speaker system of the Silang crackled again â this time, for prayer that was slowly and deliberately recited for all of its crew to hear. Most of the lines were standard fare, but a few were specific to a soldierâs life.
â Ipagtanggol mo kami sa karahasan ng mga kalaban (Defend us from the enemyâs violent ways).â The short prayer also asked God to save the Silangâs crew and their comrades in the Navy from disaster and other harms out at sea.
In the vastness of the West Philippine Sea, faith is essential â in a God who looks after a ship and her crew, in skills that her officers have earned and honed through the years, and in a steadfast commitment to defend what Filipinos have always known is theirs. â Rappler.com

title: ‘NNPP to adopt presidential candidate soon’
body: T he New Nigeria Peoples Party (NNPP) will soon announce a frontline presidential candidate from another political platform to adopt for the 2027 presidential election, according to its founder, Dr. Boniface Aniebonam. In a statement issued on Tuesday in Abuja, Aniebonam explained that prolonged litigation over the party’s national leadership left the platform with insufficient time to process a standard-bearer capable of matching major contenders. He noted that following the Independent National Electoral Commission’s (INEC) recognition of the NNPP leadership led by Dr. Agbo Major as National Chairman, the party utilized a placeholder candidate while actively shopping for a presidential contender with character and capacity. “The NNPP is firm with its manifesto and requirements for a presidential candidate. We made a mistake with Kwankwaso in 2023 and do not want to repeat it,” Aniebonam stated. “The NNPP is not desperate to rule Nigeria at all cost. We believe that God has the final say and that the Almighty decides who can lead a nation, hence our stance on politics not being a do-or-die affair.” Aniebonam revealed that national leadership will convene shortly to finalize the adoption strategy before making a formal public declaration. He stressed that party members, alongside key stakeholders in the maritime, shipping, transport, and logistics sectors, will contribute to deciding which candidate receives the party’s endorsement. Clarifying the party’s broader strategy for the upcoming election cycle, the founder affirmed that the NNPP will focus its direct electoral contests on legislative and state executive positions. “For now, the only position we will no longer be contesting for is the presidency. By 2031, we will have a presidential candidate to compete favourably with other political parties,” Aniebonam added. (NAN)

title: Forum 2000 participants to join Global Crimea International Conference in Kyiv
body:
Tetiana Zhukova, senior international advocacy manager at the ZMINA Human Rights Center, said this in a comment to Ukrinform.
“We are cooperating with them, and this year they are helping us organize the Global Crimea conference for the first time,” Zhukova said.
She explained that several participants of the Forum 2000 conference, which took place in Prague earlier this week, will travel to Ukraine.
According to Zhukova, this will help promote the issue of Ukraine more actively among countries of the Global South and provide them with information about what is happening both in occupied Crimea and in Ukraine more broadly. As in previous years, the organizers plan to take participants – including experts, academics, journalists, human rights defenders and opinion leaders – to regions of Ukraine beyond Kyiv. They will also hold meetings with local residents, politicians, journalists and others.
The conference aims to strengthen Ukraine’s dialogue with countries of the Global South – in Asia, Africa and Latin America – and discuss global security challenges, the de-occupation of Crimea, the release of civilian detainees and other issues.
ZMINA took part in the Prague forum for the third time. Two years ago, the Center organized an event on Crimea on the sidelines of the conference.
This year’s forum marked its 30th anniversary. It brought together around 850 participants from 115 countries, with Ukraine having one of the largest delegations, numbering nearly 60 people, the organizers told Ukrinform. Ukraine was one of the central topics of the conference. In addition to discussions at various panels and workshops, a separate section of the program was dedicated to Ukraine.
“They have been highlighting Ukraine as a separate item for several years now. This is very important for getting information about what is happening in Ukraine to people on different continents for whom the issue of Ukraine is quite distant,” Zhukova noted.
As Ukrinform reported, the Days of Crimea held in the Czech Republic on September 17–20 aimed to remind politicians and the public of the problems faced by people in Ukraine’s temporarily occupied territories.

title: Senators come up flat as power play fizzles
body:
OTTAWA – As captain Thomas Chabot knows, he carries a certain responsibility to evaluate his team’s performance.
Tuesday night he clearly stated his Ottawa Senators just weren’t good enough.
“Not good, not good at all,” he said. “There’s no other way to put it.”
While the season is young, Tuesday’s 7-2 loss to the St. Louis Blues is a rare misstep on an otherwise impressive start to the season for the Senators. At 5-2-0 the Senators are off to one of their best starts in more than a decade.
“We had a game for a bit and we just didn’t have it, or the execution wasn’t great,” said Chabot. “We’re aware of it as a team, as a group, as players, and that’s all that matters and we’ll make sure we answer back.”
While it would be easy to call this a one-off there are issues that have to be of some concern to the Senators.
The power play continues to struggle. Ottawa was 1-for-4 with the man advantage Tuesday and has converted on just five of 33 power-play opportunities (15.2 per cent) through seven games.
“They’re not executing their passes first of all,” said head coach Travis Green. “Simple passes. We’re passing pucks that are rolling instead of passing it flat. I think it’s just the simple things. You’ve got to do those things well before you even start doing anything about the rest of the power play.”
Last season assistant coach Daniel Alfredsson was responsible for the power play, but with his departure to the Toronto Maple Leafs Ben Sexton has taken over the special teams duties.
Sexton is also missing a key piece of his top unit, with Jake Sanderson’s absence perhaps felt most on the power play. Sanderson hasn’t played since opening night, although Green is hopeful the defenceman could return this week.
Without Sanderson the Senators have struggled to get the puck out of their own end on the power play.
“At times we’ve had some chances and at times it hasn’t been great,” Chabot said. “Let’s call a spade a spade. We’re going to keep on nailing down details and maybe keep things a bit more simple and get some guys some traffic … It’s on us as players to dig in and find a way to make a difference early in the games.”
While the Senators would like to generate more with the man advantage they also need to ensure it’s not a liability. The Blues were able to score short-handed Tuesday to open the scoring.
“Yeah, I mean that’s a really good hockey team over there, and they’re 5-2 for a reason,” said Blues head coach Jim Montgomery. “But getting that short-handed goal was really key. Our penalty kill has been very good. I thought both special teams were good for us tonight, which is a really pleasant sign in our growth as a team.”
The Senators are dealing with growing pains of their own. Already without Sanderson and Artem Zub, Ottawa also lost Nikolas Matinpalo on Monday. That left the Senators with an inexperienced blue line Tuesday, with Carter Yakemchuk, Jorian Donovan and Hoyt Stanley combining for just 18 games of NHL experience.
Yakemchuk finished the game minus-5, but played 22:25.
Green admitted guys are being asked to play big minutes.
Veteran Claude Giroux says there are lessons to be learned from games like these.
“You’ve got to take the feeling that we have right now and make sure it doesn’t happen again.”
Ridly Greig left the game midway through the third. Green said he was dealing with a bit of a strain and felt it was best to keep him out for the remainder of the game.
Ottawa has played seven games over 11 days and was playing the back half of a back-to-back.
The Senators will take Wednesday off before they’re back in action Thursday against the New York Islanders.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

title: Nigeria’s next economic test is turning stability into better living standards
body: The World Bank’s October 2026 Nigeria Development Update, Beyond the Federal Purse: How Higher Revenues Shaped State Priorities, provides a useful framework for examining Nigeria’s transition. The country’s economic debate is entering a new phase, after years in which the central policy concerns were the removal of distortions, the restoration of macroeconomic stability and the rebuilding of confidence in the naira. The question now is: What benefits are the transition delivering for businesses, workers and households? The report recognises that economic growth has remained resilient, while higher oil prices have strengthened government revenues and the country’s external position. Yet it also warns that rising global fuel prices have interrupted the progress made in reducing inflation, leaving household purchasing power under pressure even as important macroeconomic indicators improve. The challenge is no longer simply to establish whether the reforms have improved the economy’s underlying indicators. It is to determine whether the resulting gains can support faster growth, create productive employment and raise living standards across a country where many households continue to struggle with the cost of food, transport, energy and other necessities. There are reasons to acknowledge the improvement in Nigeria’s macroeconomic position. The World Bank reports that real gross domestic product grew by 4.2 per cent in the first half of 2026, compared with 3.9 per cent and 3.5 per cent in the corresponding periods of 2025 and 2024, respectively. Growth was driven largely by services, alongside a stronger contribution from agriculture. The current-account surplus also widened to $12 billion in the first half of 2026, while gross external reserves rose above $54 billion in September. Higher oil prices have helped strengthen Nigeria’s export earnings and government revenues, but the benefits depend partly on how much oil the country can produce and sell, the cost of production and the obligations attached to some future oil receipts. Consequently, an increase in the international price of crude does not automatically translate into an equivalent increase in the revenue immediately available to the government. The improvement in the external position also needs to be interpreted alongside the sources of foreign-exchange inflows. The World Bank notes that portfolio investment has contributed substantially to the accumulation of reserves. While such inflows can strengthen the foreign-exchange market, their sustainability depends partly on investor confidence and financial-market conditions, making them different from a durable expansion of non-oil exports and productive investment. Inflation remains another constraint. The rise in global fuel prices following the conflict in the Middle East, combined with seasonal food-price pressures, has interrupted the decline that began in early 2025.
