Higher fuel and transport costs affect more than the prices consumers pay directly at filling stations; they also feed into the cost of moving agricultural produce, distributing manufactured goods and operating businesses. Consequently, an economy can record stronger output, a better external balance and higher government revenues without households experiencing a corresponding improvement in their purchasing power. Macroeconomic stability creates the conditions for recovery, but it does not guarantee that the benefits will be broadly distributed. The World Bank’s examination of state finances brings the discussion closer to the quality of economic management. Between 2023 and 2025, aggregate state revenues increased by about 93 per cent in real terms, while expenditure rose by approximately 92 per cent. The share of total state expenditure devoted to capital spending increased from 46 per cent to 61 per cent, with transport infrastructure accounting for the largest increase. These figures suggest that state governments have used part of the additional fiscal space to expand investment in infrastructure and other economic activities. Better roads, reliable water supplies, functioning schools and accessible healthcare can reduce the costs faced by businesses and households, improve productivity and create conditions for private investment. However, the composition of public spending deserves as much attention as its overall size. The World Bank reports that education’s share of state expenditure declined from 14.9 per cent in 2021 to 12.1 per cent in 2025, while health spending remained broadly stable at around seven per cent. Social protection’s share increased from 1.4 per cent to 4.4 per cent. Although expenditure on education and health increased in absolute terms, their slower growth relative to economic infrastructure raises questions about whether states are allocating sufficient resources to the human capabilities required for sustained development. Infrastructure and human capital should not be treated as competing priorities. A road may improve access to markets, but the productivity of the people using it depends on their health, education and skills. Industrial expansion requires electricity and transport infrastructure, but it also requires a workforce capable of operating modern equipment, maintaining quality and adopting new technologies. There is a further concern about the capacity of states to sustain these improvements. The World Bank reports that only Lagos and Enugu generated enough internally generated revenue to cover their recurrent expenditure in 2025. The continued dependence of most states on federal allocations leaves their budgets vulnerable to changes in federation revenue and underscores the need to strengthen local revenue administration without imposing unnecessary burdens on productive economic activity.

title: Why Atiku defeated Tinubu in Kaduna in 2023-APC
body: The Kaduna State Publicity Secretary of the All Progressives Congress (APC), Mohammed Sani Haruna, has attributed the opposition’s performance in the 2023 general election in the state to dissatisfaction with the administration of former Governor Nasir El-Rufai. Haruna said the outcome of the election reflected voters’ discontent with the former governor’s style of leadership, which he accused of demolishing houses and markets, sacking thousands of workers and exploiting religious and ethnic differences in the state. He said the situation had changed under Governor Uba Sani, whose administration, according to him, had adopted an inclusive approach that brought people across religious, ethnic and political divides into the APC. The APC spokesman stated this while briefing journalists on preparations to receive President Bola Ahmed Tinubu in Kaduna State for the flag-off of the party’s 2027 presidential campaign, scheduled for October 24, 2026. “Most elections are always a referendum on leadership at a particular time in history. So, the election in Kaduna State in 2023 was a referendum on the governing style of the former governor of Kaduna State,” Haruna said. He added that the previous administration’s policies had alienated some sections of the state, particularly Southern Kaduna, where voters had traditionally supported opposition parties. “The people of the state were not happy with the governing style of that governor during that time,” he said. Haruna argued that Governor Uba Sani’s approach to governance had changed the political landscape, claiming that the APC now controlled all elective positions in the state. He said the governor had demonstrated respect for people irrespective of their religion, ethnicity, socioeconomic status or cultural background, adding that this had encouraged more people to identify with the ruling party. According to him, the APC’s current political position in Kaduna State differs from the situation before the 2023 election, when opposition parties secured significant victories. Haruna, however, expressed confidence that the APC would secure widespread support in the state during the 2027 elections, including for President Tinubu’s re-election bid. He said Governor Uba Sani had assured the president that Kaduna would deliver two million votes for him, describing the target as achievable because of the governor’s leadership and the party’s growing support. “Today, we assure Mr President and the entire APC family that Kaduna State will lead the way in securing his re-election on May 29, 2027,” he said. The APC spokesman also dismissed suggestions that the opposition could repeat its 2023 performance, insisting that the ruling party’s control of elective positions across the state reflected a shift in political alignment. He said the party was preparing to mobilise hundreds of thousands of supporters to welcome Tinubu and other APC leaders to Kaduna for the campaign flag-off. Haruna added that a dedicated media centre had been established to provide journalists with timely and accurate information about preparations for the event. He said the planned rally would demonstrate the party’s support for Tinubu and the commitment of the Kaduna APC to his re-election campaign.

title: Shekarau vows to mobilise northern votes for Tinubu
body: Ahead of the 2027 general elections, prominent northern political leaders under the banner of the Arewa for Asiwaju (A4A) movement have pledged to mobilize voters across the 19 northern states and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) to secure victory for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and the All Progressives Congress (APC). The delegation, led by the Chairman of the Board of Trustees (BOT), Senator Ibrahim Shekarau, and Deputy BOT Chairman, former Plateau State Governor Simon Lalong, met with the APC National Chairman, Dr. Nentawe Yilwatda, at the party’s national secretariat in Abuja. Presenting the group’s roadmap, Senator Shekarau explained that A4A was established to complement the official APC structure by deploying an experienced reserve of political strategists, former governors, and legislators to address voter apathy and maximize northern vote returns. “What we are doing is adding color to the APC, which is the mother of all,” Shekarau said. “We are very conscious of the number of voters in the North, which remains the largest in the country. Our objective is to ensure that our voter turnout is not only repeated but significantly expanded compared to previous elections.” Shekarau revealed that A4A has established over 20 functional directorates and appointed coordinators across all states, local government areas, and electoral wards. He added that the group has compiled a comprehensive catalog of President Tinubu’s infrastructural projects and policy achievements across the North to counter opposition narratives claiming the region has been neglected. He formally invited the party leadership to the grand commissioning of the A4A operational secretariat in Abuja, scheduled for Saturday, October 17, confirming that Vice President Kashim Shettima will perform the official commissioning. Corroborating Shekarau’s remarks, Lalong, described A4A as a strategic reserve unit composed of seasoned political veterans working in sync with the APC Presidential Campaign Council. Welcoming the delegation, APC National Chairman Dr. Nentawe Yilwatda praised the inclusivity, regional balance, and political weight of the A4A coalition, noting that the group effectively dispels claims that the North does not support the Tinubu administration. “Anyone from the North who sees the faces in this group feels included,” Yilwatda said. “Where are the people saying the North doesn’t like Mr. President? Is it the former governors, former speakers, or former senate presidents? Most of them are right here in this group. Now we have a unified voice that speaks for the North.”

title: Fire breaks out near Russian metallurgical plant after reported drone attack
body:
A fire has broken out in the Russian industrial city of Balakovo following reports of Ukrainian drone strikes on Oct. 14, according to Telegram monitoring channels.
Footage shows an explosion and subsequent fire after a reported drone strike near a large metallurgical plant in Balakovo, located in the Saratov region, according to reports by the Exilenova+ Telegram channel. The region experienced widespread power outages as a result of the attack, the channel reported.
Balakovo, a city on the east bank of the Volga River, is home to a large steel mill with a stated capacity of over 1 million tons per year, according to the Balakovo Metallurgical Plant’s website. It was not immediately clear as to whether the plant was damaged in the attack.
Saratov’s regional governor claimed that the drone attack damaged several buildings and killed one person in a statement on Telegram.
Elsewhere in Russia, a fire at an oil-loading terminal in Rostov-on-Don was reported to be burning for a fourth day following drone strikes on Oct. 10.
A reported drone strike over the weekend hit the oil terminal, which is located in the city’s industrial Zheleznodorozhny district. The terminal handles petroleum products for export, including shipments from the Novoshakhtinsk Oil Refinery.
Rostov Oblast Regional Governor Yuriy Slyusar claimed that over 100 drones had been struck down that night in a statement on Telegram.
Footage published on the Exilenova+ Telegram channel shows rising flames and a thick cloud of smoke. The fire, which has burned for three days, had died down to a smolder before flaring up again, Exilenova+ reported.
As of Oct. 13, at least eight of the Novoshakhtinsk terminal’s 12 tanks have been put out of service, according to an OSINT analysis by the independent Russian outlet Astra . The facility, which can receive and load an estimated 2.5 to 3.5 million tons of oil products a year, handles exports and also supplies the Russian armed forces, the outlet said.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the reports. No information was immediately available on the extent of the damage for either attack.
While Ukrainian officials have not yet commented on the reported attack on the terminal, Ukrainian forces have repeatedly targeted Russian energy facilities in recent months.
Last week, U.S. President Donald Trump declared an energy ceasefire, and demanded that Ukraine stop targeting Russian oil facilities. He claimed that these attacks contributed to heightened oil prices, widely attributed to the US war in Iran.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said he would be willing to agree to an energy ceasefire if Russian forces stop targeting Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

title: Slovakia delays connecting fourth power unit of Mochovce NPP to grid — agency
body:
BRATISLAVA, October 14. /TASS/. Utility Slovenske Elektrarne has decided to delay connecting the fourth power unit of the Mochovce Nuclear Power Plant (NPP) in central Slovakia to the grid, the TASR news agency reported.
Slovenske Elektrarne, the operator of two nuclear power plants in in the country, postponed the connection scheduled for Tuesday due to an unusual reaction during technical tests, according to the report.
On June 29, Slovak media reported the start of the process to bring the NPP’s new power unit online. It was also announced that the loading of nuclear fuel had begun for the reactor of the fourth power unit at the Mochovce NPP, which was built using Soviet technology. The fuel was supplied by a Rosatom subsidiary.

title: Why many Nigerians spend more on phone repairs than buying new phones
body: By Miracle Onyemuwa The rising cost of smartphones in Nigeria is forcing more consumers to repair damaged devices rather than replace them with new ones. This is more so, as inflation and the depreciation of the naira continue to push phone prices higher. At Computer Village, Ikeja, phone repair shops are seeing increasing numbers of customers bringing in devices with cracked screens, damaged charging ports and faulty batteries. At a repair centre, Kornerstone Technology, one of the engineers who spoke to TechXtra, said screen replacements currently account for about 80 per cent of the shop’s jobs. He said: “Eighty per cent of our jobs this month are screen replacements. Today’s screens are more delicate than eggs. I don’t know why phone makers are doing that. iPhone 11, iPhone 12, Samsung A32 and Samsung A23 are among the phones frequently brought in here for repairs and screen replacements.” Revealing the cost for the screens, he said the shop charges about N25, 000 for a copy screen for an iPhone 11 and N45,000 for an original screen. He also said that battery replacement costs between N10, 000 and N20,000, while charging-port repairs range from N7,000 to N15,000. For him, the increasing cost of original replacement parts has also encouraged technicians to salvage genuine components from damaged or dead phones to reduce repair costs for customers. The preference for repairs is also evident among owners of lower- and mid-range smartphones. At Divine Mercy Enterprises, also in Computer Village, another repairer said charging-port damage, cracked screens and swollen batteries were among the most common faults he handled. He said Tecno Spark and Infinix Hot models were among the phones customers most frequently brought for repairs. He explained that children sometimes damage charging ports by forcing USB cables into the phones incorrectly. Factor fuelling repairs Other factors fuelling phone repairs, according to the engineers, is the rainy season. Water-damaged phones are also flooding the repair tables . A lady who introduced herself simply as Aisha who came to repair her phone in one of the shops said her child threw her Infinix Hot 50 into the water. “I opted to repair this phone because I don’t have the money to replace it. I can’t cough out over N300,000, which I am sure this phone costs now. Even if it costs me N50,000 to repair, I am ready to pay. Cost of repairs Repair costs vary according to the phone model and the severity of the fault. Screen replacement for low- and mid-range devices generally costs between N10,000 and N40,000, while repairs for high-end phones can range from N50,000 to N150,000 or more depending on the phone model. Battery replacements cost between N5,000 and N20,000, while charging-port repairs typically range from N3,000 to N15,000. For many consumers, the difference between repair costs and the price of a replacement phone makes repairing an existing device a more practical option. Repair culture Nigeria’s long-standing repair culture has also contributed to the trend, with technicians developing skills in salvaging usable components from damaged electronics and extending the lifespan of devices rather than discarding them. The growing dependence on smartphones has further increased the importance of keeping existing devices functional. For many Nigerians, phones are used not only for communication but also for mobile banking, business transactions and point-of-sale services. The post Why many Nigerians spend more on phone repairs than buying new phones appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Tompolo warns against repeat of 2023 setback in Lagos
body: Leader of the PBAT Door-to Door Movement, Government Ekpemupolo, popularly known as Tompolo, has urged Lagos residents to ensure President Bola Ahmed Tinubu secures a convincing victory in the 2027 presidential election. Tompolo, who called on residents to obtain their Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs) ahead of the election, said the outcome of the 2023 presidential election in Lagos must not be repeated in 2027. He made the call on Tuesday during a campaign rally in Lagos, where the movement presented 57 vehicles to its state coordinators as part of efforts to mobilise support for Tinubu’s re-election. Represented by Kestin Pondi, Tompolo described Tinubu as a courageous and selfless leader who had continued to implement economic reforms despite the political implications, adding that Nigerians were beginning to benefit from the policies. “What happened in 2023 must not repeat. He must win convincingly in 2027,” he said. He urged Lagos residents to take advantage of the ongoing Continuous Voter Registration exercise by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to register and obtain their PVCs, stressing that electoral victory could only be secured through votes. Tompolo attributed Lagos’s development to the foundation laid by Tinubu during his tenure as governor of the state between 1999 and 2007, arguing that successive administrations had built on his achievements. He said Tinubu’s experience in Lagos had positioned him to replicate similar development across the country, adding that the president needed the support of his home state to sustain his reform agenda at the national level. “Lagos is the city for all Nigerians because someone stood firm to restructure and reform it. From the time he came into office in 1999 up to 2007 that he left, Lagos was the envy of other states,” he said. He added that the president’s current responsibility offered an opportunity to extend the development model associated with Lagos to other parts of the country. “Today, he has a higher responsibility, an opportunity to replicate the Lagos success story in Nigeria through reforms. There is massive development across the states today because reforms are working,” he stated. Tompolo urged members of the movement and other supporters to take the re-election campaign to households across Lagos, saying sustained grassroots mobilisation was necessary to secure Tinubu’s victory. Also speaking at the rally, Lagos State Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu expressed confidence in the Tinubu administration, saying the country was moving towards economic stability under the president’s leadership. Sanwo- Olu urged voters to reject opposition politicians whom he accused of lacking clear plans for the country, arguing that frequent movement between political parties demonstrated inconsistency in leadership. The governor also highlighted what he described as the administration’s achievements in infrastructure, workers’ welfare and education, citing road construction, support for students, the increase in the national minimum wage and the availability of funds for pension payments. “Why won’t we vote for him? The entire Lagos is for Tinubu. All our votes are for Tinubu. You’ve done it before, you’ll do it again,” Sanwo-Olu said. He urged campaign coordinators to intensify their mobilisation efforts across the state and persuade residents to support the president’s re-election bid. “We will touch every corner of Lagos with our message to reelect Tinubu. Go out and convince everyone that Tinubu is the candidate to vote,” he stated. Earlier, the National Coordinator of the PBAT Door-to-Door Movement, Sunday Asuku, called on Lagos residents to obtain their PVCs and use them to express their support for Tinubu at the polls. Asuku said the movement was committed to securing the president’s re-election through lawful electoral participation rather than intimidation. “We must stand our ground and deliver Tinubu with PVCs, not with guns or intimidation. Lagos must not put their son, Tinubu, to shame,” he said.

title: E-commerce, championing Nigeria’s digital journey?
body: •Online shopping sector jumps 15 points to 75% in new report •Customer satisfaction hits 71% despite service quality decline in key sectors •Power, Public Sector trail at 51%, 53% By Prince Osuagwu E-Commerce appears to be one sector in Nigeria where customers are not complaining as much as they used to. While poor service continues to dog several sectors of the economy, e-commerce appears to be quietly winning the hearts of Nigerian consumers. The online shopping business emerged as Nigeria’s best-performing sector in customer satisfaction in 2025, scoring 75 per cent — a remarkable 15 percentage-point jump from its 2024 score of 60 per cent. And that is not all. The sector’s 2025 performance came against a rather gloomy backdrop in which nine of the 12 sectors measured recorded lower scores than in the previous reporting period. In other words, while service quality was falling in several parts of the economy, e-commerce was going in the opposite direction. The finding is contained in the 2025 State of Customer Service in Nigeria Report, released by the Nigeria Customer Service Index, NCSI, in a review of Nigeria’s 66th Independence anniversary and the 2026 Customer Service Week. The report, powered by the West Africa Association of Customer Service Professionals, WAACSP, is based on 21,387 responses covering more than 1,500 organisations across all 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory. From the report, the numbers tell an interesting story. Nigeria’s overall Customer Satisfaction Index, NCSI, benchmark climbed from 61 per cent in 2023 to 67 per cent in 2024 and 71 per cent in 2025. But beneath that headline improvement lies a curious contradiction. Despite the national satisfaction score hitting an all-time high, the report says nine out of the 12 sectors recorded lower scores than in the previous reporting period. So, where did the satisfaction come from? E-commerce appears to have provided part of the answer. The sector did not merely retain its position among the better-performing industries. It moved decisively to the top, scoring 75 per cent, ahead of Real Estate at 72 per cent. Telecommunications also recorded modest improvement, rising by one percentage point. At the organisation level, Slot emerged number one in e-commerce, followed by Jumia and Konga. Interestingly, e-commerce has not just appeared suddenly on the customer-service radar. Jumia, Konga and Slot have featured in the NCSI every year from 2023 to 2025, showing that the sector’s major players have maintained visibility in the index over time. Why online shoppers are now happier Providing a clue, the report found that customer trust was the number-one priority in every sector, but e-commerce recorded the highest trust rating of all sectors at a striking 90 per cent. That is significant in an economy where consumers are increasingly demanding convenience, transparency and quick responses from businesses. For the online shopper, the customer journey is increasingly digital. If they are not searching for products, they are comparing prices, ordering, tracking delivery and raising complaints. The NCSI says its survey measured customer experiences across areas including trust, professionalism, competence, complaint resolution, ease of doing business, processes and procedures, staff engagement and customer-focused innovation. The 75 per cent e-commerce score therefore suggests that, despite the complaints that still surround online shopping, customers are finding enough improvement in the experience to give the sector a strong vote of confidence. But there is also another interesting twist. While Power struggles, e-commerce surges. The contrast with some other sectors could hardly be sharper. For instance, Transportation suffered the biggest decline, falling 13 percentage points, while Power and the Public Sector each dropped by 10 points. Power ended the ranking at just 51 per cent, while the Public Sector scored 53 per cent. Negative public sentiment was also highest in the Public Sector, at 44 per cent, and Power, at 43 per cent. Yet e-commerce was sitting at the other end of the table with 75 per cent satisfaction and 90 per cent customer trust. It is a striking picture of two Nigerias: one where customers are still battling service failures, and another where digital platforms are gradually learning how to make convenience part of the service. The e-commerce climb The journey becomes even more interesting when the figures are placed side by side. In 2023, Hospitality was the highest-performing sector at 73 per cent, while the Public Sector was lowest at 47 per cent. In 2024, Transportation took the lead at 73 per cent, while E-commerce was at the bottom of the table among the reported sector extremes with 60 per cent. Then came 2025, and e-commerce exploded to the top with 75 per cent. That 15-point jump is arguably the most dramatic sectoral improvement in the latest report. And it could be telling Nigerian businesses something important: customers may forgive many things, but they increasingly reward businesses that make their lives easier. But there is a warning; the e-commerce success story does not mean Nigeria has solved its customer-service problem. The NCSI and WAACSP are urging organisations to focus on trust-building, faster complaint resolution and consistent service delivery, particularly in the Public Sector and Power. They also recommend combining digital convenience with reliable traditional customer support. The report further cautions that the survey had a strong concentration in Lagos and Abuja. Of the 21,387 responses, Lagos accounted for 9,897 responses, or 46.75 per cent, while Abuja contributed 2,994, or 14.14 per cent. Together, the two locations accounted for 60.89 per cent of all responses. So, while the numbers provide a fascinating snapshot of customer sentiment, the researchers say broader participation outside Lagos and Abuja would strengthen future comparisons. Still, one message from the 2025 numbers is difficult to ignore. As traditional sectors struggle with complaints over service quality, e-commerce appears to be showing that Nigerians can still be satisfied when technology, convenience and customer experience come together. For an economy increasingly moving from the physical to the digital marketplace, that may be the beginning of an even bigger story in 2026 and beyond. title: Ex-VP challenges Wike to disclose sources of funding for broadcast media chats
body: Paul Ibe, the Special Adviser on Media to former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, has publicly challenged the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, to disclose the total cost and funding sources behind his recurring live television media chats. The demand followed Wike’s latest broadcast on Tuesday, which was transmitted live across multiple national television and radio networks. In a statement posted on his official X handle, Ibe questioned the transparency of the broadcast financing, urging the minister to publish full accounting details, including channel invoices, funding sources, and specific budget line items used to finance the airtime. According to Ibe, at least eight major broadcast stations carried Tuesday’s two-hour session live, including Channels Television, Arise News, TVC, News Central, AIT, JDK, Aso TV and Radio, and ADBN. Based on industry estimates of prime-time commercial broadcast rates, Ibe calculated that airtime costs range between N10 million and N20 million per station per hour. A single two-hour session across eight stations, he noted, could cost between N160 million and N320 million, potentially mounting to N1.92 billion to N3.84 billion annually if held on a monthly basis. “FCT residents deserve to know how much is being spent on these broadcasts and how much airtime is devoted to FCT development, rather than Wike’s political disagreements,” Ibe stated. Wike’s aide fires back The spokesperson for the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, Lere Olayinka, has challenged media adviser to former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar, Paul Ibe, to explain whether FCT residents had complained about the minister’s frequent media chats. “Did the people of FCT complain to him? Did they tell him their money is missing?” Olayinka argued that Ibe should first address questions raised by Wike about funds allegedly collected from the sale of Rivers State’s gas turbine and the reported payment for a hospital project in the Caribbean. “The minister asked questions where is the $308 million collected from the sale of Rivers State’s gas turbine? Where is the Caribbean White Hospital that he said they paid $39 million dollars?” Olayinka said. He also questioned the reported payment of $10m for communication relating to Rivers State, insisting that Ibe should urge his principals to respond to the issues raised by Wike.

title: Subscribers lament hours of disrupted mobile service
body: By Islamiyyah Adekanbi Subscribers in Lagos have lamented hours of disrupted mobile service, saying the outage affected their studies, businesses and communication with family and friends. The disruption, which was reported in Lagos, Oyo, Rivers, Delta and the Federal Capital Territory, left some users unable to access mobile data and other network services. Several subscribers said they relied on friends’ and relatives’ hotspots or alternative networks to get online. Kafayat Kokumo, a Mass Communication student, said the outage began as she was trying to send a WhatsApp message while working on a research assignment due in less than 30 minutes. She said switching on airplane mode did not restore her connection, so she eventually used a friend’s hotspot. The experience left her anxious about meeting her deadline. Kokumo said service returned after about an hour. She called for more reliable mobile service, noting that disruptions could affect people’s daily activities. Memunat Olayemi Omidiya, a student and online store manager in Abulegba, said she was unable to respond to customers after her data subscription expired and she could not buy another one. She eventually used her mother’s hotspot. Omidiya said she noticed the disruption around 5 p.m. and it continued until she went to bed after 11 p.m. She called for steps to prevent similar outages. Digital marketer, Joel Okikioluwa also said he had difficulty accessing the internet. He said he was debited after purchasing data but had not received a refund by the time of the interview. He described the experience as horrible and called for network improvement. Abdur-Rahman Awesu, a student in Lagos, said the disruption cut off his mobile data for about six hours, affecting his communication with friends and family. He relied on an alternative network and called for stronger infrastructure and backup systems, as well as timely updates to subscribers during outages. Covenant Amaechi, a student living around First Gate, Ikorodu, said he could not communicate when he needed to. Although service returned, he said the connection remained intermittent at times. He also called for better customer care. Another student, AbdulQayum Jakande, who lives in Surulere, said he lost access to mobile data for more than four hours. He called for stronger network servers. The subscribers’ accounts highlight the role of reliable mobile service in education, communication and online businesses. They called for improved network reliability and measures to minimise future disruptions. The post Subscribers lament hours of disrupted mobile service appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: EC safeguards must check partisan bias among commissioners – Osae-Kwapong
body: CDD-Ghana Fellow, Dr John Osae-Kwapong, has questioned whether internal safeguards at the Electoral Commission (EC) can prevent a partisan commissioner from advancing a political party’s interests. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, he said concerns about openly partisan appointees should also prompt scrutiny of the Commission’s internal checks. “Are there internal safeguards? Are we so worried that we are thinking one person who is publicly partisan can actually do the bidding of a political party in the midst of six other peers?” His comments follow President John Mahama’s swearing-in of Dr Joseph Kwaku Asamoah and Emelia Afi Agbenyo as EC deputy chairpersons on Monday, October 12. They filled vacancies following Dr Bossman Eric Asare’s resignation and Samuel Tettey’s retirement. President Mahama tasked the new deputies with upholding impartiality and strengthening public confidence. Dr Osae-Kwapong said other commissioners could provide a check against an individual seeking to act on partisan interests. He said he would be less worried if an appointee lacked the influence to override colleagues and pursue a party’s agenda. Beyond those safeguards, he proposed assessing appointees against standards former President Nana Akufo-Addo outlined when swearing in commissioners in 2023. He described this as the “Akufo-Addo test”. “And he talked about things like, if the person can serve with integrity, the person can serve with fairness, if the person can be professional, and if the person can show independence of mind and judgment.” For him, the appointment should be subjected to those standards to establish whether the individual could measure up. Dr Osae-Kwapong also questioned the distinction the public draws between openly partisan appointees and those who keep their political sympathies private. “The second point for me then becomes this idea of the open partisan being appointed to an independent constitutional body versus the person who could be just as partisan but is more private about his or her partisanship.” He said that visible political affiliations seemed to cause particular discomfort when an individual was appointed to an independent constitutional body. “It appears that we have a certain level of discomfort in knowing that somebody is openly partisan and being sent to an independent constitutional body.” His assessment emphasised both the appointee’s conduct and the ability of fellow commissioners to restrain partisan behaviour.

title: Nigeria loses $2bn yearly to cocoa value addition gap — FG
body: Production stuck at 300kg p/htare despite improved seedlings — CRIN Africa needs climate-resilient cocoa varieties to boost yield — IITA By Cynthia Alo & Kafayat Kokumo The Federal Government (FG) has said that Nigeria loses about $2 billion annually in potential value from cocoa because the country’s processing capacity is largely underutilised. Meanwhile, the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA), has said that West Africa needs high-yielding, climate-resilient cocoa varieties to improve productivity and protect farmers from the effects of climate change. The Minister of Agriculture and Food Security, Abubakar Kyari, stated this in Lagos at a two-day Africa Cocoa and Coffee Conference organised by the Cocoa and Coffee Farmers Alliance Association of Africa, COCEFAAA in partnership with the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security, FMAFS, and the Cocoa Research Institute of Nigeria, CRIN. Kyari, who was represented by the Deputy Director of Tree Crops at FMAFs, Mr. Ajayi Olutobaba, said Nigeria has an installed cocoa processing capacity of about 2,000 tonnes annually, but only about 30 percent is currently utilised. According to him, the FG was focused on moving Nigeria from simply producing cocoa to processing it into butter, liquor, powder and chocolate locally, adding that it would continue to position the country as a reliable cocoa exporter. He stated: “Roughly $2 billion in value addition slips away every year. It is not a shortage of resources; it is an opportunity waiting for the right investors. For cocoa and coffee, it comes down to one idea: value addition, not just volume. Our goal is to add value, not export ban and we’ll make it easy for investors to build the factories to do it’’. He further said, “We will back the renewal of aging farms and the growth of coffee with better seedlings, extension support, and enough for smallholder farmers. As we’ll make sure Nigerian produce keeps its place in the world best markets.And we must protect the harvest of tomorrow with better inputs, stronger pests and disease management, and climate-smart production.” Kyari called on stakeholders in Africa to share research, align their standards and speak with one voice in the markets that buy their crops. He stated: “Africa grows about 70% of the world’s cocoa, yet takes home only a tiny fraction of a chocolate industry worth over $130 billion. In coffee, our share of world production has fallen from 27.2% in the 1970s to about 12.5% today, and yet Ethiopia and Uganda each earned over $1.4 billion and $2 billion respectively from coffee over coffee export in 2025. “If our neighbors can do it, the continent can do it, but none of us will get there alone. “The EU deforestation regulation is no threat if we prepare early. We’ve been preparing for it.Traceability is simply how we protect our place at the table from farm to markets.” Speaking on the theme, ‘Building sustainable value chains for cocoa and coffee across West, Central and East Africa’, acting Executive Director, Cocoa Research Institute of Nigeria, CRIN, Dr. Abiodun Adedeji, said Nigeria’s cocoa productivity remained between 250kg and 300kg per hectare annually despite years of government distribution of improved seedlings. He called for better prices for farmers, greater local processing, stronger research and improved data to build a sustainable value chain. He said: “Between 2011 and 2015, we gave out 601,000 pods free to farmers. After that, we had 300,000 seedlings during COVID. Presently, Federal Government has mandated CRIN to produce and give out 1 million improved hybrid cocoa seedlings. But between that 2011 and now, the Nigerian productivity still lies between 250 and 300 kg per hectare per year.” Adedeji urged African countries to strengthen collaboration on research and development, saying the continent needed better varieties and production systems to address emerging challenges. According to him, 90 percent of cocoa proceeds and over 70 percent of coffee proceeds go to non-producing countries, while Africa shares less than 10 per cent of cocoa and less than 30 per cent of coffee. Global President & Founder COCEFAAA, and Convener of the conference, Comrade Adeola Adegoke, said Africa produces 80 percent of the world’s cocoa but captures less than 10 per cent of its value. Adegoke said the 2023-2024 season recorded the largest global deficit in 60 years, about 490,000 tons, pushing prices above $10,000 before the International Cocoa Organization, ICCO reported a surplus and prices fell by 75 per cent. “When there is bumper harvest, price goes down. When there is shock, price goes to $12,000, Robusta $15,000. Why should we produce more and earn less?” he said. Representing the Lagos State Commissioner for Agriculture and Food Systems, Abisola Olusanya, Director, Agribusiness, Lagos State Ministry of Agriculture and Food Systems, Mrs. Aramide Gansallo, said Africa must move from exporting raw cocoa and coffee beans to processing, branding and consuming its own products. Olusanya said the transformation must also make agriculture attractive to young people by presenting it as a business, technology-driven industry and career. Managing Director, Sunbeth Global Concepts, Olasunkanmi Owoyemi, who was represented by the Manager, Corporate Affairs & Communication, Abdussamad Abdurrahman said, “We have been content to be the world’s farm while others become the world’s kitchen.” He said the company is building a 70,000 metric ton processing facility at its industrial park, which will be ready by next year to boost local value addition, stressing that traceability has become critical for market access. Africa needs climate-resilient cocoa varieties to boost yield — IITA Also speaking at the conference, the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA), has harped on the need for high-yielding, climate-resilient cocoa varieties to improve productivity and protect farmers from the effects of climate change. The Institute disclosed that the region’s cocoa output had dropped by 10 per cent due to climate-related challenges, including extreme temperatures and erratic rainfall. Senior Researcher at IITA, Ranjana Bhattacharjee, who stated this at the conference, advocated the adoption of alternative varieties, particularly Liberica and Stenophylla, as climate change threatens the sustainability of established varieties. “The production of Liberica coffee is four times more than Arabica and Robusta. So, if Arabica is going down and Brazil is taking over, then you start growing Liberica and make sure that it becomes the legacy of Africa,” she said. According to her, the decline highlights the urgent need for African cocoa-producing countries to adopt improved planting materials and farming practices capable of withstanding changing weather conditions while increasing yields. She noted that ageing trees, unmanaged pests and diseases, high input costs, inadequate access to loans and international price volatility were also affecting cocoa and coffee production across the region. Bhattacharjee urged West African producers to learn from Indonesia’s rising cocoa output by adopting high-yielding varieties, improving soil nutrition, strengthening crop protection and expanding access to agricultural credit. She warned that climate pressures were worsening production challenges, particularly in Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire, where drought and cocoa swollen shoot virus disease were occurring simultaneously. The researcher also called on African policymakers to address the disparity between the income earned by cocoa farmers on the continent and their counterparts in Latin America. “Somewhere Africa gets $3,200, the farmers, while in Latin America they get $5,000. Why? My question is why? We are the highest producers of cocoa, then why should we not get that price? Farmer income 6 per cent in Africa while 31 per cent in Latin America. Why there is a system? policymakers have to fight for it,” she said. Meanwhile, stakeholders at the conference stressed the need to strengthen the entire cocoa and coffee value chain. Representing the governor of Abia State, Alex Otti , Deputy Gov. of the state , Engr. Ikechukwu Emetu said Africa must move beyond exporting raw commodities and retain more value through local processing, branding and exports. He said, “The transformation of cocoa and coffee must therefore begin at the farm, but must not end there. From improved planting materials and agronomic practice through extension, aggregation, and post-harvest management to processing, branding, and export, everything determines the competitiveness of the final product.” Also speaking, representative of Ondo State Government, Mrs. Foluke-Tunde Daramola, disclosed that the state had begun moves to revive cocoa production through improved seedlings and the rehabilitation of old plantations, alongside plans to establish 1,000 hectares of coffee at Oke-Agbe. Meanwhile, Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Agriculture and Irrigation Development, Cross River State,Dr.Joseph Odey highlighted the importance of traceability and deforestation-free production, noting that improved seedlings alone could not build a sustainable industry without reliable nurseries, extension services, processing facilities, finance and dependable markets. Representing the Cocoa and Coffee Farmers Alliance Association of Africa (COCEFAAA) Ghana, Mr. Nana Reuben challenged stakeholders to examine whether African farmers were benefiting sufficiently from the industry and whether the ageing farming population offered a sustainable future for cocoa production. The two-day conference brought together policymakers, researchers, farmers, investors and development partners to explore ways of building sustainable and competitive cocoa and coffee value chains across Africa.
