title: How the tokenisation of AI threatens African sovereignty
body: Imagine a time when you turn on your computer or connect to the internet, but you cannot freely use it. Imagine a world where you must pay for every search, every prompt, and the quality of every output. Ponder on the outlook of a society where natural intelligence, creativity, logic, and human know-how are insufficient for progression in schools and society. Consider the chilling prospect of our primary, secondary schools and universities as we have them now becoming obsolete. In this reality, the questions we can ask, the information we can source, and the quality of responses we receive will be strictly dictated by our financial resources—and how much wealth we are willing to surrender to foreign tech firms and financial institutions. Picture a lockdown where government agencies—local, state, national, and continental—are barred from accessing data essential for policy formulation, development planning, and nation-building. To gain access, they must possess either massive financial muscle or the willingness to part with pieces of their national sovereignty. While these postulations may sound like alien illusions or tropes from science fiction, they represent the precise future staring Africa in the face. To understand this shifting landscape of global technology, one must first grasp a critical, emerging concept: the tokenisation of intelligence. This modern industrial push marks a radical departure from traditional knowledge development, fundamentally changing how we interact with technology. Historically, we purchased tools as one-off assets—buying a computer or software once and owning its utility. Today, advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI) operates on a completely different model: it turns human thought, communication, and reasoning into a metered, pay-as-you-go utility. Much like water or electricity, users now pay a micro-fee for every single idea processed, word generated, or question asked. Consequently, the future of education will no longer depend on the quality of lecturers, depth of research, merit-based selection processes of recruiting talented students, the state of physical infrastructure, or the strategic leadership. Instead, an institution’s worth will be measured by the volume and caliber of raw intelligence it can financially acquire. What feels like an elusive threat is a looming reality. In March 2026, during his remarks at the BlackRock Infrastructure Summit, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman stated that the future AI business model will revolve around selling intelligence as a metered utility—similar to electricity or water—rather than merely selling software. This admission was made in the open, yet African leaders were simply not paying attention. Altman’s outlook is not isolated; it resonates with the dominant players across the tech and finance industries who view companies as “thinking factories” that sell raw intelligence by consumption. This mindset signals the death of the open web as we know it, transitioning us away from an era where information is freely accessible. For a country like Nigeria, which relies heavily on foreign technology stacks primarily from the West, this tokenisation model poses an existential threat. It risks trapping the nation in a state of chronic digital dependency. What happens if foreign firms decide to shut down our digital gateways? What happens if our smartphones collectively cease to function because Nigeria refuses to submit to Western geopolitical dictates? This is not mere paranoia; it is a terrifyingly plausible vulnerability. To protect our sovereignty, we must urgently confront the aggressive commercialisation of knowledge and intelligence. This shift will deal a fatal blow to our education ecosystem and socio-economic structure. Africa stands to be the biggest loser, as available knowledge will be locked behind commercial walls. How will underfunded African governments, research institutions, and local industries cope? African economies and institutions would be isolated from the world, and become less competitive. Currently, global tech giants harvest, collect, and store knowledge from the Global South at next to zero benefits to the locals. Tomorrow, that same data will become a premium product we can only access if we pay. This privatisation of the digital commons poses an existential threat to the African continent and the global knowledge economy. It alters how knowledge is produced, valued, and shared. It gives global conglomerates absolute power to decide what enters the world’s digital gateway. For Western powers, this is a beautiful development that positions them for advanced neo-colonialism, diplomatic leverage, and global resource control. AI models were trained by scraping billions of pages of public text, books, code, art, and history created collectively by humanity. Yet, information once freely available is now locked behind proprietary infrastructure gateways. Who owns this infrastructure? Who grants access? And where is Africa in this discussion? The dangers of this unfolding future are vast, beginning with the degradation of deep thought. When critical thinking and research are tied entirely to financial tokens, deep thought will become a luxury, and only wealthy regions will afford high-level cognitive exploration, widening the global knowledge divide. This hyper-commercialisation via ‘tokenomics’ means that under the traditional Software-as-a-Service model, you bought a tool, but under the emerging token utility model, you effectively rent your own thoughts and communication back from foreign servers. This imposes a cognitive tax on everyday life; when every word read, sentence written, or idea analysed costs a fraction of a naira, thinking will carry a literal financial toll. This will kill academic experimentation, as researchers will fear the cost of failure. Disadvantaged populations will also face cognitive redlining; just as poor neighborhoods suffer from neglected electricity grids, they will receive lower-quality data infrastructure and outdated information models. Furthermore, this model breeds cultural homogenisation and bias gatekeeping. The world’s digital infrastructure will run primarily on American and European cultural, political, and ethical biases, systematically erasing minority languages and localised histories because they do not offer a high return on investment. Corporate executives will hold an absolute monopoly over truth, wielding total control over what information is filtered, edited, or prioritised. Worst of all are the environmental exploitation and blackout risks. Africa will be exploited for the raw physical resources needed to build this infrastructure, yet remains highly vulnerable to sudden shutoffs. If a tech conglomerate decides to weaponise its utility against an African nation, it can trigger an immediate intellectual and operational blackout. Global superpowers view AI data infrastructure as the ultimate tool for national security and digital dominance. The U.S. government heavily backs American AI utilities as weapons of geopolitical alignment, exemplified by OpenAI signing agreements with the U.S. Department of Defense and War, while rival powers in Asia and Europe fund data sabotage and psychological operations. This threat extends dangerously into our national security infrastructure. As intelligence becomes tokenised, how will our ministry of defence, police forces, and intelligence agencies execute their mandates if they rely entirely on foreign software and hardware? Without technological self-reliance, our security apparatus will be rendered completely handicapped, stripping us of domestic sovereignty. Yet, while Western countries aggressively invest in the AI ecosystem to secure global control, many African leaders remain distracted, erecting billboards to showcase basic constitutional responsibilities like paving roads and building classrooms. Regrettably, when it comes to these critical developmental challenges, African governments routinely pay lip service while allocating meager resources. State funding remains aggressively active during political campaigns, electioneering, and the ostentatious display of political power. Yet, the staggering sums spent prosecuting elections stand in stark contrast to the near-total neglect of our technological infrastructure. Africa was once the cradle of civilization and the birthplace of scientific knowledge, but that has been relegated to history. In the last century, the continent has contributed less than two per cent to the global knowledge economy. If intelligence remains tokenised and commodified, access to knowledge will be determined entirely by financial capacity. In Nigeria, where 133 million citizens live in systemic poverty, and across a continent where millions more struggle to afford a daily meal, a paywall on reasoning will permanently lock the poor out of quality education. If left unaddressed, Africa’s fate over the next 20 to 30 years will be one of total, inescapable subjugation to Western investors and governments. To mitigate these risks and prevent total collapse, African governments must pivot toward assertive digital protectionism. We must deliberately act to prevent total recolonisation. If we do not take charge of our knowledge production today, our future will be dictated by forces that are already quietly breaching our shores. First, states need to enforce strict data valuation and taxation. Foreign tech companies should no longer harvest local public data for free, only to turn it into proprietary products and sell it back to us. Local data must be treated as a national economic asset. Second, African nations must aggressively restructure how they regulate the digital industry. Foreign tech giants possess immense financial muscle that easily crushes domestic competition. We must adjust entry criteria to protect local players. If we do not, the very definition and valuation of “intelligence”—from how we award university degrees to how the labour market operates—will be permanently dictated by Western tech monopolies. Predictably, these conglomerates will not invest in technologies that allow Africa to leapfrog its developmental challenges. Instead, they will fund mechanisms that entrench brain drain, impoverish the continent, and deepen foreign control. Concurrently, our university ecosystems must be radically re-engineered. Higher education requires policy interventions that grant real autonomy and independence from Western influence. We must stop designing curricula solely to compete with Western universities; instead, we must localise and Pan-Africanise our educational systems. The more we blindly Westernise, the more we lose our originality. Alongside this curricular shift, governments must change their investment models by subsidising AI compute power for public universities. State-level grants should be established specifically to purchase compute capacity and token credits. This ensures that students can experiment and innovate without carrying a crippling personal financial burden. Finally, we must actively combat cultural homogenisation by building indigenous Large Language Models. Digitising and integrating local knowledge systems across Africa’s diverse languages will safeguard our unique cultural identities from being erased by Western-centric algorithms. Ultimately, we must redefine our relationships with Western tech monopolies and foreign governments. We must rechannel our investment structures away from stomach infrastructure and into independent, sovereign digital infrastructure. If this is not done, we will awake in a few years to find that the institutions we spent decades building are worthless. We will realize we have handed over our data, natural resources, and values to foreign forces who will sell them back to us at a premium—or shut them off entirely when we refuse to kowtow to their policy directions. To some, this warning may sound alarmist. However, if these critical matters are not addressed immediately, the warnings of today will inevitably become the harsh realities of tomorrow. The clock is ticking. Africa, wake up. Now is the only time you have to determine your own destiny. We must answer these questions before it is too late. Okocha is a Professor of Journalism and Emerging Media, ICA Nigeria Chair, and Dean of the Faculty of Communication and Media Studies at Bingham University

title: Strafe: A new open-source, E2E Encrypted, and federated alternative to Discord
body:
Connect with your community on a platform that respects your privacy and freedom. No tracking, no ads, just pure communication.
Finally, a chat app that respects our privacy!
Strafe combines powerful features with a commitment to privacy and open source values.
All messages are encrypted by default. Your conversations stay private, always.
Express yourself with full markdown support, code blocks, and rich embeds.
Create and join communities. Organize with rooms, roles, and permissions.
Crystal-clear voice and video calls with screen sharing capabilities.
Share files securely without restrictions. Send whatever you need with no arbitrary limits.
No tracking, no ads, no data harvesting. Your data belongs to you.
Run your own instance with full control, isolated from our main instance.
Built for performance. Low latency messaging that scales with your community.
Use Strafe on desktop, web, or mobile. Your conversations sync seamlessly across all devices.
One app for every instance: sign in wherever Strafe runs, switch between your accounts in a click, and get calls and mentions even with the window closed. Updates install themselves.
Strafe is built on the principles of transparency, privacy, and community ownership. Our entire codebase is available under a permissive open source license.
Every line of code is open for inspection. No hidden trackers, no secret backdoors, no surprises.
Built by the community, for the community. Your contributions shape the future of Strafe.
Run Strafe on your own infrastructure. Full control, full privacy, your rules.
Your data is yours. Export, migrate, or self-host anytime without restrictions.
Transparency in everything we do, including our policies.
2026 Strafe. Open source under GNU Affero General Public License v3.0.

title: Trump unlikely to impose sanctions soon under law tightening restrictions against Moscow
body:
WASHINGTON, October 14. /TASS/. The Washington administration is unlikely to impose new sanctions in the near future under the law tightening restrictions on Russia, the Politico newspaper wrote, citing sources.
On September 18, US President Donald Trump signed a bill passed by Congress that provides for sanctions against Russia’s top political and military leadership and state-owned companies, as well as secondary sanctions against Russia’s trading partners. "The legislation requires that <…> 30 days after the bill’s signing, President Donald Trump must make a determination about what people and entities he characterizes as meeting the criteria for getting sanctioned. <…> But, as critics of the bill pointed out before its passage, the legislation also includes broad waiver authority for the White House: The president just needs to submit a document to Congress saying a waiver ‘is in the national interests of the United States’," according to the publication.
"It’s a low bar for them to just send the waiver," a Democratic Senate aide told the newspaper. "I expect that that’s what would happen, and then there would be no recourse because that’s how the bill was written," he added.
Traditionally, if the administration was planning big sanctions steps, there would be a lot of messaging from the Treasury, State and Commerce departments in the leadup, the Senate aide said. That isn’t happening now, he noted.

title: Tinubu Must Stay: The North demands answers, not slogans
body: The launch of “Tinubu Must Stay” may have come at precisely the moment when its promoters need to ask themselves an uncomfortable question: What exactly are they asking Northern Nigerians to celebrate and extend into another term? As supporters of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu prepare to counter the opposition’s “Tinubu Must Go” campaign ahead of the 2027 presidential election, they risk mistaking political mobilisation for public satisfaction and a catalogue of government projects for evidence of meaningful development. The North does not lack reasons to demand a better future; what it lacks, in the eyes of many of its citizens, is sufficient evidence that the present administration is delivering one at the pace and on the scale they expect. The central weakness of Tinubu Must Stay (TMS) is that it seeks to defend political continuity without first demonstrating that the administration’s policies have produced fair, broad-based and measurable gains. Its promoters cannot simply point to the existence of projects and treat them as conclusive evidence in favour of another term. They must explain why voters should endorse four more years if voters believe their region continues to bear enormous economic and social burdens without receiving commensurate developmental benefits. Until that case is made, the slogan amounts less to a defence of performance than to an appeal for political loyalty. There are numbers behind northern discontent. Consider the findings of the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS)’ 2022 Multidimensional Poverty Index survey. Published in November 2022, the survey estimated that 133 million Nigerians, representing 63 per cent of the population, were multidimensionally poor. Of these, approximately 86 million, or 65 per cent of the national total, live in Northern Nigeria, compared with nearly 47 million in the South. The survey also found that multidimensional poverty ranged from 27 per cent in Ondo State to 91 per cent in Sokoto State. The survey data were collected between November 2021 and February 2022, before Tinubu assumed office in May 2023. They therefore do not establish that his administration caused the North’s poverty. Rather, they demonstrate the scale of the longstanding developmental disadvantage confronting the region and the magnitude of the challenge the present administration inherited. That distinction strengthens rather than weakens the argument. A government seeking re-election must be judged not only by the problems it inherits but also by the progress it makes in addressing them. What is the current population of multidimensionally poor Nigerians, particularly in the North? If President Tinubu wins a second term, what level of multidimensional poverty can reasonably be projected in Ondo or Sokoto States for 2031? These are questions that require credible data, measurable targets and a clear account of the progress made under the present administration. This is the political danger facing TMS. Northern voters may ask why a region with enormous agricultural resources continues to struggle with food insecurity, why its young people find it difficult to obtain productive employment, and why many communities remain constrained by inadequate infrastructure and insecurity. These challenges have direct consequences for households, workers, farmers and small businesses. For example, the August 2026 inflation figures illustrate the complexity of this challenge. According to the National Bureau of Statistics, headline inflation declined from 23.14 per cent in August 2025 to 15.39 per cent in August 2026. Food inflation also declined from 25.30 per cent to 19.57 per cent over the same period. Yet the Consumer Price Index increased from 145.3 points in July to 146.3 points in August 2026. A decline in the inflation rate does not mean that prices have returned to their previous levels. It means that prices are generally rising more slowly than before. Many households may therefore continue to experience severe financial pressure even as the headline inflation rate improves. For families already struggling to afford food, transport, education and healthcare, a slower rate of price increases does not necessarily translate into an immediate improvement in living standards. Supporters of Tinubu may point to major infrastructure proposals and programmes, including the Sokoto–Badagry Superhighway and the proposed Kano–Jigawa–Katsina–Maradi railway, as evidence of the administration’s commitment to Northern Nigeria. Such projects could deliver significant benefits. Better transport links can reduce logistics costs, connect producers to markets, encourage investment and stimulate economic activity across communities. Northern Nigeria needs more than transport corridors. It needs an agricultural transformation programme that moves beyond primary production towards value addition. It needs better schools and stronger support for entrepreneurship. Above all, it needs policies that translate public investment into jobs, higher incomes, greater productivity and improved living standards. The timing of TMS is significant, but its deeper problem is the gap between political messaging and public experience. A campaign launched in response to Tinubu Must Go may successfully mobilise supporters, attract publicity and strengthen party networks. Yet these achievements do not necessarily persuade undecided voters or resolve the concerns of citizens who are economically insecure. The campaign will be too little if it offers selective statistics instead of measurable improvements in livelihoods. It will be too little if it defends economic reforms without acknowledging the continuing pressure on household budgets. And it will be too little if it treats regional dissatisfaction as a communications problem rather than a development challenge. It may be too late if its organisers assume that years of accumulated hardship and disappointment can be overcome by a slogan launched as the 2027 election approaches. Political communication can influence public opinion, but it cannot indefinitely substitute for tangible results. A serious campaign should publish a transparent national and regional development scorecard showing the administration’s commitments, the status of major projects, measurable improvements in public services and the economic outcomes citizens can reasonably expect before the end of its first term. Such a scorecard should include clear indicators of progress in poverty reduction, food security, employment, education, healthcare, infrastructure and access to economic opportunities. It should also distinguish between promises made, funds committed, projects completed and benefits actually realised by citizens. The launch of TMS reveals that the President’s supporters recognise the need to defend his record against an increasingly assertive opposition. But the contest in Northern Nigeria is about more than competing slogans. It concerns economic opportunity, distributive fairness, public confidence and the credibility of promises made to citizens. The NBS poverty figures provide a sobering reminder of the scale of the North’s longstanding disadvantages. The more recent inflation figures demonstrate why improvements in macroeconomic indicators do not automatically translate into an immediate restoration of household purchasing power. Neither set of statistics alone determines how northern voters will behave in 2027. Together, however, they illustrate the challenge facing those who wish to persuade the region to support another Tinubu presidency. The North does not need to be told merely that Tinubu Must Stay. It needs a convincing explanation of what his continued presidency would mean for its children, farmers, traders, workers and entrepreneurs. It requires evidence that the sacrifices demanded of citizens today will lead to a more prosperous and secure tomorrow. For Northern Nigeria, a late campaign of persuasion may still make a difference. But if the campaign offers less than the people expect, it will struggle to overcome the feeling that they have waited too long for too little. Before asking the North to endorse continuity through 2031, the promoters of TMS must demonstrate why continuity should be expected to deliver a different and better development outcome. As a Hausa proverb puts it, “a dog was told a celebration is coming, it said, ‘we will see it on the floor.’”

title: Mental health beyond stigma
body: World Mental Health Day is observed every October 10 to raise global awareness of mental health issues, mobilise support for those affected and reduce the stigma often associated with mental illness. The theme for the 2026 commemoration, “Lived Experiences Heard: Real Voices, Real Change,” highlights the importance of listening to people living with mental health conditions and involving them in shaping policies, services and decisions that affect their lives. The theme is a timely reminder that those affected by mental health conditions are not merely patients or recipients of care but can also contribute meaningfully to developing solutions to healthcare challenges. Undoubtedly, people feel valued and understood when encouraged to share their experiences. Their stories can provide mental health professionals, caregivers and policymakers with a deeper understanding of the realities of living with these conditions. Such engagement can also improve treatment approaches, guide funding decisions and challenge stereotypes. Unlike physical illnesses, mental health conditions are not always easy to identify. They can affect an individual’s ability to cope with the normal stresses of life, work productively and contribute meaningfully to their community. According to the World Health Organisation (WHO), more than one billion people worldwide live with mental health disorders. The most common conditions include anxiety and depression, while suicide remains one of the leading causes of death among young people. Nigeria is not immune to this growing challenge. Available data indicate that an estimated 20 million to 40 million Nigerians are affected by one form of mental health condition or another. The causes are not difficult to identify. Years of insurgency, banditry and violent crime in northern Nigeria, alongside other security challenges across the country, have left many citizens struggling with deep psychological scars. Many continue to live with trauma that either goes unnoticed or is deliberately ignored. Children have been forced to witness the killings of their parents and loved ones, while many others have endured abduction and prolonged captivity. At the same time, many men and women remain trapped in abusive and toxic relationships, with little support from a system that lacks adequate social safety nets and often expects them to endure their suffering. These challenges are compounded by economic hardship, rising poverty, unemployment and uncertainty about the future. Pressure from social media also tends to increase stress and emotional distress among young people, pushing some to the brink. These factors are by no means exhaustive, but they are enough to make mental well-being a priority for any country that takes the welfare of its citizens seriously. Beyond these causes, Nigeria lacks adequate infrastructure and personnel to address the challenge. Access to mental health services remains limited and unaffordable, particularly in rural communities, many of which also face security challenges. Consequently, people in remote areas are often left at the mercy of herbal and spiritual healers. The country also faces a severe shortage of mental health professionals. With the continued mass exodus of healthcare workers, Nigeria has an estimated 300 psychiatrists to cater to a population of more than 220 million. This situation is unacceptable. Perhaps not all these challenges can be addressed at once, but some can certainly be mitigated. Nigeria must begin to prioritise the overall well-being of its citizens, with mental health recognised as an essential component of healthcare. We therefore urge the government to ensure that budgetary allocations to the health sector reflect this reality. Beyond funding, mental health services should be integrated into primary healthcare and health insurance programmes across the country. Everyone, irrespective of location or social status, should have access to mental healthcare. One major misconception about mental health is the belief that anyone with a mental health condition is “mad” or mentally unstable. This attitude must change. Anyone can experience mental health challenges at some point in life, and those affected deserve understanding, support and appropriate care rather than ridicule or discrimination. We call for increased public awareness to combat stigma and discrimination. The National Orientation Agency should work with mental health experts, including the Association of Psychiatrists in Nigeria, to sustain public education, challenge misconceptions and promote early intervention. We also call for the full implementation of the National Mental Health Act 2021 and urge government authorities at all levels to create safe spaces where people can speak openly about their mental health without fear of discrimination.

title: Mental health beyond stigma
body: The World Bank’s October 2026 Nigeria Development Update, Beyond the Federal Purse: How Higher Revenues Shaped State Priorities, provides a useful framework for examining Nigeria’s transition. The country’s economic debate is entering a new phase, after years in which the central policy concerns were the removal of distortions, the restoration of macroeconomic stability and the rebuilding of confidence in the naira. The question now is: What benefits are the transition delivering for businesses, workers and households? The report recognises that economic growth has remained resilient, while higher oil prices have strengthened government revenues and the country’s external position. Yet it also warns that rising global fuel prices have interrupted the progress made in reducing inflation, leaving household purchasing power under pressure even as important macroeconomic indicators improve. The challenge is no longer simply to establish whether the reforms have improved the economy’s underlying indicators. It is to determine whether the resulting gains can support faster growth, create productive employment and raise living standards across a country where many households continue to struggle with the cost of food, transport, energy and other necessities. There are reasons to acknowledge the improvement in Nigeria’s macroeconomic position. The World Bank reports that real gross domestic product grew by 4.2 per cent in the first half of 2026, compared with 3.9 per cent and 3.5 per cent in the corresponding periods of 2025 and 2024, respectively. Growth was driven largely by services, alongside a stronger contribution from agriculture. The current-account surplus also widened to $12 billion in the first half of 2026, while gross external reserves rose above $54 billion in September. Higher oil prices have helped strengthen Nigeria’s export earnings and government revenues, but the benefits depend partly on how much oil the country can produce and sell, the cost of production and the obligations attached to some future oil receipts. Consequently, an increase in the international price of crude does not automatically translate into an equivalent increase in the revenue immediately available to the government. The improvement in the external position also needs to be interpreted alongside the sources of foreign-exchange inflows. The World Bank notes that portfolio investment has contributed substantially to the accumulation of reserves. While such inflows can strengthen the foreign-exchange market, their sustainability depends partly on investor confidence and financial-market conditions, making them different from a durable expansion of non-oil exports and productive investment. Inflation remains another constraint. The rise in global fuel prices following the conflict in the Middle East, combined with seasonal food-price pressures, has interrupted the decline that began in early 2025. Higher fuel and transport costs affect more than the prices consumers pay directly at filling stations; they also feed into the cost of moving agricultural produce, distributing manufactured goods and operating businesses. Consequently, an economy can record stronger output, a better external balance and higher government revenues without households experiencing a corresponding improvement in their purchasing power. Macroeconomic stability creates the conditions for recovery, but it does not guarantee that the benefits will be broadly distributed. The World Bank’s examination of state finances brings the discussion closer to the quality of economic management. Between 2023 and 2025, aggregate state revenues increased by about 93 per cent in real terms, while expenditure rose by approximately 92 per cent. The share of total state expenditure devoted to capital spending increased from 46 per cent to 61 per cent, with transport infrastructure accounting for the largest increase. These figures suggest that state governments have used part of the additional fiscal space to expand investment in infrastructure and other economic activities. Better roads, reliable water supplies, functioning schools and accessible healthcare can reduce the costs faced by businesses and households, improve productivity and create conditions for private investment. However, the composition of public spending deserves as much attention as its overall size. The World Bank reports that education’s share of state expenditure declined from 14.9 per cent in 2021 to 12.1 per cent in 2025, while health spending remained broadly stable at around seven per cent. Social protection’s share increased from 1.4 per cent to 4.4 per cent. Although expenditure on education and health increased in absolute terms, their slower growth relative to economic infrastructure raises questions about whether states are allocating sufficient resources to the human capabilities required for sustained development. Infrastructure and human capital should not be treated as competing priorities. A road may improve access to markets, but the productivity of the people using it depends on their health, education and skills. Industrial expansion requires electricity and transport infrastructure, but it also requires a workforce capable of operating modern equipment, maintaining quality and adopting new technologies. There is a further concern about the capacity of states to sustain these improvements. The World Bank reports that only Lagos and Enugu generated enough internally generated revenue to cover their recurrent expenditure in 2025. The continued dependence of most states on federal allocations leaves their budgets vulnerable to changes in federation revenue and underscores the need to strengthen local revenue administration without imposing unnecessary burdens on productive economic activity.

title: Strike: FCT council chairman begs teachers to resume work
body: The chairman of Gwagwalada Area Council of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) Kasim Mohammed Ikwa, has appealed to primary and secondary school teachers to resume classes while negotiations between labour unions and the FCT Administration over their demands continue. Ikwa made the appeal yesterday when he met with executives of the Gwagwalada branch of the Nigeria Union of Teachers (NUT) in his office. He urged the union leadership to allow schools to reopen for academic activities in the interest of parents and pupils, pending the resolution of the dispute between the Nigeria Labour Congress (NLC) and the FCT Administration. The chairman expressed concern over the impact of the prolonged school closure on children in rural communities, noting that some areas of the FCT already faced educational disadvantages. He warned that the continued disruption of academic activities could further undermine learning opportunities for pupils in such communities. Ikwa appealed to the teachers to consider the interests of pupils and students while negotiations continued, reaffirming his administration’s commitment to engaging stakeholders in the education sector to resolve the dispute. He expressed optimism that constructive dialogue would lead to an amicable resolution. In his response, the Gwagwalada branch chairman of the NUT, Comrade Abubakar Ahmed Sadiq, appreciated Ikwa’s intervention, saying teachers were equally concerned about the situation but felt compelled to join the industrial action over issues affecting their welfare and career progression. He highlighted concerns over promotion opportunities, particularly the challenges confronting teachers who had attained certain grade levels. Sadiq called for improved communication between the government and union leaders to ensure that teachers’ grievances received adequate attention.

title: 9 die, 2 injured in Abuja-Lokoja road crash
body: N ine persons died while two others were injured in a truck accident at Piri village along the Abuja-Lokoja highway. A witness, Samson Yakubu, said the accident involving a Howo truck with registration number FKY 922 XB occurred at about 5:37am yesterday. He said the truck, which was loaded with ceramic tiles, was travelling from Ajaokuta in Kogi State to Kano when the driver allegedly lost control due to fatigue and plunged into a ditch. According to him, nine of the 11 persons sitting on top of the tiles were trapped and died when the truck crashed into the ditch, while the two survivors were rescued by officials of the Federal Road Safety Corps (FRSC) and taken to the General Hospital, Kwali, for treatment. The trailer involved in the accident Yakubu said some villagers joined the FRSC rescue team to remove the tiles before the trapped bodies could be recovered. An FRSC official attached to the Yangoji Unit Command, who participated in the rescue operation, also confirmed the incident, saying all nine deceased victims were males. The official attributed the crash to fatigue and a violation of speed limits, adding that the bodies had been deposited at the mortuary of the General Hospital, Kwali, while the injured victims were receiving treatment at the same facility. The FCT Sector Commander of the FRSC, Tijjani Iliyasu, also confirmed the accident, although he said he was still awaiting detailed information from the Yangoji Unit Command. He expressed concern over the practice of some passengers travelling on top of goods loaded onto trailers, warning that it exposed them to serious danger. Iliyasu said the FRSC had consistently sensitised trailer drivers on the dangers of carrying passengers on top of goods during long-distance journeys and had sanctioned drivers caught violating the regulations. The sector commander also disclosed that the construction firm handling the dualisation of a section of the Abuja-Lokoja highway had been booked for allegedly failing to provide adequate traffic warning signs along the construction corridor.

title: Some Trump advisers express concern over livestreaming Nidal Hasan execution
body:
Hegseth's announcement last week caught Army planners off-guard, sources said.
President Donald Trump and his advisers are mulling whether to no longer livestream the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan , sources familiar with the matter told ABC News.
The discussions come amid a hesitancy over whether broadcasting the execution could super charge anti-American propaganda, particularly among Islamic-extremist groups, or simply turn the execution into a spectacle that reflects poorly on the U.S, the sources said.
Some officials, the sources said, have raised concerns about the optics of broadcasting an execution, particularly one in which a firing squad would shoot a paralyzed man confined to a wheelchair.
Hasan was paralyzed from the waist down during an exchange of gunfire with police during his 2009 rampage.
Last week Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth vowed to make the execution public and confirmed it would be livestreamed. The Pentagon maintains the livestream is moving forward, with a defense official saying Tuesday in a statement: "The Secretary is correct. It will be live streamed. Details will follow."
Multiple people familiar with the planning described concerns behind the scenes about the video being used as propaganda by extremist groups.
Hasan told Army officials after his arrest that he had hoped to die during the attack and become a martyr and said he would still consider himself a martyr if he were executed, court records show.
The president has asked a number of advisers and allies to weigh in on whether the Pentagon should move forward with livestreaming the execution. During discussions, a range of ideas have been floated, sources said.
Among the options being weighed is broadcasting the period immediately before the execution and cutting away before the firing squad shoots Hasan, an official familiar with the planning described. Another option being discussed is positioning the camera outside the execution area, potentially showing Hasan being brought in without broadcasting his death.
When asked about the livestream last week, Trump said, "They're making a determination about that," but agreed either way Hasan should die.
The White House has not yet returned a request for comment.
Additionally, Vice President JD Vance and House Speaker Mike Johnson have said they wouldn't watch the execution. Opposition or hesitancy has been less focused on Hasan's death sentence which has broad support among Republicans, but on the decision to broadcast it.
CNN was the first to report the debate among Trump and his advisers about whether to go through with the livestream.
On Nov. 5, 2009 Hasan, then an Army psychiatrist, opened fired on clusters of troops in a building at Fort Hood, killing 12 and wounding 32 others. He was sentenced to death in 2013 and has been incarcerated at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas.
Hasan described his attack as an act of jihad against American troops for the wars being waged in Iraq and Afghanistan which he viewed as immoral.
The military has not executed a death-row prisoner since 1961, when the sentence was carried out by hanging.
The Army had been preparing since at least February for the possibility of executing one or more of its four death-row inmates, including Hasan, but those plans centered on lethal injection at the federal prison in Terre Haute, Indiana, where the Justice Department carried out a series of executions during Trump's first term.
Hegseth's announcement last week that Nidal Hasan's execution would be livestreamed caught Army planners by surprise, according to three officials familiar with the preparations, adding another complication to an execution the service is already scrambling to organize.
The Army has not carried out an execution by firing squad since 1945 and is still developing procedures for doing so, including determining how many shooters would participate and what type of chair would be used to secure Hasan.
Lethal injection had been the service's only authorized means of executions since the 1980s until a 2023 rule change granting the Army secretary broad authority over the methods which death row inmates are executed.
The last public execution in the U.S. was in 1936 in Kentucky.
Public executions were gradually outlawed by some states beginning in the 19th century and has long become taboo across much of the developed world. They remain in practice in North Korea, Iran and the Taliban-controlled Afghanistan.

title: Eretz Nehederet returns with sharp election satire, Sydney Sweeney, flydubai spoof
body: Sydney Sweeney (Mishel Pru) singing “Hatikvah” was one of the few bits on this week's episode of Eretz Nehederet (Wonderful Country), Israel's popular sketch comedy show on Keshet 12, that didn't involve politics. The series, which has been on hiatus for a few months, returned just in time for the October 27 elections.Sweeney, the Hollywood star/spokesmodel, appeared on the first episode of the show's new season because she is rumored to be converting to Judaism so she can marry her boyfriend, the American-Jewish music manager, Scooter Braun.View this post on InstagramA post shared by מישל המלכה (@mishelpru)As host Eyal Kitzis pointed out, during this time of rising antisemitism, having the wildly popular sex symbol join the tribe would be a publicity coup. She entered singing the Israeli national anthem because in a recent commercial for the sports betting platform, Novig, in which she appeared nearly nude, fans thought they detected the strains of “Hatikvah” at the end, which was true: In the last seconds of the ad, Anderson. Paak's “Come Down,” a 2016 song which samples “Hatikvah,” played in the background.Sweeney walked across the set singing in Hebrew, mangling the lyrics, and singing, “Cute freckle, ship,” in Hebrew, which rhymes with the real words, “A Jewish soul yearns,” along with other malapropisms. Despite her errors, she told Kitzis she was serious about converting and that from now on, she would be modest in her commercials and that she was planning to appear in a new campaign, this time for the grocery chain Rami Levy.She showed a pair of jeans she would wear in the campaign, which was covered with chicken parts, and she said the slogan would be, “Rami Levy has great wings,” a play on her American Eagle commercials with the motto, “Sydney Sweeney has great jeans.”To no one's surprise, the show ended with a sketch based on the flydubai attempted hijacking, which was made for Eretz Nehederet. The incident featured lots of drama and action, but no one died, and it was perfect for one of their periodic Fauda spoofs – plus, one of the main Israeli heroes who saved the day was a plumber.So Lior Raz (Eran Zarachovitz) played a version of his Fauda character, reconfigured as the real-life passenger Yaniv Hayoun, who helped foil the hijacking. As the theme from Fauda wailed in the background, the plumber, armed with the tools of his trade, asked for various wrenches to subdue the terrorist.Then he told the woman helping him that he had to go to his car for a part he needed, a typical habit of plumbers. Once he had the plane under control, he drew a Jewish star with the plane's contrails.Eretz Nehederet mocks Netanyahu, Eisenkot ahead of October 27 electionsBut in between, the show was all about the elections, poking fun at each major candidate and some of the minor ones, starting with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (Mariano Eidelman) and his main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot (Yaniv Biton) of the Yashar party, who is currently leading in the polls.Eisenkot has challenged Netanyahu to a debate, which the prime minister has refused to take part in, and Eisenkot ribbed him, saying he was only 10 minutes late to the show, not 10 hours late as he was on October 7.Netanyahu, for his part, said had he taken Eisenkot's advice, the war would have ended before Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar and other terror leaders were killed. He included Dolly Parton on the list of terrorist casualties, then corrected himself, saying her death was merely “collateral damage.”Eretz Nehederet also joked about recent reports that Netanyahu ignored warnings about the deadly Hamas-led massacres on October 7. It showed the Israeli leader, supposedly in the days before the attack, even being told by a host on Master Chef and by a song on the radio that an attack was imminent – and doing nothing.In response, Netanyahu kept accusing Eisenkot of “sitting with Arabs,” meaning that he suspected that the Yashar leader would renege on his promise to create a government of only Zionist parties.Miri Regev spoof targets security failures in flydubai hijacking attemptMiri Regev (Yaniv Biton), the country's transportation minister, came in for criticism over her handling of foreign pilots flying into Israel, which led to a pilot from Oman being allowed to fly to Israel. Kitzis asked her if she would take responsibility for the tragedy that almost happened when the attempted hijacking was foiled, but she laughed and said she wasn't going to take responsibility for something that “almost” happened.Finally, she reluctantly agreed to look over some pilots' passports as she sat by a pool on one of her many work-related trips, and mistook a pilot from Oman as being from Uman, Ukraine, the final resting place of Rabbi Nachman of Breslau, a popular pilgrimage spot for hassidim.The Odyssey parody highlights struggles of exhausted IDF reservistsTHERE WAS much more about politics, and in fact, the show opened with a pointed piece of political satire, an elaborate parody of the big summer movie, Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey. Only in this case, Odysseus was a beleaguered reserve-duty soldier (Omer Etzion) trying to get home after 500 days of service.Sitting dazed on a beach, he struggled to remember his home and was approached by a robed figure, who was the prime minister (Mariano Eidelman) as Apollo. The prime minister said it all started when a Qatari statue of a camel – like the Trojan horse – that was filled with cash and weapons was dragged into Gaza. But the soldier was confused about how long it had taken to fight this war.“All of Gaza is the size of the IMAX in Rishon,” he said.The soldier then recalled an adventure in which he and his men were menaced by an ultra-Orthodox Cyclops figure and hundreds of haredi men. Maybe some of these men could help them out, replacing them on the battlefield, the soldier suggested, but the Cyclops figure was unmoved.Among his other adventures, he was addressed by a trio of sirens, one of whom was MK Tally Gotliv (Liat Harlev). The two others were the directors of NAZA, the award-winning documentary that asserts that the Israeli military callously disregarded civilian casualties in Gaza. The three hurled accusations at him, from both left- and right-wing perspectives.As he traveled, his family went broke and lost all their possessions. When he finally arrived home, dressed as a beggar, he learned that he really was a beggar – and was greeted by Sara Netanyahu (Alma Zack), instead of his own wife. In place of a welcome-home gift, she handed him a notice that he had to report for reserve duty – again.This Odyssey skit was funny, absurd, bitter, topical, and right on target for the many weary reserve duty soldiers and their families. It was a perfect example of how good Eretz Nehederet can be at its best. Expect the satire to get even sharper as Election Day approaches.

title: Russian ballistic missile strike on Kyiv kills two, injures 21
body:
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported this, according to Ukrinform.
Sixteen of the injured were hospitalized, including four in serious condition.
1 / 10 A Russian missile hit a nine-story residential building in Kyiv’s Desnianskyi district, setting apartments on fire on the first through eighth floors. Search-and-rescue operations continued as residents were evacuated from the upper floors.
A warehouse building in the same district was also set on fire, while debris from the attack caused a grass fire at a stadium in the Darnytskyi district.
The Ukrainian Air Force reported launches of ballistic missiles targeting Kyiv, prompting an air raid alert in the capital and several regions.
As Ukrinform reported, since the evening of October 12, Russian forces had attacked Ukraine with five Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles, nine Bandеrol/Dan-T loitering munitions and 108 Shahed-type attack drones. Ukrainian air defenses neutralized 88 drones.

title: Ajadi pledges ₦50m empowerment for Oyo traders
body: Ambassador Olufemi Ajadi Oguntoyinbo, the Allied Peoples Movement (APM) senatorial candidate for Oyo Central in the 2027 general election, has pledged ₦50 million in financial empowerment for traders and market women across the district. Ajadi also promised to pursue initiatives to improve access to business support and create employment opportunities for youths if elected. He made the pledge at a gathering of traders and artisans in Oyo State, where leaders of various market associations expressed support for APM candidates ahead of the 2027 elections. Ajadi said his decision to venture into politics was driven by his desire to extend his philanthropic activities to more people through effective representation, people-oriented legislation and policies aimed at improving the welfare of ordinary Nigerians. “I am a philanthropist, but I want empowerment to reach more people. That is one of the reasons I joined politics. Through good lawmaking and motions that address the needs of the people, we can create opportunities for our youths, market women, traders and other members of the electorate,” he said. He said his legislative agenda would prioritise initiatives to improve livelihoods, support small businesses and create opportunities for young people. Ajadi also urged market women to encourage their children to participate actively in politics, noting that political engagement provided an avenue for citizens to influence leadership decisions and promote good governance. He disclosed plans to provide ₦50 million in financial support to traders and market women to strengthen their businesses and improve their economic circumstances. Responding to the traders’ requests, he acknowledged the importance of accessible financing for small businesses and expressed readiness to work towards support mechanisms that could help market operators expand their commercial activities. The traders had appealed for empowerment programmes to help them manage and grow their businesses. Sanda Praises Makinde, Urges Traders to Back APM Speaking at the gathering, Hon. Sikiru Oyedele Sanda, Chairman of Egbeda Local Government, Chairman of the Association of Local Governments of Nigeria (ALGON) in Oyo State and Director-General of Ajadi’s campaign committee, commended Governor Seyi Makinde for what he described as his contribution to political understanding and harmony among aspirants in the state. Sanda urged stakeholders to recognise Makinde’s role in political reconciliation, arguing that arrangements to accommodate different interests had helped reduce disagreements among aspirants. He said accommodating political interests and assigning responsibilities without persistent hostility were important to building a united political platform. Sanda urged traders to view electoral participation not only as an exercise to elect candidates but also as an opportunity to pursue their welfare and the development of their communities. “The electoral process is not only about the candidates. It is also about the progress and well-being of the electorate. The people must look at what political participation can bring to their businesses, families and communities,” he said. The ALGON chairman also praised the Makinde administration over security, regular payment of civil servants’ salaries and the timely payment of pensions to retired workers. He said the state government’s approach to workers’ welfare had helped provide economic stability for many families and urged traders to consider governance and its wider implications when making their electoral choices. Sanda further disclosed that Ajadi’s campaign committee had resolved to engage traders in all 11 local government areas in Oyo Central Senatorial District during campaign activities. He said the initiative was intended to make the campaign more inclusive by giving market women, artisans and other traders opportunities to express their concerns and communicate their needs to the candidate. YK Abass Seeks Financial Support for Traders The Babaloja-General of Oyo State, Alhaji Asiwaju Yekini Abass Oladapo, popularly known as YK Abass, thanked participants, particularly the presidents and representatives of the traders’ associations. Abass, who said he was elected to the position by Governor Makinde, appealed to Ajadi to support traders across the state, particularly through financial assistance. He welcomed the opportunity for market associations to engage political candidates on issues affecting their members, describing financial empowerment as important to improving traders’ welfare. The appeal highlighted concerns among small-business operators over access to affordable credit, rising operating costs and inadequate capital for business expansion. Market Leaders Declare Support for APM Candidates Earlier, Alhaji Dauda Abiodun Oladepo, President of the Ibadan Joint Traders Association, conveyed greetings to APM candidates in Oyo State, particularly Ajadi. Speaking on behalf of the traders’ leadership, Oladepo said the gathering was intended to communicate the associations’ position and assure the candidates of their members’ support. He expressed confidence in the APM candidates’ prospects in the 2027 elections, saying the traders were prepared to exercise their voting rights in support of candidates they believed could advance their interests. “The purpose of this gathering is to assure all our APM candidates that the traders are with them. We believe that all the candidates will win,” he said. Stella Modupe Olabode, President of the Oyo State Artisans and Traders’ Network (OSATRIN), also expressed optimism about the candidates’ electoral prospects. She prayed for the success of the traders and the candidates, urging association members to remain united and committed to their shared objectives. OSATRIN is among the trade and artisan unions operating under the Amalgamation of Oyo Market Traders and Artisans. Similarly, Mrs Khadijat Ojolowo Sanusi, President of the Oyo State Food Canteen Association, described the gathering as the beginning of a process that the traders hoped would culminate in a thanksgiving celebration after the candidates’ anticipated victory. She said traders might not necessarily be politicians but were eligible voters whose ballots could influence election outcomes. According to her, the associations were prepared to exercise their franchise in support of APM candidates. Alhaji Mogaji Salaudeen Kamorudeen, President of Omo Ajorosun and Progressive Traders, Men and Artisans, urged the candidates to pay greater attention to the needs of traders and market operators. He specifically called for solar-powered lighting in markets across Oyo State, saying improved lighting could enable traders to extend their operating hours and support commercial activities beyond the usual daytime schedule. Kamorudeen said reliable lighting could improve convenience for traders and customers while creating additional opportunities for economic activities. He urged political leaders to consider the request as part of efforts to improve market infrastructure and strengthen the state’s commercial sector. Other market leaders at the gathering included Babaloja (Eleso) Kamardeen Olaosebikan; Alabi Olalekan, Chairman of the Nylon Cutters Association; Alhaja Sonde Saudat; and Alhaji Eniola Mutalubi, the Babaloja for Food in Oyo State. title: Oil prices climb as traders weigh Saudi supply risk, Russian diesel flow
body: Oil prices climbed on Wednesday as traders weighed supply risk from fighting between Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthis and Saudi Arabia against the ​prospect of increased diesel from Russia. Brent crude futures rose 89 cents, or 0.8%, to $106.58 a barrel by 0030 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures gained 80 cents, or 0.9%, to $94.94 a barrel. Brent fell 0.9% on Tuesday, while WTI rose 0.4%. “Supply ​concern stemming from conflict between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia is driving ​prices higher,” said chief strategist Hiroyuki Kikukawa at Nissan Securities Investment, ⁠a unit of Nissan Securities. “However, the expectation that increased Russian diesel exports ​will ease market tightness is likely to limit sharp price movement in either direction,” ​Kikukawa said, projecting WTI to trade between $90 and $100 a barrel. The Houthis attacked an administrative building belonging to state-owned oil firm Saudi Aramco in the city of Dhahran, causing a limited fire, ​Saudi Arabia’s energy ministry said on Wednesday. The group has fired ballistic missiles and ​drones at Saudi Arabia over the past week in retaliation for the kingdom’s support of ‌Yemeni ⁠government forces. Riyadh’s international airport has been hit four times, with a strike on Saturday killing 13 people. Last month, Saudi Arabia raised oil production despite disruptions to shipments caused by the US-Iran war, leading to a sharp increase in production from OPEC+ — the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and partners, including Russia — OPEC said on Tuesday. Iran is deploying new tactics to target ships in the Strait of Hormuz ​to keep oil prices high and influence US midterm elections, ​two senior ⁠Iranian officials told Reuters. In Russia, the government said on Tuesday it did not see any direct link between peace talks with Ukraine and its deal to export diesel to ⁠the US. The comment came after Reuters reported that US envoys had told Ukrainian officials on Friday that the deal was part of an attempt to draw Russia back into negotiations for a peace settlement .

title: Cody Rhodes calls for WWE return to Abu Dhabi, before Street Fighter release
body: It's been nearly nine years since WWE last staged a show in Abu Dhabi. Three-time WWE champion Cody Rhodes thinks it's time the wrestling company returned. “Love Abu Dhabi,” Rhodes tells The National . “I only get to stop in for a brief moment usually, but I feel like it’s been a minute because WWE has been over in the Middle East, but we haven’t really hit Abu Dhabi. And we should.” WWE last staged shows in the UAE capital in December 2017 , when Roman Reigns was among the stars who performed at Zayed Sports City Tennis Stadium. The company has since increased its presence in Saudi Arabia, where its next major event, Crown Jewel , takes place in Riyadh on November 7, with Reigns set to face Sami Zayn. Rhodes is speaking alongside American comedian Andrew Schulz, his co-star in the new Street Fighter film. Schulz is no stranger to the emirate as he has performed at Etihad Arena twice, first in October 2023 and again in May 2024 during the inaugural Abu Dhabi Comedy Week. “Abu Dhabi’s great. Some of the best comedy audiences in the world,” Schulz says. In director Kitao Sakurai's adaptation of Capcom's fighting-game series, Rhodes plays US Air Force fighter Guile, while Schulz portrays Dan Hibiki. Set in 1993, Street Fighter follows estranged fighters Ryu (Andrew Koji) and Ken Masters (Noah Centineo), who are recruited by Chun-Li (Callina Liang) to enter the World Warrior Tournament. Learning to perform without an audience Schulz came to the film with two decades of stand-up comedy experience, although some of the habits he had developed on stage proved less useful when working alongside other actors. “We’re not getting a big pop or a big laugh,” he says. “So I think in some ways it’s like training yourself out of waiting for the reaction. “This character’s not even looking for a laugh. He’s dead serious about what he’s saying. It might be ridiculous and absurd, but to him, it’s the most important thing in the world. It’s kind of unlearning some things that we’ve both been doing for the last 20 years.” Rhodes found more familiar territory during a tournament scene involving hundreds of extras gathered around the fighters. With Guile surrounded by competitors and spectators, there was an opportunity to draw on the showmanship he has developed throughout his wrestling career. “There is an element of peacocking to what Guile was doing,” he says. “I mean, I even challenged Schulz to an arm-wrestling contest.” Director Sakurai and representatives from Capcom were also on set, providing some of the feedback Rhodes was accustomed to receiving from wrestling audiences. Their encouragement helped him judge whether his interpretation of Guile was working and remained faithful to the character. There was also room to experiment, particularly when Schulz and Rhodes began suggesting ways to add humour to the action. During one scene, Schulz was fascinated by the aerial performers suspended above the set, some of whom were hanging by their hair. “They literally just tied a knot to their hair, and they’re just spinning around,” he says. The sight inspired an idea. Schulz and Rhodes suggested that one of the performers could descend upside down during a conversation involving Guile, interrupting the exchange before disappearing back towards the ceiling. The filmmakers liked the gag enough to include it in the finished film. “They were very willing to just hear our absurd ideas,” Schulz says. Bringing something new to familiar characters Beyond those contributions, Schulz was working within a production in which the broader creative decisions were in other people's hands – an unfamiliar position after two decades building his own comedy career. “It was very cool to be in something where you trust the creators and you just go, ‘OK, for the first time in my career, I completely submit to what your creative is, and I’m going to try to execute that to the best of my ability',” he says. Rhodes is joined in the film by fellow professional wrestlers Roman Reigns, who plays Akuma, and Hirooki Goto, who portrays E Honda. WWE has helped promote the adaptation, with Rhodes wearing Guile-inspired ring gear during his SummerSlam entrance in August. The crossover between wrestling and film offers an opportunity to reach an audience already familiar with their work, while showing fans something they haven't seen before from all three. “What I love is that when they see Roman, when they see Goto, when they see me, they won’t be seeing what they’re used to, which is a credit to what we’ve been able to do and the skills that we were able to develop before we got into this, in terms of creating a brand new character, another layer for us,” Rhodes says. Street Fighter releases in UAE cinemas on Thursday

title: Enugu opposition parties call for probe of political violence
body: By Dennis Agbo Opposition political parties in Enugu State have called on security agencies to investigate reports of violence and intimidation involving their members and supporters and take appropriate action against anyone found culpable. The parties made the call at a joint press conference attended by representatives of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA), Labour Party, African Democratic Congress (ADC) and Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC). They expressed concern over reported incidents involving opposition supporters, campaign structures and political gatherings, stressing the need to protect democratic participation ahead of the forthcoming elections. Leading the address, the PDP governorship candidate, Wakibiah Uche Nnaji, alongside other party leaders, called for peaceful political engagement, saying political contests should focus on service, performance and ideas rather than confrontation. The coalition urged political leaders, including presidential candidates, to uphold democratic principles and respect the rights of political opponents. The NDC governorship candidate, Sir Chinyeaka Ohaa, recounted incidents he said affected his supporters and campaign activities. Ohaa alleged that supporters who welcomed him at the Akanu Ibiam International Airport, Enugu, were tear-gassed and attacked by individuals he described as suspected thugs. He also alleged that some vehicles were damaged, journalists’ mobile phones were taken and several supporters sustained injuries during the incident. According to him, his campaign office was subsequently attacked, while some people reportedly suffered gunshot wounds and other injuries requiring emergency medical treatment. The NDC candidate also raised concerns over the reported arrest and detention of a young man who allegedly livestreamed and reported the incident. He called for the circumstances surrounding the arrest to be clarified. Similarly, the ADC governorship candidate, Chief Ocho Obodoeze, expressed concern over reports of attacks and threats involving members of his party. He said security agencies had a responsibility to protect citizens regardless of their political affiliations. Obodoeze added that incidents involving ADC members at public gatherings had been documented and reported to the Department of State Services (DSS). He called for effective security measures to ensure that political activities could take place without intimidation or disruption. The opposition coalition also referred to a reported incident involving the community associated with an NDC senatorial candidate, where more than 15 people were said to have been shot. The parties said several victims reportedly sustained serious injuries and required emergency medical treatment, calling for an investigation to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident. The opposition leaders urged security agencies to investigate the reported incidents, establish the facts and ensure that anyone found responsible was dealt with in accordance with the law. They also called on federal security agencies to pay attention to concerns raised by political parties and urged the international community to monitor developments relating to political participation and electoral security in the state. The coalition maintained that political violence could undermine confidence in the electoral process, calling on security chiefs to act impartially and provide a safe environment for all political parties to campaign. Despite their concerns, the opposition leaders reaffirmed their commitment to peaceful and issue-based campaigns, urging political actors to honour peace agreements and respect the electorate’s democratic rights. They also called on political leaders and security agencies to work together to preserve peace and peaceful coexistence in Enugu State ahead of the elections.
