title: 2027: Atiku should back Obi, Uzodinma can’t speak for Ndigbo — Eme Okoro
body: . Faults APC’s treatment of S’East, urges Igbo leaders to unite for Kanu’s release By Steve Oko UMUAHIA — Former Abia State Secretary to the Government, Dr Eme Okoro, has urged former Vice-President and the candidate of the African Democratic Congress, ADC, for the 2027 presidential poll, Atiku Abubakar, to support Peter Obi’s presidential ambition in 2027, arguing that equity and political strategy demand that the South be allowed to retain the presidency beyond 2027. Okoro, a former ally of Atiku and one of his key supporters in the South East, described Obi as Nigeria’s best presidential material at the moment, adding that the former Anambra State governor possesses the competence and capacity to lead the country. He insisted that the quest for the presidency required strategic thinking rather than ethnic sentiments. The elder statesman who spoke exclusively with Vanguard in Umuahia, urged Atiku to show political maturity and sagacity by supporting Obi to enable the South complete its turn before power “rotates back to the North in 2031.” The former SSG also faulted what he described as the All Progressives Congress (APC)’s unfair treatment of the South-East, while challenging the region’s political leaders to rise above partisan interests and pursue issues affecting Ndigbo collectively. He regretted that most of the key challenges of the South East had not been addressed by the APC -led federal government. Okoro particularly decried the collapse of railway services across the South-East, lamenting that the zone had been left out of the federal government’s massive railway investments, despite billions of naira reportedly borrowed to revamp rail transportation in other parts of the country. He described the situation as another glaring evidence of what he considered the APC-led Federal Government’s marginalisation of the South-East, questioning why a region whose support the ruling party would need in the 2027 elections should continue to suffer such infrastructural neglect. The former SSG argued that the APC’s treatment of the South-East had done little to inspire confidence that the ruling party genuinely valued the region’s electoral support, warning that political loyalty should not be expected where equity, inclusion and tangible development remained elusive. On the continued detention of the Indigenous People of Biafra (IPOB) leader, Nnamdi Kanu, Okoro said South-East governors and Ohanaeze Ndigbo must close ranks and mount a coordinated effort to secure his release. He criticised the region’s political leadership for failing to demonstrate the unity and determination needed to address the matter, insisting that Kanu’s case should transcend party affiliations. Okoro also dismissed claims that Imo State Governor Hope Uzodimma could speak for the entire Igbo nation on critical political questions, arguing that no individual political leader should arrogate to himself the authority to determine the collective position of Ndigbo. He maintained that the South-East must reassess its political calculations and demand fairness in the Nigerian federation rather than allow partisan considerations to undermine its interests. The former SSG’s position comes amid growing political manoeuvres ahead of the 2027 presidential election, with questions of opposition unity, regional interests and the South-East’s place in the Nigerian political equation taking centre stage. Okoro said South East geopolitical zone could achieve more politically if speak with one voice and jettison selfish interests. The octogenarian cautioned South East political elite against sacrificing the interest of the zone on the altars of their individual political ambitions. The post 2027: Atiku should back Obi, Uzodinma can’t speak for Ndigbo — Eme Okoro appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: 2027: Bende traditional rulers disown rotation agreement
body: Traditional rulers in Bende Federal Constituency of Abia State have distanced themselves from a document circulating on social media as a purported 2019 agreement on the rotation of the constituency’s seat in the House of Representatives. The document, which has featured in discussions surrounding political representation in the constituency ahead of the 2027 general elections, purportedly outlines an eight-year rotation arrangement between Bende North and Bende South. It reportedly bears the names of the Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives, Benjamin Okezie Kalu, and some traditional rulers from the two political blocs. However, the Director-General of the Benjamin Kalu Movement (BKM), Hon. Emmanuel Trumps Eke, has denied signing the document, stating that neither he nor Kalu endorsed the purported agreement. In a disclaimer, Eke said he had become aware of the document, which was being circulated as a proposal on representation and rotation in Bende Federal Constituency. “I wish to state categorically that neither I, nor my Principal, signed any such document,” he said. Eke also questioned the dates appearing on the documents associated with the purported arrangement, noting differences in the dates and raising questions about the sequence of events described. He further stated that the format of the document differed from what he expected of an official communication from the traditional rulers. According to him, the traditional rulers whose names appeared on the document had also issued separate statements distancing themselves from it. Eke urged political stakeholders to communicate their positions on representation and rotation directly to the people of Bende and encouraged members of the public to verify documents before sharing them. Traditional Rulers Issue Disclaimers Among those who have publicly distanced themselves from the document is Eze Dr Patrick Ude, Isiobu I of Umuisiobu Autonomous Community in Bende Local Government Area. Ude, whose name appeared on the document as chairman or representative of Bende South, stated in a letter dated October 9, 2026, that he was not invited to or present at any meeting where the purported agreement was discussed. “I hereby state clearly and without ambiguity to Ndi Bende, Abia State and the general public that I was never invited to, never attended any meeting where such agreement was discussed or reached,” he said. Ude added that he did not sign, thumbprint or witness any document concerning the rotation of the Bende Federal Constituency seat. He said his name and office appeared in the publication without his knowledge or consent and urged the public to disregard the document insofar as it concerned him. The traditional ruler also called for peace, equity and progress in the constituency, adding that he remained committed to maintaining cordial relations with political actors. Similarly, Eze Jerry Akpala Igwe, Aka-ji Ofo Item of Ikwueze Okoko Item Autonomous Community in Bende LGA, issued a statement dated October 10, 2026, distancing himself from the document. He said the signature attributed to him was not his and maintained that he had not participated in any such agreement. “I hereby dissociate myself from the document circulating on social media, as I was not part of such a document at any point in time, and it should be discountenanced by the general public,” he said. Also, Eze John Akaliro, Obasiukwu II of Umuonuoha, Umuibe, Ogboko Umuobasiukwu Ozuitem Autonomous Community in Bende LGA, said in a letter dated October 9, 2026, that he did not sign or witness the document bearing his name. “The document in circulation bearing my name should be discountenanced, as I did not sign or witness such a document,” he said. The statements from the traditional rulers and Eke reflect their respective positions on the disputed document and the purported rotation arrangement. The claims surrounding the document’s origin, authenticity and the existence of any formal agreement have not been independently established. The post 2027: Bende traditional rulers disown rotation agreement appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Zimbabwean author denies using AI to write award-winning story
body: Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using artificial intelligence (AI) to write his short story, which won this year’s Caine Prize for African Writing. His statement comes a week after he scooped the £10,000 ($13,000) award, and a recent article in The Atlantic said that AI-detection software Pangram had shown his work about a boy whose family is going through hard times was entirely AI-generated. “For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote The Blue Fighter,” he posted on X . The accusation has caused an uproar on social media, and Caine Prize chair Ellah Wakatama told the BBC she was shocked that the US magazine had not waited for a full investigation before publishing. “I do wish The Atlantic had spent more time investigating this so that, alongside Pangram, they did have evidence of real human investigation of it before tainting the prize and tainting this winner,” Wakatama told the BBC’s Front Row programme . The chair of the Caine Prize’s board of trustees said she had been contacted on Friday about the allegation and Vauhini Vara’s article – Yet Another Prizewinner Seems to Be AI – had been published on Sunday. It follows rows over other literary prizes this year, in particular the Commonwealth Short Story Prize, which was won by Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir despite allegations that he had used AI, and the withdrawal of Canadian-Haitian author Thélyson Orélien from France’s top literary award, the Goncourt, over allegations he used AI for his first novel, which he denies . Vara, who quoted Wakatama in her article, said her wariness of Silicon Valley was “well founded and reasonable” but she said Pangram’s internal research showed its assessments were rarely wrong. The backlash to the article on social media has included comments from African writers with suggestions that such accusations are primarily being made against non-white writers. Wale Lawal, the Nigerian founder of The Republic magazine, called out The Atlantic article for being “crazy, racist and wildly unethical” . Zimbabwean writer Joe Ruzvidzo, whose novel Welcome to Anywhere came out last year, said he stood by Kundizeza and that it was time “to fight this literary stop-and-frisk” . Nigerian publisher Modupe Daramola said it was necessary to discuss how “these AI allegations are targeting Black and African writers” and how they were often disproportionately scrutinised. “There’s something incredibly sinister about this,” the Noisy Streetss Limited publisher posted on X . “Pangram is itself AI-powered. Why should its assessment be treated as definitive?” she added. Wakatama said that, as part of an internal investigation for the Caine Prize, Kundizeza would be submitting documentation on his various drafts, and that there were ongoing conversations with all the judges and with The Shallow Tales Review, the publication that first published The Blue Fighter in 2025 . In his statement, Kundizeza said he had “a concrete, documented history” about the story’s inspiration and he set out the chronology of its development. Wakatama, who is also editor-at-large at Canongate Books, said Caine Prize submissions, all of which were previously published, were not checked for AI, but writers vouched for the originality of their work. She added that she was not against using AI per se to check entries, but she was “against is it being used as a final arbiter in this case”. Wakatama said it was also important to remember Pangram was “not yet tested”. “I am not happy for the work of writers, and in this case especially black writers, to form the testing ground for something that is at best still rough and ready.” Research has found that AI detectors can wrongly flag human writing as AI generated. Vara conceded that any AI-detection product, “including one as good of Pangram” was “not going to be 100% accurate”. In her article, as well as citing Pangram research she also quoted a recent paper by researchers at Free University of Brussels , which said it had found zero cases of Pangram, and two other AI-detection tools, getting it wrong when it came to English-language writing by non-native English speakers. The study notes that tools like Pangram should be considered “as an initial flag for further investigation”. Vara told BBC’s Front Row programme that she had also used her own judgment “to suss out these things” and that every other previous Caine Prize winning story she had put through Pangram “came out as 100% human”. “I also found an earlier 2021 story by the same author. I ran that through Pangram. It also came out as 100% human. And what struck me was that was a really good, interesting story. And tonally, it’s so different from this story, as if the same person hadn’t written both.” In response Kundizeza wrote: “To suggest that a writer cannot write in different styles or genres, or improve his writing substantially after five or more years fundamentally misunderstands the craft of writing.” For Vara, one of the stylistic issues that stood out about The Blue Fighter was that it had used sentence constructions using “X but Y”, which she says is common in AI-generated texts. “Not with anger, but with the quiet resignation of someone who had known all along this moment would come,” is an example she gave from the story that described the character of the mother. “The proliferation of those struck me,” Vara told Front Row, adding that the story also had many metaphors, which are prevalent in AI-generated writing. The day after winning the Caine Prize, Kundizeza told the BBC he was inspired after hearing a poem read by South African Vangile Gantsho at an event in Ghana last year about her father’s obsession with building fish tanks. He said he had woven that with fictionalised details from his own life around 2002 when Zimbabwe’s economic troubles began. “Much like the father in the story, my own dad… was an accountant, but he quit his job to grow tomatoes. So it kind of touches on both of our fathers,” he told BBC Newsday. On X, Kundizeza said he was heartened by “the numerous messages of solidarity from fellow writers and readers”, and ended his message by saying, “Most importantly, I will continue to write.”

title: Trump predicts new Great Depression for US if Democrats win November elections
body:
NEW YORK, October 14. /TASS/. The US will face a new Great Depression if the Democrats win the midterm elections to Congress in November, US leader Donald Trump said.
"If the Democrats win, you will have a 1929-style economic depression," he said, speaking to supporters in Alaska. "If the Republicans win, you will each receive $5,000 in your pocket and economic success for our country, the likes of which we have never seen before," Trump added.
The Great Depression was a worldwide economic downturn that began in 1929 with the stock market crash in the United States and lasted until about 1939. Industrial cities were hit the hardest, construction almost came to a halt, agricultural prices plummeted, while unemployment affected 14 mln people in the US.

title: ‘Am Yisrael Chai’: Belgian defense minister backs Israel despite government criticism
body: Belgium has been among Israel's harshest critics in the European Union since the October 7 Hamas massacre, adopting a series of measures against the Jewish state. Yet despite the Belgian government's critical stance, several senior figures in its governing coalition have emerged as outspoken supporters of Israel. In January 2026, Belgium restricted arms exports to Israel and moved to limit services for Belgian citizens living in West Bank settlements.   Against that backdrop, Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken marked the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre with a three-word message in Hebrew: "Am Yisrael Chai," meaning "The people of Israel live," accompanied by two blue-and-white hearts. The message was posted at precisely 6:29 a.m., symbolically marking the time Hamas launched its attack on Israel on October 7, 2023. Francken has long been an outspoken supporter of Israel, repeatedly criticizing previous Belgian governments over what he described as their hostile and unfair treatment of a democratic country. In November 2023, he condemned ministers in the previous Belgian government who refused to designate Hamas as a terrorist organization, as well as those advocating boycotts of Israel. In June 2025, Francken told Al Arabiya that he believed Israel should retain the monopoly on nuclear weapons in the Middle East to counter the Iranian threat to the West.   The Belgian defense minister is not Israel's only supporter within the country's governing coalition. Georges-Louis Bouchez, president of the Reformist Movement (MR), the second-largest party in Belgium's coalition, attended a memorial ceremony for the victims of October 7 this week alongside Israel's ambassador to Belgium, David Saranga. In his speech, Bouchez expressed strong support for Israel and the Jewish community. He emphasized Israel's right to defend itself against terrorism and explicitly addressed the threat posed to Israel by the Iranian regime. Last week, on October 7, Saranga presented his credentials to Belgium's King Philippe, formally beginning his tenure as Israel's ambassador. Reflecting on the significance of the date, Saranga wrote on X: "In Israel, pain and hope often share the same day. That is how it is for me today." "On the day we commemorate the October 7 massacre, I will present my credentials to the king of Belgium as Israel's ambassador. I will enter the palace carrying the memory of those murdered and our determination to live, create and prosper. Our enemies murdered our people. They did not break our spirit."   Upon taking up his post, Saranga also launched a series of artificial intelligence-generated videos introducing himself to the Belgian public in French, Flemish and Arabic. In the videos, the Israeli ambassador calls for an end to boycotts against Israel and discusses Israel's struggle against radical Islam, warning that the threat also exists on European soil in the form of dormant terrorist cells. Saranga also calls for dialogue with moderate Muslim communities. "Many in Europe already recognize the threat posed by radical Islamist organizations. These terrorist networks have existed on European soil for years, some active and others dormant. As democratic countries that cherish freedom and life, we have a responsibility to confront this challenge," he said. Saranga has been among the pioneers of artificial intelligence in public diplomacy. As early as 2023, Israel's Foreign Ministry released a series of videos under the title "AI Diplomacy," featuring Saranga speaking eight different languages in an effort to reach diverse audiences around the world. Recent technological advances have made it possible to incorporate increasingly sophisticated facial expressions and emotional nuances into AI-generated videos, providing diplomats with new ways to communicate with local populations even when they do not speak their languages.

title: Gombe 2027 : MURIC protests omission of Pantami’s name by INEC
body: By Adesina Wahab A group, the Muslim Rights Concern (MURIC) has described the omission of the name of Prof. Ibrahim Isa Ali Pantami as the governorship candidate of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) in Gombe after a court-ordered fresh primary as an act of impunity and contempt of court. The group therefore called for the immediate reinstatement of Pantami’s name, describing its omission on the list of gubernatorial candidates by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) as illegal and unjust. Addressing a press conference at its headquarters in Lagos on Tuesday, MURIC Founder/Executive Director, Prof. Ishaq Akintola, said the development was clearly unjust. MURIC recalled that Pantami was the sole governorship aspirant of the PDP in Gombe as at May 2026 and was affirmed by voice vote on May 26, 2026, at an event presided over by the PDP electoral committee chairman for the state, Gregory Yenlong. According to the group, the initial primary was nullified by a Federal High Court which ordered a fresh primary. The fresh primary was held on September 29, 2026, where Pantami scored 2,054 votes to defeat Khamisu Mailantarki and Aliyu Garry, who polled 389 and 112 votes respectively. The group claimed that INEC monitored the fresh primary, with a team led by Mr. Gambo Umar Arabi, who signed and submitted an official report. “‎While President Bola Tinubu is working very hard on economic reforms, Amupitan is pursuing his hidden agenda in INEC, namely, to weed out Islamic scholars among the candidates in the 2027 general elections, particularly those vying for higher offices like the governorship post. ‎ ‎”Incidentally, Professor Ibrahim Isa Ali Pantami is vying for the position of the governor of Gombe State under the banner of the PDP and Amupitan has special interest in him. He must explain this special interest. ‎ “‎We said it a long time ago. A man who took it upon himself to write an 80-page legal brief replete with falsehoods against Nigerian Muslims on the basis of which the United States labelled Nigeria as a country of special concern, a Christian-killer nation and a country where Christian genocide reigns supreme cannot be a good electoral umpire. ‎ ‎”If Amupitan can manufacture all those lies against Nigerian Muslims in his 80-page legal brief which he willingly sent to the United States, nothing stops him from concocting allegations against the only Islamic scholar contesting for the post of governor in today’s Nigeria, something unheard of before in this country. ‎ “On what ground is INEC disowning a process it was part of? The presence of INEC at the PDP primary which produced Pantami proves beyond any reasonable doubt that both Pantami and his party went through due process,” he stated. The Islamic human rights group accused INEC Chairman, Professor Joash Amupitan, of being responsible for the omission, alleging religious bias. The group cited examples of Christian clerics serving as governors, including Pastor Umo Eno of Akwa Ibom, Apostle Bassey Otu of Cross River, Rev. Fr. Hyacinth Alia of Benue, and Pastor Agbu Kefas of Taraba, and questioned why an Islamic scholar could not be allowed to contest in Gombe. “We put it to INEC that its chairman has a ‘Candidate of Special Concern’ and it is no other than Professor Isa Ali Pantami,” Akintola said. MURIC said it had earlier protested the appointment of Professor Amupitan as INEC chairman, along with the Supreme Council for Shariah in Nigeria (SCSN), and that the handling of Pantami’s candidature had vindicated its position. The group passed a vote of no confidence in the INEC chairman and called on President Tinubu to appoint a detribalised and religiously neutral replacement. “MURIC demands the immediate reinstatement of the name of Professor Ibrahim Isa Ali Pantami as the governorship candidate of the Peoples Democratic Party in Gombe State,” the statement concluded. MURIC stressed that it is a non-partisan Islamic human rights organisation whose interest is in the protection of the fundamental rights of Nigerian Muslims across all political parties. The post Gombe 2027 : MURIC protests omission of Pantami’s name by INEC appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: At NIFST AGM: NAFDAC DG charges food scientists on food safety, quality
body: .Says it impacts public health By Adesina Wahab The Director General of the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control, NAFDAC, Prof. Mojisola Adeyeye, has charged food scientists and others involved in the production of edible items to ensure the safety and quality of their products, saying it impacts on public health. She stated this in Lagos on Tuesday while delivering a goodwill message at the 50th Conference and Annual General Meeting of the National Institute of Food Science and Technology, NIFST. “I congratulate the institute on 50 years of impact, professional development and sustainable research that promotes safe nutrition and sustainable economic growth. You must be agents of change for products that are safe for consumption. We must improve the food system in Nigeria. “Food safety and quality are critical. Innovation and public health protection must go hand in hand. New products must be developed with regard to food safety. One of the innovations we need most is to prevent waste, as over 40 percent of food items we produced are wasted. “Collaborate with others to achieve prevention of food waste. Stop working on silos. Our laboratories are available for you to use in your research efforts,” she stated. The President of the NIFST, Dr Bola Osinowo, expressed happiness that the institute that started with five members in 1976 at the Federal Institute of Industrial Research, Oshodi, has become a big platform for food safety, security, and sound nutrition. “We are the biggest collection of food scientists on the continent of Africa. The NIFST Academy is on course and we have developed 32 training programmes and are collaborating with other research institutes across the globe. Research must be translated to enterprises to create jobs and for the economic development of our nation,” he said. The incoming president of the institute, Dr Ignatius Alaka, said his vision is to take it to greater heights. “We are grooming food scientists who are going to be involved in how edibles are produced or processed. We do not have the power to arrest those who adulterate products, there are agencies of government doing that. However, we believe that if we groom people with conscience and ethical values to be in charge of the process and system, faking of products will be a thing of the past,” he opined. Delivering a paper on “Research to Relevance”, to student members of the institute, Dr Sylvanus Ogbor, said research must create national value. “Commercialisation must become national culture, good scientists must become systems builders. Our institute is all out for food security and safety of Nigerians,” he said. As part of the event, two new persons were invested as members Trustees of the institute. They are Eze Mike Elechi of Elele in Rivers State and business mogul, Dr Cosmas Maduka. The post At NIFST AGM: NAFDAC DG charges food scientists on food safety, quality appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Even during wartime, the UAE is budgeting for the future
body: There is no denying that for many regional economies, these are uncertain times. Strikes on oil tankers and airports highlight the unresolved nature of the conflict between Iran and the US, and its ripple effects. However, a look at how the UAE is planning its future in this environment is illuminating. The country’s latest federal budget is a reminder that long-term economic ambitions cannot be put on hold every time the region faces a crisis. The decision to commit Dh292.5 billion ($79.64 billion) over the next three years is a serious statement of intent. Of particular note is its emphasis on social development, which has been earmarked as the largest area for spending. Economic strength largely depends on the people who sustain it, particularly their education, skills, health and ability to participate in a changing economy. Investing in citizens is an essential part of the UAE’s long-term competitiveness and is recognition that its most valuable asset is its people. “Our priorities remain fixed and unchanged…” Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid , Vice President and Ruler of Dubai , said on Monday. “Education, health, housing, social services, and the quality of life and stability of the citizen.” Somewhat counterintuitively, despite the months of violent and dangerous conflict in the region, the UAE is confident in its future. This is borne out by some independent projections; a report on Monday by global advisory firm Boston Consulting Group suggested that wealth in the Emirates is set to jump to $6 trillion by the end of this decade. This reflects the Emirates’ enduring appeal to investors and its accumulation of assets. The country’s long policy of diversifying its economy beyond hydrocarbons has been supported by international capital and a reputation for stability. Economic strength largely depends on the citizens and residents who sustain it This is not to be complacent. The International Monetary Fund’s recent decision to downgrade its growth forecasts for regional economies highlights the seriousness of continuing challenges. Even countries with substantial financial reserves and diversified sources of income are not wholly immune from regional shocks of the magnitude being experienced right now. The UAE’s budget can be best understood as an expression of ambition and an investment in resilience. The current regional turmoil actually supports the case for more medium and long-term planning. Funding resilience only when a crisis arrives is not the most effective strategy. It is the decisions that governments make today that will count when the chips are down. Long-term planning and strategic foresight are strengths of the UAE, and essential ingredients for its current and future success.

title: 'He irrigated the tree with his blood': West Bank olive farmers set for another deadly harvest
body: Abdul Latif Al Bazzari, 59, moved slowly and deliberately as he battled through pain to recount the last moments of his cousin, Ali Al Bazzari, at an olive grove in the pale green, dusty hills around the city of Nablus. On Monday, the scattering of olive trees among which he stood was serene. Accessible through a rough dirt track, the only sign of a world outside the grove was a light breeze that travelled through the valley. That peace was shattered last week, on October 7, when the family was subjected to the only settler attack they have faced in that area in 60 years. “He irrigated the tree with his blood,” Mr Al Bazzari said, standing near the trunk where his relative bled to death. “It will forever be the real estate of this attack by Jewish terrorist settlers.” His face barely showed emotion as he described the death of his cousin, a 44-year-old father of four. Perhaps it was too painful: his face was still bruised and covered in a fresh white dressing. Mr Al Bazzari said the settlers shot at them, beat them with metal and wooden objects and threw stones. Eight people were injured, two by gunfire. One of his cousins is still in the hospital. “They don’t want us to stay on any land, or take any of our crops. They are telling us to stay in our villages and cities, and not to go down to our trees,” he said. Palestinian olive farmers across the Israeli-occupied West Bank are facing another harvest season marred by settler violence . Unlike last year, when the crop was poor, the weather this year has been good and the trees are full. The settlers, however, are still as violent, if not more so. The harvest season officially begins on Thursday but the farmers have been out in their groves for weeks, fearing thefts from Israeli settlers who are posting social media campaigns encouraging people to steal their olives. Already, two Palestinians have been killed by settlers since farmers started heading to their trees in late September, and many more injured. The entire harvest season is in danger – a major blow to the Palestinian economy , which has been significantly damaged by violence and severe restrictions in the occupied West Bank during the three years since the Hamas-led October 7 attacks on southern Israel. The olive harvest is not only crucial to the economy but also symbolic of Palestinians' deep connection to the land. “The olive groves and the harvest are the soil of the Palestinian people. This is a strategic crop," Mr Al Bazzari said. "It’s not like wheat or barley; it’s the identity of the Palestinian people. Some of the trees are more than 500 years old, hundreds of years before Israel was established.” I was screaming. I was scared for my son. Then they threw me to the ground and I couldn’t feel anything Ghassan Ahmed Adeli, victim of settler attack Farther south, in the village of Usarin, Warda Adeli, 63, was also nursing wounds from a settler attack, with her arm in a sling and stitches stretching across her bruised right cheek. She was beaten as she rushed towards family members who were ambushed by settlers in the tiny grove outside their house 10 days ago. “I was screaming. I was scared for my son. Then they threw me to the ground and I couldn’t feel anything,” she said. Family members said her entire body is blue with bruising. One of her sons is still in the ICU in Nablus with a severe brain injury after being beaten with a metal bar. Another son, Ghassan Ahmed Adeli, seated next to Ms Adeli, has a broken shoulder and a back injury. He spoke on her behalf during most of the interview because she was still too weak and traumatised. The views from their home are spectacular, but also reveal a bleak situation: vast groves in the valley that farmers have not been able to access for years because of Israeli violence. There are also new settler outposts visible, established amid the blitz of settlement construction since the Gaza war broke out . The empty groves are a reminder of the long-term nature of the problem facing Palestinian olive cultivation under Israeli occupation. This year, however, there has been a worrying new development. The attacks on the Al Bazzari and Adeli families took place in Areas A and B, where the Palestinian Authority is supposed to have either full or partial control. In previous harvests, the attacks focused on Area C, where Israel has full security and civil occupation. In Ms Adeli’s case, the attack actually happened inside her village, in the narrow groves and streets between the homes of this close community, which turned out in great numbers to listen to her describe her ordeal. Some in Israel talk of there being a loss of control in the occupied West Bank , which has accelerated during the tenure of the far-right government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Palestinian olive farmers who have been attacked, as well as some of the few Israeli-Jewish activists who try to support them during the harvest, disagree. There has never been more Israeli military and civilian power in the territory. Military vehicles are everywhere, rushing about to open and close various checkpoints and gates installed in the past few years, while settlers travel and build at will. With Israel's general election just weeks away , there is also a heavy presence of candidates' campaign posters. Opposition candidates such as Gadi Eisenkot are visible shortly after passing the separation wall that separates East Jerusalem from the rest of the West Bank. That changes deep inside the Palestinian territory, where the only posters visible are of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and far-right members of his government, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich. Many of them and their supporters laud the “revolution” this government has achieved during its tenure. For them, the unpicked Palestinian olive trees are a sign of progress; the violence inflicted on Mr Al Bazzari, Ms Adeli and many others is not something Israel has to apologise for, but to praise.

title: Toxic Trump? President makes midterms all about him but some Republicans are inching away
body: On November 3, Americans will elect all 435 members of the House and 35 senators. President Donald Trump will not be on the ballot but he has sought to make the midterm elections all about himself . “I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot. I'm on the ballot. I'm on the ballot. Just one more time,” he said at a recent rally. “Because if we lose, you’re going to lose your border, you’re going to lose your tax cuts, you’re going to lose your safety and security, you’re going to lose your wealth.” At recent rallies, Mr Trump has campaigned on what he says are his administration’s accomplishments and made the election a referendum on his presidency. He said voters turn out in greater numbers when he is running and that Republican control of Congress is necessary to preserve his agenda. He even pledged $5,000 cheques to every American adult if Republicans retain control of Congress, calling it a “Trump dividend”. Previous similar promises related to tariffs and cuts in government spending have come to nothing and he cannot unilaterally authorise such payments. But amid low approval ratings, rising costs of living and an unpopular war with Iran, some Republican candidates have sought to distance themselves from him on major issues, raising the question of whether Mr Trump has become toxic. 'Kind of a betrayal' John Feehery, a Republican strategist, said the war with Iran presents a particular challenge for the President because it conflicts with his central message of non-intervention in conflicts abroad. “The war is very unpopular, even though it’s probably for a good cause. It hasn’t been really well explained. It’s not the Trump brand," Mr Feehery said. "And so, all these people who voted for Trump because they wanted an end to no more endless wars – it’s kind of a betrayal." Mr Trump has said that the war, which he initially claimed would last only a few weeks, would end after the midterms , and that fuel costs would go down shortly after. Control of Congress is likely to hinge on a relatively small number of contested races in Michigan, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, Iowa, Alaska and Texas. Republicans hold narrow majorities in both chambers. In the Senate, where Republicans hold a 53-47 majority, Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control. Historically, the party of the sitting president loses seats in the House. “We’re worried about Michigan. We’re worried about Texas. We’re worried about a few states. But it’s all about 35 different contests – not states, contests,” Mr Trump said at a recent rally. Midterm elections also typically draw fewer voters than presidential polls, and experts say Mr Trump's base is less motivated to vote in the midterms than Democratic supporters. “This is not going to be a high-turnout election, so you have to be very careful – you can’t run against Trump," Mr Feehery said. 'Like he has malaria' Still, some Republican candidates have been trying to distance themselves from the President's stance on Iran and other issues. Mike Rogers, the Trump-endorsed Republican Senate candidate running against Abdul El Sayed in Michigan, is running an advertisement saying: “The war with Iran needs to end – and end quickly.” Polling also suggests voters are mainly concerned about the economy and the rising cost of living, with a majority blaming Mr Trump for his handling of the issues. In Iowa, Republican Congresswoman Ashley Hinson, who is running for the Senate, focused her message on the economic impact of the war. “Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran,” she said in a statement. Heavy-handed immigration enforcement is another possible vulnerability for Republicans, with polling showing that many voters believe the Trump administration has crossed the line. In a campaign advertisement, Maria Elvira Salazar, a three-term Republican congresswoman running for re-election in Florida, said Mr Trump’s immigration enforcement efforts “have gone too far”. “Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy,” she said. “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.” Mr Trump has also dismissed criticism from lawmakers from both parties over a recent deal with Russia to supply millions of barrels of diesel to global markets after a call with President Vladimir Putin. The move appeared to be an attempt to slow the rising prices of diesel, but Republican senators said the deal may violate US restrictions imposed after Moscow's invasion of Ukraine. A bipartisan group of senators released a statement at the weekend opposing Russian diesel fuel imports. Senator Thom Tillis, one of the signatories to the statement, told NBC's Meet the Press on Sunday that "there’s a legitimate case for saying the President’s not following the law". “Well, I think these are Republicans that can't really be serious,” Mr Trump said on Monday when asked about the criticism from his own party. Recent polls put Mr Trump's approval ratings in the low 30s nationally, a historic low, and his disapproval ratings above 60 per cent. Chris Christie, the former Republican governor of New Jersey who ran against Mr Trump twice for the party's presidential nomination, highlighted the growing unease of politicians in his party. “With his current approval rating, Republicans are going to treat Trump like he has malaria by the time we get to October,” he wrote in a post on X. Mr Trump, however, appears convinced that his stamp of approval is a boost for candidates rather than the proverbial albatross. "I think we're going to do very well. I think that the rallies I'm doing are really changing around," he said on Tuesday. Mr Trump pledged to visit a different state most days until the election, and forgo playing golf on the weekends.

title: Suspected vehicle thief arrested in Ondo after fleeing Port Harcourt
body: By Dayo Johnson, Akure A suspected vehicle thief, Bamidele Rowell Lodi, has been arrested in Ondo State after allegedly fleeing Port Harcourt, Rivers State, with his employer’s car. The suspect, said to have worked as a security guard in Port Harcourt, was arrested following a complaint that a motorist purchased fuel worth ₦100,000 at a filling station in Epinmi-Akoko and drove away without paying. The complaint was reportedly lodged by Akin Thomas, prompting operatives of the Isua Police Division to launch a pursuit of the fleeing motorist. According to police sources, the suspect allegedly distracted the fuel attendant by asking him to fetch water before driving away without paying for the fuel. “Upon receiving the complaint, operatives attached to Isua Division immediately mobilised, mounted roadblocks and commenced pursuit of the fleeing suspect,” a source said. On sighting the police, the suspect reportedly diverted onto the Ise-Ikare Road in an attempt to evade arrest. However, the officers continued the pursuit and alerted soldiers at the Nigerian Army checkpoint in Auga. “Through this coordinated response, the suspect was intercepted and arrested for further investigation,” the source added. Preliminary investigations reportedly linked the vehicle recovered from the suspect to a stolen vehicle case reported by his employer in Port Harcourt. Investigators compared the vehicle’s chassis number with the number supplied to the police, and the two were said to match. Further intelligence indicated that the suspect had been employed as a security guard by the vehicle’s owner in Port Harcourt and allegedly stole the car before fleeing. Confirming the arrest, the Ondo State Police Public Relations Officer, DSP Jimoh Abayomi, said the suspect and the recovered vehicle were in police custody as investigations continued. “The recovered vehicle and the suspect remain in police custody as investigations continue to establish the full circumstances of the alleged offences, verify ownership of the vehicle, and determine whether the suspect may be connected to other criminal activities,” Abayomi said. He commended operatives of the Isua Division for their prompt response and professionalism, as well as the soldiers at the Auga checkpoint for their timely intervention and collaboration. Abayomi said the operation underscored the importance of inter-agency cooperation, actionable intelligence and swift response in tackling cross-border crime. He reassured residents that the command would continue to strengthen intelligence gathering and collaboration with sister security agencies to prevent crime, urging members of the public to report suspicious activities promptly. The police spokesman reiterated the command’s commitment to preventing Ondo State from becoming a safe haven for criminals, adding that a thorough investigation would be conducted and appropriate legal action taken. title: NDPA endorses Tinubu for second term, demands 25% derivation
body: By Samuel Oyadongha, Yenagoa The Niger Delta Progressives Alliance (NDPA) has endorsed President Bola Ahmed Tinubu for a second term in office, while calling for an increase in the derivation fund for the Niger Delta from 13 per cent to 25 per cent. The National President of NDPA, Victor Udoh, made the declaration during a stakeholders’ meeting in Yenagoa, Bayelsa State, where he assessed the Tinubu administration’s performance in the region over the past three years. Udoh said the administration had delivered more tangible benefits to the Niger Delta than previous administrations within their first three years, citing improvements in crude oil production, increased derivation revenue and federal interventions. In an address titled, “Legacy of Bold Reforms: An Evaluative Overview of the Tinubu Reforms in Three Years in Relation to the Quest for Sustainable Development in the Niger Delta,” he described the region as central to Nigeria’s history and economic development. “The Niger Delta is not a footnote in Nigeria’s story. It is the opening line,” he said, arguing that the region’s history of struggles for fiscal justice should inform its future. Udoh referenced the region’s historical contributions, from Eyo Ita’s pre-independence political activities in Calabar to the emergence of Goodluck Jonathan as president and Godswill Akpabio as Senate President. He said crude oil production had increased from 1.18 million barrels per day in August 2023 to more than 1.7 million barrels per day by late 2024, attributing the improvement largely to enhanced security in the creeks. “A secure Niger Delta earns the nation more,” he said. Udoh also disclosed that the nine oil-producing states received ₦1.51 trillion in derivation revenue in 2025, compared with ₦671.92 billion in the previous year. Despite the reported increase in revenue, he argued that the region’s development should be measured by the impact of public spending rather than the size of allocations received. He identified economic diversification beyond oil, local utilisation of gas for power generation, environmental restoration and transparent institutions as critical to achieving sustainable development in the region. The NDPA president reiterated the group’s demand for an increase in the derivation share from 13 per cent to 25 per cent, describing the demand as a key component of fiscal justice for oil-producing communities. “A larger share spent poorly is only a larger disappointment,” he warned, stressing that increased revenue must translate into tangible development for the people. Udoh also announced the introduction of a Reform Scorecard, an annual, open-source evaluation tool designed to assess the impact and sustainability of government reforms. He said the scorecard would be guided by three questions: “Does it flow? Does it reach? Will it last?” He further highlighted the South-South’s 15.8 million registered voters, representing about 15.3 per cent of the national register, as a potential instrument for demanding accountability from political leaders. “The era of docility is over, and the era of disorder was never ours,” he said, urging young people to take advantage of federal intervention programmes through agencies such as the National Directorate of Employment (NDE) and the Small and Medium Enterprises Development Agency of Nigeria (SMEDAN). He said the NDPA had been promoting such opportunities across the nine Niger Delta states through its “The Future Is Here” initiative. The alliance pledged to continue monitoring and documenting government reforms transparently and peacefully, with the aim of promoting accountability and regional unity. Tinubu’s Reforms Painful but Necessary, Youth Leader Says Also speaking at the meeting, the National Coordinator of the Niger Delta Youth Council Worldwide, Engr. Jator Abido, said Nigeria, at 66, could no longer afford to make excuses for its development challenges. “We are a mature nation that must make bold choices,” he said. Abido said previous administrations had largely managed the symptoms of the country’s economic challenges, while the Tinubu administration had taken steps to address structural problems. He identified fuel subsidy removal and the unification of the foreign exchange market as two major reforms, noting that although they had imposed hardship on Nigerians, they had also increased federal allocations to states and helped restore investor confidence. He cited Nigeria’s expenditure of about $10 billion on fuel subsidy in 2022 and the Central Bank of Nigeria’s reported $7 billion in unmet obligations at the time as evidence of the economic challenges confronting the country before the reforms. Abido acknowledged that inflation and the rising cost of living had affected residents of Niger Delta cities, including Port Harcourt, Warri and Yenagoa, but argued that the reforms had helped address underlying economic problems. He also said crude oil production, which had declined because of oil theft and pipeline vandalism, had improved to about 1.8 million barrels per day through collaboration between security agencies and private security firms. On environmental concerns, Abido cited the establishment of the Presidential Committee on Ogoni Consultations and the reconstitution of the board responsible for accelerating the Ogoni clean-up as steps towards rebuilding trust and addressing longstanding grievances. “These are steps in the right direction,” he said. Students, Stakeholders Back Tinubu’s Re-election In his remarks, the Bayelsa State President of the National Association of Nigerian Students (NANS), Mr Lucky Michael, commended the Tinubu administration for introducing the student loan scheme. He urged Nigerian students to support Tinubu’s re-election bid, saying a second term would enable the administration to consolidate its initiatives. Similarly, Chief Ubong Akpan said the administration had performed well in the Niger Delta and appealed to Nigerians to re-elect the president to enable him to complete his programmes. The endorsements came alongside the NDPA’s demand for a higher derivation allocation, with the alliance insisting that increased revenue must be accompanied by accountable spending and sustainable development across the region. title: Bank of America hit with $1.2bn fine for money laundering failings
body: Bank of America has been fined $1.2bn (£910m) for failing to detect potential money laundering and other illegal activity, the US Treasury Department said on Tuesday. The banking giant failed to report over $5bn in suspicious activity to the government, $1bn of which posed national security and illicit finance risks, the Treasury said. Those failures included not flagging transactions that possibly involved Chinese money laundering networks or trade-based laundering “with a substantial nexus to the southwest border”, according to the Treasury. “Our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators,” Bank of America told the BBC. The announcement came less 24 hours before Bank of America was due to announce its quarterly earnings on Wednesday morning. “Our third-quarter results will include a non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2 billion impacting net income by approximately 17 cents per share,” the bank said in an emailed statement. “We have already dedicated substantial personnel and resources to our ongoing remediation efforts, and those costs are in the current expense base,” it added. In announcing the fine, the third-largest the department has ever imposed, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said: “When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks.” The Treasury said the bank overly relied on inquiries from outside parties like law enforcement and other financial institutions instead of its own internal controls. This meant that it “effectively outsourced to third parties a substantial portion of its proactive detection and reporting obligations,” the department said. As part of the settlement, Bank of America admitted that it “willfully violated” the Bank Secrecy Act by failing to maintain a compliant anti-money laundering programme, conduct required due diligence on foreign correspondent accounts and file suspicious activity reports, the Treasury said. The $1.2bn fine included penalties imposed by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). The OCC’s $750bn fine marked the biggest penalty it has ever levied. OFAC said its settlement with the bank was tied to 475 apparent violations of sanctions programmes, including those on Russia and Iran, narcotics, and global terrorism. The settlement amount of $11.6m reflected the determination that Bank of America’s apparent violations were “non-egregious”, OFAC said.

title: Falana urges governors to utilise ₦267bn basic education funds
body: Human rights lawyer, Femi Falana, SAN, has urged governors of the 36 states and the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) to utilise ₦267 billion in released intervention funds and access over ₦65 billion in counterpart funding for basic education. Falana, who is the chairman of the Alliance on Surviving COVID-19 and Beyond (ASCAB), said the failure to utilise the funds undermined the right of Nigerian children to free and compulsory basic education. In a statement dated October 13, 2026, he cited a November 28, 2025, judgment of the Federal High Court in the case of Femi Falana & Anor v. Attorney-General of the Federation & 36 Ors (Suit No. FHC/L/CS/142/24), which he said affirmed the legal obligation of the Federal Government, the 36 state governments and the FCT to provide free, compulsory and universal basic education for children of primary and junior secondary school age. Falana expressed concern over figures disclosed by the Universal Basic Education Commission (UBEC), indicating that as of August 2026, about ₦267 billion in released intervention funds remained unutilised, while more than ₦65 billion in counterpart funding was yet to be accessed by states. The Executive Secretary of UBEC, Dr Aisha Garba, reportedly disclosed the figures at the opening of a month-long technical capacity-building workshop organised under the World Bank-assisted HOPE-GOV Programme in Abuja. The workshop is aimed at strengthening budget planning and execution for basic education and primary healthcare across the 36 states and the FCT. Falana called on the state governments and the FCT administration to urgently access the available funds and fulfil their statutory obligations under the Free, Compulsory Universal Basic Education Act. He also urged the Federal Government to provide at least one meal daily for schoolchildren to improve school enrolment and nutrition, in line with the National Social Investment Programme Agency Act. With political campaigns underway, the human rights lawyer called on the media to demand clear commitments from all registered political parties and their candidates on the implementation of laws guaranteeing free and compulsory basic education and the school feeding programme. He said political parties should be pressed to explain how their proposed programmes would ensure that every Nigerian child had access to basic education. Falana further called for urgent action to remove school-age children from the streets across the country, including the FCT, arguing that Nigeria had sufficient resources to address the challenge without further delay. He maintained that the effective utilisation of available education funds and the enforcement of existing laws were necessary to protect children’s right to education and expand access to schooling nationwide. title: Build Public confidence through professionalism, AIG tells police
body: By Muhammad Inuwa, Dutse The Commandant of the Nigeria Police Academy (POLAC), Wudil, Kano State, AIG Auwal Musa Muhammad, has urged police officers in Jigawa State to build public trust and confidence through professionalism, discipline and respect for citizens’ fundamental rights. Muhammad made the call while addressing officers and men of the Jigawa State Police Command during an official visit to the command headquarters in Dutse. He emphasised that discipline, integrity, professionalism and respect for human rights were essential to effective policing, urging officers to uphold these values in the discharge of their constitutional responsibilities. The commandant also urged police personnel to maintain cordial relationships with the communities they serve, noting that public cooperation was vital to strengthening security and boosting confidence in the Force. He stressed the need for continuous training, knowledge sharing and stronger collaboration between the Police Academy and operational police formations to enhance officers’ capacity and improve service delivery. Earlier, Muhammad paid a courtesy visit to Governor Umar Namadi at the Government House in Dutse, where discussions focused on strengthening cooperation between the Jigawa State Government and the Nigeria Police Academy. He said the visit was aimed at promoting police training, capacity development and institutional support to improve professionalism within the Force. In his remarks, Namadi commended police officers and other security agencies for their efforts to protect lives and property across the state. The governor reaffirmed his administration’s commitment to supporting security agencies in the discharge of their responsibilities. title: Cheap transport fare: FG visits 2 CNG vehicle manufacturing firms in Anambra, seeks collaboration
body: …Auto makers hail FG’s new policy on patronage By Vincent Ujumadu Two auto makers in Anambra State, Innoson Vehicle Manufacturing, IVM, Nnewi, and Kojo Motors Auto Assembly, Umunya, have hailed the Federal Government’s new policy that has made it mandatory for Ministries, Departments and Agencies, MDAs, to patronize locally made vehicles. Officials of the two companies, who spoke during the visit of board members of the National Automotive Design and Development Council, NADDC, to their facilities in Anambra State, said that with the new policy, there will be more patronage of their products. Secretary to the Government of the Federation, SGF, George Akume, has already issued a circular directing all government establishments to purchase their vehicles from local manufacturers. Managing Director of Innoson Motors, Chief Innocent Chukwuma, said during the visit to his facilities that he was particularly impressed with the Federal Government’s emphasis on Compressed Natural Gas, CNG, which, he added, is the easiest way for the Nigerian automobile industry to survive. According to him, it was to support the CNG project that made his company dedicate its newest massive facility to the production of only CNG trucks and electric vehicles. He said: “President Bola Tinubu visited some countries and saw the benefits of CNG, and on his return, he began to support it. According to the president’s plan, by next year, there will be CNG plants in all parts of the country because a lot of money has been invested in it. “With the rising cost of fuel, CNG is the way to go. There is so much gap between the prize of diesel and CNG gas, and that is why we want everyone to embrace it and move Nigeria forward. “We are investing massively in the automobile industry to make sure that our youths are busy. When the factory is constantly working, all categories of people are benefiting. “It does not even matter if there may not be so much return on investment. The important thing is that we are helping so many families to survive. As far as the factory is working, I am okay; after all, I was not born with any money. The money we invested here is for the public, and we are happy that they are enjoying it.” He commended the NADDC for supporting auto makers across the country, adding, however, that there is a need for backward integration in the industry so that companies can specialize in manufacturing products that they have comparative advantage. The Executive Director of Jojo Motors, Chinedu Oguegbo, informed the NADDC members that his company is focusing on commercial vehicles for transportation in Nigeria, adding that they are beginning to benefit from the Federal Government’s policy on locally made vehicles. “We brought the facility to where the customers are,” he said. He however noted that there had been serious challenges over the last few years, particularly the massive devaluation of the naira, adding that the fluctuation is such that it has been very difficult to take certain critical decisions. “We persevered, and we are actually in the first phase of our development. As it is, things are actually stabilizing, and we believe that the next time the board members come, our gas facility will be ready.” He said that the company’s main brand, Omma Bus being manufactured in its Ununya facility, may soon be exported to the rest of the world, while its natural gas facility would soon come on stream. The Director-General of NADDC, Oluwemimo Joseph, said the decision to visit the facilities was to enable the board members to get first-hand information on their needs and challenges. He said:”We know that those who are into production in Nigeria face a lot of challenges. These challenges will be reduced when we interact with the manufacturers and proffer solutions on how to overcome them. “We are reviewing our policies and putting forward new legislation to ensure smooth operation in the industry. We are therefore here to have first-hand knowledge of the operations to equip us and incorporate into the bill that is currently being prepared what we gather from the manufacturers. We also need to see the products being manufactured and get the experience of their customers who patronize them. “We are also talking about backward integration and seeing the parts they are using and the ones that others can adapt. There are certain vehicle components that can be produced in Nigeria, and by discussing with the manufacturers, we can cede the products for easy adaptation and then create the market for them. “In Anambra State, for instance, there are many small and medium enterprises (SMEs) manufacturing various products, and we need to harness them to see how they can fit into the automobile industry’s needs. “We have also taken note of complaints that the investment is not protected because of the proliferation of imported used vehicles. We know this, and we are taking it to the right quarters, especially as it concerns zero duty on CNG and electric vehicles.” Chairman of NADDC, Chief Emma Eneukwu, said the board is canvasing for a bill that would control the flooding of the market with foreign used cars, which, he observed, have been destroying the local market and the local vehicle manufacturers. “We will use the law to protect our local producers so that they can easily sell their products. Because some of these imported vehicles are tax free, our local manufacturers cannot effectively compete with them. That is why we want to liaise with the government to encourage them. “We also encourage the manufacturers to move a step higher to be able to compete effectively in the auto market. There could be a few components that could be imported, but we should be able to have our locally manufactured parts that should be used in the manufacture of vehicles.
