title: Top line carries Winnipeg Jets to 5-2 win over Wild
body:
At some point, the Winnipeg Jets are going to need some consistent depth scoring.
But if their top line can keep firing on all cylinders, they’re going to win a decent number of hockey games, such as Tuesday night in Winnipeg when Kyle Connor, Mark Scheifele and Cole Perfetti supplied most of the offence in a 5-2 win over the Minnesota Wild.
The Jets top line scored four times and combined for seven points as they bounced back from their first regulation loss of the season to conclude the three-game homestand.
Perfetti scored twice, Scheifele notched his first goal of the season and also added two assists, while Connor found the net again for the seventh time in just the first six games.
“Honestly, Fetts (Perfetti) has done an amazing job,” said Scheifele. “He’s done so many good things, good stick, good in battles. He’s been amazing and it’s always a work in progress.”
Connor also became just the fourth player in franchise history to score in each of the team’s first four home games of a season.
Cole Koepke had the other tally for Winnipeg.
The two teams went back-and-forth in the first period, and it was 2-2 after 20 minutes. But the Jets took the lead in the second frame and then scored two more times in the third for their fourth win in their first six games.
“Our detail or our execution getting out of our zone in the first wasn’t very good,” said Jets head coach Scott Arniel. “Talked about it. Looked at some things to be a little bit quicker. Thought we did a fantastic job in the second.
“And them flying in, playing last night, flying in, then we got them on their heels. We got them caught for a couple of long shifts, extended shifts in their end of the rink in that second period which really kinda wore, especially their defence more than anybody. It started to really wear them down which we had hoped to do earlier, but it just took us a little longer to get that.”
The Jets outshot the Wild 13-3 in the middle stanza.
With Josh Morrissey out of the lineup with an injury for the second straight game, Neal Pionk had almost 24 minutes of ice time and registered two assists in the win, including a nifty setup on Scheifele’s goal.
“P (Pionk) has a skill set, obviously moving up to that top power play is big,” Arniel said. “You saw that vision on Schife’s goal, the play that he made there. But we need everybody to have that sorta offensive flare.”
The opening goal came less than two minutes in. After Perfetti entered the Minnesota zone with the puck, he left it for Scheifele who then dropped it back to the point for Pionk. Pionk held it for a moment before sending a shot on goal that was tipped en route by Perfetti and past Cal Pickard at the 1:50 mark.
The goal was Perfetti’s fourth of the season in his sixth game. It took him 36 games to hit that mark last season as he worked his way back from an ankle injury.
But the Wild answered back at the 8:47 mark, taking advantage of a bad giveaway. As Dylan Samberg circled from behind his own net with the puck, he tried to pass it to his partner Dylan DeMelo. The pass was not a good one, landing in DeMelo’s skates and he was unable to corral it before Kirill Kaprizov picked it up.
He skated in alone on Stuart Skinner, who turned aside Kaprizov’s first shot before the Russian star batted the rebound into the net, a highlight-reel finish to a disastrous play from Winnipeg’s back end.
Winnipeg’s star players cashed in again with 2:06 left in the first. Connor skated behind the Wild net with the puck and along the boards before dropping it off to Pionk. Pionk then skated back around the net the other way, taking the puck above the goal line before sending a perfect backdoor pass that Scheifele deposited into an open net for his first of the season.
The lead was short-lived, however, as Kaprizov scored again 44 seconds later when he tipped a Quinn Hughes point shot past Skinner.
Minnesota wound up outshooting the Jets 13-7 in the first, including 9-1 over the final 11:43.
The score stayed deadlocked 2-2 for most of the second period but a long o-zone shift by the second line helped Winnipeg earn their first power play of the night, and they took full advantage.
After Pionk missed the net, Scheifele collected the puck near the left point. He sent the puck below the goal line to Gabriel Vilardi, who quickly steered the puck to Perfetti in the slot for a snapshot that beat Pickard high at the 16:36 mark.
It took 40 games for Perfetti to score five goals last season.
Winnipeg earned another power play less than a minute later as Isak Rosen was held during a strong net drive, but the Jets couldn’t cash in on the ensuing advantage.
Just over four minutes into the third period, the Jets extended their lead, once again thanks to their stars. Tyler Pitlick had a chance to control a loose puck in his own end, but he fumbled it, allowing it to roll to the stick of Connor near the point. He skated to his right to try and get away from Pitlick, which he was able to do after executing a tight spin with the puck.
That left Connor with a lot of space in the slot, which he used to load up and rocket a wrist shot past Pickard for his seventh goal of the season.
With just over five minutes to go, the Jets got an insurance goal from their fourth line. Vlad Namestnikov and Koepke were sprung on a 2-on-1, with Namestnikov carrying the puck into the Minnesota zone before sliding it across to Koepke, who wired it past a sliding Pickard to make it 5-2 with his first of the season.
Skinner stopped 19 shots to earn the win, though he only needed to make eight saves over the final two periods against a Wild team that had played the night before.
The Jets will head out on the road for one game, in Chicago Thursday night. Puck drop is just after 7 p.m. with pregame coverage on 680 CJOB starting around 5:15 p.m.

title: Every operational squadron flying as Royal New Zealand Air Force operations continue to pace
body:
Unfortunately you are viewing this website on an outdated browser which does not support the necessary features for us to provide an adequate experience. Please switch to a modern browser such as latest version of Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Apple Safari or Microsoft Edge.
Royal New Zealand Air Force (RNZAF) squadrons have been delivering for the country during a busy operational period - across New Zealand, the Pacific and the near Asia-Pacific region.
“It’s been a great time for our Air Force,” said Chief of Air Force, Air Vice-Marshal Darryn Webb.
“Every one of our operational squadrons has been flying in recent times in support of New Zealand and our partners, from the central North Island to the Pacific and across the Asia-Pacific region.”
Air Component Commander Air Commodore Andy Scott said that over a four-day period, there were “personnel and aircraft on operations, exercises and providing contingency responses to help people in need across Niue, the Cook Islands, Fiji, Tuvalu, Papua New Guinea, Kiribati, Vanuatu, Singapore, Australia and the United States as well as at home”.
“This highlights the breadth of work our people do on a daily basis and the importance of maintaining a well trained and equipped defence force to deliver both pre-planned and contingency operations 365 days of the year,” he said.
Recent activities have included crew from No. 5 Squadron flying the P-8A Poseidon on a search and rescue mission in the Pacific, successfully locating three Kiribati fishermen on a small boat to the east of Tarawa.
Aircraft pilot, Flight Lieutenant Stuart Glendinning, said the three men had not returned from fishing and had been located by the P-8A crew well over 160 nautical miles from shore, four days after the engine on their dinghy had failed.
“We remained on the scene after finding the men and coordinated a rescue by a vessel nearby,” Flight Lieutenant Glendinning said.
While this Pacific search and rescue was underway, crew from No. 3 Squadron with an NH90 Helicopter were conducting search and rescue training over the weekend, including winch familarisation, with New Zealand Police search and rescue personnel.
The training, involving 12 Police search and rescue members and over 2.5 flying hours, included winching personnel to a hut in the Ruahine Ranges, practising techniques used in emergencies.
Two other NH90s deployed over the weekend to Hawaii on two USAF C-17 aircraft recently exercising in NZ, to participate in exercises with Indo-Pacific Partners at the Joint Pacific Multinational Readiness Centre.
Other recent activities included personnel from No. 40 Squadron deploying a C-130J Hercules to deliver a Fire and Emergency New Zealand fire appliance to Niue to bolster response capability in the Pacific nation.
This aircraft had just returned from taking personnel and equipment between Fiji and Tuvalu for Pacific engagement ahead of COP31, the United Nations climate conference in Türkiye.
Another C-130J was also transporting Australian Defence Force soldiers from a multinational exercise in Papua New Guinea, supporting regional security cooperation.
No. 40 Squadron then started to fly New Zealand Defence Force personnel home from Penhryn in the Cook Islands, where personnel have been conducting construction and maintenance tasks, medical and dental outreach, and hydrographic surveying on Exercise Tropic Twilight.
Also in the Pacific, No. 42 Squadron personnel have been conducting maritime patrols on an MC-12K King Air in Vanuatu in support of a variety of Vanuatu Government departments and the Pacific Islands Forum Fisheries Agency, helping monitor and protect the region’s valuable fisheries resources.
Today, another P-8A will also support the Pacific Islands Forum Fisheries Agency conducting further patrols across the Pacific searching for illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing activities.
As well as this, a P-8A and personnel have joined Five Power Defence Arrangements partners on Ex Bersama Lima in Singapore, and No. 6 Squadron Seasprite helicopter crews, embarked on HMNZ Ships Te Mana and Aotearoa, have continued flying operations as part of Operation Crucible, a five-month regional presence deployment across the Asia-Pacific region.
“These missions reflect the breadth of what our people do every day: supporting those in need, contributing to regional security, strengthening partnerships, and protecting our shared Pacific interests,” Air Vice-Marshal Webb said.
“ As always, it’s the strength of our talented people that make the operations possible. My thanks to all involved, including the maintainers, support staff and families for the work they do.”

title: Aguleri/Umuoba Anam crisis: The bloody battle of close neighbours
body: …Five people killed, property worth millions of Naira destroyed in latest crisis By Vincent Ujumadu On October I, 2026, when Nigerians were celebrating the country’s 66th Independence anniversary, two neighbouring communities of Aguleri and Umuoba Anam, both in Anambra East Local Government Area of Anambra State, were busy fighting each other over the alleged right position of the boundary between them. At the last count, five people lost their lives. Part of the massive palace of the traditional ruler of Aguleri was set ablaze, while goods, mainly rice and large tubers of yam (the area is the food basket of Anambra State), were destroyed. People fled their homes, while youths of both communities fought with firearms. Several houses and shops were destroyed, set ablaze, and in a viral video, voices were heard ordering armed men to shoot at sight. Many residents of the area fled, and the ever-busy Otuocha-Umuoba Anam road has been deserted. Rice mills and hundreds of bags of rice were destroyed, and smoke was seen coming out of many residential houses, while traders were seen salvaging some of their property. Apart from the palace of Igwe Idigo, some of the other houses destroyed were those of Chief Nonso Ozemene, Chief Nnaluo Ebunu, Chief Okonkwo Umebe, and other buildings within the Aguleri-Umuoba Anam boundary, as well as shops at the Timber market in Aguleri. The cause of the clash was said to be the alleged decision of Aguleri Community to mount a signpost and Closed Circuit Television (CCTV) cameras on the boundary between the two communities, which Umuoba Anam community resisted. There were other reports that what ignited the latest battle was that the place the signpost was mounted was not the appropriate boundary between the two communities. Angered by the development, Umuoba Anam youths pulled it down, insisting that the signpost was mounted on their land. Later, dangerous weapons were freely used, leading to casualties, with five people confirmed dead and several others injured. It was gathered from the area that originally, Aguleri owned part of the area presently known as Umuoba Anam, but gave it to the Anam people in perpetuity. “One thing we should understand is that Umuoba Anam have continued to live peacefully in the portion of land bought from Aguleri ancestors in the olden days, which the new generation of Aguleri youths are insisting on taking over”, a resident of the area claimed. Recall that during a similar incident which lasted from 1999 to 2002 in the same local government area between Aguleri and Umuleri, over 300 lives were lost. The scars of that three-year war are still seen as one enters the local government. It was apparently to avoid another prolonged war that informed the quick intervention of the Anambra State Government, with Governor Chukwuma Soludo detailing his deputy, Dr. Onyekachukwu Ibezim, who is the chairman of the state boundary commission, and the state Commissioner of Police, CP Nnanna Oji Ama, to the area to quell the hostilities without delay. During the visit, Ibezim ordered a stoppage of further activity in Otuocha market until the state government completes necessary investigations and takes appropriate action against those responsible for the incident. He warned that no community leader or local government chairman has the authority to determine boundaries between communities without the knowledge of the state government, stressing that the State Boundary Commission is responsible for determining boundaries within the state. In the meantime, Professor Chukwuma Soludo has set up a Commission of Inquiry to look into the matter. The Judicial Commission of Inquiry would thoroughly examine all petitions, complaints, and historical grievances. The Commission was mandated to submit its comprehensive report within four months. At the peace summit held at the Government House in Awka, traditional rulers, Presidents-General, and community leaders from Aguleri, Umueri, and Umuoba Anam were in attendance. Also in attendance were traditional rulers from the Anambra South and Central Senatorial Districts, the Chairman of the Anambra State Traditional Rulers Council, and key government officials. Decrying the tragic loss of lives and the widespread destruction of properties, Governor Soludo emphasized that such lawlessness is entirely unacceptable to his administration. To ensure compliance, the governor directed security agencies to maintain a robust, round-the-clock presence in the affected zones, reassuring all parties that the government remains firm, fair, and uncompromising in its pursuit of lasting peace and justice across the state. The governor immediately convened an emergency peace and security meeting with key stakeholders from the two communities in an effort to decisively restore law and order in the area. Essentially, the meeting was to address the root causes of the long-standing dispute in the area and proffer suggestions that would help to achieve a lasting resolution of the crisis. After shutting down the popular Otuocha Market in the area, which some residents claim is still in contention, the governor issued a stern directive ordering both communities to cease all forms of hostilities, maintain absolute peace, and exercise restraint. He also expressed deep sadness over the level of casualties and injuries sustained during the clash, reminding the people that violence, bloodletting, and destruction of property have no place in a peaceful and prosperous Anambra State. Following extensive deliberations, the stakeholders reached a multi-point resolution to foster reconciliation and security, including an immediate ceasefire, prosecution of perpetrators, accountability for leadership, and the rebuilding of the Igwe Idigo Palace, which was torched, and condemned the attack on the traditional stool as an assault on the heritage of the state. In fact, Governor Soludo has announced that the state government will actively assist in rebuilding the destroyed Idigo palace to restore traditional dignity. “All grievances, claims, and presentations must be channeled exclusively through designated stakeholders”, the governor warned, explaining that security agencies were fully deployed to the area to enforce law and order, safeguard lives, and prevent any further breach of the peace. The governor reassured all citizens of the state of his administration’s unwavering commitment to the protection of lives and property, as well as the peaceful resolution of communal disputes across the state. The traditional ruler of Aguleri, Igwe Mike Idigo, and his Umuoba Anam counterpart, Igwe George Ekwealor, have, in the meantime, appealed to their subjects to maintain peace and allow the government to handle the matter. Former governor of Anambra State, Mr Peter Obi, has also appealed to the two communities to sheath their sword and embrace peace. In a statement , Obi said he was deeply pained by the reports of hostilities between the people of Umuoba-Anam and Aguleri. “Hostilities of the kind we are witnessing between the two communities achieve nothing but destruction. At a time when people are already finding it increasingly difficult to survive, adding the devastation of conflict is like adding fuel to the fire. “I appeal to both communities to immediately cease hostilities and embrace peace. No grievance, however serious, is worth the loss of lives, the destruction of homes and livelihoods, or the pain inflicted on families. “Let us choose dialogue over violence, reconciliation over revenge, and peace over destruction. There is always a better way to resolve our differences”, Obi appealed. The post Aguleri/Umuoba Anam crisis: The bloody battle of close neighbours appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Ministry receives over 47,500 applications for Hajj
body:
The Ministry of Endowments and Religious Affairs (MERA) in Muscat has announced full digital and administrative readiness to serve pilgrims from the Sultanate of Oman for the 1448 AH Hajj season. The ministry received 47,551 online applications requesting to perform Hajj next year. It noted that the response was overwhelmingly positive during the 14-day application period, averaging 142 registrations per hour, supported by 24/7 technical and administrative monitoring. Statistics show that the ministry processed 830 technical support requests, handled 784 phone calls, and managed 70 reports and inquiries, all while adhering to a maximum one-hour turnaround time for processing and completion. The ministry highlighted that these efforts were anchored in receiving and tracking applications, providing approved communication and support channels, resolving technical issues, ensuring continuous oversight, and streamlining procedures. Ultimately, this high level of engagement reflects significant public awareness, efficiency, and widespread confidence in the digital system.

title: Robot seized by German police after allegedly groping teenage girl
body: German police have launched an investigation into two teenagers accused of controlling a robot that allegedly groped a 16-year-old girl. Police in Cologne have confiscated the red and gold robot that allegedly grabbed the girl’s buttocks and made thrusting motions against her before she screamed and moved away. North Rhine-Westphalia Police said the robot’s 16-year-old owner and his companion, 19, are believed to have streamed the incident live on social media and commented on it. According to a police statement on Facebook, the 120cm (3.9ft) tall device approached the girl from behind while she was with her friends close to midnight local time (23:00 BST) on Saturday. The girl was in front of a fast-food outlet near the city centre when the incident took place, police said. Emergency services were alerted, and the teenage boy and the man now under investigation with him were found a block away a short time later. The robot was discovered in the back of a car, where the boy had placed it, police said. A photo released by police showed the robot wearing a black moustache, a gold-coloured chain and a white vest. Along with the robot, police seized two mobile phones belonging to the suspects. They are trying to determine whether someone was deliberately controlling the robot’s movements at the time of the incident. In a follow-up post on Facebook, police warned that some social media comments on the case “can be a crossing of the line and, in the worst case, a criminal offence”.

title: No more agitation for autonomous communities in Anambra, govt declares
body: By Vincent Ujumadu The Anambra State government has finally put to rest the agitation for the creation of new autonomous communities in the state, saying it welcomes the Supreme Court ruling on the matter. At the state’s weekly Executive Council meeting in Awka, the state government said it aligns with the apex court’s ruling that allowing it would splinter many large communities in the state and create confusion and conflict. Government advised those pushing for autonomous communities to “perish the idea” in line with the Supreme Court judgement and channel their energies to uniting and developing their communities as presently constituted. Also at the meeting, the state Executive Council debunked the insinuation that it has plans to reclaim mission schools returned to the churches. “Council debunked the fake news that government is planning to reclaim mission-returned schools. “Government has no such plan. However, Council frowned at the poor standard in which some mission-returned primary schools are run and noted that these schools were voluntarily returned by government. “It was also noted that many primary schools are currently under renovation as part of the counterpart-funding agreement between Anambra State and the Federal Government. “Council resolved to establish irreducible minimum standards of operation for both private and public primary schools in the state, after which schools that fail to meet the standards will be shut down”, the state government said. Government added that for the records, it has so far recruited 8,115 teachers for public primary and secondary schools and deployed 3,500 of them to mission-returned schools, while still paying their salaries and emoluments. The state EXCO also received update on the ongoing Onitsha Main Market regeneration project, noting that “it is on course to meet the December deadline”. Recall that the regeneration exercise embarked upon by Governor Chukwuma Soludo administration aims to restore the market’s master plan, as well as its image and reputation. The post No more agitation for autonomous communities in Anambra, govt declares appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: PPDC to Convene Access to Justice Conference in Abuja
body: Conference to focus on judicial reforms, technology, fundamental rights By Christopher Ameh, Abuja The Public and Private Development Centre (PPDC) will convene a two-day Access to Justice Conference in Abuja from November 3 to 4, 2026, to promote judicial reforms, strengthen the protection of fundamental human rights and explore how technology can improve justice delivery in Nigeria. The conference, scheduled for the Los Angeles Event Centre, Mabushi, Abuja, will bring together judges, legal practitioners, civil society organisations, technology innovators and members of the public to discuss challenges confronting the country’s justice system. It will be held under the theme, “Balancing Security with Fundamental Rights: Terrorism, Technology and Access to Justice.” The Chief Executive Officer of PPDC, Lucy James Abagi, said the conference would provide a platform for stakeholders to explore solutions to challenges in justice delivery while ensuring that national security measures did not undermine citizens’ fundamental rights. The event will combine the Access to Justice Parley with the Law for Humanity Summit, bringing together judicial officers, legal experts and other stakeholders to deliberate on reforms to improve the administration of justice. According to the organisers, PPDC’s interventions in the justice sector provided free legal representation to 20,009 detainees and facilitated the release of 8,552 people from detention without trial in 2025. The conference is expected to examine strategies for reducing delays in court proceedings, improving pre-trial processes and expanding the use of digital technologies to make justice more accessible and efficient. The Access to Justice Parley will begin with a Judges Parley featuring a keynote address, a fireside chat on judicial leadership and the launch of a Justice Sector Assessment Report. The session will also feature practical training for judges and court information and communications technology teams on JUDIC AI and Docketmaster. Participants will also be presented with PPDC’s Court Administration and Case Management Roadmap, alongside the organisation’s targets for 2027. The Law for Humanity Summit, organised in partnership with the Legal Aid Council of Nigeria, will focus on the question, “Can Technology Bridge the Access to Justice Gap in Nigeria?” The summit will feature a Law Clinic Showcase and the award of innovation seed grants of up to $1,500 to outstanding university law clinic projects. Another major highlight will be the Access to Justice Town Hall, which will provide citizens with an opportunity to engage directly with judicial officers and law enforcement agencies on issues affecting access to justice and the administration of justice in Nigeria. Participants will also discuss national security and digital privacy during panel sessions, while former detainees will share their experiences to highlight the human impact of detention without trial. The programme will further feature creative performances and the presentation of PPDC’s Access to Justice Impact Report, documenting the organisation’s interventions and their outcomes. The conference will conclude with an Access to Justice Gala and Fund Launch aimed at mobilising resources to support initiatives promoting access to justice across the country. Interested participants can register through the conference registration pages on PPDC’s official website. The post PPDC to Convene Access to Justice Conference in Abuja appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: The Supreme Court and national interest: The judiciary as a public-policy institution (1), by Usman Sarki
body: I have had the privilege of sitting beside His Royal Highness, the Emir of Lafia, Honourable Justice Sidi Dauda Bage Muhammad I, CFR, Chairman of the Nasarawa State Council of Chiefs and a retired Justice of the Supreme Court of Nigeria, on several occasions. In him, I observed the composure, dignity and calm deliberation that one instinctively associates with a judge who has served at the highest level of the justice system of our country. His interventions were measured, reflective and marked by a quiet competence that commanded attention and respect without demanding either. It was during one such encounter that His Royal Highness offered a simple but profound observation which set in motion the train of thought that resulted in this series of articles. The Supreme Court, he suggested, should not be regarded merely as the highest court and the court of last resort in Nigeria. It should also be understood as a public-policy institution. That observation remained with me because it illuminated a dimension of the Court insufficiently emphasised in public discourse in Nigeria. The more I reflected upon it, the more compelling the proposition became. The Supreme Court of Nigeria may indeed be regarded as one of the last bastions of the sovereignty, unity and continuity of our country, not primarily in the physical sense, but in the deeper metaphysical, moral and constitutional sense in which a nation recognises itself as one political community governed by common sentiments, rules and institutions. The Supreme Court is therefore not merely the highest institution within the judicial hierarchy, nor simply the final tribunal available to litigants who have exhausted every other legal avenue. In a profound constitutional sense, it stands alongside the Presidency and the National Assembly as one of the three great institutions through which state authority is expressed. The Executive governs and administers; the Legislature makes laws and gives representative expression to the political will of the people; while the Judiciary, culminating in the Supreme Court, interprets the Constitution and the law, determines the lawful boundaries of governmental authority and provides final judicial resolution when competing claims threaten to unsettle the constitutional order. Its public-policy significance therefore arises not because judges are elected to formulate policy, nor because courts should assume the functions of either the Executive or the Legislature. Rather, it arises from the consequences of constitutional interpretation. Whenever the Supreme Court determines the limits of federal or state authority, interprets the rights of citizens, resolves disputes between constituent units of the Federation, defines the constitutional powers of institutions or pronounces upon issues capable of affecting the political stability of the country, such as election results, it is doing considerably more than settling a dispute between the parties before it. It is in fact helping to define the operating principles of the Nigerian state itself. Its judgments consequently extend beyond the immediate interests of litigants. A controversy may begin as a dispute between two individuals, between a citizen and government, between political organisations, or between the Federation and one or more states. Once a fundamental constitutional question reaches the apex court, its determination may shape institutional behaviour, public authority and the constitutional inheritance transmitted to succeeding generations. This is why the Supreme Court cannot always afford to regard the cases before it merely as isolated contests involving the technical rights and liabilities of adversarial parties. Behind pleadings and procedural rules may lie questions of democratic continuity, federal balance, citizens’ rights, institutional credibility, economic organisation and, ultimately, Nigerians’ faith in the constitutional order. But there is an important qualification to be made here. Recognition of the national consequences of judicial decisions must never become an invitation to judges to substitute political calculation for law. The national interest cannot be employed as an amorphous justification for disregarding constitutional provisions, overlooking illegality or manufacturing convenient outcomes. Indeed, the first and highest national interest must be the faithful maintenance of the constitutional order itself. That was another of His Royal Highness’s observations that remained fixed in my mind. A court that bends the law today in pursuit of what appears to be stability may unintentionally weaken the basis of stability tomorrow. Once citizens believe constitutional principles can be displaced when political stakes are high, the authority of law itself becomes conditional. The Court’s contribution to national security and continuity therefore rests precisely upon its willingness to apply the law even when the surrounding political atmosphere is difficult. This leads to a larger question: what do we actually mean by constitutionalism? A constitution is a document establishing institutions, allocating powers, defining procedures and recognising rights. Constitutionalism is, however, something deeper. It is the culture by which power is exercised with wisdom and prudence, public authorities acknowledge limits, political actors accept lawful decisions they dislike, and government remains subject to rules superior to temporary holders of office. It is at this point that some reflections by John Buchan in his book The African Colony, written in the aftermath of the South African Boer War, become relevant despite the very different colonial and historical setting in which he wrote, and his prejudices against the African races. I have read the book several times. Buchan observed that a country’s constitutional requirements are not determined solely by immediate political needs. History also matters, because theories and habits of government may sink deeply into the consciousness of a people and become part of their political outlook. This insight is especially important in societies where constitutional rules must mediate deep memories, competing identities and recurring struggles over power, because durable institutions depend as much upon accepted habits of mutual accommodation as upon written provisions. There is considerable wisdom in that proposition. Constitutions do not operate in historical vacuums. They are interpreted and experienced by societies carrying memories of previous governments, political crises, conflicts, compromises and expectations. Institutions derive legitimacy not merely from text, but from confidence in their consistency and fairness. Nigeria’s Constitution must therefore be understood against the background of the extraordinary historical journey through which the Nigerian state has passed. It traversed conquest, amalgamation, colonial administration, independence, federal experimentation, political crises, military intervention, civil war, successive constitutional arrangements and eventual democratic restoration. The document under which we presently govern is part of that accumulated national experience. That historical experience leads naturally to the federal question, and to the place of the Supreme Court in holding together a political community whose diversity is both its strength and its perpetual constitutional challenge and critical weak joints.
