title: Atiku and the northern oligarchs should be careful of what they are asking for, by Rotimi Fasan
body: Our politicians are already up in arms, nagging and threatening fire and brimstone about the INEC list of politicians cleared for the January 16, 2027 election. The electoral body is being accused of bias and favouritism. There are allegations that while some names have been excluded from INEC’s list on the grounds that they did not meet the deadline to be registered members of their parties, others in the same situation who are of the ruling party or close to it have allegedly been cleared. These are still very early days since the release of the list. As the days go by, it would be clear where the truth of these claims lies and INEC explains its position, or that position is either subjected to legal challenge or legal interpretation. Once this hurdle is crossed, the next stage is the campaign. What is even probable is that any legal challenge of INEC would go apace with the campaigns, which many Nigerians are coming around to conclude have so far been mediocre. As the election draws close and the campaigns gain traction, Nigerians would need to be more attentive to the nature of the campaign and how it is prosecuted within the bounds of decency and acceptable practices. This is not only about the next election but also for the consequences it may have for future elections and the politics of this country. One of the politicians Nigerians must have their eyes on is the African Democratic Congress’ Atiku Abubakar, whose desperation to be president increasingly takes him into dangerous territories. The former Vice President’s electoral modus operandi has been the naked mobilisation of ethnicity and religion. This comes from a sense of entitlement that has seen the perennial presidential candidate stand for election for nearly three and a half decades non-stop. Atiku’s politics is motivated solely by his personal interest, which those who know him say is repugnant to integrity. From President Olusegun Obasanjo, under whom he served as Vice President, to Nasir El-Rufai, who worked under him during Atiku’s leadership of this country’s privatisation drive, the verdict has been damning. President Obasanjo only a few weeks ago had cause to remind Nigerians that one of his greatest regrets in life was choosing Atiku as his running mate. Even Babachir David Lawal, President Buhari’s SGF, a man who has very harsh words for President Bola Tinubu, somehow considers the worst of Tinubu better than the best of Atiku. He would rather embrace Bola Tinubu than shake hands with Atiku. For him, Nigeria is doomed should Alhaji Atiku Abubakar find himself anywhere close to Aso Villa. The picture he paints of an Atiku presidency is one of national ruin. He speaks of him in binary terms of good against evil, and it is clear where he thinks Atiku belongs. In a series of recent interviews, he has restated this position without any response from Atiku, who gets youthfully energised when the conversation turns to Bola Tinubu. The reason for this is very obvious. Tinubu is the only obstacle to his fading dream of becoming Nigeria’s president. He is the only politician in today’s Nigeria that he fears and loathes in equal terms. The only one that can and has defeated him in an election. Now he sees nothing good about him for purely political reasons. Should Atiku become the president right today, he would be the first to consecrate President Bola Tinubu in saintly registers. He would dress him in robes made of looms that are yet to be invented. But for as long as he occupies the position he covets, sleeps and dreams of, he cannot see anything good in him. Which is why he has added petulance to his political message that was, until recently, filtered through ethnic and religious affiliation. He calls the president by his first name during formal presentations and has not only doubled down on it but encouraged a battery of paid hands to propagate his rage-baits. It remains to be seen how well petulance looks as a political strategy on an eighty-year-old grandfather. But Atiku’s main strategy is to sell ethnicity and religion among the disaffected section of the northern electorate. He adds a dose of insults for the benefit of a president who knows the game and has refused to take his bait. How does calling the president by his first name affect a man who has been called the worst thing in the books? It is for Atiku’s own good that he has been advised to show decorum for the office he covets. His insults would not bring down the presidency. If anything, they diminish the Waziri Adamawa. How long ago did Babachir Lawal label him Kachalla to the amusement of Nigerians who didn’t know what it meant? But Atiku seems to be living up to the billing of a kachalla, a militia czar or warlord with enough followers on standby to lob insults as campaign ads. What should worry Nigerians, particularly those of northern extraction, is what Atiku Abubakar’s disregard of political rules and conventions portends for the region’s leadership of Nigeria post-2027. If, despite their antagonism, Tinubu wins the next election, what argument would they have to counter a southerner who chooses to stand for the presidency when it’s the north’s turn to produce the president? One is by no means saying the presidency should be a rotating game between the north and the south without regard for competence. What is in place now is a convention that should hopefully be terminated soon. If that ameliorative measure must end, it shouldn’t be mid-stream or soon after an eight-year, two-term presidency of a northerner and specifically a president of Fulani extraction. Is that section of the northern oligarchy pushing for a Fulani-led leadership mindful of what that might mean for Nigeria’s continued existence? We did not get to where we are today three and a half years ago. Nor can the northern oligarchy absolve itself of responsibility for the economic, social and religious condition of the northern poor. That is not a problem that can be blamed on anyone but those who have governed that region. The reforms that have aggravated the situation in the north, as in other parts of Nigeria, are for the most part necessary for the survival of the country. The conditions created by the reforms have themselves been aggravated by global geopolitics. They were not targeted at any region. We all suffer equally. To seek a solution that suggests that only a northerner or a Fulani can restore economic salvation, as Atiku Abubakar and some northern religious and political leaders have been doing, is to be short-sighted. It is dousing a tinder of wood in petrol. The post Atiku and the northern oligarchs should be careful of what they are asking for, by Rotimi Fasan appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Haaland vs Mbappe: The race to break Cristiano Ronaldo’s historic Champions League goals record
body: Erling Haaland’s two goals against Porto on the opening matchday of the 2026/27 Champions League maintained the Manchester City striker’s incredible scoring rate in the competition. Haaland has scored 59 goals from 59 games at the elite level of European club football, giving him the best goals-per-game ratio of any notable player in its history. In fact, he is the only player to have scored a significant number of goals at a rate of at least one per game. It’s also the best scoring rate of the three active players among the Champions League's all-time top scorers: Haaland, Harry Kane and Kylian Mbappe. The benchmark, however, is still some way off for all three. Cristiano Ronaldo is out in front with a staggering 140 goals from 183 appearances in the competition. So, this raises the question: Can one of this generation’s elite goalscorers actually beat Ronaldo’s record? Kane has an impressive haul of 54 goals in 70 games, but at 33, the England captain can almost certainly be ruled out of the race. Sadly for him, he stayed at Tottenham Hotspur for too long. That leaves us with Haaland and Mbappe. Both are in action on Tuesday night, with Manchester City hosting PSG and Real Madrid visiting Roma. Below is an appraisal of each man’s chances of going down as European club football’s greatest-ever goalscorer. Erling Haaland Haaland, 26, made his Champions League debut for RB Salzburg against Genk on September 17, 2019, and scored a hat-trick. Of course he did. Since then, as stated above, he has scored at a rate of a goal per game in the competition. His best return came in 2022/23, when he scored 12 times in 11 games and ended up with a winner’s medal . He currently sits seventh on the all-time list. This season will be his eighth in the Champions League. Among those, there is an outlier – 2021/22 – when he played just three games, scoring as many goals, as his then club, Borussia Dortmund, made an early exit. Every other season, he has played at least eight games. If we remove that campaign and the current one, then he has a tally of 54 goals in 55 games across six seasons, at an average of nine goals per season. By that calculation, he will need another 9.1 seasons (including the current one) to get the 82 goals he requires to break Ronaldo’s record – form, fitness and participation willing, of course. That means Haaland needs to continue scoring at the same rate until the 2035/36 season. The Norwegian star, born in July 2000, will be 35 by then. It’s a big ask to be so consistent for so long, but in this era of supreme athleticism, it’s far from inconceivable. There’s also the frightening prospect that he could still get better and increase his goal output. Kylian Mbappe Mbappe, 27, has 71 goals in 99 Champions League games following his strike in Real Madrid’s 2-1 victory over Inter Milan in their opening game of the 2026/27 competition. That took him to joint-fifth with Raul in the all-time list. He made his UCL debut on September 27, 2016, with a 13-minute cameo off the bench in Monaco’s 1-1 draw with Bayer Leverkusen. He is now into his 11th season of Champions League football. Mbappe has managed at least eight games in each of his first 10 seasons, making his average a pleasingly concise seven goals per season, with 70 goals across the 10 completed campaigns. At that rate, he will need exactly 10 more to chalk up the 70 goals he requires to surpass Ronaldo. Mbappe will be 38 heading into the back end of the 2036/37 season. It's clear he needs to speed up, and there's ample evidence to suggest that he has. His goals-per-game rate has spiked sharply since he moved to Real Madrid in 2024. The France striker managed an incredible 15 goals in 11 games last term – his best return – while he has a total of 22 in 25 games in his two completed seasons at the club. At an average of 11 per campaign, he would need another six-and-a-half seasons to potentially put him within striking distance of the record by the 2032/33 season, when he will be 34, turning 35 in December. Verdict The numbers suggest that both Haaland and Mbappe stand a reasonable chance of surpassing Ronaldo’s mark if they can stay fit and play in the majority of matches for their respective clubs. Both will be helped by the extra games offered by the competition’s new format, with teams now guaranteed eight league phase games as opposed to the six group games Ronaldo used to get before the knockouts. If anything, this exercise really underlines Ronaldo’s incredible longevity and potency in front of goal. Interestingly, he scored goal number 140 on his 183rd and final Champions League appearance in a 2-0 win for Manchester United over Villarreal on November 23, 2021. He was 36 years, nine months and 18 days old at the time. Should Mbappe manage to stay at Madrid into the twilight of his career, then you would have to give him a shot, given the number of goals he has scored since his move to Los Blancos, and their consistency in reaching the latter stages of the competition year after year. Ronaldo was 33 when he left Madrid, while Mbappe's compatriot, Karim Benzema , stayed there until he was 35. That said, averaging 11 per season to get there by the time he is 35 is a big ask, and he may need to keep playing into the second half of his 30s to eventually top the list. Haaland, 19 months younger than Mbappe, will feel that 141 is an achievable target if he can regularly play 10 or more games per season in the competition. As the younger man, and with the better goals-per-game ratio, you'd have to make the Manchester City striker a firm favourite. The X-factor is, of course, Mbappe's Real Madrid form. His 15 last season was the third most ever behind Ronaldo in 2015/16 (16) and 2013/14 (17). Either way, it seems certain that both men will finish their careers considered among the finest goalscorers in modern football history. If either eventually stands alone as the best, remains to be seen.

title: Libya could become reliable supplier of oil, gas again — envoy
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Libya is able to strengthen its role as a reliable supplier of oil and gas to global markets once again, the country’s Ambassador to Iran Ali Juma Hassan Fadil said in an interview with TASS.
"Energy security is not only an economic but also a geopolitical category now. For Libya, this situation presents both opportunities and responsibilities. The country possesses significant resources and is located in close proximity to European markets. In a stable production and investment environment, Libya is capable of strengthening its role as a reliable supplier of oil and gas," he said.
"However, it requires protecting energy infrastructure, ensuring stable production, modernizing facilities, and creating a more predictable contractual and legal environment for investors," the diplomat noted.

title: Subject EC appointment to ‘Akufo-Addo test’ – Kwapong
body: CDD-Ghana Fellow Dr John Osae-Kwapong says the latest Electoral Commission appointment should face an ‘Akufo-Addo test’ of integrity, fairness, professionalism, and independent judgment. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, he proposed assessing the appointee against standards former President Nana Akufo-Addo outlined when swearing in commissioners in 2023. “So that’s the first thing for me is subjecting the appointment to the Akufo-Addo test to say if the person can measure up to these things, fair enough.” Dr Osae-Kwapong said Akufo-Addo’s remarks offered useful guidance on the qualities expected of an electoral commissioner. “And he talked about things like, if the person can serve with integrity, the person can serve with fairness, if the person can be professional, and if the person can show independence of mind and judgment.” His comments follow President John Mahama’s swearing-in of Dr Joseph Kwaku Asamoah and Emelia Afi Agbenyo as EC deputy chairpersons on Monday, October 12. He charged them with upholding electoral integrity and strengthening public confidence. The appointments followed Dr Bossman Eric Asare’s resignation and Samuel Tettey’s retirement. Dr Osae-Kwapong also questioned the distinction the public draws between openly partisan appointees and those whose political sympathies remain private. “The second point for me then becomes this idea of the open partisan being appointed to an independent constitutional body versus the person who could be just as partisan but is more private about his or her partisanship.” He said public knowledge of an appointee’s political affiliation seemed to fuel concerns about their suitability. “It appears that we have a certain level of discomfort in knowing that somebody is openly partisan and being sent to an independent constitutional body.” Beyond those perceptions, he questioned whether the Commission’s internal safeguards could prevent an individual from advancing a party’s interests. “Are there internal safeguards? Are we so worried that we are thinking one person who is publicly partisan can actually do the bidding of a political party in the midst of six other peers?” For him, the ability of fellow commissioners to restrain partisan conduct was a key consideration. He said his concern would be reduced if the other commissioners could check an individual’s attempts to act on political bias.

title: IDF chief vows to apply October 7 lessons, pledges to pursue Israel's enemies at military ceremony
body: IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir honored the bravery and sacrifice of fallen Commando Brigade soldiers at a memorial ceremony in Modi'in on Tuesday, pledging to implement the lessons of October 7, strengthen the military, and prevent future threats to Israel's security.Addressing soldiers, commanders, and bereaved families, Zamir praised the brigade's courage, determination, and dedication, describing it as the IDF's "striking fist" at the forefront of operations against Israel's enemies. He highlighted the combined strength of its elite Egoz, Maglan, and Duvdevan units, emphasizing their professionalism, operational experience, and tactical ingenuity in carrying out complex missions on the front lines and deep within enemy territory.Zamir also stressed the military's responsibility to expand its ranks, reinforce the importance of IDF service, and recognize combat soldiers as national heroes and examples of Zionist excellence.Addressing the bereaved families, Zamir emphasized that the memory of fallen soldiers continues to guide their comrades in battle, shaping their actions and the values they uphold.Commanders and fellow soldiers "carry the memory of your loved ones with them as they head out on their missions. In decisive moments, the image of your loved ones, their fallen comrades, is present within them: how they acted, the values ​​that guided them, and the standards they set for themselves," he said.Zamir vows to overhaul IDF defense strategy based on October 7 lessonsTurning to the lessons of October 7, Zamir stressed the need to turn the military's failures and the lessons learned into concrete changes to Israel's defense strategy."We have drawn profound insights that we are committed to translating into action; we are building the IDF for the future, updating our security doctrine, and actively implementing the lessons learned," Zamir said."This is the professional and moral imperative incumbent upon us: to ensure that the lessons of October 7th remain forever before our eyes," he added.Zamir vows preemptive action to eliminate threats to IsraelZamir outlined a strategy centered on preemptively eliminating enemy capabilities before threats can materialize, while pursuing those who seek to undermine Israel's existence."We will act to preemptively destroy our enemy's capabilities, prevent threats to our future from emerging, and relentlessly pursue those who seek to deny our right to exist in our land," he declared.

title: Saudi national arrested for installing audio recording device at OpenAI office
body:
NEW YORK, October 14. /TASS/. An employee of the US technology firm OpenAI, who has been arrested on suspicion of installing a surreptitious audio recording device in its office, is a Saudi Arabian national, the US Department of Justice said in a statement.
"An employee of OpenAI has been arrested for and charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, was arrested on Oct. 9, and made his initial appearance in federal court today (on Tuesday - TASS)," the statement reads.
Meetings in the executive conference room, where the recording device was discovered, "frequently involved discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, product plans, and business-development opportunities, as well as nonpublic information about Open AI’s technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships," according to the statement.
Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025, the US Department of Justice said. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.

title: Two Nights Without Missile Warnings – Zelensky Raises Alarm as Trump Denies Intelligence Cutoff
body:
For two consecutive nights, the air raid warnings that normally give Kyiv residents precious time to seek shelter came only after Russian ballistic missiles were already approaching or striking the Ukrainian capital.
On Monday and Tuesday, Oct. 12-13, Russia launched successive ballistic missile attacks, striking civilian infrastructure and a major power plant. Ukraine received no advance warning of the launches from Western partners, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The second attack hit Kyiv’s CHP-4 thermal power plant and a nine-story residential building, killing at least two people and injuring 21, including a child.
Zelensky described Monday’s attack as “particularly vile,” saying five Russian ballistic missiles had struck civilian infrastructure in Kyiv without advance warning from Ukraine’s partners.
“Unfortunately, we received no early warning from our partners about this strike,” Zelensky said Tuesday, Oct. 13.
“Advance intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches is critical to saving lives. Early warnings give people time to seek shelter and help prevent casualties.”
In his evening address, Zelensky revealed that Ukrainian forces had detected the five missiles only seconds before impact.
“Normally, we receive advance warnings from our partners, which are crucial for our defense,” Zelensky said, stressing that intelligence sharing helps Ukraine protect civilians and prevent Russian killings.
However, Zelensky did not specify which partner had failed to provide the warnings, nor did he explicitly accuse Washington of deliberately withholding intelligence.
The consequences were immediate for civilians.
A Kyiv Post journalist recounted how a friend, unaware of the incoming missiles, was walking her dog on Kyiv’s left bank when the attack began.
“The explosions were so loud that she [the dog] was terrified,” the journalist said.
The missing warnings come at an especially sensitive moment in US-Ukrainian relations.
According to an Axios report published Oct. 9, citing a Ukrainian official, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner warned during negotiations in Miami that Washington could suspend intelligence sharing if Kyiv continued striking Russian oil refineries.
However, a US official denied that such a threat had been made, saying Washington remained a strong partner providing Ukraine with intelligence and weapons.
President Donald Trump rejected suggestions that Washington had stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine.
“We are helping them, and we are sharing intel,” Trump told reporters Tuesday, Oct. 13, adding that Washington was working with both Kyiv and Moscow to end the war.
Yet Trump’s assurances have not resolved the central question: Why did Ukraine go two consecutive nights without the early missile warnings it normally receives from its Western partners?
The Trump administration’s response was less definitive when the question reached the White House briefing room on Tuesday.
Katie Zacharia, Trump’s newly appointed press secretary, was asked directly by Fox News correspondent Peter Doocy whether the US had stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine.
“I’ll have to get back to you on that,” she replied during her first briefing.
The intelligence concerns emerged just days after Trump reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports.
On Oct. 9, the US Treasury Department issued General License 135, authorizing transactions involving the sale, delivery and importation of Russian-origin diesel fuel.
The temporary sanctions relief followed Trump’s agreement with Putin to release Russian diesel supplies onto international markets in an effort to ease rising fuel prices.
The decision has drawn criticism from lawmakers in Washington, who warn that renewed Russian energy revenues could help finance Moscow’s war against Ukraine.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Blues cool off hot Senators with 7-2 road win
body:
OTTAWA – Pius Suter, Jake Neighbours and Mason McTavish each had a pair of goals Tuesday night to lead the St. Louis Blues to a 7-2 win over the Ottawa Senators.
Adam Jiricek also scored for the Blues (3-2-1), while Joel Hofer stopped 15 shots.
Claude Giroux and Fabian Zetterlund scored for the Senators (5-2-0). Samuel Ersson, making his second start for Ottawa, made 19 saves. He’s now 0-2.
Ottawa was playing the back half of a back-to-back coming off a 4-1 win against the New Jersey Devils on Monday. The loss halted the Senators three-game win streak.
The game marked the start of a three-game road trip for the Blues.
The Blues took a 4-1 lead midway through the third when Suter beat Ersson short side from a sharp angle. Neighbours scored his second off a snap shot, McTavish scored on the power play, and Jiricek scored his first career goal to round out the scoring.
Zetterlund added a late power-play goal to make it 7-2.
St. Louis took a 2-0 lead midway through the second when Neighbours stepped in with a shot from the top of the slot and wristed a shot through traffic to beat Ersson glove side.
Giroux cut the lead in half with 2:08 remaining in the second on a beautiful feed from Tim Stutzle, but the Blues responded 33 seconds later. Some poor defensive zone coverage allowed McTavish to get a shot past Ersson from the top of the crease.
The Blues stifled the Senators for much of the second and outshot Ottawa 12-4.
The Blues opened the scoring at 14:28 of the first period with a short-handed goal. Colton Parayko won a battle along the boards and found Suter with some open space and he beat Ersson blocker side.
With another hit to the blue line Jorian Donovan will slot in for Nikolas Matinpalo who was injured Monday against the Devils. Dylan Peterson made his NHL debut with the Blues Tuesday.
With his second-period goal, Giroux recorded his 1,170th career point, tying Bobby Hull for 59th on the NHL’s all-time scoring list.
Blues: Visit the Minnesota Wild on Thursday.
Senators: Host the New York Islanders on Thursday.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

title: English football’s independent regulator would quit over Man City interference
body: The head of English football’s independent regulator says he will resign if he encounters any political interference over the future of Manchester City . As chairman of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR), David Kogan has the power to assess the suitability of club owners and executives. If an independent commission’s findings that the club broke Premier League financial rules are upheld, the watchdog could even force a sale. Last month, the Prime Minister Andy Burnham was criticised for saying he would be “really concerned” if the scandal led to Manchester City ‘s Abu Dhabi owners selling the club. “They’ve been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is,” he added. When asked about Burnham’s comments, Kogan told BBC Sport: “The Prime Minister is entirely entitled to make his own observations on anything. “We are independent. That is in the name. I am the chairman of the Independent Football Regulator and independence absolutely runs through everything we’re doing. “And no politician has tried to influence and would try to influence anything we do on that.” When asked what he would do if he did come under political pressure over the case, Kogan replied: “I would resign.” An independent commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018. Owners Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) – a private investment company belonging to United Arab Emirates vice-president and deputy prime minister Sheikh Mansour – are said to have topped up the value of commercial deals as part of a “disguised funding scheme” to the scale of £830m. City insist they are innocent and have appealed. Kogan on next steps on Man City Kogan, a former sports media rights executive, was appointed to the regulator role one year ago The prime minister initially told the BBC of his concerns, before later denying his reaction had “downplayed the seriousness of the findings”. However, some Premier League clubs were so “astonished” by Burnham’s stance that sources told BBC Sport they were “concerned” about political interference in the appeal process. Burnham’s previous role as mayor of Greater Manchester has led to questions about his relationship with City’s Abu Dhabi ownership. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch demanded all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club are released. The government released these details on Monday . Speaking at the launch of the IFR’s State of the Game report, Kogan said, “As far as we, as the regulator, are concerned, we have a very clear course of action that is governed by statute and we are going to follow that course of action, and no comment by any politician or indeed any individual is going to affect what we do”. Kogan’s hiring as IFR chair was the subject of an inquiry by the Commissioner for Public Appointments over his historic links to the Labour Party, including contributions to the leadership campaigns of former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer and culture secretary Lisa Nandy. Shadow Culture Minister Louie French has written to the government, citing “concerns about the IFR’s ability to adjudicate this case fairly, free from political interference”. In response, Kogan said: “I can tell you absolutely categorically that any politician who’s trying to meddle in this for political purposes is welcome to try and welcome to do it, but I am going to stand by the probity of the organisation that I lead. If anybody wishes to challenge those after we’ve acted, that’s entirely up to them.” ‘Very serious issues’ The independent panel will hold a sanctions hearing – which could take months to convene – to decide on City’s punishment. The club can appeal both the guilty verdicts and the sanction, leaving the league in a state of uncertainty. City’s punishment could range from a huge fine to point deductions to ejection from the Premier League. When asked how crucial it was that it be resolved as soon as possible, Kogan said, “I think it’s very important.” Kogan added that the case was “raising very serious issues if Manchester City on appeal is found to be guilty of the allegations within those findings”. “We are waiting like everybody else to see what the independent panel will do… and then we will bring in a view in terms of our own investigation and statutory powers if we need to do so. “Our powers relate to individual owners, directors and senior executives. They refer to whether people are in a position to run a club in a way that is safe, coherent and done with probity, and we will be examining those things.” When asked whether the IFR could withhold a club license from the City when it starts awarding them next month, Kogan said: “I’m not going to begin to comment on any actions we may take until we’ve had a chance to assess it.” And on whether the case had raised questions about the state-connected ownership of clubs, Kogan replied: “No, I don’t think specifically it does. We have no powers to prevent state ownership of clubs. It’s not within our remit. But I don’t think you can apply a general observation about type of ownership to one particular example.” An independent commission held a 42-day hearing in 2024 that led to the verdict announced last month, with City also guilty of all charges except one relating to non-cooperation with the Premier League investigation. The commission’s report said that “a number of important club witnesses gave false evidence in key respects and that some knowingly gave untrue and dishonest evidence”.

title: Guilty plea in connection with Kelowna teen’s death
body:
A painful day in court for the family and friends of Tristan Seeger , a Kelowna teen who was fatally run down by a vehicle three years ago.
They packed a Kelowna courtroom Tuesday as the man responsible for the 15-year-old’s death, Brandon Kazakoff, pleaded guilty to dangerous driving causing death and assault.
The guilty pleas stem from an incident on Oct. 21, 2023.
“I’m glad he admitted what he did to my son, whether or not it’s remorseful or not, only he knows,” Tristan’s father, Jason Seeger, said.
Tristan’s mother, Paule Moore, said she wanted Kazakoff to face the family.
“He killed my son with a car. He didn’t even have the guts to look him in the eye, and he needed to look us in the eye,” she said.
Court heard that shortly before the fatal collision, Tristan was part of a group of teenagers involved in an incident in which Kazakoff’s father was bear-sprayed.
After learning about the incident, Kazakoff went looking for the group.
He eventually found the teenagers and assaulted one of them, according to the court proceedings.
Kazakoff then got back into his vehicle. While stopped at an intersection, Tristan deployed bear spray toward the passenger side of the car. Kazakoff turned the vehicle around and drove into the teenager.
He fled the scene. In the days that followed, Kazakoff changed his licence plates and set his vehicle on fire along a forest service road.
Kazakoff’s defence lawyer, Glenn Verdurmen, described the incident as “one horrendous, horrible mistake.”
Verdurmen said his client feels remorse for his actions and understands the impact the case has had on the community.
“It’s ripped up a lot of people in the Rutland and Kelowna area, and the hurt has gone deep, and that’s not lost on my client,” Verdurmen said. “He tells me that this is what he thinks about every day.”
For Tristan’s family, the guilty plea means they will not have to relive the painful details of the case through a trial. But they say no outcome in court can undo their loss.
Asked what justice would look like, Jason Seeger said for him, there isn’t any.
“Bring my son back, but we know that’s not going to happen,” he said, choking back tears.
Instead, the family is left holding on to memories of a teenager they remember for his laughter, charisma and adventurous spirit.
“His cheeky grin and his devil-may-care attitude and his willingness to just do anything,” Moore said. “I miss that stuff about him. You know, we miss him every day.”
Kazakoff is expected to be sentenced at a later date, likely in early 2027.

title: Anthropic seeks rehearing of case over Pentagon’s security risk branding
body: Anthropic asked a US appeals court on Tuesday to reconsider a ruling that upheld the Pentagon’s decision to ​label the AI company as a national security supply ‌chain risk over a dispute about safety guardrails on its technology. A federal appeals court in September upheld the designation in a 2-1 decision, ​agreeing with the Pentagon that the firm’s safety restrictions ​could compromise military operations. The Pentagon’s blacklisting of ⁠the company has cost it billions of dollars in lost ​business, Anthropic has said. The court’s majority said the Pentagon acted ​reasonably after Anthropic refused to allow its AI to be used in autonomous weapons or mass surveillance, and the court rejected the firm’s ​claim that it faced retaliation by the Defense Department ​over its views on AI safety. In its petition on Tuesday to the ‌US ⁠Court of Appeals in Washington, DC, for a rehearing, Anthropic argued that the panel majority misinterpreted and transformed a federal law “aimed at hostile foreign actors into one that presumptively reaches ​every government contractor.” The ​court let ⁠the Pentagon take action against Anthropic “without any pre-designation process and despite straightforward evidence the designation ​was retaliation for Anthropic’s speech about AI safety,” ​the ⁠company said. In a separate lawsuit in August, a federal judge in California struck down a parallel designation under a different law. Anthropic CEO ⁠Dario ​Amodei has called for regulation covering ​all US frontier AI companies, while the Trump administration has favored a pro-growth ​approach.

title: Netanyahu admits Egyptian intelligence chief visited before Oct. 7, but his account doesn't add up
body: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu acknowledged for the first time Tuesday evening that Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel, one of Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi's closest associates, landed in Israel a week and a half before the October 7 massacre. In an interview with Channel 14, Netanyahu said he had not met with Kamel because he was attending a memorial ceremony for fallen IDF soldiers. According to published reports, Kamel warned at the time of "a major attack being planned by Hamas." Two days after the massacre, ynet's Smadar Perry reported, following an Associated Press report about an Egyptian warning, that according to a senior Egyptian source, Kamel had conveyed a message to Netanyahu's office warning of "something unusual, a massive operation" about to be launched from Gaza. The Prime Minister's Office denied the report.   "He didn't speak to me. Since when does an intelligence chief speak to a head of state? It's never happened to me. There's no such thing. He would always come with someone," Netanyahu said Tuesday. But just two years earlier, Netanyahu had hosted Kamel at the prime minister's residence in Jerusalem. In a video released at the time by the Prime Minister's Office, Netanyahu and Kamel were seen shaking hands and talking. Kamel was then leading a delegation of senior Egyptian officials visiting Israel. Netanyahu claimed he did not know whom Kamel met during his secret visit to Israel on Sept. 26, 2023. "Egypt's intelligence minister was here. He spent 59 minutes on the ground. I'm turning to the security and law enforcement authorities — I want to know whom he met. Someone who met with him is trying to pin this on me," Netanyahu said.   Last month, The Atlantic reported that Kamel had made a brief visit to Israel on Sept. 26, warning that Hamas was preparing a major attack and urging Israel to ease economic restrictions to prevent an escalation. According to the magazine's investigation, a chartered Cessna aircraft linked to Egyptian intelligence services landed at Ben Gurion Airport and remained in Israel for just 67 minutes before departing for Cairo. A former Israeli official who spoke to the magazine said the Egyptian intelligence chief's decision to make such an unusually brief visit should itself have made the urgency of the warning clear. As the official put it, "The messenger was the message." About two hours after the Egyptian plane landed, Netanyahu attended a ceremony in Jerusalem marking the 50th anniversary of the Yom Kippur War. "As a central lesson from that war, we do not underestimate any threat," Netanyahu said at the time. Meanwhile, The Wall Street Journal reported that Kamel called Netanyahu in early October 2023 to warn him of an impending attack from the Gaza Strip, after two previous Egyptian warnings had gone unheeded. Kamel "was growing anxious," the newspaper reported, further corroborating Smadar Perry's revelations about an Egyptian warning, published just days after the massacre.

title: Quebec’s incoming, outgoing premiers meet as transition of power begins
body:
Quebec’s transition of power is underway, with outgoing premier Christine Fréchette and premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon meeting Tuesday to discuss some of the major issues facing the province as the Parti Québécois prepares to take office.
The two leaders met for just under 50 minutes at the premier’s office in Quebec City, where they discussed the economy, employment, relations with the United States and the Churchill Falls hydroelectric agreement with Newfoundland and Labrador.
“We touched on all kinds of urgent and sensitive issues,” St-Pierre Plamondon told reporters in French after the meeting.
He said he was satisfied with the talks and thanked Fréchette’s team for its co-operation.
“We are looking at an orderly transition, marked by collaboration,” he said.
Fréchette also stressed the importance of a smooth handover. “It’s important to ensure a co-ordinated, proper transition,” she said. “Our teams will exchange information on the next steps.”
The transition comes eight days after Quebecers elected a minority Parti Québécois government in the Oct. 5 provincial election, returning the sovereigntist party to power for the first time since 2014.
The PQ won 59 seats, while the Quebec Liberals secured 40 to form the official Opposition. The Conservatives won 19 seats and Québec solidaire took nine. The Coalition Avenir Québec, which had governed since 2018, failed to elect a single member.
While the transition is underway, St-Pierre Plamondon is already signalling a different approach as he prepares to lead a minority government.
Newly elected PQ members are scheduled to be sworn in as members of the national assembly on Thursday, though it remains unclear whether St-Pierre Plamondon will pledge allegiance to the King, an issue that is facing a legal challenge .
Daniel Béland of the McGill Institute for the Study of Canada said the issue itself is not new, but questioned how prominently it will figure in the incoming government’s agenda.
“It’s not anything new,” Béland told Global on Tuesday. “At the same time, the question is to know whether he will really focus on this because he said his priorities are homelessness, the cost of living, government spending and so forth.”
A bigger challenge could be governing with a minority.
With 59 seats, the PQ will need support from other parties to pass legislation, requiring St-Pierre Plamondon’s government to find common ground with its political opponents.
Béland said the PQ could turn to different opposition parties depending on the issue.
“In terms of some issues related to government spending, reducing the size of public services, that is something they can do with the Conservatives,” he said. “When we need social issues or homelessness and so forth, certainly Québec solidaire is keen on social spending.”
The incoming government will also face a learning curve, with more than 50 PQ MNAs new to provincial politics and limited representation in Montreal and the Quebec City area.
“It’s a challenge for any new government, but when you’re in minority territory you have to be especially disciplined,” Béland said.
“And on top of it, when most of your MNAs are rookies, at least to provincial politics as elected MNAs to the national assembly, I think that this adds to the challenges that this government is facing.”
St-Pierre Plamondon and his cabinet are scheduled to be sworn in Oct. 21, when he will be able to officially move into the premier’s office.
Fréchette, meanwhile, announced the day after the election that she was resigning as CAQ leader after taking “full responsibility” for the party’s defeat.
The transition is unfolding as the PQ also challenges results in two closely contested ridings.
A party source said Tuesday the PQ is seeking a judicial recount in Champlain, in the Mauricie region, where Conservative Adriana Szalontai defeated PQ candidate René Branchaud by 191 votes.
The source said alleged irregularities were identified during the counting of ballots, with approximately 80 ballots missing from one ballot box and another 30 from a second.
Quebec election law allows a recount to be requested when the margin between the top two candidates is less than one-thousandth of the votes cast. While the margin in Champlain does not meet that threshold, the PQ official said the party believes it has sufficient grounds to convince the Court of Quebec to grant the request.
The Court of Quebec has already granted the PQ’s request for a recount in Vachon, where Liberal Affine Lwalalika defeated PQ candidate Stephan Fogaing by 10 votes.
That recount is scheduled to begin Oct. 19 and is expected to last three days.
St-Pierre Plamondon is expected to unveil his cabinet next week.

title: Kelowna residents left with costly damage after fuel tanks drilled
body:
Fuel theft is leaving Kelowna vehicle owners facing more than an empty tank, with some discovering holes drilled directly into their vehicles’ fuel tanks.
Roger Dyck says he and his wife were leaving a Walmart parking lot around 8:45 p.m. Saturday when they noticed a strong smell.
“We started smelling gas and we saw it flowing from our truck,” Dyck said.
He says the fuel was pouring out of the truck and draining into the street. His wife spotted two police officers nearby, who came over after the couple alerted them. The officers had been pursuing someone else through the parking lot and believed they may have startled the people mid-theft.
The fire department eventually arrived to clean up the spilled fuel.
For Dyck, the damage means more than losing gasoline. His 2020 Chevrolet Silverado is undergoing repairs, leaving him without his truck for another week or two while parts are sourced.
He estimates the repair could cost between $1,000 and $2,000, although he is still waiting for an official estimate. His insurance deductible is $300, and he expects to pay about $200 for towing depending on what insurance will cover.
Chris Loney experienced a different kind of fuel theft after returning from a trip to Edmonton. He discovered his 1992 Mitsubishi Pajero’s fuel cap had been pried open and a significant amount of diesel was missing.
Loney says older vehicles may be more vulnerable to siphoning because they lack the protective mechanisms found in many newer models. Newer vehicles, however, can be targeted through a more damaging method.
“Even with a cylinder lock, it doesn’t matter; they’ll pry it open,” Loney said.
A replacement fuel tank can cost around $1,000, according to Vince Minnis, a body shop manager. That figure could climb to $2,000 if a brand-new original-equipment tank is required.
With fuel costing more than $200 to fill some vehicles, Dyck says high prices may be playing a role in the thefts.
“I know it’s happening quite a bit; I don’t want to blame people these days. But I wish people would consider the damage they are causing others,” Dyck added.
Chris Loney says the experience has left him frustrated, particularly because vehicle expenses already consume much of his budget.
“I put most of my money into the vehicle and now I can’t go out and enjoy it over the weekend,” said Loney.
As fuel prices remain high, vehicle owners are left facing an unsettling possibility: the next time they return to their parked vehicle, the damage may extend well beyond the cost of gasoline.

title: Google DeepMind and Singapore Government collaborate to build fine-tuned AI model for scam detection
body:
Collaborating with the Government Technology Agency of Singapore (GovTech Singapore) to protect users without compromising privacy.
Scams, such as investment fraud, fake job offers, and impersonation of public officials make up over half of Singaporeâs reported crimes, and account for more than S$4 billion in losses since 2019 . At the same time, scam tactics have shifted from simple phishing to complex social engineering, whereby attackers manipulate victims with convincing conversations before requesting money. Such scams now account for up to 80% of all losses.
To address this, Google DeepMind and the Government Technology Agency of Singapore (GovTech Singapore) have been working together as part of our National AI Partnership with the Singapore Government. Together, we've fine-tuned a privacy-preserving, on-device scam detection model.
Generic models often struggle with local deception techniques, making scam detection harder. To address this, Googleâs lightweight Gemma model was fine-tuned on local scam conversations. These ranged from impersonations of public institutions, banks, and local figures, to trending regional schemes. This ensures the fine-tuned model will be able to distinguish benign social chatter from genuine manipulation when deployed in applications installed by citizens.
Unlike traditional threat detection, which relies on server-side scanning of messages in the cloud, this model can process conversation data directly on-device. When integrated into applications, this will allow faster analysis of conversation patterns to detect manipulative intent and help citizens act before financial or credential exposure can occur.
The roll out of the model within applications will be carefully phased and developed in partnership with the Singapore Government. When deployed, the model will only be able to access on-device conversations with the user's consent, in accordance with the terms of use of that application. As the model runs entirely on-device, neither the Singapore Government nor Google, will be able to access usersâ conversations through its deployment.
Fighting scams shouldn't mean sacrificing personal privacy. Working with Google DeepMind, we're bringing advanced AI protection directly onto citizens' devices. This allows us to catch highly targeted, local scam attempts in real time while keeping personal communications private.
When the model detects manipulative conversational patterns, it triggers a real-time warning directly on the user's device advising them to pause and exercise caution before sharing sensitive information or funds.
Running a complex scam classifier model on modern smartphones is no easy task, with battery efficiency being a critical area of concern. To do this, we're relying on a two-stage pipeline:
Presented at Singapore International Cyber Week (SICW 2026), this collaboration provides a model for messaging platforms balancing user protection with end-to-end encryption. Strict governance was maintained throughout development:
The project demonstrates how AI can help counter criminality without compromising safety or privacy. It also shows how governments and model providers can work together to build tech for public good. With this lightweight, on-device model, we've proven the ability for local, real-time scam detection while ensuring chat interactions remain secure. We look forward to sharing more soon on our collaboration with the Singapore government, as well as exploring the potential for similar technology to be deployed in other countries.

title: 'There are no dreams left': Families of two sailors missing after drone attack off Oman speak of their grief
body: Two families are “sick with grief” waiting for news of two young sailors missing days after an empty tanker was struck by a drone off Oman. The oil tanker, MT Petro Dolphin, was hit near the Sohar anchorage on Sunday. Relatives in two northern Indian villages are waiting for information on Amit Singh, 20, and Bir Bahadur Yadav, 25, who were on the main deck when the drone struck and fire spread. Of the 12 crew on the Nicaraguan-flagged tanker, nine Indians and one Bangladeshi national were rescued and two seafarers are missing, India’s External Affairs Ministry has said. It was the first sailing job for both men, and their relatives have described the incomprehensible loss they felt on learning of the attack. “Amit’s parents are in and out of consciousness, they cannot cope. It’s all finished, there are no dreams left, it’s all broken,” Amit Singh’s uncle, Ravindar Singh, told The National from Gopala village in Uttar Pradesh. “It’s as if they are dead. As long as they live, they will be in this condition, like death. We are trying to support them but what can we say to comfort them?” Maritime agency reports show that at least 12 tankers have been attacked in the Arabian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz in the past week as Iran steps up its campaign to stop US-backed efforts to move oil. There have been 24 seafarer deaths and 104 incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and the Middle East since the Iran war began on February 28, according to the International Maritime Organisation. Shattered dreams An experienced seafarer , Ravindar Singh, 40, spoke to rescued crew members to find out his nephew’s location when the drone struck. He says there is no hope of survival. “The men told me Amit was working on the main deck in the exact same place of the drone attack. We know he is no more,” Mr Singh said. “The crew were evacuated by fishermen. They went around the vessel to search in case the sailors had jumped into the sea, but found nothing.” Video shot by the crew captures the fire and smoke engulfing sections of the tanker, and a sailor can be heard crying out: “My two crew have gone, Allah, my two men have died.” Amit Singh was from a poor farming community and his family were happy when he followed his uncle into the merchant navy. He signed on with the tanker in January as an able seaman, and his work covered navigation, mooring, handling cargo and maintenance of the ship’s deck equipment. His uncle, a sailor for 20 years, spoke of the rising danger as merchant ships are targeted in the Iran-US and Russia-Ukraine wars. Ravindar Singh returned home in May after a projectile landed near his ship in the Black Sea. His nephew was due to complete his contract on October 20, and the men had planned to find a safe voyage together. “Amit was excited about coming home,” Mr Singh said. “After the Iran war, it is the worst condition for sailors. But Amit’s vessel was not in the Strait of Hormuz, it was in anchorage. How can it be that sailors are not safe near the port?” Mr Singh spoke of his nephew’s plans to build a better life for his family. “Amit was starting out in life. He wanted to save money to get his older sister married. His parents live on a small farm and he wanted a better life for them. “This is so wrong. Why should Amit be gone? We are just seamen. We are like drivers, we load and unload cargo, we do as we are told. But they are targeting us. If the ship is the target, at least give sailors a warning. Property damage can be fixed but a sailor’s life is gone.” Someone’s son, someone’s brother The family of the second sailor, Bir Bahadur Yadav, also from Uttar Pradesh in northern India, tried to shield his mother from news that he was missing , but she learnt from villagers who heard it on television. “I didn’t want to tell my mother until we were sure but now she knows, her spirit is broken. She is constantly crying,” Mantoo Yadav, Bir’s elder brother, told The National from India. He works in Abu Dhabi and was visiting home when the attack occurred. “In this war, why are sailors being killed? It is someone’s son, someone’s husband, someone’s brother who is dying. What will you get from killing our brothers?” The night before the drone attack, Bir Bahadur spoke to his family about wanting to return home. The youngest of four, he worked as a wiper, cleaning the engine room and machinery. He had four months remaining on a nine-month contract. “We had a long talk. He told us he had seen attacks and saw one ship hit nearby,” Mr Yadav said. “Bir was worried his ship would become a target. But he thought he should stay and finish the contract. We told him to come home but it was too late.” Mr Yadav, 36, said his younger brother was focused on completing seafarer certifications to earn a higher rank. “Bir wanted to work hard, finish exams to get a good position. He was serious when he spoke but could also make people laugh. He was very loving,” said Mr Yadav. The family continues to hold on to hope. “We have been told that we will know about Bir only when the ship is brought to shore and checked,” Mr Yadav said. “The crew saw the attack and know the other sailor is no more. But the crew did not see Bir. “What if he managed to jump off? There is 10 per cent hope that he is still alive. Maybe in the rescue, they will find him unconscious.” Waiting for news Manoj Yadav, general secretary of the Forward Seamen’s Union of India, spoke of the trauma families suffer as they wait for news from search operations. “It's tough. When a vessel is hit by drone or rocket, there is fire and waterlogging,” said Mr Yadav, who is not related to the missing sailor. “It takes time to search the area for missing sailors, and families may not get an answer for days.” Neither Iran nor the US has taken responsibility for the drone strike. Maritime associations have called for more protection for sailors as the war continues. “This tanker was anchored off Sohar, so what was the need to hit this vessel? The only danger is for sailors,” Mr Yadav said. “It’s a very alarming situation and the threat to sailors is growing. Families are suffering. We need strong measures to protect seafarers.” India’s External Affairs Ministry has condemned the attacks. “The recurring attacks on commercial shipping in the region are deeply concerning and risk further aggravating an already volatile situation,” the Indian government said. “Attacks on commercial vessels, seafarers and civilian infrastructure must cease.”
