title: AI could be worth $1 trillion to the Mena region, new research suggests
body: Artificial intelligence could be the key to unlocking about $1 trillion in the Middle East and North Africa region by 2030, if used efficiently, research by the World Economic Forum has shown. Two reports have been published as the WEF and the Government of Dubai host the inaugural Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders this week. The three-day event brings together hundreds of leaders and experts from around the world, who will hold intergenerational conversations aimed at tackling the problems of the future. If the region uses AI for growth in the sustainability and economic sectors, the WEF sees great potential for value by 2030. Across sectors, this could mean up to $200 billion in sustainable financing through the financial sector, $370 billion in sustainable investment flows enabled by the public sector, $250 billion in long-term asset losses avoided, $90 billion in increased valuation through improved sustainability performance for the energy sector and $100 billion in sustainable projects launched through cross-sector partnerships. Altogether, this is valued at more than $1 trillion. The region is ripe for this growth, experts say, but it will require cross-sector collaboration. "Mena has the resources, investment capacity and ambition to become a major centre of AI-led growth,” said Maroun Kairouz, managing director of the WEF. “Turning that ambition into reality will require innovation across data-centre infrastructure, energy and water systems, and the application of AI to drive sustainability solutions." Case studies showed how different UAE and regional companies used AI for sustainable initiatives, from First Abu Dhabi Bank in sustainable finance to Adnoc in the energy sector. The UAE has been at the forefront of AI investment, with the US-UAE AI Acceleration Partnership resulting in an AI campus in Abu Dhabi and a $1.4 trillion investment plan over the next 10 years. Abu Dhabi is betting big on AI, with a $3.54 billion investment to integrate the technology into the government's public services by next year. Rising energy and water demands The second report gave a warning about the consumption of resources such as energy and water through data centres, to power AI infrastructure, especially given that the region faces extreme heat and water scarcity. Data-centre cooling, which uses large amounts of water, was flagged as one of the priority areas for innovation and the incorporation of sustainable methods for long-term efficiency and resilience. The opportunities for data centres in the region, however, are plentiful, experts said. Connecting new data centres to the grid can be much quicker in the region, taking between two and five years compared with other mature markets. “Mena is uniquely positioned to lead the next wave of digital infrastructure by bringing together its energy capabilities, investment capacity and technological ambition,” said Nedaa Almubarak, managing director of SRMG Think. “The opportunity lies in aligning intelligent infrastructure with efficient resource use to build resilient, sustainable and competitive digital ecosystems that drive long-term economic growth and innovation.” The Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders in Dubai continues until Thursday.

title: Torrential rains in Libya’s Tripoli kill two
body: Torrential downpours flooded the Libyan capital of Tripoli ​on Tuesday, killing two people, ‌according to a statement by authorities and a local TV channel. Jumhouria Bank ​said an employee died due ​to an electrical shock. The ⁠Tripoli Red Crescent said in ​a statement it recovered the man’s ​body during the flooding. Rescue teams recovered the body of another man from his ​car, which was submerged in ​the floodwaters, according to a local TV ‌station. Fadel ⁠Abu Arqoub, the mayor of Central Tripoli, told the TV station that the rain lasted for ​2-1/2 hours ​and ⁠that the situation was catastrophic. The state-owned electricity company ​said it cut off power ​as ⁠a precaution in certain areas where rising water reached homes. Eyewitnesses ⁠said ​the floodwaters inundated roads ​and submerged numerous vehicles.

title: FG Unveils Fresh Interventions to Revamp Nigeria’s Education Sector
body: Blessing Ibunge in Port Harcourt The federal government has unveiled series of interventions aimed at improving infrastructure, teacher quality, digital learning and skills development as part of efforts to reposition Nigeria’s education sector. Minister of Education, Dr. Tunji Alausa, disclosed this at the opening of the 85th Joint Consultative Committee on Education (JCCE) Plenary Meeting in Port Harcourt, Rivers State, with the theme, ‘Infrastructural Development and Teacher Motivation: Panacea for Improved Learning Outcomes’. Represented by the Director overseeing the Office of the Permanent Secretary, Federal Ministry of Education, Dr. Folake Olatunji-Davies, Alausa said the administration of President Bola Tinubu is implementing targeted policies to make education more qualitative and responsive to national development needs. He said that the federal government is concerned not only about physical infrastructure, but also about teacher quality and the overall learning environment. “Through the Renewed Hope Agenda, the federal government has continued to place education at the centre of national development,” Alausa said. According to him, the Federal Ministry of Education instituted the Nigerian Education Sector Renewal Initiative to provide a coordinated framework for transforming the sector, with emphasis on quality assurance, technical and vocational education and training (TVET), STEM, digitalisation, inclusion and improved learning environments. He listed the Renewed Hope Energising Education Programme (RHEEP) and the Next Gen Student Hostel Projects at institutions including Yaba College of Technology and Lagos State University among interventions designed to improve students’ living and learning conditions. “This underscores the administration’s commitment to improving the physical conditions under which students live and learn,” he said. The minister also disclosed that the government is strengthening science, technology, engineering, mathematics and medical sciences through the rehabilitation and upgrading of medical schools, as well as engineering and technology faculties in tertiary institutions. He added that the National Digital Learning Initiative is facilitating the rollout of smart classrooms and digital learning resources nationwide to expand technology-enabled education and improve digital literacy among teachers and learners. Alausa further cited intensified efforts to reduce the number of out-of-school children through targeted enrolment campaigns, alternative learning pathways and collaboration with state governments and development partners. He said the government is also establishing and upgrading vocational and innovation hubs in federal polytechnics and colleges of education to equip students with practical, industry-aligned skills for employability and self-reliance. The minister urged state governments, local communities, development partners and corporate organisations to complement federal interventions, stressing that education is a shared responsibility. “The success of these reforms will depend not only on government policies and investments, but also on effective implementation, accountability, and sustained collaboration among all tiers of government and stakeholders,” he said. Earlier, Rivers State Governor, Siminalayi Fubara, represented by the Commissioner for Education, Dr. Peters Nwagor, described the JCCE as the country’s foremost technical and advisory body on education. Fubara said the resolutions reached at the meeting would have far-reaching implications for teaching and learning across the country. He said his administration is committed to improving school infrastructure while prioritising teacher training, capacity building and welfare. “School building is the first statement a society makes about how much it values its children. Just as important, we are committed to the welfare, training and motivation of our teachers. The teacher is the single most important factor within the school that determines whether a child succeeds,” the governor said.

title: AI, Automation: African Varsities Urged to Revamp Teaching Methods
body: Funmi Ogundare The Vice-Chancellor of the University of Ghana, Prof. Nana Aba Appiah Amfo, has called on African universities to overhaul their teaching methods and curricula to prepare graduates for a rapidly changing world shaped by Artificial Intelligence (AI), automation and emerging societal challenges. She stated that higher education institutions must move beyond traditional teaching and examination methods to prioritise critical thinking, creativity, ethical judgment, problem-solving and practical application of knowledge. She said this in her keynote address at the International Week of the University of Lagos (UNILAG), themed, ‘Re-imagining Pedagogy and Teaching for Higher Education in the 21st Century’. Amfo argued that universities must reconsider their purpose and the capabilities they seek to develop in students, rather than focusing primarily on the use of technology in teaching. According to her, the rapid advancement of AI, climate change, public health threats, migration, demographic shifts and geopolitical uncertainties are transforming professional fields faster than universities can update their curricula. She noted that African universities face the additional challenge of responding to these changes while addressing longstanding development problems, widening access to education and managing limited resources. “Before asking how we should teach, we should ask, what is higher education for in the 21st century? What should it enable our graduates to become? And what responsibilities do universities have to the societies that sustain them?” she asked. The VC acknowledged that university education remained an important pathway to professional employment, social mobility and intellectual development, particularly in African societies where families often make significant sacrifices to educate their children. While stressing that employability remained important, the VC maintained that universities must also cultivate intellectual independence, adaptability, cultural understanding and a commitment to the public good. She said graduates should be able to interrogate information, investigate problems, develop solutions, work with people of diverse perspectives and continue learning beyond formal education. “For African universities, there is an additional responsibility. Our institutions must help produce the knowledge, leadership, and capabilities needed to address the continent’s challenges, from health systems and food security to environmental sustainability, inequality, democratic governance, and technological inclusion,” she stressed. In her remarks, UNILAG Vice-Chancellor, Prof. Folasade Ogunsola, called on universities to rethink traditional teaching methods and embrace innovative, technology-driven approaches that will equip students with the skills required to thrive in a rapidly changing world. Ogunsola who declared open the university’s International Week, said higher institutions must move beyond conventional lectures and rote learning to teaching methods that promote critical thinking, creativity, innovation, problem-solving and adaptability. She said the growing influence of AI and other emerging technologies had fundamentally changed the higher education landscape, requiring universities to reconsider how they teach, assess and certify students. According to her, the question is no longer whether students have access to AI tools, but how institutions can ensure that learning remains meaningful and prepares graduates for the demands of the workplace. “Our students have access to information on the internet and AI tools that can summarise, calculate, translate and even draft essays in seconds. The question therefore is no longer whether these tools exist, but what it now means to teach, assess and certify learning in their presence,” she said. Ogunsola noted that employers were increasingly seeking graduates with competencies beyond the ability to recall facts and figures, including AI and machine learning literacy, analytical and critical thinking, problem-solving, adaptability, effective communication, emotional intelligence, creativity and innovation. Also in her remarks, the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Resident Representative in Nigeria, Ms Elsie Gyekyewaa Attafuah, urged Nigerian universities to reform their student assessment systems, faculty promotion criteria and research funding mechanisms to encourage innovation, entrepreneurship and practical solutions to national challenges. She stated that universities must align their institutional incentives with the demands of the future to ensure that investments in infrastructure translate into meaningful innovation and development. She stressed the need for institutions to reward innovative thinking, interdisciplinary collaboration and research that demonstrates public value, warning that without deliberate changes to existing academic structures, universities risk investing in new facilities while continuing to reward conventional approaches that may not adequately promote innovation. “There is a risk of placing new facilities within systems that continue to reward the same old ways of working,” she stated. To illustrate how universities could encourage innovation, Attafuah cited University College London, which recognises enterprise and external engagement in its academic career frameworks, and the University of Cambridge, where inventors and their departments share revenue generated from research licensing. She charged Nigerian universities to consider similar approaches by giving greater recognition to innovation, interdisciplinary research and initiatives that translate academic discoveries into practical benefits for society. She also advocated the provision of small, accessible grants to enable students and faculty members to experiment, test ideas and improve their solutions. According to her, “universities should explore ways to support innovation hubs and other platforms where ideas developed through original research could be tested and refined.” She added that rigorous testing and a clear contribution to knowledge should remain central to academic research, including doctoral studies. “The opportunity is to align our incentives with the future. We want our universities to create while upholding academic rigour,” she stated.

title: Stakeholders Canvass Public-Private Partnership to Reduce Out-of-school Population
body: Oluchi Chibuzor Stakeholders in the country’s education sector have called for public-private partnership to reduce the over 10 million out-of-school population. They also sought an upgrade of existing education models to meet modern world demands, to close the gap between learning and workplace realities. These were some of the recommendations made at the maiden edition of the Education that Works Summit, organised by Auctus Social Transformation Initiative, in collaboration with Khadijat Okonnu Leadership Foundation and One Million Teachers, which opened at the University of Lagos, recently. Convener of the summit and founder, Auctus Social Transformation Initiative, Prof. Akin Akinpelu, explained that with education in Nigeria, practitioners often talk about the problem without proffering solutions to them. Akinpelu, who was represented by the Programmes Manager, Dr. Omam Agboro, stated that the goal of the summit was to bring together stakeholders in the education space to proffer solutions towards strengthening education in Africa. “We discovered that many education stakeholders have been working in silos. For this pilot project, we thought about letting the teachers share their own perspective on how things can work in the sector. “That is why in the room we have students, teachers, policy makers, edtech founders and students to talk about education that works. The goal is to be able to change the trajectory of education in Nigeria and in Africa, so that education must really work,” she said. Speaking during the panel session, Education Systems and Policy Leader, Olarenrewaju Oniyitan, said that public-private partnerships in education need to move beyond takeovers of public schools by private practitioners to addressing the problem of affordable and accessible basic education. She noted that Nigeria’s education system cannot be understood simply as a choice between public and private schools. She opined that “public-private partnerships in education should direct public funding and support to affordable non-state schools already serving low-income communities, rather than transfer public schools to private operators. “In many communities, low-cost private, faith-based and community schools, as well as alternative learning centres, provide places for children who might otherwise be unable to attend school.” Delivering his paper, Finnish Education Service Consultant and Chief Executive Officer, Polar Partners, Kimmo Kumpulainen, explained that the environment also plays a critical role in education outcomes. According to him, “integrating digital tools which support learning diversity and encouraging digital learning and grading models can support students and teachers in delivering education that is inclusive for students and their teachers.”

title: Beyond Compliance: How Chrisland is Building a Culture of Safety, Safeguarding
body: For children facing bullying, abuse or situations that make them feel unsafe, speaking up can be difficult. Some members of Chrisland Schools’ management team and its Designated Safeguarding Officers told journalists, including Funmi Ogundare, how the school is working to create an environment where learners feel safe reporting concerns and seeking help. They explained how initiatives such as its Safeguarding Week, confidential reporting channels, staff training and regular risk assessments are helping to make safety and child protection a shared responsibility among learners, parents and staff across the school’s campuses For a child who is being bullied, feels unsafe or is struggling with a situation that they do not know how to handle, the hardest step can often be finding the courage to speak. At Chrisland Schools, the message during Safeguarding Week is simple: speak up, and someone will listen. Across its 16 schools, the management is seeking to make safety and safeguarding more than rules contained in a handbook or instructions delivered during an assembly. It wants them to become part of how learners think, behave, and relate to others. For the Head of Risk, Compliance, Safeguarding and Child Protection, Kemi Fajemirokun, the objective goes beyond satisfying regulatory requirements. “Our focus is beyond compliance, embedding the whole school safety culture and safeguarding culture for positive character development in every learner,” she stated. That philosophy is reflected in the school’s approach to safeguarding, which places learners, parents and staff at the centre of what Fajemirokun described as a ‘triangle of responsibility’. “The children are focused on what they should do; the parents are focused on what they should do; and the teaching and non-teaching staff are also focused on what they should do,” she explained. The approach is particularly important in a school environment where children spend a significant part of their formative years interacting with peers and adults. Rather than waiting for an incident to occur before responding, Fajemirokun said the school has deliberately built safety awareness into the everyday school experience. For about seven years, the school has held a dedicated safety and safeguarding awareness week, using different themes each term to address emerging concerns and remind the entire school community of their responsibilities. This year’s theme, ‘Beyond Compliance: Embedding the Whole School Safety Culture and Safeguarding Culture for Positive Character Development in Every Learner’, she noted, captures the school’s attempt to make safety instinctive. Fajemirokun wants learners and staff to develop what she described as a safety mindset, an internal awareness of when an action could place them or another person at risk. “We want it to become a culture where every learner, every staff member and every child has a mindset of safety and safeguarding in their DNA, that I cannot do this thing because I am going to be vulnerable; I cannot do this thing because it is going to expose me to danger,” she said. Every planned activity, Fajemirokun noted, must undergo a risk assessment before it receives clearance. “We do risk management of all our processes every time. Before we do anything, we must assess the risks. Only after you have completed the risk assessment can you clear a school to proceed with whatever you have planned. This means safety considerations are expected to precede activities rather than being introduced after something goes wrong,” she explained. One of the most significant elements of the safeguarding programme is creating safe channels for children to raise concerns. At schools in Ikeja, Idimu and Festac, Victoria Island, Designated Safeguarding Officers (DSOs) said learners are encouraged to report bullying, abuse or anything that makes them uncomfortable. They, however, noted that reporting is not always easy. Some children may be afraid of being labelled a ‘snitch’. Others may fear retaliation from the person they have reported or worry that their peers will discover that they raised the alarm. The schools therefore assured learners that confidentiality is central to the reporting process. A designated safeguarding officer at Chrisland School, Opebi, Ikeja, Abimbola Taylor, explained that where a child was uncomfortable being identified, the matter could be treated as a general observation rather than attributed directly to the child. The objective, she said, was to ensure that “nobody will even trace it to whoever has reported”. The system also recognises that not every child will be comfortable standing before an adult and narrating what happened. For such learners, safeguarding boxes have been provided where they can write down their concerns and submit them. The designated safeguarding officers then review the reports and take appropriate action. “It is a small but significant shift: giving children not just instructions about staying safe, but different avenues through which they can ask for help,” Taylor said, adding that bullying is not acceptable, and every child has the right to express discomfort and seek protection. The school’s safeguarding system does not end with awareness campaigns. Another DSO said incidents and concerns should be reported promptly, with a 24-hour window for escalation. “Dedicated incident-reporting email channels operate around the clock, allowing staff to report concerns no matter how minor they may initially appear. Don’t take anything too small or too big. No matter what, within 24 hours,” she stated. The Executive Head of School (Academics), Olusegun Ogunsola, said he believes that effective safeguarding must begin with a clear understanding of who the school exists to protect. “The child is the focus of everything we do. The child is the focus, especially since he or she is in our care. So, we owe every child the duty of care,” he stated. He noted that Chrisland has therefore invested in training staff in safety, safeguarding, child protection and risk compliance, with training provided through government agencies and external experts. “Chrisland also brings specialised facilitators into the schools to strengthen staff capacity. Safeguarding is not an annual conversation. It has to be reinforced continuously,” he stated. Ogunsola added that assemblies, meetings, competitions and other school gatherings provide opportunities to remind learners about safety, while events include specific safety moments designed to make participants conscious of their surroundings, saying, “At such events, learners and staff are reminded of emergency exits, muster points and fire-drill areas.” He said the school operates a unified safety and safeguarding calendar to ensure that learners receive consistent attention regardless of the school they attend. The second week of every term is dedicated to safeguarding awareness across the schools, with activities including talks, seminars, workshops and practical demonstrations. External experts are also invited to engage learners on different dimensions of safety and child protection. “Every school is as important as the other because every school is populated by children, and we owe everyone the duty of care and need to safeguard everybody,” the head of school said. The Principal of Chrisland College, Idimu, Olubunmi Dosunmu, stated that the school is strengthening its safeguarding culture by making safety awareness and risk assessment a shared responsibility among staff, students and parents. He noted that the initiative was particularly important because the college operates a full boarding system, requiring more intensive supervision and deliberate safety measures to protect students around the clock. He restated that safeguarding must become embedded in the consciousness of the entire school community rather than being treated as the responsibility of designated personnel alone. According to him, the school continuously assesses potential risks and reviews its systems to respond to changing circumstances, including periods when students remain on campus but have fewer academic activities. “We build a strong safeguarding culture in our schools. The entire community, staff, students and parents need to have it in their subconscious about this subject,” he said. Dosunmu explained that the boarding arrangement required the school to pay particular attention to what happens to students throughout the day and night, adding that supervision was therefore a major component of its safeguarding strategy. He stated, “Because we are a full boarding school, we have to be more intensive and more intentional. We are looking at a system that works 24/7. We look at what happens to the children during the day and when they sleep at night, and what the possible changes in school are.”

title: Nigeria Eyes Rugby League World Cup Hosting After IRL Boost
body: The Nigeria Rugby League Association has achieved a major milestone in its development after becoming the fourth country to join the International Rugby League accelerator programme. The IRL Accelerator Nation project is designed to increase the value of the Rugby League World Cup by growing the number of competitive countries through activities. France, Wales and Papua New Guinea were the initial cohort of Accelerator Nations in 2025, with the group subsequently extended to include one nation from each of the Americas and Middle East Africa regions. IRL’s Strategy Committee managed a month-long application process which produced Nigeria from four invited MEA applicants. No decision has been made on the Americas nation. Subsequently, Nigeria Rugby League Association Vice President, Ade Adebisi, joined senior officials from France and Wales as an embed on the IRL Rugby League World Cup 2026 operations team to gain experience and insights into the management of the biggest event in global rugby league. The three-week deployment is the first output of the Accelerator Nation initiative announced by IRL last year. Ade Adebisi, alongside Mathilde Marchand and Rob Deeney, are leaders in their national federations and will work at the World Cup, which provides their organizations with invaluable, unique experience at the elite level of Rugby League. “What I bring back will go straight into how NRLA operates,” said Adebisi, Nigerian rugby league’s vice Chair and general manager. “Our players have already shown they can compete internationally, and now our administration needs to match that standard. This experience will help us build stronger systems, better governance and a more professional environment for our athletes, coaches and partners.” The accelerator project objectives include the cultivation of pathways from local junior leagues to 13-a-side men’s and women’s leagues, high-quality coaching and high-performance coach development; providing opportunities for local youth or open age representative sides to assemble in training camps and experience elite-level competition through touring IRL member nations with a generally accepted higher standard of play than the Accelerator Nation; and to support selected local player secondment to elite foreign clubs to improve the selected Accelerator Nation player’s on- and off-field standards and experience. Nigeria is the first African country to join the accelerator project, which aligns with the NRLA’s big dream of bringing the world to Nigeria by hosting the International Rugby League World Cup.

title: Dangote Cement Hosts 2026 Football Tourney to Promote Inter-Community Unity
body: Dangote Cement Plc, Obajana Plant, is set to host the 2026 Unity Football Tournament, an inter-community sporting competition designed to promote peace, unity, mutual understanding, healthy competition, youth development, and sustainable relationships among its host and catchment communities. Group Head, Social Performance, Dangote Cement Plc, Mr. Wakeel Olayiwola, said the tournament represents another significant platform for strengthening relationships between Dangote Cement Plc and its host communities through sports, youth engagement, social inclusion, and active community participation. Mr. Olayiwola said the tournament shows the role of sports as a powerful instrument for bridging social differences, fostering peaceful coexistence, and building a sense of belonging among the diverse communities. He said: “The competition will bring together participating communities, namely Oyo, Iwaa, Apata, Jakura, and Obajana, at the Dangote Academy, where football will serve as a unifying platform for friendship, sportsmanship, constructive engagement, and collective development.” Plant Director, Dangote Cement Plc, Obajana Plant, Engr. Azad Nawabuddin, urged the Local Organising Committee to work closely with relevant stakeholders and participating communities to ensure effective coordination and the successful delivery of the tournament. The Plant Director emphasised the importance of transparent administration, proper player accreditation, adequate security arrangements, medical and health support, effective logistics, and strict adherence to established competition rules. He said these measures are expected to ensure that the tournament is conducted in a safe, organised, fair, and professional atmosphere that reflects the values and standards of Dangote Cement Plc. Speaking on the objectives of the tournament, Head of Social Performance at the Dangote Cement Plc, Obajana Plant, Prince Ademola Adeyemi, said the programme goes beyond winning trophies and medals. According to him, “the tournament is designed to foster lasting bonds among participating communities, encourage positive youth engagement, identify and nurture emerging football talents, and provide young people with opportunities to demonstrate discipline, teamwork, leadership, and sporting excellence.” Secretary, Local Organising Committee (LOC) Mr. Iguoba John said the tournament will officially open Friday, October 16, 2026. Mr. John said that community-based sporting activities remain valuable tools for strengthening stakeholder relationships, promoting social cohesion, and building mutual trust between corporate organisations and the communities within which they operate. Speaking on behalf of the catchment communities, Comrade Ayodele Julius, Youth Chairman and Youth Leader of Apata, assured the organisers of peaceful coordination among the youths and pledged support for an atmosphere of unity, cooperation, and mutual respect throughout the competition.

title: Super Falcons Crush Comoros 5-0, Set up Clash with Morocco
body: Marvelous David Nigeria’s Super Falcons yesterday secured a commanding 5-0 victory over Comoros in the second leg of their 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games qualifiers at the Remo Stars Stadium in Ikenne, Ogun State. The Super Falcons will now face Morocco in the third round of the African qualifiers as they continue their pursuit of a place at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games. Uchenna Kanu and Toni Payne scored twice each, while Christy Ucheibe added another goal as Nigeria completed a 7-0 aggregate victory to advance to the next round of the African qualifying series. The Super Falcons broke the deadlock in the 41st minute when Uchenna Kanu took advantage of a defensive error before setting up Toni Payne, who finished confidently to give Nigeria the lead before the break. Nigeria returned for the second half with greater attacking intensity, and Uchenna Kanu doubled the advantage in the 58th minute, heading home a cross from Folashade Ijamilusi. Toni Payne extended Nigeria’s lead in the 63rd minute after Blessing Okpe created the opportunity with an impressive run past two Comoros defenders before setting up the midfielder to score a brace in the match. Three minutes later, Uchenna Kanu completed her brace, connecting with another delivery from Folashade Ijamilusi to make it 4-0 as the Super Falcons continued to dominate proceedings. Nigeria added a fifth goal in the 71st minute after Blessing Okpe won a penalty, which Christy Ucheibe calmly converted to complete an emphatic victory for the home side. The result confirmed Nigeria’s progression to the next round with a 7-0 aggregate win, following their 2-0 victory in the first leg.

title: Presidential Message on the Birthday of the United States Navy
body: Briefings & Statements Search Select Category All News Briefings & Statements All Presidential Actions Executive Orders Nominations & Appointments Presidential Memoranda Proclamations Fact Sheets Releases Remarks Research All Briefings & Statements Presidential Actions All Executive Orders Nominations & Appointments Presidential Memoranda Proclamations Fact Sheets Releases Remarks Research For over 250 years, American sailors have defended our Nation upon the seas, forging the most lethal Navy in the history of the world. Today, on the birthday of the United States Navy, Icelebrate this incredible milestone with our active duty and reserve sailors, past and present, whose unparalleled expertise and extraordinary devotion to duty in times of war and peace have carried our Navy to these unrivaled heights. On October 13, 1775, our Navy was formally established when the Second Continental Congress authorized a pair of armed vessels to sail against the mighty British Empire, intercept enemy supply lines, and defend the cause of American liberty at sea during the Revolutionary War. Since its humble beginnings, the Navy has grown into the most formidable seafaring force the world has ever known. Today’s sailors are part of a storied legacy of maritime supremacy that has safeguarded our sovereignty in every major conflict since. Our warships are unmistakable symbols of American military might, but the most sophisticated, state-of-the-art fleet is nothing without the elite men and women who carry out every mission at home and abroad with unwavering resolve and professionalism. In home ports and on carrier decks, submarine patrols, and distant oceans, our sailor stand watch around the clock, deterring aggression, keeping the world’s great sea lanes open and free, and carrying American strength to every corner of the globe. Their skill and sacrifice keep our Republic safe and secure in the blessings of liberty, earning the everlasting gratitude of the American People. As President, I am rebuilding our incredible Navy and restoring the mighty American shipbuilding industry that sustains it, ensuring our fleet is prepared to meet every challenge of our age. Since returning to office, my Administration has secured over $150 billion in investments to usher in the Golden Age of American shipbuilding. In August, I was proud to sign a National Security Presidential Memorandum that directs the Department of War to pursue more direct investments in the American shipbuilding industrial base, expanding our capacity to build warships and creating good-paying jobs for American workers. The Memorandum further directs the Secretary of War to establish a fifth Naval shipyard, the first in more than eight decades, to increase our Nation’s submarine and aircraft carrier repair capacity. Just last week we saw the fruit of those actions as construction began on the largest new shipyard in the United States since World War II, which will build the next generation of American submarines. Under my leadership, our Navy will be bigger, better, and stronger than ever before. Since the dawn of our glorious Republic, generation after generation of valiant sailors have answered the Navy’s stern call for “faith, courage, service true, with honor over all.” Today, the First Lady joins me in saluting over two and a half centuries of American dominance upon the seas and honor the heroes who secure the freedom and safety of the American People. The post Presidential Message on the Birthday of the United States Navy appeared first on The White House .

title: Enrique Hopes City Avoid Sanctions as PSG Hit Etihad
body: Paris St-Germain boss Luis Enrique has said that he was surprised to learn Manchester City had been found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules and hopes the club can avoid sanctions. City host European champions PSG in the Champions League this evening at 8pm- their first home match since being found guilty of the majority of 115 charges . “There is a lot of noise around Manchester City and there is often noise around big clubs,” said Enrique when asked about City’s guilty verdict at a news conference at Etihad Stadium on Tuesday. “We just have to wait and see what the final decision will be. I hope everything works out well for Manchester City because I think what they have done on the pitch has been incredible over the last few years and they certainly deserved to win on the pitch all the trophies they have won. “Now we have to wait to see what the authorities decide or the judge is going to say.” An independent commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 by creating “sham” contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than £830m into their football operations. City insist they are innocent and have appealed. Luis Enrique added: “The first thing that you hear, it is a surprise, but we need to respect the process and wait for the final decision. “The authorities are responsible for making these decisions. But speaking only about football, they deserved those trophies. I love their football. Beyond that, we have to wait for the decision. “The trophies you win on the pitch remain on the pitch. They deserved to win that and I hope they can avoid the sanction. But we have to wait.”

title: Ademola Lookman Ends Goals Drought against Man Utd
body: *Osimhen fires blanks as Barcelona hammer Galatasaray 4-1 in Istanbul Marvelous David Ademola Lookman came off the bench against Manchester United last night and ended his goals drought this season as he sealed Atlético Madrid’s 2-0 win In the UEFA Champions League league phase action. The former Atlanta man profited from Manchester United’s goalkeeper’s blunder. Senne Lammens had parried Jonathan David’s initial effort into Lookman’s way only for the Nigerian international to tapped into net in the 79th minute. It was his first goal this season. Before that goal came, Diego Simeone’s men had raced into the lead in the very first minute of the UEFA Champions League league phase clash at the Metropolitano in the Spanish capital city. Alex Baena raced beyond Diogo Dalot on to a routine ball over the United defence, before squaring for the excellent Pablo Barrios, whose shot squirmed under Ayden Heaven and into the net. United’s final hope of an equaliser disappeared when Leny Yoro was sent off for tangling with substitute Jonathan David when the France defender was the last man. Head Coach, Michael Carrick made five changes to his starting line-up against United, yet the Red Devils have now gone five games without a win. The Nigerian forward made an immediate impact after coming on, providing the attacking spark Atletico needed to strengthen their position in the competition and give their supporters a reason to celebrate. Lookman’s goal underlined his importance to Diego Simeone’s side, with the forward demonstrating his ability to influence a match even when he does not start in the first eleven. His introduction gave Atletico an additional attacking option, and he took his opportunity by finding the back of the net at a crucial moment in the contest. The goal also highlighted Lookman’s growing role in the team as Atletico seek to build momentum in Europe and compete strongly against some of the continent’s top clubs. For the Nigerian international, the performance was another opportunity to prove his value on the biggest stage, while Atletico will hope the victory provides a foundation for a stronger group-phase campaign. Lookman decisive contribution ensured that the spotlight remained firmly on the Super Eagles star as Atletico Madrid celebrated a significant European victory. Elsewhere on the night, Lookman’s Super Eagles teammate, Victor Osimhen and his Galatasaray were hammered 1-4 by Barcelona in Turkey. Osimhen fired blank in the match played at the Rams Park in Istanbul. title: ‘Nanaimo’s most prolific criminal’ back on the street again
body:
A man described as “Nanaimo’s most prolific criminal” is back on the street, raising concern for residents and businesses.
Forty-one-year-old Aiden Tye was arrested in January for assaulting a coffee shop owner.
He now has 174 criminal convictions – 81 of them involving violence – including an incident where he threw a brick at a pregnant woman.
In July 2024, he was arrested over a string of aggressive outbursts at local businesses.
Public safety advocate Kevin Shaw says Tye is an obvious candidate for secure, involuntary care.
“If this person is not in a jail setting, they need to be in some sort of involuntary complex care because they can’t cope with life and we cannot have someone like this causing literally mayhem over and over and over and over again,” he said.
BC Conservative Leader Lorne Doerksen said in a social media post that if he is elected premier, he will “Amend the Mental Health Act so police can get someone like this into mandatory treatment.”
The BC NDP and BC Greens were not able to respond by the deadline for comment on this specific case.

title: NIGERIA AND THE INVISIBLE RAILS
body: Nigeria’s ₦3.4 quadrillion economy runs on telecom networks, argues JOHN EMENIKE In 2025, electronic payment transactions in Nigeria reached ₦3.458 quadrillion, according to the Central Bank of Nigeria’s Annual Report, more than triple the ₦1.078 quadrillion recorded just a year earlier. Transaction volume rose to 47.9 billion from 11.3 billion. By the first half of 2026, Point-of-Sale terminals alone had processed ₦ 41.74 trillion, a 62.5 per cent increase over the same period in 2025, across a network of 8.36 million registered POS devices, of which 5.9 million were actively deployed. AfricaNenda’s 2025 State of Inclusive Instant Payment Systems report rated Nigeria’s NIBSS Instant Payment platform as the first African instant payment system to achieve “mature” status on its Inclusivity Spectrum, with 57.7 million unique users, representing 52 per cent of the adult population. The practical question that maturity raises is: what physical infrastructure carries that volume, and who built it? The answer, for anyone who pauses to trace the chain, is telecoms. Every POS terminal, every bank transfer initiated via a mobile app, every USSD session dialled on a feature phone, and every merchant payment confirmed via a fintech platform requires, at some point in its execution, a working mobile network connection. The terminals connect to their payment processors almost exclusively via mobile SIMs. When a rider-hailing driver in Surulere accepts a digital fare, when a pharmacist in Aba confirms a transfer, when a fruit seller at Damaturu checks her POS balance at the end of the day, each of those moments depends on a signal travelling from a base station to a switch and back again. Ebenezer Onyeagwu, former Group Managing Director of Zenith Bank, captured the relationship plainly when he observed that introducing USSD changed everything for banking. “Without telecoms infrastructure,” he said, “there is no USSD code.” His observation, made before the current wave of app-based banking gathered pace, is truer now than when he made it. USSD’s share of total payment value has declined to 0.14 per cent as smartphone users migrate to banking apps, and GTCO’s *737# platform saw volumes fall from ₦987 billion in the first half of 2024 to ₦499 billion a year later. But the migration from USSD to apps deepens the economy’s dependence on telecoms infrastructure rather than reducing it. A USSD session uses the signalling layer of the mobile network, while a banking app uses the data layer, consuming more bandwidth, more consistently, across more hours of the day. The dependency has only thickened. The infrastructure sustaining that dependency is the product of sustained capital deployment across the sector. According to the Nigerian Communications Commission, mobile network operators invested more than ₦2.13 trillion in capital expenditure on network infrastructure and upgrades in 2025, while tower companies committed an additional ₦373.8 billion, bringing the sector’s total investment to approximately ₦2.5 trillion for the year. Within that total, MTN Nigeria’s ₦1 trillion full-year spend, more than double its ₦443.5 billion outlay in 2024, represented the single largest operator commitment and financed an expansion to 43,000 kilometres of fibre backbone and a population coverage footprint of 93.7 per cent. In the first half of 2026 alone, MTN deployed a further ₦620.5 billion in capital expenditure, while the NCC confirmed that operators collectively committed to more than 12,000 site additions and upgrades across the year, with nearly 3,000 delivered by mid-year and over 730 new 5G sites deployed across 27 states. Airtel Nigeria, Globacom, and the broader tower and fibre infrastructure companies that serve all four operators have each contributed to a shared physical layer that now underpins the daily flows of Africa’s largest digital payments economy. What has changed in the past decade is the number of institutions whose business models rest on that shared layer. A decade ago, the relationship was bilateral: banks used mobile channels, and telcos provided them. Today, the ecosystem includes payment service banks, mobile money operators, merchant aggregators, and lending platforms, all of which route their services through the same base stations and fibre lines that carry voice calls and WhatsApp messages. Moniepoint, which reported processing ₦412 trillion across more than 14 billion transactions in its 2025 review, claims to power eight out of every ten in-person payments made across the country. OPay, PalmPay, and Kuda serve millions more. None of them own a single base station or a metre of fibre. Their infrastructure is borrowed from telecoms operators whose investment decisions determine whether it can bear the weight that Nigeria’s digital economy now places on it. The regulatory system has begun to recognise this interdependence. The Central Bank of Nigeria now requires all POS transactions to connect to both licensed Payment Terminal Service Aggregators, NIBSS and UPSL, with automatic failover between them, a mandate that exists precisely because a single point of failure in the connectivity chain can cascade into settlement failures across thousands of terminals. The joint CBN and NCC circular of December 2024, which directed banks and telecoms companies to resolve the ₦250 billion USSD debt dispute that had accumulated since 2019, was itself an acknowledgement that the two sectors had become so structurally intertwined that a commercial disagreement between them posed a systemic risk to the national payments system. The fragility of the arrangement surfaces periodically. When network disruptions occur and affect operators at different times, POS operators report failed settlements, merchants revert to cash where they can find it, and the digital commerce layer that Nigeria increasingly depends upon contracts until the signal returns. The Central Bank’s own data shows that currency outside banks stood at ₦4.922 trillion in June 2026, enough to sustain barely two days of normal transaction volume if the digital rails went dark. An economy that has moved this far online has no offline mode. The telecoms sector contributed ₦5.2 trillion and 9.72 per cent of real GDP in the second quarter of 2026, up 10.38 per cent year on year, compared with 4.43 per cent for the overall economy. But these figures capture only the sector’s direct output. They do not capture the ₦41.74 trillion in first-half POS volumes, ride-hailing platforms, e-commerce deliveries, telemedicine consultations, and agricultural price-discovery tools that use the same infrastructure. The NCC designated telecoms towers, base stations, fibre-optic cables, data centres, and submarine cable landing points as Critical National Information Infrastructure in 2024. Whether the country treats that designation as an operational commitment will determine how resilient the ₦3.4 quadrillion economy proves to be when the next disruption occurs. Emenike is a Social Commentator and Policy Analyst

title: Libya moves past war stage, threat of new crisis remains — envoy
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Libya has moved past the stage of large-scale war, Ali Juma Hassan Fadil, Libya's Ambassador to Iran, said in an interview with TASS, adding though that the threat of a crisis in a new form exists.
"Libya’s current state can be characterized as a state of ‘relative yet incomplete stability’. The country has moved past the stage of large-scale war of previous years. However, a final political and institutional settlement has not yet been reached. The absence of a major war itself does not imply the onset of a full-fledged peace," he said.
"Today, the Libyan issue goes beyond a single dispute that can be resolved through an agreement between two individuals or institutions. It comprises several interconnected levels: the legitimacy of institutions, the constitutional and legal framework for elections, the distribution of powers and resources, the unification of sovereign and security institutions, relations between the center and regions, and national reconciliation. Therefore, a solution limited merely to the formation of a new government, without those issues being solved, risks replicating the crisis in a different form," the diplomat explained.

title: NIN CORRECTIONS AS BARRIER TO OPPORTUNITIES
body: Nigeria’s National Identification Number (NIN) was introduced to improve identity management, strengthen national planning and make citizens’ identification easier. However, the difficulties many Nigerians face when correcting errors in their NIN records are becoming a growing concern that deserves urgent attention. For citizens affected by spelling mistakes in their names, incorrect dates of birth and other discrepancies in their personal information, correcting these errors can be both financially demanding and time consuming. What should ordinarily be a straightforward administrative process has become a challenge for people who cannot afford the required charges. The question is simple: why should a Nigerian citizen struggle financially to correct an error in an official identification record that is necessary for accessing essential services and opportunities? Government exists to serve the people, and public institutions should operate in ways that promote citizens’ welfare. Although identity management requires proper procedures, verification and administrative resources, these processes should not impose unnecessary hardship on ordinary Nigerians. One major concern is the impact of incorrect NIN information on employment opportunities. Many young Nigerians are searching for jobs in an increasingly competitive environment. Unfortunately, discrepancies between NIN records and other official documents can create complications during job applications, recruitment screening and identity verification. Imagine a qualified job seeker who has spent years acquiring an education and developing professional skills but encounters difficulties because of a spelling error or an incorrect date of birth on their NIN record. For someone already struggling financially, the cost of correcting the error may become another obstacle standing between them and a potential opportunity. This is not merely an administrative concern; it is an issue that affects access to opportunities, social inclusion and the ease of doing business. A national identification system designed to make identification easier should not become a source of frustration for the very citizens it is intended to serve. The federal government and the National Identity Management Commission (NIMC) therefore need to reconsider the current challenges surrounding NIN corrections. There should be a clear distinction between genuine administrative errors attributable to the registration process and other changes that require additional verification. Where errors result from mistakes made during registration, free correction should be considered. For other categories of correction, charges should be reasonable, transparent and affordable, with clear guidelines to prevent citizens from being exploited or misinformed. Idris Rufai, idrisrufai744@gmail.com

title: THE CASE FOR UNDERUTILISED SEAPORTS
body: More functional seaports will enhance the economy On 24 September in Paris, the French capital, a Memorandum of Understanding between DP World, a private port operator, and the Ogun State Government was signed to develop the Gateway Deep Seaport and the Ogun State Blue Marine Special Economic Zone. Prominent figures who attended the event included President Bola Tinubu, Minister of Marine and Blue Economy, Adegboyega Oyetola, and the Managing Director of the Nigerian Ports Authority (NPA), Abubakar Dantsoho. Details of the deal indicated that it would attract an initial investment of over $7 billion and create more than 50,000 direct jobs when fully developed. The Gateway Deep Sea Port will have a four-kilometre berth and an 18-metre draft, which would enable it handle very large vessels. On its part, the Ogun State Blue Marine Special Economic Zone is estimated to span over 10,000 hectares, hosting numerous multi-sector businesses involved in manufacturing, processing and export-oriented operations. However, as many stakeholders have argued, the deal would mean a concentration of maritime infrastructure and operations in the South-West, with Lagos alone boasting of major ports located at Apapa, Tin Can Island, Lekki, while plans are afloat to develop Badagry Seaport. A pillar of their grouse is that the natural ports in Calabar, Port Harcourt, Onne, Sapele and Warri have largely been ignored while concerted efforts are concentrated on the Lagos ports with the attendant traffic gridlock and high cost of haulage to other parts of the country. The backlash seemingly triggered a response from Minister of Marine and Blue Economy, Adegboyega Oyetola, who announced through his official X account that four ports outside Lagos have received approval to be upgraded while six new deep seaports would be developed across the country. He identified the seaports as Onne, Port Harcourt and Calabar. The six proposed deep seaports are Ibom in Akwa Ibom State, Bakassi in Cross River State, Agge in Bayelsa State, Gateway in Ogun State, Ondo in Ondo State and Bonny in Rivers State. Indeed, over the years, the chronic congestion in the Lagos ports has inflated prohibitive logistics costs and dimmed Nigeria’s competitiveness in the maritime sector. A report by Dynanmar, a Dutch consultancy firm, revealed that Nigeria loses a staggering N20 billion daily at the ports due to poor infrastructure and inefficiencies. Benin Republic is reaping from Nigeria’s misfortune. Its port in Cotonou has remained a haven for most importers. Huge trade cargoes are also lost to Togo and other neighbouring countries from where they are offloaded and transshipped to Nigeria due to poor shipping connectivity and shallow draft of the port channels. “In the West and Central Africa region, 80 per cent of containers are destined for Nigeria, but less than 20 per cent actually arrive because of the decayed infrastructure, whether at Lagos, Port Harcourt, or other ports,” said maritime and commercial lawyer, Olisa Agbakoba, SAN. Despite the ease of doing business initiative by the federal government, Nigeria ports have been rated as among the worst in sub-Saharan Africa. With bad policies, maritime authorities have failed to position the ports among the best on the continent as a result of a series of failed policies. Years of excessive reliance on Apapa and Tin Can ports have led to crippling gridlock, corruption, inefficiency, and the collapse of traffic management systems. The problem persists despite the recent introduction of the electronic call-up system to manage the chaotic traffic. In the aftermath, most ships bringing goods to Nigeria prefer to go to other neighbouring ports, particularly Cotonou, Tema and Lome. But after decades of missed opportunities measured in trillions of naira, the federal government seems to be taking seriously the need to decentralise the country’s seaports and unlock dormant economic potential. The NPA has indicated its determination to build a maritime nation where every shoreline counts by transforming several waterways into corridors of commerce. The Lekki Deep Seaport in Lagos is a model for port modernisation. It is expectedly making a huge difference, attracting more than $20 billion in investment. It is a model worthy of replication. The country needs more seaports to trade effectively, and indeed to stop the current hemorrhage. The underutilised seaports have the capacity to significantly increase our national revenue and indeed our Gross Domestic Product.

title: Guinea-Bissau says it has not approved hepatitis B vaccine trial in newborns
body: Guinea-Bissau’s transitional government said Tuesday it has not approved a proposed clinical trial of a hepatitis B vaccine in newborns, ​denying reports that the study had been authorised. The denial followed ‌news reports that the Trump administration-funded study to assess the effects of administering the hepatitis B vaccine at birth would go ahead in the West African ​country. The proposed trial triggered outcry earlier this year, with some ​scientists arguing the study was unethical because some of ⁠the newborns involved would not get the vaccine, which is known ​to be safe and save lives, in a country with high rates ​of hepatitis B. The illness commonly transmits from mother to child during birth and can cause liver failure and cancer. The country’s health minister, Quinhin Nantote, said ​the government had not yet authorised the trial during a press ​conference in the capital on Tuesday. “Any scientific research initiative involving human beings, particularly children, ‌must ⁠strictly comply with applicable national legislation, international ethical principles, competent evaluation and approval mechanisms,” Nantote said, without providing details on the process. In January, the director general of the Africa CDC, Dr Jean Kaseya, told journalists that Guinea-Bissau officials had asked for support with a further ethical and technical review of the trial. The US Department of Health and ​Human Services also denied that the trial has been authorised. “The ​study has ⁠not been approved,” the department said in a statement. The proposed trial aimed to investigate potential “non-specific effects” of vaccines, including skin disorders and neurodevelopmental ⁠disorders, such ​as autism, according to details of the ​study posted online.

title: Transit troubles a key issue for Winnipeg voters as civic election looms
body:
Fatima Bashir’s main way of getting around was the bus, but since the new changes, she plans to buy a car.
“Buying a car wasn’t even in my plan…but now they’re (buses) late and I’m walking more now,” said Bashir, at a bus shelter on Osborne Street.
The City of Winnipeg unveiled the largest change to its transit system on June 29, 2025. The system features a spine-and-feeder model, which is composed of rapid and express lines as the central Primary Transit Network that forms the spine.
Community and connector routes links riders to a main line, which is called a feeder route. The new system has around 4,000 bus stops from 5,200 before the changes.
Many Winnipeggers feel mixed about the city’s transit, with some saying they want to go back to the old transit system.
Bashir said she wants the old transit system back.
“It’s not nice…So many people are complaining about this new system. No one is happy about it,” she said.
Mike Vogiatzakis, a mayoral candidate, pitched to change transit back within 30 days in office, at a news conference in August. Don Woodstock also pledged to “immediately cancel” the transit plan upon taking office but doesn’t mention how it will impact the current routes, according to his campaign website.
The city has spent around $20.4 million towards the implementation of the new network.
It would take “millions and millions of dollars to convert back to the old system,” said Janice Lukes, Public Works chair.
Lukes said the new grid-like transit routes are built to grow with Winnipeg’s growing population and size.
James Van Gerwen, president of the Amalgamated Transit Union Local 1505, said he doesn’t see any logic behind going back to a system that was broken.
Van Gerwen is calling for more buses and funding to support bus drivers to make transit better.
He and other advocates are also pushing for a different funding model which requires the province to step up funding for transit.
The 50-50 funding agreement is an operational bill for transit to be split between the province and the city. This model was scrapped 10 years ago, and provincial funding for transit has remained stagnant, according to the Climate Action Team Manitoba.
“We continue to increase support for municipalities year after year,” said a provincial spokesperson on behalf of Glen Simard, minister of Municipal and Northern Relations. The province did not address specific questions about the 50-50 funding model.
Functional Transit Winnipeg is advocating for more financial support from the province.
Kyle Owens, president of Functional Transit Winnipeg, said re-adopting the funding model means transit will be more reliable with frequent service and expansion of routes.
“Nostalgia is always popular in Winnipeg. It’s an easy way to get attention and get people engaged in transit to talk about the old system and the old routes, but Winnipeg Transit isn’t going back,” said Owens.
Lukes said next year the city plans on having the supporting infrastructure: benches and shelters installed to the new stops.
Around 40 new bus shelters will be installed by the end of 2026, and there are 84 shelters with polycarbonate glass panels throughout the city, according to a city spokesperson.
An Abacus Data poll (formerly Probe Research) shows around a quarter of Winnipeggers want safety and security needs to be addressed on buses.

title: Russia prepares for possible direct military confrontation with Europe by 2045, Ukrainian Intelligence says
body:
The assessment was published by Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service (SZRU), according to Ukrinform.
The report states that Russia's primary objective in Europe at present is to undermine support for Ukraine while keeping its own risks as low as possible.
To achieve this, Moscow has tools it can use more effectively than a direct invasion, the agency says. These include hybrid warfare tactics such as sabotage, cyberattacks, influence operations, disinformation, unexplained drone incursions, and espionage.
According to the SZRU, nearly 400 Russian intelligence officers are operating in Europe. Their activities allow Moscow to systematically test the limits of what other countries will tolerate while attempting to remain below the threshold that could trigger a collective NATO response.
"At the same time, it would be a mistake to assume that Russia has abandoned the prospect of a direct military confrontation with Europe. On the contrary, Moscow considers it one of the possible military conflict scenarios through 2045. Six of these scenarios are linked to Northern Europe. Scenarios involving Poland and the Baltic states are also being actively developed," the intelligence service stated.
It added that the Russian leadership needs an external enemy to justify its policies, mobilize society, and maintain control over the population.
The report emphasizes that Russia seeks to undermine European unity and discredit Europe's security architecture. One possible instrument is a controlled regional crisis on NATO's eastern flank.
According to Russian assessments cited by the Ukrainian intelligence service, the Baltic states are among the most vulnerable links in European security.
A potential scenario could involve creating a situation in which NATO is forced to make decisions amid uncertainty and severe time constraints.
The objective would not necessarily be to defeat NATO militarily, but rather to portray the alliance as incapable of responding quickly or collectively defending its members.
The SZRU also disputes the assumption that the Kremlin develops its plans without considering public opinion.
According to the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), Russians identify the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Poland, Finland, and the Baltic states as among the countries most hostile toward Russia.
At the same time, 61% of respondents believe it is time to pursue negotiations, while 59% believe Russia should intensify its aggressive actions if negotiations fail.
The intelligence service concludes that the Russian threat to Europe has long extended beyond the possibility of a direct attack. Russia is preparing for a prolonged confrontation in which its objectives toward Ukraine and Europe are closely interconnected.
Europe should therefore regard Ukraine not as a peripheral part of its security, but as an indispensable front line, the SZRU emphasizes. The underlying principle, it says, is that Ukraine's security and Europe's security are inseparable.
As previously reported, Oleh Ivashchenko, head of Ukraine's Defense Intelligence (HUR), said Russia has the military and economic resources to continue its war against Ukraine in 2027, but that these resources could be exhausted by 2028.

title: US Supreme Court to hear asylum fight involving Nigerian cook
body: The US Supreme Court agreed on Tuesday to hear a bid by President Donald Trump ‘s administration to deny asylum to a ​man who was forced to prepare meals for an apparent separatist group in Nigeria, in a case that could expand what officials ‌may deem terrorist activity under American immigration law. The justices took up the Justice Department’s appeal of a lower court’s ruling in favour of Nigerian citizen Izuchukwu Ozurumba, who was denied US asylum due to his work cooking for a group known as the Unknown Gunmen that US officials considered to be a terrorist organisation. The lower court ruled that cooking did ​not qualify as “material support” for terrorism under the immigration statute. The Supreme Court is expected to hear arguments and rule in the case by ​the end of June. The administration, in appealing the case to the Supreme Court, said that if the lower court’s ruling ⁠were allowed to stand, it would “substantially increase the burden on the government in excluding aliens with links to terrorism.” The case centres on whether Ozurumba’s work ​for the group fell under provisions of US immigration law that bar the entry of non-US citizens who have “engaged in a terrorist activity,” including actions that provide “material ​support” for such activity or “to a terrorist organisation.” “At stake in this case is whether the government can use an overly broad reading of the law to shut the door on people seeking asylum,” said Aimee Mayer-Salins, an attorney with the Amica Centre for Immigrant Rights, which is helping to represent Ozurumba. The lower court “correctly recognised that asylum should not be denied ​to immigrants who provided no meaningful support to a terrorist group,” Mayer-Salins added. Following a job tip in 2022, Ozurumba took a van to a remote camp ​outside of Lagos, according to court papers. After he was hired, he eventually learned the camp was run by the Unknown Gunmen, a group likely associated with Nigerian separatists, ‌according to ⁠court papers. Ozurumba soon “observed that the young men’s movements from the camp coincided with news reports of murder and arson,” his lawyers said in a court filing. Ozurumba sought to leave but was forced to stay without pay, they added. After six months, he escaped during an outing for supplies and eventually made his way back to Lagos, they said. Ozurumba then faced beatings and threats of death, prompting him to flee to Venezuela, where the threats continued, his lawyers said. Ozurumba then travelled to the southern US border and entered the country illegally in July 2023. Ozurumba eventually applied for asylum and other protections from deportation. ‘BASIC HUMAN NEEDS’ During Democratic former President Joe Biden’s administration, an immigration judge deemed the Unknown Gunmen a terrorist organisation and found that Ozurumba’s cooking for the group rendered him ​inadmissible, and denied him any protections from deportation. The judge concluded that the cooking helped the group accomplish its ​goals by satisfying their “basic ⁠human needs,” and that it was irrelevant that he had worked under duress. Ozurumba was deported back to Nigeria last year while his case was on appeal. The Richmond, Virginia-based 4th US Circuit Court of Appeals sided with Ozurumba in September 2025, ruling that he was a captive labourer and his cooking did not constitute material support. Ozurumba’s work “provided ⁠nothing that ​the organization could use or readily divert to plan or carry out its terrorist activities,” the ​4th Circuit ruled, but declined to order the government to return him to the US while the case proceeds. “Providing meals to a terrorist organization’s members is no less a material form of ​support than providing gasoline for its vehicles,” the Justice Department told the Supreme Court in its appeal.

title: US Army hackathon sets backdrop for an AUSA focused on autonomy
body: The Army recently wrapped up a hacking initiative that asked defense companies to break into each other’s networks and allow their autonomous machines to communicate. Operation Jailbreak, which began in May and concluded in late August, staged two major events that brought contractors, operational units and Army technical experts together to fast-track the future of unmanned tactical networks . “The completed effort dismantled longstanding system silos, proving that autonomous platforms, sensors, weapons, and command-and-control (C2) technologies can exchange real-time data seamlessly across disparate vendors,” the Army said after the final initiative concluded. The first three-week event began in May, bringing 600 people and 50 defense companies to Fort Carson, Colorado. Former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll said the idea for the initiative came after he traveled with then-U.S. Army Europe and Africa Commander Gen. Christopher Donahue to allied training sites in Germany to observe how Ukrainians integrate d drones, sensors and shooting platforms onto a single network. Driscoll resigned on Aug. 31, after allegedly butting heads with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Donahue unexpectedly relinquished command of U.S. Army Europe and Africa in July and retired in August. Driscoll and Donahue observed Ukrainian military utilizing one network that allowed different systems and technologies to exchange data and information without any software barrier. This, in turn, sped up the ability to identify and destroy targets. Within 30 days of the first Operation Jailbreak event at Fort Carson, the Army began fielding system integrations with service members in the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility. Alex Miller, the Army’s chief technology officer for Operation Jailbreak, lauded the strides in technology by describing a nightmare hypothetical involving everyday power adapters for civilians. “Imagine if every accessory you have—light bulbs, toasters, TVs—had a different way to connect,” Miller said at a May 28 media roundtable. “You couldn’t just plug the light bulb in; you had to go find a special cord to plug it into the wall.” Miller likened the scenario to the siloed information exhanges, explaining that it placed too much pressure on soldiers to act as the adapter and said communication between unmanned machines could change that. The second and final exercise, Operation Jailbreak Falcon Fury, concluded on Aug. 28 in Tampa, Florida, after a several-week sprint that began on July 27. Seventy companies utilized more than 150 pieces of technology. Major defense contractors took part, including Epirus , which showcased how its Leonidas high-powered microwave system, which melts drones, could integrate into a wide command-and-control network that hosts other autonomous systems.
