title: Schoolgirls in tears, 37 arrested: Hijab rules pit Israel-friendly Azerbaijan against ally Turkey
body: Azerbaijan's government on Tuesday defended its decision to enforce strict school uniform regulations that have sparked protests over restrictions on Islamic headscarves, and demanded that its close ally Turkey refrain from interfering in its internal affairs after Ankara criticized the measures. Azerbaijan, a former Soviet republic with a predominantly Shiite Muslim population, is officially secular. Its constitution separates religion from the state and guarantees freedom of religion. After decades under Soviet rule, the country has established itself as one of the most secular states in the Muslim world.   Last month, the government introduced new regulations prohibiting students from attending school in clothing that deviates from the official uniform or was deemed inconsistent with the secular character of public education. Although the regulations did not explicitly mention the hijab, reports soon emerged that female students and teachers wearing Islamic headscarves were being denied entry to schools. The restrictions triggered protests in recent days. On Monday, Azerbaijan's Interior Ministry said 37 people had been arrested for disturbing public order while opposing enforcement of the new rules. The ministry said protesters in the capital, Baku, had confronted school staff over the dress requirements, damaged school property and attempted to disrupt classes. Videos circulated on Azerbaijani social media showed students embracing their teachers and crying after learning that the teachers were no longer allowed to enter school because of their headscarves. Female students who had been denied admission, or who were protesting restrictions imposed on others, were also filmed crying and holding protest signs. Students at at least two schools boycotted classes in protest against the restrictions.   Amid the growing controversy, Azerbaijani social media users reported difficulties accessing online platforms on Monday. Instagram and TikTok users, where videos supporting the right to wear the hijab had been circulating, complained that videos would no longer load and news feeds had stopped updating. Some said they were able to regain access only by using virtual private networks, or VPNs. The hijab controversy has also triggered a diplomatic confrontation between Azerbaijan and its traditional ally Turkey. Azerbaijan's ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP) on Tuesday criticized Oktay Saral, an adviser to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, along with lawmakers from Erdogan's ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP), over their opposition to the new regulations. Saral wrote on X on Monday that denying Azerbaijani girls wearing headscarves their right to education was "unacceptable." "A headscarf is not an obstacle it is a religious obligation," he wrote. "We expect Azerbaijan to reverse this mistake as soon as possible." In response, YAP condemned Saral's remarks as "populist and irresponsible," warning that they could endanger relations between the two close allies. The party said the new regulations were based on the principles of equality, secularism and the rule of law. It also pointed out that Turkey itself is constitutionally secular, warning Ankara against using Azerbaijan's education policies for political purposes.   The Azerbaijani ruling party emphasized that the principle of "one nation, two states," commonly used to describe the close relationship between Azerbaijan and Turkey, did not justify interference in another country's domestic affairs or the imposition of political and ideological views. The dispute now threatens to cast a shadow over relations between the two countries, illustrating the challenges facing Baku as it seeks to enforce secularism in a predominantly Muslim society. Last week, protesters gathered outside Azerbaijan's consulate in Istanbul to demonstrate against the restrictions. On Turkish social media, some compared the developments in Azerbaijan to those in Turkey following the 1997 military intervention, when women were barred from wearing headscarves at universities and in public-sector workplaces. Those restrictions were introduced a little more than five years before Erdogan came to power and subsequently made Islam far more prominent in Turkish public life.   Azerbaijan, like neighboring Iran, has a predominantly Shiite Muslim population. Unlike the government in Tehran, however, Baku maintains warm and extensive relations with Israel. Those ties are rooted primarily in deep security cooperation, with Israel serving as a major weapons supplier to Azerbaijan's military. The two countries also share significant economic interests, particularly Israel's imports of Azerbaijani oil. Their relationship is further strengthened by positive cultural and historical connections, including Azerbaijan's ancient Jewish community and the relatively low prevalence of antisemitism in the country. Azerbaijan's close relationship with Israel frequently draws sharp criticism from parts of the Muslim world, particularly neighboring Iran, but occasionally also Turkey. In its statement Tuesday, Azerbaijan's ruling party also addressed renewed criticism from Ankara over Baku's relationship with Israel. YAP defended the bilateral ties, stressing that Azerbaijan's relations with Israel are based on international law and mutual interests.

title: Egypt’s Baha’i minority is running out of space to bury their dead
body: In a Cairo cemetery shaded by palms and tangled shrubs, pale graves are packed so tightly that in some places only narrow strips of sand and broken pavement separate one family’s ​plot from the next. This is the last remaining burial place of Egypt’s Baha’i community, a religious minority long on the margins of official life, and ‌it is quickly running out of room. As it fills, the cemetery has become a symbol for the community of the bureaucratic obstacles and restrictions they say complicate everything from school enrollment to pensions and marriage registration. “God forbid that this area becomes completely full. If that happens, we would have no other places where we can bury,” said Joumana Labib, a 25-year-old architect whose extended family is buried there. The Baha’i faith, whose members are scattered across different continents and who believe their 19th-century founder, Baha’u’llah, is a prophet, was brought to Egypt by merchants in the 1860s, not long after it originated in Iran. With current numbers in Egypt estimated in the thousands, they are a tiny minority in a mainly Muslim country of about ⁠110 million. The Egyptian constitution guarantees religious freedom, though mainstream Islamic scholars view the Baha’i faith as heretical, and officials are often reluctant in practice to recognise religions outside the main ​Abrahamic faiths. BURIAL REQUIRED WITHIN ONE-HOUR JOURNEY While Islamic tradition requires burial within a day, Baha’i practices allow a body to be moved no more than one hour from the place of death, creating ​particular challenges. Burial grounds once used by Baha’is in the port cities of Alexandria and Port Said have been filled or reassigned over the years, leaving many families to transport bodies to Cairo, according to the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), a leading Cairo-based rights group. Community members say requests for new burial grounds in Alexandria and Port Said — where much of Egypt’s Baha’i community lives — have been rejected without clear written explanations, said ​Marina Samir, who heads EIPR’s freedom of religion and belief work. “Death becomes, instead of a time when people are trying to comprehend their loss, a logistical process,” Samir said. Egypt’s government ​information agency and the governorates of Alexandria and Port Said did not respond to requests for comment. Last year, in a response to a UN human rights report, Egypt’s government said it “does not impose any restrictions ‌on personal ⁠belief or religious affiliation, including adherence to the Baha’i faith”. Based on government data, there were “sufficient burial sites to meet the needs of all citizens”, it said. President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi has repeatedly stressed the need for religious coexistence and said the state works tirelessly to fight discrimination and promote tolerance. MARRIAGE WITHOUT RECOGNITION A landmark 2009 court ruling allowed those who do not follow Islam, Christianity or Judaism to leave a dash in the religion field on their identity documents. The change allowed Baha’is to avoid declaring a faith they do not follow, but still left them facing practical ​difficulties. One of the biggest is establishing Baha’i marriages ​in official records. Baha’i couples are often ⁠registered as “single” even after decades together, which can complicate child registration, inheritance, pensions, health insurance and family records. Hanan Kamal El-Din, 65, said her identity card describes her as single, although she married in a Baha’i ceremony 45 years ago and has two children in their 40s. “What harm ​would recognising this marriage do to society?” she said. Like other Baha’is, she won an individual court ruling recognising her marriage in 2020. ​But that decision was ⁠overturned by a higher court in January this year, a ruling other Baha’i couples now fear could affect them as well. Ahmed Helmy, 49, also won a court ruling allowing his documents to show he was married, but said his wife has already been removed from the family section of his account on the government’s digital services platform. He worries that his status on his identity card will revert to “single” when he next renews it. “If I do not have proof of marriage, I cannot add my wife to health insurance,” he ​said. “Anything I own, my wife won’t be able to inherit. Anything she owns, I won’t be able to inherit.” For Labib, the community’s shrinking burial space and the bureaucratic hurdles are connected by the same demand: to be treated ​as an equal citizen. “I am not asking anyone to accept my religion,” she said. “I am asking them to accept me as a person in this country.”

title: Nigeria’s Dangote oil refinery swings to net profit ahead of IPO
body: Nigeria’s Dangote Petroleum Refinery, which is seeking to raise $1.6 billion in what would be Africa’s biggest IPO, swung to a net profit in the first nine months of 2026 as ​revenue more than doubled, according to unaudited results released on Tuesday. The company ​posted a net profit of $4.73 billion for January to September, compared ⁠with a $117.2 million loss a year earlier. The refinery has benefited from rising demand for its products amid supply disruptions linked to the war in Iran, helping it sell jet fuel into Western Europe. “Our third-quarter performance demonstrates the successful transition from commissioning and ramp-up activities to sustainable commercial operations,” Chief Executive Officer David Bird said in a statement. Revenue ​rose to $22.48 billion from $9.19 billion, while core earnings (EBITDA) jumped to $5.52 billion from $627.6 million, ​as higher crude processing rates, stronger refining margins and improved operations boosted profits. The 700,000-barrel-per-day refinery ‌generated ⁠operating cash flow of $3.68 billion, up from $364.7 million a year earlier, and ended September with cash holdings of $6.69 billion. It also moved from a net debt position of $1.73 billion a year ago to net cash of $650.8 million. The application period for the initial public offering, originally due to close on October 13, has been extended by two weeks to October 27 amid strong investor demand. Built at a cost of about $20 billion on the outskirts of Lagos, the refinery has reshaped Nigeria’s fuel market since it began operations in 2024. It aims to double refining capacity to 1.4 million bpd by 2029. The refinery has helped reduce Nigeria’s reliance on imported petroleum products and has emerged as a major supplier of refined fuels to domestic and regional markets.

title: NDC Deputy National Organizer Aspirant Hamza Umar targets grassroots mobilisation
body: Businessman and former student leader Hamza Umar has declared his intention to contest for Deputy National Organizer of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), pledging to strengthen grassroots participation and coordination within the party. Mr Umar, an activist from Tafo in the Ashanti Region, says his ambition is to improve collaboration between the party’s national, regional and constituency structures while ensuring that grassroots members have a stronger voice in decision-making. He previously served as President of the Local National Union of Ghana Students at the University for Development Studies (UDS) and has participated in constituency and regional campaigns within the NDC. He also contested for the position of Constituency Deputy Organizer in Tafo and currently serves on the constituency’s Financial Committee. Mr Umar says effective party organisation depends on an active and empowered grassroots base, identifying inclusive leadership, accountability, youth participation and party unity as the key pillars of his campaign. “Leadership is not merely about holding office,” his campaign message states. “It is about service, commitment and listening to the grassroots.” He says he intends to work with the party’s leadership and regional and constituency executives to advance the NDC’s organisational objectives. His proposed approach centres on improving communication and coordination across the party’s structures, with an emphasis on ensuring that members at the grassroots level are included in party activities and decision-making.

title: Apples to Apples: Getting Type Mappings Right in LLM-Based Code Translation
body:
What it takes for a type mapping between a source and target language to be correct — conversion soundness and round-trip preservation — and how Code Metal uses schema-based interface generators to build verified, behavior-preserving type mappings.
Ariel Kellison, Laura Titolo, and Loris D'Antoni
A major limitation of most LLM-based code translation systems is that they can generate code that compiles successfully without preserving the behavior of the source program. At Code Metal, we are addressing this challenge as we build systems for translating large and complex code bases across many source and target languages. In this post, we examine how choices about mapping types across languages contribute to this problem, what it takes for a mapping between source and target types to be correct, and how translation systems can meet that bar. Let’s begin with why choosing a target type is harder than it looks.
Deciding how types should map across languages is difficult because a choice made for one type affects how values flow through function bodies and across call sites. The right target type often depends not only on the source type itself, but also on how the program uses values of that type. A C function that takes a char * may use it to read text, write into a buffer, or access a sequence of raw bytes. Rust gives each of these uses a different type, and the C signature alone does not say which one is meant.
On the target language side, a type checker or compiler can validate that the generated code uses the chosen types consistently, but it cannot establish a correspondence between source and target values. A correctness claim about such a correspondence must begin by identifying the values for which conversion is expected to succeed. Some mappings may cover every value of the source type. Others may support only a subset and report an error for values outside it. A mapping from Python’s unbounded integers to C’s fixed-width integers, for example, cannot convert every source value.
To make this concept a little more precise, let σ be a source type in language S and τ a target type in language T , and write ⟦ σ ⟧ and ⟦ τ ⟧ for the sets of values admitted by those types. A value conversion function C S→T takes a value in ⟦ σ ⟧ and either returns ok(w) for some value w in the target language or reports an error. The value conversion function C T→S operates in the opposite direction. If σ is Python’s integer type and τ is C’s int , the value conversion function C Python→C returns the same integer when it fits in a C int and reports an error otherwise. The reverse value conversion function always succeeds because every C int has a corresponding Python integer.
For the values a conversion function supports, conversion soundness is the key requirement: every successful result must be admitted by the target type. In symbols,
v ∈ ⟦ σ ⟧ ∧ C S→T ( v ) = ok ( w ) ⇒ w ∈ ⟦ τ ⟧
The value conversion function in the opposite direction must satisfy the same property. Note that conversion soundness guarantees that a successful conversion produces a valid target value, but it does not guarantee that the value conversion function in the opposite direction recovers the original source value.
We say a mapping is lossless for a set of source values when converting any of those values to the target representation and back recovers the original source value. In our Python-to-C example, conversion is lossless for every Python integer that fits in a C int : converting the integer to C and then back to Python recovers the original value. Python integers outside that range cannot be converted to a C int , so they are not included in the set of values for which lossless conversion is promised.
More generally, this property, called round-trip preservation , is stronger than conversion soundness. Let lossless S ⊆ ⟦ σ ⟧ denote the source values for which lossless conversion is promised. Then
∀ v ∈ lossless S , ∃ w ∈ ⟦ τ ⟧ : C S→T ( v ) = ok ( w ) ∧ C T→S ( w ) = ok ( v )
Thus, every value in lossless S must convert successfully and be recovered by the reverse value conversion function. Round-trip preservation rules out value conversion functions that map different supported source values to the same target value, since the reverse value conversion function could not recover the original source value.
Taken together, the two types, the two value conversion functions, and the set of lossless values form a type mapping , which we write
M = ( σ , τ , C S→T , C T→S , lossless S )
A type mapping is correct when both value conversion functions are sound and the mapping is round-trip preserving on lossless S .
Both properties come into play when a source function is compared with the translated function on the same inputs. To compare a Python function with a C translation, a test harness has to convert every Python integer argument into a C int and convert every result back into Python. If these value conversion functions are sound but not round-trip preserving, an argument or result may change during conversion and introduce a disagreement between the two functions that is not a failure of the translation.
Now that we know what makes a type mapping correct, we need to figure out how to find one. The first step is choosing a target type for each occurrence of a source type, and the earlier char * example showed that this step is harder than it looks: the same C type can represent data used in several different ways, so the declared source type alone may not determine its Rust counterpart. We begin there.
When the declared source type does not determine the target type, how the program uses values of that type can. We call this information program context . To see how context guides the choice of a target type, consider the following C function, adapted from Hong and Ryu’s paper on Tymcrat , an LLM-based tool for translating C programs into Rust. The function increments an integer through a pointer:
A direct translation of the function inc maps the type of the C pointer p to the Rust raw pointer type *mut i32 . Dereferencing a raw pointer requires unsafe Rust, but the way the source C function uses p suggests a more idiomatic Rust type. Because inc reads and updates only a single integer at the address supplied by the caller, the type of p can be expressed in Rust as &mut i32 , a mutable reference to an integer:
The Rust compiler accepts this signature together with the translated body, but rejects one that declares p as an immutable reference, since the body writes through it.
Hong and Ryu built Tymcrat around the observation that choosing an idiomatic Rust signature can depend on how the source function uses its parameters. Before generating the body translation, Tymcrat uses the source function body to generate candidate Rust signatures and discards signatures containing type errors. It then generates a Rust function for each remaining signature, uses compiler feedback to reduce type errors, and selects a translation. This process happens in dependency order, so that the signature selected for each callee can be included in the prompt when generating callers.
Tymcrat reduced the number of type errors by 71.5 percent across 39 GNU programs, but Hong and Ryu emphasize that the absence of type errors does not establish correctness: their manual review found functions with no type errors whose translations did not preserve the original program behavior. These results show how program context can address one part of defining a type mapping: choosing target types that reflect how the source program uses values. The other part, showing that the chosen types make the mapping correct , remains open, since neither conversion soundness nor round-trip preservation follows from successful target compilation alone.
Once a target type has been chosen, the next question is whether source values survive the trip into the target language and back. Two types may look equivalent, and code that uses them may compile, while the target type still fails to distinguish values that the source type keeps apart. When that happens, round-trip preservation is out of reach: two different source values are forced onto the same target value, and the reverse value conversion function cannot tell them apart any longer. The authors of Oxidizer , an LLM-based tool for translating Go programs into Rust, give a concrete example. Consider the following Go structure with a field of type []int :
A plausible Rust translation gives the field Addenda05 the type Vec<i64> :
Both the types []int and Vec<i64> contain sequences of integers, but a Go []int value can be either nil or an empty sequence, while a Rust Vec<i64> value has only one empty representation. These two distinct Go values must therefore be mapped to the same Rust value. The Rust structure is well typed, and functions that use it may compile, but a value conversion function into Vec<i64> cannot be round-trip preserving for both Go values.
To detect this mismatch, Oxidizer introduces a notion of type compatibility . A target type is compatible with a source type when the source values being considered can be converted to the target type and back, with each round trip recovering the original source value. In the terminology of this post, a target type is compatible with a source type when there exists a type mapping between the two types that is lossless for a selected set of source values.
More concretely, Oxidizer instruments the source project and runs the project’s tests to collect input and output values for functions — i.e., the lossless S set of the mapping. Oxidizer then implements the two value conversion functions between Go and Rust through JSON. The value conversion function C Go→Rust serializes a Go value as JSON and deserializes the result into the proposed Rust type, and C Rust→Go serializes the Rust value and deserializes it back into Go. Using slightly abused notation, the recorded value v satisfies round-trip preservation when C Rust→Go ( C Go→Rust ( v )) = v .
In the example above, the nil value of type []int has no distinct counterpart in Vec<i64> : either C Go→Rust fails on it, or it produces the empty vector, which C Rust→Go maps back to an empty, non- nil sequence rather than to nil . Either way, round-trip preservation fails for that value. Because the recorded values come from the project test suite, Oxidizer establishes round-trip preservation only for values observed while running the tests. It does not explicitly define a type mapping or otherwise characterize the values for which the mapping is correct beyond those reached by the tests. To move beyond this limited guarantee, we need a type mapping whose supported values are specified independently of a project’s tests and whose correctness can be established for all of those values.
At Code Metal, we translate between many source and target languages, and we want to avoid writing, and proving, the same value conversion functions once for every pair of languages. A language-independent specification of values, shared by all languages, lets each language connect to the specification once instead of to every other language. Schema-based interface generators provide such a construction: they are commonly built around an interface definition language , or IDL, in which a schema describes structured values, paired with a serialization format that defines how the values described by that schema are represented as bytes. Together, the schema and the format form a language-independent specification of structured values and their valid serialized representations. A generator then produces language-specific data types, serializers, and deserializers that implement this specification.
Our approach, schema-based type mappings , uses the components of schema-based interface generators to construct a type mapping. It starts with a source type and its corresponding schema in the IDL; that is, a description of the structure of the type’s values, such as the fields of a record, the type of each field, and which fields are optional or repeated. From this schema, the generator for each supported language produces a type representing the schema values, together with serializers and deserializers for that type. For a particular source and target language, the generated types provide the two types in a mapping. The source serializer followed by the target deserializer provides the value conversion function in one direction, while the target serializer followed by the source deserializer provides the conversion in the other direction. The values described by the schema determine the source values for which round-trip preservation is promised. One possible gap remains between the generated source type and the type used in the source program, but their equivalence can be validated separately.
Protocol Buffers provide a familiar example of schema-based interface generators. Returning to the earlier EntryDetail example shows the value of this approach: the Go field has type []int , which admits both a nil slice and a non- nil empty slice, while the proposed Rust type Vec<i64> has only one empty-vector value. Converting both Go values to Rust would therefore lose a distinction that the source program can observe, while a correct type mapping must preserve this distinction.
A schema-based approach can preserve this distinction. To see how, consider the following Protocol Buffers schema, which represents the sequence inside an IntList message:
In this schema, addenda05 may be absent or may contain an IntList . When it is present, the values field may be empty or may contain elements. The schema therefore distinguishes the three cases needed to represent a nil Go slice, a non- nil empty slice, and a nonempty slice. For each supported language, a generator uses this schema to produce an EntryDetail type and serializers and deserializers for that type. The generated type must represent all three possibilities for addenda05 . For Rust, a bare Vec<i64> therefore remains insufficient.
To describe this construction for arbitrary schemas and supported languages, let Σ denote a schema. In the example above, Σ is the Protocol Buffers description of EntryDetail and IntList . We write σ Σ and τ Σ to denote the types generated from the schema Σ for the source language S and target language T , respectively. Let W Σ denote the valid byte representations determined by Σ and the serialization format. In the Protocol Buffers example, these are the valid binary representations of messages described by the schema. Finally, we write E Σ S and D Σ S for the serializer and deserializer generated for the source language S , and E Σ T and D Σ T for those generated for the target language T . Conversion from the representation in language S to the representation in language T proceeds as follows:
In the terminology of the first section, this construction yields the type mapping
M Σ S,T = ( σ Σ , τ Σ , D Σ T ∘ E Σ S , D Σ S ∘ E Σ T , lossless Σ S )
where lossless Σ S contains the generated source-language values corresponding to values described by Σ . For the mapping M Σ S,T to be correct, each serializer must produce a valid encoding of the structured value represented by its input, and each deserializer must reconstruct that same structured value from any valid encoding of it. When these requirements are satisfied by the serializers and deserializers generated for S and T , they establish conversion soundness. For every value in lossless Σ S , they also establish round-trip preservation: conversion to another language and back recovers the original value. These guarantees apply to values described by Σ , rather than to arbitrary values of native types.
Schema-based interface generators have also appeared as a solution to a related problem in LLM-based translation systems. CrossCrate , an LLM-based tool for translating Go programs into Rust, uses them to validate translations involving opaque library types. CrossCrate uses an LLM to synthesize a Protocol Buffers schema for source types that may contain opaque library types, as well as adapters connecting the source Go type and translated Rust type to types generated from that schema. It states a universal round-trip property requiring every value of the source Go type to survive conversion to Rust and back, and checks this property on values observed while running tests. CrossCrate demonstrates the practical value of a shared schema when source and target library types cannot be compared directly.
At Code Metal, we embrace schema-based type mappings as a general component of our translation systems. Our system makes each mapping explicit and separate from the code generated by a language model. It consists of a language-independent data description language and a generator for each supported language. These generators produce corresponding types, serializers, and deserializers for C, C++, Rust, Python, TypeScript, CUDA, OpenCL, Octave, and VHDL. The same mapping can therefore be used throughout the translation and validation of a large code base, including whenever source and translated functions are compared on corresponding inputs.
While schema-based interface generators are a major strength of our approach, they also pose a potential risk. For each supported language, one generator produces types, serializers, and deserializers for every supported schema. This means that a defect in a single generator can affect every mapping involving the language. The fact that every such mapping uses code produced by the same generator also lets us address this risk in one place. A single machine-checked proof can establish, once and for all, that for every supported schema the generator produces serializers and deserializers whose conversions are sound and recover every value promised to be lossless after a round trip. Ye and Delaware demonstrate the fundamentals of this approach in A Verified Protocol Buffer Compiler , using Rocq to verify a generator that produces serializers and deserializers for a supported subset of Protocol Buffers.
More broadly, this reflects how we build translation systems at Code Metal. We use language models to generate idiomatic code from program context while carving out core components that can be statically generated and formally verified. Type mappings and conversion code form one such crucial component. Without them, we can check that the translated code compiles, but we cannot compare its behavior with the source program on corresponding inputs. Getting type mappings right is what turns the comparison between a program and its translation into an apples-to-apples comparison: only when values are known to correspond across languages can we conclude that the translation preserves the behavior of the source program.

title: Bru: Send and read SMS from the browser
body:
Short version: Bru is an Android app and web client that lets you read and send SMS messages from your browser, via your phone. It is currently available from the IzzyOnDroid app repository, but hopefully soon on F-Droid, and possibly Google Play.
Since the start of the summer this year I have tinkered with Bru . The b idirectional r emote u plink for your Android phone. Bru is also the Norwegian word for bridge . And yes, the name is of course a backronym. Since I started using a T9 phone as my daily driver, I have more than once wished I could break out into a full qwerty keyboard when typing out long messages or having a longer conversation. Don't get me wrong, I love the tactile buttons, but for me, nothing beats an actual keyboard when writing. Another thing I wanted to solve was that every SMS was a prompt to take my phone out, opening the door for endless distractions. And yes, this could have been solved with notification settings, self discipline and yada yada...
The best code is no code at all. Every new line of code you willingly bring into the world is code that has to be debugged, code that has to be read and understood, code that has to be supported. Every time you write new code, you should do so reluctantly, under duress, because you completely exhausted all your other options.
While my first instinct was "oooh I can build thing", I recognized that this might be a problem others have had and solved before me. I did some searching, and tested some alternatives. It is quite possible I have left out several good candidates, but these are the ones I looked at.
The default SMS app from Google actually has a "Device pairing" option. Sign in to https://messages.google.com/web and pair your phone, and it works pretty well. But for one, it is limited to the Google app, and I have ( very ) gradually tried to limit my reliance on big G. With that said, my only real gripe is that you have to re-pair very frequently. Often enough that during my limited testing I was quite annoyed. But if you are using Google Messages anyway, this might be the right solution for you.
Sigh. I really wanted this to be the solution. The ambitions are great. KDE is great! Open source! It even has a MacBook client, being a Linux-adjacent project. But I could not get it to work reliably. The pairing process was buggy. Sometimes connectivity would break, even with the phone and laptop on the same network. I found the options for configuration overwhelming, and in good Linux-fashion, there is ample room for some UX improvements. But the biggest problem was that I found the whole experience ... clunky? For all I know the Linux client is leaps and bounds better than the Mac one, though. Maybe this is the right solution for you?
Pushbullet has been around for a long time. And to be fair, I didn't really give them a fair chance. I tried it years ago, and found it aggravatingly unreliable and buggy. Dropped notifications, SMSes reported as "sent" never ended up actually sent, messages I had already answered suddenly triggering notifications again. Things may have improved, I didn't bother to check. I am listing it here for completeness' sake.
Okay, so I might have really wanted to build this thing just for the sake of it, regardless of the alternatives.
I decided on some goals for the project:
I started out with the obvious problem: how can I get the phone and the browser to talk to each other? Being familiar with WireGuard, I first thought about baking that into an app on the phone that could serve a REST(ish) endpoint that a client on the same network could access. As an easy way to start prototyping I installed Tailscale on my phone and on my laptop, as Tailscale is WireGuard under the hood, and gives you a stable IP address for the devices on the network. The architecture at that point was polling based, the web client would poll the server running on the phone periodically and look for new messages. While I had a nagging feeling that this might not be optimal for many reasons (battery life on the phone for one) I just wanted something that worked to iterate on.
After some evenings of hitting my head against the wall that is Android development I had a rudimentary app working, running in the background on the phone and serving the available SMS threads, secured with a hard-coded token just in case. With that in place I could start working on a client.
As stated, I wanted to build this as a statically hosted web app, and without any web framework. I wanted to get a feel for how it is to develop like this in 2026. Having relied almost solely on React professionally, and SvelteKit in my spare time, I wanted to do something different. I first imagined the client as a typewriter with the paper sticking out of the top sort of thing, but ended up turning the skeuomorphism down a few notches. I kept the monospaced Courier font and off-white though.
The client is built as index.html files in a folder hierarchy, an increasingly unmaintainable style.css and typed JavaScript with ESM modules and custom elements for the reused components like header and footer. This does mean the components are rendered client side instead of being baked into prerendered static pages which I would have preferred. There are no architectures without tradeoffs, and the alternative would have been to copy-paste the shared code across several pages and remembering to keep them in sync. Not horroble, but not great either.
While the prototype worked, there were some things I needed to figure out. For my own personal use, depending on Tailscale as an additional app was not a problem, but it would greatly reduce the number of other people that would bother to install it. And while solving problems for myself is enough by itself, creating something that others might find useful as well is very rewarding. Embedding the WireGuard tunnel library seemed like a logical step, but before I started on that, I found Iroh.
Sometimes the stars align. A post announcing Iroh 1.0.0 came up in one of my feeds, and I knew this could be the right fit. In essence, Iroh is a dumb pipe. You put stuff in at one end, it comes out the other. "Dial keys, not IPs" is the mantra. And being built with Rust, it works in the browser when compiled to WebAssembly. And with the Android SDK available, it was exactly what I needed.
Iroh works by establishing a direct peer-to-peer connection between your devices. It does this with the help of relays, servers that both devices can reach. When a device starts up, it connects to a relay. When one device wants to talk to another, they first swap addresses through the relay. Then both start firing packets at each other at the same time. Each router sees the incoming traffic as a reply to something it sent out itself, and lets it through. This is called hole punching, and works in most network topologies. When it doesn't, say on a locked-down corporate network, the traffic is forwarded via the relay.
Browsers aren't allowed to send raw UDP packets, so hole punching isn't possible there, and the Bru web client always goes through a relay. The connection is still end-to-end encrypted, so the relay can't read your messages. A desktop application, or a terminal based one, would be able to do actual peer-to-peer communication.
The juicy center of the client, the Iroh-related code, is written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly with wasm-pack . The module exposes a single Bru struct that the JavaScript code can use. It has methods for opening a connection, sending and receiving data, health checks and so on. Having wasm-pack generate the bindings and glue code makes using WebAssembly as easy as any other JS module.
Since the Iroh relay is open source and can be run on whatever server you want, and the client is simple static files, the whole stack can be self-hosted if one is so inclined. There is a settings menu in both the client and the Android app to configure the relay in use.
The "protocol" is also open, and there is no reason why a user could not build their own client. I am hoping someone will. Maybe a CLI, desktop app, AI agent integration (or maybe that is not a good idea?) or maybe something completely different. If I get the drive to do it, I might extract the relevant code into a self-contained library others can use.

title: Number of drones downed on approach to Moscow since start of day reaches 96
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. The Russian Defense Ministry’s air defenses have shot down another 21 UAVs heading to Moscow, Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said on his Max channel.
"An attack by 21 more UAVs has been repelled by the Defense Ministry’s air defenses. Emergency services are working at the scene of the fall of debris," he wrote.
This brings the number of UAVs downed by air defense systems while approaching Moscow since the start of the day to 96, according to TASS calculations.

title: Sen. Jon Ossoff: ‘I’m not running for president’
body: Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff said Tuesday he will not run for president in 2028 and committed to serving a full six-year Senate term if reelected. “I have zero interest in running for president. I’m not running for president. I’m running for reelection to the Senate,” Ossoff said during a Georgia Senate debate against Republican Rep. Mike Collins. Asked by Greg Bluestein of The Atlanta Journal-Constitution whether he would serve his full term if he wins in November, Ossoff replied: “Yes, I will.” The remarks are Ossoff’s most forceful rejection yet of a potential 2028 presidential bid even as his name has repeatedly surfaced in national Democrats’ conversations about possible contenders for the party’s nomination. His public commitment to a full Senate term on Tuesday is the latest of his campaign’s many efforts to tamp down that speculation. Ossoff gained national attention this year given his strong fundraising numbers , his consistent lead in public polling against Collins and his ability to generate viral moments on the campaign trail, particularly through his attacks on President Donald Trump. Democrats are bullish about Ossoff’s ability to hold onto his Senate seat — so much so that the Democratic-aligned Senate Majority PAC said Tuesday it was removing its ad spending in Georgia for the week. He’s also taken steps to boost the state Democratic party in Georgia, a perennial battleground that has been and will be key to winning the presidency. If November brings historic wins up and down the ballot, Ossoff will get some of the credit — and he’ll have confirmed his status as a leader in the swing state.

title: Ghana’s Vivies Academy wins six awards in South Africa, earns Croatia 2027 finals slot
body: Vivie’s Dance and Theatre Academy (VDTA) has secured six awards at the Dance Star qualifiers in Johannesburg, South Africa, with dancers from the Ghanaian academy qualifying for the World Dance Championship finals in Croatia. The academy earned honours in contemporary dance, lyrical dance and acrobatics, with dancer and teacher Daniel Appah receiving recognition in the Senior Contemporary Solo category and the competition’s Personality Award. Rita Abankwah and Anna Bashiru placed second in the Senior Contemporary Duo category, while the quartet of Rita Abankwah, Hillary Oppong, Anna Bashiru and Michelle Kassis finished third in the Senior Contemporary Quartet category. Rita Abankwah also placed second in Senior Acrobatics Dance. Michelle Kassis, the youngest member of the delegation, secured third place in Children’s Lyrical Dance, competing against more than 20 dancers. The team’s routines were developed under the direction of Omoyemi Davies, the academy’s Head of Academy and Choreographer. He attributed the achievement to the dedication required to turn ambition into performance. “When you dream, dream big, but make sure it doesn’t end as just a dream. Fight till you see that dream become a reality,” he said. The academy said the results reflected the combined efforts of its choreographer, teachers and dancers, whose training and preparation helped secure recognition on the international stage. Founder and Chief Executive Officer Vivian Boateng said the achievement went beyond the awards, demonstrating the potential of Ghanaian talent and the importance of creating opportunities for young performers. “I have always believed in Ghana’s creative industry and the extraordinary talent we have in this country. Opportunities like this allow us to showcase Ghanaian talent on the world stage and demonstrate that our young people have a place in the global creative ecosystem,” she said. Ms Boateng expressed hope that the team’s success would encourage young Ghanaians interested in the arts to continue developing their abilities. “My hope is that this experience inspires every young person in Ghana with a passion or gift for the arts to keep learning, training and honing their craft. Talent must be nurtured, discipline must be developed, and young people must be given opportunities to discover just how far their gifts can take them,” she said. She added that the experience should help the academy’s students recognise their potential to compete internationally. “For our own students, I want them to understand that the world is not beyond their reach. They belong in the global conversation. They have a place on international stages, and with the right training, commitment and opportunities, they can compete and contribute meaningfully.” VDTA offers training in ballet, contemporary dance, Ghanaian dance, acrobatics, drama and musical theatre, with a focus on developing versatile performers. The academy said participation in international competitions exposes students to different artistic standards while helping them build confidence, resilience, teamwork and the ability to perform under pressure. As the dancers prepare for the finals in Croatia, the academy plans to build on their experience in Johannesburg to strengthen their performances. It also acknowledged the contribution of teachers, parents and the wider VDTA community in supporting the team’s international participation. “This is bigger than winning awards. It is about expanding possibilities for young people and showing what Ghana’s creative industry can offer the world,” Ms Boateng said.

title: CIA was aware of plans of Nord Stream pipelines sabotage, did not oppose it — journalist
body:
HAMBURG, October 14. /TASS/. The Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) was aware of the plan to sabotage the Nord Stream and Nord Stream 2 gas pipelines and had nothing against it, German investigative journalist Oliver Schrom told the NTV television channel.
"According to our sources, the CIA knew [of the sabotage plans] at an early stage. Its officers on the ground initially had no objections to the plan, and they even admitted financial participation," said the journalist who co-authored a book dedicated to the attack on the pipelines with Ulrich Thiele. The Americans’ position changed after Dutch intelligence learned of the plans, he noted.
"However, according to our sources, the CIA men never told the organizers with such great emphasis to drop it," the journalist said, adding that there was no fundamental objection from the CIA "at the working level," though responsibility for an operation of such scale could not have rested with the staff on the ground.
"When the organizers decided to blow up the pipelines, they turned to their American contacts," he said.
The first trial against a suspected perpetrator of the Nord Stream explosions, Ukrainian citizen Sergey K., begins in Hamburg on Wednesday. Sergey K. is suspected of a war crime involving prohibited methods of warfare, including attacks on civilian objects, carrying out an explosion, destruction of structures and disruption of public utilities.
The German Federal Prosecutor General’s Office believes that Sergey K., whom German media have identified as the head of the sabotage group, and his accomplices planned the pipeline blasts on orders from Ukrainian government agencies.
On September 26, 2022, unprecedented damage was recorded on three strings of the Nord Stream pipelines and the never-commissioned Nord Stream 2 pipeline. The Russian Prosecutor General’s Office opened a criminal case over an act of international terrorism.

title: US Army, Navy research labs team up to combat Arctic cold
body: For much of recorded military history, the through line between mission success and failure came down to the basics, including adequate latrine facilities to keep disease vectors at bay. Despite massive technological shifts, that paradigm still holds, which is why the U.S. Army and Navy have teamed up to keep systems operational — even in the extreme cold of the Arctic . As the Department of Defense eyes greater operability in the far north, these low temperatures can wreak havoc on equipment and machinery (and toilets), with ice becoming enemy No. 1. Which is why the Naval Facilities Engineering and Expeditionary Warfare Center, or NAVFAC EXWC, and the Cold Regions Research and Engineering Laboratory, or CRREL, began working with both branches to field a rapidly deployable Triple Container rigid-wall shelter system usable in temperatures as low as -50 degrees Fahrenheit. The already fielded version can operate in temperatures as low as -15 degrees Fahrenheit. The team focused on different configurations of thermal wrappings, insulation and other components to ensure that parts of the kit’s components that are particularly vulnerable to cracking and freezing — hoses, valves, bladders and pumps — were able to withstand the greater threshold for cold, according to a recent Army release. The result, per the release, far exceeded the objectives, with the TRICON-based system staying operational down to -65 degrees Fahrenheit. Testing took place in CRREL’s New Hampshire-based Extreme Cold Chamber, a 288-square-foot cold room capable of reaching temperatures as low as -90 degrees Fahrenheit, per the release. While military units typically have to wait until the Alaskan winter reaches its peak to simulate similar conditions, the controlled environment allowed the research team to create conditions similar to those of the real world. “Our armed forces live and operate in extremely cold and difficult conditions, so having these facilities operational is important for their physical and mental health while serving in the Arctic and other high-north environments,” said Dr. Dan Tague, a research chemist at CRREL, one of seven U.S. Army Engineer Research and Development Center laboratories. In 2024, the DoD released its “ Arctic Strategy ,” citing “Major geopolitical changes are driving the need for this new strategic approach to the Arctic, including Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the accession of Finland and Sweden to the NATO Alliance, increasing collaboration between the People’s Republic of China (PRC) and Russia, and the accelerating impacts of climate change.” The region, according to the report, had become “a venue for strategic competition,” and a space where the United States intends to build a more persistent presence . The latest successes with TRICORN-based systems provide, beyond the obvious comforts for personnel stationed in the Arctic — Toilets! Laundry! Showers! — an expanded operational footprint for the U.S. military as a whole, according to James Pilkington, a project manager in NAVFAC EXWC Expeditionary Technical Department. “This extends the operational range of base camps in terms of geographic locations and durations,” said Pilkington. “In turn [it] extend[s] force posture.”
