In 2024, the DoD released its “ Arctic Strategy ,” citing “Major geopolitical changes are driving the need for this new strategic approach to the Arctic, including Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the accession of Finland and Sweden to the NATO Alliance, increasing collaboration between the People’s Republic of China (PRC) and Russia, and the accelerating impacts of climate change.” The region, according to the report, had become “a venue for strategic competition,” and a space where the United States intends to build a more persistent presence . The latest successes with TRICORN-based systems provide, beyond the obvious comforts for personnel stationed in the Arctic — Toilets! Laundry! Showers! — an expanded operational footprint for the U.S. military as a whole, according to James Pilkington, a project manager in NAVFAC EXWC Expeditionary Technical Department. “This extends the operational range of base camps in terms of geographic locations and durations,” said Pilkington. “In turn [it] extend[s] force posture.”

title: 50 DAF Battle Network Programs Rolled into Single, $4.5B ‘Megatron’ Contract Vehicle
body: The Department of the Air Force is consolidating more than 50 programs supporting its efforts to create a vast battle network into a single $4.5 billion contract vehicle to streamline software and technology integration. The contract, dubbed “ Megatron ” in reference to the lead villain in the Transformers toy and movie franchise, is a multiple award, indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity vehicle to get technology now and in the future into the DAF Battle Network. Brig. Gen. Joshua Williams, the department’s new portfolio acquisition executive for command, control, communications, and battle management, highlighted the Megatron program at AFA’s Air, Space, & Cyber conference in September. “The DAF Battle Network depends on an industrial base that can innovate, integrate, and deliver at the speed of relevance, and we need to build business mechanisms to enable their ability to do that,” Williams told reporters at the conference. The contract vehicle will cover software delivery, commercial solutions to Battle Network challenges, and other tech needs, Williams said. The draft notice for Megatron was posted in August, with a final request for proposals expected to be released this quarter. Multiple contract awards are planned for fiscal 2027 under the new “master plan,” Megatron Contracting Officer Julianne Payne told Air & Space Forces Magazine, “which span from sensor integration and connectivity to applications and secure data processing.” “Key efforts include maturing our digital architecture, fielding secure processing at the edge, and delivering applications that put the operator at the center,” Payne added. Brig. Gen. Joshua Williams, Department of the Air Force Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Command, Control, Communications and Battle Management, moderates a panel about Next Generation Battle Management on Sept. 15, 2026, at the Air and Space Forces Association’s Air, Space & Cyber conference. Air Force photo by Senior Airman Malia Heemsoth Merging Efforts Past contract vehicles often created multiyear contracts tied to fixed requirements and hardware delivery. That doesn’t work in a world of rapid software updates, new sensors, and modes of communication needed for the DAF Battle Network. “When a specific mission need arises, we can quickly compete delivery or task orders within this pool, compressing our acquisition timeline from over a year to a matter of months to get critical capabilities to the field faster,” Payne said. “For years, our sensors, command and control nodes, and warfighters have operated in stovepipes, making it difficult to share information quickly.” The C3BM office’s decision to take this new contract approach isn’t happening in a vacuum. Payne noted that adversaries such as China are already building highly sophisticated capabilities to disrupt U.S. military networks. The larger effort to connect all operational capabilities via the battle network and ultimately to the larger Combined Joint All Domain Command and Control network must happen faster. Soliciting, buying, and implementing standalone platforms for a single aircraft or satellite, common practice for decades, won’t cut it. “If our systems do not integrate, they do not fight. That realization is what led to the creation of C3BM in 2022 to bring all those fragmented authorities under one roof,” Payne said. “Ultimately, that’s what drove us to the DAF Battle Network concept, and Megatron is the vehicle that is going to deliver it.” Megatron combines two current IDIQ contracts: the Advanced Battle Management System IDIQ and the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center’s architecture and integration directorate’s XA IDIQ. The ABMS contract launched in 2020 and was planned for an initial five-year run, allowing the Air Force to award multiple contracts for ABMS work across the force. The Air Force used the ABMS IDIQ to conduct live operational demos for real-time hardware and software testing in field conditions. Contractors participating ranged from small software companies to large defense primes. The XA IDIQ was a planned 10-year effort from 2022-2032 to bring together early-stage concepts for the network’s architecture and integration. But even with two large IDIQs, the Air Force had a problem. A company might bring a great concept to AFLCMC via the XA IDIQ but not have a contract under the ABMS IDIQ, creating a bottleneck between capability growth and deployment. A New Approach PAE C3BM intends to use the new Megatron contract to find the “best-of-breed” option across six lines of effort for the Battle Network: Digital Architecture & Standards Sensor Integration Secure Data Processing (including Cloud, AI, and Machine Learning) Network Connectivity (Line-of-Sight, Beyond-Line-of-Sight, and anti-jamming) Software Applications Synthetic Environments (computer-simulated training and development) Col. Freddie Robinson, the Joint Air Component Coordination Element team director for the 186th Air Operations Group, facilitates communication with the Combined Joint Task Force and 1st Lt. Kaitlin Volk, an air battle manager, during Project Convergence Capstone 5 at the National Training Center, Fort Irwin, California. (Air Force Photo by Morgan Brown) Staying Relevant With rapid upgrades across the tech industry, the Megatron contract, and larger C3BM efforts, the goal is to bring the best tech into the system while keeping it secure and standardized across the network. The PAE’s secure processing strategy works across multiple security classification levels, Payne said. “This capability applies to form factors ranging from enterprise data centers to tactical edge hardware,” Payne said. “The contract mandates that vendors deliver compatible, mission-tailorable solutions, utilizing bare metal, virtualization, or cloud-based services.” Across the Department of Defense, information technology managers and decision-makers face the burden of maintaining legacy technology and software while merging old but sometimes linchpin systems with new software and hardware. With Megatron, officials seek to prevent “technical debt,” or the continued use of legacy systems that can’t be upgraded, and avoid future “vendor lock,” which allows a single vendor to control vital software or hardware because of proprietary constraints. “If a contractor’s solution becomes obsolete or creates technical debt, we can recompete future delivery orders or task orders among the other qualified vendors in our pool. This continuous competition at the order level incentivizes contractors to deliver open, modern, and cost-effective solutions,” Payne said. The post 50 DAF Battle Network Programs Rolled into Single, $4.5B ‘Megatron’ Contract Vehicle appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

title: ‘This little bit of perfection’: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk on seeing Earth from space
body:
Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk says his first two weeks aboard the International Space Station have been unforgettable as he adjusts to life in microgravity and begins research into the effects of long-term space travel on the human body.
“It’s one of the most amazing things I’ve ever seen,” Kutryk said of looking back at Earth from the station.
Growing up in northern Alberta, Kutryk was familiar with the northern lights, but he said seeing them from above offered an entirely different perspective.
“To see the whole Earth, the curvature of the Earth, just embraced by this blanket of dancing fluorescent oranges and yellows and pinks — magical,” he said.
Kutryk, 44, launched Oct. 1 as part of NASA’s four-person Crew 13, arriving at the space station in just under eight hours.
The former CF-18 fighter pilot is serving as a mission specialist during the six-month mission, which will include scientific experiments, research and critical maintenance work.
“It is important for Canada to be here,” Kutryk said Tuesday while answering questions from Canadian journalists in Longueuil, Que.
“We take a lot of benefits from these missions and it’s something that we hope we can continue.”
Kutryk said the launch itself was exhilarating and spectacular, adding that no amount of training could fully prepare him for the experience.
“Everything about being here for the first couple weeks is very special,” he said.
“You just feel so lucky and fortunate to be living this experience.”
But living in space also requires an adjustment. Kutryk said even routine tasks such as eating, sleeping and moving around can take practice in microgravity.
“You have to sort of learn to do everything again, almost like you’re a child,” he said. “How you eat, how you move around, how you sleep, how you fall asleep, what do you do with your neck when you’re sleeping, what do you do with your hands.”
Kutryk has already begun experiments, several of which are related to the physical challenges astronauts experience during extended periods in space. He said he has lost five pounds since arriving at the station.
“Humans on a six-month mission lose a lot of bone, a lot of muscle and come back to Earth, frankly, a lot older physiologically and not very healthy,” Kutryk said. “So it’s a big concern of ours.”
The mission includes Canadian-led studies examining how space travel and microgravity affect human health. During Tuesday’s orbital press conference, Kutryk was wearing equipment for the AstroFit research project, which monitors his health and is aimed at finding ways to allow humans to spend longer periods in space.
The space station is a long way from the Alberta cattle farm where Kutryk grew up, but a small piece of his family’s history is there with him.
A pocket watch his relatives brought with them when they immigrated to Canada from Ukraine four generations ago had been sent to the station ahead of him.
Kutryk said the watch sits near where he sleeps. Holding it makes him think about how much technology has changed over the past century and how his ancestors could never have imagined the journey he is now taking.
His own journey to space was a lifelong goal, and Kutryk said it was difficult to describe the first time he saw Earth from orbit.
“It’s just one world. It’s one thing hanging in the blackness of space and you don’t see all the countries and the problems and all the challenges,” he said.
“You just see this little bit of perfection that we should really, really be trying to protect.”
Kutryk’s mission comes in the same year Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen travelled aboard the Artemis II mission in April. The 10-day lunar fly-around marked humanity’s first journey to the moon in more than 50 years.
Kutryk said Canada’s presence aboard the space station demonstrates what the country can accomplish when it pursues ambitious goals and takes risks, while encouraging Canadian industry, academia and commercial interests to take part in space exploration.
“That’s how we innovate, that’s how we develop new technologies, that’s what we want to be doing,” he said.

title: Pope Leo had lobe of lung removed as doctors found cancer, Vatican says
body: Pope Leo was diagnosed with lung cancer after surgeons removed a part of his right lung on Tuesday, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin, marking a significant health setback for the 71-year-old pontiff.The pope has adenocarcinoma, a common form of lung cancer, with tissue tests conducted during the operation confirming what doctors had suspected from preparatory examinations, the bulletin said.Leo was admitted to Rome's Gemelli hospital on Tuesday for surgery to remove the growth that doctors had discovered in a recent health checkup.The Vatican said earlier on Tuesday evening that the operation had been successful, then provided a more detailed update from the pope's lead surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, and his personal physician, Dr. Luigi Carbone."In order to make the procedure curative, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique," the medical update said, making clear that the aim was to eliminate all cancerous tissue.Human lungs have five lobes - three in the right lung and two in the left.Medical experts said that in order to assess the pope's case, they would need to know the size of the tumor removed from him and whether the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes, information the Vatican did not immediately provide."While we have the diagnosis, we do not yet have the stage. This is critical to prognosis and treatment," said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown University in Washington and division chief of hematology-oncology at MedStar Georgetown University Hospital."If this is a small lung cancer with no lymph nodes involved, surgery itself is likely to be curative," he told Reuters. "But if final analysis reveals a greater extent of cancer involvement, this indicates a poorer prognosis."Resting in his hospital roomTuesday's surgery lasted about 90 minutes and was successful with no complications, the Vatican said. The pope has woken up normally and is resting in his hospital room.Leo left the Vatican shortly before 1 p.m. (1100 GMT) in Rome, ahead of the surgery, and was seen waving from the back of a black SUV as his convoy drove about 9 km (5.6 miles) north of the Vatican to the Gemelli.Upon arriving at the hospital, Leo shook hands with several officials, walked in front of a waiting crowd of well-wishers, some of whom shouted 'Auguri' (best wishes), and entered through the main entrance.The Vatican said earlier this week that the pope was expected to recover in hospital for about a week. All his public events have been canceled until October 20.Leo, elected by the world's cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to smoke or have had recent health issues.The late Pope Francis, Leo's predecessor, was hospitalized several times as he grew frail in his later years. He died aged 88 in April 2025.Leo, who spoke in a firm, clear voice at his only public event on Monday, keeps a very busy schedule. He is due to make an 11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17, but it was unclear whether he would still go ahead.Vatican operations continue without pope's approval during illnessThe pope is the ultimate earthly authority for the world's 1.4 billion Catholics and has no deputy who steps in when he is sick.When a pope is incapacitated, the business of the Vatican's vast bureaucracy carries on as usual, holding off on any decisions that require papal approval.Leo, born in Chicago in 1955 as Robert Prevost, served for decades as a missionary and bishop in Peru before becoming pope. In 1985, when he was a young priest, he came down with typhoid fever in Chulucanas, Peru, and was hospitalized.He recounted the experience in his only major interview given as pope, in a book for Penguin Peru.Leo said the pain was so bad that he asked God to die rather than continue suffering. He took his survival as a sign from God that "We need you here (on Earth)," he said."I never looked back," said Leo.

title: Tajikistan’s Shohin Airlines Unveils First Plane
body: Shohin Airlines, a new private airline in Tajikistan that says it has regional ambitions, recently unveiled the first fixed-wing aircraft in its fleet and also signed an agreement under which its staff will study at the Turkish Airlines Flight Academy in Turkey. The memorandum of understanding with Turkish Airlines provides for academy training for flight and ground personnel from Shohin Airlines, the Tajik airline said this week. Shohin Airlines described the agreement as an important step in the professional development of its employees. Earlier this month, Shohin Airlines unveiled an L 410 NG turboprop aircraft as part of a plan to develop regional passenger service, including in the mountainous terrain that covers much of Tajikistan. The L 410 NG is the latest model of the L 410 aircraft family developed by Czech firm Aircraft Industries. Representatives of Tajikistan’s Civil Aviation Agency attended the unveiling. The agency said the L 410 NG can operate on relatively short runways, which it described as a “crucial capability for local airports in the mountainous regions of Tajikistan.” Shohin Airlines, which was established last year, has flown the new aircraft from Dushanbe, the capital, to Khorog, capital of the Gorno-Badakhshan Autonomous Region in southeastern Tajikistan. Previously, the airline’s operations had consisted of helicopter flights. Shohin Airlines has said it will acquire four planes from the Airbus A320neo line of aircraft, reflecting plans for a significant expansion into commercial passenger traffic. However, delivery plans for the Airbus aircraft have yet to be announced. The airline’s plans to grow coincide with an effort by the Tajik government to expand the country’s role in regional and international aviation. As part of that project, the government introduced an “Open Skies” policy last year that lifted many market restrictions in an effort to generate competition and improve service.

title: Iran shifting tactics to step up attacks on shipping before US vote, officials say
body: Iran is deploying new tactics to target ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz as it seeks to keep oil prices high and influence the US midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters. Tehran has tried to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz since the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran on February 28 . It has restricted passage through the waterway, which carried about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade before the war, in an effort to gain leverage over Washington. Its threats and attacks have severely curtailed traffic through the strait, driving up oil prices, though some oil has continued to transit. Must Read Iran says US response to its proposal to reopen Hormuz ‘insufficient’ The two officials declined to provide details of the new strategy, but one said that Iran had started using different offensive tactics against vessels it considered in violation of its restrictions about 10 days ago, adding that this had led to an increase in attacks on such ships. The strategy included a change in the type as well as the pace of attacks, with one goal being to influence the outcome of the US vote, they said. “The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices,” one of the two officials said. The decision to adopt the new strategy had been taken at the highest levels of Iran’s leadership and was fully coordinated across the country’s ruling system, the officials said. Iran using spotters A US military official, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed that Iran had changed tactics in one significant way: after the US destroyed much of Iran’s radar capabilities, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had started using unarmed spotters in small boats to identify potential targets, including US naval vessels, the official said. Last week, in a previously unreported incident, the US military determined that Iranian spotters were operating from a dhow, calling in targets to the IRGC, the official said. US forces confronted the vessel, told its occupants to abandon ship and then destroyed it. There were no casualties, the US official said. Unwilling to risk its remaining fast boats, Iran had been unable to prevent a ramp-up in oil exports through the strait, the official said, particularly after US strikes devastated its navy. The war — and its $3 billion monthly price tag — has become a key issue on the US campaign trail for November’s midterm elections, which will decide control of Congress. US President Donald Trump has been weighing next steps against Iran, but has said he will not attack again before the vote . The US has meanwhile been pressing its own naval blockade of Iranian ports and extending sanctions as it tries to pile economic pressure on Tehran to reach a deal to end the conflict. The standoff over Hormuz has left global energy markets exposed to further disruption, with the threat of attacks and high shipping and insurance costs complicating efforts to restore normal traffic. Must Read The Middle East crisis: From the Strait of Hormuz to your dining table In recent days, attacks on commercial ships still sailing through the strait have surged to their highest level since the war began, according to independent data. There have been at least five incidents in the past 48 hours involving tankers and other commercial ships around the Hormuz area, including drone strikes, according to data analysis from maritime security sources and incidents reported to British navy-affiliated agency United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO). That approximately mirrored the rate of attacks on October 3-5, pointing to a new escalation, according to data from the UN shipping agency, the International Maritime Organization. “There is a tempo increase in strikes, which looks deliberate,” one maritime security source said. Attacks over an expanded area As part of the new strategy, Tehran will also expand the geographical scope of its operations beyond the Strait of Hormuz to the Gulf of Oman and waters further afield, the officials said. Analysis by maritime security sources based on attacks reported to UKMTO and maritime security companies in the region suggest this may already be happening. They show Iran targeting ships in areas beyond the Strait of Hormuz, including waters off the coast of Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, in recent days. The second Iranian official added that Tehran would not allow Trump to bring down oil prices before the November elections. “Just when they think they are getting close to the point where prices will fall, we will push them away from it. This is a game of chess,” the second official said. “Such vessels would be safe nowhere, even outside the Strait of Hormuz.” The Pentagon and Iran’s Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Complete closure of Hormuz soon, says Iranian official Both Iranian officials said Tehran is moving toward a situation in which no vessel violating its restrictions would be able to pass through the strait. “It will be complete closure soon,” one of the officials said. In its latest report on Sunday, the US Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) said the threat to merchant shipping in the Strait of Hormuz remained “severe”, the second-highest level. “IRGC attacks, attempted attacks, and/or harassment activity persisted including UAV overflight, targeted surveillance of merchant shipping, and occasional VHF hailing,” JMIC said. – Rappler.com Must Read Gasoline prices up again, diesel prices down on October 13

title: Pletenchuk: Russian naval drones pose threat to Black Sea countries
body:
Dmytro Pletenchuk, spokesperson for the Ukrainian Navy, made the remarks during a televised broadcast, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
"In terms of the physical domain, yes, both aerial drones and naval drones could be involved. We have encountered the naval drones that we consider a genuine threat in our waters and have dealt with them accordingly by destroying them. One hundred percent of the naval drones used against Ukraine this year have been destroyed," he said.
Pletenchuk also commented on potential hybrid threats to Bulgaria, Romania, and other countries bordering the Black Sea. He said the readiness of other states to respond to such developments must be assessed in light of their respective areas of responsibility.
"The hybrid aspect lies solely in the information campaigns accompanying these operations, when they genuinely try to spin events in some way to their own advantage," the spokesperson explained.
He noted that he had not seen Russia publicly commenting on these attacks in general. However, while Russia's name was not mentioned in connection with an earlier incident, this time the Russian ambassador to a third country had been brought into the discussion.
According to Pletenchuk, the emergence of specific details in the information space indicates that it is becoming clearer who benefits from such actions and who may be carrying them out in the Black Sea.
"In fact, even open sources show that various aircraft are operating over the sea constantly, primarily those belonging to NATO member states," he said.
He explained that activity is difficult to conceal in a relatively small maritime area, but the use of small unmanned vehicles creates additional risks.
Meanwhile, Russia continues to attack civilian vessels in international waters. Similar incidents have not been recorded in the territorial waters of NATO member states, he said.
Pletenchuk recalled that most of Ukraine's grain corridor passed through the territorial waters of Romania, Bulgaria, and Turkey before reaching the Bosphorus Strait. Security along this route remains at a high level, and Russia is excluded from operating in these waters, he said.
At the same time, Russia continues to terrorize civilian shipping in international waters, according to the spokesperson. Such actions demonstrate, in his assessment, that Moscow is not committed to ensuring safe navigation in the Black Sea and raise concerns about the possibility of similar attacks in other maritime regions.
As Ukrinform reported, on October 5, Romanian broadcaster Digi24 reported an incident involving a vessel carrying grain from Ukraine to Italy near Romania's coast in the Black Sea. Two crew members reportedly died, while another 11 were rescued.
On October 6, Bulgarian broadcaster Nova reported that drones had attacked two merchant vessels in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea.
According to Novinite, Bulgarian Prime Minister said two merchant ships had been hit by drones in separate incidents near Bulgaria. One sank east of the village of Krapets, while the other survived an attack east of the town of Byala.
Zhelyazkov also announced plans to hold talks with Russian Ambassador to Bulgaria Eleonora Mitrofanova and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.

title: Space Force Activates Component Under Special Operations Command
body: The Space Force has officially established its component to U.S. Special Operations Command, creating a ninth component charged with presenting space expertise to commanders in the field. The service activated the component Oct. 7, according to a Sept. 29 memo confirmed to be authentic by Air & Space Forces Magazine, and it plans to hold a formal ceremony in the coming weeks. The Space Force has had a special forces element operating at SOCOM headquarters at MacDill Air Force Base, Fla., but not a formal component field command. The announcement comes more than 18 months after U.S. Special Operations Command revealed plans to create a space component. Congress pressed pause on that process in the fiscal 2026 National Defense Authorization Act, blocking funding for the move until the Space Force provided more details on its plans . A Space Force spokesperson did not immediately respond to questions about who would lead the component or provide details on its organizational structure. Axios first reported on the activation. Space capabilities and forces have played a critical role in recent operations, according to senior defense officials. Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine identified space forces as a “first mover” during the early days of Operation Epic Fury. And in a speech last month at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference, Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess highlighted electronic warfare operations performed by Guardians deployed with the Space Force’s 42nd Electronic Warfare Detachment, which supports U.S. Central Command and Space Forces Central. Standing up components under every unified combatant command has been a focus of the Space Force since its establishment in 2019. Along with Space Forces Special Operations, or SPACEFOR-SOC, the service has component field commands within U.S. Northern Command, Southern Command, Pacific Command, Space Command, and Central Command. It also has a combined component for European Command and Africa Command, and sub-unified components in Japan and Korea. As the Space Force looks to more than double its number of uniformed Guardians over the next five years—increasing its ranks from about 11,000 to 25,000 by fiscal 2031—officials have said the size of its component organizations must increase to meet operational demand. “As we walked forward and stood up U.S. Space Force components—now with almost every combatant command around the planet—each one of those was sized to get off the ground and start doing the integrated work that we’ve seen,” Lt. Gen. Dennis Bythewood, commander of U.S. Space Forces-Space, the service’s SPACECOM component, told reporters in March. “But we already see that in stressing times, we’re having to surge people forward.” To support future surge needs, Bythewood said at the time, components must grow to make sure that Guardian deployments don’t disrupt regular operations. He noted that his component has growth plans “already laid in” over the next few years. The post Space Force Activates Component Under Special Operations Command appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

title: ‘Catastrophic’ brake failure led to Columbia Icefield rollover that killed 3 people
body:
A fatality inquiry report into a deadly tour bus rollover in Jasper National Park says it was the result of a “catastrophic” brake failure and neglected repairs.
The Ice Explorer bus lost control on a road leading to the Athabasca Glacier at the Columbia Icefield in July 2020, tumbling about 50 metres down an embankment before coming to rest on its roof.
Three people died and 14 others were seriously injured.
“In short the brakes suffered a catastrophic failure because they were worn, improperly inspected and concerns with respect to the brakes functioning were not attended to,” Justice Vaughn Myers wrote in his 13-page report.
The inquiry held a year ago, heard the driver of the bus complained the vehicle, which had air brakes, was not stopping quickly enough.
The report from the Alberta Court of Justice judge said the bus was in neutral when it stopped at the top of the hill and then reached speeds of nearly 50 kilometres an hour when it raced down.
The top speed for the Ice Explorer in 4th gear is limited to 14 kilometres an hour.
“There are two primary contributing factors. The first is the driver, for reasons unknown, negotiating the lateral moraine in neutral and without the six-wheel drive engaged,” he wrote.
“Unable to use engine power to slow the bus, the driver would have to rely on conventional braking. We know that the driver attempted to brake as a result of the sounds of the airbrakes. We can safely assume she applied the brakes because she said she did and it would be the natural human reaction to do so.”
Myers also noted that there is no requirement on the bus to have seatbelts and those who died were thrown out of the vehicles as it rolled down the embankment.
A fatality inquiry cannot assign blame but makes recommendations to prevent similar deaths.
Dionne Durocher, 24, of North Battleford, Sask., as well as Kamleshbai Patel, 58, and Griva Patel, 28, of Edmonton, died in the crash.
Myers made a number of recommendations, including that future inspection reports should be dated, as well as identify and detail what work was done during the inspections.
His report listed other contributing factors in the deaths due to the lack of seatbelts and the slope of the hill, which at 40 per cent is above the maximum grade specifications of 36 per cent set out by the manufacturer.
Brewster, also known as Pursuit, conducted its own internal investigation of the crash. The company added seatbelts to its buses and made changes to training for its drivers.

title: US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle resigns amid bribery, corruption allegations - report
body: US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned on Tuesday following a request from the White House amid allegations of bribery, corruption, and other misconduct, ABC News reported.The White House "has received Ms. Guilfoyle's formal resignation," an official confirmed later Tuesday, according to the report.Newly appointed White House press secretary Katie Zacharia announced the administration's decision during her first press briefing on Tuesday morning."We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign," Zacharia said. "She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well."Guilfoyle subsequently acknowledged her departure in a post on X/Twitter, while reaffirming her loyalty to US President Donald Trump.Guilfoyle issued a vague X/Twitter post amid her resignation as ambassador"While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end," she wrote.Serving as the United States Ambassador to Greece has been the honor of a lifetime. I will forever be grateful to President Donald J. Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio for entrusting me with the extraordinary privilege of representing the greatest country in the history of the world. From my first day as Ambassador, I have worked tirelessly to advance President Trump's America First agenda, strengthen our strategic alliance with Greece, and deliver meaningful victories for the American people. During my tenure, we have helped secure historic agreements to expand American liquefied natural gas exports to Europe, advanced the Vertical Corridor to reduce Europe's dependence on Russian energy, strengthened our defense and security partnership with a critical NATO ally, and expanded opportunities for American businesses and investment throughout the region. I am especially proud of the role our Embassy has played in strengthening American energy dominance, advancing economic cooperation, and ensuring that the United States remains the indispensable leader in Southeast Europe. These accomplishments are a testament to President Trump's bold leadership, Secretary Rubio's commitment to American diplomacy, and the extraordinary men and women who serve our country every day. I also want to address the recent allegations against me. These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity. I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional. I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service. My gratitude and respect for President Trump and Secretary Rubio remain unwavering. I am proud of what we accomplished together, and I will always be a loyal supporter of President Trump and his mission to Make America Great Again. While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end. It has been the honor of my lifetime to serve the United States of America. My deepest heartfelt appreciation to the people of Greece for their hospitality, partnership, and welcoming me with open arms. God bless President Trump, God bless our incredible diplomats and service members, and God bless the United States of America.— Kimberly Guilfoyle (@kimguilfoyle) October 13, 2026"It has been the honor of my lifetime to serve the United States of America," Guilfoyle added.She strongly denied the allegations against her, describing them as "false" and pledging to "vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity...I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service."Guilfoyle also expressed her "deepest heartfelt appreciation to the people of Greece for their hospitality, partnership, and welcoming me with open arms," during her tenure as ambassador.Guilfoyle accused of offering access to Trump administration in exchange for cashGuilfoyle has faced mounting scrutiny in recent days after reports alleged she offered Trump donor Eric Deters access to senior administration officials in exchange for financial assistance.According to reports, Guilfoyle asked Deters to pay a $100,000 credit card bill in July 2025, just days before her Senate confirmation hearing, allegedly in exchange for helping him gain access to senior Trump administration officials.Additional allegations include using her diplomatic position to promote private business interests, facilitating lobbying access for a Greek energy company, accepting lavish gifts, and fostering a hostile work environment.Her conduct was also described in reports as "pushing the bounds of what is considered appropriate for a top US representative."Guilfoyle's attorneys have rejected the allegations, maintaining that the money sought from Deters was payment for services, public appearances, and speaking engagements that predated her nomination as ambassador.Addressing separate allegations involving travel aboard private aircraft, her lawyers said Guilfoyle “sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the Department's travel regulations” before every trip.“Ambassador Guilfoyle has served, and will continue to serve, with integrity, honor and distinction. We are evaluating all available legal remedies to collect this debt and any other potential causes of action,” her lawyers said.Trump, Rubio reportedly angered by misconduct allegationsA senior administration official told the Associated Press on Monday that both Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were "extremely pissed off" over the allegations.Rubio was reportedly particularly frustrated because he had recently visited Athens, where Guilfoyle attended all his official events and "greeted him on his arrival with a bear hug as the allegations swirled."Trump also publicly expressed dissatisfaction with the reports on Monday when asked whether he was considering dismissing Guilfoyle.“Well, we're looking at it,” Trump told reporters at the White House. “We're not happy.”The allegations have also drawn the attention of the State Department's inspector general. A US official said the watchdog was examining the claims, although the precise status and scope of any formal investigation remain unclear.A spokesperson for the US Embassy in Athens previously defended Guilfoyle's conduct, saying she had "faithfully followed State Department ethics and gift reporting guidelines."Her resignation comes amid growing calls for scrutiny of her conduct, including demands from congressional Democrats and Greek opposition politicians to investigate the allegations.Guilfoyle has denied wrongdoing, and no criminal charges against her have been reported. The allegations remain subject to scrutiny by US authorities, with questions surrounding her dealings with political donors and private business interests still unresolved.Jonah Davidov contributed to this report.

title: 97% of US soldiers complete brain health assessment
body: Nearly all U.S. soldiers completed a mandatory test meant to track the effects of blast exposure and monitor brain health across the Army, the service said in a release . The test, or Neurocognitive Assessment Tool, is computer-based and records neurological activity, such as attention, concentration, reaction time, memory, processing speed and decision-making. Testing started in 2024 in response to reports about the effects that routine weapons training can have on the brain, including traumatic brain injury. Active-duty, National Guard and Reserve soldiers in high-risk military occupational specialties, including combat engineers and explosive ordnance technicians, as well as troops operating heavy weapons systems, must take the assessment every year, starting soon after they enlist. All other soldiers are required to test every three years. Medical professionals use the data to monitor service members’ cognitive health throughout their military careers, allowing them to spot significant changes, including potential brain injuries. “[The NCAT] is an important part of taking care of soldiers, but what this does is, it sets a baseline for reaction times and for memory,” Jordan Gillis, assistant secretary of the Army for installations, energy and environment, said in a release. “By establishing a baseline for all soldiers, we’re able to monitor brain health, as well as … let medical providers help with treatment, if required.” According to the Sept. 30 release, the Army is expected to publish a directive about the Neurocognitive Assessment Tool and a broader overpressure program, which includes hazard assessment, exposure tracking, risk mitigation, cognitive monitoring, information management, illness and injury reporting and training and education. “The takeaway is we are trying to take care of soldiers and monitor their health,” Gillis said. “And if there is an impact, we’ll be able to treat them.” Reaching the milestone of 97% of soldiers being tested on the NCAT “demonstrates our commitment to cognitive safety, medical readiness and warfighting capability,” Gillis added. The announcement of the milestone came just one month after the Government Accountability Office released the findings of its investigation into the ability of military services to provide the baseline cognitive assessments. Across the services, the Defense Department is hampered by staff shortages and a lack of technology needed to conduct the assessments, the GAO found. The Pentagon announced in April that it will begin a one-year pilot program to test a new cognitive assessment tool, an app that service members can use to complete assessments. DoD officials said the app will be less resource-intensive than current assessments and will help improve the services’ ability to track exposures.

title: Bomb threat grounds second Delta plane from New York to Tel Aviv in one day
body: A Delta Air Lines plane scheduled to depart from New York for Israel was held before takeoff at John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) in New York following a bomb threat. Flight DL234 was scheduled to depart at 10:40 p.m. Israel time.The aircraft was denied clearance for takeoff after police received a phone call claiming that a bomb had been planted on board. Authorities suspect that the caller may be the same individual who earlier claimed that a bomb had been placed on a Delta flight that landed at Ben-Gurion Airport on Tuesday morning. That aircraft was searched, and the incident ended without any unusual findings.The flight was only permitted to depart once US security authorities had completed their inspections and clearance had been granted by Israeli security.Earlier incident on Delta flight landing at Ben-Gurion AirportThe incident follows a similar bomb threat earlier on Tuesday, when a Delta aircraft arriving at Ben-Gurion Airport from New York was moved to an isolated parking area after the Israel Airports Authority (IAA) received an anonymous report of a suspicious object on board that could contain explosives.All passengers were evacuated from the aircraft, and security personnel conducted searches to rule out the possibility of an explosive device.No suspicious objects or explosives were reported. Although security officials assessed the threat as likely a hoax, they decided to thoroughly inspect the aircraft as a precaution.The IAA later confirmed the incident was resolved, stating, "The incident ended with no unusual findings."Shortly after foiled flydubai hijacking attemptThese bomb threats come just weeks after the co-pilot of a flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv attempted the hijack the plane. The attempt was foiled by the quick thinking passengers and pilot who fought off the hijacker and saved the flight.The pilot-hijacker stabbed the lead pilot and tried to crash the plane before four passengers restrained him.The passengers say that had the Indian lead pilot not managed to open the door during the attack, they would not have been able to stop the plane from crashing.

title: Partisan appointment cycle will persist without meaningful reforms – Osae-Kwapong
body: CDD-Ghana Fellow, Dr John Osae-Kwapong, has warned that partisan appointments to independent constitutional bodies will persist unless meaningful institutional reforms break the cycle. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, he said both the NDC and NPP had questioned such appointments. Yet the practice continued as power changed hands. “Both parties – NDC and NPP – have had opportunities to express a view about openly partisan persons being appointed to certain institutions, but we see this cycle being repeated, through the rotation and election turnovers.” His comments follow the swearing-in of two new Electoral Commission deputy chairpersons, Dr Joseph Kwaku Asamoah and Emelia Afi Agbenyo, on Monday, October 12. President John Mahama charged them with upholding impartiality and strengthening public confidence. The appointments followed Dr Bossman Eric Asare’s resignation and Samuel Tettey’s retirement. For Dr Osae-Kwapong, the political response to the appointments points to a deeper institutional problem. He recounted a conversation with a partisan friend about the lesson political actors were drawing from the controversy. “Her response to me was that this tells us that whenever we have the chance, we should pack independent Constitutional bodies with partisans,” he said. Dr Osae-Kwapong warned that this thinking would sustain the practice without reforms to check partisan appointments. Asked whether the latest development damaged the EC’s credibility, he said it did little to rebuild confidence. “So for an institution that is already struggling in the eyes of the public, you mentioned the Afrobarometer on the question of trust.” “I feel like this doesn’t help to restore that kind of trust, that the institution itself really needs to build back up.” Dr Osae-Kwapong also raised a distinction between appointees whose political sympathies remain private and those whose affiliations are publicly known. “But again, the one question I’ve been reflecting on is: you could have a privately partisan person being appointed to the EC,” he said. His concern was the discomfort surrounding publicly partisan figures entering an independent institution while it was struggling to secure public confidence.

title: Montreal announces new metro security measures, 5% service increase
body:
The City of Montreal and its public transit agency are rolling out a series of measures aimed at improving safety in the metro network, including hiring more special constables, increasing surveillance and adding social workers.
The plan comes as transit advocates say many passengers continue to feel unsafe using the metro.
“We know that one rider on two doesn’t feel safe in the metro,” said Brian Nash of Trajectoire Québec.
Six measures are being introduced, including a $6.5-million investment to hire more special constables and $3 million to improve electronic surveillance. The city also plans to increase collaboration with Montreal police and add more social workers in the metro system.
Dimitrios Jim Beis, a member of Montreal’s executive committee, said more than 50 constables will be added by the end of 2027.
“We are clearly responding to the insecurity that folks are feeling,” Beis said.
Starting this fall, St. John Ambulance will help provide social workers, with two teams operating seven days a week during the winter and one team during the summer months.
Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada said the approach is intended to ensure different situations receive different responses.
“If you have a person that is in a homelessness situation, with a personal situation or a crisis, that doesn’t need to have the SPVM to come,” she said. “Maybe it’s the St. John Ambulance, the intervention of a social team that will come.”
Alongside the safety measures, city officials and the STM plan to increase metro service by five per cent as of 2027, with most of the additional service coming in the evenings.
“We see a lot more people having schedules outside of rush hour, so it is good news for them,” Nash said.
The service increase is expected to cost $8 million.
“The cost of not doing it is bigger than the cost of doing it,” Martinez Ferrada said.
Transit advocates welcomed the new measures but said more investment is still needed, particularly for bus service.

title: Iran uses oil prices as leverage in 'game of chess' with Trump ahead of US midterms
body: Iran is deploying new tactics to target ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz as it seeks to keep oil prices high and influence the U.S. midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters. Tehran has tried to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz since the U.S. and Israel launched strikes against Iran on February 28. It has restricted passage through the waterway, which carried about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade before the war, in an effort to gain leverage over Washington.   Its threats and attacks have severely curtailed traffic through the strait, driving up oil prices, though some oil has continued to transit. The two officials declined to provide details of the new strategy, but one said that Iran had started using different offensive tactics against vessels it considered in violation of its restrictions about 10 days ago, adding that this had led to an increase in attacks on such ships. The strategy included a change in the type as well as the pace of attacks, with one goal being to influence the outcome of the U.S. vote, they said. "The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices," one of the two officials said. The decision to adopt the new strategy had been taken at the highest levels of Iran’s leadership and was fully coordinated across the country’s ruling system, the officials said. Iran using spotters A U.S. military official, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed that Iran had changed tactics in one significant way: After the U.S. destroyed much of Iran’s radar capabilities, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had started using unarmed spotters in small boats to identify potential targets, including U.S. naval vessels, the official said. Last week, in a previously unreported incident, the U.S. military determined that Iranian spotters were operating from a dhow, calling in targets to the IRGC, the official said. U.S. forces confronted the vessel, told its occupants to abandon ship and then destroyed it. There were no casualties, the U.S. official said. Unwilling to risk its remaining fast boats, Iran had been unable to prevent a ramp-up in oil exports through the strait, the official said, particularly after U.S. strikes devastated its navy. The war — and its $3 billion monthly price tag — has become a key issue on the U.S. campaign trail for November's midterm elections, which will decide control of Congress. U.S. President Donald Trump has been weighing next steps against Iran, but has said he will not attack again before the vote. The U.S. has meanwhile been pressing its own naval blockade of Iranian ports and extending sanctions as it tries to pile economic pressure on Tehran to reach a deal to end the conflict. The standoff over Hormuz has left global energy markets exposed to further disruption, with the threat of attacks and high shipping and insurance costs complicating efforts to restore normal traffic. In recent days, attacks on commercial ships still sailing through the strait have surged to their highest level since the war began, according to independent data. There have been at least five incidents in the past 48 hours involving tankers and other commercial ships around the Hormuz area, including drone strikes, according to data analysis from maritime security sources and incidents reported to the British navy-affiliated agency United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO). That approximately mirrored the rate of attacks on October 3-5, pointing to a new escalation, according to data from the U.N. shipping agency, the International Maritime Organization. "There is a tempo increase in strikes, which looks deliberate," one maritime security source said. Attacks over an expanded area As part of the new strategy, Tehran will also expand the geographical scope of its operations beyond the Strait of Hormuz to the Gulf of Oman and waters further afield, the officials said. Analysis by maritime security sources based on attacks reported to UKMTO and maritime security companies in the region suggests this may already be happening. They show Iran targeting ships in areas beyond the Strait of Hormuz, including waters off the coast of Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, in recent days. The second Iranian official added that Tehran would not allow Trump to bring down oil prices before the November elections. "Just when they think they are getting close to the point where prices will fall, we will push them away from it. This is a game of chess," the second official said. "Such vessels would be safe nowhere, even outside the Strait of Hormuz." The Pentagon and Iran's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Complete closure of Hormuz soon, Iranian official says Both Iranian officials said Tehran is moving toward a situation in which no vessel violating its restrictions would be able to pass through the strait. "It will be complete closure soon," one of the officials said. In its latest report on Sunday, the U.S. Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) said the threat to merchant shipping in the Strait of Hormuz remained "severe," the second-highest level. "IRGC attacks, attempted attacks, and/or harassment activity persisted including UAV overflight, targeted surveillance of merchant shipping, and occasional VHF hailing," JMIC said.

title: Navy Unveils Secret Homegrown Sea Drone
body: ATHENS, October 2026 — The Hellenic Navy unveiled the Pyrpolitis USV on Tuesday at Skaramangas, showing its first fully home-built unmanned surface vessel after six months of secret work. Defence Minister Nikos Dendias opened a new unmanned-systems training centre at the Palaskas base for the ceremony. Because officers and NCOs worked outside their daily duties, teams finished the Pyrpolitis USV under strict secrecy, Kathimerini reported. It is five metres long and can hit 40 knots. Crews can use it for intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, surface attack and kamikaze strikes. “All these initiatives are one piece of a single plan,” Dendias said, linking innovation, training, production and use at sea. As a result, he said Greece aims to lead the European Union by 2030 in operational use of autonomous vehicles. Pyrpolitis USV production plan Mass production of the Pyrpolitis USV is now the next step. Then the navy plans to induct it into the fleet. However, the display went wider than one craft. The Corsair from US firm Saronic, already used near the Strait of Hormuz, was also shown. In addition, the navy has lined up two Italian Pluto Plus Plutino Miki underwater craft for mine hunting and kamikaze roles. Wider unmanned fleet Three surface boats from the defence staff research centre cover surface missions. Kanaris 1, Kanaris 2 and MESE run from 1.8 to 6.5 metres. Greek firm Altus LSA supplies the Niriis for surveillance and environmental data. Still, the Naval Cadet School runs a Blue Boat hydrographic craft under the TRITON program with MIT. Cadets wrote new AI software for that boat. They also wrote new software for the Portuguese Flexus system after finding its original code closed. Greek City Times earlier reported that Greece was seeking Italian minehunters as the navy deepens its unmanned push. Dendias said future operations will need new platforms on and under the sea. Specifically, Greece must design and build systems at home, not only buy them abroad, he said. That path sits under the Ministry of National Defence Agenda 2030 plan. Further fleet detail sits with the Hellenic Navy . Source: Kathimerini The post Navy Unveils Secret Homegrown Sea Drone appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Bake a Batch of Finikia, the Honey-Soaked Greek Biscuits, for National Dessert Day
body: This finikia recipe offers a sweet way to mark National Dessert Day on Wednesday 14 October: orange-scented semolina biscuits dipped in hot honey syrup and topped with chopped walnuts. Finikia at the Greek Festival, St George Greek Orthodox Church, Piscataway, New Jersey, in 2011. Photo: Richard Arthur Norton / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0 A finikia recipe for National Dessert Day National Dessert Day falls on 14 October each year, according to National Day Calendar . In 2025, Greek City Times marked the occasion with a semolina halva recipe , the simple 1:2:3:4 pudding of oil, semolina, sugar and water. This year, the choice is finikia. The finikia recipe here comes from Allrecipes, where home cooks rate it 4.6 out of 5. It makes about five dozen biscuits, so there is plenty to share with family and neighbours. Finikia sit very close to melomakarona, the honey biscuits that fill Greek homes at Christmas. In fact, many cooks use the two names for the same treat , although some families keep finikia for a slightly different, lighter version. Still, the shared flavours are clear: orange, cinnamon, cloves, honey and walnuts. The name may also have deep roots. According to TasteAtlas , some trace the biscuits to ancient Phoenicia. Greek City Times has also reported on melomakarona’s place among the world’s top sweets , where finikia earn a mention as a close relative. What goes into finikia The finikia recipe has two parts: a soft biscuit dough and a spiced honey syrup. Here is the full shopping list for the finikia recipe, with metric amounts in brackets. For the dough, you need: 1/2 cup (about 115 g) butter, softened 1/2 cup caster sugar Grated zest of one orange 1/2 cup (125 ml) corn oil 2 1/2 cups plain flour 1 1/2 cups semolina 4 teaspoons baking powder 1 teaspoon each of ground cinnamon and ground cloves 1/2 cup (125 ml) orange juice For the syrup and topping, you need: 1 cup (250 ml) water 1 cup white sugar 1/2 cup honey 1 cinnamon stick 2 teaspoons lemon juice 1/2 cup finely chopped walnuts Each biscuit comes to about 100 calories, according to the Allrecipes nutrition panel. Because the dough uses both butter and oil, the biscuits stay tender, while the semolina gives them a light crunch. How to bake and dip them The finikia recipe on Allrecipes lists 45 minutes of preparation and 25 minutes of baking, plus time for the biscuits to cool. Before you start, heat the oven to 175°C (350°F) and grease two or three baking trays. Beat the butter, caster sugar and orange zest in a large bowl, then slowly add the oil and beat until light. Mix the flour, semolina, baking powder, cinnamon and cloves in a second bowl. Add the dry mix to the butter mix in batches, alternating with the orange juice. Once the dough thickens, tip it onto a floured bench and knead it until firm. Roll tablespoons of dough into balls or ovals and space them 5 cm apart on the trays. Bake for about 25 minutes until golden, then let them cool completely on the trays. For the syrup, boil the water, sugar, honey, cinnamon stick and lemon juice for 10 minutes, then remove the cinnamon stick. Dip each cool biscuit into the hot syrup until covered, set it on a wire rack and sprinkle with walnuts. Put baking paper under the rack to catch the drips. Finally, store the finished biscuits in a sealed container at room temperature. Tips from home cooks Reviewers on Allrecipes say the orange and cinnamon pairing is what makes this finikia recipe stand out. One cook, Nick, wrote: “I followed the directions and they came out exactly like my grandmother’s.” Several reviewers also shared advice on the syrup. In particular, one warned that boiling it for too long turns it into a hard, candy-like coating. Another said syrup that is too hot can make the biscuits fall apart, so his mother let them sit in it for only two or three seconds. Patience helps as well, because the finikia recipe rewards a little waiting. The same cook noted that finikia taste better after a day, since the syrup soaks through evenly. Similarly, a third reviewer suggested freshly squeezed orange juice for a brighter flavour. For a neater finish, one baker dipped the tops in syrup and then rolled them straight in the walnuts, so more nuts stuck. Overall, home cooks agree that the finikia recipe is worth the effort, whether for National Dessert Day or the Christmas table. Readers who want the festive cousin can try Greek City Times’ traditional melomakarona , while the original Allrecipes page lists every review and photo. Source: Allrecipes The post Bake a Batch of Finikia, the Honey-Soaked Greek Biscuits, for National Dessert Day appeared first on Greek City Times .
