title: Russia detains Japanese journalist on espionage charges
body:
Japanese journalist Yuki Imai was arrested on charges of espionage on Oct. 13, according to Russian court records.
Russia's Security Service (FSB) said that a Japanese citizen working for the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper was arrested in the country's far east near islands disputed by Russia and Japan before being taken to Moscow.
The outlet has a dedicated team covering Japan-Russia relations, territorial disputes between the two countries, and Russia's war against Ukraine.
FSB footage circulated by Russian state media appears to show the journalist pinned to the ground as Imai is handcuffed before being forced to power on his laptop in front of officers.
Russia's FSB claims the suspect collected data on the number of mobilized soldiers and volunteers in Russia's war against Ukraine for Japanese intelligence among residents living on the disputed islands controlled by Moscow.
Russia regularly brings politically motivated charges against opposition figures, journalists, and foreign citizens.
Russia has banned independent media outlets and is currently detaining dozens of journalists and media workers, according to Reporters Without Borders.
On Oct. 4, Moscow police detained about 60 people at an authorized Communist Party rally after demonstrators began chanting anti-Kremlin slogans, according to the party and Russian rights group OVD-Info.

title: Anthropic opens Singapore office and signs MOU with the Government of Singapore
body:
Today, we are expanding our Asia-Pacific operations by opening a new office in Singapore—our fifth in the region—and signing a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the Singapore Ministry of Digital Development and Information. Singapore is one of our most active markets anywhere in the world, and Claude is already powering Singaporean business and government services used by millions of people every day, like GovTech Singapore, Grab, and DBS. Our growing local team will ensure these organizations and many more stay on the frontier with safe, capable AI.
“We’re committed to Singapore for the long term,” said Dale Finlay, General Manager of ASEAN at Anthropic. “Our customers here hold AI to an extremely high standard, especially when it comes to reliability and security. Having a team on the ground means we can get even closer to the organizations putting Claude to work on their hardest problems.”
Kai Fong Chng, Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Digital Development and Information, and Anthropic co-founder Ben Mann signed the MOU on the sidelines of Singapore International Cyber Week. Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo and Michael Sellitto, Anthropic Head of APAC Policy, witnessed the signing. It sets out areas of cooperation in AI safety, security, and model evaluation; research on AI adoption and its impact; and responsible adoption across the public and private sectors.
“Singapore has been a leader in responsible AI, with a long track record of investment in model testing and evaluation,” said Mann. “We founded Anthropic on the belief that capability and safety have to go hand in hand. With this MOU, we’ll partner with Singapore to help ensure the transition to powerful AI goes well here, across Asia-Pacific, and around the world.”
“Singapore’s approach to AI has always been to enable innovation while keeping pace with its evolving risks. Trust is critical for businesses, workers, and the public to use AI with confidence,” said Chng. “This partnership with Anthropic reflects the Government’s commitment to scaling up the responsible adoption of AI, deepening capabilities in our companies and government agencies, and delivering impact for Singapore.”
Our work with Singapore goes back to 2023, when we joined the Generative AI Evaluation Sandbox run by the Infocomm Media Development Authority and the AI Verify Foundation. We later partnered with them on a red-teaming project in English, Mandarin, Malay, and Tamil.
Under the MOU, we plan to hold technical exchanges with Singapore’s AI safety, security, and assurance institutions on model evaluation, testing standards, and incident response. We do similar work with safety institutes around the world, where sharing technical information provides governments with a clearer view of frontier AI capabilities and risks, while helping developers build safer models.
We’ll also look for ways to strengthen AI skills in Singapore, help small and medium-sized businesses adopt AI responsibly, and support the government’s goal of building AI capability among public officers. We plan to share research and data with the government, including from the Anthropic Economic Index , and to offer technical and policy expertise as Singapore develops its rules for AI.
In our latest Economic Index , Singapore ranks second of 121 countries in Claude.ai usage relative to its population, at nearly six times what its size alone would predict.
In the public sector, more than 1,500 engineers and technical staff at the Government Technology Agency of Singapore (GovTech Singapore) have adopted Claude Code to modernize government systems and speed up software delivery. This has helped GovTech Singapore teams build, maintain, and enhance digital services more efficiently at national scale. The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore is exploring how Claude could help strengthen the country’s cyber defense.
In financial services, DBS, Southeast Asia’s largest bank, works with Claude across a range of use cases in its Singapore operations—including software development and day-to-day productivity—as part of its broader AI innovation efforts. These applications operate within the bank’s strict security and governance framework. GIC, Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund, is rolling out Claude across its investment and corporate services teams. Organizations in regulated sectors like financial services can now run Claude with in-region inference on Amazon Bedrock, helping them meet strict data processing requirements.
Singapore’s largest technology companies and startups are building with Claude too. Grab powers BriX, its sales assistant, with Claude. The assistant saves Grab’s sales teams approximately 40,000 hours every quarter and surfaces new sales opportunities. Sea—the business behind Shopee, Garena, and Monee—works with Claude to help Shopee’s customer service chatbot respond faster and more accurately, and thousands of its employees write and debug code with Claude. And Supabase—the developer platform with strong roots in Singapore—is building with Claude Code.
This week, senior leaders from Anthropic are in Singapore to open the office and meet with customers, developers, and policymakers.
Today, we hosted Builder Summit Singapore, bringing more than 300 developers together with engineering and product leaders from Anthropic. Earlier in the week, Singapore’s Claude community ambassadors held a meetup for more than 700 local builders.
Our Singapore office is now open and hiring. To learn more about joining the team, visit our careers page .

title: [OPINION] How the Philippine Left lost its way
body: In his Vantage Point column on September 1, 2026, “ What’s left for the Philippines’ Left? ,” Val Villanueva proposed some explanations for the demise of the revolutionary Left in the Philippines. One is that the ideology of fighting for socialism went out of fashion globally, with China and Vietnam’s turn towards capitalism. Another is that the Left’s position on EDCA and Pax Silica has aligned it with China geopolitically, thus discrediting it as well as allegedly revealing its ignorance of the economic benefits that could come to the country. In short, global developments have left the Philippine Left behind. My sense, however, is that the principal cause of the Left’s decline lies in three things: its misreading of domestic political realities after the collapse of the Marcos dictatorship, a bloody internal purge that took several thousand lives, and a very deep split in the leadership of the revolutionary movement. The way these factors came together is illustrated in the life of former New People’s Army (NPA) cadre Eddie Quitoriano, whose memoir published by Ateneo de Manila University Press, just came out. Let me share a review I did of that book as a way of illustrating why the Left’s decline was really a complex—and tragic—process. At the launch of his book Deeper Ground, Darker Shadows ** in Manila a few weeks ago, Eddie Quitoriano asked, “How did the NPA’s image change from being the ‘Nice People Around’ to one of being only interested in imposing revolutionary taxes and obtaining weapons?” This was Eddie’s diplomatic way of asking, “How did the Philippine revolution lose its way?” Answering that question was undoubtedly a key motivation for writing his memoir. In the process of fleshing out his life in over 300 pages, he provides the reader a fascinating personal odyssey that is meshed with a larger, tragic odyssey, that of the national democratic movement. Eddie as an individual reaches his Ithaca, which is reconciliation with a family he had neglected out of devotion to the revolution. The movement, however, has not, and is still adrift, growing more marginal to Philippine politics by the day. This is a book that should be required reading for the global left, for it is a sobering affirmation of the truism that efforts to realize good intentions, if not grounded in a firm belief in the intrinsic value of individuals, balanced by good institutional checks, and guided by plain common sense, can go badly awry. Cadre The offspring of a struggling family in Mindanao, the Philippines’ second biggest island, Eddie grows up in a frontier area peopled by Christian settlers, indigenous peoples, and Muslims. It is the early seventies and, like many in his generation, he is repelled by Ferdinand Marcos Sr. ’s declaration of martial law and attracted to the national democratic revolution radiating outwards from Manila to the rest of the country. He is drawn into activist circles, resulting in his being railroaded from the seminary where he has been training to be a Catholic priest. Recruited into the reestablished Communist Party of the Philippines (CPP), he proves his mettle as an organizer, one who is able to skillfully navigate both the perils of encounters with the military and internecine conflicts within the fledgling party. With the establishment of the party’s Mindanao Commission and the growth of the CPP’s armed wing, the New People’s Army , in the movement’s most promising expansion area, Eddie becomes a seasoned NPA fighter and trainer, even as he fathers a family and, along with his wife, Agnes, rotates in and out of military and police detention. His performance attracts the attention of Romulo Kintanar, the chief of the NPA and a fellow Mindanaoan, and he and his family are brought to Manila for his integration into the people’s army’s General Command. In the first part of the book, the excitement of revolutionary organizing and the dedication of CPP and NPA cadres come across despite the author’s understated style of writing and his reluctance to tell the reader about his talents and capabilities. Still, there are things that bother him that he registers. One is the lack of warmth with which he is received by “Tagalog” cadres in Manila; indeed, their reluctance to extend personal assistance contrasts with the spontaneous solidarity of comrades in Mindanao. Another is a disconcerting distrust among the top leadership of the party and NPA, which leads to non-sharing of vital information like his pending assignment to overseas work. The third is the most alarming, which is news from home about an internal purge taking the lives of many veteran cadres in Mindanao beginning in 1985. War with the NPA, war without end The voyage out But before he can wrap his head around what came to be known as “Kampanyang Ahos,” or “Garlic Campaign,” he is sent off on a mission to raise money and purchase arms abroad by Kintanar, who comes across in these pages as a dynamic, take-charge personality. Over the next seven years, the mission brings him to Syria, North Korea, Nicaragua, Libya, Cuba, Yugoslavia, Greece, Yugoslavia, the Netherlands, Vietnam, to name just a few stops. He is unable to procure weapons, but does get some money, and is able to arrange for the training of NPA combatants in Pyongyang and Libya. In the process, along with top leaders of the party and NPA, he gets to meet the mercurial Libyan chief Muammar Khadaffy, who gives the NPA one million dollars, and the ailing North Korean leader Kim Il-Sung, who promises weapons but wants assurances the NPA can work out a way of receiving them, which it can’t. Since his mission is not sanctioned by the party leadership but only the NPA General Command, it is not surprising that Eddie eventually gets entangled in the transnational feud between Kintanar in Manila and the party leadership in exile domiciled in Utrecht, the Netherlands, led by Joma Sison , whom Eddie initially accords the respect due to one who has been a key founder of the party and its prime ideologue. The feud stems from jurisdictional, political, ideological, and personal conflicts. An explosion waiting to happen, animosities accumulate and erupt over the mixing of counterfeit dollars provided by the Japanese Red Army (JRA) for NPA operations with Khadaffy’s gift of real dollars. US authorities have spotted the counterfeit dollars, resulting in a major headache for the NDF’s international representatives. Along with another comrade, Eddie is tried by what he describes as a kangaroo court in the Dutch City of Maastricht, with Sison leading the prosecution while denying his own role in authorizing the use of fake dollars for revolutionary ends. Admitting his own role in the foolhardy enterprise, Eddie is dismayed by obvious efforts by others to make him the fall guy. Play Video Stormy voyage back… Judged guilty and “banned” from again setting foot in Western Europe, Eddie is on his own, subsisting on funds periodically given to him by a Japanese Red Army contact codenamed “Nadia,” who is later revealed to be the legendary Fusako Shigenobu , founder of the Japanese Red Army (JRA). His travels bring him to, among other places, Havana, where hospitable Cuban comrades arrange for cosmetic surgery. He is on the run from US and international police authorities owing to the counterfeit dollars affair and needs a new nose to look like someone of Native American descent from the Andes. The Cuban surgeon botches the first operation, forcing him to return for a second, which succeeds. As he explains, “I had to disappear. I was no longer with the CPP or the NPA and I wasn’t prepared to join the JRA, but I wanted to survive, even as a different person if need be.” Surprisingly, at a time that he is deserted by his own party, it is the JRA that remains faithful to Eddie, generously providing cash for his subsistence and travels even when meaningful reciprocal support for “joint actions” from the increasingly disorganized NPA General Command is no longer feasible. The grateful Eddie does try to repay the favor by scouting for and securing safehouses in Latin America for the JRA, which is finding its Eastern European safehouses becoming less and less secure with the collapse of socialist governments there at the turn of the nineties. Eddie hints at casual encounters with the opposite sex on the winding way back home, but if he does indulge in them, like Odysseus he does not allow any Circe or Calypso derail him from what has now become his obsessive goal of reaching hearth and home. After an odyssey of nearly seven years, Eddie finally gets back to the Philippines in 1993. No longer with the party and NPA, his priority is to provide his two children and wife with the stability that his revolutionary commitments deprived them when they were growing up. He is able to fend off the military’s efforts to send him to prison, but he cannot avert his eyes from the tragedy that has engulfed the movement he has cut ties with. …to the heart of darkness It turned out to be a stroke of luck that Eddie was absent from the Philippines during the period 1986 to 1993. For it was during this period that the CPP literally descended into madness. The scale of the purges in Mindanao that he had first heard about when he left in 1986 shocked him upon his return. Thousands of trained cadres of the party and NPA had been executed by their own comrades owing to the panic that swept the ranks that were triggered by unverified rumors that the military had been able to infiltrate its agents into the movement. Ironically, methods of summary justice CPP cadres had employed against “bad elements” in the barangays or villages were now turned against their own comrades. Mindanao was turned into a howling wilderness in just a few months in 1985 to 1986 by Kampanyang Ahos , and, failing to absorb the lessons of a purge that went out of control, party and NPA units in Luzon stumbled into the same bloody process, with the purges known as Operation Missing Link and Project Olympia, which Robert Francis Garcia, a victim, documented in his classic 2001 account To Suffer Thy Comrades . When Marcos was overthrown in February 1986 and Corazon Aquino assumed power, the NDF was immobilized and stood on the sidelines, partly because it had adopted a policy of boycotting the rigged polls that triggered the mass insurrection against the dictator. But the bigger reason was that it was in no position to intervene because its ranks had been depleted and demoralized by successive purges. The bloodletting at the base took place in parallel with a fierce struggle at the top for the leadership of the party, with Sison regaining unchallenged control of the party and NPA and driving out those he labeled military adventurists like Kintanar and as well as other factions that questioned his leadership or rejected a return to the classic Maoist strategy of protracted people’s war. Filemon Lagman was assassinated in 2001, Kintanar in 2003, and Arturo Tabara in 2004, though the NPA admitted only to the killing of Kintanar. All had been top leaders of the CPP. In 2005, the names of 14 “counter-revolutionaries” or, as we joked then, candidates for execution, were published by the CPP journal Ang Bayan (among them my own, most likely because I was among the first to do an empirical investigation and publish an analysis of the purges). Purges are not, of course, uncommon in revolutionary movements. Still, there are those like the Vietnamese Communist Party, that have been able to evolve a collective process to resolve intra-party disputes relatively peacefully. During the Chinese Revolution, Mao Tse-tung dealt with his rivals not by executing them but by relieving them of their positions and isolating them in “criticism-self-criticism” sessions designed to get them to “reform.” Among those famously subjected to this treatment were influential cadres such as Zhou En Lai and Deng Hsiao Ping, who was purged twice. Stalin, of course, executed thousands of his Bolshevik comrades and their factional followers, but this took place long after the triumph of the Russian Revolution in 1917. The uniqueness of the purges in the Philippines was that the mass executions took place before the left even had a real chance to come to power. As Patricio Abinales aptly put it, the purges resulted in “the revolution devouring its own children before victory.” Indeed, the purges eliminated thousands of trained, loyal cadres who would have been indispensable actors had the movement been in a position to take over the state. Must Read Ed Quitoriano: The life, travels, and travails of a promdi rebolusyonaryo A distant reckoning The tragedy has been compounded by the fact that none of those who led the purges, whether they later aligned with Sison’s “reaffirmist” line or against it by joining the “rejectionist” camp, have stepped forward to take responsibility for the purges, hoping perhaps that memory of the bloody campaigns would be erased with the passage of time. It’s been 40 years since the killings, yet the collective refusal to own up to the collective madness persists. This is understandable, though inexcusable, since most of those in national or responsible regional leadership positions in the then still unified party knew about the ongoing purges but did little or nothing to halt them, though some of them did apologize to the incredulous relatives of the victims. “ Kahos (purge) only stopped when there were no more comrades to execute,” Eddie writes. Eddie is right that the actual number of cadres whose lives were taken will never be really known, though a hint was provided by a party document that acknowledged that in the immediate post-Marcos years, the number of party members abruptly dropped from 9,000 to 3,000. For him, the real measure of the scope of the purge is the “silence of the NPA guns and the collapse of guerrilla fronts and party organizations.” Having been central in building the party and NPA infrastructure in Mindanao, an endeavor that took years, Eddie is understandably aghast at a campaign that demolished it in just a few months. It is only when he talks about the question of accountability for Ahos that bitterness seeps into Eddie’s writing. People responsible for the purges “have not been held to account because they continue to perform essential duties for the organization. Some have found new lives in government, academia, or the private sector. I am sure they know what happened and what their role was but choose to pretend they have done nothing wrong.” One can sense a smoldering desire to name names instead of the pseudonyms that people went by, but out of a remnant of comradely respect, he refrains from doing so. The moral high ground surrendered Revolutions succeed for a variety of reasons. But one of the ingredients of success is that among the people, the revolutionaries are seen as holding the moral high ground. Ahos and the other purges demolished that for all sections of the Philippines left, and it is doubtful that in the foreseeable future they will be able to reclaim that once quaint popular description of them as “the nice people around.” The question, however, might arise among some readers: How reliable is Eddie’s account? Fairly reliable, I would say. It’s not just the level of detail and complexity with which he describes his experiences, which could not have simply been conjured out of thin air. Just a few pages in, you realize that what you’re reading is not a polemical ideological tract nor an account by someone with an axe to grind but an honest attempt by one who spent 20 years in the revolution as an ordinary cadre to find an answer to one question, one that is asked by many who came into political maturity during a memorable era and became part of something bigger than themselves: Was it all worth it? Like the response to Eddie’s query of how many young lives were snuffed out by the purges, the answer to this question is not likely to be definitively settled. But to again become a real force in the country’s politics, the revolutionary left must reckon with rather than avoid its past. – Rappler.com Walden Bello, a retired professor at the University of the Philippines and the State University of New York at Binghamton, is the author of Global Battlefields: My Close Encounters with Dictatorship, Capital, Empire, and Love (Ateneo de Manila University Press, 2025). ** Deeper Ground, Darker Shadows: The Making of a Mindanao Rebel ( University of Wisconsin Press 2025 and Ateneo de Manila University Press 2026) Play Video

title: ‘This cycle isn’t going to be broken any soon’ – Osae-Kwapong on appointments to independent institutions
body: CDD-Ghana Fellow Dr John Osae-Kwapong says partisan appointments to independent constitutional bodies will persist unless meaningful institutional reforms break the pattern. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, he said both the NDC and NPP had questioned such appointments, only for the cycle to continue when power changed hands. “Both parties – NDC and NPP – have had opportunities to express a view about openly partisan persons being appointed to certain institutions, but we see this cycle being repeated, through the rotation and election turnovers.” His comments follow President John Mahama’s swearing-in of Emelia Afi Agbenyo and Dr Joseph Kwaku Asamoah as EC Deputy Chairpersons on Monday, October 12. They fill vacancies left by Dr Bossman Eric Asare and Samuel Tettey. Mahama charged them with upholding impartiality and prioritising the national interest. Dr Osae-Kwapong illustrated his concern with an exchange he had with a partisan friend earlier that day. He had asked what the biggest lesson was. “Her response to me was that this tells us that whenever we have the chance, we should pack independent Constitutional bodies with partisans,” he said. For him, that response exposed why the practice keeps recurring. He warned that “this is not a cycle that is going to be broken any soon” without meaningful institutional reforms. Asked whether the latest appointment damaged the EC’s credibility, Dr Osae-Kwapong said it did little to rebuild public confidence. “So for an institution that is already struggling in the eyes of the public, you mentioned the Afrobarometer on the question of trust. I feel like this doesn’t help to restore that kind of trust, that the institution itself really needs to build back up.” He also drew attention to the distinction between private political sympathies and publicly demonstrated partisanship. A person appointed to the EC could privately hold partisan views, Dr Osae-Kwapong observed. “The public discomfort arose when someone openly associated with a party entered an institution whose independence was already under scrutiny,” he stated. That concern, he added, came “at a time when that institution is struggling to have the fullest confidence of the Ghanaian public.”

title: Pope Leo diagnosed with cancer as doctors remove part of lung
body: VATICAN – Pope Leo was diagnosed with lung cancer after surgeons removed the lower lobe of his right lung during surgery on Tuesday, October 13, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin. The 71-year-old pontiff has lung adenocarcinoma, a common form of lung cancer, with tissue tests conducted during the operation confirming what doctors had suspected from preparatory examinations, the bulletin said. The surgery to remove a small growth discovered during a recent routine health check lasted about 90 minutes and was successful, with no complications, according to Leo’s lead surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, and personal physician, Dr. Luigi Carbone. “In order to make the procedure curative, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique,” they said, indicating that the aim was to eliminate all cancerous tissue. The pope was admitted to Rome’s Gemelli hospital earlier on Tuesday for the procedure. The Vatican had said his recovery was expected to take about a week. Leo regained consciousness normally after the operation and returned to his hospital room, where he was resting, the medical bulletin said. The Vatican said earlier this week that the pope was expected to remain in hospital for about a week. All his public events have been cancelled until October 20. A medical expert said more information was needed to assess the pope’s condition, including the size of the tumor and whether the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes, details the Vatican did not immediately provide. “While we have the diagnosis, we do not yet have the stage. This is critical to prognosis and treatment,” said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown University in Washington and division chief of hematology-oncology at MedStar Georgetown University Hospital. “If this is a small lung cancer with no lymph nodes involved, surgery itself is likely to be curative,” Liu said. “But if final analysis reveals a greater extent of cancer involvement, this indicates a poorer prognosis.” Leo left the Vatican shortly before 1 pm (1100 GMT) on Tuesday and was seen waving from the back of a black SUV as his convoy traveled about 9 km north to the hospital. Upon arrival, Leo shook hands with several officials and walked past a crowd of well-wishers, some of whom shouted “Auguri” (best wishes), before entering through the main entrance. Elected by the world’s cardinals in May 2025, Leo is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to be a smoker or to have had recent health issues. The late Pope Francis, Leo’s predecessor, was hospitalised several times as he grew frail in his later years. He died aged 88 in April 2025. Leo, who spoke in a firm, clear voice at his only public event on Monday, October 12, maintains a busy schedule. He is due to make an 11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17, though it was unclear whether the trip would still go ahead. The pope is the ultimate earthly authority for the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics and has no deputy who steps in when he is sick. When a pope is incapacitated, the Vatican’s bureaucracy continues its work, holding off on decisions that require papal approval. Born in Chicago in 1955 as Robert Prevost, Leo served for decades as a missionary and bishop in Peru before becoming pope. In 1985, when he was a young priest, he contracted typhoid fever in Chulucanas, Peru, and was hospitalized. He recounted the experience in his only major interview as pope, published in a book by Penguin Peru. Leo said the pain was so severe that he asked God to let him die rather than continue suffering. He took his survival as a sign from God that “We need you here (on Earth),” he said. “I never looked back,” Leo said. – Rappler.com

title: MI5 reports 50-plus arrests in Iran-linked UK operations, warns of threats to Jewish communities
body: More than 50 people have been arrested in Britain over the past year in operations linked to Iran, MI5 Director General Sir Ken McCallum revealed Tuesday, warning that Tehran is expanding its hybrid campaign against the United Kingdom, with much of its aggression directed at Jewish communities. He also warned that terrorists could exploit artificial intelligence to develop biological weapons. Delivering his annual threat assessment at MI5 headquarters in London, McCallum described how Britain is confronting hostile states, including Iran and Russia, in a new era of national security. He compared the scale of the changes facing the intelligence service to the transformation that followed the September 11 attacks.    McCallum described Russia as Britain's leading state aggressor, while identifying Iran as another country seeking to outsource violence on British soil. He said he had been warning about the Iranian threat since 2022, particularly Tehran's use of criminal proxies to intimidate opposition figures, Iranian media organizations and Israeli targets. According to McCallum, 2026 has seen Iran, like Russia, attempt to expand its hybrid campaign against Britain. Over the past 12 months, MI5 operations connected to Iran have resulted in more than 50 arrests across the country. He expressed solidarity with Britain's Jewish communities, saying they had been among the principal targets of Iranian-linked aggression. He pointed to the recent arrest and charging of two Iranian nationals over an alleged plot targeting Manchester's Jewish community.   McCallum also referred to a wave of arson and sabotage attacks during the spring against Jewish communities in Britain and elsewhere in Europe. The incidents included attacks on ambulances, synagogues and businesses. Responsibility for the attacks was claimed by a group calling itself the Islamic Movement of the Companions of the Right. McCallum said members of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps were behind the organization. He explained that both the group and the IRGC had since been designated under Britain's National Security Act, giving authorities additional powers to disrupt their activities and pursue prosecutions. McCallum warned that those seeking to carry out violence on British streets, whether criminals recruited locally or the foreign actors directing them, would face a determined response. Addressing the wider terrorist threat, McCallum said MI5 continued to confront threats from Islamist extremists, the far right, the far left and groups associated with Northern Ireland. Although sustained counterterrorism operations have weakened the leadership of the Islamic State group, he said both ISIS and al-Qaeda continue to direct and inspire attacks. He stressed that MI5 was still dealing with attempts to carry out mass-casualty attacks in Britain. In February, three Islamist extremists were convicted of plotting to use automatic weapons against Manchester's Jewish community. McCallum also revealed that MI5 is now devoting more resources to threats posed by hostile states than it did during the Cold War. Another major concern, he said, is the growing ability of terrorists and hostile actors to exploit artificial intelligence. AI is already intensifying the struggle between attackers and defenders in cyberspace, helping produce propaganda and extremist recruitment material, and allowing hostile groups to improve their intelligence-gathering capabilities and attack planning. McCallum said MI5 had encountered terrorists seeking to use AI to improve reconnaissance and attack methods, while AI-enabled drones were creating additional security challenges. He warned that an even more serious potential threat was the use of artificial intelligence to advance the development of biological weapons, including the possibility of new biological agents. Although that particular threat has not yet materialized, he said the technology could place dangerous knowledge within reach of people who previously lacked the expertise to obtain or use it. McCallum also raised concerns about the broader implications of artificial intelligence, noting that humanity has never before faced the prospect of an adversary capable of outthinking human beings. His remarks came after two Iranian nationals appeared in a London court earlier this month accused of plotting an attack against the ultra-Orthodox Jewish community in Salford, Greater Manchester. Rahman Salehi, 34, of Salford, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, of Liverpool, face charges of engaging in conduct in preparation for terrorist acts, including allegedly planning or assisting an attack around Yom Kippur last month. The two were arrested on September 20 on Newton Street in Manchester's Northern Quarter, as thousands of British Jews were preparing to observe the holy day. Prosecutors allege the suspects conducted hostile reconnaissance of Manchester's Jewish community, identifying potential targets including the Manchester Jewish Museum and the Heaton Park synagogue. The prosecution says the two men planned to use an improvised explosive device and had been in contact with a third person overseas, believed to be operating from Iran, who allegedly provided instructions for the attack. At a hearing at Westminster Magistrates' Court on October 3, prosecutors alleged that the defendants had obtained a document containing instructions for making a homemade bomb, along with video material explaining how to manufacture or assemble an improvised explosive device. They are also accused of obtaining liquids, components and equipment needed to construct the device, as well as researching potential targets and acquiring maps and photographs of locations they allegedly intended to attack.

title: Donetsk region to introduce extended curfew starting November 1
body:
Oleksandr Honcharenko, head of the Kramatorsk City Military Administration, announced the decision on Facebook , according to Ukrinform.
The decision was approved during a regular meeting of the regional Defense Council.
"We have agreed to expand the area covered by the extended curfew. Starting November 1, the curfew will run from 16:00 to 11:00 throughout the Ukrainian-controlled territory of Donetsk region, except for the Oleksandrivka and Cherkaska communities," Honcharenko said, citing Donetsk Regional Governor Vadym Filashkin.
As previously reported, the area subject to the mandatory evacuation of children from certain parts of Kramatorsk has been expanded.

title: Sara Duterte amid trial: ‘I will not resign. I will never resign.’
body: There have been allegations here and there against Vice President Sara Duterte. She has an ongoing impeachment trial that could oust her from the vice presidency and prevent her from running for president in 2028. There are alleged deliveries of millions of pesos to her as claimed by former cop Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. And there’s this claim about her alleged link to companies that do business with China. Cale88 Food Corporation , tied to Duterte and husband Mans Carpio, allegedly received remittances from Chinese state-owned firms. So, is resignation the answer to all her problems? “No, no, no. I will not resign. I will never resign from the Office of the Vice President,” said Duterte during a chance interview with reporters on Tuesday, October 13. Even before, Duterte’s defense lawyers said resigning is not option for the Vice President: “ Never pa namin napag-usapan ng ating Bise Presidente ‘yung resignation (The Vice President and I have never talked about resignation). So, I don’t think we even have to discuss that issue,” said defense spokesperson and counsel Michael Poa. A resignation, until now, would be a gamble for Duterte. There’s no assurance that her resignation will stop the Senate impeachment court from continuing her trial. House prosecutors have been firm that a Duterte resignation won’t stop the trial, and by extension, the impeachment court’s judgment. “Even if she resigns, for example, it will not absolve, it will not even terminate the impeachment trial because the only way to terminate the impeachment trial is for the court to finally reach a decision,” said House prosecution Zia Alonto Adiong earlier. Duterte remains to be the most popular presidential aspirant because based on Pulse Asia’s September survey, she received a 50% voter preference rating. This is perhaps what keeps her holding on to her presidential dream. But this number does not guarantee her political survival. If she gets convicted, it will mean nothing nor be of any use. And at the rate things are going, the odds might no longer be in Duterte’s favor. Play Video First, the Senate impeachment court already adjusted the voting threshold — it will count only the votes of senator-judges who are “legally and factually capable” of participating in the proceedings at the time of the vote. This is bad news for Duterte because with 20 active senators at present, two-thirds of the denominator would mean 14 (the required number of conviction votes). And this rule, so far, still stands because the Supreme Court dismissed the three petitions challenging the decision to adjust the threshold. Second, the prosecution already dropped three of four articles of impeachment against her . The prosecutors said their evidence on her alleged unexplained wealth is sufficient to convict Duterte. “We believe that evidence is substantial and compelling, and warrants the respondent’s removal from office for culpable violation of the Constitution and betrayal of public trust,” lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro said. What could this mean? It’s possible the prosecution has the numbers to convict her — and the dropping of the three articles is a telltale sign that the end of her vice presidency is coming. “Whether or not I become the next president of our country remains to be seen. Hindi natin alam (We don’t know). And perhaps my purpose has always been bigger than the position itself,” said Duterte. – Rappler.com

title: Partisan appointments won’t help restore trust in EC – Osae-Kwapong
body: Appointing openly partisan figures to the Electoral Commission (EC)will not help rebuild public trust, CDD-Ghana Fellow Dr John Osae-Kwapong has warned. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, he said such appointments deepen concerns about an institution already struggling to regain public confidence. “So for an institution that is already struggling in the eyes of the public, you mentioned the Afrobarometer on the question of trust. I feel like this doesn’t help to restore that kind of trust, that the institution itself really needs to build back up.” His comments follow President John Mahama’s swearing-in of two new EC deputy chairpersons on Monday, October 12. They are Dr Joseph Kwaku Asamoah and Emelia Afi Agbenyo. They fill vacancies left by Dr Bossman Eric Asare, who resigned, and Samuel Tettey, who retired. At the ceremony, President Mahama urged the appointees to strengthen public confidence through impartiality, transparency and accountability. Dr Osae-Kwapong placed the controversy within a recurring pattern involving both major political parties. “Both parties – NDC and NPP – have had opportunities to express a view about openly partisan persons being appointed to certain institutions, but we see this cycle being repeated, through the rotation and election turnovers.” He argued that changes in government had failed to break the practice. Instead, the cycle risked encouraging parties to fill independent constitutional bodies with their supporters whenever they gained power. He illustrated the problem with a conversation he had with a partisan friend that afternoon. “Her response to me was that this tells us that whenever we have the chance, we should pack independent Constitutional bodies with partisans,” he recounted. For him, meaningful institutional reforms are needed to interrupt that cycle and address concerns about openly partisan appointments. Dr Osae-Kwapong also drew a distinction between private political preferences and publicly known party affiliations. An appointee could privately support a party, he noted. The public concern, however, becomes sharper when an openly partisan person joins an independent institution already facing questions about its credibility. His central concern was the EC’s need to rebuild confidence. Appointments that raise fresh doubts about its independence, he argued, do little to support that task.

title: Spiro Unveils Growth Plans for Nigeria, Says New MD
body: Bennett Oghifo Spiro, Africa’s leading electric mobility company and recipient of the West Africa Sustainable Award (WASA), has reaffirmed its commitment to accelerating Nigeria’s transition to sustainable transportation. This was revealed by the newly introduced Country Head/Managing Director of Spiro Nigeria, Mr Prasad Sane at the second edition of the Media Connect organised by the company in Lagos. Building on the success of its inaugural edition, the event brought together leading business, technology, mobility, and sustainability journalists for an exclusive update on Spiro’s growth journey, the expansion of its battery-swapping infrastructure, and its long-term vision for the Nigerian market. This year’s Media Connect highlighted Spiro’s strategic focus on its three priority markets: Lagos, Ogun, and Oyo States, where the company continues to strengthen its operational footprint through expanded battery-swapping stations, enhanced rider support services, and strategic partnerships. A key highlight of the event was the formal introduction of Mr. Prasad Sane, who now leads the company’s operations and growth strategy in the country. Addressing members of the media, Mr. Sane emphasized Spiro’s commitment to transforming mobility across Nigeria. According to him, “today is about progress, partnership, and purpose. A year ago, we shared our vision for electric mobility in Nigeria. Today, we are demonstrating tangible results and a clear path forward. My mandate is simple: to make Spiro the most trusted, affordable, and accessible electric mobility solution for Nigerians, beginning with Lagos, Ogun, and Oyo States. “We are moving beyond electric bikes to build a complete ecosystem centered on our promise of ‘Energy on the Move.'” He added that “with our battery-swapping technology, riders can replace depleted batteries in under a minute and get back on the road without worrying about fuel costs, charging time, or excessive maintenance expenses. “This model not only reduces carbon emissions but also creates economic opportunities, supports small businesses, and improves livelihoods. Electric mobility is no longer the future. It is the present, and Nigeria is poised to lead the transition.” Mr. Sane outlined the company’s key priorities for the coming year to include deepening of Infrastructure in focus states , accelerating the deployment of battery-swapping stations and service centres across Lagos, Ogun, and Oyo States to ensure riders have convenient access to support and services wherever they operate. On expansion of geographic presence, he said the company intends to extend its footprint beyond its current focus markets by entering additional states and bringing clean, affordable mobility solutions to more Nigerians. Spiro, he added, intend to enhance the country’s battery-swapping network to improve operational efficiency, reliability, and customer convenience. It also plans to deepen partnerships with financial institutions, logistics companies, and rider communities to make electric motorcycles and Battery-as-a-Service solutions more accessible to Nigerians. The Managing Director also said Spiro projects to scale local assembly operations, technical training programs, and after-sales support services to create employment opportunities, particularly for Nigerian youth and women. The event featured live product demonstrations, operational showcases, and unveiling of Spiro Ekon M1 Version 3

title: Russia to convene Arria-formula meeting on human rights violations in Ukraine on Oct. 14
body:
UN, October 14. /TASS/. The UN Security Council will hold an informal Arria-formula meeting at Russia’s initiative on October 14, focused on human rights violations in Ukraine, according to the Security Council’s work program.
The meeting is titled "Piercing the Blind Spots of Violations of International Humanitarian Law and International Human Rights Law in the Context of the Ukrainian Crisis."
The Arria-formula meetings provide interested council members an opportunity to engage in a direct dialogue with high representatives of governments and international organizations, as well as non-state parties, on matters with which they are concerned and which fall within the purview of responsibility of the Security Council. The process is named after Ambassador Diego Arria of Venezuela, who initiated the practice in 1992. The format suggests the participation of all members of the Security Council.

title: Shakhtar Dream of Champions League Return to Ukraine as London Keeps War in Spotlight
body:
Shakhtar Donetsk dream of one day taking Champions League football back to Ukraine but a temporary home at Chelsea’s Stamford Bridge helps keep the war-torn nation’s struggles “visible”, according to the club’s chief executive Sergey Palkin.
The Ukrainian champions entertain AEK Athens on Wednesday before hosting Sporting Lisbon, Fenerbahce and Real Madrid with west London their latest base.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Shakhtar were forced to flee their home city in 2014, just two years after hosting the European Championship, after war broke out in the Donbas region but could still play their European games in western Ukraine.
However, since Russia’s invasion in 2022, all European club matches and national team games have taken place abroad due to the security situation.
Poland, Germany and Slovenia have played host to Shakhtar in recent years, but Palkin believes the switch to “the football capital of the world” helps to keep the Ukrainian cause in the spotlight.
“We are representing our country and want to be visible for Ukraine,” Palkin told the BBC.
“We need support from the democratic world.
“We cannot fight alone. Part of our role when we play in London and other cities in Europe is to send these messages and remind people what’s going on.”
Yet the choice of Stamford Bridge has raised eyebrows.
Chelsea enjoyed a golden era of success under Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich between 2003 and 2022 before Britain sanctioned the oligarch for his close ties to the Kremlin and froze his assets.
Abramovich was forced to sell Chelsea as a result but retained the support of many fans who chanted his name following the British government’s action.
On the field, Shakhtar have proven remarkably resilient in the face of such upheaval.
They reached the semi-finals of the Conference League last season and the last four of the Europa League in 2020.
Despite the war, the club remain a hothouse for developing Brazilian talent with 14 players among the current squad from the South American nation.
Shakhtar have also maintained a reputation for nurturing up-and-coming young coaches.
Tottenham boss Roberto De Zerbi and Lyon coach Paulo Fonseca are among those to have taken charge during their period in exile.
Former Turkey and Atletico Madrid midfielder Arda Turan is the latest promising manager making waves at Shakhtar.
“We are looking on the positive side of being (in London) but we are dreaming of the day that we can play in Ukraine again,” Turan said on Tuesday.
“My players taught me how to live at war without showing excuses, always going on with the fight.
“I have an excellent group, not just the players but the staff, everyone in Ukraine.
“We are carrying the hopes of people. It’s not just for football purposes.”

title: Woman accused of stabbing husband and son to death at family resort: Complaint
body:
The incident occurred at the Great Wolf Lodge in the Poconos, police said.
A Pennsylvania woman allegedly stabbed her husband and 3-year-old son to death at a family resort in the Poconos before trying to take her own life, according to a criminal complaint.
Monroe County District Attorney Mike Mancuso called the incident a "violent domestic tragedy" while announcing homicide charges against the woman on Tuesday.
Authorities responded to a room at the Great Wolf Lodge in Scotrun, Pocono Township, on Monday for a suicidal caller, according to the complaint.
The 911 caller -- identified in the complaint as 27-year-old Metallica Rose Harrison of Towanda -- reported that she was "too weak to stab my neck" and "I need police," according to the complaint.
During the call, Harrison allegedly said she had knives but they were "not working," and that she needed "help dying," according to the complaint. When asked if she was alone, she allegedly said that "my husband and son are already gone in the bed," and, "They're already gone, I'm sorry," and did not at any point on the call request help for them, according to the complaint.
Harrison allegedly told responding officers that she "wanted to be with her husband and son," who were both found dead on mattresses in the room, according to the complaint. Her husband, Charles Harrison, had multiple stab wounds to his chest, while her son, identified in the complaint as T.H., appeared to have a single stab wound to his chest, according to the complaint.
Harrison had cuts on her left wrist and "superficial punctures about the neck," according to the complaint. She was transported to a local hospital for treatment of her injuries. During the ambulance ride, she allegedly said she took medication to help thin her blood and "expressed verbal frustration that the blood was clotting when [it] wasn't supposed to," the complaint stated.
"Everyday, I work so hard. To be the best person, the best mother, the best wife. It wasn't supposed to end like this. I was supposed to have my happy family. That's what I envisioned since I was a child," she allegedly said, according to the complaint.
When a detective advised Harrison of her Miranda warning and asked to speak to her about what brought her to the hospital, she allegedly responded that she was "suicidal, not stupid," and advised that she was not willing to speak with police, according to the complaint.
Authorities did not observe defensive wounds on her body, according to the complaint, which charges her with two counts of criminal homicide.
"This case is an isolated domestic tragedy and there is no threat to the community," the Pocono Township Police Department said in a statement .
Harrison was denied bail during her arraignment on Tuesday and is in custody awaiting a preliminary hearing, according to police. The online court docket does not list any attorney information for her at this time.
The Monroe County coroner said the autopsies for the victims are set to take place later this week.
According to the complaint, the family checked in to the lodge on Sept. 21, and were due to check out on Tuesday. A "large butcher kitchen knife" and smaller knife were found in the bathroom, according to the complaint. Resort staff confirmed that neither knife was the type kept by the lodge, according to the complaint.
The Great Wolf Lodge said the resort was "cooperating fully with local law enforcement as they conduct their investigation."
"We are deeply saddened and heartbroken by a tragic domestic incident that occurred yesterday in a guest room at our resort in the Pocono Mountains," the company said in a statement on Tuesday. "Our thoughts are with the family and loved ones of those affected."
If you are struggling with thoughts of suicide or worried about a friend or loved one, call or text the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 for free, confidential emotional support 24 hours a day, seven days a week.
24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

title: Who is Sofya Rozenfeld, the internationally renowned Russian ornithologist sentenced to three and a half years for donating to Alexey Navalny’s Anti-Corruption Foundation?
body: Sofya Rozenfeld has spent her life studying Arctic birds: traveling to Russia’s Far North on expeditions, following flocks of geese in a seaplane, and fighting to protect rare species. Now the scientist, one of Russia’s leading ornithologists with a doctorate in biological sciences, has been sentenced to three and a half years in a penal colony for two donations of 1,000 rubles each to the Anti-Corruption Foundation (FBK). Rozenfeld admitted guilt in part, saying she had been unable to cancel her recurring payments because she was on an expedition and out of contact. T-invariant examined why she refused to leave Russia, how her trial unfolded, and what Russian science stands to lose with her imprisonment. Meduza is translating the article with minor edits. ‘They put on quite a show’ Sofya Rozenfeld learned of the criminal investigation on December 5, 2025, shortly after returning from Israel, where she had been visiting her father. The 50-year-old scientist was charged with financing an “extremist” organization over two transfers of 1,000 rubles each to the Anti-Corruption Foundation in August and September 2021. “She was here in Israel visiting me. And she went back to Moscow sometime in late November. Literally the next day or the day after, they searched her home and made her agree in writing not to leave town without permission. They did leave her passports, though, and took copies of them,” Sofya’s father, Boris Rozenfeld, told T-invariant. During the search, officers seized her phone and two laptops. Then came months of waiting. Rozenfeld continued working and going on expeditions. “The first hearing was scheduled six months later. But the witness didn’t show up, so it was postponed. The next one was, too. Then they read out the charges. It was all very pleasant. Nice young women read out the charges, and the lovely investigator kept calling, asking how she was doing, how her health was, what was new. Everything was more or less civil. And there was no sign that anything terrible was coming. Though I think they’d decided everything long before. They put on quite a show,” said Sergey, a friend of Sofya Rozenfeld’s whose name has been changed. Before each hearing, Rozenfeld packed a bag in case she was taken into custody in the courtroom. “She knew a prison sentence was possible. But she thought a fine or forced labor was much more likely. The lawyers thought so, too. That’s where they went wrong. I suspect there are general instructions for cases like these. This is already the third recent case in which women have been given prison time,” Boris Rozenfeld said. “Of course it was stressful. But for some reason, we went to the last hearing feeling relaxed. They’d even let her go on an expedition before that, beyond the Arctic Circle, to the Polar Urals, to tag musk oxen. There was a TV report about her. She only got back on October 2,” Sergey said. “We last spoke a few weeks ago. She wasn’t making any plans, just waiting to see what would happen next. There was one hearing after another, and she came to every one with her things packed. But they kept being postponed. The last one ended with her being put in handcuffs,” Rozenfeld’s friend and former university classmate, science journalist Ilya Kolmanovsky, told T-invariant. Rozenfeld’s friends said the court was unhappy that she had admitted guilt only in part. “The judge and the prosecutor were extremely unhappy that Sonya had only partly admitted guilt. Here’s the situation she was in: She’s a field biologist who spends six months or more a year on expeditions. And most of those expeditions are to the Far North, where they’re working out in the field with only satellite communications. She had all the evidence showing that she was away on a research trip when FBK was declared an extremist organization — there was confirmation from the institute. But none of that mattered to the court. The lawyer even asked: Why go after her? The banks were transferring the money, knowing those payments had been deemed criminal, even though they’re perfectly capable of blocking unwanted and suspicious payments and regularly do so in other cases. Why not go after the bank? The judge let that pass. You could see that long speeches irritated him, period. It seemed none of the defense’s arguments had any bearing on his decision. He’d already received his instructions, and he wasn’t interested in the circumstances of the case,” said Anna, a friend of Sofya Rozenfeld’s whose name has been changed. “If she’d admitted guilt in full, they’d have knocked a couple of months off. There were three sentences like that this week. Before this, though, they’d left women alone. I think they’re all trying to curry favor now. I can’t see any other reason for such terrible sentences, literally ‘for three ears of grain’ [an allusion to a 1932 Stalin-era law under which people were imprisoned for taking a few ears of grain from collective farm fields],” Sergey said. In court, Rozenfeld did in fact admit guilt only in part: “I categorically deny, first, that I share extremist views and, second, that I had any criminal intent. When I decided to start supporting FBK, my sole motivation was to fight corruption. I believe we need all the help the public can give. Because even in my own work, in scientific research and conservation, I’ve seen the monstrous forms this evil can take. And I felt that any help in fighting corruption would be a good thing.” She acknowledged signing up for recurring donations to FBK. Because she was on a lengthy scientific expedition with no access to communications when the foundation was declared “extremist,” she canceled her donations as soon as she returned. Her lawyers even submitted a letter she had sent to FBK requesting the cancellation. But this did not reduce her sentence. On October 7, Rozenfeld was taken into custody in the courtroom at Moscow’s Gagarinsky District Court. She is now being held at Moscow’s Pechatniki pretrial detention center. She was not allowed to take her packed bag from the courthouse, so she initially had none of her personal belongings. ‘Geese are my thing’ Sofya Rozenfeld holds a doctorate in biological sciences and is a senior researcher at the Russian Bird Ringing Center at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of Ecology and Evolution. She is one of the best-known specialists in Arctic waterfowl. Rozenfeld has said she decided to become a biologist when she was just 5. She grew up in a Moscow family: Her father, Boris Rozenfeld, is a mathematician; her mother is an engineer; and her grandfather, Iosif Rozenfeld, was a full member of the Academy of Sciences with a doctorate in chemistry. Sofya attended a school specializing in French. In the late 1980s, the family moved to Israel, but a year and a half later, Rozenfeld, then 15, returned to Moscow. “I didn’t think I had the right to force a 15-year-old to stay. When we were leaving, she said she didn’t want to go. And really, why would she want to leave? Everything was great, she had friends at school, and it was a good school with an intensive French program. And anyway, why the hell are you going anywhere? You have everything: an apartment, a car, jobs. I worked at the Academy of Sciences. And I told her, ‘Listen, we can’t leave you here on your own. But if you want to come back, I won’t stand in your way.’ I promised her that. And a year and a half later, she did come back. Of course we were worried, especially during the coup. That was 1991. Yes, fun times. But then everything was fine,” Boris Rozenfeld said. “Her parents talked her into going for at least a year, to see what life was like there. She went. And a year later, she packed her suitcase and said, ‘I’m leaving. I don’t want to abandon my country at a difficult time.’ She came back, finished school, and enrolled in the biology department. She’s a very determined person,” Anna said. In Moscow, Sofya lived with her grandmother and aunt and, by her own account, was constantly bringing animals home. Besides a dog, the apartment housed snakes, frogs, fish, and birds. In 1993, Rozenfeld enrolled in Moscow State University’s biology department, choosing zoology. “We met in our first year. I heard about her before I saw her: People were saying there was someone very unusual in our class. You could tell there were, well, students, and then there was someone you already knew was a scientist. For her, science was a calling, something she was deeply committed to,” Ilya Kolmanovsky said. At university, Rozenfeld took up photography because she wanted to photograph birds in the Arctic. She also played guitar, studied languages, and pursued show jumping at a professional level. But polar birds remained her greatest passion from her student years onward. “Geese are my thing. These birds amazed me: Their unique social behavior sets them apart from other birds. Geese are like people. All geese and swans are monogamous. Pairs stay together for many years, sometimes even for life. The young always make their first migration with their parents, who show them where to fly. Those bonds sometimes last for many years, too,” she said . Rozenfeld began traveling to the Arctic for fieldwork while she was still a student. “She was the master of those enormous expanses, where there isn’t another person for thousands of kilometers. She could go somewhere in Kazakhstan and sleep in a tent where, on a spring night, it’s minus 16 Celsius [about 3 Fahrenheit]. And see 15,000 geese through her binoculars that no one before her had seen. Make a discovery, find out that there’s a huge population stopping there during migration. She’s a scientist of enormous stature. From day one, you could tell she was working on something extraordinarily significant. And anyone who has ever met her has enormous respect for that,” Kolmanovsky said. From Meduza’s archives ‘Yes, I regret going’: Russian IT specialist returned to Russia to visit his ailing father and was charged with treason over €30 sent to his ex-girlfriend in Ukraine. ‘This must be a terrible mistake’ Russia doesn’t have enough doctors — but that hasn’t stopped the authorities from arresting physicians on dubious charges What comes next The Russian authorities want to designate Alexey Navalny’s political and anti-corruption network as ‘extremist.’ This would be the legal fallout. In 1998, Rozenfeld began doctoral studies at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ A. N. Severtsov Institute of Ecology and Evolution, where she still works. Her main research areas are waterfowl ecology and migration, as well as migratory bird conservation. During migration, birds travel tens of thousands of kilometers, crossing borders between countries with different conservation laws. In 2016, Rozenfeld and her colleagues began following flocks of birds in a homemade seaplane, photographing and counting them. The light aircraft can fly at the same speed as the birds and take off from and land on water, ice, and small patches of ground. The data allow scientists to estimate population sizes, identify threats to their survival, and develop recommendations for protecting migratory species. “Sonya has devoted her whole life to migratory birds. She actually followed them by plane. She’s an incredible expert in this field. That’s the kind of person she is. There was no point talking politics with her. Of course she understood everything. All the terrible injustice around her. But her priority is migratory birds. That’s what she lives for, and she can talk about nature for hours,” Andrey Rostovtsev, a friend of Sofya Rozenfeld’s father and a co-founder of the independent online community Dissernet, told T-invariant. “She’s a very well-known biologist who worked on joint projects in the U.S. and Canada, and French researchers took part in her expeditions. She presented at all the most important conferences in her field. Sonya is devoted to wildlife conservation. She’s a real patriot, not a fake one. She fought to protect all the rare animal species in the Red Data Book and to eliminate exemptions in hunting laws. In the end, she managed to convince the State Duma that she was right. She’s an incredible fighter,” Anna said. Rozenfeld was the first to count migratory birds systematically. Previously, researchers had estimated their numbers by counting individual birds in one area, then extrapolating the results across the entire territory. Accurate counts are essential both to understanding species’ spatial ecology and to conserving their populations, said Alexandra Panyutina, a researcher at Tel Aviv University’s School of Zoology: “Say you have a place on the ocean coast where huge numbers of migratory birds gather. And it’s a crucial site. If something is disrupted there, it will affect bird populations in many countries, across an enormous area. Disrupting migration routes and stopover sites changes where a species lives and how many birds there are. That’s why research in this area is so important.” Waterfowl are a difficult group to study: They are hunted, which affects their population sizes and reproduction. Many species also live in remote northern regions where field research is difficult. “There’s a strong Russian group there working on shorebirds. And the people we called the ‘goose people.’ That’s it. Sonya is the scientific mind behind all this work on waterfowl. And you can’t replace someone of that caliber. She’s the person who designs the research, who has the whole thing in her head. You can’t replace her with a robot. When a researcher leaves, no one automatically takes over their work. And an education isn’t enough — you need to understand where research on that particular problem stands and know who else is doing what. And of course, no one will be able to take over her research in three and a half years,” Panyutina said. Sofya Rozenfeld had big plans for the coming months: filming “Gusi Rossii” (“The Geese of Russia”) and working on an atlas of geese. “It’s a comprehensive atlas with descriptions, illustrations, and maps. It’s supposed to cover every goose species found in Russia. She left us all her contacts. We have to finish this work without her,” Sergey said. ‘You can’t study geese from prison’ Rozenfeld’s friends and colleagues said she adamantly refused to leave Russia. “There are things she’s completely unbending about. Leaving is one of them. For her, it was absolutely not up for discussion, non-negotiable. She understood all the risks, but nothing was more frightening than leaving and finding herself unable to return to the birds she studies. She can’t do her research anywhere else, because the species she studies live only in the Russian Arctic,” Kolmanovsky said. Alexandra Panyutina tried more than once to talk to Rozenfeld about leaving Russia, but Rozenfeld avoided the subject. “To me, the situation was perfectly clear from the start. But in all that time, I never managed to talk to her about it. She was very afraid of being set up. Especially since her lawyers were telling her the outlook was good, because she was only required to get permission before leaving town, and she was a woman with a doctorate,” Panyutina said. According to Panyutina, serious research into waterfowl migration is currently possible in Russia and Canada. “Until relatively recently, you could work freely in Russia. That’s not the case in most other countries. Scientists face restrictions at every turn — any work requires an incredible number of permits and licenses, and special funding for specific tasks. Besides, moving to another country almost always means a huge step down for a scientist. Here, you’re a leading specialist; there, you’re basically nobody. You start working as an assistant in some lab. No one’s going to give you your own lab right away. It’s very hard to get the chance to do your own research. But then again, you can’t study geese from prison either,” Panyutina said. The administration of the Russian Academy of Sciences’ A. N. Severtsov Institute of Ecology and Evolution is not commenting on Sofya Rozenfeld’s sentence. “They gave the court a good character reference. But after the sentence, they decided to save their own skins. Of course I think they’ll fire her. How can they not fire her if she isn’t coming to work? They’ll fire her. Maybe they’ll wait for the appeal,” Boris Rozenfeld said. Alexandra Panyutina has little hope for the appeal. In her view, Rozenfeld will not be the last scientist to face political persecution. “Fortunately, the FSB [Russia’s Federal Security Service] hasn’t come for biologists yet. Things are already very bad in physics. I don’t know a single sane person who would go into hypersonics today. You’d have to be suicidal. In Sonya’s case, we can’t say she’s being persecuted as a scientist. We’re talking about the persecution of a citizen who cares about her country’s future. What’s more, she was simply a victim of circumstances. When FBK was banned, she was on a remote expedition with no access to communications and couldn’t even find out about the ban on donations, let alone cancel them. As soon as she returned, she canceled all the payments. So she didn’t break any Russian law. There’s some hope that on appeal, the court will take into account the importance of Sofya’s research and her important role in the Russian Academy of Sciences,” she said. “I feel like this state is now devouring everything alive, at home and abroad. The regime sees a threat in people who can put two and two together and refuse to compromise their judgment. Scientists have things they value above all else: science, nature, geese, and zoology. Many people can compromise, but scientists can be extraordinarily stubborn in this respect. What happens next to Russian science? I think it faces what the late ayatollah called a ‘jihad of knowledge,’ in which every scientist has to prove their usefulness to the Islamic Revolution in its struggle against the West. Now all scientists and all fields of science have to prove their usefulness in the war Russia has declared on civilization,” Kolmanovsky said. According to Haaretz, Israel declined to intervene in Rozenfeld’s case, despite her having an Israeli passport. After she was charged, she sought help from the Israeli Embassy in Moscow, but was told that Israeli authorities could not intervene in decisions by Russian law enforcement because she also holds Russian citizenship. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
