But the main question that lies ahead is: would a potential mandate from FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro differ significantly from his fatherâs? Or can Lula still pursue his agenda in the face of such an adverse governing framework in 2027? If FlÃ¡vio wins, he will enjoy much more goodwill from markets and the legislative houses (Chamber of Deputies and Senate) for his projects. He is clear about seeking the annulment of his fatherâs 2025 judicial conviction for plotting a coup whilst allies foresee a pardoning for those involved in the invasion of Congress on 8 January 2023 . Some experts raised concerns about the future of the judiciaryâs independence as the Senate could impeach Supreme Court justices and PL now has a third of the house. Regionally, FlÃ¡vio will also enjoy a much more favourable ideological environment , as most countries in South America are now led by right-wing governments.
Internationally, the scenario is more blurred. China is in direct technological, resource and trade competition with the US, especially in Latin America, becoming Brazilâs main trade partner in 2009 . Recently, China has expanded its focus to mining, infrastructure and energy Chinaâs MMG agreed to acquire Anglo Americanâs nickel operations in 2025, and China Nonferrous Metal Mining Group acquired MineraÃ§Ã£o Taboca for tin and niobium extraction. In terms of infrastructure, Chinaâs CRRC in a consortium with a Brazilian company will build an intercity railway between SÃ£o Paulo and Campinas. Therefore, reducing the Chinese influx of investments in favour of the US (especially in critical minerals) will be a tough task in case of a victory for FlÃ¡vio. Likewise, an expansion of Chinese investment in case of Lulaâs victory could also be quite difficult, as he will face the widest opposition to his government. The relationship with Europe will be marked by the implementation of the EUâMercosur trade agreement and by how environmental protection is championed by the future administration , as deforestation is a non-trade barrier for the EU . With the US, organised crime and tariff negotiations might dominate bilateral dialogues. In 2025, Trump imposed 50% tariffs on several Brazilian exports alleging unbalanced trade and political persecution of Jair Bolsonaro . Although the US Supreme Court annulled Trumpâs presidential order , tariffs returned in 2026 and both countries agreed to create a working group to negotiate a relief deal.
The strong dominance of right-wing parties in legislative houses and a potential reduction of judiciary counterweight will not stop the advance of a conservative agenda, regardless of who occupies the Alvorada Palace. If a FlÃ¡vio victory might make legislativeâexecutive relationships much less convoluted in comparison to a Lula victory, the expectation is that clashes with the judiciary will be the main source of tension. In any scenario, Brazilâs following years promise breathtaking events with local and global repercussions.

title: Industrial Next wants factory robots to switch tasks in minutes, not weeks
body:
In most factories, automation is fixed: robots and machines are programmed for one specific task and product. Changing a line means reprogramming and physical retooling, or swapping out equipment, which can take weeks or months. San Francisco-based Industrial Next says it’s changing that.
The startup, which presented today on the Startup Battlefield stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, builds AI-driven, self-contained robotic stations powered by proprietary foundation models that connect vision, task context, and motion. The company says this lets a production line be retooled in minutes rather than weeks without traditional programming. The goal is to let manufacturers automate complex and delicate tasks that traditionally require human labor.
The company announced onstage that it’s partnering with BMW Group Technology Office to evaluate Industrial Next’s AI-powered dexterous manipulation for manufacturing.
Industrial Next was founded in 2021 by Lukas Pankau and Allen Pan, both of whom previously worked at Tesla. Pankau served as a lead electrical architect at Tesla before moving on to Waymo. Pan led Tesla’s autonomous factory efforts and later became a chief architect at autonomous driving company Neolix.
The pair came up with the idea for Industrial Next while working together at Tesla. Pankau’s first encounter with Pan was literally tripping over him as Pan was asleep on a factory catwalk after pulling an all-nighter. Although the two didn’t get along at first, they soon realized they shared an obsession with getting things done and had complementary skills.
After years of watching cutting-edge vehicle and self-driving technology get held back by decades-old factory equipment, the founders realized that manufacturing needed to be rebuilt.
“We had all these fancy things that we could do on cars. I could run machine learning algorithms to design a car for me. But I couldn’t figure out how to program a robot, and this was pretty common for engineers at Tesla,” Pankau said. “You had this massive divide, right? You had people who are really good at what they’re doing — designing cars and designing self-driving systems — and then you had them effectively stumped at the factory looking at this equipment from the 1980s. And so we started rethinking what this should look like using the technology that we have today and using everything that we know today.”
The two kept thinking about their frustrations with industrial equipment even after moving on to their next jobs. They stayed in touch, often reminiscing about the machines that never functioned the way they wanted, and eventually decided they could do better.
“I was at Waymo at the time, kind of bored out of my mind because I was missing that pace of Tesla,” Pankau said. Pan, he added, was in a similar position at Momenta, a developer of self-driving systems in China. Pan recalled their conclusion: “We’re like, we’re not getting any younger, and we’re still obviously passionate about it. We still keep complaining about industrial technology. Like, this is three years later, we should start the company.”
Pankau notes that traditional industrial robots are typically programmed to perform highly specific, repeatable tasks. As a result, even a small change in the process or product can cause the robot to fail or trigger costly downtime, which forces manufacturers to simplify their products for repeatability.
Making robots truly flexible presents a different challenge. They need enormous amounts of training data and, unlike AI models trained on the internet, robotics lacks the vast datasets needed to teach machines how to perform complex physical tasks.
“We can make robots do all these cool things like dance around, because there’s data for that, but we can’t make them assemble high-precision things,” Pankau explained. “This is where we’ve made a lot of progress on using simulated environments to do these high-precision and high-dexterity tasks. The secret sauce for the robots that we have is that we have given them an understanding of the process in general, but we build that understanding using an extremely high-fidelity simulation engine that is close to the real dynamics to where we can let the robot do these kinds of high-precision tasks almost without seeing the parts at all.”
In other words, the robots practice in a highly detailed virtual world that closely mimics real-world physics. Industrial Next’s robotic stations can be reconfigured, combined, and redeployed across product lines. New tasks are taught through simulation and demonstration, rather than hard-coded scripts.
Pankau explained that some of the startup’s workstations are already used in making one of the world’s most popular smartphones. They handle tasks that manufacturers had tried and failed to automate for years, such as threading a delicate flex cable and snapping a tiny connector cap into place. (He wasn’t at liberty to disclose the customer.) He also described a “film peeling” station, where their AI-powered robots strip protective film off camera modules and buttons at or above human speed with 100% accuracy, even when moved to a new phone model and production line they have never seen.
“We started this company because that is the kind of performance that we wish we had at Tesla, where we were bypassing robot stations because we couldn’t program them effectively enough using traditional technologies,” Pankau said. “Now we want to take this to more complicated tasks than just building a phone. We ultimately want to take this to building a full car end-to-end without any human touching ever.”
To check out more of the Startup Battlefield — along with a slate of established founders and VCs whose takes on the industry you won’t want to miss — join us at Disrupt , happening this week in downtown San Francisco.

title: Future Economy Will Reward Skills, Not Certificates, Jamiu Tells Graduates
body: Gbenga Sodeinde in Ado Ekiti Chairman of the Ekiti State House of Assembly Committee on Youths, Sports Development and Job Creation, and former Deputy Speaker of the state House of Assembly, Rt. Hon. Hakeem Jamiu, has urged Nigerian undergraduates to look beyond academic certificates and equip themselves with practical skills, warning that the future economy will reward competence, innovation and entrepreneurship rather than paper qualifications. Jamiu stated this while delivering a lecture titled ‘Equipping Ekiti Youth for the Modern Economy’ at the Bamidele Olumilua University of Education, Science and Technology (BOUESTI), Ikere-Ekiti. Addressing students and members of the university community, the lawmaker said that the rapidly changing global economy has made it imperative for young people to embrace digital literacy, vocational skills, entrepreneurship and critical thinking to remain relevant in an increasingly competitive labour market. He stressed that while academic degrees remain important, they are no longer sufficient to guarantee employment or career success. “The future belongs to graduates who possess relevant skills, can solve problems, create value and adapt to changing realities. Certificates may open doors, but it is skills, innovation and character that will keep those doors open,” he said. Jamiu urged students to begin preparing for life after graduation by acquiring marketable skills alongside their academic pursuits, noting that employers now place greater value on competence, creativity and the ability to deliver results. He encouraged the students to take advantage of opportunities in technology, agriculture, manufacturing, the creative industry and entrepreneurship, describing them as sectors driving economic growth and job creation across the world. The lawmaker also challenged educational institutions to complement academic learning with practical training capable of producing graduates who are job creators rather than job seekers. According to him, Nigeria’s economic future depends largely on a generation of young people equipped with the skills needed to compete globally and contribute meaningfully to national development. Jamiu further urged governments, educational institutions and the private sector to strengthen collaboration in providing platforms that expose young people to innovation, digital technology, mentorship and enterprise development. He maintained that investing in youth skills development remained one of the most effective ways of tackling unemployment, poverty and other socio-economic challenges confronting the country. The lecture attracted students, academic staff and other stakeholders, who commended Jamiu for highlighting the urgent need to align higher education with the realities of the 21st-century economy. Participants described the session as insightful and inspiring, saying it challenged students to rethink success beyond the acquisition of certificates and embrace lifelong learning, innovation and skills development as pathways to sustainable careers.

title: US Army suspends longtime hometown recruiter assistance program, faces cancellation
body: For years, Army recruiters have enjoyed flagging a special perk for new Advanced Individual Training graduates: an opportunity to return to their hometowns for 14 days with pay prior to their first duty station, with the understanding they’ll help local recruiters during that time and tell the Army story. But according to the head of U.S. Army Recruiting Command, the new soldiers struggled to hold up their end of the deal. The service’s decades-old Hometown Recruiter Assistance Program has been suspended, Lt. Gen. Johnny Davis confirmed at a forum hosted by the Association of the United States Army. And while he said it’s being “looked at” for possible next steps, he also described the built-in problems keeping the service from getting its money’s worth. “I would tell you, when the program was initiated and really delivered to the Army years ago and executed, that we had some good return on investment — about, you know, one or two percent,” Davis said in response to a question at the forum. “But, bottom line, what we’ve learned over the years is that 20, 30,000 young superstars, when they were headed back home, were good; they got to go home,” he added. “But they weren’t really working with the recruiters as much as we wanted them to.” Davis said leaders understood the “human element” of what was happening, in that new graduates were eager to reconnect with family and friends in what amounted to additional uncharged leave. But, he added, the Army had to consider what it was getting out of the arrangement. Likewise, he said, the Army has in the past allowed National Guard and Reserve soldiers to return home for non-charged leave during the holiday break known as the Christmas Exodus on the understanding that they would support Army recruiting as ambassadors during that time. “During that Christmas holiday, was there a lot of recruiters in the recruiting stations working with them? No,” Davis said. “So we’re really thinking through: is this return on investment, and is it worth the cost to the Army? Or can we take those funds and spend them in other ways to help our men and women.” Davis said leaders were now “looking at other ways” to help soldiers get coveted hometown leave apart from the hometown recruiting program. Army recruiting social media pages began discussing the suspension of the Hometown Recruiter Assistance Program in January, though the service has not publicly addressed the move until now. HRAP dates to the 1980s. In its most recent form, soldiers had to be selected and approved for the program by a company commander. In a 2022 Army news release, a recruiting center station commander in Missouri, Staff Sgt. Colton Dunbar, said the success of the program came down to “how the soldiers are leveraged.” “We try to get the most out of them while they’re here by bringing them to the high school where they graduated and their communities to show everyone that this person was in your community six months ago as a civilian, but look at them now,” he said in the release. ”It helps to break down any barriers because they know that person in uniform — it helps show we are people just like everybody else.” But from early on in the program, a lack of success metrics and specific service requirements have limited HRAP’s success. A 1983 study from the U.S. Army Research Institute for the Behavioral and Social Sciences found that it was hard to evaluate the usefulness of program participants, because it was hard to track their impact outside of foot traffic to the recruiting office. It also suggested, though, that there were nevertheless non-quantifiable benefits to having new soldiers present and visible in their hometown. “Aides are credited for individuals they brought to the recruiter who subsequently enlist, but the total effect of the aide’s efforts is more subtle than the sum of their recruits,” the study found. “For example, aides can ‘plant seeds’ or lay the groundwork months in advance of an enlistment decision and receive no credit for an enlistment that occurs months after his or her departure.” The Army hasn’t said when it will make final decisions on the way forward for HRAP.

title: Firm Unveils Customer Service Week Marketing Campaign
body: Ebere Nwoji CHI Life Assurance Limited, a subsidiary of Consolidated Hallmark Holdings Plc, has unveiled a new brand marketing campaign titled The Legacy: Golden Key of Assurance”. The company said this is part of activities marking this year’s Customer Service Week. CHI said the campaign, built around the promise “Always There. When Legacy Matters,” positioned CHI Life as the golden key to protecting what matters today while helping individuals and families secure a more confident future. Managing Director/CEO, CHI Life Assurance Limited, Mr Tope Ilesanmi , said the campaign highlighted CHI Life’s assurance and wealth preservation solutions, including its Rent Secure Plan and Value Plus Plan, designed to help customers protect their financial aspirations and plan for the future. Ilesanmi, said CHI Life placed its own people at the centre of the creative execution, adding that ahead of the launch, employees were invited to submit their photographs and videos for possible inclusion in the campaign. He said the response exceeded expectations, with staff members contributing enthusiastically to the initiative. According to Ilesanmi, the selected entries have been transformed into cinematic, movie-inspired campaign visuals featuring the real faces and voices of CHI Life employees. He said the result was a campaign that sought to tell the story of legacy through the people who represent the brand every day.

title: The true story behind Moscow’s new big-budget racing movie: How Imperial Russia’s first Monte Carlo Rally team crossed Europe in 1912 without a windshield
body: Andrey Nagel and Vadim Mikhailov in Monaco. 1912 On October 8, Ilya Malanin’s film “Bitva motorov” (“Battle of the Motors”) opened in Russian theaters. Starring Yura Borisov and Ivan Yankovsky, it tells the story of a Russian team that competed in the 1912 Monte Carlo Rally in a Russo-Balt car. The historical adventure drama draws heavily on real events, though its creators emphasize that it takes plenty of artistic liberties. Writing for Meduza, history educator Andrey Aksenov, creator of the podcasts “Zakat imperii” (“Twilight of the Empire”) and “Vremya i dengi” (“Time and Money”), explains how the race actually unfolded. The film’s protagonist is race car driver and Avtomobil magazine publisher Andrey Nagel (Ivan Yankovsky). He dreams of creating a Russian car, but no one believes in his idea. Officials laugh at him, as does his competitor Gustav List (Yehezkel Lazarov), a supplier of German Benz cars. Nagel travels to Riga, where he persuades Mikhail Shidlovsky (Alexey Guskov), chairman of the board of the Russian-Baltic Wagon Works, to build a car. During its development, Nagel meets Dmitry Bondarev, a taciturn mechanic. Together, they assemble a team of fellow enthusiasts and try to build the Russo-Balt. When the project threatens to fall apart, Nagel decides to enter the famous Monte Carlo Rally, a 3,000-kilometer (about 1,860-mile) race, to prove the Russo-Balt’s worth. He and Bondarev set off for Monaco from St. Petersburg, getting stuck in snow and mud along the way but heroically finishing the rally. Reviewers say the makers of “Battle of the Motors” take liberties with history. The most conspicuous departure is that Nagel’s actual teammate was Avtomobil employee Vadim Mikhailov, rather than Bondarev. The film’s main villains are foreigners scheming against the Russian project. Emperor Nicholas II (Sergey Volkov) is a charming jokester — and a “deus ex machina”: “Nothing short of a fairy-tale vision of an ideal government in the Russian Empire,” RBC said. The film “plays it safe” with historical parallels. The race itself takes up the final 30 to 40 minutes; the opening focuses on the drama of building the car. The filmmakers care far more about the technical details of creating the Russo-Balt than about the characters’ relationships or politics, Kinopoisk said . Several authentic cars were built specifically for the shoot using actual blueprints. Why was the 1912 Monte Carlo Rally important for Russia’s auto industry? Today, the Monte Carlo Rally is just one round of the World Rally Championship , but a century ago, the race followed entirely different — and surprising — rules. Its aims were different, too. In 1912, a Russian team entered the rally in a Russo-Balt. One reason the event became legendary was that it marked the first appearance of a Russian team in the race. Drivers Andrey Nagel and Vadim Mikhailov were in the most technologically advanced and fastest car ever built in the Russian Empire. Their route was the longest : It began in St. Petersburg and ended in Monaco, covering about 3,200 kilometers (1,990 miles). They traveled in winter in an open car, without detailed road maps. Both the car and its drivers needed painstaking preparation. Their result was a major achievement for Russian motorsport. Here’s how it all worked. Were cars really a luxury back then? In early 20th-century Russia, cars were no longer a novelty. They could be seen in every Russian city, from St. Petersburg to Verny, now Almaty. Still, they remained an expensive, prestigious way to get around. A car owner was seen as either someone of high social standing or an enthusiast for technological progress. The average worker in the Russian Empire earned about 20 rubles a month. A standard Russo-Balt Model C cost about 8,000 rubles — a hefty sum even for the middle class in the capital. Only 350 of these cars were ever made. The cheapest car of the day, the Ford Model T, cost 2,500 rubles, also well beyond many people’s means. In the major cities, Moscow and St. Petersburg, streetcars were the main form of transportation. Horse-drawn cabs came second, and cars third, though most people preferred to walk. City streets were littered with manure and horseshoe nails, and sometimes even dead horses. The nails seriously hampered the spread of cars by puncturing tires. Some places even introduced special vehicles equipped with electromagnets to pick up nails from the ground every day. Nizhny Novgorod, 1898 Alongside private cars, taxi fleets were already appearing in cities. At the time the film is set, St. Petersburg had about 300 taxis and Moscow roughly 80. There were trucks, too: Some businesses, such as Blandov’s dairy company, bought them to deliver food, in large part for the marketing benefits. This helped the company build a reputation as modern, technologically advanced, and “forward-looking.” In 1911, when Nagel and Mikhailov set off for Monaco in their Russo-Balt, Russia manufactured only one make of car: the Russo-Balt itself. The Russian-Baltic Wagon Works in Riga had been assembling the cars since 1909. Production was small-scale: The factory specialized mainly in railroad cars, while automobiles remained a promising sideline. Mikhail Shidlovsky, chairman of the board, oversaw the automobile business; in 1908, he had recruited a chief designer from Switzerland. A Model C 24/55 before the start of the rally in Monaco. Andrey Nagel and Vadim Mikhailov are in the car. 1912 In 1912, another manufacturer emerged in St. Petersburg: Ivan Puzyrev. He intended to build a technologically sophisticated car using only Russian components. His cars did have some innovative features, including an aluminum gearbox with a novel design. Before World War I began, however, Puzyrev managed to produce only about 40 cars. Russia lagged disastrously behind Europe and the United States in both car production and use. In 1913, the newspaper Moskovskiye Vedomosti reported that the United States had 196 factories, Britain 100, and Germany 50. Russia had just two, and the total number of cars ever produced in the country was no more than 600. Ford’s factory in Michigan sold 70,000 cars in 1911 alone. By 1914, it had sped up its assembly line so much that the famous Ford Model T could be built in an hour and a half. Annual sales reached 300,000 cars. At that point, people in Russia owned no more than 8,000 cars altogether. Why hold long-distance motoring runs? Long-distance motoring runs are now a thing of the past, but in the early 20th century, they were very important. The biggest problem with cars at the time was reliability. Traveling several hundred kilometers without a single breakdown was almost inconceivable. Imagine being stranded in the forests around Pskov with a broken carburetor when the nearest repair shops were in St. Petersburg and Riga. Then there were punctured tires: Changing wheels along the way was routine. These problems put off potential buyers. Organizers held long-distance runs to demonstrate cars’ reliability and show that the roads were passable. If a car could make it from St. Petersburg to Sicily and back, it could certainly get you to your summer house in Kuokkala or Malakhovka — you could go ahead and buy one. Cars were also still a rarity in the provinces in the early 20th century. Enthusiasts and car geeks wanted to show that automobiles were fast, convenient, and fashionable, rather than frightening or dangerous. Motoring runs and races also attracted tourists. That was precisely why, in 1909, Prince Albert I of Monaco came up with the idea of holding an international competition that would finish in Monaco. Monte Carlo was a popular resort among the aristocracy and the bourgeoisie. Motorsport was a fashionable and, just as importantly, expensive hobby that would draw wealthy visitors to his principality, he reasoned. A poster for the 1911 Monte Carlo Rally Winter was also the off-season in Monaco, so a major event would help fill Monte Carlo’s hotels and casinos. And so it did — which was why the Russian team had to travel from St. Petersburg to Monaco in January. They completed the journey in a little over eight days. The rules of the Monte Carlo Rally In its early years, the rally had rather surprising rules. You could enter from any city and start right from home. All participants had to finish in Monaco, and teams were expected to arrive at roughly the same time. Yes, this bears no resemblance to racing as we know it. Andrey Nagel and Vadim Mikhailov started in St. Petersburg and had the longest route. Their main rivals, the Germans Karl von Esmarch in a Dürkopp and Julius Beutler in a Berliet, set off from Berlin several days later. The team from Turin had the shortest journey. Each team’s starting time was calculated separately: The judges assumed an average speed of 10 kilometers per hour (about 6 mph), meaning teams would need to cover 240 kilometers (about 150 miles) a day. Remember that many roads were unpaved then, and in Russia, they were covered in snow to boot. Rally participants before the start in Paris But arriving first wasn’t enough to win. The winner was determined by total points. Teams earned points for the distance traveled — a category Nagel and Mikhailov automatically won — as well as for speed, additional passengers, and the car’s condition at the finish. To earn the maximum points for speed, teams had to average more than 25 kilometers per hour (about 16 mph). That may not sound very fast, but it was the average for the entire journey, including stops. Nagel and Mikhailov drove for roughly 14 to 18 hours a day: They had to eat, sleep, and pull the Russo-Balt out of snowdrifts. Each person in the car other than the driver earned two extra points. Some rally entrants didn’t drive themselves: They rode in the passenger seat while hired chauffeurs took the wheel. The car’s appearance and elegance at the finish were also judged. Remember, these cars were intended for very wealthy people, and the rally was essentially an advertising campaign. Repairs to the engine and chassis components were forbidden along the way. Those parts were therefore sealed at the start, and officials inspected each team at designated checkpoints, where they also recorded its time. The Russian crew: Who were Andrey Nagel and Vadim Mikhailov — and Bondarev, who appears in the film? Nagel Andrey Platonovich Nagel was born in 1877 and was 34 at the time of the race. A car geek who promoted motoring to the public, he entered his first race while still at university. After graduating, he founded Russia’s first publication devoted entirely to cars, a magazine simply called Avtomobil. Before that, you could read about cars in sports magazines, but more often in the tabloids, which gleefully recounted every collision with a carriage and every pedestrian run over. City dwellers saw cars as luxurious but frightening status symbols. Owners were viewed with suspicion: A rich man had connections and could cover up any incident, while an enthusiast was crazy — and it wasn’t clear which of the two was more dangerous. It’s no coincidence that in “Zolotoy telenok” (“The Golden Calf”), Adam Kozlevich complained that the only people who rode in his taxi were embezzlers who drank vodka and swam naked in the moonlight. The wealthy usually hired chauffeurs because driving was difficult then. It involved more than shifting gears and turning the wheel: A chauffeur had to understand how the car was built and be able to fix everything from the gearbox to the acetylene lamps . Andrey Nagel drove himself. In 1907, Nagel and Avtomobil held Russia’s first auto show. The magazine proudly reported: For the first time in our country, the mainstream press and people outside motoring circles took an interest in the machines of the future. Throughout May, newspaper columns were filled with articles about automobiles, most of them favorable — something that had never happened before. Before the exhibition, newspapers discussed automobiles only to accuse chauffeurs of running over ordinary citizens; they covered nothing else. Ivan Petrovich Puzyrev, who would later establish Russia’s second carmaking operation, also attended the exhibition. He was so impressed that he decided to go into the automobile business: At the show, he signed a contract with a German parts supplier and became its distributor in Russia. In the early 20th century, Russia was a promising market for European companies, so they were happy to take part in Nagel’s auto show. Moscow, 1908 Afterward, Andrey Nagel began taking part regularly in long-distance motoring runs. He drove to Paris and back, organized a race from St. Petersburg to Riga, and won a gold medal in the imperial race from the capital to Kyiv and back. In 1910, he traveled from Russia to Italy with the famous photographer Karl Bulla, climbed Mount Vesuvius, and returned through Germany. Vadim Mikhailov accompanied him on this trip, too. Nagel drove to Italy in a brand-new Russo-Balt Model C 24/30. The following year, the Riga factory would create a special racing version of its car, and Nagel would propose a partnership to enter the Monte Carlo Rally. His excellent relationship with the factory’s chairman, Mikhail Shidlovsky, also helped. Mikhailov We know almost nothing about Vadim Mikhailov, Andrey Nagel’s teammate in the race. His participation is, in fact, the most notable detail of his life. He worked at Avtomobil and was one of the very first car owners in St. Petersburg — and that’s about all. Apparently, this is why engineer Dmitry Bondarev took his place in “Battle of the Motors.” Bondarev, by contrast, was every bit as legendary as Andrey Nagel. Bondarev Dmitry Bondarev was the same age as Nagel and headed the automobile department at the Russian-Baltic Wagon Works. In 1911, Nagel invited Bondarev to join him in the Monte Carlo Rally, but the engineer declined. Bondarev organized Russo-Balt production, helped design the largest aircraft of World War I, the Ilya Muromets, and, just before the revolution, became director of the AMO automobile factory then under construction in Moscow. In Soviet times, it became known as ZiL. Bondarev lived in the Soviet Union. In 1937, he was accused of belonging to a counterrevolutionary Right-Trotskyist terrorist organization and then shot. Nagel emigrated after the revolution and died in 1956. What did Nagel and Mikhailov drive? A closer look at the cars Nagel and Mikhailov made their journey in a heavily modified Russo-Balt Model C 24/30 convertible. What does 24/30 mean, anyway? It was a common designation that everyone understood at the time. The 24 stood for the engine’s rated horsepower , and the 30 for its maximum horsepower. Those were good figures for the period. Racing, however, required improvements. Andrey Nagel and Vadim Mikhailov in Monaco. 1912 The car was upgraded in several stages. First, to boost power, engineers increased the engine’s displacement from 4.5 to 5 liters, lightened the body, and installed another fuel tank. The racing Russo-Balt’s engine could now produce up to 50 horsepower. In tests in May 1911, the car reached 91.5 kilometers per hour (about 57 mph); a standard Russo-Balt could manage 75 to 80 kilometers per hour (about 47 to 50 mph). Several more changes followed. For example, the pistons were replaced with aluminum ones, a rarity even in Europe. This further increased the engine’s output to 55 horsepower. A French carburetor was then installed. In this configuration, the Russo-Balt could reach 113 kilometers per hour (about 70 mph). To help it get through snowdrifts, the designers made it possible to fit two additional wheels to the rear axle — the rally rules didn’t prohibit this. Electric headlights replaced the acetylene ones, and special skis were packed in the trunk. These could be attached to the wheels and, in theory, help the car get out of the snow. Now they could set off for Monaco. There was one final change: The Russian inscription “Russko-Baltiysky” on the radiator was replaced with the French “Russo-Baltique.” Only two Russo-Balts have survived the past century. One is in Moscow’s Polytechnic Museum; the other is on display at the Riga Motor Museum. Soviet and Russian motorsport historian Lev Shugurov spent several decades gathering information about the Russian-Baltic Wagon Works and the Russo-Balt car. In his book “Pogonya za Russo-Baltom” (“In Pursuit of the Russo-Balt”), he recalled how what appeared to be Nagel and Mikhailov’s actual racing car once turned up at Monaco’s automobile club. It later proved to be only a replica. Still, Shugurov managed to trace the original car’s history. After the race, in the spring of 1912, engineers continued improving it — it was, after all, a test vehicle. They replaced its body with a streamlined one and removed the fenders, earning the car the nickname “Russian Cucumber.” The “Cucumber” could now reach 116 kilometers per hour (about 72 mph). At the end of 1912, it received newly designed aluminum pistons and a modified exhaust system, bringing its output to 58 horsepower. To reduce drag, a pan was fitted beneath the engine and a wedge-shaped “air splitter” in front of the radiator. On May 28, 1913, the newly upgraded Russo-Balt entered a short race and set a Russian national speed record of 129.744 kilometers per hour (about 81 mph). The record stood for 25 years, until 1938. In the winter of 1913–1914, the car was upgraded again. The cylinders were enlarged once more, and the body was redesigned with a long, narrow tail. World War I began soon afterward. According to some accounts, Nagel and Mikhailov’s car was handed over to the military authorities. Its trail went cold: It disappeared during either World War I, the revolution, or the Civil War. The tires were a particular source of pride While Russian-made cars couldn’t compete with Western ones, Russian tires enjoyed phenomenal popularity. The company’s advertising materials said: Russian engineers were the first to propose that a herringbone pattern with alternating tread directions would keep a car from skidding. This was borne out in practice in Russia’s vast steppes , on the level roads of England and continental Europe, and in the mountains of Switzerland and Spain. At the time of the 1912 rally, the Riga company Provodnik was the world’s second-largest tire manufacturer, behind only Michelin. Yet just 10 years earlier, the rubber-goods factory had been in deep trouble, shaken by constant strikes. In 1900, its management decided to invest in a new product: automobile tires. The industry was growing, and it looked promising. Provodnik began making tires without additives, using only pure rubber and sulfur. They proved exceptionally durable. And because rubber made from natural latex is easy to color, the factory could produce tires in any color. London’s red double-decker buses, for example, ran on stylish red Provodnik tires to match. The racing Russo-Balt also used tires from the Riga factory, sold under the Kolumb brand. The name Provodnik was clearly visible on the spare-wheel cover on the car’s right side. After finishing in Monte Carlo, Andrey Nagel proudly wrote back to Russia: “The engine is running just as it did when we set off. The tires still have St. Petersburg air in them. A tremendous success.” The remark about St. Petersburg air means they hadn’t had a single puncture during the journey. An incredible achievement for the time. Read more ‘Ford v Ferrari’ gets a tsarist makeover in ‘Battle of Motors,’ a lavish Russian drama about a race from St. Petersburg to Monte Carlo How did the race unfold? Andrey Nagel published a detailed account of the race in his magazine, Avtomobil. Lev Shugurov’s research also allows us to reconstruct it. Nagel and Mikhailov set off on December 31, when the temperature in St. Petersburg was minus 16 degrees Celsius (about 3 degrees Fahrenheit). They wore fur coats, felt boots, hats, and goggles. Their convertible had no windshield — it would only have gotten in the way, since cars then had neither windshield wipers nor heaters. Until they reached somewhat warmer territory, it was critical for them to be able to get to a heated garage. There were only two along their route: one in St. Petersburg and one in Riga. Nagel and Mikhailov therefore planned to reach Riga within the first 24 hours. But the snowdrifts made fast driving impossible: Their average speed was no more than 13 kilometers per hour (about 8 mph). The skis attached to the wheels proved utterly useless and were removed. Their driving goggles kept fogging up, so the crew took those off, too. The Russian crew on the way to Monaco A truck traveled alongside the Russo-Balt, clearing the road from Riga to the German border. The Russian-Baltic Wagon Works had supplied it, too, and again, the rules didn’t prohibit this. With that help, Nagel and Mikhailov reached the German border without too much trouble. Nagel wrote that along the way, Vadim Alexandrovich even “knocked back about three shots of cognac and warmed up completely.” Germany was warmer, but not by much. Nagel and Mikhailov stayed overnight in hotels but woke up every hour and a half to warm the engine. Still, the cold wasn’t their biggest problem. Mikhailov couldn’t drive: A few days before the start, he had either broken or badly bruised his arm while trying to start the engine. Nagel suggested that he stay in St. Petersburg, but Mikhailov flatly refused, saying he would help steer with one hand. That’s what they did, but Andrey Nagel did most of the work. Navigation was another problem. Driving through Russia was relatively straightforward: There weren’t many roads, so it was generally clear which way to go. Germany’s road network was much more extensive, however, and road signs were extremely rare. The crew asked locals for directions, which sometimes led them into dead ends. Mikhailov wrote that once, as they sped past a mason who had previously sent them the wrong way, they “offered heartfelt thanks in the kind of language a Russian uses when he’s angry.” On the fifth day, Nagel and Mikhailov passed through Berlin and stopped for the night in Heidelberg. Their main competitors didn’t leave Berlin until the following morning. To pick up speed, the drivers decided to lighten the car by getting rid of the tire chains. That was a mistake. In the Alps, the Russo-Balt couldn’t climb one of the slopes: Without chains, it kept sliding back down. They had to search the area for replacements. A local winemaker had some, but they still had to haggle with him. Soon after crossing the mountains, the crew ran out of gasoline and had to transfer some from the reserve tank. The rest of the journey through southern France was easy. A day later, Nagel and Mikhailov crossed the finish line. I breathed a sigh of relief when I saw Monaco, the flags, the arches, the signs. […] I shot like a bullet into the square where the finish was supposed to be, and only the applause and congratulations told me that I was first. It later turned out that Beutler arrived six hours afterward. But, as you’ll remember, arriving first didn’t mean winning. The main prize was awarded on total points. In the “elegance” category, the Russo-Balt, which had traveled 3,200 kilometers (about 1,990 miles), fared poorly. The team also failed to earn points for average speed: Theirs was just 16.7 kilometers per hour (about 10 mph), slower than their competitors’. The German Julius Beutler took first place in a Berliet, with an excellent average speed of 29 kilometers per hour (about 18 mph). The Russian crew placed only ninth out of 58, receiving prizes for the longest route and endurance. After a leisurely drive through southern France and Italy in the Russo-Balt, the drivers decided to return to Russia by train. The car also traveled back by rail, in a wooden crate. Nagel wrote in Avtomobil: In this extraordinarily difficult competition, it was only thanks to the flawless performance of the car and tires that I managed to arrive first in Monaco… Maintaining the car involved nothing more than adding gasoline and oil, and just once — in Lyon — topping up the water (2–3 glasses). The tires required no attention whatsoever: All four set off with St. Petersburg air in them, and with that same air they are now traveling back by rail with the car. The engine did not falter once during the entire journey. At both minus 19 degrees Réaumur on heavy gasoline and plus 15 degrees Réaumur on good, light gasoline, it delivered the same power, started with a quarter-turn, and ran equally smoothly at low speed and full speed… Honor and glory to the Russian-Baltic Wagon Works and to the Provodnik company’s Kolumb tires. title: Lawmakers ask FAA to pause use of new AI tool in Washington-area flight management
body: More than two dozen lawmakers asked the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to pause the use of a new AI tool in the Washington area to assist air traffic controllers, citing safety concerns.The lawmakers, including Democratic Representatives April Delaney, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Don Beyer, said in a letter they were concerned with the FAA pilot project "as we have not seen any safety evaluation and testing reports, nor have we been made aware of any efforts to train aviation safety personnel on how best to use the tool."The letter seeks an answer by Oct. 19. "Air traffic control leaves zero margin for error," Ocasio-Cortez said Tuesday, calling for the pause.Last month, the FAA began using a new software-based AI tool that uses predictive analytics to ​improve how flights ​are managed."We are deeply concerned about the integration of any AI-enabled system into air traffic control systems, where decisions are literally a matter of life or death," said the letter that was also signed by Senator Chris Van Hollen and Representatives Jamie Raskin, Raja Krishnamoorthi and Kweisi Mfume.FAA awards $875 million contract for SMART systemThe FAA in June awarded an $875 million, 12-year contract ​to Air Space Intelligence for a system dubbed Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories, or SMART, ‌which uses ⁠data to analyze airline schedules, weather, airport capacity, airspace conditions, and operational constraints to predict traffic flows and identify potential conflicts before they occur.The FAA ⁠is initially using the AI tool in ​the ​airspace ⁠around Washington, D.C. and ​plans to ​gradually ⁠expand it to other parts ⁠of ​the country.Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Tuesday called the tool essentially "dumb AI" and emphasized that controllers, not the software, remain in charge. "Air traffic controllers will always control the airspace. This is just giving additional tools for controllers to better manage weather and other issues," Duffy said on Fox Business' "Big Money in the Morning."The system uses over 200 data streams, creates data visualizations, and produces scheduling recommendations for operations experts to consider passing along, but the US Department of Transportation said it does not involve active management of planes in the sky.FAA Administrator touts benefits of AI in airspace management"It's going to be transformational," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told Reuters earlier. "We'll ​make much better decisions if we have better decision-making tools."The plan is to initially use it to more effectively reschedule ​flights that were canceled due to bad weather, with plans to expand to other ​tasks such as strategically coordinating schedules and trajectories before aircraft depart.

title: Somerville, Massachusetts city council moves to enact Israel divestment vote
body: The issue of divestment from Israel returns to the Somerville City Council in Massachusetts on Tuesday night as lawmakers plan to discuss how to implement a nonbinding ballot question on the matter that passed last year.The divestment push has divided the city of more than 84,000 residents, which has a long-standing Jewish population. It is located between Cambridge, home to Harvard University, and Medford, a city with which it shares the Tufts University campus.After ballot Question 3 on divesting from Israel passed with 55.7% of the residents' vote in November 2025, the City Council that same month passed a resolution committing to work toward a binding ordinance within a year to enact the ballot's goals. An initial ordinance, introduced in June, would bar the city from investing in or procuring labor, services, or goods from companies that support entities identified by the ordinance as violating international law, including Israel. Unlike the divestment proposal awaiting a November ballot vote in Providence or the binding human rights divestment ordinance passed by Medford's city council in 2025, the Somerville ordinance specifically mentions Israel and Palestine.Petition for a hearing submitted, with concerns about impact on the cityIn response to the push for a binding ordinance, 74 registered voters in Somerville submitted a petition for a hearing, which was held in September, before final action was taken, citing concerns about its impact on the city. The issue has now moved to the city's Legislative Matters Committee, which is meeting Tuesday night.Among the groups opposing divestment is Shalom Somerville, which submitted the September petition stating that “the sense of belonging and safety experienced by Jewish, Israeli and other residents of diverse backgrounds” is at risk as a result of the ordinance. Sam Gechter, co-founder and president of Shalom Somerville, said that the ordinance singles out Jews who support Israel, which makes it antisemitic. Deputy City Solicitor David Shapiro also advised in November 2024 that such an ordinance would be “likely invalid,” according to a letter from the Anti-Defamation League and the Louis D. Brandeis Center for Human Rights Under Law.“I think it's incredibly irresponsible,” Gechter said, suggesting that the ordinance would slow down governmental action. “But the biggest thing for me is that it makes Jews feel unwelcome in Somerville.”Somerville for Palestine driving force for ballot, ordinanceA local organization, Somerville for Palestine (S4P), has been a driving force behind both the ballot question and the ordinance, which the group developed in collaboration with sponsoring city councilors Ben Ewen-Campen, Ben Wheeler, Wilfred N. Mbah and Jon Link. “It's what people voted for,” said Mo Katz-Christy, a member of S4P's leadership and Jewish Caucus. “We want to follow the will of the people.” The ADL issued a statement condemning the ordinance in June. It also joined the Brandeis Center in issuing a letter calling the proposal an unconstitutional intrusion into foreign affairs. Other Jewish organizations disagree. Jewish Voice for Peace Boston has worked closely with S4P to back the measures. “I don't think that those objections have validity,” said Eli Gerzon, a longtime member of JVP. “As a Jewish organization, we are especially concerned that 'never again' really means what it says: never again, that we never let a Holocaust, a genocide happen.”

title: Meta Launches Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full: Benchmarks, Pricing and How to Use It
body: Meta has released Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full , its most capable models so far. Muse Wonder is a frontier model from Meta built for personal and professional AI agents. Both models target long-running agent work: coding, legal and finance tasks, and computer use. Muse Wonder is live now on the Meta Model API and Muse Code . Muse Wonder Full is limited to paid Muse Code plans. TL;DR Size: 1M-token context , input of text, image, video and audio, output of text. Runs on: Meta’s cloud only, via the API or Muse Code CLI (macOS, Linux, Windows). Performance: Muse Wonder Full leads 6 of 14 rows in Meta’s benchmark table. It trails Claude Opus 5.5 on several. Best: Muse Wonder scores 85.6 on MemoryBench, the top result among all 5 models listed. Worst: Muse Wonder scores 50.0 on ProgramBench, against 70.5 for Claude Opus 5.5. What is Muse Wonder? Muse Wonder follows Muse Spark on Meta’s scaling ladder. Meta team states that it was trained at its Prometheus data center , with gains across pretraining and reinforcement learning. Meta credits a larger base model for better results on unfamiliar tasks. Two named behaviors define the release: Active Memory: carries user context across conversations and pulls back the details a task needs. Active Focus: keeps working on hard tasks, tries alternatives, and checks in before important actions. For developers, Muse Wonder plans long tasks and delegates to sub-agents. It also operates browsers, desktop and mobile apps. How does Muse Wonder perform on benchmarks? All scores below come from Meta’s published table at max reasoning effort. Several rows use third-party sources such as Artificial Analysis, Vals AI and Datacurve. Benchmark Muse Wonder Full Muse Wonder Claude Fable 5.1 GPT-6 Astra Claude Opus 5.5 Personal Superintelligence Index (internal) 59.1 54.3 49.9 54.5 55.2 Harvey LAB-AA 13.1 10.0 6.4 8.6 4.2 Vals Finance Agent V2 59.1 56.6 58.9 53.5 58.6 AutomationBench-AA 45.4 39.1 32.1 41.6 41.2 OSWorld V2.1 (partial) 78.4 72.6 80.7 75.8 81.8 MemoryBench (internal) 85.5 85.6 79.0 81.4 81.5 Terminal-Bench 4.0-AA 57.1 52.0 52.0 59.1 59.6 DeepSWE 1.1 79.0 78.8 67.4 74.1 74.2 SWE-Marathon 57.5 (xhigh) 53.1 45.6 42.5 46.3 ProgramBench 59.0 50.0 55.5 52.5 70.5 AA Intelligence Index v4.3 56 52 53 53 58 Note: PSI, MemoryBench and FocusBench are internal Meta evaluations. The model card says competitor runs are best-effort and may not be tuned. SWE-Marathon results for rivals used Codex and Claude Code, so it is not a common-harness comparison. window.addEventListener("message",function(e){var d=e.data;if(d&&d.mtpMwHeight){var f=document.getElementById("mtp-mw-frame");if(f&&e.source===f.contentWindow){f.style.height=d.mtpMwHeight+"px";}}}); Muse Wonder vs Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra Feature Muse Wonder Muse Wonder Full Claude Opus 5.5 Claude Fable 5.1 GPT-6 Astra Developer Meta Meta Anthropic Anthropic OpenAI Parameters Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Context 1M 1M 1M 1M 1.05M Input modalities Text, image, video, audio Text, image, video, audio Text, image Text, image Text, image Open weights No No No No No API price (in / out per 1M) $4 / $20 Subscription only $4 / $20 $10 / $50 $10 / $50 Access Model API, Muse Code Muse Code Power ($50) or Maximum ($200) Claude API Claude API OpenAI API DeepSWE 1.1 78.8 79.0 74.2 67.4 74.1 How to use Muse Wonder: step-by-step for new users Step 1: Open dev.meta.ai. Click Start building to sign in. The Muse Code install command sits on the same page. Step 2: Pick your model. Muse Wonder costs $4 input, $0.20 cached and $20 output per million tokens. Muse Wonder Full needs a Muse Code plan : Power at $50 or Maximum at $200 per month. Step 3: Sign in with your Meta account. Confirm your name, accept the Model API terms, and click Get started . Step 4. Add billing, then create an API key. New accounts see a “No payment method” banner, and Create API key stays disabled. Add a card under Billing , then open API keys and select Create API key . Export it as MODEL_API_KEY , per the quickstart . Step 5. Test it in the Playground. Open Chat , pick muse-wonder-1.0 , and set temperature, max tokens and reasoning effort. Step 6. Copy working code. Click Get code for a curl or Python snippet. It calls the Responses endpoint at https://api.meta.ai/v1/responses . The API is OpenAI-compatible, so the OpenAI SDK works with a new base URL: Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser import os from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI(base_url="https://api.meta.ai/v1", api_key=os.environ["MODEL_API_KEY"]) resp = client.responses.create(model="muse-wonder-1.0", input="List 3 risks in this lease clause: ...") print(resp.output_text) Step 7: Or use Muse Code in your terminal. On Mac, install with curl -fsSL https://dev.meta.ai/install.sh | bash . On Windows, use irm https://dev.meta.ai/install.ps1 | iex . Run muse in your project folder, trust the workspace, and sign in. The default model is muse-spark-1.2 . Switch with /models , or launch with muse --model muse-wonder-1.0 . Key Takeaways Muse Wonder ships at $4/$20 per million tokens with 1M context. Muse Wonder Full leads DeepSWE (79.0) and SWE-Marathon (57.5). Claude Opus 5.5 still leads ProgramBench, OSWorld and Terminal-Bench. Wonder Full is Muse Code only, from $50 per month. No parameters, open weights or full safety report yet. Check out the research blog , model card and developer docs . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. title: UN General Assembly adopts pandemic declaration, urges stronger global cooperation
body:
The United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) has adopted a political declaration on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response, reaffirming the need for stronger international cooperation and sustained investment to protect the world against future pandemics.
The declaration was adopted on Tuesday following a vote in which 153 countries voted in favour, three against and two abstentions, according to the voting record provided.
The United States, Israel and Argentina voted against the declaration, while New Zealand and Paraguay abstained.
The declaration outlines measures to strengthen disease surveillance, improve national health systems and ensure equitable access to vaccines, treatments and other essential medical products during health emergencies.
It also calls on countries to strengthen their preparedness and response capacities, particularly in addressing weaknesses exposed by the COVID-19 pandemic.
The World Health Organisation (WHO) welcomed the adoption, describing it as a renewed commitment by countries to work together to prevent and respond to future pandemics.
WHO Director-General Tedros Ghebreyesus urged member states to translate their commitments into action, particularly by concluding negotiations on the Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing (PABS) system.
“WHO welcomes this strong commitment by UN Member States to continue working together on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response,” he said.
Mr Ghebreyesus said concluding negotiations on the PABS annex would be an important step towards opening the Pandemic Agreement for signature, followed by ratification and its eventual entry into force.
The declaration was considered by member states at the second UN General Assembly High-level Meeting on Pandemic Prevention, Preparedness and Response on 25 September 2026 before being referred to the full General Assembly for adoption.
The declaration calls for sustained investment in national, regional and global capacities to prevent, detect and respond to emerging pandemic threats.
It also frames pandemic preparedness as a development, economic and security priority that requires coordinated action beyond the health sector.
Among its priorities are stronger disease surveillance and monitoring systems, improved national preparedness capacities and implementation of the amended International Health Regulations (2005).
The declaration further calls for greater community participation, equitable access to pathogens and benefit-sharing arrangements, expanded local and regional manufacturing capacity, increased investment in research and development, and sustainable financing for pandemic preparedness and response.
These measures are intended to help countries identify emerging threats earlier, respond more effectively to outbreaks and improve the availability of essential health products during emergencies.
The emphasis on equitable access also reflects concerns about disparities in the availability of vaccines, treatments and other medical countermeasures during global health emergencies.
The declaration identifies the conclusion of negotiations on the PABS annex as an urgent priority for member states.
The outcome of the negotiations is expected to be considered at the next World Health Assembly in May 2027, or earlier through a special session.
Concluding and adopting the annex would clear a key outstanding hurdle in the process towards the Pandemic Agreement’s entry into force.
The agreement is intended to strengthen international cooperation in preventing and responding to future pandemics, including through improved coordination and arrangements for sharing the benefits derived from access to pathogens.
WHO said the declaration provides a framework for strengthening global health security through collective action, solidarity and equity.
However, its impact will depend on countries translating their political commitments into practical action through adequate financing, stronger health systems and sustained cooperation at national, regional and international levels.
The COVID-19 pandemic exposed significant weaknesses in global health systems, including inadequate disease surveillance, limited emergency preparedness and unequal access to essential medical products.
Many countries, particularly those with limited manufacturing capacity, experienced difficulties obtaining vaccines, diagnostic tools and treatments during the pandemic.
These challenges prompted renewed international efforts to strengthen health security and establish mechanisms for more coordinated responses to future outbreaks.
The WHO Pandemic Agreement was developed as part of these efforts, with a focus on international cooperation, equity and improved preparedness.
Although the newly adopted UN declaration reinforces these commitments, it is a political declaration rather than a legally binding agreement.
Its effectiveness will therefore depend on the steps taken by member states to fulfil their commitments, including increased financing, stronger health systems and sustained international cooperation.

title: Lisandro Martinez issues scathing attack on Man Utd board – has he made things worse?
body: Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez has launched a blistering attack on the club’s hierarchy for failing to strengthen the squad after qualifying for the Champions League. Tuesday’s 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid means United have now gone five games without a win. Their most recent victory was against Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK on 10 September. United’s only other win in nine matches this season came against newly promoted Ipswich at Old Trafford, when they had to come from behind. The Red Devils finished third in the Premier League last term, sealing a Champions League return for the first time in three years. They won 12 of Michael Carrick’s 17 games in interim charge following the dismissal of Ruben Amorim in January, which was enough to earn the former United midfielder a permanent two-year contract as head coach . “We did a fantastic season last season and now we expect more from the top, more players to compete because many teams bring many players as well,” Martinez told Amazon Prime. “Atletico have an amazing team and they deserved to win today. “I expect more [investment]. 100%. I expect more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox]. “I have to be honest, as players we have to do more, but it is also important, when you make a strong squad, to be ready for this kind of night. “Tonight it is easy to [blame] the coach, easy to say the players, but also we have to see other areas.” Martinez’s view has been echoed by many external observers and has also been mentioned by some inside Old Trafford. The failure to bring in striking support for Benjamin Sesko and competition at left-back for Luke Shaw have both been highlighted in a summer when United spent £155m on three midfielders to the exclusion of any other position. Minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe was sitting next to United chief executive Omar Berrada in the Metropolitano Stadium on Tuesday. They have sacked managers in the past two seasons after backing them the previous summer, with Erik ten Hag dismissed in October 2024, and Amorim shown the door in January 2026. “You can’t keep changing, changing, changing the manager,” said Martinez. “What about other areas? I can’t say more. “Last season we did everything; we created the base to create an amazing team.” Martinez’s comments echo those made by his Argentina defensive partner, Cristian Romero, against the Tottenham board last season. Ironically, Romero was in Atletico’s side against United after his summer move to Spain. Martinez, meanwhile, has one year left on his United contract and has yet to agree to an extension. ‘That will rip the dressing room apart’ Former United players Wayne Rooney and Ashley Young were in Madrid for the game. Discussing Martinez’s comments on Amazon Prime, both said the defender had gone too far and the damage inside the dressing room could be significant. “Something like that will rip that dressing room apart,” said Rooney. The former England and United captain recalled his own public criticism of the club in 2010 which drew a fierce response from boss Sir Alex Ferguson. Rooney said it had been a mistake which he had apologised for. “It is disrespectful to his team-mates,” he said. “He is saying his team-mates aren’t good enough. “Bruno [Fernandes] is the only one with any right to say that. Behind closed doors, it happens – but that interview isn’t going to help… “[Martinez] has tried to speak on behalf of the players but done it the wrong way. “It looks like a player trying to look after himself. It was very premeditated. It is sad because you need everyone to stick together, you need to be as one.” Tielemans – who United bought from Aston Villa for £35m in July – also spoke to the host broadcaster but opted not to respond to the question. Commentating on the game, and speaking before Martinez, former England striker Alan Shearer said he felt Carrick had been let down. Young feels Martinez should have kept his counsel. “We know recruitment has to work and be better but players have to be better,” he said. “They are the ones who have to produce. “There’s going to be no change now. That could create [issues] all week after what was a good performance.” Speaking on BBC Radio 5 Live, former England keeper Paul Robinson said he could understand Martinez’s point. “I question his timing because with the noise around Manchester United at the moment, positivity needs to come out of the dressing room,” he said. “But on the flip side, I actually quite like it – a player being honest. “Manchester United fans don’t need their players coming out saying ‘we’re doing OK, the squad’s strong enough’. “Everyone can see they didn’t recruit well enough and they need more players and the squad’s not strong enough.” Does Martinez have a fair point? Manchester United minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe (left), with chief executive Omar Berrada (centre) and director of football Jason Wilcox Although United were much improved on their tepid display against Tottenham at the weekend, conceding inside the first minute did not reflect well on Carrick. And they have now gone five games without a win for the first time since 2024-25, when it happened under both Ten Hag and Amorim. Carrick remains under intense pressure, although Martinez’s words will bring renewed focus on Wilcox. The former Southampton executive’s appointment as football director is starting to be questioned, as are the decisions taken by Ratcliffe and Berrada since the Glazer family stepped back ,despite remaining majority shareholders. In addition to sacking Ten Hag and Amorim, they also dismissed highly respected Dan Ashworth in December 2024, just five months after his appointment as sporting director. Ratcliffe has also been blamed for increasing ticket prices and for launching what the club said was a ticket-touting investigation among season ticket holders, but which fans felt was an attempt to drive them out in favour of ‘tourist’ supporters. In their latest set of accounts, United’s overall debt stood at £1.1bn, with some fans criticising the decision to spend £63.5m on land for a new 100,000-capacity stadium – which is set to cost in excess of £2bn – rather than use the money to strengthen Carrick’s squad. United have only qualified for the Champions League in successive seasons twice sinceFerguson retired in 2013. Amorim told Wilcox to concentrate on his own job in a blistering final news conference as United boss , when he suggested too much attention was paid to external “noise” from the likes of ex-player Gary Neville. Carrick was initially asked for his response to Martinez’s remarks live on TV, before heading to the post-match news conference, where three reporters questioned him about the comments. “I haven’t seen the interview,” he said. “I’ve half heard about it. It’s a bit about the game’s emotions. “Straight after the game is not the time to talk about that interview, and I can’t really comment on that. It’s important for us to move forward quickly. “As a group, I don’t doubt the togetherness and us wanting to win. I know results-wise, it’s easy to look and think there’s something deeply wrong, but the players have been great in their willingness.” Asked if he would speak to Martinez about his comments, Carrick said: “I need to find out a bit more about it before I can say if and what is going to be done.” ‘Brave’ or ‘shocking’ – what you thought Mark: Wow, very brave for Martinez for call out the upper management like that. I’m sure it won’t go down well within Manchester United but I am also sure fans will be happy that someone in the club is finally saying it in public. Stuart McLean: Martinez is right, refreshing to hear an honest assessment. Rooney and Young being unhappy and ‘should be kept in the boardroom’ are so wrong, we pay their astronomical wages. We should praise the honesty, as we all know the problems. Ben Dutton: Martinez saying what most of the fans think. The rot starts at the top, and the squad is not up to the task. Rare honesty from a modern player! Andrew Mitchell: Might be the best thing Lisandro has done in a United shirt. But the ownership are still there against the wishes of nearly every United fan, they continue to run the club the way they want (to its detriment), so there’s no need to think Martinez’s words will move them. Joel Sparks: Martinez might be correct about the people at the top not doing enough. But their lack of activity is not causing his poor performances. Solanke didn’t get the better of him on Saturday because of a lack of subs. He needs to give his head a wobble. Dave Barry: It feels shocking to hear Martinez speak so openly. Those are criticisms fans have been chatting about in the pub for years – hearing it from a player’s mouth is staggering.

title: ‘Anyone Who Attempts Suicide And Fails Will Go To Jail,’ Says Akpabio
body: The Senate has passed, for second reading, a bill seeking to establish a national framework for suicide prevention, decriminalise attempted suicide and provide rehabilitation for survivors, despite opposition from Senate President Godswill Akpabio, who insists that the act should remain punishable by imprisonment. Sponsored by Senator Asuquo Ekpenyong, representing Cross River South, the bill seeks to address what he described as a contradiction in Nigeria’s laws. Ekpenyong argued that while the National Mental Health Act recognises attempted suicide as a psychiatric emergency requiring treatment, Section 327 of the Criminal Code and Section 231 of the Penal Code still criminalise the act. He said decriminalisation without accessible care would be incomplete, stressing that suicide has complex causes and requires a humane, health-focused response. “At the heart of this bill is a simple question: when a Nigerian survives a suicide attempt, should the first response of the state be prosecution or protection?” he asked. The senator said criminalisation discourages people from seeking help, forces families to conceal suicide attempts and contributes to poor data on the problem. He warned that continued punishment could create a situation in which people experiencing distress feel compelled to ensure their attempts are fatal to avoid prosecution. The bill proposes replacing imprisonment with mandatory assessment, referral, treatment and follow-up support. It also provides for crisis helplines, training for police officers, teachers and health workers, public education and a national data system for suicide prevention. However, Akpabio maintained that attempted suicide should remain a criminal offence, arguing that removing the penalties could encourage the act. “If you attempt suicide, make sure you die. Anyone who attempts and fails will go to jail,” the Senate President said. Akpabio added that the issue involves both the Criminal Code and the Penal Code, requiring input from State Houses of Assembly during a public hearing to avoid legal conflicts. The bill has been referred to the Senate Committees on Judiciary and Health for further legislative action and a public hearing. title: Greek Deputy Minister Visits Orthodox Cathedral in Tirana
body: Greek Deputy Interior Minister for Macedonia and Thrace Kostas Gioulekas visited the Orthodox Cathedral of the Resurrection of Christ in Tirana alongside business leaders, academics and representatives of three regions of northern Greece attending the Greek-Albanian Forum to promote bilateral cooperation. Iconographer Christos Papanikolaou guided Gioulekas and the delegation through the cathedral, its chapel, the tomb of the late Archbishop Anastasios and an underground amphitheatre that seats 635 people and serves as a cultural centre. The visit highlighted the cathedral’s religious and cultural significance in Albania, as well as its connection to the legacy of Archbishop Anastasios, the former head of the Orthodox Church of Albania who initiated its construction. Cathedral Attracts Visitors from Across Albania and Abroad Construction of the Orthodox cathedral began in 2004 and took seven years to complete. It has since become one of Albania’s most visited landmarks, with more than 70 tour groups visiting daily, according to Papanikolaou. The cathedral complex includes the main church, a chapel and the underground amphitheatre, which hosts cultural activities. Anastasios invited Papanikolaou to Tirana in 1997 to organise an arts school specialising in fresco painting and portable icons. Papanikolaou has remained in the Albanian capital since then. He also undertook the chapel’s iconography, which he considers the work of his life. Greek Delegation Promotes Bilateral Cooperation Gioulekas visited the cathedral as part of the Greek-Albanian Forum, which brought together business representatives, academics and officials from three regions of northern Greece to encourage closer bilateral cooperation. Greek Deputy Ambassador to Albania Vasiliki Bafi accompanied the minister during the visit. Earlier, Gioulekas met Greek Ambassador Lambrini Komini at the Greek Embassy in Tirana.
