Airlie said that probably 90% of contributors are using LLMs now. Many of them, he said, fear being caught up in an anti-LLM witch hunt. He suggested adding a requirement that models read all of the kernel's documentation into an AGENTS.md file. Torvalds thought many submitters were simply ashamed to admit that they were using those tools. Gleixner suggested, not entirely seriously, adding a Not-assisted-by tag instead; Arnd Bergmann said he would find that a useful indicator of developers he should put time into helping. Torvalds said that the tag requirement might scare people away from using LLMs, and that he would be happy to drop the requirement; Brauner added that it is pointless now. Khan said that she still found Assisted-by to be useful, but there was a strong consensus in the room that the tag had outlived any purpose it may have had, and that the requirement could be dropped. That said, there was also a general interest in knowing how patches are created. Some would like to see which models were used, or where in the development process they were brought in. Maintainers still want to know if there is a human involved in the development process. There was agreement, though, that this information does not need to be recorded in the changelog; the suggestion came out of the discussion is that this information should be put into the cover letter instead. Security issues and urgent fixes The advent of LLMs has resulted in the discovery of huge numbers of security-relevant bugs, leading to a lot of fixes. Kroah-Hartman, who plays a central role in responding to those bugs, said that there are many more coming. Current tools find a lot of vulnerabilities, he said, but they are also wrong half the time; he has students working on improving that performance. He also has people and funding to help with handling the resulting fixes. We can work through this pile of problems, he said, but it will take a while. That is what the next year of work will be focused on. Levin added that LLMs do two things that are new. One is that they are good at developing an exploit from a patch; the other is that they can be used to monitor mailing lists and figure out which fixes have security implications. The result is machines that are automatically cranking out exploits. As soon as a problem has been detected, he said, any embargo is already over. There are thousands of known exploits out there at the moment. Kroah-Hartman said that the only thing that can be done is to get the fixes into the mainline as quickly as possible. Brauner pointed out that this leads to large pull requests after -rc1, which Torvalds has complained about. Torvalds, though, said that pull requests full of fixes are fine as long as they come from people who he can trust to have verified them to be fixes for real problems. The cost to him of doing a pull is almost zero; it's his job. Pinchart said that, while fixing bugs is good, what is really needed is ways to prevent the addition of new bugs. Kroah-Hartman said that increased use of Rust would help in that regard; many bugs are in error paths, and Rust has better ways of handling those. There is also an effort to scale up the work on hardening C code. Some of that work is landing in the newest versions of the compilers, but developers often do not have easy access to them, and linux-next does not either. Ojeda said there is work underway to increase the availability of prebuilt toolchains that developers can use to test their code. Kroah-Hartman said that security bugs are being immediately copied to maintainers now rather than being kept secret; it is the only way to keep up with the flood. But, he cautioned, maintainers should not be telling their employers about those bugs before they are public; otherwise the project as a whole risks running into trouble with government agencies worldwide. Once a fix has been pushed, though, the embargo ends. Starovoitov said that there are lists of vulnerabilities that have been discovered by LLMs, many of which have reproducers available. He wondered what the best way was to get those fixes into the mainline. Torvalds said that, when there are real kernel developers involved, the most urgent patches can go directly to him, bypassing maintainers and avoiding adding to their workload. Hildenbrand worried that maintainers would lose the opportunity to review fixes in their subsystems, and that they would lose control, but Torvalds answered that reviewing all those fixes just adds stress for everybody involved. Pain points Prior to the Summit, Torvalds asked each of the participants to prepare a one-minute summary of their biggest pain point for the group. These presentations would happen over a half hour, with no discussion until everybody had said their piece. The "no discussion" rule held most (but not all) of the time. In the order they were presented: Kroah-Hartman : subsystems that do not add CC: stable@vger.kernel.org tags to patches, but which still expect the stable team to pick up the important fixes anyway. The stable maintainers are overwhelmed as it is and are not doing that. Pinchart has heard from developers that they submit code, but do not know when their patches have been applied or to which tree. More maintainers should send emails when they apply patches, he said. Eric Biggers : patches that cannot easily be applied, and which do not specify a base to which they can be applied. A lot of patches cannot be properly reviewed without applying them first, he said. Rafael Wysocki : insufficient feedback on patches in general. People often have opinions, but do not always share them. Airlie asked his sub-maintainers; most of them identified him as the biggest pain point. More seriously, it was that the DRM subsystem is still seeing too many regressions. There is a push within the subsystem to move development to GitLab in order to use its CI features; he is not standing in the way because he wants to see how it turns out. Ts'o : prioritization, and having too many things to look at. He would love to add a priority tag to patchwork that maintainers could set to help identify what needs attention first. Ryhl : not knowing how long she needs to wait after sending a version of a patch before concluding that she does not need to worry about problems with it. Me : huge number of patches touch the documentation directory, and it is hard to know which ones I should apply and which to leave to others. A lot of time is spent digging through linux-next to see if patches have been picked up by somebody else. Torvalds said that he often has the same problem. Khan complained about the same problem; it is often not clear who will pick up test patches. Hildenbrand : the high review load. Review cannot just be handed off to a bot; most changes need input from developers. Somehow, the subsystem needs to develop more experts, but it is hard to identify people who can grow in that way. Bergmann said that the review process is breaking down. When he replies to patches, he tries to teach contributors how to do better, but he has become discouraged because people using LLMs do not learn. So now those who might learn are not getting the feedback they need. The opposite problem happens too: a submitter sends 50 versions (literally) of a patch and responds to comments, but Bergmann thinks that the patch should not exist in the first place. Starovoitov : maintainers should not be looking for bugs or coding-style problems; bots will do that now. Instead, reviews should be strictly focused on the "why" of a patch, whether the fix is made in the right place, and is in good taste. Ryabitsev : the last entry in the MAINTAINERS file, titled " THE REST ", directs every patch to the linux-kernel mailing list. That generates millions of outgoing emails every day, leading to constant delivery problems. He asked whether that entry could be removed or changed to redirect patches to the patches@vger.kernel.org list. He later submitted a patch to get_maintainer.pl , causing it to only add linux-kernel if no other list has been identified as a recipient for a patch. Levin : subsystems are diverging in their practices, and many now have a manual on how to interact with them. That makes life hard for developers working across subsystems; he would like to see the community come back together. Hellwig : the Sashiko review workflow is broken, causing people to continually resend patches. There is no obvious answer to this problem, but something needs to improve. Brown asked subsystems with tests to actually build and run them so they don't break in linux-next. Kosina : there needs to be a better way to prioritize the handling of submissions. He liked Ts'o's idea, but without using patchwork. Will Deacon : the process is not much fun anymore; maintainers try to explain to contributors how they could improve, but are ignored. Danilo Krummrich does not mind seeing multiple versions of a series in a short time, but submitters are just feeding the Sashiko reviews into their LLM to create those new versions. A way needs to be found to encourage submitters to engage and talk to maintainers. Abeni : the infrastructure is not keeping up with what the subsystem needs. Networking runs its own version of Sashiko, which produces better results, but it can't be run for every networking subsystem. That creates extra friction for maintainers. Eric Dumazet announced that he had just retired, and that all of his pain points have vanished. Gushchin : Sashiko has gone from an experiment to a widely used tool in the community. There is a lot of work involved beyond developing the bot itself; he has to obtain tokens to run it, explain its value to management, and more. He could really use more people and more feedback. He only knows a few kernel subsystems; if people don't tell him about problems with the others, he will never know. Julia Lawall does not know if her work, much of which has involved finding and fixing bugs in the kernel, will have any relevance in the future. Five years ago she would have asked for more feedback from developers, now she isn't sure if it matters. Ojeda : tree-wide refactoring work can be tricky, and the advent of more Rust code seems set to make it harder. Gleixner has spent much of his time looking at design patterns and explaining them in lengthy emails. Developers used to appreciate that work, but more recently it is mostly ignored, and he wonders if it is still worth doing. In the LLM world, people say that they don't have time for design and, besides, the code works. He has spent 25 years doing cleanups, and does not want to merge more stuff that will just have to be cleaned up in the future. Brauner : code removal. The time has come to fix less code and to remove more of it. The idea was that these pain points would be discussed after the presentation, but that did not really happen. Instead, the conversation took a rather different direction. Succession Torvalds let it be known that he was about to go on vacation for two weeks, which is a bit awkward given that there is a merge window coming. So he was considering extending the merge window for a third week in response. There was not a lot of opposition to that idea in the room. He went on to talk about succession plans. The 2025 Summit included a discussion on that topic that was focused mostly on what should happen if Torvalds abruptly became unable to continue leading the project. This year, he said that, while he is not going anywhere anytime soon, it is not too early to think about how a graceful transition to a Torvalds-less future might happen. To help that process along, he has started actively ignoring more emails and stepping back a bit from development questions. He is curious to see how the community will react. There followed a wide-ranging but inconclusive discussion about the role Torvalds plays in the community and how things might operate when he finally decides to move on to something else. The two chief aspects of that role of can be described as "patch monkey" (executing pull requests) and resolution of conflicts between developers — which he professed to be bad at. In the future those roles could perhaps be split apart. The project could name a new benevolent dictator, or perhaps move to some sort of committee model. No decisions were made — none are needed now, and none were expected. But Torvalds clearly feels that it would be better to think about these things well ahead of time rather than under pressure. There will be a mailing list created, initially with the Summit attendees as members, where the discussion can simmer. At the end, Gushchin pointed out that the world looks quite different now than it did one year ago; with the current rate of change, it is going to be hard to make meaningful plans for an event that is expected multiple years in the future. Metadiscussion The closing topic was about the Maintainers Summit itself, and how it might be improved in the future. It started with a reference to this August thread where James Bottomley questioned whether the event should continue to exist at all. Few people seem to think it should be abolished, but there were concerns expressed about the process for selecting attendees, with some people describing it as a closed clique. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the maintainers in the room, all of whom had received invitations, did not see a lot of problems with that process. High-level process discussions tend to need the high-level maintainers in the room. As Brauner pointed out, that group is always going to seem a bit elitist. But, he said, getting that group into the same room once each year is helpful for the management of the project as a whole. Torvalds said that the older format of the Kernel Summit, which topped out at about 150 participants, was simply not manageable. The smaller group is at least able to have constructive discussions, he said. Hildenbrand said that one problem is a widely held impression that proposing a topic for the Summit will necessarily result in an invitation; he suggested that the call for topics next year should be rephrased. Ts'o said that colocating the Summit with the Linux Plumbers Conference (LPC) works well, and that holding the Summit afterward works best. That allows the participants to gather information from others and bring it into the more focused group. Hellwig put in a request for a different sort of gathering where developers from one subsystem can hold "office hours" to talk with others. That sort of happens at conferences now but, he said, the time at those events is too structured and there are too many other distractions happening. Bergmann pointed out that the LPC kernel-summit track has become less relevant over the years, and suggested that some of that track's time could be repurposed; that idea was reasonably well received. There was also talk of using a videoconference server to host subsystem-specific office hours at other times. The meeting closed with a general agreement that its format works fairly well, and that the office-hours idea might improve it. The biggest change might be in the call for topics, which may be rewritten to provide more information about how the selection process works and to make it clear that people can nominate others to attend. There was, finally, a suggestion that the ksummit mailing list could be used more. There are usually interesting discussions there in the lead-up to the event, but then it goes quiet the rest of the year; there is no reason why discussions of that type can't happen there at other times as well. Rust and error paths Posted Oct 15, 2026 13:59 UTC (Thu) by daroc (editor, #160859) [ Link ] (4 responses) Specifically, not handling an error (by discarding a Result value) currently gives a compiler warning, and Miguel Ojeda works hard to keep the kernel's Rust code warning-free, so that's noticeable. In a future version of the language, it may be possible to make not handling an error a compile-time error; there's work in progress on the language features required to enable that. In addition, Rust has shorthand for propagating errors (the ? operator) and facilities for carrying additional information as part of errors, which can make handling them easier in the cases where propagating the error is not appropriate. Also, in C one must read the documentation to figure out whether a function returning an int can return an error (although it often can); in Rust, that information is part of the type of the function, which makes it easy to see at a glance. It's really a whole bunch of little things that work together to make writing error-handling code in Rust a bit more pleasant and hard to screw up. There was agreement, though, that this information does not need to be recorded in the changelog; the suggestion came out of the discussion is that this information should be put into the cover letter instead. Security issues and urgent fixes The advent of LLMs has resulted in the discovery of huge numbers of security-relevant bugs, leading to a lot of fixes. Kroah-Hartman, who plays a central role in responding to those bugs, said that there are many more coming. Current tools find a lot of vulnerabilities, he said, but they are also wrong half the time; he has students working on improving that performance. He also has people and funding to help with handling the resulting fixes. We can work through this pile of problems, he said, but it will take a while. That is what the next year of work will be focused on. Levin added that LLMs do two things that are new. One is that they are good at developing an exploit from a patch; the other is that they can be used to monitor mailing lists and figure out which fixes have security implications. The result is machines that are automatically cranking out exploits. As soon as a problem has been detected, he said, any embargo is already over. There are thousands of known exploits out there at the moment. Kroah-Hartman said that the only thing that can be done is to get the fixes into the mainline as quickly as possible. Brauner pointed out that this leads to large pull requests after -rc1, which Torvalds has complained about. Torvalds, though, said that pull requests full of fixes are fine as long as they come from people who he can trust to have verified them to be fixes for real problems. The cost to him of doing a pull is almost zero; it's his job. Pinchart said that, while fixing bugs is good, what is really needed is ways to prevent the addition of new bugs. Kroah-Hartman said that increased use of Rust would help in that regard; many bugs are in error paths, and Rust has better ways of handling those. There is also an effort to scale up the work on hardening C code. Some of that work is landing in the newest versions of the compilers, but developers often do not have easy access to them, and linux-next does not either. Ojeda said there is work underway to increase the availability of prebuilt toolchains that developers can use to test their code. Kroah-Hartman said that security bugs are being immediately copied to maintainers now rather than being kept secret; it is the only way to keep up with the flood. But, he cautioned, maintainers should not be telling their employers about those bugs before they are public; otherwise the project as a whole risks running into trouble with government agencies worldwide. Once a fix has been pushed, though, the embargo ends. Starovoitov said that there are lists of vulnerabilities that have been discovered by LLMs, many of which have reproducers available. He wondered what the best way was to get those fixes into the mainline. Torvalds said that, when there are real kernel developers involved, the most urgent patches can go directly to him, bypassing maintainers and avoiding adding to their workload. Hildenbrand worried that maintainers would lose the opportunity to review fixes in their subsystems, and that they would lose control, but Torvalds answered that reviewing all those fixes just adds stress for everybody involved. Pain points Prior to the Summit, Torvalds asked each of the participants to prepare a one-minute summary of their biggest pain point for the group. These presentations would happen over a half hour, with no discussion until everybody had said their piece. The "no discussion" rule held most (but not all) of the time. In the order they were presented: Kroah-Hartman : subsystems that do not add CC: stable@vger.kernel.org tags to patches, but which still expect the stable team to pick up the important fixes anyway. The stable maintainers are overwhelmed as it is and are not doing that. Pinchart has heard from developers that they submit code, but do not know when their patches have been applied or to which tree. More maintainers should send emails when they apply patches, he said. Eric Biggers : patches that cannot easily be applied, and which do not specify a base to which they can be applied. A lot of patches cannot be properly reviewed without applying them first, he said. Rafael Wysocki : insufficient feedback on patches in general. People often have opinions, but do not always share them. Airlie asked his sub-maintainers; most of them identified him as the biggest pain point. More seriously, it was that the DRM subsystem is still seeing too many regressions. There is a push within the subsystem to move development to GitLab in order to use its CI features; he is not standing in the way because he wants to see how it turns out. Ts'o : prioritization, and having too many things to look at. He would love to add a priority tag to patchwork that maintainers could set to help identify what needs attention first. Ryhl : not knowing how long she needs to wait after sending a version of a patch before concluding that she does not need to worry about problems with it. Me : huge number of patches touch the documentation directory, and it is hard to know which ones I should apply and which to leave to others. A lot of time is spent digging through linux-next to see if patches have been picked up by somebody else. Torvalds said that he often has the same problem. Khan complained about the same problem; it is often not clear who will pick up test patches. Hildenbrand : the high review load. Review cannot just be handed off to a bot; most changes need input from developers. Somehow, the subsystem needs to develop more experts, but it is hard to identify people who can grow in that way. Bergmann said that the review process is breaking down. When he replies to patches, he tries to teach contributors how to do better, but he has become discouraged because people using LLMs do not learn. So now those who might learn are not getting the feedback they need. The opposite problem happens too: a submitter sends 50 versions (literally) of a patch and responds to comments, but Bergmann thinks that the patch should not exist in the first place. Starovoitov : maintainers should not be looking for bugs or coding-style problems; bots will do that now. Instead, reviews should be strictly focused on the "why" of a patch, whether the fix is made in the right place, and is in good taste. Ryabitsev : the last entry in the MAINTAINERS file, titled " THE REST ", directs every patch to the linux-kernel mailing list. That generates millions of outgoing emails every day, leading to constant delivery problems. He asked whether that entry could be removed or changed to redirect patches to the patches@vger.kernel.org list. He later submitted a patch to get_maintainer.pl , causing it to only add linux-kernel if no other list has been identified as a recipient for a patch. Levin : subsystems are diverging in their practices, and many now have a manual on how to interact with them. That makes life hard for developers working across subsystems; he would like to see the community come back together. Hellwig : the Sashiko review workflow is broken, causing people to continually resend patches. There is no obvious answer to this problem, but something needs to improve. Brown asked subsystems with tests to actually build and run them so they don't break in linux-next. Kosina : there needs to be a better way to prioritize the handling of submissions. He liked Ts'o's idea, but without using patchwork. Will Deacon : the process is not much fun anymore; maintainers try to explain to contributors how they could improve, but are ignored. Danilo Krummrich does not mind seeing multiple versions of a series in a short time, but submitters are just feeding the Sashiko reviews into their LLM to create those new versions. A way needs to be found to encourage submitters to engage and talk to maintainers. Abeni : the infrastructure is not keeping up with what the subsystem needs. Networking runs its own version of Sashiko, which produces better results, but it can't be run for every networking subsystem. That creates extra friction for maintainers. Eric Dumazet announced that he had just retired, and that all of his pain points have vanished. Gushchin : Sashiko has gone from an experiment to a widely used tool in the community. There is a lot of work involved beyond developing the bot itself; he has to obtain tokens to run it, explain its value to management, and more. He could really use more people and more feedback. He only knows a few kernel subsystems; if people don't tell him about problems with the others, he will never know. Julia Lawall does not know if her work, much of which has involved finding and fixing bugs in the kernel, will have any relevance in the future. Five years ago she would have asked for more feedback from developers, now she isn't sure if it matters. Ojeda : tree-wide refactoring work can be tricky, and the advent of more Rust code seems set to make it harder. Gleixner has spent much of his time looking at design patterns and explaining them in lengthy emails. Developers used to appreciate that work, but more recently it is mostly ignored, and he wonders if it is still worth doing. In the LLM world, people say that they don't have time for design and, besides, the code works. He has spent 25 years doing cleanups, and does not want to merge more stuff that will just have to be cleaned up in the future. Brauner : code removal. The time has come to fix less code and to remove more of it. The idea was that these pain points would be discussed after the presentation, but that did not really happen. Instead, the conversation took a rather different direction. Succession Torvalds let it be known that he was about to go on vacation for two weeks, which is a bit awkward given that there is a merge window coming. So he was considering extending the merge window for a third week in response. There was not a lot of opposition to that idea in the room. He went on to talk about succession plans. The 2025 Summit included a discussion on that topic that was focused mostly on what should happen if Torvalds abruptly became unable to continue leading the project. This year, he said that, while he is not going anywhere anytime soon, it is not too early to think about how a graceful transition to a Torvalds-less future might happen. To help that process along, he has started actively ignoring more emails and stepping back a bit from development questions. He is curious to see how the community will react. There followed a wide-ranging but inconclusive discussion about the role Torvalds plays in the community and how things might operate when he finally decides to move on to something else. The two chief aspects of that role of can be described as "patch monkey" (executing pull requests) and resolution of conflicts between developers — which he professed to be bad at. In the future those roles could perhaps be split apart. The project could name a new benevolent dictator, or perhaps move to some sort of committee model. No decisions were made — none are needed now, and none were expected. But Torvalds clearly feels that it would be better to think about these things well ahead of time rather than under pressure. There will be a mailing list created, initially with the Summit attendees as members, where the discussion can simmer. At the end, Gushchin pointed out that the world looks quite different now than it did one year ago; with the current rate of change, it is going to be hard to make meaningful plans for an event that is expected multiple years in the future. Metadiscussion The closing topic was about the Maintainers Summit itself, and how it might be improved in the future. It started with a reference to this August thread where James Bottomley questioned whether the event should continue to exist at all. Few people seem to think it should be abolished, but there were concerns expressed about the process for selecting attendees, with some people describing it as a closed clique. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the maintainers in the room, all of whom had received invitations, did not see a lot of problems with that process. High-level process discussions tend to need the high-level maintainers in the room. As Brauner pointed out, that group is always going to seem a bit elitist. But, he said, getting that group into the same room once each year is helpful for the management of the project as a whole. Torvalds said that the older format of the Kernel Summit, which topped out at about 150 participants, was simply not manageable. The smaller group is at least able to have constructive discussions, he said. Hildenbrand said that one problem is a widely held impression that proposing a topic for the Summit will necessarily result in an invitation; he suggested that the call for topics next year should be rephrased. Ts'o said that colocating the Summit with the Linux Plumbers Conference (LPC) works well, and that holding the Summit afterward works best. That allows the participants to gather information from others and bring it into the more focused group. Hellwig put in a request for a different sort of gathering where developers from one subsystem can hold "office hours" to talk with others. That sort of happens at conferences now but, he said, the time at those events is too structured and there are too many other distractions happening. Bergmann pointed out that the LPC kernel-summit track has become less relevant over the years, and suggested that some of that track's time could be repurposed; that idea was reasonably well received. There was also talk of using a videoconference server to host subsystem-specific office hours at other times. The meeting closed with a general agreement that its format works fairly well, and that the office-hours idea might improve it. The biggest change might be in the call for topics, which may be rewritten to provide more information about how the selection process works and to make it clear that people can nominate others to attend. There was, finally, a suggestion that the ksummit mailing list could be used more. There are usually interesting discussions there in the lead-up to the event, but then it goes quiet the rest of the year; there is no reason why discussions of that type can't happen there at other times as well. That said, there was also a general interest in knowing how patches are created. Some would like to see which models were used, or where in the development process they were brought in. Maintainers still want to know if there is a human involved in the development process. There was agreement, though, that this information does not need to be recorded in the changelog; the suggestion came out of the discussion is that this information should be put into the cover letter instead. Security issues and urgent fixes The advent of LLMs has resulted in the discovery of huge numbers of security-relevant bugs, leading to a lot of fixes. Kroah-Hartman, who plays a central role in responding to those bugs, said that there are many more coming. Current tools find a lot of vulnerabilities, he said, but they are also wrong half the time; he has students working on improving that performance. He also has people and funding to help with handling the resulting fixes. We can work through this pile of problems, he said, but it will take a while. That is what the next year of work will be focused on. Levin added that LLMs do two things that are new. One is that they are good at developing an exploit from a patch; the other is that they can be used to monitor mailing lists and figure out which fixes have security implications. The result is machines that are automatically cranking out exploits. As soon as a problem has been detected, he said, any embargo is already over. There are thousands of known exploits out there at the moment. Kroah-Hartman said that the only thing that can be done is to get the fixes into the mainline as quickly as possible. Brauner pointed out that this leads to large pull requests after -rc1, which Torvalds has complained about. Torvalds, though, said that pull requests full of fixes are fine as long as they come from people who he can trust to have verified them to be fixes for real problems. The cost to him of doing a pull is almost zero; it's his job. Pinchart said that, while fixing bugs is good, what is really needed is ways to prevent the addition of new bugs. Kroah-Hartman said that increased use of Rust would help in that regard; many bugs are in error paths, and Rust has better ways of handling those. There is also an effort to scale up the work on hardening C code. Some of that work is landing in the newest versions of the compilers, but developers often do not have easy access to them, and linux-next does not either. Ojeda said there is work underway to increase the availability of prebuilt toolchains that developers can use to test their code. Kroah-Hartman said that security bugs are being immediately copied to maintainers now rather than being kept secret; it is the only way to keep up with the flood. But, he cautioned, maintainers should not be telling their employers about those bugs before they are public; otherwise the project as a whole risks running into trouble with government agencies worldwide. Once a fix has been pushed, though, the embargo ends. Starovoitov said that there are lists of vulnerabilities that have been discovered by LLMs, many of which have reproducers available. He wondered what the best way was to get those fixes into the mainline. Torvalds said that, when there are real kernel developers involved, the most urgent patches can go directly to him, bypassing maintainers and avoiding adding to their workload. Hildenbrand worried that maintainers would lose the opportunity to review fixes in their subsystems, and that they would lose control, but Torvalds answered that reviewing all those fixes just adds stress for everybody involved. Pain points Prior to the Summit, Torvalds asked each of the participants to prepare a one-minute summary of their biggest pain point for the group. These presentations would happen over a half hour, with no discussion until everybody had said their piece. The "no discussion" rule held most (but not all) of the time. In the order they were presented: Kroah-Hartman : subsystems that do not add CC: stable@vger.kernel.org tags to patches, but which still expect the stable team to pick up the important fixes anyway. The stable maintainers are overwhelmed as it is and are not doing that. Pinchart has heard from developers that they submit code, but do not know when their patches have been applied or to which tree. More maintainers should send emails when they apply patches, he said. Eric Biggers : patches that cannot easily be applied, and which do not specify a base to which they can be applied. A lot of patches cannot be properly reviewed without applying them first, he said. Rafael Wysocki : insufficient feedback on patches in general. People often have opinions, but do not always share them. Airlie asked his sub-maintainers; most of them identified him as the biggest pain point. More seriously, it was that the DRM subsystem is still seeing too many regressions. There is a push within the subsystem to move development to GitLab in order to use its CI features; he is not standing in the way because he wants to see how it turns out. Ts'o : prioritization, and having too many things to look at. He would love to add a priority tag to patchwork that maintainers could set to help identify what needs attention first. Ryhl : not knowing how long she needs to wait after sending a version of a patch before concluding that she does not need to worry about problems with it. Me : huge number of patches touch the documentation directory, and it is hard to know which ones I should apply and which to leave to others. A lot of time is spent digging through linux-next to see if patches have been picked up by somebody else. Torvalds said that he often has the same problem. Khan complained about the same problem; it is often not clear who will pick up test patches. Hildenbrand : the high review load. Review cannot just be handed off to a bot; most changes need input from developers. Somehow, the subsystem needs to develop more experts, but it is hard to identify people who can grow in that way. Bergmann said that the review process is breaking down. When he replies to patches, he tries to teach contributors how to do better, but he has become discouraged because people using LLMs do not learn. So now those who might learn are not getting the feedback they need. The opposite problem happens too: a submitter sends 50 versions (literally) of a patch and responds to comments, but Bergmann thinks that the patch should not exist in the first place. Starovoitov : maintainers should not be looking for bugs or coding-style problems; bots will do that now. Instead, reviews should be strictly focused on the "why" of a patch, whether the fix is made in the right place, and is in good taste. Ryabitsev : the last entry in the MAINTAINERS file, titled " THE REST ", directs every patch to the linux-kernel mailing list. That generates millions of outgoing emails every day, leading to constant delivery problems. He asked whether that entry could be removed or changed to redirect patches to the patches@vger.kernel.org list. He later submitted a patch to get_maintainer.pl , causing it to only add linux-kernel if no other list has been identified as a recipient for a patch. Levin : subsystems are diverging in their practices, and many now have a manual on how to interact with them. That makes life hard for developers working across subsystems; he would like to see the community come back together. Hellwig : the Sashiko review workflow is broken, causing people to continually resend patches. There is no obvious answer to this problem, but something needs to improve. Brown asked subsystems with tests to actually build and run them so they don't break in linux-next. Kosina : there needs to be a better way to prioritize the handling of submissions. He liked Ts'o's idea, but without using patchwork. Will Deacon : the process is not much fun anymore; maintainers try to explain to contributors how they could improve, but are ignored. Danilo Krummrich does not mind seeing multiple versions of a series in a short time, but submitters are just feeding the Sashiko reviews into their LLM to create those new versions. A way needs to be found to encourage submitters to engage and talk to maintainers. Abeni : the infrastructure is not keeping up with what the subsystem needs. Networking runs its own version of Sashiko, which produces better results, but it can't be run for every networking subsystem. That creates extra friction for maintainers. Eric Dumazet announced that he had just retired, and that all of his pain points have vanished. Gushchin : Sashiko has gone from an experiment to a widely used tool in the community. There is a lot of work involved beyond developing the bot itself; he has to obtain tokens to run it, explain its value to management, and more. He could really use more people and more feedback. He only knows a few kernel subsystems; if people don't tell him about problems with the others, he will never know. Julia Lawall does not know if her work, much of which has involved finding and fixing bugs in the kernel, will have any relevance in the future. Five years ago she would have asked for more feedback from developers, now she isn't sure if it matters. Ojeda : tree-wide refactoring work can be tricky, and the advent of more Rust code seems set to make it harder. Gleixner has spent much of his time looking at design patterns and explaining them in lengthy emails. Developers used to appreciate that work, but more recently it is mostly ignored, and he wonders if it is still worth doing. In the LLM world, people say that they don't have time for design and, besides, the code works. He has spent 25 years doing cleanups, and does not want to merge more stuff that will just have to be cleaned up in the future. Brauner : code removal. The time has come to fix less code and to remove more of it. The idea was that these pain points would be discussed after the presentation, but that did not really happen. Instead, the conversation took a rather different direction. Succession Torvalds let it be known that he was about to go on vacation for two weeks, which is a bit awkward given that there is a merge window coming. So he was considering extending the merge window for a third week in response. There was not a lot of opposition to that idea in the room. He went on to talk about succession plans. The 2025 Summit included a discussion on that topic that was focused mostly on what should happen if Torvalds abruptly became unable to continue leading the project. This year, he said that, while he is not going anywhere anytime soon, it is not too early to think about how a graceful transition to a Torvalds-less future might happen. To help that process along, he has started actively ignoring more emails and stepping back a bit from development questions. He is curious to see how the community will react. There followed a wide-ranging but inconclusive discussion about the role Torvalds plays in the community and how things might operate when he finally decides to move on to something else. The two chief aspects of that role of can be described as "patch monkey" (executing pull requests) and resolution of conflicts between developers — which he professed to be bad at. In the future those roles could perhaps be split apart. The project could name a new benevolent dictator, or perhaps move to some sort of committee model. No decisions were made — none are needed now, and none were expected. But Torvalds clearly feels that it would be better to think about these things well ahead of time rather than under pressure. There will be a mailing list created, initially with the Summit attendees as members, where the discussion can simmer. At the end, Gushchin pointed out that the world looks quite different now than it did one year ago; with the current rate of change, it is going to be hard to make meaningful plans for an event that is expected multiple years in the future. Metadiscussion The closing topic was about the Maintainers Summit itself, and how it might be improved in the future. It started with a reference to this August thread where James Bottomley questioned whether the event should continue to exist at all. Few people seem to think it should be abolished, but there were concerns expressed about the process for selecting attendees, with some people describing it as a closed clique. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the maintainers in the room, all of whom had received invitations, did not see a lot of problems with that process. High-level process discussions tend to need the high-level maintainers in the room. As Brauner pointed out, that group is always going to seem a bit elitist. But, he said, getting that group into the same room once each year is helpful for the management of the project as a whole. Torvalds said that the older format of the Kernel Summit, which topped out at about 150 participants, was simply not manageable. The smaller group is at least able to have constructive discussions, he said. Hildenbrand said that one problem is a widely held impression that proposing a topic for the Summit will necessarily result in an invitation; he suggested that the call for topics next year should be rephrased. Ts'o said that colocating the Summit with the Linux Plumbers Conference (LPC) works well, and that holding the Summit afterward works best. That allows the participants to gather information from others and bring it into the more focused group. Hellwig put in a request for a different sort of gathering where developers from one subsystem can hold "office hours" to talk with others. That sort of happens at conferences now but, he said, the time at those events is too structured and there are too many other distractions happening. Bergmann pointed out that the LPC kernel-summit track has become less relevant over the years, and suggested that some of that track's time could be repurposed; that idea was reasonably well received. There was also talk of using a videoconference server to host subsystem-specific office hours at other times. The meeting closed with a general agreement that its format works fairly well, and that the office-hours idea might improve it. The biggest change might be in the call for topics, which may be rewritten to provide more information about how the selection process works and to make it clear that people can nominate others to attend. There was, finally, a suggestion that the ksummit mailing list could be used more. There are usually interesting discussions there in the lead-up to the event, but then it goes quiet the rest of the year; there is no reason why discussions of that type can't happen there at other times as well. In a future version of the language, it may be possible to make not handling an error a compile-time error; there's work in progress on the language features required to enable that. In addition, Rust has shorthand for propagating errors (the ? operator) and facilities for carrying additional information as part of errors, which can make handling them easier in the cases where propagating the error is not appropriate. Also, in C one must read the documentation to figure out whether a function returning an int can return an error (although it often can); in Rust, that information is part of the type of the function, which makes it easy to see at a glance. It's really a whole bunch of little things that work together to make writing error-handling code in Rust a bit more pleasant and hard to screw up. Security issues and urgent fixes The advent of LLMs has resulted in the discovery of huge numbers of security-relevant bugs, leading to a lot of fixes. Kroah-Hartman, who plays a central role in responding to those bugs, said that there are many more coming. Current tools find a lot of vulnerabilities, he said, but they are also wrong half the time; he has students working on improving that performance. He also has people and funding to help with handling the resulting fixes. We can work through this pile of problems, he said, but it will take a while. That is what the next year of work will be focused on. Levin added that LLMs do two things that are new. One is that they are good at developing an exploit from a patch; the other is that they can be used to monitor mailing lists and figure out which fixes have security implications. The result is machines that are automatically cranking out exploits. As soon as a problem has been detected, he said, any embargo is already over. There are thousands of known exploits out there at the moment. Kroah-Hartman said that the only thing that can be done is to get the fixes into the mainline as quickly as possible. Brauner pointed out that this leads to large pull requests after -rc1, which Torvalds has complained about. Torvalds, though, said that pull requests full of fixes are fine as long as they come from people who he can trust to have verified them to be fixes for real problems. The cost to him of doing a pull is almost zero; it's his job. Pinchart said that, while fixing bugs is good, what is really needed is ways to prevent the addition of new bugs. Kroah-Hartman said that increased use of Rust would help in that regard; many bugs are in error paths, and Rust has better ways of handling those. There is also an effort to scale up the work on hardening C code. Some of that work is landing in the newest versions of the compilers, but developers often do not have easy access to them, and linux-next does not either. Ojeda said there is work underway to increase the availability of prebuilt toolchains that developers can use to test their code. Kroah-Hartman said that security bugs are being immediately copied to maintainers now rather than being kept secret; it is the only way to keep up with the flood. But, he cautioned, maintainers should not be telling their employers about those bugs before they are public; otherwise the project as a whole risks running into trouble with government agencies worldwide. Once a fix has been pushed, though, the embargo ends. Starovoitov said that there are lists of vulnerabilities that have been discovered by LLMs, many of which have reproducers available. He wondered what the best way was to get those fixes into the mainline. Torvalds said that, when there are real kernel developers involved, the most urgent patches can go directly to him, bypassing maintainers and avoiding adding to their workload. Hildenbrand worried that maintainers would lose the opportunity to review fixes in their subsystems, and that they would lose control, but Torvalds answered that reviewing all those fixes just adds stress for everybody involved. Pain points Prior to the Summit, Torvalds asked each of the participants to prepare a one-minute summary of their biggest pain point for the group. These presentations would happen over a half hour, with no discussion until everybody had said their piece. The "no discussion" rule held most (but not all) of the time. In the order they were presented: Kroah-Hartman : subsystems that do not add CC: stable@vger.kernel.org tags to patches, but which still expect the stable team to pick up the important fixes anyway. The stable maintainers are overwhelmed as it is and are not doing that. Pinchart has heard from developers that they submit code, but do not know when their patches have been applied or to which tree. More maintainers should send emails when they apply patches, he said. Eric Biggers : patches that cannot easily be applied, and which do not specify a base to which they can be applied. A lot of patches cannot be properly reviewed without applying them first, he said. Rafael Wysocki : insufficient feedback on patches in general. People often have opinions, but do not always share them. Airlie asked his sub-maintainers; most of them identified him as the biggest pain point. More seriously, it was that the DRM subsystem is still seeing too many regressions. There is a push within the subsystem to move development to GitLab in order to use its CI features; he is not standing in the way because he wants to see how it turns out. Ts'o : prioritization, and having too many things to look at. He would love to add a priority tag to patchwork that maintainers could set to help identify what needs attention first. Ryhl : not knowing how long she needs to wait after sending a version of a patch before concluding that she does not need to worry about problems with it. Me : huge number of patches touch the documentation directory, and it is hard to know which ones I should apply and which to leave to others. A lot of time is spent digging through linux-next to see if patches have been picked up by somebody else. Torvalds said that he often has the same problem. Khan complained about the same problem; it is often not clear who will pick up test patches. Hildenbrand : the high review load. Review cannot just be handed off to a bot; most changes need input from developers. Somehow, the subsystem needs to develop more experts, but it is hard to identify people who can grow in that way. Bergmann said that the review process is breaking down. When he replies to patches, he tries to teach contributors how to do better, but he has become discouraged because people using LLMs do not learn. So now those who might learn are not getting the feedback they need. The opposite problem happens too: a submitter sends 50 versions (literally) of a patch and responds to comments, but Bergmann thinks that the patch should not exist in the first place. Starovoitov : maintainers should not be looking for bugs or coding-style problems; bots will do that now. Instead, reviews should be strictly focused on the "why" of a patch, whether the fix is made in the right place, and is in good taste. Ryabitsev : the last entry in the MAINTAINERS file, titled " THE REST ", directs every patch to the linux-kernel mailing list. That generates millions of outgoing emails every day, leading to constant delivery problems. He asked whether that entry could be removed or changed to redirect patches to the patches@vger.kernel.org list. He later submitted a patch to get_maintainer.pl , causing it to only add linux-kernel if no other list has been identified as a recipient for a patch. Levin : subsystems are diverging in their practices, and many now have a manual on how to interact with them. That makes life hard for developers working across subsystems; he would like to see the community come back together. Hellwig : the Sashiko review workflow is broken, causing people to continually resend patches. There is no obvious answer to this problem, but something needs to improve. Brown asked subsystems with tests to actually build and run them so they don't break in linux-next. Kosina : there needs to be a better way to prioritize the handling of submissions. He liked Ts'o's idea, but without using patchwork. Will Deacon : the process is not much fun anymore; maintainers try to explain to contributors how they could improve, but are ignored. Danilo Krummrich does not mind seeing multiple versions of a series in a short time, but submitters are just feeding the Sashiko reviews into their LLM to create those new versions. A way needs to be found to encourage submitters to engage and talk to maintainers. Abeni : the infrastructure is not keeping up with what the subsystem needs. Networking runs its own version of Sashiko, which produces better results, but it can't be run for every networking subsystem. That creates extra friction for maintainers. Eric Dumazet announced that he had just retired, and that all of his pain points have vanished. Gushchin : Sashiko has gone from an experiment to a widely used tool in the community. There is a lot of work involved beyond developing the bot itself; he has to obtain tokens to run it, explain its value to management, and more. He could really use more people and more feedback. He only knows a few kernel subsystems; if people don't tell him about problems with the others, he will never know. Julia Lawall does not know if her work, much of which has involved finding and fixing bugs in the kernel, will have any relevance in the future. Five years ago she would have asked for more feedback from developers, now she isn't sure if it matters. Ojeda : tree-wide refactoring work can be tricky, and the advent of more Rust code seems set to make it harder. Gleixner has spent much of his time looking at design patterns and explaining them in lengthy emails. Developers used to appreciate that work, but more recently it is mostly ignored, and he wonders if it is still worth doing. In the LLM world, people say that they don't have time for design and, besides, the code works. He has spent 25 years doing cleanups, and does not want to merge more stuff that will just have to be cleaned up in the future. Brauner : code removal. The time has come to fix less code and to remove more of it. The idea was that these pain points would be discussed after the presentation, but that did not really happen. Instead, the conversation took a rather different direction. Succession Torvalds let it be known that he was about to go on vacation for two weeks, which is a bit awkward given that there is a merge window coming. So he was considering extending the merge window for a third week in response. There was not a lot of opposition to that idea in the room. He went on to talk about succession plans. The 2025 Summit included a discussion on that topic that was focused mostly on what should happen if Torvalds abruptly became unable to continue leading the project. This year, he said that, while he is not going anywhere anytime soon, it is not too early to think about how a graceful transition to a Torvalds-less future might happen. To help that process along, he has started actively ignoring more emails and stepping back a bit from development questions. He is curious to see how the community will react. There followed a wide-ranging but inconclusive discussion about the role Torvalds plays in the community and how things might operate when he finally decides to move on to something else. The two chief aspects of that role of can be described as "patch monkey" (executing pull requests) and resolution of conflicts between developers — which he professed to be bad at. In the future those roles could perhaps be split apart. The project could name a new benevolent dictator, or perhaps move to some sort of committee model. No decisions were made — none are needed now, and none were expected. But Torvalds clearly feels that it would be better to think about these things well ahead of time rather than under pressure. There will be a mailing list created, initially with the Summit attendees as members, where the discussion can simmer. At the end, Gushchin pointed out that the world looks quite different now than it did one year ago; with the current rate of change, it is going to be hard to make meaningful plans for an event that is expected multiple years in the future. Metadiscussion The closing topic was about the Maintainers Summit itself, and how it might be improved in the future. It started with a reference to this August thread where James Bottomley questioned whether the event should continue to exist at all. Few people seem to think it should be abolished, but there were concerns expressed about the process for selecting attendees, with some people describing it as a closed clique. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the maintainers in the room, all of whom had received invitations, did not see a lot of problems with that process. High-level process discussions tend to need the high-level maintainers in the room. As Brauner pointed out, that group is always going to seem a bit elitist. But, he said, getting that group into the same room once each year is helpful for the management of the project as a whole. Torvalds said that the older format of the Kernel Summit, which topped out at about 150 participants, was simply not manageable. The smaller group is at least able to have constructive discussions, he said. Hildenbrand said that one problem is a widely held impression that proposing a topic for the Summit will necessarily result in an invitation; he suggested that the call for topics next year should be rephrased. Ts'o said that colocating the Summit with the Linux Plumbers Conference (LPC) works well, and that holding the Summit afterward works best. That allows the participants to gather information from others and bring it into the more focused group. Hellwig put in a request for a different sort of gathering where developers from one subsystem can hold "office hours" to talk with others. That sort of happens at conferences now but, he said, the time at those events is too structured and there are too many other distractions happening. Bergmann pointed out that the LPC kernel-summit track has become less relevant over the years, and suggested that some of that track's time could be repurposed; that idea was reasonably well received. There was also talk of using a videoconference server to host subsystem-specific office hours at other times. The meeting closed with a general agreement that its format works fairly well, and that the office-hours idea might improve it. The biggest change might be in the call for topics, which may be rewritten to provide more information about how the selection process works and to make it clear that people can nominate others to attend. There was, finally, a suggestion that the ksummit mailing list could be used more. There are usually interesting discussions there in the lead-up to the event, but then it goes quiet the rest of the year; there is no reason why discussions of that type can't happen there at other times as well. Rust and error paths Posted Oct 15, 2026 13:59 UTC (Thu) by daroc (editor, #160859) [ Link ] (4 responses) Specifically, not handling an error (by discarding a Result value) currently gives a compiler warning, and Miguel Ojeda works hard to keep the kernel's Rust code warning-free, so that's noticeable. In a future version of the language, it may be possible to make not handling an error a compile-time error; there's work in progress on the language features required to enable that. In addition, Rust has shorthand for propagating errors (the ? operator) and facilities for carrying additional information as part of errors, which can make handling them easier in the cases where propagating the error is not appropriate. Also, in C one must read the documentation to figure out whether a function returning an int can return an error (although it often can); in Rust, that information is part of the type of the function, which makes it easy to see at a glance. It's really a whole bunch of little things that work together to make writing error-handling code in Rust a bit more pleasant and hard to screw up. The advent of LLMs has resulted in the discovery of huge numbers of security-relevant bugs, leading to a lot of fixes. Kroah-Hartman, who plays a central role in responding to those bugs, said that there are many more coming. Current tools find a lot of vulnerabilities, he said, but they are also wrong half the time; he has students working on improving that performance. He also has people and funding to help with handling the resulting fixes. We can work through this pile of problems, he said, but it will take a while. That is what the next year of work will be focused on. Levin added that LLMs do two things that are new. One is that they are good at developing an exploit from a patch; the other is that they can be used to monitor mailing lists and figure out which fixes have security implications. The result is machines that are automatically cranking out exploits. As soon as a problem has been detected, he said, any embargo is already over. There are thousands of known exploits out there at the moment. Kroah-Hartman said that the only thing that can be done is to get the fixes into the mainline as quickly as possible. Brauner pointed out that this leads to large pull requests after -rc1, which Torvalds has complained about. Torvalds, though, said that pull requests full of fixes are fine as long as they come from people who he can trust to have verified them to be fixes for real problems. The cost to him of doing a pull is almost zero; it's his job. Pinchart said that, while fixing bugs is good, what is really needed is ways to prevent the addition of new bugs. Kroah-Hartman said that increased use of Rust would help in that regard; many bugs are in error paths, and Rust has better ways of handling those. There is also an effort to scale up the work on hardening C code. Some of that work is landing in the newest versions of the compilers, but developers often do not have easy access to them, and linux-next does not either. Ojeda said there is work underway to increase the availability of prebuilt toolchains that developers can use to test their code. Kroah-Hartman said that security bugs are being immediately copied to maintainers now rather than being kept secret; it is the only way to keep up with the flood. But, he cautioned, maintainers should not be telling their employers about those bugs before they are public; otherwise the project as a whole risks running into trouble with government agencies worldwide. Once a fix has been pushed, though, the embargo ends. Starovoitov said that there are lists of vulnerabilities that have been discovered by LLMs, many of which have reproducers available. He wondered what the best way was to get those fixes into the mainline. Torvalds said that, when there are real kernel developers involved, the most urgent patches can go directly to him, bypassing maintainers and avoiding adding to their workload. Hildenbrand worried that maintainers would lose the opportunity to review fixes in their subsystems, and that they would lose control, but Torvalds answered that reviewing all those fixes just adds stress for everybody involved. Pain points Prior to the Summit, Torvalds asked each of the participants to prepare a one-minute summary of their biggest pain point for the group. These presentations would happen over a half hour, with no discussion until everybody had said their piece. The "no discussion" rule held most (but not all) of the time. In the order they were presented: Kroah-Hartman : subsystems that do not add CC: stable@vger.kernel.org tags to patches, but which still expect the stable team to pick up the important fixes anyway. The stable maintainers are overwhelmed as it is and are not doing that. Pinchart has heard from developers that they submit code, but do not know when their patches have been applied or to which tree. More maintainers should send emails when they apply patches, he said. Eric Biggers : patches that cannot easily be applied, and which do not specify a base to which they can be applied. A lot of patches cannot be properly reviewed without applying them first, he said. Rafael Wysocki : insufficient feedback on patches in general. People often have opinions, but do not always share them. Airlie asked his sub-maintainers; most of them identified him as the biggest pain point. More seriously, it was that the DRM subsystem is still seeing too many regressions. There is a push within the subsystem to move development to GitLab in order to use its CI features; he is not standing in the way because he wants to see how it turns out. Ts'o : prioritization, and having too many things to look at. He would love to add a priority tag to patchwork that maintainers could set to help identify what needs attention first. Ryhl : not knowing how long she needs to wait after sending a version of a patch before concluding that she does not need to worry about problems with it. Me : huge number of patches touch the documentation directory, and it is hard to know which ones I should apply and which to leave to others. A lot of time is spent digging through linux-next to see if patches have been picked up by somebody else. Torvalds said that he often has the same problem. Khan complained about the same problem; it is often not clear who will pick up test patches. Hildenbrand : the high review load. Review cannot just be handed off to a bot; most changes need input from developers. Somehow, the subsystem needs to develop more experts, but it is hard to identify people who can grow in that way. Bergmann said that the review process is breaking down. When he replies to patches, he tries to teach contributors how to do better, but he has become discouraged because people using LLMs do not learn. So now those who might learn are not getting the feedback they need. The opposite problem happens too: a submitter sends 50 versions (literally) of a patch and responds to comments, but Bergmann thinks that the patch should not exist in the first place. Starovoitov : maintainers should not be looking for bugs or coding-style problems; bots will do that now. Instead, reviews should be strictly focused on the "why" of a patch, whether the fix is made in the right place, and is in good taste. Ryabitsev : the last entry in the MAINTAINERS file, titled " THE REST ", directs every patch to the linux-kernel mailing list. That generates millions of outgoing emails every day, leading to constant delivery problems. He asked whether that entry could be removed or changed to redirect patches to the patches@vger.kernel.org list. He later submitted a patch to get_maintainer.pl , causing it to only add linux-kernel if no other list has been identified as a recipient for a patch. Levin : subsystems are diverging in their practices, and many now have a manual on how to interact with them. That makes life hard for developers working across subsystems; he would like to see the community come back together. Hellwig : the Sashiko review workflow is broken, causing people to continually resend patches. There is no obvious answer to this problem, but something needs to improve. Brown asked subsystems with tests to actually build and run them so they don't break in linux-next. Kosina : there needs to be a better way to prioritize the handling of submissions. He liked Ts'o's idea, but without using patchwork. Will Deacon : the process is not much fun anymore; maintainers try to explain to contributors how they could improve, but are ignored. Danilo Krummrich does not mind seeing multiple versions of a series in a short time, but submitters are just feeding the Sashiko reviews into their LLM to create those new versions. A way needs to be found to encourage submitters to engage and talk to maintainers. Abeni : the infrastructure is not keeping up with what the subsystem needs. Networking runs its own version of Sashiko, which produces better results, but it can't be run for every networking subsystem. That creates extra friction for maintainers. Eric Dumazet announced that he had just retired, and that all of his pain points have vanished. Gushchin : Sashiko has gone from an experiment to a widely used tool in the community. There is a lot of work involved beyond developing the bot itself; he has to obtain tokens to run it, explain its value to management, and more. He could really use more people and more feedback. He only knows a few kernel subsystems; if people don't tell him about problems with the others, he will never know. Julia Lawall does not know if her work, much of which has involved finding and fixing bugs in the kernel, will have any relevance in the future. Five years ago she would have asked for more feedback from developers, now she isn't sure if it matters. Ojeda : tree-wide refactoring work can be tricky, and the advent of more Rust code seems set to make it harder. Gleixner has spent much of his time looking at design patterns and explaining them in lengthy emails. Developers used to appreciate that work, but more recently it is mostly ignored, and he wonders if it is still worth doing. In the LLM world, people say that they don't have time for design and, besides, the code works. He has spent 25 years doing cleanups, and does not want to merge more stuff that will just have to be cleaned up in the future. Brauner : code removal. The time has come to fix less code and to remove more of it. The idea was that these pain points would be discussed after the presentation, but that did not really happen. Instead, the conversation took a rather different direction. Succession Torvalds let it be known that he was about to go on vacation for two weeks, which is a bit awkward given that there is a merge window coming. So he was considering extending the merge window for a third week in response. There was not a lot of opposition to that idea in the room. He went on to talk about succession plans. The 2025 Summit included a discussion on that topic that was focused mostly on what should happen if Torvalds abruptly became unable to continue leading the project. This year, he said that, while he is not going anywhere anytime soon, it is not too early to think about how a graceful transition to a Torvalds-less future might happen. To help that process along, he has started actively ignoring more emails and stepping back a bit from development questions. He is curious to see how the community will react. There followed a wide-ranging but inconclusive discussion about the role Torvalds plays in the community and how things might operate when he finally decides to move on to something else. The two chief aspects of that role of can be described as "patch monkey" (executing pull requests) and resolution of conflicts between developers — which he professed to be bad at. In the future those roles could perhaps be split apart. The project could name a new benevolent dictator, or perhaps move to some sort of committee model. No decisions were made — none are needed now, and none were expected. But Torvalds clearly feels that it would be better to think about these things well ahead of time rather than under pressure. There will be a mailing list created, initially with the Summit attendees as members, where the discussion can simmer. At the end, Gushchin pointed out that the world looks quite different now than it did one year ago; with the current rate of change, it is going to be hard to make meaningful plans for an event that is expected multiple years in the future. Metadiscussion The closing topic was about the Maintainers Summit itself, and how it might be improved in the future. It started with a reference to this August thread where James Bottomley questioned whether the event should continue to exist at all. Few people seem to think it should be abolished, but there were concerns expressed about the process for selecting attendees, with some people describing it as a closed clique. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the maintainers in the room, all of whom had received invitations, did not see a lot of problems with that process. High-level process discussions tend to need the high-level maintainers in the room. As Brauner pointed out, that group is always going to seem a bit elitist. But, he said, getting that group into the same room once each year is helpful for the management of the project as a whole. Torvalds said that the older format of the Kernel Summit, which topped out at about 150 participants, was simply not manageable. The smaller group is at least able to have constructive discussions, he said. Hildenbrand said that one problem is a widely held impression that proposing a topic for the Summit will necessarily result in an invitation; he suggested that the call for topics next year should be rephrased. Ts'o said that colocating the Summit with the Linux Plumbers Conference (LPC) works well, and that holding the Summit afterward works best. That allows the participants to gather information from others and bring it into the more focused group. Hellwig put in a request for a different sort of gathering where developers from one subsystem can hold "office hours" to talk with others. That sort of happens at conferences now but, he said, the time at those events is too structured and there are too many other distractions happening. Bergmann pointed out that the LPC kernel-summit track has become less relevant over the years, and suggested that some of that track's time could be repurposed; that idea was reasonably well received. There was also talk of using a videoconference server to host subsystem-specific office hours at other times. The meeting closed with a general agreement that its format works fairly well, and that the office-hours idea might improve it. The biggest change might be in the call for topics, which may be rewritten to provide more information about how the selection process works and to make it clear that people can nominate others to attend. There was, finally, a suggestion that the ksummit mailing list could be used more. There are usually interesting discussions there in the lead-up to the event, but then it goes quiet the rest of the year; there is no reason why discussions of that type can't happen there at other times as well. Rust and error paths Posted Oct 15, 2026 13:59 UTC (Thu) by daroc (editor, #160859) [ Link ] (4 responses) Specifically, not handling an error (by discarding a Result value) currently gives a compiler warning, and Miguel Ojeda works hard to keep the kernel's Rust code warning-free, so that's noticeable. In a future version of the language, it may be possible to make not handling an error a compile-time error; there's work in progress on the language features required to enable that. In addition, Rust has shorthand for propagating errors (the ? operator) and facilities for carrying additional information as part of errors, which can make handling them easier in the cases where propagating the error is not appropriate. Also, in C one must read the documentation to figure out whether a function returning an int can return an error (although it often can); in Rust, that information is part of the type of the function, which makes it easy to see at a glance. It's really a whole bunch of little things that work together to make writing error-handling code in Rust a bit more pleasant and hard to screw up.
