Prior to the Summit, Torvalds asked each of the participants to prepare a one-minute summary of their biggest pain point for the group. These presentations would happen over a half hour, with no discussion until everybody had said their piece. The "no discussion" rule held most (but not all) of the time. In the order they were presented: Kroah-Hartman : subsystems that do not add CC: stable@vger.kernel.org tags to patches, but which still expect the stable team to pick up the important fixes anyway. The stable maintainers are overwhelmed as it is and are not doing that. Pinchart has heard from developers that they submit code, but do not know when their patches have been applied or to which tree. More maintainers should send emails when they apply patches, he said. Eric Biggers : patches that cannot easily be applied, and which do not specify a base to which they can be applied. A lot of patches cannot be properly reviewed without applying them first, he said. Rafael Wysocki : insufficient feedback on patches in general. People often have opinions, but do not always share them. Airlie asked his sub-maintainers; most of them identified him as the biggest pain point. More seriously, it was that the DRM subsystem is still seeing too many regressions. There is a push within the subsystem to move development to GitLab in order to use its CI features; he is not standing in the way because he wants to see how it turns out. Ts'o : prioritization, and having too many things to look at. He would love to add a priority tag to patchwork that maintainers could set to help identify what needs attention first. Ryhl : not knowing how long she needs to wait after sending a version of a patch before concluding that she does not need to worry about problems with it. Me : huge number of patches touch the documentation directory, and it is hard to know which ones I should apply and which to leave to others. A lot of time is spent digging through linux-next to see if patches have been picked up by somebody else. Torvalds said that he often has the same problem. Khan complained about the same problem; it is often not clear who will pick up test patches. Hildenbrand : the high review load. Review cannot just be handed off to a bot; most changes need input from developers. Somehow, the subsystem needs to develop more experts, but it is hard to identify people who can grow in that way. Bergmann said that the review process is breaking down. When he replies to patches, he tries to teach contributors how to do better, but he has become discouraged because people using LLMs do not learn. So now those who might learn are not getting the feedback they need. The opposite problem happens too: a submitter sends 50 versions (literally) of a patch and responds to comments, but Bergmann thinks that the patch should not exist in the first place. Starovoitov : maintainers should not be looking for bugs or coding-style problems; bots will do that now. Instead, reviews should be strictly focused on the "why" of a patch, whether the fix is made in the right place, and is in good taste. Ryabitsev : the last entry in the MAINTAINERS file, titled " THE REST ", directs every patch to the linux-kernel mailing list. That generates millions of outgoing emails every day, leading to constant delivery problems. He asked whether that entry could be removed or changed to redirect patches to the patches@vger.kernel.org list. He later submitted a patch to get_maintainer.pl , causing it to only add linux-kernel if no other list has been identified as a recipient for a patch. Levin : subsystems are diverging in their practices, and many now have a manual on how to interact with them. That makes life hard for developers working across subsystems; he would like to see the community come back together. Hellwig : the Sashiko review workflow is broken, causing people to continually resend patches. There is no obvious answer to this problem, but something needs to improve. Brown asked subsystems with tests to actually build and run them so they don't break in linux-next. Kosina : there needs to be a better way to prioritize the handling of submissions. He liked Ts'o's idea, but without using patchwork. Will Deacon : the process is not much fun anymore; maintainers try to explain to contributors how they could improve, but are ignored. Danilo Krummrich does not mind seeing multiple versions of a series in a short time, but submitters are just feeding the Sashiko reviews into their LLM to create those new versions. A way needs to be found to encourage submitters to engage and talk to maintainers. Abeni : the infrastructure is not keeping up with what the subsystem needs. Networking runs its own version of Sashiko, which produces better results, but it can't be run for every networking subsystem. That creates extra friction for maintainers. Eric Dumazet announced that he had just retired, and that all of his pain points have vanished. Gushchin : Sashiko has gone from an experiment to a widely used tool in the community. There is a lot of work involved beyond developing the bot itself; he has to obtain tokens to run it, explain its value to management, and more. He could really use more people and more feedback. He only knows a few kernel subsystems; if people don't tell him about problems with the others, he will never know. Julia Lawall does not know if her work, much of which has involved finding and fixing bugs in the kernel, will have any relevance in the future. Five years ago she would have asked for more feedback from developers, now she isn't sure if it matters. Ojeda : tree-wide refactoring work can be tricky, and the advent of more Rust code seems set to make it harder. Gleixner has spent much of his time looking at design patterns and explaining them in lengthy emails. Developers used to appreciate that work, but more recently it is mostly ignored, and he wonders if it is still worth doing. In the LLM world, people say that they don't have time for design and, besides, the code works. He has spent 25 years doing cleanups, and does not want to merge more stuff that will just have to be cleaned up in the future. Brauner : code removal. The time has come to fix less code and to remove more of it. The idea was that these pain points would be discussed after the presentation, but that did not really happen. Instead, the conversation took a rather different direction. Succession Torvalds let it be known that he was about to go on vacation for two weeks, which is a bit awkward given that there is a merge window coming. So he was considering extending the merge window for a third week in response. There was not a lot of opposition to that idea in the room. He went on to talk about succession plans. The 2025 Summit included a discussion on that topic that was focused mostly on what should happen if Torvalds abruptly became unable to continue leading the project. This year, he said that, while he is not going anywhere anytime soon, it is not too early to think about how a graceful transition to a Torvalds-less future might happen. To help that process along, he has started actively ignoring more emails and stepping back a bit from development questions. He is curious to see how the community will react. There followed a wide-ranging but inconclusive discussion about the role Torvalds plays in the community and how things might operate when he finally decides to move on to something else. The two chief aspects of that role of can be described as "patch monkey" (executing pull requests) and resolution of conflicts between developers — which he professed to be bad at. In the future those roles could perhaps be split apart. The project could name a new benevolent dictator, or perhaps move to some sort of committee model. No decisions were made — none are needed now, and none were expected. But Torvalds clearly feels that it would be better to think about these things well ahead of time rather than under pressure. There will be a mailing list created, initially with the Summit attendees as members, where the discussion can simmer. At the end, Gushchin pointed out that the world looks quite different now than it did one year ago; with the current rate of change, it is going to be hard to make meaningful plans for an event that is expected multiple years in the future. Metadiscussion The closing topic was about the Maintainers Summit itself, and how it might be improved in the future. It started with a reference to this August thread where James Bottomley questioned whether the event should continue to exist at all. Few people seem to think it should be abolished, but there were concerns expressed about the process for selecting attendees, with some people describing it as a closed clique. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the maintainers in the room, all of whom had received invitations, did not see a lot of problems with that process. High-level process discussions tend to need the high-level maintainers in the room. As Brauner pointed out, that group is always going to seem a bit elitist. But, he said, getting that group into the same room once each year is helpful for the management of the project as a whole. Torvalds said that the older format of the Kernel Summit, which topped out at about 150 participants, was simply not manageable. The smaller group is at least able to have constructive discussions, he said. Hildenbrand said that one problem is a widely held impression that proposing a topic for the Summit will necessarily result in an invitation; he suggested that the call for topics next year should be rephrased. Ts'o said that colocating the Summit with the Linux Plumbers Conference (LPC) works well, and that holding the Summit afterward works best. That allows the participants to gather information from others and bring it into the more focused group. Hellwig put in a request for a different sort of gathering where developers from one subsystem can hold "office hours" to talk with others. That sort of happens at conferences now but, he said, the time at those events is too structured and there are too many other distractions happening. Bergmann pointed out that the LPC kernel-summit track has become less relevant over the years, and suggested that some of that track's time could be repurposed; that idea was reasonably well received. There was also talk of using a videoconference server to host subsystem-specific office hours at other times. The meeting closed with a general agreement that its format works fairly well, and that the office-hours idea might improve it. The biggest change might be in the call for topics, which may be rewritten to provide more information about how the selection process works and to make it clear that people can nominate others to attend. There was, finally, a suggestion that the ksummit mailing list could be used more. There are usually interesting discussions there in the lead-up to the event, but then it goes quiet the rest of the year; there is no reason why discussions of that type can't happen there at other times as well. Every word I post online is hand typed by me, but it's almost always been critiqued by an LLM. They are extraordinarily good at fixing spelling and grammar mistakes, and good at doing fact checking and checking reasoning, but bat well below 50% at thinking up novel ideas or viewpoints and will usually refuse to take them at face value. However, you can mostly convince them those rejected ideas are sound, and in the process make your reasoning clearer to human readers as well. On the odd occasion I can't convince them, I usually drop the post. I figure if I can't explain the rationale to an LLM, I'm probably not going to convince a human either. Explaining the rationale means you have to convince the LLM that its initial summary of the internet hive mind its stochastic parrot spat out is wrong. You do that in the usual way - with evidence and deductions from that. If the evidence matches what they know (they know an awful lot, so if you're right you don't have to give citations, you just have to give them enough so that same stochastic parrot can dig up the facts it's already seen), they are completely capable of checking the reasoning you used to arrive at your deductions. Used well, an LLM can get a single poster closer to the editorial standard LWN achieves with its team. It's the same sort of force multiplier Linus is saying he gets with coding. Like all force multipliers, it can be used to polish rubbish into the flood of slop we see today. Yes, LLMs enabled that flood, but I don't see why that's a good reason to eschew them. In a future version of the language, it may be possible to make not handling an error a compile-time error; there's work in progress on the language features required to enable that. In addition, Rust has shorthand for propagating errors (the ? operator) and facilities for carrying additional information as part of errors, which can make handling them easier in the cases where propagating the error is not appropriate. There was, finally, a suggestion that the ksummit mailing list could be used more. The idea was that these pain points would be discussed after the presentation, but that did not really happen. Instead, the conversation took a rather different direction. Succession Torvalds let it be known that he was about to go on vacation for two weeks, which is a bit awkward given that there is a merge window coming. So he was considering extending the merge window for a third week in response. There was not a lot of opposition to that idea in the room. He went on to talk about succession plans. The 2025 Summit included a discussion on that topic that was focused mostly on what should happen if Torvalds abruptly became unable to continue leading the project. This year, he said that, while he is not going anywhere anytime soon, it is not too early to think about how a graceful transition to a Torvalds-less future might happen. To help that process along, he has started actively ignoring more emails and stepping back a bit from development questions. He is curious to see how the community will react. There followed a wide-ranging but inconclusive discussion about the role Torvalds plays in the community and how things might operate when he finally decides to move on to something else. The two chief aspects of that role of can be described as "patch monkey" (executing pull requests) and resolution of conflicts between developers — which he professed to be bad at. In the future those roles could perhaps be split apart. The project could name a new benevolent dictator, or perhaps move to some sort of committee model. No decisions were made — none are needed now, and none were expected. But Torvalds clearly feels that it would be better to think about these things well ahead of time rather than under pressure. There will be a mailing list created, initially with the Summit attendees as members, where the discussion can simmer. At the end, Gushchin pointed out that the world looks quite different now than it did one year ago; with the current rate of change, it is going to be hard to make meaningful plans for an event that is expected multiple years in the future. Metadiscussion The closing topic was about the Maintainers Summit itself, and how it might be improved in the future. It started with a reference to this August thread where James Bottomley questioned whether the event should continue to exist at all. Few people seem to think it should be abolished, but there were concerns expressed about the process for selecting attendees, with some people describing it as a closed clique. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the maintainers in the room, all of whom had received invitations, did not see a lot of problems with that process. High-level process discussions tend to need the high-level maintainers in the room. As Brauner pointed out, that group is always going to seem a bit elitist. But, he said, getting that group into the same room once each year is helpful for the management of the project as a whole. Torvalds said that the older format of the Kernel Summit, which topped out at about 150 participants, was simply not manageable. The smaller group is at least able to have constructive discussions, he said. Hildenbrand said that one problem is a widely held impression that proposing a topic for the Summit will necessarily result in an invitation; he suggested that the call for topics next year should be rephrased. Ts'o said that colocating the Summit with the Linux Plumbers Conference (LPC) works well, and that holding the Summit afterward works best. That allows the participants to gather information from others and bring it into the more focused group. Hellwig put in a request for a different sort of gathering where developers from one subsystem can hold "office hours" to talk with others. That sort of happens at conferences now but, he said, the time at those events is too structured and there are too many other distractions happening. Bergmann pointed out that the LPC kernel-summit track has become less relevant over the years, and suggested that some of that track's time could be repurposed; that idea was reasonably well received. There was also talk of using a videoconference server to host subsystem-specific office hours at other times. The meeting closed with a general agreement that its format works fairly well, and that the office-hours idea might improve it. The biggest change might be in the call for topics, which may be rewritten to provide more information about how the selection process works and to make it clear that people can nominate others to attend. There was, finally, a suggestion that the ksummit mailing list could be used more. There are usually interesting discussions there in the lead-up to the event, but then it goes quiet the rest of the year; there is no reason why discussions of that type can't happen there at other times as well. In a future version of the language, it may be possible to make not handling an error a compile-time error; there's work in progress on the language features required to enable that. In addition, Rust has shorthand for propagating errors (the ? operator) and facilities for carrying additional information as part of errors, which can make handling them easier in the cases where propagating the error is not appropriate. Also, in C one must read the documentation to figure out whether a function returning an int can return an error (although it often can); in Rust, that information is part of the type of the function, which makes it easy to see at a glance. It's really a whole bunch of little things that work together to make writing error-handling code in Rust a bit more pleasant and hard to screw up. Succession Torvalds let it be known that he was about to go on vacation for two weeks, which is a bit awkward given that there is a merge window coming. So he was considering extending the merge window for a third week in response. There was not a lot of opposition to that idea in the room. He went on to talk about succession plans. The 2025 Summit included a discussion on that topic that was focused mostly on what should happen if Torvalds abruptly became unable to continue leading the project. This year, he said that, while he is not going anywhere anytime soon, it is not too early to think about how a graceful transition to a Torvalds-less future might happen. To help that process along, he has started actively ignoring more emails and stepping back a bit from development questions. He is curious to see how the community will react. There followed a wide-ranging but inconclusive discussion about the role Torvalds plays in the community and how things might operate when he finally decides to move on to something else. The two chief aspects of that role of can be described as "patch monkey" (executing pull requests) and resolution of conflicts between developers — which he professed to be bad at. In the future those roles could perhaps be split apart. The project could name a new benevolent dictator, or perhaps move to some sort of committee model. No decisions were made — none are needed now, and none were expected. But Torvalds clearly feels that it would be better to think about these things well ahead of time rather than under pressure. There will be a mailing list created, initially with the Summit attendees as members, where the discussion can simmer. At the end, Gushchin pointed out that the world looks quite different now than it did one year ago; with the current rate of change, it is going to be hard to make meaningful plans for an event that is expected multiple years in the future. Metadiscussion The closing topic was about the Maintainers Summit itself, and how it might be improved in the future. It started with a reference to this August thread where James Bottomley questioned whether the event should continue to exist at all. Few people seem to think it should be abolished, but there were concerns expressed about the process for selecting attendees, with some people describing it as a closed clique. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the maintainers in the room, all of whom had received invitations, did not see a lot of problems with that process. High-level process discussions tend to need the high-level maintainers in the room. As Brauner pointed out, that group is always going to seem a bit elitist. But, he said, getting that group into the same room once each year is helpful for the management of the project as a whole. Torvalds said that the older format of the Kernel Summit, which topped out at about 150 participants, was simply not manageable. The smaller group is at least able to have constructive discussions, he said. Hildenbrand said that one problem is a widely held impression that proposing a topic for the Summit will necessarily result in an invitation; he suggested that the call for topics next year should be rephrased. Ts'o said that colocating the Summit with the Linux Plumbers Conference (LPC) works well, and that holding the Summit afterward works best. That allows the participants to gather information from others and bring it into the more focused group. Hellwig put in a request for a different sort of gathering where developers from one subsystem can hold "office hours" to talk with others. That sort of happens at conferences now but, he said, the time at those events is too structured and there are too many other distractions happening. Bergmann pointed out that the LPC kernel-summit track has become less relevant over the years, and suggested that some of that track's time could be repurposed; that idea was reasonably well received. There was also talk of using a videoconference server to host subsystem-specific office hours at other times. The meeting closed with a general agreement that its format works fairly well, and that the office-hours idea might improve it. The biggest change might be in the call for topics, which may be rewritten to provide more information about how the selection process works and to make it clear that people can nominate others to attend. There was, finally, a suggestion that the ksummit mailing list could be used more. There are usually interesting discussions there in the lead-up to the event, but then it goes quiet the rest of the year; there is no reason why discussions of that type can't happen there at other times as well. In a future version of the language, it may be possible to make not handling an error a compile-time error; there's work in progress on the language features required to enable that. In addition, Rust has shorthand for propagating errors (the ? operator) and facilities for carrying additional information as part of errors, which can make handling them easier in the cases where propagating the error is not appropriate. Also, in C one must read the documentation to figure out whether a function returning an int can return an error (although it often can); in Rust, that information is part of the type of the function, which makes it easy to see at a glance. It's really a whole bunch of little things that work together to make writing error-handling code in Rust a bit more pleasant and hard to screw up. Torvalds let it be known that he was about to go on vacation for two weeks, which is a bit awkward given that there is a merge window coming. So he was considering extending the merge window for a third week in response. There was not a lot of opposition to that idea in the room. He went on to talk about succession plans. The 2025 Summit included a discussion on that topic that was focused mostly on what should happen if Torvalds abruptly became unable to continue leading the project. This year, he said that, while he is not going anywhere anytime soon, it is not too early to think about how a graceful transition to a Torvalds-less future might happen. To help that process along, he has started actively ignoring more emails and stepping back a bit from development questions. He is curious to see how the community will react. There followed a wide-ranging but inconclusive discussion about the role Torvalds plays in the community and how things might operate when he finally decides to move on to something else. The two chief aspects of that role of can be described as "patch monkey" (executing pull requests) and resolution of conflicts between developers — which he professed to be bad at. In the future those roles could perhaps be split apart. The project could name a new benevolent dictator, or perhaps move to some sort of committee model. No decisions were made — none are needed now, and none were expected. But Torvalds clearly feels that it would be better to think about these things well ahead of time rather than under pressure. There will be a mailing list created, initially with the Summit attendees as members, where the discussion can simmer. At the end, Gushchin pointed out that the world looks quite different now than it did one year ago; with the current rate of change, it is going to be hard to make meaningful plans for an event that is expected multiple years in the future. Metadiscussion The closing topic was about the Maintainers Summit itself, and how it might be improved in the future. It started with a reference to this August thread where James Bottomley questioned whether the event should continue to exist at all. Few people seem to think it should be abolished, but there were concerns expressed about the process for selecting attendees, with some people describing it as a closed clique. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the maintainers in the room, all of whom had received invitations, did not see a lot of problems with that process. High-level process discussions tend to need the high-level maintainers in the room. As Brauner pointed out, that group is always going to seem a bit elitist. But, he said, getting that group into the same room once each year is helpful for the management of the project as a whole. Torvalds said that the older format of the Kernel Summit, which topped out at about 150 participants, was simply not manageable. The smaller group is at least able to have constructive discussions, he said. Hildenbrand said that one problem is a widely held impression that proposing a topic for the Summit will necessarily result in an invitation; he suggested that the call for topics next year should be rephrased. Ts'o said that colocating the Summit with the Linux Plumbers Conference (LPC) works well, and that holding the Summit afterward works best. That allows the participants to gather information from others and bring it into the more focused group. Hellwig put in a request for a different sort of gathering where developers from one subsystem can hold "office hours" to talk with others. That sort of happens at conferences now but, he said, the time at those events is too structured and there are too many other distractions happening. Bergmann pointed out that the LPC kernel-summit track has become less relevant over the years, and suggested that some of that track's time could be repurposed; that idea was reasonably well received. There was also talk of using a videoconference server to host subsystem-specific office hours at other times. The meeting closed with a general agreement that its format works fairly well, and that the office-hours idea might improve it. The biggest change might be in the call for topics, which may be rewritten to provide more information about how the selection process works and to make it clear that people can nominate others to attend. There was, finally, a suggestion that the ksummit mailing list could be used more. There are usually interesting discussions there in the lead-up to the event, but then it goes quiet the rest of the year; there is no reason why discussions of that type can't happen there at other times as well. In a future version of the language, it may be possible to make not handling an error a compile-time error; there's work in progress on the language features required to enable that. In addition, Rust has shorthand for propagating errors (the ? operator) and facilities for carrying additional information as part of errors, which can make handling them easier in the cases where propagating the error is not appropriate. Also, in C one must read the documentation to figure out whether a function returning an int can return an error (although it often can); in Rust, that information is part of the type of the function, which makes it easy to see at a glance. He went on to talk about succession plans. The 2025 Summit included a discussion on that topic that was focused mostly on what should happen if Torvalds abruptly became unable to continue leading the project. This year, he said that, while he is not going anywhere anytime soon, it is not too early to think about how a graceful transition to a Torvalds-less future might happen. To help that process along, he has started actively ignoring more emails and stepping back a bit from development questions. He is curious to see how the community will react. There followed a wide-ranging but inconclusive discussion about the role Torvalds plays in the community and how things might operate when he finally decides to move on to something else. The two chief aspects of that role of can be described as "patch monkey" (executing pull requests) and resolution of conflicts between developers — which he professed to be bad at. In the future those roles could perhaps be split apart. The project could name a new benevolent dictator, or perhaps move to some sort of committee model. No decisions were made — none are needed now, and none were expected. But Torvalds clearly feels that it would be better to think about these things well ahead of time rather than under pressure. There will be a mailing list created, initially with the Summit attendees as members, where the discussion can simmer. At the end, Gushchin pointed out that the world looks quite different now than it did one year ago; with the current rate of change, it is going to be hard to make meaningful plans for an event that is expected multiple years in the future. Metadiscussion The closing topic was about the Maintainers Summit itself, and how it might be improved in the future. It started with a reference to this August thread where James Bottomley questioned whether the event should continue to exist at all. Few people seem to think it should be abolished, but there were concerns expressed about the process for selecting attendees, with some people describing it as a closed clique. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the maintainers in the room, all of whom had received invitations, did not see a lot of problems with that process. High-level process discussions tend to need the high-level maintainers in the room. As Brauner pointed out, that group is always going to seem a bit elitist. But, he said, getting that group into the same room once each year is helpful for the management of the project as a whole. Torvalds said that the older format of the Kernel Summit, which topped out at about 150 participants, was simply not manageable. The smaller group is at least able to have constructive discussions, he said. Hildenbrand said that one problem is a widely held impression that proposing a topic for the Summit will necessarily result in an invitation; he suggested that the call for topics next year should be rephrased. Ts'o said that colocating the Summit with the Linux Plumbers Conference (LPC) works well, and that holding the Summit afterward works best. That allows the participants to gather information from others and bring it into the more focused group. Hellwig put in a request for a different sort of gathering where developers from one subsystem can hold "office hours" to talk with others. That sort of happens at conferences now but, he said, the time at those events is too structured and there are too many other distractions happening. Bergmann pointed out that the LPC kernel-summit track has become less relevant over the years, and suggested that some of that track's time could be repurposed; that idea was reasonably well received. There was also talk of using a videoconference server to host subsystem-specific office hours at other times. The meeting closed with a general agreement that its format works fairly well, and that the office-hours idea might improve it. The biggest change might be in the call for topics, which may be rewritten to provide more information about how the selection process works and to make it clear that people can nominate others to attend. There was, finally, a suggestion that the ksummit mailing list could be used more. There are usually interesting discussions there in the lead-up to the event, but then it goes quiet the rest of the year; there is no reason why discussions of that type can't happen there at other times as well. There followed a wide-ranging but inconclusive discussion about the role Torvalds plays in the community and how things might operate when he finally decides to move on to something else. The two chief aspects of that role of can be described as "patch monkey" (executing pull requests) and resolution of conflicts between developers — which he professed to be bad at. In the future those roles could perhaps be split apart. The project could name a new benevolent dictator, or perhaps move to some sort of committee model. No decisions were made — none are needed now, and none were expected. But Torvalds clearly feels that it would be better to think about these things well ahead of time rather than under pressure. There will be a mailing list created, initially with the Summit attendees as members, where the discussion can simmer. At the end, Gushchin pointed out that the world looks quite different now than it did one year ago; with the current rate of change, it is going to be hard to make meaningful plans for an event that is expected multiple years in the future. Metadiscussion The closing topic was about the Maintainers Summit itself, and how it might be improved in the future. It started with a reference to this August thread where James Bottomley questioned whether the event should continue to exist at all. Few people seem to think it should be abolished, but there were concerns expressed about the process for selecting attendees, with some people describing it as a closed clique. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the maintainers in the room, all of whom had received invitations, did not see a lot of problems with that process. High-level process discussions tend to need the high-level maintainers in the room. As Brauner pointed out, that group is always going to seem a bit elitist. But, he said, getting that group into the same room once each year is helpful for the management of the project as a whole. Torvalds said that the older format of the Kernel Summit, which topped out at about 150 participants, was simply not manageable. The smaller group is at least able to have constructive discussions, he said. Hildenbrand said that one problem is a widely held impression that proposing a topic for the Summit will necessarily result in an invitation; he suggested that the call for topics next year should be rephrased. Ts'o said that colocating the Summit with the Linux Plumbers Conference (LPC) works well, and that holding the Summit afterward works best. That allows the participants to gather information from others and bring it into the more focused group. Hellwig put in a request for a different sort of gathering where developers from one subsystem can hold "office hours" to talk with others. That sort of happens at conferences now but, he said, the time at those events is too structured and there are too many other distractions happening. Bergmann pointed out that the LPC kernel-summit track has become less relevant over the years, and suggested that some of that track's time could be repurposed; that idea was reasonably well received. There was also talk of using a videoconference server to host subsystem-specific office hours at other times. The meeting closed with a general agreement that its format works fairly well, and that the office-hours idea might improve it. The biggest change might be in the call for topics, which may be rewritten to provide more information about how the selection process works and to make it clear that people can nominate others to attend. There was, finally, a suggestion that the ksummit mailing list could be used more. There are usually interesting discussions there in the lead-up to the event, but then it goes quiet the rest of the year; there is no reason why discussions of that type can't happen there at other times as well. Metadiscussion The closing topic was about the Maintainers Summit itself, and how it might be improved in the future. It started with a reference to this August thread where James Bottomley questioned whether the event should continue to exist at all. Few people seem to think it should be abolished, but there were concerns expressed about the process for selecting attendees, with some people describing it as a closed clique. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the maintainers in the room, all of whom had received invitations, did not see a lot of problems with that process. High-level process discussions tend to need the high-level maintainers in the room. As Brauner pointed out, that group is always going to seem a bit elitist. But, he said, getting that group into the same room once each year is helpful for the management of the project as a whole. Torvalds said that the older format of the Kernel Summit, which topped out at about 150 participants, was simply not manageable. The smaller group is at least able to have constructive discussions, he said. Hildenbrand said that one problem is a widely held impression that proposing a topic for the Summit will necessarily result in an invitation; he suggested that the call for topics next year should be rephrased. Ts'o said that colocating the Summit with the Linux Plumbers Conference (LPC) works well, and that holding the Summit afterward works best. That allows the participants to gather information from others and bring it into the more focused group. Hellwig put in a request for a different sort of gathering where developers from one subsystem can hold "office hours" to talk with others. That sort of happens at conferences now but, he said, the time at those events is too structured and there are too many other distractions happening. Bergmann pointed out that the LPC kernel-summit track has become less relevant over the years, and suggested that some of that track's time could be repurposed; that idea was reasonably well received. There was also talk of using a videoconference server to host subsystem-specific office hours at other times. The meeting closed with a general agreement that its format works fairly well, and that the office-hours idea might improve it. The biggest change might be in the call for topics, which may be rewritten to provide more information about how the selection process works and to make it clear that people can nominate others to attend. There was, finally, a suggestion that the ksummit mailing list could be used more. There are usually interesting discussions there in the lead-up to the event, but then it goes quiet the rest of the year; there is no reason why discussions of that type can't happen there at other times as well. Metadiscussion The closing topic was about the Maintainers Summit itself, and how it might be improved in the future. It started with a reference to this August thread where James Bottomley questioned whether the event should continue to exist at all. Few people seem to think it should be abolished, but there were concerns expressed about the process for selecting attendees, with some people describing it as a closed clique. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the maintainers in the room, all of whom had received invitations, did not see a lot of problems with that process. High-level process discussions tend to need the high-level maintainers in the room. As Brauner pointed out, that group is always going to seem a bit elitist. But, he said, getting that group into the same room once each year is helpful for the management of the project as a whole. Torvalds said that the older format of the Kernel Summit, which topped out at about 150 participants, was simply not manageable. The smaller group is at least able to have constructive discussions, he said. Hildenbrand said that one problem is a widely held impression that proposing a topic for the Summit will necessarily result in an invitation; he suggested that the call for topics next year should be rephrased. Ts'o said that colocating the Summit with the Linux Plumbers Conference (LPC) works well, and that holding the Summit afterward works best. That allows the participants to gather information from others and bring it into the more focused group. Hellwig put in a request for a different sort of gathering where developers from one subsystem can hold "office hours" to talk with others. That sort of happens at conferences now but, he said, the time at those events is too structured and there are too many other distractions happening. Bergmann pointed out that the LPC kernel-summit track has become less relevant over the years, and suggested that some of that track's time could be repurposed; that idea was reasonably well received. There was also talk of using a videoconference server to host subsystem-specific office hours at other times. The meeting closed with a general agreement that its format works fairly well, and that the office-hours idea might improve it. The biggest change might be in the call for topics, which may be rewritten to provide more information about how the selection process works and to make it clear that people can nominate others to attend. There was, finally, a suggestion that the ksummit mailing list could be used more. There are usually interesting discussions there in the lead-up to the event, but then it goes quiet the rest of the year; there is no reason why discussions of that type can't happen there at other times as well. In a future version of the language, it may be possible to make not handling an error a compile-time error; there's work in progress on the language features required to enable that. In addition, Rust has shorthand for propagating errors (the ? operator) and facilities for carrying additional information as part of errors, which can make handling them easier in the cases where propagating the error is not appropriate. Also, in C one must read the documentation to figure out whether a function returning an int can return an error (although it often can); in Rust, that information is part of the type of the function, which makes it easy to see at a glance. It's really a whole bunch of little things that work together to make writing error-handling code in Rust a bit more pleasant and hard to screw up. The closing topic was about the Maintainers Summit itself, and how it might be improved in the future. It started with a reference to this August thread where James Bottomley questioned whether the event should continue to exist at all. Few people seem to think it should be abolished, but there were concerns expressed about the process for selecting attendees, with some people describing it as a closed clique. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the maintainers in the room, all of whom had received invitations, did not see a lot of problems with that process. High-level process discussions tend to need the high-level maintainers in the room. As Brauner pointed out, that group is always going to seem a bit elitist. But, he said, getting that group into the same room once each year is helpful for the management of the project as a whole. Torvalds said that the older format of the Kernel Summit, which topped out at about 150 participants, was simply not manageable. The smaller group is at least able to have constructive discussions, he said. Hildenbrand said that one problem is a widely held impression that proposing a topic for the Summit will necessarily result in an invitation; he suggested that the call for topics next year should be rephrased. Ts'o said that colocating the Summit with the Linux Plumbers Conference (LPC) works well, and that holding the Summit afterward works best. That allows the participants to gather information from others and bring it into the more focused group. Hellwig put in a request for a different sort of gathering where developers from one subsystem can hold "office hours" to talk with others. That sort of happens at conferences now but, he said, the time at those events is too structured and there are too many other distractions happening. Bergmann pointed out that the LPC kernel-summit track has become less relevant over the years, and suggested that some of that track's time could be repurposed; that idea was reasonably well received. There was also talk of using a videoconference server to host subsystem-specific office hours at other times. The meeting closed with a general agreement that its format works fairly well, and that the office-hours idea might improve it. The biggest change might be in the call for topics, which may be rewritten to provide more information about how the selection process works and to make it clear that people can nominate others to attend. There was, finally, a suggestion that the ksummit mailing list could be used more. There are usually interesting discussions there in the lead-up to the event, but then it goes quiet the rest of the year; there is no reason why discussions of that type can't happen there at other times as well. Rust and error paths Posted Oct 15, 2026 13:59 UTC (Thu) by daroc (editor, #160859) [ Link ] (4 responses) Specifically, not handling an error (by discarding a Result value) currently gives a compiler warning, and Miguel Ojeda works hard to keep the kernel's Rust code warning-free, so that's noticeable. In a future version of the language, it may be possible to make not handling an error a compile-time error; there's work in progress on the language features required to enable that. In addition, Rust has shorthand for propagating errors (the ? operator) and facilities for carrying additional information as part of errors, which can make handling them easier in the cases where propagating the error is not appropriate. Also, in C one must read the documentation to figure out whether a function returning an int can return an error (although it often can); in Rust, that information is part of the type of the function, which makes it easy to see at a glance. It's really a whole bunch of little things that work together to make writing error-handling code in Rust a bit more pleasant and hard to screw up. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the maintainers in the room, all of whom had received invitations, did not see a lot of problems with that process. High-level process discussions tend to need the high-level maintainers in the room. As Brauner pointed out, that group is always going to seem a bit elitist. But, he said, getting that group into the same room once each year is helpful for the management of the project as a whole. Torvalds said that the older format of the Kernel Summit, which topped out at about 150 participants, was simply not manageable. The smaller group is at least able to have constructive discussions, he said. Hildenbrand said that one problem is a widely held impression that proposing a topic for the Summit will necessarily result in an invitation; he suggested that the call for topics next year should be rephrased. Ts'o said that colocating the Summit with the Linux Plumbers Conference (LPC) works well, and that holding the Summit afterward works best. That allows the participants to gather information from others and bring it into the more focused group. Hellwig put in a request for a different sort of gathering where developers from one subsystem can hold "office hours" to talk with others. That sort of happens at conferences now but, he said, the time at those events is too structured and there are too many other distractions happening. Bergmann pointed out that the LPC kernel-summit track has become less relevant over the years, and suggested that some of that track's time could be repurposed; that idea was reasonably well received. There was also talk of using a videoconference server to host subsystem-specific office hours at other times. The meeting closed with a general agreement that its format works fairly well, and that the office-hours idea might improve it. The biggest change might be in the call for topics, which may be rewritten to provide more information about how the selection process works and to make it clear that people can nominate others to attend. In a future version of the language, it may be possible to make not handling an error a compile-time error; there's work in progress on the language features required to enable that. In addition, Rust has shorthand for propagating errors (the ? operator) and facilities for carrying additional information as part of errors, which can make handling them easier in the cases where propagating the error is not appropriate. Also, in C one must read the documentation to figure out whether a function returning an int can return an error (although it often can); in Rust, that information is part of the type of the function, which makes it easy to see at a glance. It's really a whole bunch of little things that work together to make writing error-handling code in Rust a bit more pleasant and hard to screw up. Torvalds said that the older format of the Kernel Summit, which topped out at about 150 participants, was simply not manageable. The smaller group is at least able to have constructive discussions, he said. Hildenbrand said that one problem is a widely held impression that proposing a topic for the Summit will necessarily result in an invitation; he suggested that the call for topics next year should be rephrased. Ts'o said that colocating the Summit with the Linux Plumbers Conference (LPC) works well, and that holding the Summit afterward works best. That allows the participants to gather information from others and bring it into the more focused group. Hellwig put in a request for a different sort of gathering where developers from one subsystem can hold "office hours" to talk with others. That sort of happens at conferences now but, he said, the time at those events is too structured and there are too many other distractions happening. Bergmann pointed out that the LPC kernel-summit track has become less relevant over the years, and suggested that some of that track's time could be repurposed; that idea was reasonably well received. There was also talk of using a videoconference server to host subsystem-specific office hours at other times. The meeting closed with a general agreement that its format works fairly well, and that the office-hours idea might improve it. The biggest change might be in the call for topics, which may be rewritten to provide more information about how the selection process works and to make it clear that people can nominate others to attend. There was, finally, a suggestion that the ksummit mailing list could be used more. There are usually interesting discussions there in the lead-up to the event, but then it goes quiet the rest of the year; there is no reason why discussions of that type can't happen there at other times as well. Rust and error paths Posted Oct 15, 2026 13:59 UTC (Thu) by daroc (editor, #160859) [ Link ] (4 responses) Specifically, not handling an error (by discarding a Result value) currently gives a compiler warning, and Miguel Ojeda works hard to keep the kernel's Rust code warning-free, so that's noticeable. In a future version of the language, it may be possible to make not handling an error a compile-time error; there's work in progress on the language features required to enable that. In addition, Rust has shorthand for propagating errors (the ? operator) and facilities for carrying additional information as part of errors, which can make handling them easier in the cases where propagating the error is not appropriate. Also, in C one must read the documentation to figure out whether a function returning an int can return an error (although it often can); in Rust, that information is part of the type of the function, which makes it easy to see at a glance. It's really a whole bunch of little things that work together to make writing error-handling code in Rust a bit more pleasant and hard to screw up. Rust and error paths Posted Oct 15, 2026 13:59 UTC (Thu) by daroc (editor, #160859) [ Link ] (4 responses) Specifically, not handling an error (by discarding a Result value) currently gives a compiler warning, and Miguel Ojeda works hard to keep the kernel's Rust code warning-free, so that's noticeable. In a future version of the language, it may be possible to make not handling an error a compile-time error; there's work in progress on the language features required to enable that. In addition, Rust has shorthand for propagating errors (the ? operator) and facilities for carrying additional information as part of errors, which can make handling them easier in the cases where propagating the error is not appropriate. Also, in C one must read the documentation to figure out whether a function returning an int can return an error (although it often can); in Rust, that information is part of the type of the function, which makes it easy to see at a glance. It's really a whole bunch of little things that work together to make writing error-handling code in Rust a bit more pleasant and hard to screw up. Rust and error paths Posted Oct 15, 2026 13:59 UTC (Thu) by daroc (editor, #160859) [ Link ] (4 responses) Specifically, not handling an error (by discarding a Result value) currently gives a compiler warning, and Miguel Ojeda works hard to keep the kernel's Rust code warning-free, so that's noticeable. In a future version of the language, it may be possible to make not handling an error a compile-time error; there's work in progress on the language features required to enable that. In addition, Rust has shorthand for propagating errors (the ? operator) and facilities for carrying additional information as part of errors, which can make handling them easier in the cases where propagating the error is not appropriate. Also, in C one must read the documentation to figure out whether a function returning an int can return an error (although it often can); in Rust, that information is part of the type of the function, which makes it easy to see at a glance. It's really a whole bunch of little things that work together to make writing error-handling code in Rust a bit more pleasant and hard to screw up. In a future version of the language, it may be possible to make not handling an error a compile-time error; there's work in progress on the language features required to enable that. In addition, Rust has shorthand for propagating errors (the ? operator) and facilities for carrying additional information as part of errors, which can make handling them easier in the cases where propagating the error is not appropriate. Also, in C one must read the documentation to figure out whether a function returning an int can return an error (although it often can); in Rust, that information is part of the type of the function, which makes it easy to see at a glance. It's really a whole bunch of little things that work together to make writing error-handling code in Rust a bit more pleasant and hard to screw up. On the odd occasion I can't convince them, I usually drop the post. I figure if I can't explain the rationale to an LLM, I'm probably not going to convince a human either. Explaining the rationale means you have to convince the LLM that its initial summary of the internet hive mind its stochastic parrot spat out is wrong. You do that in the usual way - with evidence and deductions from that. If the evidence matches what they know (they know an awful lot, so if you're right you don't have to give citations, you just have to give them enough so that same stochastic parrot can dig up the facts it's already seen), they are completely capable of checking the reasoning you used to arrive at your deductions. Used well, an LLM can get a single poster closer to the editorial standard LWN achieves with its team. It's the same sort of force multiplier Linus is saying he gets with coding. Like all force multipliers, it can be used to polish rubbish into the flood of slop we see today. Yes, LLMs enabled that flood, but I don't see why that's a good reason to eschew them. Rust and error paths Posted Oct 15, 2026 13:59 UTC (Thu) by daroc (editor, #160859) [ Link ] (4 responses) Specifically, not handling an error (by discarding a Result value) currently gives a compiler warning, and Miguel Ojeda works hard to keep the kernel's Rust code warning-free, so that's noticeable. In a future version of the language, it may be possible to make not handling an error a compile-time error; there's work in progress on the language features required to enable that. In addition, Rust has shorthand for propagating errors (the ? operator) and facilities for carrying additional information as part of errors, which can make handling them easier in the cases where propagating the error is not appropriate. Also, in C one must read the documentation to figure out whether a function returning an int can return an error (although it often can); in Rust, that information is part of the type of the function, which makes it easy to see at a glance. It's really a whole bunch of little things that work together to make writing error-handling code in Rust a bit more pleasant and hard to screw up. Rust and error paths Posted Oct 15, 2026 13:59 UTC (Thu) by daroc (editor, #160859) [ Link ] (4 responses) Specifically, not handling an error (by discarding a Result value) currently gives a compiler warning, and Miguel Ojeda works hard to keep the kernel's Rust code warning-free, so that's noticeable. In a future version of the language, it may be possible to make not handling an error a compile-time error; there's work in progress on the language features required to enable that. In addition, Rust has shorthand for propagating errors (the ? operator) and facilities for carrying additional information as part of errors, which can make handling them easier in the cases where propagating the error is not appropriate. Also, in C one must read the documentation to figure out whether a function returning an int can return an error (although it often can); in Rust, that information is part of the type of the function, which makes it easy to see at a glance. It's really a whole bunch of little things that work together to make writing error-handling code in Rust a bit more pleasant and hard to screw up. A big issue is if it’s affordable to do so; our tool is simpler than sashiko (at the cost of less accuracy, I suspect) and can be run with a standard LLM subscription using the coding agent tool. Sashiko can too of course. So this option to run it yourself *mostly* solves the many series with repeated small changes problem for us. Randomness means the posted patch still sometimes gets some other stuff, but dramatically less. Another option we’re probably going to implement is a service folks can submit to if they can’t afford/don’t want to use their own subscription. But ours is a much smaller community with open but gated participation; drive by is much harder. But to my but, Sashiko is already freely reviewing every submitted patch in the kernel. Anyway, perhaps some part of these ideas could be useful to the kernel.

Moreover, training a brand new model is not that terrible. The largest released Nemotron model from NVidia (it's a "sample" model with open weights and the training set) would take about 5 million GPU-hours to retrain from complete scratch. Assuming a reasonable amount of disruptions and restarts, there are about 5000 hours within one year. So a cluster of 1000 Blackwell GPUs can train it within 1 year. At about $2 per hour for these kinds of GPUs, that's around $10 million. This number will fall down by 3-4x within years, as new generations of GPUs become available with better training methods. That's just not a lot of money for even a large university, never mind a government.

This may well be a temporary problem, not because LLMs are going to go away (they're not) but because there are only a finite number of humans, a tiny proportion of the population, who think it's "cool" to get their name in the changelog. LLMs have lowered the barrier to being able to create a kernel patch but they haven't increased the number of people who know that it is possible to contribute patches to the kernel. It's also likely that the perceived reputation value of having your name in the changelog will go down due to more LLM submissions. So I suspect the supply of "vanity patches" will end up drying up but that there will continue to be a higher level of submissions from people who are trying to solve a real problem they are running into but who wouldn't have contributed before without LLM assistance. If this means more bugs being fixed that's probably a good thing.

Rust and error paths Posted Oct 15, 2026 13:59 UTC (Thu) by daroc (editor, #160859) [ Link ] (4 responses) Specifically, not handling an error (by discarding a Result value) currently gives a compiler warning, and Miguel Ojeda works hard to keep the kernel's Rust code warning-free, so that's noticeable. In a future version of the language, it may be possible to make not handling an error a compile-time error; there's work in progress on the language features required to enable that. In addition, Rust has shorthand for propagating errors (the ? operator) and facilities for carrying additional information as part of errors, which can make handling them easier in the cases where propagating the error is not appropriate. Also, in C one must read the documentation to figure out whether a function returning an int can return an error (although it often can); in Rust, that information is part of the type of the function, which makes it easy to see at a glance. It's really a whole bunch of little things that work together to make writing error-handling code in Rust a bit more pleasant and hard to screw up. title: Greece Honours Team Hellas Athletes After Mediterranean Games
body: Athletes, coaches and sports officials gathered at the Hellenic Olympic Committee (HOC) in Athens on 8 October to celebrate Greece’s achievements at the Taranto 2026 Mediterranean Games, where Team Hellas won 71 medals and finished third among 26 nations. The Greek delegation secured 26 gold, 26 silver and 19 bronze medals, marking one of Greece’s most significant performances in the history of the Mediterranean Games. The ceremony honoured the athletes’ achievements and recognised Public Power Corporation (DEI) for its support of Greek sport. HOC President Isidoros Kouvelos congratulated the athletes and highlighted the importance of planning, organisation and sustained investment in sporting success. “Taranto 2026 leaves an important legacy. It sends a strong message that when there is planning, organisation and meaningful support, Greece can achieve great results and play a leading role in international sport,” Kouvelos said. He praised DEI’s contribution as a strategic partner of the HOC and announced that, for the first time, medal-winning athletes and their coaches at the Mediterranean Games would receive financial rewards through the partnership. The initiative will distribute €250,000 in bonuses to recognise their achievements and dedication. Antonis Nikolopoulos, head of the Greek delegation, praised the team spirit displayed by the 393 athletes and coaches who represented Greece in Taranto. “I saw a team of 393 athletes and coaches become one, supporting one another in the stadiums and swimming pools and representing the Greek colours with unparalleled ethos and professionalism,” he said. Nikolopoulos also thanked DEI for helping the delegation meet the logistical and financial demands of such a large team. As the HOC’s exclusive sponsor in the energy category, DEI supports Team Hellas by covering preparation, equipment and travel costs. The partnership also provides financial rewards for Olympic achievements and forms part of the company’s wider commitment to promoting teamwork, dedication and sporting excellence. Elena Christopoulou, DEI Group’s director of sponsorships and partnerships, congratulated the athletes and reaffirmed the company’s commitment to supporting their preparations for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games. “We are particularly proud that, as DEI, we stand alongside the Hellenic Olympic Committee and DEI Team Hellas, providing tangible support to our athletes on their journey towards Los Angeles 2028,” Christopoulou said. She wished the athletes continued success as they pursued their sporting ambitions. Athletes Share Their Experiences The medal winners also reflected on their experiences in Taranto and the hard work behind their achievements. Antonis Tantalidis, who won gold in artistic gymnastics, thanked the HOC and DEI for recognising the athletes’ dedication. “Behind every achievement and every medal are many hours of hard work, sacrifices, moments of joy and difficulties,” Tantalidis said, adding that the recognition encouraged athletes to continue pursuing their dreams. Swimmer Anna Ntountounaki, who won two gold medals and one silver, highlighted the significance of reaching the podium at her third consecutive Mediterranean Games. She said she felt particularly pleased to win medals in her individual events and thanked the HOC and DEI for helping make the experience enjoyable for the Greek delegation. The ceremony concluded with the presentation of certificates to Team Hellas athletes who won medals at the Taranto 2026 Mediterranean Games. HOC President Isidoros Kouvelos presented the certificates alongside Christopoulou, HOC Secretary-General Stefanos Handakas, International Olympic Committee member and European Olympic Committees President Spyros Capralos, Greek delegation head Antonis Nikolopoulos, and deputy heads of mission Theodoros Tsavdaridis and Dora Palli-Petralia. The post Greece Honours Team Hellas Athletes After Mediterranean Games appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Gordon scores as Barcelona beats Galatasaray
body: Anthony Gordon scored his first Champions League goal for Barcelona as the Spanish side came from behind to beat Galatasaray in Istanbul. Barcelona sought to extinguish the febrile atmosphere early on by controlling possession, but fell behind after Galatasaray’s first proper attack. Seconds after Gordon’s penalty claim was ignored, Rafael Leao charged down the left wing and cut the ball back into the path of Aleksey Batrakov, who found the bottom corner after a deflection off Joao Cancelo. Galatasaray thought they had doubled their lead six minutes later when Baris Alper Yilmaz diverted Victor Osimhen’s header past Joan Garcia, but the goal was disallowed for a marginal offside after a video assistant referee (VAR) check. Barcelona steadied themselves and silenced the frenzied home support two minutes before the break, as Dani Olmo deflected the ball into the path of Joao Cancelo who curled a strike into the corner past Turkish goalkeeper Ugurcan Cakir. Any vulnerability the visitors showed in the first half quickly evaporated in the second as Hansi Flick’s side scored twice in quick succession. Fermin Lopez headed in from a Lamine Yamal cross in the 50th minute, and three minutes later a supreme piece of close control from the latter set up Gordon to fire in his first Champions League goal for Barcelona three days after netting for the club for the first time. Fellow summer signing Karim Adeyemi replaced Gordon and arrowed in Barcelona’s fourth goal from the left side of the penalty area after Gabriel Jesus touched a Lamine Yamal cross into his path. Barcelona have scored 84 goals in 28 Champions League matches under Flick, giving them the highest goals-per-game ratio (3) in the competition among clubs with 20 or more games under a specific manager since 1992-93. Barcelona have six points after thrashing Feyenoord 5-1 in their league phase opener, and will now travel to France to face Paris St-Germain on Tuesday, 20 October (20:00 BST). After losing 3-1 to Sporting CP last month, Turkish Super Lig leaders Galatasaray will look to claim a first win of the campaign when they face Lille on Wednesday, 21 October (17:45 BST).

title: Organizers of Kanye West’s canceled St. Petersburg concerts say prosecutors found no evidence of fraud
body: Prosecutors found no evidence of fraud in a review of Say Agency, which was organizing rapper Kanye West’s concerts in St. Petersburg. Say Agency representative Alexander Panin said investigators “found no evidence of fraud because, in fact, there isn’t any.” The agency’s CEO and founder, Anna Subcheva, said law enforcement officers had received answers to all their questions and that “if I’m talking to you, that means they were satisfied with the answers.” News of a police and prosecutorial inquiry into the organizers of West’s canceled concerts emerged in late September. The inquiry began after a St. Petersburg resident who had bought a ticket to a show filed a complaint. Two West concerts at St. Petersburg’s Gazprom Arena were scheduled for October 10 and 11. The organizers said they had sold more than 100,000 tickets. After the concerts were announced, lawmakers and pro-war activists began speaking out against the rapper’s visit to Russia. Even the Kremlin discussed whether the concerts should go ahead or be canceled. In September, Gazprom Arena representatives said there was no agreement to rent the stadium for West’s concerts and that they would not take place. Announcements for the concerts in Russia later disappeared from the rapper’s website. Say Agency said in late September that the concerts were canceled. After the cancellation, ticket buyers began demanding refunds from Say Agency, along with compensation for travel expenses and emotional distress. The agency began issuing refunds in October.
