title: Greece Counts 2,100 Wolves and 760 Bears as Wildlife Conflicts Grow
body: Greece estimates its wolf population at approximately 2,100 and its brown bear population at around 760, as wolf numbers across the European Union have nearly doubled over the past decade, raising concerns about livestock losses, public safety and the coexistence of wildlife and human activities. Michele Nori, a policy officer at the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Agriculture and Rural Development (DG AGRI), presented the EU figures at a conference in Thessaloniki titled Human Coexistence with Large Carnivores in Greece: Public Dialogue and Policy Co-creation. The National Platform for Large Carnivores organised the event. Nori said large carnivores that prey on livestock create a significant disincentive for extensive grazing in 12 EU member states. Their impact also extends to animal welfare, biodiversity management and ecosystem conservation. Sheep account for approximately 90% of animals killed by wolves, Nori said, highlighting the substantial indirect costs that often go unrecognised. According to his assessment of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) Strategic Plans, 18 of the 28 member states covered by the analysis use CAP funding to support preventive measures and promote coexistence with large carnivores. These measures include fencing, deterrent devices, livestock guardian dogs, protective enclosures, and funding for labour, maintenance and operating costs. The EU also allows member states to cover up to 100% of direct and indirect damage caused by protected species, including livestock losses, damage to agricultural infrastructure and equipment, and veterinary expenses. Nori reported that EU countries spent approximately €18.7 million annually on compensation for wolf-related damage in 2022. Greece Estimates 760 Brown Bears and 2,100 Wolves Dr George Mertzanis, a specialist scientist at the Large Carnivore Observatory, estimates Greece’s brown bear population at approximately 760. Authorities and researchers have recorded 300 incidents of illegal bear killings since 1996. However, scientific estimates suggest that recorded cases represent only about one-third of actual deaths. Dr Nikoleta Karaiskou of the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki’s Department of Biology said genetic monitoring could provide a more accurate assessment of bear populations, but researchers need funding to carry out the work. Karaiskou also presented research into wolf attacks on beehives, based on hair and faecal samples collected across an area extending from Doirani to Lake Mikri Volvi. Her analysis identified a single wolf moving through the area and causing damage, demonstrating how genetic tools could help authorities identify and manage individual animals responsible for repeated incidents. Dr George Iliopoulos, a specialist scientist working with the environmental organisation Callisto, estimates Greece’s wolf population at around 2,100. However, he noted that researchers do not conduct systematic monitoring across sufficiently large areas. Iliopoulos described wolves as opportunistic animals that do not live exclusively in mountainous areas. Their population growth depends on several factors, including the food they find in peri-urban areas. Wolves and Bears Raise Concerns in Rural and Urban Areas Dr Yiannis Kazoglou of the Hellenic Livestock Association, who lives in Prespes, highlighted the growing concerns among rural residents. Although local communities live alongside wildlife, he said bear faeces appeared in the village square at Laimos, Prespes, in December last year, making residents afraid to walk around without a car. Filothei Mela, head of the Thessaloniki Forest Service, said wolves had entered the metropolitan forest because the area offers food sources, including wild boar, stray cats and dogs, as well as food that people leave out for animals. When wildlife began appearing in urban areas, particularly Panorama, the forest service worked with Callisto to deploy deterrents and encourage wolves to return to their natural habitat. Mela said the service also maintains contact with local authorities and police and informs residents how to respond if they encounter wildlife. Greece Prepares €3 Million in Preventive Measures The Greek Ministry of Rural Development and Food is preparing an intervention package worth approximately €3 million to prevent damage caused by large mammals and improve coexistence between wildlife and human activities. Evangelos Delis, an agronomist working with the ministry’s Pillar I Intervention Monitoring Unit, said officials would finalise the measures after consulting relevant organisations before issuing calls for applications. The programme aims to: Prevent damage to crops, livestock farms and beekeeping operations. Improve coexistence between human activities and wildlife. Reduce human-caused deaths among protected species. Support biodiversity conservation. Eligible agricultural holdings must lie within the habitats of large mammals, including bears, wolves, jackals and deer. Qualifying land may support maize, sunflowers, vineyards, orchards, vegetables, cereals and alfalfa, as well as beehives or livestock facilities. Eligible expenditure may include purchasing and installing permanent electric fencing, wooden, plastic or metal fence posts, and modern deterrent lights known as Fox Lights to discourage large mammals from entering protected areas. Officials Call for Cooperation and Reliable Public Information Green Fund Director George Protopapas said effective coexistence between people and large carnivores requires cooperation among government authorities, scientists, environmental organisations and local communities. Efstathios Stathopoulos, secretary-general for forests at the Ministry of Environment and Energy, also stressed the importance of cooperation among all stakeholders. Panayiotis Parashos, a forester and organisational secretary of the board of the Geotechnical Chamber of Greece, said coexistence requires planning, cooperation and shared responsibility. Participants also discussed who should provide reliable information when wildlife approaches populated areas. Representatives from hunting, animal welfare, environmental and forestry organisations agreed that an official body should provide accurate public information about such incidents. Kyriakos Skordas of the Hellenic Hunting Confederation, Dr Christina Nomikou, president of the Panhellenic Animal Welfare and Environmental Federation, Dr Nikitas Fragkiskakis of the Macedonia–Thrace Forest Policy Implementation Inspectorate, and Dr Tasos Chovardas of the EU-funded CoCo project stressed the need to examine reports of wildlife encounters carefully to prevent misinformation. The post Greece Counts 2,100 Wolves and 760 Bears as Wildlife Conflicts Grow appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: How to Use Meta’s Rebalancer for Task Placement & Optimization
body:
In this tutorial, we implement the Rebalancer , Meta’s assignment solver, with a C++ core and a Python binding. We describe objects, containers, dimensions, scopes, and partitions, add constraints and goals, then choose local search or the exact mixed-integer solver HiGHS. We build a small datacenter, drain a busy host, and compare the two solvers on toy models, mutually exclusive hosts, synthetic clusters, and 60 published OR-Library instances. We judge every plan by recounting the returned assignment rather than by the solver’s flags. In this build, across 24 solves, the solved flag read True in 14 solves that still left memory over capacity. HARD under local search returned a violating start without raising; misspelled spec keys were ignored silently, and enum names are rejected. The timings come from an Apple M4 with the macOS wheel, and Colab’s Linux wheel may time differently. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser import os import re import sys import json import math import time import random import hashlib import platform import tempfile import statistics import traceback import subprocess import collections import urllib.request RESULTS = {} # step -> headline (or the failure), saved to results.json after every step CLAIMS = [] # (step, claim, held) rows for the ledger in the last cell SOLVE_SECONDS = collections.Counter() # step -> seconds spent inside solve() CURRENT = ["1"] def banner(title): print("
" + "=" * 78) print(title) print("=" * 78) def section(name): def wrap(fn): def run(*a, **kw): CURRENT[0] = name.split(".")[0] banner(name) t0 = time.time() try: out = fn(*a, **kw) RESULTS[name] = out if isinstance(out, str) else "ok" return out except Exception as e: RESULTS[name] = f"SKIPPED / FAILED -> {type(e).__name__}: {e}" print(f"
[!] {name} did not complete: {type(e).__name__}: {e}") traceback.print_exc(limit=3) return None finally: print(f"
[{time.time() - t0:.1f} s]") json.dump({"results": RESULTS, "claims": CLAIMS, "solve_seconds": SOLVE_SECONDS}, open("results.json", "w"), indent=1) return run return wrap def claim(text, held): CLAIMS.append((CURRENT[0], text, bool(held))) return held banner("1. Install rebalancer 1.0.4, check the build, and solve one small model with both solvers") assert (3, 12) <= sys.version_info[:2] <= (3, 14), "the 1.0.4 wheels exist for Python 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14 only" assert (sys.platform.startswith("linux") and platform.machine() == "x86_64") or \ (sys.platform == "darwin" and platform.machine() == "arm64"), f"no rebalancer 1.0.4 wheel for {sys.platform} {platform.machine()}" subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", "--retries", "5", "--timeout", "120", "rebalancer==1.0.4"], check=True) import importlib.metadata as md import rebalancer.specs as S from rebalancer import ProblemSolver # The binding takes every enum as its Thrift integer. The type stubs advertise the names ("HARD", "HIGHS"), but a name # raises '"" is not a valid int', and an out-of-range integer is accepted silently, so the integers live in one table. POLICY = {"DEFAULT": 1, "HARD": 2, "SOFT": 3} LIMIT = {"ABSOLUTE": 1, "RELATIVE": 2} FORMULA = {"LINEAR": 1, "SQUARES": 2, "MAX": 3, "IDEAL": 4} PACKAGE = {"XPRESS": 0, "GUROBI": 1, "HIGHS": 2} MAX_BOUND = 1 END = {1: "OPTIMAL", 2: "HIT_TIME_LIMIT", 3: "HIT_MOVE_LIMIT", 4: "HIT_STOP_CONSTRAINT", 5: "HIT_PLATEAU_TIME", 6: "NO_SOLUTION_FOUND", 7: "HIT_STAGE_MOVE_LIMIT", 8: "HIT_EXCEPTION", 9: "UNABLE_TO_FIND_MORE_MOVES", 10: "HIT_MIN_CYCLE_OBJECTIVE_IMPROVEMENT", 11: "UNABLE_TO_FIND_IMPROVING_MOVES"} NESTED = {"limit": "Limit", "conflictInfoList": "ScopeItemConflictInfo", "conflictingScopeItemsWithOverlap": "ConflictingScopeItemInfo"} def check_keys(name, fields, where): cls = getattr(S, name) unknown = set(fields) - (cls.__required_keys__ | cls.__optional_keys__) if unknown: raise KeyError(f"{where} has no field {sorted(unknown)}; the binding would ignore it silently") for key, value in fields.items(): sub = "AssignmentAffinity" if (where, key) == ("assignmentAffinitiesSpec", "affinities") else NESTED.get(key) for item in (value if isinstance(value, list) else [value]): if sub and isinstance(item, dict): check_keys(sub, item, f"{where}.{key}") def spec(arm, **fields): """One union arm, e.g. spec("capacitySpec", name=..., scope=..., dimension=...). The binding ignores unknown keys without a warning, so the keys are checked against the TypedDicts in rebalancer.specs: the arm's own keys and the nested limit, affinities and conflict lists used in this notebook.""" check_keys(arm[0].upper() + arm[1:], fields, arm) return {arm: fields} MOVES = {"single": {"singleMoveTypeSpec": {}}, "swap": {"swapMoveTypeSpec": {}}, "triple": {"tripleLoopMoveTypeSpec": {}}, "kl": {"klSearchMoveTypeSpec": {}}} def local_search(seconds=2, seed=0, moves=("single", "swap"), **extra): return spec("localSearchSolverSpec", moveTypeList=[MOVES[m] for m in moves], solveTime=int(seconds), randomSeed=seed, **extra) def highs(seconds=5): # solverPackage 2 is HiGHS, the only MIP solver compiled into the pip wheel. suppressLogs removes a banner that the # optimal path otherwise prints to stdout. return spec("optimalSolverSpec", solverPackage=PACKAGE["HIGHS"], solveTime=int(seconds), suppressLogs=True) def new_problem(assignment, objects="task", containers="host"): p = ProblemSolver(service_name="rebalancer_tutorial", service_scope="marktechpost") p.set_log_level("ERROR") # silences ~50 log lines per solve; never "OFF", which exits the process p.set_object_name(objects).set_container_name(containers) # names first, then the assignment, then dimensions p.set_assignment(assignment) # every container must be listed, empty ones too return p def solve(p): t = time.perf_counter() sol = p.solve() dt = time.perf_counter() - t SOLVE_SECONDS[CURRENT[0]] += dt return sol, dt # Independent checks: everything below reads only the returned assignment, never the solver's own verdict. def where(container_to_objects): return {o: c for c, objs in container_to_objects.items() for o in objs} def by_container(object_to_container, containers): out = {c: [] for c in containers} for o, c in sorted(object_to_container.items()): out[c].append(o) return out def load(object_to_container, values): out = collections.Counter() for o, c in object_to_container.items(): out[c] += values.get(o, 0.0) return out def excess(object_to_container, values, caps): L = load(object_to_container, values) return {c: max(0.0, L[c] - caps[c]) for c in caps} def moved(before, after): return sum(before[o] != after[o] for o in before) def ends(sol): return "/".join(END.get(r["endReason"], str(r["endReason"])) for r in sol["solverSummaries"]) def goals(sol): return [round(g["value"], 6) for g in sol["finalGlobalObjective"]["goals"]] def clean(e, n=90, typed=True): msg = re.sub(r"[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}", "
", str(e)).strip()[:n] return f"{type(e).__name__}: {msg}" if typed else msg def cpu_name(): if os.path.exists("/proc/cpuinfo"): for line in open("/proc/cpuinfo"): if line.startswith("model name"): return line.split(":", 1)[1].strip() if sys.platform == "darwin": r = subprocess.run(["sysctl", "-n", "machdep.cpu.brand_string"], capture_output=True, text=True) if r.stdout.strip(): return r.stdout.strip() return platform.processor() or platform.machine() def ram_gb(): if os.path.exists("/proc/meminfo"): kb = next(int(l.split()[1]) for l in open("/proc/meminfo") if l.startswith("MemTotal")) return kb / 1024 ** 2 r = subprocess.run(["sysctl", "-n", "hw.memsize"], capture_output=True, text=True) return int(r.stdout) / 1024 ** 3 if r.stdout.strip() else float("nan") VERSION = md.version("rebalancer") HW = f"{cpu_name()}, {os.cpu_count()} logical CPUs, {ram_gb():.0f} GB RAM" print(f"rebalancer {VERSION} python {platform.python_version()} {platform.system()} {platform.machine()}") print(f"hardware: {HW}") assert VERSION == "1.0.4", "this notebook is written against rebalancer 1.0.4; restart the runtime after installing" def two_tasks(solver_spec, policy=None): # Two 10 GB tasks on host0, two hosts of 15 GB: the start breaks capacity and one task has to move. p = new_problem({"host0": ["t0", "t1"], "host1": []}) p.add_object_dimension("memory", {"t0": 10.0, "t1": 10.0}) p.add_container_dimension("memory", {}, default_value=15.0) kw = {} if policy is None else {"policy": policy} p.add_constraint(spec("capacitySpec", name="memory_capacity", scope="host", dimension="memory"), **kw) p.add_solver(solver_spec) return p GATE = {} for label, make in [("local search", lambda: two_tasks(local_search(2))), ("HiGHS (solverPackage=2)", lambda: two_tasks(highs(2)))]: try: sol, dt = solve(make()) per_host = load(sol["assignment"], {"t0": 10.0, "t1": 10.0}) GATE[label] = sol print(f"{label:<28} -> host loads {dict(sorted(per_host.items()))} GB, endReason {ends(sol)}, " f"{dt * 1000:.1f} ms") except Exception as e: GATE[label] = None print(f"{label:<28} -> FAILED {clean(e)}") print("
What the build refuses (each is caught here; the message is the binding's own):") for label, make in [("OptimalSolverSpec() default", lambda: two_tasks(spec("optimalSolverSpec", suppressLogs=True))), ("solverPackage=1 (Gurobi)", lambda: two_tasks(spec("optimalSolverSpec", solverPackage=1, suppressLogs=True))), ('policy="HARD" (a name)', lambda: two_tasks(local_search(2), policy="HARD")), ('solverPackage="HIGHS"', lambda: two_tasks({"optimalSolverSpec": {"solverPackage": "HIGHS"}}))]: try: solve(make()) print(f" {label:<28} -> accepted") except Exception as e: print(f" {label:<28} -> {clean(e, 60)}") try: spec("localSearchSolverSpec", timeLimitMs=500) except KeyError as e: print(f" spec(..., timeLimitMs=500) -> {e.args[0]}") def gate_ok(sol): # solved means OPTIMAL and, by recount, no host above its 15 GB return (sol is not None and ends(sol) == "OPTIMAL" and len(sol["assignment"]) == 2 and max(load(sol["assignment"], {"t0": 10.0, "t1": 10.0}).values()) <= 15.0) HIGHS_OK = gate_ok(GATE["HiGHS (solverPackage=2)"]) if not gate_ok(GATE["local search"]): raise RuntimeError("local search did not solve the two-task model; nothing below can run on this runtime") print(f"
GATE: local search solved; HiGHS {'solved' if HIGHS_OK else 'FAILED (steps that need it will say so)'}") RESULTS["1. Install, check the build, solve one small model with both solvers"] = f"rebalancer {VERSION}, Python {platform.python_version()}, {HW}; HiGHS {'ok' if HIGHS_OK else 'failed'}" We install rebalancer 1.0.4 and print the Python version and hardware, because every timing depends on them. The binding rejects enum names and silently ignores unknown spec keys, so the notebook passes integers from one table and checks each spec before solving. A gate then solves a two-task model with both solvers, each moving one task, in 0.8 ms with local search and 0.9 ms with HiGHS. The cell also confirms that this build refuses the default XPRESS solver and the Gurobi package. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser README_TASKS = {f"task{i}": 10.0 for i in range(4)} README_CAPS = {"host0": 20.0, "host1": 20.0} def readme_model(start, solver_spec): p = new_problem(start) p.add_object_dimension("memory", README_TASKS) p.add_container_dimension("memory", {}, default_value=20.0) # No limit given: the capacity limit is RELATIVE 1.0, i.e. 100% of each host's memory dimension. p.add_constraint(spec("capacitySpec", name="memory_capacity", scope="host", dimension="memory")) p.add_solver(solver_spec) return p @section("2. The README model: four 10 GB tasks, two 20 GB hosts, and a recount instead of the solver's verdict") def readme_step(): start = {"host0": ["task0", "task1", "task2"], "host1": ["task3"]} sol, dt = solve(readme_model(start, local_search(2))) before, after = where(start), sol["assignment"] ex0, ex1 = excess(before, README_TASKS, README_CAPS), excess(after, README_TASKS, README_CAPS) l0, l1 = load(before, README_TASKS), load(after, README_TASKS) ic, fc = sol["initialConstraint"], sol["finalConstraint"] print(f"start: {start}") print(f"final: {by_container(after, README_CAPS)}") print(f"host loads {l0['host0']:.0f}/{l0['host1']:.0f} GB -> {l1['host0']:.0f}/{l1['host1']:.0f} GB " f"against 20 GB; recounted excess {sum(ex0.values()):.0f} -> {sum(ex1.values()):.0f} GB") print(f"solver's own report: brokenCount {ic['brokenCount']} -> {fc['brokenCount']}, brokenVal " f"{ic['brokenVal']:g} -> {fc['brokenVal']:g}, solved={fc['solved']}") print(f"tasks moved (diff against the start): {moved(before, after)} movesSummary entries: " f"{len(sol['movesSummary'])} endReason {ends(sol)} solve {dt * 1000:.1f} ms") print(f"result keys: {', '.join(sorted(sol))}") balanced = {"host0": ["task0", "task1"], "host1": ["task2", "task3"]} sol_b, _ = solve(readme_model(balanced, local_search(2))) sol_z, _ = solve(readme_model(start, local_search(0))) mb, mz = moved(where(balanced), sol_b["assignment"]), moved(before, sol_z["assignment"]) exz = sum(excess(sol_z["assignment"], README_TASKS, README_CAPS).values()) print(f"
control, start already 2-2: {mb} tasks moved, endReason {ends(sol_b)}") print(f"control, solveTime=0 on the 3-1 start: {mz} tasks moved, endReason {ends(sol_z)}, recounted excess " f"{exz:.0f} GB, solved={sol_z['finalConstraint']['solved']} <- 0 means no time, not 'no limit'") claim("README model: recounted excess reaches 0 GB", sum(ex1.values()) == 0) claim("README model: a 2-2 start is left alone", mb == 0) claim("README model: solveTime=0 makes no moves", mz == 0) return (f"3-1 start -> {l1['host0']:.0f}/{l1['host1']:.0f} GB, excess {sum(ex0.values()):.0f} -> " f"{sum(ex1.values()):.0f} GB, {moved(before, after)} task moved; solveTime=0 moved {mz}") readme_step() We solve the README example, four 10 GB tasks on two 20 GB hosts with three tasks on one host, and recount the result instead of trusting the solver. Local search moves one task in 0.3 ms, and the recount drops the excess from 10 GB to 0. The solver’s own brokenCount also falls from 1 to 0 and endReason reads OPTIMAL. A control makes the point about the flag: with solveTime=0 the solver moves nothing, still leaves 10 GB over capacity, and reports solved=True. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser HOSTS = [f"host{i}" for i in range(8)] RACK = {h: f"rack{i // 2}" for i, h in enumerate(HOSTS)} # Python add_scope maps container -> scope item JOB_OF = {f"job{j}_t{k}": f"job{j}" for j in "ABCD" for k in range(4)} TASK_CPU, TASK_MEM, HOST_CPU, HOST_MEM = 4.0, 16.0, 16.0, 64.0 DC_START = {h: [] for h in HOSTS} DC_START["host0"] = [t for t, j in JOB_OF.items() if j in ("jobA", "jobB")] DC_START["host1"] = [t for t, j in JOB_OF.items() if j == "jobC"] DC_START["host2"] = [t for t, j in JOB_OF.items() if j == "jobD"] def datacenter(solver_spec, start=DC_START, rack_rule=True, formula="LINEAR", drain=None, movement_tuple=None, limit_type="ABSOLUTE"): p = new_problem(start) p.add_partition("job", {j: [t for t in JOB_OF if JOB_OF[t] == j] for j in sorted(set(JOB_OF.values()))}) p.add_scope("rack", RACK) p.add_object_dimension("cpu", {t: TASK_CPU for t in JOB_OF}) p.add_object_dimension("mem", {t: TASK_MEM for t in JOB_OF}) p.add_container_dimension("cpu", {}, default_value=HOST_CPU) p.add_container_dimension("mem", {}, default_value=HOST_MEM) p.add_constraint(spec("capacitySpec", name="cpu_capacity", scope="host", dimension="cpu", bound=MAX_BOUND)) p.add_constraint(spec("capacitySpec", name="mem_capacity", scope="host", dimension="mem", bound=MAX_BOUND)) if rack_rule: # at most one task of each job per rack, as an ABSOLUTE limit (step 3 shows what RELATIVE does) p.add_constraint(spec("groupCountSpec", name="one_task_per_job_per_rack", scope="rack", partitionName="job", bound=MAX_BOUND, limit={"type": LIMIT[limit_type], "globalLimit": 1.0})) if drain: p.add_constraint(spec("toFreeSpec", name=f"drain_{drain}", containers=[drain])) p.add_goal(spec("balanceSpec", name="cpu_balance", scope="host", dimension="cpu", formula=FORMULA[formula]), weight=1.0, tuple_pos=0) if movement_tuple is not None: p.add_goal(spec("minimizeMovementSpec", name="tasks_moved", scope="host", dimension="task_count", doNotNormalize=True), weight=1.0, tuple_pos=movement_tuple) p.add_solver(solver_spec) return p def dc_check(o2c, drain=None): cpu, mem = load(o2c, {t: TASK_CPU for t in JOB_OF}), load(o2c, {t: TASK_MEM for t in JOB_OF}) per_rack_job = collections.Counter((RACK[o2c[t]], JOB_OF[t]) for t in JOB_OF) live = [h for h in HOSTS if h != drain] util = [cpu[h] / HOST_CPU for h in live] return {"cpu": sum(max(0.0, cpu[h] - HOST_CPU) for h in HOSTS), "mem": sum(max(0.0, mem[h] - HOST_MEM) for h in HOSTS), "rack": sum(n - 1 for n in per_rack_job.values() if n > 1), "per_host": [sum(1 for t in JOB_OF if o2c[t] == h) for h in HOSTS], "umax": max(util), "umin": min(util), "complete": sorted(o2c) == sorted(JOB_OF)} @section("3. A small datacenter: racks, jobs, CPU and memory capacity, one task per job per rack, CPU balance") def datacenter_step(): before = where(DC_START) c0 = dc_check(before) print(f"start: tasks per host {c0['per_host']} (host0 holds jobA and jobB: {c0['umax']:.0%} CPU)") print(f"start, recounted: CPU excess {c0['cpu']:.0f}, memory excess {c0['mem']:.0f}, " f"extra tasks of a job sharing a rack {c0['rack']}") runs = [] for _ in range(3): # three fresh builds of the same model sol, dt = solve(datacenter(local_search(3))) runs.append((sol, dt)) sol = runs[0][0] c1 = dc_check(sol["assignment"]) print(f"
final (build 1): tasks per host {c1['per_host']}, CPU use {c1['umin']:.0%}..{c1['umax']:.0%}") print(f"final, recounted: CPU excess {c1['cpu']:.0f}, memory excess {c1['mem']:.0f}, rack duplicates " f"{c1['rack']}, every task placed once: {c1['complete']}") print(f"tasks moved {moved(before, sol['assignment'])}, endReason {ends(sol)}, balance objective " f"{goals(sol)}, solver brokenCount {sol['initialConstraint']['brokenCount']} -> " f"{sol['finalConstraint']['brokenCount']}") same = [goals(s) == goals(sol) and moved(before, s["assignment"]) == moved(before, sol["assignment"]) for s, _ in runs] ms = statistics.median(dt for _, dt in runs) * 1000 print(f"3 fresh builds: same objective and move count in {sum(same)} of 3; median solve {ms:.1f} ms") sol_c, _ = solve(datacenter(local_search(3), rack_rule=False)) cc = dc_check(sol_c["assignment"]) print(f"
control without the rack rule: rack duplicates {cc['rack']}, tasks per host {cc['per_host']} " f"(the checker sees the rule only when the solver is not enforcing it)") sol_r, _ = solve(datacenter(local_search(3), limit_type="RELATIVE")) cr = dc_check(sol_r["assignment"]) print(f"control, the same rule with limit type RELATIVE: brokenCount at the start {sol_r['initialConstraint']['brokenCount']}" f" (ABSOLUTE: {sol['initialConstraint']['brokenCount']}), rack duplicates after the solve {cr['rack']}") ok = c1["cpu"] == c1["mem"] == c1["rack"] == 0 and c1["complete"] claim("datacenter: every constraint holds by recount", ok) claim("datacenter: removing the rack rule brings back rack duplicates", cc["rack"] > 0) claim("datacenter: a RELATIVE group limit leaves rack duplicates", cr["rack"] > 0) return (f"violations CPU/mem/rack {c0['cpu']:.0f}/{c0['mem']:.0f}/{c0['rack']} -> {c1['cpu']:.0f}/" f"{c1['mem']:.0f}/{c1['rack']}, {moved(before, sol['assignment'])} tasks moved, {ms:.1f} ms; " f"without the rule {cc['rack']} rack duplicates, with a RELATIVE limit {cr['rack']}") datacenter_step() We build eight hosts in four racks, four jobs of four tasks each, and start with host0 at 200% CPU and 12 rack duplicates. We add CPU and memory capacity, a one-task-per-job-per-rack rule, and a CPU balance goal. The solver moves 13 tasks to leave two per host with no violations, with a median solve of 2.5 ms over three fresh builds. Without the rack rule, the recount finds 5 rack duplicates, and a RELATIVE limit on it also ends with 5, so it enforces nothing here. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser @section("4. What 'solved' means: the constraint policies under local search and HiGHS, checked by recount") def policy_step(): cases = {"F (fixable)": ({f"t{i}": 10.0 for i in range(4)}, {"host0": ["t0", "t1", "t2"], "host1": ["t3"]}), "I (infeasible)": ({f"t{i}": 20.0 for i in range(3)}, {"host0": ["t0", "t1", "t2"], "host1": []})} caps = {"host0": 20.0, "host1": 20.0} def build(sizes, start, policy, solver_spec): p = new_problem(start) p.add_object_dimension("memory", sizes) p.add_container_dimension("memory", {}, default_value=20.0) p.add_constraint(spec("capacitySpec", name="memory_capacity", scope="host", dimension="memory"), policy=POLICY[policy]) p.add_solver(solver_spec) return p rows, stable, solved_but_broken, cells = [], [], 0, 0 print(f"{'case':<15}{'policy':<9}{'solver':<14}{'outcome':<36}{'moved':>6}{'broken':>9}{'solved':>8}" f"{'brokenVal':>11}{'excess GB':>11}") for case, (sizes, start) in cases.items(): for policy in ("DEFAULT", "HARD", "SOFT"): for solver_name, solver_spec, reps in [("local search", local_search(1), 3), ("HiGHS", highs(2), 1)]: outs = [] for _ in range(reps): cells += 1 try: sol, _ = solve(build(sizes, start, policy, solver_spec)) ex = sum(excess(sol["assignment"], sizes, caps).values()) fc, ic = sol["finalConstraint"], sol["initialConstraint"] solved_but_broken += fc["solved"] and ex > 0 outs.append({"out": "returned, " + ends(sol), "moved": moved(where(start), sol["assignment"]), "broken": f"{ic['brokenCount']}->{fc['brokenCount']}", "solved": fc["solved"], "bv": fc["brokenVal"], "ex": ex, "sol": sol, "sizes": sizes}) except Exception as e: outs.append({"out": "raised: " + clean(e, 30, typed=False), "moved": "-", "broken": "-", "solved": "-", "bv": None, "ex": None}) o = outs[0] if reps > 1: stable.append(len({(x["out"], x["moved"], x["broken"], x["bv"]) for x in outs}) == 1) bv = "-" if o["bv"] is None else f"{o['bv']:g}" exs = "-" if o["ex"] is None else f"{o['ex']:.0f}" print(f"{case:<15}{policy:<9}{solver_name:<14}{o['out']:<36}{o['moved']!s:>6}{o['broken']:>9}" f"{o['solved']!s:>8}{bv:>11}{exs:>11}") rows.append((case, policy, solver_name, o)) print(f"
local-search repeats (3 per row) identical in {sum(stable)} of {len(stable)} rows") print(f"cells where solved=True although the recount still finds excess memory: {solved_but_broken} of {cells}") # What does brokenVal measure? Three candidate formulas, tested on the first returned result of every row above and # on four starts read before any move: two hosts over capacity, and three starts with hosts of different sizes. probes = [({"host0": ["t0", "t1", "t2", "t3"], "host1": ["t4", "t5", "t6"], "host2": [], "host3": []}, {"host0": 20.0, "host1": 20.0, "host2": 20.0, "host3": 20.0}), ({"host0": ["t0", "t1", "t2"], "host1": []}, {"host0": 20.0, "host1": 40.0}), ({"host0": ["t0", "t1", "t2", "t3"], "host1": ["t4", "t5", "t6", "t7"]}, {"host0": 20.0, "host1": 30.0}), ({"host0": ["t0", "t1", "t2"], "host1": ["t3", "t4", "t5", "t6"], "host2": ["t7"]}, {"host0": 20.0, "host1": 30.0, "host2": 100.0})] samples = [(o["sol"]["assignment"], o["sizes"], caps, o["bv"]) for *_, o in rows if o["bv"] is not None] for start, pcaps in probes: sizes = {t: 10.0 for objs in start.values() for t in objs} p = new_problem(start) p.add_object_dimension("memory", sizes) p.add_container_dimension("memory", pcaps, default_value=0.0) p.add_constraint(spec("capacitySpec", name="memory_capacity", scope="host", dimension="memory")) p.add_solver(local_search(0)) probe, _ = solve(p) bv = probe["initialConstraint"]["brokenVal"] samples.append((where(start), sizes, pcaps, bv)) ex = excess(where(start), sizes, pcaps) print(f"start {[f'{load(where(start), sizes)[h]:.0f}/{c:.0f}' for h, c in pcaps.items()]} GB (load/capacity): " f"excess {sum(ex.values()):.0f} GB, brokenVal {bv:.4g}") cands = {"total excess in GB": lambda e, c: sum(e.values()), "sum over hosts of excess / that host's capacity": lambda e, c: sum(e[h] / c[h] for h in c), "total excess / mean capacity of all hosts": lambda e, c: sum(e.values()) / (sum(c.values()) / len(c))} match = [name for name, f in cands.items() if all(abs(f(excess(a, s, c), c) - title: U.S. Navy Developing Much Needed New Tomahawk Missile with Bunker Penetration Capabilities
body: The U.S. Navy is preparing to move a new variant of the Tomahawk cruise missile with a bunker-busting warhead into low-rate initial production, with the new weapon expected to allow for long range attacks on hardened and underground targets. At the heart of modifications is the development of the Joint Multiple Effects Warhead System (JMEWS), which will combine penetration and blast-fragmentation effects in a two-stage design, allowing a single missile to engage targets requiring different destructive effects. The U.S. Armed Forces’ difficulties targeting reinforced structures, bunkers and underground facilities, has been highlighted in the recent U.S.-led assault on Iran, where the country’s heavily fortified military bases have allowed it to sustain its war effort against America and its allies for over six months with relatively little damage to its key missile forces. The program represents an effort to expand the capabilities of an established long-range strike weapon rather than introduce an entirely new missile. Existing Tomahawk Block IV missiles carry a unitary warhead in the 1,000-pound class, while the Block Vb configuration is intended to incorporate JMEWS. The new warhead could therefore allow the Navy to exploit the existing Tomahawk launch infrastructure while adding a specialised capability against targets that may be difficult to destroy using conventional unitary warheads. The actual effectiveness of the system against deeply buried facilities will depend on factors including the depth and construction of the target, the warhead’s penetration performance and the accuracy of the missile’s terminal guidance. The Tomahawk arsenal is currently in the most critical state in its history due to hostilities with Iran, with the Navy by the final week of March estimated to have expended close to 1,000 of the cruise missiles, of a total arsenal of between 3,000 and 4,500 in its total inventory. The United States in May indefinitely suspended the delivery of Japan’s first 400 RGM-109 Tomahawk cruise missiles, due to serious shortages of the missiles. Stockpiles have only become more constrained since then, reflecting a broader serious depletion of American arsenals which have for many categories of armaments been much more severe. The Tomahawk Block V has an estimated 1,700 kilometre range, and flies at low altitude using terrain-following guidance, making interception difficult. Modern variants combine GPS navigation with Terrain Contour Matching, Digital Scene Matching Area Correlation, two-way satellite communications and in-flight retargeting capability. Operators can redirect the missile after launch, command it to loiter while awaiting updated target information, and even receive post-strike battle damage data. The Tomahawk is nevertheless limited to flying at low subsonic speeds, and lacks stealth capabilities, which makes it relatively straightforward to shoot down for advanced multi-layered air defence networks.

title: How to avoid military conscription and pressure to sign an army contract in Russia
body: How to avoid military conscription and pressure to sign an army contract in Russia In September 2022, Grigory Sverdlin, the former director of Nochlezhka, an organization that helps homeless people, launched Idite Lesom (“Get Lost”). The project helps Russians avoid mobilization or desert the military. Over four years, more than 85,000 people have used its services. Meduza has already published a detailed guide to avoiding being sent to the front. Now we’ve asked the Idite Lesom team to share the advice they give people who turn to them for help. Don’t wait for a draft roundup or pressure to sign a military contract Gather your medical records and have your diagnoses confirmed. Check whether you qualify for a deferment or exemption. Find out how to apply for alternative civilian service (ACS). Keep copies of all applications and medical records you submit to the military enlistment office. If your city has a network of facial recognition cameras (Moscow, St. Petersburg, Nizhny Novgorod), avoid the subway and walk or take taxis. Avoid public places and, if possible, don’t live at your registered address. Carry notarized copies of your passport and military registration certificate, along with two completed ACS applications. Save contact details for human rights advocates and our help bot on your phone. Give someone close to you power of attorney to sign and file a lawsuit challenging administrative decisions on your behalf. Include the right to delegate that authority. If necessary, they can work with a lawyer to bring your case to court. Start with your medical history and symptoms Review your childhood and adult outpatient records, hospital discharge summaries, specialists’ reports, and test results. Write down the symptoms you’re currently experiencing and see the appropriate specialists. A test result isn’t a diagnosis. An MRI, ultrasound, CT scan, or blood test gives a doctor information they can use to make a diagnosis. Once you have one, check it against the current Schedule of Diseases used to assess fitness for military service. What matters isn’t just the name of the condition but also how much it affects your ability to function, how often it flares up, and other criteria. Related reading Four years after Putin announced a ‘partial mobilization,’ rumors of another wave are spreading. Meduza asked lawyers how Russians can protect themselves. For students: Check whether you qualify for an education deferment and whether it has been formally granted Being a student doesn’t always entitle you to a deferment. Before enrolling or transferring to another institution, find out whether you’ll retain that right. If you’re already studying, check both the certificate from your institution and the draft board’s decision. Request an extract from the military register: It should list the number of the decision granting your deferment and its start and end dates. If you qualify for a deferment but it hasn’t been formally granted, submit the original certificate from your institution’s military registration office to the military enlistment office. Alternative civilian service is possible We hear from people facing conscription who don’t believe they can get approval for alternative civilian service: The military enlistment office won’t accept their application, they’ve missed the deadline, their family doesn’t support them, or the draft board pressures them. But people do get approved for ACS. Applications do get considered. Rejections can be appealed. We’ve helped people facing conscription prepare applications, autobiographies, and character references, explain why they missed the deadline, and prepare to appear before the draft board. We’ve also helped them go to court to get the draft board to review their documents. Even if you’re scared and the military enlistment office pushes back, you have the right to pursue ACS. Read more ‘Our focus is weakening the Russian army’: For four years, Grigory Sverdlin’s aid group has helped Russians evade the draft and desert What happened to the Russians Putin mobilized four years ago? Meduza follows two of them — one still at the front, the other now a deserter in Spain. Don’t go to the military enlistment office without a reason A phone call, an ordinary text message, an email, or a message on a messaging app does not, on its own, count as a summons. Requests relayed through relatives to come in “just to sign something,” “check your details,” or “talk” don’t mean you’re required to go, either. A document dropped in your mailbox or taped to your door does not, on its own, mean a summons has been properly served. But a summons may already have been sent by another method, including electronically. Don’t go in person to clear things up. Save the message or photograph the document, check the Summons Registry, and seek advice. If the summons is considered served under the law, that’s a different situation. Consult human rights advocates about whether you’re required to appear and what to do next. Don’t sign anything unless you understand the document and its consequences Be especially careful if it includes the words “contract,” “BARS,” “volunteer unit,” or “unmanned systems forces.” You may be offered a military contract under the guise of “alternative service,” with promises of a quiet posting, a job as a cook or drone operator, or work at a computer. Signing a military contract instead of serving as a conscript is not ACS. Don’t believe promises of a short-term contract “For three months,” “for six months,” “for a year” — the stated term doesn’t mean you’ll be able to leave when it ends. During mobilization, contracts remain in force after their stated terms expire. You can be discharged only on grounds specified by law. You may be told in your unit that you can terminate your contract at any time. Don’t believe it. For conscripts: What should you do if you’re pressured to sign a contract? Submit a written statement to your commanding officer in advance declaring that you do not plan to sign a contract and intend to be discharged when your compulsory military service ends. Keep a copy and proof of submission. Your written refusal may remain in your personnel file. If you’re later pressured to sign, the document could serve as evidence that your decision wasn’t voluntary. It doesn’t guarantee protection from pressure. If you’re being forced to sign a contract, tell someone close to you immediately and contact human rights advocates. Prepare in case you’re detained Agree with people close to you on what they’ll do if they stop hearing from you. Save contact details for human rights advocates on your phone and separately on paper. Keep your phone charged and carry a portable charger. If you’re detained, try to let someone close to you know where you are as soon as possible. Don’t get into a confrontation or try to fight the people who detained you. Don’t sign a contract, and contact human rights advocates. If you’re already in the military and want to desert, don’t act on your own. Contact Idite Lesom first: Together, we can work out a plan and reduce the risks. Telegram help bot: @iditelesom_info_bot . Help is free and anonymous. At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication. If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at reports@meduza.io . To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter .

title: Bumble bought for $1.3bn in ‘bet on the future of humanity’
body: Dating app Bumble has been bought for $1.3bn (£980m) in what the new owners called “a bet on the future of humanity”. Investment firm Ithaca Holdings is taking over the loss-making firm and it directors, Ravi Gupta and John Hegeman, will become co-chief executives of the company which once differentiated itself by having a “women-first” chat rule. Bumble ditched the rule in August this year. Whitney Wolfe Herd, Bumble’s founder and current chief executive, said she would remain “actively involved” in the business she founded 12 years ago. While it is unclear what Wolfe Herd’s role at the dating app will be, she said she will work closely with the new owners. Gupta and Hegeman said they wanted to use technology to “renew and accelerate businesses…in a world transformed by AI”. They said: “Technology should work in service of our deepest source of fulfilment, human connection, and this investment is a bet on the future of humanity.” This contrasts with a recent debate over the safety of AI, with some experts claiming the speed of its development threatens the future of humanity . Bumble’s share price has soared as news of the deal began to emerge. The jump lifted its company valuation to over $580m but that is still far below a peak of more than $14bn it reached after it floated the business on the Nasdaq stock index in 2021 . Since becoming a public company, it has made an annual pre-tax profit only once, in 2023. In the following two years, it reported steep losses, though during that period Bumble had been working to incorporate new technology, including AI, into its app. Its chief executive in 2024, Lidiane Jones, told the BBC she believed AI had “exciting potential” for safety in dating apps, and that Bumble had been reviewing research showing Gen Z and millennials were interested in AI assistance with creating profiles. This year, the dating app unveiled several new AI features, including profile guidance to help people create dating profiles. Bumble was launched in 2014 by Wolfe Herd, who built the brand around a distinctive feature that only allowed women to initiate conversations with matches. It recently abandoned that rule , prompting debate among users over whether the app had lost what set it apart from rivals. “Today, our community is asking for more flexibility, less pressure, and more opportunities to create real, meaningful connections and that is what this new experience provides,” Wolfe Herd said in August. Dating apps like Bumble have come under pressure in recent years as some younger users have grown disillusioned with the process of browsing for dates. Bumble said in 2025 that it would cut almost a third of its workforce as the industry grappled with what Wolfe Herd described as an “inflexion point” in online dating. Investments in other dating companies have also soured as apps have struggled to convince users to pay for their services. Match Group – which owns apps including Tinder, OkCupid and Hinge – has also seen its shares fall sharply from their peak in 2021. According to a 2025 report by the media watchdog Ofcom, adults in the UK were spending less time on dating apps than three years earlier. Some single people are instead turning to board game get-togethers , book clubs and other group activities in the hope of finding a partner.

title: Bayern Held By Viking After Olise Red Card In 3-3 Champions League Draw
body: Bayern Munich were held 3-3 at Viking in the Champions League on Tuesday with the Norwegian champions equalising late through Herman Haugen after Michael Olise was sent off. Bayern trailed 2-0 at halftime thanks to goals from Gianni Stensness and Peter Christiansen. Harry Kane seemed to have dragged Bayern to victory as he scored twice and set up another for a 3-2 lead, but Olise picked up two yellow cards in the space of a minute. Viking made the most of their advantage with Haugen scoring in the final minute to snatch the Norwegian champions a shock draw against the German giants. Olise’s red means he will miss next week’s blockbuster clash with English champions Arsenal in Munich. Kane scored for the ninth straight Champions League match, equalling a club record set by Robert Lewandowski and drawing two behind the record of 11 set by Cristiano Ronaldo. Just days after conceding the fastest goal in Bundesliga history in Saturday’s 2-2 draw at Augsburg, Bayern were again behind early. With just 72 seconds gone, Stensness headed in an outswinging corner to give the hosts a shock lead. Bayern ramped up the pressure but could not break through, with Kane twice heading into the arms of Viking goalie Arild Ostbo. Not content to absorb Bayern pressure and cling to a narrow lead, Viking launched a lightning-fast counter-attack and doubled their advantage with 38 minutes gone. Top goalscorer Christiansen finished off a slick move to give Viking a 2-0 lead. Bayern were handed a lifeline when Konrad Laimer was felled in the box just after the break, bringing Kane to the spot. After a stuttering run up, the 33-year-old guided the ball into the bottom right of the goal, past the fingertips of Ostbo. On the hour, Kane lost his marker and heading in a Joshua Kimmich cross to lock up the scores. Luis Diaz had an effort ruled out for offside just a minute later but the Colombian was the beneficiary of a Kane pass 10 minutes later. Kane lofted a ball to Laimer, whose saved shot rebounded into Diaz’s path. The England captain appeared to have saved Bayern, until Olise was sent from the pitch. The France winger saw yellow for a foul and then picked up another for dissent, leaving Bayern a man down with 16 minutes left. Viking pushed and Haugen scored in the 90th minute to help the hosts to a memorable draw. title: US DoW selects Avon Protection System: MITR-M1 Half Mask and MITR-PG1 Powered Goggle
body:
The United States has become the latest nation to place an order for Avon Protection’s MITR System. The recent order by the Department of War (DoW) incorporates the MITR-M1 Half Mask and MITR-PG1 Powered Goggle for its Special Operations Forces and includes both MITR-PF Particulate Filter and MITR-RF Riot Filter for mission-specific modularity, and integrated helmet and communication system accessories.
The MITR System delivers modular protection for eyes, nose and mouth as an alternative to full-face respirators, allowing users in tactical threat environments to scale up their protection during dynamic, fast-paced missions.
The NIOSH-certified MITR-M1 Half Mask with MITR-PF Filter provides users with lightweight, flexible respiratory protection for the nose and mouth. With a sleek flush-fitting curved profile, the wearer retains weapon sighting ability and maintains communications via voice amplification/projection units. The half mask clips directly to the wearer’s helmet via the MITR-M1 Helmet Mount Kit, enabling the mask to be donned without removing the helmet.
MITR-PG1 has been designed to integrate seamlessly with the MITR-M1 Half Mask, providing ocular protection against riot agents. With an integrated air purging system that constantly purges air, the goggle’s lightweight, fog-resistant, tactical-black design provides clear vision and operational readiness in the most demanding conditions. Lightweight andcomfortable for extended wear, MITR-PG1 is compatible with combat helmets andnight vision systems.
Avon Protection’s MITR-PF Compact Particulate Filter is a low-profile design with a particulate filter containing a pleated, high-efficiency filter element for protection against biological and pharmaceutical agents. The MITR-RF Compact Riot Filter combines the pleated, high efficiency filter with activated carbon layer for additional riot agent vapor protection. Both filters provide NIOSH P100 protection, removing greater than 99.97% of harmful airborne particulates.
With this order, the U.S. has become the second FVEY nation to select the MITR-M1 Half Mask, following Canada’s selection in May 2026.
Steve Elwell, President, Avon Protection, said: “This award culminates nearly four years of working collaboratively with end-users developing a solution that meets their mission requirements. Securing the U.S. DoW as another customer for the MITR System demonstrates continued focus on protecting the health of personnel, both in the short-term and the long-term.
“For tactical operators, MITR is not just about protection during today’s mission, it is about reducing lifetime exposure to hazardous particulates that can contribute to long-term health issues and helping ensure those who serve remain healthy long after their careers end. This award represents an important step in bringing this capability to a wider community of users.”
AVON Protection is represented in South Africa by ECM Technologies, which had this MITR system on display at the recent Africa Aerospace and Defence exhibition.

title: Apple’s HomeView ad is confusing to everyone except parents
body:
Apple’s ad introducing its new HomeView smart display is a little unusual. It’s fast-paced and unruly, depicting a family of five as they rush through the morning routine. There’s yelling and mess, misplaced keys and discarded eggshells. Apple’s typical vibe is clean, simple, orderly; this commercial is chaos.
But the spot has parents — those with teen children in particular — feeling seen.
[Media: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hkrYiZ_g9tw]
I’ll admit that it stressed me out the first time I watched it, too. Mornings getting my five-year-old out the door are a special breed of chaos, and usually culminate in us playing whatever ad-libbed game will get him to put his shoes on. But it’s not quite as intense as this one, which features dad making French toast, mom losing and finding keys in her pocket, a proxy battle over the thermostat, a teenage boy helping himself to whipped cream from a can, and an unexpected video call. There’s also a microdrama about the daughter’s ride to school with a boyfriend nobody knew about that ends with everyone gathered around the HomeView watching the security camera feed of the two of them departing the porch. It’s a lot for just over three minutes of screentime.
If I know anything, though, I know to trust my colleague Jen Tuohy, senior reviewer and parent to two teens, on matters of the home. Her take? “The most unrealistic part of the video is that no one is holding an iPhone.”
Other parents of teens shared similar reactions on Threads. When tech analyst Benedict Evans posted about the ad feeling stressful and confusing, CNET editor at large Bridget Carey chimed in to defend it, saying “It was exactly what my morning is like and it was the most real ad I’ve ever seen from Apple.” Others agreed, saying it “accurately captured” real life and that it “hit home,” no pun intended, at least I think.
Even if Apple didn’t need to do much to heighten the stakes of a family getting out the door, there is of course plenty of sleight of hand at work when it comes to making the HomeView appear so essential. The family has seemingly drilled a hole directly into the middle of their kitchen island to accommodate the charging cable, for one. And what sibling is going to check a text message from a secret boyfriend on the communal kitchen screen with their brother sitting at arm’s length? I don’t believe any teenager trusts Apple’s privacy features that far.
[Image: You gotta really like that screen on a speaker to drill a hole in your nice kitchen furniture for it. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/family_kitchen.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
The confusion about the commercial is understandable. This is a far cry from the quiet luxury lifestyle everyone seems to enjoy in Apple’s Vision Pro ads. There’s also Evans’ observation that the HomeView doesn’t really solve any of the problems that come up throughout the course of the video. In the case of a spontaneous FaceTime call from the grandparents, the screen in the middle of the kitchen seems to make things worse.
But maybe morning chaos isn’t the problem that’s being solved. If the alternative is five people all interacting with their own phones, then the HomeView presents a different picture where everyone gets the essential information they need from one shared screen and stays more present.
A screen that makes you be more present is a lovely idea, but the real test will come when it’s in real households. Is the HomeView going to be enough to convince families to put their personal devices down? Will everyone just ignore it and keep scrolling on their own iPhones? These are questions worth answering before you start drilling holes in your kitchen island! In any case, an ungovernable morning routine is probably a feature of a busy household, not a bug. Just ask a parent.

title: Emergency order by US to 'prevent blackouts' could affect data centres
body: The US Department of Energy has issued an emergency order to try to prevent power cuts amid increasing demand. Monday's order prompted PJM Interconnection , a corporation that transmits electricity in parts of the US, to " direct data centres and other large-load customers to switch to back-up generation resources, if necessary". Data centres in the US are commonly blamed for a surge in electricity prices and have driven public opinion on AI to sour, according to polls. In issuing its emergency order, the Energy Department also gave "a high rate of planned generator outages during the autumn maintenance season" as a possible cause of blackouts. PJM has issued a Maximum Generation Alert and Load Management Alert for Oct. 13 ahead of expected tight system conditions caused by unusually warm fall weather and planned equipment outages required for maintenance and construction. This alert does not require any action from… pic.twitter.com/zH8QXo2Jwm — PJM Interconnection (@pjminterconnect) October 12, 2026 The order remains in effect until October 16. Energy Secretary Chris Wright was confident in his decision to order utility companies and others to take emergency measures. "This order will help ensure millions of American families and businesses across the mid-Atlantic have access to affordable, reliable and secure electricity by making additional power generation, including back-up power, available to use as needed," Mr Wright said. The Department of Energy said in a statement that the US had 35 GW of unused back-up generation available nationwide. PJM issued a maximum generation alert for October 13 and 14: "Emergency procedures took place as above-normal temperatures are forecast across much of the PJM region. Additional emergency procedures may be necessary pending system conditions." The company said the alert does not "require any action from customers". The warnings come before the US midterm elections, where energy policy, AI and data centres are key issues. Any blackouts or failure to adequately address them could add to friction between residents in the US and utility companies, as well as AI firms. President Donald Trump has repeatedly dismissed critics of AI in recent weeks and accused them of "hoaxes". But in February he tried to ease the strain data centres were putting on the grid by signing a non-binding ratepayer protection pledge in which technology and data centre companies would provide their own electricity to operate. Meanwhile, the Department of Energy has pushed for the construction of more nuclear reactors to address AI energy needs.

title: Greek National Tourism Body Wins International Marketing Award
body: The Greek National Tourism Organisation (GNTO) has won the Marketing Partnership of the Year 2026 award at the annual Jet2 Marketing Awards in Leeds, England. The award recognises the quality and effectiveness of the GNTO’s joint advertising programme with Jet2holidays for 2026, according to an official announcement. The partnership supports the GNTO’s strategy to develop more effective and targeted collaborations with British tour operators. This year’s campaign combined traditional marketing methods, including radio advertising, programmatic advertising, video-on-demand content and articles in major national media, with targeted initiatives designed to engage British travellers in new ways. These initiatives included: Travel agent engagement: The GNTO and Jet2holidays strengthened Greece’s presence among a network of 80 independent travel agents in southwest England through a joint event in Bristol. Greek gastronomy promotion: The campaign showcased Greek recipes through The Greek Kitchen at the BBC Good Food Show in Birmingham, reaching 26,000 visitors. Interactive marketing: A dedicated Greece-themed game on the Jet2 app recorded more than 700,000 plays in just one week and attracted 13% new customers. Influencer marketing: Six popular British influencers visited six different Greek destinations on a familiarisation trip, generating 104 social media posts and 5.4 million views, significantly expanding the campaign’s digital reach. Elena Skarveli, head of the GNTO’s United Kingdom and Ireland Office, said the use of more creative and interactive marketing tools was transforming the traditional joint advertising model with tour operators. She explained that connecting awareness of Greece with audience engagement increased the GNTO’s return on investment (ROI) and helped strengthen bookings to Greece throughout the year. Angela Tzifa, deputy head of the GNTO’s United Kingdom and Ireland Office, accepted the award on behalf of Greece. The ceremony took place during the Jet2 Destination Partnerships event, where the GNTO participated to deepen professional relationships and further promote Greece in the British tourism market. Senior executives from Jet2.com and Jet2holidays attended alongside more than 40 representatives of national and regional tourism organisations from Europe and North Africa. Representatives from 12 British airports also took part to strengthen connections between destinations, airports and Jet2. The event featured presentations and panel discussions on key tourism industry issues, including public responses to tourism development, emerging trends in the British market, changing consumer behaviour and ways to improve joint advertising programmes. Participants also explored the opportunities artificial intelligence and new digital technologies offer for tourism marketing. Separate breakout sessions featured representatives from Google, Meta, Adobe and Mail Metro Media. Discussions focused on emerging technologies, data-driven marketing, personalisation tools and specialised campaigns to improve the promotion of tourism destinations. title: Ex-gang leader sentenced to 40 years to life in prison for Tupac Shakur murder
body: A former gang leader was sentenced to 40 years to life in prison on Tuesday for orchestrating the 1996 drive-by shooting death of hip-hop star Tupac Shakur in Las Vegas, capping the prosecution of a long-unsolved murder that shaped the golden age of rap music.Duane "Keffe D" Davis, 63, found guilty of first-degree murder in August, received the penalty during a hearing in a Las Vegas courtroom.Until Davis' 2023 arrest, the killing of Shakur, shot dead in the passenger seat of an SUV driven by his record executive, Marion "Suge" Knight, had stood for nearly three decades as one of America's most notorious cold cases.The murder, which silenced one of rap's most commercially successful and influential artists, heightened the image of violence permeating 1990s hip-hop culture while stoking the infamous East Coast-West Coast "gangsta" rap feud of the era.Despite Davis' conviction, the question of who pulled the trigger in the fatal shooting of the 25-year-old rap legend has never been conclusively decided.Davis was tried and convicted for masterminding the murder to avenge the beating of his nephew by Shakur and members of the rapper's entourage inside the MGM Grand casino on the Las Vegas Strip on September 7, 1996.Davis has said he would appeal his conviction.Fatal shooting sparked by casino brawlThe clash at the casino stemmed from hostility between two Los Angeles-area street gangs - the South Side Compton Crips, of which Davis was the self-described leader, and Mob Piru, associated with Shakur, Knight, and their music label, Death Row Records.Members of both groups were in Las Vegas that night to see a world heavyweight title boxing match between Mike Tyson and Bruce Seldon.Within hours of the casino brawl, Davis ushered his nephew and two other associates into a white Cadillac and went looking for Shakur and Knight, determined to settle scores, according to an account Davis later gave police in an unrelated investigation and that prosecutors cited during his murder trial.Davis said he passed a gun to the two men seated behind him in the Cadillac, one of whom opened fire through the window when they caught up with, and pulled alongside, Knight and Shakur's vehicle in traffic.Shakur was struck four times and died in a hospital six days later. Knight, who suffered a minor injury from a bullet fragment that grazed his head, is now serving a 28-year prison term on an unrelated voluntary manslaughter conviction.Authorities initially lacked sufficient evidence for charges despite suspicionsAuthorities said they long believed Davis was involved in Shakur's killing but lacked sufficient evidence to charge him.That changed when he went public with his story in media appearances and a memoir that, along with tapes of his secret meetings with investigators, formed the bulk of the prosecution's murder case.In his book, Compton Street Legend, Davis himself wrote that he was considered a suspect in the murders of both Shakur and Christopher Wallace, a rival rapper.Wallace, who performed as the Notorious B.I.G. under the New York-based Bad Boy Entertainment label, was shot dead in Los Angeles in March 1997.Although the Wallace killing remains unsolved, there has long been speculation that he was gunned down in retaliation for Shakur's killing months earlier.While Davis was never accused of actually firing the shots that killed Shakur - Nevada law allows someone to be charged with murder as a participant in the crime - prosecutors have never named a suspected gunman.All three other men in the Cadillac with Davis that night have since died.

title: Imagination Africa, Mentors Chess Academy to host second African Genius Chess Championship at Ghud Park
body: Imagination Africa and Mentors Chess Academy will host the second African Genius Chess Championship on Saturday, 24 October 2026, at Ghud Park, Accra Mall. The competition uses chess to develop young minds, promote inclusion and create equal opportunities for children from different socio-economic backgrounds. “Talent and potential are not determined by a child’s social or economic circumstances. On the chessboard, every child starts with the same pieces and the same chances, and that is the opportunity we want to give them,” said Mariam Mahamah, co-founder of Imagination Africa. The maiden edition, held at Legon City Mall in 2024, attracted more than 150 young players from over 15 schools across Ghana. Participants competed in age categories ranging from Under-8 to Under-20. Twelve-year-old Dave Chief Quansah Acheampong was the standout performer, going unbeaten in four rounds against older players from Presec, the University of Ghana, DPS International and ARIS to win the Under-20 title. The 2024 event was attended by a representative of the Ministry of Education and the High Commissioner of India to Ghana. Parents also praised the initiative for providing a conducive environment for children to learn and play chess. This year’s competition will feature different age categories, with trophies, medals and gift prizes for top finishers and the best girl in each category. The organisers say chess can help young people develop critical thinking, concentration, discipline, confidence and problem-solving skills. They have encouraged chess enthusiasts to participate. Imagination Africa plans to make the championship an annual event and is seeking partners to expand its reach and support youth development, social inclusion and intellectual growth. Imagination Africa is a non-profit organisation that identifies, develops and showcases young people’s talent in Ghana through sports, arts and academics, creating opportunities for underprivileged children to reach their full potential.

title: Paradigm Initiative steps up calls over digital rights, internet freedom in Africa
body: Paradigm Initiative (PIN), a pan-African digital rights organisation, is stepping up calls for stronger protection of human rights online as African policymakers and human rights institutions gather in Senegal for a key regional meeting. The organisation is participating in the 89th Ordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (ACHPR), taking place at the King Fahd Palace Hotel in Dakar from 12 to 21 October. PIN says it will use the session to draw attention to growing concerns about digital rights and internet freedom across Africa, including the slow development of artificial intelligence (AI) policies, restrictions on media freedom and violations of children’s rights online. Its advocacy will draw on ongoing monitoring of digital rights violations and findings from its Londa report, which examines the state of digital rights and freedoms across the continent. Representing PIN at the session are Bridgette Ndlovu, Partnerships and Engagements Officer, and Moussa Waly Sene, Programmes Officer for Francophone Africa. The organisation will make a statement during discussions on the human rights situation in Africa, highlighting issues it believes require greater attention from governments and regional institutions. As internet access and digital technologies become increasingly important to everyday life, concerns about how they are governed and used are growing. AI systems are developing rapidly, raising questions about accountability, privacy, discrimination and the protection of fundamental rights. PIN is concerned about the slow pace of AI policy development in Africa and the need for frameworks that protect people as the technology expands. Media freedom is another priority. The organisation intends to draw attention to threats to the free flow of information, the importance of protecting journalists, and the need to ensure that people can access reliable information. Children’s rights online will also feature in its advocacy, with a focus on making digital spaces safer while ensuring that young people can benefit from the opportunities technology offers. Through its engagement with the African Commission, PIN aims to encourage stronger action by governments and human rights institutions to protect fundamental freedoms in both digital and physical spaces. Events to focus on elections, inclusion and disinformation Beyond its formal engagement with the Commission, PIN will host a series of activities in Dakar with partners, bringing together human rights institutions, journalists and other stakeholders to examine emerging digital rights challenges. On 13 October, PIN and the Network of African National Human Rights Institutions (NANHRI) will convene a session on digital rights and internet freedom, focusing on the role of national human rights institutions in monitoring elections. The discussion will draw on PIN’s Digital Rights and Elections in Africa Monitor Toolkit (DREAMT) , which is designed to support efforts to monitor digital rights during elections. The session will also feature The Signal , a short film on digital accessibility and inclusion, followed by discussions on how to make digital spaces more accessible to people across Africa. On 14 October, PIN will organise a Digital Rights Academy for journalists and media practitioners. The training will focus on information integrity, equipping participants to better understand the challenges surrounding the accuracy, credibility and responsible sharing of information. The programme will continue on 15 October with a session on information integrity based on PIN’s research project, Africa Facing Down Disinformation . The session will present research findings on information disorders in Senegal and outline recommendations to address disinformation and strengthen the information environment. The activities reflect PIN’s wider efforts to connect digital rights advocacy with practical action, including election monitoring, media development and the promotion of inclusive digital spaces.

title: Mark Carney to attend ‘Forever Canadian’ rallies ahead of Alberta referendum
body:
Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to attend two Forever Canadian rallies in Alberta this week, just ahead of the province’s referendum .
On Oct. 19, Albertans will vote on the whether to stay in Canada or hold a future separation referendum. There are also nine other questions involving constitutional and immigration issues.
The “Forever Canadian” campaign, launched by Alberta’s former deputy premier Thomas Lukaszuk, seeks to encourage Albertans to vote to stay in Canada.
The organization’s website says Carney was invited to one rally in Calgary on Oct. 15 and another in Edmonton on Oct. 16. The Prime Minister’s Office confirmed Carney will attend both.
“We want the country’s leader to see what we see every day: Albertans from every walk of life standing up for a united Canada,” says the Forever Canadian website.
Carney, who grew up in Alberta, focused his Thanksgiving Day message on Alberta’s upcoming separation referendum , saying Canada is “worth fighting for.”
“This year, Thanksgiving is a bit different,” he said in a video message posted Monday and filmed at his old high school in Edmonton.
“A week from today, Albertans will have the opportunity to make an important decision about their future: whether to remain part of Canada or begin a long and uncertain process through which Alberta could separate from Canada.”
Carney said the federal government is building “big things” in Alberta — including a planned new pipeline to the West Coast — but Canada can’t achieve those goals if the country is divided.
“You can’t build big things on fault lines,” he said.
Carney also said Canadians are “stronger together” as they face down threats to their economy, security and culture.
“Generations of Albertans helped build this country. It’s yours, it’s ours, and it’s worth fighting for,” he said.
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is expected to deliver his own speech supporting Canadian unity in Calgary on Friday.
Poilievre is set to speak during the Canada Strong and Free Network conference on Oct. 16 in Calgary. His speech is expected to be followed by an address from Alberta Premier Danielle Smith.
— With files from David Baxter and Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

title: Honeywell Aerospace doubles supply of key Abrams engine part, removing fleet availability bottleneck
body: Honeywell has invested nearly $100 million across its AGT1500 engine supply chain and production network over the past three years. That spending includes supplier development, equipment and tooling upgrades, material reserves and expanded in-house manufacturing. “Supporting the venerable AGT1500 requires more than just ordering parts from suppliers,” said Kathy Worthen, senior vice president and chief supply chain officer at Honeywell Aerospace. “It requires sustained investment across the entire industrial base that supports them.” “We are strengthening manufacturing capacity, investing in our supply chain and expanding critical capabilities across the AGT1500 ecosystem to ensure Abrams operators have the support they need today and well into the future,” Worthen said. The company announced further investment in the program but did not give a separate amount for the additional spending. Honeywell qualified its precision machining Center of Excellence to manufacture the AGT1500 compressor impeller. The additional source supports the Army’s Total Integrated Engine Revitalization, or TIGER, program. Engineering, manufacturing, supply chain and customer support teams worked together to accelerate qualification and production. Honeywell said hardware was delivered months ahead of schedule, doubling the component’s supply. The AGT1500 gas turbine has powered the M1 Abrams family since the early 1980s. It produces 1,500 horsepower and, according to Honeywell, can propel a 72-ton tank to speeds of up to 42 miles per hour. The compact engine can operate on multiple fuels and supports cold starting. Honeywell also identifies rapid acceleration and quiet operation among its features. AGT1500 engines have accumulated more than 40 million operating miles with Abrams fleets worldwide. Honeywell continues to support modernization and sustainment through TIGER, with upgrades intended to improve reliability, performance and operational availability.

title: Please stop hashing the public key first (or: ML-DSA's µ annoys me)
body:
13 October 2026 · updated 13 October 2026 · Permalink
A goal one might have when designing a signing algorithm is to prevent signing a message one has not seen.
Signing a message one hasn't seen might sound difficult at first, but most classical signature algorithms , as commonly used, sign a hash of the message, rather than the message itself. This kind of arrangement is necessitated by the fact that the underlying algorithms are only capable of signing messages of a limited size. You might not have seen the message, but you might have seen the hash of it, or another signature which encodes said hash. In many protocols, this lets you produce a valid signature on a message you've never seen. That's rarely a problem in practice, but it can be surprising, and it's a pitfall for the unsuspecting protocol designer.
More recent algorithms take steps to prevent this:
This can complicate your signing code, particularly when dealing with HSMs or smart cards, but it doesn't require majorly reworking your signing process. Unfortunately, on the verification side things are less rosy.
As a general rule of thumb, we should avoid touching the body of a signed message until we've verified the signature. Also as a general rule of thumb, cryptographic protocols where there are multiple signers put the signer's identity within said body (X.509, most JWT and CWT usages, SAML, I'm looking at all of you, but you're not the only ones).
This means the verification process ends up being
Often (JWT, CWT and SAML again), there's either no key identifier present in the signed message, or it's permitted for multiple signing keys to share a key identifier † . This means that, if the issuer has multiple keys, you may have to do multiple trial-verifications to work out if the message is actually valid.
One nice property that all of these protocols have (except XML Digital Signatures, but nobody thinks XML Digital Signatures were a good idea) is that they carry the signing method in a header. So, with a traditional signing algorithm, you have the option of
Unfortunately, it has the slight flaw that it doesn't work with either Ed25519 or ML-DSA as defined.
For ML-DSA, it would have been quite easy to re-arrange matters. If we instead computed SHAKE-256(0x00 || len(ctx) || ctx || m || SHAKE-256(PubK, 64), 64) (i.e. we put the public key hash in at the end ), then we can hold our SHAKE-256 context around and copy it for each trial verification. We'd end up keeping just over 200 bytes of SHAKE-256 context around (instead of 64 bytes of output), but that's not too bad. Unfortunately, that's not the choice that was made and we'll just have to deal with it.
Ed25519 is slightly more challenging. If we reversed the hash computation to be SHA-512(M || R || PubK) instead, it would be vulnerable to length extension attacks (for any SHA-512(X) you can extend it into SHA-512(X || some predictable garbage || Y) for any arbitrary Y).
Fixing that when Ed25519 was published in 2011 would be somewhat tricky, though the easiest option without truncating the hash is just to sign SHA-512(SHA-512("ed25519 domain separation" || M || R || PubK)) .
Since we don't have a time machine, it's all a bit academic. In 2026 you can just avoid the problem by using SHA-3, BLAKE2, a truncated SHA-2 variant, or any other modern hash function which isn't vulnerable to length extension attacks.
In the meantime I'll just sigh and hope we can reduce the number of signatures we pass around, given they're really becoming rather large and expensive.
† You may be thinking it somewhat defeats the purpose of having a key identifier if they aren't unique. I don't disagree!
