title: Adebutu’s Omission: ‘Don’t set Ogun on fire’ – PDP candidate warns INEC
body: By James Ogunnaike, Abeokuta The Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), candidate for Ifo Constituency I in the Ogun State House of Assembly, Adebari Adekunle, has cautioned the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), over the omission of the party’s gubernatorial candidate from the election. Adekunle also warned the All Progressives Congress, APC, gubernatorial candidate, Senator Solomon Adeola, popularly known as Yayi, against actions that could heighten political tension in the state. The final list, signed by INEC Secretary, Rose Oriaran-Anthony, contains the candidates of 13 political parties, including the APC. However, PDP is missing from the list. Adekunle, while reacting to the development, said the exclusion of Oladipupo Adebutu and his running mate, Lateefat Sowunmi-Kolapo, from INEC’s list had gone beyond the two candidates and had become a matter of concern for the entire state. He recalled that President Bola Tinubu expressed displeasure over the desperation of some political associates, warning that their actions could damage his administration’s image and democratic legacy. According to Adekunle, the Presidency’s comment is a “great indictment” on INEC and raises serious questions about its credibility and Yayi’s role in the controversy. The Assembly candidate cautioned INEC against undermining public confidence in the electoral process and urged the commission to act transparently and reverse the omission. Adekunle insisted that Ogun State must not become a battleground for desperate political interests ahead of the 2027 elections. “A situation where APC party members would be celebrating that they would remove names from the INEC list even before it actually happened was a reckless one,” he said. Adekunle said many residents, angered by what they perceive as an attempt to undermine their choice, had threatened to protest, while elders and stakeholders were appealing for calm to prevent a breakdown of peace. “Ogun State must not become a battleground for desperate political interests. Political ambition should not take precedence over democratic principles. People are already burdened by economic hardship, are looking towards 2027 for change and will resist any attempt to deny them a fair opportunity to choose their leaders. Peace must not be mistaken for weakness,” he warned. He urged the Presidency to ensure that no individual uses the President’s name to advance personal ambition and stain his efforts at credible elections. The Assembly hopeful also urged INEC to act transparently and address the controversy without delay, stressing that peace must not be mistaken for weakness and the people’s patience must not be taken for granted. title: Schools in Azerbaijan are barring girls who wear hijabs from class. Some of their male classmates are refusing to attend in solidarity.
body: A woman wearing a hijab on a street in Baku, January 18, 2011 In late September, Azerbaijan approved new school uniform rules, including a ban on “items inconsistent with the principle of secularism.” Inspections soon began at schools, and girls wearing hijabs were barred from classes. Protests broke out in Baku and other cities, with schoolgirls and their classmates demanding that everyone’s right to an education be upheld. On October 12, 37 people were detained in Baku. The Interior Ministry said protesters had tried to “grossly disrupt public order.” Meanwhile, users began reporting that they could not access TikTok and Instagram — the country’s two most popular social networks. Here’s a closer look at what is happening in Azerbaijan and what may be behind the ban. Azerbaijan’s Cabinet of Ministers introduced the new school uniform rules in a September 21 decree . The decree prohibits “wearing items of clothing that disrupt the uniformity of the prescribed school uniform,” as well as clothing that is “inconsistent with the principle of secularism in general education.” The decree does not explicitly mention hijabs. But during school inspections that began on October 9, girls with their heads covered were barred from classes , even though the decree does not authorize such measures. Female teachers were also required to remove their headscarves, Jam News reported . Protests then broke out in Baku and other Azerbaijani cities. At some schools, boys also refused to attend classes in solidarity with girls wearing hijabs. In a village in Baku’s Sabunchu district, students protested with a sign bearing the slogan: “A hijab does not stand in the way of an education.” A source at a Baku school told the BBC that boys in the upper grades were also required to shave their beards — even though, like hijabs, beards are not mentioned in the cabinet decree. Videos of the protests appeared on social media. One shows students trying to smash school windows. The Telegram channel Minval Politika reported that a school principal’s car had been set on fire in the Garadag district. On October 12, Azerbaijan’s Interior Ministry said it had detained 37 people for actions “grossly violating public order.” The ministry said “a group of individuals” had created “a conflict situation” with school staff over “compliance with a uniform dress code” and damaged schools. Authorities opened a criminal investigation into allegations of organizing acts that disrupted public order, an offense punishable by up to three years in prison . The ministry provided no further details, and it is unclear whether any of those detained are minors. As the protests unfolded, Azerbaijanis began reporting that they could not access Instagram and TikTok — the country’s two most popular social networks. Some users could access them only through a VPN. Some directly link the disruption to the protests, although the authorities have not confirmed blocking the platforms. Azerbaijan has seen protests against a hijab ban before. Jam News reported that a similar protest took place outside the Education Ministry in May 2011 and led to a criminal investigation. That same year, authorities detained activist Abgul Suleymanov, who was known for taking part in protests against the hijab ban. He was later sentenced to 11 years in prison on charges he denied. The reasons for the current ban are unclear, the BBC reported . Neither the cabinet nor the Education Ministry has explained them or responded to journalists’ inquiries. Journalist Afgan Mukhtarli, a critic of the authorities, believes that hijabs pose no problems but that Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev “needs the specter of radical Islam to strengthen his hold on power.” Supporters of the authorities, by contrast, see the ban as part of “strengthening the sovereignty of a country trying to free itself from the influence of other states.” It is unclear what influence they mean, but many believe Aliyev was referring to Turkey when he recently spoke about countering ideological interference from abroad, the BBC reported. On October 3, protesters gathered outside Azerbaijan’s consulate in Istanbul to demand an end to the ban on wearing hijabs in Azerbaijani schools. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication. If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at reports@meduza.io . To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter .

title: AlphaNIST
body:
From AlphaGo to AlphaZero , reinforcement learning produced strategies that surprised expert players. AlphaZero learned from experience at scale, without human demonstrations.
AlphaNIST brings this philosophy to contact-rich, high-precision robotic assembly in simulation. An end-to-end policy learns how to complete the task, without prescribed manipulation stages.
Four successful ten-part runs, using a policy trained separately from the single-component policy below.
The NIST board has twenty assembly tasks, with parts as small as 4 mm. Fitting one part can take several changes of grasp and orientation. Tight clearances leave little room for error: a tilted nut can jam or cross-thread.
With several parts, the robot also has to choose an order. An installed component may block the gripper’s next move.
Trying to prescribe every maneuver means anticipating how the robot should respond as contacts and obstructions change. A two-finger gripper may also need solutions quite different from those that come naturally to a human hand.
Perhaps the answer is to stop telling the robot how we think the task should be done, and let it learn how to get there. We give it a binary task reward for success and train it through vast amounts of diverse experience. That leaves room for the robot to discover solutions we might never have thought to teach.
One policy trains across twenty heterogeneous assemblies, starting from loose parts, in-hand grasps, and partial assemblies cached in simulation.
Near-complete starts let the robot practice finishing an assembly before it can solve the whole task. The cache supplies starting states, not demonstrations.
Beta sampling favors starting states the policy solves about half the time, while giving every state a chance. Progress on one state can make another solvable; its sampling weight then changes with new outcomes.
With binary task rewards, one policy trained across all twenty tasks reaches higher training success than twenty separate specialists. Adding rewards for reaching and alignment reduces success in this experiment.

title: As Army I Corps gets parts of NGC2 ecosystem, ‘tyranny of distance and disruption’ in the Pacific are top of mind for commander
body: As the Army shifts parts of its Next Generation Command and Control System to I Corps, the organization’s top officer acknowledged that the new ecosystem will operate across vastly larger distances than previously tested given the unit’s focus on the Pacific. Having been prototyped across two divisions over the last year — both smaller tactical echelons than I Corps — the Army’s ecosystem is working its way to more immense environments. “What’s really different is the scope and scale,” Lt. Gen. Matt McFarlane, head of I Corps, said at the annual AUSA conference Tuesday, referencing the Pacific theater. “Instead of across an island or two islands next to each other, at the corps level it’s command posts in Honshu in Japan and in Brisbane in Australia.” He said that I Corps’ primary challenge is the “tyranny of distance and disruption,” an allusion to the significant expanses U.S. forces will have to operate across should a war with China occur in the Pacific. McFarlane said NGC2 would help synchronize effects and data, and provide his units better survivability across that type of theater. I Corps has used some elements of NGC2 over the last nine months, according to McFarlane, but now has started a “deliberate rollout” of the system at the corps headquarters and its “enabling” brigades. “As we make that transition … the mission of Next Gen C2 fundamentally pivots from the tactical to the operational level,” he said at a separate media roundtable on the sidelines of the AUSA conference. “Corps echelons do not fight localized gun battles or tactical fights. My job as the corps commander is to orchestrate through theater-wide multi-domain campaigns, allocate joint fires, manage operational endurance, and synchronize all-domain effects across thousands of miles of maritime domain in the Indo-Pacific.” A top priority for the Army, NGC2 is meant to give commanders the ability to make decisions and act upon them faster than an adversary, as service officials drum beat about how quick access to data flowing from a suite of new sensors will be decisive on future battlefields. NGC2 tools were put through their paces this summer in the Mojave Desert during the Army’s Project Convergence Capstone 6 exercise. Afterward, senior leaders dubbed the event a success, but acknowledged that some equipment failed in the desert heat. “We are fielding or equipping right now with the systems that were validated during PCC6,” McFarlane said. “So things that weren’t working or weren’t ready, we are not rolling out at I Corps at the operational level with my team.” McFarlane did not name specific hardware systems that were validated or not validated during PCC6, when asked about them by DefenseScoop. “As we train and then certify ourselves on those [NGC2] systems, the ruggedization and the requirement for that is incredibly important in the Pacific as you look at the different kind of environments we fight in, from the frozen Arctic terrain in Alaska to the high heat, high humidity, extreme dense triple-canopy jungles in the first island chain in the Pacific. So, the ruggedization is obviously really important for us as we look at operating that forward in small, distributed nodes, where mobility is a key aspect of survivability for our command posts,” McFarlane said. “What I can tell you is the systems that enable Next Generation Command and Control provide me [with] decision dominance at the operational level in the Pacific. And so that’s the [data and communications] transport so I can talk from anywhere on the face of the Earth with any other point on the face of the Earth that’s got the transport that’s part of the Next Gen Command and Control package,” McFarlane said. The tech can also drive faster “detector-to-effector” or “sensor-to-shooter” cycles in the kill chain, he noted. “And then amongst all of that are the applications that allow me to see myself, see the enemy, predictive analysis, some modeling tools to help me make decisions faster than our adversary makes decisions, and then take action faster than our adversary,” he added. “The ones that we’re fielding were validated at the tactical level, and so I think there’ll be some room as Next Gen C2 continues to work with industry to identify the right apps and maybe additional pieces of equipment that we need at the operational level,” McFarlane said. Over the next six months, some of his focus areas will include interoperability among the joint force and allies, across multiple classification levels or information levels, McFarlane told reporters. How quickly NGC2 capabilities can be scaled will depend on the resources that are available, he told reporters. “The key aspect here for me is as we employ at the corps level, driving operational maneuver, [is] making sure we’re optimizing the apps, the different tools to include transport as we deal with contested electromagnetic spectrum, to ensure we can quickly move from one transport to another — fiber to radio, the different connectivity there, LEO and milsat — without humans having to be in that loop, is an example of an app that we’re excited about because it’ll drive our assured comms there and resilient comms that we need at the distances we need them,” McFarlane said. The post As Army I Corps gets parts of NGC2 ecosystem, ‘tyranny of distance and disruption’ in the Pacific are top of mind for commander appeared first on DefenseScoop .

title: INEC Explains Omission Of Some 2027 Governorship Candidates
body: The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) has explained that it omitted some candidates from the final list for the 2027 governorship elections because their political parties failed to submit membership registers as required by law. The clarification comes amid reactions from affected parties and candidates following the publication of the final list, which excluded prominent aspirants, including the Peoples Democratic Party’s (PDP) governorship candidates in Gombe and Ogun states, Isa Pantami and Ladi Adebutu, respectively. Pantami’s omission came after he won a court-ordered rerun of the PDP governorship primary in Gombe, while Adebutu’s name and that of his running mate were also missing from the list. The Ogun PDP subsequently accused the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) of mounting pressure on INEC, while human rights lawyer Inibehe Effiong called on the commission to demonstrate its impartiality. In a statement on Tuesday signed by INEC National Commissioner and Chairman of the Information and Voter Education Committee, Mohammed Kudu Haruna, INEC said the omissions followed the Supreme Court’s September 24, 2026, judgment in INEC v. Zenith Labour Party, Appeal No. SC/CV/495/2026, which upheld the constitutionality of Section 77(5)–(7) of the Electoral Act, 2026. The provisions require political parties to submit their membership registers to the commission within the stipulated period. The court also upheld INEC’s timetable requiring parties to submit the registers between April 21 and May 10, 2026. According to the commission, the Supreme Court held that parties that failed to comply with the requirements were ineligible to sponsor candidates in the elections. INEC said it applied the judgment in finalising the governorship candidates’ list in accordance with Section 287(1) of the 1999 Constitution, as amended. The commission noted that the final lists of presidential and National Assembly candidates had been published on September 12, 2026, 13 days before the Supreme Court delivered its judgment. It added that, under Section 32(2) of the Electoral Act, 2026, political parties that believe their candidates were wrongly omitted have 14 days from the date of publication to notify the commission. INEC fixed October 24, 2026, as the deadline for such notifications. The commission reaffirmed its commitment to transparency, the rule of law and the credibility of the electoral process. The post INEC Explains Omission Of Some 2027 Governorship Candidates appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Airbus Details Progress With Lakota Connector Uncrewed Cargo Helicopter
body: Airbus U.S. Space and Defense has been actively developing and iterating the technology for its Lakota Connector, an uncrewed, autonomous variant of the multi-mission UH-72B Lakota helicopter. This includes testing under Team Lakota Connector, that has brought together Shield AI, L3Harris Technologies, and Parry Labs in a prototyping phase for the U.S. Marine Corps. title: Saudi man charged with planting ‘sophisticated’ recording device in OpenAI office
body: A Saudi national has been charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI’s offices in California, federal prosecutors announced. Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked at the AI firm as an engineer, was charged federally with using or endeavouring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. OpenAI said it had discovered a “sophisticated recording device” hidden in their San Francisco office and alerted the FBI. The company said it used its AI models to track that it had been planted by an employee. Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room. OpenAI, the maker of the popular chatbot ChatGPT, said that it has no indication that source code, model weights or customer data were inappropriately accessed or taken in the incident. It said the employee has been fired. According to the complaint, Alfozan “allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer’s executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications,” FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement. Patel said that the alleged goal was to capture information about the company’s AI product. Alfozan has been working as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors say. On 30 September, OpenAI employees discovered the device – two days after prosecutors say it had been installed. The device was encrypted, prosecutors said. OpenAI said they were able to use their AI models “to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier”. According to the FBI, the suspect used a “productivity tool” and a “chatbot” to research sensitive locations at OpenAI and how to secretly place audio equipment. Chatbot prompts that he is alleged to have searched include “building, customising, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device”, prosecutors allege. He is also accused of using the chatbot to ask about “‘build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,’ ‘customiz[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,’ ‘improv[ing] audio and live listening,’ and ‘encrypt[ing] the SD card'”. The device was allegedly concealed in toilet paper On 5 October, prosecutors say he allegedly returned to inspect the device in the office room. Prosecutors used CCTV camera footage to link him to the scene. That same day, Alfozan left a bag unattended in a different part of the building. A security team for OpenAI opened it to find his wallet and ID, as well as another recording device that was similar to the one found in the office conference room, prosecutors said. Alfozan appeared in court on Tuesday. It’s unclear whether he has legal representation. If found guilty, he faces up to five years in prison and a fine of $250,000 (£187,000).

title: Pope Leo has lung cancer diagnosed after surgery, Vatican says
body: Pope Leo XIV has had lung cancer diagnosed after surgeons ⁠removed a part of his right lung on Tuesday, the Vatican said. The Pope , 71, has adenocarcinoma, ​a common form of lung cancer , with tissue tests conducted during the operation confirming what doctors had suspected from preparatory examinations, the Vatican said. He was admitted to Rome's ⁠Gemelli Hospital for surgery to remove the growth that doctors had discovered in a recent health check-up. The Vatican said earlier on Tuesday that the operation had been successful, before providing a more detailed update from the Pope's lead surgeon and personal physician. "In order to make the procedure ⁠curative, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique," the medical update said, making it clear that the aim was to eliminate ​all cancerous ⁠tissue. Medical experts said that in order to assess the Pope's case they would need to know the size of the tumour ​removed from him and whether the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes. Pope Leo is due to make an 11-day tour of ⁠Uruguay, Argentina and Peru starting from November 6 to 17, but it was not clear if this trip would still go ahead. The Vatican has cancelled all of his audiences until October 21 to give him time to recuperate. The American-born pontiff revealed during his regular Sunday blessing on October 11 that doctors had discovered the nodule. The late Pope Francis, Pope Leo's predecessor, was admitted to hospital several times as he grew frail in his later years. He ​died aged 88 in April ‌2025. Pope Leo was elected leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Roman Catholics in May 2025. He has left his mark on the papacy by addressing the social and ethical implications of artificial intelligence and has grown increasingly critical of US military actions, challenging the administration of President Donald Trump's argument that God was on the side of the US in its conflict with Iran.

title: ‘Alice is still chugging along, though she’s showing clear signs of a personality breakdown’: Meduza readers describe how attacks on Yandex data centers are changing their work and daily lives
body: After repeated Russian attacks on data centers in Ukraine , Ukrainian forces began striking Yandex’s data centers. From October 8 to 11, Ukrainian drones reached three of the company’s data centers: in Sasovo in the Ryazan region, Kaluga , and Vladimir . A major outage followed, affecting Yandex’s services and companies that used Yandex Cloud storage. Millions of people in Russia and other countries felt the effects: Many couldn’t use taxi services or maps, for example, and lost access to their cloud files and money in Yandex Pay. It took until October 13 for Yandex Pay to be partially restored . Meduza asked readers how disruptions to Yandex products and other businesses connected to the company had affected their daily lives and work. We received hundreds of letters and are publishing the most interesting ones. Warning : This article contains statements that some readers may find offensive. Meduza’s Russian-language newsroom checked all letters for AI-generated content, but even the most thorough screening can’t rule out manipulation entirely. Please keep that in mind. Natasha Moscow On Sunday [October 11], everything looked okay at first when I ordered a taxi, but then all I could see on the screen were two messages: “Searching for a car” and “Loading trip details.” It stayed that way for half an hour. When I gave up and headed for the subway, the driver called and asked where to pick me up. Apparently, he’d noticed my location marker moving away. I asked for the car’s license plate number, found the car, and we got where we were going. Then I discovered that the payment method had switched from card to cash, and I didn’t have any cash on me. I couldn’t switch it back because the app was still showing the same “Searching for a car” and “Loading details” messages. Restarting it didn’t help. I said, “Can I send you a bank transfer?” The driver said, “To Yandex Bank.” I opened the banking app, and there was a message saying, “We’ll have everything fixed soon”… It turned out the driver’s other accounts were blocked. Luckily, I managed to reach some friends nearby who had cash. And that ride still isn’t in my trip history. During those 30 minutes [while I was waiting for the car], I tried downloading other taxi apps from Google Play, but they all seemed to go down at once. Maybe because they’re somehow connected to Yandex too. I didn’t risk ordering a taxi by phone — the local taxi companies have really bad reviews. That evening, some friends booked a cargo van with almost no trouble. It’s still in their trip history, but they can’t download the receipt, and I don’t think they were charged. On Monday, Yandex Maps wasn’t showing me bus schedules or the buses themselves. Everything was working properly for my friend, but I was either getting nothing or getting wrong information that didn’t match hers. Ivan Yekaterinburg I can’t access my photo and video archive on Yandex Disk. My whole life is in there — from when I was young to photos of my kids. Right now, you can’t download anything, only view it. And some files look like they’re gone for good — they won’t even open in preview mode. I’ve already bought myself a NAS . I’d wanted one for a long time but kept putting it off, and now I’m paying for it. I hope I can save the data. I used to have a backup on Google Drive, but paying for it now is a whole ordeal. Now it all depends on how well Yandex designed its recovery system [ for restoring files after an outage — Meduza ]. I’d like to believe they’ve taken all the necessary steps on their end. Either way, Putin and his gang bear all the responsibility. Stanislav Nizhny Novgorod I couldn’t make a payment on my credit card from another bank because all my money is in a Yandex savings account. I had to borrow from people I know to avoid getting hit with interest. It’s not like you can explain to the other bank why you can’t pay. Hundreds, probably even thousands, of people are in the same situation. Many can’t make their mortgage or loan payments or pay their rent. All of this will damage their credit histories and cause financial problems, because if you don’t meet your credit card’s terms, you can get hit with outrageous interest. I’m definitely moving half my money to another bank, even if the terms aren’t as good. Kirill Novosibirsk I’m a taxi driver. It’s my main source of income. My work has come to a standstill. Passengers say they spend 30 minutes trying to order a car without any luck. We drivers aren’t getting notifications about ride requests, and when we do, the location is wrong. Nobody knows how long this will last. There are no alternatives. Yandex has taken over the entire market. I have nothing fit to print to say about what’s going on. Hi, I’m Vladislav Gorin. I’m the host of Meduza’s daily Russian-language news podcast. This summer, the Russian authorities opened a criminal case against me — not for committing a crime, but for telling the truth about Russia and its war against Ukraine. Because the Kremlin has branded me a criminal, I can’t go home. I also can’t safely travel to countries like Turkey — even though it’s a NATO member — because I could be arrested and extradited to Russia. I can’t even renew my passport at the consulate anymore. None of this is going to stop me. I know there are hundreds of thousands of people in Russia who don’t want this war and who still believe in freedom and democracy, and they deserve access to independent journalism. Please support Meduza so I can keep reaching them. Alex Balakovo, Saratov region Taxi drivers are waiting at bus stops, store registers are glitching, Kinopoisk isn’t working, and neither is Alice. I wanted to download my data from cloud storage, but no luck. I’ll buy an 18-terabyte drive and keep all my files on it. I used to think Google Drive and iCloud were a bit expensive, but now I understand what you’re paying for. I’m going to stop using Yandex services. Our whole family has been planning to quit them for a long time anyway. Ukraine was the final nail in the coffin for Yandex. I’m sick of all this, especially all those “majors” from the security services prying into our private lives. Dodging responsibility whenever something beyond your control happens is a way of life in Russia. It’s cheap and underhanded, though predictable. Our family, like the rest of the world, stopped recognizing Russia’s government as legitimate long ago, so whatever they come up with over there [in the Kremlin] is their business alone. There have never been so many spectacular idiots in the State Duma — the concentration of insanity is off the charts. When is Ukraine finally going to start hitting their dachas on Rublyovka?! Anonymous reader Italy Edvibe , the service for teachers and tutors known in Russia as ProgressMe, isn’t working, even though they present themselves as an international platform. I’ve always paid for it in dollars and had no idea it was connected to Yandex. Now lessons have been disrupted, and the materials are unavailable. I feel completely drained and have no idea what to do next. Part of what my students were paying for was a convenient platform that was pleasant to use during and after lessons. There are no alternatives to Edvibe — everything else on the market is awful, with lag and terrible design. Edvibe isn’t perfect, but it’s still a decent option. I don’t want any connection to Yandex or to Russia at all. Rustam Tashkent, Uzbekistan Yandex dominates a lot of areas in Uzbekistan — it’s the biggest delivery service, taxi service, and so on. At one point, it either drove all the local competitors out of the market or bought them up. It scorched the earth and left nothing alive behind it. So when it went down completely, everything went down. Today [October 12], everything started working again, but badly. Basically, it’s become clear that Uzbekistan depends far too much on Yandex. If anything else happens to it, everything will grind to a halt again. I used WB Taxi today, but it’s awkward to use. You have to admit that Yandex knows how to make user-friendly products people want to use. Well, what else are they going to do but say they’re not responsible for events beyond their control? At least everyone knows now: If something happens again tomorrow, Yandex will wash its hands of it. Marat We’re a small IT company whose services ran largely on Yandex servers. After the first attack [October 8], some of our services stopped working for our clients. We got everything back up on Saturday [October 10], but overnight into Sunday, they went down again after an attack on another data center . We can see that many of our major clients’ corporate services were also hosted on Yandex’s cloud — so for now, they’ve got bigger things to worry about than taking us to task. Yandex hasn’t just disclaimed responsibility — it’s still charging for hosting that it’s effectively no longer providing. Yandex has always had the highest prices on the hosting market, but it’s practically the only provider that meets all the requirements of major clients. Now nobody cares about that anymore — they just want the system to work. I think other data centers will soon raise their prices sharply. They’d be foolish not to. Vasily Lisbon, Portugal I’m the founder of a service that advises parents of children under 3. For example, we give advice on children’s sleep and nutrition. Our Russian servers are in the Vladimir region. On the night of the [third] attack , we had to rush to restore data from backups and move it to another platform. We managed to do it. Now we’ll use Timeweb Cloud and several other backup providers in case Timeweb gets hit. We won’t use Yandex Cloud again, even if they restore something there. It’s not clear yet what we can use instead of Yandex Direct for advertising, but I think we’ll find new advertising channels . Putin’s regime bears all the responsibility. Yandex shouldn’t have to take responsibility for the consequences of decisions made by a deranged former KGB man surrounded by criminal oil wheeler-dealers from a St. Petersburg back alley. Dmitry Tallinn, Estonia After the strike on the data center in Vladimir [October 11], the Yandex Metrica web analytics system stopped working. It’s not critical, of course, but it’s extremely inconvenient, because its competitor, Google Analytics, reports website traffic with a delay of up to 48 hours. The problems with Yandex Metrica made it impossible to assess website traffic in the hour or two after publication, which in turn made it harder to manage traffic. I’ve actually been using both analytics services for a long time, but now I’ll have to rely solely on Google Analytics for a while. I’m not happy with it at all, because of the delay, its bad interface, and how poorly it works on smartphones. And the Google Analytics app is a useless mess that tells you nothing. Yevgeny Tomsk I’m a developer at Yandex. After the strike on Sasovo [October 8], everyone was working at a fairly calm pace because we regularly held drills where a randomly selected data center was taken offline. There were some problems, but the staff on call dealt with them quickly. After the strike on Vladimir, things descended into chaos because our internal messaging app and all our monitoring systems went down. That meant the automated systems didn’t kick in and the right on-call staff weren’t notified. There was no internal communication at all. Developers are working around the clock, trying to stabilize services and free up hardware in the last surviving data center in Kaluga. Technically, there are more data centers, but in practice, all of Yandex’s services run on three — in Kaluga, Sasovo, and Vladimir. So far, nobody has any idea what will happen next. There are rumors that Yandex is considering moving some of the infrastructure to outside providers’ data centers. Even though I work at Yandex, I try not to use its products. I only use Yandex Eats, Taxi, and Maps, and I don’t plan to switch to alternatives for now — because there aren’t any. Read more Ukraine strikes Russian tech giant Yandex’s data centers for a second straight day as new peace talks involving Kyiv, the U.S., and Europe get underway in Miami Ukraine strikes Yandex data center housing two of the company’s supercomputers Russia keeps attacking Ukrainian data centers, calling it a ‘mandatory digital detox’ Yaroslav St. Petersburg I work as a courier for Yandex Delivery . On October 11, no orders came in from the middle of the night until 3 p.m. I completed a few [existing] orders, but the money still hasn’t been credited to my balance, and it probably won’t be. Paying couriers will be the last thing Yandex gets around to — if it does at all, of course. The first thing Yandex restored after the outage was the system that makes couriers lose priority points for turning down orders. That way, couriers couldn’t avoid penalties for skipping [unprofitable] orders and would have to take orders with pickup locations 20 to 30 minutes away. We don’t get paid separately for that travel time. Unfortunately, there are no good alternatives to Yandex Delivery. Alina Korolyov, Moscow region I work in support for Yandex couriers. In the first few days, we got a huge number of inquiries, mostly about the app: Various functions weren’t working, orders and the bonuses for them weren’t being credited, the map wasn’t working, and they couldn’t start their shifts. I found out about the third attack [October 11 in Vladimir] before the news came out. At 4 a.m., all our work tools suddenly died, and our work email and corporate messaging app went blank. No way to reach management or colleagues. They restored the messaging app by morning, but it was impossible to work — people just sat through their shifts with nothing to do. Some of our work tools have now been restored, and everything more or less works. The couriers we support still have lots of problems with the app and instant payouts. Some had tax deducted twice; they were promised their payouts would be recalculated later. We’re trying to help and apologize. I think Yandex Delivery lost a huge amount of money because of disrupted orders. I rarely use Yandex services myself. Anonymous reader Moscow I work at an IT company, and some of our infrastructure was hosted in those very data centers destroyed by drones. Getting jolted awake by a phone call in the early hours, connecting remotely, and restoring everything from backups at another data center while the business is rapidly losing money is, of course, inconvenient. We were prepared for something like this, but a disaster is still a disaster. Fortunately, Yandex is not the only cloud provider in the country, but other providers’ data centers are under threat too. Add the equipment shortage caused by the AI boom, along with exorbitant prices and long delivery times because of sanctions imposed over the war. The outlook is so bleak it could give you an anxiety disorder. Yandex may be a company full of fucking assholes, as everyone knows, but responsibility for the drone attacks lies with a well-known group of people who seized power in Russia and are systematically making life in our country worse. Inna Moscow I flew out of Russia this weekend. My dog stayed in Moscow, where my sister is getting her ready to move. Since she’s an older dog, we’re getting the tests she needs done, and now she’s also been prescribed physical therapy three times a week. Last week, I submitted a request through the Sobaka-Gulyaka pet-care service. A pet sitter was due to come today [October 12] to take my little girl to an appointment with a rehabilitation specialist, but this morning I received this message from the service: Good morning! Unfortunately, we have temporarily suspended operations because of the widespread Yandex outage. For now, we’re not accepting new requests and can’t handle existing orders because we can’t view them. We apologize for the inconvenience — as soon as everything is restored, we’ll be able to resume work on your order. My sister and I tried to find a pet sitter in our neighborhood on Avito, but it’s obvious that the people there have no experience. Oleg Odintsovo, Moscow region After a walk in the park, my wife and I rented a couple of Yandex scooters. Almost immediately, she said hers was broken. I checked — the wheels were locked. I opened the app, selected the first scooter, and only then did the rental start, even though it should have started right away. A few seconds later, without us doing anything else, the second scooter beeped to life too. We checked the brakes and headed home. Twenty seconds into the ride, the motor on my clunker cut out. That happens when the GPS glitches. I fiddled with the throttle. Nothing. My speed dropped to four kilometers an hour [about 2.5 mph]. I pushed off with my foot and tried the throttle again, with no luck. I let go of the throttle and took my hands off the brakes, then turned to see how my wife was doing as I got ready to stop. But just then, the satellite connection came back — and the scooter suddenly accelerated on its own. I panicked, didn’t brake in time, lost control, and crashed into a roadside barrier. I ended up with ripped jeans, a scraped leg, and badly bruised ribs. There are other inconveniences too. For example, taxi receipts aren’t being generated, so I couldn’t finish the expense paperwork for my business trip. Support is useless in every case. Almost none of my Smart Home devices work. The app is a blank page asking me to add my first device. All four Alice devices suggest the same thing. But the switches sometimes work, including as part of complex automation routines . Whoosh barely operates in my area. Rebuilding a Smart Home setup with dozens of devices is too much. Artur London, U.K. I’ve been researching my genealogy and building a family tree for almost a year. I’ve put hundreds of hours and quite a bit of money into it. I kept most of the information I’d found on the Genotek website. After the first two attacks, I decided I should back up that data. But by the morning of October 11, the site was already down. I don’t know whether all my work has survived or when I’ll be able to access it. The company still hasn’t made any official statements. I haven’t been hit nearly as hard as many people, but I still can’t believe that the work I put in during all those sleepless nights could be wiped out so easily. If I can regain access, I’ll move all the data to a foreign website. Businesses can’t and shouldn’t be held responsible for drone attacks. The government bears full responsibility to both businesses and their customers. Still, Yandex is an accomplice of the regime, so I have no sympathy for it. Anonymous reader Smolensk I use Yandex Delivery to order stock for my business from Moscow to Smolensk. On October 9, after my latest order, I noticed that my supplier’s delivery times had increased. Goods used to arrive in the usual two or three days, but now delivery is scheduled for October 20. I don’t know whether this is directly connected to the strikes on the data centers or just a coincidence, but the result is obvious: The service has gotten noticeably worse. We’ll try switching to CDEK. At home, Alice and the Smart Home app stopped working. Even simple commands like “Set a timer for ten minutes” are a struggle for her. We’re back to turning the lights on and off by hand. Sorry for sounding like a snob, but you get used to the convenience pretty quickly. Personally, I feel bad for Yandex — they have good services. But looking at the bigger picture, I understand that war is war, and [for the enemy] anything goes. After the attacks on Wildberries and Ozon warehouses, this was to be expected. Sofia Vladivostok I’m homeschooled through an online school. As I understand it, they used Yandex Cloud to store course materials, because after the Ukrainian attack, we lost access to lecture recordings, homework, and lots of other things. Drone attacks affecting my education were the last thing I expected, especially since I’m so far from the front. Teachers are holding classes on MTS Link — not the most convenient platform. The school administration won’t let them use anything better, like Zoom or Telegram. Yandex, like Ozon and Wildberries, has a monopoly. They know people will be angry for a couple of weeks and then come back, because there are no alternatives with comparable quality and convenience. Kristina Da Nang, Vietnam I’m taking a course through Yandex Practicum . I haven’t been able to study since Thursday [October 8] because the coding practice tools aren’t working. And the students further along than me can’t access the training databases, so they can’t submit their projects. Practicum has pretty strict rules, with deadlines and expulsions, so this [the current outages] is a real problem. The course coordinators aren’t saying anything except that “the team is looking into it.” I don’t know of any alternatives that match Practicum’s quality. So there’s nothing to do but wait and worry. All Yandex services treat their customers terribly, but for some reason I had faith in Practicum. Yelizaveta Chicago, U.S. The Ozon app isn’t working [ the marketplace used Yandex Cloud to store data — Meduza ]. With a VPN, without one — nothing works at all. I can’t buy groceries and medicine for my mom and have them delivered. I’m her only source of money. I’m terribly worried. Wildberries doesn’t work from the States: Ozon accepts my American card, but Wildberries doesn’t. Sofya Moscow I’m a teacher. All my tests for students are on the Online Test Pad platform. Because of the .com domain, I was sure it was a foreign site, but it turned out to be a Russian project. Its servers are in a Yandex data center. Now the site is down. Colleagues who contacted [Online Test Pad’s] tech support got this reply: “…there is a very high likelihood that all materials from the past 2.5 years will be lost.” Unfortunately, I don’t have copies of those tests — I wrote everything directly on the site. Creating that many new original tests would take me about a month of daily work. Some teachers have lost even more materials. Now I’ll look for a new platform for making tests. Dmitry St. Petersburg Yandex NeuroLawyer went down at work. Too bad — it was a fairly useful service. It could check documents for errors, didn’t make up court rulings, and helped me with wording a couple of times… Alice is still chugging along, though she’s showing clear signs that her personality is disintegrating. I probably won’t switch to alternatives. If this happened to the biggest domestic provider, what can you expect from the smaller guys? And I don’t really need to anyway. If it comes to it, we’ll go back to searching through court ruling databases by hand, the old-fashioned way… Nikita St. Petersburg Just my luck — this is exactly when I needed to set up business email for my small company. Yandex 360 is the easiest way to do it. But for several days now, the service has barely let me do anything. The project is stuck. I can either wait or use VK WorkSpace, which is worse. I also use Yandex Disk a lot. Right now, you can’t play audio files there at all — you can only view images. Uploading files to the drive works on and off. It seems to have gotten better now, but as recently as yesterday [October 11], I had to wait a couple of hours just to log into my account. Ironically, I had to use Telegram, which is blocked, to store and transfer files. It still works perfectly with a VPN. Then there are the little things everyone’s already talking about: You can’t order from Yandex Lavka, you can’t get a taxi, and the maps aren’t showing public transit or traffic. Switching from one Russian service to another won’t make any difference to data security, so ease of use makes Yandex my first choice. Within Russia, its services are the most convenient for most tasks. And sometimes they’re the only ones. Whenever I have the chance to use foreign services, I take it. Gmail has been my main email for years. I can’t even imagine using Yandex search instead of Google. Most foreign services you can still access are usually more pleasant to use than Yandex products. But it’s no surprise that Yandex has become part of every Russian’s daily life. Everyone noticed when it went down. If Ukrainian forces wanted to once again disrupt the comfortable lives of Russians who are indifferent to the war, they succeeded. title: Ongoing explosions in Riyadh, Aramco headquarters as Saudi coalition intercepts Houthi attacks
body: The Saudi-led coalition said that it intercepted three missiles and two drones fired by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi terrorists on Tuesday towards Riyadh and Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran.The initial interception announcement regarding Dhahran came after loud booms were heard in the area, six sources told Reuters on Tuesday, with the coalition saying that missile fragments fell in a nearby residential area.Aramco made no official comment or confirmation.One source said the Aramco headquarters was on fire. An evacuation order for the building had been issued, four of the sources said.A source with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters the Aramco headquarters had been struck, adding that it was unclear whether the building was hit directly or by falling debris.Aramco employees were instructed to work from home on Wednesday, a direct source told Reuters.Early warning issued for Riyadh, booms heard in citySaudi Civil Defense issued an early warning for the country's eastern province earlier on Tuesday, then issued another for Riyadh shortly after the Dhahran interceptions.A loud boom was heard in the Saudi capital following the warning.Four people were injured and 15 homes sustained limited damage in Riyadh after debris from two intercepted missiles fell on the Saudi capital, the state news agency SPA reported on Wednesday, citing the Civil Defense spokesperson.The missiles were launched by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group and were intercepted and destroyed, the spokesperson said, adding the injured included two women, a man and a child.

title: Netanyahu, Trump discussed possibility of renewing strikes against Iran before elections - report
body: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spoke to US President Donald Trump last week to discuss the possibility of a renewed military campaign against Iran before Knesset elections are held at the end of October, according to an Axios report on Tuesday.The potential joint US-Israel operation could target Iran's nuclear and military sites, sources reportedly said.Senior US officials told Axios that Netanyahu cited alleged Iranian efforts to rebuild nuclear capacity as the reason for launching new strikes.If military operations against Iran do reignite, it could have an impact on both the Israeli election and US midterm elections in early November.Despite Trump's earlier public statements that he has not yet decided how to proceed with Tehran, sources said both the IDF and US Central Command (CENTCOM) are on alert and are finalizing preparations in case he decides to order strikes.One US official told Axios that Trump told Netanyahu to “go ahead and get ready,” but noted there was no firm commitment to restart military operations.A White House official denied that the two leaders had talked about resuming the war and asserted that Trump has said that the US will not attack Iran before midterm elections.The Prime Minister's Office confirmed that Netanyahu maintains regular contact with Trump but did not comment to Axios on the content of their talks.Support for renewed strikes mixed, officials sayOne Israeli official said Trump initially seemed willing to join renewed strikes before growing hesitant, and another US official said Trump was still on the fence.Additional sources familiar with the discussions told Axios that US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and CENTCOM leadership are among the strongest backers of plans to resume the war.Much of the Trump administration, however, reportedly favors maintaining economic and political pressure on Tehran over military action."They claim this economic choking is working better and better. Let's keep it up," a US official told Axios.Trump says decision on Iran coming 'very soon'Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Tuesday, Trump said the US would decide on its next move regarding Iran “very soon.”"Iran is a failed country," Trump said. "They have no economy, they have 300% inflation, they have no money, they're not paying their troops, they're not paying anybody."

title: Libya to participate in Russia-Africa summit in Moscow — envoy
body:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Libya will take part in the Russia-Africa summit in late October, though the level of its delegation’s representation will be officially announced later, Ali Juma Hassan Fadil, Libya's Ambassador to Iran, said in an interview with TASS.
"The level of Libya’s representation and the specific choice of participant fall exclusively within the sovereign competence of authorized Libyan authorities. Therefore, it would be wrong to preempt an official announcement or name a specific individual before a respective decision is made," he said when asked about the delegation’s participation in the upcoming summit and its level of representation. "The substance of Libya’s participation is more important than the name of the representative," the diplomat added.
Libyan-Russian relations "have political, economic, educational, and historical dimensions," he said, adding that there exists "significant potential for their development based on mutual interests and respect for Libya’s sovereignty and unity."
"It seems appropriate to focus Libya’s participation on practical areas that can be transformed into specific cooperation programs, such as reconstruction and infrastructure, energy and the oil and gas sector, food security and grain supplies, education, professional training, university programs, transport and logistics, as well as the expansion of economic ties between Russia and North Africa," the ambassador explained.
"Libya’s relations with Russia should develop within the framework of a balanced foreign policy open to cooperation with all partners," he concluded.
The third Russia-Africa summit will take place in Moscow on October 28-29. Director of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s Sub-Saharan Africa Department Anatoly Bashkin told TASS earlier that more than 30 African nations had confirmed that they would participate in the event.

title: 2027: No real tension between Wike, APC governors - Morka
body: The All Progressives Congress (APC) spokesperson, Felix Morka, has dismissed reports of a rift between the party’s governors and Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, saying there was no real tension between them. Morka said the perceived disagreement was a “false battle” because both the APC governors and Wike were committed to President Bola Tinubu’s re-election bid ahead of the 2027 general elections. He spoke on Tuesday during an interview on Arise Television’s News Day , following Wike’s inclusion in the APC presidential campaign council. “It was a false battle to begin with. I mean, I don’t think there was any real tension between those positions because they united in their extraordinary commitment to the re-election of the president,” Morka said. He noted that the Progressive Governors Forum comprised governors elected on the APC platform, while Wike, a former Rivers State governor, was a member of Tinubu’s cabinet and a vocal supporter of the President. According to him, their shared political interest made reports of a disagreement between them largely insignificant. Morka said the publication of the presidential campaign council list had also clarified the roles of those involved in Tinubu’s re-election campaign. He pointed to the inclusion of governors who do not belong to the APC, describing it as evidence of Tinubu’s ability to attract support across party lines. “Governors, who are not of the APC, now [are] front and centre, coordinating some of our activities in their respective jurisdictions,” he said. The APC spokesperson described the development as a new phase in Nigeria’s democratic politics, arguing that the President was bringing politicians from different parties together around a common objective. “What we’re witnessing today in our country is novel. It’s really a new dawn for democracy,” Morka said. He argued that the collaboration was unusual in a presidential system, where political parties are generally expected to compete against one another. According to Morka, Tinubu was transcending party differences by building a coalition of political actors to support his administration and re-election campaign. “We’re seeing a president who is transcending all of the divides and really nullifying what I call the politics of difference between these partisans and bringing them together under the same umbrella to pursue a common agenda for the good of the people,” he said. The post 2027: No real tension between Wike, APC governors - Morka appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Ghana wins UN Human Rights Council seat as calls grow for action against atrocities
body: Ghana has been elected to the United Nations Human Rights Council for the 2027–2029 term, placing the country at the centre of renewed demands for stronger international action to prevent mass atrocities and protect vulnerable populations. The UN General Assembly elected Ghana and 14 other countries on October 13, 2026. The other elected members are Brazil, Burundi, the Dominican Republic, Germany, Ireland, Japan, Jordan, Kuwait, Nepal, Nigeria, the Republic of Moldova, Ukraine, Uruguay and Zambia. For Ghana, the seat brings an opportunity to influence international scrutiny of human rights abuses, support investigations and help turn warnings of potential atrocities into preventive action. It also carries clear obligations. Under UN General Assembly Resolution 60/251, Council members must uphold the highest human rights standards and cooperate fully with its mechanisms and procedures. In its assessment of the elections, the Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect urged incoming members to translate commitments into practical, consistent action against genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity. The organisation said that, in 2027, 23 of the Council’s 47 members would be “Friends of the Responsibility to Protect” — countries that have appointed a national focal point and/or joined the relevant diplomatic groups in New York and Geneva. Ghana’s election comes as the Council faces questions over its credibility. The Global Centre criticised Burundi’s re-election, citing its documented history of atrocity crimes, continuing serious human rights violations and failure to cooperate with Council mechanisms. It also warned that political selectivity, double standards and weak follow-up on investigations undermine the Council’s ability to protect populations at risk. These concerns frame the challenge facing Ghana and its fellow incoming members: ensuring that human rights scrutiny produces sustained political action. The Council’s tools include the Universal Periodic Review, independent experts, commissions of inquiry and fact-finding missions. These mechanisms can expose patterns of abuse, identify perpetrators and recommend reforms before violations escalate. According to the Global Centre, the Council has established 42 investigative bodies since becoming operational in 2006 and referred to states’ responsibility to protect their populations in at least 98 resolutions since 2008. The organisation urged members to strengthen early-warning assessments, support investigations, protect human rights defenders, and maintain investigative mandates until risks have clearly subsided. It also called for closer coordination between the Council in Geneva and UN institutions in New York, including the Security Council. For Ghana, the three-year term offers a platform to champion accountability and amplify victims’ voices. The central test will be whether that diplomatic influence helps secure timely, consistent responses when communities face the threat of mass atrocities.
