title: 12 Senators Sign Bipartisan Letter Urging Trump to Rescind Russian Diesel Deal
body:
A bipartisan group of 12 US senators signed a joint letter on Tuesday, Oct. 13, urging US President Donald Trump to rescind his diesel agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin, calling it a gift to Moscow and a betrayal of Ukraine.
The letter , led by Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal, was signed by six Republican and six Democratic senators. The Republican senators include Thom Tillis, Susan M. Collins, Alan Stuart Armstrong, Lisa Murkowski, Christopher A. Coons and John Cornyn. Blumenthal was joined on the Democratic side by Jeanne Shaheen, Richard J. Durbin, Sheldon Whitehouse, Jack Reed and Mitch McConnell.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies; it should be rescinded,” the senators wrote.
The senators reaffirmed their support toward ending Russia’s war, arguing that any peace must uphold Ukraine’s sovereignty and security. In their view, the deal fails that test and does very little for Americans.
They took aim at the Treasury Department’s General License No. 135, which formally lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports immediately after Trump arranged the deal with the Kremlin.
The license, they wrote, “only provides Putin with more fuel to finance his war machine and enables Russia to continue its brutal attacks on Ukrainian civilians.”
While the lawmakers did acknowledge the pressure on US fuel prices from the war with Iran, they said Russian diesel would offer “limited to no relief” to American citizens.
The revenue, they warned, would instead fund Moscow’s war effort, deepen its security ties with China, Iran and North Korea, and endanger US troops deployed in Operation Epic Fury.
The letter also reminded Trump that he signed the sweeping Lindsey Graham sanctions into law, after it passed both chambers with broad bipartisan support.
The law, signed just three weeks before Trump struck a deal with Putin, requires him to apply significant economic pressure on Russia and its main backers, particularly China.
“Putin is a tyrant. Withdraw from this agreement, rescind General License No. 135, and execute the authorities provided under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026,” the senators wrote.
Blumenthal said that the deal rewards the Kremlin and noted that Putin’s response to Trump’s proposed energy infrastructure truce would be the first test of peace efforts.
“Once again, he’s playing Trump for a fool & hoping to weaponize a freezing, starving, bloody winter against Ukraine,” he wrote on X, as Russia continued striking Ukraine’s power grid and civilian infrastructure nationwide.
Trump announced the agreement following a telephone call with Putin on Oct. 9, saying Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to US and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons after that.
The Treasury Department then authorized the sale and import of Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
Analysts have questioned whether Russia can deliver the promised volumes, with its refineries running at about 60% of capacity after repeated Ukrainian drone strikes.
Ukraine and its Western allies condemned the move, calling it a mistake. “Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged,” President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
The deal was announced while the Ukrainian delegation was in Miami , hoping to reach a breakthrough in ending Russia’s war with senior US envoys Steve Witkoff and Steve Kushner.
During the meeting, Witkoff and Kushner reportedly warned Ukrainian negotiators that Washington could restrict intelligence sharing if Kyiv kept striking Russian oil refineries.
Those concerns grew after Russia fired ballistic missiles at Kyiv late on Monday, when Zelensky said Ukraine had received no advance warning of the launches from its partners.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the next day that intelligence cooperation with Washington continues , attributing the delayed alert to the type of weapon Russia used.
On Tuesday, Trump denied claims that Washington has stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine . “No, we haven’t,” he said, adding “We are helping them.”
The US had reportedly also raised the possibility of limiting weapons purchases through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), under which European allies buy American arms for Ukraine.
US NATO Ambassador Matthew Whitaker later said that there had been “no change” to deliveries through the mechanism.
Around the same time, Trump announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, despite neither Kyiv nor Moscow confirming any agreement and Russian strikes continuing against Ukrainian facilities.
“They agreed because I said they agreed, and that thing has to get settled,” he said on Monday, speaking to reporters outside the White House before departing for Ohio.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Athens Hosts Global Push Against Tax Evasion
body: Tax transparency meetings in Athens from 12 to 15 October put Greece at the centre of OECD peer reviews as AADE hosted a global tax information forum. AADE Governor George Pitsilis opened the 25th meeting of the OECD Global Forum’s Automatic Exchange of Information Peer Review Group. He said public bodies must earn citizens’ trust. In an interconnected world, tax authorities cannot stop at national borders, he said. Because of the Common Reporting Standard, countries exchanged data on more than 171 million financial accounts in 2024. Those accounts held nearly €13 trillion, Pitsilis said. He also said rules must keep pace with financial innovation. Then he pointed to the amended CRS and the new Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework. As a result, AADE is investing in digital tools, data use and compliance systems, he said. No country can face these challenges alone. Tax transparency Athens agenda Maria José Garde, head of the Global Forum Secretariat, thanked the Greek hosts for organising the Athens meeting. She said the forum is in one of its busiest periods. Peer review work is bearing fruit, she said. In particular, delegates are due to discuss 20 consolidated jurisdiction reports as part of an assessment of CRS effectiveness. What delegates will weigh Greek City Times earlier reported that the Greek tax authority seized 9,100 litres of fuel and four tankers in a separate enforcement case. Background on the Common Reporting Standard is available on the OECD automatic exchange pages . AADE publishes authority news via aade.gr . Still, tax transparency Athens remains the focus while peer reviewers weigh how jurisdictions apply the global standard. Pitsilis closed by stressing that tax transparency Athens work succeeds only when countries share expertise and best practices. Source: Athens-Macedonian News Agency The post Athens Hosts Global Push Against Tax Evasion appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Russian, Vietnamese deputy defense ministers hold another strategic dialogue round
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Deputy defense ministers Vasily Osmakov of Russia and Nguyen Truong Thang of Vietnam held another round of bilateral strategic dialogue, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
"Russian Deputy Defense Minister Vasily Osmakov and Deputy Minister of National Defense of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam Colonel General Nguyen Truong Thang held a regular round of the Russian-Vietnamese strategic dialogue on defense," it said.
According to the ministry, the parties reaffirmed their commitment to making the most effective use of their existing capabilities to deepen military cooperation in the spirit of a comprehensive strategic partnership. The meeting took place in a constructive, warm, and friendly atmosphere, it added.

title: Drone Forge and Arkeus announce Warden hyperspectral optical radar partnership
body: Australian autonomous systems integrator Drone Forge has signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Arkeus to explore the deployment of Warden, Arkeus’ hyperspectral optical radar technology, across Drone Forge’s growing portfolio of autonomous systems. Warden is designed to provide highly detailed spectral information about objects and environments, creating opportunities for applications where conventional imaging technologies may not provide sufficient information. For Drone Forge, the partnership represents an opportunity to incorporate emerging sensing technologies into its broader platform and solutions offering, while working directly with Arkeus to identify where Warden can deliver the greatest operational value. The companies will initially focus on opportunities across the broader Asia-Pacific (APAC) region, with discussions also extending to potential international applications. Drone Forge Founder, Thomas Symes, said the partnership reflects the company’s focus on bringing leading technology together to solve real-world customer requirements. “The feedback we’re hearing from customers is clear. They need more from their uncrewed platforms. It’s no longer just about collecting imagery, but finding, identifying and tracking what matters, and delivering intelligence fast enough to act on it. Warden is a proven autonomous perception capability that responds directly to those needs, with demonstrated performance on leading uncrewed aerial systems. Through our partnership with Arkeus, we’re focused on rapidly integrating this technology into our platforms and delivering the enhanced situational awareness and mission effectiveness our customers are demanding.” The collaboration will include opportunities to undertake joint flight operations, data gathering and demonstrations, while the companies continue to explore potential customer applications and commercial pathways. For Arkeus, the partnership provides a pathway to introduce Warden to new aerial applications and markets through Drone Forge’s platform capabilities and customer relationships. Simon Olsen, Arkeus CEO, said: “The future of mission effectiveness depends on how quickly platforms can turn what they sense into what they know. Warden is already demonstrating that advantage on leading uncrewed aerial systems, combining advanced hyperspectral sensing with edge AI to detect, recognise and track targets across wide areas without relying on operators to interpret endless streams of data. Autonomous perception is fundamentally changing what’s possible for uncrewed systems. Drone Forge brings deep expertise in developing and operating these platforms, along with a strong understanding of customer requirements. Together, we’re building on Warden’s proven performance to accelerate deployment and deliver the decision-ready intelligence operators need to act faster and with greater confidence in complex and contested environments.” For Editorial Inquiries Contact: Editor Kym Bergmann at kym.bergmann@venturamedia.net For Advertising Inquiries Contact: Group Sales Director Simon Hadfield at simon.hadfield@venturamedia.net

title: Nana B passport claims a diversionary tactic — Abu Jinapor
body: The Ranking Member on Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee, Samuel Abu Jinapor, has dismissed allegations that the Member of Parliament for Bosome Freho, Nana Asafo-Adjei Ayeh, lobbied Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa over a passport for New Patriotic Party (NPP) Second Vice-Chairman Henry Nana Boakye, popularly known as Nana B, describing them as a diversionary tactic. Mr Jinapor said the allegation was intended to distract from the Minority’s concerns over expenditure on Ghana’s evacuation of citizens from South Africa, for which it is demanding an independent audit. Speaking on Eyewitness News on Tuesday, October 13, Mr Jinapor said Nana B had never held a diplomatic passport and had surrendered his service passport in accordance with a directive issued by the new government. “Let me say that that allegation is a complete diversionary tactic, and it’s a rule in the old book, you know it, I know it, and we should not allow ourselves to be distracted,” he said. Mr Jinapor said he had spoken to Mr Asafo-Adjei Ayeh, who told him that Nana B had formally requested the transfer of a valid visa from his old passport to a new one. “He had a valid visa in the passport, and he made a requisition, a formal requisition, that the visa be transferred to his new passport, which the minister committed to work on,” Mr Jinapor said. He added that Mr Asafo-Adjei Ayeh followed up with the minister once and was told the matter was still being processed, after which he did not pursue it further. The comments follow allegations by the Majority Caucus on Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee that Mr Asafo-Adjei Ayeh pressured Mr Ablakwa to allow Nana B to retain a service passport he was allegedly not entitled to hold. Salaga South MP Hajia Zuwera Mohammed Ibrahimah made the allegation, claiming that Mr Asafo-Adjei Ayeh and Nana B had sought an exception from the minister. She said Mr Ablakwa rejected the request because Nana B’s former positions as NPP National Youth Organiser and Board Chairman of the National Food Buffer Stock Company did not qualify him for a service passport. Mr Jinapor also rejected attempts to link the passport issue to the Minority’s scrutiny of the South Africa evacuation expenditure, insisting that the caucus had not accused the minister of wrongdoing. Credit: citinewsroom.com

title: Use of machine learning to enhance transient astronomical phenomena
body:
You have full access to this open access article
Transient, star-like point sources that appear and vanish over short timescales are described in astronomical images prior to launch of Sputnik. We have reported that transient numbers diminish significantly in Earth’s shadow (shadow deficit) and are more likely within (+/-) one day of nuclear testing (nuclear window). These findings remain debated; some argue transients identified via existing automated pipelines are simply plate defects. Machine learning (ML) was used to enhance transient identification accuracy and validate the phenomenon. The model was trained against 250 transient image pairs taken 30 min apart classified as real versus plate defect by expert visual review; it demonstrated good discrimination (out-of-fold AUC = 0.81; sensitivity = 0.71, specificity = 0.71). After deployment in a dataset of 107,875 previously-identified transients, the model assigned each a probability of being real. After controlling for ML-identified artifacts, transient counts were significantly elevated for dates within a nuclear window ( p = 0.024); transients with the highest probability of being real were more likely to occur within a nuclear window ( p <0.0001). The shadow deficit was significant ( p <0.001) and largest in the highest probability transients relative to lower probability transients ( p =0.003). Results support existence of an unrecognized population of transient objects in historical astronomical plates warranting further study.
Transient, star-like phenomena exhibiting point spread functions have been identified by comparing sequential images over short timescales in the Palomar Observatory Sky Survey (POSS-I) and other historical sky surveys 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 . Their morphology suggests they may persist on sub-second timescales (i.e., brief flashes) 8 . These short-lived transients are absent in images taken immediately before the transients appear and in all images from subsequent surveys 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 (see Fig. 1 for example). They do not correspond with known objects in optical catalogs (e.g. Gaia, Pan-STARRS) and cannot be accounted for by known satellites or orbital launch debris, as all images were obtained prior to launch of the first artificial satellite 1 , 3 .
The left image presents examples of three transients (green circles) identified on the POSS-I red plate taken on August 11, 1953 (RA = 339.8697437 and Dec = 38.4411717). The image at right is the same region in a POSS-II red image taken on September 3, 1989. The yellow circle indicates a plate defect on the left image.
The nature and origin of transients are unclear and difficult to elucidate due to their historical nature. Modern attempts to capture similar phenomena are fraught due to the quantity of satellites and launch debris currently in orbit. Nonetheless, recent findings point to potentially intriguing transient characteristics. Transient numbers have been reported to diminish by ~ 30% when located within Earth’s shadow, suggesting a “shadow deficit” consistent with some transients representing highly reflective objects in orbit 5 , 9 . Furthermore, transients are significantly increased when within a “nuclear testing window” (+/- one day of historical above-ground nuclear weapons tests) relative to days with no nuclear testing 9 , 10 , 11 . Such contemporaneous correlates of transients potentially provide information for better characterizing their nature.
Validity of these findings has been debated based largely on the potentially high (and unknown) level of false positives in existing transient data given their automated identification on scanned photographic plates more than 50 years old likely prone to plate defects (e.g., emulsion errors, dust, scratches) 12 , 13 , 14 . Both the shadow deficit and nuclear testing association were identified in a dataset of 107,875 transients developed by Solano et al. using an automated pipeline 1 , with no visual inspection to document validity of individual transients identified (which was not feasible due to the extensive work required).
To address the unknown false positive rate in transient identification using existing automated methods, the current study used machine learning (ML), specifically a supervised learning approach, to quantify the probability that each transient of the n = 107,875 previously identified reflected a real object versus plate defect. To validate the resulting ML model against external criteria, we tested two a priori hypotheses based on our prior findings 5 , 10 . Both were predicated on the assumption that if transients represent real phenomena, decreased statistical noise due to reduction of false positives in the ML-vetted dataset would enhance signal to noise ratio and increase effect sizes. Specifically, we hypothesized that both the magnitude of the shadow deficit reported in Villarroel et al. 5 and the strength of the transient-nuclear testing association reported in Bruehl & Villarroel 10 would be largest in the subgroup of transients that the ML model determined to be most likely to be real.
The training set for ML-based supervised learning comprised 250 image pairs (red versus blue POSS-I images taken 30 min apart) classified as containing at least one transient appearing only on the red plate based on the Solano et al. automated pipeline 1 , 5 , 14 . This training set was manually inspected by an astronomer with expertise in the transient phenomenon (BV); 134 were labelled likely real transients and 116 as plate defects. The ML model included 23 morphometric and other predictors extracted solely from the red plate (see Methods for ML details). No spectral features or red-blue plate comparisons were included in the model. Shapley (SHAP) values quantifying relative contributions of each predictor to the final ML model are displayed in Fig. 2 .
SHAP values for the 23 machine learning predictors of real transients versus plate defects relative to expert classification based on manual inspection of 250 transient candidates from the original n = 107,875 transient dataset. SHAP values indicate the relative contribution of each predictor to the model. Features are listed in descending order of mean absolute SHAP value. The 23 ML model predictors are detailed in the Methods.
The final ML model demonstrated good overall discrimination relative to manual labelling, with an area under the curve (AUC) value of 0.81 +/- 0.04 across 5-fold cross-validation. The sensitivity was 0.71 (probability of being classified as a real transient if manual inspection categorized the transient as likely real) and specificity was 0.71 (probability of being classified as a plate defect if manual inspection classified the transient as a defect). The ML model was then deployed in the original n = 107,875 transient dataset that was analyzed in our prior work 5 , 10 , assigning each transient a probability of being labelled a real transient. All transients were assigned to 10 equal-sized bins (deciles) of increasingly greater ML-derived probability that the transients contained in each bin reflected real transients (lowest probability transients were in Decile 0 and the highest probability transients were in Decile 9).
Table 1 summarizes transient probabilities by deciles. Of the transients in the original dataset, only the upper 20% (Deciles 8 and 9) exceeded a 0.66 probability of being a real transient. Only 10% of the original sample (Decile 9) approached or exceeded at least a 0.80 probability of being a real transient. While the majority of transients occurred in isolation, multiple transients were not uncommon. When considering only the highest confidence group of transients (Decile 9) within 10 arcmin of each other on the same night of observation, we found that there were 549 doublets (transient pairs), 143 triplets, and 190 larger groupings.
Key features of transients (from red FITS images) classified into the highest probability (Decile 8 and 9) and lowest probability deciles (Deciles 0 and 1) by the ML model are summarized in Table 2 . Distribution of apparent magnitudes (Cousins R) across the highest and lowest probability transients is presented in Fig. 3 . High probability transients were approximately 4.8 times fainter (higher magnitude), narrower (full width half maximum; FWHM), and less elliptical than transients classified by the ML model as artifacts; they also displayed a lower red image signal to noise ratio (SNR). High probability transients were significantly further from the edge of photographic plates than those classified as likely artifacts, consistent with plate edges being more susceptible to plate defects.
Distribution of apparent magnitudes between highest probability transients (Deciles 8 and 9) and lowest probability transients (i.e., likely artifacts; Deciles 0 and 1) as classified by the ML model.
As described in Villarroel et al. 5 , the number of transients in Earth’s shadow was expected to decrease substantially relative to sunlit regions to the extent that transients represent orbital objects exhibiting specular reflections. If the ML model were successfully removing plate defects and increasing the relative signal of real transients, the shadow deficit previously reported 5 was expected to be largest in the subset of transients with the highest ML-derived probability scores (Decile 9). That is, transients most likely to be real would show the largest shadow deficit, with this physical property validating both the transient phenomenon and the ML model. Details of the shadow deficit calculation methodology are described in the Methods and in Villarroel et al. 5 . In the current work, shadow deficit analyses compared the observed number of transients in Earth’s shadow (the shadow fraction) to the number theoretically-expected given a random geometric distribution (0.692% expected; see Methods).
Figure 4 presents the observed shadow deficit across the 10 ML-derived probability deciles. Note that to facilitate interpretation in context of the current hypotheses and prior work, Fig. 4 displays the shadow deficit , reflecting the difference between the observed shadow fraction and the expected random geometric distribution shadow fraction. However, all related analyses focus on the shadow fraction itself as the dependent variable.
Magnitude of the shadow deficit across ML-based probability deciles. The range of probability values within each decile is indicated on the X axis in parentheses below each. The Y axis displays the shadow deficit expressed as a percentage. Calculation of this shadow deficit is detailed in the Methods. In brief, the fraction of retained transient candidates falling within the Earth’s shadow was compared to the fraction expected to appear based on geometric expectations for a uniform sky distribution. The shadow deficit for each decile of probability values (i.e., increasingly stringent definitions of a transient) was calculated as: (observed shadow fraction – control shadow fraction)/control shadow fraction, expressed as a percentage. Increasing deciles reflect greater probability that the transients within each decile reflect real objects rather than plate defects. *** p < 0.001, ** p < 0.01, * p < 0.05 for one-sided binomial tests comparing the observed shadow fraction in each decile against the plate-aware Monte Carlo expected rate of 0.692%.
A series of binomial tests was conducted to compare the observed shadow fraction for each decile to the expected shadow fraction for a random geometric distribution. Results of these binomial tests for Deciles 1, 5, 6, and 9 exceeded the Bonferroni-corrected significance threshold of p < 0.005, indicating that there was a significant shadow deficit compared to expectations for transients assigned to these probability deciles. However, the smallest shadow fraction (0.31%), corresponding to the largest shadow deficit (55.2%) compared to expectations, was observed in the decile with the highest probability of reflecting real transients based on the ML model (Decile 9); p <0.001), a finding significant at the 5 sigma level. Given the current study hypotheses, it is notable that the shadow fraction in Decile 9 was significantly smaller than the pooled mean of all other deciles (two-proportion z test = 2.78, p = 0.003). Moreover, follow-up Bonferroni-corrected pairwise tests between the highest probability decile (Decile 9) and the two deciles with the lowest probability of being real transients (Decile 1 and Decile 2) confirmed that the shadow fraction was significantly smaller for the highest confidence transients (exceeding the Bonferroni corrected significance threshold of p = 0.0056). These results all support our findings as indicating that the largest shadow deficit occurred in the transient subgroup that the ML model determined to have the highest probability of reflecting real transients.
Of the 370 POSS-I observation nights, 26 fell within a United States (U.S.) nuclear weapons testing window (+/- 1 day of a nuclear test; see Methods for rationale). This definition was adopted for consistency with our prior related work 10 . In the current work, we tested the hypothesis that if the ML model were successfully eliminating false positive transients, the strength of association between nuclear testing and number of transients would increase as the ML-derived probability that transients were real increased (i.e., across increasing probability deciles). The percentage of transients observed within a nuclear window is presented by probability decile in Fig. 5 . Inspection of this figure clearly indicates that the association between transients and nuclear testing strengthens linearly as the probability that transients are real increases. There was an approximately 65% higher rate of transients occurring within a nuclear window for the highest probability decile (Decile 9; 13.6%) relative to the lowest probability decile (Decile 0; 8.3%). The percentage of transients in Decile 9 that fell within a nuclear window significantly exceeded the pooled mean percentage falling within a nuclear window across the remaining nine deciles (11.1%; two-proportion z-test, z = 7.40, p < 0.0001). The latter statistical findings should be considered descriptive only rather than hypothesis testing due to potential confounds that are addressed in the primary analyses below.
The ratio of number of transients that occurred on dates falling within a nuclear window (+/- 1 day of a nuclear weapons test) relative to the number of transients falling outside of a nuclear window, expressed as a percentage and presented by ML-based probability decile. The sample reflects n=370 days of POSS-I observations.
In primary analyses, we tested the nuclear-transient hypothesis using a non-parametric permutation testing approach (i.e., no distributional assumptions) with observation dates as the independent unit of analysis. This focus on dates as the unit of analysis avoided possible confounding of results inherent in several other potential analytic approaches that might be biased by temporal clustering of transients (non-independence within dates). For each date, the sum of ML-assigned probabilities across all transients on that date was computed, yielding a probability-weighted transient count that represented the estimated number of real transients on that date. Each permutation test evaluated whether the summed probability values for dates within a nuclear window differed significantly from the summed probability value expected for a random distribution of nuclear labels (i.e., the label indicating whether there was a nuclear test on that date) based on 10,000 permutations. See the Methods for the rationale and additional details. This permutation test confirmed that probability-weighted transient counts were significantly higher for dates within a nuclear window compared to the value expected based on a random distribution ( p = 0.024). A follow-up Mann-Whitney U test, which also makes no distributional assumptions but is more powerful statistically, confirmed that probability-weighted transient counts were significantly higher for dates within a nuclear window compared to non-nuclear dates ( p = 0.002). These findings indicate that even when the influence of artifacts in the original transient sample is controlled for, there are significantly more transients recorded on dates within a nuclear window.
Post-hoc sensitivity analyses were conducted to examine the temporal specificity of the nuclear-transient association across all probability deciles. We examined a series of lags from 3 days before to 3 days after each nuclear test date. These analyses were conducted to determine whether the nuclear-transient signal is sharply localized around test dates or broadly distributed, with a highly specific signal providing further support for the effect representing a genuine physical association rather than a spurious correlation (e.g., due to observation scheduling). A series of permutation tests were conducted for the series of lags noted above. The probability-weighted transient count (summed probabilities for each date) was significantly higher than expected compared to 10,000 random distributions for both the day of the nuclear test ( p = 0.0355) and one day before the nuclear test ( p = 0.0288). The lagged permutation test focused on the day after the test also approached significance ( p = 0.078). Magnitude of these effects can be expressed as the ratio of probability-weighted mean transient count for the nuclear testing time frame targeted to transient count for days with no nuclear testing. Figure 6 displays this nuclear-transient effect size from 3 days before the nuclear test to 3 days after the nuclear test. The largest effect was one day before the nuclear test (ratio = 2.57), with analyses on the day of the nuclear test having only a slightly smaller ratio of 2.36. For comparison, this ratio of weighted probability scores for nuclear test dates to non-test dates was 1.70 for the analysis of the day after a nuclear test (which approached significance), but ranged from 0.31 to 1.37 for all other lagged tests (all of which were nonsignificant, p’s > 0.19). The pattern of findings in these sensitivity analyses indicated that the nuclear-transient association was highly specific temporally, consistent with it reflecting a physical association. We note that the lagged finding for one day prior to a nuclear test which exhibited the largest effect must be interpreted cautiously, as the POSS-I plates were exposed overnight whereas the nuclear tests were generally conducted the following morning. Thus, the lag one day before a nuclear test actually reflects transients that were present closest in time to the nuclear test itself (e.g., several hours before the test).
Ratio of the number of probability-weighted transients observed after a nuclear test relative to number observed on dates with no nuclear testing presented from lags reflecting 3 days before to 3 days after a nuclear test. We note that only the nuclear-transient associations for the lag one day before a test and the concurrent association on the day of the nuclear test are statistically significant. * = p<.05 based on a permutation test.
Several potential confounds warranted consideration. Atmospheric effects of solar radiation (e.g., Aurora Borealis) or cosmic rays might produce some transients via direct impact on the photographic emulsion or effects of Cherenkov-type phenomena in the upper atmosphere. Cosmic rays may originate from increased solar activity (typically low-energy particles, mainly protons), but they may also originate from galactic sources (with much higher energies). As solar activity increases, galactic cosmic rays decrease because the enhanced solar wind shields the Earth from incoming galactic cosmic rays. If cosmic rays contributed to point-like transients, solar energetic particles might be expected to produce point-like sources more efficiently than typically higher-energy galactic cosmic rays, as their lower energies increase probability of depositing a larger fraction of their energy within the photographic emulsion.
We examined associations between daily probability-weighted transient counts and three daily solar activity indices (F10.7, sunspot number, and Kp) in the two highest probability deciles. Results revealed a small but statistically-significant association between elevated sunspot number (i.e., increased solar radiation) and decreased transients (rho − 0.15, p = 0.01). This anticorrelation disagrees with direct influences of solar radiation on transient counts, but could support a small effect of galactic cosmic rays on transient counts. However, comparable associations for the overall solar radiation measure of 10.7 cm solar radio flux (F10.7; rho − 0.09, p > 0.10) and the Kp index (rho − 0.05, p > 0.10) were nonsignificant.
We also hypothesized that if solar activity/cosmic rays were contributing selectively to artifactual transients, higher solar activity should be associated with lower ML-derived probability scores. This hypothesis received modest support, with higher overall solar activity (F10.7 index) exhibiting a small but significant association with lower ML-derived probability scores (rho − 0.13, p = 0.023); sunspot number and Kp index analyses were nonsignificant.
Finally, we directly tested whether solar activity influenced the observed nuclear-transient association. Because the Mann-Whitney U test does not permit covariates in the model, we used an alternative approach. We first generated a probability-weighted transient count variable residualized for the three solar activity indices by entering the latter into a linear regression model to predict nightly probability-weighted transient counts. Residuals from this analysis were then saved as the new analytic variable, reflecting variance in transient counts not accounted for by solar activity (which accounted for only 4.5% of variance in transient counts). Next, a Mann-Whitney U test was performed examining associations between nuclear testing and residualized probability-weighted transient counts, indicating that when solar activity influences were statistically-controlled, transient counts remained significantly ( p = 0.003) elevated when in a nuclear window relative to other days (compare to p = 0.002 in primary results). Thus, even if galactic cosmic rays might modestly influence nightly transient counts, they do not confound the nuclear-transient association reported in primary analyses. We note also that lunar phase and associated illumination differences did not significantly affect probability-weighted transient counts (rho = −0.06, p = 0.25).
Transients are short-lived, star-like objects of unknown origin that have been identified in the POSS-I and other historical sky surveys 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 15 . A significant barrier to accepting transients as real astronomical phenomena and to understanding their nature and origin is the unknown and potentially high rate of false positive transient identifications using the existing published automated pipeline 1 , 14 . These false positives comprise plate defects due to dust, hair, scratches, and emulsion errors on scanned archival astronomical plates. This study for the first time attempted to reduce these false positives and optimize identification of true astronomical transients via a supervised learning ML approach.
Results indicated the ML model displayed good discrimination between real transients and plate defects based on classification via expert visual inspection (AUC = 0.81). Some have argued that all purported transients are simply plate defects 12 , 13 . Our results clearly argue against this possibility. If true, the supervised learning approach employed would have trained the ML model to recognize plate defects randomly labelled as true transients versus plate defects. In this scenario, ML model discrimination would be expected to approximate random levels (AUC = 0.50), contrasting sharply with the observed AUC = 0.81.
Inspection of the range of probability values for each of the 10 increasingly stringent deciles confirm the original n = 107,875 dataset from the Solano et al. pipeline 1 , 14 contains many false positives (only 20% exceeded a 0.66 probability of being a real transient). Overall, only a small subset of the original n = 107,875 dataset were judged by the ML model to have high likelihood of reflecting real objects rather than plate defects, highlighting the issue of statistical noise in the existing pipeline but also the value of incorporating this ML model into future transient studies.
Given the model’s accuracy in discriminating likely transients from artifacts, we next evaluated two a priori hypotheses to validate the model against external criteria. First, Villarroel et al. 5 reported that transient numbers were significantly lower (∼7.6 sigma) when located in Earth’s shadow compared to expectations given actual sky coverage (i.e., shadow deficit). In the current study, we found that the shadow deficit was largest (and the shadow fraction smallest) in the subgroup with the highest ML-derived probability of reflecting real objects, consistent with our hypothesis. Our findings provide additional support for the previously proposed hypothesis that a subset of transients exhibit features consistent with those expected of highly reflective objects in orbit 5 , 8 .
Our second means of validating the ML model was to test the a priori hypothesis that associations between nuclear testing and transients reported in our prior work 10 and confirmed by others 9 , 11 would be strongest in the subgroup of transients the ML model judged most likely to be real objects rather than plate defects. Results confirmed this hypothesis as well. The probability-weighted transient count (which controls for any influence of the high percentage of likely plate defects in the sample) was significantly higher for dates within a nuclear test window than the transient count expected based on a random distribution (reflecting 10,000 permutations). Sensitivity analyses further indicated that associations between increased transient counts and nuclear testing were specific to the day of the nuclear test and the day immediately prior. That transients were increased most strongly on the day before a nuclear test rules out all explanations for the nuclear-transient association that are dependent on the effects of the nuclear blast itself (e.g., bomb debris, acute radiation effects). The temporal specificity of the nuclear-transient association and the fact that this association is statistically significant even when plate artifacts are controlled both confirm and strengthen our prior findings 10 .
Taken together, results of this study argue strongly against claims that all transients are plate defects. If this were true, the magnitude of both the shadow deficit and the nuclear-transient association would not have shown any systematic association with ML-derived probability values. The fact that the shadow deficit and the nuclear-transient association were each significantly larger in transients with the highest ML-derived probability of being real supports the transient phenomenon, the shadow deficit, and the nuclear-transient association all as reflecting real physical phenomena rather than being due to spurious associations arising from plate defects.
So how should the two key findings in the current study be interpreted? A number of potential explanations for each of these findings when considered in isolation have been addressed previously 5 , 10 , 14 . It is not difficult to accept that the shadow deficit finding, considered on its own, might imply that there is an unknown population of previously undiscovered natural objects in orbit with high specular reflectivity and flat surfaces. But how can this interpretation account for the finding that this same group of high-probability transients is observed more often around the dates of nuclear weapons testing? Does one simply disregard the latter finding because it does not fit within current scientifically-accepted models?
Several explanations for the current findings are potentially plausible if one does not require that the explanation account for all key study findings and observed transient characteristics simultaneously. For example, the nuclear-transient association (but not the shadow deficit) might be due to observation balloons launched at the time of nuclear tests. While theoretically plausible, balloons can be ruled out as an explanation based on geometrical and optical grounds. First, because POSS-I images tracked the celestial sphere during 50 min exposures, any nearby balloon would produce a streak rather than a stationary point source. Even distant balloons would appear as streaks over a 50 min exposure because balloons are nearly always constantly moving, either ascending skyward or moving laterally with the wind. Second, observational geometry suggest that the balloon explanation is implausible. Mount Palomar is approximately 480 km from the Nevada nuclear test site, and a stratospheric balloon has a typical ceiling of ≈ 130,00 feet (39.6 km). It would therefore only be visible from Mount Palomar when viewed very close to the horizon, at approximately 4° elevation. As indicated in Supplemental Fig. 1 , virtually no transients in the entire dataset were observed at such a low viewing angle, with nearly 80% observed within 30° of the zenith rather than near the horizon. The number of transients seen during nuclear tests also argues against the balloon hypothesis. The probability-weighted transient count within a nuclear window averaged 196.9 transients. The proposition that hundreds of balloons were launched from the Nevada test site to monitor a single nuclear test is implausible prima facie . For the reasons above, we believe the balloon hypothesis can be rejected as a plausible explanation for the nuclear-transient association.
Other possible prosaic explanations for transients should be considered. The U-2 aircraft was flown from August of 1955 onward and had a ceiling of 70,000 feet (21.3 km). However, at that altitude, even a stationary U-2 would appear unfocused in the Samuel Oschin telescope used for POSS-I observations, as it was focused on infinity and objects observed at fewer than several hundred kilometers would be out of focus. Moreover, the U-2 was constantly moving in flight and would thus appear as a streak during the POSS-I 50 min exposure.
Another potential explanation is cosmic rays. High energy particles under the right conditions might produce a point-like appearance, similar to the transients reported in this study. However, cosmic rays interact directly with the photographic plate and therefore should not be influenced by whether the telescope is pointing through the Earth’s shadow at geostationary altitudes (i.e., the shadow deficit). Influence of lower energy solar cosmic rays (which would be more likely to produce a point source rather than a streak) is ruled out by the small anticorrelation observed between solar activity and transient counts. This anticorrelation is potentially consistent with galactic cosmic rays, but its small magnitude and the fact that the anticorrelation was observed for only one of three solar activity measures argue against their having a substantial effect on transient counts. Moreover, any such effects were found to be linked most strongly to transients classified by the ML model as artifacts. Finally, statistical control of possible galactic cosmic ray influences did not substantively alter the significant nuclear-transient association reported in our primary findings. Thus, neither solar activity nor galactic cosmic rays can plausibly account for the increased number of transients during nuclear test windows. Differences in lunar illumination also did not significantly confound transient detection.
If one accepts that both key findings in this study represent real phenomena and their interpretation is necessarily limited to hypotheses that can simultaneously account for both findings, we are left with a very small set of provocative hypotheses that would be considered highly implausible by most. For example, is it possible that unknown to the public there were multiple launches of artificial satellites long before Sputnik with some launches timed to coincide with U.S. nuclear tests? Or rather, do the current findings represent detection of a non-human technosignature? Finally, might our results represent detection of an entirely new yet unknown physical phenomenon? Due to data limitations, such hypotheses cannot be subjected to falsification. Ultimately, it must be left to the reader to determine the most plausible explanation for the current findings. Regardless, replication of our findings using scanned images from sky surveys obtained at other observatories worldwide during the same time period (1949–1957) could independently corroborate validity of the associations reported here. More work in this regard needs to be carried out.
Prior critiques had previously disputed interpretation of transients identified in historical astronomical images as representing an unrecognized population of real transient astronomical phenomena distinguishable from plate defects 12 , 13 . However, together with several recent replications of our prior work 9 , 11 , the current findings provide compelling data that argue for at least considering high probability transients as real astronomical phenomena worthy of further study. Our findings further suggest that ML can be successfully used to extract higher quality astronomical data from historical sky surveys that often are underutilized. For example, having sequential images as in POSS-I of the same sky region over relatively short timescales (30 min apart) that have in effect been digitally cleaned via ML could potentially enhance their utility for time domain astronomy (e.g., detection of asteroids and Kuiper belt objects, monitoring novae).
The current study addresses several limitations of our prior work. Arguments that all transients are plate defects 12 , 13 have been addressed by developing and validating an ML approach permitting quantitative discrimination between real transients and plate defects via ML-derived probability scores. Comments that previously reported associations between presence/absence of nuclear testing and presence/absence of transients 10 were simply due to coincidental correspondence between POSS-I observation schedules and nuclear testing schedules (potentially reflecting common weather patterns) 13 were addressed by: (1) limiting nuclear-transient analyses only to recorded dates of POSS-I observation ( n = 370) with no assumptions regarding transient presence/absence on other dates, and (2) targeting nightly transient counts as the variable of interest, which unlike presence/absence of transients, should not exhibit spurious association with nuclear testing schedules or common weather patterns influencing both observing conditions and nuclear test schedules. Finally, the current work used a 3D topocentric model for calculating shadow deficits rather than the 2D model used in our initial work 5 , in order to permit more accurate estimation of the shadow deficit.
This study also has limitations. It is limited by reliance on scanned POSS-I images rather than original plates, which have not been made publicly available. The primary limitation was reliance upon subjective expert opinion to determine the classification of training sample images as real transients versus plate defects. This was unavoidable due to the absence of any objective gold standard for determining the validity of a given transient image. While there is potential for classification error with this approach, this situation parallels challenges routinely encountered in research in other fields. For example, in developing the widely used Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders III-Revised, validation research employed expert clinical opinion regarding diagnosis as the gold standard 16 , 17 . This approach was necessary given absence of clear biomarkers for the disorders targeted, a situation paralleling the transient classification issues in the current work. We note that the individual primarily responsible for performing the manual inspection of transient images (BV) is the co-discoverer of the phenomenon and therefore well-qualified to make classification decisions.
In conclusion, our study provides further support for the idea that a population of previously unknown transient objects were detected on photographic plates by historical astronomical surveys, although their nature remains unexplained. Results confirm that a ML approach can be used to optimize discrimination of real transients from plate defects. Findings that transients classified by the ML model as likely real exhibit the largest shadow deficit and the strongest associations with nuclear testing both validate the ML model and the transient phenomenon itself. What these two findings taken together might reveal about the nature of the transient phenomenon remains to be confirmed, although additional research on this topic is clearly warranted.
The VASCO transient catalog was first presented in Solano et al. 1 as an intermediate data product consisting of > 298,000 transient candidates, and was later refined into a filtered transient catalog of 107,875 transient objects (see Villarroel et al. 8, 14 ), with duplicates, asteroids, high-proper-motion stars, and other spurious entries removed. The catalog was originally constructed to include all transients detected in only a single image. The catalog consists primarily of point-like sources detected in the red images of the POSS-I survey that are absent from the Pan-STARRS1 survey and the Gaia catalogue. Nevertheless, the VASCO catalog was not systematically subjected to visual inspection and therefore still contained a significant level of contamination from plate defects, hairs, and even ordinary stars. The VASCO catalog should not be confused with the sample of 5,399 vanishing-star candidates presented in Solano et al. 1 , which addresses a different scientific question (the search for a single vanishing star-candidate) and is a heterogeneously filtered dataset that exhibits a different spatial distribution.
The transient dataset to which ML was applied consisted of 107,875 transients from the VASCO catalog occurring between 11/19/49 and 4/28/57 identified in publicly-available scanned images from the POSS-I survey available on the DSS Plate Finder website ( https://archive.stsci.edu/cgi-bin/dss_plate_finder ). The process used initially to identify these transients and eliminate misidentifications was conducted via an automated workflow detailed in Solano et al. 1 and further clarified in Villarroel et al. 14 . In brief, transients were defined as distinct star-like point sources exhibiting point spread functions that were present in POSS-I Red images but that were absent both in images taken immediately prior to the POSS-I Red image and in all subsequent images from other surveys. A final criterion for classifying an object as a transient was that there were no optical counterparts either in PanStarrs DR1 or Gaia DR3 at less than 5 arcsec (see Villarroel et al. 5 for additional details).
Apparent magnitudes were derived from a per-plate characteristic curve calibrated against field stars with known Gaia-based reference magnitudes. For each plate, instrumental magnitudes were transformed to standard Cousins R using that plate’s own photometric standards, which simultaneously corrects for plate-to-plate differences in exposure and emulsion sensitivity. This yields calibrated apparent magnitudes on a common photometric system rather than a relative brightness proxy. As supplemental analyses to check for influence of nonlinearity of magnitudes on comparisons of high and low probability transients, we restricted the comparisons to only transients within 0.5 magnitudes of the pooled median across groups (see Supplemental Table 2). Differences in SNR, FWHM, ellipticity, and distance from the plate edge between groups were maintained and became larger in magnitude.
Replication of the nuclear testing-transient association reported in Bruehl & Villarroel 10 employed public data sources. Dates of all U.S. above ground nuclear tests during the study period noted above were obtained from the US Department of Energy (DOE/NV-209 Rev.16). As in our prior work 10 , the nuclear testing variable was again a nuclear testing window reflecting whether each date fell within one day of any nuclear weapons test (test date +/- 1 day). This window was chosen to balance sensitivity to the effects of interest with a reasonable degree of specificity, given numerous anecdotal reports of unidentified aerial phenomena both during and shortly before or after historic nuclear tests 18 .
Machine learning (ML) model development was conducted in Python 3.11 using the scikit-learn (v1.7.2), XGBoost (v3.1.2), and SHAP (v0.50.0) libraries. Transients targeted for model development in the current study were all identified solely on red POSS-I plates. The ML model included 23 predictors extracted from the red FITS images and the VASCO v4 catalog. Seven catalog-level morphometric features were included: signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), point spread function (PSF) ratio, elongation, compactness, sharpness, number of comparison stars, and candidate score (described in Solano et al. 1 ). The ML model also included 6 plate-aggregate features: a plate quality indicator, plate-level SNR fraction, SNR standard deviation, mean elongation, and high-SNR source count. Finally, the model included 10 morphometric features identified by the ML model in the red FITS images themselves: PSF Full Width at Half Maximum (PSF FWHM), ellipticity, sharpness, connected pixel count, aperture flux, distance to plate edge, symmetry score, gradient magnitude, proximity to bright star, and FITS-measured SNR. The ML model did not include any spectral features or red-blue plate comparison. Descriptive statistics for the 23 predictors are presented in Supplemental Table 1. Abbreviations used in Fig. 2 which displays the ML model results are as follows: plate_low_snr_frac = Plate-level: fraction of candidates on the same plate with SNR < 5; plate_quality_GOOD = Plate-level: binary, plate rated as GOOD (one-hot encoded); plate_quality_MODERATE = Plate-level: binary, plate rated as MODERATE (one-hot encoded); plate_elongation_mean = Plate-level: mean elongation of all candidates on the same plate; plate_snr_std = Plate-level: standard deviation of SNR across all candidates on the same plate; candidate_score = Candidate-level: original pipeline quality score from Solano et al. detection algorithm; red_gradient_magnitude = Red FITS: magnitude of the intensity gradient at candidate position (edge sharpness); red_n_connected_px = Red FITS: number of contiguous pixels above threshold in the source footprint; red_fits_fwhm = Red FITS: full width at half maximum of the candidate PSF profile (point-source width); red_aperture_flux = Red FITS: total flux within the measurement aperture centered on the candidate; red_dist_to_edge_px = Red FITS: distance from candidate to nearest plate edge, in pixels; plate_n_high_snr = Plate-level: count of candidates on the same plate with SNR > 15; red_symmetry_score = Red FITS: radial symmetry of the candidate light profile (1 = perfect symmetry); red_sharpness_2nd = Red FITS: second-order sharpness (curvature of the PSF peak; point sources vs. extended); red_fits_snr = Red FITS: signal-to-noise ratio measured directly from the FITS pixel data; red_ellipticity = Red FITS: ellipticity of the source (0 = circular, 1 = elongated); psf_ratio = Candidate-level: ratio of candidate FWHM to plate-median FWHM (PSF consistency check); snr = Candidate-level: signal-to-noise ratio from the original detection pipeline (catalog-level); sharpness = Candidate-level: sharpness from the original detection pipeline; elongation = Candidate-level: elongation from the original detection pipeline; compactness = Candidate-level: compactness from the original detection pipeline; n_comparison_stars = Candidate-level: number of comparison stars used for PSF calibration on that plate; red_near_bright_star = Red FITS: binary flag, candidate is near a bright cataloged star (halo/diffraction risk).
The criterion for training and determining accuracy of the ML model was a training set of 250 POSS-I image pairs (red versus blue) taken 30 min apart and previously identified by the Solano et al. pipeline as containing at least one transient on the red image 1 , 14 . The training set was chosen to include exemplars of either true astronomical transients or a variety of clearly-identifiable plate defects (e.g., dust, hair, scratch, emulsion defect, exposure problems). Each image pair was manually inspected by an astronomer with expertise regarding the transient phenomenon (BV); 134 were labelled likely real transients and 116 as plate defects. To enhance classification consistency over time, a second reviewer (SB) who was trained by the primary evaluator periodically reviewed a subset of the images assigned to the primary reviewer, with any disagreements discussed with the primary reviewer and resolved. Supplemental Table 1 displays the characteristics of transients classified as likely real versus plate defect based on expert visual inspection.
The ensemble ML classifier detailed in this study combined four tree-based models (XGBoost, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, LightGBM), each trained with 300 trees and identical hyperparameters, with final classification predictions based on the unweighted mean of the four models’ predicted probabilities. For analytic purposes, transients were distributed into 10 bins of equal size (probability deciles) with each increasing decile reflecting a higher probability that transients in that decile reflect real transients based on the ML model (see Table 1 ). Isotonic probability calibration was attempted but collapsed the probability distribution; raw mean ensemble probabilities were therefore used as the primary candidate probability scores described in analyses (i.e., likelihood that each transient would be classified as real). Additional details regarding the ML methods can be provided upon reasonable request to the authors. The final machine learning script can be found at: https://github.com/dca-doherty/VASCO-ML .
Transients appear as point sources rather than streaks during a 50-minute plate exposure, and therefore calculation of the shadow deficit assumed that transients were at geostationary orbit altitude, 35,786 km (GEO). In our prior work 5 , we employed the Nir et al. 2D EarthShadow model ( https://github.com/guynir42/earthshadow ) to calculate the shadow deficit. In the current work, we used a 3D model in order to more accurately capture the hypothesized shadow deficit. Specific advantages of the 3D model were that it enabled the shadow boundary to be computed correctly for any assumed orbital altitude, it permitted anchoring of the model at Mount Palomar’s actual coordinates, and it accounted for the impact of Earth’s penumbra on shadow deficit results.
Each transient’s angular separation (based on recorded sky position) from the center of Earth’s penumbra was computed using the topocentric anti-solar direction as seen from the coordinates of Palomar Observatory, with candidate coordinates precessed from j2000.0 to the observation epoch using the IAU 1976 formulae. The primary model was the 3D topocentric penumbra, which has an angular radius of 8.96 degrees at GEO and represents the boundary at which solar illumination is fully restored. Transients falling within this angular radius were classified as in-shadow; all others were classified as sunlit.
The fraction of retained transient candidates falling within the shadow zone was compared to the fraction expected to appear based on geometric expectations for a uniform sky distribution. The latter plate-aware control sample was generated as follows. Individual plates were identified by spatial clustering of transient positions per observation date (complete linkage, 15-degree threshold), yielding 626 plates. For each plate, 100 random sky positions were generated within the plate field of view using the plate center coordinates and observation time, with no reference to actual transient positions. Of 62,600 total control positions, 433 (0.692%) fell within Earth’s geometric shadow at geosynchronous orbit altitude, establishing the expected shadow fraction of 0.692%. The shadow deficit for each decile of probability values (i.e., increasingly stringent definitions of a transient) was calculated as: (observed shadow fraction – control shadow fraction)/control shadow fraction, expressed as a percentage. See Villarroel et al. 5 for additional details.
All statistical analyses were conducted in Python 3.11 using the statsmodels, scipy, and scikit-learn libraries. To demonstrate the discrimination accuracy of the ML model, we examined sensitivity (True Positive/True Positive + False Negative), specificity (True Negative/True Negative + False Positive), and area under the curve (AUC), all based on 5-fold cross-validation with final results comprising cross-validated out-of-fold values. Sensitivity and specificity were also derived from pooled out-of-fold values. All tests of ML model discrimination used manually-classified transients as described above as the reference standard. Given that both study hypotheses were a priori and based on our prior findings, we used one-tailed probability values to determine statistical significance ( p <0.05) for the two a priori hypothesis tests; all post-hoc and confound analyses used two-tailed p values.
The shadow deficit quantifies extent to which transients are underrepresented in Earth’s shadow relative to geometric expectations. The shadow deficit is presented in Fig. 3 for consistency with our prior work 5 but all analyses focused solely on observed shadow fraction values. For each probability decile, the observed fraction of transients falling within Earth’s shadow was compared to a plate-aware Monte Carlo control expectation of 0.692% using a one-sided binomial test. Because ten simultaneous tests were conducted, a Bonferroni-corrected significance threshold of p < 0.005 was applied. To test whether the highest-probability transients showed a disproportionately larger shadow deficit compared to lower probability transients, the shadow fraction of the upper decile (D9) was compared to the pooled shadow fraction of all other deciles (D0 through D8) using a two-proportion z-test.
Primary analyses of hypothesized transient-nuclear testing associations were restricted in this study to U.S. nuclear tests, which were most often conducted at the Nevada test site, a location only 435 km from Mount Palomar Observatory (in California) from which all POSS-I transients were identified. In contrast, the bulk of remaining worldwide nuclear tests were conducted by the Soviet Union in Semipalatinsk, Kazakhstan, which is 10,617 km from Mount Palomar. This focus on U.S. nuclear testing in the current study was intended to address questions raised in response to our prior work 10 regarding mechanistic plausibility of nuclear-transient associations if nuclear tests were conducted vast distances from the observatory from which transients were identified.
The nuclear-transient association was tested in primary analyses using a non-parametric permutation approach (i.e., no distributional assumptions) with observation dates as the independent unit of analysis ( n = 370 dates of POSS-I observations). This focus of analyses on dates as the unit of analysis avoided possible confounding of results using other available analytic approaches due to temporal clustering of transients (non-independence within dates). For each date, the sum of ML-assigned probabilities across all transients on that date was computed, yielding a probability-weighted transient count that represents the estimated number of real transients. The mean probability-weighted count for nuclear dates (those falling within one day of a US nuclear test, 26 of 370 dates) was compared to the comparable count on non-nuclear dates. Statistical significance was assessed via 10,000 random permutations of the nuclear window labels (i.e., the label indicating whether each date was within a nuclear window). This analytic approach therefore tested how often randomly-shuffled nuclear window label assignments produce a mean difference for summed probability values as large as what was actually observed. A confirmatory non-parametric Mann-Whitney U test was also conducted given that it has more statistical power for detecting shifts within continuous distributions. To parallel the shadow deficit analysis above, we compared the percentage of transients in a nuclear testing window for the upper decile (D9) to the pooled percentage of transients in a nuclear testing window for all other deciles (D0 through D8) using a two-proportion z-test.
To assess the temporal specificity of nuclear-transient associations identified, we repeated the primary permutation test approach above for different lagged time periods, from 3 days before a nuclear test date to 3 days after a nuclear test date. This sensitivity analysis tested whether the nuclear-transient signal was sharply localized around test dates or broadly distributed, which may better distinguish a genuine physical association from confounding by seasonal patterns or observation scheduling. For purposes of comparing the size of the nuclear-transient association between different lags for significant analyses, we report the unadjusted ratio of the mean probability-weighted transient count on nuclear-window dates to the mean on non-nuclear dates.
The final dataset reflecting all analyzed variables including the machine learning-derived probability scores will be made available by the authors upon reasonable request to Dr. Stephen Bruehl (stephen.bruehl@vumc.org).

title: Pope Leo diagnosed with cancer as doctors remove lobe of lung, Vatican says
body: Pope Leo was diagnosed with a common form of lung cancer after doctors removed ​a lower lobe of his right lung in surgery on Tuesday, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin. The 71-year-old pontiff ‌has lung adenocarcinoma, with tissue tests conducted during the operation confirming what doctors had suspected from preparatory examinations, the bulletin said. The pope was admitted to Rome’s Gemelli hospital on Tuesday for surgery to remove a growth on his lung that doctors found in a recent health checkup. The Vatican had said earlier on Tuesday evening that the ​surgery had been successful before providing a more detailed update from the pope’s lead surgeon, Professor Stefano Margaritora, the chief of ​thoracic surgery at the Gemelli. “In order to make the procedure curative, the lower lobe of the right lung was ⁠removed using a video-assisted technique,” said Margaritora’s update. “A rapid intraoperative histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, as had been suspected from ​the pre-operative tests,” it said. Tuesday’s surgery lasted about 90 minutes and was successful with no complications, the Vatican said. The pope has woken up normally ​and is resting in his hospital room.

title: ANA prepares to receive first Boeing 737 MAX in December after years of delays
body:
All Nippon Airways (ANA) is preparing to receive its first Boeing 737 MAX 8 in December, more than five years after deliveries of the new narrowbody jet were originally expected to begin.
ANA announced its selection of the 737 MAX 8 in January 2019, initially planning to introduce the aircraft between fiscal years 2021 and 2025. The decision came shortly before the worldwide grounding of the MAX following the crashes of Lion Air Flight 610 and Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302.
The Japanese airline eventually formalized an order for 20 aircraft in 2022, after the MAX had returned to service. The delivery schedule continued to change in subsequent years amid production constraints and quality problems at Boeing.
ANA had more recently expected its first aircraft in May 2025 and then in June 2026. The current schedule calls for deliveries to start in December, according to Nikkei Asia .
Follow Air Data News: WhatsApp | Instagram | LinkedIn | Twitter | Facebook
The airline has expanded its commitment during the long wait. ANA now has 38 737 MAX 8s on firm order and options for another four aircraft.
Production of the first aircraft is now well underway at Boeing's Renton plant in Washington state.
The first MAX 8 intended for ANA, expected to receive the Japanese registration JA030A, made its maiden flight on August 29. A second aircraft, JA031A, had completed final assembly by late September, while a third, JA032A, was progressing through the production line.
ANA personnel have been conducting on-site inspections during production. The airline told Nikkei Asia that its inspectors monitor specific stages of assembly and check whether Boeing's manufacturing work complies with contractual requirements.
The inspections extend to ground and flight testing before delivery. ANA personnel can also request additional checks when production records identify a nonconformity.
The process comes as Boeing continues efforts to improve manufacturing quality following increased regulatory scrutiny of its 737 production system. ANA's inspections, however, are part of the airline's aircraft acceptance process and do not indicate that problems have been identified with its first MAX aircraft.
The 737 MAX 8s will be used primarily on ANA's domestic network and will gradually replace older 737-800s.
ANA Wings, the regional subsidiary of ANA Holdings, is expected to operate the aircraft. Introducing 38 MAX 8s will give the group a substantial new-generation narrowbody fleet for domestic routes.
ANA's original 2019 commitment covered 20 aircraft with ten options. The airline subsequently increased its firm order through additional purchases and the conversion of options, bringing the total to 38 aircraft, with another four options remaining.
ANA will not be the first Japanese airline to operate the 737 MAX despite having been the first in the country to announce an order for the type.
Skymark Airlines received its first 737 MAX 8, JA738A, in April 2026 and introduced it on commercial services on May 28, initially between Tokyo Haneda and Fukuoka. The carrier plans to operate 13 MAX 8s and seven MAX 10s.
If the latest schedule is maintained, ANA's first delivery in December will come almost eight years after the airline announced its MAX selection and more than five years after the beginning of its original delivery window.

title: Zelensky says Ukraine’s Western allies again gave no warning before Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv. It’s the second time in two days.
body: Ukraine’s Western partners again failed to warn it ahead of another Russian ballistic missile strike on Kyiv on the evening of October 13, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said. He said the strike primarily targeted the city’s energy infrastructure, specifically the combined heat and power plant known as CHP-4. A residential building was damaged and caught fire. A Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. Once again, no early warning from our partners. The main target was energy infrastructure, specifically CHPP-4. Unfortunately, it was hit. A residential building was also damaged, and rescuers are currently putting out a fire there. Our… pic.twitter.com/6FKPx8PuFG — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) October 13, 2026 Russia is preparing further missile strikes on Ukraine, Zelensky said, citing Ukrainian intelligence. The previous day, Zelensky said Ukraine had received no warning from its Western allies about the Russian missile strike on the evening of October 12. Politico reported that the U.S. told Ukraine it had not provided intelligence because of bad weather. Last week, the U.S. threatened to stop sharing intelligence with Ukraine unless Kyiv agreed to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, the Financial Times reported . Washington has made no official announcement that it intends to stop sharing intelligence. Read more European allies publicly back Zelensky after Trump says Ukraine needs a new president Russian missile strike on apartment building in Ukraine kills 14, including four children. Zelensky calls it the Russian army’s ‘birthday gift’ to Putin. Trump claimed that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an energy truce. Neither side stopped the strikes. title: Joint statement on UK’s attribution of Iranian involvement in RAF Fairford incident
body: The text of the following statement was released by the Governments of the United States of America, the United Kingdom, Australia, Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Canada, Croatia, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, and Sweden. The United States of America, the United Kingdom, Australia, Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Canada, Croatia, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, and Sweden condemn in the strongest terms Iran’s use of violent attacks, including the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners. We recognize the United Kingdom’s attribution of Iran’s involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford on 27 September. title: Deputy defense minister notes special role of Korean army in liberation of Kursk Region
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Russia’s Deputy Defense Minister, Colonel General Vitaly Shulika has noted the special role of Korean military personnel in liberating the Kursk Region from the Ukrainian army, in demining and restoring infrastructure.
Shulika took part in a solemn reception marking the 78th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between Russia and North Korea. He said that today Russian-Korean relations experience one of the best periods in their entire history. The strategic partnership is based on the alignment of fundamental national interests, shared views on the international situation and the world order, a high level of mutual trust, and the preservation of long-term good-neighborly relations for the benefit of the peoples of the two countries.
"Colonel General Vitaly Shulika, on behalf of the defense minister of the Russian Federation expressed gratitude to the leadership of the DPRK and personally to Chairman of the State Affairs of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, Comrade Kim Jong Un, noting the special role of Korean military personnel in liberating the Kursk Region from the armed formations of the Kiev regime, demining, and restoring infrastructure facilities on Russian soil," the Russian Defense Ministry said.
