title: Legal Aid Commission takes free legal services to Techiman main lorry terminal
body: The Ghana Legal Aid Commission has launched its 2026 Legal Aid Week with a bold new approach to closing the country’s access-to-justice gap, bringing free legal services directly to the people who need them most. Under the theme “ Justice at Your Doorstep ,” the Commission has rolled out a pilot outreach initiative that takes legal aid out of formal offices and into the heart of everyday Ghanaian life: markets and lorry terminals. The program specifically targets traders, commercial drivers, and vulnerable citizens who cannot easily leave their workplaces to seek legal assistance. For years, access to justice in Ghana has been hindered by a simple but stubborn barrier: geography and economics. Traders in busy markets and drivers at lorry terminals often cannot afford to abandon their livelihoods for a day to visit a legal aid office -assuming they even know such services exist. “We see justice not to be a commodity to be sold to the highest bidder,” said Justice Seidu Anafure, Senior Legal Aid Officer at the Commission’s Bono East Regional Office. “The traditional approach has been for people to come to us. But we realized the most vulnerable cannot leave their work to come to our offices. So we decided to reverse the equation; we are taking justice to them.” The initiative was officially launched in Accra, with planned stops at the Tema Station lorry terminal, Kaneshie Market, and Kasoa Market. But the program is not confined to the capital. Regional offices across the country are rolling out similar localized outreach efforts. Today, the Bono East Regional Office stormed the Techiman Main Lorry Terminal, where citizens consulted directly with lawyers, received legal education, and got assistance with dispute resolution, including Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR)—all free of charge. The ADR component is particularly significant. By focusing on out-of-court settlements, the Commission offers a faster, less adversarial, and more accessible path to resolving conflicts that might otherwise drag through Ghana’s overburdened court system for years. For many who attended the Techiman outreach, it was their first-ever interaction with a lawyer. One commercial driver, who stopped to listen between loading trips, said the session had been eye-opening. “I came here to load my vehicle, but I ended up getting free legal advice,” he said. “This is very helpful. I wish they could do this regularly, maybe every month. We have so many issues among ourselves, and sometimes we don’t know where to go.” A trader who consulted with a lawyer on a long-standing dispute expressed similar gratitude. “I didn’t know I could get legal help for free,” she said. “I thought lawyers were only for the rich. Today, I’ve registered my case, and they are going to help me. I’m very grateful.” The session also featured an open question-and-answer segment, where participants raised concerns ranging from landlord-tenant disputes to family and commercial matters. The Commission’s message is clear: justice should not be a privilege reserved for those who can afford it. “Whether you are a driver, a trader, a farmer, or a vulnerable citizen, if you have a legal problem, we are here to help,” Anafure said. “Justice at your doorstep is not just a theme. It is our commitment.”

title: Jailed Russian historian Yury Dmitriev, who uncovered Soviet mass graves, is sent back to prison without a diagnosis after a suspected stroke, supporters say
body: Historian Yury Dmitriev, 70, has been returned to Penal Colony No. 18 in Mordovia from a prison hospital, the human rights group ZPCh said, citing his support group. He was taken to the hospital in late September with a suspected stroke. “He’s not feeling very well. They suspected a stroke, but there’s been no diagnosis: the hospital doesn’t have the equipment to diagnose it. Dmitriev was given a course of injections. We don’t know what they gave him,” the support group said. Dmitriev’s supporters said he was prescribed bed rest until October 28. But until recently, staff at the penal colony were unaware of this and would not let him lie down, a woman from the support group told ZPCh. “It’s hard to keep count of how many times he’s been put in a punishment cell. One time it’s because the top button on his shirt isn’t fastened, another because he sat on his bed, another because he fed a cat. Being in a damp, unheated room doesn’t do his health any good,” the support group said. Yury Dmitriev is a historian and the former head of Memorial’s Karelia branch. In 1997, he discovered mass graves of victims of Soviet political repression in the Sandarmokh forest. He also compiled lists commemorating victims of political repression in Karelia. Dmitriev has been imprisoned since 2016, when he was charged with producing pornography involving his underage adopted daughter, committing lewd acts against her, and illegally possessing a firearm component. The case stemmed from photographs of his daughter found in his possession. He denied the charges and said he had taken the photographs solely for medical purposes, to track her development. In 2018, a court acquitted him on two of the charges. For the weapons possession offense, he received only a noncustodial sentence of 3.5 years of restricted freedom. Karelia’s Supreme Court later overturned that verdict. Authorities opened another criminal investigation into Dmitriev, this time for sexual assault. He was sentenced to 13 years in a penal colony in that case. In December 2021, a court in Petrozavodsk combined his sentences and ordered him to serve 15 years in a high-security penal colony. Dmitriev denied the charges in both cases. Memorial considers him a political prisoner. Scholars, cultural figures, and Nobel laureates have spoken out in his support. title: Oshkosh starts production of JLTV-based Kaaiman patrol vehicle prototype for Netherlands
body: The Dutch Expeditionary Patrol Vehicle has upgraded suspension and mobility, maritime corrosion protection and modular protection options. Other changes include environmental upgrades and integrated mission systems. “The start of DXPV prototype production is an important step in delivering next-generation capability to the Netherlands,” said Jeff Heggemeier, vice president and general manager of Oshkosh Defense. “Just as importantly, it demonstrates the strength of an active production base and our ability to continuously evolve proven vehicle technologies to address the changing needs of our customers and their missions.” The prototype is being built on Oshkosh Defense’s active production line. The company said using an existing, fielded platform would shorten development timelines and reduce lifecycle risk. Kaaiman’s modular architecture is designed to accommodate future upgrades and different mission configurations. Oshkosh said the vehicle’s enhancements were developed in close collaboration with customers. “Production readiness matters,” Heggemeier said. “Because we’re building on a mature platform from an active production line, we can move from concept to prototype much faster than traditional vehicle development.” “That allows us to deliver capability quickly while maintaining the quality and reliability our customers expect,” Heggemeier said. The same production operations are also manufacturing JLTV-based counter-drone vehicles to meet an urgent customer requirement. Oshkosh Defense Europe B.V. and Oshkosh Defense, LLC jointly announced the start of prototype production. They did not disclose a completion date, delivery schedule or contract value.

title: Lancer Unmanned Ground Vehicles in Demand in Ukraine
body:
Ukrainian military forces have praised the performance of Forterra ‘s Lancer Unmanned Ground Vehicle (UGV) in moving dozens of 155mm artillery shells and other soldier supplies in front-line areas.
Since last year, Ukrainian forces have used more than 100 Lancers, Forterra said, for 1,500 missions, and it appears that Ukraine wants more, should funding materialize.
“The short answer is yes,” Patrick Acox, Forterra’s vice president of defense, said in a Tuesday interview at the Association of the United States Army conference in Washington, D.C. when asked whether there was a way for Ukraine to get more Lancers in spite of the ending of U.S. military aid to Ukraine. “The tactics are being translated right back out to the rest of the world…I know NATO’s interested. Between them, the capability coalitions–the SAG-U, and the localization, we have three main avenues.”
SAG-U is the Security Assistance Group-Ukraine, created nine months after the Russian invasion in February, 2022 to coordinate weapons shipments, other military equipment, logistics, and training for Ukraine. U.S. European Command recently announced a reorganization to move SAG-U tasks to NATO Security Assistance and Training for Ukraine in which Europe would take the leading role.
The gas powered Lancer UGVs, often used under the cover of night to shield them from Russian one way attack drones, can carry 65 155mm shells or other supplies several dozen kilometers. In addition, the Lancer has provided at least 88 medical evacuations so far, according to Forterra.
Ukrainian forces have installed cages on Lancers at times, and in one instance that cage withstood hits from four Russian first person view (FPV) “kamikaze” drones, although there have also been losses of Lancer due to Russian FPVs.
In July, the Maryland-based Forterra said that it had “produced and deployed 105 autonomous Lancer vehicles, in support of Ukrainian forces in the Russo-Ukrainian War.”
“Completing full delivery in under six months, the company designed and built, and deployed the Lancer, a multi-mission autonomous ground vehicle, to provide logistical and combat support on the battlefield,” according to Forterra. “This effort was developed under a U.S. government program in 2024 and was on contract by March of 2025.”
The Lancer is based on the Polaris Ranger 1500 utility vehicle by Minnesota-based Polaris, Inc.

title: El-Rufai Earmarked $600,000 To Settle EFCC Officials, DSS Witness Tells Court
body: A forensic investigator with the Department of State Services (DSS), Segun Kayode, on Tuesday alleged that former Kaduna State Governor Nasir El-Rufai and some of his associates earmarked $600,000 to pay officials of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) and intermediaries. Kayode, the first prosecution witness in the ongoing trial, made the allegation while testifying before the Kaduna State High Court sitting in Kawo, Kaduna, presided over by Justice Darius Khobo. The witness told the court that $500,000 and $100,000 were allegedly set aside for the payments. He added that forensic audio recordings captured conversations involving El-Rufai and some of his suspected associates. According to Kayode, the recorded conversations centred on alleged efforts to frustrate an EFCC investigation into a company identified as Singularity. He said a Senior Advocate of Nigeria, one other individual; and Bashir El-Rufai among those allegedly mentioned in the conversations. The investigator told the court that the Senior Advocate and the other individual were allegedly directed to meet one Ahmadu Sule to obtain a template previously used to liquidate another company, with the intention of applying a similar process to Singularity. Kayode further alleged that the discussions included plans to liquidate the company in Nigeria and Mauritius, where it was reportedly under investigation by the Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit. He also alleged that the recordings contained discussions about preventing the EFCC from investigating a company, which he said was listed on the New York Stock Exchange. The allegations formed part of the prosecution’s evidence against the former governor and have yet to be established by the court. Proceedings lasted nearly eight hours, from 12:26 pm to 8:18 pm, with about two hours devoted to playing the recorded conversations. Earlier, El-Rufai’s lead counsel, Paul Erokoro (SAN), objected to Kayode’s testimony, arguing that the witness’s name and summary of evidence were not included in the prosecution’s proof of evidence. Erokoro argued that the omission undermined his client’s right to a fair hearing, insisting that the defence was entitled to know the evidence it was expected to answer. However, counsel for the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC), Ayodeji Adedipe (SAN), told the court that Kayode was a subpoenaed witness and that the omission did not automatically render his testimony inadmissible. Adedipe said the subpoena was issued and signed by the court on June 30, 2026, adding that the defence would have the opportunity to cross-examine the witness. He also cited judicial authorities in support of his argument. In response, Erokoro maintained that the issue was not whether the witness could testify but whether the defence had been adequately informed to prepare for his evidence. He relied on Section 210 of the applicable Administration of Criminal Justice Law, 2017, arguing that the prosecution should have served the subpoena on the defence. In its ruling, the court acknowledged that the witness’s name and summary of evidence were absent from the proof of evidence but held that the records showed he had been subpoenaed. Justice Khobo ruled that the omission did not automatically make the testimony inadmissible, provided the defence was allowed to cross-examine the witness. After Kayode submitted a hard copy of his findings to the court clerk, the defence complained that the document should have been served earlier to enable it to study its contents. The judge, however, ruled that the defence could obtain a certified true copy of the document admitted as Exhibit One for examination. The court adjourned the case until November 30 and December 1, 2026, for continuation of the cross-examination, following agreement by the prosecution and defence. El-Rufai arrived at the court premises at about 11:50 am, ahead of the scheduled noon hearing, amid tight security. He was accompanied by the African Democratic Congress (ADC) governorship candidate in Kaduna State, Isah Ashiru. His appearance followed an order by Justice Khobo directing the ICPC to produce him in court for the resumed proceedings. The hearing resumed days after the Court of Appeal in Kaduna dismissed El-Rufai’s appeal challenging the refusal of bail by the state high court. In its judgment delivered on October 9, the appellate court upheld the lower court’s decision, ruling that the former governor had failed to establish sufficient grounds to warrant interference with the refusal of bail. El-Rufai has been in ICPC custody since February 18, 2026, over allegations of financial misconduct linked to his administration of Kaduna State between 2015 and 2023. title: Cementing Russia-North Korea partnership contributes to global stability
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Strengthening the Russian-Korean partnership makes an invaluable contribution to international stability, said Russia’s Deputy Defense Minister, Colonel General Vitaly Shulika.
Shulika took part in a solemn reception marking the 78th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between Russia and North Korea.

title: Nana B denies seeking passport favour, accuses Ablakwa of failing to account for GH¢16.4m
body: National Vice Chairman of the New Patriotic Party (NPP) Henry Nana Boakye, popularly known as Nana B, has denied seeking a favour from Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa to retain his service passport. He insisted that the controversy is being used to divert attention from questions over GH¢16.4 million allegedly spent on evacuating Ghanaians from South Africa. In a statement issued on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, Nana B rejected claims by the Majority in Parliament that Deputy Ranking Member of the Foreign Affairs Committee, Nana Asafo-Adjei, was pursuing a personal vendetta against Mr Ablakwa over the passport issue. The Majority had alleged that Mr Asafo-Adjei’s criticism of the Minister stemmed from his refusal to grant a request for a former NPP national organiser to retain his service passport. However, Nana B described the allegation as “weak, diversionary, unreasonable and a red herring” intended to cover up what he said were concerns about possible corruption raised by Mr Asafo-Adjei. He clarified that he had possessed only a service passport and had never held a diplomatic passport, adding that he surrendered the service passport in compliance with the President’s directive as published by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. According to him, his request to Mr Ablakwa was for a formal letter to notify embassies whose visas were in the service passport so the visas could be transferred to his ordinary passport. Nana B said Mr Ablakwa personally asked him to get Mr Asafo-Adjei to follow up on the letter, which he did. “Okudzeto Ablakwa personally requested that I inform Hon. Asafo Adjei to follow up on the letter, which I did, but after one visit, Hon. Asafo Adjei was informed the letter was not ready; hence, I abandoned it and applied for new visas,” he said. He maintained that Mr Asafo-Adjei had not sought any special favour from the Minister but had followed up on the letter at Mr Ablakwa’s request. “I never requested to retain the passport because doing so would have been unreasonable as a national executive of the opposition party,” Nana B added. The NPP official also expressed concern that the Majority had displayed the biographical data page of his service passport, which he said was in the custody of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Turning to the evacuation expenditure, Nana B accused the Majority of attempting to shield Mr Ablakwa from accountability over the GH¢16.4 million. He argued that the concerns raised by Mr Asafo-Adjei were based on data submitted by the Minister himself and should not be dismissed as a personal dispute. “The majority should not take discerning Ghanaians for fools by suggesting that a member of Parliament’s exposition on possible corruption to the tune of GHS16.4 million, based on data submitted by Okudzeto himself, is a personal vendetta,” he said. Nana B called on the Majority to demand explanations from Mr Ablakwa over what he described as serious inconsistencies in documents relating to the evacuation expenditure. “President Mahama promised Ghanaians accountability, and the majority should call Okudzeto Ablakwa to answer the serious inconsistencies in the documents submitted regarding the expenditure on the evacuation of citizens,” he said. The statement did not provide a detailed breakdown of the alleged inconsistencies in the evacuation expenditure. The claims of possible corruption and the alleged failure to account for the funds remain allegations in Nana B’s statement.

title: Wike defends cross-party coalition for Tinubu’s re-election
body:
The Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, has defended the growing cross-party political alliance backing President Bola Tinubu re-election in 2027.
Mr Wike, who made this known during a monthly media chat in Abuja on Tuesday, dismissed claims of internal crisis.
He described the rainbow coalition as “a movement bringing together figures from the All Progressives Congress (APC), All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA), Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), and other political platforms to support Tinubu”.
He emphasised that support for the presidency transcends individual party cards, adding that he would be leading Tinubu’s re-election campaign in FCT and Rivers despite being in the PDP.
Highlighting key figures driving the coalition across various states, Mr Wike pointed out Governor Charles Soludo of Anambra State, a member of APGA serving as a key campaigner for Tinubu in his state.
“In Osun, Governor Ademola Adeleke (PDP) is supporting the president at the national level while maintaining party identities sub-nationally,” he said.
Replying to critics who see a contradiction in political figures backing the presidential candidate of one party while contesting sub-national seats under another, Mr Wike dismissed the perceived friction as a “problem that does not exist.”
“Why would anybody say there is a problem there? Take Soludo—he is supporting Mr. President, but that does not mean his party will not field candidates for the House of Representatives or state assembly.
“It tells you leadership capacity. If you speak to your people and they listen, that is political strength,” the minister said.
Addressing opposition figures and state governors who have publicly acknowledged the president’s performance, Mr Wike singled out the Governor Bala Mohammed of Bauchi State for praising national infrastructure and governance strides despite belonging to an opposition party.
He urged politicians to put national progress above blind partisanship
“Time has come, not because of your political party, to just say the chief manager of the country has done nothing for the sake of politics. Politics must be a do-or-die affair.
“For us, whether anybody likes it or not, Mr. President has done well,” he said.
Earlier on Tuesday, Messrs Wike, Soludo and Adeleke had been named as members of the APC Presidential Campaign Council despite belonging to PDP, APGA and Accord Party. They are to coordinate President Tinubu’s re-election campaign in their respective states.

title: PostEra (YC W20) Is Hiring AI Researchers for Drug Discovery
body:
PostEra is building an AI-first biotech. We use Proton, our AI platform for medicinal chemistry, to accelerate the discovery of new medicines for patients. PostEra is advancing an internal pipeline focused on Women's Health and Fertility, and has used Proton to nominate multiple clinical candidates across PMOS and Fertility. PostEra also advances small molecule programs through partnerships with pharma. We've closed over $1B in AI partnerships including 4 multi-year agreements with Pfizer and Amgen . PostEra is also leading an antiviral drug discovery center for pandemic preparedness , funded by one of the largest grants in NIH history.
We believe time spent navigating complex hierarchies in organizations is better invested in the pursuit of novel technology and scientific discoveries. As such, our organizational structure is intentionally minimalist.
In this role, you will develop the agentic research vertical at PostEra, using agentic systems to automate the development of mechanistic models for biochemical and physiological processes, and analyse biological data for target validation. You will interact closely with chemists and biologists to use these models to drive drug discovery decisions.
You will also develop machine learning methods that can rapidly adapt to new drug discovery problems from limited labeled data. A particular focus is molecular and tabular in-context learning and building foundation models from PostEra’s proprietary multimodal data. You will build models that use the context of drug discovery effectively, determine which prior examples and tasks are relevant, quantify when transfer is helpful or harmful, and provide reliable predictions under distribution shift.
You will help drive the full research loop: defining tasks, constructing datasets and evaluation episodes, developing strong baselines, training and scaling models, performing rigorous ablations, and translating successful methods into capabilities used by PostEra’s scientists. Prior drug discovery experience is not required, but you should be motivated to learn the domain and work closely with medicinal chemists, computational chemists, and other scientists.
Agentic Research for Chemistry and Biology: Develop and benchmark agentic systems to automate the development of quantitative models to simulate biological and physiological processes, and the analysis of biological data.
Research Direction and Execution: Independently identify, formulate, and lead research projects involving in-context learning, agentic systems, few-shot adaptation, tabular foundation models, and molecular machine learning.
In-Context Learning for Molecules: Design and train models that adapt to new assays, endpoints, targets, or chemical series using limited labeled context and heterogeneous historical data.
Benchmarking: Rigorously compare new approaches against strong baselines, curating test cases that deconfounds impact of different sources of bias.
Cross-Functional Collaboration: Work with scientists to connect modeling objectives and evaluation metrics to practical decisions in potency modeling, ADME prediction, selectivity, lead optimization, and the design of early clinical studies.
Model Training and Scaling: Develop efficient training and data pipelines and, where appropriate, scale models across large collections of molecular and tabular tasks.
Research Engineering: Produce readable, reproducible research code; maintain well-tracked experiments; and contribute through code review, documentation, and shared modeling infrastructure.
Scientific Dissemination: Publish results in leading machine learning, medicinal chemistry, or computational biology venues. You will be an ambassador of PostEra to the scientific community.
PhD degree in machine learning, or STEM research involving the development of novel machine learning approaches
Track record of high-quality research, such as publications and open-source contributions
Strong research or engineering experience in modern machine learning, deep learning, or statistical modeling, backed by understanding of the theory behind machine learning algorithms
Demonstrated expertise in at least one relevant area: agentic workflows for science, machine learning approaches to bioinformatics and clinical data modelling, in-context learning, tabular learning, few-shot learning
Hands-on experience training, debugging, and evaluating ML models in Python using frameworks such as PyTorch or JAX
Ability to independently translate ambiguous scientific or technical problems into well-defined ML projects, including datasets, task definitions, baselines, metrics, and validation schemes
Ability to design careful experiments, benchmarks, and ablations that distinguish improvements from biases, and understand which aspects of the model led to the improvements
Comfort working in a startup environment where priorities evolve, data is imperfect, and high-quality judgment matters as much as raw model complexity
Candidates are more likely to succeed in this role if they also have experience with one or more of the following:
Training tabular foundation models, particularly for sparse, heterogeneous, small-data, or high-missingness settings
Developing molecular in-context learning systems or adapting general-purpose in-context models to molecular or scientific data
Large model training, including 1B+ parameter models, distributed training, sharding, data parallelism, model parallelism, and large-scale data pipelines
The development of AI “co-scientist” systems for physical or biological problems
Hands-on experience in modelling biological, biochemical or clinical data using machine learning approaches
Moving research models into production scientific software or computational workflows

title: Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps took the lessons of the failed 2023 counteroffensive into Operation Vivaldi. It fought small, and won.
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi has succeeded because ground commanders thought small instead of big Rather than hoping for a major breakthrough, they fought incrementally and with heavy support from the air Contrast Operation Vivaldi's small but successful thinking with the big thinking of Ukraine's failed 2023 counteroffensive Five months after launching Operation Vivaldi, a local counteroffensive in northern Donetsk Oblast, the Ukrainian 3rd Army Corps has eliminated the Russian bridgehead on its most important long-term objective: the Zherebets River, which flows south through eastern Ukraine and forms a natural defensive barrier east of the last big free cities in Donetsk: Sloviansk and Kramatorsk. Attacking methodically under strict secrecy, the 3rd Army Corps has pushed back the Russian 20th and 25th Combined Arms Armies and returned 176 sq km of northern Donetsk to Ukrainian control as of 30 September, according to Ukraine's presidential office. The figure could not be independently verified. Operation Vivaldi netted the Ukrainians hundreds of Russian prisoners and erased 18 months of Russian advances toward Sloviansk. "Ukrainian forces have defeated the 2026 Russian campaign to seize Donetsk Oblast," the Institute for the Study of War in Washington concluded . It's a remarkable feat for the overall outgunned and outmanned Ukrainian forces. Equally remarkably, the Ukrainians deftly dodged several potentially fatal traps as they flanked the 20th and 25th CAAs. They didn't get stuck in the Russians' dense minefields. They didn't expose themselves to devastating air attack. Perhaps most importantly, they didn't set their sights on distant objectives. They thought small instead of big, stacking small gains on top of small gains until those wins amounted to a big victory. Explore further Armored assaults aren’t dead. Robots got the credit, but it was Ukrainian infantry in armored trucks that reversed a year of Russian gains near Lyman A trio of US Army officers—Col. Timothy Price, Capt. Patrick Visser, and Capt. Andrew Carter—described this achievement in academic terms. The corps' defeat of the Russian bridgehead on the Zherebets "had little to do with maneuver warfare," the officers wrote for the Modern War Institute at the US Military Academy in West Point, New York. In military parlance, "maneuver" generally involves heavy ground forces supported by air strikes and artillery decisively breaking through enemy lines and then rushing vehicles and troops into the panicking enemy's unguarded rear area to quickly inflict maximal destruction and achieve maximal territorial gains. That's not what the 3rd Army Corps did in its five-month—and ongoing—counteroffensive. No, the Ukrainians "won through systematic, geometric interdiction and positional pressure," Price, Visser, and Carter wrote. Put plainly, the corps carefully probed for tree-covered assault lanes toward key settlements, deployed unmanned ground vehicles to clear mines and explode the most important nearby Russian strongpoints, and then rushed in armored vehicles carrying infantry. Settlements Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps says it liberated during Operation Vivaldi north of Lyman, Donetsk Oblast, Ukraine, as of 28 September 2026. Map: ISW They marched step by step, incrementally liberating a kilometer at a time instead of running a marathon toward a major objective tens of kilometers away. In that way, Operation Vivaldi is the very opposite of Ukraine's failed 2023 summer counteroffensive, which massed tanks for what commanders hoped would be a decisive breakthrough around the village of Mala Tokmachka in southern Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia Oblast. The objective at that time was to break into the Russian rear and speed tanks 80 km to the occupied city of Melitopol near the Sea of Azov. That never happened. The Ukrainians got mired in minefields around Mala Tokmachka, suffered badly from Russian air attacks, and, after a grueling season of costly attacks, lost momentum just 10 km south of Mala Tokmachka. Later Russian counterattacks erased even those modest Ukrainian gains. Explore further In Ukraine’s Vivaldi offensive, nobody rides in the BTR-60s. Bulgaria’s old troop carriers go into Russian bunkers packed with mines Old thinking versus new The planners of the failed 2023 counteroffensive were stuck in an old way of thinking about maneuver warfare. The planners of the successful 2026 counteroffensive shrugged off obsolete ideas. They thought smaller—and, ironically, achieved much more as a result. The 3rd Army Corps couldn't, and didn't, do it alone. Indeed, the corps depended on the Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces to fray the Russians' supply lines, electronic warfare teams to jam Russian drones, and the Ukrainian air force to bomb Russian drone operators the EW teams couldn't suppress. By contrast, the Ukrainian forces attacking south from Mala Tokmachka in 2023 did so without much aerial support. The aerial and electronic preparation was a prerequisite for each of the 3rd Army Corps' incremental advances this spring and summer. The lesson, the officers argue, is that "higher headquarters must degrade key enemy capabilities" before a smaller ground formation can expect to gain ground and keep it. If the support falters, the ground forces won't be able to hold. Think small. Prepare hard. Now that the Ukrainians know this is how to win on the ground, can they repeat Operation Vivaldi's success? There's some evidence they're already doing so in the southeast, where a clutch of Ukrainian air assault brigades has been pushing back the Russian 29th Combined Arms Army.

title: B-2 Stealth Bomber Returns to Base After Depot Maintenance
body: One of the Air Force’s critical B-2 Spirit stealth bombers has returned to Whiteman Air Force Base, Mo., after an extensive course of maintenance to restore its stealth coating and preserve its structural integrity. The B-2, which bears the tail number 93-1086 and is nicknamed the Spirit of Kitty Hawk, underwent programmed depot maintenance at Air Force Plant 42, a highly secure facility in Palmdale, Calif., the Air Force said in an Oct. 10 statement. Northrop Grumman, which originally built the B-2 when it was called the Northrop Corp. and today builds B-21 Raiders at Plant 42, managed the Spirit’s depot maintenance. Programmed depot maintenance is a regularly scheduled, labor-intensive process for thoroughly inspecting, overhauling and repairing Air Force aircraft. It becomes increasingly important as aircraft age and more maintenance troubles emerge. The Spirit of Kitty Hawk touched down Oct. 7 at Whiteman, which is home of the 509th Bomb Wing. But it’s not returning to service just yet—it will now move to the 509th’s modification line to receive advanced stealth and communications upgrades. The Air Force officially records 20 of the stealthy long-range B-2s in its inventory. But another B-2, called the Spirit of Hawaii, had a fiery crash in 2022 after its landing gear collapsed, which sparked a fire that ignited the bomber’s fuel tanks. The Air Force later said it planned to retire the Spirit of Hawaii, which would leave the service with 19 B-2s. With so few B-2s in its fleet , the Air Force said, returning even one bomber responsible for some of the service’s core functions back to the field “represents a significant boost to readiness.” “The B-2 is a small fleet,” Lt. Col. Jeffrey Lembrick, air vehicle and systems management materiel leader for the B-2 program office, said in the statement. “Every time we return a jet to the field, it represents an additional strategic option available for the President of the United States. When you talk about aircraft availability, one thing we know is that a jet can’t be used if it’s sitting at PDM. So, completing PDM and returning to the field is a big deal.” Depot maintenance for the B-2 typically involves restoring its low-observable stealth coating, inspecting its fuel system for leaks, and maintaining its blade seals, which are strips of metal that seal gaps when doors for weapons bays, landing gear, or other compartments close. In recent years, B-2s have taken about 15 to 16 months to go through programmed depot maintenance, although in 2024, one B-2 finished the process a little more than a year after it began. This time, the Air Force said, the Spirit of Kitty Hawk’s depot maintenance included replacement of its hot trailing edge, “a critical structural assembly designed to withstand the extreme thermal and acoustic fatigue generated by the bomber’s four engines.” Maintainers also spotted and fixed several unexpected maintenance problems while the B-2 was going through the depot. This included carrying out “a strategic part swap” with another B-2 that was coming into the Palmdale depot, and manufacturing another replacement part on-site, a B-2 program office official said. The post B-2 Stealth Bomber Returns to Base After Depot Maintenance appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

title: ‘My only home.’ Russian journalist Leonid Ragozin spent 12 years building a life in Latvia. Now he’s afraid to return.
body: Latvia’s Foreign Ministry said on October 6 that it had added a Russian citizen to its list of personae non gratae . It did not name him. According to Delfi and Politico , he is journalist Leonid Ragozin, who moved from Russia to Latvia after the annexation of Crimea, obtained permanent residency there, and writes for Western media outlets. Ragozin appears set to become the first independent journalist opposed to the war on Latvia’s persona non grata list, which includes more than 150 Russians. He would find himself alongside numerous Russian propagandists and prominent supporters of Russia’s aggression, including filmmaker Nikita Mikhalkov, singer Larisa Dolina, television presenter Tina Kandelaki, and the singer known as SHAMAN, whose real name is Yaroslav Dronov. Meduza spoke with Ragozin about his views on the war, his conflict with the Latvian authorities, and his love for the Baltic country. Leonid Ragozin’s conflict with Latvian politicians began long before the Foreign Ministry’s latest decision. In 2019, Ragozin coauthored a story with Sanita Jemberga, a journalist at the investigative journalism center Re:Baltica, about ties between members of Latvia’s National Alliance party and both Ukrainian far-right groups and Russian neo-Nazis. After its publication, he faced criticism and threats of deportation. In 2022, after Ragozin gave an interview about Russian journalists’ attitudes toward the war, Latvian Defense Minister Artis Pabriks called him a “possible Russian agent of influence” and said he was repeating Russian propaganda narratives. Four years later, in late September 2026, on the eve of parliamentary elections, Latvian Interior Minister Jānis Dombrava called on Foreign Minister Baiba Braže to declare Ragozin an “undesirable person.” He accused Ragozin of justifying Russian aggression and discrediting Ukraine. Dombrava is a member of the National Alliance, the party Ragozin wrote about. The ministers publicly argued over who should decide whether to expel the journalist. Other politicians joined the calls for the Foreign Ministry to act. Rihards Kols, a member of the European Parliament from the same party, said that if the Interior Ministry banned Ragozin from entering Latvia, he could challenge the decision in court. To avoid that, Kols said, the journalist should be declared persona non grata. (Notably, it was Latvia’s Interior Ministry that banned former TV Rain presenter Alexey Korostelev from entering the country in 2022 amid the public controversy surrounding the channel.) Many Russian-speaking and English-speaking journalists have come to Ragozin’s defense. Sabīne Sīle, the head of Media Hub Riga, which supports journalists from Russia and Belarus who have found refuge in Latvia, believes the situation sets a dangerous precedent because Ragozin has no way to defend himself in court. On October 12, Russian journalists in exile published a letter defending Ragozin, addressed to two U.N. special rapporteurs . At the time of publication, 143 people had signed it. Meanwhile, on October 7, the Latvian investigative center Re:Baltica published a statement saying it had not worked with Ragozin since 2019 and considered some of his social media statements “unacceptable and condemnable.” Anastasija Tetarenko-Supe, chair of the board of the Latvian Association of Journalists, told Novaya Gazeta Europe that the organization stood with Re:Baltica. Ragozin himself does not know whether he has officially been added to the list of personae non gratae; the authorities have not contacted him. Latvian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Līga Jermacāne confirmed to Meduza that the ministry had begun the process of adding “a citizen of the Russian Federation” to the list, but it remains unclear whether that person is Ragozin. The Foreign Ministry’s full response to Meduza follows: Under Article 104, Part 3, Paragraph 1 of the Republic of Latvia’s Immigration Law, and in close cooperation with the relevant authorities, the Foreign Ministry decides whether to add individuals to the list of persons whose presence in the Republic of Latvia is undesirable. In some cases, the Foreign Ministry makes this information public. We confirm that another citizen of the Russian Federation was added to this list on October 7, 2026. The ministry will not provide further information about the decision-making process or the identity of the individual added to the list. Latvia condemns in the strongest terms Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, which began in 2014, and its violation of Ukraine’s territorial integrity, as well as its unprovoked and unjustified full-scale war against Ukraine. Meduza also contacted Latvia’s Interior Ministry. “The Foreign Ministry has already answered this question within its remit,” the ministry said. — You’re not in Latvia right now. Did you leave because of the efforts to declare you persona non grata, because of the threats you’ve written about, or for other reasons? Do you plan to return? — I was already outside Latvia when all this happened, for reasons unrelated to the situation. And I can’t go back right now. Even though the government hasn’t contacted me directly or publicly named me as someone added to the list of personae non gratae — no such announcement has appeared on the Foreign Ministry’s website — there’s a substantial risk that if I turn up in Latvia, they’ll start deportation proceedings against me. And they would deport me specifically to Russia. The people who set all this in motion have spent years threatening to deport me specifically to Russia, because they understand that it’s a way to put me in prison. — How did you feel when you learned about the decision? — I’d lived with these threats for years and always understood that something like this could happen. I had a pretty realistic understanding of Latvian politics and how these things get decided. On the other hand, the sadism of this decision is shocking, of course. It’s going to take some serious emotional work to get through this and process my feelings about it. Because Latvia is a place I sincerely loved and considered my home. And of course I’d like to contribute something to Latvia. I’m not a threat to this country. I think the threat to Latvia comes from the people who alienate people like me, break the law, engage in political repression outside the courts, and punish people harshly for their honestly held views, for trying to give an intellectually honest analysis of the political situation and the military conflict. All this was shocking to me, but there’s also a sense of liberation… Liberation from self-censorship, too. I didn’t talk about Latvia for a very long time. And I have a great deal to say about it. But I’m not going to smear Latvia. I love this country, its culture, and its language. And I’ll try to act in ways that don’t harm it. — You’ve lived in Latvia since 2014. Why did you move in the first place? And why Latvia specifically? — We decided to leave on the day of the referendum in Crimea. My ex-wife and I decided that this chapter was over, that we had to leave Russia, that we simply couldn’t be associated in any way with what was happening. Latvia wasn’t a random choice. It’s the land of my ancestors, and I feel very much at home in Riga, partly because I like Latvian culture and the language. I think it’s the most beautiful language in the world. [Moving to Latvia] was a dream, and quite a long-standing one — going back to when I took part in the democratic revolution of 1991 and defended the White House in Moscow. Even then, my political priorities were tied to the idea of Baltic independence. One of the largest rallies in Moscow — in the entire history of Moscow and Russia, really — was held in January 1991 in support of Baltic independence. Leonid Ragozin. Moscow, 2016 So Baltic independence and the possibility of living in the Baltic countries, specifically Latvia, always had a place in my heart. — How did your feelings about the country and about life in Europe more broadly change? — I learned a lot about Latvian society that I probably never wanted to know. It didn’t change my views on Latvia’s independence, the Soviet occupation of Latvia and the other Baltic countries, or the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact. My views just became much more complex, informed, and nuanced. My fundamental beliefs stayed the same. I oppose all violence as a matter of principle. I consider the seizure of territory an occupation. But over the years, of course, I’ve accumulated a pile of questions — just a little Everest-sized pile — about the motives of various figures and organizations in the West, various politicians, their role in this conflict, and their attitudes toward Ukraine. I went through the same process with Ukraine, where I also worked a great deal and spent a lot of time. ‘I’m just an easy target they use to solve their political problems’ — Your career has taken some turns: You trained as a hydrogeologist and a translator, then spent many years as an international affairs journalist before writing for Lonely Planet guidebooks. What was your life like when you decided to leave Russia? — I worked as a journalist in Russia from 1998 to 2013. Almost all that time was at the BBC, apart from three or three and a half years at Russian Newsweek. I worked in various roles for Britain’s public television and radio broadcaster. First in the monitoring service, then in the Russian service, and toward the end as a producer for English-language television. I was coming around to the idea of trying freelance work, of becoming a self-employed journalist. A few years before that, I’d more or less stopped traveling all over the world and realized I wanted to focus on the countries I had ties to — Russia and Ukraine. I started traveling extensively around both countries and getting a better grasp of Ukrainian politics in particular. In 2013, I got the chance to write a Lonely Planet guide to Ukraine, but I also wanted to spend a substantial amount of time there, do some political reporting, and lay the groundwork for working in Ukraine. Of course, I had absolutely no idea what was going to happen there [Maidan]. Partly because at that point I was only beginning to develop my expertise on Ukraine. But I don’t think anyone expected it. Back then, Ukraine was something of a dream for me. A country much more tolerant than Russia, and much more diverse, too. A country where the two main languages coexist — you know, soccer matches where one commentator speaks Russian and the other Ukrainian. A country with many faiths and cultures. Even then, I supported Ukraine’s movement toward Euro-Atlantic integration, the European Union, and NATO. In that sense, Ukraine seemed like a beacon to me, one Russia might eventually follow. Ukraine could set an example for Russian society, show that a better life was possible. I arrived in Ukraine in late June 2013. My last story for the BBC was about Edward Snowden at Sheremetyevo Airport. I pretty much drove straight from Sheremetyevo to Ukraine. Then I traveled around Ukraine in 2013 and watched the whole story unfold. At first it seemed very clear to me: Ukraine was moving toward the European Union… Then it became less and less clear… I started digging deeper and deeper. By the fall, I was one of a small number of English-speaking journalists on the Maidan when the student protests were broken up. After that, I got a lot of calls from all sorts of media outlets. I had quite a few options about who to work with. I ended up working with Bloomberg, but I also tried freelancing for various major outlets. — When you started working as a journalist, what mattered most to you about the profession? Has your understanding of journalism changed over the years? — I had very nuanced views on a range of issues, but I was also clearly a fairly typical pro-Western Russian liberal. Very radical on some issues. When Arkady Babchenko talked about Estonian tanks on Red Square, it occurred to me that I’d used that exact phrase, half-jokingly, 10 to 15 years before him. Russia could have followed the path of Euro-Atlantic integration, too, like other countries. In many ways, my political views led me into journalism. And then, simply because I’m generally inclined to go to pretty extreme lengths in pursuit of objectivity, my views became more nuanced and changed a great deal. When I realized that my views didn’t reflect reality at all, I adjusted them. — You said that at some point you decided to focus on Ukraine and made it your journalistic specialty. Why did Ukraine interest you more than Russia? — Ukraine was relatively unexplored territory back then, while plenty of excellent journalists, both Russian and Western, were covering Russia. I tried different kinds of journalism. For example, I investigated yet another corrupt official in Putin’s circle, a deputy governor of St. Petersburg, and found a four-star hotel he owned in Prague. I published a story about it for the BBC Russian Service. But I just found that kind of work boring. At some point — I can’t say exactly when — I settled on a principle that’s now in my Twitter bio: I want to tell people what they need to know, rather than what they want to hear. And I think that’s now the main difference between journalism about Russia and journalism about Ukraine. Journalism about Russia is good journalism. People are still reporting on Russia’s military and corruption. I’m not diminishing the work of those journalists in the slightest. But it’s what the audience wants to hear. It’s a kind of confirmation bias . Ukraine is a different story, because there are so many untold stories there. When you talk to Ukrainians, especially people in the political establishment, you realize they’re very aware of this. In private conversations, including at very senior levels, they say things that completely contradict what they say in public. Then some of it comes out in stories like that of Yuliya Mendel , Zelensky’s former press secretary, who began expressing entirely different views. My sources are primarily in Ukraine, and to a much lesser extent in Russia. I have people I can talk to in private and, to some extent, have heart-to-heart conversations with. The picture of Ukraine I get from conversations with my sources, from what Ukrainians say, is very much at odds with the story being told in the mainstream right now. People tell horrifying stories about mobilization, and they themselves have been hiding at home for years. Political sources at very senior levels agree with my analysis of the war and talk a great deal about corruption. There are lots of people like Hetmantsev, but within Ukraine, only [Danylo] Hetmantsev and [Oleksiy] Honcharenko speak out [publicly]. — It sounds as though, when you went to Ukraine, you were idealizing the country to some extent. — There was a lot of idealization. Actually, I was mostly idealizing the West. I’d always done that. To a great extent, what drove my journalism career was my understanding of Western ideals — or, more precisely, the ideals of a liberal democratic society. The problem was that I tried to follow those ideals to the letter. And when you start doing that, you find yourself in serious conflict with people who claim to uphold those ideals, with organizations and entire countries that consider themselves the embodiment of them. — What happened after 2022, when, as I understand it, you could no longer travel to either Russia or Ukraine? — I could no longer report from either country. I’d spent quite a long time reporting for Bloomberg. At the same time, I wrote columns for Al Jazeera and some pieces for bigger outlets, The Washington Post, for example. And I tried my hand at investigative journalism in Latvia and Ukraine. In Latvia, I wrote a story about the Harmony Party, which represented the interests of the Russian-speaking minority. It was very well received and, I think, contributed somewhat to the change of government in Riga and the end of the whole Harmony era there. Another story concerned the far-right party [National Alliance] of the current interior minister [Jānis Dombrava], who’s the one most eager to deport me. It was an investigation into his party’s ties to Russian National Socialists whom I’d met in Kyiv and written other stories about. We now know them as part of the Russian Volunteer Corps — back then, they were all simply connected to Azov. One of them is the Russian neo-Nazi Alexey Lyovkin, a key figure in the Wotanjugend platform. They [National Socialists in Russia] organized the world’s largest National Socialist black metal festival. And in 2019, these people from Wotanjugend were distributing a Russian translation of the manifesto of the man who carried out the terrorist attack in Christchurch, New Zealand — who killed 51 people in mosques. The translation was posted [on their website] suspiciously soon after the attack. An 80-page document in Russian. A Latvian journalist and I established a connection between this political party [National Alliance] and Russian neo-Nazis who’d settled in Kyiv. That seemed pretty shocking, of course. It doesn’t anymore. Another, much bigger project was an investigation by the Ukrainian outlet Zaborona into the murder of Pavel Sheremet, which I took part in. I think those investigations were the main reason I became a target for forces that probably didn’t want what was best for Ukraine — that were more interested in simply having a war happen. There’s a lot to say about the nationalists, but of course many people in Ukraine wanted to fight and win. Arms industry lobbyists wanted a war, too, and that was very noticeable. — Recently, you’ve been publishing in The American Conservative , writing your own analysis blog on Substack, and continuing to publish with Al Jazeera. Why these particular platforms? — Like many other people, I have a big problem with where mainstream journalism has ended up in its coverage of the conflict in Ukraine. But I think my colleagues in America and Europe have had an even bigger problem with coverage of the conflicts in Gaza and Iran. Though the coverage of Russia’s war against Ukraine has also been rather peculiar. So I have complicated views on mainstream journalism. I’ve stepped back from it a little for now. That doesn’t mean I don’t respect major news organizations. I’m a product of the BBC myself. It’s where I learned journalism, my alma mater. [But] now I publish where I can express my thoughts. There’s barely any room left for free thought and free discussion, especially about the Russian-Ukrainian conflict. All these years, people with an interest in keeping the war going have been working to destroy that space in various ways: intimidation, online harassment on Twitter, where most politicians, journalists, and experts are. Thinking objectively and talking honestly about this conflict makes you a target — one these people and organizations want to destroy. And that explains why I’ve become one of their targets. — Let me ask you directly: Have other outlets refused to publish your work? — No, we’ve been drifting apart. I wouldn’t say it’s an unbridgeable divide. I’m still in touch with journalists and editors at mainstream outlets. We have good relationships. I just don’t really agree with their editorial policies right now. As for The American Conservative, they represent a very specific strand of American conservatism known as paleoconservatism . They matter to me because they oppose American interventionism. Their foreign policy analysis really speaks to me and overlaps quite a bit with my own approach, which is more left-liberal. So I’m grateful to them for the opportunity to publish. But you see, my most recent piece was in Jacobin , an outlet more closely associated with democratic socialism in the United States, with Senator [Bernie] Sanders — though I actually criticize Senator Sanders in that piece — and with politicians like [Zohran] Mamdani, the mayor of New York. Leonid Ragozin’s column in Jacobin There’s a very interesting process happening right now that I write about in my articles. Largely in an effort to counter the far-right populists and extremists they constantly compete with, mainstream politicians in Western countries are adopting [equally radical positions]. As a result, mainstream politicians’ own views are becoming quite extreme. It’s most apparent in foreign policy, in their attitudes toward the Russian-Ukrainian conflict and, to a considerable extent, toward Gaza and Iran. Paradoxically, their rivals in far-right parties, like Germany’s AfD, are starting to sound like the voice of reason. Like people who don’t want a nuclear war to wipe us all out. Who don’t want us to spend our entire lives in this endless war, with a front line running through Europe all the time. — Have you ever caught yourself self-censoring? For example, after what happened to TV Rain. Did that worry you at the time, by the way? — I should say that before what happened to TV Rain, exactly the same thing had happened to me. And exactly the same figures in Latvian politics were involved. In my case , Latvian Defense Minister Artis Pabriks wrote an official letter about me [to two media regulators: Latvia’s Public Electronic Mass Media Council and National Electronic Mass Media Council], accusing me of being a Kremlin agent of influence. Then exactly the same thing happened to TV Rain, six months later. In my case, nothing came of it at the time. For TV Rain, it ended with the channel being forced to leave Latvia. Of course I felt I was censoring myself. It seemed to me that I was doing it all the time. At some point, many years ago now, I stopped writing or saying anything about Latvia out of concern for my personal safety. At the same time, as many of my friends know, self-censorship and I don’t get along very well. In any situation, in life or in politics, I tend to say what I think. I think both the attack in 2022 and the current one were entirely about Latvia’s elections . Back then, the defense minister [Artis Pabriks], who published the letter and tried to get me deported, was in a party [Development/For!] that lost the election badly. Now it’s two parties that started this discussion in the final week before the election. In theory, they might not have made it into the Saeima [Latvia’s parliament]. They were fighting to keep their seats. In the end, they got in, but finished in the last two places among the parties that won seats. Now they’re fighting to join the governing coalition. There’s a good chance they’ll get in as two small parties joining the large party [United List] that won the election. I’m caught up in all this almost by chance. I’m just an easy target they use to solve their political problems. The other thing is that one of the parties also has a long-standing personal score to settle with me. They campaigned against me for a very long time, seven years, practically every day, without stopping. It was a nonstop campaign of abuse and smears on Twitter: daily threats and mockery, constant public denunciations sent to Latvia’s State Security Service, and the publication of photos of me taken surreptitiously in Riga. They were shaping public opinion about me. It was an industrial-scale campaign of character assassination . Later, Ukrainian psyops joined in. An InformNapalm article published my 78-year-old mother’s full address in Moscow. The article came out in 11 languages, and the Latvian version appeared on the website of Raivis Zeltīts’s new party [Rising Sun for Latvia]. And now they’ve got what they wanted. — On Latvia’s list of personae non gratae, you’re alongside people like Tina Kandelaki, Dmitry Guberniev, Nikita Mikhalkov, Valery Gergiev, Denis Matsuev, Yekaterina Andreyeva, Polina Gagarina, Shaman… How does that feel? — You’ve listed people who are connected to Putin’s regime and work for it. I don’t work for Putin’s regime. I’m disgusted by it, which is why I left. But I think the people persecuting me politically in Latvia are cut from the same political cloth as Putin’s regime. And unfortunately, they’re taking Latvia in the same direction. It’s very sad, of course. I think the threat of Eastern Europe and all of Europe becoming more like Putin’s Russia, of security concerns being used to justify more control, of whole countries being taken over by political police and intelligence officers, as happened in Russia — all of that has been a very strong motivation for me to warn about this danger. I really wouldn’t want that to happen. Fortunately, it hasn’t happened yet. But there are very strong signs, including in my own case, of a creeping shift toward Putin-style rule. ‘I’m only human, and I probably tend to say more than I should’ — You wrote about a “character assassination campaign involving far right infowar and fake news outfits” intended to “destroy my life” and “put a gag on me as a notable voice in public debate on the Russo-Ukranian war.” What did you mean? — I mean the outlet Visegrád 24 . An outlet with an audience of two million used my interview with Aaron Maté to put words in my mouth that I never actually said. The Russian “opposition journalists” Leonid Ragozin is threatening his new “home country” Latvia again. Speaking on Aaron Maté’s anti-Western propaganda show, he staged that Russia is “compelled” to respond with brutal force to “actions that changes the landscape in the former… — Visegrád 24 (@visegrad24) October 5, 2026 It wasn’t my best interview, but they interpreted it in a way that distorted my thoughts beyond recognition. — You’re talking about your appearance on the podcast “Useful Idiots,” where Aaron Maté and Katie Halper interviewed you. Could it be connected to your being declared persona non grata? — I have no idea whether that interview could have anything to do with the Latvian authorities’ decision. I’ve said all sorts of things over the years. And I’m often not happy with what I’ve said. I haven’t always expressed my thoughts well or clearly. I’m only human, and I probably tend to say more than I should. I think there are information warfare groups on social media that have always looked for a reason to pick apart something I’ve said. Their goal is simply censorship, to shut me up and stop me from saying what I think. To keep my analysis out of the public sphere altogether. The main thing here is the way I’m being banished from Latvia, from my only home. This is a decision made outside the courts. And the people involved talk openly on Twitter about why they chose that particular way of banishing me. They want to keep all this out of Latvia’s court system. Let me quote Rihards Kols, a senior National Alliance politician and member of the European Parliament who could even become [Latvia’s] foreign minister if the party gets that post: He wrote that it’s very important to do this through a persona non grata designation, because that kind of decision can’t be appealed in Latvian courts. It’s a decision made entirely outside the courts. But if they simply revoke my residence permit, then I’ll sue and Latvia will lose, Rihards Kols wrote. You can go look up his post before he deletes it. — One of your most widely discussed statements on the podcast was that Russia sees itself as being under constant pressure from the West, which “compels them to respond” to Western actions in the post-Soviet region. If you say the Russian authorities were forced to act, does that mean you’re absolving them of responsibility? — In that passage, I’m conveying what I think the Kremlin thinks. I’m describing the Kremlin’s motives in my own words — how the Russian government sees its situation, its position in this conflict. They, I say, feel they’re the “weaker side.” And as the weaker side, they feel compelled to compensate by striking first, with a preemptive, devastating blow, a disproportionate response. The “stronger side” can afford to act calmly, to take small, relatively inconspicuous steps, to use salami tactics to force the weaker side into a disproportionate response. That isn’t what Leonid Ragozin thinks. That’s what, in Leonid Ragozin’s view, the Kremlin thinks. — Many people heard it as a justification of Russian aggression. — No, I’m interpreting the Kremlin’s understanding of this situation, explaining it to a Western audience. But you see, this was a live interview. You can pick apart any live interview. The people attacking me, including politicians and experts, say an insane amount of incendiary nonsense. If they were in my position, they’d be thrown out of their countries every two minutes. I’m generally pretty careful about what I say. But I’m human, and some days I feel better than others. I give interviews from time to time. Sometimes I express myself better, sometimes worse. If someone says something awkwardly or unclearly, instead of asking what they meant, what they actually wanted to say, do you really have to punish them in such a completely draconian way? Take away their home, throw them out of the home they’ve spent 12 years building and making their own, turn them into a homeless person? But I want to repeat: We don’t know, and most likely never will know, the grounds for throwing me out. Judging by how Latvian courts have handled such cases, this decision most likely won’t even be made available to the court itself. Because it’s classified. What does it say? Something intelligent, or some nonsense? I don’t know. I can see that the people accusing me over this interview weren’t directly connected to Latvia. And Latvian politicians were actively retweeting all those stories. I was also subjected to the most bizarre allegation that I’d traveled to Russia after 2022. This is being done through various mouthpieces of information warfare. And nobody says it directly, probably because they’re all afraid I’ll just sue for defamation. One politician who talks about this deliberately misspells my surname with an “o,” so that later he can say he wasn’t talking about me at all, but about Dmitry Rogozin, for example. Of course I can respond to all these allegations, but they’re being made on Twitter. They’re not being made in court or before official bodies. This whole thing is about denying me access to justice. I’m accused of all sorts of outrageous sins, but it’s not happening in a courtroom or in government offices. I don’t understand what exactly I’m being accused of. I’ve been denied access to justice in Latvia. Read more Russian-speaking Latvians who back Ukraine and value their language are heading into an election without an obvious political home A new law in Latvia is forcing Russian and Belarusian workers out of hospitals, railways, and power companies — with no severance and no exceptions — One of the public allegations against you concerns your blaming the West for obstructing peace talks. You openly write that the aim of Western strategy now is “not a better Russia or Ukraine, but conflict itself.” You argue that prolonging the conflict benefits Western arms manufacturers and is being used to weaken Russia. — You see, there’s always a danger in talking about very complicated things in simple terms. The West isn’t a single entity, of course. And right now it’s particularly fragmented. The United States, for instance, is very different from the countries of Europe. But I have serious doubts about the motives of a significant part of the Western political establishment in this war. I have a strong sense that the fate of Ukraine and Ukrainians, which is very important to me, isn’t a priority [for part of the Western political establishment]. The priority is the conflict with Russia itself and some illusory goal of weakening Russia and achieving a strategic victory over it. You can find all sorts of quotes from Western politicians, starting with Lindsey Graham, who actually talked about fighting to the last Ukrainian. Quite a few politicians and experts also talk about a strategic victory over Russia as a goal, one that seems less and less achievable. For me, the priority is human life. And I’d really like to see the Ukraine I remember and love exist again. A Ukraine that included Crimea and the Donbas — precisely the regions I know best. That country became something of an ideal for me, or a potential ideal. But right now, I think the priority is preserving what’s still left in Ukraine. Over this summer, [for example,] Ukraine’s steel industry was completely destroyed . — How do you see the war between Russia and Ukraine ending under the current circumstances? — After the enormous loss of life, economic damage, and territorial losses Ukraine has suffered, I don’t see a way to achieve what President Zelensky calls a just peace. Let alone a way to regain the occupied territories. However much I’d like that. I probably shouldn’t say this as a journalist, but I will — this is my position. Given the circumstances, the morally right decision now would be to end the war and try to start some sort of political process that might, over time, restore justice. I have doubts about this [my position], as I think most people do. But ideally, I’d probably like all of that. I can describe possible bargaining scenarios, but I don’t think it’s my role to tell politicians how to negotiate with one another. And of course I deeply regret that the war wasn’t ended earlier, when it could have ended on much better terms for Ukraine. ‘The life I built in Latvia is my real home, my ideal home’ — What kind of life did you build in Latvia, and who has been part of your circle of friends and loved ones lately? What are you losing with this order declaring you “undesirable” in the country? — I don’t want to name my friends, because I’m afraid it might harm them in some way. Probably the only people I want to mention are Lena Nemirovskaya and Yuri Senokosov [who moved to Latvia in 2021], who’ve become very close to me. And I know they feel the same way about me. They founded the School of Civic Education, an organization that was declared “undesirable” and a “foreign agent” in Russia. People who, at the age of 80, were thrown out of Russia and forced into exile. I have quite a lot of friends from all sorts of backgrounds. At some point, half of Moscow descended on Riga. I mean journalists, people I’d met at the Pussy Riot trial, on trips with [Alexey] Navalny when I interviewed him. They expanded my social circle. People who’d always been hard to meet up with in Moscow, because meeting up and arranging anything in Moscow is difficult in general, suddenly turned out to be a 10-minute walk away here. And that’s wonderful, of course. But originally, my social circle in Latvia was very Latvian, very Latvian-speaking. Many of us later went our separate ways politically, but I still have a lot of very good friends who are Latvian citizens. — You said you came to feel that Latvia was your only home. — Yes, I think that will stay with me for the rest of my life. Latvia has a very special place in my heart. And the life I built in Latvia is my real home, my ideal home. I’ve invested a great deal in it emotionally. So much happened there — dramatic things and good, wonderful things. So yes, it’s a great personal tragedy. And that’s why, above all, what’s being done to me seems sadistic. Pointless, stupid, and very sadistic. — You consider yourself a victim of persecution for your political beliefs. But Latvia and other European countries have real reasons to fear Russian influence. In that case, how should a state distinguish an independent journalist with unpopular views from someone knowingly participating in another state’s information campaign? And what is it entitled to do in the latter case? — First, I think that in a country governed by the rule of law, a person should have the right to defend themselves. And that’s a right I’ve been denied. I have no way to defend myself in court against being designated persona non grata. Whether I’m a threat to Latvia, whether I’m spreading certain narratives — though Latvian law doesn’t actually prohibit any narratives, at least none I’ve heard of — is something a court should decide, one way or another. And the second thing that’s probably important to say is this: When people start being punished, especially outside the courts, for inconvenient opinions, whatever those opinions may be, that’s where the rule of law ends. That’s where freedom of speech and constitutional freedoms end. That probably matters. Because what’s at stake is the future of a very complex, imperfect civilization governed by law, but still the best one we have. Whatever comes after that, I’m afraid, will look more like Putin’s Russia. — Can you talk about your plans, about where you intend to settle? Aren’t you afraid you could lose your home yet again there? — No, I’m not going to give the people who continue to persecute me a chance to make my life even worse. So I’m not commenting on my whereabouts. As for plans, they’re very fluid. I’ll have to respond to circumstances as they develop. One way or another, I’ll have to build a new life. But I’ll keep doing my work. That’s what matters most to me. I’ve had a very interesting life so far. The people persecuting me couldn’t even dream of the kind of life I’ve had. Something tells me my life will carry on much the same way — happy and good overall, by my definition of happiness.
