title: LaNeve Redesignates Army’s FCC To Be New Futures and Autonomous Systems Command
body:
The Army’s acting chief of staff announced Tuesday said he has redesignated the service’s Futures and Concepts Command (FCC) to become the recently-announced Futures and Autonomous Systems Command (FASCOM).
Gen. Christopher LaNeve, who also serves as vice chief, approved the move after Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle signed a memo on Oct. 1 to establish FASCOM, with the service detailing the new command’s initial set of projects and plans to develop corps-level autonomous capabilities and formations based around unmanned capabilities.
“We are incorporating autonomous and unmanned systems at every single echelon across the formation with the force structure to match, including introducing UAS and robotics military specialties to integrate these technologies at the point of need,” LaNeve said in remarks at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual conference in Washington, D.C.
The Army’s move on creating FASCOM follows Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s recent announcement on plans for the Pentagon to stand up a new four-star Autonomous Warfare Command (AutoWarCom) ( Defense Daily , Sept. 30).
“The Department of War is committed to not only experimenting, testing and rapidly fielding advanced technologies, but to also proliferate proven technologies throughout our formations,” LaNeve said in his speech.
Along with FASCOM, the Army’s recent memo also called for establishing a new Program Acquisition Executive (PAE) for Autonomy focused on efforts to rapidly field such capabilities by fiscal year 2028 ( Defense Daily , Oct. 5).
“This goes beyond drones,” LaNeve said in a separate statement on Tuesday. “FASCOM will pioneer operational concepts that harness autonomous capabilities across all warfighting functions.”
The Army confirmed that FASCOM will be led by a three-star general officer and the new command will consolidate the work done by the current Combat Capabilities Development Command, Medical Research and Development Command, 75th Innovation Command, Joint Modernization Command and the Transformation Decision Analysis Center.
“This change unifies expertise that the new Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Autonomy will depend on to meet Acting Secretary Telle’s directive to rapidly integrate autonomous technologies across the Army,” the service said in a statement.
The redesignation of FCC comes less than a year after it was officially activated in February ( Defense Daily , Feb. 20).
Lt. Gen. Michael McCurry is the current commanding general of FCC, which functions as a major subordinate command along with Army Recruiting Command and Combined Arms Command under the newly-formed Transformation and Training Command, which was created after the merging of Army Futures Command with Training and Doctrine Command.
The Army said LaNeve has given FASCOM an initial task to develop corps-level autonomous capabilities, noting the service’s five corps will “test equipment, evaluate tactics and make recommendations on accomplishing autonomous mission sets.”
“This approach leverages experimentation to validate concepts that can then be scaled across the Army,” the Army said.
Initial projects for FASCOM’s autonomous development plan include “the testing of an autonomous fires battery and autonomous watercraft company in I Corps, an autonomous armored reconnaissance company in III Corps, an autonomous breaching company in V Corps, autonomous aerial ISR and lift companies in XVIII Airborne Corps and the pairing of manned and unmanned rotary wing aircraft in 8th Army,” according to the Army.
On the last of the five projects, the Army said the idea was formulated at the Army Aviation Center in Fort Rucker, Alabama, and is intended to give “attack aviation pilots direct control of UAS sensors to enable over-the-horizon targeting and synchronize manned-unmanned fires.”
“Fort Rucker is unique in that we can bring together warfighting experts and cutting-edge commercial capabilities to test technology the way we intend to fight it. To ensure that we move swiftly to achieve the Army’s autonomy goals, as of today Fort Rucker will serve as our UAS Autonomy Center of Excellence,” LaNeve said in a statement.
LaNeve has also directed FASCOM to work on creating new capability-based formations built around autonomous long-range fires, protection, tanks, logistics and obstacle breaching, the Army noted.
“These capabilities were specifically selected for their role in enabling operational maneuver and are aligned to the four elements of convergence, strike, close battle, and endurance outlined in the operational warfighting guidance released by the U.S. Army last week,” the Army said.

title: EU cannot be trusted with tournaments after denying visas to gymnasts — minister
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. The politically motivated refusal of visas to Russian gymnasts for participation in the World Championships shows that EU countries cannot be trusted to host international competitions, Russia’s Sports Minister, head of the Russian Olympic Committee Mikhail Degtyarev said.
The Netherlands refused to issue visas to Olympic champions Angelina Melnikova and Victoria Listunova, as well as Anna Kalmykova. The World Artistic Gymnastics Championships will be held from October 17 to 25 in Rotterdam.
"The politically motivated refusal of visas to the Russian gymnasts by the Netherlands again shows that big sports have no place in Europe. Today Europeans have disregarded the decisions of international organizations (the IOC and World Gymnastics) and denied Russians visas, and next they will deny entry to someone else. Russia has always advocated and continues to advocate for equal access for all athletes to compete under its flag without any discrimination. EU countries cannot be trusted with international competitions," Degtyarev wrote on Telegram.
Earlier, TASS reported that gymnasts Daniel Marinov, Arsenii Dukhno, Sergey Naidin, and Alena Glotova, who received Schengen visas, arrived in the Netherlands. Five more athletes included in the main roster of the Russian national team for the World Championships - Lyudmila Roshchina, Milana Kayumova, Ilia Zaika, Savelii Sieedin, and Mukhammadzhon Iakubov - are also awaiting decisions on their visa applications.
The World Championship in Rotterdam will be the first stage of the team qualification for the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles. Based on its results, the three best men’s and three best women’s teams will receive Olympic quotas.

title: Sudan urges France to reopen embassy in Khartoum
body: Sudan’s foreign minister has urged France to reopen its embassy in Khartoum and restore its cultural centres, as the army-aligned government seeks to rebuild diplomatic ties following its return to the capital. Foreign Minister Muhyi al-Din Salim held talks in Khartoum on Tuesday with Jean-Marie Safa, France’s special envoy for Sudan and the Horn of Africa, according to the state-run Sudan News Agency (SUNA). Salim said Sudan wants a new phase in relations with France based on transparency, integrity and facts. He urged Paris to assess conditions in Sudan directly rather than rely on what he described as false narratives promoted by groups seeking to return to power. He cited allegations that the Sudanese army had used chemical weapons as an example of what he called misinformation. The United States accused the Sudanese army of using chemical weapons and announced sanctions in May 2025, including restrictions on U.S. exports to the country and access to credit lines. Khartoum has denied the allegations and repeatedly called on Washington to disclose its evidence. The war between Sudan’s army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which began in April 2023, has devastated large parts of the country, displaced millions of people and disrupted essential services. عُقد أول لقاء في الخرطوم مع وزير الخارجية، محيي الدين سالم، بحضور دبلوماسي فرنسي قدم من باريس. وجرى التأكيد على الرغبة في العمل من أجل جميع السودانيين، إلى جانب بحث سبل إطلاق حوار وطني شامل يمهّد إلى تحقيق المصالحة الوطنية بين أبناء السودان. كما تناول اللقاء تبادل وجهات النظر… pic.twitter.com/hscnonG2fg — La France au Soudan (@FranceauSoudan) October 13, 2026 Salim said Sudan is nearing the end of a difficult period and called for the reopening of France’s diplomatic mission and cultural centres, which he described as important institutions in Sudan’s cultural life. Most European embassies suspended operations or relocated staff after fighting erupted in Khartoum on April 15, 2023. Some Arab and African countries have since reopened their missions in the capital, where security has improved, although fighting continues elsewhere in Sudan. The talks also covered bilateral relations and efforts to promote peace and stability in Sudan and the wider Horn of Africa, SUNA reported. On relations with Ethiopia, Salim said Sudan is open to dialogue with Addis Ababa if it stopped what he described as support for the RSF and actions threatening Sudan’s security. He said Sudan is committed to peace because it understood the suffering caused by war. Envoy Safa said France wants to establish transparent relations with Sudan and help bridge divisions among Sudanese through dialogue aimed at reconciliation, SUNA reported. He expressed hope that Sudanese people could ensure the current conflict would be the country’s last war. A committee is consulting Sudanese political and other groups ahead of a proposed comprehensive dialogue inside the country, an initiative supported by the army-aligned government. Efforts to reach a political settlement face major challenges amid continued fighting and divisions over Sudan’s future. The post Sudan urges France to reopen embassy in Khartoum appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Mack enjoying career season with Edmonton Elks
body:
Reuniting with Cody Fajardo is paying huge dividends for Austin Mack.
Through 16 games in his first season with the Edmonton Elks, Mack has established career highs in catches (79), yards (1,229) and touchdowns (eight). Mack last had numbers like these in his first CFL campaign with the Montreal Alouettes in 2023 (78 receptions, 1,154 yards, four TDs).
The constant in both equations, though, is Fajardo. The veteran quarterback was with Montreal in 2023, leading the team to a Grey Cup championship that season.
This year, Edmonton (12-4) will return to the CFL playoffs for the first time since 2019. It will also host its first post-season contest since 2015.
If Edmonton can split its remaining two regular-season games (Friday versus Winnipeg, at Saskatchewan on Oct. 24), it will cement first in the West and host the division final Nov. 7. The Elks downed Calgary 45-31 in the 2015 West finale before beating Ottawa 26-20 in the Grey Cup, their last CFL title.
The six-foot-one, 208-pound Mack spent his first three CFL seasons with Montreal and finished his ’25 campaign playing in the club’s 25-17 Grey Cup loss to Saskatchewan. He was released Jan. 26 ahead of being due a reported $45,000 roster bonus.
But, with Fajardo’s persistence, the 29-year-old Mack signed a two-year deal with Edmonton three days later.
“It’s funny because Cody never calls anybody in the off-season because he’s with his family,” Mack said. “But he called me every single day until I signed.
“There was a lot that went into it … I wanted to make sure it was the right fit and was a decision me and my family made together even though I had my guy shooting me texts. I think had I gone anywhere else our friendship would’ve probably ended and it’s a good thing we didn’t have to go down that road.”
Fajardo immediately contacted Mack after learning he’d been released by Montreal.
“There was a reason why I called him 360 times to try and get him here,” Fajardo said. “I just know how good he is and how good he was for me in Montreal.
“Everything I thought he’d do here he has done and exceeded. I’m just really happy he’s on the green and gold with me.”
But Fajardo isn’t the only reason for Mack’s success in Edmonton. First and foremost, Mack has remained healthy and been a nice fit in offensive coordinator Jordan Maksymic’s scheme.
“Austin came to his new organization as advertised,” said Kenny Kim of Summit Athletes, Mack’s Florida-based agent. “He’s a prolific receiver in this league and shows it game in and game out.
“A true family man off the field, Austin has exceeded all expectations this year. I know he’ll continue to perform at a very high level and lead his team deep into the playoffs.”
Edmonton earned a 27-12 road win in Hamilton on Friday to clinch a home playoff contest. It was the Elks’ second straight victory over the Ticats and sixth in seven games overall.
Finishing the regular season versus West rivals shouldn’t faze Edmonton, which is 6-2 within its division. The Elks are 1-1 versus Saskatchewan and have already won the season series with Winnipeg (2-0).
Heady stuff for a team that posted a 7-11 record last season to finish fifth in the West. But general manager Ed Hervey signed such veterans as defensive lineman Robbie Smith, defensive back Tyrell Ford and running back Justin Rankin to extensions before getting Fajardo, 34, to put off retirement in December.
Then in free agency, Hervey added such veterans as offensive linemen Coulter Woodmansey, Brendan Bordner and Jordan Murray, receivers Mack, Brendan O’Leary-Orange and Joe Robustelli and defensive lineman Malik Carney.
“This locker room has many great guys who want to win, who want to sacrifice,” Mack said. “It’s a lot of team guys and you need that in this league.”
That’s not to downplay the impact of the Mack-Fajardo chemistry. But the biggest returns on familiarity and time together usually come in big games, especially those in Canada in late October and November.
“Everyone says Canada is cold, and it can be, but the best part about playing football in the cold is you’re playing meaningful games,” Mack said. “One reason why I wanted to come to this team was to contribute to helping this offence be more explosive and be in games and I believe that’s what I’ve done.
“We’ve still got to make sure we secure (a West final home berth) and that’s our biggest focus. If we could, that would be amazing and I’d hope we’d see 60,000 people in Commonwealth (for a division championship game).”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

title: Young girls demand climate action, stronger protection against child marriage
body: Young girls have called for increased investment in education, healthcare and protection as climate change exposes more of them to risks, including child marriage, during Plan International Ghana’s Girls’ Takeover Day on Tuesday, October 13, 2026. The event formed part of activities to commemorate the 2026 International Day of the Girl Child, observed globally on October 11, and featured the launch of Plan International’s State of the World’s Girls 2026 report. The report examines the links between climate change, sexual and reproductive health and rights, and child marriage. The Girls’ Takeover initiative saw children and young people assume leadership roles at Plan International Ghana and UNICEF Ghana to amplify calls for girls’ rights and greater participation in decisions affecting their futures. Speaking at the event, 14-year-old Priscilla, who took over as Country Director of Plan International Ghana for a day, said climate-related disasters were making life increasingly difficult for girls. She said floods, droughts and extreme heat could disrupt education, limit access to healthcare and expose girls to violence, exploitation and pressure to marry at a young age. “We are children. We should be learning, playing and dreaming about our future, not worrying about how climate disasters will affect our lives,” she said. The children outlined five key recommendations to address these challenges, including keeping girls in school during climate-related emergencies, investing in girls’ health and ensuring access to essential services during disasters. They also called for targeted support for girls at greater risk, including those with disabilities, girls from minority communities and those displaced from their homes. The fifth recommendation urged leaders to include girls in climate-related decision-making, arguing that their experiences and ideas should inform policies affecting their lives. “Even though we are young, we understand the challenges we face, and we deserve to be part of decisions about our future,” the children said. Juliet, 21, who took over as UNICEF Ghana’s Officer in Charge for a day, said the initiative provided an opportunity for young people to demonstrate that their voices mattered in discussions about their rights and future. The children also called for an end to child marriage and greater investment in girls’ rights as part of activities marking the 2026 International Day of the Girl Child. They urged stakeholders to work towards a future in which every girl could access education, healthcare and protection, regardless of the climate challenges facing her community. At the close of the event, the substantive Country Director of Plan International Ghana and UNICEF Ghana’s Officer in Charge assured the children that their proposals would be considered for action. The assurance followed the girls’ calls for stronger measures to protect their rights and ensure their participation in decisions affecting them. “Our future matters. Our voices matter. And it is time to #ChangeHerForecast,” they said, as they formally launched Plan International’s State of the World’s Girls 2026 report.

title: Ex-gang boss sentenced to 40 years for orchestrating Tupac Shakur’s murder
body: Former gang boss Duane “Keffe D” Davis has been sentenced to at least 40 years in prison for orchestrating the murder of Tupac Shakur. A jury found Davis, 63, guilty in September of one count of murder with a deadly weapon for the rap superstar’s death in a drive-by shooting in Las Vegas on 7 September 1996. He has said he will appeal the verdict. Prosecutors argued that although Davis did not fire the gun himself, he was the ringleader of the group that committed the murder. He admitted in his memoir that he had provided the gun used in the crime. Davis’ conviction was the first in a cold case that has intrigued hip-hop fans for nearly 30 years. Prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo argued during Tuesday’s sentencing hearing that Davis spent years “publicly grandstanding” and bragging about his role on Shakur’s death, which he said, “had wide-ranging effects upon the world”.

title: From near-deferral to three awards: UMaT graduate’s academic journey
body: Solicity Amankwa-Taylor, a graduate of the University of Mines and Technology (UMaT), has earned three academic awards after financial difficulties nearly forced her to defer her studies, a challenge she says was eased by the MTN Bright Scholarship. Solicity, who studied Environmental and Safety Engineering, faced growing financial pressure after her father lost his job, leaving her mother’s business as the family’s main source of income. With her elder brother also pursuing tertiary education, meeting tuition, accommodation and other university expenses became increasingly difficult. She said the situation left her considering external financial support or deferring her studies until her family’s circumstances improved. “Things became tough financially to the point that I had to either find a means of financial support or defer. When I found out I had been selected as an MTN Bright Scholar, I had hope in achieving my dreams again,” she said. The scholarship provided financial support for tuition and accommodation, easing the burden on her family and allowing her to concentrate on her academic work. “The scholarship helped me channel all my focus on my studies. With a sound mind, I was also able to help some of my colleagues academically,” she added. Solicity’s academic performance earned her three awards during her university journey. At the 9th Ghana Mining Industry Awards, she was named Best Level 200 Female Engineering Student. She also received the Prof. Newton Attah Amegbey Award for Best Graduating Student in the Department of Environmental and Safety Engineering and the Prof. Douglas Boateng Award for Best Graduating Student in the Faculty of Geosciences and Environmental Studies at graduation. She is currently undertaking her national service as a Health, Safety and Environment (HSE) personnel at YILPORT-ATSL in Takoradi, where she is applying the knowledge and skills acquired during her studies. Her experience forms part of stories highlighting the impact of the MTN Bright Scholarship as MTN Ghana marks 30 years of operations in the country under the theme, “30 Years of Progress, Power to You.” The scholarship, an initiative of the MTN Ghana Foundation, supports brilliant but financially disadvantaged students in public tertiary institutions. It covers tuition, accommodation, stipends for reading materials and a laptop to help beneficiaries pursue their education. Solicity’s journey illustrates how financial assistance can help students overcome barriers to completing their education and prepare for professional careers.

title: Pope Leo XIV diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, which was successfully removed
body:
VATICAN CITY, October 13. /TASS/. Pope Leo XIV has undergone surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, according to a statement by his doctors Luigi Carbone and Stefano Margaritora that was released by the Holy See Press Office.
"An intraoperative histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma (cancerous tumor - TASS), as suspected from the preoperative examinations," the statement says. "To ensure a radical resection, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique."
The 71-year-old pontiff was in the operating room for about three hours.

title: Court overrules El-Rufai’s objection to DSS forensic witness
body: A Kaduna State High Court on Tuesday has overruled an objection by former Governor Nasir El-Rufai’s defence team to the testimony of the Department of State Services (DSS) digital forensic expert. The presiding Judge, Justice Darius Khobo ruled that the prosecution could call the witness, who was subpoenaed by the court, despite his name and evidence summary being absent from the prosecution’s witness list. The judge held that the defence’s right to fair hearing could be protected by allowing it to cross-examine the witness. The ruling followed objections by El-Rufai’s senior counsel, Paul Erokoro, who argued that the defence had not received the witness’s evidence summary or the subpoena. Erokoro submitted that the omission denied the defence adequate notice to prepare for cross-examination and understand the case it was required to answer. The ICPC prosecution counsel, Ayodele Adedipe, however, argued that failure to include a subpoenaed witness in the proof of evidence did not automatically render the testimony inadmissible. In its ruling, the court confirmed that the witness had been subpoenaed through an order signed by the court on June 30, 2026. Khobo said the prosecution’s position reflected the applicable law, citing previous cases in support of the ruling. The judge held that the witness’s absence from the prosecution’s witness list and evidence summary did not prevent him from testifying because he had been subpoenaed. He added that the defence’s fair-hearing concerns could be addressed by allowing it to cross-examine the witness. Earlier, the DSS digital forensic examiner, Shegun Kayode, testified about a forensic examination of communication records and audio recordings allegedly linked to the defendant. Kayode told the court that specialised software revealed two-way communications involving El-Rufai and suspected associates, including Bashir El-Rufai and another person, between October. 25 and 28, 2025. He said the findings prompted further analysis of audio recordings received from a communication intelligence server. The witness explained that he immediately created a forensic image of the original audio file, sealed it and secured it to preserve its technical integrity. Kayode said subsequent software examination showed that the audio was authentic and had not been artificially generated or manipulated using artificial intelligence. The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that El-Rufai arrived at the court amid heavy security, accompanied by his wife, Asiya El-Rufai, and Isa Ashiru Kudan, the governorship candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) in Kaduna State. El-Rufai was brought to court for the continuation of his trial over alleged corruption in a suit filed against him by the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC). During the proceedings, an audio recording of his interrogation by the DSS concerning the alleged importation of about 10 kilogrammes of thallium sulphate, a highly toxic and strictly regulated substance, into Nigeria was played. The recording, which lasted about one hour and 30 minutes, contained the interrogation and other exchanges. The case was adjourned until November. 30 and December 1 for continuation of the cross-examination of the DSS witness by the defence counsel. Speaking with journalists after the court proceedings, Adedipe said the prosecution had opened its case by calling its first witness, a forensic expert. He said the witness testified and tendered a forensic investigation report before cross-examination commenced. Adedipe explained that the proceedings took considerable time because of objections and legal arguments but said the prosecution was able to conclude its presentation with the witness for the day. He confirmed that the case had been adjourned until November 30 and December 1 for continuation of cross-examination. Erokoro, counsel to El-Rufai, said the prosecution had opened its case and called its first witness, adding that the lengthy proceedings showed the parties’ commitment to ensuring the trial progressed. He expressed confidence that his client would be discharged and acquitted of all the charges. Erokoro said the defence had begun examining the witness’s testimony and would continue to scrutinise the evidence when the court reconvened. He maintained that the next hearing would provide the defence with an opportunity to test the accuracy and credibility of the prosecution’s evidence. The post Court overrules El-Rufai’s objection to DSS forensic witness appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Vatican says surgery confirms Pope Leo has lung cancer, lower lobe of right lung removed
body: Pope Leo XIV’s surgery confirmed that he has lung cancer and he had the lower lobe of his right lung removed, the Vatican said Tuesday. The tests confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin after the surgery. It said the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests and was confirmed during surgery.   The 71-year-old was in the operating room for about 3 hours, the statement said. The surgery itself lasted approximately 90 minutes. “The surgery was successful, and there were no complications,” the statement said. Leo underwent surgery Tuesday to remove a lung nodule and the Vatican said the operation was completed “successfully, on schedule and as planned.” Leo had walked into Rome's Gemelli hospital through the main entrance earlier in the day and waved to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered to greet him. The surgery was performed by a team led by Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.   The American pontiff has offered a rare level of transparency about the first publicly disclosed major health problem of his 17-month papacy. He revealed the discovery of the small, localized nodule during his Sunday noon prayer and announced that he would have it removed. Oncologists said prior to the operation that even if the nodule turned out to be cancerous, Leo’s prognosis is “excellent” since it will have been removed at an early stage. The Vatican on Monday canceled all Leo’s audiences through Oct. 20. While Gemelli has a specific papal apartment that past popes have used, complete with a private chapel on the 10th floor, Leo will actually be staying in a nearby room since the papal apartment is currently undergoing renovations, according to the Vatican press office. The nodule was discovered during regular checks, the Vatican has said. “I think he has had a bit of luck. They found something that was asymptomatic — a lung nodule, possibly a tumor. He might call it something else we call it luck,” he said.

title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1693: Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv before air raid sirens, as fears grow that the US could cut launch warning data
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Exclusives “Now it’s your turn”: US envoys planned to show Moscow a refinery pause and a diesel deal, then ask for something back, a source tells Reuters . Ukraine’s part of that exchange was to stop striking Russia’s oil plants, a request Kushner repeated at the Miami meeting. Military Ukrainian scouts used a captured Russian soldier’s radio to gather intelligence for four days . Recon soldiers shared stories about their daily lives with ArmyInform. No contact with command, a comrade maimed by a mine. A former TV director fought—and halted the Russians . He saved three soldiers in six months, ArmyInform says. One wounded comrade he could only hear on the radio. Ukraine says it hit 12 Russian refineries in September. No refinery strikes reported since Trump’s “energy ceasefire” . Zelenskyy said Russia’s attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities continued after Trump’s announcement, while Moscow had yet to confirm a ceasefire. The night Trump announced a diesel deal with Putin, drones knocked out more than half the tanks at a Russian fuel-export terminal . The Rostov-on-Don site, which loads oil products onto river and sea tankers, burned for two days and was still smoking on the third. “We don’t need to hit the entire plant”—Ukraine’s drones go for refinery parts sanctions make hard to repair . Of 54 strikes The Washington Post examined, more than half appear to have damaged the units that start turning crude into fuel. Intelligence and technology Ukraine’s swimming robot can tow 10 tons, its maker says. Hook up a gun, and the shells ride aboard . It has already swum across the Desna River, its team says, and Ukraine’s Defense Ministry cleared it for use in 2025. Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv before sirens, gap that lands hard amid fears that Washington could cut data that warns of launches . The alert came late because Ukrainian radar detected the missiles only during the attack, with no advance data on launches, the Air Force says. Kinzhal is 90% identical to Iskander-M: Ukraine’s intelligence identifies 58 companies in production chain . Russia is developing a modified version of the Kinzhal missile, equipped with a warhead that strikes targets with fragments and a blast wave. Built by Ukraine’s ex-defense minister and unit that wrecked $12 billion of Russian gear, new interceptor downs two jet drones over Kyiv . Mykhailo Fedorov and Lasar’s Group commander Pavlo Yelizarov developed the drone in a month, Fedorov says. Russia is building satellite network that could put all of Europe in reach, defense executive warns . Oleksandr Danyliuk, head of the European defense-tech firm Destinus, called Russia’s Rassvet system an extraordinary threat, first to Ukraine and then to Europe. International Ukraine wins seat on UN Human Rights Council, vows to seek accountability for Russian abuses . Elected with 162 votes, Ukraine says it will focus on documenting violations, protecting prisoners of war and unlawfully detained civilians, and returning children taken by Russia. Finland calls for EU tourist visa ban on Russians until Moscow ends war against Ukraine as bloc weighs tougher restrictions . As suspected Russian sabotage and other hybrid operations spread across Europe, EU officials are weighing tighter restrictions on Russian travel, diplomats, and former combatants to reduce security risks. Germany works to organize a Coalition of the Willing meeting as Russia strikes Ukraine’s energy sector . Ukraine and Germany have also agreed to hold a meeting of national security advisers in the E3 format. France seizes Russian shadow fleet tanker in Indian Ocean, vows to combat illicit oil trade “wherever it may be in the world” . The French Navy intercepted the DF Peak in the Indian Ocean over suspicions it was sailing under a false flag. Russia relies on shadow fleet tankers to keep oil revenues flowing despite Western sanctions. Germany detains two Turkish nationals suspected of torching a Polish Starlink station that helps route internet to Ukraine . Polish radio reports that two more people who may be tied to the arson are in German custody. Russia’s sabotage of Europe should bring Ukraine more weapons through US purchase scheme, with clear statement of where its red lines lie, NATO’s top European commander says . The PURL program lets allies fund US-made weapons for Ukraine and drew nearly $5.5 billion in pledges before May. EU blacklists 1,569 Russian arms suppliers and their bosses in its biggest sanctions round ever, as Trump eases up on Moscow . Most of the listed firms feed the supply chain behind the ballistic missiles Russia fires at Ukrainian cities, and EU ministers vowed to keep up the pressure despite the US-Russia fuel arrangement. Humanitarian and social impact Russia used civilians as human shields, then shelled them near Kupiansk, Ukraine’s Khartiia says . Aerial reconnaissance footage recorded casualties among a group that included two women and a child, according to Khartiia. The Ukrainian corps says Russian media could use the incident to accuse Kyiv of attacking civilians. Russian strike collapses a Kharkiv apartment stairwell and kills three, days after the US waived sanctions on Russia’s diesel . Rescuers dug through the night to reach the people buried in the four-story building, while the White House still wants Kyiv to stop striking Russian refineries. Ukraine’s largest steelworks begins cold shutdown after extensive damage from Russian strikes, saying safe operation is impossible while war continues . The plant will spend two months shutting down safely before mothballing its industrial assets, with any restart dependent on conditions after the war. Political and legal developments Energy truce with strings attached: Kyiv reportedly told to spare Russian refineries or lose US intelligence and arms . EU loans ease Ukraine’s budget, yet satellite data, Patriot interceptors, and US-made weapons still hinge on Washington, giving US President Donald Trump room to squeeze Kyiv. US continues sharing intelligence with Ukraine, Trump says amid Russia deal backlash. Questions remain over missed warning for latest attack . Ukraine received no advance warning before Russia launched five ballistic missiles and more than 100 drones, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, raising questions about how intelligence support was functioning. Frozen assets, embargoes, entry bans: Ukraine names the pressure it wants the EU to put on Moscow . Kyiv says it is ready for energy, food-security, and full ceasefires—and that Moscow has to be forced to agree. “Zelenskyy is helping Democrats”: Trump’s MAGA base accuses Ukraine of trying to swing US midterms, says journalist in US . The narrative runs across all levels of the US information space, from anonymous accounts to national television. Bipartisan US senators say Trump’s Russian diesel deal conflicts with 2022 ban, as he presses Kyiv to spare Russian refineries . The administration says the deal will lower fuel prices, but lawmakers warn it could help finance Russia’s war against Ukraine. For years, Hungary tied Ukraine’s whole EU course to ethnic Hungarians’ language rights. Kyiv has now passed the schooling law meant to lift the block . Hungary had blocked four stages of Ukraine’s membership process over the matter. Zelenskyy says Ukraine could hold elections if Russia agrees to 60-day ceasefire. Moscow counters with truce lasting only voting day . Spokesperson Dmitry Peskov says Ukraine needs the 60 days not to hold elections but to heal its wounds and keep fighting. title: OpenAI employee arrested for allegedly planting a bug in a conference room
body:
An OpenAI engineer was arrested after the company said it discovered a “sophisticated recording device” hidden in one of its offices. The employee was identified as Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national. Alfozan is charged with using or endeavoring to use a device to intercept oral communications, according to a press release from the Department of Justice.
OpenAI’s post about the incident says it used its AI models to “understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier.”
As noted by the DOJ, OpenAI found the device plugged into a TV’s USB port in an executive conference room, where discussions about “highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information” often take place.
Alfozan didn’t have access to this room, but CCTV footage allegedly showed him “near the executive conference room on multiple dates prior to the device’s discovery,” according to the DOJ. Footage also captured Alfozan appearing to look behind the TV where the device was installed, federal prosecutors claim.
[Image: A photo allegedly showing Alfozan looking behind the TV where the device was installed. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-13-at-5.24.17-PM.png?quality=90&strip=all]
The device was covered in toilet paper and installed on or around September 28th. Its contents were encrypted. Additionally, the DOJ claims OpenAI security discovered a bag Alfozan left in another room inside the company’s office, where they found his wallet, ID, and another recording device.
OpenAI says it fired the employee and referred the incident to the FBI. Alfozan was arrested Friday and has remained in custody since, appearing in federal court for the first time on Tuesday.
> We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices. We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work.
> At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated.
> We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance. Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats.
[Media: https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28813506-openai-listening-device-us-v-abdulrahman-alfozan-complaint/]
[Media: https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28813505-govuscourtscand48082920-1/]
Update, October 13th: Added information from the DOJ.

title: The weaponisation of yesterday, By Umar Yakubu
body:
If Nigeria is to break this destructive cycle, we must transition from what Nietzsche termed “reactive” history to a critical history — a deliberate practice that scrutinises past structural failures, disarms historical grievances, and prioritises civic nation-building over score-settling… Until we stop using yesterday as a weapon to fight today’s political battles, we will remain trapped in Hegel’s grim reality: a nation that speaks of its history incessantly, yet learns absolutely nothing from it.
An excess of history makes life wither and degenerate – Nietzsche
During the recent presentation of the book, Emirs of Zazzau: A Biographical Study (1808–2025), in Zaria, Professor Usman Bugaje made a compelling case for the imperative of historical knowledge. He reminded the audience of the indispensable need to study history if we are to understand our present and navigate our future.
His call echoes a familiar refrain heard across our public space: we must study history so that we do not repeat it. Yet, as the contemporary state of our country so vividly demonstrates, this moral maxim is flawed in its popular execution. Do we truly learn from history in Nigeria? Or do we absorb the past merely to stock an arsenal of grievances, inciting new hatreds under the guise of remembrance?
When examined through the lens of political philosophy, Nigeria’s fraught relationship with its past reveals a tragic paradox: historical knowledge, rather than serving as a lamp for national building and institutional enlightenment, has too often been transformed into a flame for social division.
In his Lectures on the Philosophy of History , the German philosopher Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel made a stark observation that remains unnerving in its precision: “What experience and history teach is this — that nations and governments have never learned anything from history, or acted upon principles deduced from it.”
Hegel’s insight was born, not out of structural critique of human governance. States rarely act out of wisdom derived from old textbooks. In Nigeria, this Hegelian paradox is visible in the cyclical nature of our political and economic crises. The structural failures that precipitated the tragic collapse of the First Republic — unbridled regionalism, electoral fraud, state-sanctioned corruption, and the politicisation of everything serious, such as the security and economy — are continuously replicated by successive generations of political elites. Each generation claims to understand the national tragedies of the past, yet each reproduces the exact institutional dynamics that triggered those ruptures.
We quote history in anniversaries and public lectures, but our approach to governance largely remains unchanged. Some will argue that it is worse. We do not learn from history because we treat historical knowledge as an ornamental academic exercise, rather than an imperative for structural reform.
When history is weaponised…memory becomes a catalyst for retribution instead of being a teacher of reflection, caution and progress. Every new generation is taught whom to mistrust based on acts committed long before they were born.
If we do not extract constructive lessons from the past, what then do we do with it? We seem to have turned it into a weapon.
In his essay On the Use and Abuse of History for Life , Friedrich Nietzsche distinguished between historical memory that serves human flourishing and history that poisons the present. Nietzsche warned against an obsession with the past that creates a “reservoir for grievances” — a state wherein a society becomes so intoxicated by old injuries that it loses the capacity to build a viable future.
This, for me, is the central dilemma of modern Nigeria. I have often told a few friends that I sympathise with people who possess retentive memories, because most of them use that gift to remember grievances, rather than the good. The engagement with our past has largely devolved into a competitive accounting of historical injury. The 1966 military coups and the devastating Civil War are rarely examined through an objective, institutional framework meant to foster structural reconciliation. Instead, they are routinely weaponised in daily political discourse to justify ethno-regional marginalisation or to cultivate sub-national resentment.
Across the geopolitical zones, historical narratives of pre-colonial dominance, colonial favour, and post-independence betrayals are invoked not to build empathy, but to validate contemporary prejudice, resource hoarding, and political exclusion. And who benefits from all this chaos? The people or the elite?
As my friend Husein Adeto Bello succinctly observed, the underlying issue lies in why people engage with the past in the first place: many study history merely to acquaint themselves with historic grievances and inherit legacy talking points, without ever pausing to ask what they can do to ensure their generation — and the next — does not perpetuate those same grievances.
When history is weaponised in this manner, memory becomes a catalyst for retribution instead of being a teacher of reflection, caution and progress. Every new generation is taught whom to mistrust based on acts committed long before they were born.
This brings us to a fundamental question in the philosophy of history: Whose history is actually being told?
History is never a neutral recording of facts; it is an interpretive narrative shaped by power and context. In a multi-ethnic federation formed through arbitrary colonial amalgamation, there is no singular, universally accepted “Nigerian narrative.” There exists, instead, a contested marketplace of competing ethnic, regional, and religious memories.
When history is learnt through the narrow lens of tribal insularity, it fails to construct a shared civic identity. Instead, it codifies “us versus them” dynamics, ensuring that the act of remembering directly incites more hatred. And we can’t grow with such history.
The historical decision to remove history from the basic school curriculum for years left a critical void. A generation grew up learning their past not from rigorous, critical academic inquiry, but from informal, highly partisan narratives. These informal histories function primarily as national myths of triumph and victimisation:
When history is learnt through the narrow lens of tribal insularity, it fails to construct a shared civic identity. Instead, it codifies “us versus them” dynamics, ensuring that the act of remembering directly incites more hatred. And we can’t grow with such history.
The continuous cycle of political instability, inter-communal conflict, and ethnic polarisation in Nigeria validates the fear that knowing the past can easily degenerate into nursing old wounds.
If Nigeria is to break this destructive cycle, we must transition from what Nietzsche termed “reactive” history to a critical history — a deliberate practice that scrutinises past structural failures, disarms historical grievances, and prioritises civic nation-building over score-settling.
Until we stop using yesterday as a weapon to fight today’s political battles, we will remain trapped in Hegel’s grim reality: a nation that speaks of its history incessantly, yet learns absolutely nothing from it.
Umar Yakubu is the executive director of the Center for Fiscal Transparency and Public Integrity.

title: LaNeve to industry: ‘We are not walking away from modernization’
body: The U.S. Army’s top officer sought to reassure industry leaders that the service remains committed to modernization and autonomous systems, announcing a new name for the command charged with shaping the future force during remarks at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, D.C. Acting Army Chief of Staff Gen. Christopher LaNeve said that the Futures and Concepts Command has been redesignated as U.S. Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command, or FASCOM. The change comes as the Army aligns its weapons purchases, force structure and training around new “How the Army Fights” guidance, which was published last week and explains how the service intends to wield land power in future wars. “We are not walking away from modernization,” LaNeve said, addressing the industry partners directly at one point in his speech. “We are sprinting towards, it,” he said, adding “and we are doing so responsibly with a recognition that resources are not endless.” LaNeve has charged FASCOM with developing corps-level autonomous capabilities through experimentation and testing. According to a Tuesday release, the three-star command will have “capability-based formations centered on autonomous long-range fires, protection, tanks, logistics and obstacle breaching,” and will include some of the Army’s first 390A Robotic Technicians , which were activated this month. The Army said it chose those capabilities based on their ability to affect maneuver and their alignment to the “four elements” of land power outlined in last week’s guidance: convergence, strike, close battle and endurance. “This goes beyond drones,” LaNeve said in the release, “FASCOM will pioneer operational concepts that harness autonomous capabilities across all warfighting functions.” The Army has come under fire recently after shuttering its experimental drone battalion in Europe less than a year after launching the novel unit to test how such a formation could operate. According to The Wall Street Journal , the decision to end the experiment — the brainchild of LeNeve’s predecessor, Randy George — came as part of LeNeve’s broad “back-to-basics” approach. In September, a bipartisan group of lawmakers signed a letter expressing concern about eliminating the 600-member “Unmanned Assault Battalion,” which was created as part of the 173rd Airborne Brigade. The legislators questioned how the U.S. would continue to learn drone warfare from Ukraine. In a September media roundtable, Maj. Gen. Christopher Norrie, the acting Commanding General of U.S. Army Europe and Africa, said the future of the U.S. Army’s drone warfare is spread across formations, not condensed into one unit. “In Ukraine and Russia you’ve seen those armies create brigades and entire unmanned systems forces, whereas the U.S. Army’s approach has been to decentralize; to accelerate learning across all units,” he said, adding that the Army is aiming to push one-way attack drones to the squad level in the near future.

title: Nigeria Mourns 140 Migrants Killed in Djibouti Boat Tragedy, Calls for Action Against Irregular Migration
body: Michael Olugbode in Abuja The Federal Government has expressed condolences to Djibouti following the death of nearly 140 migrants, including 15 children, in a boat disaster off the country’s coast, calling for urgent collective action to address the root causes of irregular migration. Nigeria, in a statement issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Abuja, said the boat capsized between October 8 and 9, 2026, leaving scores of people missing, according to the International Organisation for Migration (IOM). The government expressed sympathy to the bereaved families and solidarity with the government and people of Djibouti over the tragedy, describing the incident as a grim reminder of the dangers confronting migrants who undertake perilous journeys in search of economic opportunities. The statement, signed by the ministry’s spokesperson, Oluwafemi Adeniyi, said the disaster underscored the urgent need to tackle the underlying factors driving irregular migration, strengthen the fight against migrant smuggling and human trafficking, and promote safe, orderly and regular migration. It stressed that efforts to prevent such tragedies must align with relevant African Union frameworks and applicable international instruments. Nigeria further emphasised that protecting migrants, particularly children and other vulnerable persons, was a shared responsibility requiring sustained cooperation among countries of origin, transit and destination, as well as regional and international organisations. According to the government, stronger collaboration is essential to prevent further loss of life, protect migrants’ fundamental rights and dignity, and ensure that migration is managed safely and humanely. The Federal Government reaffirmed its commitment to working with the United Nations, the African Union and other relevant stakeholders to strengthen migration management, raise awareness about the dangers of irregular migration and develop practical measures to address its root causes. It also called for renewed international cooperation to safeguard human life along migration routes across Africa and beyond. The tragedy adds to concerns over the risks faced by migrants travelling along dangerous routes in pursuit of better economic prospects, reinforcing calls for stronger action against criminal networks that facilitate irregular journeys and for more sustainable solutions to the factors compelling people to leave their homes. Nigeria reiterated its deepest sympathies to all those affected by the disaster and urged collective efforts to prevent similar tragedies.

title: Israelis aren’t afraid of Iran, they’re afraid of supermarket prices, Zelekha says - interview
body: The Economic Party leader promises sweeping changes to living costs within three months of becoming finance minister—and threatens to bring down any government that gets in his way.Israel's young people have faced Iran, Hezbollah, and Hamas, but the price of filling a shopping cart still frightens them, Economic Party leader Yaron Zelekha told The Jerusalem Post on Tuesday.“Our young people deserve to live, not just survive. They are not afraid of the Iranians. They were not afraid of Hezbollah or Hamas. But they are afraid of a trip to the supermarket.”Their mothers, he added, fear their children will leave Israel because they cannot afford to buy a home. Those pressures drive his campaign to become finance minister - and, he warned, keeping a government together would not take priority over addressing them.“If anyone gets in my way, I will bring down their government,” he said, stating he would demand control of the Finance Ministry and the Competition Authority in coalition negotiations.It is a warning he would apply to either political bloc. Whether Benjamin Netanyahu, Naftali Bennett, or Gadi Eisenkot becomes prime minister, Zelekha said he would insist on the authority to implement his economic program and would be prepared to bring down the government if obstructed.Zelekha's five-step plan to lower cost of living as soon as he takes the helmHis opening offer to voters is equally bold: five measures to tackle living costs, with a difference households would feel within three months of his taking office.“I plan to take five steps as the opening move in a fight against the cost of living that will last throughout the government's term,” Zelekha said.The first two would abolish all tariffs, without exception, and eliminate import quotas.The third would prevent monopolies in domestic production from also acting as importers. Zelekha argued that companies operating in both markets use their control of imports to block competition against their locally produced goods.His fourth measure would prohibit exclusive import agreements and prevent an importer controlling imports from one major international manufacturer from also taking control of imports from another manufacturer that should compete with it.Finally, he would move the Competition Authority into the Finance Ministry, placing it under his supervision so that he could oversee enforcement of competition law.Zelekha described the package as an opening intervention that would produce a significant change on its own, followed by further reforms throughout the government's term.Asked how quickly people would notice the difference, he gave a timeline of months, not years.“Within three months from the day I take my seat, you will not recognize the country,” he said. Zelekha further insisted that his premise would not require any funding, and would actually generate money.Like its citizens, the government also pays inflated prices for its purchases, he argued. Meanwhile, households spending more on necessities have less money available for other economic activity, slowing the economy and limiting growth in tax revenues.Lowering those costs, he maintained, would benefit public finances as well as consumers.Zelekha's willingness to negotiate with either bloc comes with an insistence that the identity of the prime minister would not change his economic strategy.“None of them will change my strategy, because implementing it will be entrusted to me. I will be finance minister, and I will not allow any of them to interfere.”If a prime minister obstructed him, he said, he would not hesitate to bring down the government and move to the opposing bloc. He presented his independence from both camps as a source of negotiating power.“Although my positions are right-wing, my conditions are substantive matters of principle.”Beyond control of the Finance Ministry and Competition Authority, Zelekha set two further conditions.“We will not sit in a government that includes Arab parties, and we will not sit in a government that allows draft evasion.”He called for Arabs to perform national service and haredim to serve in the military, saying the state should create frameworks that allow haredi recruits to preserve their religious beliefs.Those arrangements, he said, should be accompanied by higher pay for regular soldiers and better conditions for reservists. At the same time, he argued that people avoiding service should not continue receiving state benefits.For Zelekha, demanding broader participation in service also means finding the money to support those who serve. He criticized an approach that relies on aggressive rhetoric against population groups without providing the resources needed to improve daily life.A partnership rooted in rejecting the status quoThat connection between service and economic policy is central to his partnership with Yoaz Hendel, which Zelekha said followed more than half a year of discussions.“Neither of us is willing to let the status quo continue.”He described their shared objective as shaking a system in which some benefit from connections between wealth and political power while others maintain arrangements allowing them to avoid military service.Hendel, he said, brings plans to improve reservists' conditions and establish military frameworks capable of accommodating haredim. Zelekha would seek the financial resources to implement them.Asked whether either had made concessions to establish the alliance, he said their agendas reinforced each other. Both, he added, hold right-wing positions, oppose a Palestinian state, and support strengthening settlement in the West Bank.Zelekha pointed to the haredi campus at Ono Academic College as an example of a framework that allowed students to enter the workforce while maintaining their religious identity. He argued that suitable military frameworks could follow the same principle.“But those plans require money. I know how to bring in the money.”

title: Report: Airlines will face shortage of new airplanes until at least 2030
body: Airlines waiting for new airplanes face several more years of delivery shortages, with engine availability, supplier bottlenecks and certification delays expected to constrain production until at least 2030. That is the outlook from aviation analytics company Cirium, which released its annual fleet forecast on October 13, 2026, as the company expects manufacturers to remain unable to meet airline demand throughout the remainder of the 2020s. “Long-term aircraft demand remains strong, but the pace of growth increasingly depends on the industry’s ability to deliver,” said Stephen Burnside, Global Head of Cirium Ascend Consultancy. Cirium forecasts about 43,000 deliveries of new commercial passenger and cargo aircraft between 2026 and 2045, worth $3.2 trillion at 2026 prices. These jets and turboprops will allow airlines to expand their fleets and replace aging aircraft. But the wait for replacements is already growing more expensive. The International Air Transport Association (IATA) said in June 2026 that airlines were short of more than 5,000 fuel-efficient aircraft they had expected to receive by now. With fewer replacements available, carriers are keeping older airplanes flying longer, spending more on maintenance and paying higher lease rates. They are also missing out on the lower fuel bills newer aircraft would bring. IATA said the order backlog exceeded 18,000 aircraft and the average fleet age had reached a record 15.2 years. It estimated that supply chain failures cost airlines at least $11 billion in 2025, with higher fuel prices adding to the burden. IATA said engine durability issues, spare-parts shortages and limited maintenance capacity were disrupting operations as well. It has urged manufacturers to provide earlier warnings of delays and give airlines more options for obtaining approved parts and repairs. Despite those pressures, Cirium expects the global passenger fleet to exceed 50,000 aircraft by 2045. Higher fuel costs, geopolitical disruption and trade uncertainty could alter airlines’ expansion plans, but the forecast still points to sustained demand for new airplanes, the company said. title: Show HN: Stack Tender, supplement tracking and product scanning
body:
