title: IDF to protect Israel ‘from the river to the sea,’ Netanyahu vows in visit to West Bank seam line
body: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu decried the Tulkarm refugee camp as a “terrorist stronghold” during a Tuesday visit to the West Bank seam line, vowed that the IDF will remain in control of the area, and promised to safeguard Israeli territory “from the Jordan River to the sea.”In a video statement released by the Prime Minister's Office, Netanyahu referenced a Sunday High Court of Justice order for the state to provide a timeline for the return of displaced Palestinians to refugee camps in the area.“I heard that someone at the High Court of Justice says the residents should be brought back here. These are not residents; they are terrorists,” he claimed. During the visit to the West Bank border, IDF, Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency), and Border Police commanders briefed Netanyahu on security measures in the area and ongoing efforts to address threats of terrorism that may emerge from the refugee camps. Netanyahu praised the IDF for their efforts to clear Tulkarm of extremism through extensive counterterrorism operations, saying that troops did an “excellent job.”“There will be no Arab army west of the Jordan River; there will be the IDF,” he continued. “The one who will control this territory and remain in it is the IDF.” Netanyahu warns that Israel's enemies may test security ahead of electionsThe prime minister emphasized Tulkarm's proximity the the coast, describing the strip of Israeli territory between the West Bank border and the water as a “narrow waist.”“We are safeguarding the area from the Jordan River to the sea. Our country, our control,” Netanyahu declared. “Israel's narrow waist will no longer be narrow.”Netanyahu also warned that Israel's enemies may try to “test” security measures ahead of the upcoming Knesset elections. “We are prepared for any scenario,” he assured, adding that the IDF and Defense Minister Israel Katz have briefed him on security plans. “I do not advise our enemies to test us. You will encounter a force here that you never dreamed of,” he said. “We will continue to safeguard the security of Israel here, at the seam line, and everywhere.”

title: Grafana MCP for Claude Code: Query Dashboards, Metrics, and Alerts Directly
body:
When something breaks in production, the usual Claude Code loop is: open Grafana, find the right dashboard, squint at a spike, copy a PromQL query or a chunk of Loki logs, paste it into the terminal, and repeat when Claude asks for a wider time range. You end up as a slow, lossy copy-paste bridge between your metrics and your agent. Grafana MCP is Grafana Labs’ official MCP server. It lets Claude Code search your dashboards, run PromQL against Prometheus and LogQL against Loki, read alert rules and their firing state, and look up incidents on its own. It works with self-hosted Grafana 9.0+ and Grafana Cloud, and it’s open source (Apache 2.0). Pair it with our Sentry MCP guide : Sentry tells Claude which error is happening, Grafana shows when it started and what the metrics were doing around it. Quick Start Create a Grafana service account token with the Viewer role (Administration → Users and access → Service accounts), then run: claude mcp add --scope user --transport stdio grafana \ --env GRAFANA_URL = http://localhost:3000 \ --env GRAFANA_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN =
\ -- uvx mcp-grafana --disable-write Replace
with your token, and swap the URL for your Grafana Cloud address ( https://myinstance.grafana.net ) if you use Cloud. Restart Claude Code and run claude mcp list . Total time: about 5 minutes. ⚡ Copy This Prompt: Let Claude Code Install and Verify It For You Skip the manual steps below and hand the whole job to the agent instead: You have shell access and the `claude mcp` CLI on this machine. Connect the Grafana MCP server (grafana/mcp-grafana) to Claude Code in read-only mode and report back. Do not tell me it's done unless step 5 actually confirms it: 1. Run `uvx --version`. If uv is missing, install it with the official installer for this OS (macOS/Linux: `curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh`, Windows PowerShell: `powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"`), then re-check. 2. Run `claude mcp list`. If a grafana entry already exists, stop and show me its config instead of adding a second one. 3. Ask me for two values: my Grafana URL (e.g. http://localhost:3000 or https://myinstance.grafana.net) and a service account token. Tell me to create the token in Grafana under Administration > Users and access > Service accounts, with the Viewer role. Never echo the token back in chat or write it to any file other than the Claude Code config. 4. Add the server for all projects, read-only: `claude mcp add --scope user --transport stdio grafana --env GRAFANA_URL=
--env GRAFANA_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN=
-- uvx mcp-grafana --disable-write` 5. Run `claude mcp list` and confirm grafana shows Connected. Then call the Grafana search tool and list the first 5 dashboard titles. If any step fails, give me the exact error and the command that produced it. A 400 "id is invalid" error on datasource tools means Grafana is older than 9.0, so say that instead of retrying. Do not skip ahead. The agent can’t create the service account token for you, so the prompt stops and asks for it. That’s intentional: you decide what role the token gets. What You’ll Need Requirement Why You Need It Time Grafana 9.0 or later (self-hosted or Cloud) Datasource tools use API endpoints that were added in 9.0 0 min A service account token How the server authenticates to Grafana. Viewer is enough for read-only use ~2 min uv installed The Quick Start runs the server with uvx mcp-grafana , no global install needed ~1 min Claude Code installed The client that calls the Grafana tools 0 min Step-by-Step Setup Prefer to do it by hand instead of delegating to the agent? Here’s the manual version. Step 1 — Check uv (and optionally start a test Grafana) ~1 min Confirm uv is available: uvx --version No Grafana to test against? Start a throwaway local one with Docker, then sign in at http://localhost:3000 (admin / admin): docker run -d --name grafana -p 3000:3000 grafana/grafana Step 2 — Create a service account token ~2 min In Grafana, go to Administration → Users and access → Service accounts , select Add service account , give it the Viewer role, then Add service account token and copy it. You won’t see it again. Want Claude to create dashboards or silence alerts later? Give the account the Editor role instead and drop --disable-write in Step 3. Step 3 — Add the server to Claude Code ~1 min --scope user makes it available in every project. Everything after -- is passed to the server, which is where --disable-write goes: claude mcp add --scope user --transport stdio grafana \ --env GRAFANA_URL = http://localhost:3000 \ --env GRAFANA_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN =
\ -- uvx mcp-grafana --disable-write Real run, October 2026, Claude Code 2.1.291. Keep the server name before the --env flags: placed after them, Claude Code reads it as one more variable and stops with Invalid environment variable format . Connected means the server started; it only calls Grafana when a tool runs. Step 4 — Turn on extra datasources (optional) ~1 min Prometheus, Loki, dashboards, alerting, and incidents are on by default. Other datasources are off until you enable them with --enabled-tools , for example sql , cloudwatch , elasticsearch , or influxdb . You can also switch off categories you never use, such as --disable-oncall , to keep Claude’s tool list short. Claude Code queries the same dashboards, metrics, and alerts you check during an incident. What Each Piece Does Tool Group What Claude Can Do With It Dashboards Search dashboards, get a compact summary, pull a single property with JSONPath, and read each panel’s queries Prometheus Run instant and range PromQL queries, list metric and label names, and compute p50/p90/p95/p99 from histograms Loki Run LogQL log and metric queries, list labels, and pull detected log patterns Alerting List alert rules with their state (firing, normal, error) and read notification policies and contact points Incidents & Sift Search incidents and, on Grafana Cloud, run Sift checks for error patterns in logs and slow requests --disable-write Removes every create, update, and delete tool, so the agent can look but not touch Verify It’s Actually Working claude mcp list ✔ grafana uvx mcp-grafana –disable-write – Connected ! grafana 401 Unauthorized → token is wrong or was deleted; create a new one ✘ grafana Failed to connect → run uvx mcp-grafana --help to see the real error Then give Claude a real question: Search my Grafana dashboards, pick the one for the API service, and tell me if the error rate changed in the last 6 hours If Claude calls a dashboard search tool, then a Prometheus or Loki query tool, and answers with actual numbers from your data, the token, the URL, and the datasource access are all working. Common Mistakes to Avoid Giving the token Admin because it’s easier. An AI agent with an Admin token can delete dashboards and alert rules. Start with Viewer and --disable-write , and move up only when you need a write tool. Putting server flags before the -- . --disable-write belongs to mcp-grafana , not to claude mcp add . Placed before the double dash, Claude Code rejects it or ignores it. Using the old GRAFANA_API_KEY variable. It still works but is deprecated. Use GRAFANA_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN for new setups. Asking for a whole dashboard. Full dashboard JSON can eat a large chunk of the context window. Ask for the summary or specific panels instead; the server has dedicated tools for exactly that. Running Grafana older than 9.0. Datasource tools fail with 400 … “id is invalid” . The fix is upgrading Grafana, not reconfiguring the server. Q&A Is it free? Yes. The server is open source under Apache 2.0. You need a Grafana instance, and the free Grafana Cloud tier or a self-hosted OSS install both work. Does it work with Grafana Cloud? Yes. Set GRAFANA_URL to your stack address, such as https://myinstance.grafana.net , and use a service account token from that stack. Some tools, like Sift investigations, only exist on Cloud. Can Claude change my dashboards or alerts? Not with the setup in this guide. --disable-write removes the write tools, and a Viewer token can’t write anyway. Remove both only if you want Claude to edit things. I don’t use uv. Are there other ways to run it? Yes. The project also ships a Docker image, prebuilt binaries, and a Helm chart. The README’s Usage section covers each one. How do I remove it? claude mcp remove grafana --scope user , then delete the service account token in Grafana so it can’t be reused. Official Resources grafana/mcp-grafana on GitHub — README, full tool list, and every CLI flag Grafana service accounts — how to create the token and pick a role Claude Code MCP docs — claude mcp add options and scopes Originally published at quickpromptco.com , where the guide is kept up to date.

title: My wife and I lost our Apple Walkie-Talkie app, so I'm building my own
body: For years, my wife and I talked through our watches. One tap, one sentence, a quick instant voice connection. Then iOS 27 arrived and Walkie-Talkie was gone. I build software for a living, so I'm doing the obvious thing: building a replacement, and documenting it every step of the way. Part 1 of my Public Build Series My favourite app on my Apple Watch was never a fitness tracker or a fancy watch face. It was a simple but effective Walkie Talkie app to chat to my wife when we needed to. It did one thing really good. You tapped a contact, held a big yellow button, and talked. On the other side, your voice came out of their wrist. No typing, no phone, no waiting for a reply. iOS 27 and WatchOS 27 released, and I eagerly updated my watch, rookie mistake I know. Few days later, my wife tried to reach me via the Walkie Takie app, and she couldn't reach me, maybe just a bad connection or sometimes it was buggy. The next day, I tried to reach her via the Walkie Takie app, and saw it's no longer there? Confusion, then shock, then a quick google here, and a claude chat there, only to be discovered it's no longer there. I got to my pc and went on the official site and read through the change logs and discovered it's no longer supported and have been removed. Why such a small app mattered The Walkie Talkie app was never about long conversations. It was for the small stuff. "On my way." "Do you want some coffee" or "Food is ready". Those messages are too small for a phone call and a bit annoying to type on a watch. A quick voice note from your wrist sits right in the middle. It feels more personal than a text, and it takes two seconds. And you can hear your partners voice. When it disappeared, it wasn't the same. That's usually a good sign that something is worth building. What I'm attempting to build The idea is simple: a walkie-talkie app that puts the Apple Watch first. It can use the iPhone too, but the watch is the main hardware. Think of it as somewhere between Apple's Walkie-Talkie and Zello. Here's how I have it in my mind how I would like it to work: You open the app, pick a contact, and tap Connect. Their watch buzzes, even if the app is closed, and asks them to accept. If they accept, you're connected. Hold the button to talk, let go to listen. If they don't answer, you see "Not available" and that's it. That's the first version. Voice messages for when the other person is busy, groups, and other extras can come later. I'd rather ship something small that my wife and I use every day than something big that never gets finished. The catch I know this would not be a quick weekend project, I have worked on native device tooling before, its never "just a quick thing". An Apple Watch is built to save battery, so it's strict about what apps can do. A watch app can't sit in the background waiting for someone to talk. It can't keep a live connection open whenever it wants. And Apple's own push-to-talk toolkit only exists on the iPhone, not the watch. So how do you wake up someone's watch and start talking straight away? The answer is to borrow the way phone calls work. When you tap Connect, the other watch gets a special notification that wakes the app, and the session runs like a call. That's what keeps it alive with the screen off. Some form of alive state. The trade-off is that the incoming screen will look a bit like a phone call. Not ideal, but I will find something cool I can make it look better. Working within the platform's rules beats fighting them, and those rules shaped this design more than any feature list did. Why I'm building it in public I'm going to write about every step: the decisions, the mistakes, what it costs to run, and what I learn along the way. Some of it will work the first time. A lot of it won't. I expect more failures than successes the first time around. Part of the reason is accountability. If I tell you I'm building it, I have to finish it. The other part is that I couldn't find many projects about building a real Apple Watch app from scratch, so maybe this helps someone else. It doesn't have a name yet The app has no name, and I'd love your help to suggest something that we can turn into a real product. And if you used Walkie-Talkie too, tell me what you miss most about it. In the next part, I'll pick the name, claim it on the App Store, and set up the project. Follow along to see if a two-person walkie-talkie makes it all the way to the App Store. If you are interested in following the journey, follow me, like this article and share your journey, would love to see what you are building

title: Build a stock sentiment watchlist in Go with Adanos SDK 1.0.0
body: You are building a stock watchlist in Go. Alongside prices, you want to see which tickers people discuss on Reddit, how they talk about them on X, and which companies attract news coverage. We released Adanos Go SDK 1.0.0 for that work. You can query stock sentiment, inspect mentions and compare companies through typed Go methods. The SDK covers the API 1.54.0 contract, including 53 operations and 113 schemas, and uses the Go standard library without third-party dependencies. Get your first stock trends Use Go 1.26 or newer. Create a project and pin the release: mkdir sentiment-watchlist cd sentiment-watchlist go mod init example.com/sentiment-watchlist go get github.com/adanos-software/adanos-go-sdk@v1.0.0 Get an API key from Adanos , set ADANOS_API_KEY in your environment, and save this as main.go : package main import ( "context" "fmt" "log" "os" "time" adanos "github.com/adanos-software/adanos-go-sdk" ) func main () { client , err := adanos . NewClient ( adanos . Config { APIKey : os . Getenv ( "ADANOS_API_KEY" ), }) if err != nil { log . Fatal ( err ) } ctx , cancel := context . WithTimeout ( context . Background (), 5 * time . Second ) defer cancel () stocks , err := client . Reddit () . Trending ( ctx , & adanos . TrendingOptions { Limit : new ( 5 ), }) if err != nil { log . Fatal ( err ) } for _ , stock := range stocks { fmt . Printf ( "%s buzz=%.1f sentiment=%.2f \n " , stock . Ticker , stock . BuzzScore , stock . SentimentScore ) } } Run go run . . You get ticker, buzz and sentiment values from the API. The context gives the request a five-second deadline. The SDK defaults to https://api.adanos.com . Query the source that fits your question For a watchlist, you can query Reddit stock discussions and X sentiment, then inspect News coverage for the same ticker. You can query Polymarket stock activity or Reddit crypto sentiment through separate service clients. Inside the same Go program, with client and ctx in scope, you can filter News trends by publisher: news , err := client . News () . Trending ( ctx , & adanos . NewsTrendingOptions { Source : new ( "Reuters" ), Limit : new ( 10 ), }) if err != nil { log . Fatal ( err ) } fmt . Println ( news ) Or compare two tickers on X: comparison , err := client . X () . Compare ( ctx , [] string { "AAPL" , "MSFT" }, nil ) if err != nil { log . Fatal ( err ) } fmt . Println ( comparison ) You can inspect mentions behind a trend, query supported date windows, and group stock trends by sector or country. Check the package documentation for the methods and response fields for each source. Each source has its own coverage and metrics. Keep those distinctions when you compare results. Analyze a headline you supply You can submit your own text through the sentiment endpoint. An optional target identifies the company you want to analyze: analysis , err := client . Sentiment () . Analyze ( ctx , "Goldman Sachs cuts Apple price target" , & adanos . SentimentAnalyzeOptions { Target : new ( "Apple" )}, ) if err != nil { log . Fatal ( err ) } fmt . Println ( analysis ) Use this in a headline ingestion job or add sentiment analysis to a research dashboard. Keep the original text beside the response so you can review how the analysis relates to the headline. Keep control of your requests We kept the client close to Go's HTTP conventions. You pass context.Context to each method and can inject your own http.Client through adanos.Config . Optional query fields use pointers. A nil field omits the parameter; new(0) sends zero and new(false) sends false. That distinction matters for pagination and the IncludeInherited filter on Reddit mentions. Go 1.26 supports the new(value) syntax in these examples. For a failed API request, inspect *adanos.APIError with errors.As . You can read its status code, detail and response headers, including Retry-After when the server supplies it. You decide whether to retry and how long to wait. The SDK performs no automatic retries. Build something you can inspect A useful first project is a watchlist digest. Query trends, retain the timestamp and source with each result, and show changes between snapshots. Add a link to the underlying mentions so readers can inspect the discussion. For a research dashboard, put Reddit and News results in separate panels. You can spot a ticker that attracts discussion and check whether publishers cover the same company. For crypto, use client.Crypto() to inspect token mentions and market sentiment. You can use these observations as inputs to your own research. A sentiment score measures language in the covered data; it does not establish a future price move. We maintain the SDK under the MIT license. Start with the pinned release, browse the Go documentation , and use the API reference for endpoint access and request limits. You can report bugs or propose examples in the GitHub repository .

title: Zénit: a desktop workspace for code, AI assistance and real execution
body: Moving a file to a second monitor should not disconnect it from the rest of your work. Asking an assistant about a selection should not quietly send the whole file. And a Run button should tell you what actually happened. Those are the workflows behind Zénit , a desktop coding workspace built with a Python backend, a JavaScript frontend, Monaco and native webview windows. I’m sharing its 0.5.4 R5 public preview , now with Apache-2.0 licensing and a clearer path for contributors. One workspace, more than one window Zénit keeps the editor, explorer, terminals and assistance together, but it does not force them onto one monitor. Detach an editor and its terminal sits directly below the code. Resize it, detach the terminal separately, or use the terminal in the main application instead. The important part is the shared buffer. Unsaved edits and saves synchronize between the application and the external editor. Concurrent conflicts are kept for resolution rather than silently overwritten. Appearance and project-tree changes also update across the views. This takes more than rendering a second page: document revisions, shell input, active-view terminal resizing and window ownership all need to agree. Melody: make the scope visible Melody is the development assistant in the workspace. Connect a local engine or a supported provider and model; Zénit does not bundle a hosted AI subscription. R5 makes the request’s destination and context visible. For questions, choose Selection or file , Whole file or No code . This fixes a concrete problem: the old context selector existed, but the question path still included the file. There is also a separate Edit file mode for live buffer changes. It uses the complete file because an edit must preserve the surrounding code. A reviewed selection suggestion, by contrast, can replace only the range captured with the request. If the buffer changed afterwards, the stale proposal is rejected. Undo remains available. File plans can create, update or delete named session files with recovery copies and review. I’m careful to separate testing that workflow from claiming that a model is universally reliable: deterministic transport tests verify context and file behavior, not the intelligence of a provider. Forge: close the execution loop Forge is the execution workspace. Its main Run action saves the current file, prepares the configured runtime and starts an interactive terminal. Python also has Run buffer for unsaved editor content; C/GDB has its own debugging action. Try this small file: def greet ( name : str ) -> str : return f " Hello, { name } ! " print ( greet ( " Zénit " )) Open it in Forge and select Run Python . The terminal shows the program’s output; the execution card reports elapsed time and the real exit code. Run again repeats the captured file. Stop ends that tracked process without closing unrelated terminal sessions. Design is part of the workflow R5 uses coordinated headers, quieter surfaces, clear primary actions and visible keyboard focus. There are light, dark and forest palettes. Motion respects reduced motion settings; scrolling works without permanently visible scrollbar chrome. The welcome screen and My activity provide another route back into a project. The screenshots here are the running application with a small demo workspace; Forge output is real, and no simulated AI answer is presented as a model result. Try it and help shape the next iteration The current verified binary is Windows 10/11 x64 , with Edge WebView2. The release offers an installer, portable ZIP, manifest and SHA-256 checksums. Preview binaries are unsigned. The IDE has its own Python runtime; project toolchains and AI integrations are configured separately. Zénit is still a preview. VS Code extension compatibility is partial, regex/bulk replace are future work, and current Linux/macOS packages need separate build and verification. Original code and documentation use Apache-2.0; the independent ASM worker and dependencies retain their existing licenses. Explore the code and screenshots Download the R5 preview See working features and boundaries Contribute a focused improvement I’d especially like feedback on detached-window editing, terminal behavior at different DPI settings, and whether Melody’s context controls make the request scope understandable. What part of the edit → run → inspect loop would you improve first?

title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
body:
Updated October 15 to include more detail on the projects that pioneered many of the techniques we use in Scion.
At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research. Claude is able to autonomously iterate on research loops, micro-optimize complex programs, and build new services from the ground up at a speed and scale we haven’t seen before. The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI.
In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce.
In order to support this growth, we built Scion, an in-house version control system, and fully migrated our monorepo from git in five months. We also built and shipped a code review surface (called Antique), code search, a rich source control IAM system, novel ways of managing and landing large amounts of reviewed code, and more, all in that same time period. In this post, we’ll focus on how we built Scion specifically. It makes for an interesting case study: Claude’s ability to write code was both what put us in this situation in the first place and how we were able to quickly build a high-quality, scalable system to deal with it.
Before we explore what we built, we should acknowledge how unusual our workload is. Unsurprisingly, Anthropic uses Claude to write software far more than almost any other company, so we’re often the first to see where tools built for human scale start to strain. Source control is just one example of this. While we don’t expect many organizations to have these problems in the very near term, we suspect it won’t be too long before others who use AI coding tools experience these same pressure points, which is why we wanted to share what we built and what we learned.
Git is a decentralized system: every clone is a complete, self-contained repository that can compute diffs, read history and blame, and check out any revision while fully offline. For the vast majority of repositories, this is the right design, and it’s a large part of why git became the standard.
As our monorepo grows, it increasingly doesn’t fit that design space. The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day.
Git offers tools for working with a slice of a repository, such as shallow clones, sparse checkouts, and promisor remotes. Beyond these, there are standard workarounds for large monorepos, like internal git mirrors and repository snapshots (seeds) kept in blob storage. We’ve used all of them—at our peak, we operated several hundred internal git mirrors to deal with the load. This bought us time, but they became harder to operate as our merge rate increased. Seeds fell further from the tip of main between refreshes, and it took more and more care to keep operations that depend on history, like diff and blame, working on partial clones.
Taking a step back, we noticed that, like most companies, we were using git as a centralized system with one authoritative copy, but nearly all of our clients were agents and jobs that are online by definition. The properties that make git excellent for distributed, offline work were actively undermining our ability to scale as the repo grew. So we asked ourselves: if we designed source control with the fact that agents are always online in mind from the start, what would it look like?
With agentic coding, many common assumptions about how software is developed are evolving. We embraced these changes when building Scion, which allowed us to take a fundamentally different approach than git on several core principles. Source control for huge monorepos has prior art, notably Google’s Piper and Meta’s Sapling , 2 so we were able to build Scion with their hard-won lessons in mind. Our principles are:
Clients are always online. Git assumes that clients work offline and need a complete copy of the repository. Since nearly all of our clients are agents and jobs, we designed Scion’s client and protocols around a server that is always reachable, and have clients fetch data when they need it.
Client-server asymmetry. In git, every client is capable of being a full-fledged server. In Scion, the server answers questions about file history and blame, creates commits, performs merges and rebases, and so on. The client maintains a bounded local object cache, lays out the working copy files on disk, monitors for filesystem changes, and gives users an ergonomic way to work with the server. It can compute very little on its own but, in exchange, it requires much less data locally.
A comprehensive source control service can power many novel applications. With git, a CI job or tool that needs to ask a question about the repository, such as who last changed a line or how two commits are related, has to maintain a local copy of the repo or hope that vendor-specific APIs provide the answer. With Scion, all of the source control queries the client uses are also exposed via API, so in many cases jobs don’t need a local repository at all. Many internal tools, such as our automated bisect and revert pipelines, wouldn’t be practical at scale without this cheap, programmatic access to source control.
Everything must be horizontally scalable. At our peak, we ran several hundred git mirrors, which significantly strained capacity and no longer scaled once the repo outgrew the mirrors’ disks or memory limits. In Scion, the repository’s data is distributed, and every component is independently scalable; there is no fully materialized copy of the repo anywhere, even on the server. There is no equivalent of packfiles (git’s compressed bundles of objects), so no repository maintenance is needed.
Commits must be cheap, incremental, and lock-free. In git, you commit locally and then push to share your work. In Scion, every commit, rebase, or merge happens on the server, so there’s nothing to push, but each of those operations needs to be fast. The cost of creating a commit and updating its downstream data structures has to scale with the size of the change, not the overall size of the repo, or the server can’t keep up. The development lifecycle in Scion discourages refs (pointers to commits, such as branches and tags), except for the main ref or release branches, because global state that every server has to agree on is a looming scaling problem.
The working copy is optional, and sparse by design. Because our monorepo is so large, and because we check out code tens of millions of times a day for CI, we wanted to avoid checkouts whenever we could. With Scion, a CI job that needs the diff between a commit and its merge base, for example, can ask the server for it. The same goes for writes: many write workloads can also skip the checkout and function entirely via API. Scion’s protocol is centered around sparse checkouts, which only contain the directories the client asks for, and virtualized checkouts, which materialize files on demand, so when a job does need files on disk, the client only pays for what it actually reads.
It’s helpful to understand how these principles came together in practice when building Scion. These insights can apply to other source control systems or, more broadly, to other stages of the software development lifecycle.
In Scion, the unit of work is a “changeset,” an entry in a write-ahead log. A changeset stores most of what you’d expect from a commit in git. But where a git commit stores a pointer to the tree, a changeset stores a list of the files that changed relative to its first parent, 1 along with content-addressed pointers to the compressed file contents in blob storage. Changesets are created server-side and are available everywhere, instantly.
This structure lets us accept changesets with very high throughput because there are no packfiles to accept, no locking or cross-server coordination, and no refs to move around. Scion does technically support refs, but since neither creating nor fetching commits involves them, moving one is a compare-and-swap on a single Spanner row that happens separately from creating changesets.
A changeset records only what’s changed, so on its own, it can’t quickly answer questions like who last edited a line or which commits affected a file. To answer those, Scion builds additional data structures from the changesets, including dedicated structures for file blame and path history and skip lists for the commit graph. We call everything that isn’t directly part of the changeset “derived data,” and we compute it all through one generic mechanism. Each type of derived data is defined recursively, so its value for a changeset is computed from its values for that changeset’s parents.
This mechanism has three benefits. First, we can easily add a new type of derived data when a new data structure would make some operation faster. Second, for each type, we can choose whether to compute it eagerly or defer the work, so we avoid materializing data we don’t need. And third, because the client never sees the internals of these data structures, we can optimize them without changing the client. We’ve added new types of derived data many times as the system has grown, such as new indices for performing copy detection or path-based file search.
A small fleet of Scion servers provides source control APIs for any operation a client needs, such as getting changesets, computing diffs, finding merge bases, and fetching blobs. All source control data is content-addressed, so a piece of data never changes once it’s stored, and any server can cache it without checking with the others. As a result, the servers are horizontally scalable and require little coordination. They are essentially large caches that can also compute derived data on the fly and write the results back to Spanner.
Scion’s many consumers no longer need to maintain local repositories of their own. Fetching and maintaining the repository used to be a significant maintenance burden for CI jobs or tools that needed to ask source control questions, particularly about commit ancestry and blame. Early in the migration, before we had our own client, repo format, or protocols, Scion only answered these “metadata” queries. Fetching file contents and materializing working copies are far more data-intensive operations, and they needed a design of their own.
Scion’s scn client deviates from git’s fetch protocols in several important ways and, as a result, lends itself to a highly scalable architecture that requires significantly less CPU than git servers. Scion’s negotiation doesn’t tell the server what the client already has; instead, it operates exclusively on trees and blobs the client wants. Starting from a root tree, the client checks its local store for missing trees and requests them recursively, then repeats the process for blobs. Every request is for a specific object that never changes, so any cache can answer it, and the architecture closely resembles traditional tiered caches. The process is also efficient and resumable, because there is no single multi-gigabyte packfile response. Sparse and even virtualized checkouts don’t need special support, because the client simply doesn’t ask for trees it doesn’t want.
In the fleet, the client talks over a socket to a daemon, scion-daemon, that stores objects for the whole node. Most of our nodes need access to the monorepo, and jobs on the same node reuse most of the same objects. Each daemon starts from a periodically refreshed snapshot, then talks only to the tree and blob cache servers in its region, called scion-cache. These cache servers stream objects directly from memory, in the disk format that the daemon will consume, so they don’t need to spend time computing the client’s missing objects or performing delta compression. When a cache is missing an object, it asks the authoritative scion-servers, which read from Spanner or cloud storage as needed.
The scion-daemon, scion-cache, and scion-server all respond to identical RPCs for this protocol, so the client doesn’t need to know the cache topology. Any tier could theoretically talk to any other, but we strictly enforce the tiering to isolate failure domains. We want to avoid a situation where a failure in a regional scion-cache overwhelms the upstream scion-servers and brings down the entire system.
Each tier of this system maintains a cache hit rate of over 99% and does not require long-lived state, so it’s easy to scale up if needed. Our Scion infrastructure footprint is now 200x smaller than our previous git mirroring infrastructure in terms of CPU and memory requirements. CI and research jobs check out code two orders of magnitude faster (in seconds rather than minutes), which frees up a sizable amount of capacity across the fleet; CI alone realized a 25% CPU capacity win. Neither clients nor caches need to perform repository maintenance, which simplifies the lifecycle management of our jobs.
We started building Scion around the same time as Claude Mythos Preview and Claude Tag became available internally. Both of these releases simultaneously amplified the need for Scion and meaningfully accelerated how quickly we could build it.
Here’s a particularly striking example. Earlier in the year, we had largely handwritten the first version of the git-to-Scion ingestion pipeline as a prototype. We thought it was good—until we got our hands on an early internal snapshot of Claude Mythos Preview. We asked it to rewrite the whole thing, and with no further instructions, it produced a version that consumed 20x less memory and was 4x faster, while preserving all of the implicit invariants around ingestion ordering and data structures.
What we learned building and operating Scion offers some interesting lessons for what building agent-scale software could look like.
Rapid development with a small team will become more common. A team of seven people built both Scion and Antique (our code review tool, which we could easily write a whole other blog post about), not to mention half a dozen related systems, and fully migrated to them in five months. We did all this while the volume of code merged per day increased by 10x. In the past, developing and deploying a source control system like this would have taken a company years of iterative migration, with many more engineers. We think this sort of fast, nimble migration will become more common in the future.
Engineers are no less valuable, but their work is changing. All of the engineers who worked on this system would now rate Claude as better at writing code than them. But our engineers still supplied the invaluable understanding of the high-level inter-system components and the design-level tradeoffs, making informed choices around the problems we wanted to solve and the scale we knew we needed to achieve. Very often, we found that the role of the engineers was to tell Claude “no.” Agents will sometimes violate core system constraints to satisfy a pattern that should never have been allowed in the first place. This was particularly common in our migration. For example, there were multiple systems that tried to brute force looking up when a change merged to main by linearly reading the commit log instead of asking our code review tool. Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns. For example, one such review was overly defensive about trusting another internal service, which resulted in Claude adding excessive validation and complexity. Our team members still review every change request for the system, but they now examine the intent of the change as opposed to reading every line of code.
We were able to substantially improve optimization and quality. By virtue of Claude’s ability to write immense amounts of code much faster than we could ourselves, Scion is among the most well-tested and well-defended codebases we have ever worked on. Even on our tight timeline, we were able to build hermetic simulations of every non-trivial infrastructure and source control interaction we’ve ever encountered, as well as fuzzing and sophisticated rate limiting. Claude also casually found significant optimizations—for example, an algorithmic optimization to ancestry queries that missed one of our indexes—that would have taken an expert days or weeks of analysis and tuning… and then did it all again the next day.
We laid the groundwork for new forms of monorepo security. Managing safety, security, and compliance in a massive monorepo is as important as managing the size and scale. We built Scion with these in mind from the start. It supports rich access control on repositories, as well as the ability to apply permissions to individual directories in order to protect the most sensitive code without losing the benefits of a monorepo. Furthermore, the code review tooling we built can express complex semantic constraints on approvals, which lets us differentiate simple things like comment-only changes from sensitive logical changes, so that human reviewers can focus on the most consequential changes.
A new level of operational excellence is possible. Our team uses Claude Tag heavily, which has helped us monitor each component of the system. For example, we created Slack channels where we tasked Claude with being obsessively focused on the health of a single component. We call these Claudes “superfans.” We have a scion-daemon superfan, a scion-cache superfan, an Antique merge queue superfan, and so on. They have access to our telemetry and logs, and act like an experienced engineer who has nothing better to do than to refresh charts and look for anything strange. We also have traditional alerts for all of our systems, but our superfans can detect subtle and novel issues that make these alerts seem one-dimensional by comparison.
We’re completely rethinking our priors. This project prompted us to take a very hard look at other workflows designed for human scale. A proper merge queue, for example, doesn’t make much sense at agent scale. What does CI even mean when hundreds or even thousands of changes can merge while tests are running? We haven’t been able to effectively replicate the industry standard of a global repository lock on the merge queue, so instead, we’ve invested in post-merge and pre-deploy automated testing. This does mean that concurrent changes can conflict, but Claude can typically fix these conflicts faster than humans can even identify them.
We see Scion as just one part of the answer to the scaling concerns that increasingly capable AI agents have raised. We’re sharing these details as an example of how teams can tackle similar challenges, though we don’t expect our solution, or our considerations, to suit every case.
Scion is by no means a suitable replacement for git for general use. The concepts we’ve outlined here really only make sense for truly enormous monorepos, with either tens of thousands of engineers or swarms of agents prolifically writing code. Plus, Anthropic is unique in that our ability to spend tokens for internal use far exceeds what any other business would realistically want to spend. We do this both to address our own software development needs, and to test Claude’s capabilities.
Practically speaking, it’s difficult to offer Scion in a form that would be broadly useful to other organizations. It diverges significantly from git, meaning companies would need to migrate every piece of the development lifecycle, and it requires its own code review, code search, and CI. Our internal versions of these components are highly bespoke, so they would be difficult for other organizations to adopt, and we worry that attempting to build a public version that tries to please everyone wouldn’t actually be very useful.
However, we anticipate that this class of problems will become more commonplace over the next six to 12 months, and it would be an inefficient use of engineering resources for every company using git to face similar challenges alone. Given that, we think the most impactful thing we can do is to share our thinking, so that other developers can apply some of the most successful parts of Scion to git without departing from the overall model. A git server doesn’t have to work the same way as a git client does; novel server architectures exist that provide significant scaling improvements. Git platforms can provide comprehensive server-side RPCs like Scion, perhaps even in a standardized way across forges that the git client can learn to talk to. The negotiation protocol doesn’t have to look exactly like it does today, either, and the various sparse and shallow features in git can be made to compose well.
Lastly, we want to acknowledge that the git community has spent nearly two decades scaling the platform for millions of developers. Our contribution is far narrower: sharing our early view into how agentic software development interacts with these systems, so that we can partner with GitHub, GitLab, and the OSS community to support the changing needs of developers. We’re all in it together as the software development lifecycle intersects with the AI exponential.
01 Storing changed files relative to the first parent of a merge is a stylistic choice; in practice, we’ve found that people only care about history or blame for commits on the main line in trunk-based development in a monorepo.
02 Specifically, the server component of Sapling, Mononoke . It pioneered many of the techniques we use in Scion, in particular the Bonsai data model.
Written by Nick G. and the source control team: S.G., R.K., Dan C., Garrett H., Ben L., Colin M., Joe P. We’re grateful to Vilas J. and Sergiu D. for supporting the source control team on this ambitious journey and Amir O. for early contributions to Antique.

title: General Atomics’ Mojave Drone Completes Austere Testing in Korea
body: General Atomics Aeronautical Systems (GA-ASI) and Hanwha Aerospace completed operations in a simulated battlefield scenario with the Mojave short take-off and landing (STOL) drone on September 16. The testing formed part of a Defense Drone Technology Exhibition and included Mojave operating from an austere short runway at the Seungjin Training Field in Pocheon-si. The flying portion of the trials also saw the Mojave operating down at low level to demonstrate its ability to terrain mask to avoid potential threats and to support ground forces at close quarters. TWZ’s Jamie Hunter spoke to Matt Petraitis, senior manager of U.S. Army programs at GA-ASI, at the AUSA 2026 trade event being held this week in Washington D.C. about how the Mojave landed on a rough maneuver trail typically used by tanks and artillery vehicles, and about the company’s plans for Mojave in partnership with Hanwha Aerospace. The post General Atomics’ Mojave Drone Completes Austere Testing in Korea appeared first on TWZ .

title: Judge orders OpenAI to turn over hiring records in Apple trade secrets case
body:
A judge has ruled that Apple will gain expedited access to OpenAI’s hiring materials in the trade secrets-focused lawsuit the iPhone maker filed against OpenAI in July.
Specifically, the court will allow Apple to view documents associated with OpenAI’s interviews with former Apple employees who applied for roles within its consumer hardware and robotics groups ahead of the rumored launch of OpenAI’s first hardware device.
These documents could include interview checklists, guides, instructions, manuals, and scripts, as well as technical presentations and records showing that interview discussions had included references to Apple technology or components.
The court gave OpenAI five days to turn over materials it has already collected and 14 days for any other materials related to this request, agreeing with Apple that these documents should be expedited.
The case comes as OpenAI develops a consumer hardware device that could one day potentially rival the iPhone — or smartphones more generally — if the AI device becomes a central part of consumers’ lives and how they engage with software and services.
In its lawsuit, Apple accused OpenAI of a pattern of theft, which includes direct complaints about former employees using Apple laptops to download confidential material and files that contained information about unannounced technologies, features, and products, including technical specifications, engineering presentations, and proprietary project data.
Apple also said that former Apple employees at OpenAI coached others considering leaving Apple for OpenAI on what information to bring to their interviews, among other allegations.
U.S. District Judge Edward Davila didn’t greenlight all of Apple’s requests for expedited access to OpenAI documents and messages relevant to the case. But he did rule that Apple could access the interview materials, alongside private LINE messages (from a messaging app) between individuals named in the case, including OpenAI employees Chang Liu and Alyssa Peng.
The judge also approved depositions for Liu and Peng, along with a third individual, OpenAI’s chief hardware officer, Tang Yew Tan. All three are former Apple employees.
However, the judge denied Apple’s request to expedite its access to OpenAI’s research and development in specific areas, like metal finishes and power management. He also denied several of Apple’s broader discovery requests, like access to OpenAI’s hardware research or information about what its former employees created while working at OpenAI.
That denial isn’t final, though; the judge left the door open for Apple to narrow its requests and try again.

title: Mastering Git: From Basics to Pro‑Level Workflows
body:
Git has become the de‑facto version‑control system for modern software development. Whether you’re a solo coder, a startup founder, or part of a multinational engineering team, mastering Git can dramatically improve code quality, collaboration speed, and deployment confidence. In this post we’ll walk through the essential concepts, showcase practical workflows, and sprinkle in a few advanced tricks that most beginners miss. Grab your terminal, and let’s dive. 1. Why Git? Git isn’t just another tool – it’s a distributed VCS that gives every developer a full copy of the repository history. This design provides: Speed – most operations are local, so commits, diffs, and branch switches happen in milliseconds. Safety – the reflog and object database act as an accidental‑delete safety net. Flexibility – you can rewrite history, cherry‑pick commits, or rebase without breaking the shared code base. 2. Getting Started # Install Git (macOS, Linux, Windows) # macOS (brew) brew install git # Ubuntu/Debian sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install git # Windows – use the installer from git-scm.com After installation, configure your identity – Git embeds this metadata into each commit. git config --global user.name "Your Name" git config --global user.email "you@example.com" You can verify everything with: git --version git config --list --show-origin | grep user 3. Core Concepts 3.1 Repository A repository is a .git directory that stores objects, refs, and configuration. Create one with: git init my‑project cd my‑project 3.2 Staging & Committing Git separates staging (the index) from the actual commit. This lets you craft precise snapshots. echo "Hello, Git!" > README.md git add README.md # stage git status # see staged changes git commit -m "Add initial README" 3.3 Branches Branches are lightweight pointers to commits. The default branch is usually main (or master ). git branch # list branches git checkout -b feature/login # create + switch to new branch 3.4 Merging vs. Rebasing Merging creates a new commit that ties histories together. Rebasing rewrites the base of a branch, yielding a linear history. # Merge example git checkout main git merge feature/login # fast‑forward or three‑way merge # Rebase example git checkout feature/login git rebase main # replay commits on top of main Pro tip: Use git pull --rebase for a clean history when pulling remote changes. 4. A Practical Feature‑Branch Workflow Sync with remote – always start from the latest main . git checkout main git pull --rebase origin main Create a feature branch . git checkout -b feat/payment‑gateway Commit often – small, logical commits make reviews easier. git add src/payments.js git commit -m "Implement payment API client" Push for a Pull Request . git push -u origin feat/payment‑gateway Open a PR on GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket. Request reviews, add labels, and let CI run. Address feedback – add more commits or amend existing ones. Squash & merge – keep main tidy. git checkout main git pull --rebase origin main # ensure up‑to‑date git merge --squash feat/payment‑gateway git commit -m "feat: payment gateway integration" git push origin main Delete the branch locally and remotely. git branch -d feat/payment‑gateway git push origin --delete feat/payment‑gateway 5. Advanced Tips & Tricks 5.1 Stashing Temporary Work When you need to switch context without committing: git stash push -m "WIP: refactor auth" git stash list # view saved states git stash apply stash@ { 0 } # restore 5.2 Bisect – Find the Bad Commit Git can binary‑search through history to locate a regression. git bisect start git bisect bad # current HEAD is bad git bisect good v1.2.0 # known good tag/commit # Git checks out a midpoint; test, then mark good/bad # Repeat until the culprit is identified 5.3 Reflog – Recover Lost Commits Even after git reset --hard , the reflog retains a record. git reflog # show recent moves of HEAD git checkout
# recover 5.4 Hooks – Automate Checks Git hooks are scripts that run at specific points. A simple pre‑commit hook to enforce eslint : # .git/hooks/pre-commit (make executable) #!/bin/sh npm run lint if [ $? -ne 0 ] ; then echo "Linting failed – commit aborted" exit 1 fi Place it in the repo or use a tool like husky for cross‑platform support. 6. Git in CI/CD Pipelines Most CI systems clone the repo shallowly for speed: # Example GitHub Actions snippet actions/checkout@v3 : with : fetch-depth : 1 # shallow clone When you need the full history for version bumping or changelog generation, set fetch-depth: 0 . 7. Common Pitfalls & How to Avoid Them Pitfall Symptom Fix Accidentally committing large files Repository size balloons, CI slows Add a .gitignore and use git rm --cached
Merge conflicts proliferate Team spends hours resolving Rebase feature branches onto main frequently History becomes noisy git log hard to read Squash commits before merging, or use git commit --amend for tiny fixes Lost work after reset “Oops, I reset too far” Run git reflog immediately and checkout the desired SHA 8. Conclusion Git is more than a set of commands – it’s a mindset about incremental, reversible development. By mastering the basics, adopting a disciplined feature‑branch workflow, and sprinkling in a few advanced techniques, you’ll unlock a smoother collaboration experience and a cleaner project history. Keep experimenting with rebasing, hooks, and bisect; the more you explore, the more Git will feel like an extension of your brain rather than a separate tool. Happy coding!

title: Sending a NuVotifier vote with nothing but the Python standard library
body:
Minecraft server lists reward players for voting: the list sends a small message to the game server, and a plugin like VotingPlugin hands out the reward. The protocol behind this is Votifier , today mostly in its fork NuVotifier . If you run a server, the most common question is "is my Votifier actually reachable, and is my token right?". So we wrote a tiny test client, and it turned out to be a nice little exercise in sockets, HMAC and even raw RSA. All code below runs on Python 3.8+ without any packages. The v2 handshake When you open a TCP connection to the Votifier port (default 8192), the server speaks first: VOTIFIER 2 4f0c1b8e6d... The third token is a challenge . It ties your vote to this one connection, so a captured vote can't be replayed later. def read_greeting ( sock ): data = b "" while not data . endswith ( b " \n " ): chunk = sock . recv ( 1 ) if not chunk : break data += chunk return data . decode (). strip () # "VOTIFIER 2
" Building the signed message The vote itself is a JSON object, serialized to a string. That string is signed with HMAC-SHA256 using the server's token, and both go into an outer JSON object: payload = json . dumps ({ " serviceName " : " votifier-test " , " username " : " Notch " , " address " : " 127.0.0.1 " , " timestamp " : int ( time . time () * 1000 ), " challenge " : challenge , }, separators = ( " , " , " : " )) signature = base64 . b64encode ( hmac . new ( token . encode (), payload . encode (), hashlib . sha256 ). digest () ). decode () message = json . dumps ({ " payload " : payload , " signature " : signature }). encode () Note that the payload is a JSON string inside JSON. The server verifies the HMAC over the exact bytes of that string, so you must not re-serialize it on the way. Framing: a magic number and a length NuVotifier v2 frames the message with two big-endian 16-bit integers: the magic 0x733A and the length of the message. packet = struct . pack ( " >HH " , 0x733A , len ( message )) + message sock . sendall ( packet ) The server answers with one JSON line: {"status":"ok"} or {"status":"error","cause":"CorruptedFrameException","error":"Signature is not valid (invalid token?)"} . That error message is exactly what you want a test tool to show, because "wrong token" is the number one setup mistake. Protocol v1: RSA without a crypto library Old Votifier (v1) has no token. Instead, the vote is a plain text block VOTE
encrypted with the server's 2048-bit RSA public key using PKCS#1 v1.5 padding, and sent as 256 raw bytes. No reply. The key file ( rsa/public.key ) is a base64 X.509 SubjectPublicKeyInfo. Getting the modulus and exponent out of it only needs a minimal DER reader: def der_read ( data , pos ): tag = data [ pos ]; pos += 1 length = data [ pos ]; pos += 1 if length & 0x80 : n = length & 0x7F length = int . from_bytes ( data [ pos : pos + n ], " big " ); pos += n return tag , data [ pos : pos + length ], pos + length SubjectPublicKeyInfo is a SEQUENCE of an AlgorithmIdentifier and a BIT STRING; the BIT STRING (after one "unused bits" byte) contains another SEQUENCE with the modulus and the exponent. PKCS#1 v1.5 encryption padding is 00 02
00
, filled up to the key size, and the encryption itself is one line thanks to Python's three-argument pow : k = ( n . bit_length () + 7 ) // 8 padding = bytes ( b for b in os . urandom ( k * 2 ) if b != 0 )[: k - 3 - len ( message )] block = b " \x00\x02 " + padding + b " \x00 " + message cipher = pow ( int . from_bytes ( block , " big " ), e , n ). to_bytes ( k , " big " ) (Don't use hand-rolled RSA for anything that protects secrets. Here it only reproduces what a server list sends, and the server decrypts it with a proper library.) Testing it We tested three things against a fake listener in unit tests (the v1 test decrypts with the cryptography package) and then against a real NuVotifier 2.7.3 on Paper 1.21.11: v2 with the right token: OK v2 with a wrong token: Signature is not valid (invalid token?) v1 with the public key: the console logs Got a protocol v1 vote record The whole script is about 200 lines and MIT licensed: https://github.com/nickynice1/bestmcserverlist/tree/main/votifier-tester Disclosure: this is written by the team behind BestMCServerList, a Minecraft server list, and the script came out of testing our own vote delivery. The code and this article were written with the help of an AI assistant; every result shown here was actually run and checked.

title: Energy Software Has a Consistency Problem
body:
Renewable-energy systems produce information through many different components.
Sensors collect measurements. SCADA systems display operational conditions. Maintenance platforms store interventions, while separate applications may manage training, documentation and reporting.
Each system can work correctly on its own while still creating a larger problem: inconsistency.
The same equipment condition may be described differently across two applications. Status values may follow different rules, timestamps may use different formats and essential context may remain stored in a separate system.
For developers, this is not simply a database issue. It is a meaning issue.
A stronger digital workflow needs consistent terminology and clearly defined states.
These principles become increasingly important when data may later support automation or artificial intelligence.
AI systems do not automatically understand operational meaning. If the underlying information is inconsistent, additional volume may only increase the inconsistency.
Not every renewable-energy platform needs to manage every part of this sequence. However, systems should make their responsibility within the sequence clear and preserve enough context for information to remain understandable.
The long-term opportunity is not a single universal dashboard. It is a more consistent digital environment in which different people and systems can understand what a particular record represents.
The Voltalix project is exploring part of this challenge through structured SCADA-oriented activities, consistent terminology and visible review stages. Its potential contribution is to help organise participant-generated information so that its source, context and validation status remain clearer as the platform develops.
More about the project can be found at voltalix.com.

title: Phantom Defense Buys Developer of KARAKURT Drone Net Launchers
body:
Ukrainian defense technology group Phantom Defense has bought the developer of KARAKURT drone net launchers, adding a low-cost, non-explosive interceptor that frontline units have already used in more than 50,000 kits over the past six months.
The company wrote that the deal covers the entire business and its team. It did not name the developer or the size of investment.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The acquisition extends Phantom Defense beyond its core of electronic warfare (EW), target detection, kinetic interception and battle management software, and into the physical capture of drones, according to the press release .
A KARAKURT module throws a net over a target drone, entangling its rotors and ending the flight. The company wrote that enemy reconnaissance or strike drones lose control and come down largely intact. Because nothing explodes, it argued, downed drones can be examined or potentially reused by Ukraine’s Defense Forces, and the risk of collateral damage to critical and civilian infrastructure is lower. It added that net launchers cost less to make and maintain than missile- or artillery-based air defense, making large-scale deployment along the front line feasible.
The product comes in two main configurations. Versions for DJI Mavic, Matrice and Autel platforms, in the M3, M4 and A4 variants, drop a net vertically from above, which the company wrote allows crews to neutralize enemy drones waiting on rooftops or on the ground. FPV and LS variants fire a net forward with a target retention mechanism to catch fast-moving targets. The company wrote that modules weighing as little as 201 g have virtually no effect on the carrier drone’s maneuverability or flight endurance.
The performance figures come from Phantom Defense itself and have not been independently verified. The company wrote that it has recorded more than 5,000 video-confirmed interceptions under a program that gives units free replacement consumables in exchange for footage of a successful kill.
It framed the scheme as a way to cut costs for the military while feeding operational data back to developers. According to Phantom Defense, a single crew of the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine intercepted more than 500 enemy drones with net modules over six months.
The press release quoted an unnamed Phantom Defense representative as saying that folding KARAKURT into the company’s ecosystem meets demand among military units for effective but affordable short-range interception, and opens the way to scale a product with combat experience behind it.
Alongside the deal, Phantom Defense introduced MANGAL, a close-range net interception system that it has integrated into its counter-UAS ecosystem. The company wrote that the system is designed to provide point-defense protection for military vehicles, stationary positions and unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs).
MANGAL pairs artificial intelligence with daylight and thermal imaging cameras to detect aerial threats and identify targets automatically. The company wrote that the interval between detection and net launch is one second. The modular system carries six net launchers and has an effective engagement range of five to 15 meters. Its built-in battery provides at least eight hours of autonomous operation, and it can also run on an extra battery module or a combat vehicle’s onboard electrical system.
Phantom Defense wrote that it employs more than 620 people and operates nine production facilities with a combined capacity of more than 100 drones and 200 electronic warfare devices per day.
Olena Hrazhdan is the Business Reporter at Kyiv Post, covering Ukraine’s markets, business, and economic policy. While she reports broadly on economic issues, her core focus is banking, finance, monetary and fiscal policy. Olena previously wrote for leading Ukrainian business media and became a Fellow of the International Monetary Fund’s Journalism Fellowship in 2024.

title: n8n Adds Native OpenTelemetry Tracing for Workflow and Node-Level Visibility
body: n8n has introduced native OpenTelemetry tracing for its automation platform, giving teams a way to follow workflow executions from their trigger through downstream actions. Announced on June 8, 2026, the capability can emit a trace for every workflow run and, optionally, a child trace span for every node. That provides a production-focused view of automations that connect services such as CRMs, payment systems, API gateways, and AI agents . The update matters because workflow failures are often difficult to isolate once an automation crosses several applications. A failed run may be caused by a slow external API, an incorrectly mapped data field, a payment event, or a later step in a process. With OpenTelemetry, n8n can send execution data to a compatible observability backend, so teams can investigate workflow behavior alongside the rest of their software stack. The details are set out in n8n's official OpenTelemetry tracing announcement . What native OpenTelemetry support changes in n8n OpenTelemetry is an open standard for collecting telemetry data, including traces. In this case, n8n uses tracing to represent the path of a workflow execution. Each run produces a root span , which acts as the top-level record for the execution. Users can also enable child spans for individual workflow nodes. That distinction is important. A workflow-level trace can show whether a process completed and how long the complete execution took. Node-level spans add diagnostic detail by showing where time was spent and where an error occurred. Rather than treating an automation as a single opaque task, teams can examine its component actions in a centralized tracing tool. The announcement describes exports to OTLP-compatible collectors and backends, including: Jaeger Tempo Datadog Honeycomb New Relic Grafana Cloud This interoperability is a significant part of the release. n8n users with an existing OpenTelemetry-compatible observability setup can use that environment for workflow traces rather than adopting a separate, proprietary monitoring layer. The capability applies across n8n workflows and is designed for both self-hosted and cloud deployments. Workflow-level and node-level trace data Tracing level What n8n emits Practical use Workflow execution A root span for every workflow execution Follow the end-to-end path, status, and timing of an automation run. Individual nodes Optional child spans for each workflow node Identify the specific step that is slow or producing an error. The two levels are complementary. A root span establishes the broad execution path, while node spans help explain the outcome. For a workflow that receives a customer request, checks a database, updates a CRM, and sends a response, node-level tracing can reveal which action created a delay or failure. Configuration and contextual attributes n8n documents configuration through Settings > OpenTelemetry . The documentation also covers trace export and custom span attributes that can be applied at the project, workflow, and node levels. Those attributes are made available in the connected observability backend. Custom attributes give teams a way to add relevant context to traces. Depending on how a workflow is organized, that can make it easier to filter and investigate executions by project, workflow, or the step that requires attention. The feature is therefore more than a basic execution log. It creates trace data that can be queried and viewed within tools built for operational investigation. Why the update is useful for businesses running automations For businesses that depend on n8n to move data between applications, an automation is part of an operational process, not simply a background convenience. Delays or errors can affect lead handling, customer communications, payment-related processes, and internal data updates. Native tracing can shorten the path from noticing a problem to locating the affected workflow step. The strongest practical benefit is faster incident diagnosis . A team can use the trace to see the complete call path and then narrow its investigation to the node that failed or performed slowly. This is especially useful where multiple systems are involved and each system has its own monitoring data. The release can also support more informed performance work. End-to-end traces make it possible to see where execution time accumulates, rather than assuming that n8n itself is the source of a delay. If an external service call is the slowest point in a workflow, the trace should make that relationship visible in the chosen backend. For smaller teams, the ability to use an existing OTLP-compatible backend may reduce the friction of adding workflow observability. The value will depend on whether the business already operates compatible tooling and on how critical its workflows are. The supplied announcement focuses on tracing capabilities and configuration, rather than setting out separate pricing terms for the feature. If n8n workflows support customer-facing or time-sensitive processes, Scalevise can help turn them into more dependable operations through production-ready n8n workflow setup . We can connect business applications, design error handling and monitoring around critical workflow paths, and reduce the manual effort needed to diagnose failures. This helps teams retain the speed of automation while gaining clearer operational control. Discuss your n8n automation project with Scalevise. Frequently Asked Questions What is n8n's new OpenTelemetry capability? n8n can emit OpenTelemetry traces for every workflow execution, with an option to emit child spans for individual nodes. The traces show execution paths, timing, and status in a compatible observability backend. Which observability backends can receive n8n traces? n8n states that its traces can be exported to OTLP-compatible collectors and backends, including Jaeger, Tempo, Datadog, Honeycomb, New Relic, and Grafana Cloud. How do users enable OpenTelemetry tracing in n8n? The n8n documentation describes configuration through Settings > OpenTelemetry. It also covers trace export and custom span attributes at the project, workflow, and node levels. Can tracing identify a failing n8n workflow node? Yes. When node-level child spans are enabled, teams can inspect individual workflow steps to identify the node that is slow or producing an error. Conclusion n8n's native OpenTelemetry support brings workflow execution data into standard observability systems. By pairing a trace for each automation run with optional node-level detail, the release gives teams a clearer way to investigate failures and performance issues across connected business systems.

title: ECOWAS Defence Chiefs seek sustained Nigerian support for regional security
body: By Kingsley Omonobi The outgoing and incoming Chairmen of the ECOWAS Committee of Chiefs of Defence Staff (CCDS) have called for sustained Nigerian support to strengthen regional security cooperation and address growing threats across West Africa. The two military chiefs made the appeal on Tuesday during a courtesy visit to the Chief of Defence Staff (CDS), General Olufemi Oluyede, at the Defence Headquarters in Abuja. The outgoing Chairman, Lieutenant General Amara Idara Bangura, who is Sierra Leone’s Chief of Defence Staff, expressed appreciation to Nigeria for its continued support for the ECOWAS defence framework and regional security initiatives throughout his tenure. Bangura disclosed that he and his successor had spent the previous two days conducting formal handover activities ahead of the transition in the leadership of the ECOWAS defence committee. He commended Nigeria’s longstanding contributions to peace and stability in West Africa, particularly its support for Sierra Leone during the country’s civil war and subsequent peacebuilding efforts. He also highlighted Nigeria’s contributions to regional peacekeeping operations, counter-terrorism cooperation and logistical support, describing the country’s role as critical to the security of the sub-region. The outgoing chairman urged Oluyede to extend the same level of cooperation and goodwill to his successor to ensure continuity in regional security efforts. In his remarks, the incoming Chairman of the ECOWAS Committee of Chiefs of Defence Staff and Senegal’s Chief of Defence Staff, Vice Admiral Oumar Wade, thanked the Nigerian military leadership for the warm reception accorded the delegation. Wade identified terrorism, violent extremism, transnational organised crime and maritime insecurity as some of the complex and evolving threats confronting ECOWAS member states. He described Nigeria as a key regional power and an anchor of security in West Africa, stressing that its continued guidance, participation and support would be essential to the committee’s ability to fulfil its mandate. Responding, Oluyede thanked the two defence chiefs for their commendation of Nigeria and its Armed Forces, describing their visit as a demonstration of solidarity and a shared commitment to regional peace and security. The CDS called for stronger unity, cooperation and mutual understanding among ECOWAS member states, urging countries to set aside political differences, divergent interests and bilateral disputes to confront common security threats. He emphasised that security was indivisible, noting that no country could effectively guarantee its own safety in isolation from its neighbours. Oluyede reaffirmed Nigeria’s commitment to supporting ECOWAS security initiatives, citing the country’s determination to promote regional peace, integration and development. He also assured Wade of Nigeria’s full support during his tenure as chairman, expressing confidence that sustained cooperation among member states would strengthen the region’s collective security architecture. The post ECOWAS Defence Chiefs seek sustained Nigerian support for regional security appeared first on Vanguard News .
