title: Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis sentenced for orchestrating Tupac Shakur’s murder
body:
Duane “Keffe D” Davis was sentenced Tuesday to 40 years to life in prison for orchestrating the murder of rap icon Tupac Shakur who was gunned down off the Las Vegas Strip over 30 years ago.
Davis, 63, was convicted in August of first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon. He is the only person ever charged in the death of Shakur, whose popularity was peaking at age 25.
Prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo said Tuesday that whatever sentence the court imposes, Davis is “guaranteed to die” behind bars.
“It’s not just about losing a family member,” DiGiacomo said as Shakur’s sister Sekyiwa “Set” Shakur nods her head in the audience.
The killing went unsolved for years until Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips, gave interviews and published his role in the shooting in his 2019 tell-all memoir.
DiGiacomo said Davis was trying to profit off a killing that he committed, and for that he does not deserve the minimum sentence.
“In my mind he deserves the maximum possible sentence,” DiGiacomo said.
Davis spoke briefly in court, telling Judge Carli Kierny he wants items back that police took from his house, including his pictures. Asked if there was anything else he wanted to say, Davis said: “No I’m good.”
Davis’ lawyer, Michael Sanft said he plans to appeal the verdict. Sanft said prosecutors waited too long to bring the case.
On the night of Sept. 7, 1996, Shakur was in the passenger seat of a black BMW with music mogul Marion “Suge” Knight when a white Cadillac pulled up at a red light, and shots erupted. Shakur was shot multiple times and died six days later, while Knight survived.
Shakur is considered one of the most influential and versatile rappers of all time and had a burgeoning film career as an actor at the time of his death. His legend has only grown since. His songs still resonate among fans with themes of hardship, love and Black struggles.
In his memoir, Davis explained how Shakur and his entourage beat up Davis’ nephew hours before the shooting in Las Vegas. He said he sought retaliation, and that he was in the passenger seat of the Cadillac and passed the gun to the backseat, where shots were fired. Davis had spoken to detectives years before but avoided prosecution because of an agreement he made with law enforcement.
During the weekslong trial, prosecutors relied on Davis’ own statements he made to law enforcement and documentarians. They argued Davis orchestrated the shooting and provided the gun used in Shakur’s death, which was the result of a rivalry between the South Side Compton Crips and Mob Piru. Davis’ defence lawyer pointed to a lack of physical evidence that connected his client to the 30-year-old crime, and he portrayed Davis as a liar who was trying to make money.
After nine days of hearing testimony in August, the jury deliberated for three hours before turning over the guilty verdict.
Shakur’s family spoke at the sentencing, including his siblings Maurice “Mopreme” Shakur and Sekyiwa “Set” Shakur.
Following the verdict, prosecutor Binu Palal said that to many people, Shakur was an icon or an idea, “but to the family, Tupac Shakur was a brother, a son, a cousin, a loved person ripped from them 30 years ago.”
Palal said the family had to sit through years of Davis “bragging about killing someone they loved.”
“They loved that man. And the arrogance that Mr. Davis had in expressing his joy in killing that man ultimately was his undoing,” Palal said.
Davis is the only person to be charged and convicted in the killing of Shakur. The three other people who allegedly were in the Cadillac — including Davis’ nephew Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson who Davis said was the one who pulled the trigger — have died.
Sean “Diddy” Combs and his alleged role were brought up often throughout the trial. Witnesses testified Combs used members of the South Side Compton Crips for security for Bad Boy Records. In his book and public statements, Davis alleged Combs offered him money to kill Shakur and Knight. Combs, who is serving a four-year prison sentence after being convicted of prostitution-related offenses, has repeatedly denied any involvement in the death of Shakur.
Clark County District Attorney Steve Wolfson has said his office doesn’t believe it has sufficient evidence to charge anyone else.
“But like any other case, if we come into more information, more evidence, we can always consider filing additional charges,” he said following the guilty verdict. “But today, we don’t believe that’s the appropriate move to make.”

title: Kwara: Truck Driver kills student in accident, flees
body: The Kwara State Police Command is searching for a Conoil truck driver and his motor boy over the death of a Kwara State Polytechnic student. His body was allegedly dumped on a bridge after a road crash and buried as an unidentified corpse. The Commissioner of Police, Ojo Adekimi confirmed the incident to Daily Trust during a telephone chat on Tuesday. He said a tricycle operator who allegedly handed the body to the truck driver had been arrested. It was gathered that the deceased, identified as Sheu, was reportedly hit by the truck around the Government Secondary School area of Ilorin, on Friday. A family member, who spoke to Daily Trust anonymously, said the deceased had borrowed a motorcycle from one of his brothers to buy clothes for his side business when the incident occurred. Sheu, who hailed from Eyombo Anabi compound in Ilorin, lived with his mother in Shao, Moro local government area, and helped with her clothes business. His family, however, became worried when he failed to return the motorcycle on the fateful day. A relative of the deceased who confided in our correspondent said the owner of the motorcycle later called his phone after 9pm, but an unidentified person answered. He added that they heard a voice in the background questioning why he had picked up the call before the line went off. Repeated attempts to reach him later failed. The development prompted the family to search for him. The family later learnt that a body had been found on a bridge in the Oko-Olowo area of Ilorin. Residents had alerted the police after they suspected that the deceased had fallen from a moving vehicle. The body was classified as unidentified and buried by local government health officials. The family said it identified him from a photograph taken before the burial before they exhumed the body for confirmation. A family member told Daily Trust that a tricycle operator, Basit, who witnessed the accident helped to convey the body to the University of Ilorin Teaching Hospital (UITH), where doctors confirmed that the deceased was brought in dead. He said that the tricycle operator later claimed to be the deceased’s brother, took custody of the body and handed it to the truck crew after leaving the UITH. The family questioned why the operator did not alert hospital personnel that he had merely assisted in conveying the body. “We want justice and to establish whether the operator handed over the body out of ignorance or for financial gain. The Commissioner of Police has directed that they produce the drivers of the Conoil truck,” the family member said. The relative added that the family found the motorcycle at the Kulende Police Station during its search. Confirming the incident, Commissioner of Police, Ojo Adekimi said efforts were underway to arrest the truck driver and motor boy, who were employees of Conoil. “Yes, we are trying to arrest the drivers now,” he said. The commissioner said the body was initially classified as unidentified before the police sent its photograph to the family, which identified the deceased. “We later discovered an abandoned corpse on top of a bridge and sent the picture to the family of the deceased for identification. “But before then, it was classified as an unknown corpse and had to be buried. The body was later exhumed, and they confirmed it was him,” he said. “He confirmed that the tricycle operator handed the body to the truck driver but said he claimed not to know where it was taken afterwards”, the commissioner said

title: Solutions to the risks posed by the global pet trade could be enacted quickly
body: The global pet trade, particularly in exotic reptiles and amphibians, poses significant biodiversity and potential human health risks, scientists say; yet compared to other pressing crises like climate change, the solutions are relatively simple — if only governments would act on them. Susan Lieberman, vice president for international policy at the Wildlife Conservation Society, based in the U.S., and Sandra Altherr, co-founder and head of science at Pro Wildlife, in Germany, join the Mongabay Newscast this week to discuss these solutions, which they’ve outlined in a commentary published in the journal Nature. “The international wildlife trade for pets, reptiles, amphibians, and other species is a massive experiment,” Lieberman says. “It’s an experiment to see what diseases can come from one part of the world into another part of the world, and ‘let’s see what happens.’ I think it’s an experiment we should not be undertaking.” But the “exotic pet trade could be regulated very quickly, and this risk could be reduced very quickly,” Altherr adds. Both guests discuss what they identify as the main legal gaps that world governments could close, such as the fact that countries of origin have no or little legal recourse for species sold outside their borders. Another gap is that the CITES, the global convention on the wildlife trade, is often poor at taking a proactive approach to protect species before they become threatened, the authors argue. And species being pushed toward the brink of extinction don’t have the luxury of time for the long…This article was originally published on Mongabay

title: Photos: Mahama commissions 85-bed Police Hospital ward, donates two ambulances
body: President John Mahama has commended the Ghana Police Service for improvements in public safety and crime investigations, while urging the Service to sustain efforts to protect lives and property. He made the remarks on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, at the commissioning of a new 85-bed ward complex at the Ghana Police Hospital in Accra. The facility, named the Christian Tetteh Yohuno Ward Complex after the Inspector-General of Police (IGP), is expected to improve healthcare for police personnel, their families and the general public. The President praised IGP Christian Tetteh Yohuno and the Police Administration for their work in maintaining peace and security across the country. He said investment in police healthcare was essential because officers regularly face physical and psychological demands in the line of duty, including exposure to violence, emergencies and other traumatic situations. President Mahama stressed that officers injured during operations must receive timely and quality medical care, adding that their welfare was closely linked to their ability to protect the public effectively. He urged the hospital’s management and staff to maintain high standards of hygiene, patient safety and professional care, while ensuring that the new facility and its equipment were properly maintained. To strengthen emergency response and patient care, the President also donated two new ambulances to the hospital. He further assured the Police Service of additional logistical support, including more armoured vehicles, as part of efforts to improve operational effectiveness and officer safety. The commissioning forms part of efforts to expand the Police Hospital’s capacity to serve both security personnel and the wider public. Inspector-General of Police Christian Tetteh Yohuno welcomed the new facility, describing it as an important step towards improving healthcare delivery for officers, their families and other patients. He said the additional beds and expanded facilities would enable the hospital to provide more specialised care on site, reducing the need to transfer patients to other health facilities and easing the associated costs and inconvenience. The IGP reaffirmed the Police Administration’s commitment to maintaining the complex and ensuring that it continued to provide quality healthcare to all who needed its services.

title: White Nile launches breast cancer awareness campaign
body: Sudan’s National Health Insurance Fund in White Nile State on Sunday launched a breast cancer awareness campaign at White Nile Oncology Hospital in Kosti, in partnership with community initiatives. The campaign seeks to raise awareness of breast cancer and encourage early detection as conflict-related disruption places additional pressure on health services, including access to diagnosis and treatment. Haider Hashim, director of the fund in the state, said health insurance centres and diagnostic facilities in several localities, including El Geteina, Ad Douiem and Kosti, provide free clinical examinations and laboratory tests. Hashim said the fund is committed to supporting patients throughout their treatment and stressed the importance of sustained public awareness, including sharing the experiences of cancer survivors. Naji Suleiman, director of the Kosti Oncology Centre, said social stigma and misconceptions about cancer remained barriers to seeking medical care, with some people viewing the disease as a death sentence. He said these attitudes contributed to delays in seeking treatment and stressed that early detection was important for improving treatment outcomes. Lamia Mutawakkil, a media professional who said she was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2016, shared her experience as a survivor and urged women to seek early screening. Mutawakkil said the chances of recovery are significantly higher when breast cancer is detected at an early stage. The post White Nile launches breast cancer awareness campaign appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Show HN: Fold a sheet of paper until it reaches the Moon
body:
One sheet of paper. One very bad sense of scale.
Fold to the Moon is a free interactive paper folding simulator about a number that feels wrong even after you have seen the math. Start with a sheet of paper just 0.1 mm thick. Guess how many times you would need to fold it in half to reach the Moon, then fold it one step at a time and find out.
Each fold doubles the thickness. The first few barely seem to change anything. Keep going, and your stack grows past everyday objects, buildings and mountains. The view pulls back as folded-paper figures put each new height into perspective. Eventually, a sheet of A4 becomes a very unreasonable way to travel through space.
This paper folding game turns exponential growth into something you can watch rather than just calculate. Your original guess stays on screen as the scale changes. Reach the Moon to see how close your prediction was, then keep folding toward the edge of the observable universe. No download or signup needed. If numbers that defy intuition fascinate you, see how a single number can anchor your judgment .
Choose one of the suggested guesses or enter your own number of folds. Press Let's fold and find out to start with a single sheet.
Tap the fold button, click an empty part of the scene or press Space to fold once. Each step doubles the stack's thickness and layer count. Watch the changing scale and the comparisons beside the paper.
At fold 42, the game pauses to show the Moon result and compare it with your guess. Choose Keep folding to continue all the way to fold 103, or Guess again to return to the beginning. You can turn the paper sounds off at any time.
With a starting thickness of 0.1 mm, it takes 42 theoretical folds to exceed the Moon's average distance from Earth. After 41 folds, the paper would be about 219,902 km thick. One more fold doubles that to about 439,805 km, beyond the Moon's average distance of roughly 384,400 km.
The calculation is simple: thickness after n folds = 0.1 mm × 2ⁿ. The surprising part is how quickly repeated doubling catches up with an enormous distance. This simulator uses that idealized calculation; it does not model the force, sheet size or material limits needed to fold real paper.
Adding another sheet gives you a steady increase. Doubling the whole stack gives you an accelerating one. The difference is easy to miss when the starting number is tiny: after seven folds, 0.1 mm has only become 1.28 cm. But the same rule keeps working when the stack is kilometres tall.
Making a guess before you start lets you compare your intuition with the result. There is no timer and no penalty for being wildly off. It is a quiet little visual experiment about how far a very ordinary rule can take you.
No. The 42-fold result is a mathematical thought experiment assuming thickness doubles with every fold. A real sheet runs out of usable area and becomes too stiff to keep folding long before that.
Starting at 0.1 mm, 41 doublings produce about 219,902 km of thickness, short of the Moon's average distance. At 42 doublings, the thickness is about 439,805 km, which exceeds that distance.
There is no single limit for every sheet. Around seven folds is a familiar practical limit for ordinary paper folded by hand, but larger, thinner or specially prepared sheets can go further. This game explores theoretical doubling, not a physical folding record.
Yes. The result is the starting thickness multiplied by 2 for every fold. This game fixes the starting thickness at 0.1 mm; thicker or thinner paper would change when each distance is reached.
Yes. Choose Keep folding on the Moon result screen. The experience continues to fold 103, when the theoretical thickness exceeds the diameter of the observable universe.
Yes. Play free in your browser without an account. Tap to fold on a phone or use your mouse or Space key on desktop.

title: GTEC directs Ghana’s public universities to reopen by October 16 and begin lectures on October 19
body: The Ghana Tertiary Education Commission (GTEC) has directed all public universities to reopen their campuses for the 2026/2027 academic year by Friday, October 16, despite any earlier decisions to postpone reopening. In a letter dated October 13, 2026, and signed by Deputy Director-General Prof. Augustine Ocloo on behalf of the Director-General, the Commission said academic activities, particularly lectures, must commence on Monday, October 19. The directive was issued on the authority of the Minister for Education. GTEC has also directed university managements to ensure that halls of residence, academic libraries, departmental registration desks and other essential student support facilities are fully staffed and operational by Thursday, October 15. Vice-Chancellors are required to submit comprehensive academic reopening readiness reports to the Commission by Wednesday, October 14. The directive comes amid an industrial dispute involving the Ghana Association of University Administrators (GAUA) and the Technical University Administrators Association of Ghana (TUSAAG). GTEC acknowledged the administrative challenges arising from the industrial action but warned that the continued suspension of academic activities had far-reaching implications for students’ academic progression, university operations, tertiary education delivery and international academic partnerships. The Commission said the government, through the Ministry of Education, Ministry of Finance and Fair Wages and Salaries Commission, had initiated engagements with GAUA’s leadership to facilitate the resolution of outstanding grievances. It has asked members of GAUA to resume their administrative duties while good-faith negotiations continue. “The Commission expects strict compliance with the stipulated timelines,” the letter stated. GTEC further directed institutions that anticipate difficulties meeting the deadlines to notify the Commission immediately in writing, outlining the challenges and measures being taken to address them. The directive follows a meeting between Education Minister Haruna Iddrisu and the leadership of GAUA and TUSAAG on Monday, October 12, during which the Minister expressed optimism that the strike would be called off in the coming days. GAUA, however, said it needed to consult its members before announcing a decision. The industrial action, which began on August 10 and was reactivated on September 15, centres on disparities in the Interim Market Premium (IMP) between teaching and non-teaching senior members. The strike has disrupted administrative operations at public universities, including admissions, registration and accommodation allocation. The University of Ghana and Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) have postponed their reopenings indefinitely. Under the latest directive, universities are expected to reopen by October 16 and begin lectures three days later, while negotiations over the outstanding grievances continue. title: Licube wants to be the fuel provider to the fusion power industry — see how at TechCrunch Disrupt
body:
If fusion power pans out, and there are signs that it will , the world will need a lot more lithium.
That’s the bet behind Licube , a startup that has licensed technology from Hirosaki University in Japan, to purify lithium-6, the form of lithium that fusion plants need to make their own fuel, out of naturally occurring lithium.
The reason comes down to the fuel supply. A lot of things have to go right for fusion power to hit the grid, and one of them is the fuel. Most planned plants would run on a mix of two fuels, deuterium and tritium. Deuterium is easy to come by, but tritium is extremely rare in nature, and it’s an open secret in the fusion world that there isn’t enough of it to power every planned plant.
The proposed workaround is to make tritium on site, inside the power plant itself. A fusion reaction gives off a stream of fast-moving particles called neutrons. Startups plan to surround the reactor with a blanket of lithium, so that when a neutron strikes a lithium atom, the atom splits into helium and tritium. The tritium can then be collected, purified, and fed back into the reactor as fuel.
Not all lithium does this job equally well. It comes in two slightly different forms, lithium-6 and lithium-7, named for their weights. Lithium-6 is far better at capturing neutrons and producing tritium, but it makes up only about 7.5% of natural lithium, and the rest is the heavier lithium-7. Separating the two is difficult, and there is little capacity to do it today, so the world doesn’t have enough lithium-6 either.
Licube sees a big market in solving that problem. “If fusion comes online, it should be a $50 billion market by 2040,” Yohei Kiguchi, co-founder and CEO of Licube, told TechCrunch.
Licube is one of 20 startups that are presenting onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco as part of the Startup Battlefield pitch competition.
While fusion has the potential to capture a significant chunk of the multitrillion-dollar energy market, fusion startups are still years away from building their first power plants.
“Fusion is the biggest market in the future, but we also understand the future might be late by a few years,” Kiguchi said.
Until fusion becomes a major market, Licube plans to use the same technology to purify lithium for use in semiconductor, pharmaceutical, fission reactors, and spacecraft industries.
The core technology is based on the electrolyzer, a device that uses electrical current to drive chemical reactions. In Licube’s case, lithium is dissolved in a liquid on one side of a ceramic membrane. As electrical current flows from one side of the membrane to the other, lithium-6 moves faster. Licube can then draw off that liquid and separate the lithium-6.
The goal is to enrich the lithium to at least 99.995% lithium-6. Fusion companies can feed that highly enriched lithium into their fuel breeding systems.
Kiguchi was inspired to start Licube after visiting ITER, the experimental fusion reactor being built in the south of France. He said he was living a couple of hours’ drive away in Monaco after retiring from his previous company, Enechange, an energy-switching platform network in Japan.
“I found out that I was too young to retire,” he said. “I’m an energy guy. I want to do something bigger.”

title: Princeton Researchers Find a Lower-Energy Route to Fusion Ignition
body: A new model for nuclear fusion has potentially discovered a significantly more energy-efficient way to achieve nuclear fusion, and flipped everything we thought we knew about the fusion process. The scientists' modelling also flips the traditional order of operations for managing and sustaining plasma in a controlled fusion experiment. Traditionally, fusion processes start by compressing plasma for higher density, and then heating it to superhot temperatures. However, new modelling from the United States Department of Energy's Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory PPPL shows that reversing this order of operations could drastically reduce the energy inputs necessary to achieve ignition.  This is big. Ignition refers to when a fusion experiment creates more energy than it consumes. To date, this has been the biggest and most elusive challenge of achieving fusion  the process which powers our own sun  here on Earth. The first ever successful ignition was achieved in 2022 at California's Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. And while this achievement has been repeated and other instances of ignition have occurred, the sector is still a far cry from creating enough net energy to be anywhere close to practical and commercial application.  Unlocking the secret to commercially scalable nuclear fusion would solve much of the world's energy problems essentially overnight. Fusion provides a near-limitless source of clean energy and yields none of the hazardous and radioactive spent nuclear fuel associated with nuclear fission. It's therefore viewed as a 'holy grail' of clean energy. This is why finding more energy-efficient pathways toward ignition is such a big deal, even if they are  at this point  purely theoretical.  But the team at PPPL didn't just discover how to make fusion easier. They also discovered a way to make fusion much, much more difficult  and found that it could be a major stumbling block for many of the nuclear fusion experiments and startups racing to achieve commercial nuclear fusion. The team found that the incorporation of just a tiny amount of the element tungsten in the fusion process  as small as one part of tungsten in 10,000 within the plasma  could cause the pressure needed to achieve ignition to double, creating major issues for efficiency and stability.  This is highly relevant for many next-gen fusion experiments which use tungsten in the design of their reactors. According to reporting from Interesting Engineering, "More than a dozen next-generation fusion machines have selected tungsten for their inner walls because the metal can withstand extremely high temperatures." If the tiniest bit of this tungsten enters the plasma, achieving fusion quickly becomes much more difficult, and could even make the experiment unstable.  Discovering this risk now may avoid a lot of wasted energy and expenditures going forward. And, happily, those tungsten-based reactors don't need to be scrapped; they just need to be coated, such as with liquid lithium, to ensure that the tungsten doesn't contaminate the plasma.  "While more study is needed, we are excited by these results, and they suggest a clear path forward for future research in this area," PPPL physicist Jonathan Menard told Interesting Engineering.  PPPL is far from alone in its enthusiasm for fusion research and its disruptive potential. After a century of slow and painstaking progress from very few players, the field of nuclear fusion is now exploding as investors take note of the accelerated developments in the field, and the AI boom causes VC money to flood into all kinds of alternative energies. As a result, startups are starting to crowd into the sector, creating more competition and leading to increased innovation.  Some of the tech sector's biggest names and deepest pockets are heavily involved in the burgeoning fusion sector. Microsoft's Bill Gates and OpenAI's Sam Altman are vocal advocates for and financial backers of nuclear fusion research as a critical solution to the energy monster their own companies are creating through the hyperscaling of AI data centers. Altman has admitted that the world simply doesn't have enough energy to support the tech sector's growth trajectory in a business-as-usual scenario.  "There's no way to get there without a breakthrough," he said at the 2024 World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland. "It motivates us to go invest more in fusion."  By Haley Zaremba for Oilprice.com

title: The world’s distorted view of Israel is built on persistent myths - opinion
body: If one had to choose a single word that characterizes the prism through which the world sees Israel and internalizes its feelings about us these days, that word would be “canard.” The prism is the vehicle that makes it possible for the viewer to see the truth bent to one's own liking, while the canard provides the basis that attempts to propagate the lie.The dictionary states that a canard primarily refers to an unfounded rumor, a false story, or a deliberate hoax. The word is derived from the French canard (meaning “duck”), tracing back to the old French expression “vendre un canard à moitié” (“to half-sell a duck”), meaning to trick or cheat someone.Of course, some would say that given France's frequent negativism about Israel, it should not be surprising that the word that describes the world's preference for internalizing lies about Israel has its source in French.Examples abound as to how this plays out in real life.Last week, in a debate between US senatorial candidates in Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed was asked multiple times by a debate moderator which country he considers a bigger threat to the US: Iran or Israel? Each time, he parried.“That's a ridiculous hypothetical because here's what's happening right now: Our ostensible ally in Israel has lobbied us to go to war with Iran. I don't consider an ally a country that takes us to wars we don't need to fight, and I don't want to be fighting wars we don't need to fight,” he said, describing both as “kind of dangerous.”The canard that Israel is responsible for America's decision to attack Iran has surfaced so often since the start of the war on February 28 that it is regularly stated as fact. It reminds one of the words commonly attributed to Joseph Goebbels, the propaganda minister of Nazi Germany, though there is no evidence he ever actually said or wrote those exact words.'Illusion of truth effect'While the formulation is a paraphrase rather than a direct historical citation, psychologists study this concept as the “illusion of truth effect,” which shows that people are more likely to believe information is true simply because they have heard it before.The fact is that Israel has urged every American president for the last 40-plus years to take the Iranian nuclear threat seriously and do something about it. No US president prior to the current one has ever chosen to authorize military action against Iran to neutralize their nuclear capability.However, it was the current US president who chose to invite Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to the White House briefing room to hear his pitch, but it was US President Donald Trump who decided to launch military action against Iran.Regardless of how it turns out, it is a canard to blame Israel for taking the US to war against Iran, even if the Netanyahu government was in favor of such action.However, a canard can be manipulated for other purposes as well. Last week, a decision was made by the Nobel Prize Committee to award this year's peace prize to South African Jurist Navanethem “Navi” Pillay. Among other anti-Israel positions in her history, she is famous for believing the canard that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza.While she has done worthwhile work in helping advance a more comprehensive international legal order and, as the Committee noted, “played a central role in ensuring that issues such as war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are brought to justice,” her activities regarding the supposed genocide by Israel in Gaza dramatically tarnish her reputation.Elisha Wiesel, in an op-ed in The Free Press, wrote: “My father, Elie Wiesel, received the Nobel Peace Prize for ensuring the Holocaust wouldn't be forgotten. By honoring Navi Pillay, who accused Israel of genocide, the committee has betrayed his legacy.”Yet the canard is that Israel, which vaccinated over one million residents of Gaza against polio, enabled millions of kilograms of food to enter the strip during the war (most of which was stolen by Hamas and then resold at inflated prices), put its own troops at risk by having them enter buildings to ensure only combatants were attacked, not civilians, and notified the Gazan population of every significant military operation to come with instructions for moving to safer zones, is somehow guilty of genocide.A truthful look at the facts will show that it is actually Hamas that was engaged in genocide against Israel given their attack on October 7, intent on killing as many Jews as possible. This, in keeping with their original 1988 founding charter explicitly calling for the killing of Jews, which draws on religious texts to justify violence against Jewish people globally.While a revised document released in 2017 removed this specific language, Hamas did not formally revoke or repudiate the original charter. Organizations like Genocide Watch and various genocide scholars have stated that Hamas's October 7, 2023, attacks against Israeli civilians and statements by its leadership reflected genocidal intent and acts.Yet the canard that Israel is guilty of genocide continues, with large portions of the world's diplomatic corps agreeing with or remaining silent about this blatant misstatement of facts.Former US president John F Kennedy said: “The great enemy of the truth is very often not the lie, deliberate, contrived, and dishonest, but the myth, persistent, persuasive, and unrealistic.”When it comes to Israel, the world too easily accepts the myth rather than seek the truth. Our job, the job for all of us, is to shatter the prism that enables the myths to fester and do so at every opportunity. That is our obligation as a community.The writer, a 42-year resident of Jerusalem, is a former national president of the Association of Americans and Canadians in Israel, a past chairperson of the board of the Pardes Institute of Jewish Studies, and a Board Member of the Israel-America Chamber of Commerce (AMCHAM).

title: Greek Students Camp Outside Parliament as Rent Crisis Deepens
body: Students have pitched tents in Athens’ Syntagma Square, directly outside the Greek Parliament, to protest soaring rents and the rising cost of university education, warning that housing costs are making it increasingly difficult for young people to begin or continue their studies. Around twenty camping tents have been set up in Syntagma Square in central Athens on Tuesday by university students demanding affordable student housing and measures to tackle the rising cost of living. A rally is planned for later. Photos: Daphne Tolis @greekcitytimes pic.twitter.com/kgnXB8NxHa — Daphne Tolis (@daphnetoli) October 13, 2026 Despite heavy rain and difficult weather conditions, students from dozens of university associations have maintained their protest, turning the central square into an overnight demonstration against Greece’s worsening student housing crisis. The mobilisation on Tuesday, October 13, includes a march to the Ministry of Finance, where students plan to present their demands, followed by an overnight stay in the square and a concert featuring Greek artists. The students say high rents, limited university accommodation, rising food prices, transport costs and expensive educational materials are placing mounting pressure on them and their families. Students Face Rents of €600 for a Studio Nina Nifakou, president of the Student Association of the School of Administrative, Economic and Social Sciences at the University of West Attica, says the cost of studying has reached an unsustainable level. Greek student housing crisis photo by Daphne Tolis Speaking to Orange Press Agency, she explains that students established the protest camp after repeated attempts to draw attention to their financial difficulties. “Today, being a student has become a struggle for survival,” Nifakou says. She argues that the housing shortage is particularly severe for students who move to Athens from other parts of Greece and cannot live with their families. Nifakou claims existing student accommodation meets less than four per cent of demand. She also points to the University of West Attica, one of Greece’s largest universities, as an example of the shortage, saying students there have no dedicated student residence. As a result, she says, some students face rents of around €600 for a studio apartment. The expense comes on top of everyday costs, including groceries, petrol, energy, meals and the materials required for university courses. Housing Costs Threaten Access to Higher Education The protesters argue that the housing crisis is no longer simply a financial burden for families. They say it threatens students’ ability to access higher education and complete their degrees. For young people who must relocate to attend university, accommodation can represent one of their largest expenses. When rent consumes a substantial share of a household’s income, some families struggle to support their children’s studies away from home. Nifakou also claims that hundreds of students do not enrol in their chosen university programmes because of the financial pressures associated with studying. The demonstration seeks greater public support for student accommodation and measures to reduce the overall cost of university life. Student Housing Protests Spread Across Europe The Athens demonstration comes amid wider disputes over housing affordability across Europe. Spain has experienced repeated demonstrations over rising rents, shortages of affordable housing and the impact of short-term tourist accommodation on local housing markets. Portugal has also seen protests demanding greater protection for tenants and measures to make housing more affordable. Although conditions vary between countries, housing costs have become a major concern for younger generations seeking financial independence. In Greece, students say the combination of high rents and limited university accommodation is placing their education and future prospects at risk. Students Warn of Further Protests The protesters have vowed to continue their campaign, arguing that immediate measures are needed to improve access to affordable housing and provide greater financial support for students. Nifakou criticises government spending priorities, arguing that resources must also be directed towards meeting social needs. She says the student associations intend to escalate their mobilisation, with another rally planned for Syntagma Square the following Wednesday, October 21. The students are calling on others to join the overnight protest and support their demands through further demonstrations organised by university associations. With tents set up outside Parliament, the protesters are making their position clear: for many students, the cost of accommodation has become a barrier to university life itself. The post Greek Students Camp Outside Parliament as Rent Crisis Deepens appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Russia says Kiev disguises military supply channel by concern for global food security
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. The Kiev regime, supposedly concerned about the global food security, wants to have a reliable maritime supply channel for its army, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said.
"After the effectiveness of Russia’s retaliatory strikes against the military and economic potential of the Zelensky regime became obvious, and the delivery of weapons to the Ukrainian armed forces through the Black Sea ports was effectively blocked, various proposals began to emerge from all sides - proposals to agree on ‘maritime’, ‘energy’, and ‘air’ truces, to establish ‘maritime security corridors’, and so on," the diplomat stated in response to a question from journalists.
In her view, this is linked to "Zelensky’s desire, together with his handlers, to find ways to reduce the intensity of strikes by the Russian armed forces. Their goal is obvious - under the formal pretext of concern for the global food security, to secure a protected maritime supply channel for weapons to the armed forces of Ukraine and to create yet another mechanism of political and economic pressure on Russia," Zakharova said, adding that "the Black Sea artery supplying Zelensky’s regime is very important for its sponsors."

title: 2027: Hamzat unveils policy agenda, promises reforms in transport, housing, security
body: The Deputy Gov. of Lagos State, Dr Obafemi Hamzat, has unveiled a policy agenda for the state, promising reforms in transportation, housing, security, technology, food distribution and justice delivery ahead of the 2027 governorship election. Hamzat made the commitments while presenting his Promise Agenda, tagged, ‘An Afternoon to Discuss the Facts and Figures of Lagos State: The 8th Largest Economy in Africa’. The event was organised by the Lagos Chamber of Commerce and Industry (LCCI) in collaboration with the Contact and Mobilisation Committee, Formal Sector for PBAT and KOH on Tuesday in Victoria Island, Lagos State. . Hamzat, the All Progressives Congress (APC) governorship candidate for the 2027 elections, described it as a social contract with Lagos residents, which he pledged to implement from May 29, 2027, if elected governor. He said the agenda was designed to establish measurable targets for government, enabling residents to assess performance and hold the administration accountable for its promises. Hamzat said transportation remained one of Lagos most pressing challenges, noting that traffic congestion costs the state an estimated economic losses of N1 trillion annually, with residents spending an average of four hours daily in traffic. He said Lagos had a vehicle density of 212 vehicles per kilometre, compared with the national average of 16, making the development of alternative transportation systems imperative. According to him, the state has identified 63 traffic junctions for improvement and addressed 33 of them, while plans are underway to expand Bus Rapid Transit services, improve terminals, develop rail infrastructure and increase water transportation. He said his administration would prioritise waterways to reduce pressure on roads, including developing ferry terminals and improving connections between communities such as Ikorodu, Badagry and other parts of Lagos. Hamzat also promised improved pedestrian walkways, greener public spaces and better organised bus terminals to separate commuters from vehicular traffic. He said the state aimed to plant 10 million trees within four years. On water supply, Hamzat said the completion of an ongoing water infrastructure project would provide additional access to water for six million people. On Jobs, technology and business growth, the APC candidate said the Lagos State Employment Trust Fund had supported businesses and activated about 340,000 jobs since 2019. He added that his administration if elected, would strengthen mentorship and business management support to help small enterprises survive and expand. He said the state had proposed four industrial parks in Epe, Badagry, Ikorodu and Ojo under its 2025–2030 industrial policy. Hamzat also pledged to harmonise government levies and regulatory processes to reduce the burden on businesses, while reviewing charges imposed on petty traders and micro-enterprises. On technology, he described Yaba as a major technology hub, saying its technology ecosystem had developed into a 15.3-billion-dollar economy with about 2,000 start-ups. He noted that Lagos was implementing a 1,000-kilometre fibre-optic cable network, with plans to expand it to 6,000 kilometres, while reducing broadband costs and supporting local technology companies. The deputy governor further added that the state would adopt a local-first procurement approach by giving qualified Nigerian technology firms the first opportunity to supply products required by the government. On food security and creative economy, Hamzat said the state was developing a 420-hectare food logistics hub and cold-chain network to reduce food wastage, improve storage and cut transportation costs between farmers and markets. He said: “The cold-chain facilities in Mushin and Gbagada has helped market women reduce logistics costs by 40 per cent while government is expanding medium-scale markets across the state.” “Also, the state will support farmers through a proposed N500 billion guarantee scheme, alongside arrangements in facilitating the purchase and distribution of locally produced food.” On the creative industry, Hamzat said Lagos would strengthen training in contract negotiation and intellectual property to enable artists and other creative professionals to earn better returns from their work. On Justice, inclusion and social welfare, the APC governorship candidate said the state was working with the judiciary to increase the civil jurisdiction of magistrates courts from N10 million to N15 million to reduce the backlog of cases in the High Courts. He said the government also wanted landlord-tenant disputes resolved within three months, adding that more courts would be established to improve access to justice. He disclosed that about 198 people had been prosecuted for domestic violence, stressing the need to strengthen support for survivors and encourage more victims to seek justice. On inclusion, Hamzat said women-led enterprises performed well among small businesses, adding that the government planned to allocate five per cent of its business support to women-led enterprises. He also promised to certify artisans and other skilled workers in their preferred languages and establish an online platform where customers could assess their services through reviews. He said the government would pay 40 per cent of the stipends of trainees placed in companies under its vocational and technical training programmes to encourage businesses to employ them. Hamzat added that the state would strengthen child protection by ensuring that children below 18 years were either in school or acquiring vocational skills. On security, he said Lagos had about 6,800 personnel in its safety agency and was recruiting an additional 2,500, adding that the personnel could form a foundation for state policing if the necessary constitutional approval was secured. He said the state had increased insurance benefits for police officers who died in service to N4 million for junior officers and N10 million for senior officers, stressing the need to improve support for their families. Hamzat also called for stronger climate adaptation measures, including improved drainage, community protection and early-warning systems to prepare residents for extreme rainfall and flooding. On housing, the deputy governor said the state would collaborate with private developers to increase the supply of affordable homes, noting that the average period for an African to build a house was about 17 years. According to him, we will explore housing and mortgage arrangements that enabled young people and low-income earners to secure decent accommodation without sacrificing other basic needs. Hamzat said the commitments would be assessed against measurable targets to ensure accountability, adding that government, businesses and residents must work together to achieve a more inclusive and prosperous Lagos. Earlier, the LCCI President, Mr Leye Kupoluyi, stated that the engagement provided an opportunity for the business community to assess the economic policies and development priorities of prospective political leaders. He said: “it gives us direct impact of government policies on investment, operating costs and business growth.” Kupoluyi identified five key priority areas for the next administration, which included reducing the cost of doing business, improving infrastructure and mobility, reforming the tax and regulatory framework, promoting economic growth and investment, and empowering small and medium-scale enterprises (SMEs). He said addressing high energy and logistics costs, traffic congestion, freight bottlenecks and regulatory challenges would improve productivity and create a more conducive business environment. The LCCI president also called for improved access to capital, technology and markets for SMEs, emphasising the need for stronger collaboration between government and the private sector to unlock Lagos State economic potential. He reaffirmed the Chamber’s commitment to constructive, evidence-based engagement with political leaders and future administrations. The LCCI Deputy President, Mr Knit Ulvmoen, emphasised the need to strengthen local manufacturing and reduce Nigeria’s dependence on imported finished goods. He noted that the country had the people, market and raw materials required to produce more goods locally. He cited the transformation of Nigeria’s cement industry from heavy reliance on imports to local production and exports as evidence of the benefits of adding value to domestic resources. Ulvmoen called for greater investment in sectors such as agriculture, pharmaceuticals, textiles, petrochemicals and renewable energy, while stressing that education and skills development are essential to preparing Nigerians for industrial growth and economic self-sufficiency. In his goodwill message, the Managing Director of Sterling Bank, Mr Abubakar Suleiman, identified Lagos State real estate sector as a major untapped source of capital. Suleiman urged the government to make land assets more accessible to investors through funding. He added that Lagos possessed a unique economic advantage as a financial hub, with substantial lending and investment activities already concentrated in the state. According to him, unlocking real estate value can significantly expand development funding. “If the government can do this, I am confident that the initiative could attract more domestic investment, boost development and strengthen Lagos ambition to become a leading global financial centre,” he said. The post 2027: Hamzat unveils policy agenda, promises reforms in transport, housing, security appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Russian drone debris falls on Lutsk shopping mall, setting roof on fire
body:
According to Ukrinform, Roman Romaniuk, acting head of the Volyn Regional Military Administration, reported this on Telegram .
“The enemy launched a ‘Shahed’ jet drone at the region. After it was shot down in mid-air, debris fell onto the grounds of the ‘Adrenaline City’ entertainment center in Lutsk. A fire broke out on the roof of the entertainment center,” the message reads.
Firefighters from the State Emergency Service have already managed to contain the fire .
No one was injured—there were no fatalities or injuries.
As reported by Ukrinform, the Russians attacked the Lviv region with drones during the day—houses were damaged, and three people were injured.

title: Star Oil donates GH¢1million towards construction of new CID facility
body: Oil marketing company Star Oil has donated GH¢1 million to support the construction of a new facility for the Criminal Investigations Department (CID) of the Ghana Police Service. The new facility, estimated at GH¢11 million, is expected to improve the CID’s investigative and operational functions when completed. The project will provide office accommodation, interrogation rooms, and detention facilities for the department. Chief Executive Officer of Star Oil, Philip Tieku, said the donation was in recognition of the CID’s contribution to addressing security challenges facing the company’s nationwide operations. He noted how the Department’s work has helped Star Oil improve security monitoring at its more than 280 locations across the country, explaining that this has reduced the need for physical security personnel at some lower-risk stations. “The CID has been very supportive in that effort. They’ve assisted us in almost every situation that comes up, and we’ve gotten to the point where that collaboration has allowed us to operate a remote security monitoring system supported by the CID,” he said. Mr. Tieku added that the company considered it important to support the department’s infrastructure needs, having benefited from its services over the years. Receiving the donation, Director-General of the CID, COP Lydia Yaako Donkor, said the new facility would address longstanding challenges associated with the department’s lack of adequate detention space at its headquarters. She explained that the department often has to rely on other police stations for the detention and interrogation of arrested persons, placing additional pressure on those facilities. “For a while now, we’ve not had that facility within this headquarters, and it is also a matter of concern for us. We have to be sending people to other stations, and those stations are also burdened,” she said. The contractor for the project, David Mawuli of Delta Plus, said the facility will include eight detention cells for male and female suspects, as well as a separate cell for juveniles. The building will also accommodate interrogation rooms, investigation offices, and IT facilities, with a cafeteria planned for the top floor. Construction is expected to take 12 months, provided the required resources are made available.

title: The secrets hiding in our environment, By ‘Tope Fasua
body:
In several of my books I have agonised over our environment and the need for us to take a keen view and obsess about how we present ourselves. I recall writing a few articles with titles such as “It’s The Environment, Stupid!” (in the style of the famous Clintonian campaign slogan around the Economy in 1998), and “We Cannot Emphasise the Environment Enough” , among others. I pushed the matter in the public space to the extent that Nigeria – and most of Africa – really have little business for now, with the big Climate Change discussions which is the new obsession among developed countries who love to set agenda for everyone. I believe that being corralled into the Climate Change agenda may distract us from what really matters for us, and what is immediately achievable, which is the subject of how we can really take care of our own environment and pick up after ourselves. You cannot enroll for a PhD when you should be learning the ropes in primary school.
My many urban sojourns within Nigeria in recent times has compelled me to write on the environment, again. There seems to be an explosion of urban waste in places like Lagos, Abuja, Port Harcourt, Kano, and perhaps every state capital and large cities across Nigeria, with varying degrees of success in terms of their management. Refuse dumps have been occurring in different places where they hadn’t been in the past. At some point, it looked like deliberate sabotage – and that could be valid because all over the world one of the easiest ways to bring down governments is for whatever mafia that controls waste management to strike. We’ve seen this in the US (New York, New Jersey, California etc), in Italy (Napoli) and in the UK (Birmingham, London) etc.
Driving up the bridge from Bank Anthony way towards the local airport, there is a new refuse dump right at the beginning of the ramp. I recall when people from Old Ojo Road would rush across the express road to dump refuse on the rail track that was being constructed but hadn’t been commissioned. I recall the refuse dumps that assail the eyes when you take the train ride from Yaba to Abeokuta or Ibadan. Even in Gbagada, the green areas have been assaulted. This gives one great concern. In Abuja, many incidences of fly-tipping are recorded; people dumping their trash anywhere, perhaps at night. Large roundabouts are a popular spot. Also, the streams and waterways that snake through Abuja are favorite dumping spots. Even some prime lands which owners have abandoned over time are good spots for the dumping of waste. It’s just overwhelming!
Now, the reason they call some countries ‘shit-hole’ countries is because of their management of urban waste. No matter how adept a nation gets in building fantastic structures and infrastructure, the inability to get on top of waste management is a dead giveaway. Waste management and environmental sanity are therefore arduous tasks, especially because they require unending attention and action. But the approach whereby the government is the victim, running everywhere to pick up after people, and being vulnerable to sabotage, to political vendetta and such, can no longer be the solution. The new approach must actively involve everybody. The incentives must change and be enhanced. Can streets take responsibility for their own outlook? Can communities get rewarded for doing the right thing? Can everyone become a watchdog against improper behaviours? Can the structure we currently have for waste management be expanded urgently, with more equipment, more staff, more technology, and better logistics? Can waste management, and the obsession with a clean environment all over Nigeria be declared as an emergency?
Because what we see as chaos presently, with which political opposition can take digs against incumbent governments, is actually telling us something. It masks great secrets for where we must now head as a people.
The first secret is that an explosion of urban waste actually means urban growth, and probably better standards of living for the people. This World Bank article confirms this theory, meaning that the poverty narrative around Nigeria may not be the reality. The larger part of our urban waste consists of plastics, cartons, food waste, clothing, and such like. The ubiquity of waste management issues should therefore not be seen simply as a disadvantage but as a sign that standards of living are increasing, therefore justifying the larger investments we must now make.
In some of my earlier books, I espoused how Nigeria could launch a large program which encompasses several ministries and which may be titled “Cleanest, Safest, and Most-Organised Nation in Africa Project”. I’ve been thinking about this for over a decade now and it keeps coming back. It is a project that allows us to work on the brains, minds and hearts of our people, to help us gain ownership of our country, one and all, to attract global respect, new investment and tourism, and help take the sail away from the incessant security challenge that we have. I cited the Broken-Windows Theory as an underpinning theoretical framework around such a project, because we need to understand that the bad habits that have now become a culture instead and so must be tackled at a high and comprehensive level.
The environment holds the secret to our greatness as a people. Whereas many Nigerians actively work towards the undoing of the country, but the efforts and striving of the true patriots who want her to make real progress will be enhanced if our environment is spick and span – or tending close to that. Nigeria needs investments. But before investments, we need our respect back from the world. This respect will not be obtained by force of arms but gently and quietly through how we reposition ourselves – especially our environment.
This is why I respect the work being done by people like Tokunbo Wahab in Lagos State. He gets it. Without those valiant efforts, that state – the most urbane in Nigeria and one which qualifies as a middle-income economy – would easily drown in filth and waste. The work hasn’t been fully grappled though. There is still so much to do. Tokunbo can see that it’s a big battle, as he tackles even larger issues of impunity, indiscriminate buildings that block water ways, and such like, and indiscriminate waste dumping everywhere.
A lot more investment is needed in new systems that will allow for waste evacuation. I urge governments at all levels to squeeze out the required money – even if they have to enter into Public-Private arrangements that allow them to spread the investment over time. The waste management business may look unappealing from a distance, but a closer look reveals a lucrative opportunity for everyone across the value chain—from collectors, recyclers and manufacturers to investors, governments and the Nigerian people. Waste is not merely a disposal problem; it is an economic resource waiting to be unlocked. It creates jobs, generates revenue, supplies raw materials, protects public health and improves the environment. In the circular economy, what one person throws away can become another person’s wealth. No investment is a waste—pardon the pun!
We need a national program though; one upon which we can anchor the emotions of our people, one around which we can rally the energy of millions of Nigerians. It is about visioning. It is about optics. We cannot keep inviting foreigners into this country while we leave our environment to chance. We already are coming from a position of disadvantage as a people. The world distrusts us. Around kitchen tables, they talk about Nigeria with suspicion, a little disdain, sometimes pity. Many are unable to express themselves openly about Nigeria because of our status. We are important. But we can do better by starting to position ourselves as a decent nation.
To this extent, as I’ve always asserted, Nigeria can employ and engage millions of her people around environmental work. We can nitpick about our environment. We can expand the circular economy and capture more of our solid waste for recycling. We can enforce more. Our people should be afraid to throw trash from their cars and buses or simply litter the streets. There should be a standing environmental taskforce. Those environmental workers of old (the wolewoles ) did a great service to rewire our people’s mentality. Honestly, we need that back today. We haven’t yet graduated from that level to begin to self-regulate. We can see the reality because our now exploded population has become even more careless with the way we keep our environment. As we say in Nigeria, the ‘anyhowness’ is just galling. A renewed focus on the environment, the recruitment of millions of especially young people into sustainable careers there will achieve the following:
I have proposed over time that Nigeria could launch a campaign titled “The Cleanest, Safest, Most-Organised Country in Africa” project. We could call it the COSMOS Project for want of something snazzy. This gives us a programme around which we can rally our efforts and set our vision in a renewable fashion. Of course, we don’t have to achieve this in a jiffy, but a lot will start changing in a short while. I dream about that day. I believe strongly that this is possible. And countries around us are getting smarter. I visited Benin Republic months back for the first time and I saw something similar on the streets of Cotonou. An American lady who came to Nigeria for holidays also visited Benin and was so incensed with Nigeria upon her return. Our population is not an excuse. Our minds, our vision, our standards are the problem. But those can be fixed. I write as an economist. I know that this is a sure bet to permanently reposition our economy for the long term. Not everything is anchored on electricity and natural resources. Sometimes the real solutions are much more subtle, and are there in the open, beckoning on us to act.
