title: BC Conservatives move from fractured to front runners, new poll finds
body:
A new Ipsos poll shows that while the BC Conservatives appeared in disarray one month ago, they have now gained a five-point lead over the BC NDP.
The poll, conducted in partnership with Global BC, shows the BC Conservatives have the support of 43 per cent of decided voters, which puts them five-points ahead of the BC NDP, which have 38 per cent of support.
The BC Green Party is up one point, now sitting at 11 per cent, followed by OneBC at four per cent and CentreBC at two per cent.
The poll found that 18 per cent of voters are still undecided and seven per cent have no preference for which party is in power.
“The BC Conservatives are now up on the NDP by five points,” Kyle Braid, senior vice president of Ipsos, said on Tuesday morning.
“And if anything, their lead is firming up and expanding. And so if it wasn’t obvious before, it’s very clear now from these numbers that calling this election an early election might turn out to be a giant miscalculation.”
The race remains very close in Metro Vancouver, however, with the BC Conservatives leading by three points with 42 per cent, while the BC NDP has 39 per cent, but the NDP does have a substantial lead on Vancouver Island with 47 per cent to the BC Conservatives’ 27 per cent, according to those polled.
The BC Conservatives have a 21-point lead in the Southern Interior and in the northern part of the province, with 53 per cent to the BC NDP’s 32 per cent.
“The Conservatives are doing really well with men,” Braid said.
“The gender gap that we often see in B.C. has returned, so the Conservatives lead by big margins with men, the NDP with women, the Conservatives are doing really well with the 35- to 54-year-old age group, and of course, as always, they’re doing really well in the Interior and north of the province.”
Nearly one in four voters, 23 per cent, who say they have a current party preference said there is still a “good chance” they will change their mind and vote for some other party’s candidate in the election.
The poll also found that half of residents, which is up slightly from the previous poll , believe it is time for another provincial party to take over, with that number now at 50 per cent.
Three-in-10, 31 per cent, of residents continue to say the Eby government has done a good job and deserves re-election.
Two-in-10 people, 19 per cent, are undecided.
“There’s probably about 25 per cent of the voters who are still up for grabs,” Braid said.
“Some of them undecided, some of them have a choice now but are not certain of it, so that’s a fairly large number at this point of the campaign. Some of that is driven by the fact that the Conservative Party is kind of new, different than the Conservative Party we had in the last election and they also have a new leader.”
When it comes to the favourability of the leaders, Eby continues to come out ahead at 35 per cent viewing him favourably, with BC Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson sitting at 26 per cent. However, Eby’s unfavourable rating is at 38 per cent, while Doerkson’s is at 24 per cent, according to the poll.
“The leadership question is an open one here,” Braid said.
“People just know David Eby, and his numbers actually are not that bad. We’ve seen premiers and politicians have numbers that are in the 50 or 60 per cent negatives. He’s got almost as many favorables as unfavorables, so they’re still open to hearing from David Eby. They just don’t know Lorne Doerkson yet, which suggests that the debate that’s coming up is going to be extremely important.”
British Columbians will have the opportunity to hear from the three major party leaders ahead of the provincial election on Oct. 24.
The B.C. provincial leaders’ debate will take place on Wednesday, Oct. 14, from 6:15 p.m. to 8 p.m. and will be live on Global BC, BC1 and online.
Eby, Doerkson and BC Green Party leader Emily Lowan will be taking part.
Shachi Kurl, president of the Angus Reid Institute, will be the moderator.
“David Eby has two tasks in the leaders’ debate,” Braid said.
“One is to create some sense of risk for people for electing a BC Conservative government. And the other is to try to persuade some of those voters who are considering either the NDP or the Greens that a vote for the NDP is the correct choice.
“Lorne Doerkson’s main thing is simply to introduce himself to voters in the province. Most people don’t know him. The other thing is quite simply just to stand up and look like a premier. That’s it.”
These are the findings of an Ipsos poll conducted in partnership with Global BC from Oct. 7 to 11, 2026. For this survey, a sample of 1,356 adult British Columbians were surveyed both online through sample sourced through the Ipsos panel (n=1,001) and by phone with live interviewers (n=350) using both cellphones and landlines. Data was weighted by B.C. region, age, gender and education, in accordance with Census proportions. The precision of Ipsos polls, including online samples, is measured using a credibility interval. In this case, the overall poll is accurate to within ±3.1 percentage points, 19 times out of 20. Questions asked only of online respondents are accurate to within ±3.7 percentage points, 19 times out of 20. The credibility interval will be wider among subsets of the population. All sample surveys and polls may be subject to other sources of error, including, but not limited to, coverage error and measurement error.

title: IMF warns about major economic risks and a ‘disorderly’ rise in bond yields
body:
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) released its October Global Financial Stability Report on Tuesday, which outlines three major threats to global economies: an AI market correction, spiking government bond yields and cyberattacks.
Although global economies have proven mostly resilient so far, the IMF’s directors are urging policy makers and business leaders to take immediate action to mitigate the risk from these potential “shocks.”
“Directors broadly concurred that risks to the outlook remain skewed to the downside,” the report said.
Rising bond yields have been a warning sign for financial markets in recent months amid the Iran war’s risk to global economies, and the IMF says those risks are becoming more of a concern.
Bonds are essentially loans, where governments or companies look to borrow money from the general public, and those bond purchasers expect a return or interest on that borrowed money, which is known as the yield on those bonds.
Those yields fluctuate regularly, based on various economic factors as well as supply and demand for those bonds, and yields have been spiking in recent months amid economic uncertainty and geopolitical conflicts, rising inflation and government debt, and expectations of higher interest rates .
The yield on the 10-year U.S. government treasury was at 5.22 per cent as of publication, down from a peak of more than 5.3 per cent last week and up from 4.24 per cent six months ago.
The IMF said bond market risks have worsened since its April report, as higher energy prices have driven government bond yields up.
“Resurgent inflation or fiscal concerns could trigger a sharp rise in sovereign bond yields and spark broader market turmoil given the foundational importance of sovereign bonds. High public debt and rollover risks remain unresolved, increasing the chances that a rise in yields could occur in a disorderly manner,” the report said.
“These developments suggest that bond market risks have worsened since the April 2026 Global Financial Stability Report. A crystallization of these fragilities could lead to market turmoil.”
Artificial intelligence companies have attracted trillions of dollars in investment from stock markets and governments in just a few years. That rate of growth has led some analysts to bet on an AI bubble bursting in the near future.
The IMF report highlights the risk of an AI market correction, which happens when a business, industry or sector is considered overvalued. That sudden realization may trigger a mass selloff of people’s stocks and other assets in technology companies.
If that happens, the IMF report says there could be a dramatic ripple effect that will hurt global economies because of the amount of money invested in AI.
“Weaker or less durable AI investments and profitability could be a shock that triggers a market correction. Growing evidence suggests that AI capabilities can be delivered at lower investment levels or that potential economic gains may not be as large as expected,” the report said.
Athanasios Vamvakidis, deputy director in the IMF’s Monetary and Capital Markets Department, at a press briefing in Bangkok said, “an AI market correction will affect the real economy.”
He said while global risk sentiment was very strong, underpinned by solid earnings and optimism about AI, such “resilience is not necessarily safety.” An AI correction would have impacts on wealth and investment that could spill into broader markets, he said.
The risk of such a selloff, as well as a spike in sovereign bond yields or a major cyberattack, were among “plausible near-term catalysts” that policymakers should monitor, the IMF said in its report.
On cyber threats, the IMF said that a lack of resources, particularly in emerging markets, and a growing reliance on a small number of critical providers was making cyber defence more difficult.
Canadian academics have also warned AI hack attempts are going to become more common unless policy makers and industry leaders take decisive action.
The IMF says cyber threats are not only becoming more common because of how quickly economies have shifted to a digital world, but the emergence of AI within that digital environment has “expanded the attack surface.”
“Cyber threats constitute a growing systemic risk as financial services become more digital and interconnected. For their part, frontier AI models are emerging as both powerful enablers of cyberattacks and critical defensive tools,” the report said.
“These risks by themselves do not necessarily threaten financial stability, but they could become a systemic risk—impairments to key financial intermediation and credit provision, with serious negative economic effects— if they are amplified by financial vulnerabilities.”

title: Diplomatic reshuffle: Josh Huck takes over as interim US chargé d’affaires in Athens
body: The US Embassy in Athens is undergoing a major transition following Kimberly Guilfoyle’s resignation as ambassador. To maintain continuity and prevent a diplomatic vacuum in US-Greece relations, Deputy Chief of Mission Josh Huck has assumed the role of interim chargé d’affaires. Huck will lead the embassy in the coming months while the formal process of selecting, nominating, and confirming a permanent ambassador by the US Senate takes place. Diplomatic sources indicate he is unlikely to be named as the permanent successor, as the interim role is primarily institutional and administrative. Experienced career diplomat Josh Huck joined the US Foreign Service in 2001. He has served in Shanghai, Tokyo, Sofia, Rangoon, Taipei, and Hong Kong, and held key Washington posts, including in the Bureaus of Chinese and Korean Affairs and as Chief of Staff to Kurt Campbell, then Assistant Secretary of State for East Asian and Pacific Affairs. He previously served as Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Southern Europe and the Caucasus and as Director of the Office of Southern European Affairs, overseeing Cyprus, Greece, Malta, and Turkey. Huck holds degrees from Johns Hopkins University, a master’s from the International University of Japan, and a certificate from the Johns Hopkins SAIS campus in Bologna. He speaks Mandarin Chinese, Japanese, Burmese, and Bulgarian. New ambassador expected to take months Selecting and confirming a permanent US ambassador to Greece is expected to take several months. The process requires Senate confirmation, and the upcoming US midterm elections may further delay hearings and final approval, potentially pushing the arrival of a new ambassador into early 2027. The post Diplomatic reshuffle: Josh Huck takes over as interim US chargé d’affaires in Athens appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: 'Furious' judge extends order to bar Trump admin from cutting trees at DC golf course
body:
She wants to know if the government deliberately tried to evade previous orders.
A federal judge on Tuesday extended her order barring the Trump administration from carrying out any further tree removals at Washington's East Potomac Golf Course until at least Oct. 26, court records show.
D.C. District Judge Ana Reyes erupted at Trump administration attorneys on Monday after they told her that more than 400 trees had been felled at the Washington D.C. public course that President Donald Trump wants to turn into one that can host professional tournaments.
The attorneys had previously pledged to provide notice to plaintiffs in the case about any irrevocable harm that would occur at the golf course through government actions.
"More than just being upset and furious right now, I am just beyond disappointed in the government. I have done everything humanly possible to give the government the benefit of the doubt in this case. I have done it repeatedly. I have done it for months," Reyes vented Monday after attorneys for the government told her how many trees had been cut down.
The golf course has been the subject of litigation brought by the D.C. Preservation League in response to President Donald Trump's efforts to turn it into a course that could host professional tournaments.
Reyes is expected to grill Interior Department official Gregory Wischer, a political appointee who has been a point person on many of Trump's major D.C. beautification projects, and acting director of the National Park Service Jessica Bowron in next Monday's hearing.
She also ordered written briefs from both the D.C. Preservation League, which is suing the government to stop the project, and the government over whether she should grant a more extensive preliminary injunction that would block the administration from making further renovations to the course as litigation plays out.
Reyes repeatedly pressed for answers in Monday's hourslong hearing on who within the Trump administration had ordered the removal of the trees.
"I am just at a total loss to understand what has happened here ... that the government precisely intended to do precisely what it has done, which is intentionally delaying letting the plaintiffs in the court know what was happening, so they could put a plan in place to clear hundreds and hundreds of trees."
The government provided notice to the plaintiffs at 4:55 p.m. last Friday that tree-cutting would occur at the golf course over the Columbus Day/Indigenous Peoples Day holiday weekend.
The National Park Service began cutting down trees on Saturday and the D.C. Preservation League filed for a temporary restraining order on Sunday.
Marissa Ann Piropato, a Justice Department attorney admitted to the court in Monday's hearing that 430 trees were cleared over weekend.
"I had said at the May hearing that I didn't want 10 trees chopped down without someone having notice," Reyes said. "On what universe did anyone in your office think that that was acceptable?"
"Your Honor, we did our best in providing notice," Piropato said.
"You did not do your best! You did your absolute worst!," Reyes interrupted.
The government testified that the plan to cut down trees was part of a plan put in place in 2019 to remove dead, dying and hazardous trees around the golf course.
"No one else can say what the basis of the urgency was and when this idea was first identified, because we are talking now with potential multiple misrepresentation to the court and the only reason -- the only reason I have not yet entered a show cause on contempt is that I never put this in a formal order," Reyes said. "Which, believe you now, I am regretting."
Reyes says she wants clarity on who specifically gave the orders to remove the trees on Saturday and whether it was a deliberate effort to evade her previous orders issued in the case as litigation remains ongoing.
"The questions go to whether or not I've been lied to," Reyes said during Monday's hearing. "Whether I've been lied to in declarations about the plans, whether or not I've been lied to about the timing of things ... I am beyond disappointed in the government right now. I wanted you all to be better than you have been."
Reyes had warned Justice Department lawyers of "serious consequences" if the administration began major work at the course without getting approval and notifying the court in advance.
"I'm going to say this one more time, and I do not want a situation where something has happened and then I'm being told by the government or by a foundation or by a bulldozing company that it's too late to do anything about it," she said. "If anything like that happens ... there are going to be serious consequences."
Trump promises the course, which he said will be renovated and redesigned through a public-private partnership, will be "one of the Greatest Golf Courses anywhere in the World" on the site and said it will be open to the public.

title: Trump again attacks Rep. Ilhan Omar, a US citizen, over immigration allegations
body:
Vance said he wasn't warned about the search of her home.
President Donald Trump again attacked Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar on Tuesday, calling her a "terrible person" a day after federal authorities searched her Washington, D.C.-area residence.
The investigation into Omar -- a sitting member of Congress who is up for reelection in just three weeks -- relates to her immigration paperwork, sources told ABC News.
Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, is the first Somali American in Congress. Born in Somalia, Omar became a naturalized U.S. citizen in 2000.
Asked whether he wants to see Omar deported after the Homeland Security Investigation's search at her residence on Monday, Trump said he doesn't "take a position" on the matter. It's not clear whether deportation is on the table for Omar.
"I don't take a position. I think she's a terrible person. I think she's a terrible congresswoman. I don't think she loves our country at all, but I don't take a position," Trump said as he departed the White House Tuesday morning.
Omar has denied wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime.
In recent history, the Justice Department's practice has been to advise prosecutors not to take any overt investigative steps against members of Congress or candidates within 60 days of an election.
Trump has targeted Omar in the past, saying in social media posts earlier this year that Omar "should be in jail" and "sent back to Somalia."
Omar released a statement on social media earlier on Monday, saying that the search at her residence is "an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement." She added, "I will not be silenced."
During a rally in Ohio on Monday night, Trump called Omar a "disaster."
"She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military, where all they do is shoot each other. And she comes into our country, and she says, 'I have a constitutional right,'" Trump said of Omar, who is a naturalized American citizen from Somalia.
Trump later assailed Somalia and claimed that Somali immigrants at large "cheat on everything" without providing evidence.
Trump has repeatedly criticized Somali immigrants, describing them as "garbage" and saying during a December 2025 Cabinet meeting that he didn't want them in the United States; the comments sparked backlash at the time.
Vice President JD Vance told reporters on Tuesday that he didn't have any warning about the search of Omar's residence.
"I did not have advance notice that her home was being raided. Look, I never -- we try to run our Department of Justice in a fair and honest way. We try to let the law follow the facts rather than creating facts just to prosecute people we don't like. And because of that, I think the president and I largely try to stay out of Department of Justice investigations and other prosecutions," Vance said.
Vance added that "we're going to look into" allegations against Omar.
"If there's a real case there, we're going to follow the facts. If there's not a real case there, then we won't," Vance said.
Speaker Mike Johnson weighed in on the search of Omar residence during an interview on Fox News on Tuesday morning, saying "we have to reserve judgment and let the system play out as it does."
"Maybe the timing's unfortunate for her or others, but this is the legal system, and it operates independently of the political system. So, we do our jobs, and we let the people decide," Johnson said.
ABC News' Lauren Peller contributed to this report.
24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

title: Appeal court to issue date for fresh hearing of SERAP’s appeal against SSS’ N100m defamation judgement
body:
The Court of Appeal in Abuja on Tuesday vacated an earlier order reserving judgement in the defamation appeal involving the Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project (SERAP) and two State Security Service (SSS) officers, directing that case be reschuled for fresh hearing.
Vanguard newspaper reported that the Judge Danlami Senchi-led panel of the court issued the directive during hearing into two related appeals filed by SERAP and its deputy director, Kolawole Oluwadare, against the 5 May N100 million judgement of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) High Court in Abuja holding them liable for defaming two SSS operatives.
The appeals are marked CA/ABJ/CV/1114/2026 and CA/ABJ/CV/1105/2026.
“All the two files are hereby returned to the Presiding Justice, Abuja Division … for decision on a date for hearing of both appeals that is going to be communicated to the parties,” Mr Senchi said.
He also vacated the order reserving appeal CA/ABJ/CV/1114/2026 for judgement.
During Tuesday’s proceedings, Mr Oluwadare’s lawyer, Oluwatosin Adesioye, sought permission to amend the prayers in an application concerning additional records of appeal and an extension of time to challenge the lower court’s decision.
But Mr Senchi said the court was “finding it difficult to grant the prayers” and advised the lawyer to refine the application.
Mr Adesioye subsequently withdrew it, and the court struck it out without objection from the respondents.
The court also considered applications by Columbia University, the United Nations Special Rapporteur on the rights to freedom of peaceful assembly and of association, and the Southern Africa Litigation Centre to participate in the appeal as amici curiae, or friends of the court.
Lawyer for the applicants said the case raised questions about constitutional and fundamental rights with implications beyond Nigeria.
Mr Senchi noted that the applicants were not parties to the original suit and that their participation was subject to the court’s discretion. After he indicated that their involvement was not considered necessary, the applicants withdrew their applications.
The court struck out the applications without objection from SERAP or the respondents.
The presiding justice of the Abuja Division of the Court of Appeal is to determine a fresh hearing date for both appeals and communicate it to the parties.
In the judgement being challeged on appeal, Judge Yusuf Halilu of the FCT High Court awarded N100 million in damages against SERAP and Mr Oluwadare in favour of two SSS officers, Sarah John and Gabriel Ogundele, for defamation.
The suit arose from publications SERAP made on its website and X account on 9 September 2024, alleging that DSS operatives had invaded its Abuja office and harassed a staff member.
The trial court held that the publications were defamatory. It also ordered the defendants to publish apologies in two national newspapers, on two television stations and on SERAP’s website.
The court awarded N1 million in litigation costs and imposed 10 per cent annual interest on the judgment sum until payment.
SERAP and Mr Oluwadare are asking the Court of Appeal to overturn the decision.
Their lawyer, Tayo Oyetibo, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN), challenged the trial court’s jurisdiction and questioned the identification of one of the claimants.
Mr Oyetibo argued that the judgement was in favour of Sarah John in respect of a person identified as Sarah David.
He also questioned how the claimant’s identity was established through a description of a “tall, large, dark-skinned” woman without a photograph.
He urged the appellate court to set aside the judgement.
But O. S. Kehinde, lawyer to the first and second respondents, urged the court to dismiss the appeal.
He argued that SERAP had not established that Sarah John and Sarah David were different people and that the issue had not been raised before the trial court.
On identification, Mr Kehinde stated that a publication did not have to name a person expressly to be defamatory if people who knew the person could identify them from the description.
He added that a claimant’s witness had testified that the officers could be identified from the descriptions in the publications.
Lawyer for the third respondent did not address the court.
During the trial, Mr Oluwadare testified that SSS operatives entered SERAP’s Abuja office, prompting the organisation to issue a public statement.
He said staff members, including a front-desk officer, a security guard and a lawyer, had reported the operatives’ presence.
Under cross-examination, he acknowledged that no one had been physically assaulted and no doors had been damaged.
He maintained that the manner in which the operatives entered the premises and their use of unmarked vehicles prompted the organisation’s statement.
He also noted that SERAP had CCTV footage of the incident and rejected the suggestion that the organisation existed merely to criticise the government.
He stated that its work focused on promoting and protecting human rights.

title: "If US ships approach Hormuz Strait, we will sink them"
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 13 (MNA) – General Ali Ozmaei, Commander of the IRGC Navy, has warned the US warships not to get close to Hormuz Strait otherwise they will be drowned.
In his first televised interview, the Commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy General Ali Ozmaei stressed the smart control of the Strait of Hormuz, saying: The Americans claim today that the Strait of Hormuz is open and that they have control over it, but this claim is far from the realities on the ground. If they want to know whether the Strait of Hormuz is open or closed, they must come to the field and see who controls this strait.
Referring to the situation of the US fleet in the region, the Commander of the IRGC Navy stated: Today, the US army and its seven fleets have become fuel smugglers. The reality is that their $13 billion aircraft carrier has become useless and acts like an airport runway located 700 to 800 kilometers from the Strait of Hormuz, because it is vulnerable and does not dare to come close and be within the range of our fighters.
Ozmaei clarified: The Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf are under the control of the IRGC Navy, and our dear brothers in the Navy of the Islamic Republic of Iran's Army also control the Sea of ​​Oman. In fact, the blockade continues outside the Sea of ​​Oman and in the Arabian Sea, and our brothers in the Navy also control that area. He explained how the Strait of Hormuz is controlled: Our control is smart control; that is, vessels that must pass through this route must obtain permission from us. Vessels whose origin or destination is Iran are issued permits to travel through Iranian waterways, depending on the conditions.
The IRGC Navy Commander continued: The Americans are encouraging the law-breaking vessels to secretly leave the region with their lights off.
Referring to the high costs of transporting oil to West Asia, Ozmaei said: “Today, everyone must realize that the cost of transporting oil to West Asia is about $150 per barrel, and this is a staggering cost.”

title: Trezor reduces resellers as a ‘preventative step’ amid Ledger tampering reports
body:
CCO Danny Sanders said he had notified certain hardware wallet resellers that they would be removed from Trezor’s list of authorized entities starting Jan. 1.
Hardware wallet producer Trezor announced it would reduce its number of resellers as a “preventive step, taken out of an abundance of caution,” following reports that malicious implants had been installed in devices made by competitor Ledger.
In a Tuesday X post, Trezor said there was “not a single piece of evidence that [its] devices have been compromised” after reports that Ledger hardware wallet users had found malicious implants that exposed recovery phrases.
However, Trezor said that it would reduce the number of its resellers, citing “recent supply-chain incidents.” Chief commercial officer Danny Sanders added that he had notified certain resellers that they would be removed from the company’s list of authorized entities on Jan. 1, and would halt shipments of Trezor devices starting on Tuesday.
Trezor’s response came just days after Ledger confirmed that at least one of its devices purchased by a Southeast Asian reseller contained an unauthorized hardware implant, potentially leading to millions of dollars in losses for users. The wallets, sold by reseller CryptoBilis, captured recovery phrases and transmitted them over cellular networks.
“Our setup checks are built to catch counterfeit devices and modified firmware,” a Trezor spokesperson told Cointelegraph. “The implant found in a device bought from CryptoBilis works differently. This is a unique way of tampering with the device, which doesn’t modify the firmware, but reads information on the screen and later sends it to the attacker. So far, we have not seen this specific type of attack on Trezor devices in the real world.”
Related: Ledger investigates fund losses linked to Southeast Asian reseller, warns users
During the investigation, CryptoBilis, an authorized Trezor reseller, suspended all hardware wallet sales. The parent company of European electronics retailer MediaMarkt also announced that it had removed all Ledger products from its physical stores and online platforms “as a precautionary measure.”
Blockchain sleuths are still investigating the extent of losses for hardware wallet users, but research from two individuals suggested between $72 million and $86 million. Ledger reported on Tuesday that it had “not confirmed the total number of affected users or the total value lost” due to the breaches.
The Trezor spokesperson advised users to buy products directly from the company, “checking the seal is intact,” and consider a multisignature wallet “with devices from different makers, so one compromised device can’t move funds on its own.”

title: Kimberly Guilfoyle resigns as US Ambassador to Greece
body: Kimberly Guilfoyle has resigned as US Ambassador to Greece after the White House asked her to step down following reports of misconduct. White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia confirmed the request on Tuesday. President Trump said she “was doing a good job” but that he “didn’t like what I read.” Guilfoyle later confirmed her departure on X, calling the post “the honor of a lifetime” while denying the allegations as false and vowing to defend her reputation. The reports, mainly from the Wall Street Journal, alleged she sought $100,000 from a donor to pay a credit card bill in exchange for access to Trump officials, promoted a Greek energy company’s interests, accepted improper gifts, and made threats involving the Greek government. A State Department review of embassy staff complaints was also reported. The Greek government has not commented. Opposition PASOK spokesman Dimitris Mantzos said the resignation raises serious unanswered questions about Greece’s role. During her tenure Guilfoyle signed US LNG and energy deals, appeared on Vogue Greece, and publicly called for China to sell its stake in the Piraeus port. The post Kimberly Guilfoyle resigns as US Ambassador to Greece appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: What could happen to home prices if the foreign buyers ban expires?
body:
The federal foreign homebuyers ban is scheduled to expire on Jan 1, 2027, which has real estate experts questioning whether home prices could be at risk of rising sharply if there is pent up demand from non-residents after being closed off for several years.
More buyers in the housing market creates more demand, which typically results in higher prices if new homes aren’t being built fast enough to meet that demand. But experts say Canada’s housing market is not as hot or attractive to buyers as a few years ago when the ban was put in place.
“It’s been an issue that was a hot topic several years ago, but has since died down quite a bit, and there was a lot of debate whether it was in fact an issue that really had an impact on housing affordability at the time,” says Robert Hogue, assistant chief economist at Royal Bank of Canada.
“Foreign buyers might have had a little bit of an impact in certain neighborhoods of Canada’s urban areas, like in Vancouver and Toronto in particular, but the evidence of the impact of foreign buyers was still very debatable at the time.”
The federal government has said it is looking into “options” for the foreign homebuyers ban as the expiration deadline approaches.
“That’s a measure … that has been in place for some time. The market is evolving,” Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne told reporters last week.
“We’re looking at all the options that we have in front of us, considering where the market is going, what has happened over the last few years, always keeping in mind that we want to make sure that we have a higher stock of housing opportunities for Canadians.”
Canada’s real estate market has been on a dramatic roller-coaster ride ever since the COVID-19 pandemic.
At the time, mortgages were more affordable because interest rates were at historic lows.
The Bank of Canada lowered its benchmark borrowing rate at the time to as low as 0.25 per cent, in order to help support struggling businesses and consumers while social distancing and other measures kept a lot of consumers at home and businesses shut down.
This ultimately led to a spike in demand for homes, which drove up sale prices dramatically. There were also many reports of bidding wars that drove up prices even faster.
Some of those placing bids were reportedly from foreign buyers looking to invest in Canada’ real estate market while demand was high, and more often in hotter urban areas like Toronto and Vancouver.
“When home prices were going up 10 per cent, 12 per cent, 14 per cent a year, it was a very attractive place for overseas investors to park their money,” says Mike Moffatt, founding director of the Missing Middle Initiative at the University of Ottawa.
To help cool the housing market, a multi-prong approach was needed.
The Bank of Canada began raising its borrowing rate quickly beginning in March 2022, increasing it from 0.25 per cent to a peak of five per cent by July 2023 — where it stayed until June 2024. This was comparable to putting the red-hot housing market on ice.
The federal government also initiated a ban on foreign buyers on Jan. 1, 2023, and after similar measures were put in place by individual provinces. The federal ban was in place for two years, and was extended for another two years until Jan. 1 2027.
Inflation in Canada was also spiking to multi-year highs as supply chains experienced intense bottlenecks from pent up consumer demand stemming from the pandemic years. Russia’s war with Ukraine, which began in 2022, also sent shockwaves through global economies and drove up energy costs for businesses and consumers.
“Once home prices started to fall, not only were they not wanting to buy in Canada, they were actually wanting to pull their money out of Canada — it just no longer made sense to be in this market,” says Moffatt.
The foreign homebuyers ban was launched at a time when the Bank of Canada was aggressively raising interest rates and as other global economic factors weighed on homebuyers. This means the effects of the ban may have been clouded, especially by the central bank’s monetary policy having arguably more of a cooling effect on the housing market.
“We saw a massive increase in interest rates and that absolutely not just cooled the housing market but sent in a very deep freeze in many parts of Canada, and in fact, some markets like Toronto and Vancouver are still struggling to recover from that big shock, and so that kind of triggered this cooling,” says Hogue.
According to Statistics Canada, non-residents made up a very small fraction of property owners in major markets like Ontario and British Columbia in recent years.
Prior to the ban, non-residents owned roughly 2.75 per cent of all properties in Ontario in 2021, 2022 and 2023. In 2024, that number dipped slightly to 2.62 per cent.
In B.C., non-residents owned about 4.5 per cent of all properties in 2021, just over four per cent in 2022 and 2023, and 3.8 per cent in 2024.
It isn’t clear if these dips in 2024 in particular were because of the foreign buyers ban, or because of other factors like higher interest rates and other economic factors at the time making it harder for many Canadians and non-residents to afford a mortgage.
Since it isn’t clear whether the ban had a meaningful impact on housing affordability or supply, Hogue says it’s no surprise the government is reviewing the ban’s viability.
“Government has to think real hard whether having this extra measure in place to address an issue that was a hot topic years ago, whether it’s worth maintaining,” says Hogue.
The federal government has launched other measures to tackle home affordability, including Build Canada Homes , which aims to build more housing units on federal lands, as well as eliminating the GST portion on some new home sales of up to $1 million for first-time buyers.
Hogue says it is unlikely that if the foreign homebuyers ban was abandoned, a wave of new buyers would result.
“I don’t think the conditions are there for it,” he says.
“Canada’s housing market will continue to recover very slowly, and it will likely to be a very bumpy journey.”
Moffatt says although letting the plan expire will have no short-term impacts on prices, there is also a case to keeping it, with modifications.
“It will have no noticeable impact on prices 12, 24 months from now, regardless if we keep it or don’t keep it — it’s basically a non-factor,” he says.
“I do think there is merit as well to keeping it, but making significant reforms to make sure that we can, builders and developers, can get oversee capital to help them build new projects.”
– with a file from Global News’ Alex Boutilier

title: Agency and the Making of History | Podcast Highlights
body: Listen to the podcast or read the full transcript here . Adam Omary: I’m Adam Omary, a research fellow at HumanProgress.org. I’m honored to be joined by Dr. Martin Seligman, director of the Positive Psychology Center at the University of Pennsylvania. Dr. Seligman is widely credited with founding the modern positive psychology movement and has been called by my graduate advisor, Steven Pinker, “perhaps the world’s greatest living psychologist.” He’s the author of many books, including, most recently, Agency: The Psychological History of Human Progress , which we’ll be speaking about today. I’m also joined by my colleague, Johan Norberg, a senior fellow in the Center for Global Liberty and Prosperity at the Cato Institute and a historian of human progress. Being a psychologist myself, I plan to discuss agency with Dr. Seligman from the psychological perspective, and Johan will discuss human progress from the historical perspective. Before we start our panel, Dr. Seligman, I’d love to hear an overview of the book from you. I’m trying to found a new field, Adam, the field that Isaac Asimov called psychohistory. And it has two aims: to show that psychological states profoundly influence historical events, and then to use what we know about history to try to predict the future. And the psychological state I deal with in this book is agency. Agency for me has three components. The first is efficacy, the belief that you can accomplish your goal. Optimism, the belief that you can do this into the distant future. And imagination, the range of goals that you can possibly achieve. And the historical hypothesis is that progress and innovation occur when civilizations believe in human agency, and when that belief is absent, we see stagnation and regression. The book culminates with AI. Is AI going to destroy us, or is it the most technologically important aid to human agency of my lifetime? I believe the latter. Adam Omary: I’m excited to get to AI, but I want to begin with conceptions of progress. As you describe in Agency , and as we outline with data on HumanProgress.org, we’re living in the most extraordinary time of human history. We’re wealthier and freer. Lifespan is longer than ever. Disease and mortality rates are falling. And yet, despite these improvements, so many people seem pessimistic about the future. Why is that? I think there are at least two answers. One is ideological. It’s become beneficial politically to argue that we’re in one crisis after another, and that only I, the political candidate, can solve that crisis. And the other is journalism. A hundred years ago, if you were a farmer in Nebraska, you might find out a month later that the Titanic went down. Right now, if you watch CNN all day long, you’re going to hear about one horrible thing after another. If it bleeds, it leads. So I think that political ideology and journalism are two of the factors that lead people to believe that progress is a myth. Johan Norberg: I thank you for this incredibly important book. I recommend it to everyone. I think you’ve documented the rise and fall in the belief in human agency throughout history very well. But societies with a widespread belief in human agency, such as ancient Athens, Renaissance Italy, the Dutch Republic, Britain after the Glorious Revolution, and the American Experiment, also had other things in common. They were, compared to other contemporary civilizations, relatively free and open, and had relatively limited governments. And I have yet to find one example of a very despotic, regimented society with high levels of agency. So, is agency really the independent variable, or might it be that agency is what we observe when people are more or less liberated and have the incentives to create, adapt, and change? Great question. I want to speculate about the relationship between freedom and agency. Freedom is a fact about the world, and agency is a belief about oneself. Now, when we live in a relatively free world, technology advances, science advances, literature gets better, quality of life gets better, more progress occurs, and that impacts agency itself. That is, it makes you believe you can do more, and if you believe you can do more, that produces more freedom in the world. So I think the relationship is reciprocal. Agency increases freedom, and freedom increases agency. Adam Omary: Dr. Seligman, you’re famous for your work on learned helplessness, which is essentially the opposite of agency. Again, paradoxically, despite living in the freest and most prosperous time in history, we see a lot of this learned helplessness, especially among young people and especially on social media. Do you worry that certain cultural trends are reducing our sense of agency? Victimology really gets in the way of agency. So learned helplessness is the belief that nothing I do matters. And quite a lot of ideology about why suffering occurs in the world, why inequality occurs in the world, very easily leads to the belief that you’re a victim of a malign environment or a malign system. Under that assumption, when things go wrong and when we suffer, it’s not because of our character or our decisions or actions; it’s because we’re victims. Adam Omary: From an evolutionary perspective, it seems strange that people could even have learned helplessness. Could it be what social psychologist Rob Henderson calls a luxury belief? In other words, only in a society that is prosperous enough for one to get away with learned helplessness can we see that type of mindset evolve? No, I wouldn’t go that far. Learned helplessness is not only quite real in the laboratory and in real life, but over the last 25 years, my colleague Steve Maier, who died recently, was able to trace out the brain circuitry for learned helplessness. And to simplify it, there is a structure in the human brain called the dorsal raphe nucleus. And when it fires, that’s when you see passivity and giving up. That seems to be the default response to bad events. However, when we learn hope and mastery, that triggers a set of circuits in the forebrain which inhibit the dorsal raphe nucleus. So helplessness is a very real phenomenon, and if it’s not inhibited by hope, it leads to profound passivity, cognitive deficits, poor health, and premature death. Johan Norberg: Why is that? What’s the evolutionary benefit of giving up? Well, if you’re a reptile or a bird and a predator jumps on top of you, you don’t have a lot of cognitive mechanisms to deal with it. And by curling into a ball and giving up, you conserve energy. As mammals, we’ve inherited underneath our frontal cortex a set of biological mechanisms that incline us to give up. And it requires a belief in agency, a belief in hope, an experience of mastery and coping to turn off that reptilian tendency. Johan Norberg: You also have a wonderful way of explaining our negativity bias. You write that we inherited a bad weather brain. Our ancestors who were anxiously looking towards the horizon for bad weather or predators probably survived and passed their stressed-out genes to us, so we pay more attention to what’s bad than what’s good. On the other hand, you also document that political candidates who are more hopeful and optimistic about the future usually win. Why is it that we want bad news but hopeful politicians? Another good question. Let’s see if we can make sense of it. So first, there is a negativity bias, and it comes from our ancestors in the Ice Ages. Pessimism comes naturally to us. And we are attracted to optimism, empirically. I could run an experiment where I give you a speech to deliver on the telephone, either in a highly depressive cadence or in a very chirpy cadence. Just wait to see how long it takes for people to hang up on you during your depressed speech. Misery loves company, but company does not like misery. We’re attracted to optimistic people. I’m not sure I can say more deeply why. Politically, this also seems to be the case, at least in American elections. We’ve looked at the last 120 years of elections, and for the most part, the more optimistic candidate wins. We looked deeply at that in the Trump-Harris election. You might think that Trump was the more pessimistic candidate. He was the darker candidate. He cites four times as many bad events as Harris. But we decided to look at how he explains those bad events versus Harris, and we tracked this throughout the campaign. During the first debate, Trump and Harris are equally pessimistic, and Trump cites more bad events. But right through October 31st, Trump gets more and more optimistic. And by the end, he’s massively more optimistic than Harris. And we put our prediction about the election in a sealed envelope, and we sent it to our reporter friends, and we predicted a Trump victory. So humans like optimists, and we want to be led by them. Adam Omary: How do you distinguish agency from ambition? What does high agency look like in an individual who chooses to live a quiet life centered on family? Good question. I’ve never been asked this before, so I’m winging it. So the first component of agency is that you believe that your actions will produce results. Well, to be ambitious, you’d have to have that. To be agentic, you also have to believe that you can succeed at your goals in the far future. And again, to be ambitious, you have to believe that as well. And thirdly, to be agentic, you have to entertain a large range of possible goals. And being ambitious, merely desiring fame and fortune, by no means guarantees imagination. So that’s the difference. Ambition is shallow. Johan Norberg: One thing that keeps me awake at night is the problem that you write about: pessimism and despair seem to be self-fulfilling. If you think that there’s nothing to be gained from trying, you don’t try. Similarly, if people don’t understand that objective indicators of living standards are improving, that could undermine progress. Can you talk to us about the importance of understanding past progress for agency and for human flourishing? It’s crucial to believe in human progress. I’m in a constant struggle with my English department and my history department at the University of Pennsylvania, both of which are pervaded by the belief that human progress is a myth. And the cost of not believing in human progress is not trying. The cost of alarmist pessimism, for example, about the climate, is not trying to do something about the climate. For me, this has to do with education. We have to teach history differently. Human history is not just the history of victims and suffering; it’s the history of the rise from illiteracy, poverty, and death to literacy, wealth, and long lives. There’s been a huge increase in human well-being, measured by any objective measure of human well-being I know. And the measures that defy that trend are measures of depression and pessimism. And that’s one way of naming, Johan, the problem with misteaching the history of the world. Adam Omary: Dr. Seligman, you began this conversation by pointing towards artificial intelligence as the next major step of human progress. Artificial intelligence increasingly allows us to delegate decisions and tasks that once required our own knowledge and effort. When does that delegation expand our freedom, and when does it weaken our confidence or ability to act for ourselves? I am delighted to address that question. I deal with Claude and ChatGPT roughly six hours a day. In fact, I’m so excited by them, I feel like I’m 21 again. Let me give you two examples from my life in which AI hugely expands my own agency. AI has produced more love in my life, contrary to those who say it’s dehumanizing. I have two four-year-old grandsons, Denny and Max. I’m 80 years older than they are, and I noticed, starting at around age two, that I was becoming invisible to them. They walk faster than I can run. I can’t throw a football around with them. So I went to Claude and to Chat, and I said, “Help me write stories in which Max and Denny are the guardians of the world and the heroes.” And now I’m on volume six, chapter 24: Max and Denny tour the solar system. Well, I’m visible to them now. I have more love in my life. Number two, and much more importantly, AI has increased my own creativity. Let me just give you one example of a discovery that I made with Claude that no human being could have made. This is the paradox of the Axial Age. Across the globe, around 1000 BCE, Greece, Israel, Persia, India, and China were backwaters: villages, illiteracy, minimal technology, etc. Five hundred years later, all of those cultures are thriving. What happened during those 500 years across the globe? Well, I had a hypothesis, and that was that they invented new words. They conceived, for the first time in human history, words about human agency, as opposed to divine agency. Well, interesting hypothesis, but I knew no human being could test it. There’s no human being who knows ancient Sanskrit, ancient Persian, ancient Chinese, ancient Hebrew, and ancient Greek. But Claude and ChatGPT do. So I gave them a hypothesis. We worked for a day together, and sure enough, the words don’t exist or barely exist in the five cultures in 1000 BCE, but by 500 BCE, they’ve invented the words. So, for example, in Hebrew, the word teshuva is invented. It’s not in the Torah. It’s invented later on. Teshuva means repentance. It means you can actually do things to change your life. And once you have new words, new things can occur. Take sexual harassment, for example. People were harassed sexually in the office for generations, but there was no word for it until about 1970. Once there was a word for it, it opened up lawsuits, mandatory training, and ways of counteracting it. So when we have new words, we invent new things. And that’s an example in which AI made a discovery that could not have been made by human beings. Adam Omary: There is some concern that, if we are having agents think for us, particularly for young students, it will harm our own ability to think. Do you think of agency like a muscle? Certainly it can be developed, but is it also a matter of ‘use it or lose it’? That is one doomsayer hypothetical I agree with. They call it de-skilling. Let’s take writing. So I’ve been writing for 70 years. I’ve made hundreds of thousands of decisions between “perhaps” and “maybe.” And so at age 84, I’ve got the skill of writing, and I’m delighted to have Claude, who writes better than I do, help me along and edit. It’s not de-skilling me. But if, starting at age six, I have my writing done by the machines, I’m never going to learn how to write. Adam Omary: Another audience question. How do different philosophical ideas, such as religious versus secular worldviews and individualist versus collectivist ethics, drive the cultural adoption or rejection of agency? Let me give two examples. I’ll start with the obvious Marxist one. Believing that history unfolds as a result of historical forces that are beyond our control is a recipe for passivity. And it suggests that Marxism is an ideology that leads to passivity, a sense of victimhood, and a lack of progress. In terms of religion, I spent a lot of the book documenting different religious views. Let’s take early Catholicism and early Christianity before Augustine. So early Christianity after Jesus, up to about 300 AD, is very optimistic. You can become holy, and in fact, your encounter with God after you die is about, “Did you do the things that would make you acceptable for salvation?” Under that kind of belief, you get agentic action. Then Augustine comes along and says, “Hold it, that’s Pelagianism.” Pelagius believes that you can contribute to your own grace. Augustine says that’s nonsense. Any time you do something good, it’s only by the grace of God. That’s the opening gate for the stagnation of the Middle Ages. Then, after the Renaissance, Catholicism once again becomes highly agentic. Erasmus argues that we’re like toddlers. When we fall down, God lifts us up, but we have to have motive power of our own to be so lifted. Luther says that’s nonsense, and in his retort to Erasmus on the bondage of the will, he tells us about predestination, about the lack of human will, and Calvin even goes further. With the Restoration and the influence of Arminian Protestantism, which believes you have to assent to grace, progress gets resuscitated. So, that’s a long-winded way of saying that your ideology and religious faith modulate your agency, and most importantly, the achievement of entire cultures. The post Agency and the Making of History | Podcast Highlights appeared first on Human Progress .

title: Zelensky announces “good decisions in support of Ukraine” expected this week
body:
He made this announcement in an evening address published on the Office of the President’s YouTube channel, according to a Ukrinform correspondent.
“This week brings negotiations with the European Union. There will be support packages for Ukraine, and we are moving forward in the negotiations on accession to the European Union. This week also marks the opening of two clusters; two were already opened this summer. And by the end of the year, we plan to open all six negotiation clusters—that is our plan, and it is a priority. This is political and moral support for our people; it is proof of the irreversibility of Ukraine’s course toward becoming a normal, strong, and European country,” Zelensky stated.
The Ukrainian head of state assured that the Ukrainian government is working to ensure full financial support for Ukraine and Ukrainians, as well as to fulfill Ukraine’s agreements with Europe.
“Today, I want to thank the members of parliament and our government officials: this week, the necessary decisions have been made—the necessary laws and the necessary government decisions. Thank you,” the President said.
In addition, he announced positive decisions in support of Ukraine this week.
“We are preparing them now. I continue to maintain contact with all our partners who can help us and who are always effective. I will speak with Denmark today, and I will speak with Lithuania—with the prime ministers. Tomorrow, there will be important talks in the UK,” Zelensky noted.
As reported by Ukrinform, all EU countries have agreed to open the second and third clusters in the negotiations on Ukraine’s accession.

title: Russia says declarations without clear mechanisms not to advance settlement on Ukraine
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Memorandums and declarations without clear mechanisms for their implementation are unlikely to advance the Ukrainian settlement, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said commenting on the maritime truce initiatives.
"Our experience shows that the conclusion of memorandums and declarations without creating clear mechanisms for their implementation is unlikely to contribute to a real improvement in the situation," the diplomat noted. "Kiev regularly violates what it signs.".

title: Xbox is officially embracing the chaos of AI-powered game ports
body:
Retro gaming is going through a wild time at the moment, thanks to decompilations and recompilations that are letting gamers port classic titles to new devices, or merge code from two different games into a single new experience. Microsoft has witnessed skateboarding being modded into Call of Duty and Halo being played in a web browser, and the company is now officially embracing the chaos of this new AI-powered era of game modding.
Microsoft is putting together a new Xbox Labs group to explore the rapid emergence of these mods, many of which use AI models to help modders remix games in ways we’ve rarely seen before. Xbox Labs will be a “small group of game makers, engineers and scientists whose job is to turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience,” says Xbox CEO Asha Sharma. “We’ll build in the open, learn from what people do, and measure success by whether more people are playing and creating.”
Sharma thinks the experiments we’ve seen in recent weeks, where Windows PC builds have been translated to run on Apple Silicon or ported to run inside browsers, “challenge long-held assumptions about our industry: the tether between software and hardware, the boundary between creation and play, and how people discover and experience games.”
“While it is hard to predict the future of gaming, it is easy to see the possibilities in making great games easier to access, giving old games new life and allowing more players to become creators and co-creators,” says Sharma. “These are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models.“
Modders are now doing the type of work that Microsoft has been doing for decades with its Xbox backward compatibility program, letting old games run on modern hardware. But they’re doing it without the business model restrictions that Microsoft is tied to. It’s starting to feel like we’re just a model or two away from even more breakthroughs that decouple more modern games from their intended hardware.
Sharma clearly sees an opportunity here, particularly for AI agent use at Xbox. “I think Xbox has an important role to play here,” says Sharma. “Coding became the first major workload for agents because they can write, run, and test software. Games share many of those same properties, and people spend more than 72 billion hours a year playing XBOX games, roughly five times the estimated time spent writing code worldwide.”
Xbox Labs is clearly a way for Microsoft to experiment with how AI will shape where games are played, and Xbox will share any tools and learnings with developers. The bigger question is how Microsoft will respond to decompiles and recompiles of games where modders take its precious IP and make it freely available. Modding is fun, but I can’t see Microsoft and other publishers seeing the fun side if modern console games start to appear where they shouldn’t.
I asked Microsoft to comment about unauthorized IP use, but the company didn’t respond in time for publication.
Here’s Sharma’s full memo:
> Team,
> The first video games emerged some 75 years ago. In the time since, there have been booms and busts, but every year there are more great games to play, more devices to play them, and best of all, more people than ever playing. That growth helped make XBOX what it is today, and we’ve helped shape the industry in return, from bringing hard drives to consoles and online gaming through Xbox Live to Game Pass and cloud gaming, alongside franchises that have brought millions of people together.
> In recent weeks, we’ve seen games rapidly decompiled and rebuilt to run on hardware they were never originally designed to support. Windows PC builds have been translated to run on Apple Silicon or ported to run inside a browser through WebAssembly and WebGPU, the latter now approaching 90% global browser support. Perhaps more surprisingly, we’ve seen many of the biggest games in the world have been remixed into the source code of another.
> These experiments challenge long-held assumptions about our industry: the tether between software and hardware, the boundary between creation and play, and how people discover and experience games. While it is hard to predict the future of gaming, it is easy to see the possibilities in making great games easier to access, giving old games new life and allowing more players to become creators and co-creators. These are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models.  To explore these possibilities, I’ve asked Scott to stand-up XBOX LABS, a small group of game makers, engineers and scientists whose job is to turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience. We’ll build in the open, learn from what people do, and measure success by whether more people are playing and creating. 
> I think XBOX has an important role to play here. Coding became the first major workload for agents because they can write, run, and test software. Games share many of those same properties, and people spend more than 72 billion hours a year playing XBOX games, roughly five times the estimated time spent writing code worldwide. We’ve spent 25 years learning how to make great games, and I want our game makers to help shape what these new technologies make possible. As we learn, we’ll share the tools we build with developers across the industry, just as we always have.
> Our priorities aren’t changing. We remain committed to the 4Cs, to making great games, to our hardware and to being responsible stewards of IP and the communities built around it. LABS gives us a way to explore new technology without abandoning the work already underway.
> Asha

title: Dan Levy calls out Shane Gillis for ‘misogynistic’ SNL monologue
body:
Schitt’s Creek co-creator and star Dan Levy is criticizing comedian Shane Gillis’ recent SNL monologue after he said women who go to the gym dress like “whores.”
Gillis, who hosted SNL over the weekend, was fired from the sketch comedy show in 2019, five days after being cast as a regular when clips of him using racial slurs during a podcast interview resurfaced.
The stand-up comic, who has hosted SNL several times since, said Saturday: “I haven’t been to the gym in so long, I didn’t know women just dress like whores now?”
Levy called out Gillis’ comments in an Instagram reel , saying, “Women wearing short shorts to the gym does not make them whores. It makes the men calling them whores misogynists.”
“By the way, I’ve seen more men’s nipples at the gym than I’ve ever seen women showing their bodies off,” he continued, adding that he was “speechless” that a remark like that could make it onto live national television.
“More men need to be standing up in opposition to it because it’s complacency that has created the environment with which women are sexually assaulted and it’s a ‘conversation’ as opposed to a ‘crime.'”
Women are “not objects,” he said, “they are superior human beings to men.”
“I am sorry if this gets me in trouble with the internet…but f**k.”
The Emmy Award-winning actor and writer, who hosted SNL in 2021, said this was an “everybody” issue because the more men speak about women this way in the media, the more men will treat them like “objects.”
The video, which has been viewed more than two million times, received praise from high-profile individuals including Viola Davis and Elizabeth Banks, who both commented in support of Levy’s message.
Gillis also talked about his “friend” podcaster and UFC commentator Joe Rogan’s private gym, which he said he prefers because he can work out there with no one else around.
Rogan is a controversial figure in the podcast space. He has been known to promote unproven treatments for COVID-19 and for repeatedly using racial slurs while hosting.
SNL, which is currently in its 52nd season, has said goodbye to a couple of titular cast members in the past year, including fan favourite Bowen Yang , who ended his eight-season run last Christmas, and Chloe Fineman , whose final episode was in May.
Barrie, Ont., native Veronika Slowikowska joined the SNL cast in 2025 as a featured player; she is the first Canadian cast member since the mid-90s. The show’s creator, Lorne Michaels, is from Toronto.
Other notable Canadian comedians, including Martin Short and Mike Myers, have also appeared as regular cast members.
In March, Myers returned for a surprise appearance where he showcased his impersonation of tech billionaire Elon Musk .
During the closing credits, he was spotted wearing a black T-shirt that read “Canada is not for sale,” with a Canadian flag in the middle, beside Shane Gillis, who was hosting the episode, and musical guest Tate McRae .

title: Jewish ex-Harvard admin. files discrimination suit over termination after Rosh Hashanah leave
body: A former Harvard University finance administrator has filed a federal lawsuit against the institution, alleging religious discrimination after taking paid time off to observe Rosh Hashanah.Daniel Lilienthal filed the complaint last Friday in the US District Court for the Southern District of New York, naming the president and fellows of Harvard College as the defendants. According to the filing, Lilienthal worked remotely from New York as the associate director of the Finance and Grants Administration at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health's Center for Biostatistics in AIDS Research (CBAR).Lilienthal, who previously worked for Harvard for eight years before returning in September 2024, alleged that his direct supervisor, Jackie Blake, approved his request for paid time off on October 3 and 4, 2024, to observe the Jewish High Holy Day.However, the lawsuit claims that immediately following his disclosure and observance of the day, he faced sudden heightened scrutiny and manufactured performance concerns. According to the complaint, Blake contacted human resources on the first day of his holiday leave to voice concerns, despite providing no prior negative feedback during his initial business days.Increased scrutiny after returning from Rosh Hashanah holidayUpon returning to work, Blake confronted Lilienthal over uncompleted training modules that carried no prior deadlines and allegedly told him, “I don't want you thinking you can just take off time whenever you want.”On October 16, 2024, just the 15th business day of his tenure, Lilienthal was terminated via a Zoom call.When he asked if he was being fired for performance or wrongdoing, Blake allegedly responded, “No.” A day later, HR provided a termination letter citing a lack of “skills or aptitudes,” which the lawsuit calls a pretextual justification.Lilienthal is suing under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the New York State Human Rights Law, and the New York City Human Rights Law, seeking damages for financial loss, emotional distress, and career damage, alongside a jury trial. Harvard has faced mounting public scrutiny and litigation regarding allegations of antisemitism and campus climate issues since early 2024.Harvard did not respond to a request for comment by publication time.

title: Niobia takes the guesswork out of some of tech’s most expensive mistakes
body:
San Francisco-based startup Niobia is betting big on a critical but often overlooked part of battery and chip making: helping engineers understand how and why things go wrong. Its AI software flags production defects and lets engineers ask a chatbot what caused them, aiming to deliver answers in minutes rather than days.
How it works (broadly): The company’s customers place AI agents on their production lines to look for defects, then loop in human engineers to work out what might cause a product to fail. The agents run on self-contained GPUs mounted directly on manufacturing equipment, much like a sensor. They can spot pinhole-sized flaws such as scratches. Niobia’s AI also gathers all the data in one place so engineers can ask a chatbot what went wrong and dig deeper into the cause.
Speed is so critical because chips and batteries are some of the world’s most important products, while also increasingly in short supply. As manufacturers continue to develop and improve their technologies, things inevitably go awry during research and development. Engineers then spend days or longer figuring out a fix before they can restart production. Each flaw or mistake can prove costly — sometimes running into the millions of dollars — and set back manufacturing timelines.
Niobia co-founders Gaurav Jha and Harveen Kaur both have PhDs in chemistry and have worked at chipmakers and battery manufacturers, giving them firsthand experience with the challenges within the industry. In a call ahead of TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, where the company is a Battlefield finalist, Jha explained that while what Niobia does is specialized, it serves a multibillion-dollar market that includes some of the biggest battery and semiconductor makers today.
“It’s extremely niche; maybe people will never know about it,” said Jha, speaking of the battery and chip manufacturing market that his company aims to serve. “But it’s like behind the scenes, this is powering everything… we just don’t see it in the regular world.”
“Every product around you, like glasses or shoes, slippers, wallets, and headphones — these processes touch every single part of it,” added Jha.
Niobia’s agents run on open source models that the company trains further with battery and chip research and other data. That training is what lets them identify pinhole-sized defects. Jha said that Niobia chose open source models largely because its customers don’t want their highly sensitive company information going into a public AI cloud where it might be used to train the model.
“None of our customers want their proprietary data to go to the cloud, even if we tell them it’s safe,” said Jha. The startup also outlines how it approaches cybersecurity, given the high-stakes race among adversarial nations to innovate in the battery and chip space. Niobia, for instance, lets its customers hold their own encryption keys so that the startup cannot decrypt the customers’ data.
Jha said that the company’s priority for now is to focus on three specialties, such as film coating, electroplating (which is coating a surface with metal using an electric current), and fluidized bed reaction (a chemical process where solid particles are suspended in a gas or liquid).
He said that the company also wants its technology to become more autonomous, with the eventual aim of building out a fully self-driving factory for its customers.
If you’re curious to learn more, Niobia will present onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt this afternoon in San Francisco. Join us to catch the company and the 19 startups against which it’s competing as part of our storied Startup Battlefield competition, happening today, Tuesday, through Thursday, October 15.

title: Guyana Oil Exports Set to Surpass 1 Million Barrels per Day for First Time
body: Guyana, one of the world's newest oil exporters, is poised to surpass one million barrels per day in crude oil exports for the first time this December, marking another extraordinary milestone for the small South American country.  According to Bloomberg, December's preliminary loading schedule includes 33 million barrels of crude exports, equivalent to approximately 1.06 million bpd. The first shipment of the country's new Uaru crude grade is scheduled for December 1112, with total Uaru exports expected to reach four million barrels during the month.  The achievement is particularly remarkable considering the country produced virtually no crude oil just seven years ago.  From First Oil to One Million Barrels per Day  Guyana's hydrocarbon development began in 2015, when ExxonMobil discovered significant oil resources in the offshore Stabroek Block. Commercial production followed in December 2019, with the Liza Phase 1 development and its Liza Destiny floating production, storage and offloading FPSO vessel initially designed to produce 120,000 bpd.  The expansion has been relentless ever since.  In February 2022, ExxonMobil brought the Liza Unity FPSO online, adding approximately 220,000 bpd of capacity. November 2023 saw the arrival of Prosperity at the Payara development, followed by the ONE GUYANA FPSO at Yellowtail in August 2025, adding another 250,000 bpd.  By November 2025, ExxonMobil had confirmed that production had reached 900,000 bpd.  The latest milestone follows another historic achievement in September 2026, ExxonMobil announced that cumulative production from the Stabroek Block had surpassed one billion barrels.  Three More FPSOs Are Coming  And Guyana's production boom is only just getting started.  The next major addition is the $12.7 billion Uaru project, developed around the Errea Wittu FPSO, which arrived off the coast of Guyana in August 2026. Built by Japan's MODEC, the vessel has a production capacity of 250,000 bpd and storage capacity of approximately two million barrels. Its December export debut will mark Guyana's fifth producing development.  The sixth project, Whiptail, is scheduled to begin operations in late 2027. Its Jaguar FPSO, being developed by Dutch company SBM Offshore, will add another 250,000 bpd, potentially lifting national production capacity toward 1.3 million bpd.  The seventh development, Hammerhead, received final investment approval in September 2025. The $6.8 billion project is slated to begin producing in 2029, adding another 150,000 bpd through a new FPSO.  Beyond that, ExxonMobil is advancing Longtail, its eighth development, targeting startup in 2030. Unlike earlier projects, Longtail will focus heavily on natural gas and condensate production. While the export destinations for Longtail's gas and condensate remain unknown, ExxonMobil may use some of the gas to inject into its current production wells in order to maximize output. Guyana's government is currently reviewing its development plan and production license application.  Together, the eight developments could lift installed production capacity to approximately 1.7 million barrels per day by 2030.  Hydrocarbons boost economic growth in Guyana  The expansion is transforming Guyana's economy. In its October 2026 assessment, the IMF reported that Guyana's economy grew more than 19% in 2025, with its Natural Resource Fund accumulating approximately $3.3 billion by year-end.  As Oilprice.com previously reported, Guyana's emergence as a major non-OPEC producer has become particularly significant amid Middle Eastern supply disruptions and mounting concerns over the security of oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.  For a country that only entered the global oil market in 2019, crossing the million-barrel export threshold represents a remarkable achievement. And with several more massive FPSOs scheduled to arrive before the decade is over, Guyana's rise as a global oil powerhouse may only be getting started.  By Tom Kool for Oilprice.com

title: KATH Mother and Baby Unit construction stalled for 14 months over unpaid contractor arrears
body: The 509-bed Mother and Baby Unit designed to save the lives of mothers and babies is gathering dust at the Komfo Anokye Teaching Hospital (KATH), as contractors have yet again suspended construction for 14 months over unpaid arrears. Despite millions of dollars invested, the facility remains incomplete, with some procured materials now deteriorating and warranties expiring. Parliamentary Committee on Health is raising concerns over the prolonged delay, warning against the waste of taxpayers’ money as expectant mothers wait for a facility intended to transform maternal and child healthcare in the Ashanti Region and beyond. Expectant mothers in the Ashanti Region and beyond were anticipating a sigh of relief when contractors commenced construction of the mother and baby unit at the Komfo Anokye Teaching Hospital. The building was expected to have been completed within three (3) years of its initiation in 2019 after demolition of the original 44-year-old block. However, construction works have suffered intermittent setbacks, with the project now exceeding its intended timelines. Parliament Select Committee on Health inspected the facility as part of its working visit to the region’s largest referral hospital. The abandoned structure is now approximately 70 per cent complete but remains suspended for about 14 months over non-payment of Interim Payment Certificates to the contractor. Project Consultant Emmanuel Fobi Asabre noted that the project had experienced two major suspensions, with the first lasting approximately 18 months, following which work resumed steadily before the new suspension. “The first suspension came during the domestic debt exchange programme (DDEP). We worked for another 12 months when we resumed work after the first suspension. Now, we have suspended again over the non-payment of IPCs to the contractor,” he noted. The hospital project was initially estimated at a budgetary allocation of $138.5 million, but the prolonged suspensions had resulted in additional costs. The physical construction is currently 56 per cent complete, with procurements standing at 75 per cent while demolition of the entire old block has been completed. The suspension has since affected the state of some procured materials and installations for the facility, with others losing their insurance warranties. “Some materials have already expired.
