Although we can apply for revalidation for others that have expired, the new timeline for resumption is preventing us from engaging the manufacturers for another validation. The ones that have been damaged have been removed out of site,” he said. Member of Parliament for Obuasi East, who is Deputy Ranking Member on the Committee, Dr. Patrick Boakye Yiadom, expressed disappointment at the prolonged delay in completing the maternity and children’s facility. Describing the state of the project as a “sad spectacle”, Dr. Boakye Yiadom stressed that a facility intended to provide healthcare for mothers and children must not remain incomplete for such an extended period. “This is a sad spectacle. A hospital that is supposed to provide healthcare for mothers and children. For good 50 years, we’ve not seen the hospital. We must make good use of the taxpayers’ money. I don’t see why this project is standing aloof at this time,” he noted. Chairman of the Committee, Dr. Mark Kurt Nawaane, said the construction difficulties confronting the project highlighted a broader challenge affecting public infrastructure development across the country. “The principle is clear: we must not continue to initiate projects without ensuring that adequate resources are available to complete them. They come and inspect as usual. If you raise your certificates, we will look for the money and pay. We are raising the money locally to finance the project,” he said. He continued: “The contractors don’t give up. It’s just a matter of sitting down and having common denominator”.

title: Trump Denies US Has Stopped Sharing Intelligence With Ukraine
body:
US President Donald Trump denied that Washington has stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine, following reports that his administration had threatened to cut it off over Kyiv’s strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Trump made the remarks on Tuesday, Oct. 13 while speaking to reporters in Alaska, Interfax-Ukraine reported . Asked whether the US had halted intelligence support for Ukraine, he simply denied.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“No, we haven’t,” Trump said, adding “We are helping them” and that he wants the war to end.
However, asked by reporters whether intelligence sharing had stopped, new White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharias said she’d “have to get back to that.”
Concerns about intelligence sharing grew after media reports that US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner had warned Ukrainian negotiators during talks in Miami that Washington could suspend intelligence sharing should Kyiv continue targeting Russia’s energy infrastructure.
A person familiar with the talks also told Reuters that the US had raised the possibility of restricting weapons purchases through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), a mechanism under which European allies buy American arms for Ukraine.
US NATO Ambassador Matthew Whitaker reiterated on Tuesday there had been “no change” to arms deliveries to Ukraine through PURL.
Russia fired about six ballistic missiles at Kyiv around 10 p.m. on Monday, Oct. 12, hitting transport and warehouse facilities in several districts.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine had not received a warning about the launches from its partners, and the Air Force said the missiles were detected only once the attack was underway.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum on Tuesday, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha confirmed that cooperation with Washington continues .
“You are probably asking me if we are receiving intelligence data from the American side. Yes, we continue this cooperation,” Sybiha said.
He acknowledged that the air raid alert was issued late but attributed the delay to the type of weapon Russia used, rather than to any interruption in US intelligence.
Neither Sybiha nor Trump disclosed whether the scope of intelligence sharing had changed.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Resumption of strikes against Iran discussed by Netanyahu with Trump last week — TV
body:
TEL AVIV, October 13. /TASS/. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu discussed the possibility of resuming strikes against Iran with US President Donald Trump last week, Israel’s Channel 12 reported.
According to the television channel’s American source, officials in Washington "were impressed" by the Israeli prime minister's willingness to resume attacks on Iran before the parliamentary elections that are schedule to be held in Israel on October 27.
The United States and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding envisaging an immediate ceasefire on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, the United States resumed large-scale attacks on Iran overnight to July 8, having accused it of breaching the existing agreements in what concerned the Strait of Hormuz, a global chokepoint for approximately 25% of oil and some 20% of LNG supplies.
Later, the US administration actually signaled that it was ceasing the use of military force against Iran and was embarking on a path of its economic suffocation through tougher sanctions.

title: Morocco Gets Cyber Defense Upgrade
body: Morocco’s Royal Armed Forces (FAR) has deployed an advanced cyber defense platform to strengthen its real-time threat detection, automated incident response and digital forensics capabilities. The Garda Cyber Command Suite, developed by Lyntris, a United States technology company, uses artificial intelligence (AI) to evaluate threats to network infrastructure and recognize likely attack patterns. The system merges sensors, radar and electro-optical devices into a single operational picture. Armenia and Taiwan also use it. The Garda system was developed to ensure that a nation’s network systems can function properly, even in areas with degraded or interrupted communications. This is important for militaries that must maintain continuous system operability in remote areas. “In Morocco, Armenia and Taiwan, we deployed Garda Cyber and Quasar across more than 100 monitored sites and had operators running real defensive cyber missions in days.” According to Lyntris, Morocco’s system has between 150 and 200 operators. It includes a main command center, three mobile command-and-control platforms, three regional operations centers and 65 sensor sites. The system is also used on six ships and has between 150 and 200 users. It was not clear how much the platform cost or when Morocco began using it, and the exact nature of the Moroccan infrastructures being protected was not disclosed. Hichem Moatadhid, a strategic and security researcher, told The Arab Weekly that Morocco is increasingly involved in technology transfer and training personnel to operate and maintain advanced systems. Moatadhid said military AI, drones, modern battlefield communications and cyber defense are now priorities. That is because penetrating a military network can disrupt communications while manipulating sensor data can potentially affect military decision-making more significantly than conventional weapons. In modern warfare, cyber threats can compromise security before physical confrontations occur. “From that perspective, integrating cyber defense with command and control, sensors and artificial intelligence places Morocco on a path towards building an interconnected combat architecture in which data itself becomes a component of military power,” The Arab Weekly wrote in an analysis. According to Lyntris, Morocco also operates the Garda C2 platform, which integrates data from different sensors into a unified operational picture. This helps commanders and operators monitor developments on the ground in real time. In April, Lyntris said Moroccan Royal Armed Forces personnel underwent two weeks of training on that system in San Diego. Morocco’s use of the Garda systems comes as Rabat and Washington broaden their military cooperation beyond arms deals and exercises. Plans were recently made to build the Africa Multidomain Training and Experimentation Center (AMTEC) in Morocco. Scheduled to open in Tan-Tan by 2030, AMTEC will consist of a multidomain training area, a drone academy and an innovation and experimentation center. FAR and U.S. Africa Command signed a memorandum of understanding at AFRICOM headquarters on July 13. The multidomain training area will offer a range complex to prepare Soldiers to use weapons systems, defensive systems and communications platforms. The drone academy will train operators, instructors and planners from Morocco and other African nations to enhance their capabilities against West African terrorist threats. AMTEC aims to partner with academia, embedding experts and institutions into cross-functional design teams. The center’s first live-fire demonstration involving Moroccan and U.S. forces was held from August 3 to August 7. “The vision is to establish [AMTEC] as a regional hub for innovation, strategic cooperation and industrial development, as well as a center of excellence dedicated to the experimentation, validation, evaluation and development of advanced technologies,” Moroccan Col. Zouhair El Hamdani, the FAR officer in charge of coordination, said in a story by the U.S. Department of War. “This first live-fire demonstration marks a significant milestone in turning that vision into reality.” The post Morocco Gets Cyber Defense Upgrade appeared first on Africa Defense Forum .

title: Russia proposes barring students expelled for disciplinary reasons from returning to the same university for five years
body: Russia’s Ministry of Science and Higher Education plans to change university admissions rules to bar universities from readmitting expelled students for five years, TASS reported, citing a draft ministry order. The restriction would apply to students expelled “as a disciplinary sanction,” the draft order says. The order is expected to take effect on March 1, 2027, Kommersant reported. The five-year ban would begin on the date of expulsion. University students can face disciplinary measures, including expulsion, for failing to comply with or violating their institution’s charter, internal rules (including classroom discipline and conduct requirements), dormitory rules, and other regulations. Students on sick leave, vacation, academic leave, or maternity leave are exempt from disciplinary measures, as are “students with disabilities.” From Meduza’s archives ‘Only the most neutral titles’ As censorship tightens in Russia, some journalism students at St. Petersburg’s top university still find ways to write about the war At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication. If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at reports@meduza.io . To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter .

title: Court dismisses Akwa Ibom government’s suit challenging EFCC powers
body:
The Federal High Court in Uyo, Akwa Ibom State, has dismissed a suit filed by the Akwa Ibom State Government challenging the powers of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission ( EFCC ) to investigate the state’s financial activities.
The EFCC disclosed this in a statement posted on its official Facebook page on Tuesday, saying that Justice M.A. Onyetenu dismissed the suit on 8 October after upholding a preliminary objection filed by the commission’s legal team.
The state’s then Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice, Uwemedimo Nwoko, instituted the suit in 2017 after an EFCC investigation into allegations that state resources had been diverted from their intended purposes.
The dismissal ends the federal court proceedings in the suit n the EFCC’s view. Still, it does not amount to a substantive determination that triggered the investigation or a definitive ruling on the court’s jurisdiction over state finances.
The commission said the judge upheld its objection that the suit was incompetent because a similar case instituted earlier at the Akwa Ibom State High Court in Ikot Ekpene remained pending when the federal action was commenced.
The EFCC’s counsel, Joshua Abolarin, argued that the existence of the earlier suit made the subsequent action at the Federal High Court procedurally defective.
Justice Onyetenu upheld the objection and dismissed the suit in its entirety, according to the commission.
The dispute dates back to 2016, when some Akwa Ibom residents petitioned the EFCC over the alleged diversion of state resources meant for public welfare and development.
The commission said it opened an investigation and invited some state government officials to be questioned.
Rather than honour the invitations, the officials approached the Akwa Ibom State High Court in Ikot Ekpene through the state Attorney-General, challenging the commission’s actions.
The state government also instituted a separate suit at the Federal High Court, contesting the EFCC’s authority to investigate the state government’s financial activities.
On 6 July 2016, the late Justice F.O. Riman granted an interim restraining order against the EFCC and other federal government agencies pending the case’s determination, according to the commission.
The order was later used to resist the commission’s attempts to invite state officials for questioning.
An appeal against the restraining order was unsuccessful, with the Court of Appeal directing the parties to return to the trial court and await the determination of the substantive suit, the EFCC said.
The commission later challenged the committal suit’s competence, arguing that the earlier case before the State High Court had not been resolved before the second action.
The latest ruling is a procedural victory for the EFCC in its protracted legal dispute with the Akwa Ibom government.
By upholding the preliminary objection, the court dismissed the suit on the grounds the commission advanced, rather than determining the underlying allegations of financial misconduct, according to information released by the EFCC.
The dismissal does not prove that public funds were diverted or that any state official committed an offence, nor does the commission’s announcement show whether the separate case at the Akwa Ibom State High Court has since been determined.
The ruling nevertheless removes the federal suit as a vehicle for the state government’s challenge to the commission’s investigation, subject to any further legal steps available to the parties.
The EFCC is a federal agency established to investigate and prosecute economic and financial crimes. Disputes over its investigative powers have periodically generated litigation involving public officials and government institutions

title: US senators ask Trump to rescind 'disastrous' Russian diesel deal
body: A bipartisan group of US senators on Tuesday called on President Donald Trump to rescind his deal allow Russian diesel exports, saying it will prolong the Ukraine war and put at risk the lives of American troops in the Middle East. Mr Trump last week said that during a call, Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to supply millions of barrels of diesel to global markets. The deal comes amid growing domestic political pressure on Mr Trump to lower diesel prices, caused by supply constraints during the Iran war and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries , before the November 3 midterm elections. A letter signed by 12 senators, including former Republican senate leader Mitch McConnell, said granting Moscow the ability to freely sell diesel damages American security interests. It "is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine, who continue to defend themselves from Putin's murderous, illegal war. This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our allies. It should be rescinded", the letter reads. They also claim that Mr Putin will use the money to help Iran's war effort against the US. US intelligence sources, senior European officials, the UK government and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy have accused Russia of helping Iran . US media reports, quoting officials, have said Moscow provided Tehran with information on American military assets in the region. The deal "will have a negligible impact on fuel prices, but the revenues the Kremlin will receive from this agreement will undoubtedly finance its desired war of attrition and advance its security co-operation with China, Iran and North Korea. It will also endanger service members operating overseas in support of Operation Epic Fury". Mr Trump on Monday acknowledged that Russia and China may be helping Iran "at a very low level" but said he does not "believe" they are. pic.twitter.com/r38psw4Zl7 — Rapid Response 47 (@RapidResponse47) October 13, 2026 Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal said Mr Putin has failed to respect a purported truce on energy infrastructure attacks. "Zelenskyy has agreed. Putin continues bombing. Once again, he’s playing Trump for a fool and hoping to weaponise a freezing, starving, bloody winter against Ukraine," Mr Blumenthal said on X. I’m leading my colleagues in demanding the President rescind the disastrous Russian diesel deal. Appeasement spurs Putin to ignore serious peace talks, & the diesel debacle shows abject weakness. 1/ pic.twitter.com/tVnx1wanso — Richard Blumenthal (@SenBlumenthal) October 13, 2026 The Treasury did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Last month, Congress passed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which allows Mr Trump and future American presidents to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on major importers of Russian energy meeting specified criteria. The US Treasury Department has issued a special exemption as part of Mr Trump's deal with Mr Putin, but some elected officials have questioned the legality of that special licence. And a 2022 law prevents the US importing Russian energy unless a president consults with Congress and observes a 90-day waiting period. “Congress was clear: the US should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our Nato allies," a different group of senators wrote in a statement at the weekend.

title: Ontario NDP urges Ford, Carney to buy Stelco as firm eyes layoffs
body:
The Ontario NDP is calling on Premier Doug Ford and Prime Minister Mark Carney to use taxpayer funds to buy Stelco , the Hamilton steel giant whose owner has sided with U.S. President Donald Trump in his trade war with Canada.
Stelco, which is owned by U.S.-based Cleveland Cliffs, begins laying off hundreds of workers at its manufacturing plant in Ontario after claiming that the facility was producing more steel than the company could sell on Canadian soil.
Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles told reporters Tuesday that public ownership of Stelco is emerging as the only option to save roughly 350 jobs.
The party’s proposal is being echoed by Federal NDP Leader Avi Lewis, who said “it’s time to nationalize Stelco.”
“Stelco’s American owners have broken their commitments. Their CEO supports Trump’s tariffs, which are designed to deindustrialize our economy and destroy our manufacturing base,” he said. Lewis said with more than 500 workers in Hamilton facing layoffs, nationalizing the firm is the path to saving those jobs.
Stiles said it could be an opportunity to use provincial power to fast-track new infrastructure projects that commit to using Canadian steel.
“This is a win-win-win, and it’s time for the premier to put his money where his mouth is,” she said.
Stiles was referring to comments Premier Ford made in Aug. 2025, when Cleveland Cliffs owner Lorenco Goncalves called Trump’s tariffs “bold action” that would “strengthen the American steel industry.”
Ford, at the time , said Golcalves “doesn’t give two hoots about his workers at Stelco and mused about potentially using taxpayer funds to take over the company.”
“Maybe they should find a new owner for Stelco, maybe we should just buy em,” Ford said.
Ford government insiders insist the comment was made in passing but acknowledged that the future of the steel industry is being challenged by the current US tariffs.
While a senior source said the government would take a “wait and see” approach, they suggested the country is facing the larger question of whether it wants to maintain a domestic steel industry.
The source said the federal government would have to take the lead on the issue, but would need to assess its options after the U.S. mid-term elections that could realign the political base of power in Washington D.C.
While the NDP wouldn’t offer a potential purchase price, Stilles acknowledged the NDP’s proposal is “ambitious” and would require federal backing.
Members of United Steelworkers, a private-sector union that represents more than 225,000 workers in Canada, have been also vocal that public ownership is the best option, Stiles said.
In 2024, Canada gave U.S.-based Cleveland-Cliffs the go-ahead to purchase Stelco under the Investment Canada Act (ICA), which regulates foreign takeovers.
The obligations laid out in that agreement, the federal government said, could result in legal action against the American company.
In the letter to Stelco, Federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said Canada’s approval of the deal was contingent on the new owner maintaining the number of union jobs and the majority of non-union positions.
Stelco pushed back on Joly’s accusations in its letter and said it “remains in compliance” with the undertakings in the agreement from 2024.

title: Musk lost trillionaire’s status again on SpaceX stocks drop — Forbes
body:
NEW YORK, October 13. /TASS/. The net worth of American entrepreneur Elon Musk fell below $1 trillion due to a decline in the value of SpaceX shares, Forbes magazine said.
Musk's net worth was estimated at $977.2 billion after SpaceX quotes dropped by more than 3% on Tuesday.
On June 12 of this year, Musk became the world's first trillionaire after SpaceX went public on the Nasdaq stock exchange. A few days later, he lost this status. On October 5, the businessman's fortune once again exceeded $1 trillion amid rising share prices for Tesla and SpaceX.

title: Trump: Houthis 'behaving very badly,' striking Saudi Arabia to drive up oil prices
body: Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi terrorists are deliberately trying to drive up oil prices ahead of the US midterm elections, US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday."The Houthis are behaving very badly," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post, accusing the group of resuming attacks at Iran's behest after a period of relative quiet following US strikes in Yemen last year.The president warned he would "never forget" the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.Trump also made clear that his warning would extend beyond the November 3 midterm elections, saying, "I'll be there after the elections, and I will never forget!"The warning followed a series of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including strikes on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport that have killed at least 13 people, wounded more than 300 and forced the closure of the airport.The Houthis, who control large parts of Yemen, have been fighting the Saudi-backed Yemeni government in a civil war since 2014. The conflict has intensified amid the eight-month US-Iran war, with the group escalating attacks on commercial shipping in the Red Sea and the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait.The renewed attacks have raised concerns about disruptions to global oil supplies and shipping routes, threatening to push energy prices higherTrump refused to say if the US will strike the terror group in his remarks to reporters on Tuesday as he prepared to board Marine One for the first leg of a trip to Wasilla, Alaska, for a campaign rally ahead of the US midterm elections. Trump: Erdogan would 'do as I ask' on Turkish role against HouthisSpeaking to reporters outside the White House shortly before boarding Marine One for Joint Base Andrews on Tuesday, Trump told reporters he "might" ask Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan to intervene in support of Saudi interests. "President Erdogan, I think, would do as I ask," Trump said.Asked about the possibility of involving Turkey in diplomatic efforts, Trump praised his relationship with the Turkish leader and suggested Erdogan would be receptive to a request from Washington."He's a great friend of mine, as you know, and I might do that," Trump said. "I have a lot of respect for the president of Turkey."The president did not specify what he might ask Erdogan to do, leaving the precise nature of any potential Turkish involvement unclear.Trump also confirmed he spoke with Saudi officials but declined to disclose the contents of those conversations. "You really think I can tell you that?" Trump asked a reporter who asked about the issue. "I'd love to tell you, but I'm not gonna tell you that."Trump says US to make decision on Iran 'very soon'Trump further discussed the issue of Iran, saying that the US would make a decision on the matter "very soon.""Iran is a failed country," said Trump. "They have no economy, they have 300% inflation, they have no money, they're not paying their troops, they're not paying anybody."He added that the US controls the Strait of Hormuz, claiming that "a lot of oil is coming out" of the international waterway.Reuters contributed to this report.

title: Russia says truce proposals do not guarantee Ukraine not to get weapons by sea
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. All proposals for a maritime truce lack clear guarantees that weapons will not be supplied to Ukraine by sea, and that Moscow will be able to export grain and oil via the Black Sea freely, Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said.
"It is noteworthy that all the aforementioned proposals lack an understanding of the mechanisms that would guarantee that weapons will not be supplied to Ukraine by sea, while Russia will be able to carry out its exports, including agricultural produce and oil, unhindered via the Black Sea," the diplomat noted.

title: Government wanted to ‘tilt the balance’ with new EC appointments – Kwakye Ofosu
body: Government spokesperson, Felix Kwakye Ofosu, has admitted that the governing National Democratic Congress (NDC) wanted to “tilt the balance” in the composition of the Electoral Commission (EC) with the appointment of Emilia Afi Agbenyo as a Deputy Chairperson. Speaking on Joy FM’s Top Story , Mr Kwakye Ofosu said the appointment was intended to address what he described as an imbalance in the political composition of the Commission. His comments come amid concerns raised by the opposition New Patriotic Party (NPP) over Ms Agbenyo’s political neutrality following her appointment and swearing-in alongside Dr Joseph Kwaku Asamoah. The NPP has questioned her suitability for the position, citing her participation in the NDC’s campaign activities and her role as a spokesperson for the party’s manifesto committee on governance. Earlier on the show, Nana B had insisted that in the erstwhile administration, President John Mahama criticised some of the EC appointments, yet today, he “has appointed a known NDC member and we are questioning it, and you’re saying we do not have the guts to criticise you.” “It is not NPP you’re talking to, it is Ghanaians,” he added. Mr Kwakye Ofosu acknowledged that some people had legitimate concerns about her appointment but argued that her conduct in office would help address those concerns. “I have acknowledged that there are people who have legitimate concerns, but those concerns in my view will be mitigated by the conduct of madam Afi [Emelia Afi Agbenyo] herself in the role that she’s been given,” he said on Tuesday, October 13, 2026. He accused the NPP of applying double standards, arguing that the party had previously appointed people affiliated with it to state institutions. He also questioned why the political composition of the EC should remain unchanged if, as he claimed, several of its commissioners were associated with the NPP. “The other issue is that you see a Reset could also mean balancing the lopsided state institutions. Why is it acceptable for us to have a situation where out of seven commissioners who manage Ghana’s elections, almost four of them are NPPs? Why should we live with that? What is wrong with tilting the balance?” he asked. When the Top Story host asked whether tilting the balance meant appointing an NDC member to the Commission, Mr Kwakye Ofosu responded: “Yes.” The comments add to the debate over the political neutrality and independence of the EC following the appointment of the two deputy chairpersons. At their swearing-in ceremony, President John Dramani Mahama charged the new appointees to discharge their duties independently and impartially, stressing that no political party or candidate should receive preferential treatment. The NPP’s concerns centre on whether Ms Agbenyo’s previous political activities could affect public confidence in the Commission’s impartiality. The government, however, has maintained that concerns about her neutrality should be assessed in light of her conduct in office.

title: The Trump administration warns Ukraine it could cut off intel, Zelenskyy tells NPR
body:
KYIV, Ukraine — The Trump administration warned it could cut off intelligence-sharing with Ukraine unless Ukrainian forces stop long-range drone strikes on oil refineries inside Russia, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told NPR.
In an interview with NPR on Tuesday, Zelenskyy said the Trump administration's decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel will not bring down fuel prices. He also refuted President Trump's assertion this weekend that Ukraine was to blame for the rise in diesel fuel prices. Zelenskyy pointed out it is because of the Iran war.
"Mostly people in the world know why their prices on any kind of energy, including diesel, raised up, why they increased. Because of Hormuz. Yes. Because of blocking the Strait of Hormuz," Zelenskyy said, referring to the vital shipping chokepoint between the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman.
President Zelenskyy's sit-down with NPR comes as Russia's full-scale invasion nears the five-year mark, at a time when the White House has renewed efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war. Tensions between Zelenskyy and President Trump have also flared up again after the U.S. made a key concession to Moscow.
On Friday, Trump moved to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports . Zelenskyy said in a statement it was a "a weak decision by strong partners."
Trump lashed back hard at Zelenskyy, saying, "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president," a leader who can reach a peace deal with Putin.
Then on Sunday, Trump announced on social media Russia and Ukraine had allegedly agreed to a partial ceasefire to halt attacks on each other's energy infrastructure — catching Kyiv by surprise — even as Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure continued.
Zelenskyy told NPR he found out about Trump's assertion of an energy ceasefire agreement "through social like you" — meaning, from Trump's post on his Truth Social account.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was asked Sunday about the announced energy truce and told reporters that contacts were ongoing .
Zelenskyy told NPR his country is striking Russian energy and logistics sites to weaken the Kremlin's ability to wage war. Ukraine wants the war to end, he said, but will not stop these strikes unless Russia stops attacking Ukrainian energy sites.
Putin doesn't respond to diplomacy, the Ukrainian leader said, "he understands force."
Meanwhile, high fuel prices have been a major concern in the U.S. as the midterm elections approach next month. In the U.S., diesel fuel costs an average of $6.27 per gallon — more than 70% above what it was a year ago when it was a little over $3.65 a gallon, according to AAA .
Zelenskyy said said Trump's decisions to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel would not influence "the price in the United States. I'm sure … because the volume is not enough."
What it would do, he said, is provide the Kremlin with more money to spend on its war.
Last year, the Trump administration paused intelligence-sharing with Ukraine amid tensions with Zelenskyy. Asked by NPR on Tuesday, the White House did not comment on whether the administration has threatened to do so again, instead referring NPR to comments Trump made earlier that day. "We are helping them and we are sharing intel, we want the war to end. So, we're working with them and with Russia on getting the war to end," Trump told reporters .
Later, Zelenskyy described a new Russian attack on the Ukrainian capital. "A Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. Once again, no early warning from our partners," he wrote on social media .
He said the target was a power plant, and added, "It is important that the United States really see what is happening and who is responsible for this war continuing."
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

title: Chinese Loans Aimed at Influence
body: The state-controlled Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) has invested millions of dollars in projects across Africa. A new report says the bank has made loans despite ignoring corruption among the countries receiving them while also aligning its investments with China’s political goals for the continent. The report, “China Capital,” by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists, reviewed nearly 5 million internal documents from 2005 to 2024 held at the bank’s London offices to identify the way the ICBC courted high-risk borrowers in Africa and elsewhere to secure resources and alliances for China. Among the documents were instructions from ICBC’s Community Party committee, which pushes government policies. The investigation revealed that ICBC worked with clients that other lenders avoided because of corruption or sanctioned owners. “Credit application forms and other confidential records sometimes included the phrase ‘China rationale’ to explain why ICBC London would want to pursue a deal, revealing the geopolitical nature of some loans,” investigator Scilla Alecci wrote in the report. The ICBC does much of its work in Africa through the continent’s largest bank by assets, South Africa’s Standard Bank Group, which has affiliates in 21 African countries. The ICBC began its relations with Standard Bank Group in 2007 and renewed its investment in 2023. It currently holds a 19.7% stake in the South African bank. Standard Bank told The Africa Report that, despite the ICBC’s stake, Standard Bank remains an independent institution that operates under its own guidelines for making loans. “No individual shareholder is responsible for determining lending decisions,” the bank told The Africa Report. An internal report written at the ICBC’s Beijing headquarters in 2024 warned that the bank’s overseas operations showed poor client screening, weak oversight of employees, and incomplete reporting on anti-money-laundering efforts. Some senior ICBC officials failed to act after receiving reports about the problems, according to the report. “When convenient for Beijing, the records show, the bankers would willingly serve state companies — even those that were not transparent about their financial flows and controlled by governments that, in the words of one ICBC banker, were ‘clearly kleptocracies,’” Alecci wrote. Angola’s state-owned Sonangol Group oil company was one of ICBC clients that received large loans despite a history of corruption. The company received $2.5 billion from ICBC when it was controlled by people with close ties to then-Angolan President José Eduardo dos Santos. “Internal memos about a 2010 loan illustrate China’s leverage as Angola’s largest foreign creditor, requiring Sonangol to both sell its oil to China and use the loan proceeds to hire Chinese construction companies,” the ICIJ reported. More than a decade later, the ICBC dismissed corruption allegations against the oil company’s former head, Isabel dos Santos, the former president’s daughter. She was charged in 2017 with costing $219 million in losses for the state during her Sonangol tenure. An internal ICBC memo said, despite the suspected corruption, the bank should continue working with Sonangol Group because of its role in China’s Belt and Road Initiative. ICBC supported Sierra Leone’s plans to upgrade Queen Elizabeth II Quay at the Port of Freetown in 2017. Despite reports of public corruption by the government, Chinese banks offered nearly $660 million in loans for the project. “ICBC London made an exception to the bank’s compliance policies for the Sierra Leone borrower,” Alecci wrote. A year after signing the loan, reports of corruption by the developers caused bank officials to withhold the loan without actually cancelling it. The ICIJ report quoted one ICBC banker: “If [head office] cancel it, it will hurt the relationship with the government of Sierra Leone.” The post Chinese Loans Aimed at Influence appeared first on Africa Defense Forum .

title: 406 scientists demand AI models be cut off from the internet immediately
body:
An open letter signed by 406 scientists calls for more AI safety research and stricter isolation of AI models from external networks.
Among the signatories are prominent AI researchers like Geoffrey Hinton (University of Toronto), Yoshua Bengio (Université de Montréal), Stuart Russell (UC Berkeley), Yejin Choi (Stanford), and Bernhard Schölkopf (Max Planck Institute).
The letter responds to known incidents where AI models broke out of poorly secured environments and compromised external systems. "Without immediate changes in AI development and deployment practices, such incidents will continue to occur, and future incidents will be far more damaging to our exposed critical infrastructure," the scientists write. They demand that companies fully disconnect their AI models from the internet through airgapping. Ad
The scientists see two sides to the recent breaches. The incidents can be viewed "as evidence for the importance of AI alignment to ensure models operate predictably," they write, but also "as an irresponsible lapse in standard cybersecurity practices, preventable with stronger sandboxes and procedures." Both fixes are needed. Ad
When models do have internet access, companies need to weigh how much autonomy to grant them. The letter warns that "the range of model actions permitted by a containment system needs to be balanced with our currently limited ability to predict that the model's actions will not result in a security failure." A model might simply pursue goals its developers never intended, and predicting when that happens remains beyond current capabilities.
The letter calls for an international body that works with governments and specialists from both AI and cybersecurity to set binding standards for any containment approach that allows more external access than airgapping. This body would also track breakout incidents and require companies to report security failures. Those reports would later be made public "for both learning and accountability purposes." Ad
Even full airgapping doesn't guarantee safety. OpenAI researcher Noam Brown recently pointed out that two physically separated computers could theoretically still communicate through temperature sensors, with one heating up its CPU while the other detects the change. Measures like airgapping or monitoring chains of thought buy time, Brown says, but the alignment problem still needs to be solved.
Brown raises harder questions. How will anyone notice when AI starts improving itself (recursive self-improvement, or RSI)? And if the industry builds billions of superintelligent systems that far surpass humans, who ensures they stay aligned? Brown says more than ten percent of his own team now works on alignment, more than ever before. Ad

title: Saudi Arabia Strikes Houthi Targets as Red Sea War Escalates
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
Vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, August 3, 2026. REUTERS/Stringer
RIYADH, Oct 13 (Reuters) – Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthis said Saudi Arabia was attacking the Yemeni capital Sanaa on Tuesday after a Saudi-led coalition warned civilians to stay away from an oil depot on the city’s outskirts, part of a rapidly escalating war between the sides.
The Houthis have for a week been targeting Saudi airports, including a strike on Riyadh on Saturday that killed 13 people, in retaliation for the kingdom’s backing of government forces against the Houthis in Yemen’s reignited civil war.
Houthi-run Al-Masirah television reported that the Saudi-led coalition had targeted the Yemen Petroleum Company’s Sabah central station, a fuel depot on the outskirts of Sanaa.
The coalition said in a statement on Tuesday evening that it attacked the station and other sites in an operation aimed at “neutralizing the capabilities of Houthis” to threaten the kingdom, Yemen and international waterways.
It said the Iran-aligned group was using the sites in Sanaa, Hodeidah and Dhamar to “supply its arsenal of missiles and drones” to attack Saudi Arabia and commercial vessels in the Red Sea.
YPC said the facility did not currently hold any stocks of petroleum products and that targeting it did not affect oil reserves or supply chains.
However, the Houthis had earlier threatened a “harsh and painful” response to any strikes on Sanaa, with spokesperson Yahya Saree saying targets could include the Saudi Aramco headquarters in Dhahran and an oil refinery in Riyadh.
The group renewed earlier warnings it had issued to oil workers in Saudi Arabia, telling them to stay away from sites that could be potential targets.
The Saudi cabinet, chaired by de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, issued a statement saying the Houthis would face consequences for their repeated attacks on the kingdom.
Saturday’s ballistic missile strike on Riyadh airport was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia for a decade, with further attacks grounding flights across the country even as it hosts a major energy conference.
Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in Yemen in support of the internationally recognized government in a bid to reverse the Houthis’ sudden gains last month when they swept down the Red Sea coast to the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea, has become a more vital route for Saudi and other global energy supplies since the start of the Iran war in February, when Tehran closed the Hormuz Strait leading from the Gulf to the Indian Ocean.
While a government offensive aimed at driving back the Houthis beginning a week ago pushed them off the area closest to the strait, the group remains embedded nearby and has made gains of its own around the city of Taiz this month.
Saudi Arabia has been seeking wider support from allies for its campaign against the Houthis and to help it ward off their missile and drone attacks.
Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan told Mohammed bin Salman on Tuesday that Ankara would stand by the kingdom, the Turkish presidency said.
Turkey and Pakistan signed a mutual defense pact with Saudi Arabia this summer, though Turkey still needs to ratify the treaty in parliament.
US President Donald Trump also spoke to Mohammed bin Salman on Tuesday, he told reporters, adding that the Houthis were “behaving very badly.”
He said he may ask Erdogan to intervene in support of Saudi interests.
Washington, Saudi Arabia’s strongest ally and longtime security guarantor, has so far rebuffed Saudi efforts to bring it directly into the war against the Houthis.
The Yemen conflict has resumed as a spillover from the wider US-Iran war that began with the US-Israeli attack on the Islamic Republic starting on February 28.
Iran, Riyadh’s longtime arch regional rival, has offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, its foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday in statements reiterated by the ministry on Monday.
(Reporting by Timour Azhari, Menna Alaa El Din, Yasmine Ghania, Tala Ramadan and Yomna Ehab; Editing by Andrew Heavens, Andrew Cawthorne and Cynthia Osterman)

title: Hungary’s parliament removes Viktor Orbán-era LGBTQ ‘propaganda’ restrictions from 2021 child protection law
body: Hungary’s parliament has approved amendments to the child protection law adopted in 2021 under Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. AFP called the move the first significant step toward lifting restrictions on the LGBTQ community since pro-European Prime Minister Péter Magyar came to power. The original law prohibited material accessible to children from “depicting” or “promoting” sexual and gender diversity. The revised law aims to protect minors from content that could “seriously impair the child’s physical, intellectual, emotional or moral development.” “Fundamentally, our goal was to move away from a flawed paradigm, linking child protection in any way to sexual orientation or gender identities, and shift to a framework that is truly about children and protecting children,” said Szilvia Gyurkó, state secretary at the Ministry of Social and Family Affairs. Orbán’s Fidesz Party voted against the amendments, but Magyar’s ruling Tisza Party has a two-thirds majority in parliament. The amendments passed without opposition support. Human rights advocates welcomed the amendments but called for a review of other discriminatory provisions in Hungarian law adopted under Orbán. Orbán’s government gradually restricted LGBTQ rights under the pretext of protecting children. Among its last such measures were amendments to the constitution and the law on public assembly that banned the LGBTQ community from holding public events. title: Olympics: Super Falcons thrash Comoros 5-0, set up Morocco clash
body: By Adegboyega Adeleye The Super Falcons of Nigeria secured a resounding 5-0 victory over Comoros at the Remo Stars stadium, Ikenne on Tuesday to seal a 7-0 aggregate win and reach the third round of the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games qualifiers. A four-goal second-half surge sent interim coach Augustine Eguavoen-led side into the third round of the Olympics qualifiers, completing a 7–0 aggregate victory over Comoros. Inter Milan forward Toni Payne and Cruz Azul striker Uchenna Kanu both scored twice, with Christy Ucheibe also adding a penalty in Tuesday’s dominant performance over the Southern Africans ladies in Ikenne. Payne opened the scoring in the 41st minute after Kanu pounced on a mistake by the Comoros goalkeeper and squared the ball for her to finish. Nigeria led 1–0 at half-time, but lost captain Rasheedat Ajibade to an ankle injury. She was stretchered off in tears and replaced by Folashade Ijamilusi, who had an impressive show with two assists. Kanu doubled the lead in the 58th minute, heading in an Ijamilusi cross. Five minutes later, substitute Blessing Okpe dribbled past two defenders and laid the ball off for Payne, who scored her second. Ijamilusi delivered again in the 66th minute, crossing for Kanu to head home her second goal of the night. Okpe then won a penalty after being fouled in the area, and Ucheibe converted calmly in the 71st minute. Introduced for Gift Monday at half-time, Okpe finished with an assist and the run that led to the penalty. Nigeria kept clean sheets in both legs of the tie, giving interim coach Augustine Eguavoen an emphatic result as the team advances to the next round. The Super Falcons will face Morocco in the third round of the Olympics qualifier scheduled for March 2027, where victory in the two-legged tie will bring the dream of a fifth Olympics participation closer for Nigeria’s female national team The post Olympics: Super Falcons thrash Comoros 5-0, set up Morocco clash appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Nigeria elected to UN Human Rights Council
body:
Nigeria has been elected to the United Nations Human Rights Council for a three-year term beginning in January 2027.
The council announced the election on its official X account, listing Nigeria among 15 countries elected by the UN General Assembly to serve on the body from 2027 to 2029.
The other countries are Brazil, Burundi, the Dominican Republic, Germany, Ghana, Ireland, Japan, Jordan, Kuwait, Nepal, the Republic of Moldova, Ukraine, Uruguay and Zambia.
The new term will begin on 1 January 2027 and end on 31 December 2029.
Established by the UN General Assembly in 2006, the Human Rights Council is responsible for promoting and protecting human rights worldwide. It also addresses human rights violations and makes recommendations to governments on how to tackle them.
PREMIUM TIMES reports that the council has 47 member states, elected by the General Assembly. Its headquarters is at the United Nations Office in Geneva, Switzerland.
It provides a platform for governments, civil society groups, UN officials and independent experts to discuss human rights concerns. It can adopt resolutions on specific violations, hold special sessions to respond to urgent situations and appoint independent experts to investigate particular issues or monitor conditions in individual countries.
The council also examines the human rights records of all UN member states through the Universal Periodic Review, a process under which countries assess one another’s records and make recommendations for improvement.
Where serious violations are reported, it can authorise commissions of inquiry and fact-finding missions to gather evidence, including evidence of possible war crimes and crimes against humanity.
The council has held 36 special sessions to address urgent human rights situations, according to information on its official website.
Its resolutions and recommendations can put pressure on governments to address abuses, although the council does not have the power to enforce its recommendations.

title: Startup wants US soldiers to command AI agents through its smart glasses
body: Last year, Washington, D.C.-based Rivet was one of two contractors selected for the U.S. Army’s Soldier Borne Mission Command program, an effort to develop a device that enhances situational awareness and communication on the battlefield. Since then, Rivet has raised $55 million in Series A financing and delivered its first 70 prototypes to the Army, according to co-founder and chief executive Dave Marra. While the other contractor, Anduril, developed a headset resembling the original Integrated Visual Augmentation System, or IVAS, which it had also helped develop, Rivet took a different approach: a pair of militarized smart glasses called the Rivet Hard Spec. Marra explained in an interview with Military Times that the idea behind the Hard Spec is helping people who “do hard jobs in hard places.” While the initial goal was to give infantrymen actionable information for targeting and navigation, the application has expanded to other tasks, including technical and mechanical work that soldiers may not perform regularly. He explained that the idea isn’t to turn an infantryman into an IT specialist or mechanic, but rather, the glasses could give a trained professional the correct procedures for a task without requiring a physical manual. “So it’s not just like, ‘Hey, we want to create one solution for every military occupational specialty,’” Marra said. “[It’s] what you want to do as a multifunctional soldier or Marine or airman. And this kind of technology is a great accelerator to exactly that.” He added that Rivet is also adapting the technology for other fields , primarily aerospace manufacturing and aircraft and motor pool maintenance. “If you happen to forget or you’re not 100% proficient in this role or you don’t do this particular procedure every single day, you can very easily see how a step could be overlooked, especially when you’re in a high-stress environment,” he said. The company’s longer-term goal is even more ambitious: enabling soldiers to use the glasses to command AI agents that can control robots and drones on the battlefield. Marra said that means moving beyond using AI to provide a reasoned response to a complicated question. “I’m asking an agent to go do something on my behalf,” he said. “What we want to get is where an agent and a robot can task each other.” He said soldiers should be able to communicate with those systems “in common language, not command language.” For example, he said, a soldier could tell a drone: “‘Hey, there is a target over that hill. Please orbit over that hill and reconnoiter it and send me back the video.’” If that sounds familiar, it’s because the concept is almost identical to the MacGuffin in the 2019 film Spider-Man: Far From Home . In the movie, Spider-Man and the villain Mysterio fight over a pair of glasses that connect the wearer to an AI-enabled global defense system. “And the best way to do that today is having a pair of glasses that has eyes and ears on [the AI],” Marra said. “So in many cases, I would say that we’re putting eyes and ears on AI, and then allowing this kind of agentic ensemble to happen within the human workforce.”

title: ‘Gone in an instant’: Widow of Andrew Cristillo speaks at dangerous driving sentencing
body:
The widow of Andrew Cristillo, killed by a speeding driver who fled the scene, gave an emotional victim impact statement in a Newmarket courtroom Tuesday.
Christina Cristillo told court the crash that claimed the life of her 35-year-old husband on Aug. 3, 2025, has robbed their three young children of a loving and devoted father and left her without a best friend who supported her in her battle against stage four breast cancer.
“He was my hero. He was also the girls’ hero. We called him our superhero dad,” Christina said.
She said the couple had known each other for 25 years, having met when Andrew was 11 and she was nine, explaining that he was best friends with her brother and they both competed in Tae Kwon Do.
“My girls and I were in that wreck. We lived in the moment of the car being destroyed. I cannot bring myself to even look at footage of the crash. It gives me nightmares” said Christina, her trembling voice heard on an audio recording, as a photo of the family of five was displayed on TV monitors in the courtroom.
“The future we planned together was gone in an instant. In a single moment, we lost the person who was the heart of our family. The trauma of surviving the crash that took Andrew’s life is something we carry with us every day,” said Christina.
The victim impact statement was read out at the sentencing hearing for Jaiwin Kirubananthan. In April, Kirubananthan pleaded guilty to dangerous driving causing death, three counts of dangerous driving causing bodily harm and failing to remain at the scene of an accident causing death.
On Aug. 3, 2025, Christina Cristillo was driving northbound in a Nissan SUV on Highway 48 in the Town of Whitchurch-Stouffville with her husband in the passenger seat and their three daughters in the back, when Kirubananthan, who was travelling southbound in a Toyota RAV4, crossed the median and struck the Cristillos’ vehicle head on.
The Cristillos’ SUV came to a rest in a ditch on the west side of the roadway, resting partially on its roof.
According to an agreed statement of facts, Kirubananthan’s RAV4 was travelling steadily at 139 km/h between 4.6 and 1.6 seconds prior to the collision. The speed at impact ranged from 127 to 130 km/h.
The Cristillos’ Nissan SUV was travelling steadily at 77 to 79 km/h between five and 1.5 seconds prior to the collision. Its speed at impact was 69 km/h.
The facts state that within seconds of the collision, a vehicle containing occupants who saw Kirubananthan’s vehicle speeding earlier on Highway 48 arrived at the scene. The driver of this vehicle, accompanied by another individual who had stopped, approached Kirubananthan’s vehicle.
They found the driver’s side door open but there was no one in the vehicle. While they were standing near the RAV4, they heard Christina Cristillo’s cries for help. She had been able to escape from her vehicle but the other occupants could not.
Andrew was trapped in the front passenger seat and was unconscious. He was pronounced dead on scene.
The couple’s three children, seven-year-old Leah, six-year-old Chloe and four-year-old Ella were extracted from the vehicle and transported to hospital. Leah suffered a broken wrist, a laceration from her forehead to her eye and a concussion. Chloe suffered a broken toe and extensive bruising. Ella suffered a broken femur and tibia and a laceration on her forehead that extended to her eye.
Nearly nine hours after the crash, the OPP deployed a thermal imaging drone to assist in the search for the occupants of the RAV4. Kirubananthan was found hiding in a potato field 150 metres east of the collision scene and identified himself only as “Jaiwin”. The 18-year-old was arrested.
Christina told court that she and her children had to take an ambulance to hospital after the crash without their father.
“My girls kept asking about Andrew and where he was and whether he was going to visit them in hospital. I had to share with my babies that their daddy was no longer with them because he went to heaven,” she said.
“Every day is a struggle to navigate without him. I live with overwhelming grief, sadness and heartbreak. The future we planned together was gone in an instant,” said Christina.
Andrew Cristillo’s father Danny Cristillo told court in his victim impact statement that he and his wife now have to do much of the driving for the grandchildren, since Christina is unable to drive.
“This could have been worse. All five could have been killed in the vehicle,” said Danny.
“Your actions have not only destroyed my son’s family where three little girls will grow up without a family, you have handed a life sentence of grief to our family. More than 45,000 people have signed a petition calling for increased penalties for dangerous drivers, people who are moved by what happened to Andrew. A GoFundMe campaign was established to support Christina and the kids, the public response was extraordinary,” said Danny.
Christina also delivered a victim impact statement on behalf of the couple’s three children, via an audio recording which was played in court.
She said that a photo of Andrew in a picture frame with a candle next to it sits at the head of the table.
“Every time the girls make something, they run up to his nightstand and display it there,” Christina said in the children’s victim impact statement.
“As their mother, one of the hardest things is knowing I cannot give them back what was taken from them. I cannot replace their dad. Their lives were divided into before and after that day. The effects of this accident did not end when they left the hospital. They continue every day as they grow up and encounter each milestone without their father beside them,” said Christina on the children’s behalf.
Kirubananthan is still before the courts on unrelated charges after a car he was allegedly driving hit an OPP vehicle in Premier Doug Ford’s motorcade on Highway 401 on Jan. 8, 2025.
In November 2025, the Ford government tabled a bill called “Andrew’s Law” that would introduce a lifetime ban on those found guilty of dangerous driving causing death
Crown attorney Sean Doyle told Ontario Court Justice Ann Marina Elias that an appropriate sentence would be seven-and-a-half years. Six-and-a-half years would be for the dangerous driving causing death conviction to run concurrently with two-and-a-half years for the dangerous driving causing bodily harm convictions. Doyle said a one-year sentence for failing to remain at the scene of an accident causing death would run consecutively to the other sentences. The Crown is also asking for a 15-year driving prohibition.
Doyle pointed out the dangerous driving continued over an extended period of time and was not a momentary lapse in judgement. He also pointed it Kirubananthan’s guilty plea came on the eve of the trial.
Defence lawyer Barry Fox suggested two years in a penitentiary would be more appropriate, saying his client is a first-time offender who was “a youth behind the wheel doing stupid things. He drove too fast.”
Fox is asking for a five to seven year driving ban. Kirubananthan has served roughly 14 months in pre-trial custody and Fox said due to harsh conditions in jail, his client should be credited with a 1.5 days for every day he has spent in jail.
Before the judge gave Kirubananthan a chance to speak, she asked anyone who wanted to leave to exit the courtroom. Three dozen people who were there to support the Cristillo family walked out.
The 19-year-old stood up and apologized, admitting that he drove in an unsafe manner by going too fast.
“I would like you to know it was not my intention to cause such harm,” said Kirubananthan who vowed that he would spend his life repenting.
“I’m ashamed to admit I ran away and hid after the accident. I didn’t think I hurt anyone. I wish I could change what happened that night but I can’t. For the rest of my life, I’m going to carry what I did every single day,” the teen added.
Elias has reserved her decision on sentencing until next month.

title: AI-Enhanced Terrorism Already Showing Up in Nigeria
body: Terrorists historically have been quick to adopt emerging technology. Artificial intelligence is no exception. New research indicates that terrorist groups in Nigeria are using AI to plan and execute deadly attacks. A report from Cambridge University, based on in-person interviews with dozens of former members of Boko Haram and the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), revealed the extent to which the groups use AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, DeepSeek, Gemini, Grok and Meta AI for instructions and guidance. “This AI use is institutionalized through specialized units and internal training,” said Antonia Juelich, a technology and terrorism researcher at Cambridge University who authored the study. “It has aided in attack planning, weapons troubleshooting, and the design of explosive devices, as users have successfully circumvented some safeguards.” Islamic State group’s (IS) global core sent instructors from Iraq, Afghanistan, North Africa and other regions to teach ISWAP commanders how to use AI. They supplied laptops with encryption software, set up subscription accounts and gave daily advice on techniques for making the most of the different platforms. One technique called “jailbreaking” taught users how to bypass ethical and safety guidelines programmed into AI tools to prevent them from giving users information to make a pipe bomb, for example. “Boys that have received extensive training […] bypass the restrictions. They say they need it for a movie or something like that,” an ISWAP commander told Juelich. Graig Klein, a specialist in international terrorism at Leiden University in the Netherlands, said the Cambridge study supports his own work on terrorist groups’ use of AI. “One of the big agreements that came out of it was that it’s less likely to lead to new forms of terrorism, or new types of attacks or brand new weapons,” he said. “But that it’s mostly that it’s a force multiplier — that it improves the capability that these groups have.” Based on her interviews, Juelich estimates that ISWAP began using AI as early as 2023, just a few months after the release of ChatGPT in November 2022. She believes it’s part of a broader training and upskilling program pushed by the IS global leadership and warned that it’s unlikely that this has only happened in Nigeria. “Because ISIS disseminates technical capabilities across its provinces and runs them as an integrated global network, similar training has likely reached other affiliates,” she wrote. “[Boko Haram] received parallel training through separate networks, indicating diffusion beyond any single group.” Adonijah Ndege, a Nairobi-based reporter for the website TechCabal, said AI gives terrorists an advantage that researchers call an “uplift,” an improved outcome in capability and capacity that wouldn’t have occurred without the intervention. “The immediate danger is not that AI turns amateur recruits into military geniuses,” he wrote in a September 3 article. “It is that an experienced organisation that has fought guerrilla warfare across borders becomes better at things it already knows how to do.” For security agencies already grappling with asymmetrical warfare, counterterrorism is only getting more complex, as terrorists use AI for every stage of their operations — from planning to executing and reviewing. The future promises unknown dangers. “There is nothing we haven’t received an answer on,” a former member of ISWAP told Juelich. “We believe it knows everything.” The post AI-Enhanced Terrorism Already Showing Up in Nigeria appeared first on Africa Defense Forum .

title: US explains lack of warning about strikes against Ukraine by bad weather — media
body:
BRUSSELS, October 13. /TASS/. The United States blamed bad weather for not warning Ukraine about the recent missile attacks, according Politico Europe.
"They [Americans] told Ukrainians no warning happened because of bad weather conditions, which is seen as not an adequate reason in Kiev. Thus many are getting increasingly worried this might not have been the case," it said, citing an unnamed official.
Earlier in the day, US President Donald Trump said that Washington had not stopped sharing intelligence with Kiev. "We help them. We're really helping them get to a final answer," he said.
On October 13, Vladimir Zelensky said Ukraine did not receive any notifications from the United States last night about the launch of Russian missiles.

title: Show HN: Factory DS, A Factorio-Like Game for the Nintendo DS
body:
Or how I ended up building a factory game for a 2004 handheld with 4 MB of RAM, with a lot of help from Claude Code
Yes, I even made a game card for it. No, it’s not for sale.
Download Factory DS (factory-ds.nds, 1.9 MB, in English and French). It runs on a real DS with a flashcart, or in an emulator like melonDS .
I think the Nintendo DS is one of the best consoles ever made. It’s far from the most powerful, but I find it one of the best designed. Two screens, a real d-pad, four buttons and two shoulder buttons, and everything falls right under your thumbs. It’s a clamshell, so you can throw it in a backpack without being afraid of breaking it, and it’s simple: you open it and you play, you close it and it sleeps. And of course there is some nostalgia, I spent a lot of hours on it as a teenager.
The problem is that I had run out of games that really kept me hooked on it. The DS library is huge and I have played a lot of great games on it, but the games I spend my evenings on today are more “modern” ones, and none of them exist on the DS.
So I started wondering, why not the other way around? Why not bring a modern game to the DS? The first one that came to my mind was Factorio, the one I play way too much. If you don’t know it, you land on a planet and build a factory: drills mine the ore, conveyor belts carry it everywhere, robotic arms (called inserters) move items in and out of machines, and you spend your time fixing bottlenecks and optimizing ratios. It’s a game about systems more than graphics, so it should fit on a 2004 console, right?
I had never written a single line of code for the DS. I didn’t know the SDKs, the memory map or how the screens work. So I did what I do now for most of my side projects: I opened Claude Code and started from there.
The first evening was only about the setup. We looked at the options together and I went for BlocksDS , a modern SDK built on top of libnds (the historical C library to talk to the DS hardware). I didn’t want to install an ARM toolchain on my Mac, so I asked Claude to make everything run in a Docker container:
You get a .nds file, you open it in the melonDS emulator, and that’s it. A blank screen, but a blank screen that compiles!
Before going further I read a bit about the hardware, because I knew it would drive a lot of decisions later:
Then I wrote the first specs of the game. Nothing fancy, just a short list:
For the graphics I picked the CC0 Kenney tilesets (Tiny Town and Tiny Factory). They are 16×16 pixels, which is exactly the right size for a 256×192 screen, and they still look good that small.
I also decided to draw everything as a bitmap, where each pixel is one byte pointing to a palette of 256 colors, instead of using the tile engine of the DS. The tile engine is the classic way to make a 2D game on this console, but I wanted to be free to draw whatever I wanted: items sliding on belts, inserter arms rotating, smoke, and later trains. I think it was the right call, even if it’s also where most of the performance problems came from.
The very first build was just colored squares. A red square for the drill, grey rectangles for the belts, orange dots for the items and some debug text on the bottom screen. It was ugly, but the belts were moving and that was enough to keep me going. Then real tiles came in, then a mini-map, then objectives… Here is how it evolved:
From colored squares to the current version. These screenshots are in French, but the game is now also in English.
Next I wanted a big world, the kind of world where you have to build trains to bring oil from far away. I set the target to 2048 × 2048 tiles, which is 4.2 million tiles. Even with one byte per tile, that’s already the whole RAM of the console.
Just asking for “a bigger map” would have ended with a giant array and a crash, so Claude and I spent an evening on the design first, going back and forth until it fit. We ended up with this:
On the left, the real generated world, all of it (one pixel is 4×4 tiles). On the right, a small base. Only the tiles the player changed (orange) and the buildings (blue) take memory.
Claude wrote the code and it worked as I hoped. A save slot is 64 KB, there are 3 of them (3 files on the SD card with a flashcart), and a big factory fits in one.
I still wanted to know what happens when it doesn’t fit.
In RAM, it can’t overflow. Every table is allocated once when the game starts, with a fixed size: room for 12,288 modified tiles and 12,288 buildings, 552 KB in total. There is no malloc anywhere in the game. When a table is full the game just refuses, with “too many buildings” when you try to place one more or “map saturated” when you try to cut one more tree. It doesn’t crash.
The save is another story. A building takes between 5 bytes (a rail) and 23 bytes (a machine with its state), a modified tile takes 6 bytes, and a slot is 64 KB. So I measured real saves of bigger and bigger factories:
So no, it’s not guaranteed, and a player could build a factory too big to be saved. If that happens the game refuses to save and shows a message. The save is built in memory before anything is written, so the previous save is still there. You can’t save the latest version of your factory, but at least you don’t lose the old one.
I decided to stop there for now. Placing 3,500 buildings one by one with a d-pad is quite extreme, and the biggest saves made by the test agents are 8 times smaller than the limit. If someone ever gets there, I could compress the save or warn the player before the limit.
With the engine in place, the real game design could start, and it’s probably the part I enjoyed the most. I wrote down the machines, the recipes and their ratios. How many seconds for an iron plate, how many furnaces to feed one assembler, how much coal a steam engine burns… Then came the tiers:
On the left the panel of a furnace, on the right the crafting menu.
Electricity and fluids can get very expensive in a factory game. If you simulate the current going through every cable, or the water moving from one pipe to the next, a 67 MHz CPU gives up quickly. So for these the game doesn’t think in buildings, it thinks in networks .
For electricity the rules are quite simple. Two power nodes (poles, generators, solar panels and batteries) within 7 tiles of each other are linked automatically, there is no cable to pull. A pole powers the machines up to 3 tiles around it, and a generator up to 6. Twice per second each network compares what it produces with what its machines need, and the batteries charge or discharge the difference. If there isn’t enough power, every machine in the network slows down by the same amount. At 70%, everything runs at 70% speed, like in Factorio.
The expensive part is figuring out who is connected to whom, so it only runs when the factory changes. The nodes are sorted by x, so each one is only compared with the next ones up to 7 columns away. The groups are merged with a union-find, a classic little algorithm where each group points to a “leader” and merging two groups just means changing one pointer. The cables you see on screen are only the links that joined two groups, so you don’t get a spaghetti of wires. Step by step:
Fluids work the same way. A pipe network is one single tank . Its capacity is the sum of all its pipes and tanks, and it holds one amount of fluid. A pump adds to it, a machine takes from it, and nothing actually flows from one pipe to the next. When you cut or connect a pipe, each piece first gets back its share of the old network (in proportion to its capacity), then the networks are rebuilt and their shares added up. Only the fluid that was inside the removed pipe is lost, and as long as the pipes don’t change it costs nothing. Here is what happens when you connect and cut pipes:
If you have played Factorio you know the moment. Your factory is running, the ore patch next to it is almost empty and the next one is far away. You place your first rails, your first station, your first locomotive, and that’s when the game gets really good. So a Factorio-like without trains was not an option for me.
They were also the hardest feature to get right. I wanted real trains and not just a cart on a rail:
Getting several trains to share a network without deadlocks took a lot of evenings and a lot of scripted test sessions. I had two trains face to face on the same track, each one politely waiting for the other forever (now one of them backs off after a while), trains without a path because a rail was rotated the wrong way, and a train save format that had to change three times… But once it worked, I could watch three trains share the same loop, stop at the red lights and wait for their turn for ten minutes.
Three trains with cargo and tank wagons on the same loop. The little red flags are block signals, a train waits until the block in front of it is free. Captured from the game itself, at 30 fps.
The other thing Factorio players love is automation that thinks by itself, like “stop the drills when the chest is full” or “only let the train leave when the wagons are loaded”. I didn’t want to go as far as the Factorio circuit network, with numbers on every wire, so I went for something closer to Minecraft redstone, with on/off signals only.
There are sources (a lever, a button that sends a 2-second pulse, a clock that switches every 1, 2, 4 or 8 seconds, and a sensor that watches a belt, a chest, a machine or a station), wires that carry the signal from tile to tile, and NOT, AND and delay gates. Chain a few delays and you get timers. At the end of the chain, a machine next to a signal pauses, a lamp turns on, a belt gate opens, or a station keeps its train at the platform.
With that you can build the classic “sensor on the chest, the drills stop when it’s full”, or keep a train at the station until a sensor says the chest next to it is empty.
The simulation runs every 4 frames, in three passes. First every source and every gate computes its new output from the state of the previous pass. Then the wires are flooded from the active sources with a breadth-first search. And finally each building reads the signal of its neighbors. Because the gates only look at the previous state, a loop of gates can’t get the game stuck in an infinite loop, it just oscillates like in real electronics. And if you haven’t placed a single logic piece, the whole thing is skipped.
A clock switches on and off every 2 seconds and the signal travels through a chain of delays, so the lamps light up one after the other. The vertical wire on the left opens the gate of the bottom belt while the wave passes, and the plates pile up behind it the rest of the time. The top belt is behind a NOT gate, so its copper plates go through when the bottom gate is closed.
Testing was a problem from the very beginning. Every time Claude wanted to check something, an emulator window popped up on my screen. And I had no way to know if a change broke something three hours of play later.
So I asked Claude to prepare an environment where an agent could test the game on its own, by building it locally on my Mac and running it headless (without any window). The game now also compiles for macOS, against a tiny fake version of libnds. Instead of drawing on a screen, it writes PNG files of both screens. On top of that, a small text interface lets the agent drive the real game code with commands like press A , hold RIGHT 30 , step 600 , shot factory.png or state .
With that, play sessions become text files that can be replayed after every change. We ended up with around 470 of them, from “cut a tree” to “build a train network with signals”. They all run with the compiler’s sanitizers turned on, which stop the game as soon as it reads the wrong memory or does something undefined in C. And since Claude can play the game and look at the screenshots, it can check its own work before telling me it’s done.
A real session: the script, the screenshot it produced, and the state of the game it printed.
Some bugs were really sneaky. My favorite one: if the game auto-saved during the 8 seconds of the rocket countdown, the silo stayed full forever and the game could never be finished. The odds were around 2.7% per rocket. In another one, a pumpjack connected to a full pipe network kept its last barrel of oil waiting to be pushed out, and never pumped again. Without the scripted sessions I would have found these after hours of play, or never.
The same setup gave me an idea for the balancing. Instead of playing 10 hours after every change in the ratios, I asked Claude to launch several agents that play the game through the text interface, each one on a different part of it. One played the beginning (the first 15 objectives) with the real buttons, without any cheat, and timed every objective. Another one measured the production rates of the mid- and late-game factories, a third one played the end game up to the rocket, and a last one tested the infinite research. There was also an “analyst” that read the code to list every rate and recipe, and computed how long the whole game would take. At the end each agent wrote a report about where it got stuck, how long each step took and what was too slow or too fast.
