Then I read the reports and decided what to change. Cheaper labs here, a shorter objective there, an oil patch closer to the start… The agents play badly, and where they get stuck a new player probably will too.
Then my first big factory arrived, and it could not hold 60 frames per second. Walking around stuttered. A 67 MHz CPU is not much when you want to simulate thousands of machines and redraw a full screen 60 times per second.
Before changing anything I wanted numbers, but printf does not go anywhere on a DS! So I asked for a benchmark mode in the game. It loads several test factories and writes its timings into a buffer in RAM, and a small Python script reads that buffer through the debugger connection of melonDS (its GDB stub). melonDS runs in the background with the sound off and its JIT disabled (the JIT makes the emulator faster by translating the DS code for my Mac, but then the timings mean nothing). melonDS is very accurate, but it’s still an emulator, and I’ll come back to that at the end.
Then we went through the problems one by one. Measure, fix the worst one, measure again.
The ground. Redrawing the whole ground every frame was way too slow. The DS video hardware can stack several layers and scroll each of them by itself, so I split the top screen into two layers. A large 512×256 ground layer lives in video memory, and only the new tiles entering the view are drawn into it. The hardware scrolls it during the vertical blank (the short pause between two frames when the screen is not being drawn), so scrolling is free. Buildings, items and the player are drawn on a second layer on top, where color 0 is transparent. This alone removed more than 5 ms per frame and the stuttering disappeared.
The two real layers of the top screen, pulled out of the game. The ground layer is bigger than the screen, so the tiles around the view are already there when you walk.
Night for free. The game has a day and night cycle, and my first thought was that at dusk I would have to redraw everything darker, including the big ground layer. But each pixel is not really a color, it’s an index in a palette of 256 colors. So night is not drawn at all! When the light changes, the game recomputes the 256 colors of the palette, a bit darker and a bit bluer each time, and the hardware applies them to every pixel of the screen at once. That’s 256 values to write instead of 49,152 pixels. The few colors used by the interface and the cursor are never darkened, so they stay readable at night. The only things actually drawn are the lights: the glow of the lamps and furnaces, and the fireflies.
The same frame, rendered once with the day palette and once with the night palette. 97% of the pixels have exactly the same value in both images (the other 3% are the lights), only the colors below change.
Fast memory. The ITCM is 32 KB of memory right next to the CPU, much faster than the main RAM. The hot loops go there: the simulation of the machines, the belts and the drawing of the buildings. 32 KB is not much, so I only put there what runs every frame, and every new feature in one of these loops means checking the size of the .itcm section again (22 KB are used today).
No division. The ARM9 has no division instruction. The DS has a separate division unit, but a plain / in C becomes a slow software routine. When infinite research arrived, it added a harmless-looking time * 20 / (20 + level) per machine and per frame. The benchmark caught it, the number of slow frames in the stress test almost doubled. We replaced it with a multiplication by a precomputed fixed-point factor, and the slow frames went from 581 back to 312.
The interface. Even the bottom screen became a problem when I redesigned the menus (more on that below), a full redraw took 14 ms. The rectangle function was checking every single pixel, and every letter of text went through it. Clipping once and writing whole rows at a time brought it down to 4 ms.
The intro. The splash screen was stuttering too. A nebula was computed pixel by pixel every frame (105 ms!). Computed once at startup, it takes 6 ms.
Average time per frame, measured on melonDS with the JIT off. The DS screens refresh at about 60 Hz (59.8 to be exact), so a frame has 16.7 ms. Below that, the game runs at full speed. A lot of 3D DS games actually run at 30 fps, but for a 2D game with belts everywhere I really wanted 60.
On melonDS, a factory of almost 900 buildings runs at a steady 60 fps. The stress test with 3,630 buildings is under 16.7 ms on average, but about 300 of its 1,200 frames are still too slow. That’s way bigger than what you can reasonably build with a d-pad though (and more than what a save can hold anyway).
These are melonDS numbers. The real console is a bit slower, more on that at the end.
Once everything was there, I played. A lot. And every session ended with a list of things I didn’t like, that I sent to Claude, often with a screenshot.
Designing an interface for a d-pad and 256×192 pixels is hard, and the bottom screen was rewritten many times. A selection frame was covering the number of items, two lines of the same description were in two different whites, some texts were too long for their box (they now scroll back and forth)… Removing a building used to need a “remove” tool, which I found painful, so now it’s a long press on B and the tool is gone. And START and SELECT were the other way around compared to most DS games.
Then I went through every screen, one by one, for a complete redesign. The first menus were plain text on a purple background, and every screen got rebuilt with cards, drawn buttons and icons, so you always know which key does what.
The options menu, before and after the redesign.
On the left the world map, on the right the research tree, with the infinite research in the top right corner.
I spent (too much) time on graphic styles. I asked Claude for several palettes and tile variants and kept the ones I liked. The Kenney one stayed the default, and there is also a blueprint style, a flat one and an industrial one, that you can switch at any time from the menu. There was a Game Boy palette too, but I killed it.
For the sounds, I asked Claude to find a few CC0 candidates on Freesound for each one, and I picked them by ear. Then they were all normalized to the same loudness, because the DS speakers are tiny and some sounds were inaudible next to the music. I also added rain, snow, sand wind in the desert, butterflies and fireflies (there were birds at some point, but they were distracting).
The game was first written in French, so at the end I asked Claude to translate it into English too, around 1,300 texts in total. They had to stay as short as the French ones to fit in the little boxes of the interface. The language follows the setting of your console, and you can switch it at any time from the title screen or the options menu.
And finally a small cinematic when you start a new game. Your ship drifts between the stars, the engine dies, and you wake up in the grass next to it. The first version was very “epic”, with big flashes and shaking, but I wanted something calmer and more dreamy, so we toned it down until I liked it. Everything is drawn with code, there is no video in the ROM.
You can now play Factory DS from start to finish, from cutting your first tree to launching rockets, and keep going after that. The ROM is under 2 MB.
But there is one thing melonDS didn’t tell me. On my own DS, with a flashcart, the game’s frame counter showed around 30 fps instead of 60, all the time. So I ran the benchmark ROM on the real console, it writes its results to the SD card, and compared them with melonDS line by line.
The real DS is about a third slower than the emulator for this game. The factory of 890 buildings takes 12.2 ms per frame instead of 9.1 ms, and clearing the big buffer of the top screen takes 4 times longer, writing to the main memory is much slower on the real hardware than in melonDS. That’s still under the 16.7 ms of a frame most of the time.
The 30 fps came from somewhere else, and it’s a bit funny. The frame counter is shown in the statistics screen, and this screen was fully redrawn on every frame. On the real console that alone took almost 16 ms, so as soon as you opened the statistics, the game dropped to 30 fps… and showed you 30 fps. The screen now refreshes 8 times per second and the counter shows the real speed. Small and medium factories run at 60 fps on the real console, and only very big ones slow down a bit.
There is still some margin to win on the real hardware, starting with that buffer that is cleared on every frame, and I’ll probably write a second part about it. In the meantime you can already try the game on your own DS or in melonDS. And maybe one day I’ll try local wireless multiplayer, with two DS building the same factory!
Download Factory DS (factory-ds.nds, 1.9 MB, in English and French). It runs on a real DS with a flashcart, or in an emulator like melonDS .

title: AU chairperson invites Sudanese dialogue committee to Burundi
body: Burundi’s President Évariste Ndayishimiye, chairperson of the African Union (AU), has invited Sudan’s Preparatory Committee for the inter-Sudanese dialogue to visit Burundi as part of efforts to advance talks aimed at resolving the country’s ongoing crisis. Burundi’s ambassador to Sudan, Omar Ntezimbere, conveyed the invitation during a meeting with the committee at its headquarters in Khartoum on Tuesday. Osman Mirghani, the committee’s official spokesperson, said the committee had accepted the invitation and would visit Burundi as soon as possible. He said the initiative reflects Ndayishimiye’s efforts to foster understanding among Sudanese political groups and advance consultations on ways to resolve the crisis. Mirghani welcomed Burundi’s support for the dialogue process, saying the committee had observed a serious commitment from the Burundian side to advancing the initiative. He said the visit would provide an opportunity for further consultations on preparations for an inclusive inter-Sudanese dialogue. The preparatory committee was formed to lay the groundwork for a Sudanese-led dialogue aimed at addressing the country’s political crisis. However, civilian and anti-war groups have questioned its independence and inclusiveness, warning that the process could favour political forces aligned with the military while excluding other groups. The committee says it is consulting political parties, civil society organisations and community representatives, including displaced people, refugees, women and young people, to build consensus ahead of a proposed dialogue conference. Sudan’s political forces remain divided over how to end the war, which erupted in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. The conflict has triggered a major humanitarian crisis, displaced millions of people and complicated efforts to secure a negotiated settlement. The post AU chairperson invites Sudanese dialogue committee to Burundi appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Saudi-led coalition and Houthis trade threats over oil installations
body: The war between the Saudi-led coalition and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels escalated further on Tuesday, as the two sides traded threats against oil installations. The coalition announced that it had carried out an operation against energy sites in Houthi-held areas of Yemen, including Al Sabahah station in the capital Sanaa and piers used for loading fuel at the port of Hodeidah. Coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malki said the Houthis had been using civilian infrastructure to support their military operations and supply their arsenals. He added that the operation had been focused on neutralising the Houthis’ ability to threaten Saudi Arabia, Yemen, the Red Sea and international shipping lanes. Earlier in the day, the coalition had urged civilians to leave Al Sabahah, owned by the Yemen Petroleum Company, before what it described as a “special operation”. The order was published on social media by Maj Gen Al Malki, alongside a map of the area. In response to the strikes, the Houthis announced that oil installations in Saudi Arabia would be considered legitimate targets and that any civilians working at those sites should stay away. The coalition also said it had intercepted three missiles launched towards Saudi Arabia on Monday evening and yesterday. One of the projectiles was aimed at Riyadh, while the others were heading towards the city of Khamis Mushait, Maj Gen Al Malki said. In the past weeks, Saudi Arabia has faced repeated Houthi attacks on civilian infrastructure, including a strike on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Saturday that left 13 people dead and 308 injured. However, although the attacks have disrupted travel and forced schools in Riyadh to switch to remote learning, the city’s roads remained crowded yesterday, offices were open and sporting events took place as planned, residents told The National . “The usual traffic is there. The streets are full of cars,” said Christina, a Lebanese citizen who lives in the Saudi capital. “I’m working from the office and the roads look completely normal on my way to work.” Meanwhile, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty held a call with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi yesterday, during which he pushed for an immediate halt to all attacks on Saudi Arabia, his ministry said in a statement. Mr Abdelatty was quoted as saying that there could be no justification for the attacks.

title: Angry Tema Community 25 residents threaten to sleep at GWL over water shortage
body: Residents of Tema Community 25 and surrounding communities have threatened to occupy the head office of the Ghana Water Limited (GWL) and sleep there until a reliable water supply is restored. The residents say they have endured persistent water shortages for years, forcing many households to rely on water tankers and boreholes at high cost. They issued the warning after a previous visit to the company’s Tema office and assurances of intervention failed to improve the situation. They are demanding urgent intervention from the government and Ghana Water, warning that they would bring their families and mattresses to the company’s head office and remain there until water supply is restored. “We have given the government two weeks. If we don’t get the water, then we’re going to take action. We would come and sleep at the Ghana Water Limited office till we get water,” they warned. The residents said they had visited the company’s regional office twice and received responses but were yet to see a lasting solution that would ensure a reliable supply to all affected households. In an interview with JoyNews, one resident lamented the situation. “Since 2022, in fact, it has been an unbearable situation within this community. We’ve not been having water. We depend on tankers that supply us water almost every day,” the resident said. The resident added that the shortage had also affected four fire hydrants serving the community and surrounding areas, raising concerns about access to water during fire outbreaks. Another resident, who has lived in the community for eight years, said she had relied on borehole water throughout her stay and had invested nearly GH¢30,000 in a reverse osmosis filtration system because of concerns about water quality. She said the water crisis had also affected her rental property, which had remained vacant for a year, resulting in lost income. Other residents said some households spend between GH¢1,000 and GH¢1,200 monthly to purchase water, describing the situation as financially burdensome. They accused the water company of charging estimated bills despite the absence of water in their taps.

title: BoG takes financial literacy drive to Techiman, vows to protect depositors
body: The Bank of Ghana (BoG) has reaffirmed its commitment to deepening engagement with stakeholders across the country, emphasizing collaboration and shared responsibility in sustaining Ghana’s economic stability. In its first-ever stakeholders’ engagement in Techiman, the Bono East Regional capital, the Central Bank brought its message of financial literacy, consumer protection, and inclusive dialogue directly to traders, market women, and business owners under the theme “ Strengthening Stakeholder Relations Through Dialogue and Engagement .” Speaking at the event, Director of Communications at the Bank of Ghana, Bernard Ato Otabil, explained that the initiative forms part of a broader strategy to strengthen collaboration between the Central Bank and local stakeholders. “This engagement is about inclusiveness. It’s about letting the people know the operations of the Bank of Ghana,” he said. “We want to build trust and ensure that every Ghanaian understands what we do and how it affects their daily lives.” The engagement covered a range of critical topics, including: · The role and mandate of the Bank of Ghana · Responsible borrowing and consumer protection · Dud cheques: causes, implications, and prevention · Currency education: identification and proper handling of banknotes The Regional Director of the Bank of Ghana for the Sunyani office, Lawal Abubakari, who oversees the Bono, Bono East, Ahafo, and parts of the Upper West Region, noted that the feedback received from the engagement will strengthen the bank’s output across all regions—not only in the Bono East. “The feedback we have gathered here today is invaluable. It will help us refine our approach and improve our services not just in Techiman or the Bono East Region, but across the entire country,” he said. “This is why we are committed to listening to the people. Their experiences and concerns shape the policies and interventions we design.” His remarks underscored the Bank of Ghana’s broader vision of using regional engagements as a feedback loop to enhance its operations nationwide. While participants lauded the Bank of Ghana’s decision to educate them on its operations, some expressed deep-seated concerns about their inability to identify genuine financial institutions. Many traders in the region still bear the scars of past experiences where financial institutions collapsed, taking with them monies belonging to hardworking traders. The memories of those losses have left many afraid to entrust their savings to banks. Queenmother of the Techiman Fishmongers Association, Nana Grace Tina, voiced the concerns of many when she appealed to authorities for help. “We want the authorities to help us identify reliable financial institutions that will help us do our business without fear,” she said. “We have suffered before. We don’t want to suffer again.” Responding to these concerns, Mr. Otabil offered reassurance, explaining that the Central Bank has put in place robust measures to protect depositors. “With the current measures put in place by the Central Bank, the customer is protected. No such thing can happen where customers will lose their deposits,” he assured. “We have strengthened our regulatory framework, and we continue to monitor all financial institutions to ensure compliance.” He encouraged participants to verify the status of any financial institution with the Bank of Ghana before committing their funds. The Ghana Union of Traders Association (GUTA) commended the Bank of Ghana for organizing the program and called for it to be held regularly. The Regional President of GUTA, Yeboah Asuamah Kyimeh, said the initiative would help traders understand financial inclusion and ultimately contribute to poverty alleviation. “This program is commendable. We wish it could be held intermittently to help educate traders in this area to understand the financial inclusion that will help alleviate poverty,” he said. The event concluded with an interactive question-and-answer session, where participants had the opportunity to seek clarification on various concerns, including how to identify counterfeit currency, the process for reporting dud cheques, and the steps to take when dealing with unlicensed financial institutions. Hundreds of participants showed up for the engagement, reflecting the strong appetite for financial education in the region. The Bank of Ghana says the Techiman engagement is just the beginning. The Central Bank plans to extend the dialogue to other regions across the country, ensuring that every Ghanaian, regardless of location, has access to information about the Central Bank’s role and their rights as consumers. For the traders of Techiman, the event offered not only knowledge but also hope—hope that with continued engagement and stronger regulation, their money will be safe, and their businesses will thrive.

title: Tokyo uses reporters to gather data to undermine Russia’s security — Foreign Ministry
body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Japan relies on journalists working in Russia to collect information intended to weaken Russia’s security, Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said.
"Tokyo’s attempts to use its correspondents who are in Russia and have the status of foreign journalists to gather information with the aim of undermining the security of our state are regrettable. We cannot fail to point out that today’s event is not an isolated case," she said on the ministry’s website.

title: ‘Stop the distractions’ – Akosua Manu demands answers over GH¢49.7m South Africa evacuation cost
body: Akosua Manu, an advisor to NPP flagbearer Dr Mahamudu Bawumia, has demanded answers to questions surrounding Ghana’s GH¢49.7 million South Africa evacuation exercise, warning against shifting the public debate towards political disagreements over service passports. In a Facebook post on Tuesday, October 13, Ms Manu said the public deserved a transparent account of the expenditure, particularly in light of concerns about payment registers, alleged ghost names and discrepancies in flight records. She described the development as “an insult to the intelligence of Ghanaians”, arguing that allegations concerning Nana Boakye’s service passport did not address the substance of the financial questions. Ms Manu’s comments come amid a public disagreement involving the Majority on Parliament’s Foreign Affairs and Regional Integration Committee and its Deputy Ranking Member, Nana Asafo-Ayeh, over criticism of Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa. The Majority has accused Mr Asafo-Ayeh of pursuing a campaign of “character assassination” against the Minister. It claims the tension stems from Mr Ablakwa’s refusal to grant a service passport to Nana Boakye, popularly known as Nana B, a former NPP National Youth Organiser and now NPP 2nd Vice Chairman and former Board Chairman of the National Food Buffer Stock Company. According to the Majority, the Minister acted in accordance with a presidential directive requiring holders of diplomatic and service passports to return them. Salaga South MP Zuwera Ibrahimah Mohammed has defended the Minister’s position, arguing that public officials must operate within the law when dealing with requests for favours. Ms Manu, however, insists that the passport controversy must not displace scrutiny of the evacuation expenditure. She maintains that the records should be made available for proper examination so the public can establish how the funds were used. “If there is nothing to hide, an independent audit should be welcomed,” she said, renewing her call for accountability and insisting that the documents should provide the answers Ghanaians seek.

title: Zero to Calc in Six Days: Inside XBOW's Chrome Full Chain
body:
On Wednesday October 28 at 10am PT / 1pm ET, I’ll walk through how we built this chain in six days. Join me for the live webinar →
The final chain combined a V8 compiler bug, an animated-WebP decoder bug, and a memory-safety bug in Crashpad. Together they turned JavaScript execution in an ordinary Chrome tab into code execution outside the renderer sandbox.
Google awarded this chain the first $250,000 Chrome full-chain reward under the VRP rules introduced in April 2026. Our separate announcement covers the award and what it means for XBOW. This post is about the exploit: the boundaries it crossed, the root cause of each vulnerability, and the interfaces that connected them.
A web page in signed Chrome Beta launches Calculator via XBOW’s full chain exploit.
One thing is talking about speed and how offensive is accelerating and another is to experience it first hand. Pre-LLMs a Chrome full chain would take a team of four around 6-9 months to be produced, our first submission took 2 months. The awarded one? six days. The speed is challenging even for us trying to understand how security is changing.
We built the chain in six days, from Sunday, August 2, through Friday, August 7. Rather than ask one agent to produce an exploit end to end, we split the work into parallel campaigns with narrower goals: broad vulnerability search, V8 memory corruption, a V8 sandbox escape, a renderer sandbox escape, and integration. AI agents using OpenAI's gpt-5.6-sol model searched source code, tested hypotheses, built proofs of concept, and developed exploit stages; XBOW researchers chose targets, supplied context, challenged results, redirected searches, and decided which components to join. We also developed backup routes and gave each stage a clean interface, so that we could replace one component without rebuilding the rest of the exploit. Reconstructing usage from the archived Codex logs puts the six-day campaign at roughly $40,000 in API charges. We will cover the chronology and orchestration at Unprompted at the end of October; here, we focus on the vulnerabilities and the exploit mechanics that connected them into a full chain.
V8 first contains JavaScript-engine corruption inside an in-process sandbox . Most JavaScript heap objects live in a reserved 4 GiB region, and many pointers are represented as offsets within that region. References to native objects and executable code receive additional protection. A V8 memory corruption bug can therefore give an attacker extensive control inside the cage without immediately yielding native code execution. V8 describes this design in The V8 sandbox.
Chrome then contains the renderer itself inside an operating-system process sandbox . Even an attacker with native code execution in the renderer cannot freely access the rest of the machine. Chromium's sandbox design document describes this outer boundary.
The chain crossed both boundaries in three vulnerability stages:
The animated-WebP stage was a V8 sandbox escape , but rather than attacking the sandbox itself we exploited a property that the V8 sandbox deliberately does not enforce and that Blink incorrectly assumed it could trust. Finally, the exploit used an overflow in Crashpad to cross the final the outer process boundary and achieve unsandboxed code execution on the host.
The first vulnerability was in Maglev, V8's mid-tier optimizing compiler. To understand it, we need to look at deoptimization.
Optimized code operates under assumptions about the values and objects it handles. When an assumption stops being true at runtime, V8 must reconstruct ordinary JavaScript objects and continue in less specialized code. Some of those objects never existed in memory while the optimized code was running; the compiler had represented them only as values. Deoptimization must materialize them.
A JavaScript object field with a double representation needs a HeapNumber when V8 materializes the object. The vulnerable Maglev path created one old-space HeapNumber for the virtual value and stored the object itself in the deoptimization literal array:
That code is from the vulnerable maglev-code-generator.cc . The other half of the bug was in the generic materializer. For a field marked kStoreHeapObject, it wrote the object held by the translated slot directly into the reconstructed owner:
This is the corresponding code from translated-state.cc .
The first block turned a mutable object into a literal. The second copied that object's identity, not merely its numeric value, into each reconstructed owner. With nested activations, V8 could therefore create distinct JavaScript objects whose double fields shared one mutable HeapNumber .
That behavior violated a compiler invariant stated elsewhere in V8 :
The vulnerable path made a mutable number look like exactly the sort of immutable constant that the compiler was allowed to reuse.
The exploit used the disagreement against Array.prototype.at() . One compiler observation saw a safe index and approved an in-bounds access. Another observation of the nominally same constant supplied the actual load offset. Changing one object's double field could therefore change the offset used by optimized code without invalidating the earlier bounds reasoning.
Three optimized load functions were enough to disclose nearby V8 pointers, recover the layout of a packed-double array, and obtain a reference to an attacker-described array. That forged array was then used as a bootstrap to rewrite the metadata of a real Uint8Array , extending ordinary indexed access across V8's entire 4 GiB cage.
Finding stable object addresses required one more step. The exploit stored a reference in V8's large-object space to whichever JavaScript object it needed to locate. V8 itself updated that reference during garbage collection, so the exploit could recover a current in-cage address without pinning movable objects.
At this point, the exploit had reliable memory access from JavaScript throughout the V8 sandbox.
V8 removed the literal-object special case. Virtual HeapNumber s now follow the ordinary captured-object materialization path, and Maglev explicitly prevents their deduplication. Each deoptimization materializes a fresh box:
The code is from the fixed revision . The complete patch is V8 change 8255554 , and the public root-cause report is Chromium issue 547819997 .
When we went looking for V8 sandbox escapes, we made a conscious decision to avoid attacking the sandbox itself. Instead, we thought a bit about its threat model and chose to look for things that were “allowed” but seemed likely to be problematic. We focused on obligations that the V8 sandbox threat model imposes on downstream consumers: namely, that all such code must guard against the capabilities an in-cage attacker has, like concurrent modification of in-cage objects, swaps between pointers of the same type, etc.
The vulnerability we found is precisely an example of this: WebCodecs can give an ArrayBuffer to ImageDecoder by transferring it. Under ordinary JavaScript semantics, transfer detaches the old buffer and its views. Blink can then wrap the backing store without making a copy and treat the bytes as its exclusive input.
But the V8 sandbox has a different threat model: once an attacker controls memory inside the cage, V8 assumes that the attacker can corrupt objects and bookkeeping there. It does not promise to make a detached ArrayBuffer semantically immutable against that attacker. Enforcing that property would require moving or copying the backing store, or adding checks to hot paths that the sandbox was designed to avoid.
In the full chain, the exploit used an in-cage write supplied by the first stage to remove a live Uint8Array view from its JSArrayBuffer 's detach-notification chain. When ImageDecoder transferred the buffer, V8 detached the views it still knew about. Optimized writes through the omitted view remained usable. Blink believed it owned the bytes exclusively; the attacker could still change them.
That broken ownership assumption manifested in WebP decoding as a time of check / time of use (TOCTOU) vulnerability.
The proof of concept placed two same-length, independently valid animated WebP files in the same backing store:
WEBPImageDecoder::DecodeSingleFrame() initialized the external buffer's stride and size from the cached rectangle. It then advanced the output pointer independently to that rectangle's top-left pixel ( code ):
The next statement passed that descriptor to WebPIUpdate() .
For the ASAN reproducer, the bitmap stride was 256 bytes and the complete allocation was 16,384 bytes. GetAddr(16, 0) advanced the output pointer by 64 bytes, leaving 16,320 bytes. That was exactly enough for A's cached rectangle:
Blink nevertheless advertised all 16,384 bytes. B's 64-pixel-wide payload therefore passed libwebp's external-buffer size check:
WebPIUpdate() wrote the pixels before Blink compared the decoded dimensions with the cached rectangle. The decoded footprint extended 64 bytes past the native SkBitmap allocation. ASAN caught a 256-byte conversion write starting at the first byte beyond the allocation.
Both WebPs were valid on their own. The unsafe state existed only because Blink combined A's cached geometry with B's current bytes.
The production exploit used the same bug with geometry selected for PartitionAlloc. A two-pixel frame started at x = 124 on a 126-pixel canvas. The 504-byte pixel allocation and a 496-byte WebPIDecoder occupied adjacent slots in the 512-byte bucket. Advancing the output pointer by 496 bytes left only eight bytes, while the decoder still believed it had 504.
The pixel write replaced the live decoder's native fields with pointers to two WebPDecBuffer records already staged in a native network buffer. When decode completed, the genuine WebPCopyDecBufferPixels() routine followed the false source and destination descriptions. It copied one chosen 64-bit value to one chosen native address.
That single write was the entire interface between the image exploit and the next stage.
The first landed fix set rgba , stride , and size together and limited the advertised extent to the retained rectangle. A follow-up removed a subtler assumption: rather than calculating what the allocation ought to contain, the decoder now takes its stride and extent from the ImageFrame bitmap itself:
The code appears in the follow-up revision . The root-cause report and ASAN reproducer are in Chromium issue 548509153 . The two landed fixes are Chromium change 8266257 and Chromium change 8352899 .
Stage 2 produced one selected native write outside the V8 cage. The chain still needed to turn that write into arbitrary native code execution without modifying a protected code-pointer entry.
A hot WebAssembly function resolves its target through V8's process-wide Wasm Code Pointer table. The exploit changed the writable base used to locate that table and supplied a replacement entry with the correct type.
We adapted an island-hopping technique from our previous full chain . That exploit linked instruction fragments encoded in JIT double constants with short jumps. This time, we used 13 64-bit immediates in Liftoff-generated Wasm code and a Windows loader ABI.
After WebPCopyDecBufferPixels() changed the Wasm Code Pointer table base, the next Wasm call passed the signature check and resolved the replacement entry. The entry pointed to a jmp rcx instruction in chrome.dll ; RCX pointed to the first instruction island.
Each island contributed up to six bytes of the loader, followed by a short jump over the compiler-generated instructions before the next island. Together, the 13 islands formed a roughly 70-byte loader. It allocated writable memory, copied the Crashpad payload, changed the mapping to executable, and called it.
Chrome’s Crashpad handler runs outside the renderer sandbox. When it receives a snapshot request, it suspends the renderer and reads data structures from the renderer’s address space. The handler creates ScopedProcessSuspend , which calls NtSuspendProcess() , before telling the snapshot machinery that the target is suspended.
In the revision immediately before the fix , one of Crashpad’s remote-memory helpers, ProcessMemoryWin::ReadUpTo() , contained the following recovery path:
At first glance, the error appears to be simply that short_read is not limited to size . But the calculation was safe under the assumption Crashpad believed it had established: that the suspended process’s address space could not change.
The fallback was intended for a read that begins in one readable page and crosses into an inaccessible page. If a request for size bytes crosses that boundary, the number of bytes remaining in the first page must be smaller than size . Retrying only those bytes therefore fits in the caller’s destination buffer.
With stable page protections, there are three ordinary cases:
The code therefore used the first failure as evidence about the geometry of the source mapping. That inference stopped being true when the renderer could change the mapping between the two reads.
Windows allows a thread created with the THREAD_CREATE_FLAGS_BYPASS_PROCESS_FREEZE flag to continue running across NtSuspendProcess() . Before requesting a snapshot, the native renderer payload created such a thread. The exploit used flags 0x42 : BYPASS_PROCESS_FREEZE together with SKIP_THREAD_ATTACH . Exactly why Windows has this feature remains a mystery, but it provides the essential assumption violation we need here by letting us modify page protections in between the read and its retry.
While Crashpad treated the renderer as suspended, that thread repeatedly changed attacker-controlled source pages between PAGE_NOACCESS and PAGE_READWRITE . The winning sequence was:
For the call site used by the exploit, the numbers were:
The original 0xb8 -byte request ended well before the page boundary. It could produce the required error only because the whole page was inaccessible at that instant. Once the renderer made the page readable, the 0x168 -byte retry succeeded and overran the allocation.
To make the race reliable, the payload supplied 48 candidate reads in one snapshot request. One freeze-exempt worker cycled their pages between readable and inaccessible states. The other helper threads remained parked, keeping the thread population—and the Crashpad allocations associated with it—stable.
The oversized retry could corrupt only the allocation immediately after its 0xc0 read-buffer slot. The payload arranged for that allocation to contain a live SnapshotMinidumpMemoryWriter , which Crashpad would later use to read a memory range from the renderer and send the bytes through its output path.
To create that adjacency, the payload exposed a readable process and loader graph containing memory ranges in a chosen order. Crashpad allocated a writer for each range, then coalesced contained ranges and freed their writers. The ordering left one freed 0xc0 writer slot immediately before a writer that remained live; the next 0xb8 -byte read buffer reused the freed slot. Writers for threads, TEBs, and readable stacks affected the allocation sequence, so the payload counted those inputs and adjusted the number of ranges to keep the same bucket position.
On the CET-capable systems we tested, the handler used a user shadow stack, while CFG restricted indirect calls to approved targets. To avoid running afoul of these mitigations, we used a normal call and return sequence and directed the substituted virtual calls to existing CFG-valid functions.
The vulnerable retry-read rewrote the first 0xa8 bytes of the live writer. At offset 0x00 it wrote back the SnapshotMinidumpMemoryWriter vtable; at 0x70 it set the writer’s state to writable; and at 0x78 it replaced the MemorySnapshot::Delegate vtable with a shifted CopyingOutputStreamAdaptor vtable, so the delegate callback entered the adaptor’s buffered-write path. The overwrite ended immediately before memory_snapshot_ at offset 0xa8 .
Crashpad later entered the writer’s WriteObject () through its first vtable. WriteObject() called Read() through the preserved snapshot pointer, which read a controlled 0xd0 -byte range from the renderer. The callback through the second vtable copied those bytes to a writable address in chrome.exe and treated the same address as the adaptor’s underlying output stream.
The copied bytes constructed both a one-method output stream and a fallback-launcher object. When the adaptor flushed, the stream’s virtual Write() entered Chrome’s FallbackUnhandledExceptionFilter() , a CFG-valid target. The bytes also pointed Chrome’s fallback-launcher global at the copied object and supplied its command and startup fields. The filter called FallbackCrashHandlerLauncher::LaunchAndWaitForHandler() , which passed cmd /k calc.exe to CreateProcessW . These calls maintained the shadow stack.
Because Windows ASLR randomizes modules once rather than for each process (a consequence of the decision to use relocations rather than PIC/PIE code), it mapped chrome.exe at the same address in both the renderer and the handler. This meant that the renderer payload could derive the handler addresses from the image base in its own process, as well as validating the exact build using the image timestamp and size in order to apply any build-specific offsets (given Chrome’s rapid release schedule, we had to be able to quickly retarget the chain as new versions were released).
The fixed implementation removed Crashpad’s dependence on the target remaining unchanged between the two reads. The retry is now limited by both the source-page boundary and the caller’s original request:
The clamp is necessary defensive programming, but it is best understood as removing a temporal assumption: even if the source changes between the failed read and the retry, Crashpad can no longer write beyond the destination.
The same patch hardened the generic caller by rejecting any ReadUpTo() result larger than the remaining requested count before advancing the destination pointer. That check appears in process_memory.cc .
The complete fix is Chromium change 8267322 , and the public report is Chromium issue 545820931 .
Now that everyone – including Google – is pointing LLMs at codebases like Chrome, bug collisions are a major risk. To guard against this, we designed the exploit with modular stages and tried to have backup vulnerabilities ready for each piece. This strategy paid off when the first version of our chain, which used a Gin vulnerability for its V8 sandbox escape, turned out to be a duplicate of issue 542670566 . After a very stressful few hours we managed to replace the Gin-based V8 escape with the animated WebP stage described in this post; this replacement stage rescued the chain and Google confirmed that the chain popped calc .
What should we conclude from this chain, which (to the best of our knowledge) is the first rewarded full chain Chrome exploit of the LLM era? We have a few thoughts:

title: Moscow court hands blogger Michael Naki a second prison sentence in absentia, bringing his combined term to 14 years
body: Moscow’s Basmanny District Court sentenced blogger Michael Naki in absentia to five years in a penal colony for publicly calling for activities aimed at undermining Russia’s security (Article 280.4, Part 2, Paragraph “c” of the Criminal Code). It also barred him from administering websites for five years. The prosecution stemmed from a video posted on Naki’s channel on May 7, 2024. According to Mediazona, the video was titled “Putin can now be eliminated. The day Putin stopped being president.” Prosecutors said the video contained signs of “incitement to overthrow the government in Russia.” This is Naki’s second sentence in absentia. In 2023, the Basmanny District Court sentenced him to 11 years in a penal colony for spreading “fake news” about the army (Article 207.3, Part 2, Paragraph “d” of the Criminal Code). That case concerned a video in which Naki and Conflict Intelligence Team founder Ruslan Leviev recapped the ninth day of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The court combined portions of the sentences in the two cases to impose a total term of 14 years in a penal colony. At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication. If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at reports@meduza.io . To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter .

title: How Are Ukrainians Coping With Russia’s Attacks on Ukraine’s Energy Grid?
body:
For Ukrainians, talk of an energy truce doesn’t mean one is coming.
As US President Donald Trump touted an immediate energy ceasefire , blackouts persisted across parts of Ukraine as Moscow continues pounding Ukraine’s energy grid – the rumored deal covers refineries only, while Kyiv insists on a bilateral truce that also protects the grid.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
But for Ukraine, power is only half the problem.
While Kyiv residents interviewed by Kyiv Post reported blackouts of varying intensity, people in other regions, from Odesa and Mykolaiv in the south, to Ternopil in the west, said they had yet to experience major disruptions.
In Kharkiv to the east, blackouts appear to be a limited problem.
“In October, the lights were turned off twice: the first time for about an hour, the second time from the morning until exactly 4 p.m.,” Maksym, a 39-year-old PhD student, told Kyiv Post.
But back in the capital, blackouts have been “almost daily” in October for Khrystyna, a 27-year-old head of sales who works remotely.
“Currently, they last up to five hours at a stretch,” she told Kyiv Post.
Kateryna, a 34-year-old data scientist, reported similar problems – which were complicated by Russia’s attacks on bridges spanning the river that cuts through the Ukrainian capital.
“I had initially planned to work from an energy-independent office on Kyiv’s right bank during power outages. However, since I live on the left bank, attacks on the bridges raised concerns about whether I would even be able to get to the office,” she told Kyiv Post.
This photograph shows vehicles with headlights on a non-illuminated road during a power outage in Kyiv on Jan. 20, 2026, following Russian missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. (Photo by Roman PILIPEY / AFP) Advertisement
This photograph shows vehicles with headlights on a non-illuminated road during a power outage in Kyiv on Jan. 20, 2026, following Russian missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. (Photo by Roman PILIPEY / AFP)
But some in Kyiv are luckier, such as Oleksandr Burdeinyi, a 20-year-old creative marketing manager, who said blackouts haven’t been as severe for him as for his friends, because of nearby critical infrastructure.
“I got lucky living near critical infrastructure – only two power cuts in the last two weeks. Meanwhile, most of my friends and family are dealing with daily blackouts,” he told Kyiv Post.
Ukrainians are no stranger to blackouts due to Russian attacks – in the summer of 2024, as temperatures soared above 30°C (86°F), Russia took out over half of Ukraine’s power-generation capacity.
Then, in the winter of 2025-26, Russia targeted more power plants and heating systems, sending household temperatures to single digits in subzero conditions .
Now, Ukrainians are bracing for similar situations – but worse.
Vadym, a 37-year-old operations director at a company that maintains and oversees boiler rooms and utility systems at 60 buildings and residential complexes in Kyiv, said he has already received numerous requests this month.
“Autumn 2026 has brought many of the same challenges for the utility sector, and we have already received numerous emergency service requests throughout October,” he said.
Almost everyone Kyiv Post interviewed voiced concerns about water supplies in Kyiv and beyond.
“I’m worried about poor mobile coverage and water supply issues. I reckon a complete freeze in the water supply would spell an inevitable disaster,” said Sara, a 24-year-old business analyst in southern Ukraine’s Odesa.
Oleksii Masaltsev, a 44-year-old sound engineer from Khorostkiv in western Ukraine’s Ternopil region, said he is also bracing for water shortages despite experiencing no major blackouts so far.
“I’m preparing for this by stocking up on water, power banks and a charging station,” he told Kyiv Post.
In Kyiv, two months before the cold spell, authorities reported disruptions to water supplies. They urged locals to stock up on food and water on Sunday, Oct. 11, after a Russian attack left over half of Kyiv’s households without running water.
Without power, the water pumps can’t run – meaning there’s no water to flush the toilet, as Kyiv residents told Kyiv Post during the previous winter.
People ride the tram along a non-illuminated street during blackout hours in Kyiv on Nov. 21, 2025, following Russian missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. (Photo by Tetiana DZHAFAROVA / AFP) Advertisement
People ride the tram along a non-illuminated street during blackout hours in Kyiv on Nov. 21, 2025, following Russian missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. (Photo by Tetiana DZHAFAROVA / AFP)
“As last year, power outages are causing a range of problems for the buildings we maintain… and in some cases, sewage pumping stations also shut down, disrupting the drainage system,” Operations Director Vadym explained.
Some in Kyiv are bracing for similar conditions.
“I also plan to buy a portable shower, a metal bucket that can be heated on a stove, a portable washbasin, and an electric blanket that can run on power from a portable battery or power bank,” Kateryna said.
A blackout is one thing; not having running water is another.
“We’ve gotten somewhat used to living without electricity – you can buy rechargeable lamps or other light sources. But living without water would be nearly impossible,” Khrystyna said.
As Kyiv and Moscow go tit-for-tat with strikes on logistics warehouses , Ukraine’s food and medicine supplies have become the latest victims as pharmaceutical warehouses have also been targeted.
And getting enough food for winter is a concern for some.
“What I fear most is food shortages, as the enemy has already started targeting food storage facilities,” 20-year-old Burdeinyi told Kyiv Post.
Vadym, speaking from his experience at a utility service company, said not everything can be fixed at once.
“Once the power comes back on, a technician often has to visit the building in person to restart the equipment. This creates logistical and communication challenges for a company like ours, especially when outages affect multiple buildings simultaneously,” he said.
Then comes the workforce issue, as many Ukrainian men are mobilized to defend the country.
“The average age of our plumbers and electricians is over 60, and training younger specialists takes considerable time,” he continued.
“The vocational schools we have approached have struggled to provide graduates with the practical skills we need. Qualified specialists are increasingly difficult to find, and in some highly specialized roles, there are very few left in the labor market,” he added.
The temporary solution, he said, is training residents to do some of the work.
“To ease the workload on our staff, we ask homeowners’ associations to appoint a technically skilled resident and provide them with additional training,” he said.
“This allows residents to handle minor equipment problems and restart systems after scheduled power outages, reducing the need to call our emergency repair teams.”
Almost everyone has some form of backup power to keep the essentials running.
“I’ve had fiber-optic broadband installed, my flat’s on the sunny side, and I’ve got plenty of power banks,” Sara in Odesa said.
“Yes, we have a portable power station to keep the internet running and charge our work devices. We also have several flashlights and a supply of water for household needs,” Khrystyna in Kyiv said.
In Kharkiv, Maksym said the situation is likely better than in Kyiv, though he and his family are prepared nonetheless.
“The situation with light and heat is traditionally better in Kharkiv than in Kyiv. But my family and I are, of course, preparing for the winter as best we can: We bought power banks, and use a stove with a gas cylinder to cook if there is no light for a long time,” he said.
This photograph shows a power generator outside a restaurant during blackout hours in the center of Kyiv on Jan. 18, 2026, amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. (Photo by Sergei SUPINSKY / AFP)
This photograph shows a power generator outside a restaurant during blackout hours in the center of Kyiv on Jan. 18, 2026, amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. (Photo by Sergei SUPINSKY / AFP)
But portable power stations can be costly. A Chinese-made Marstek Venus E, with enough capacity to keep a house running for over 24 hours under normal use, costs over Hr. 61,990 ($1,376) – with prices sure to rise as demands surge in winter.
Kateryna in Kyiv said she has resorted to installments to get a smaller power station.
“I… had to find a way to secure a reliable power supply at home as quickly as possible. I ordered a BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 portable power station with a 2,600-watt output and a 2,073 watt-hour capacity,” she said.
“Like many Ukrainians, I couldn’t afford such a major purchase upfront, so I had to buy it on an installment plan.”
“My winter and blackout prep is basically just planning to move out of Kyiv next month. I honestly think living and working here under these conditions is going to be extremely tough,” Burdeinyi said.
But elsewhere in Ukraine, some are also playing a game of wait and see.
“It will be possible to assess the situation once it happens, but the outlook is troubling. What worries me most is a possible energy collapse,” Yurii, a 63-year-old geologist in southern Ukraine’s Pervomaysk, Mykolaiv region, told Kyiv Post.
This question has taken on new urgency after President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv was lagging behind other regions – including frontline areas – in implementing its resilience plan. He warned that even a single Shahed strike can leave a significant part of the capital without power and water, and said decisions were being prepared on protecting critical infrastructure and changing how Kyiv is managed.
Asked about how they think the authorities could help brace their cities for the unforgiving winter, many interviewed by Kyiv Post mentioned Ukraine’s “Points of Invincibility” – tents erected nationwide that provide shelter, power and warm drinks to locals.
“Increase the number of resilience points, rather than shifting this responsibility onto businesses, such as the situation where everyone goes to the Nova Poshta post office to dry their hair,” Sara said, recalling previous blackouts.
People come and go at a tent of Point of Invincibility in Kyiv on Jan. 11, 2026, where they can charge devices and warm themself, following Russian missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure amid the Russian invasion in Ukraine. (Photo by Tetiana DZHAFAROVA / AFP)
People come and go at a tent of Point of Invincibility in Kyiv on Jan. 11, 2026, where they can charge devices and warm themself, following Russian missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure amid the Russian invasion in Ukraine. (Photo by Tetiana DZHAFAROVA / AFP)
“Develop resilience centers with electricity supplies, backup internet and stocks of drinking water. Implement anti-corruption reforms, despite the war,” Masaltsev in western Ukraine’s Ternopil region said.
Others emphasized the need to provide water supplies when the pumps fail.
“If water stops flowing to homes, I believe local authorities should ensure access to it in every district or neighborhood,” Khrystyna in Kyiv said.
“For instance, they should equip public water kiosks with backup power, as they currently rely on electric pumps… People need water for basic household needs, even if it isn’t potable.”
Khrystyna said water supplies should be provided via the “Points of Invincibility” as well.
Some also called for the government to decentralize the energy and heating system – an ongoing discussion since 2024 – while ensuring backup power at critical facilities.
“Perhaps it would be wise to set up small, autonomous boiler houses – each serving a few buildings – and equip them with backup power,” Khrystyna said, adding that it would ensure a single attack can’t cut off supplies to entire districts.
“It would probably be a good idea to look into alternative power sources, ensuring generators for boiler rooms and backup power for the water supply,” Sara added.
“Local authorities could be doing much more to develop decentralized energy systems, install cogeneration units, and provide backup power for critical infrastructure,” Kateryna in Kyiv said.
But Vadym noted that households can also help prepare buildings for cold spells, as Kyiv Post covered during the past winter.
New valves and pumps inside a restored heating unit in a Kyiv residential building in January 2026. (Photo by Sergii Kostezh / Kyiv Post)
New valves and pumps inside a restored heating unit in a Kyiv residential building in January 2026. (Photo by Sergii Kostezh / Kyiv Post)
“Some associations in Kyiv have also installed rooftop solar panels through grant programs and municipal co-financing schemes, helping their buildings become more energy-independent,” he said.
“Combined with other upgrades to building utility systems, these measures can significantly improve a building’s resilience and help it get through the winter, even if the city’s power grid suffers a complete collapse.”
And older buildings, Vadym said, can sometimes function when the grid fails – if local authorities do their job.
“Older residential buildings can sometimes continue operating without electricity, provided that the district pumping stations supplying them with cold water and central heating have backup power,” he said.
“Ensuring these facilities have reliable backup power is the responsibility of municipal authorities.”
Leo Chiu is a journalist and editor based in Eastern Europe since 2015. He has witnessed two presidential elections in Belarus and traveled widely to conflict zones and contested regions, producing reporting that bridges the gap between major developments and local realities.
Julia is a Deputy Head of News and correspondent for Kyiv Post who has previously worked as a parliamentary editor, journalist, and news editor. She has specialized in covering the work of the Ukrainian parliament, government, and law enforcement agencies.
Yuliia Zavadska is a news writer at Kyiv Post. She has experience in breaking news coverage, fact-checking, and digital journalism, with a focus on fast, accurate reporting and clear storytelling. Before joining Kyiv Post, she worked as a news feed editor for several leading Ukrainian media outlets.

title: Varus opens new supermarket in Vinnytsia
body:
Ukraine's Varus supermarket chain opened a new supermarket in early October at the MIR shopping center, located at 57 Keletska Street, Vinnytsia, the company's press service reported.
The new store offers a wide selection of Ukrainian and imported products, including fresh meat and fish, vegetables and fruit, dairy products, sweets, delicacies and everyday food items. The shelves also feature hundreds of products under the company's private-label brands.
A significant portion of the store's floor space has been allocated to prepared meals. At VARUS CAFE, customers can choose breakfast, lunch or dinner without having to prepare food at home. The menu includes salads, meat dishes, side dishes, desserts and other ready-to-eat items.
In addition to conventional checkout lanes, the new VARUS store has self-checkout stations and offers the Scan&Go service through the VARUS app. Customers can also place orders for home delivery or collect them at the store.
Varus is a national supermarket chain operating in Ukraine's grocery retail market through Omega. Its first store opened in Dnipro in 2003. The chain currently has a total of 125 supermarkets in various Ukrainian cities. It operates several formats, including traditional supermarkets, To Go stores and the Varus.ua online store.
Omega LLC is owned by Cyprus-registered Weigant Enterprises Limited, with Valeriy Kiptyk and Ruslan Shostak as its ultimate beneficial owners.
In 2025, Omega LLC increased its revenue by 20% compared with the previous year, to UAH 24 billion, while net profit rose by 37.8%, to UAH 41.4 million.

title: Bradley’s Old TOW Launchers Get New Teeth With Spike Missile Adapter
body: Rafael USA and Leonardo DRS have presented a capability that would allow fighting vehicles equipped with legacy Tube-launched, Optically tracked, Wire-guided (TOW) missile launchers to fire Rafael’s Spike LR2 anti-armor missiles. The effort builds on a demonstration dating back to 2021, with the companies now presenting a more mature adapter solution designed to integrate the Israeli-made missile into existing platforms. Roman Palaria, Rafael’s vice president for marketing and business development in its land and naval division, discussed the system in an interview with TWZ at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention . He explained that the earlier demonstration, part of Project Convergence 2021 , used a version of the adapter that had not yet reached its final configuration. Leonardo DRS, Rafael’s U.S. partner, subsequently developed the mechanical and electrical components needed to connect the Spike LR2 to the TOW launcher and the vehicle’s existing systems. The Rafael/Leonardo adaptor that allows TOW missile launchers to fire Rafael’s Spike LR2 anti-armor missiles. Howard Altman The approach is intended to avoid replacing the launcher or radically overhauling the vehicle’s gunner station. Instead, the adapter provides the mechanical interface for loading the Spike LR2 missile and the electrical connections needed to communicate with the vehicle. Additional electronic components are installed within the vehicle to support the missile’s functions. The adaptor configured for TOW (left) and Spike LR2 (right) missiles. Leonardo DRS “We’re doing minimum changes to the vehicle,” Palaria said, describing the goal of making the integration as seamless as possible for the operator. The Bradley infantry fighting vehicle is a prominent potential application, although the companies say the capability could extend to other platforms that use TOW launchers. The Army has operated TOW-equipped vehicles for decades, creating a substantial installed base of launch systems that could potentially benefit from the approach. As for the Bradley, the Army effort to replace its TOW missiles has been a long one, but is yet to produce any real results . A U.S. Army M2A4 Bradley. The TOW launcher can be clearly seen on the side of the turret. U.S. Army photo by Sgt. Austin Steinborn Spike LR2 was successfully test-fired from M2A4 Bradley equipped with Multi-Purpose Missile Launcher (MPML), developed by Rafael and DRS. Adapters allow the system to remain compatible with existing TML/UTML launchers. Spike LR2 has also been proposed for the CCMS-H and XM30. pic.twitter.com/KB9EYwi6BI — Ronkainen (@ronkainen7k15) October 13, 2026 After a missile is fired, its launch tube remains in the launcher and can be removed to accommodate another missile. The central attraction of the system is the ability to combine existing launcher infrastructure with the Spike LR2’s unique engagement capabilities. During Project Convergence 2021, two Spike missiles were fired from a TOW launcher, and both reportedly hit their intended targets. The adapter now being presented reflects subsequent development work by Leonardo DRS, including refinement of the mechanical interface and vehicle electrical integration. An M2A3 Bradley uses its twin-tube, turret-mounted launcher to fire a BGM-71 TOW anti-tank missile. U.S. Army photo by Spc. Brandi Frizzell The system is designed to preserve the vehicle’s existing TOW capability while adding the option to use Spike LR2. That would give commanders another missile option without necessarily requiring wholesale replacement of installed launcher equipment. The extent to which individual vehicles could use both missile types would depend on the completed integration and applicable qualification requirements. Another view of the Rafael/Leonardo Spike LR2 adaptor. Howard Altman Howard Altman The Spike LR2 offers capabilities that differ substantially from those of the legacy TOW missile. Palaria cited a maximum range of approximately 5.5 kilometers (3.4 miles) and highlighted the missile’s day/night imaging seeker, which provides video to the operator during flight. The longest-range TOW missile versions max out at around 4.5 kilometers (2.8 miles). In contrast, Spike LR2’s imaging capability supports engagement of targets beyond the operator’s direct line of sight, as well as observation of the target area during the missile’s approach. Depending on the engagement, the operator can acquire a target through the missile’s seeker, adjust the engagement, or select a different target while the missile is in flight. These features contrast with the traditional TOW’s semi-automatic command to line-of-sight (SACLOS) guidance, in which the gunner tracks the target through the launcher’s observation system and guides the missile throughout its flight. Spike LR2’s onboard imaging provides a different set of options for engagements in which direct observation is limited or target conditions change after launch. This can also include striking targets behind cover. Palaria also described the LR2’s two warhead options. The first of these is a tandem-charge anti-tank warhead, which Rafael claims is able to penetrate any modern main battle tank. It consists of a precursor warhead and the main warhead, which are designed to penetrate the reactive armor, and the main armor, respectively. The second option is a multi-purpose configuration. It has a programmable fuze, which allows the missile to be employed against different target types. Depending on the selected mode, the warhead can be configured for direct-impact or timed-detonation effects, for example, detonating above the ground for anti-personnel missions, or penetrating a building, in which case the first charge will make a hole in a wall, and then the second charge will go inside and explode after a short delay. The adapter offers a potential route to adding new missile capabilities to existing Army vehicles while limiting changes to their launcher hardware and crew interface. Operator training would obviously be necessary. Although the gunner would continue using the vehicle’s existing console and displays, Palaria acknowledged that Spike LR2 introduces additional functions, controls, and engagement procedures. Slovenian soldiers engage targets with a Spike LR anti-tank missile during a live-fire exercise. U.S. Army photo by Visual Information Specialist Davide Dalla Massara/Released For the Army, the proposition is straightforward: retain a familiar launcher architecture while potentially adding a missile with greater reach, onboard imaging, and more flexible engagement options that exceed line-of-sight tracking. The adapter’s significance lies in making that combination possible without starting from a clean sheet. Whether that capability becomes a fielded upgrade will depend on the Army’s requirements, testing, integration decisions, and procurement plans. But the widespread uptake of the Spike series of missiles around the globe, combined with the very large existing TOW missile operator base, means the adapter solution could well be of interest to customers outside the U.S. Army, too. Contact the author: thomas@thewarzone.com The post Bradley’s Old TOW Launchers Get New Teeth With Spike Missile Adapter appeared first on TWZ .

title: Russia Targets Zimbabwean Youth to Fight Against Ukraine
body: Russia needs manpower to support its invasion of Ukraine and has implemented an elaborate recruitment campaign to lure young Africans to the frontlines. In Zimbabwe, the Kremlin’s syndicates have tapped former Zimbabwean military, police and intelligence personnel to help recruit and lightly train young people for deployment, Zimbabwe’s Bulawayo 24 News reported. Lured by online advertisements, potential recruits are offered $7,000 to $10,000 salaries with travel-related expenses paid upfront. Vetting and basic tactical training are allegedly being conducted by former military personnel in Bulawayo, Harare and Masvingo. A senior Zimbabwe National Army officer said former colleagues were approached in 2024 and offered consultancy fees to identify young men for private security work in Russia. “By the time the boys land, the contract has changed,” the officer anonymously told Bulawayo 24. Zimbabwean officials have made a series of recent arrests on charges of human trafficking as they investigate the recruitment scheme. Investigators believe Edward Kachingwe, a 36-year-old Zimbabwean, recruited five men before he was arrested at Harare’s Roadport Bus Terminus and charged with human trafficking and operating an unregistered employment agency in late June. Prosecutors say Kachingwe worked with a Russian accomplice identified as “Roman,” who has not been detained and allegedly plans to “unlawfully recruit victims to join the Russian army where they will be forced to fight in the armed conflict between the Russian Federation and Ukrainian Forces.” Also in June, Russian national Leonid Koftev appeared in court on trafficking charges after allegedly arranging a Zimbabwean man’s travel to Russia. Zimbabwean Information Minister Zhemu Soda has said the recruits receive little combat training before they are deployed. Authorities said they rescued Zimbabweans in Tanzania and South Africa who were in transit to Russia. “Some of those who have been recruited were mostly Uber drivers recruited in South Africa with no army experience and are trained for seven days then deployed,” a local recruit now fighting for Russia told The Zimbabwean newspaper. It is difficult for recruits to escape their situation. “When they reach the front line, they [the Russians] take their passport and only promise to give it back after a year,” the recruit said. In Dar es Salaam, victims reportedly gave relatives false hotel addresses to avoid detection, but their locations were revealed by digital forensics. Some rescued men told investigators they had travelled with former military personnel who were also victimized by the Russian networks, Bulawayo 24 reported. In Tanzania, investigations revealed that rather than using messaging apps and social media to lure recruits, Russia used former soldiers, Chidawa said. According to a September investigation, at least 3,066 Africans from 40 countries were recruited into Russia’s military since October 2022. By June 2026, 502 of them had died, Kenyan newspaper The Star reported. Kenya’s National Intelligence Service previously reported that more than 1,000 of its citizens had been recruited. Kenyan officials have said recruiters targeted former military and police personnel and civilians with promises of well-paying jobs, bonuses and Russian citizenship. In March, Musalia Mudavadi, Kenya’s prime cabinet secretary and foreign and diaspora affairs cabinet secretary, announced that Russia had agreed to stop enlisting Kenyans and would place Kenya on a military recruitment “stop list.” While some Kenyans have been repatriated, others remain on the front lines. On October 6, more than 30 families of Kenyans trafficked to Russia gathered in Nairobi to urge President William Ruto to push for the return of survivors, recover the bodies of Kenyans killed in the war and disclose what happened to those who remain missing. Ruto is expected to attend the Africa-Russia Summit in Moscow in late October. The families claimed that recruitment of Kenyans has continued. “As recent as last month, there is information that the recruitment is still ongoing,” a representative of one of the families told The Star. “Yet we know that in other countries, they have repatriated their nationals back.” This year, Russia plans to recruit 18,500 foreign fighters, nearly a six-fold increase since the start of the war, according to a report by the war crimes watchdog Truth Hounds. The post Russia Targets Zimbabwean Youth to Fight Against Ukraine appeared first on Africa Defense Forum .

title: Pope Leo’s Lung Operation ‘Successfully Completed’ — Vatican
body: Pope Leo XIV’s underwent an operation at a Rome hospital Tuesday to remove a nodule from his lung that was “successfully completed”, the Vatican said. Pope Leo XIV entered the hospital smiling and waving on Tuesday morning hours before the surgery to remove the growth that looks like a coin on the lung. “The procedure was successfully completed, within the expected time and in the planned manner,” the Vatican said in a brief statement. “The Holy Father has returned to his room,” it said, adding that more details would be given later. The surgery marks the 71-year-old Leo’s first hospitalisation since he became head of the Catholic Church on May 8, 2025. Vatican officials who saw the pope on Monday said he appeared relaxed about the hospital stay. In a surprise announcement following Angelus prayers on Sunday, Leo told crowds in St Peter’s Square that doctors had discovered the nodule “at a very early stage” during medical checks. “The doctors believe it would be right to intervene,” he said. The Vatican has historically been very secretive about the health of popes, but began to be more transparent during the illness of Leo’s predecessor Francis, an Argentine who freely discussed his ailments. People outside the hospital expressed concern over the pope’s condition. Giorgia Fei, a 57-year-old Italian, said she had been worried by the news. “However, the Holy Father is in very good hands here at the hospital because we have some outstanding doctors,” she said. “I will pray a lot for him.” Giuseppe Purpura, 72, said he was also concerned. “He’s still quite young and I really wasn’t expecting this. I thought he was in better health,” he said, noting that “thankfully it was caught in time.” The Vicar General for the Diocese of Rome, Cardinal Baldassare Reina, led a rosary prayer for the pope inside the hospital chapel which was broadcast by the Vatican. Dozens of people attended and Reina asked all the city’s parishes to join in. Ahead of the surgery, the Vatican said the pope’s recovery time was expected to be about a week. His audiences have been cancelled until October 20. The Vatican secretary of state, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, told ANSA news agency that Leo had been “very calm” about his condition when they met on Monday. Routine Health Checks Chicago-born Leo, the first US pope, is sporty and believed to generally be in good health. He is scheduled to travel to South America from November 6-17 to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It was not immediately clear what would happen if the pope was forced into a longer recovery. Under Church law, a figure known as the Cardinal Camerlengo — or chamberlain — takes over administrative duties if the pope dies, but pontiffs do not have a deputy to replace them if they become incapacitated. Marco Scarci, a thoracic surgery expert in the UK, told AFP it was not “a particularly risky operation” and he expected Leo’s recovery to be quick. Most pulmonary nodules are benign, or non-cancerous, but a small percentage can be an early indication of lung cancer. The Vatican told AFP the nodule was found during routine health checks, and there were no symptoms that led to checking the pope’s lungs. ‘Coin Lesion’ A small nodule is called a “coin lesion” because on X-rays it looks like a coin, Professor Federico Venuta, head of thoracic surgery at the Policlinico Umberto 1 hospital in Rome, told AFP. Small nodules tend not to cause symptoms, but larger ones can cause shortness of breath, chest pain and persistent coughing — sometimes with blood. Such nodules “could be a whole range of benign lesions — inflammatory, infectious, autoimmune, or congenital — or they could be malignant,” Venuta said. Removing the nodule can take place under general anaesthetic with the patient breathing through a tube. Even if the nodule was not benign, the pope’s outlook would be “very positive”, Venuta said. “For a generally healthy person, the prognosis for lung cancer caught at such an early stage — specifically a pulmonary nodule with no distant spread — is absolutely favourable,” he said. AFP The post Pope Leo’s Lung Operation ‘Successfully Completed’ — Vatican appeared first on Channels Television .
