title: Northrop Grumman to upgrade U.S. Army’s IBCS for greater mobility and battlefield survivability
body: The new Integrated Collaborative Environment uses a van with extendable sides to provide more room for soldiers, equipment and mission systems. It accommodates six operator workstations and four staff operation stations. The design is intended to improve survivability and reduce the time needed to set up or dismantle the workspace. Its configurable interior will allow units to adjust to changing mission requirements. “Our sustained investments in innovation are turning IBCS into an ever-more capable combat multiplier for the warfighter,” said Kenn Todorov, vice president and general manager of command and control and weapons integration at Northrop Grumman. “By boosting the Integrated Collaborative Environment’s survivability and mobility, we’re giving warfighters greater protection and faster access to advanced command and control technology as they face increasingly complex and dynamic battlespaces.” IBCS combines sensor information into a single air picture and supplies fire-control-quality data for engagements. It is replacing legacy command-and-control systems, including those associated with Patriot, as the Army moves toward a common system for integrated air and missile defense. Its “any sensor, best shooter” approach connects sensors and weapons across the network. Operators can use information from multiple sources to assess threats and select an interceptor. Composite tracking uses several sensors to maintain target tracks where individual sensors have coverage gaps. The communications architecture uses a self-healing mesh network designed to avoid single points of failure. IBCS has demonstrated integration with Patriot, Sentinel, F-35 sensors, Common Anti-Air Modular Missile and Giraffe radars. Further integration work covers the Lower Tier Air and Missile Defense Sensor, Indirect Fire Protection Capability and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense. The system achieved U.S. initial operational capability and approval for full-rate production in April 2023. The Army has since fielded it in U.S. European Command and U.S. Indo-Pacific Command. Poland uses IBCS for medium- and short-range air defense and declared full operational capability in December 2025. Partner countries can configure the system for their requirements through its modular, open architecture. Northrop Grumman is also developing smaller configurations, software updates and additional automation, including AI-enabled battle management. Those efforts are intended to improve mobility and help operators assess threats and make decisions faster. The company said more than $10 million in internal investment and cost-sharing is supporting IBCS development and reducing integration risk. The Army’s latest contract adds a more protected workspace to those upgrades while retaining room for ten operating and staff stations.

title: Russia sends diesel fuel to entire global market — Trump
body:
WASHINGTON, October 13. /TASS/. Russia is directing diesel fuel not specifically to the United States but to the global market for all countries, US President Donald Trump said.
"That's a diesel deal, not for us. That's being released into the world. That's not being released to us. That's a diesel deal that is going to be released into the world, for the world market because the world market suffered with high prices, and when you knock out diesel refineries, that's not a great thing," Trump told reporters.
"But they're not releasing that to us. They're releasing it to the entire world," the US leader added.

title: Detribalised does not mean what most Nigerians think it means, By Temitope Lakisokun
body:
To most of us, even the very educated, a Nigerian is “detribalised” because he has demonstrated that he can relate to those beyond his ethnic group. But notice what the word actually means: The admirable Nigerian is one who is detached from his particular identity!
In Nigeria, this is almost always a compliment.
It is what we say about the politician who has friends from every part of the country, the businessman whose boardroom is a miniature Nigeria, the public servant who does not appoint only people from her village, or the man who married a woman from another ethnic group. He eats everybody’s food, speaks a few Nigerian languages and feels at home anywhere in the country.
He is, we say approvingly, so detribalised.
Except that detribalised does not mean any of those things.
The Cambridge Dictionary defines detribalise as “to make members of a tribe stop following their traditional customs or social structure.” (I checked. No dictionary records the meaning Nigerians give it.)
In other words, it describes a process by which a person or community becomes detached from the customs, social structures, and institutions associated with the group to which they belong. In colonial Africa, European officials and scholars used “detribalisation” particularly in discussions of Western education and Africans who no longer fitted neatly into the social structures through which colonial authorities sought to govern them.
In Nigeria, the British described educated Nigerians, including descendants of Africans who had been enslaved and later liberated, and people who emerged from early Christian missionary activity, as “detribalised natives.” Even when a Nigerian had become sufficiently educated and Westernised to escape the category of “tribal”, he was still, apparently, a native!
At some point in Nigeria, we turned the word into a compliment. Recently, Senate President, Godswill Akpabio, mourning the late Alhaji Bamanga Tukur, reached for it. In a statement, he described Tukur as “a detribalised Nigerian, great patriot and towering national figure whose contributions to the country transcended ethnic and political boundaries.” It was meant as praise.
Another thing we ought to be careful with is the word tribe itself. We use it constantly in Nigeria to describe Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, Tiv, Ijaw, Efik, Kanuri and hundreds of other peoples. But tribe is a very imprecise word for what we are trying to describe. These are peoples and ethnic communities, with their own languages, histories, political traditions, religions, social institutions and internal differences. Many also contain numerous subgroups with identities of their own. “Ethnicity” is the more useful term, in my opinion.
And there is also the incongruity of singing “Though tribe and tongue may differ, / In brotherhood, we stand” as part of our national anthem. I know the colonial anthem is making a point about national unity despite differences of language and ethnic identity. The incongruity is that we are using “tribe” as a shorthand for ethnicity in 2026.
A closer examination of the word makes our Nigerian usage of detribalised rather peculiar. British indirect rule relied heavily on chiefs, customary authorities and institutions that colonial officials classified as “traditional”. At the same time, urbanisation and Western education were producing Africans who did not fit neatly into those structures. Detribalised belonged to a world in which Europeans were deciding what counted as “tribal”, what counted as “modern”, and how Africans who moved between those worlds should be understood.
We have carried the word on our heads long after the colonisers left.
To most of us, even the very educated, a Nigerian is “detribalised” because he has demonstrated that he can relate to those beyond his ethnic group. But notice what the word actually means: The admirable Nigerian is one who is detached from his particular identity!
The underlying assumption is stranger still. Knowing less about your own history does not make you more enlightened. Familiarity with another culture does not require estrangement from your own. Nor should our former colonisers remain the final arbiters of sophistication or morality. The last bit is a Nobody Asked Me, But …for another day. For now, let’s talk about detribalisation.
We have taken tolerance and called it detribalisation . We have taken broadmindedness and called it detribalisation . We have taken the simple ability to see another Nigerian as an equal and given it a word that suggests the shedding of one’s own identity.
And because we have never examined the word closely, almost no one notices the contradiction, and the word has been carrying a meaning completely alien to it.
So I have a small linguistic suggestion: Can we say what we actually mean?
If a person does not discriminate against Nigerians from other ethnic groups, say so. If he has friends from everywhere, say so. If he believes Nigeria belongs to all of us, by all means, say so. If he can be proudly Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, Ijaw, Tiv or whatever else he is, without believing that his identity makes him superior to anyone else, say that too.
Maybe the ideal is not the “detribalised” Nigerian, but the Nigerian who is confident in who he is and has no problem making room for those who come from elsewhere.
Temitope Lakisokun , a political consultant, historian, and chair of Trustees of The Tarihi Trust Foundation, writes from Lagos. Tarihi Trust is a Pan-African foundation for memory, history, and civic understanding.

title: Royal Australian Navy Maintainers Learn U.S. Submarine Sustainment
body: JOINT BASE PEARL HARBOR-HICKMAN, Hawaii – In the summer of 2025, in a corner of a machine shop at Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard & Intermediate Maintenance Facility (PHNSY & IMF), Able Seaman Colby Morley disassembled a pressure valve for testing. It’s the kind of hands-on job he’d rarely get to do back home as an avionics technician with the Royal Australian Navy. As part of a first-of-its-kind training rotation, Morley was one of 20 Royal Australian Navy Fleet Support Unit (FSU) sailors who trained in Hawaii to learn how to maintain U.S. nuclear-powered attack submarines. The cross-functional team was stationed in Pearl Harbor from June through October of last year and completed an intensive U.S.-led training rotation before returning home to support USS Vermont’s (SSN 792) submarine maintenance period at HMAS Stirling in Western Australia in November 2025. “The team is a small but very important cog in the wheel for AUKUS. Our main goal is making sure Australia is self-reliable when it comes to the maintenance of these newer assets,” said Royal Australian Navy Chief Petty Officer Steven Sheakey, the deployed maintenance team’s senior technical officer. “The fleet support units are going to play an important role in delivering maintenance to the U.S. assets that are going to be rotating through HMAS Stirling. So, the knowledge, experiences and cohesive relationships we’ve got with U.S. personnel—both civilian and in uniform—are going to play a vital role moving forward to ensure we’re interoperable in the future.” In the U.S., the FSU team’s mission was to gain maintenance experience on U.S. platforms, build technical interoperability and prepare to sustain U.S. and U.K. nuclear-powered submarines. Under the AUKUS agreement, the U.S. and U.K. are supporting Australia’s efforts to acquire, maintain and sustain its own sovereign fleet of conventionally armed, nuclear-powered submarines—a departure from Australia’s current fleet of diesel-electric submarines. Submarine Rotational Force-West, or SRF-West, is one of the AUKUS partnership’s key outcomes. The initiative will see U.S. Virginia-class and U.K. Astute-class submarines rotate out of the Royal Australian Navy’s submarine base in the Indian Ocean, HMAS Stirling , for an extended period, starting in 2027. Strategic Sustainment Starts with People The team sent to Hawaii was drawn from across the Royal Australian Navy’s five FSUs and selected through a competitive, skills-based screening process. The sailors’ specialties range from electronics to propulsion to weapons, reflecting the future workforce Australia will need to support Australian-flagged nuclear-powered submarines. “We needed a team that could embed anywhere, adapt quickly and represent the full scope of Navy engineering,” said Royal Australian Navy Lt. Zachery Telfser, officer in charge of the deployed maintenance team. “This isn’t just submarine work—it’s about building a broad, interoperable sustainment workforce that can flex with future mission demands.” Some sailors, like Morely, are outside the traditional submarine pipeline. But as Australia expands its readiness to support nuclear propulsion, the Royal Australian Navy is pulling from across its engineering enterprise to identify who can contribute to the overall mission. “We’re stress-testing the system,” Sheakey said. “In Australia, we multi-train our sailors so they can wear more than one hat. That kind of flexibility is essential to building interoperable teams who can deliver complex submarine maintenance packages at SRF-West.” Fleet Support Unit-West sailors will serve as SRF-West’s primary uniformed maintenance workforce. More than 200 personnel from the Australian Submarine Agency’s civilian sustainment partner, ASC Pty. Ltd., are also training in Hawaii to lead intermediate- and depot-level maintenance work on Australia’s future fleet of fast-attack submarines. Both the Fleet Support Unit and ASC teams put their newfound skills to the test during the November 2025 submarine maintenance period at HMAS Stirlingin Western Australia. “This joint workforce approach combining the U.S. Navy, Royal Australian Navy and Australian civilians is central to how SRF-West will operate,” said Elizabeth Tolin, the deputy division head for SRF-West at the U.S. Navy’s AUKUS Integration and Acquisition program office. “Our work with Australia is enabling us to build a cohesive, interoperable sustainment enterprise.” These joint efforts align directly with the Department of War’s May 2026 announcement formally establishing Naval Support Activity Stirling and reestablishing Submarine Squadron 3. PHNSY &IMF, which was previously named the lead maintenance activity for SRF-West, is actively preparing to deploy its maintenance detachment to Western Australia where American personnel will continue working alongside their FSU and ASC maintenance counterparts. Learning to Work Together, Technically and Culturally For Royal Australian Navy Leading Seaman Jayden Webb, an electronics technician, the rotation was his second stint working with the U.S. Navy, and another opportunity to refine shared maintenance insights. “We’re doing more than just fixing systems,” he said in an interview alongside Morely last August. “We’re learning how the U.S. Navy thinks about readiness, risk and reporting. That’s what it’ll take to maintain and sustain these platforms safely and confidently back in Australia.” Webb embedded with the U.S. Navy’s Performance Monitoring Team, which performs rigorous testing and diagnostics aboard submarines. Others, like Morely, worked in the shipyard’s machine shop, rebuilding and testing valves under the mentorship of experienced U.S. tradesmen. “At home, we’re used to getting a tech order that tells us what’s wrong,” Morely said. “At Pearl, we’re learning how to troubleshoot from scratch. It’s taught me to be more comfortable with uncertainty and more deliberate about communication.” From Pearl Harbor to Perth In October 2025, the team returned to Western Australia to complete their mission by performing maintenance aboard USS Vermont during its planned submarine maintenance period . The submarine maintenance period, which lasted through November, marked a historic milestone underscoring the momentum of AUKUS and its vision for enhanced deterrence and industrial resilience in the Indo-Pacific. For Australia, it’s also an opportunity to evaluate its long-term investment in submarine sustainment and sovereign capability. “The submarine maintenance period was a big step forward from when we had a U.S. submarine tender, USS Emory S. Land (AS 39) across the pier from USS Hawaii (SSN 776) in August 2024 to oversee and execute the submarine tendered maintenance period,” said Rear Adm. Doug Adams, director, AUKUS, International & Systems. “For Vermont, we had a larger work package, a truly blended maintenance workforce led by Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard and Intermediate Maintenance Activity, and when that boat left to operate in the Indo-Pacific region, it was ready for any tasking.” As Australia continues to build capacity to own, operate and maintain nuclear-powered submarines, sailors from the FSU will continue to support U.S. submarine maintenance periods, including the next one scheduled to occur in Western Australia by the end of 2026. “We’ve still got a lot of work ahead,” said Sheakey. “Australia’s got to grow its infrastructure, procedures and people. But, we’re proving we’re up to the task, and that we’re a capable, committed partner.” For sailors like Morely and Webb, the experience has also reshaped how they think about their roles in a trilateral security framework. “To me, AUKUS is about bringing our forces together, not just in strategy, but in day-to-day operations,” said Webb. “It’s exciting to be part of something this big.” “This was my first time outside Australia,” Morely added. “To be in Hawaii, working with the U.S. Navy on something that’s going to have such a big impact back home—that means a lot.” From Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard & Intermediate Maintenance Facility, Oct. 9, 2026 The post Royal Australian Navy Maintainers Learn U.S. Submarine Sustainment appeared first on Seapower Magazine .

title: 2027: INEC meets security agencies, party leaders, others in Lagos
body: The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) in Lagos State on Tuesday met with security agencies, political parties and other stakeholders to strengthen collaboration and ensure peaceful conduct of the 2027 General Elections. Speaking at the stakeholders’ meeting in Lagos, Prof Ayobami Salami, Resident Electoral Commissioner (REC), said the meeting also aimed at mobilising public support for effective implementation of the commission’s electoral plans. Salami said the commission was intensifying preparations in logistics, personnel deployment, election security, voter education and accessibility. He said INEC had moved from strategic planning to active operational implementation, with nine of the 14 scheduled milestones for the 2027 elections already accomplished as of Oct. 6. “At the national level, the Register of Voters currently stands at approximately 103 million. “Preparations are also advancing in critical areas, including the procurement and delivery of 57,000 additional Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) devices, software upgrades, battery optimisation and biometric calibration. “Similarly, extensive logistical arrangements are being made for the deployment of over 100,000 vehicles and 4,000 boats nationwide,” he said. The REC added that recruitment of approximately 1.4 million election personnel through the INECPRES portal was ongoing, with the application window scheduled to close on Nov. 18. He said Lagos, with 7,488,633 registered voters, remained strategically important to the electoral process, requiring meticulous planning and coordinated deployment of resources across its 20 Local Government Areas (LGAs). According to him, the state has 245 Registration Areas and 13,325 Polling Units, making effective logistics and inter-agency cooperation essential to the successful conduct of the elections. Salami said the commission was taking account of Lagos’ peculiar challenges, including traffic congestion, densely populated communities, commercial activities, difficult-to-access settlements and riverine locations. “Beyond these figures are the distinctive operational realities of Lagos: a large and mobile population, densely populated urban communities, extensive commercial activities, traffic challenges, some difficult-to-access settlements and riverine locations. “These peculiarities demand careful planning and solutions tailored to the circumstances of individual communities. “Our commitment is to ensure that these challenges are anticipated and addressed through timely, coordinated and effective operational arrangements,” he said. He said preparations included transportation planning, timely deployment of election materials, activation of Registration Area Centres (RACs) and assessment of the readiness of election personnel and facilities. The REC added that INEC was strengthening internal coordination and monitoring mechanisms to identify potential operational challenges early and address them before they affected election activities. He said the commission would also provide assistive materials, including Braille ballot guides, EC30 PWD posters and magnifying glasses, where applicable, to promote participation by persons with disabilities. Salami urged organisations representing persons with disabilities to continue engaging with the commission and providing recommendations to improve accessibility and inclusion. On election security, he said INEC would continue working with relevant security agencies through the Inter-Agency Consultative Committee on Election Security (ICCES), led by the Nigeria Police Force, to identify and mitigate potential electoral risks. “Our collective priority is to safeguard voters, election personnel, observers, electoral materials and facilities throughout the electoral process. “Particular attention will be given to prevention of electoral violence, intimidation, vote-buying, ballot snatching and other unlawful activities capable of undermining the credibility of elections. “In collaboration with relevant law enforcement and anti-corruption agencies, appropriate preventive and enforcement measures will be pursued in accordance with the law,” he said. The REC called on political parties, candidates and their supporters to conduct their activities responsibly, respect electoral laws and avoid actions capable of disrupting public peace. He stressed that political competition should not be used to justify violence, intimidation or other unlawful conduct, adding that protecting citizens’ right to participate freely in elections was a shared responsibility. Salami also raised concerns about misinformation, disinformation and the misuse of artificial intelligence to circulate manipulated images, fabricated reports, synthetic audio and video recordings, deepfakes and voice clones. He urged political actors, media practitioners, civil society organisations and members of the public to verify election-related information through authorised INEC communication channels before sharing it. The REC reiterated that the collation and declaration of election results must follow established legal procedures and be undertaken only by duly authorised electoral officials. He said unverified figures and speculative reports should not be presented as official results, warning that false information could generate confusion, heighten political tensions and undermine public confidence in the electoral process. Salami emphasised that the successful conduct of the elections required the commitment of all stakeholders, noting that INEC could not achieve the objective of credible elections acting alone. “Political parties have a great responsibility to promote peaceful competition, respect electoral regulations and encourage responsible conduct among their members and supporters. “Security agencies must continue to provide a safe and enabling environment for electoral activities. “Traditional rulers, religious leaders, youth organisations, and community institutions remain important partners in promoting civic responsibility, peaceful coexistence and public participation,” he said. He also urged civil society organisations to intensify voter education and public enlightenment, while calling on the media to uphold accuracy, fairness and professionalism in reporting electoral activities. The REC appealed to stakeholders to encourage registered voters to verify their details on the Register of Voters, collect their Permanent Voter Cards, when available, and obtain electoral information from authorised sources. He said INEC remained committed to professionalism, transparency, inclusivity and effective implementation of its constitutional responsibilities as preparations for the 2027 General Elections gathered momentum. “Our objective is clear: to ensure that every stage of the electoral process is properly planned, effectively implemented and conducted in a manner that strengthens public confidence in the Commission and the integrity of elections. “With your continued cooperation, constructive engagement and shared commitment, I am confident that Lagos State can contribute significantly to the successful conduct of a peaceful, credible, transparent and inclusive General Elections,” he said. The post 2027: INEC meets security agencies, party leaders, others in Lagos appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Black Queens thrash Mauritius 7-0 to advance 10-0 on aggregate in Olympic Qualifiers
body: The Black Queens produced a scintillating performance to demolish Mauritius 7-0 in the second leg of the second round of qualifiers for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games at the Essipong Stadium on Tuesday. The emphatic victory secures a 10-0 aggregate win for Ghana, having won the first leg 3-0 in Mauritius last Thursday. Head Coach Kim Lars Björkegren’s side dominated from start to finish, overwhelming the visitors with pace, power and precision in the final third. Captain Portia Boakye opened the scoring for the Queens before Evelyn Badu doubled the lead. Ajegipina Zakaria made it 3-0 for Ghana going into the break. After the recess, the Queens continued to pile pressure on Mauritius, with substitutes making an instant impact. Benedicte Simon marked her introduction with a goal in the 73rd minute, before Jennifer Cudjoe added the fifth in the 87th minute. Nancy Amoh and Mukarama Abdulai completed the rout with two late strikes to make it 7-0. The result underlines Ghana’s determination to secure a historic first qualification for the Women’s Olympic Football Tournament. With the win, Ghana progresses to the third round of the qualifiers in search of a ticket to LA 2028.

title: KHA’s K1000ULE Achieves Award-Ready Status Through Army DevX Autonomy Marketplace
body:
Award-ready designation gives U.S. government agencies a faster route to pursue long-endurance unmanned aircraft capability
Kraus Hamdani Aerospace (KHA) today announced that its K1000ULE platform is award-ready on the Army Applications Laboratory’s DevX Autonomy Marketplace. For government teams that need airborne awareness and connectivity, the designation creates a potential direct-to-award pathway to acquire the aircraft without starting a new competitive solicitation.
The fully electric K1000ULE is the world’s longest-endurance fully electric Group 2 UAS, delivering persistent intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance (ISR), resilient communications, and electronic warfare capabilities from a single autonomous platform. The open architecture and modular payload integration enable the K1000ULE to adapt to evolving mission requirements while extending awareness and connectivity at the edge.
Through DevX Autonomy, the K1000ULE solution has completed a competitive assessment process and is available for government customers to review. Agencies with an applicable requirement and funding can engage KHA on their mission needs and work with their contracting activity on scope, milestones, and a potential award. This direct-to-award pathway may allow them to proceed without a new competitive solicitation under the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR), subject to agency contracting review.
The marketplace is available beyond the Army. Other U.S. government agencies, including the Air Force, Navy, Coast Guard, and Department of Homeland Security , can request access and pursue an award against the same K1000ULE solution.
Government customers with a .mil or .gov email address can request access through Army Applications Laboratory DevX Autonomy , search for Kraus Hamdani Aerospace, and view the six-minute K1000ULE solution video.
Kraus Hamdani Aerospace (KHA) builds AI-powered unmanned aerial technologies delivering resilient airborne intelligence, communications, and autonomous mission capabilities for defense and commercial customers worldwide. Its technologies provide persistent airborne infrastructure across sea, land, air, and space when communications fail, infrastructure breaks down, and mission success depends on continuous intelligence and connectivity. Trusted by customers including the U.S. Army, U.S. Air Force, U.S. Navy, MARSOC, and Petroleum Development Oman (Shell Oil & Gas), KHA advances autonomous systems through proven technology, operational experience, and strategic partnerships. Learn more at khaero.com .
DevX Autonomy is a digital repository of post-competition, award-ready pitch videos supporting autonomy and unmanned systems development. All solutions are assessed through rigorous scoring criteria and competitive procedures and are available to government customers with a DevX Autonomy account.

title: Gemini 4 Argon is now available worldwide as Google's most capable frontier model
body:
Google is rolling out Gemini 4 Argon globally, making its new flagship AI model available to developers, businesses, and consumers starting today.
Gemini 4 Argon is accessible through the API in AI Studio and the Gemini platform , according to Google. Google AI Ultra subscribers can use the model in Google Antigravity , while AI Ultra and Pro subscribers get access through the Gemini app and Google Search's AI mode .
Not everyone benefits equally, though. Free Gemini users and paying Plus subscribers now only have access to the weaker Flash models under a new model tier structure . Argon replaces the Gemini Pro class as Google's new frontier series. Google says more Gemini 4 models will follow, which likely means updated Flash variants that would eventually trickle down to free and Plus users as well. Internally, Google is reportedly already testing a potential successor codenamed " Carbon ," which is supposed to outperform Argon at coding in particular. Ad
Pricing and benchmark results remain as previously reported : $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens at the introductory rate, with a 95 percent discount on cached inputs. Argon holds the top spot on the Vals Index, but it still trails Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 in independent overall rankings. And because Google waited roughly two weeks to ship, it now also sits behind Meta's Muse Wonder Full , which launched just yesterday. Ad
*Google doesn't state this figure explicitly but says the cache is 95 percent cheaper than the regular input token price.
Google shared some internal numbers with the launch, though they're self-reported. Software engineers using Argon increased agent-driven code submissions by more than 35 percent, while code rollbacks dropped by nearly a third, the company says. Ad
In the Chromium project, Argon helped the Chrome team complete an architectural refactor across hundreds of files within the 40-million-line codebase. Work that would have taken months was finished in a few weeks. For users, the payoff is that web pages can move between tabs, sidebars, and floating windows without needing to reload.
Working with Google's open-source Agent Development Kit , Argon ran autonomously overnight and found optimizations that cut session preparation time by 40 percent and sped up cold imports by 21 percent. Inference speed for the open Gemma models on an A100 via vLLM jumped by a factor of 2.85, from roughly 37,900 to over 108,000 tokens per second. The changes are visible in upstream pull requests . Ad
Argon can also generate complex 3D models, games, and animations in pure code that run directly in the browser. One demo features a raytracing engine written entirely in Python with no external libraries. Google published the source code . Ad
In the demo below, Argon starts from a single image in Antigravity and controls Blender via MCP in an autonomous loop. It modeled gothic architecture and set up audio-reactive lighting to produce a finished 3D scene, Google says.
3D remains a weak spot for Meta's Muse models, which according to Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang were not specifically trained for 3D demo games.
Google is also offering 10,000 researchers the highest usage tier of Google Antigravity free for six months. Spots are awarded on a rolling basis depending on eligibility, capacity, and selection. Applications are open now.
Cybersecurity defenders can apply separately for the Fairwind program , which grants access to Argon without cyber safeguards. Google plans to expand the program to hundreds of additional partners.
On the safety side, Google calls Argon's architecture its strongest to date. External red teaming in the bio domain bypassed fewer than 1 percent of tested safety checks, and on an adversarial set, violations dropped by nearly half compared to earlier Gemini models.
On agent alignment, attempts to take unauthorized shortcuts fell to 2 percent. An automated misalignment monitor analyzes the agent's reasoning and actions in real time.
Argon also scored the lowest attack rate on the Gray Swan Indirect Prompt Injection benchmark, with a successful attack rate of just 0.7 percent across 15 adaptive attempts. In the previous Gray Swan test , GPT-6 Astra hit 8.5 percent and Claude Opus 5 came in at 4.8 percent. Google's write-up doesn't make clear whether the exact same tests were used, though. More safety details are available in the model card .

title: Oil spill: Delta govt commences medical outreach in Odidi Federated communities
body: THE Delta State Government has commenced an emergency free comprehensive medical and surgical outreach to residents of Odidi Federated Communities along the Trans-Forcados Pipeline in Warri South-West Local Government Area, following the oil spill that has affected the communities. The State Commissioner for Health, Dr. Joseph Onojaeme, who led the medical team, said the initiative was in compliance with the directive Governor Sheriff Oborevwori. He noted that the outreach would carry out multidisciplinary interventions, including surgeries, eye checks, dental care, laboratory investigations, medical outpatient care and others. The Commissioner commended the people of Odidi Federated Communities for the peaceful manner they had conducted themselves since the oil spill occurred. He appealed to residents to cooperate with the medical team, stressing that all drugs, mosquito nets and treatments being administered were completely free. Onojaeme highlighted the Governor’s keen interest in the well-being of Deltans, which said, had led to the construction and renovation of primary health care facilities across the state, as well as increased funding for these facilities. He assured that the government would continue to ensure that healthcare is easily accessible to all Deltans. Speaking on behalf of the Odidi Federated Communities, a community leader, Mr. Faith Mamamu, commended the Delta State Government for its prompt response to the oil spill crisis, which he said has disrupted the economic life of the communities. He said the people of Odidi were deeply grateful for the Governor’s concern and swift intervention. Beneficiaries of the outreach who spoke also commended Governor Oborevwori for his prompt response and for the free drugs and care provided to them, expressing appreciation that the government had come to their aid at a difficult time. Recall that Governor Oborevwori, on October 6, 2026, directed the Commissioner for Health to immediately deploy medical personnel to the affected communities to assess residents and determine the health implications of the pollution. The post Oil spill: Delta govt commences medical outreach in Odidi Federated communities appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Trump's Middle Corridor Plans Face Russian and Iranian Roadblocks
body: More than a year has passed since Armenia and Azerbaijan signed the Washington agreement under the direct mediation of President Trump. Nevertheless, the TRIPP project, an approximately 40-kilometer route that would constitute the shortest segment of the Middle Corridor, has yet to be implemented, leaving the broader project incomplete. Notably, the principal obstacles to its implementation originate neither in Armenia nor Azerbaijan but are predominantly external factors that continue to impede the project's realization.  BACKGROUND  In August 2025, the Trump administration initiated a process aimed at normalizing relations between Armenia and Azerbaijan, in which an enhanced U.S. strategic presence in the South Caucasus, particularly in Armenia, was expected to play a significant role. A central element was the proposed Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity TRIPP on Armenian territory, which would provide Azerbaijan with a direct connection to its Nakhchivan exclave without transiting Iran. The TRIPP would also offer Armenia and Azerbaijan an opportunity to strengthen their integration into the Middle Corridor, connecting Central Asia with Europe via the Caspian Sea, the South Caucasus, and Turkey.  In other words, the TRIPP would facilitate the development of the Middle Corridor through Armenia and Azerbaijan, which, according to the Trump administration, would contribute significantly to the normalization of Armenian-Azerbaijani relations. From a strategic perspective, the route also offers the prospect of transporting Central Asian energy resources to Europe while bypassing Russia and Iran. At the same time, it would provide Central Asian states with greater opportunities to diversify their export routes and reduce their dependence on China. Kazakhstan has shown particular interest in the project, as reflected in its deepening relations with Armenia, alongside its traditionally close ties with Azerbaijan.  Nevertheless, the project has experienced significant delays despite sustained efforts by Washington to advance its implementation. The U.S. has allocated financial resources for infrastructure development, established a dedicated fund to support the project, and appointed a manager with extensive knowledge of Armenia and its business environment, as well as direct ties to the Trump administration. Despite these measures, construction has yet to begin, and little information has been made available regarding the implementation process. The clearest indication of a potential timeline came from Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev, who recently stated that construction on Armenian territory may begin in early 2027.  IMPLICATIONS  Developments over recent months provide a broader picture of the factors that have delayed the implementation of the TRIPP project on Armenian territory and, consequently, the project as a whole. The first concerns Iran. The U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has fundamentally altered the regional security environment, with Tehran targeting U.S. military bases and other facilities in neighboring states within range of its missile capabilities. Against this backdrop, TRIPP represents a U.S.-backed strategic transport route running directly along Iran's northern border, in some places only a few hundred meters away. Its location and strategic significance have generated considerable concern in Tehran, which has publicly expressed its opposition to the project.  It therefore cannot be ruled out that the delays are partly linked to the negotiations between Iran and the U.S. and uncertainty over their outcome. In the event of renewed hostilities, the route could potentially become a target for Iran despite being located on the territory of a third country. Moreover, prior to the proposed implementation of TRIPP, Iran provided Azerbaijan with its shortest transit route to the Nakhchivan exclave, creating a degree of Azerbaijani dependence on Tehran that TRIPP would substantially reduce. Iran therefore also has an economic and geopolitical interest in the project's development. Yet another significant obstacle concerns the railway component of TRIPP. A functioning rail connection is central to the project's ambition to facilitate trade between Central Asia and Europe and is therefore of critical logistical importance to the viability of the corridor as a whole.  However, Armenia's railway network remains under concession to the state-owned Russian Railways, with the agreement set to remain in force for a considerable period. Russia has shown little willingness to relinquish control, although recent developments suggest that the issue may be subject to negotiation. When the possibility of returning the railway network to Armenian control was raised, the head of Russian Railways emphasized that Russia had invested approximately US$ 400 million in Armenia's railway infrastructure. This statement can be interpreted in two ways. Moscow may be signaling that it expects compensation for its investments as a condition for terminating the concession. Alternatively, it may indicate an interest in participating in the TRIPP project itself, with its existing investment potentially forming the basis for such involvement. In either case, control over Armenia's railway infrastructure introduces a significant Russian dimension into the implementation of TRIPP.  This considerably complicates the situation, as both Moscow and Tehran are capable of exerting pressure on Armenia, albeit in different ways and in pursuit of their respective strategic interests. Any potential Russian participation in TRIPP would not, however, be a matter for Yerevan and Baku alone, as Washington and Moscow could potentially reach a separate agreement on Russia's role in the project. At present, however, Iranian security concerns and Russia's control over Armenia's railway infrastructure remain among the principal external factors hindering the implementation of TRIPP.  CONCLUSIONS  At present, Armenia and Azerbaijan have limited scope to advance the implementation of TRIPP independently. The outcome of potential negotiations between the U.S. and Iran, and ultimately the termination of hostilities, may prove critical to the project's future. Should the parties pursue a diplomatic settlement, TRIPP may need to form part of a broader package of agreements between Washington and Tehran. The Russian dimension is equally complex. Moscow may seek compensation for its investments in Armenia's railway infrastructure, a substantial burden for Armenia, or demand some form of participation in the project. The latter would present Washington with a strategic dilemma whether to accommodate Russian involvement in a transport corridor whose broader geopolitical rationale includes reducing regional dependence on Russia.  In either case, the Trump administration would need to engage in substantive negotiations with Moscow, whether to agree on compensation or determine the terms of potential Russian participation in the project. The implementation of TRIPP therefore depends on a broader set of political and strategic agreements extending well beyond Armenia and Azerbaijan. Without such arrangements, the corridor will continue to entail significant geopolitical and security risks, potentially undermining its attractiveness to businesses seeking reliable routes for transporting goods between Central Asia and Europe.  By Central Asia-Caucasus Analyst via Eurasianet

title: France buries FCAS and moves alone on Rafale’s successor
body:
France is no longer waiting for Germany. After the collapse of the Franco-German track around the future combat aircraft, Paris is preparing its own path towards a sixth-generation fighter. The key date is not 2029 because a new aircraft will be ready then, but because France wants to launch the development of the operational aircraft in 2029, after a new demonstrator phase beginning in 2027.
This is the most important point in the new French calendar. The successor to the Rafale is not around the corner, and 2029 does not mean entry into service. Paris is trying to protect the original timeline after the breakdown of the NGF track inside FCAS. The objective remains a first operational capability in the early 2040s, but France has decided that it cannot allow another European negotiation to delay the aircraft that will eventually sit at the centre of its combat aviation.
The shift began earlier than the latest French reports suggest. Defence Minister Catherine Vautrin said that already in July 2026 France decided to launch national work on the critical path of what was previously called the NGF. This means Paris did not wait for a new European format after the Franco-German failure. It moved to secure the most important technologies, industrial work and schedule under national control.
This does not mean that France wants to isolate itself completely. The new model is different: France defines the aircraft first and may later accept partners who fit its operational requirements. That is a major change from the old FCAS logic, where France, Germany and Spain were supposed to define the future fighter together. The new approach is closer to the Rafale model, where French requirements are first, and partnerships are later.
The reason is quite simple: France has two non-negotiable requirements that cannot be diluted. The future aircraft must be able to carry the ASN4G nuclear missile and operate from the future aircraft carrier France Libre. Germany did not need a carrier fighter or a national nuclear strike platform. This gap was not a technical detail. It was one of the reasons why the Franco-German fighter project became increasingly difficult to sustain.
Rafale will not disappear in 2040, and that is the part often missed in headlines. France is simultaneously preparing Rafale F5, a major mid-life upgrade linked to new sensors, connectivity, combat cloud, UCAS cooperation and ASN4G. In 2029, the same year France plans to launch the development of the operational sixth-generation fighter, it is also expected to order another batch of 45 Rafales. The future aircraft will therefore enter a force structure in which Rafale remains active for decades.
The true story is not that France has found an easy replacement for FCAS. It has not. And again, Paris is taking back control of the fighter question. The technology base exists – and is quite extensive. Dassault, Safran, Thales and MBDA give France a national ecosystem that few European states possess.
France is now trying to finance Rafale F5, UCAS, ASN4G, the future carrier and a sixth-generation fighter at the same time. Some partners may still come later (but Paris must be open to sharing technology with India or the United Arab Emirates). But this time, they will join a French-defined programme, not rewrite it from the beginning.

title: I don’t miss the camera on the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses
body:
The other day I whizzed past several people while running in the park, my playlist blasting at full volume. The next morning, I smiled at a barista while ordering a caramel apple-flavored matcha latte. Afterward, I sat on a park bench reading a book, called up a pal to chat about her recent trip to Prague, and then asked my Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses what meetings were coming up on my calendar. The chipper AI voice said I hadn’t connected my Google Calendar yet (I had) and asked if I would like help connecting. I sighed and then asked it to play an upbeat song. It picked Kendrick Lamar’s “Not Like Us.”
These past few days, dozens of people have seen or interacted with me while wearing smart glasses. Not a single person noticed. Probably because these audio-only versions look just like normal glasses. They come in a retro Clubmaster look — like the ones pictured in this review — or a more Wayfarer-esque Burbank style. Honestly, people usually don’t notice when I wear camera glasses either. But for once, I didn’t feel like a creep.
[Product: Ray-Ban Meta Audio | https://www.meta.com/ai-glasses/ray-ban-meta-audio/]
The audio-only Ray-Bans aren’t a novel concept. Seven years ago, I strutted around Manhattan taking calls and listening to tunes in the Bose Frames, which also combined Bluetooth audio with stylish sunglasses. Nobody noticed me in the Bose back then, either. What makes this pair notable is that it’s 2026, they’re made by Meta, and, well, there’s been vigorous discourse about whether smart glasses are a form of spyware.
Let’s get privacy out of the way. During setup, all the privacy and data opt-out disclosures were much more prominent than when I’ve previously tested Meta glasses. A screen explained how visual data from AI experiences is handled. (You can opt out of Meta using that data to improve AI; voice data, however, is still used.) There’s no visual data from these glasses — this is simply the new messaging for any pair of Meta glasses. You can also opt out of sharing “additional data” with Meta as well, which is enumerated in a separate document online. This is a good thing, though it doesn’t address what makes people uncomfortable about smart glasses: the uneasy feeling that someone else is recording you.
You know what sort of does, though? Removing the camera. The Bose Frames never triggered the same level of distrust because they were “just” sunglasses-shaped headphones. That applies here too. Frankly, I felt much lighter wearing these out into the world precisely because I couldn’t record footage of anyone. (Even if I feel lame saying “Hey Meta” in public.)
[Image: You can see the small, customizable action button on the right-hand temple arm. I programmed it to bring up Meta AI so I don’t have to say “Hey Meta” in public. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/rayban_meta_audio_3.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
I can imagine people still distrusting these Ray-Bans because they have always-listening capabilities for waking up the AI assistant. However, you can disable the wake word in settings and use a customizable button on the right temple arm instead. (This automatically feels 10 percent less silly if you “must” talk to AI assistants outside the home.) There’s no native way to record a conversation directly from the glasses. Any other audio-based feature, like live translation, has to be manually started.
I’m not saying these can’t be modded or used for evil out of the box. Where there’s a perverse mind and ill will, there’s a way. I’m saying it’d take more effort because these glasses simply don’t do very much.
At least, not yet.
Meta’s Muse AI is eventually coming to the glasses, but it’s not available right now. Right now, the glasses ship with the less powerful Muse Spark model. It’s better than what was on the Ray-Bans in 2023, but it’s still meh unless you’re using it for accessibility reasons. In which case, these glasses may not be the best use of $350. A camera-equipped model is more helpful for low-vision and blind users. For hard-of-hearing users, the FDA-cleared hearing assistance feature isn’t available yet, and for deaf users, the Meta Ray-Ban Display may be more useful because they support live captioning.
[Image: Without a camera, the temple arms are much thinner, too. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/rayban_meta_audio_9.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
For everyone else, Muse Spark is nerfed without the camera but can still come in handy. For example, granting access to your messaging apps, Google Calendar, and email lets it do some light scheduling and correspondence on your behalf. If you enable location sharing, you can send where you are to the group chat. It’s fine for these tasks, but not great. It’s adept at short queries like “What’s my next calendar event?” or “Set a reminder to update my editors at 12PM.” With more complex asks, I’ve found Muse Spark gets confused, and it’s faster to whip out my phone. I ended up mostly asking it to set reminders for to-dos I remembered while in the middle of something else.
Muse Spark can also give you local recommendations and turn-by-turn audio directions while walking. As I’ve written before, that’s great if you’re traveling. Less so if you’re familiar with your local haunts. In my neighborhood, I already know which coffee shops have the best Wi-Fi and snacks — and it wasn’t the one Muse Spark suggested. As for walking directions, they’re not something I need that often. When I did, I found using Google Maps on my phone more helpful for getting my bearings.
I’m sure Muse will open up more possibilities when it arrives later this year. Then again, I’ve seen demos, and I’m still skeptical that agentic AI will be the thing that convinces people to buy smart glasses.
So what do I like about these? They’re simply a good pair of open-ear headphones.
I said good, not great. Sound quality is decent, but you’re still dealing with all the tradeoffs that come with this form factor. They struggle at louder volumes. The trebles start to get tinny, and bass can sound distorted. There’s inevitably sound leakage. My spouse frequently reminded me that they could hear everything I was listening to, all of the AI’s responses, and my phone calls. Conversely, even at top volume, ambient noise can still drown out your content. These won’t cut it on a loud subway, for instance.
Still, it’s nice to listen to audiobooks around the house without jumping out of my skin anytime my spouse or cats want my attention. On my daily walks, I’m less afraid of my maniac neighbors mowing me down in their murder mobiles. (New Jersey drivers, man.) It’s not mind-blowing, but it’s a meaningful improvement to my day-to-day routine. And I don’t have to think too hard about it.
[Image: You can’t really tell that these are smart glasses unless you look really closely at the transparent portion of the arms. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Rayban_meta_audio_6.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
At 43 to 47g, these are also much comfier than every other pair of Meta glasses I’ve tried. So far, I’ve worn them for two full days, including a 30-minute run and multiple walks, with zero issues. My Clubmaster review unit also has nose pads — huzzah for anyone with a low nose bridge. That also made for a huge improvement in call quality since the mic for calls wasn’t smushed up against my schnoz. The temple tips can also be adjusted for a better fit.
I usually ding smart glasses for not supporting my -10 prescription and severe astigmatism. These support a range of -12 to +6 — I’m still waiting on a prescription pair, but at least my garbage eyeballs don’t preclude me from wearing these as my daily glasses. All in all, these glasses will fit a much broader range of faces and vision needs.
Battery life is also phenomenal. I was able to eke out two full workdays without sticking the glasses back into the case.
Okay, I lied — one more gripe. These feel expensive for headphone glasses that don’t do much yet. The Meta Glasses, for example, now start at $250 and technically do more. These are $100 more for what, exactly? The Ray-Ban branding? The privilege of not worrying about freaking out other people? If these were $150 or $200, I’d say these would be a no-brainer. Starting at $350 without prescription lenses, without the hearing assistance features, without Muse? That feels off.
But pricing complaints aside, I didn’t miss the camera. (I only ever use it to take cat videos anyway.) Muse Spark isn’t what I’d call the most compelling AI model, but it’s useful now and then. For the casual user, the headphones are the most useful part of smart glasses.
[Image: This is me wondering how my beat went from tracking steps to discussing wearable surveillance and hoping bystanders won’t punch me. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/Rayban_meta_audio_7.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
I wish I could just thrust these into the air and declare that nixing the camera solves the privacy problem. I can’t. Yes, I’m relieved that I don’t have to worry about people punching me in the face if I wear these out and about. I don’t think most people want more than this right now. Still, I’d be lying if I said I didn’t personally know several people who would miss the camera. Not because they’re perverts, but because they find them to be genuinely useful tools for candid home videos, content creation, accessibility, or multimodal AI. For those people, this type of smart glasses isn’t a real option.
Besides, who’s to say Meta won’t add more ambient listening features down the line? Then what? The lack of a camera is only a comfort for now. It doesn’t negate the need for continued, thoughtful discussion about AI wearables, the definition of recording, and what role these gadgets ought to play in our lives.
Photography by Victoria Song / The Verge
---
Agree to Continue: Ray-Ban Meta Audio
Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate.
To use the Ray-Ban Meta Audio smart glasses, you’ll need a Meta account and the Meta AI app downloaded onto your phone. A Meta account works across platforms like Meta, Instagram, and Quest and comes with its own terms of service and privacy policy. Should you decide to integrate with services like WhatsApp, Messenger, Instagram, Apple Music, Apple Health, Garmin, Strava, Amazon Music, and Spotify, you also agree to those terms and privacy policies. You may also be asked to give permissions related to Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, location services, and voice data. If you choose to get a pair of prescription lenses, you may also be asked to share that information with Ray-Ban and/or LensCrafters.
If you are concerned about privacy, you can access the Glasses Privacy menu in the glasses’ settings. There you can view the voice activity log as well as the “Share additional data” toggle. To access the visual data opt-out toggle, go to the glasses’ settings and navigate to the Meta AI menu.
The smart glasses also come with supplemental terms of service and privacy policies / notices, including:
* Supplemental Meta Platforms Technologies Terms of Service
* Supplemental Meta Platforms Technologies Privacy Policy
* Meta AI app terms
* Meta AI glasses privacy settings
* United States Regional Privacy Notice
* Health and Safety Information
* Voice Controls Privacy Notice
* Meta AI Third-Party Notices
Final tally: Two mandatory agreements, eight supplemental agreements and notices, and several optional agreements.
---

title: Rochas Okorocha denies arrest but police insist he was arrested for forgery
body:
A former governor of Imo State, Rochas Okorocha, has denied being arrested by the police.
PREMIUM TIMES earlier reported that the Force Spokesperson Aniete Iniedu said the police arrested Mr Okorocha, a former senator, on Monday night at REIZ Continental Hotel in central Abuja.
Mr Iniedu, a chief superintendent of police, also said that the former governor was later released on bail after being interrogated for an hour.
But in a statement on Tuesday by his media aide Sam Onwuemeodo, Mr Okorocha claimed he was never arrested.
“(The) story that Owelle Okorocha was arrested, and released after one hour, is also not true. And we equally stand to be contradicted.
“There was no bail. There was no statement,” he claimed.
However, when contacted on Tuesday afternoon, the force spokesperson, Mr Iniedu, insisted that Mr Okorocha was arrested on Monday and granted bail.
“We released him on personal recognition. He is supposed to report to Force Headquarters later today. But up till now, we have not sighted him at the headquarters,” Mr Iniedu told PREMIUM TIMES at 2:45 p.m. on Tuesday.
Our reporter asked the spokesperson the reason for the arrest of the former governor.
“We received a petition of forgery and conspiracy against him.
“The Nigeria Police Force has sent the former governor Owelle Rochas Okorocha about three invitations which he ignored which necessitated our men to arrest him,” he responded.
Meanwhile, Mr Okorocha in the Tuesday statement also claimed that the Imo State Government was behind the story of his arrest which he described as false.
The former governor said the Commissioner of Information in Imo State, Declan Emelumba, on Monday, released a press statement captioned, “Bench warrant: Okorocha’s lies.”
The politician claimed the press statement came after he challenged those circulating the report to make public the bench warrant of arrest issued against him.
He claimed the information commissioner attached a copy of the purported bench warrant dated 9 September 2026.
“The same court order was vacated by the same court on 14 September, 2026,” he claimed.
Checks by PREMIUM TIMES showed that Mr Emelumba indeed issued the press statement and attached a copy of the bench warrant issued against the former governor.
However, this newspaper could not verify Mr Okorocha’s claim that the warrant of arrest against him dated 9 September 2026 had been vacated by the court on 14 September 2026.
Still in the Tuesday statement, Mr Okorocha claimed he had been quiet “in this matter” because the matter “is before a court of competent jurisdiction.”
“All these stampedes and lies could be adjudged subjudice and deliberate efforts to arm-twist the court which is very unfortunate,” he claimed.
The former governor was not specific about “the matter” before the court.
Mr Okorocha was an APC aspirant for Imo West District.
The APC’s primary for the district was organised by the party on 18 May.
Governor Hope Uzodimma of Imo State won the primary and was later recognised by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).
However, there was controversy when a different document emerged which showed that Mr Okorocha had won the same APC primary.
The disputed document listed Mr Okorocha as the successful candidate with 150,780 votes despite the fact that initial results showed Mr Uzodimma scored 230,464 votes, while Mr Okorocha received 1,098 votes.
In October this year, INEC’s Imo State Office petitioned the SSS and the Nigeria Police Force over the disputed document.
In letters dated 5 October and 8 October, Mr Ibeziako, a lawyer, described the document naming Mr Okorocha as the winner as “fictitious”.
INEC maintained that the authentic report of the 18 May primary identified Mr Uzodimma as the winner and that the APC had forwarded his name to the electoral body as its candidate.
The commission then attached copies of both the official report and the disputed document to its petitions and asked the security agencies to investigate the document’s source and authenticity.
Meanwhile, in August, Mr Okorocha filed a suit at the Federal High Court in Abuja against INEC, Mr Uzodimma and the APC.
The politician asked the court to determine whether INEC was bound by reports from its officials who monitored the 18 May senatorial primary and whether the commission was right to recognise Mr Uzodimma as the winner.
The former governor also raised a constitutional question concerning Mr Uzodimma’s eligibility to contest the 2027 senatorial election while still serving as governor.
Mr Uzodimma’s second term in office will elapse by January 2028 while the next Senate is expected to be inaugurated in June 2027.
Section 183 of the 1999 Constitution provides that a state governor cannot, while holding office, hold another executive office or paid employment.
However, PREMIUM TIMES understands that Mr Uzodimma had perfected plans to resign his position as governor before expiration of his tenure to switch to the Senate if he wins in the general election.
A report recently surfaced online which suggested that a “senior magistrate court” in Abuja on 9 September issued a bench warrant of arrest against Mr Okorocha and a former Senator, Ifeanyi Araraume as well as two others.
But Mr Okorocha refuted the report and challenged those circulating the report to make the warrant public.

title: Who is behind ‘Black Rus,’ the mysterious group claiming responsibility for an armed incursion into Latvia from Belarus?
body: A group calling itself “Black Rus” (Chyornye Rusy) has claimed responsibility for an incident on the Latvia-Belarus border in which armed, masked men threatened Latvian soldiers overnight on October 6. The men, who were accompanying a group of migrants, later crossed from Belarus into Latvia, damaged an electrical distribution panel, stole surveillance cameras, and returned to Belarus. LSM reported on October 12 that a video statement on the group’s behalf had been posted on a Telegram channel. In it, a man with his face covered and his voice altered says: This was just a test, and Latvia failed it. Soon you’ll see something similar elsewhere along our border. The European Union and NATO are a colossus with feet of clay that will collapse after our first strike. Experts interviewed by Latvian journalists called Black Rus “a project of the intelligence services.” Among other things, they said such a group could not exist in either Russia or Belarus without the authorities’ knowledge. Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko said Latvia itself had orchestrated the border incident to “get money from the European Union.” He said the Belarusian authorities had nothing to do with it. “Operations like this, involving entry into a neighboring country, are impossible without the president’s approval. Nothing like this was cleared with me. That means no such operations took place. I know that for a fact,” Lukashenko said, according to Belarus’ state news agency BelTA. Latvia and other European countries bordering Belarus have repeatedly blamed Minsk for the migration crisis. They believe the Belarusian authorities are behind attempts by groups of migrants to cross the border illegally and enter the EU. Minsk denies this. Latvian Interior Minister Janis Dombrava said about 12,000 people attempting to cross illegally from Belarus had been prevented from entering Latvia since the start of 2026 under Operation Werewolf (Vilkatis). He also said several incidents involving damage to surveillance equipment on the Latvian side of the border had been recorded, Delfi reported . Dombrava suggested that Russian or Belarusian intelligence services were responsible but emphasized that this was only a theory and that there was no evidence yet. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
