title: Russia’s Rassvet Satellites Could Give Drones Space-Based Control, Former HUR Official Warns
body:
Russia’s growing Rassvet satellite network could eventually allow its forces to control long-range drones over Ukraine in real time, a former senior Ukrainian intelligence official warned on Tuesday, Oct. 13.
Major General Ilya Pavlenko, who served as deputy chief of the Defense Ministry’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) from 2015 to 2020, made the remarks in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine .
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
He cautioned against writing off the project because of problems with its first satellites , arguing that the real question is whether Moscow can make the system reliable enough to support regular military communications over Ukraine. The network, he said, could also be used as another tool for hybrid warfare against NATO countries.
“For Europeans, this is a direct threat,” Pavlenko said, explaining that Russia is moving its jet drone factories underground. This could further limit Ukraine’s ability to break manufacturing cycles or destroy the drones – already hard to intercept due to their speed – before they can even be deployed.
“Fitted with a compact Rassvet terminal, such a drone, launched from a civilian vessel in the English Channel or from a rented trailer in Europe, will be able to strike targets in London or Paris unhindered, controlled directly from the Kremlin,” Pavlenko continued, arguing that Europe simply does not have enough Patriot interceptors to repel Russia’s large-scale attacks conducted by cheap satellite drones.
Built by the Russian company Bureau 1440, Rassvet is a low-orbit satellite broadband service that users can connect to through dedicated terminals that relay data to satellites overhead.
As such satellites sit far closer to Earth than geostationary ones, the signal’s travel time is significantly shorter, which could improve performance. According to Pavlenko, a satellite at about 500 kilometers (approximately 311 miles) could offer delays of roughly 30 milliseconds, compared with close to 70 at the planned 800 (roughly 497 miles).
The only trade-off is that each satellite passes quickly over any given spot, so continuous coverage of a large area requires hundreds of them. Higher orbit, although with possible delays in speed, could allow each satellite to cover more ground.
Bureau 1440 says the finished system will operate at an altitude of about 800 kilometers (497 miles), deliver speeds of up to 1 Gbps with delays of up to 70 milliseconds, and use 5G non-terrestrial network standards and laser links between satellites.
Actual speeds in combat would also depend on network load, routing, ground stations and the number of users sharing a channel, Pavlenko noted, so the advertised 1 Gbps should not be read as what each terminal will receive.
Kyiv Post could not independently verify these figures.
Russia carried out two launches of 16 Rassvet-3 satellites each in 2026, both on Soyuz-2.1b rockets from the Plesetsk cosmodrome. However, not all of the roughly 32 spacecraft are working as intended, Pavlenko said; one dropped out of its orbit, while others failed to climb to their planned altitude.
Moscow aims to launch 292 satellites in 2027 and 924 by 2035, according to The Moscow Times .
Russia’s push for its own satellite system sped up after it launched its full-scale invasion against Ukraine in February 2022, particularly because Starlink proved its value to Ukrainian Defense Forces on the battlefield.
For the Russian military, a secure satellite link would mean sharing data between units, streaming video and reaching platforms operating beyond ground networks.
A small constellation can still be military useful, Pavlenko said. Even without constant coverage, a satellite passing over the right area at the right time opens a short “access window” that may be enough to send a video feed, issue a command or adjust a drone’s mission.
That scenario has already been tested, according to Ukrainian intelligence sources cited by Janes in August 2026, who said Russia used its first batch of Rassvet satellites to communicate over Ukraine for several hours.
The biggest concern is drones. Most Russian long-range drones today fly preset routes or rely on civilian mobile networks via a SIM card. With a satellite link, an operator could watch live footage and change a drone’s course or target mid-flight.
Pavlenko said large strike drones, particularly jet-powered models, are the most likely candidates since they can carry the necessary terminals.
Russia began using jet-powered drones extensively in recent months, as they can reach speeds of up to 400-600 kilometers per hour (roughly 250-370 miles per hour), making them significantly harder to intercept.
He identified three main risks for Ukraine: drones gaining a communication channel independent of ground networks, better coordination between dispersed units, and smaller future terminals that could fit on more types of weapons.
There are limits, however. Each drone would need a compatible terminal, antenna, power supply and software, and a satellite link alone would not improve navigation or protect a drone from electronic warfare or air defenses.
Jamming Rassvet will not be so simple, Pavlenko said, noting that effective countermeasures require detailed knowledge of its frequencies, protocols and terminal design – much of which is not public.
Terminals with electronically steered antennas can track satellites quickly and hold a steadier connection, while reprogrammable chips let engineers update satellites with new software after launch.
And shooting down satellites is not much easier. A large constellation can absorb the loss of a few spacecraft, and destroying them creates debris that endangers other objects in orbit, Pavlenko said.
On Aug. 28, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha announced that Kyiv has petitioned the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) to exclude Ukraine’s territory from the service areas of Rassvet, arguing that the system is used solely to support Russia’s war effort.
“The purpose for Russia to use such satellites over the territory of Ukraine is absolutely clear and it has nothing to do with civilian purposes,” Sybiha said, adding that Moscow intends to use the system to support its war effort and commit “genocidal crimes.”
The following day, the Digital Transformation Ministry, the Foreign Ministry and the Ukrainian State Center of Radio Frequencies filed objections to the Rassvet-1 and Rassvet-3 systems.
Nonetheless, Pavlenko acknowledged that the ITU cannot enforce its decisions. But, if Rassvet’s registration were to be revoked, the system would effectively operate illegally, strengthening the case for jamming it and striking its ground infrastructure.
Rassvet’s reach could extend well beyond Ukraine’s frontline, Pavlenko said, warning that Russia is planning to sell the system’s access in 70 countries across the Global South.
This could essentially put the service in the hands of criminal groups, including Somali pirates using unmanned boats against merchant ships and Latin American cartels trying to evade US surveillance.
Ukrainian intelligence also believes Russia deliberately registered Rassvet on frequencies that overlap with Iridium, a satellite system used by the Pentagon. If so, any Western attempt to jam Rassvet could disrupt allied military communications as well.
Amid sweeping sanctions imposed by the EU, Russia has already shifted from Western components obtained through grey-market channels to primarily Chinese electronics.
That is a demanding switch for space hardware, which must withstand radiation and extreme temperatures and cannot be repaired after launch. New components would also mean reworking software and testing equipment, Pavlenko said.
Beyond sales, Beijing gains much from the arrangement as Russia’s war offers a live testing ground for Chinese technology and imposes a steady demand for electronics, optics and communications gear.
Pavlenko singled out Shanghai Fudan Microelectronics, a Chinese chipmaker the US Commerce Department added to its Entity List in September 2025 for supplying technology to Russian military end users. There is no evidence, however, that its components are used in Rassvet satellites.
He also linked the acceleration of Russia’s defense industry to Andrei Belousov, who became defense minister in May 2024.
According to Pavlenko, Belousov was given authority over the wider defense industry and reoriented it toward Chinese chips, optics, thermal imagers and carbon fiber.
He claimed that 90% of the Russian defense sector’s financial settlements now run through the yuan and Chinese banks, although the figure could not be independently verified.
President Volodymyr Zelensky separately warned on Monday, Oct. 12, that Beijing is assisting Russia’s efforts in building Rassvet .
“We know that China works on satellites, works on the possibility of helping Russia with a system similar to Starlink,” he told the Financial Times , adding that “they are getting closer, and they are passing it on to Russia.”
A delegation of bipartisan US lawmakers has backed expanding Ukraine’s access to SpaceX’s Starlink satellite network and urged an effort to win over the company’s owner, Elon Musk, during their visit to Kyiv on Oct. 9.
Musk has repeatedly refused to allow its use inside Russia over fears of nuclear escalation.
Currently, SpaceX allows Ukraine to use Starlink on Ukrainian-controlled territory, including Russian-occupied areas such as Crimea. However, the service inside Russia is completely blocked .
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Russian telecom giant Rostelecom offers smaller internet providers relief from surveillance costs. In exchange, it wants their customers — and most of their revenue.
body: Russia’s largest nationwide telecommunications operators, Rostelecom and TransTeleCom, have begun offering small regional providers service agreements under which the providers would hand over their infrastructure and subscriber bases, Kommersant reported after reviewing the presentations. Under Rostelecom’s proposal, regional operators would transfer their subscribers, communications lines, and technical support to the company. In return, they would keep 30–40% of revenue and no longer have to cover SORM costs (up to 15 million rubles a year), payroll (up to 16 million rubles a year), or contributions to the universal service fund (at least 1 million rubles a year). The proposal also promises to reduce their exposure to regulatory risk. TransTeleCom’s proposal outlines fixed virtual network operator (FVNO) models. Under these models, regional operators would no longer need a license or have regulatory obligations. In return, they would receive a share of revenue and retain the “last mile.” A source told Kommersant that the proposals involve “strictly commercial and voluntary” cooperation. Representatives of small providers say that under these terms, operators would “effectively become installers.” Rostelecom used to “at least buy companies,” but now it is effectively offering terms under which it “takes 60% of the business” without investing anything, said Yaroslav Dubovikov, executive director of the Association of Telecommunications Companies. In April 2026, reports emerged that the Ministry of Digital Development was discussing stricter requirements for telecommunications operators with industry representatives. Among other measures, the ministry proposed introducing three types of licenses that could cost between 1 million and 50 million rubles, depending on the category. The Association of Telecommunications Operators warned that the proposal could leave 27 regions without local internet providers. title: Military Plane Crash: Traditional ruler cries out as decaying bodies ‘pollute’ community’s source of drinking water
body:
A humanitarian crisis may hit Igbokoda, the headquarters of Ilaje Local Government Area of Ondo State, following the pollution of the source of water for the community by decaying bodies of the victims of the Nigeria Air Force (NAF) plane that crashed there last week.
The traditional ruler of the community, Afolabi Odidiomo, told PREMIUM TIMES on Tuesday that the body of water has been polluted, leaving the people with contaminated water both for drinking and other domestic uses.
He also said the crash destroyed economic trees and fish, which are the community’s source of livelihood.
The NAF plane crashed into the swamp in the area on Monday, 5 October, killing the 25 people on board.
Efforts by divers and rescue teams to retrieve the wreckage of the plane and the bodies of the victims have been largely unsuccessful because of the terrain.
The search and rescue efforts deployed by a combined team of NAF, the Nigerian Navy, the police, the Igbokoda community and the state government about a week ago have only succeeded in retrieving pieces of human body parts as well as the broken parts of the airplane.
Officials confirmed that the main body of the airplane is yet to be located, as it is suspected to be deeply submerged in the underlay of the swamp where the crash occurred.
However, concerns have shifted from the initial shock following the crash to fresh fears of water pollution.
The body of water where the crash occurred is the same source of water for the Igbokoda community.
Rescuers have indicated that working on the site at the moment is hazardous as the area stinks badly of decayed human flesh littering the water.
The traditional ruler of Igbokoda, Mr Odidiomo, who spoke to PREMIUM TIMES at his palace on Tuesday, said the water has been polluted, leaving the people with contaminated water both for drinking and other domestic uses.
“The concern of everybody in this community today is that our government spent time, energy, money, and effort looking for people that had been chopped into pieces by the crash. The pieces that are floating everywhere in our rivers. The pieces that have decayed left so much stench that is unbelievable.
“Going close to the river is so scary now for children who usually go to swim when they return from school, because they see human flesh everywhere as they swim. Fish are also dying everywhere.
“So, the river that used to be friendly with children has become scary, as we wonder why the government cares so much for the dead rather than the living.
“This same river where the plane crashed into is what supplies our drinking water. We have a water treatment machine at Aboto about seven kilometres away from here. The water doesn’t come every day, and when it comes, it is this same water that flows there, pumped to be treated for our drinking.
“So, it means whatever happens, pollution is already in the river, either as a result of decayed bodies or as oil that dropped into the river, and any other pollution that went into the water thereof.”
The traditional ruler called for immediate clean-up of the water in order to prevent a worse disaster in the form of an epidemic due to the polluted water.
He said the lack of a plan to protect the people from the inherent pollution was unfair to the people, as the government could have cordoned off the area so that the polluted water could be kept back from flowing into the main river.
Mr Odidiomo said that besides the pollution, the crash also destroyed economic trees and fish, which are the community’s source of livelihood.
“We are asking the government for cleanup. We are asking the government for remediation, a kind of restoration of the environment. The restoration now does not mean that we want the trees planted back, but we want the government to still do something in memory of those that died just as we have in Lagos and Ogun states,” he said.
He also said efforts should be made, in addition to cleaning up the water, to also provide an alternative source of clean drinking water.
Also speaking on the pollution, Benjamin Omoyele, a resident of Igbokoda and a 100 Level student of Civil Engineering at the Federal University of Technology, Akure (FUTA), said the water pollution arising from the crash is a genuine concern that the people expect the government to look into urgently.
According to him, the body parts still left in the water are creating health concerns and contamination in the water, which might affect residents who depend largely on it.
However, Odunsola Dada, popularly called General at Igbokoda, said he believed that since the water is deep and keeps flowing down into the ocean, it would clean itself with time.
Mr Dada said the water would clean itself with time and that he did not see any present danger to the community.
“We are all humans, and what happened is a tragedy. We will all also die at our time. The water is deep and flowing steadily. It is not a well or a pool. It is a flowing river. In a short while everything will flow into the sea and people will be able to use it as before,” he said.
Meanwhile, excavations are ongoing at the site with more machinery being deployed to assist in the removal of the remaining parts of the aircraft.
The search for the black box is the new focus of the operation as directed by the Chief of Air Staff, Sunday Aneke, during his visit to the site last week.

title: AI Researchers Are Smoking Cigarettes to Prove AI Will Cure Cancer, Says Palantir Exec
body:
Nothing says "I trust the future of medicine" quite like lighting a Marlboro and waiting for the chatbot to fix your lungs. That is the habit Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar says is spreading among AI researchers, who have supposedly started smoking cigarettes to prove how confident they are that AI will cure cancer.
"So many AI researchers have started smoking as a way of signaling to other researchers how much they believe in AI," Sankar said in an interview on CBS News' " Face the Nation " on Sunday. "I believe so much in AI that it's going to cure cancer. So I'm showing you my chips are all in."
He did not name a single researcher, cite a survey, or explain how he knows. The remark landed as an aside while host Margaret Brennan pressed him on why he was so focused on the topic.
He pointed to FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried as the effective altruist most Americans know, calling the movement a "millenarian doomsday cult." He also invoked Pascal's idea of a god-shaped hole in every human heart, which he suggested some of these researchers are filling with a machine god called AGI.
The medical record is less enthusiastic than the thesis. The CDC says smoking causes roughly one in three cancer deaths in the United States, and cigarette smoke contains at least 69 chemicals known to cause cancer.
Smokers face about 25 times the lung cancer risk of non-smokers, according to the agency. Quitting lowers the risk of 12 types of cancer, and the added lung cancer risk drops by half 10 to 15 years after stopping.
The cancer pitch is not new in this industry. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said in August that promising AI will cure cancer has become “more a cliche than it is inspiring,” and that only actually curing it would earn the public's trust.
2/2 Second, on the messaging around AI. I do not agree that my messaging has been disproportionately negative. In fact it has been about equally balanced between risks and benefits: I’ve written one major essay about each, and even in interviews where I discuss the risks, I…
— Dario Amodei (@DarioAmodei) August 15, 2026
That trust is thin. In the CBS poll Brennan cited, 50% of Americans said AI will create more problems than it solves, 29% said it will solve more than it creates, and 21% were unsure.
About 45% said they want the government to restrict AI's use and development. Smoking to show faith in the technology does not obviously help that number, but it does help AI bros bond with each other. "When you're smoking, you're networking by accident," Revamp AI cofounder Stephen Campbell told Business Insider last month.
The IMF's Kristalina Georgieva recently warned that AI could hit 40% of jobs , and insiders expect a major AI incident within a year. Indirectly causing a lung cancer outbreak was probably not on their bingo card.
Palantir sells data-analysis software to governments and militaries. Most of its business relies on AI.

title: Energy truce with strings attached: Kyiv reportedly told to spare Russian refineries or lose US intelligence and arms
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine has loosened its reliance on Washington but still depends on the United States in three military areas that let US President Donald Trump keep pressuring Kyiv, The Telegraph wrote on 12 October. That pressure now centers on the energy ceasefire Trump declared on 11 October, with US officials reportedly warning Kyiv not to hit Russian energy during the truce. Kyiv backs a mutual truce, but Moscow has not confirmed it, and Russian strikes on Ukraine’s grid have continued. The paper named three such ties: satellite intelligence, Patriot interceptors, and American weapons bought with European money. A pause in any of them would hit just as Russia’s winter campaign begins. Ukraine says an intercepted document reportedly lays out up to 1,000 Russian missiles, drones, and bombs for 60 critical sites this winter, so any pause in US intelligence, interceptors, or PURL deliveries would land as that campaign gets under way. Satellite intelligence: the US still holds the key The Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and other US services still pass precise satellite data that help Ukrainian forces hit targets inside Russia, by the paper’s estimate. Trump briefly suspended that flow in March 2025 to pressure Zelenskyy. A Ukrainian official told Axios that Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner threatened during 9 October talks in Miami to cut off US intelligence. Explore further Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv before sirens, gap that lands hard amid fears that Washington could cut data that warns of launches Patriot interceptors: no quick substitute The Telegraph called interceptor missiles the second and probably sharpest dependency. Only American Patriot systems can down Russia’s most powerful missiles, which strike Ukrainian cities daily, the paper wrote. Kyiv’s PAC-3 stocks ran dry mainly because US reserves were diverted to the Middle East after America’s war against Iran, the paper added. Kyiv had warned in March that a long Middle East war would squeeze its PAC-3 supply. Five European defense firms—Destinus, MBDA Deutschland, Safran, Airbus, and Thales— signed a letter of intent in July to develop a joint interceptor, but a testable prototype is not expected before next year, the paper wrote. Ukraine is also building its own interceptor with European allies under the FREYJA program. US officials have reportedly warned Europe that Trump may halt those supplies if Ukraine keeps striking Russian oil refineries. title: Senate Passes Bill to Provide Legal Framework for Kano varsity
body: The Senate on Tuesday passed a bill to provide a legal framework for the Yusuf Maitama Sule Federal University of Education, Kano, Kano State. The bill sponsored by the Deputy Senate President Barau I. Jibrin (APC, Kano North), was passed during plenary presided over by Senate President Godswill Akpabio. It seeks to provide the statutory foundation for the effective management and administration of the institution. Recall that in September 2024, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu approved the conversion of the Federal Colleges of Education in Kano and Zaria into federal universities of education. Following Senator Barau’s request, President Tinubu, on May 10, 2025, also approved the renaming of the institution as the Yusuf Maitama Sule Federal University of Education, Kano. To give the institution a legal framework, Senator Barau sponsored the bill, which passed through the legislative process and was approved by the Senate for second and third readings. The bill scaled first reading on Wednesday, March 25, 2025. While leading the debate on the bill, Barau said the legislation was necessary to give legal backing to the institution. He commended President Tinubu for approving the institution’s upgrade and renaming, explaining that the bill would provide a legal framework for the promotion and development of teacher education and make comprehensive provisions for the university’s management and administration. He said: “Mr Senate President, this institution has already been established by the President of the Federal Republic of Nigeria. “You may recall, my colleagues, that in the last Senate, I made efforts to facilitate the establishment of these institutions, including the Federal College of Education, Zaria, which was to be upgraded to a full-fledged university, as well as Alvan Ikoku College of Education and Adeyemi College of Education. The bills were passed and transmitted to the late President Muhammadu Buhari, but they were not assented to. “When President Bola Ahmed Tinubu assumed office, I approached him and conveyed the desire of my people to have the Federal College of Education, Kano, upgraded to a full-fledged university. He assured me that, since it was the request of the people, it would be done. The President subsequently approved the upgrade of the institution. “But we were not done yet. At the request of my people, I returned to the President to seek approval for the institution to be named after the late Yusuf Maitama Sule. The President immediately approved the request. Today, the institution is a full-fledged university offering degrees in various fields of education. “We cannot thank Mr President enough. He loves Kano and has consistently acceded to our requests. Beyond this institution, he has also approved the establishment of the Federal University of Science and Technology in Kabo and the Federal Polytechnic in Rano. We cannot thank him enough for these interventions.” In his remarks, Akpabio commended Barau for sponsoring the bill and thanked senators for supporting its swift passage. He expressed optimism that President Tinubu would assent to the bill upon its transmission to him, thereby providing the university with the necessary statutory and regulatory framework to fulfil its mandate and continue contributing to national development.

title: Orqa U.S. Awarded $38 Million for U.S. Department of War Drone Dominance Gauntlet II Competition
body:
Award will support U.S.-based production of drones, expanding domestic capacity to deliver compliant unmanned systems to the U.S. Government at scale
Orqa U.S., a U.S.-owned and independently controlled unmanned systems company, has been awarded a $38 million contract to manufacture drones for the Department of War’s Drone Dominance Gauntlet II program, expanding its ability to deliver compliant, American-made unmanned systems.
The award builds on Orqa U.S.’s delivery of 240 drones under an earlier $1.5 million award and its performance in the close-quarters portion of the Drone Dominance Gauntlet II competition. Orqa U.S. was selected as one of nine participants in the program.
“Placing second globally in the close-quarters competition and now being selected for this award is an important milestone for Orqa U.S.,” said Charles Phillips, Chief Executive Officer of Orqa U.S. “It shows that proven drone technology, combined with the ability to onshore and manufacture in the United States, can meet the needs of the U.S. Government. We’re proud to work with By Light to bring these systems into production and deliver them at scale.”
Orqa U.S. was established through a partnership between Orqa and By Light Professional IT Services LLC. Orqa provides the drone technology, while By Light supports manufacturing and compliance. By Light will manufacture the systems at its 180,000-square-foot facility in Port Orange, Florida, which supports UAS assembly, advanced manufacturing, testing, quality control and onshoring.
The selected system is from the MRM2 suite of products and features an 8-inch indoor drone and Orqa’s ground control system. The company has developed and refined the technology over the past decade to enable users to develop, test and integrate it with their platforms and systems in demanding operational environments, including real-world combat conditions.
With the award, Orqa U.S. is excited to expand production of the MRM2 in the United States and deliver the system to support the U.S. Government’s growing demand for domestically manufactured, compliant unmanned systems.

title: The Hague’s visa denial to Russian athletes seen as attempt to weaken Russian team
body:
THE HAGUE, October 13. /TASS/. Russian Ambassador to The Netherlands Vladimir Tarabrin has criticized the Dutch authorities’ decision to deny entry visas to Russian gymnasts as an attempt to weaken Russia’s team at the upcoming world championships.
"By deliberately denying visas to our top female athletes to compete in the World Artistic Gymnastics Championships, the Dutch authorities have once again shown complete disregard for one of the fundamental principles of world sports - fair play. This is a clear and willful attempt to weaken our team through political and bureaucratic means," he told TASS, adding that the Russian side was indignant over this decision.
The press service of the Russian Gymnastics Federation said earlier that the Dutch embassy refused to issue visas to Olympic champions Angelina Melnikova and Victoria Listunova, as well as Anna Kalmykova, giving their alleged status as a "threat to international relations" as a reason.
The World Artistic Gymnastics Championships will be held in Rotterdam from October 17 to 25 and will mark the first stage of team qualification for the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles.

title: ‘Like Mad Max’: Yemen desert battle footage emerges as Saudi-led airstrikes resume | Watch
body: Saudi Arabia has resumed its strikes in Yemen, with the Saudi-led coalition carrying out airstrikes against oil facilities west of the capital, Sanaa, according to reports Tuesday by the Houthi-affiliated Al-Masirah television channel and residents of the Yemeni capital. Saudi media also reported a strike in Hodeidah. Meanwhile, unusual footage circulating on social media shows direct fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed forces in a barren desert area of Yemen. U.S. President Donald Trump also commented on the developments, saying: "The Houthis are behaving very badly. I thought they had learned their lesson a year ago when we bombed them and stopped at their request. They were quiet for a long time, but now they've raised their heads again, probably on Iran's orders."   "They have returned to behaving in a particularly nasty way, attacking Saudi Arabia and deliberately trying to drive up oil prices, probably ahead of the elections in the United States. Not nice! Someone should explain to them that I'm not running in the elections. I already won, in a huge landslide, but I'll still be here after the elections, and I'll never forget!" British newspaper the Daily Mail reported that the footage was believed to show Houthi rebels pursuing pro-Saudi forces. The precise location was not disclosed, but the videos show a Saudi convoy of armored vehicles attempting to storm Houthi positions in the desert. The British newspaper described the fighting as reminiscent of "Mad Max," the post-apocalyptic action film. In one video, a body can be seen flying through the air, apparently following a strike by an anti-tank weapon, before crashing to the ground. Another video shows a pickup truck speeding across the sand, with soldiers riding in the back bouncing violently up and down. One of them is thrown from the vehicle and left behind as the others continue driving. Meanwhile, Al-Masirah reported the resumption of airstrikes in Yemen. Witnesses in Sanaa said they heard explosions, although it was not immediately clear which oil facilities had been hit. Earlier, coalition forces issued an evacuation warning for the al-Sabaha oil facility and nearby storage areas. The site is located on a hill west of Sanaa overlooking the capital. According to the Associated Press, the area is uninhabited.     Shortly after the warning, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree announced that any Saudi strike on Sanaa would be met with a "decisive and painful" response in Riyadh. Saree claimed the al-Sabaha facility was empty of petroleum products and was "militarily worthless as a target." The Yemen Petroleum Company also said it had "already taken all necessary precautions to deal with any emergency, with the aim of ensuring stable supplies and continuing to meet residents' needs without disruption." According to the company, "The al-Sabaha facilities currently contain no petroleum products, and targeting them will not affect oil reserves or supplies." The Houthis responded by issuing their own evacuation warning to civilians near facilities belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco. Saree linked the threat against Sanaa to Aramco, saying: "The Houthi forces call on all civilians to evacuate immediately and stay away from the targets that the forces will strike if Saudi Arabia carries out its threat regarding Sanaa." The sites listed in the Houthi announcement were Aramco's headquarters in Dammam, Saudi Arabia King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, which recently suffered a devastating strike and Aramco's refinery in Riyadh. A map accompanied the warning.   The exchange of threats comes as Saudi Arabia investigates how its air defense systems failed to prevent Saturday's unprecedented deadly strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, which killed at least 13 people and injured more than 300. The Houthi missile attacks on Saudi airports mark a dramatic turning point in the long-running conflict between the two sides. The Houthis' ability to enforce an air blockade on Saudi Arabia has been a major humiliation for the kingdom's authorities, with no end to the situation currently in sight. The disruptions are placing additional pressure on the aviation industry, which has already been struggling in recent years with the consequences of wars across the Middle East and soaring fuel prices. Saudi Arabia had expected the United States to intervene more directly in Riyadh's war against the Houthis. For now, however, the Americans have limited their involvement to providing intelligence, identifying targets and assisting in the planning of Saudi attacks, without carrying out their own direct strikes in Yemen. On Saturday, Trump signaled that he might change that position and take a more active role in supporting Saudi Arabia's military campaign.

title: EFCC chair warns Nigerian girls against sextortion
body:
The Chairman of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC), Ola Olukoyede, has warned Nigerian girls against sextortion and online fraud, urging them to protect themselves from criminals who exploit personal relationships to extort money.
Mr Olukoyede gave the warning in Abuja on Monday at an event organised by the African Girl Guide to mark the International Day of the Girl Child.
“Girls need to be careful about relationships and not fall into the antics of criminals and sextortionists,” he said in a statement by the agency.
Mr Olukoyede, who was represented by Aisha Muhammed, head of the EFCC’s Enlightenment and Re-orientation Unit, also cautioned girls against cybercrime, particularly allowing fraudsters to use their bank accounts to receive or transfer illicit funds.
“If you engage in cybercrime; if you become an account mule for ‘Yahoo boys’; if you blackmail people online, you are not just committing a crime, you are destroying Nigeria’s image,” he said.
He urged the girls to acquire skills that could help them earn a living legally, listing coding, tailoring, baking and content creation as options. He also advised them to save part of their earnings and learn to distinguish between their needs and wants.
“Don’t let anyone use your account to commit fraud. That account in your name can take you to prison,” he warned.
Sextortion involves threatening to share a person’s intimate images or videos unless the victim meets certain demands, such as paying money or providing more sexual material. The United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) has warned that perpetrators may manipulate children into sharing sexual images and then use threats to exploit them.
Mr Olukoyede said the EFCC had established Integrity Clubs and Zero Tolerance Clubs in schools across Nigeria to promote ethical conduct among young people. He urged the girls to become ambassadors of integrity in their schools and communities.
Also speaking at the event, Denen Petronella, executive assistant to Jindu Peter, founder of the African Girl Guide, said girls needed education, mentorship, protection and opportunities to develop their abilities.
Ms Petronella announced the launch of the African Girl Guide’s Camp Amani School Club, which she said would provide girls with opportunities to build confidence and develop leadership and life skills throughout the school year.
“Our responsibility therefore is not simply to tell girls they can succeed. It is to help create the support systems that make that success possible,” she said.
Representatives of government ministries, departments and agencies, institutions, and students from secondary schools in Abuja attended the event.
The organisers held the event under the theme, “Invest in Her, Empower Her and Let Her Lead.”

title: Netflix secures broadcasting rights for FIFA 2030 World Cup in Spain, Andorra
body: Netflix said on Tuesday it had secured the rights to broadcast the FIFA 2030 World Cup in Spain, which is co-hosting the tournament, and Andorra.It would be Netflix's first broadcast of a major men's international tournament in Spain, the company said. The 2026 World Cup was aired there by the national channel TVE.California-based Netflix did not disclose financial terms.Under the deal, one game per matchday will be free to watch in Spain. Netflix will also offer a national free-to-air channel that will broadcast a package of matches including all of Spain's games, both the semi-finals and the final.Netflix did not name the channel.TVE declined to comment on whether it would be interested in purchasing a package of matches.Spain, which won the World Cup in North America this year, will co-host the 2030 edition with Portugal and Morocco, although Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay will stage inaugural matches marking the tournament's 100th anniversary.Uruguay hosted the first World Cup in 1930.Spanish state-owned network broadcast 2026 tournament's matchesSpain's state-owned television network, TVE, broadcast the Spanish national team's matches during this year's tournament, while the private platform DAZN, which carried Mediapro's pay-TV World Cup channel, showed all 104 games.Netflix holds the rights in the US and Canada for the 2027 Women's World Cup, hosted by Brazil, and the 2031 edition, staged jointly by Costa Rica, Jamaica, Mexico, and the US.The deal in Spain is more evidence of Netflix's push into the sports broadcasting world, with NFL, MLB, WWE, boxing and MMA all appearing on the streaming platform.

title: FrontierML: A challenging, end-to-end machine learning benchmark
body:
One desirable property of human-run frontier AI labs is that they can consistently improve their models with increased access to capital. As agents begin doing machine learning work, the same question applies: given more money, can an agent build a better model?
FrontierML is a benchmark that measures how well agents turn capital into model performance on challenging, end-to-end machine learning tasks. Our benchmark makes several key advancements in capturing the real-world complexity of modern machine learning:
Overall, FrontierML faithfully measures whether or not agents can autonomously train other models, end-to-end, while handling the complexity and applying the judgment a human research team would.
In the real world, researchers might spend $10 or $200 or $50,000 toward a given task, with performance improving as budget scales. FrontierML measures whether agents can train better models as we scale the money they are given.
FrontierML tasks are designed to give agents control over the full model development process, creating opportunities to turn additional capital into better model performance through larger training runs, better data, or more algorithmic experimentation.
In our experiments, we find that stronger agents are able to reliably improve their submissions with greater access to capital.
Like real-world machine learning work, FrontierML tasks define a problem without prescribing a solution. Agents build and submit their own inference server, which we evaluate by sending requests and scoring its responses. This leaves the entire development process open-ended: agents decide what model architecture to build, what data to use, which GPUs to rent and for how long, which experiments to run, and how to serve the result.
Agents adopt different approaches for each task, resulting in a wide band of scores.
Open-ended long-horizon tasks have a large reward hacking surface, which we address with the following:
Air-gapped solution execution . The agent has internet access during development, but must submit a standalone package of serving code and model weights that runs with no internet access, on a single H100 machine.
Extensive held-out test set . To disincentivize overfitting, we provide limited validation samples and evaluate on a large out-of-distribution held-out test set, not shown to the agent, for each task. For example, for the Ternary PTQ task , we only tell the agent two of four benchmarks we will evaluate on (public: GPQA-Diamond, LCB v6; held-out: MMLU-Pro, MATH-500). In the SVG generation task , we make the held-out samples substantially more complex than the validation samples.
LLM judge review . After each task is complete, we spin up a review agent with access to the submission and the agent’s trajectory, which checks for cheating, including:
Strict time limits . We set an allowable evaluation time limit to bound the allowed inference compute for each submission. If the submitted server doesn’t return answers for each held-out sample within the limit, the agent scores 0 on the task.
FrontierML contains 21 end-to-end tasks spanning language, vision, audio, and games, inspired by research at frontier labs, neolabs, and academic institutions. Tasks range from converting an autoregressive LLM into a text diffusion model to building a streaming end-of-turn detector for voice assistants to writing a bot that plays competitive Pokémon battles.
Each task provides the agent with the same setup: a 12-hour CPU sandbox, a wallet with $10, $50, or $200, a few validation samples, and a task description. For each task, we also provide several constraints to ensure tasks are not trivially solvable, for example by restricting use of already-trained public specialist models or training on the test split of any public benchmark.
We provide the minimal amount of information required to complete the task. After submission, a review agent is given a sandbox to review the submission and agent’s trajectory to ensure the constraints were followed.
When evaluating each agent, we use the reasoning effort that provided the best score on other agentic benchmarks for each respective agent. Each model runs in the harness its developer used for agentic benchmarks on its model card, mirroring day-to-day use.
Before submitting, agents can test their work with frontier selfcheck , which runs the current submission on the grading infrastructure against the public validation samples, up to four times per trial.
Evaluating an agent on all 21 tasks costs up to $ 5,460 in wallet spend, not including model API costs.
To give each agent simple access to compute and synthetic data generation, we created Spin , an open-source CLI tool and service that allows agents to purchase on-demand compute from 17 different compute providers, and metered tokens from OpenRouter. We provide a hosted version with zero fees for ease of evaluation.
Because compute prices fluctuate, we fix the price of each GPU type across all evaluation runs. We took a snapshot of on-demand compute prices on September 29, 2026, calculated the median price across providers and saved the result. We price GPUs by form factor, with H100 SXM, H100 PCIe and H100 NVL each having their own fixed price. The snapshot used for evaluation is available as a JSON file. When running the evaluation, we set compute to the price captured in the snapshot by default.
Because FrontierML keeps tasks open-ended and allows agents to do whatever they think will produce the best model, agents design their own architectures and produce their own data.
In 28% of trajectories, agents add newly trained parts to pretrained models or train a new model from scratch.
Of the 735 runs that trained a model, 14% used only data they generated with an LLM, a local model, or a renderer or simulator, 44% combined public datasets with data they generated themselves, and 35% used public datasets only. 7% trained on the task's own data alone.
Agents almost always write their own training loop: 87% of training runs use a hand-written PyTorch loop, and 8% use the Hugging Face Trainer. 26% of runs train a LoRA through the PEFT library.
On average, agents only spend 45% of the capital in their wallet, even when they are explicitly told there is no penalty for using their entire wallet. No individual agent uses more than 80% of the capital available to it at any budget.
While FrontierML provides agents with a maximum time limit of 12 hours, agents often submit much earlier. On average, frontier models only spent half of the available time, while no model spent more than 9 hours on average.
Agents rarely researched their options before spending money, instead relying on prior knowledge to choose models for synthetic data generation and GPUs to rent.
Synthetic data: agents almost always chose models for synthetic data generation from memory, without searching for newer models beyond their knowledge cutoff. Only 3 runs listed the set of available models on OpenRouter before generation. Over 67% of all calls to OpenRouter for synthetic data were to models more than 1 year old.
GPU selection: across all agents, the vast majority of compute was in H100s, with 60% being spent on H100 SXM GPUs. Over all runs, only two web searches were performed about which GPU to use, both of which were from Grok 4.7.
The goal of FrontierML is to capture the real-world complexities of modern machine learning.
FrontierML is the most open-ended capabilities benchmark for agentic machine learning. Unlike existing benchmarks, we directly give agents access to money which they can use to purchase any type of GPU reservation, and tokens from any model on OpenRouter to generate synthetic data.
FrontierML's general task interface (submit any code that runs on an H100 and serves the model) allows agents to start from any public model and architecture, just as a human researcher could.
Agents must decide how to allocate spend between compute and synthetic data, which experiments to run, whether to start from a pretrained model, which public datasets to use or what data to generate, and whether to adopt existing architectures and learning algorithms or create their own.
Existing benchmarks are narrower in scope and give up task diversity or realism. We summarize the key differences below:
PostTrainBench is the closest work to ours. It does not give models freedom to design model architectures or generate synthetic data like FrontierML does. Because tasks are limited to LLM post-training, they do not provide a holistic evaluation of machine learning capability, reducing model separation compared to FrontierML. For example, PostTrainBench does not test architecture design, synthetic data generation, or non-language-modeling tasks.
Overall, FrontierML more faithfully measures whether or not agents can autonomously train other models, end-to-end, while handling the complexity and applying the judgment a human research team would.
Current runs use budgets of $10, $50, and $200. At present, some machine learning tasks are intractable with these budgets, limiting the set of tasks available. We are working on tasks with larger budgets, ranging from $1,000 to $100,000. In combination, we are also working on tasks that require multi-node training and significantly more complex infrastructure.
Each agent was only run at one reasoning effort. In future releases, we plan to run evaluations on multiple reasoning efforts to provide a more granular Pareto frontier across total spend.
Agents are currently limited to spending on on-demand AI neoclouds and OpenRouter. We plan to give the agent access to more paid services, such as Tinker and human talent marketplaces.
As agents take on more end-to-end economic work, capital efficiency will become a defining measure of capability. Models must be evaluated on the full cost of completing a task: not just token cost, but also the resources they provision. Resource allocation is a new axis of scaling, where providing an agent with more capital results in better performance.
Thank you to Sungjin Hong and Shayaan Emran for contributing tasks, and to Adrien Morisot, Jeffrey Li, and Edward Zhang for reviewing early versions of this work.

title: No, Ukraine's strikes on Yandex data centers didn't cripple Russian influence ops
body:
Ukrainian drone strikes against Russian data centers sparked viral claims about a sudden drop in Russian influence operations on social media — even as experts see no evidence to support this.
Kyiv struck data centers run by Yandex — Russia's "answer to Google" — in three different regions between Oct. 9 and 11, a response to Russian strikes against similar facilities in Ukraine.
Yandex acknowledged the attacks, noting that its data center in Vladimir Oblast had to be shut down due to damage and reported disruptions to various online services within Russia.
Soon after, commentators on social media began reporting an alleged decrease in activity by "Russian bots" online, linking this to Ukrainian strikes on Yandex.
President Volodymyr Zelensky even alluded to this in his address to the Warsaw Security Forum, saying it is "a little easier to breathe on many social media platforms."
Yet beyond anecdotal examples circulating online, there is no data showing that the attacks on Yandex disrupted Moscow-backed disinformation and influence operations.
At least some of the claims appear to stem from a simple confusion of terms.
The source of this confusion is a chart from the internet company Cloudflare showing that bot activity from Yandex's network dropped to 54.7% after a Ukrainian strike on a data center in Ryazan Oblast.
The rate then plummeted to 0.3% after the third data center was hit in Vladimir Oblast .
But the chart simply shows automated web page requests from Yandex's own infrastructure, primarily its search crawlers — bots that browse and index web content.
It has nothing to do with activity by what is commonly referred to as Russian bots or trolls on social media.
"No reliable graph can consolidate bot and troll activity across multiple social media platforms without their internal data that measures telemetry, traffic, and behavior," Roman Osadchuk, the director of Threat Intelligence at the LetsData tech company, tells the Kyiv Independent.
Osadchuk acknowledges a moderate dip in social media comments and posts, both by bots and real users, over the weekend, but regards it as a coincidence.
By popular demand: A follow-up thread on Russian bots, Yandex, Cloudflare, MAGA, AfD and "breathing easier" on social media. 1️⃣ We see no "dramatic drop" in traffic of Kremlin-aligned human trolls-for-hire targeting Russian domestic users (which we have been tracking for years). pic.twitter.com/QGtEdZ6bXR
This decrease "could be explained by tech complications on the side of companies that run influence operations like SDA or Structura, or it could simply be lower output from the weekend shift on the troll/bot farm, or a general fluctuation in comments."
No major fact-checking or disinformation-monitoring organizations reported a radical drop in Russian disinformation activity on social media, though some European officials echoed the claims.
In Poland, Tomasz Siemoniak, a minister coordinating the work of special services, claimed he had received exclusive information from the country's internal security service, the ABW, about a "radical decline in Russian bot activity online" due to the strikes.
But no such data has been published, and local disinformation monitors report no drop in Moscow-backed influence operations.
The Disinformation Analysis Center at Poland's state-run Research and Academic Computer Network (NASK) recorded no significant decrease in activity by disinformation accounts between Sept. 30 and Oct. 11.
"Only isolated cases of individual accounts becoming inactive were observed, but there is no basis for conclusively linking these instances to the attacks in question," the center's Daria Tomczuk told the Kyiv Independent.
Nor is there convincing evidence in other European countries.
Czech Member of the European Parliament Tomas Zdechovsky shared a graph purportedly linking the Ukrainian attacks to a drop in online activity around the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.
But the German technology website Rohtext disputed this, noting that the graph does not list a source or explain a methodology. Rohtext reported no links between AfD activity and Yandex centers.
Another theory that appeared online is that damage to Yandex data centers may have disrupted the infrastructure supporting Moscow's influence operations.
However, Russian disinformation is believed to heavily rely on decentralized networks of proxies abroad, which would not be disrupted by strikes against Russian data centers.
"There's a lot of documented evidence that these troll operations operate in other countries like North Macedonia or the Philippines," Dave Troy, a disinformation researcher and investigative journalist, told the Kyiv Independent.
Given the blockade on the Russian internet imposed by the outside world and heavy domestic restrictions, it simply makes more sense to run disinformation operations from abroad, he adds.
This proxy strategy also makes it hard to pinpoint a drop in activity that is decisively Russian.
One commentator pointed to a drop in impressions under posts linked to Storm-1516, a Kremlin-backed disinformation group.
But Bot Blocker , a group monitoring Russian disinformation, countered that the bot network used by Storm-1516 is most likely a neutral commercial engagement-for-hire provider, not affiliated with a particular state.
"This engagement amplifying network is quite unlikely to be run from Yandex data centers," Bot Blocker told the Kyiv Independent.
Troy warns that misstating the impact of Ukrainian strikes on Russian data centers could pose a strategic risk by itself.
"The danger is thinking a specific victory has been achieved, but in reality the threat lies elsewhere and must still be assessed and fought," he adds.

title: HMS Protector towed into Devonport with her future uncertain
body:
HMS Protector, the Royal Navy’s only ice patrol ship, was towed into Devonport by tugs today for, what officials say is to allow “ investigations into a defect to take place”. She remains part of the fleet for now, but it is likely she is beyond economical repair.
Protector’s difficulties began well before this summer. She entered dry dock at UK Docks on Teesside in May 2025 for her five-yearly docking, left the dock in August and sailed in December, arriving back at Devonport on 12 December for trials ahead of deployment. She did not go south for the 2025-26 summer season as would have been expected and remained in the UK. She was back on Teesside for much of this year but did not leave under her own power and was towed by tugs for the whole journey home. Other than preparation for disposal, it is hard to understand what can be achieved in Devonport that could not be done in Middlesbrough.
Protector was originally completed in October 2001 as the MV Polarbjørn, a polar research and subsea support vessel for GC Rieber Shipping. She was chartered by the RN in April 2011 as a three-year stop-gap, commissioned that June and bought outright in September 2013 for £54M, including one year’s contract support. She is now 25 years old, typical of the maximum service life commercial ships of her type are built for.
She has worked hard in RN service; between 2015 and 2019 she was based in the southern hemisphere, maintained in South Africa with crews rotating to keep her deployed around 330 days a year, and her tasks ranged from the first RN patrol of the Ross Sea in 80 years to the search for the Argentine submarine ARA San Juan in 2017. A propulsion defect in the Caribbean in 2019 brought her home for a £14M, ten-month refit on Teesside and she missed the 2020-21 season. The 2025 docking ran to seven months and was followed by a further spell in the same yard this year.
After her 2020 refit, she split her year between the poles. In June 2021 she reached 80°41’N in the Greenland Sea, within 1,050km (567nm) of the North Pole and further north than any RN surface ship in recent memory, before returning to the Antarctic that winter for the first time since 2019. She made her first visit to Canada in 2022. In the summer of 2024, she worked through the Hudson Strait into Hudson Bay with a Canadian Coast Guard ice adviser embarked. She then went through the Panama Canal and joined Exercise UNITAS off Chile ahead of a 2024-25 Antarctic season that ended at Punta Arenas in February 2025.
The RN has been here before. When HMS Endurance was put out of action due to accidental flooding off Chile in December 2008, no ice patrol ship went south for the next two seasons, and it was 2013 before the MoD accepted she was beyond economical repair. She lay at Portsmouth until June 2016, when she was towed to Turkey for scrap. Operating a single second-hand ship on a shoestring means there will be gaps in availability in the event of unforeseen incidents or more frequent defects emerging as a ship gets older.
Fortunately, the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) has its own logistic support ship, RRS Sir David Attenborough, to resupply its stations. Protector’s role was primarily to conduct work that falls to a government vessel, carrying observers inspecting foreign stations under the Antarctic Treaty as well as fishery inspections in the Southern Ocean, and hydrographic surveys of waters now increasingly busy with cruise ships. Argentina and Chile, whose claims overlap the British Antarctic Territory, both send naval icebreakers south each season. The MoD claims that demonstrating sovereignty over this area and treaty obligations can be met by occasional overflights by RAF aircraft flying from the Falklands.
The Defence Investment Plan published in June commits the MoD to replacing Protector with what ministers describe as “a more modern variant”, intended for the Arctic as well as the Antarctic. Adding the requirement to patrol the Arctic complicates matters. More than a single vessel is needed to sustain a presence in both polar regions.
In July, the Defence Readiness Minister, Luke Pollard, told Parliament that funding had been allocated but the timeline depended on a procurement route not yet chosen. Asked in September when those decisions would be made, he said only that “decisions on the method of procurement and the exact replacement timeline will be taken in due course”. The assumption was that Protector would keep going until a successor arrived. Another stopgap solution might be to again charter an existing ice-class vessel.

title: TMG vs TMS: The communication dilemma over Tinubu’s future, By Yushau A. Shuaib
body:
As a student and practitioner of public relations, I believe the battle for public opinion in the months ahead will not be won by the side that shouts loudest, marches furthest, or commands the most digital noise. It will be won by the side that builds the most credible narrative around verifiable reality.
I was reluctant to make this disclosure. For weeks, I weighed silence against the obligation to be transparent. In the end, a video forced the matter: footage of my brotherly friend, Omoyele Sowore, leading a “Tinubu Must Go” procession. It reminded me that this dilemma has a public dimension I can no longer keep to myself.
Let me begin with context. Sowore and I have maintained a cordial relationship despite our different orientations — his rooted in activist journalism, mine in strategic communication. When I was removed from the federal public service after my well-documented altercation with then Finance Minister Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, Sowore used his platform, energy, and resources to defend me at a time when few were willing to be publicly associated with the controversy. That kind of solidarity is hard to forget.
When I later served as a communications consultant to a sensitive office and our media placements appeared on SaharaReporters , which he still publishes, a misunderstanding followed. During my transit in New York on my way to Las Vegas, he declined to see me, suspecting, I believe, that I had come to compromise his editorial independence on behalf of the then National Security Adviser, Colonel Sambo Dasuki. He treated the man the same way.
Ironically, he and Dasuki later found common ground in a SSS detention cell, and were released the same day. I have never sought a favour from Sowore that he refused, except for one occasion when he confronted me over an article supporting Okonjo Iweala’s World Trade Organisation (WTO) aspiration. I respected his candour then, as I do now.
I offer this context not to demonstrate proximity to power on either side, but because the dilemma I am about to describe only makes sense against this background.
A few weeks ago, Kashifu Inuwa — a highly respected technocrat from the North and a strong supporter of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and the First Lady, Remi Tinubu — invited me to his office. Known nationwide for championing digital literacy and transformation that has empowered training centres and young people, Kashifu came straight to the point: he wanted my professional guidance in building a movement.
Before I could respond, he named it: “Tinubu Must Stay — for Continuity, Stability and Prosperity.”
I asked why the framing was not simply “Tinubu Should Stay.” His explanation was strategic, not sentimental. The movement was intended as a counter-narrative to the “Tinubu Must Go” campaign, which he believed had gained momentum from northern opposition quarters aligned with former Vice President Atiku Abubakar. He needed a response that matched the opposition’s framing without conceding its terms.
He asked me to commit within 24 hours. I requested more time, but he held firm. I told him I would return with an assessment. The question was not whether I supported the President. The question was whether I could support a campaign on terms that were professionally defensible.
I asked my team to run a perception index and sentiment analysis on recent campaigns around the President. Using PRrev — PRNigeria’s cross-platform media monitoring software supported by NITDA — the findings were sobering. Negative sentiment, especially on social media, was not just high; it showed a level of public disaffection that no honest communicator could mask with slogans or rallies.
I then consulted a cohort of young communicators — professionals in their late twenties and early thirties, from different regions and with no political affiliations. I asked if they would support the Tinubu Must Stay campaign. Their initial response was lukewarm. But I pressed further. I asked them to independently assess the administration’s verifiable achievements against the weight of public grievance. What they brought back was more instructive than I anticipated.
They found that Tinubu facilitated the takeoff of new medical universities — not only in the South, but also in Tsafe and Funtua in the North — institutions many Nigerians hardly know exist. They noted hundreds of housing units commissioned across northern states and a marked rise in federation account allocations to states and local governments, funds that previous administrations often diverted into federal intervention schemes like PTF, DFRRI and SURE P. Security improvements were equally notable: new military divisions, acquisition of sophisticated armaments, and better personnel remuneration.
These were concrete, documented, verifiable facts that had not penetrated public consciousness because communication around them had been, to put it mildly, inadequate — buried in technical statistics and figures that ordinary citizens rarely engage with.
Three of the young communicators who had been most reluctant became the most thorough in their research. By the end of the exercise, they joined the movement voluntarily, without inducement. To me, that was more significant than any polling data. It suggested that the deficit was not in the administration’s record — it was in the communication of that record.
When I returned to Kashifu, I recommended that the campaign be strictly evidence-based: facts, data, documented outcomes, and verifiable comparisons. I also cautioned against attacks on opposition personalities and confrontational posturing toward anti-government movements. No hired crowds. No orchestrated demonstrations. No manufactured street energy. No faking.
The forum would contribute intellectual rigour to the national conversation, not spectacle. A communication campaign built on verifiable facts does not need to shout down its critics. It simply needs to be heard.
Then, as I finalised my position, Sowore’s video emerged. My brotherly friend — the man who stood with me when others did not — was now supporting the very movement my professional guidance was retained to counter. I do not know whether he will formally align with the Atiku Abubakar camp, based on endorsements from initial conveners in the North.
As a student and practitioner of public relations, I believe the battle for public opinion in the months ahead will not be won by the side that shouts loudest, marches furthest, or commands the most digital noise. It will be won by the side that builds the most credible narrative around verifiable reality.
If the administration’s achievements are as substantial as the data suggest, then failing to communicate them is a failure of professional execution — not a failure of governance. And that failure can be corrected.
Yushau A. Shuaib is the author of An Encounter with the Spymaster and NIPSS: MNI Versus MNIPR-Tackling Institutional Bullying . Email: [email protected]

title: Sybiha to Wadephul: Ukraine ready for German businesses to be among leaders in accessing Ukrainian technology
body:
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha met with German Federal Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul; they discussed the situation on the battlefield, Ukraine's urgent needs for air defense, and the capability to launch long-range strikes; Sybiha stated his readiness to grant German companies access to Ukrainian defense technologies.
"Andriy Sybiha briefed the German foreign minister on the situation on the battlefield, peace efforts, and Ukraine's defense needs, placing particular emphasis on protecting our airspace and strengthening our capabilities to launch long-range strikes," according to a statement by the Ukrainian Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Telegram on Tuesday evening.
The foreign minister also briefed his German counterpart on Russian attacks on civilians and critical infrastructure. Over the past week, at least 150 people have been killed, and more than 700 have been wounded. At least eight Ukrainian children were killed during the last two massive attacks.
Sybiha said Russia's barbarism and escalating terror require a decisive and principled response, and noted that Ukraine welcomed the EU's largest sanctions package and discussed further steps to increase pressure on Moscow.
"As a leading supporter of Ukraine, Germany should also lead in defense partnerships with Ukrainian companies. We are ready to see German businesses among leaders in access to Ukrainian technology and recovery projects," Sybiha said.
"Our partnership is a two-way street. Ukraine's experience, technology, and resources will contribute to Germany's economic strength and stability. I am grateful to Johann for his personal engagement in developing our strategic partnership," the foreign minister said.

title: Laplace Intelligence red-teams robots and self-driving cars before they hit the real world
body:
If there’s one lesson the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident taught us, it’s that AI agents can be unpredictable.
“Imagine if something like that happened in the physical world,” Howie Sun, CEO and co-founder of Laplace Intelligence , told TechCrunch. “AI agents are moving from computers into the real world, and we don’t really want physical AI to fail in the real world.”
Ann Arbor-based Laplace is building automated red-teaming — essentially, stress-testing a system by deliberately trying to make it fail — for robotics and physical AI. The company is betting that the only way to make sure physical AI is safe is to have AI test it.
“Our goal is to help companies discover and fix problems before deployment — and, over time, build a shared foundation of evidence that customers, insurers, and regulators can trust,” Sun said.
Laplace is one of 20 startups competing in Startup Battlefield 200, the startup pitch competition taking place at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco this week, October 13-15. It will present on the Disrupt Stage Tuesday afternoon , October 13.
Sun, alongside his co-founder and chief scientist Henry Liu, founded Laplace a year ago out of the University of Michigan. Sun has spent the last eight years in academia researching how to challenge autonomous driving AI in simulation. In 2023, he and Liu — his then-PhD adviser — published a paper on the subject that made it onto the cover of the top scientific journal Nature. That’s when the calls started coming in from autonomous vehicle companies interested in implementing their ideas.
“I realized that I wanted to build this and take it from purely academic research into a product that’s useful in the real world,” Sun said.
Using their academic research as a base, Sun and Liu built Laplace, so named for “Laplace’s demon,” an 1814 thought experiment by French scholar Pierre-Simon Laplace, who imagined that if you knew the exact state of everything in the universe, you could predict the future with total precision.
“We are essentially using simulation to predict the real world’s future,” Sun said.
At the startup’s core is a high-fidelity simulation reconstructed from the real world, paired with an AI agent that constantly probes for weaknesses and failure points. The goal is to ensure that any physical AI — be it a robot, autonomous vehicle, or smart city solution — is safe in simulation before it’s deployed in the real world.
The simulation environment is a post-trained version of Nvidia’s Cosmos, an AI world simulation platform, which is grounded in the real world, allowing Laplace to reconstruct anything from an Arizona highway to a Paris pedestrian crossing. Simulations are generated by blending a mesh of different real-world information. A Google Street View image could serve as a reference from which an entire street is generated. But rather than generating something random, the simulator combines real-world map data to re-create an environment that’s true to scale.
Developers can then use language prompts to change the setting in real time, like adding in afternoon traffic. Sun says Laplace pulls real-time traffic and congestion information from navigation providers like TomTom.
Within Laplace’s simulations, not only is the environment simulated, but also the behavior of other actors. For example, during a demo, Sun directed the test agent vehicle to swerve into oncoming traffic. The car it would have hit — or driven through, as is common among some generative world models — moved out of its way to avoid a collision.
“It’s truly an interactive simulation environment,” Sun said. “Everyone is reacting to everything … This is more like a world model with interactive participants.”
While the simulated environment is an important part of Laplace’s product, the real unique selling point is the AI agents the startup is developing to automatically design corner cases (tricky, rare scenarios that could trip up an AI system), moving the human further out of the loop.
“They can design from the news, from police reports on collisions — all kinds of information to actively challenge the autonomous vehicles and other physical AI agents,” Sun said.
Today, autonomous vehicle developers mostly train an AI to handle edge cases using recorded footage that they then turn into a simulation, or by relying on humans to come up with new ideas and design them. While many AV companies have done what Laplace is pitching and started embracing AI to create edge cases for training — self-driving truck company Waabi comes to mind — the need for this kind of technology will really become apparent when we start placing generalized robots in the real world.
“There’s less data on generalized robotics,” Sun said. “No one knows what the edge cases will be in the real world.”
Despite Sun and Liu coming from academia, with no shiny Silicon Valley tech company pedigrees, the two have managed to start generating revenue and even turn a modest profit. Most of the money is coming from autonomous driving use cases, with customers including Texas-based autonomous trucking firm Bot Auto and a major Japanese automotive manufacturer.
Laplace is also working with Nvidia and T-Mobile on a free smart city pilot for San Jose, California, to provide high-level traffic operations. Laplace is also in the early stages of working with partners building humanoid robotics for warehouses.
Most of Laplace’s customer contracts are project-based today, and the company is working toward turning that into recurring revenue. The startup’s near-term goal — which it hopes will be aided by competing at Disrupt — is to raise funds and scale so it can compete with its rivals.
Chief among its rivals is Applied Intuition , a buzzy late-stage startup that’s raised $1.2 billion to date at a $15 billion post-money valuation.
Sun isn’t too worried. He believes Laplace’s core methodology of using AI to test AI is a “new paradigm that changes the testing of physical AI entirely,” turning it into a “dynamic interactive testing process.”
“That will be the biggest moat,” he said.
This article has been updated to clarify Laplace’s relationship with Nvidia.

title: Argentina Takes Falklands Oil Fight to International Tribunal
body:
Oil Prices Plunge 7% as U.S. and Iran Signal Room for Diplomacy
Julianne Geiger is a veteran energy journalist and market analyst with more than a decade of experience covering the global oil and gas sector. Her…
Argentina has moved its fight over Falklands oil from threats to the courtroom, asking an international maritime tribunal to halt development of Sea Lion, the islands’ first commercial oil project.
The government filed for provisional measures with the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea on Tuesday, seeking to stop British-authorized hydrocarbon activity in the Northern Falklands Basin.
The specific project in question is Sea Lion, a 315-million-barrel development operated by Navitas Petroleum with Rockhopper Exploration. The companies reached FID last December and are targeting first oil in 2028. Peak production is expected to be around 50,000 barrels per day.
The UK government said Argentina’s filing does not invalidate licenses issued by the Falkland Islands government or require oil development to stop. Britain will participate in the tribunal proceedings and is also preparing legal measures to protect companies from Argentine sanctions and other domestic enforcement actions.
Argentina has been tightening the screws for weeks.
President Javier Milei warned in September that Argentina would take Britain to the maritime tribunal unless work on Sea Lion stopped. His government has also proposed tougher penalties against companies and individuals involved in oil development around the islands without Argentine authorization.
That pressure has already reached the oilfield-services business.
Halliburton said earlier this month that it would not participate in Sea Lion or other oil and gas development around the Falklands after contacts with Argentine authorities involving potential criminal, civil and regulatory enforcement.
Navitas and Rockhopper have maintained that development will proceed. Navitas CEO Ian Ramsey welcomed Britain’s latest commitment to defend companies involved in the project.
Sea Lion has already spent more than 15 years trying to move from discovery to production, with high development costs and political risk repeatedly complicating the project.
Now the companies have financing, project approval and a 2028 production target.
