title: Home health tests aim to tackle disease before it strikes
body: At-home blood tests that can identify potential health risks years before symptoms emerge are to become more easily available in the UAE as healthcare providers shift their focus from treatment to prevention. Health assessments starting from about Dh200 can offer patients insights into their future risk of disease and the lifestyle changes they can make to potentially prevent or delay its onset. More comprehensive services analyse hundreds of biomarkers, while DNA testing costing several thousand dirhams can provide a directory of detailed genetic information. The growing market reflects a wider push towards preventive healthcare in the UAE, with new government initiatives in Dubai and Abu Dhabi encouraging residents to take greater control of their long-term health. Dubai recently launched the Dubai Longevity Authority to encourage people to live healthier lives, free of chronic disease and mental decline. Abu Dhabi has also put preventive healthcare and pre-emptive screening at the forefront of multiple initiatives implemented by the Abu Dhabi Public Health Centre and the Department of Health Abu Dhabi. Private operators have also stepped up their focus on wellness rather than on responding to ill health. For Dh599 ($163), Aster promises a home assessment that can help identify health risks based on more than 120 biomarkers extracted from a blood test and a urine sample. The test promises a comprehensive, personalised health assessment that could help people make more informed lifestyle decisions. “Once the system has your genetic code and understands what's happening with your microbiome, along with your blood work, it can give a very comprehensive view on where your predispositions may be or some vulnerabilities,” said Alisha Moopen, managing director and chief executive of Aster DM Healthcare. “It can show how you can address them way earlier to delay or prevent them becoming a problem. But in the wider longevity, 80 per cent of the work needs to be done by the individual. “If you have the sleep, nutrition, movement and stress management under control, you can benefit from all the other exciting things science is offering. “People can't go in and sit in a hyperbaric oxygen chamber or talk about doing stem cells or cleansing the blood if you don't have the basics right. Longevity can get you to an amazing health outcome, but just doing the shiny things is throwing away money.” Full body check The service is the latest in a long line aiming to capitalise on the booming demand for longevity medicine. Medcare Hospitals offer a Lab at Home service where qualified technicians visit homes to collect blood and diagnostic samples across Dubai and Sharjah. Elsewhere, Vesta Care and Health 24/7 offer full-body check-ups, vitamin, hormone and thyroid panels, and routine blood tests at your doorstep, delivered by qualified nurses, with results in 24 hours. The tests form part of a wider switch in attitudes towards a more preventive health strategy. Ms Moopen said insurance companies are also beginning to change their approach and support disease prevention. “My father started off the Aster business being reactive to ill people, but today we can't just be a sick care company,” she said. “There are companies that sponsor enhanced insurance plans which think about prevention, we do see employers being a lot more pro-employees' health and managing that much more closely. We're seeing that shift, especially in the UAE.” The recently formed Dubai Longevity Authority is aiming for 31 per cent annual growth in the longevity sector and a Dh35 billion ($9.53 billion) economic boost over the next decade. Experts, however, said it could be difficult for some to buy into the reality of wellness programmes and avoid being blinded by slick marketing campaigns that fail to deliver results. The House of Longevity is a research and community platform hoping to capitalise on demand. The platform translates clinical and scientific research into practical guidance across seven pillars of sleep, movement, nutrition, mental health, preventative care, healthy environments, and purpose. Alex Zagrebelny, founder and CEO of R.Evolution, the company behind the project, said where we live can have a significant impact on how long we live. “Longevity itself is not an industry,” he said. “As prevention, wellbeing and quality of life become greater priorities, existing industries will need to develop new services, products and infrastructure around them. “The sheer volume of claims, often based on different levels of evidence, makes it difficult for consumers to understand what is genuinely supported by science and what is simply good marketing.” Healthy homes Researchers at the non-profit Global Wellness Institute said property focused on health and wellness was on the rise. Global investment has increased from $151 billion in 2017 to $$876 billion in 2025, the report says. While longevity may have become a buzzword in healthcare and real estate, Dr Eli Abirached, an expert in recovery and biohacking at Dubai’s Restore Fitness, said consumers should do their own research into what works for them. “Whenever there is demand, there's always a clever entrepreneur somewhere coming up with the next problem solving and devised path you must take,” he said. “If you do not have it, you are behind everyone else. Fear of missing out is a great selling, anchor. However, when it comes to biohacking (in health), the equation is incredibly simple. “When you get a longevity device or sign up to a programme, if you do not have a reason for getting it, then you’re the sucker.” “If you have a reason, but you're also trying to track the changes that are happening, you've moved from the sucker to adding real value to your life.”

title: UAE universities must change to equip students in AI age, say leaders and students
body: UAE universities must overhaul their courses and teaching methods to keep pace with artificial intelligence and the rapidly changing demands of the jobs market, the acting Minister of Higher Education and Scientific Research has said. Dr Abdulrahman Al Awar called for closer collaboration between universities and industry. He warned that emerging technologies were transforming the skills employers require and creating an urgent need to rethink how students are taught. He was speaking at the Zayed Education Foundation’s Partnerships for the Future event, in Abu Dhabi, where 12 institutions came together to strengthen collaboration and expand opportunities for home-grown scholars. “Economies and job markets are undergoing a radical and rapid change, and it is happening at a very rapid pace,” Dr Al Awar said. “New technologies, including artificial intelligence, are creating new opportunities and changing the skills that the market needs. “Fundamental changes must happen in engaging higher education institutions and economic sectors and redesigning the curricula and the skills of both faculty and students.” He said the ministry’s Outcome-Based Evaluation Framework was challenging universities to meet those demands and become more competitive in shaping the future of higher education in the UAE. “The UAE vision for higher education is centred on creating a vibrant higher education ecosystem that is future-ready, globally competitive and connected to the needs of our students, our economy, and our society,” he said. An updated guidebook for the framework was released earlier this year following consultations involving 735 representatives from higher education institutions across the country. Hopes for future Change has not just been called for from the top, but also by students. The National spoke to two Ruwwad Zayed Scholars about their hopes for the future of higher education. Noor Odeh, a UAE resident from Jordan, is a member of the first cohort of the masters scholars and is studying computational data science at Khalifa University. She scrapped her plans to study at an Australian university to stay in the UAE. “I want to be a changemaker. So it's not just the degree that I got excited about when I was accepted [for the scholarship]. It was more that will get to do something for my community because I will receive guidance,” she said. She believes the future of higher education will rely on hands-on experiences and skills rather than grades and metrics. “We need to put less focus on numbers like GPA [grade point average], and more about the skills that you're learning. What has helped me the most was not just the knowledge that I got from my degree, but the skills that I gained,” Ms Odeh said. Fellow Ruwwad Zayed Scholar Jassem Alkhoori is studying digital transformation at Zayed University. He agrees that higher education needs to be agile and keep pace with technological development. “I think currently the education system follows guidelines that are very outdated. Now that AI is actually overtaking most simple tasks such as screening papers, I think there should be more education on how to use these tools to help with research,” he told The National . Hidden talents The push for a competitive higher education sector has accelerated in recent years and has taken major steps since the founding of the country's first university, the United Arab Emirates University, 50 years ago. Zayed Education Foundation hopes to create opportunities for 100,000 students by 2035 and recently announced the first cohort of 50 Ruwwad Zayed Scholars – exceptional Emirati and Arab students who will pursue master’s degrees at universities in the UAE. Saeed Al Nazari, secretary general of the Great Arab Minds initiative – which recognises and empowers exceptional Arab scholars, scientists and innovators – told The National that the talented minds from the region must be nurtured. “With whatever happening around us – conflicts, news, social media, AI – sometimes we even forget to look up to our people in this region who are doing brilliant stuff,” he said. “This region has always been part of the momentum to move educational research forward globally. The good thing is that we have so many people who are willing to invest in knowledge economy. We just sometimes need to connect the dots.”

title: Fubara Commends IGP Disu’s Professionalism During Political Crisis In Rivers
body: Rivers State Governor, Siminalayi Fubara, has commended the Inspector-General of Police, Olatunji Disu, for his professionalism and commitment to duty while serving as Commissioner of Police in Rivers State during a period of political crisis. The Governor spoke at Government House, Port Harcourt, on Tuesday, when the IGP, accompanied by senior police officers, including Commissioners of Police from Rivers, Bayelsa and the Eastern Port Command, as well as heads of sister security agencies, paid him a courtesy visit. Governor Fubara expressed delight at Disu’s elevation, recalling how he discharged his responsibilities despite the difficult circumstances at the time. “While he was here as a Commissioner, he was here at the peak of crisis. But I can tell you that he did his work, not minding the situation. He tried as much as he could to balance all the areas.” The Governor said Disu’s performance in Rivers State demonstrated the value of professionalism and earned him recognition, describing his return as Inspector-General of Police as a moment of pride. “I feel very happy that somebody who left here in a very difficult situation, in a very trying time, did wonderfully well is here today visiting us in a higher capacity.” Governor Fubara also wished the IGP success in addressing the country’s security challenges, particularly with the 2027 general elections approaching. He expressed confidence that Disu would overcome the challenges ahead and prayed for greater success in his new position. Earlier, IGP Disu said his visit combined attendance at the book launch of retired Deputy Inspector-General of Police Dame Stella Obuoforibo Okuyiga (formerly Opuiyo) with an opportunity to return to Rivers State, where he previously served as Commissioner of Police. He said Dame Okuyiga (formerly Opuiyo) was among the first 20 women to join the Nigeria Police Force, describing her as an important figure in the history of the police and Rivers State. “I’m here in this wonderful state, this wonderful city, today to attend the launch of a book presented by Dame Stella Obuoforibo Okuyiga, a retired Deputy Inspector-General of Police, who was among the first set of 20 women to join the Nigerian Police Force,” the IGP told the governor. The IGP also thanked the Governor and the people of Rivers State for their cooperation and support during his previous assignment. He noted that effective policing requires collaboration with the state government and other security agencies. “Without the cooperation of the state government, without the cooperation of the Governor, the job of policing will be very, very difficult,” he said. Disu expressed appreciation for the assistance given to the police and other security agencies, saying the support contributed to maintaining peace in the state. In September 2026, the memoirs of Dame Stella Obuoforibo Okuyiga (formerly Opuiyo), titled “Origin of Policewomen in Nigeria and My Journey in the Nigeria Police Force (1955–1986)”, were published, capturing her trailblazing career as one of Nigeria’s first 20 pioneering female police officers. The post Fubara Commends IGP Disu’s Professionalism During Political Crisis In Rivers appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Tinubu transmits bills on genocide, war crimes prosecution to House of Reps
body:
President Bola Tinubu has transmitted two bills to the House of Representatives seeking to strengthen Nigeria’s legal framework for prosecuting genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.
The bills, which were forwarded to the House for consideration, seek to domesticate key international legal instruments and establish provisions for punishing serious international crimes under Nigerian law.
The president’s letter, dated 6 October and addressed to the Speaker of the House, Abbas Tajudeen, was read during plenary on Tuesday.
Titled “Transmission of the Geneva Conventions and Additional Protocols Bill, 2026 and the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (Enforcement) Bill, 2026 for consideration”, the letter invoked Section 58(2) of the 1999 Constitution, as amended.
“Pursuant to Section 58(2) of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (as amended), I forward herewith the Geneva Conventions and Additional Protocols Bill, 2026 and the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (Enforcement) Bill, 2026 for the kind consideration of the House of Representatives,” Mr Tinubu said.
According to the president, the Geneva Conventions and Additional Protocols Bill seeks to repeal the existing Geneva Conventions Act, Cap. G3, Laws of the Federation of Nigeria, 2004, and give effect to the four Geneva Conventions of 12 August 1949 and two Additional Protocols adopted on 8 June 1977.
The Geneva Conventions establish rules for the protection of people during armed conflicts, including wounded and sick members of armed forces, prisoners of war and civilians. The Additional Protocols expand these protections and provide further rules governing the conduct of hostilities.
The proposed legislation would update Nigeria’s domestic legal framework for implementing these international humanitarian law obligations.
The second bill, the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (Enforcement) Bill, 2026, seeks to give effect to the Rome Statute, which established the International Criminal Court (ICC).
The proposed law would provide for the enforcement and punishment of genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and related offences in Nigeria. It would also establish a legal basis for Nigeria to cooperate with the ICC in carrying out its mandate.
Genocide generally involves acts committed with the intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group. Crimes against humanity involve certain widespread or systematic attacks against civilian populations, while war crimes are serious violations of the laws governing armed conflict.
The ICC prosecutes individuals accused of these crimes when the conditions for its jurisdiction are met. The proposed Nigerian legislation seeks to strengthen the country’s capacity to address such offences through its domestic legal system while facilitating cooperation with the international court.
Mr Tinubu urged the House to consider the bills expeditiously.
“While I trust that the House of Representatives will consider the request expeditiously, please accept, Rt. Hon. Speaker, the assurances of my highest regards,” the president said.
The bills will now be subject to legislative consideration by the National Assembly.

title: How the Russian army is learning from Ukraine and NATO
body:
British army soldiers work at a command post during the Allied Spirit 25 military exercise at the U.S. Army’s Hohenfels training area in Hohenfels, Germany, on March 12, 2025. (Alex Kraus/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The Russian army entered its full-scale war against Ukraine with a reputation as one of the strongest in the world, but the first weeks of the invasion showed that this assessment was wrong. The reasons were sought in logistics, equipment, training, and motivation, but most of the failures stemmed from an inability to make sound decisions on the battlefield.
The Russian army found itself in a war in which commanders had to operate in situations where orders from above were either absent or no longer reflected battlefield conditions.
This was when the fundamental problems with Russian military education became clear. For decades, it had trained officers to carry out tactical tasks and work with staff documents, but not to think and act independently.
In this respect, Russian and Western ( NATO ) military training systems differ in ways that go far beyond methods and training procedures. They reflect different command cultures and, consequently, different views of a commander's role in modern warfare, and we saw this firsthand in our study.
One of the core ideas of NATO's military doctrine is mission command, a command philosophy built on trust, a shared understanding of the mission, and disciplined initiative by commanders at every level.
A senior commander defines the objective, intent, and key constraints but does not attempt to prescribe every step their subordinates must take, leaving them free to choose how to accomplish the mission in response to the situation.
This allows decisions to be made at the level with the clearest understanding of conditions on the ground, without depending on constant instructions from above.
The Ukrainian Defense Forces have recently been moving more decisively toward this kind of command culture. This is clearly reflected in the Leadership Principles recently issued by Ukraine's Commander-in-Chief.
The principles identify an understanding of the commander's intent, initiative, responsibility, the development of subordinates, and the ability to learn and adapt as key leadership requirements.
Essentially, the goal is to build a culture in which a lower-level commander does not wait for detailed instructions at every step but acts on a clear understanding of the mission and takes responsibility for the outcome.
The Russian military tradition, by contrast, has historically followed the opposite logic: rigid centralized control inherited from the Soviet military school and rooted in the state's broader autocratic culture of governance.
Western researchers call this a top-down command system and argue that it leaves lower-level commanders with virtually no ability to make decisions independently. Its weaknesses were evident early in the full-scale war, including during the battle for Hostomel Airport, the crossing of the Siverskyi Donets River, and the deployment of Russian equipment at the Chornobaivka airfield.
Waiting for orders from above, units lost time or repeated actions that were clearly doomed to fail.
No command philosophy can work without institutions to support it. For mission command, that institution is the professional non-commissioned officer (NCO) corps.
In NATO armies, NCOs serve as the backbone connecting officers with enlisted personnel. They train subordinates, pass on practical experience, maintain discipline, and carry out much of the day-to-day leadership.
NCOs also build the trust that mission command requires, which is why particular attention is paid to their training and expanded authority. The Russian army is far less suited to this model.
Duties assigned to NCOs in NATO armies have traditionally been performed in the Russian military by junior officers, primarily lieutenants commanding platoons. In this system, sergeants have little scope for leadership or mentorship. Their job is to follow orders and handle organizational matters.
This creates a problem for the Russian army when it comes to delegating initiative to lower levels: sergeants and junior commanders are not trusted to act independently in complex situations. This is particularly paralyzing for combat units when conditions change rapidly.
The differences between NATO and Russian military training models are also evident in how they approach learning from mistakes. NATO places greater emphasis on critical thinking, operating amid uncertainty, and analyzing outcomes.
The main methodology is the After Action Review (AAR), a structured review conducted after a training exercise or operation. It revolves around four questions: "What was planned?", "What happened?", "What worked and what didn't?", and "What should change?" The essential condition for this approach is the ability to discuss mistakes honestly without fear of punishment, so that lessons can be learned and improvements identified.
The Russian system also has mechanisms for analyzing combat experience. Its biggest problem, however, lies in the logic of its top-down management system, which tends to punish "failures." This is why there is so much lying and embellishment in reports sent up the chain of command: admitting a mistake means facing punishment.
The result is distorted information reaching senior leadership, an unwillingness to take initiative at lower levels, and a growing fear of deviating from instructions — all of which directly contradict mission command.
Russian officers themselves acknowledge this problem. In 2023, the journal Military Thought (Voennaya Mysl) published the results of a survey of more than 100 artillery officers, most of them at the tactical level. About 81% had combat experience. Only 12% of respondents favored a policy of "intelligent initiative."
Among the obstacles, 40% cited "excessive micromanagement and commanders' distrust of subordinates," while only 30% supported a ban on punishing unsuccessful initiatives. The researchers also identified a problem with military education: the concept of "initiative" is absent even from the document governing educational activities at Russian Defense Ministry universities.
It would be convenient to reduce the differences in military training to the formula "flexible NATO vs. inflexible Russia," but the war in Ukraine has shown that reality is more complex.
The Russian armed forces are capable of learning and adapting their tactics fairly quickly under pressure. Even in Russia's public discourse, military analysts have openly reflected on the Russian military's key mistakes.
After suffering losses in 2022, Russian forces restructured their logistics in response to HIMARS strikes, changed how they used armored vehicles in response to the threat posed by FPV drones, integrated commercial (unmanned aerial vehicles) UAVs into reconnaissance on a massive scale, shortened the "detect-to-strike" cycle, and began using small assault groups more extensively.
These groups have created considerable problems for Ukrainian commanders by infiltrating the rear of Ukrainian forces.
Adaptation has also become visible at the personnel level. There have been more cases of junior commanders identifying the most experienced and motivated soldiers among their subordinates and informally transferring some responsibility to them.
Some principles resembling mission command are being absorbed less through doctrine than through the pressures of war itself.
The fastest changes are taking place in technology and specific combat procedures. Russia is developing command, control, communications, computers, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance systems (C4ISR), training UAV operators, and transferring front-line experience into its higher education system.
Military educational institutions — including the Mikhailovskaya Military Artillery Academy, the Military Academy of Air Defense, the Military Academy of Communications, and the Military University of Radioelectronics — are adjusting their curricula, testing new equipment, and maintaining contact with graduates who have combat experience.
Particularly telling is that military education in Russia is no longer limited to professional military training but is increasingly penetrating the general education system. At the same time, its ideological and propagandistic component is spreading even into preschool education.
Of course, these "cosmetic changes" do not mean that the Russian army will become like Western armies. Its most fundamental difference remains its attitude toward service members. The value placed on their lives and expertise remains low.
The Soviet model continues to serve as the benchmark for a victorious army.
The Soviet command sacrificed 27 million people in the war against Nazism. The principle of "we won't spare any expense" — a Russian expression meaning that no price is too high — makes the system even more dangerous.
Russia could build an even harsher model of military training adapted to modern warfare, combining new technologies, total control, and a generation of ideologically conditioned soldiers whom it will readily throw into new wars.

Liubov Tsybulska is a strategic communications expert and a leading authority on hybrid threats in Ukraine. As the founder and current director of NGO "Join Ukraine," she leverages her extensive expertise to address critical national security challenges. Previously, she served as the inaugural Head of the Centre for Strategic Communication and Information Security under Ukraine's Ministry of Culture and Information Policy.

title: Massive fire at industrial plant in Russia's Rostov Oblast spreads to 9,000 square meters
body:
A massive fire broke out at an industrial plant that produces parts for specialized vehicles in Russia's Rostov Oblast on Oct. 13, spreading across 9,000 square meters, Russia's Emergency Situations Ministry reported.
The blaze erupted at warehouses on the premises of the Aksaykardandetal plant in the town of Aksay, near Rostov-on-Don . A warehouse wall collapsed as the fire spread, according to Russian state-controlled news agency Interfax.
The Aksaykardandetal plant manufactures drive shafts and metal components for agricultural and specialized machinery. The facility also has metalworking capabilities, including stamping and heat treatment, which could potentially be used to manufacture components for military equipment .
The ministry said firefighters received a report of a fire at a warehouse storing plastic products at 4:10 p.m. local time. Personnel were evacuated from the premises.
According to the ministry, 98 emergency personnel and 36 vehicles were deployed to combat the blaze. Strong winds and large quantities of flammable materials complicated firefighting efforts.
Footage shared by the Telegram channel Exilenova+ showed thick columns of black smoke rising above the area. Another video showed local residents lining up at a gas station as smoke from the fire filled the sky in the background.
The cause of the fire remains unclear. The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the claims.

title: Obaasima Summit: ‘AI is not a spiritual attack’ — Rev. Dr. Ofori-Boateng urges young women to embrace technology
body: Young women have been urged to embrace artificial intelligence (AI) and continuous learning as technology reshapes the world, with an Anglican priest cautioning against interpreting AI as a spiritual threat. Director of Programmes for the Anglican Diocese of Accra, Rev. Dr. Akua Buabema Ofori-Boateng, gave the advice at the 2026 Obaasima Summit, where speakers encouraged young women to prepare for leadership and build on the achievements of previous generations. She said the rapid pace of technological change made lifelong learning essential for anyone seeking to remain relevant and effective in leadership. “Embrace lifelong learning. I hold many degrees, and I’m still learning,” she said. Rev. Dr. Ofori-Boateng stressed that academic qualifications should be viewed as the beginning, rather than the end, of the learning process. “Your education does not end when you walk across the stage and they hand you a certificate. It begins there because the world is changing rapidly, and those who lead the world never stop being students,” she said. Citing artificial intelligence as an example of a technology young women need to understand, she urged them to approach it with openness rather than fear. “So, for instance, AI is here. And let me tell you on my authority as a priest, AI is not a spiritual attack,” she added. Gomashie challenges women on values and mentorship Meanwhile, Minister for Tourism, Culture and Creative Arts Abla Dzifa Gomashie challenged women to reflect on the values, knowledge and principles they pass on to younger generations. She questioned whether the lessons being imparted to young people were appropriate for their development and whether the recipients were prepared to learn from them. “Teach a child the way they should grow. And when they grow, they will not depart from it. But what are we passing on now? And those we are passing the things on to, are they ready to receive it?” she asked. Drawing on the familiar analogy of leading a donkey to water without being able to force it to drink, the minister highlighted the limits of guidance when the person receiving it is unwilling to learn. Her remarks underscored the role of mentorship and personal responsibility in preparing younger generations to take up leadership positions. Women leaders share experiences The summit also featured contributions from former Electoral Commissioner Charlotte Osei, Administrator of the Ghana Medical Trust Fund Secretariat Obuobia Darko-Opoku, and Special Aide to President John Dramani Mahama Joyce Bawa Mogtari. The speakers shared experiences from their professional journeys and encouraged young women to develop their abilities, overcome barriers and take advantage of opportunities to contribute to national development. Founded by Ama Pratt, Press Secretary and Spokesperson to the Vice President, the summit was held under the theme, “Legacy and Leadership: Ghanaian Women Shaping the Past, Guiding the Future.” The event focused on sustaining the contributions of women in leadership while equipping younger generations with the knowledge, values and skills needed to carry that legacy forward.

title: Ekiti recruits 8,358 workers, generates N88.4bn IGR in four years – Gov Oyebanji
body:
The Ekiti State Governor, Biodun Oyebanji, on Tuesday, disclosed that the state government has employed no fewer than 8,358 workers into the state civil service, local governments, security outfits, among others in the last four years.
He also said that the state generated N88.4 billion as the Internally Generated Revenue (IGR) in the last four years.
Mr Oyebanji spoke while delivering the state of the state address at the Ekiti State House of Assembly complex, in Ado Ekiti, the state capital.
The governor, who said that the economy of Ekiti State continues to hold an exciting promise in all ramifications, added that a quick summary of Ekiti’s GDP performance from the recently released NBS Report indicates that the overall State GDP moved from 2.4 trillion in 2019 to 4.6 trillion in 2023, a growth of 90 per cent.
He said recent projections suggest that Ekiti GDP now inches towards the N8.8 trillion mark.
“This has moved Ekiti from the 33rd position to the 28th since APC was given the mandate to govern the state. Similarly, our contribution to the national GDP grew from 1.3 per cent to 1.6 per cent. Apparently, our economy is largely driven by trade, which contributed 1.7 trillion (37 per cent) and agriculture, which contributed 1.05 trillion (23 per cent). Both sectors contribute 60 per cent to the state’s economy,” he said.
On the employment created in the past four years, the governor said, “Since we assumed office, we have employed qualified persons in strategic places of need. The Civil Service Commission employed 41 senior officers in 2025 and the Office of Establishment and Service Matters has employed 340 junior officers.
“Similarly, the Local Government Service Commission also employed 774 persons to fill consequential vacancies in 2025. So far, this administration has employed 6,530 teachers into both the public primary and secondary schools in the state. We employed 3,530 into the Teaching Service Commission and 3,000 into the State Universal Basic Education Board.
“In the security sector, we employed another set of personnel numbering over 600 to join the Ametokun Corps and the newly created Agro Marshal Corps, respectively, while Ekiti State Traffic Management Agency also took in an additional 73 traffic officers,” he said.
Speaking on the state IGR, Mr Oyebanji said when he took over in 2022, the average IGR of the state hovered around N650 million to N700 million monthly, totaling N8.7 billion in 2022, and that by the end of 2023, it had surged to N12 billion.
“The trend continued in 2024 with a reconciled figure of N17.6 billion; in 2025, we grossed N27.1 billion. As at the last reconciliation in June this year, we have already attained N15.6 billion, with all indications that we would near the N32billion mark at the end of the year, as we currently do average of N2.6 billion monthly.
“The growth per year indicated 38 per cent in 2023, 47% in 2024, 53 per cent in 2025 and about 60 per cent in 2026. Cumulatively speaking, we have generated the sum of N88.4billion as IGR in the last four years.
“The independent data from the Joint Revenue Board confirmed that 2025 was an exceptional year for Ekiti State’s revenue administration. The state grew Internally Generated Revenue (IGR) by 62.13 per cent, faster than any other state in the South-west and faster than 26 other States and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT).
“We increased our share of the national Internally Generated Revenue (IGR) and now fund a third of our total expenditure from our IGR. We hope to maintain this momentum going forward.
The governor attributed the achievements to the institutional re-organisation, transformation of the tax administration and improved business environment.
“All of this is possible because of the impact of the institutional re-organisation, digital transformation of tax administration, expansion of the tax net and improved business environment.
“It is for this reason that we have intentionally given more attention to trade, investment and agriculture since they have proved to be areas of our comparative advantage. With our deliberate investment in aviation and tourism, we hope to further diversify our economic base in the new tenure,” he said.

title: SpaceX and Google both said no. Now his software is riding a SpaceX rocket next to Google’s
body:
The way Rama Afullo tells it, he saw orbital data centers coming.
The Kenyan American engineer previously worked in Google’s cloud computing business before a brief stint at SpaceX’s Starlink communications network in 2024. His experiences convinced him that there was untapped potential for computers in space.
“When I was at SpaceX, I tried to pitch this internally. They said no. When I was at Google, I tried to pitch this internally. They said no,” he tells TechCrunch.
So he left SpaceX and co-founded Satlyt , a new company with headquarters in Sunnyvale, California, and Nairobi, to build software for satellites that he hopes will let many satellites share the work of large computing jobs in space. The company has raised an $8 million seed round, Afullo exclusively told TechCrunch.
The timing looks good for him. SpaceX has since gone all-in on orbital data centers, and Satlyt’s software is set to launch Thursday on a SpaceX rocket alongside the first prototype for Google’s space data center effort, Project Suncatcher.
Unlike SpaceX, Google, or startups like Starcloud and Cowboy Space Company, Satlyt isn’t planning to build its own spacecraft. Afullo’s team is building the software to operate AI models on satellites, comparing his approach to VMware and Snowflake — companies whose platforms let users run complex software without worrying about the underlying infrastructure.
“The folks like SpaceX who are doing orbital data centers — if they are the iPhone, we’ll build Android as a horizontally integrated, open ecosystem,” he said. In other words, Satlyt wants to offer software that works across many companies’ satellites.
Satlyt has already flown its software on two demonstration missions. The initial focus is finding operational efficiencies for spacecraft, which typically depend on flight controllers on the ground to solve any problems that arise. Sending data back to Earth, known as downlink, is expensive and often slow, so using AI to make decisions on the spacecraft can mean real savings, either when resolving anomalies or by processing sensor readings on the spacecraft instead of on the ground.
Earlier this year, Satlyt deployed Google DeepMind’s Gemma AI model onboard a spacecraft operated by Momentus. The model cut the size of a transmission about onboard software errors by more than 60%, the kind of efficiency that Afullo says can save hundreds of thousands of dollars per satellite each year.
A launch will put Satlyt’s software to work onboard a spacecraft built by TakeMe2Space, an Indian startup that builds computing hardware for satellites. The mission involves three customers: NASA, which is paying the company to test protocols for cloud computing in space; Stellerian, a startup focused on space surveillance (tracking objects in orbit) that wants to test image processing workloads; and TakeMe2Space itself, to show the satellite can host other companies’ software.
Right now, few high-powered GPUs are in orbit. For now, the most likely opportunity lies in the kinds of workloads Satlyt is working on. But the company’s next project is to show that it can create a shared computing system — a cloud — spanning two different satellites, which it expects to attempt next year. If successful, it will allow the company to build a true compute cloud in orbit as a third-party provider to spacecraft builders.
The way to think about it is that we turn your satellite into a revenue-generating managed service,” Afullo said.
Satlyt’s seed round was led by Houston-based Non Sibi Ventures, where partner Bernard Harris, who served as a NASA astronaut for more than 20 years, helped ground the firm’s conviction in a novel, space-based business.
One reason the firm invested was that Satlyt doesn’t depend on a highest-octane vision of space data centers, which faces uncertain economics and a launch bottleneck. “We don’t need data centers in space for Rama to be wildly successful, right?” Non Sibi partner Kent Lucas told TechCrunch. “It can just be driven by the number of satellites going up.”
Afullo’s hope is to be live on 20% of satellites by the end of the decade, when he expects virtually every spacecraft builder to be putting GPUs and similar advanced processors in their satellites.
“If you’re putting up a satellite without putting up a GPU on it, at the very least, you’re doing yourself a disservice, right?” he says.
This story was originally published on October 1. Satlyt is among dozens of other startups vetted by TechCrunch and appearing at Disrupt as part of our broader Battlefield competition happening this week in downtown San Francisco. It all kicks off on Tuesday. Learn more here .

title: Dangote Swings to $4.7 Billion Profit Ahead of Africa’s Biggest IPO
body:
Oil Prices Plunge 7% as U.S. and Iran Signal Room for Diplomacy
Julianne Geiger is a veteran energy journalist and market analyst with more than a decade of experience covering the global oil and gas sector. Her…
Nigeria’s Dangote refinery has gone from losing money to posting a $4.73 billion profit in less than a year, just as it asks investors for $1.6 billion in what would be Africa’s largest IPO.
Dangote Petroleum Refinery reported net profit of $4.73 billion for the first nine months of 2026, reversing a $117.2 million loss during the same period last year.
Revenue more than doubled to $22.48 billion from $9.19 billion. EBITDA jumped to $5.52 billion from $627.6 million as the refinery processed more crude and captured higher refining margins.
Disruptions to Middle Eastern refining and fuel exports sent product margins sharply higher this year, particularly for diesel and jet fuel. Dangote increased exports into those shortages, including jet fuel shipments to Western Europe.
The 700,000-barrel-per-day refinery generated $3.68 billion in operating cash flow through September, compared with $364.7 million a year earlier. Cash holdings reached $6.69 billion.
Its balance sheet has moved just as quickly. Dangote finished the period with $650.8 million in net cash after carrying $1.73 billion in net debt a year earlier.
Those numbers landed in the middle of the refinery’s IPO.
Dangote is seeking to raise $1.6 billion in an offering that values the refinery at roughly $47 billion . The subscription period, originally scheduled to close October 13, has been extended through October 27 after heavy investor demand overwhelmed some Nigerian investment platforms when the offering opened.
The money is earmarked partly for Dangote’s next expansion.
The company wants to double refining capacity to 1.4 million bpd by 2029, which would put the Lagos complex among the world’s largest refineries. Dangote has already increased capacity from its original 650,000 bpd and was running near 660,000 bpd earlier this year.
The refinery has also cut West Africa’s dependence on imported fuel, with Nigerian product exports increasingly displacing barrels that previously arrived from Europe, the Middle East and the United States.
A year ago, Dangote was still absorbing commissioning costs. Nine months into 2026, it has $4.73 billion in profit, $6.69 billion in cash, and investors lining up for a piece of it.

title: Herzog honors Israel Bonds for raising billions post-Oct 7 while mourning northern school tragedy
body: The festive ceremony celebrating the conferring of the Presidential Medal of Honor on Israel Bonds was overshadowed on Monday evening by the tragic outcome of a school excursion in the North in which one pupil was killed, and 23 students and teachers were lightly to critically wounded.President Isaac Herzog, in his address to the International Leadership Delegation of Israel Bonds, said that he could not begin without offering a prayer for the safety of the pupils and the speedy recovery of the wounded.Israel Bonds, whose official title is the Development Corporation for Israel, is a vital component in Israel's economic engine,Over the years, it has invested $58 billion in Israel's economy – with $1b. invested in the first month following the October 7 catastrophe. Since then, an additional $8.5b. has been raised. The organization keeps breaking its own records.Harking back to the beginnings of Israel Bonds, in which Herzog's uncle Abba Eban – then Israel's ambassador to the United States – played a prominent role, Herzog said that the founders had created the organization with multiple motivations in mind, the first being to generate financial support for the nascent state.Israel Bonds sold in US, Canada, Europe, Central AmericaIsrael's founders saw in post-war America “a nation as generous as its vast landscapes, committed to fighting for freedom, prosperity, and liberty for all. They saw a devoted Jewish community aching to be connected to the redemption of the Land of Israel after 2,000 years of yearning from afar, and they saw an opportunity to deepen the ties of friendship with the American people through these coupons and interest-bearing bonds,” Herzog said, adding that the success of Israel Bonds had exceeded their wildest dreams.Although Israel Bonds were originally primarily sold in the United States, it did not take long for the organization to expand its activities to Canada, Europe, and Central America.Among members of the International Leadership Delegations were representatives from the US, Mexico, Canada, the UK, other European countries, and several Latin American nations.In commending the work of Israel Bonds Global President and CEO Dani Naveh, a former health minister, Herzog commented that they had been friends since they served in the same unit in the army. He hastened to add that this was not the reason that he was presenting Naveh with the medal.Noting the relationship between Israel Bonds and the US, Herzog said: “Throughout the years, the United States has proved to be our most steadfast, our  most important friend and ally; and the Israel Bonds provided an anchor of support throughout.”  Listing some of the areas in which proceeds from Israel Bonds have been utilized, Herzog cited construction, the development of infrastructure, and advancements in science and technology, and he declared Israel Bonds to be a vital network of support during times of crisis.Herzog criticizes Nobel Prize committee“This has never been more evident than in the last few years of uncertainty, of loss here in Israel since October 7,” he said.Herzog also used the occasion to criticize the ignoble decision by the Nobel Prize committee to award the Nobel Peace Prize to Navi Pillay, whom he characterized as “one of the leading proponents of the genocide lie.” To reward her for her so-called efforts  'to promote peace and international law' was, in Herzog's perception, “a cynical decision by the Nobel Committee which celebrates a shameful display of moral erosion and is an affront to any life-affirming, peace-loving people, particularly the victims and survivors of the October 7 murders.”Naveh said that his Holocaust survivor mother, who died recently at the age of 101, used to worry that he and Israel Bonds in general were working too hard.  She wondered if what they did was appreciated by the Israeli population.  After being honored by the No. 1 citizen of Israel, Naveh said he could finally assure his mother that the work was appreciated. He emphasized that the honor bestowed by the president belonged to every single person who had ever invested in Israel Bonds, regardless of how much or how little.Naveh also mentioned that he had launched a special campaign with instant results on October 7. He had not waited for a day or a week to pass. In addition, he expressed appreciation to the Finance Ministry for its long-standing cooperation.Dr. Andrew Hutter, US and International Chairman of the Board of Directors of Israel Bonds, said that over the years, he had shaken many hands and received many awards, but nothing compared to shaking the hand of the president of Israel, in his official residence, and receiving the Presidential Medal of Honor.“This was more emotional than I anticipated,” he said.A short Israel Bonds film was screened. Naveh said that there had been photographs from the launch in New York by Israel's founding prime minister David Ben-Gurion, but no movies until AI became available.The film opens with Ben-Gurion and Albert Einstein sitting on a park bench, discussing their individual visions for the future. All of a sudden, a young woman appears out of nowhere. Einstein asks who she is, while Ben-Gurion goes off to do one of his favorite things – to stand on his head – this time, wearing a suit and not in his swimming trunks.The mysterious woman takes Einstein time-traveling through Israel's crisis periods when Israel Bonds consistently came to the rescue. The punchline involves Einstein remarking that he would have to rewrite his Theory of Relativity

title: Luxembourg's excuse for de-listing Russian oligarch Mikhail Fridman fails to convince
body:
LUXEMBOURG — Luxembourg's prime minister defended his government's September push to delist Mikhail Fridman from EU sanctions in the country's parliament on Oct. 12, primarily by showing a lack of awareness of EU rules.
In September, the EU took the controversial decision to delist two Russian oligarchs, Mikhail Fridman and Alisher Usmanov , after a threat by France, Luxembourg, and Slovakia to otherwise let all 3,000 of the bloc's Russia sanctions expire.
The sanctions were due for renewal, and that required unanimity to proceed, allowing the three countries to plausibly make this threat.
In Luxembourg's foreign affairs committee, whose meetings are not made publicly accessible, Prime Minister Luc Frieden justified the move in terms of national interest, two lawmakers, Franz Fayot from the social democrats and Sam Tanson from the green party, told the Kyiv Independent.
Frieden said that the national interest was to try and make an arbitration case initiated by Fridman for $16 billion go away, "given the exceptionally high amount of his claim relative to Luxembourg's national budget," Tanson explained.
With Slovakia pushing for the delisting of Usmanov and Fridman, and France doubling down specifically over Usmanov, Frieden explained to lawmakers that he made the "opportunistic" calculation that getting Fridman delisted now might cause him to drop the arbitration and thus benefit Luxembourg in the long run, Fayot said.
However, as Fayot and Tanson explained and Luxembourg's leading newspaper the Luxemburger Wort also reported, there was no contact between the Luxembourgish government with Fridman or his legal team, and so far, that arbitration proceeding has not been withdrawn.
"Luxembourg appears willing to weaken the EU sanctions regime in response to a potentially enormous financial liability without having established that delisting would eliminate it," Tanson said.
The move might even have weakened Luxembourg's case in any eventual arbitration proceeding, Fayot added.
This could be interpreted as an "admission that Luxembourg had a say ... contrary to what was pretended," Fayot said.
Frieden's fears also do not hold ground, given the EU clarifying with every sanctions package that countries do not have to abide by any legal ruling to compensate sanctioned Russian companies or individuals if sanctions are the reason a deal or contract could not be carried out.
A European Commission spokesperson told the Kyiv Independent that the EU's sanctions regulations include a "no-claims clause" to that effect, adding that the latest sanctions packages included a range of additional safeguards to allow those who uphold sanctions to recover damages incurred in doing so.
However, that did not stop Frieden from saying there was "no solidarity at EU level for any damage," Fayot said.
Tanson told the Kyiv Independent that the solidarity question was not discussed in detail, but that it appears to be "the government's general position ... that Luxembourg would have to bear the financial burden alone if it were ordered to pay compensation."
Tanson explicitly asked Frieden about EU rules that would protect Luxembourg from having to compensate Fridman after a future court ruling, to which he replied "he was not aware of such a rule," an exchange also confirmed by Fayot.
The Kyiv Independent asked Prime Minister Frieden's head of communications about these comments and asked for a reaction but had not received any response at the time of publication.
The Luxemburger Wort also reported that Luxembourg's Bilateral Investment Treaty (BIT) with Russia was cited as a basis for having to respect the ruling of an arbitration in Fridman's favor.
In comments made separately to the Luxemburger Wort, Tanson said she asked if it would not make sense to terminate the treaty, but that Foreign Minister Xavier Bettel opposes this.
In the EU, there have been some conversations about a coordinated ending of the bloc's BITs with Russia , of which 17 still exist, but even so the comments made by the EU about an obligation to not comply with legal rulings that undermine sanctions also extends to these treaties.
Instead, Fayot told the Kyiv Independent that he fears Luxembourg has "set a dangerous precedent," as other Russian oligarchs may push to get the same treatment.
The move "weakens the position of smaller countries," and risks creating a "regulatory chill" Fayot warned.
"If a single (small) member state can be put under sufficient financial pressure through judicial or arbitration proceedings to push for an individual's delisting, this risks undermining the entire sanctions system," Tanson said.
Tanson added that the sanctions delistings send the "wrong signal to both Russia and Ukraine."
For her, the move tells Moscow that EU unity is fragile, and for Ukraine, "it raises serious questions about the reliability of European support."
Fayot also said "he's sure the Ukrainians aren't crazy about this," a fact confirmed shortly after the committee meeting.
That same morning, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha met with Prime Minister Frieden , then immediately headed for a meeting of EU foreign ministers, where he told journalists "our position is that the delisting of the two Russian oligarchs was a wrong step, it was a wrong decision."
"That's why we will propose to impose sanctions on an additional 10 Russian oligarchs. It was a wrong step," Sybiha repeated.

title: Freshworks To Acquire Torii To Expand AI Spend Governance Offerings
body: Nasdaq-listed SaaS major Freshworks has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Torii, a SaaS management platform, to extend its IT service management tool, Freshservice, into AI and software spend governance. The transaction is expected to close in the quarter ending December 2026. Founded in 2017 by Uri Haramati, Uri Nativ and Tal Bereznitskey in New York, Torii helps enterprises track AI consumption at the token level, attribute usage to specific internal teams, forecast spend trajectories, and set operational budget limits. By integrating its SaaS management capabilities into Freshservice, Freshworks aims to enable organisations to have better visibility of their AI usage. The system provides IT and finance departments with continuous oversight, replacing manual spreadsheet reconciliation with real-time analytics. “Modern IT teams are being asked to govern more of the business than ever, with less visibility into what it costs. Freshservice already gives IT one place to see everything they run. With Torii, that same view now extends to software and AI spend — what’s running, who’s using it, and what it costs, so finance and IT stop reconciling spreadsheets and start making decisions together,” said Freshworks CEO and President Dennis Woodside. Founded in 2010 by Girish Mathrubootham and Shanmugam Krishnasamy, Freshworks offers a suite of cloud-based software to help companies manage customer engagement, sales, IT service management and marketing. After Mathrubootham exited the company in 2024, it has sought to reinvent itself as an AI-native enterprise platform under Woodside’s leadership. Apart from introducing AI-led offerings like vertical AI agents and workflow automation tools, it also underwent a major restructuring earlier this year, trimming 11% of its workforce or around 500 employees, citing automation of work. Growing adoption of its AI products helped Freshworks get back into the black in the quarter ended June 2026 . The company reported a net profit of $3.2 Mn as against a net loss of $1.7 Mn in the year-ago period and a net loss of $4.8 Mn in the previous quarter. Meanwhile, its revenue grew 16% YoY to $237.4 Mn. The post Freshworks To Acquire Torii To Expand AI Spend Governance Offerings appeared first on Inc42 Media .

title: Enemy attacks Pavlohrad with drones; one killed, two wounded – administration
body:
Russian occupation forces struck Pavlohrad (Dnipropetrovsk region), killing one civilian, according to Head of the regional military administration Oleksandr Hanzha.
"The enemy attacked Pavlohrad with drones. One person was killed, and two were wounded," he said on Telegram on Tuesday evening.
According to the regional military administration, a fire broke out in the city center.

title: GHS to distribute 80,000 pairs of locally-made protective footwear to health workers
body: The Ghana Health Service (GHS) will distribute 80,000 pairs of protective footwear to health professionals implementing the Free Primary Healthcare programme, following a donation by Sanford, World Shoe Ltd. and Samaritan’s Feet Ghana. The shoes are manufactured in Ghana using lightweight EVA foam and feature antimicrobial properties intended to help prevent infections. They are also designed to be biodegradable. Director-General of the Ghana Health Service, Dr Samuel Kaba Akoriyea, said the Service would work with its regional and district teams to ensure the shoes reach the intended beneficiaries. “We will communicate with our regional and district teams and support a process that is organised, transparent and consistent with the purpose of the donation,” he said. Vice President of Sanford World Clinic, Karoliina Slack, said the initiative was inspired by the sacrifices health workers make, often in facilities with limited equipment and infrastructure. “We wanted to give them a piece of something, a piece of hope, something that they will wear when they go to work, and they remember that across the ocean, in the US, there are lots of people that think of them and value them and understand the sacrifices that they make every day,” she said. Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of World Shoe and Samaritan’s Feet International, Manny Ohonme, said the donation demonstrates how locally manufactured products can address healthcare needs while creating jobs and supporting economic growth. “Our solution is not just about providing the shoes. So the shoes that you saw here today, 80,000, means people are employed,” he said. The organisations say they hope to build on the partnership to attract more stakeholders to support healthcare delivery and improve the well-being of health workers in Ghana.

title: Reps panel backs Tinubu, NNPC, PINL over pipeline security gains
body:
The House of Representatives Committee on Host Communities has passed a vote of confidence in President Bola Tinubu, the management of the Nigerian National Petroleum Company (NNPC) Limited and Pipeline Infrastructure Nigeria Limited (PINL), citing improvements in crude oil recovery and pipeline security.
Chairman of the committee, Dumnamene Dekor (APC, Rivers), announced the resolution on behalf of the lawmakers following the adoption of a subcommittee report on a petition against PINL at a special sitting on Tuesday.
The committee also recommended that the federal government extend PINL’s pipeline surveillance contract after dismissing allegations of financial mismanagement and other improprieties against the company and its Managing Director, Osahon Okunbor, as unsubstantiated.
The decisions followed the adoption of a subcommittee report on a petition against PINL at a special sitting of the committee on Tuesday.
The petition, dated 5 September, was filed by the Niger Delta Oil-Producing Communities Reform Movement (ND-OCRIM), which accused the company of improper contract implementation, mismanagement of contract funds, neglect of surveillance personnel and alleged personal expenditure linked to Mr Okunbor.
The petitioners also called for a forensic review of PINL’s finances.
However, the subcommittee said the petitioners failed to appear despite three invitations issued on 14 September, 22 September and 5 October. It added that they neither sent representatives nor submitted documentary evidence to support their allegations.
PINL appeared before the subcommittee and submitted a written report titled The Impact of PINL Operations on Oil Production and Stability of the Niger Delta, alongside geotagged photographic evidence.
Based on the submissions, the subcommittee concluded that the allegations against the company and its managing director had not been substantiated. It recommended that the committee dismiss the petition and discontinue further investigation into the issues raised.
The report also recommended a vote of confidence in Mr Tinubu, the National Security Adviser, NNPC Limited’s management and the pipeline surveillance contractors covered by the report.
A key finding highlighted in the report was an increase in the proportion of crude oil reaching the Bonny Terminal through the Trans Niger Pipeline (TNP), according to data submitted by PINL.
The company reported that the proportion rose from three per cent in May 2022 to 98 per cent in September 2026.
The subcommittee also noted that “Oil Mining Lease (OML) 11, which had been shut in for 18 months, resumed operations within 90 days of PINL’s engagement.”
It further recorded that 2,049 illegal connections had been remediated and 1,010 illegal refinery clusters destroyed.
According to the company’s submission, its operations began in August 2022 and covered 215 host communities, with more than 35,600 surveillance guards deployed to support pipeline protection.
The operations were supported by 28 forward bases, 130 boats, 175 vehicles, 25 drones and 454 personnel from government security agencies.
The subcommittee attributed the reported operational gains to efforts to protect oil infrastructure and improve stability in the Niger Delta.
Beyond pipeline security, the report highlighted PINL’s community development initiatives, including more than 5,000 scholarships and skills training for over 4,000 women and girls.
The company also reportedly provided flood relief to more than 10 communities in Rivers State.
The committee commended NNPC Limited’s management for providing an enabling environment for pipeline security operations and urged PINL to sustain its engagement with host communities.
It also called on the company to maintain attention to the welfare of surveillance personnel.
The lawmakers’ position comes as Nigeria continues to pursue higher crude oil production amid persistent concerns about crude theft, pipeline vandalism and the underutilisation of oil assets.
According to production figures attributed to the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC), crude oil production stood at approximately 1.50 million barrels per day in August 2026, while output including condensates was about 1.68 million barrels per day.
Average production reportedly rose from 1.388 million barrels per day in the first quarter of 2026 to 1.525 million barrels per day in the second quarter.
Despite the reported improvement, production remained below the 2026 budget benchmark of 1.84 million barrels per day.
The gap highlights the continuing challenge of increasing output to meet budget projections and strengthen government revenue and foreign exchange earnings.
The subcommittee consequently recommended that the federal government extend PINL’s pipeline surveillance contract and urged the company to sustain its operational performance and community development programmes.
The report will be presented to the House of Representatives in plenary for consideration and adoption.

title: Russian court orders Japanese journalist held on espionage charges
body: Further reading Who is Yuki Imai, the Japanese journalist Russia has arrested on espionage charges? A Japanese journalist was detained in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk on suspicion of espionage, TASS reported. The journalist is a correspondent for the newspaper Hokkaido Shimbun. His name was not disclosed. Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) said the journalist was gathering information “related to defense capabilities.” He was detained shortly before he was due to fly out of Russia and taken to Moscow. Ostorozhno, Novosti reported that the journalist is Yuki Imai, 34, who arrived in Russia this summer. He visited Primorsky Krai, including Vladivostok and Nakhodka. Imai was interested in the Soviet-Japanese War of 1945 and relations between Russia and Japan. Kommersant reported that Moscow’s Lefortovo Court had already ordered Imai held in custody on October 13 on espionage charges under Article 276 of Russia’s Criminal Code. title: Supertankers Turn From Gulf Oil Transfer Hub Amid Iran’s Attacks
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
A file image from March 2, 2024, shows the Chinese-flagged VLCC supertanker Cosnew Lake, which exited the Red Sea via the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on July 23, 2026. VLADIMIR TONIC/Handout via REUTERS
A growing number of empty supertankers have been turning away from the Persian Gulf as escalating Iranian attacks threaten a critical transfer hub for wartime oil shipments.
At least 10 very large crude carriers and several Suezmax vessels approaching the port of Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates have stopped or reversed course in recent days, according to tanker-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg.
While other vessels are still continuing on their journeys into the region, the retreat of these tankers amid near-daily attacks around the Strait of Hormuz — some near Fujairah itself — raises fresh concerns over the sustainability of oil flows through the waterway.
Fujairah is commonly signaled as an interim destination by vessels ultimately sailing to the Gulf of Oman — where they can collect cargoes via ship-to-ship transfer — or onward into the Persian Gulf. That makes the number of ships heading toward the port a broader indicator of tanker operators’ appetite for approaching the waterway.
The shift threatens a key workaround that has helped Persian Gulf oil exports recover to near prewar levels. Large crude carriers can wait off Fujairah and in Omani waters outside Hormuz while shuttle tankers make the riskier transit through the strait, bringing out crude and transferring it for onward shipment to buyers.
The system depends on a steady supply of receiving tankers, so a significant retreat from the region by empty VLCCs could slow the flow of crude, tying up the shuttle vessels for longer when tanker availability is already tight.
The pullback is particularly striking given the financial rewards on offer. A global tanker shortage has pushed shipping costs to extraordinary levels. For example, hiring a vessel to haul oil from the US to China now costs more than launching a rocket into space.
