title: Natural language security queries at Orca Security using Amazon Bedrock
body: Security analysts need fast answers about their cloud infrastructure without deep familiarity with domain-specific query languages. Orca Security ’s tool covers over 900 cloud models (the resource types Sonar tracks, such as an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance or an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket). Querying that data required precise model names, nested relationship navigation, and selection from 18 operators (comparison functions like equals or contains used to filter results). To solve this, Orca Security partnered with AWS to build Discovery AI, a natural language query agent on Amazon Bedrock . Orca provides context-aware security for cloud, code, and AI, and Sonar is its domain-specific query system where users search, filter, and explore across the entire data graph. In this post, we share the architecture and results of Discovery AI, which converts a natural language question into a Sonar query. As a result, Orca reduced query costs by 90 percent, input tokens by 93 percent, and latency by 75 percent compared to the initial baseline. Bridging natural language and structured queries Orca Security’s Sonar query system supports 900+ cloud infrastructure and application models with complex relationships between them. To query this data, users construct JSON objects that specify exact model names, select from 18 operators, and navigate parent-child hierarchies across cloud providers. Doing this well requires deep familiarity with the Sonar schema. To build this capability, the Orca team set out to build a natural language interface that can generate valid Sonar queries from plain text. Their initial proof of concept loaded the full Sonar schema into a single prompt on the largest available model. This included over 900 model definitions, every relationship type, and a generous set of example queries. The output quality was strong (design partners and internal users responded positively) but three significant drawbacks emerged at production scale. Token consumption was inefficient, at roughly 2 million input tokens per workload, which drove up cost. Latency was high, with end-to-end response times of around 60 seconds per workload. Accuracy on complex, multi-model queries was limited because nested relationships and multi-condition queries often required additional refinement. The Orca team validated that the concept worked. The next challenge was making it cost-effective, fast, and accurate enough for production. To address this, the Orca team designed and deployed a solution that handles thousands of queries per day at 15-second response times using Amazon Bedrock. Solution overview Orca designed Discovery AI as a hybrid solution on Amazon Bedrock that combines Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) with schema-aware query construction. The system converts natural language questions into valid Discovery filters through a multi-stage pipeline, with each stage matched to the most appropriate Amazon Bedrock model. Orca chose Amazon Bedrock because it provides multi-model access through a single API, letting the team allocate different foundation models to each pipeline stage without managing separate integrations. Amazon Bedrock also inherits AWS governance controls through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoints, and AWS CloudTrail, meeting Orca’s security requirements. The model-agnostic architecture meant the team could swap in newer model versions as they became available without rearchitecting the pipeline. The following diagram illustrates the nine-stage pipeline architecture. Figure 1: Multi-stage Discovery AI pipeline architecture showing the flow from natural language input to validated Discovery filter queries using foundation models on Amazon Bedrock The Discovery AI pipeline converts a natural language request into a validated Discovery filter through nine steps. Request Entry and Context Setup: The pipeline starts by combining the user’s natural language request with relevant context, including the user’s organization, connected cloud providers, and request metadata. This context helps the pipeline interpret the request accurately and generate a Discovery filter that matches the customer’s environment. Quick Deterministic Matcher: The Quick Matcher identifies structured inputs such as IP addresses, Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs), ARNs, file hashes, Amazon Machine Image IDs, Oracle Cloud Identifiers, EC2 IDs, URLs, and alert IDs. It uses regex and rule-based matching to detect high-confidence patterns.When a match is found, the pipeline can return a predefined Discovery filter through a fast path, without using large language model (LLM) inference. When no match is found, the request continues to the next step. LLM Guardrail Screening: The Guardrail component checks whether the request is safe, relevant, technical, and supported. It blocks prompt injection attempts, off-topic requests, and unsupported inputs before they reach the rest of the pipeline. Requests that fail the guardrail checks are rejected with an appropriate error. Approved requests continue to example retrieval. Embedding-Based Semantic Candidate Recall: The pipeline searches for relevant previously validated query examples using Amazon Titan Text Embeddings. It retrieves the 20 nearest examples from the vector store based on semantic similarity. These candidates provide the pipeline with examples of how similar natural language requests were previously translated into Discovery filters. Neural Relevance Reranking: The retrieved candidates are reranked using Cohere Rerank 3.5 on Amazon Bedrock. It identifies the examples that are most relevant to the current request and selects the five highest-signal examples. When an exact or high-confidence match is found, the pipeline can reuse the known-good filter directly. Otherwise, the reranked examples are passed to the generative stages. LLM-Driven Relevant Model Selection: Model Selection narrows more than 900 Sonar models to the small set relevant to the request. It considers the user’s request, connected providers, and retrieved examples when selecting the appropriate models. The selected models are provided to the Generator using the appropriate schema level, ranging from compact micro schemas to more detailed mini schemas. This reduces unnecessary context and makes generation more efficient. Tool-Augmented Agentic Filter Generation: The Generator uses a tool-augmented agent to construct the final Discovery filter. It reasons over the selected model schemas, retrieved examples, user context, and available tools. The agent can iteratively refine the filter as it works toward a valid representation of the user’s request. Static and API-Backed Validation: The generated filter is checked for syntactic and semantic correctness. The pipeline first applies static validation and then verifies the filter against Orca’s Sonar API. When validation fails, the validation error is returned to the Generator so the agent can correct the filter and try again. If the maximum number of retries is reached without producing a valid filter, the pipeline returns an invalid-filter response. The Generator is constrained to the reranked examples and selected schemas. Static validation resolves every model, field, and operator back to those schema definitions. Each validation error goes back to the agent with the offending element identified, so retries re-ground rather than re-guess. Post-Processing and Response: After a valid filter is produced, whether through the Quick Matcher, reuse of a known-good example, or agentic generation, the pipeline prepares the final response.The team allocated different foundation models on Amazon Bedrock across components based on each stage’s requirements. Anthropic Claude Haiku 4.5 powers the Model Selector and Generator. These components require strong reasoning for accurate query construction. Amazon Nova 2 Lite handles the Guardrail and Validator, where fast inference at lower cost is prioritized. Amazon Titan provides embeddings for semantic search in the Example Retrieval component. Cohere Rerank 3.5 reranks retrieved candidates to maximize relevance. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Regional availability by models . Maximizing relevance and diversity in example retrieval Example retrieval emerged as the single biggest accuracy lever in the pipeline. Strong examples teach the Generator how to translate questions into Sonar queries more efficiently than schema alone, so the Orca team benchmarked several retrieval strategies on Amazon Bedrock. Each strategy traded off relevance, diversity, or speed in a different way, and comparing them directly showed which combination worked best. Pure top-K semantic search on Amazon Titan embeddings performed quickly, but it tended to return near-duplicate examples that starved the Generator of diversity. Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) improved diversity, but it traded off relevance when the top candidate was actually the right answer. Retrieving a larger candidate set and then reranking it pulled in a broader pool and used a reranker to select the most relevant subset, which pointed toward the winning approach. The winner was top-20 nearest-neighbor retrieval using Amazon Titan embeddings. Orca then reranked these results with Cohere Rerank 3.5 down to the top five. This approach gives the Generator a small, diverse, highly relevant set of examples without forcing a trade-off between coverage and precision at retrieval time. Loading over 900 models into context A core constraint shaped the architecture. It wasn’t feasible to include 900+ Sonar model schemas into every prompt. Even with long-context models, doing so degrades both cost and accuracy. The Model Selector resolves this. Running on Anthropic Claude Haiku 4.5, it works against compact, semantically rich representations of each model (name, purpose, key fields, and key relationships). Given the user’s question, it returns only the models the Generator actually needs. The Generator then receives full schema detail only for those selected models plus the relationships that connect them. Evaluation methodology To iterate confidently, the Orca team built a continuous evaluation harness early in the project. The harness combines a curated dataset, an automated scoring layer, and a slice-based measurement approach so the team can trust every change before it ships. Together these elements turn evaluation into a routine step rather than an afterthought. The curated evaluation dataset spans the question types, model families, and complexity tiers seen in production, so it reflects real usage. An LLM-as-judge scoring layer grades generated queries on correctness, completeness, and semantic equivalence to a reference query, which gives the team a consistent quality signal. The measurement methodology then breaks deltas down by slice, allowing the team to identify exactly where regressions occur and what to correct. Every change to a prompt, a model, a retrieval parameter, or an example flows through the harness before it ships to production. Domain-expert-in-the-loop labeling system for continuous improvement Sustaining accuracy as customer environments evolve and new question patterns emerge required more than a strong initial deployment. The Orca team built an internal labeling tool for product managers, support engineers, and security researchers. With the tool, they can flag queries, correct outputs, and push corrections into the example bank in one action. Furthermore, the system automatically collects production queries with low-confidence matching examples and routes them to the appropriate domain expert for daily labeling. The next pipeline run retrieves the new example through Cohere Rerank 3.5, and accuracy on that class of question improves the same moment, with no deployment. “The labeling UI is the single most important investment we made for long-term quality. It turns Discovery AI from a static deployment into a living system, with our domain experts continuously improving it inside their normal workflow.” — Or Gabay, Director of AI, Orca Security Combined with end-to-end pipeline observability and shared dashboards spanning product, engineering, and customer-facing teams, this feedback loop is what keeps Discovery AI improving after initial launch. Results After deploying Discovery AI to production, the new solution outperformed the initial baseline across cost, latency, and accuracy. Input token usage fell by 93 percent, from approximately 2 million tokens down to 140,000 per comparable workload. Overall cost fell by 90 percent, driven by that lower token consumption together with per-stage model allocation across Amazon Bedrock. Latency also improved, with end-to-end response times dropping by 75 percent, from approximately 60 seconds to 15 seconds. Accuracy on complex, multi-model queries also improved, measured continuously through the team’s evaluation harness. Discovery AI now handles thousands of queries per day in production since March 2026, with internal subject matter experts and customer feedback validating quality. Conclusion In this post, we shared how Orca Security built Discovery AI on Amazon Bedrock. The solution reduced query costs by 90 percent, input token usage by 93 percent, and latency by 75 percent compared to the initial baseline. The solution combines several key technologies. These include RAG-based example retrieval with Cohere Rerank 3.5, per-stage model allocation across Anthropic Claude Haiku 4.5 and Amazon Nova 2 Lite, and semantic search powered by Amazon Titan. Additionally, a continuous human-in-the-loop labeling system provides ongoing improvement. This combination allowed Orca to turn a working prototype into a production-grade solution that is both cheaper to run and more accurate. To get started building similar solutions, explore Amazon Bedrock for foundation model (FM) access, Cohere Rerank on Amazon Bedrock for retrieval optimization, and Amazon Titan for embeddings. To learn more about Orca Security’s cloud security tool, visit orca.security . To learn more about how Orca Security applies AI across its framework, see how Orca drives security outcomes with AI and how Orca secures AI adoption, including Amazon Bedrock . For more on the techniques used in this post, read related posts on the AWS Machine Learning Blog . About the authors Deniz Yilmaz Deniz is a Machine Learning Engineer at the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center. She partners with enterprise customers across EMEA to design and deploy production-grade generative AI solutions, from proof of concept through to scaled deployment. Her work focuses on agentic architectures, retrieval-augmented generation, and evaluation methodology for building reliable AI systems in production. Natalie Tarasova Natalie is a Machine Learning Engineer in the AWS Custom Model Optimisation team. She focuses on LLM fine-tuning, continued pretraining, and post-training. She is the author of SWE-InfraBench , a benchmark for LLMs on infrastructure-as-code. Julia Wagner Julia is a Senior AI Strategist at the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center. She partners with large enterprises and innovative startups across multiple industry verticals to define and implement generative and agentic AI strategies and products. With over a decade of product and technology leadership experience, she helps organizations automate complex workflows, accelerate R&D, and build the organizational capabilities needed for scaled AI adoption. Barak Tarab Barak is the AI Team Lead at Orca Security, driving the development of advanced artificial intelligence capabilities. His professional focus centers on building scalable AI solutions and robust infrastructure. Saurav Hiremath Saurav , Software Engineer at Orca Security. Lead and built API Security suite at Orca and now transitioned to building Agentic AI systems for enterprise customers. Occasionally spotted contributing to OSS (prev. Facebook’s Jest, React Hermes)

title: Germany works to organize a Coalition of the Willing meeting as Russia strikes Ukraine’s energy sector
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Germany is preparing a new meeting of the Coalition of the Willing to coordinate further support for Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 12 October following a conversation with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Russia continues to strike Ukraine’s energy infrastructure despite US President Donald Trump’s claim that Moscow has agreed to an energy truce. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is initiating a meeting of European leaders to discuss assistance to Ukraine in this situation. Kyiv and Berlin have also agreed to hold a meeting of national security advisers in the E3 format, with Ukraine participating, according to the statement. The format involves an informal grouping of three leading European countries: the United Kingdom, France and Germany. Zelenskyy and Merz discuss energy truce and support for Ukraine During the conversation, the two sides also discussed US President Donald Trump’s proposal for an energy truce and Russia’s subsequent actions. Russian forces continue to attack Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, Zelenskyy noted. “This is exactly how the Russians behave when pressure eases. It is very important that Europe continue to act on principle,” Zelenskyy stressed. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz speaks online with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, 12 October 2026. Photo: Volodymyr Zelenskyy/X Germany is coordinating preparations for a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing, the Ukrainian president noted. The two sides also discussed support for Ukraine’s financial stability. Further steps are to be coordinated in greater detail during a meeting scheduled for this week, Zelenskyy said. The Coalition of the Willing seeks additional support for Ukraine The Coalition of the Willing was initiated by the United Kingdom and France, which held talks with representatives of 37 countries in March 2025 on supporting Ukraine in the event of a peace agreement. The initiative envisaged financial assistance and the deployment of troops, air forces or naval forces to protect Ukraine against renewed Russian aggression, Bloomberg reported . The latest meeting of the Coalition of the Willing took place on 24 August and was the 16th meeting, according to a statement on the website of the President of Ukraine. Zelenskyy called on partners to strengthen Ukraine’s air defense and provide at least 300 missiles for Patriot systems for the winter, the statement said. The Patriot PAC-3 surface-to-air missile system. Photo: Swedish Ministry of Defense The president also proposed bringing forward part of the European loan financing planned for 2027 so that Ukraine could receive the funds this year. He separately stressed the need to find a mechanism for using frozen Russian assets to defend Ukraine and to unblock the maritime corridor in the Black Sea. “We value this format—the Coalition of the Willing. It brings together countries that are ready not only to talk about security but also to act. We need this—to act and build real security together,” Zelenskyy stressed. A ceasefire in words, but fresh attacks on energy infrastructure in practice Ukraine and Russia had allegedly agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire, US President Donald Trump said on Truth Social on 11 October. However, at the time of publication, neither Kyiv nor Moscow had confirmed such an agreement, Ukrainska Pravda reported. Ukraine supports the ceasefire and is awaiting details from the US side, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on X the same day. Russia must also agree to halt the strikes, he stressed. Ukrainian forces had received the relevant orders, and Kyiv was ready to refrain from striking Russian energy infrastructure provided Russia reciprocated, Zelenskyy said in his evening address on 11 October. Russia continued attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure after the ceasefire was announced, including striking a gas production facility and a petrol station, Zelenskyy said on his official Telegram channel on 12 October. Moscow had shown no willingness to abide by the ceasefire, the president added. title: Trezor Reduces Number of Resellers Following Ledger Drainage Incident
body: Bitcoin Magazine Trezor Reduces Number of Resellers Following Ledger Drainage Incident Hardware manufacturer Trezor has said it has reduced the number of resellers it works with following supply-chain incidents related to its competitor Ledger. The Prague, Czech Republic-based company added in a Tuesday post on X that it was in the process of checking which vendors it works with. It added that there were no reports of any issues with Trezor devices. “Let us be very clear: there is not a single piece of evidence that Trezor devices have been compromised,” the company wrote. “This is a preventive step, taken out of an abundance of caution.” Signing device manufacturer Ledger last week said it had started an investigation after customers in South East Asia reported they’d lost funds after buying from Malaysia-based reseller, CryptoBilis. Following recent supply-chain incidents, we decided to reduce the number of resellers so we can more effectively check those we work with. Let us be very clear: there is not a single piece of evidence that Trezor devices have been compromised. This is a preventive step, taken… https://t.co/pKF4tCHo5c — Trezor (@Trezor) October 13, 2026 Ledger then said that one of the impacted users’ devices contained an unauthorized hardware implant. More reports of what appear to be tampered devices have since surfaced on social media but Ledger said Tuesday that only devices sold through CryptoBilis have been linked to lost funds. It added that it had only confirmed an unauthorized hardware implant in one affected user’s device. The implant, according to Ledger, was able to read a seedphrase when it appeared on the device. Ledger did not reveal how much money had been lost but blockchain investigator Specter said $86 million had been drained from devices. “We have not confirmed the total number of affected users or the total value lost,” Ledger added on X. “Figures circulating online come from third parties and Ledger has not fully verified them.” Ledger did not respond to Bitcoin Magazine’s questions. CryptoBilis has also stopped selling devices, Ledger added, and advised customers who bought from CryptoBilis to not set up their devices and contact the Ledger support team. Criminals have been targeting hardware wallets this year. Hackers in July were able to steal close to $120 million in bitcoin from Coldcard users due to a firmware bug in the devices. Canadian company Coinkite, which makes the popular products, said that the bug led to faulty seed generation, allowing hackers to guess investor seedphrases. In a separate incident, hardware wallet manufacturer Trezor last month reported that close to 81,000 customers had their details leaked after its third-party fulfillment partner had data stolen. Scammers earlier this year were able to get hold of customer information via crypto wallet Ledger’s payment processor Global-e to send phishing emails. This post Trezor Reduces Number of Resellers Following Ledger Drainage Incident first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Mathew Di Salvo .

title: Gemini 4 Argon debuts with a unified 1M input/output token limit
body: On Tuesday, Google made Gemini 4 Argon , the company’s new flagship model, available to developers on the paid tier of the Gemini API through Google AI Studio, as well as in several of the company’s other developer and consumer tools. Google announced the model on September 30. Initial external access was limited to selected cyber defenders in its Fairwind Program and other trusted testers; Google employees were also using it internally. Gemini 4 Argon pricing Google is giving the model a competitive price. Developers will pay an introductory $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens through November 30, with a single 1 million-token budget for input and output combined. That’s the same price as OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol. After that date, Google’s new model will cost $4 and $20 per million tokens, matching Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 . Cached input tokens are 95 percent off during the introductory period. During the introductory period, Argon also costs a fifth of what Anthropic charges for Claude Fable 5.1 and OpenAI charges for GPT-6 Astra , which both list at $10 and $50 per million tokens. Developers can call the model as gemini-4-argon through Google’s Interactions API, with support in the google-genai SDKs. Android developers can also build it into their apps through Firebase AI Logic. One budget for input and output Argon’s unified 1 million input/output token limit covers both what goes into the model and what comes out of it, according to Google. That’s markedly different from how Google described it in the original Sept. 30 Argon announcement. At the time, it called the limit an output cap of 1 million tokens, up from 64,000 in earlier Gemini models. With what is now a shared budget, the equation changes a bit because a long prompt can now eat into how much the model can write back. For example, if a request loads 800,000 tokens of code, that leaves only 200,000 for the response. In comparison, Claude Opus 5.5 combines the standard 1 million-token context window with a separate output cap of 128,000 tokens. Google says the extra room will let Argon keep working on long, multistep coding, science, and agent jobs. Today we are rolling out Gemini 4 Argon globally in the Gemini API, to Pro + Ultra in Gemini App, and Ultra subs in Antigravity! Argon is a huge step forward for Gemini, and a labor of love. This model has been battle tested by over 100,000 people at Google over the last month,… — Logan Kilpatrick (@OfficialLoganK) October 13, 2026 Gemini 4 Argon benchmarks Google says Argon ranks first on the Vals Index , which scores models on finance, coding, legal, and tax work and weights each sector by its share of U.S. GDP. On Embodied Reasoning Question Answering (ERQA), a test of physical and spatial reasoning, Google reports Argon scored 87 percent. That puts it ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 at 82.3 percent, GPT-6 Astra at 81 percent, and Claude Fable 5.1 at 74 percent. Gemini 4 Argon ERQA benchmark. Credit: Google. Bloomberg reported Sept. 30 that some Google employees with access to the model said it struggled with certain coding tasks, particularly front-end design. Google told Bloomberg it would be “inaccurate to say that Gemini 4 is underperforming in areas such as coding.” For now, we don’t have a full set of new benchmarks to better compare Argon to other models. Like some other frontier labs, Google focused its announcement more on “feels” than data. Benchmarks never tell the full story, but we’ll update this post once we hear more. Artificial Analysis published an evaluation on September 30: Argon scored 53 on its Intelligence Index, matching GPT-6 Astra at the models’ tested reasoning settings. However, there’s no guarantee the model released on Tuesday is precisely the same as the one tested on September 30. Argon in Antigravity Where else Argon is available is a bit complicated. For coding, Google is also making Argon available in Antigravity , its platform for running coding agents across the editor, terminal, and browser. Argon is available in the Antigravity desktop app for macOS, Windows, and Linux and in the Antigravity CLI, but only for Google AI Ultra subscribers and eligible Gemini Enterprise plans. AI Pro subscribers get Argon in the Gemini app, but not in Antigravity. Google is also bringing Antigravity’s coding interface into the Gemini app for macOS, so users can move between chatting and coding without switching tools. Anthropic and OpenAI do the same with their Claude and ChatGPT/Codex desktop apps , but nobody has found an elegant way to combine these chat and coding tools into a single interface. In Android Studio Canary, developers can sign in to Antigravity from the agent tool window, and a new Android CLI plugin gives the agent access to local Android build tools. More than 100,000 Googlers use Argon each month in an in-house build of Antigravity, the company says. Over four weeks, code submitted by agents rose 35 percent while post-submit rollbacks fell 30 percent. Google says more than half of its Cloud sales staff and almost half of its finance team now use Antigravity. Gemini 4 Argon is here. It’s available globally today for developers and enterprises in the paid tier of the Gemini API and the Gemini platform, for Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity, and Ultra and Pro subscribers in the Gemini app and Search. Hope you all enjoy it! pic.twitter.com/2jyAgqoylU — Sundar Pichai (@sundarpichai) October 13, 2026 Argon in the Gemini app Subscribers on Google’s AI Pro and Ultra plans now also get access to Argon in the Gemini app and in AI Mode in Search. In addition to the new model, the Gemini app is also getting a new toggle that lets users turn a chat into a task, which Gemini can then keep working on after the user steps away from the computer. Gemini 4 Argon is amazing for knowledge work and coding – and it’s super fun to build with! We asked it to create this wizard chess game and it's so cool to see Argon's physics understanding & 3D modelling capabilities, makes me nostalgic for Battlechess on the Amiga – fun times!… pic.twitter.com/nVADBiXYDe — Demis Hassabis (@demishassabis) October 13, 2026 Cyber defenders and agent safety Google is also expanding Fairwind , the program it launched September 2 to give vetted security teams early access to its cyber models. Selected Fairwind partners can access Argon without its cyber guardrails, and Google says it’s adding hundreds more partners to the more than 650 the program had when it launched. For the public model now available, Google says it trained Argon to check with a person before doing anything it can’t undo and to report when it hits a wall instead of working around it. On coding evaluations, Argon tried unauthorized shortcuts 2 percent of the time, the company says, its lowest rate for any Gemini model (though 2 percent still isn’t zero, and when thousands of agents work together, 2 percent is still quite a few agents that could go rogue). Google also runs a separate monitor that reads the agent’s reasoning and actions as it works and blocks unintended workarounds. The company says it ran that monitor during training without penalizing the model for what it was thinking, so its reasoning stays readable. According to Google, Argon also leads Gray Swan’s indirect prompt injection benchmark, with attacks succeeding 0.7 percent of the time across 15 adaptive attempts. Developers have until November 30 to test Argon at the introductory rate. After that, Argon and Opus 5.5 cost the same per token. The post Gemini 4 Argon debuts with a unified 1M input/output token limit appeared first on The New Stack .

title: Why Diesel Prices Are So Much Higher Than Gasoline
body: There was a time when diesel fuel was usually cheaper than gasoline in the United States. That relationship began to change about 20 years ago, and since then diesel has generally traded at a premium. Today, that premium is not just persistent but unusually large, which raises an obvious question how did we get from gasoline typically costing more than diesel to diesel costing substantially more than gasoline  The answer has two parts. The first is structural and goes back to the mid-2000s, when changes in fuel specifications, taxes, refining economics, and global demand fundamentally altered the relationship between gasoline and diesel prices.  The second is more immediate. In 2026, refinery disruptions, geopolitical conflicts, low inventories, and reduced exports from major suppliers have pushed the global diesel market into an unusually tight position. Understanding the difference between those long-term and short-term forces explains both why diesel usually costs more and why the gap is so large right now.  Diesel Was Once The Cheaper Fuel  Before the mid-2000s, diesel was often cheaper than regular gasoline in the United States. There were exceptions, particularly during cold winters when heating-oil demand strengthened, but the longer-term pattern generally favored diesel. That began to change around 2004, and according to the Energy Information Administration, on-highway diesel prices have been higher than regular gasoline prices almost continuously since September of that year.  That shift is clearly visible in the historical data I examined in my 2023 article on the subject. In the decade before 2005, gasoline generally traded at a small premium to diesel. After that, the relationship reversed, and diesel became the more expensive fuel in most years. The timing is important because it coincided with a major change in the way U.S. refiners had to produce highway diesel.  Ultra-Low-Sulfur Diesel Changed The Economics  Beginning in the mid-2000s, U.S. refiners had to dramatically reduce the sulfur content of highway diesel. That was an important environmental improvement because sulfur emissions contribute to air pollution and acid rain, but it also made diesel more expensive to produce. Refineries invested billions of dollars in new hydrotreating and sulfur-removal equipment, and those investments increased capital and operating costs and made compliant diesel more expensive to produce and distribute.  My earlier article focused heavily on this transition because the timing lines up closely with the point at which diesel's historical discount disappeared. EIA now describes the persistent diesel premium as the result of several factors working together, including strong global demand for diesel and other distillates, the higher cost of producing low-sulfur diesel, and federal taxes that are six cents per gallon higher on diesel than on gasoline.  None of those factors explains every short-term price movement, but together they created a structural premium that had not existed to the same degree before 2004. Once diesel became more expensive to produce and more tightly linked to global distillate markets, the old relationship with gasoline never really returned.  Diesel Became A Global Commodity  Another important change has been the globalization of the diesel market. Gasoline is also traded internationally, but diesel and other middle distillates occupy an especially important role in the global economy because they power trucking, agriculture, construction, mining, shipping, industrial equipment, and heating systems. Strong demand in Europe, China, India, and the United States has kept pressure on global distillate balances for years.  That means U.S. diesel prices are increasingly influenced by events far beyond U.S. borders. Even when domestic production is strong, refiners can export diesel into higher-priced international markets, tying domestic prices more closely to global supply and demand. This is one reason it is misleading to look only at U.S. crude oil production and assume that abundant domestic oil should automatically translate into cheap diesel.  The United States can produce plenty of crude while still facing tight supplies of refined products. Crude oil has to be processed in the right refineries, into the right products, and then moved through the right transportation system. Those constraints matter just as much as the amount of oil coming out of the ground.  2022 Showed How Quickly The Premium Can Explode  The most dramatic recent example came in 2022, when Russia's invasion of Ukraine disrupted global energy markets. Diesel was hit particularly hard. Russia was a major supplier of crude oil, refined products, and feedstocks to Europe and other markets, so sanctions and trade restrictions forced a rapid reshuffling of global flows. Gasoline prices rose sharply as well, but diesel supplies tightened even more, pushing the diesel premium to record levels.  In my earlier article, I noted that the gasoline-diesel spread reached a record in 2022. At the time, the disruption from Russia explained why a structural premium suddenly became an extreme one. The market eventually adjusted as trade routes shifted, refinery operations stabilized, and inventories recovered, but that normalization did not last.  Why The Gap Is So Large Again In 2026  The current situation resembles 2022 in one important respect global diesel supply has again been disrupted more severely than gasoline supply. EIA recently reported that global distillate supplies are tight because of reduced refining activity in Russia, China, and the Middle East. At the same time, U.S. refiners have been running near maximum utilization, with domestic distillate production averaging about 5.1 million barrels per day through August, the highest level since 2019.  That point is worth emphasizing because it shows that the current problem is not simply a collapse in U.S. refinery output. American refiners are producing large volumes of diesel, but global demand for those barrels has increased at the same time that supplies elsewhere have fallen. As exports increased, U.S. inventories declined, and by mid-September distillate inventories were about 13% below the five-year seasonal average even though summer is normally a period when inventories build ahead of winter.  Since then, the global situation has become even tighter. Russia has restricted diesel exports as refinery infrastructure has been damaged, China has curtailed fuel exports to protect domestic supplies, and Middle Eastern refining and shipping have been disrupted by the conflict involving Iran. Tanker costs and insurance rates have also risen, making it more expensive to move refined products around the world.  The result is a global scramble for middle distillates. Both gasoline and diesel are affected by higher crude prices, but diesel is being squeezed more severely because the product itself is in shorter supply relative to demand. That is why the diesel-gasoline spread has widened so dramatically.  The Price Gap Is Now Extraordinary  As of October 5, the national average price of on-highway diesel was $6.199 per gallon, compared with $4.354 for regular gasolinea spread of about $1.85 per gallon. Diesel reached a nominal record of $6.29 per gallon in September, according to EIA, and remained above $6 nationally in early October.  That gap is not primarily the result of a sudden increase in diesel taxes or some new change in fuel specifications. Those structural factors help explain why diesel usually costs more than gasoline, but they do not explain why the premium is so large today. The current premium reflects a very tight global distillate market layered on top of the long-term changes that already made diesel the more expensive fuel.  That distinction is important because it separates the underlying reason diesel normally carries a premium from the temporary forces that can cause that premium to explode.  Refining Margins Are A Consequence, Not A Cause  Refining margins have risen sharply, and major refiners are benefiting from the tight market. But those high margins are a consequence of constrained diesel supply relative to demand rather than the original cause of the shortage.  When refinery capacity is disrupted, exports are curtailed, and inventories fall, the value of the remaining barrels rises. Refiners that can continue producing diesel benefit from that scarcity, but the scarcity comes first. This distinction is important because high margins are sometimes cited as evidence that refiners decided to raise prices, when in reality the margin expansion is largely the market's response to a shortage of refined product.  Diesel Is A Different Market Than Gasoline  The broader lesson is that gasoline and diesel may come from the same barrel of crude oil, but they are not interchangeable products. They serve different markets, have different seasonal demand patterns, require different processing, and face different global supply pressures. A refinery cannot simply turn every barrel of crude into whichever product happens to be most expensive that day because refinery configuration, crude quality, product specifications, and physical operating limits all constrain what can be produced.  That is why abundant crude oil does not guarantee cheap diesel. The United States can produce record amounts of oil, run refineries near capacity, and still face expensive diesel if global product markets remain tight.  Twenty years ago, gasoline was often the more expensive fuel. Then diesel moved to a structural premium, and today that premium has widened dramatically because the global market for diesel and other middle distillates is again under severe strain. Until those supply constraints ease, diesel is likely to remain much more expensive than gasoline.  By Robert Rapier

title: Russia responsible for Starlink sabotage, says Poland
body:
Polish authorities on Oct. 12 blamed Russian intelligence services for an arson attack on a Starlink ground station in Poland on Sept. 23, and said two Turkish citizens had been detained as suspects in Germany.
The two suspects had been arrested on behalf of Polish services on Oct. 10 under suspicion of having set fire to the station in Wola Krobowska, in Poland's Masovian Voivodeship, said Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk in a post on X . He called the attack “another act of hybrid warfare.”
Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister coordinating Polish special services, made Russia responsible for the attack, reported AP .
“We have no doubt that Russian intelligence services are behind this act of sabotage,” he said, according to AP.
He also said that "​It is worth adding that Russian services are increasingly turning ​to individuals linked ‌to the criminal underworld," according to Deutsche Welle .
On Sept. 24, Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski told reporters that a fire at a Starlink ground station in Poland may have been a deliberate attempt to disrupt internet access used by Ukrainian forces at the front.
The station is operated by the state-owned telecommunications company Exatel and serves as an internet hub that carries traffic through Poland , including to Ukraine, Gawkowski said.
He suggested Russia could be behind the incident, describing it as potentially part of Moscow's hybrid warfare .
Polish authorities are also investigating an alleged assassination plot targeting Tusk and his deputy, Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, Jacek Dobrzynski, a spokesperson for Polish intelligence agencies, said on Oct. 11.
Police received numerous reports of a possible assassination attempt, after which a meeting was called between representatives of the Interior and Administration Ministry, the State Protection Service, and the Internal Security Agency.
"We are taking this matter very seriously," Kosiniak-Kamysz said at a press briefing on Oct. 11.

After months sitting on the sidelines of the frontier AI race, Google has finally launched its long-awaited Gemini 4 Argon model, claiming it can compete with the best the industry has to offer.
Google says Argon delivers “frontier reasoning and improved performance across complex workflows,” while cutting down on hedging, repetition, and the cliches that continue to plague AI chatbots. The company claims Argon outperforms rival models like GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1, and Claude Opus 5.5 across a range of benchmarks, including coding, cybersecurity, science, finance, and law.
Google says it’s already putting Argon to use internally, such as finding and patching cybersecurity vulnerabilities, halving the computing power needed to power YouTube’s comments section, and debugging the drone physics simulator for Alphabet’s drone delivery company Wing.
The model is rolling out today to Google’s higher-tier Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app and AI mode in Search, as well to Ultra subscribers on its agentic development platform Antigravity. It is not clear when — or if — Argon will be available to Plus subscribers or free users.
Google is pricing Argon very competitively. The model is launching with an introductory price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, around a fifth the cost of OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra and Anthropic’s Fable 5 models. Even after those costs double at the end November — when the introductory period finishes — Argon will still be significantly cheaper than its frontier rivals on a per-token basis, though this doesn’t necessarily translate to lower costs in practice, as models can use different numbers of tokens for the same tasks.
The launch fills in some of the blanks left behind from when Google first teased Argon a few weeks ago. In line with other recent frontier model releases, the public rollout follows a limited release to a select set of “trusted cyber defenders” to be tested for potential risks.
Argon is Google’s first major frontier release since Gemini 3 in late 2025. In the intervening months, impressive models from Anthropic and OpenAI have seen Google trail far behind its rivals. Seismic internal shakeups raised further doubts about the company’s ability — or desire — to reclaim its position and compete at the frontier of AI.
But Argon’s arrival suggests we can’t count Google out of the AI race just yet. Landing just a day after Meta announced its own frontier model , Muse Wonder Full, Argon is a reminder of how quickly the balance of power can shift in AI, and that the frontier is far from a two-horse race.
